Hüseyin Bulut (born 29 March 1999) is a Turkish professional footballer who plays as a right-back or winger for Süper Lig club Çorum. Born in Dortmund, Germany, he spent most of his youth career with Borussia Dortmund before beginning his senior career with Borussia Dortmund II. He has represented Turkey at under-16 and under-17 level. [ref: Hüseyin Bulut – Player Details, Turkish Football Federation]

==Club career==

===Borussia Dortmund===
Bulut was born in Dortmund, Germany, and played youth football for TuS Eving-Lindenhorst before joining the youth system of Borussia Dortmund in 2010. [ref: Hoş geldin Hüseyin Bulut, Altınordu F.K.]

He progressed through Borussia Dortmund's youth teams. His development was interrupted by a hip injury during the 2016–17 season, which caused him to miss much of the campaign. [ref: Hüseyin Bulut: Das türkische Talent in den Reihen von Borussia Dortmund, [[Goal (website)] He returned to feature in the final stages of Borussia Dortmund's German under-19 championship-winning campaign.

In September 2017, Bulut attracted attention after scoring twice for Borussia Dortmund's under-19 team in a 5–3 victory over Real Madrid in the UEFA Youth League. A profile published by Goal.com following the match examined his development at Dortmund, injury history, technical ability and positional versatility.

Bulut later progressed to Borussia Dortmund II. During the 2018–19 Regionalliga West season, he made nine league appearances and scored three goals. [ref: Huseyin Bulut – Player profile, German Football Association]

In 2019, Turkish sports outlet Ajansspor published a separate profile and analysis of Bulut, discussing his development at Borussia Dortmund, positional versatility and playing characteristics. [ref: Hüseyin Bulut Analizi, Ajansspor]

===Göztepe and return to Germany===
Bulut moved to Turkey in July 2019 and joined Göztepe. He did not make a league appearance for the club, but appeared twice in the Turkish Cup, scoring once. [ref: Gel de kahrolma!, Yeni Asır]

Yeni Asır reported in July 2020 that Bulut had struggled for first-team opportunities under managers Tamer Tuna and İlhan Palut and had requested permission to leave the club in order to continue his career in Germany. His contract with Göztepe was terminated by mutual consent on 14 July 2020.

He subsequently returned to Germany and joined Sportfreunde Lotte, making 11 Regionalliga West appearances and scoring once. In January 2021 he moved to Rot-Weiß Oberhausen, where he made 28 league appearances over two seasons and scored one goal.

Bulut joined Rot Weiss Ahlen for the 2022–23 season, scoring seven goals in 29 Regionalliga West appearances. The following season he played for Wuppertaler SV, recording four goals in 25 league appearances.

===Altınordu===
In May 2024, Bulut returned to Turkey and signed a three-year contract with Altınordu. He became one of the club's leading attacking players during the 2024–25 TFF Second League season.

By May 2025, Bulut had scored 13 goals during the regular league season. Demirören News Agency described him as Altınordu's leading scorer and reported that his goals had played an important role in the club qualifying for the promotion play-offs. [ref: Altınordu'nun kozu Hüseyin Bulut, Demirören News Agency]

He finished the campaign with 15 goals in 36 appearances across the league and promotion play-offs. [ref: Hüseyin Bulut, Maçkolik] In June 2025, DHA reported that his performances had attracted transfer interest and that Altınordu had placed a reported €600,000 valuation on him. [ref: Altınordu'da Hüseyin değerini katladı, Demirören News Agency]

===Keçiörengücü===
Bulut joined Keçiörengücü in September 2025. He made 29 appearances and scored four goals in the TFF First League during the 2025–26 season.

During his time with Keçiörengücü, he increasingly featured in a defensive role on the right side, having spent much of his earlier career in attacking wide positions.

===Çorum===
On 11 July 2026, newly promoted Süper Lig club Çorum signed Bulut from Keçiörengücü on a two-year contract with an option for a further season. [ref: Çorum FK, Hüseyin Bulut'u kadrosuna kattı, Demirören News Agency] The transfer was announced with Bulut described as a right-back.

His registration with Çorum took effect on 14 July 2026, with the Turkish Football Federation listing his contract as running until 30 June 2028.

==International career==
Bulut represented Turkey at youth international level. He made three appearances for the Turkey under-16 team in 2015. He scored for Turkey in a 3–1 defeat against Mexico at the Montaigu Tournament on 4 April 2015. [ref: U16 Milli Takımı, Meksika'ya 3-1 mağlup oldu, Turkish Football Federation]

Later that year, Bulut represented the Turkey under-17 team, making three appearances. He was part of the Turkey squad that competed at the St George's Park Tournament in England in August 2015. [ref: U17 Milli Takımı İtalya'ya 2-0 yenildi, Turkish Football Federation]

==Playing style==
During his youth career, Bulut was primarily used as an attacking player. In its 2017 profile, Goal.com described him as capable of playing on either wing or through the centre, highlighting his technical ability, dribbling, movement and work rate.

Hannah Lew is a Bay Area-based musician, filmmaker, and visual artist best known as the bassist and co-vocalist of the post-punk trio Grass Widow (2007–2013) and as the founder of darkwave group Cold Beat (~2012-present). [ref: WAMU's Bandwidth Presents: Cold Beat, NPR] She also runs a record label, Crime on the Moon, and co-founded Contact Records, a record store in Oakland, California. Her self-titled solo album was released on April 10, 2026.

== Early life ==
Hannah Lew is the daughter of Rabbi Alan Lew. Her family moved often when she was a child. At one point, her family lived in New York City during the week, went to Monroe, New York on weekends, and "lived in the basement for Shabbat." [ref: With dad’s legacy as inspiration, rabbi’s daughter uses music to heal] Her family moved to San Francisco when Hannah was 11, just after the Loma Prieta earthquake. Alan Lew later became the leader of Congregation Beth Sholom in San Francisco, California.

Lew started her first band at age 19. She worked as a visual artist until the September 11 attacks changed her perspective. Lew wanted to "do something that was accessible, that everyone could have." Early in her career, Lew worked at a video store called Lost Weekend. In her twenties, she played moog synthesizer in a band, The Insides, where she was the only girl.

== Grass Widow ==

Lew co-founded Grass Widow with Raven Mahon and Lillian Maring in 2007. [ref: Grass Window: Past Time, Pitchfork]
[ref: Grass Widow, a band in perfect harmony, Washington Post] In one interview, Lew described the band's process as highly collaborative, adding, "We collaborate on songs, each writing parts and all singing. We have band meetings where we make decisions together. We don't have a band leader. It's a very empowering project and it takes a lot of work." Songs were created together in their San Francisco practice space and all members contributed equally to the work of the band. [ref: Grass Widow interview: "Our own internal logic", Dummy] They would often tour for two weeks at a time, in order to remain connected to their friends and family. [ref: Grass Widow [band], The Believer]

Members of the band were often asked about the fact that the band is all-women and about their feminism, and responded with a quote from Gina Birch: "And you ask me if I’m a Feminist? Why the hell would I not be?!" [ref: Grass Widow, Interview] They cited influences like Neo Boys, Kleenex, The Move, and The Kinks as major sources of inspiration. [ref: Grass Widow, Kill Rock Stars]

The band dissolved circa 2013, with members moving on to pursue other projects. [ref: Cold Beat [band], BOMB Magazine] [ref: On figuring out how to do whatever you want, The Creative Independent]

== Cold Beat ==

Lew started Cold Beat after the death of her father, when she felt the collaborative style of Grass Widow (which was already on hiatus) would not work for her. [ref: Grass Widow's Hannah Lew formed new group Cold Beat, releasing debut album in July, BrooklynVegan]
Cold Beat's name comes from a song by the British post-punk group The Sound. The project began as a solo vehicle for Lew, and evolved into a four-piece band. [ref: Cold Beat Dodges the Ghosts of San Francisco, Dives Into Surf-Kissed Post-Punk, Spin] Cold Beat has released five studio albums and two EPs on Crime on the Moon (Lew's own label), Dark Entries Records, DFA Records, and Like LTD. [ref: Cold Beat's Dreamy Synth-Pop Song '62 Moons' Takes Off, NPR All Songs Considered] [ref: Cold Beat discuss the inspirations behind their new album 'War Garden', BrooklynVegan] The album Mother (2020) was recorded while Lew was pregnant. [ref: Indie Basement (2/28): Caribou, Real Estate, Juniore, The Orielles, Cold Beat, Pictish Trail, David Roback's Rainy Day, BrooklynVegan]

== Filmmaking ==
Lew has directed dozens of music videos for her own bands and other acts, including Erase Errata, Tony Molina, and The Mantles. [ref: Music Videos, HannahLew.com] She has also made and released several short films. In 2009, she received both the Leo Diner and Robin Eichman Awards for her short films Stoplight and Over the Hill. [ref: Hannah Lew and Chris Stewart Just Want to Connect., Talkhouse]

== Other projects ==
Lew released San Francisco is Doomed, an anthology of local bands, on her label Crime on the Moon. She released a self-titled album in April 2026, which was named Bandcamp's "Album of the Day" and positively reviewed in The Guardian and BrooklynVegan. [ref: Add to playlist: the maximalist melancholy of Hannah Lew and the week’s best tracks, The Guardian] [ref: Indie Basement (4/10): Squarepusher, My New Band Believe, more]

{Infobox baseball
| name = Baseball Pitch Recognition Timeline

Pitch recognition in baseball refers to the perceptual ability of batters to detect visual cues from a pitcher’s pitching motion, arm angle and hand position at pitch release, and spin of the ball to identify the pitch type thrown (e.g. fastball, curveball, slider, changeup). Batters subconsciously generate predictions about the trajectory and speed of different pitch types to anticipate where and when the ball will cross the hitting zone. [ref: Müller, S. & Abernethy, B. “Expert Anticipatory Skill in Striking Sports: A Review and a Model.” *Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport* 83(2): 175–187 (2012).]

Pitch recognition helps batters decide whether to execute a full bat swing or a checked swing based on anticipating that the pitch will or will not be in the strike zone. Because batters often must check a swing mid-motion, the decision whether to swing usually must occur very early in the pitch’s trajectory.

== Timing constraints ==

Sports scientists estimate that a batter typically needs **about 150 milliseconds** to initiate and complete a swing. Given that a 95 mile-per-hour fastball takes roughly **400 milliseconds** to travel from pitcher to home plate, this leaves only about **250 milliseconds** for recognition and decision making (i.e. “the blink of an eye”). [ref: Adair, Robert K. The Physics of Baseball (2002).]

Because of highly constrained swing decision time, many hitting coaches teach a mental sequence of “yes, yes, YES,” describing hitters' intent to swing unless pitch recognition cues contradict it, changing the hitters' intent to “yes, yes, NO” if the pitch is clearly outside the strike zone. [ref: The Batter's Box Mindset: How to Win Every Battle at the Plate in Baseball and Softball]

== Pitch repertoire and deception ==

Pitch recognition is both more difficult and more critical because modern professional pitchers often throw five or more types of pitches, each with distinct velocity, movement, and spin signatures. For instance, a cut fastball may travel only a few mph slower than a pitcher’s fastball but exhibit late horizontal movement in the opposite direction of the pitcher's pitching arm. The subtle, late nature of such movement increases difficulty for hitters to distinguish early signals. [ref: Cut fastball, MLB.com]

An example of pitch movement deceiving hitters is Mariano Rivera, whose reliance on a cut fastball contributed to his dominance as a relief pitcher. [ref: Cut fastball, The New York Times]

== Conceptual contrasts ==

=== vs. Plate discipline ===
Plate discipline is a measure of a batter’s ability to swing at strikes and refrain from swinging at balls. One statistic often used is the walk-to-strikeout ratio (BB/K). A BB/K of 1 walk per 2 strikeouts (0.5) is generally acceptable, while a ratio greater than 1 is rare and denotes strong plate discipline. Historical examples of hitters with elite career BB/K ratios include:

- Ted Williams: ≈ 2.85
- Wade Boggs: ≈ 1.90
- Tony Gwynn: ≈ 1.84
- Joe Morgan: ≈ 1.82
- Barry Bonds: ≈ 1.66
- Juan Soto: ≈ 1.08 [ref: MLB Hitters Sorted By Best Walk To Strikeout Ratio For Career]

While plate discipline can be measured as an outcome, pitch recognition refers to the underlying perceptual skill that influences not only swing decisions but also swing adjustments. Historically, Tony Gwynn of the San Diego Padres was notable for making solid contact with a variety of pitch types and locations. [ref: Tony Gwynn was a pure contact hitter]

=== vs. Visual skills ===
Visual faculties such as dynamic tracking, contrast sensitivity, and peripheral vision are often considered the hardware; pitch recognition is the software that interprets sensory input, matches patterns, and activates decision pathways. Both can be trained, but they are conceptually distinct and may require separate assessment and training. [ref: Tremblay, M., Couëpel, B., Abboud, J. et al. "What are the Individual Characteristics or Skills Associated with Baseball Batting Performance? A Scoping Review." *Sports Med* Open 11, 150 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-025-00947-1.]

David Sinclair is an American professional athlete competing in Nordic skiing, ski mountaineering, and trail running.

Sinclair has represented Team USA in ski mountaineering (skimo) and trail running. [ref: David Sinclair, Team USA] [ref: Nordic Skiing, Ultrarunning Prepared David Sinclair To Take A Shot At A Lifelong Olympic Dream In Skimo, Team USA]

== Early life and career ==

Following college, Sinclair transitioned to elite trail running and ultramarathons. In 2018, he won the USATF 50-km Trail Championships. [ref: Vermonters Enman and Sinclair win rain-soaked Ragged 50K, Trail Running, Ultrarunning, USATF, USATF Championships] He has represented Team USA at the World Mountain and Trail Running Championships in 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2025. [ref: Catching Up with David Sinclair About Trail Running and Ski Mountaineering, Trail Runner Magazine]

Despite primarily competing in trail running, Sinclair qualified for the 2020 US Olympic Marathon Trials with a time of 2:16:18 at the 2016 California International Marathon. [ref: David Sinclair, US Olympic Team Trials Athlete Bios]

He was rated Ultra Running Magazine's number 3 men's ultrarunner of 2024. [ref: David Sinclair Named #3 Ultrarunner of the Year, Ultrarunners of the Year]

In 2025, he joined the Craft Elite Run Team as a sponsored athlete. [ref: Craft Sportswear Welcomes New Trail Athletes to Its Elite Run Team, Outdoor Industry Association]

Draft: Oil and Gas Free Zones Authority

Draft text:
Oil and Gas Free Zones Authority (OGFZA) is the federal government of Nigeria agency responsible for the regulation of oil and gas free zones. It was established in 1996 under the Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act. The Act designated the Onne/Ikpokiri area of Rivers State as an oil and gas export free zone. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

== History ==

The Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act was enacted on 29 March 1996. The Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Authority to operate and manage Onne Oil and Gas Frr Zone. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

== Regulatory jurisdiction ==

Regulators and free-zone operators are at odds over the geographic and sectoral scope of OGFZA's mission.

A media analysis in The Guardian Newspaper suggested the debate centered on ambiguities and overlaps between the OGFZA and NEPZA laws. It further mentioned that instead of combining OGFZA with NEPZA, the federal government had kept it as a distinct organization in response to a previous public-sector reform initiative. [ref: OGFZA and NEPZA bills: Matters arising, The Guardian]

In subsequent years, the two free-zone regulators' disagreement persisted. Punch revealed in 2021 that a Senate committee had criticized the ongoing disputes between NEPZA and OGFZA and demanded changes to their enabling legislation to make their different roles more clear. [ref: NEPZA, OGEFZA crisis, an economic sabotage, says NASS, Punch]

== Disputes involving free-zone operators ==

In the oil and gas free-zone system, OGFZA has also been involved in regulatory issues with operators.

An audit of Intels Nigeria Limited's operations from 2006 to 2016 was mandated by OGFZA in 2017. The authority claimed violations of free-zone rules, according to The Guardian Newspaper. The claims were refuted by Intels. [ref: Fresh trouble for Atiku's INTELS as OGFZA alleges rules' violation, The Guardian]

Intels later vowed to sue the authority, according to Punch Newspaper. The company contested a number of issues, including the renewal of its operating license, OGFZA charges, and regulatory rulings pertaining to foreign employees employed by businesses in the One Free Zone. [ref: Intels threatens to sue OGFZA over malicious allegations, Punch]

Following OGFZA's revocation of operating licenses, the case subsequently entailed immigration action against foreign workers of Intels and a number of related businesses. [ref: FG revokes residence permits of expatriates in Atiku, others' firms, Punch]

== Petroleum-sector regulatory overlap ==

Nigeria's post-2021 petroleum regulatory framework has also raised concerns about OGFZA's jurisdiction.

A jurisdictional dispute between OGFZA and the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority was resolved in June 2026 by the Senate Committee on the Downstream Petroleum Sector. According to Punch, the committee was looking for a framework to address statutory obligations that overlap between the two bodies. [ref: Senate promises to end conflict between petroleum sector regulatory agencies, Punch]

The disagreement centered on whether the regulatory framework run by petroleum-sector organizations or the free-zone laws of OGFZA applied to operations conducted within oil and gas free zones. [ref: Senate promises to end conflict between petroleum sector regulatory agencies, Punch]

== Functions ==

The authority is tasked with overseeing the designated export free zone and managing authorized businesses within it under the Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act. Its statutory powers include approving firms, issuing licences, enacting regulations and managing provisions governing the movement of commodities and allowed activities within the free zone. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

Additionally, the Act permits the authority to assume duties previously carried out by NEPZA in relation to the export of gas and oil from Nigerian export processing zones. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

== Free Zones Under OGFZA ==

# Onne Oil and Gas Free Zone, Rivers State
# Warri Oil and Gas Free Zone, Delta State
# Notore Industrial City, Rivers State
# Eko Support Services Free Zone, Lagos State
# Liberty Oil and Gas Free Zone, Akwa Ibom State
# Brass Oil and Gas City, Bayelsa State
# BESTAF Industrial Free Zone, Lagos State
# Secured Bunkering Anchorage Free Zone, Lagos State
# Orashi Special Energy Free Zone, Imo State
# Dangote Industries Free Zone, Lagos State

The Onne/Ikpokiri area in Rivers State was the free zone specifically designated by the 1996 Act. [ref: Oil and Gas Export Free Zone Act, Laws of Nigeria]

The zone grew out of the logistics and services related to oil and gas operations at Onne Port. Its management served as the foundation for OGFZA's subsequent attempts to exert regulatory authority over additional Nigerian free zones connected to oil and gas. [ref: 20 Years After, NEPZA to Hands off Oil and Gas Free Zones, ThisDay]

Draft: Highly Optimized Object-oriented Many-particle Dynamics

Draft text:
[https://hoomd-blue.readthedocs.io/en/v7.1.2/ HOOMD-blue] (Highly Optimized Object-oriented Many-particle Dynamics—blue edition) is a general-purpose particle simulation engine designed primarily for nano- and colloidal-scale modeling. It serves the scientific purpose of probing the structure, dynamics, and self-assembly of complex matter. The software executes on single or multi-core central processing units (CPUs) as well as graphics processing unit (GPU) hardware architectures. Its principal research fields focus on soft matter physics, polymers, colloids, self-assembly, and active matter. [ref: HOOMD-blue: A Python package for high-performance molecular dynamics and hard particle Monte Carlo simulations, Computational Materials Science] It is also enlisted in the list of different tools for molecular modelling in the table.

== History and development ==
Development began in March 2007 at Iowa State University to explore the computational potential of graphics processing units for coarse-grained polymer simulations. The initial implementation achieved accelerated execution using C++ and CUDA code targeting single NVIDIA GPUs. In published benchmark evaluations, single-GPU execution produced computational performance comparable to approximately 30 CPU cores for equivalent benchmark systems. [ref: General purpose molecular dynamics simulations fully implemented on graphics processing units, Journal of Computational Physics] In August 2008, HOOMD was released as open-source software. Shortly after, developers added a high-level Python scripting interface, transforming HOOMD-blue into an extensible Python package that integrates natively into the scientific Python ecosystem. [ref: HOOMD-blue version 3.0 A Modern, Extensible, Flexible, Object-Oriented API for Molecular Simulations, SciPy 2020]

== Capabilities ==
HOOMD-blue supports molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in constant-volume (NVE, NVT) and constant-pressure (NPT, NPH) thermodynamic ensembles. For particle motion, the software provides separate equations of motion, including Langevin, Brownian, and overdamped dynamics. It evaluates interaction potentials such as short-range pair cutoffs, angular or dihedral force fields, embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials, and Finnis-Sinclair (FS) metallic terms. [ref: Implementation of metal-friendly EAM/FS-type semi-empirical potentials in HOOMD-blue: A GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics software, Journal of Computational Physics] Additionally, the Hard Particle Monte Carlo (HPMC) framework supports two-dimensional and three-dimensional simulations in constant-volume (NVT) and constant-pressure (NPT) ensembles. [ref: Scalable Metropolis Monte Carlo for simulation of hard shapes, Computer Physics Communications] Supported HPMC shape classes include disks, spheres, convex polygons, concave polyhedra, spheropolygons, and ellipsoids. The high-level Python interface completely decouples simulation setup, particle initialization, and control loops from the low-level compiled backend.

== Architecture and performance ==
The engine pairs a user-facing Python API with a compiled C++/CUDA backend optimized for hardware execution. While early versions were restricted to single-GPU workstations, the engine transitioned to distributed-memory execution using spatial MPI domain decomposition. This spatial decomposition divides the global simulation box across multiple parallel processor targets. Performance evaluations demonstrate scaling across parallel supercomputing architectures. For molecular dynamics, published benchmark studies tested simulations on up to 3,375 GPUs and systems containing as many as 108 million particles. [ref: Strong scaling of general-purpose molecular dynamics simulations on GPUs, Computer Physics Communications] For Hard Particle Monte Carlo simulations, multi-GPU scaling tests demonstrated performance across up to 2,048 GPUs for systems containing 16.8 million hard polyhedra.

== Distribution and licensing ==
HOOMD-blue is distributed as open-source software under the permissive BSD 3-Clause licence, which permits free use, modification, and redistribution. [ref: License - HOOMD-blue 7.1.2 documentation, hoomd-blue.readthedocs.io] The source code repository, documentation, and user tutorials are publicly hosted online. Researchers can extend the software by writing separately compiled C++ and Python plugins. This plugin system allows developers to introduce custom pair forces, novel particle shapes, constraint algorithms, and external potential fields without modifying the core codebase.

Regalias Digitales LLC is a Bay Area-based independent music publishing administration and royalty collection company founded in 2014. The company provides royalty collection, publishing administration, and rights management services for songwriters, recording artists, producers, and music publishers. [ref: Josh Norek Is on a Mission to Help Musicians, Hispanic Executive] Regalias Digitales was the leading representative of artist and songwriter victims whose royalties were stolen in the $23 million Mediamuv scandal. [ref: YouTube Thieves Ordered to Pay $3M of Stolen Royalties Back to Bad Bunny, Julio Iglesias & Other Latin Musicians, Billboard]

Regalias Digitales was founded by music executive Josh Arón Norek, a former vice president of Nacional Records, co-founder of the Latin Alternative Music Conference (LAMC), [ref: Latin Alternative Music's Movers and Shakers Meet, The New York Times] and co-host of the syndicated public radio program The Latin Alternative. [ref: Josh Norek shines a light on alternative Latino music, Times Union] Although Regalias Digitales initially focused on representing Latin music creators and rights holders, the company subsequently expanded its roster to include artists and publishers across multiple musical genres.

Regalias Digitales' music publishing clients include hip-hop artists like Big Boi (Outkast), Lloyd Banks, Lil Gnar, OMB Peezy, Eric Bobo (Cypress Hill, Beastie Boys) [ref: Publishing Briefs: Reservoir Makes a 'Key' Move in Egypt, Plus Concord Signs Wyoming Rapper, Billboard] and SOB x RBE; rock acts like Primus, Ween, The Warning [ref: Publishing Briefs: Foreigner's Mick Jones Signs to WCM, Barry Weiss Announces Bossy Songs, Billboard] and The Used; Latin artists such as Daddy Yankee, Los Tigres del Norte, Los Tucanes de Tijuana, Grupo Codiciado, Canserbero [ref: Publishing Briefs: Kacey Musgraves On Another 'Merry Go 'Round' With Warner Chappell, Billboard]); EDM acts Said The Sky and Bonnie X Clyde; and the publishing catalogs of Regional Mexican labels like Afinarte. Regalias Digitales also represents reggae acts SOJA, Stick Figure, Collie Buddz, Steel Pulse, Tribal Seeds and Mo'Kalamity [ref: Publishing Briefs: UMPG Signs 'Poor Things' Composer Jerskin Fendrix, Billboard]; and popular Caribbean / dancehall artists such as KES The Band, Machel Montano, Travis World and Destra.

Norek's ties with the Argentine music industry date back to the 1990's, [ref: Josh Norek Is on a Mission to Help Musicians, Hispanic Executive] and the company represents the heirs of many of the country's most iconic tango, rock and folkloric artists including Astor Piazzolla, Soda Stereo, Carlos Gardel and Mercedes Sosa.

In recent years Regalias Digitales has acquired the music publishing catalogs of several artists, including Likybo, Juan Gotti, J Swey, Bill $aber, Beeda Weeda, producer Branden Cox (Icewear Vezzo, Young Thug) and Swifty Blue. [ref: Publishing Briefs: Laufey Renews Deal With Warner Chappell Music, Plus Claudia Brant & More, Billboard]

U!REKA European University is a European university alliance. The name U!REKA stands for ‘Urban Research and Education Knowledge Alliance’. The alliance brings together higher education institutions with a focus on applied sciences, professional education, and cooperation in teaching, research, and innovation.

=== Member institutions ===
As of 2024, the alliance comprises eleven member institutions:

* Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences (The Netherlands),

* Edinburgh Napier University (Scotland),
* Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences (Germany),
* HOGENT University of Applied Sciences and Arts (Belgium),
* Metropolia University of Applied Sciences (Finland),
* New Bulgarian University (Bulgaria),
* Odessa National Economic University (Ukraine),
* UAS BFI Vienna (Austria),
* Universidade Politécnica de Lisboa (Portugal),
* University of Bari Aldo Moro (Italy)
* VSB Technical University of Ostrava (Czech Republic).

Together, the member institutions represent approximately 123,000 students and 13,000 staff members.

=== Funding ===
The alliance is supported through the European Union's Erasmus+ programme [ref: The European Universities alliances in action - European Education Area, education.ec.europa.eu], which funds cooperation in higher education, research, innovation, and societal engagement. Following its designation as a European University alliance, the U!REKA SHIFT project received co-funding from the European Union [ref: European Universities alliances and their partners - European Education Area, education.ec.europa.eu] for an initial four-year period. The programme also provides opportunities for transitional funding between EU budget periods.

=== Objectives and activities ===
U!REKA promotes cooperation among its member institutions in the fields of teaching, research, innovation, and academic mobility. The alliance develops joint initiatives and projects related to urban challenges, including the Urban Commons Lab [ref: U!REKA Lab: Urban Commons – Collaborative Challenge Based European University Education] and the U!REKA Change Agents programme [ref: U!REKA Change Agents engage students in challenge-based learning to develop skills for innovation, Metrospective]. It also organizes an annual networking event known as U!REKA Connects. [ref: EURASHE at the U!REKA Connects meeting, EURASHE]

The alliance's activities are centred on supporting the transition towards climate-neutral and smart cities. This focus is linked to the European Union's Mission Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities, which aims to support 100 European cities in achieving climate neutrality by 2030 [ref: EU Mission: Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities, research-and-innovation.ec.europa.eu]. Several cities associated with member institutions, including Amsterdam, Helsinki, and Lisbon, participate in the mission. [ref: 112 Mission Cities striving for climate neutrality by 2030, NetZeroCities]

=== History ===

==== Formation ====
U!REKA was established in Amsterdam in November 2016 by six higher education institutions [ref: Explore our journey, U!REKA]:

* Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences (Netherlands)
* HOGENT University of Applied Sciences and Arts (Belgium)
* Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences (Germany)
* Metropolia University of Applied Sciences (Finland)
* Edinburgh Napier University (Scotland, United Kingdom)
* Oslo and Akershus University College of Applied Sciences (Norway; later renamed OsloMet)

In 2020, the alliance expanded with the addition of Politécnico de Lisboa (Portugal) and VSB Technical University of Ostrava (Czech Republic). OsloMet subsequently withdrew from the consortium in 2021.

=== Recognition as a European University Alliance ===
In 2023, U!REKA was selected by the European Commission under the third call of the European Universities Initiative, obtaining official recognition as a European University alliance. [ref: ]

In January 2024, four additional institutions joined the alliance:

* UAS BFI Vienna (Austria)
* University of Bari Aldo Moro (Italy)
* Odessa National Economic University (Ukraine)
* New Bulgarian University (Bulgaria)

=== Partnerships ===
U!REKA cooperates with regional authorities, municipalities, European networks, and other organizations. Its partners include [ref: Our U!REKA Moment: Co-Creating Sustainability Education Across Urban European Contexts, UAS Journal]:

==== Cities and municipalities ====
* Amsterdam
* Cascais
* Espoo
* Frankfurt
* Ghent
* Helsinki
* Lisbon
* Oeiras
* Ostrava
* Vantaa

==== Regional authorities and public bodies ====
* Helsinki-Uusimaa Regional Council
* Hessian Ministry of Science and Research, Arts and Culture
* District of Offenbach
* Moravian-Silesian Innovation Centre
* Province of East Flanders

==== European networks ====
* ERRIN (European Regions Research and Innovation Network)
* EURASHE (European Association of Institutions in Higher Education)

==== Other organizations ====
* POLITEC&ID
* Waag FutureLab
* Platform Talent voor Technologie / Katapult

Enzo Cacciola (born 12 December 1945) is an Italian artist associated with Analytical Painting. Since the 1970s, his work has incorporated industrial materials including cement and asbestos, later extending to materials such as Multigum and denim. [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia processo e provocazione, Il Giornale dell'Arte] He participated in the international exhibition Analytische Malerei in Düsseldorf in 1975 and in documenta 6 in Kassel in 1977. [ref: Angela Madesani, curator, The Golden Nightingale. Ricostruzione di una mostra, Progettoarte-Elm, Milan, 10 May–29 June 2018, reconstructing Palma Bucarelli's project for the third Golden Nightingale prize in Platres, Cyprus, in 1973, https://www.progettoarte-elm.com/eng/exhibitions/the-golden-nightingale-ricostruzione-di-una-mostra (accessed 14 July 2026); Klaus Honnef and Catherine Millet, Analytische Malerei (Genoa: Edizioni Masnata/La Bertesca, 1975); documenta, documenta 6, 24 June–2 October 1977, https://documenta.de/en/retrospective/documenta-6 (accessed 14 July 2026).]

== Life and career ==
Cacciola held his first solo exhibition at Galleria La Bertesca in Genoa in 1971. In 1973, Palma Bucarelli included him with Paolo Cotani, Marco Gastini, Carmengloria Morales and Gianfranco Zappettini in her project for the third Golden Nightingale prize in Platres, Cyprus. [ref: Gli analitici di Palma, Il Gionale delle Arte]

In 1975, Cacciola participated in Analytische Malerei in Düsseldorf, curated by Klaus Honnef and Catherine Millet. Two years later, he took part in documenta 6 in Kassel. [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia processo e provocazione, Il Giornale dell'Arte]

Cacciola has also been active in local government in Rocca Grimalda. He served as mayor from 1995 to 2004, returned to the office in 2020, and was elected again in May 2026. [ref: Le elezioni comunali nei paesi dell’Alessandrino: tutti i sindaci eletti, La Stampa] [ref: Comune di Rocca Grimalda, www.comune.roccagrimalda.al.it]

== Work ==

=== Early geometric and analytical work ===

During the late 1960s and early 1970s, Cacciola developed geometric-concrete works incorporating elements such as neon. His attention to the division of pictorial space led to multipart works in which the wall behind the individual elements formed part of the composition. In the Superfici integrative of the early 1970s, the work therefore depended on its surrounding architectural context. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 9–10; Corà, Uncini Cacciola, 9–10.]

Cacciola's work developed within the Italian current of Analytical Painting, whose practitioners examined painting through its material and structural components rather than through representation. His particular focus was the relationship between the support, the physical surface, the materials used and the sequence of operations through which the work was made. [ref: Meneguzzo, Pittura Analitica. I percorsi italiani 1970–1980; Giorgio Bonomi et al., Pensare Pittura. Una linea internazionale di ricerca negli anni '70 (Cinisello Balsamo: Silvana Editoriale, 2009).] In the Asbesti works of 1974, he combined asbestos-containing mixtures with a restricted range of muted pigments. [ref: Enzo Cacciola tra materia, processo e provocazione - Il Giornale dell'Arte, Il Giornale dell'Arte] From 1975, he applied unpigmented cement directly to canvas, with the resulting layers and drips retaining visible traces of the working process. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 12.]

In his text Processo operativo (1975), Cacciola described the materials, manual procedures, and working times involved in producing his cement paintings, treating the process itself as a constituent element of the work. [ref: Corà, Uncini Cacciola, 9–11; Salvatore Russo, "Enzo Cacciola Interviewed," Art International Contemporary Magazine, no. 3 (May–June 2022): 14.]

Photography became integral to this process. Cacciola photographed successive stages in the application of cement and displayed the resulting sequences as components of the work itself. He later extended the combination of photography and painting to the site-related cycles begun in 1979. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 16–17.]

In a diary entry published in KUNSTFORUM International in 1975, Klaus Honnef wrote that, despite his initially ambivalent response to Cacciola's work, the artist's method corresponded closely to the principles Honnef had formulated for Analytical Painting. [ref: Klaus Honnef, "Tagebuch," KUNSTFORUM International 14, no. 3 (1975): 168; reproduced and translated in Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 13–14.]

At documenta 6, Cacciola delegated the selection of the work shown in his allotted space to Honnef and Weiss. The curators chose a sixteenth-century Venetian Venus attributed to Titian's workshop from the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum in Cologne. It was accompanied by Cacciola's Processo operativo, which explained the transfer of the artist's decision-making role to the curators. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 14–15; documenta 6, vol. 1, 58.]

In the early 1980s, Cacciola temporarily turned to figurative painting; works from this period were included in Achille Bonito Oliva's Pittura in radice in 1981. [ref: Valenti, "L'incessante sperimentazione," 18–20; Bonito Oliva, Pittura in radice.]

Linxens is a French technology company that manufactures components and develops technologies used in smart cards, identification products, radio-frequency identification (RFID), and other electronic applications. Its products have included microconnectors, antennas, RFID inlays and tags, and components used in payment cards, SIM cards and identification products. [ref: Linxens France SA, Bloomberg]

Linxens originated from the Microconnections division of French connector manufacturer FCI. In 2011, the division was sold to private equity firm Astorg and established as a stand-alone business. The company was later renamed Linxens and was acquired by CVC Capital Partners in 2015. In 2018, Tsinghua Unigroup agreed to acquire Linxens from CVC.

== History ==

=== Microconnections and Astorg ===

Linxens originated from the Microconnections division of FCI, a French manufacturer of electrical connectors. In 2011, private equity firm Astorg acquired the division from FCI, separating Microconnections from its former parent and establishing it as a stand-alone business. [ref: Astorg Partners scelle le rachat des microcircuits de FCI, L'Agefi]

FCI had previously been the connector subsidiary of the French industrial group Areva before being acquired by Bain Capital in 2006. [ref: Astorg négocie en exclusivité le rachat des microconnexions de FCI, L'Agefi]

At the time of the Astorg transaction, Microconnections had reported revenue of €202 million for 2010. L'Agefi described it as the world leader in the production of flexible connectors for smart cards.

The business was subsequently renamed Linxens. [ref: REFILE-LPC-Banks line up around 1 bln euros of debt for CVC Linxens buy, Reuters]

=== Acquisition by CVC Capital Partners ===

In 2015, CVC Capital Partners entered into an agreement to acquire Linxens from Astorg. [ref: CVC to Buy French Tech Firm Linxens in $1.7 Billion Deal, The Wall Street Journal] [ref: CVC valoriserait 1,5 milliard d’euros son LBO sur le français Linxens, L'Agefi]

The Wall Street Journal reported that the transaction valued Linxens at approximately €1.5 billion ($1.66 billion) and that CVC had pre-empted an auction process being run by Astorg.

Reuters reported that Linxens had approximately 1,100 employees, five manufacturing facilities and three research and development centres in Europe and Asia at the time.

Between 2010 and 2014, Linxens's annual sales increased from approximately €200 million to €253 million, according to L'Agefi. The company had manufacturing operations in France and Singapore and had also acquired Thai company KNL, which specialized in contactless technology.

L'Agefi reported that Linxens was benefiting from the expansion of smart-card use in China and the United States. Europe and Asia accounted for approximately 49 percent and 51 percent of its sales respectively.

=== Acquisition by Tsinghua Unigroup ===

In 2018, Chinese semiconductor company Tsinghua Unigroup moved to acquire Linxens from CVC. [ref: Chinese chipmaker Tsinghua Unigroup to buy France's Linxens for $2.6 billion - sources, Reuters]

The proposed acquisition received coverage in the French press. Le Figaro described Linxens as a French technology "pépite" and reported on the proposed transaction. [ref: Un chinois convoite Linxens, une pépite de la tech française, Le Figaro]

Reuters reported that Tsinghua Unigroup had agreed to acquire Linxens for approximately €2.2 billion. The proposed acquisition also raised questions over whether the French government would regard Linxens as a strategic company and therefore subject the transaction to foreign-investment controls.

The French government did not object to the transaction. According to a Finance Ministry official cited by Reuters, Linxens was not considered strategic because it manufactured passive components rather than semiconductors. [ref: France not objecting to sale of Linxens to Chinese group, Reuters]

=== Tsinghua restructuring ===

Tsinghua Unigroup later experienced serious financial difficulties and defaulted on bond obligations in 2020. The group entered a court-supervised restructuring process in China in 2021. [ref: China's Tsinghua Unigroup says creditors back restructuring plan, Reuters]

A consortium led by Wise Road Capital and JAC Capital was subsequently selected as the strategic investor in Tsinghua Unigroup's restructuring.

The restructuring was completed in 2022, with Wise Road Capital and JAC Capital among the investors in the reorganized group.

== Operations ==

Linxens manufactures components used in smart cards and other electronic products. Its smart-card products have included connectors used in banking cards, SIM cards, identification cards and health cards.

The company also develops Internet of Things (IoT) and RFID technologies. Bloomberg describes Linxens France's activities as including IoT modules, authentication and traceability platforms, and RFID inlays and tags.

Bloomberg lists automotive, logistics, luxury goods, transportation, supply chain, food and beverage, and healthcare among the sectors served by Linxens France.

The company has operated manufacturing and research facilities in Europe and Asia.

== Tsinghua Unigroup International litigation ==

Linxens Holding SAS was involved in legal proceedings in the British Virgin Islands arising from the liquidation of Tsinghua Unigroup International Co. Ltd. (TUI).
[truncated]

Remzi Gökdağ (born 1968 in Istanbul) is a Turkish journalist and author.

==Journalism career==

Gökdağ was born in Istanbul in 1968. [ref: Following Footsteps] While studying journalism at Istanbul University, he began his journalism career as a reporter for Cumhuriyet in 1989. [ref: Efsane isimlerin izinde 'Başka Şehirler', Aydınlık] He covered Istanbul's urban development and municipal affairs. [ref: Belediye muhabiri gökdelene karşı, EP Medya] [ref: Bir kent suçunun belgesel öyküsü, Cumhuriyet Kitap Eki]

In the early 1990s, Gökdağ reported for Cumhuriyet on the controversies surrounding the Park Hotel and the Süzer Building, known as "Gökkafes." [ref: Gökkafes haberi suç değil, Cumhuriyet] A lawsuit seeking 2 billion lira in damages was filed against Gökdağ and other defendants over the reporting. The court dismissed the case. [ref: Gökkafes'in sahibinin açtığı dava reddedildi, Cumhuriyet]

In 1993, he received an award from the Contemporary Journalists Association [ref: ÇGD ödülleri sahiplerini buldu, Cumhuriyet] and an honorable mention in the Çetin Emeç Journalism Encouragement Awards [ref: Emeç Ödülleri sahiplerini buldu, Cumhuriyet] for his story about "Matmazel," an elderly member of Istanbul's Rum community living alone in Beyoğlu. [ref: Son sahneyi oynuyor matmazel, Cumhuriyet]

Gökdağ later worked abroad, serving as the Moscow correspondent for Kanal D and Radikal. [ref: Kaliforniya'da Bir Türk Gazetesi, VOA Türkçe] In Los Angeles, he continued reporting for Cumhuriyet [ref: Başka şehirlere zaman yolculuğu, Diken]; by 2005 he had become editor-in-chief of the newly launched California Turkish Times, a Turkish-language newspaper based in California. [ref: ABD'de yeni Türk gazetesi, Cumhuriyet] Cumhuriyet later published his reporting from Zurich [ref: Avrupalı göçmenlerin ekmek kapısı, Cumhuriyet] and Dubai. [ref: Remzi Gökdağ / BAE (Dubai), Cumhuriyet]

Shaheed Dr Syed Muhammad Ali Naqvi (28 September 1952 – 07 March 1995) was a prominent Pakistani Shia leader, medical practitioner, and community organizer from Lahore. He is widely recognized as the principal founder of the Imamia Students Organization (ISO) Pakistan, the largest student organization for Shia youth in Pakistan. [ref: Rieck, Andreas. The Shia of Pakistan: An Assertive Minority. Oxford University Press, 2015, pp. 214–225. ISBN 978-0190240967.] [ref: Khan, Tasleem Raza. Safeer-e-Inqilab: Biography of Shaheed Dr. Muhammad Ali Naqvi. Youth Progressive Publications, 2002.] He was also a key figure in the formation of Tehreek-e-Jafaria Pakistan (TJP) and a close associate of Allama Arif Hussain Hussaini. He played an instrumental role in shaping Shia student activism, anti-imperialist awareness, and socio-religious reforms in Pakistan. [ref: Fuchs, Simon Wolfgang. Inverted World: Shi'i Thought and Activism in Modern South Asia. Harvard University Press, 2019, pp. 165–170. ISBN 978-0674980792.] [ref: ISO founder Dr Naqvi remembered, Dawn]

== Early life and education ==
Dr. Syed Muhammad Ali Naqvi was born in Ali Raza Abad, Lahore on 28 September 1952. He received his early education in Lahore and spent parts of his childhood in East Africa, where his father served as a preacher. [ref: Khan, Tasleem Raza. Safeer-e-Inqilab: Biography of Shaheed Dr. Muhammad Ali Naqvi. Youth Progressive Publications, 2002.] He completed his higher secondary education at Government College, Lahore before enrolling at King Edward Medical University, where he earned his Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree. [ref: ISO founder Dr Naqvi remembered, Dawn]

== Founding of ISO Pakistan and activism ==
On 22 May 1972, while studying at King Edward Medical College, Dr. Naqvi alongside fellow Shia students founded the Imamia Students Organization (ISO Pakistan) to unify Shia youth, promote religious literacy, and provide educational and social assistance. [ref: Remembering Dr Muhammad Ali Naqvi: Tribute paid to ISO founder, The Express Tribune] Under his leadership, ISO grew into a nationwide network across Pakistani universities, colleges, and schools. [ref: Dr Naqvi remembered on anniversary, The Nation]

He was a staunch follower of Ruhollah Khomeini and the ideology of the Islamic Revolution, advocating for Islamic unity and social justice while actively organizing anti-imperialist rallies and educational workshops across the country. [ref: Fuchs, Simon Wolfgang. Inverted World: Shi'i Thought and Activism in Modern South Asia. Harvard University Press, 2019, pp. 165–170. ISBN 978-0674980792.]

== Political activism and major events ==
During his student life and medical practice, Dr. Muhammad Ali Naqvi was deeply involved in grassroots political organizing and public mobilizations in Pakistan:

* 1980 Islamabad Demonstration: In July 1980, when the Shia community organized a massive sit-in in Islamabad against Zakat and Ushr Ordinance enforcement under General Zia-ul-Haq's regime, Dr. Naqvi played a crucial role on the ground in organizing logistics, student volunteers, and medical first-aid teams. [ref: Rieck, Andreas. The Shia of Pakistan: An Assertive Minority. Oxford University Press, 2015, pp. 214–225. ISBN 978-0190240967.]
* Formation of Tehreek-e-Jafaria (TJP): Dr. Naqvi was key in connecting student activism with national religious leadership, working closely with Allama Arif Hussain Hussaini to organize political awareness rallies across Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during the 1980s. [ref: Fuchs, Simon Wolfgang. Inverted World: Shi'i Thought and Activism in Modern South Asia. Harvard University Press, 2019, pp. 165–170. ISBN 978-0674980792.]
* Establishing Free Healthcare: Alongside political rallies, he operated healthcare clinics and free medical outreach programs in Lahore for underprivileged communities. [ref: Khan, Tasleem Raza. Safeer-e-Inqilab: Biography of Shaheed Dr. Muhammad Ali Naqvi. Youth Progressive Publications, 2002.]

== Death ==
On 7 March 1995, Dr. Syed Muhammad Ali Naqvi was assassinated at Yateem Khana Chowk in Lahore. [ref: Remembering Dr Muhammad Ali Naqvi: Tribute paid to ISO founder, The Express Tribune] He was laid to rest in his ancestral cemetery at Ali Raza Abad, Lahore. [ref: Dr Naqvi remembered on anniversary, The Nation]

== References ==

Open systems theory (OST) is a conceptual framework for active socioecological adaptation and democratic self-management developed by the social scientists Fred Emery and Merrelyn Emery. It provides both a theoretical view of organizations and their environments and practical methods for organisational and community design and planning. It is an amalgamation of research on sociotechnical system by the Tavistock Institute of Human Relations, Ludwig von Bertalanffy's general systems theory (GST), and the conceptualisation of the environment as Causal Textures by Fred Emery and Eric Trist.

== Core concepts ==
Two concepts are central: the genotypical organizational design principles, which describe two different places where the responsibility for control and coordination lies: over the work (known as DP1) or with the people doing it (known as DP2). DP1 produces dominant hierarchies while DP2 produces self-managing groups.

The other is the ecological view in which people and their environments co-evolve, so that active adaptation requires changing the system and environment together.

==Applications==
The framework is used for organizational unified design and change, using methods like the Search Conference for strategic planning and the Participative Design Workshop to design a DP2-based organisational structure. These can be combined to form a two-stage method for active adaptation. OST has been applied in democracy programmes in both the private and public sectors, in community planning, and in a wide range of research projects.

==Reception==
Baburoğlu tracks the development of the framework from the 60s through the mid-1990s. Mike Jackson places OST within the wider systems thinking tradition. OST methods are also treated in surveys of Dialogic Organization Development.

Lamin Sillah (born 6 June 2006) is a Gambian professional footballer who plays as a striker for EFL League Two club Gillingham, on loan from Nottingham Forest. He previously played for Steve Biko in The Gambia and the under-19 side of Greek club Olympiacos, and has represented The Gambia at under-20 level.

==Club career==

===Early career===
Sillah began his career with Steve Biko in the Gambian First Division. He made a strong start to the 2023–24 season, scoring nine goals in his first ten league appearances and providing three assists. [ref: Sillah, Mustapha open up on GFF Division 1 Golden boot race, The Alkamba Times] Sillah said that he had taken on greater goalscoring responsibility following the departure of Adama Bojang from the club.

He finished the season as the league's top goalscorer with 14 goals. [ref: Title favorites, new signing, drop in goal ratio and relegation battle, The Alkamba Times] In May 2024, Sillah also scored as Steve Biko beat Elite United 2–0 to reach the semi-finals of the Gambia Football Federation Cup. [ref: Medina Utd, Steve Biko, Team Rhino cruise to FF Cup semis, The Point]

Sillah subsequently moved to Greece, signing a four-year contract with Olympiacos in October 2024. Three days after signing, he scored the winning goal on his debut for the club's under-19 side in a 2–1 victory over Panathinaikos. [ref: Λαμίν Σιλά: Υπέγραψε την Πέμπτη 4ετές συμβόλαιο στον Ολυμπιακό και την Κυριακή έκρινε το ντέρμπι «αιωνίων» Κ19, Sportal]

Sillah scored nine goals and provided five assists in 17 U19 Super League appearances during his season with Olympiacos. [ref: Forest sign Sillah, Nottingham Forest F.C.] He was also part of the club's squad in the 2024–25 UEFA Youth League. [ref: UEFA Youth League 2024–2025 – Knockout Round 32, Olympiacos F.C.]

===Nottingham Forest===
On 16 July 2025, Sillah moved to England to sign for Nottingham Forest on a contract until the summer of 2028, initially joining the club's B team.

He became a regular in Forest's development side during the 2025–26 season and also made three appearances for the club's under-21 team in the EFL Trophy. [ref: Gills snap up striker on loan, Kent Sports News] On 24 May 2026, Sillah was named in a Nottingham Forest senior matchday squad for the first time, remaining an unused substitute in a 1–1 Premier League draw with Bournemouth. [ref: Nottingham Forest vs. Bournemouth Match Report – Sunday May 24, 2026, FBref]

===Loan to Gillingham===
On 27 August 2026, Sillah joined EFL League Two club Gillingham on loan for the remainder of the 2026–27 season. He had scored in both of Forest B's opening two matches of the season prior to the move, including an equaliser against Gateshead in the National League Cup.

Sillah made his English Football League debut two days after signing, replacing Ronan Hale in the 81st minute of a 1–1 draw with Northampton Town at Priestfield. [ref: Live Commentary – Gillingham vs Northampton, Sky Sports] On 5 September 2026, Sillah scored his first goal in the EFL in a 4–1 away win against Rochdale. [ref: Rochdale 1-4 Gillingham Report, Gillingham F.C]

==International career==
Sillah was selected for the Gambia under-20 squad for the 2024 WAFU Zone A U20 tournament in Liberia. [ref: Gambia U-20 gaffer announces squad ahead of WAFU U-20 tourney, The Point]

He scored as Gambia came from behind to draw 2–2 with defending champions Senegal in the group stage. [ref: Gambia draws Senegal at Wafu U-20 tourney, The Standard] Sillah scored again in a 3–0 victory over Guinea in the third-place play-off as Gambia finished the tournament in third place. [ref: Gambia U20 vs Guinea U20, Global Sports Archive]

==References==

Boeotia Football Clubs Association (Greek: Ένωση Ποδοσφαιρικών Σωματείων Βοιωτίας) is the governing body of association football in the regional unit of Boeotia, Greece. [ref: Ε.Π.Σ. Βοιωτίας, Ελληνικό Ποδόσφαιρο] Based in Livadeia, it is a member of the Hellenic Football Federation (HFF). It is responsible for organizing local league championships and the local Cup, as well as youth championships. It also coordinates the regional representative teams (Youth and Children), which compete at the national level.

== History ==
It was founded as an independent association in 1973; [ref: Ιστορική Αναδρομή, EPS Boiotias] in previous years, specifically from 1928 to 1973, teams from the Boeotia region participated in competitions organized by the Euboea Football Clubs Association (as the Euboea–Boeotia FCA).

Under its jurisdiction are the regional Cup and league competitions. In the men's category during the 2024–25 season, two divisions existed: the A Category with 11 clubs [ref: Βαθμολογία, EPS Boiotias], and the B Category with two groups of 12 and 14 clubs each.

Draft: Crossley-Kegresse half-track

Draft text:
----

The Crossley-Kégresse half-track was an experimental half-track using the Kégresse track tested by the British army in the late 1920s. The production vehicles were produced by Crossley Motors in the United Kingdom and delivered to the army from 1926. The Kégresse track was licensed from Citroën in France, which employed its inventor Adolphe Kégresse.

== Development ==

Kégresse half-tracks were also extensively used by the French army, [ref: ] [ref: ] including the later Citroën P17 and P107 utility half-tracks. [ref: Le grand album des Citroën-Kégresse sous l'uniforme, Histoire & Collections] In 1923, the British army purchased Kégresse half-track vehicles from Citroën for testing, but ultimately decided they were not satisfactory for its purposes and commissioned Crossley Motors to produce a new vehicle using the licensed track from Citroën.

In the British army, the Crossley vehicle could replace horses for haulage work that otherwise only animals could do, one of the first such attempts in the world. The Kégresse track had a two-speed gearbox while the standard gearbox had four speeds, giving a total of eight forward speeds. It was otherwise driven like a truck. It was used as a general service vehicle, a staff car, and an artillery tractor. [ref: ]

== Service history ==

=== Trials and field exercises ===

Test trials began at least as early as October 1924. [ref: ] In February 1925 comparative cross-country and road trials took place in which the Crossley-Kégresse half-track placed first, ahead of the fully tracked Vickers Light Dragon Mark II. By November 1925, it had been found "capable of traversing the most difficult country at a very fair speed" in government trials. [ref: ] In later trials, it proved capable of pulling a heavy QF 4.5-inch howitzer across open country, including through a stream. [ref: ] In 1926, it was demonstrated to the heads of government of the British Dominions at Camberley, equipped to tow a QF 3.7-inch mountain howitzer.

It was among the first vehicles used to equip the British army's interwar Experimental Mechanised Force (EMF), the first mechanised combined arms brigade in the world. At the Force's formation in 1927, the Crossley half-track was used by the machine-gun battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry, [ref: ] and the 9th Field Brigade of the Royal Artillery, allowing these previously non-mechanised infantry and artillery units to manoeuvre alongside the 3rd and 5th battalions of the Royal Tank Corps in a prototype of a modern combined arms mechanised force. Operating with the 'fast group' it maintained a daily average cross-country speed of 10 mph over 30 miles. This was "the first mechanised formation to be born in the world, and was the mother of all 'armoured divisions'".

=== Shanghai deployment ===

Between February and May 1927, tensions arose in China. The EMF's 11 and 80 batteries, armed with QF 18-pounder guns, were re-equipped with Crossley-Kégresse half-tracks and Burford-Kégresse half-tracks, replacing their fully tracked Vickers Light Dragon Mark IIs, and shipped to China as part of the Shanghai Defence Force. This Force was withdrawn in January 1928. In 1928 and 1929, the remaining Vickers Light Dragon Mark IIs towing artillery in the EMF in the UK were also replaced with Burford- and Crossley-Kégresse half tracks.

== Legacy ==

In 1927, the British War Office ordered a related Crossley vehicle in which drive wheels could be fitted with chain tracks, intended to reproduce the functionality of the Crossley-Kégresse vehicle in a more flexible format. [ref: ] The half-track Crossley-Kégresse left British army consideration in the early 1930s, as part of a general shift away from half-tracks to fully tracked vehicles by the army.

At least two examples of the half-track have survived and been preserved, one by the Norfolk Tank Museum and another by the British army's Royal Logistics Corps Museum, both in the United Kingdom. Official Ministry of Supply photographs of the vehicle are held in the collections of the Imperial War Museum. [ref: ]

== References ==

* Moving the Guns: The Mechanisation of the Royal Artillery, 1854-1939, HMSO
* British Military Transport, 1829–1956, HMSO
* Men, Ideas and Tanks: British Military Thought and Armoured Forces, 1903–39, Manchester University Press
* The Tanks: The History of the Royal Tank Regiment and its Predecessors Heavy Branch Machine-Gun Corps Tank Corps & Royal Tank Corps 1914–1945 (1914–1939), Praeger

Draft: Volunteers in Technical Assistance (VITA)

Draft text:
Volunteers in Technical Assistance (VITA) was an American nonprofit organization that provided technical assistance for international development. It emerged in 1959 from a group of scientists and engineers linked to General Electric. VITA became an early organization associated with appropriate technology. [ref: Imagining the future through revisiting the past: the value of history in thinking about R(R)I's possible future(s), Journal of Responsible Innovation]

==History==
VITA developed from discussions among scientists and engineers at General Electric in Schenectady, New York. Some also taught at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. [ref: Engineering and Sustainable Community Development, Morgan & Claypool Publishers series SYNTHESIS LECTURES ON ENGINEERS, TECHNOLOGY, AND SOCIETY] The group began receiving requests for technical advice from charities. The United States Agency for International Development contracted it to study solar cookers in 1960. [ref: Imagining the future through revisiting the past: the value of history in thinking about R(R)I's possible future(s), Journal of Responsible Innovation]

VITA later expanded outside the United States. It had affiliated groups in several countries by 1968. In 1969, the Office of Economic Opportunity commissioned VITA to undertake work in the United States.

== Activities ==
VITA maintained a roster of volunteers used by more than 120 private relief organizations by 1991. These included CARE, the Red Cross, Catholic Relief Services and Save the Children. [ref: DOCTORS WHO RESPOND TO SUFFERING ABROAD, The Washington Post] VITA also used computer networks to distribute technical information. The Washington Post in 1993 reported that the organization used the Internet in its work. It advised countries on subjects such as crop production and water facilities. [ref: GETTING CAUGHT UP IN THE INTERNET, The Washington Post]

The organization also worked on projects linking development with environmental conservation. The Christian Science Monitor in 1995 reported on VITA's work near the Perinet nature reserve in Madagascar. VITA trained local guides for ecotourism. It also oversaw a program that directed part of national park revenue to village projects. [ref: Poor Nations Confront Choice of Trees or Jobs, Christian Science Monitor]

== Merger ==
VITA in 2005 joined with EnterpriseWorks Worldwide. The combined organization became known as EnterpriseWorks/VITA. [ref: Simple Ways to Keep Food Cool, Voice of America] EnterpriseWorks/VITA later merged with Relief International in 2009. [ref: ]

Draft: Pavel Florjančič

Draft text:
Pavel Florjančič (born 11 August 1947) is a Slovenian painter known primarily for his work in realism, photorealism, and hyperrealism. His work is particularly associated with still-life painting, with an emphasis on light, reflections, and the material qualities of depicted objects. [ref: Pavel Florjančič »V iskanju univerzalne lepote«, Sokolski dom Škofja Loka] [ref: Pavel Florjančič, Loški muzej Škofja Loka]

== Early life and education ==
Florjančič was born on 11 August 1947 in Virlog near Škofja Loka, Slovenia. From 1962 to 1966, he attended the School of Design in Ljubljana, where he studied applied graphic design. He later continued his education at the Department of Art Education of the Pedagogical Academy in Ljubljana.

Between 1970 and 1975, he worked as an art teacher at an elementary school in Škofja Loka. In 1975, he obtained the status of an independent cultural worker as a painter, and in 1977 he received a state scholarship for further artistic training in Paris.

In 1979, together with artists including Franc Berčič - Berko, Herman Gvardjančič, Franc Novinc and Ive Šubic, he became one of the founding members of the Association of Artists of Škofja Loka (Združenje umetnikov Škofja Loka, ZUŠL). [ref: Zgodovina ZUŠL, Združenje umetnikov Škofja Loka]

From 1986 onward, he collaborated with galleries in Munich and later exhibited elsewhere in Europe and in the United States. He lives and works in Škofja Loka.

== Artistic work ==
Florjančič's painting is based on close observation of the physical world and a highly detailed realist painting technique. Still lifes form a central part of his body of work. Recurring motifs include glass, fruit, flowers, bottles, drinking glasses, musical instruments and other everyday objects.

Light is an important element in his work. Art historian and critic Damir Globočnik, writing in connection with the exhibition V iskanju univerzalne lepote ("In Search of Universal Beauty"), highlighted Florjančič's treatment of light, reflections on glass surfaces and the realistic depiction of the material qualities of objects.

In 2007, art historian Boštjan Soklič wrote about Florjančič's work in the journal Loški razgledi on the occasion of the artist's 60th birthday. [ref: Razstava Pavla Florjančiča ob umetnikovi 60. letnici, Loški razgledi]

== Exhibitions ==
Since the 1970s, Florjančič has participated in numerous solo and group exhibitions in Slovenia and abroad. His solo exhibitions have included presentations at the Ivan Grohar Gallery in Škofja Loka, galleries in Linz and Vienna, an exhibition in New York in 2016, and an exhibition at the Šivec House Gallery in Radovljica in 2019.

In 2007, the Ivan Grohar Gallery in Škofja Loka organised an exhibition marking his 60th birthday. The exhibition and his work were also covered by the Slovenian newspaper Gorenjski glas. [ref: Tihožitja, ki so živa, Gorenjski glas]

In 2020, his exhibition V iskanju univerzalne lepote was presented at the Sokolski dom Gallery in Škofja Loka.

== Awards and recognition ==
In 2020, the Association of Artists of Škofja Loka, with the support of the Municipality of Škofja Loka, awarded Florjančič the Grohar Award for his lifetime artistic achievement and his contribution to the association.

== List of ferns of West Virginia==
The term "Ferns" is here used in the historical sense and includes Ferns, Spikemosses, Clubmosses, and Quillworts.

This checklist was compiled from the following sources: WVU Herbarium, SERNEC, iNaturalist, USDA Plants and PteridoPortal records. For the most part, the nomenclature used in this list follows that in "Ferns, Spikemosses, Clubmosses, and Quillworts of Eastern North America" by Emily Sessa.

Draft: Ipe Akoko

Draft text:
Ipe-Akoko (historically called Ukue, Ukpe, or Uqwe) is a town in the Akoko South-East Local Government Area of Ondo State, Nigeria. [ref: Social and Economic Development of Akoko Society under Colonial Rule, West Bohemian Historical Review]

== History ==
Oral tradition states that the people of Ipe-Akoko migrated from Ife. During early regional conflicts, the community moved to a rocky hill called Uloke for protection. [ref: Inter-Group Relations in Akoko, 1800–1960, Ibadan University Press]

After the conflicts ended, residents moved back down to the flat land. The Ibà quarter descended first. This relocation was completed by around 1928, but colonial administrative files and early church records show the town was already established long before. [ref: National Archives Ibadan (NAI), Colonial Secretary's Office (CSO) Files on Akoko District Assessment Reports (1910–1930).] [ref: The History of Evangelism and Church Growth in Akoko, Ondo State, Journal of Religion in Africa] The Uloke stone site still exists in the town layout.

== Monarchy ==
The king of Ipe-Akoko is known as the Olupe of Ipe-Akoko. Local tradition names Oba Ajagbi as the first king. The current ruler is Oba Ajiyinrere Francis Makanjuola Apata JP (Arogunbola II).

The monarchy rotates among several royal families across the town quarters:
* Abamido (Ibà quarter)
* Odepo (Ibà quarter)
* Odovie Ute (Igbede quarter)

== Quarters ==
The town contains 11 traditional quarters: Ibà-Ute, Ibà-Peju, Okun, Isinodo, Ilegbe, Igbede, Ugbe, Itoto, Ipaso, Uwi, and Uthakpe.

== Language and Culture ==
The native name of the town and its people is Ukue. Over time, neighboring communities began referring to the settlement as Ipe.

The indigenous language is Ukue (also referred to as Ipe), which belongs to the Edoid language family. [ref: Comparative Edoid: Phonology and Lexicon, University of Port Harcourt Press] Linguistic studies on the Ipe language demonstrate historical vocabulary contact and borrowing with English, Yoruba, and Edo. [ref: Aspect of Borrowing in the Ipe and Yoruba Languages, EBSU Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities] Most residents are also fluent in Yoruba. Cultural events in the town include the Chegba festival, which features traditional rites and virginity dances (*Uge*), alongside the Uheni, Ella, and Opara festivals. [ref: Chegba festival: Ipe-Akoko showcases widest beans cake, The Hope Newspaper]

== Infrastructure ==

=== Healthcare ===
* General Hospital, Ipe-Akoko: A public secondary medical facility in Ibà quarter, established in 1979. [ref: Healthcare and Community Development in Ondo State, Tribune Online] [ref: General Hospital Ipe Akoko - Healthcare Services Directory, Medpages]
* Igbede Primary Health Care Centre: A local public health clinic serving Igbede quarter.

=== Education ===
* Ipe High School: A public secondary school established in September 1976.
* Olawale International Model Secondary School: A private secondary institution.
* Dynamic Excellent College: A private secondary school operating as a regional examination centre.

== Notable People ==
* Prof. Olanrewaju Olu-Adeyemi – Professor of Political Science at Adekunle Ajasin University.

Draft: Grzegorz Zwoliński

Draft text:
Grzegorz Zwoliński is a Polish technology entrepreneur. He is the founder and chief executive officer of ARES Shield, a company developing high-power microwave (HPM) systems intended to protect satellites. [ref: Polish startup ARES Shield hired to protect data center satellites with high-power microwave weapons, Space.com] [ref: Ares Shield has a big ambition – and a long way to go, XYZ] He previously co-founded and led the satellite manufacturer SatRev (formerly SatRevolution) [ref: Polish space startup puts first nanosats into orbit, eyes satellite constellation and production facility, SpaceNews] and co-founded the mobile-game developer T-Bull. [ref: Producent gier mobilnych z Wrocławia wkrótce zadebiutuje na giełdzie, Gazeta Wyborcza]

== Career ==

=== T-Bull ===
In 2010 Zwoliński co-founded T-Bull, a mobile-game developer, together with Damian Fijałkowski and Radosław Łapczyński. The company debuted on the NewConnect alternative market in Warsaw in November 2016 [ref: Doskonały debiut T-BULL na NewConnect, Polskie Radio Jedynka] and moved to the main market of the Warsaw Stock Exchange in August 2018.

=== SatRev ===
In 2016 Zwoliński co-founded the nanosatellite company SatRevolution, later renamed SatRev, and served as its chief executive officer. The company designed and manufactured nanosatellites for Earth observation and commercial missions. In 2019 it launched Światowid, described by the Polish Press Agency as Poland's first commercial Earth-observation satellite. [ref: Two Polish satellites have left the International Space Station, Science in Poland ([[Polish Press Agency] SatRevolution announced plans for an Earth-imaging constellation and in December 2021 received a Series B investment from Virgin Orbit. [ref: Virgin Orbit Invests in Customers Hypersat, SatRevolution to Expand Markets, Via Satellite]

In January 2023 the company's STORK-6 satellite was lost in the failure of Virgin Orbit's first LauncherOne mission from the United Kingdom. [ref: First Virgin Orbit U.K. launch fails, SpaceNews] Following Virgin Orbit's collapse later that year, SatRev came under financial and operational pressure. In 2025 investor January Ciszewski took control of the company; Zwoliński sold his shares and stepped down as chief executive. [ref: Kolejne zmiany w SatRev. Odchodzi CEO firmy, Evertiq] [ref: Jeszcze więcej Ciszewskiego w SatRev. Inwestor przejmuje 42% akcji spółki i chce budować kosmiczny ekosystem, MamStartup] He later acknowledged that SatRev's communication about the scale of its plans had at times run ahead of the company's ability to deliver, describing this as a lesson for his subsequent work.

=== ARES Shield ===
Zwoliński founded ARES Shield around the turn of 2025 and 2026. According to the company, its system combines sensors, AI-based analytics and a high-power microwave emitter in a module attached to a client satellite, designed to disable threatening spacecraft electronically without creating space debris. Zwoliński said the company initially raised 1 million PLN and later a further 1.4 million PLN from private investors.

In August 2026 the American company Lonestar Data Holdings contracted ARES Shield to protect its orbital data-storage satellites, in a deal reported to be worth up to US$6 million (about 22 million PLN). The agreement initially covers three satellites, with the first systems expected to be delivered in 2028 or 2029. At the time, the technology was at Technology Readiness Level 4, having been tested only under laboratory conditions, and Zwoliński estimated that around 80 million PLN in further funding would be needed to bring it to operational use. Industry commentators described the concept as technically plausible but subject to high technological risk, noting a long path from a laboratory demonstrator to an operational system in orbit, and Polish space-industry observers said they were following the venture with interest but caution in light of SatRev's record.

Zwoliński has also co-founded other Polish ventures, including the airborne wind energy startup Njord Energy [ref: Latawiec, który generuje prąd. Polski start-up walczy o rynek w USA, Gramwzielone.pl] and the artificial-intelligence startup GrantBot.AI. [ref: GrantBot.AI kończy męki przedsiębiorców związane z wnioskami o dotacje, 300Gospodarka]

== References ==

The World Youth Choir (WYC) is an international youth choir. The choir was created in 1989. it is a project choir reformed through auditions each year, consisting of singers aged between 17 and 26 from up to 75 different countries.

The choir is organised by the WYC Foundation [ref: Stichting World Youth Choir, KVK], based in Amsterdam, which is a cooperation between Jeunesses Musicales International, the International Federation for Choral Music, and since 2002 Europa Cantat [ref: World Youth Choir, World Youth Choir], which merged into the European Choral Association.

In 1996, the World Youth Choir was names UNESCO Artist for Peace [ref: UNESCO Artists for Peace, portal.unesco.org]. The choir performed at a number of notable events, including twice at the Olympic Games (Summer 1992, 2008) and the Nobel Peace Prize Ceremony (2011) [ref: Video - The 2011 Nobel Peace Prize Award Ceremony, NobelPrize.org].

Draft: Wa Mao

Draft text:
The Wa Mao (), also known as the Tile Cat, is a traditional apotropaic roof ridge ornament found on folk residences in Yunnan province, China. [ref: Tile cats: Yunnan's native ridge beasts, Yunnan.cn] Typically crafted from clay, shaped, and then glazed and fired in a kiln, the Wa Mao serves a dual symbolic purpose: to ward off evil spirits and to attract wealth and good fortune to the household. [ref: Yunnan Wa Mao "Leaps" into Daily Life, People's Daily Online]

Despite its name, the Wa Mao is not modeled after a domestic cat, but rather after a fierce tiger. [ref: Tracing the Wa Mao: A Mysterious Symbol Across Yunnan's Rooftops, Our China Story] This design philosophy is often described in Chinese folklore as having a "cat's appearance but a tiger's energy" (). [ref: The "Guardian" on the Rooftop: Yunnan Wa Mao, Yunnan Chinese Channel] The figure is characteristically depicted with a wide-open mouth and bulging, alert eyes, symbolizing its ability to swallow evil spirits and misfortune from all directions while welcoming prosperity. [ref: Yunnan Clay Sculpture "Wa Mao": The Cultural and Creative Revival of the Eaves Guardian, Daai Television]

== Appearance and symbolism ==

The Wa Mao is a unique form of folk ceramic sculpture. Although it is called a "cat," its visual features are heavily stylized to embody the ferocity and fearlessness of a tiger, which is traditionally regarded in Chinese culture as the king of beasts capable of devouring ghosts and malevolent entities. The typical Wa Mao features an exaggerated, wide-open mouth, wide eyes, and a grounded, seated posture mounted on a roof tile.

In traditional Yunnan belief systems, the rooftop is considered a threshold between the human dwelling and the outside world. Placing the Wa Mao at the highest point of the house, such as on the main roof ridge, flying eaves, or above the main gate, is believed to guard the household from harm, suppress negative influences, and prevent misfortunes such as fire. The ritual of installing a Wa Mao, sometimes referred to as "consecration," traditionally involves a ceremonial offering (such as dripping a rooster's blood on the figure) to endow it with spiritual power.

== Distribution and history ==
The cultural practice of using Wa Mao is widely distributed across Yunnan province, with notable variations in style and craftsmanship among different regions and ethnic groups. It is particularly prevalent in Yuxi, Qujing, Dali, Chuxiong, Wenshan, and the areas surrounding Kunming.

The tradition of placing these ceramic guardians on rooftops has a history spanning over a century in Yunnan. Historically, the craft was often carried out on a household or village basis by local pottery artisans. While the basic form remains consistent, regional variations exist; for example, some Wa Mao figures feature a Bagua (Eight Trigrams) diagram on their chest, while others may be made of stone (known as "Stone Cats") instead of clay in certain localities.

== Intangible cultural heritage ==
In recognition of its historical, artistic, and cultural value, the Yunnan Wa Mao was officially listed as a provincial-level intangible cultural heritage in 2023. In recent years, there has been a cultural and creative revival of the Wa Mao. Local artisans and designers have begun adapting the traditional motif into modern souvenirs, decorative art, and cultural products, ensuring the preservation and continuation of this unique folk tradition in contemporary society.

* Roof charm
* Feng shui
