Draft: The Castillejos Oppidum

Draft text:
----

The settlement of Los Castillejos, located in the municipality of Sanchorreja in the province of Ávila in Spain, was a hill fort or oppidum (also known as a castro) where people lived between the late Chalcolithic or Early Bronze Age and the fifth century BC. Although some archaeological excavations have taken place, the ruins are hardly visible here. [ref: Guía. Castro de Los Castillejos. Sanchorreja, Ávila]

The oppidum of “Los Castillejos” is one of the most important archaeological sites in the province of Ávila. The stratigraphic sediments have a depth of 2.0 meters. The range of the sediments can be traced from the late Chalcolithic or early Bronze Age until the fifth century BC, when the settlement was gradually abandoned by its inhabitants without any signs of cultural Romanization. [ref: Vetones: historia y arqueología de un pueblo prerromano, UAM Ediciones]

These people are considered as the predecessor of what would become later the Vettones, who founded new relevant settlements in the province of Avila like La Mesa de Miranda, Las Cogotas, Ulaca or El Raso.

The first archaeological excavations took place in the decade of 1930 by Joaquín María de Navascués, Emilio Camps Cazorla, and Juan Cabré. But the first findings were not published until 20 years later by Juan Maluquer [ref: El Castro de los Castillejos en Sanchorreja. Estudio de las excavaciones realizadas por D. Juan Cabré, D. Joaquín María de Navascués, y D. Emilio Camps, de 1931 a 1935]. An additional archaeological excavation took place later in the years 1981, 1982 and 1985 by F. J. González-Tablas Sastre.

The archaeological findings include many different types of ceramics, personal items made of bronze (buttons, needles, brooches, belt buckles), and utensils made of iron (axes, knives).

Some metal recipients found in the settlement, the ceramic techniques and types used, as well as one of the belt buckles with the representation of a griffin, are typical samples of western cultures like the Phoenicians, which had colonies around the Mediterranean area of the Iberian Peninsula at that time. Therefore, those items found at Los Castillejos are a confirmation that there was some type of exchange between the people who lived here and the coastal inhabitants of the Peninsula.

== References ==

GONZÁLEZ-TABLAS SASTRE, F.J. y DOMÍNGUEZ CALVO, A.; Los Castillejos de Sanchorreja. Campañas de 1981, 1982 y 1985. Acta Salmanticensia 117. Salamanca. 2002.

Chandanbati Shiva Mandir (locally known as Chandaneshwar Shib Mandir) is a Hindu temple located in Chandanbati village within the Sagardighi Community Development Block of Murshidabad district, West Bengal, India. [ref: District Statistical Handbook 2014: Murshidabad, Department of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Government of West Bengal] The site features a modern superstructure enclosing a basalt stone Shiva lingam, which local tradition associates with the regional Pala Empire heritage of the area. [ref: Bengal District Gazetteers: Murshidabad, Bengal Secretariat Book Depot]

== Location ==
The temple is situated in Chandanbati village in the Jangipur subdivision of Murshidabad district (PIN: 742226). It is located approximately 1.78 kilometres (1.11 mi) from Sagardighi railway station and roughly 7.52 kilometres (4.67 mi) from the Morgram junction connecting NH-12 and NH-114A. [ref: District Census Handbook: Murshidabad, Directorate of Census Operations, West Bengal]

== Historical context ==
The site reflects the historical settlement patterns of the Northern Rarh region, where early medieval ritual sites transitioned into rural community centers following regional trade realignments and shifts in river courses. [ref: Banglar Mandir Sthapatya O Bhaskarya, Pustak Bipani] The basalt lingam has remained under continuous local religious worship.

== Architecture ==
The temple consists of a single-chamber masonry sanctum topped with a stepped pyramidal shikhara. Over time, the structure has undergone multiple renovations:
* Earlier phase: A monolithic masonry sanctum finished in lime plaster, featuring hand-painted devotional murals flanking the entrance under a stepped tower.
* Modern phase: Renovation with ceramic tiles, an updated stepped pyramidal shikhara with an ornamental brass kalasha (finial), and a perimeter boundary railing.

== Governance and festivals ==
The site's physical infrastructure, civil maintenance, and religious observances are managed by the Chandanbati Shib Mandir Parichalana Committee. The temple serves as a focal point for regional religious gatherings, with peak congregations occurring during Maha Shivaratri and throughout the Bengali month of Shraavana.

== References ==

Wojciech Jan Jurczak (born August 9, 1966, in Kraków, Poland) is a Polish hematologist. His research focuses on the diagnosis and treatment of lymphoid malignancies [ref: Osobowość Roku 2020. Wojciech Jurczak: Poskromić chłoniaka, dać nadzieję i siłę pacjentom, Dziennik Polski], including lymphomas [ref: ], chronic lymphocytic leukemia and multiple myeloma. [ref: BRUIN CLL-313: Pirtobrutinib Demonstrates PFS Benefit in Relapsed/Refractory Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia or Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma, Asco Daily News] He is a professor of hematology and a Chair of the Department of Lymphoid Malignancies at the Maria Skłodowska‑Curie National Research Institute of Oncology in Kraków. [ref: ] He is a member of European Hematology Association (EHA) [ref: Wojciech Jurczak EHA 2022, memoinOncology], the American Society of Hematology (ASH) [ref: Wojciech Jurczak MD PhD; ASH 2025: Big Study Suggests Non-Covalent BTK Inhibitor Pirtobrutinib Could be New Standard-of-Care for Patients with Untreated Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia, audiomedica.com] and the American Society of Clinical Oncology. [ref: prof. dr hab. n. med. Wojciech Jurczak – Department of Hematology MC JU, hematologia.cm-uj.krakow.pl]

== Education and career ==
Jurczak graduated with distinction from the Medical Academy in Kraków in 1990, and completed additional coursework in mathematics and physics at the Jagiellonian University. [ref: dr hab. Wojciech Jurczak, uniwersytetdladzieci.eu] He joined the academic staff of the Department of Hematology at the Jagiellonian University Medical College (UJ CM), where he led the lymphoma treatment team from 1992 and served as the Head of Department from 2018.

== Research ==
His early researches focused on the development and clinical application of monoclonal antibodies in B‑cell lymphomas, including studies on radioimmunotherapy, as well as practical aspects of stem cell transplantation. [ref: Pratia Kraków: leading the way in Clinical Research, Pratia] Jurczak is a co‑author of publications that contributed to the approval of therapeutic agents used in lymphoid malignancies, including Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors [ref: Prof. Wojciech Jurczak: Chemioterapia jest jak stanowisko z karabinem, Rzeczpospolita], phosphatidylinositol‑3‑kinase (PI3K) inhibitors [ref: PI3Kδ Inhibition by Idelalisib in Patients with Relapsed Indolent Lymphoma, New England Journal of Medicine], BCL‑2 antagonists (venetoclax) [ref: Ibrutinib plus venetoclax for relapsed/refractory mantle cell lymphoma: Final analysis of the phase 3 SYMPATICO study, British Journal of Haematology] and HDAC inhibitors (belinostat). [ref: Belinostat in Patients With Relapsed or Refractory Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma: Results of the Pivotal Phase II BELIEF (CLN-19) Study, Journal of Clinical Oncology: Official Journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology]

His work has also included research on combination regimens and targeted treatment strategies currently shaping lymphoma therapeutics. [ref: Celowany atak w chłoniaka, www.medexpress.pl]

Jurczak’s research has been published in The New England Journal of Medicine, Blood, Journal of Clinical Oncology, The Lancet, The Lancet Oncology, and Annals of Oncology. [ref: Wojciech Jurczak - Publications - Bridge of Knowledge, Bridge of Knowledge - your knowledge portal] Jurczak has authored and co‑authored clinical research articles, including works on molecularly targeted therapies for lymphoid malignancies, ADC (antibody drug conjugates) and immunotherapies. [ref: ] [ref: ]

Scott McCullough is an American writer, director, cinematographer and editor of films, commercials, music videos and concert films. His work includes projects for Prince, 70mm NASCAR films and narrative and nonprofit projects. [ref: Top VFX Specialist Richard Kidd Joins Artemple-Hollywood Along With Scott McCullough, Deadline] [ref: Top 10 Innovative Minds Disrupting The Entertainment Space - LA Weekly] McCullough has been a member of the Directors Guild of America since 2001. [ref: Profile, www.dga.org]

== Early life and career ==
McCullough grew up in the Twin Cities area of Minnesota and attended the University of Minnesota, initially studying architecture and then advertising at the School of Journalism. He subsequently moved into camera work, music videos and commercial production in Minneapolis. [ref: Spotlight: Scott McCullough, PRN Alumni Foundation]

== Work with Prince and music videos ==
During the early 1990s, McCullough worked with Prince and associated artists across music videos, films and documentary projects. [ref: The director formerly with Prince / Industry signs third director, Screen]

His work also appeared on three Prince home-video releases: Gett Off, Sexy M.F. and Diamonds and Pearls Video Collection.

A later PRN Alumni Foundation profile described his Gett Off-era work as well as his filming of Prince's Special Olympics rehearsals and European concert material. Decades later, archival material from that period was released, including Live at Glam Slam and This Thing Called Soundcheck. [ref: Prince & The New Power Generation's 'Diamonds And Pearls' Expanded Reissue With Previously Unreleased Tracks & HD Concert Footage, Legacy Recordings]

On January 11, 1992, Prince and the New Power Generation performed at Glam Slam in Minneapolis. The film remained unreleased in Prince's vault for more than three decades. The complete concert was released in 2023 as Prince and the New Power Generation: Live at Glam Slam. [ref: Watch Rare Prince Performance of 'Nothing Compares 2 U' - PAPER Magazine, www.papermag.com] [ref: Prince / The New Power Generation: Diamonds and Pearls (Super Deluxe Edition), Pitchfork] The 2023 release identifies McCullough in its original-crew credits as director and cinematographer, a credit also carried in the accompanying hardcover book. [ref: Diamonds and Pearls Super Deluxe Edition, NPG Records / Paisley Park Enterprises / Sony Music Entertainment / Warner Records] In coverage of the release, PAPER interviewed McCullough about filming the "Nothing Compares 2 U" performance, identifying him as the concert film's director, cinematographer and camera operator.

Variety described Prince and the New Power Generation as being in peak form during the 90-minute performance, [ref: Prince's 'Diamonds and Pearls' Deluxe Edition Delivers Rare Gems From His Last Blockbuster: Album Review, Variety] while The Current called the Glam Slam concert "the real prize of the set". [ref: Digging for '(Diamonds and) Pearls' in Prince's expanded reissue, www.thecurrent.org]

His early Paisley Park work included Eric Leeds' "Little Rock." In 2000, the Chris Cummings video "That'll Teach Her" reached number 1 on RPM’s Video & Instant Top Forty chart. [ref: Video and Instant Top Forty, RPM] Screen also discussed McCullough's work with Cummings during that period. [ref: Variety Is the Spice - Director/cameraman doesn't want to be pigeonholed, Screen]

== Commercial and advertising work ==
While continuing music-video work, McCullough moved into commercial directing during the 1990s. Adweek credited him as director of Target Stores' 1995 "Single Step" campaign. [ref: New Campaigns, Adweek] In 1998, the magazine included the Jesse Ventura for Governor campaign spot "The Thinker," also directed by McCullough, in its "Best Spots" coverage. [ref: Best Spots - November, Adweek] [ref: CAMPAIGN REFORM HELPED 'THE BODY' SLAM RIVALS, The Washington Post]

His work expanded into automotive and motorsports filmmaking. For R.J. Reynolds and the NASCAR Winston Cup Series, McCullough created, directed, photographed and edited the large-format films No Bull and 100%, filming NASCAR Winston Cup drivers across multiple race weekends for the traveling Thunder Theater experience. [ref: "100%" in 70mm, www.in70mm.com] The films were photographed in 65mm five-perf for 70mm exhibition.

McCullough's commercial work includes campaigns for General Motors, Coors Light and Pepsi. For General Motors, McCullough directed and photographed automotive work for Buick, Pontiac and GMC, including a five-commercial GMC package for Boston agency Digitas. [ref: ] In 2008, Reel Chicago reported that McCullough directed Story's largest production to date, a 23-day, two-country automotive shoot divided between Los Angeles and Buenos Aires. [ref: PRODUCTION CENTRAL, Reel Chicago News]

McCullough's motorsports work later extended to open-wheel Champ Car racing. He directed and photographed a campaign featuring Paul Newman and Newman's Champ Car racing team. LA Weekly later described the project as Newman's final filmed appearance and reported that Newman had requested McCullough as director.

Jiangang "Jim" Dai (戴建岗) is an operations researcher and applied probabilist known for work on stochastic processing networks, queueing theory, and fluid and diffusion approximations. He is the Leon C. Welch Professor of Engineering in the School of Operations Research and Information Engineering at Cornell University. [ref: Jim Dai, Cornell Duffield Engineering] Dai received the 2024 John von Neumann Theory Prize for contributions to stochastic systems theory [ref: Jim Dai, INFORMS] and the 2018 ACM SIGMETRICS Achievement Award for his analysis of queueing networks. [ref: Dr. Jim Dai 2018 ACM SIGMETRICS Achievement Award, ACM SIGMETRICS]

== Education and career ==

Dai earned bachelor's and master's degrees in mathematics from Nanjing University and a doctorate in mathematics from Stanford University in 1990. [ref: DAI, Jiangang Jim, School of Data Science] He joined the faculty of the Georgia Institute of Technology in 1990 and remained there until moving to Cornell in 2012. At Georgia Tech, he held the Chandler Family Chair in Industrial and Systems Engineering. At Cornell he became the Leon C. Welch Professor of Engineering.

Dai has also held appointments at Tsinghua University, the National University of Singapore, Aarhus University, Stanford, and the University of Wisconsin–Madison. At the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, he has served as dean and later honorary dean of the School of Data Science. He was editor-in-chief of the journal Mathematics of Operations Research from 2013 to 2018.

== Research ==

Dai's research concerns mathematical models for allocating resources in processing networks, including communication and computer systems, manufacturing systems, data centers, call centers, hospitals, and transportation services. His work develops fluid and diffusion approximations for analyzing the stability and control of such networks.

In a 1995 paper, "On Positive Harris Recurrence of Multiclass Queueing Networks: A Unified Approach via Fluid Limit Models", Dai established a general connection between the stability of deterministic fluid models and positive recurrence of stochastic processing-network models. INFORMS described the result as a foundation for later work on stochastic-network stability. His later research has addressed heavy-traffic diffusion approximations, reflected Brownian motion, max-weight scheduling, and quantitative approximation bounds based on Stein's method.

With J. Michael Harrison, Dai wrote the monograph Processing Networks: Fluid Models and Stability, published by Cambridge University Press in 2020. [ref: Processing Networks: Fluid Models and Stability, Cambridge University Press]

== Awards and honors ==

INFORMS awarded Dai the 2024 John von Neumann Theory Prize for "fundamental and sustained contributions" to stochastic systems theory, particularly stochastic-network stability and heavy-traffic diffusion approximations. The prize recognizes a body of fundamental, sustained theoretical work in operations research and the management sciences. [ref: John von Neumann Theory Prize, INFORMS]

The ACM SIGMETRICS Achievement Award recognized Dai's contributions to fluid and diffusion analysis of queueing networks and their applications to computer, communication, and processing systems. He is an elected fellow of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics and of INFORMS. His earlier honors include the 1998 Erlang Prize and the 1997 and 2017 Best Publication Awards from the INFORMS Applied Probability Society.

Goran Gatalica (born 2 September 1982) is a Croatian writer, poet and haiku poet. He has also worked in physics, chemistry and education. He is a member of the Croatian Writers' Association and Matica hrvatska. [ref: Gatalica Goran, Društvo hrvatskih književnika]

== Life and work ==

Gatalica was born in Virovitica, Croatia, and completed his elementary and secondary education in Daruvar. He studied at the University of Zagreb, where he obtained master's degrees in Physics and Chemistry Teaching in 2009 and Chemical Engineering in 2011. He subsequently enrolled in doctoral studies. He has worked at the Institute of Physics, the Ruđer Bošković Institute and the Faculty of Chemical Engineering and Technology of the University of Zagreb.

Gatalica writes poetry in Croatian, including in the Kajkavian dialect, as well as haiku. His work has appeared in Croatian and international literary journals, collections and anthologies.

His poetry has been discussed in Croatian literary criticism. In Vijenac, Ljerka Car Matutinović reviewed his collection Kozmolom, discussing its prose-poetry form, metaphorical imagery and existential themes. [ref: Kozmičko iščitavanje svijeta, Vijenac]

Darija Žilić discussed Gatalica's collection Odsečeni od svetla in Vijenac, including its use of the Kajkavian dialect and its distinctive vocabulary and imagery. [ref: Ares briše svet med zvezdami, Vijenac]

Ružica Martinović-Vlahović reviewed Noćni jasmin / Night Jasmine in Kolo, discussing the collection's 113 haiku, its organization around the four seasons and its relationship to traditional and contemporary haiku. [ref: Zbirka poetskih trofeja, Kolo]

His first poetry collection, Krucijalni test, was published in 2014 by Matica hrvatska Daruvar. In 2015, it received the Slavić Award for the best first book published in 2014. [ref: Nagrada Dana hrvatske knjige – Slavić, HRČAK]

His second collection, Kozmolom, was published in 2016. In 2017, it received the Kvirin Award at the Kvirin Poetry Meetings in Sisak. The award was reported by Novi list. [ref: Kvirinovi susreti: Miroslavu Mićanoviću plaketa, nagrađen i Goran Gatalica, Novi list]

In the same year, Gatalica received the Dragutin Tadijanović Poetry Award from the Foundation of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts. The award was reported by the Croatian news agency HINA. [ref: Pjesnik Goran Gatalica laureat ovogodišnje Nagrade "Dragutin Tadijanović", HINA]

His third poetry collection, Odsečeni od svetla, was published in 2018 by the Croatian Writers' Association and received the Katarina Patačić Literary Award for the best Kajkavian book published in 2018.

His fourth collection, Jezero zmešaneh noči, was published in 2020. His fifth book, Noćni jasmin / Night Jasmine, was published in 2022. The collection received the Krunoslav Sukić recognition for Book of the Year 2021/2022 from the Center for Peace, Nonviolence and Human Rights in Osijek. [ref: Goranu Gatalici priznanje Krunoslav Sukić za knjigu godine 2021./2022., SiB.hr]

Gatalica has received awards in international haiku competitions. The Bashō-an International English Haiku Competition in Japan lists him among its award recipients. [ref: Bashō-an International English Haiku Competition, Koto City Culture and Community Foundation]

In 2023, Gatalica received the Katanogahara Monogatari Award at the fourth Star Haiku Contest in Katano, Japan. The award was reported by Croatian Radiotelevision. [ref: Pjesnik Goran Gatalica osvojio nagradu Katanogahara Monogatari, Hrvatska radiotelevizija]

In 2025, Gatalica received the John Bird Dreaming Award at the third John Bird Dreaming Haiku Competition in Australia. Croatian Radiotelevision reported the award. [ref: Hrvatskom književniku Goranu Gatalici prva nagrada za haiku u Australiji, Hrvatska radiotelevizija]

His sixth poetry collection, Povratak u Getsemani / Returning to Gethsemane, was published by Tonimir in Varaždinske Toplice in 2025. The Croatian National Bibliography records the publication as an 88-page volume. [ref: Hrvatska nacionalna bibliografija: Niz A – knjige, 2025, National and University Library in Zagreb]

The book was selected as one of the finalists for the 2025 Tin Ujević Award of the Croatian Writers' Association. [ref: Izabrano 11 finalista Nagrade Tin Ujević, Društvo hrvatskih književnika] It subsequently received the Duhovno hrašće Award at the Poetry Meetings in Drenovci. [ref: Šlisuriću Povelja Visoka žuta žita, Gatalici Duhovno hrašće, Večernji list]

Gatalica has also worked as an editor of haiku publications. Since 2020 he has edited the Haiku Meridians column in Iris magazine, and since 2021 he has edited the Haiku Circles column and a monthly haiku competition in Lanterna magazine.

Ameen Muhammad Laghari (Sindhi:امين لغاري also spelled Amin Laghari/Leghari) is a Sindhi author and researcher [ref: امين لغاري, انسائيڪلوپيڊيا سنڌيانا]. He has served as In-charge secretary of the Sindhi Language Authority an autonomous body under the Government of Sindh and Its deputy director of research and publication. [ref: "Secretories - Sindhi Language Authority", Sindhi Language Authority] [ref: "Introduction to Contributors", Kalachi Research Journal (Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai Chair, University of Karachi)].

== Early life and education ==
Laghari was born on 7 June 1966 in Sanghar, Sindh, Pakistan [ref: "امين لغاري", SindhSalamat Kitab Ghar]. He did his early schooling from primary school of village and completed his matriculation, Intermediate education and BA from high school and Degree College Sanghar. He pursued master's degree in mass communication from University of Sindh in 1991.

== Career ==
In 1992 Laghari joined Sindhi Language Authority (SLA), Statutory body of Government of Sindh as Research Assistant. From 14 March to 23 May 2018, he served as In-charge Secretary of Sindhi Language Authority and again from 9 February to 22 June 2023. [ref: "سيڪريٽري", Sindhi Language Authority]. During his tenure he served under renowned scholars and literary figures including Dr NA Baloch, Dr Ghullam Ali Allana and Ishaq Samejo [ref: Sindhi Language Authority hosts farewell in honour of Deputy Director Amin Leghari, The Nation] [ref: Sindhi Language & Literature at a Glance, Scribd]. As deputy director of Research and Publication he was involved in Research and Publication on Sindhi Language including contributing to authority's Sindhi Boli Research Journal. He also participated in conferences on Sindhi language and its revival [ref: "Sindhi language, Indus Script and Endangered Indigenous languages", UNESCO International Decade of Indigenous Languages 2022–2032] [ref: Sindhi Language, Indus Script and Endangered Indigenous Languages International Conference – Proceedings / Program, sl.sindhila.org]. Laghari retired from Sindhi Language Authority on December 22, 2025 [ref: "Sindhi Language Authority Hosts Farewell In Honour Of Deputy Director Amin Leghari", UrduPoint].

Süleyman Gazi Erçel (February 20, 1945 – June 13, 2022) was a Turkish economist who served as 18th Governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey (1996-2001). [ref: Governors of the CBRT, www.tcmb.gov.tr] He previously served as Director General of the Ministry of Treasury and Finance of Turkey as well as chairman of Tütünbank. [ref: Turkish stock market: Time to clean things up, www.euromoney.com] [ref: Former Central Bank Governor Gazi Erçel has passed away., [[The Independent]

==Early life and education==
Erçel was born on February 20, 1945 in Istanbul, Turkey. [ref: Gazi Erçel, former governor of the Central Bank, has passed away., www.bankadunyasi.com] He earned his bachelor's degree from the Department of Finance and Economics of Ankara University in 1967 and his master's degree from Vanderbilt University in 1976.

==Career==
Erçel began his career in 1967 at the Turkish Ministry of Treasury and Finance where he held several roles, including Deputy Director General of the Treasury, as well as various roles in the economic research, banking and foreign exchange, IMF, and World Bank departments.

From 1982 to 1986, Erçel left the ministry to serve as Deputy Executive Director of the IMF. He returned in 1987 upon appointment as Director General of the Treasury.

In 1989, Erçel left civil service to pursue a career in the private sector. He was a board member at Yaşar Holding as well as Tütünbank, where he became chairman in 1994.

Erçel was appointed governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey in 1996 by the cabinet of Turkish President Süleyman Demirel. [ref: Turkey names new Central Bank governor, www.upi.com] Three weeks into his term, Erçel addressed the Institute of International Finance in Istanbul, remarking that his two primary goals as governor would be to reduce inflation and to prepare the Turkish economy for entry into the EU Customs Union. [ref: Remarks by Gazi Erçel, Governor, The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, at the Spring Meeting of IIF, Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey]

In December of 1999, Erçel announced an IMF-backed disinflation program with a three-year horizon, aimed at tackling an inflated consumer price index, lowering real interest rates, and redistributing resources throughout the Turkish economy. [ref: Disinflation Program for the Year 2000: Implementation of Exchange Rate and Monetary Policy, Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey] In 2000, Erçel secured $7.5 billion in loans from the IMF to help replenish the central bank's reserves after growing government deficits led to a liquidity shortage. [ref: Turkey markets calmer with IMF cash to boost reserves, www.cnn.com] In response to the 2001 Turkish economic crisis, Erçel resigned as governor on moral grounds, asserting that Turkey needed a reconstituted negotiating team to establish a new IMF agreement. [ref: Turkey's sparring leaders meet, www.news.bbc.co.uk]

After leaving the Central Bank of Turkey, Erçel became a financial columnist for several Turkish newspapers and served as a lecturer on the Faculty of Economics and Administrative Sciences at Istanbul Aydın University. He died at home on June 13, 2022 at the age of 77. [ref: Gazi Erçel kimdir? Gazi Erçel neden vefat etti?, www.cnnturk.com]

Julius Yasir Ballo (born April 20, 2003), known as JuJu Ballo, is an American professional boxer from San Diego, California, of Iraqi and Chaldean Catholic descent. A multi-time USA Boxing National Champion and 2021 Junior Pan American Games gold medalist as an amateur, he turned professional in 2025 after signing with Top Rank. He was undefeated through his first four professional fights as of August 2026. He frequently appears on the same fight cards as his cousin, fellow professional boxer Jonathan "Jonny" Mansour.

== Early life ==
Ballo was born in San Diego and raised in the city's East County area, including the communities of Lakeside and El Cajon. [ref: East County boxer Julius Ballo set to make pro debut, FOX 5 San Diego] [ref: El Cajon cousins will fight Saturday in Detroit, The San Diego Union-Tribune] His father, Yasir Ballo, immigrated to the United States from Iraq and boxed as an amateur before opening Bomber Squad Boxing Academy in El Cajon, where Julius trains under Berlin Kerney. [ref: Julius Ballo has a plan, and it doesn't involve settling for less than No. 1, BoxingScene] Ballo has said he began boxing at age three. The Ballo family also owns El Pueblo Mexican Food, a restaurant chain with five locations. The family is of Iraqi and Chaldean Catholic descent, part of a Chaldean community with a significant presence in both San Diego and Detroit; San Diego County is home to the second-largest Chaldean community in the United States, and Detroit the largest. [ref: Undefeated boxing cousins to make Detroit debut at Fox Theatre in August, ClickOnDetroit / WDIV Local 4]

== Amateur career ==
Ballo won USA Boxing's National Championships in 2021, 2022, and 2023, and has been described in later coverage as a three-time national champion. [ref: Julius Ballo signs co-promotional deal with Overtime Boxing and Top Rank, BoxingScene] He was named USA Boxing's Youth Athlete of the Year for 2021. He won gold at the 2021 Junior Pan American Games in Cali, Colombia, and closed his amateur career with the 2024 National Golden Gloves championship. The Ring reported that Ballo had more than 200 amateur bouts while representing Team USA; [ref: Julius Ballo, backed by Top Rank, in store for big plans, [[The Ring (magazine)] BoxRec lists his amateur record at 51 wins and 8 losses. [ref: Julius Ballo, BoxRec] Ballo's promotional team has described him as having been ranked the No. 1 pound-for-pound amateur boxer in the United States out of an estimated 55,000 amateur competitors, though this ranking has not been independently verified.

Among his amateur wins was a decision over Jahmal Harvey, who was already a world amateur champion at the time and went on to represent the United States at the 2024 Paris Olympics. Ballo did not qualify for the Olympic roster himself, an outcome he later described as one of the more disappointing results of his amateur career.

== Professional career ==

=== Signing with Top Rank ===
In January 2025, Ballo signed with Top Rank. He is managed by James Prince and his father, Yasir Ballo. By 2026, Ballo's own social media following was reported by his team at more than 1.2 million combined across Instagram and TikTok.

=== 2025: Professional debut ===
Ballo made his professional debut on July 26, 2025, at the Madison Square Garden Theater in New York, defeating Brandan Ayala by unanimous decision over four rounds. [ref: Julius Ballo, BoxRec] Ahead of the fight, he told TMZ Sports he intended to "make my name up there in the pound-for-pound list." [ref: Team USA Boxer Julius 'Juju' Ballo Vows to Make Statement In Pro Debut, TMZ Sports]

On December 13, 2025, Ballo defeated Juan Centeno by unanimous decision over six rounds in Hollywood, California. Centeno stepped in as a late replacement opponent, and Ballo moved up two weight classes to make the fight; all three judges scored the bout 60-53. [ref: Chaldean boxing prospects Jonny Mansour and Julius Ballo win professional bouts on same night in Los Angeles, SyriacPress] [ref: Chaldean cousins Mansour, Ballo deliver knockout show for fans, Times of San Diego]

=== 2026: SD Fight Night and Detroit debut ===
On April 18, 2026, Ballo headlined an event billed as SD Fight Night at Frontwave Arena in Oceanside, California, a card he co-promoted with his father, defeating Roman Reyes by unanimous decision over six rounds to improve to 3-0. [ref: Julius Ballo breaks down Roman Reyes over six rounds, BoxingScene] [ref: SD Fight Night full card set for Saturday in Oceanside, CA, FIGHTMAG] Discussing his motivation for continuing to box, Ballo told BoxingScene, "I don't have to do this. I drive a quarter-million-dollar car, and live in a multi-million-dollar house. I don't have to do this sport. I do it because I love it, and I am addicted to that winning feeling." [ref: Julius Ballo boxes because he wants to, not because he has to, BoxingScene]

Lewis G. Burton is a London-based performance artist, DJ, cultural producer and activist. They are the founder of INFERNO, a queer techno rave and performance-art platform established in 2015, and a founding organiser of London Trans+ Pride. Burton's work combines performance, club culture and community organising. [ref: Lewis G. Burton on the Magic of Change, Mission Magazine] [ref: 5 photographers on INFERNO, London's most 'chaotic, beautiful' rave, Dazed] [ref: The right to dance: Queer nightlife in 2026, [[Time Out (magazine)]

==Career==

===Performance art===
Burton began working as a performance artist in the early 2010s. In 2014, Burton collaborated with artist Victor Ivanov on FLESH, a performance project centred on a bodysuit constructed from preserved chicken skins. The project received coverage in the Evening Standard, which reported on Burton performing in the suit in public spaces across London. [ref: Video: man in chicken flesh gimp suit shocks London commuters, Evening Standard]

In December 2022, Burton presented TRANSPHORIA, an interdisciplinary performance work combining theatre, performance art and club culture, at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London. [ref: TRANSPHORIA, Institute of Contemporary Arts]

===INFERNO===
Burton founded INFERNO in London in 2015 as a club night combining techno with performance art. In a 2024 feature, Dazed examined INFERNO's influence on London's queer techno-rave culture through the work of photographers who had documented the night over nine years.

INFERNO subsequently developed programming beyond its regular club nights. In 2022, it staged a late-night takeover at the Institute of Contemporary Arts alongside an INFERNO Summit focused on queer and trans artists and nightlife culture. [ref: INFERNO Rave, Institute of Contemporary Arts] In July 2026, Dazed reported that INFERNO was operating at The Distillery in London and continued to provide a space for artists and designers within the city's nightlife scene. [ref: London's dying nightlife is killing the fashion club kid, Dazed]

===London Trans+ Pride===
Burton is a founding member and organiser of London Trans+ Pride. [ref: 'We have the right to live with dignity': More than 55,000 people march for London Trans+ Pride, The Big Issue] At the 2026 march, which ended at Trafalgar Square for the first time, organisers estimated attendance at 150,000. ITV News identified Burton as a founding member and reported their remarks at the event. [ref: 150,000 march through London in 'world's largest trans pride', organisers say, ITV News]

[ref: Latinos en Metro: Para la ingeniera Eleanor Sillerico, cada tunel es un desafio fascinante, Hispanic LA newspaper] Her brother Rodrigo Sillerico Mayta is a violinist and conductor of the Bolivia Clasica orchestra and an associate of the concert pianist Ana-Maria Vera.

Walter Gonzalez incentiva la excelencia académica, El Diario newspaper] She received her degree as a civil engineer from the Higher University of San Andrés (Universidad Mayor de San Andres) in La Paz, Bolivia in 2002. Walter Gonzalez incentiva la excelencia académica, El Diario newspaper] She completed advanced studies at the Centro de Estudios y Experimentacion de Obras Publicas (CEDEX) and the Technical University of Madrid (UPM), earning master's degrees in geotechnics and tunneling engineering. Rachel Ann Pepper is a Judge at the Land and Environment Court of New South Wales, Australia. She was appointed to the Court in 2009. [ref: Judicial officers and decision makers, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

== Early life and education ==
Rachel Pepper was born in Canada and immigrated to Australia in the early 1980s. She completed her secondary education at Swanbourne Senior High School in Perth, Western Australia, graduating in 1984. [ref: SWEARING IN CEREMONY OF RACHEL ANN PEPPER AS A JUSTICE OF THE LAND AND ENVIRONMENT COURT OF NEW SOUTH WALES, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

She graduated from the Australian National University with a Bachelor of Arts, majoring in French, in 1992 and a Bachelor of Laws with First Class Honours in 1994. [ref: Judicial speeches and papers, Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]

== Legal career ==
Pepper practised as a solicitor with Allen Allen & Hemsley in 1995. In 1996, she served as associate to Justice Michael McHugh in the High Court of Australia. [ref: ANU]

She was called to the New South Wales Bar in 1997, reading with John Marshall and Justin Gleeson. She practised as a barrister at 7 Wentworth Chambers and 12 Wentworth Selborne Chambers until her appointment to the Court in 2009. [ref: LEC Swearing in ceremony]

Between January 2017 and April 2018, Pepper served as Chair of the Scientific Inquiry into Hydraulic Fracturing of Onshore Unconventional Gas Reservoirs and Associated Activities in the Northern Territory. [ref: Home, Northern Territory Government]

In 2021, she was made a fellow of the Australian Academy of Law. [ref: Rachel Pepper, Australian Academy of Law]

== Professional activities ==
Pepper serves on the editorial board of the Australian Journal of Administrative Law and is the Environment Section Editor of the Australian Law Journal. [ref: Environmental Law, The Australian Law Journal]

From 2009 to 2018, she was a Co-Consulting Editor of the Australian Environment Review published by LexisNexis. [ref: Co-consulting Editors, Australian Environment Review]

She has served on the committee of the Australian Institute of Administrative Law and was its President. [ref: National Executive, Australian Institute of Administrative Law] She is also a member of the Ngara Yura Committee of the Judicial Commission of NSW [ref: Ngara Yura Committee members, Judicial Commission of New South Wales] and a judicial member of Football Australia. [ref: Constitution, Football Australia]

Pepper served as Secretary of the Australian Association of Constitutional Law from 2013 to 2017 and as Vice President from 2017 to 2018. [ref: UNSW]

She was elected to the NSW Bar Council in 2000 and served until her appointment to the bench in 2009, including as Secretary from 2005 to 2009. [ref: ANU alumnae trailblazers in law: an intimate discussion, Australian National University]

From 2019 to 2023, Pepper was a board member of Twenty10. She also served as Vice President of ACON from 2001 to 2003. [ref: ACON Annual Report 2001/2002]

Pepper has authored and edited books, journal articles, book chapters and other publications in the fields of environment, administrative, constitutional, criminal and discrimination law [ref: Thomson Reuters]. She has also participated in the teaching and training of judges from overseas in environmental law and environmental dispute resolution through programs supported by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Asian Development Bank. [ref: 2022 IUCN Academy of Environmental Law Colloquium]

== Academic appointments ==

Pepper is an Adjunct Professor at the University of Sydney Law School [ref: University of Sydney Law School].

She has been a judicial fellow and visiting scholar at the Australian National University College of Law [ref: ANU Law School] and Melbourne University Law School [ref: Melbourne University Law School]. She has also taught law courses at the University of New South Wales, the University of Technology Sydney and the University of Sydney. [ref: University of Sydney Law School]

----In mathematics, the {\mathbb
J}-transform [ref: {{Cite journal|url=http://www.jaac-online.com//en/article/doi/10.11948/20180258|title=BEYOND SUMUDU TRANSFORM AND NATURAL TRANSFORM: $ {\mathbb J} $-TRANSFORM PROPERTIES AND APPLICATIONS|first1=Weidong|last1=Zhao|first2=Shehu|last2=Maitama|date=August 15, 2020|journal=Journal of Applied Analysis & Computation|volume=10|issue=4|pages=1223–1241|via=www.jaac-online.com|doi=10.11948/20180258}}] is an integral transform introduced as a modification of the well-known Sumudu transform [ref: Sumudu transform: a new integral transform to solve differential equations and control engineering problems, International Journal of Mathematical Education in Science and Technology] and the Natural transform [ref: Theory of Natural Transform, MESA] for solving differential equations arising in applied physical sciences and engineering. The {\mathbb
J}-transform possesses several useful properties that distinguish it from the Sumudu transform and the natural transform, and it can be applied to problems that may be difficult to handle using either transform independently. The {\mathbb
J}-transform was introduced by Shehu Maitama and Weidong Zhao in 2020. Since its introduction, it has been applied to the solution of various ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and partial differential equations (PDEs), including problems involving fractional-order models and real-life applications in the physical science and engineering. [ref: A novel tempered fractional transform: theory, properties and applications to differential equations, Fractals] [ref: A survey of (2+1)-dimensional KDV-MKDV equation using nonlocal Caputo fractal-fractional operator, Results in Physics]
== Formal definition ==

The {\mathbb J}-transform of the function f(t) of exponential order is defined over the set of functions, A=\left\{f(t):\exists N, \xi_{1}, \xi _{2}>0,\; \text{such that}\; \left|f(t)\right|

by

{\mathbb J}\left[f(t)\right](\mu,\nu)=F(\mu,\nu)=\nu\int _{0
}^{\infty}\exp\left(\frac{-\mu t}{\nu}\right)f(t)dt
=\nu\lim_{\alpha\rightarrow\infty}\int _{0
}^{\alpha}\exp\left(\frac{-\mu t}{\nu}\right)f(t)dt.

Here, \mu>0 and \nu>0, provided the limit of the integral
exists, and \mu\,\,and \,\,\nu are the {\mathbb
J}-transform variables.. The {\mathbb
J}-transform converges to Laplace transform when the variable \nu=1.

== Inverse {\mathbb
J}-transform ==

Let F(\mu,\nu) be
the {\mathbb J}-transform of the function f(t), then the inverse {\mathbb J}-transform is defined as

{\mathbb J^{-1}}\left[F(\mu,\nu)\right]=f(t),\, \,
\text{for}\,\,t\geq0.

Equivalently, the complex inverse {\mathbb J}-transform is
defined as
{\mathbb J^{-1}}\left[F(\mu,\nu)\right]=f(t)=\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\alpha-i\beta}^{\alpha+i\beta}\frac{1}{\nu^2}\exp\left(\frac{\mu t}{\nu}\right)F(\mu,\nu)d\mu

=\sum
\text{residues of}\,\,
\frac{1}{\nu^2}\exp\left(\frac{\mu t}{\nu}\right)F(\mu,\nu)\,\,\text{at the poles of}\,\,F(\mu,\nu).

Here, \mu is a complex number and \alpha is a real number.

== Properties of {\mathbb
J}-transform ==

Linearity property:
Let the functions f(t) and w(t) be in set A. Then, the following linearity property holds

{\mathbb J}\left[\alpha f(t)+\beta w(t)\right]
=\alpha{\mathbb J}\left[f(t)\right]+\beta{\mathbb J}\left[w(t)\right],
where \alpha and \beta are two constant parameters

First translation or shifting property:

\frac{\mu-\alpha}{\mu}F\left(\mu,\frac{\mu}{\mu-\alpha }\right),\,\,\text{when}\,\,\nu=1,\,\,\text{Laplace transform}&\\

F\left(1,\frac{\nu}{1-\alpha \nu}\right),\,\,\text{when}\,\,\mu=1,\,\, \text{Elzaki transform}.

It is evident that for \nu=1, we have the Laplace transform [ref: Electronic Signals and Systems, Macmillan Education UK] and for \mu=1 we have the Elzaki transform [ref: A comparative study of elzaki and laplace transforms to solve ordinary differential equations of first and second order, Journal of Physics: Conference Series] correspondingly.

The 2027 CONCACAF Champions Cup will be the 62nd season of the CONCACAF Champions Cup, the premier club association football tournament for North, Central America, and the Caribbean organized by CONCACAF. It is a five-round knockout tournament, with 27 teams qualified based on their national and zonal League and Cup competitions; the first four rounds are played as a two-legged series at the home stadiums of the respective teams, ending with a one-legged final. [ref: 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup: Qualified Clubs, CONCACAF]

The winner will qualify for the 2029 FIFA Club World Cup and the 2027 FIFA Intercontinental Cup.

== Qualification ==
Twenty-seven teams will qualify for the tournament, with five qualifying directly to the round of 16. The remaining 22 teams enter in round one.

In addition to national league competitions in the United States, Mexico, and Canada, 12 of 27 berths are determined by international competitions, including the 2026 Leagues Cup (three), 2026 CONCACAF Caribbean Cup (three) and 2026 CONCACAF Central American Cup (six).

Two Canadian Premier League teams qualify automatically, while the United States-only 2026 U.S. Open Cup knockout competition and Canada-only equivalent, the 2026 Canadian Championship, provide one berth each.

The winners of the three international competitions, along with the winner of MLS Cup 2026 and the champion of the 2025–26 Liga MX season, receive byes into the round of 16.

=== Distribution ===
Twenty-seven teams qualify for the tournament.

* North American Zone: 18 teams (from 3 associations)
* Central American Zone: 6 teams
* Caribbean Zone: 3 teams

Five teams receive a bye into the round of 16.

* The champion of the regional competition for each of CONCACAF's constituent zones; North American, Central American and Caribbean
* The champions of Liga MX of Mexico and Major League Soccer of the United States and Canada (Liga MX has a split Clausura and Apertura system, so the champion team with the higher aggregate points will take this place. If a team won both Apertura and Clausura, they will take this place.)

The remaining 22 teams enter in round one.

* The runners-up and third-place team from the MLS–Liga MX Leagues Cup
* The runners-up and third-place team from the Caribbean Cup
* The runners-up, remaining semifinalists, and two play-in winners from the Central American Cup
* The U.S. Open Cup winners
* The Canadian Championship winners
* The Canadian Premier League regular season winners and playoff champions
* The remaining winner with the worse record, two runners-up, and the two best next clubs by season aggregate from Liga MX
* The MLS Supporters' Shield winners
* The remaining MLS Conference regular-season leader, and the next two teams in the Supporters' Shield table

Draft: Network discovery and reconciliation

Draft text:
----

Network discovery and reconciliation is a set of operational practices used by telecommunications network operators to keep a network inventory system aligned with the actual physical and logical state of the network it is supposed to describe. [ref: TM Forum. "TMFC045 Resource Discovery and Reconciliation v1.0.0." https://www.tmforum.org/resources/technical-specification/tmfc045-resource-discovery-and-reconciliation-v1-0-0/] In practice this means two things happen in sequence: automated tools collect data directly from network equipment and from the management systems that oversee it, and that data is then compared, record by record, against whatever already exists in the operator's inventory database. [ref: Breitbart, Y., Garofalakis, M., Jai, B., Martin, C., Rastogi, R., Silberschatz, A. "Topology Discovery in Heterogeneous IP Networks." Proc. IEEE INFOCOM, 2000, pp. 265–274. Extended version: "Topology discovery in heterogeneous IP networks: the NetInventory system," IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking, vol. 12, no. 3, 2004, pp. 401–414. https://doi.org/10.1109/TNET.2004.828963] Where the two disagree, the discrepancy is either corrected automatically or set aside for a person to review, depending on how the operator has configured the process.

The practice exists because large telecommunications networks are rarely static. [ref: TM Forum Inform. "Introducing TM Forum's Autonomous Network Mission: The roadmap to true autonomy in telecom." July 2025. https://inform.tmforum.org/features-and-opinion/introducing-tm-forums-autonomous-network-mission-the-roadmap-to-true-autonomy-in-telecom] A typical operator's network combines equipment from many vendors, mixes physical hardware with virtualized and cloud-hosted functions, and changes continuously as equipment is installed, links are re-patched, and old hardware is retired. Under these conditions, an inventory record maintained only by hand tends to become more inaccurate over time, from what is deployed. [ref: Donnet, B., Friedman, T. "Internet topology discovery: a survey." IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials, vol. 9, no. 4, 2007, pp. 56–69. https://doi.org/10.1109/COMST.2007.4444750] Network discovery and reconciliation was developed to close that gap, by treating the network's own reported state, rather than a person's notes about the network, as the source of truth.

The process is applied across most of the domains a modern operator runs, including IP and MPLS networks, optical transport networks, passive optical and DSL access networks, mobile radio access networks, and software-defined wide area networks. [ref: TM Forum. "TIP (Operations Management) Interfaces." https://www.tmforum.org/standards/standarized-interfaces-apis/operations-management-interfaces/] It has also been formalized as a named, standardized function, Resource Discovery and Reconciliation, within TM Forum's Open Digital Architecture, an industry reference architecture used across the telecommunications sector by both network operators and their equipment and software suppliers.

== Background ==

Before automated discovery tools became common, telecommunications operators generally relied on manually maintained inventory databases: engineers recorded what equipment was installed, where it was connected, and how it was configured, and updated those records whenever a change was made in the field. This worked reasonably well while networks were smaller and changed infrequently, but it scales poorly. A large operator's network can span tens of thousands of physical elements across multiple vendors and technology generations, and any of them can be touched during a routine maintenance window, an outage repair, or a planned upgrade. Every one of those changes is an opportunity for the paper or database record to fall out of sync with reality.

The consequences of that inaccuracy are practical, not abstract. Plan a network expansion around a stale inventory record and the numbers can be wrong in either direction: capacity that looks available may already be gone, or capacity that exists may never make it into the plan at all. Fault investigations run into the same wall from the other side, time lost hunting for a piece of equipment the inventory places in one location when it was physically moved months earlier. Neither failure mode is unusual. It's the accumulation of small, ordinary mismatches like these, more than any single dramatic outage, that pushed discovery and reconciliation from a niche tool used by a handful of large operators into a standard part of telecommunications operations generally.

== Historical background ==

The practice grew out of two separate lines of development that only later converged: internet-standard network management protocols on one side, and telecommunications-industry efforts to standardize operational support systems (OSS) on the other.
[truncated]

Emmanuel Magembe (born 25 December 1992) is a Ugandan former footballer who played as an attacking midfielder and winger. He is also known for his fox sprints and speed, free kick specialist and a dribbler. He was regarded as a highly talented attacking midfielder/winger, capable of playing centrally or on either flank. He developed through youth football in Uganda, including the Kampala Kids League, and later played for several Ugandan and European clubs. His senior career included spells with Victors FC, KJT, Vipers SC, KCCA FC, Proline FC, Franö FK and Ishavsbyen FK

== Early life and youth career ==
Emmanuel Magembe was born on 25 December 1992 in Kampala, Uganda. He began playing football at a young age in Mutundwe, in Rubaga South Division. He played football while attending primary school, where his ability in the sport helped him obtain a bursary to continue his education.

Magembe began his early academy football in Nalukolongo. He played for Super Cubs before moving to Young Express, also known as Wembley. He later joined the Kampala Kids League (KKL), where he developed as a youth footballer and gained opportunities to participate in international youth tournaments.Magembe later joined the Kampala Kids League (KKL), where he developed as a youth footballer and gained experience in international youth competitions. By 2007, he was listed among players produced by KKL, which had won tournaments including the Gothia and Tivoli Cups in Europe. [ref: https://www.newvision.co.ug/news/1518522/kkl-transformed-ugandan-football]

Magembe represented KKL in international youth competitions in Europe. He travelled with the team to tournaments in Denmark, England, Peru, Spain, Sweden and Norway and was among the players who gained international experience through KKL. [ref: KKL transformed Ugandan football, New Vision] [ref: KKL Tivoli Cup, New Vision] [ref: KKL roll on at Gothia Cup, New Vision]

In 2005, Magembe joined Old Kampala Senior Secondary School as a student and footballer. He initially developed with the school before progressing to the senior team. During this period, he continued to develop through school and youth football. [ref: Ali finds gift in unbreakable spirit, Daily Monitor] [ref: Magembe ready to revive career at Proline, Kawowo Sports] [ref: Old Kampala SSS are the U-16 Secondary School Champions, Uganda Radio Network]

Magembe later transferred from Old Kampala Senior Secondary School to St. Mary's Kitende, where he continued his education while playing football for the school team. In 2010, he was part of the St. Mary's Kitende team that travelled to Nakuru, Kenya, for the Federation of East Africa Secondary Schools Sports Association (FEASSA) competition, which Kitende won.

== Senior career ==
In 2011, Magembe joined Victors FC in the Uganda Premier League. He later moved to PDRM in Malaysia, where he played during the 2012–13 period. [ref: Express faces player exodus, New Vision] [ref: Hippos Prepare as Opponent Win 3-Nation tourney, Uganda Radio Network]

In 2012, Magembe was summoned to the Uganda Hippos under-21 team. He subsequently spent a period away from active football following a contractual dispute involving a football agent.In 2012, Magembe was summoned to the Uganda Hippos under-21 team. [ref: Afrikansk landslagsspiller klar for norsk 3.-divisjon, Aftenposten] [ref: 2012/13 Super League Club Preview: Vipers Sports Club, Kawowo Sports]

== International career ==
Magembe was involved with the Uganda under-21 national team. In 2012, he was listed among the players in the Uganda Hippos camp preparing for the African Youth Championship qualifying campaign. [ref: Hippos Prepare as Opponent Win 3-Nation tourney, Uganda Radio Network] In 2015, a Norwegian report stated that Magembe had made under-21 international appearances for Uganda and had played against Ghana. [ref: Afrikansk landslagsspiller klar for norsk 3.-divisjon, Aftenposten]

In 2014, Magembe joined Rwenshama/KJT, a club competing in the FUFA Big League. He was part of the team that earned promotion to the Uganda Premier League and contributed goals and assists during the campaign. [ref: KJT / Rwenshama dumps Mutundwe out, faces Jinja S.S / Kirinya, Kawowo Sports] [ref: Rwenshama Books Slot In FUFA Super League, ChimpReports]

Magembe later continued his career in Europe. He played for Franö FK in Sweden before moving to northern Norway, where he joined Ishavsbyen FK. During his time in Norway, he played under the name "Em" and scored goals for the club. [ref: Afrikansk landslagsspiller klar for norsk 3.-divisjon, iTromsø] [ref: Afrikansk landslagsspiller klar for norsk 3.-divisjon, iTromsø]

In 2016, Magembe joined KCCA FC under coach Mike Mutebi. He was part of the KCCA team that won the 2015–16 Uganda Premier League title. He later moved to Proline FC, but injuries, including knee and ankle problems, limited his ability to play.In 2016, Magembe joined KCCA FC and was part of the club's 2015–16 league-winning side. [ref: https://www.monitor.co.ug/uganda/magazines/score/kcca-triumph-amidst-mediocrity-1651940] He later joined Proline FC on a two-year deal. [ref: https://kawowo.com/2016/09/01/magembe-ready-to-revive-career-at-proline/] Magembe left Proline in 2017 after limited playing time, with injury contributing to his lack of game time. [ref: https://kawowo.com/2017/06/14/magembe-confirms-departure-proline/]

Draft text:
Lieutenant-Colonel Arthur William Valentine Plunkett (4 May 1868 – 17 April 1903) was a British Army officer who served as a major in the Manchester Regiment and held the local rank of lieutenant-colonel while commanding the 2nd Battalion of the King's African Rifles. He was killed during the Dervish War at the Battle of Agaarweyne, also known as Gumburu. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.]

== Early life and education ==

Arthur William Valentine Plunkett was born on 4 May 1868, the son of Lieutenant-Colonel G. T. Plunkett, CB. [ref: Churchill and the Mad Mullah of Somaliland: Betrayal and Redemption 1899–1921, Pen and Sword Military] [ref: A Manchester Officer's Will, Manchester Evening News] He attended the Royal Military College, Sandhurst from 1886. [ref: Dover college register, 1871-1894,, ST George's Press]

Plunkett was commissioned as a second lieutenant in the Manchester Regiment on 14 March 1888 and was promoted to lieutenant in November 1889. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.] [ref: Hart's Annual Army List, Militia List, and Imperial Yeomanry List] He was promoted to captain in 1897. [ref: Dover college register, 1871-1894,, ST George's Press]

== Military career ==
=== British India service ===
Plunkett first saw active service in 1891, when he took part in the Second Miranzai Expedition with the 2nd Battalion of the Manchester Regiment. For his service in the expedition he received a medal with clasp. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.]

During the North-West Frontier campaigns of 1897–1898, Plunkett served as assistant to the divisional transport officer with the Malakand expeditionary force. He participated in operations in Bajaur and the Mohmand country, for which he received the India Medal with clasp. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.]

Plunkett subsequently served as assistant transport officer of the 1st Division during the Tirah campaign. During the campaign he took part in the capture of the Sampagha and Arhanga passes, operations against the Khani Khel, and operations in the Bazar Valley in December 1897. His service earned him an additional clasp to his medal. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.] [ref: Churchill and the Mad Mullah of Somaliland: Betrayal and Redemption 1899–1921, Pen and Sword Military]

=== Central Africa, Uganda and Gambia service ===

In March 1899, Plunkett was seconded for service in Central Africa and joined the 2nd (Central Africa) Battalion of the King's African Rifles. He subsequently served in Uganda and Central Africa. In 1901, Plunkett took part in a British expedition in the Gambia. He was mentioned in dispatches for his service and received a medal with clasp. [ref: Churchill and the Mad Mullah of Somaliland: Betrayal and Redemption 1899–1921, Pen and Sword Military] [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.]

In June 1901, Plunkett was promoted to the substantive rank of major. In August 1902, Plunkett was granted the local rank of lieutenant-colonel. Although he continued to hold the substantive rank of major in the Manchester Regiment, he now commanded the 2nd Battalion of the King's African Rifles as a local lieutenant-colonel. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.]

== Dervish War and death ==

After service in Uganda and Central Africa, he accompanied the battalion to British Somaliland during the campaign against the Dervish movement. Plunkett subsequently served in Colonel Eric Swayne's column during the fighting at the Battle of Erego. Contemporary newspapers credited his bravery with helping to prevent the engagement from becoming a more serious defeat. [ref: Mainly About People, [[The Star (1888-1960)]

The Battle of Agaarweyne began on 15 April 1903 after Captain Olivey, while conducting a scouting mission from Colonel Cobbe's position, reported a large body of mounted and dismounted Dervish forces approximately four miles from the camp.
Cobbe sent Plunkett with a company of the 2nd King's African Rifles, 50 men of the 2nd Sikhs and two Maxim guns to reinforce Olivey and assist his return. Although his orders were confined to bringing Olivey's company back, Plunkett continued the advance after joining him and was drawn into contact with the main Dervish force. The Dervishes repeatedly charged the square from several directions, with cavalry attacking its front and flanks while spearmen and dismounted riflemen attacked from the rear. Neither rifle nor Maxim fire succeeded in stopping the repeated assaults, which continued as British casualties mounted and their ammunition diminished. Plunkett was among the first officers wounded and subsequently received a spear thrust, but continued fighting. [ref: Somaliland, Hutchinson and Co.] [ref: The Mad Mullah of Somaliland, Herbert Jenkins Limited]

Draft: Midwest Express Airlines Flight 007

Draft text:
----

Midwest Express Airlines Flight 007 was a scheduled domestic passenger flight that was involved in a near Mid-Air collision on September 11, 2001, leading to a series of rapid descents and four minor injuries. The flight passed within 30-300 feet of United Airlines Flight 175. [ref: Incident McDonnell Douglas DC-9-32 N207ME, Tuesday 11 September 2001, aviation-safety.net]

==Aircraft==
The aircraft involved was a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-32, manufactured in 1979 for Garuda Indonesia and sold to Midwest Express in 1995 as N207ME.
==Crew==
The flight was operated by Captain Gerald Earwood and first officer Eric Fjelstad (who had joined Midwest less than a year prior). [ref: Gerald Earwood Archives, International Center for 9/11 Justice] Earwood was well known at Midwest for his tendency to "joke" with his fellow crew members; also on board were three flight attendants. [ref: User Clip: Gerald Earwood 9-11 Response | Video | C-SPAN.org]

==Flight==
===Radio issues===
While the aircraft was on NYC radar, several calls to air traffic control (ATC) were missed. This led to the crew believing they might have had an unserviceable VHF communications radio. The missed calls occurred at the same time as American Airlines Flight 11 crashed. [ref: Changing Terror's Course; Book Details How Midwest Plane Avoided Sept. 11 Crash, Redorbit]

===Near miss===
As the aircraft was nearing the Hudson river, United Airlines 175 was also approaching at the same attitude. ATC was focused on vectoring both a Delta and a TWA flight; Midwest 007 was left to fly as previously instructed. The controller was alerted to a conflict between two aircraft and directed Midwest 007 to turn left; the crew complied with this instruction. The controller, on seeing that United 175 was less than a mile from collision told the Midwest crew to "Roll Right". At this time the First officer could see the United aircraft and sent the DC-9 into a right hand dive. [ref: The untold story of 9/11: extract from The Only Plane in the Sky, www.thetimes.com] [ref: ] The aircraft quickly lost altitude and they had to pull up after around 1000 feet. United 175, now on its final descent, was still on a collision course with the DC-9. Once again the crew were forced to dive. This time four people (two passengers and two cabin crew) were injured. The aircraft dropped around 2000 feet in a second dive to the right, allowing Flight 175 to pass an estimated above.

==Aftermath==
The DC-9 landed safely with no further issues. N207ME received temporary repairs in NYC before flying a group of Midwest Express crew members back to Milwaukee on September 13, where it was fully repaired. The aircraft is currently stored in Mexico. [ref: https://imgproc.airliners.net/photos/airliners/4/3/9/1526934.jpg?v=v40 ] Both pilots continued to fly for Midwest Express until 2010, when the airline ceased operations; Earwood would later be hired by JetBlue as a first officer on the A321. [ref: Gerald Earwood Obituary - Frisco, TX, Dignity Memorial]

==In popular culture==
The book Touching History by Lynn Spencer includes the flight along with a number of others.

Ady Arie (Hebrew: עדי אריה; born: 1963) is an Israeli electrical engineering scientist.

He is a professor in the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering in the Fleischman Faculty of Engineering at Tel-Aviv University (TAU), where he holds the Marko and Lucie Chaoul Chair in Nano-Photonics. [ref: Prof. Ady Arie, quantum.tau.ac.il]

Arie's research focuses on nonlinear optics, electron optics, and light–electron interactions. He is a fellow of Optica. [ref: ]

== Early life and education ==
Ady Arie was born in Israel in 1963. He received his B.Sc. in mathematics and physics from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1983, in the framework of Talpiot project, followed by an M.Sc. in physics (1986) and a Ph.D. in engineering (1992), both from Tel Aviv University. His M.Sc. advisors were Prof. Shmuel Goldstein and Prof. Moshe Tur, and his PhD advisor was Prof. Moshe Tur. [ref: Team, NONLINEAR OPTICS AND WAVE PROPAGATION LABORATORY]

From 1991 to 1993, he held Wolfson and Fulbright postdoctoral fellowships under Prof. Robert L. Byer at Stanford University. [ref: Laser heterodyne spectroscopy of 127I2 hyperfine structure near 532 nm, Edward L. Ginzton Laboratory, Stanford University]

== Academic career ==
Arie joined the Department of Physical Electronics in the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering in the Fleischman Faculty of Engineering at Tel-Aviv University in 1993. He became a full professor in 2006. Arie served as the Vice Dean of Research of the Faculty of Engineering from 2011 to 2013 and as the head of the School of Electrical Engineering 2013 to 2017. [ref: KLA-Tencor ישראל תרמה מלגות ל-37 סטודנטים למקצועות טכנולוגיים -, אנשים ומחשבים - פורטל חדשות היי-טק, מיחשוב, טלקום, טכנולוגיות]

He is also the co-founder and head of the TAU Center for Light Matter Interaction since 2016. [ref: Our People, lmicenter.tau.ac.il]

Arie has supervised more than 80 Postdoctoral, Ph.D., and M.Sc. students. [ref: Team, adyarie] [ref: Past Students, adyarie]

== Professional experience ==
In 2001, Arie was a co-founder and chief technology officer of ZettaLight Inc. [ref: השקעה ראשונה לקרן רנוויי טלקום ונצ'רס: גיוס סיד של 1.5 מיליון דולר בזטהלייט - וואלה כסף, וואלה] He is chair of the national steering committee of the Israeli Planning and Budgeting Committee on Quantum Science and Technology and a member of the national science advisory board of the Israel National Quantum Initiative. [ref: מינוי מחליף ליו"ר ועדת היגוי המייעצת לוות"ת לנושא מדע וטכנולוגיה קוונטיים, המועצ]

Arie served as a Topical Editor of Optics Letters (2008-2014) and as an Associate Editor of Optica (2018-2024).  Since 2025, he has been a Deputy Editor of Optics Express. [ref: Optics Letters Editorial Board Members, opg.optica.org] [ref: Editors and Staff, opg.optica.org] [ref: Optic Express, opg.optica.org]

== Research ==
Arie's research spans optics, electron microscopy, light–electron interactions, plasmonics and the propagation dynamics of special wavepackets. [ref: חוקרים מאוניברסיטת תל אביב הצליחו למדוד חבילות גלים מחזוריות, Ynet] [ref: סדרת מחקרים חשפה: תורת הקוונטים משפיעה על תהליך פליטת האור, Ynet]

His research has included the development of nonlinear optical holography for generating and controlling structured light, including Airy and optical vortex beams. [ref: The electron sheepdog, The Statesman] [ref: יצירה ושליטה על אלומות לייזר מאיצות (Airy Beams) בעזרת גבישים פוטוניים לא ליניאריים, הידען - Hayadan] Drawing on an analogy between spin and sum-frequency generation, he proposed and helped demonstrate an all-optical Stern–Gerlach effect, both in space and in time. [ref: מחקר ישראלי: אם אין מגנטים – תשתמשו באור, Ynet]

He developed quasiperiodic nonlinear photonic crystals for phase matching multiple nonlinear optical processes and to periodically poled ferroelectric crystals for efficient frequency conversion across a broad spectral range. [ref: Photonic quasicrystals for general purpose nonlinear optical frequency conversion, Physical Review Letters] [ref: Green and ultraviolet quasi-phase-matched second harmonic generation in bulk periodically-poled KTiOPO4, Optics Communications]

In electron optics, his team produced the first electron Airy beam and developed masks for shaping electron beams, later applying this to correct spherical aberration and improve resolution in electron microscopy. [ref: Researchers develop electron-based Airy Beam, EDN] Using surface gravity water waves as a model system, his group also made the first observation of the Kennard phase of wave packets in a linear potential. [ref: חוקרים ישראלים פתרו תעלומה מדעית בת 93 שנה, ynet]

== Honors and awards ==
Arie received several awards, including the Fulbright and the Wolfson Fellowships for postdoctoral scholars and the Alon Fellowship.

In 2010, he was elevated to a fellow of Optica “for significant contributions to the development of periodic and quasi-periodic nonlinear photonic crystals”.

In 2015, he was named to the Marko and Lucie Chaoul Chair in Nano-Photonics at Tel Aviv University.
[truncated]

The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reported on his return to competition and identified him as a Milwaukee Bucks minority owner. [ref: Milwaukee hosts USA Summer Nationals: Takeaways from the world's largest fencing tournament, Milwaukee Journal Sentinel]

[ref: Largest fencing tournament in the United States heads to Milwaukee, CBS 58]

Weber has been involved with the Carter Burden Network, a New York nonprofit serving older adults. He has served on the organization's board and has been recognized by the organization for his service. [ref: 2025 Campaign & Senior Prom, Carter Burden Network]

Zingroll is an American streaming platform for AI-generated films and series. The platform is known for it's short-form and episodic content produced with generative video tools.

The company was founded by Harshit Yadav, who had previously built the consumer applications Airfeed and LitFeed. It maintains offices in San Francisco and Delhi.

Its investors include Accel, Andreessen Horowitz's Speedrun programme, Google, Z Fellows and Network VC.

== History ==

Zingroll was founded by Harshit Yadav, an entrepreneur based in San Francisco who had previously built 2 consumer applications, Airfeed and LitFeed. The platform launched on iOS and subsequently on Android. Its early positioning centred on free access to movies and series. The application was later repositioned around personalised generation, allowing a user to appear as the protagonist of a movie generated from a single photograph.
== Atoms AI Cohort ==

In March 2026, Zingroll was named one of five startups selected for the Atoms AI Cohort 2026, a partnership between Accel and Google's AI Futures Fund announced in November 2025 to support early-stage companies building AI products connected to India. The programme received more than 4,000 applications and each selected company became eligible for up to $2 million in funding from Accel and the AI Futures Fund together with up to $350,000 in Google cloud and AI compute credits.

Accel partner Prayank Swaroop told TechCrunch that roughly 70% of the rejected applications were "wrappers" and that many of the remainder fell into crowded categories such as marketing automation and AI recruitment. Jonathan Silber, co-founder and director of Google's AI Futures Fund, said the selected companies aligned with areas where Google expected deeper real-world adoption of AI. The Free Press Journal characterised Zingroll as the creative outlier of the group.

The cohort opened on 11 March 2026 at Google's Ananta campus in Bengaluru with virtual speaker series running through April and May 2026 and a concluding programme in Mountain View, California in June. Announcing the selection, Accel described Zingroll as a streaming platform for AI-native films and shows. The selection was also reported by The Indian Express, YourStory, Analytics India Magazine, Moneycontrol and IT Voice.

== Platform and technology ==

Zingroll distributes films and series produced with generative tools. The application is distributed free of charge, offers trailers and original series, with in-app purchases. The application allows a user to upload a photograph and receive an episodic film in which they appear as the lead character.
== Funding ==

Zingroll raised $250,000 in pre-seed funding. In November 2025, the Ukrainian-American firm Network VC announced an investment in the company. Its founder, Oleksandr Soroka, said the firm backs founders who change how audiences create and experience content. Its listing
with a16z Speedrun names Accel, a16z Speedrun, Google and Z Fellows among its backers, and it appeared among the companies presenting at the a16z Speedrun 2025 demo day. Selection for the Atoms AI Cohort in March 2026 carried eligibility for up to $2 million in further investment and up to $350,000 in Google compute credits.

Draft text:
China Everbright Bank (Europe) S.A. is a credit institution incorporated in Luxembourg. It serves as the European subsidiary of China Everbright Bank (中国光大银行), a Chinese joint-stock commercial bank founded in August 1992, headquartered in Beijing, and listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE: 601818) and the Hong Kong Stock Exchange (SEHK: 6818).

When China Everbright Bank set up its Luxembourg operation in 2017, it did so through two separate legal structures: the subsidiary covered in this article, and a directly operated branch, the China Everbright Bank Luxembourg Branch. At the time, this made China Everbright the seventh Chinese bank with a presence in the Grand Duchy. Academic research on Chinese banks' European expansion has noted that Luxembourg's early diplomatic ties with China, dating to 1972, and its role as a financial gateway have made it a recurring choice for Chinese lenders structuring their EU market entry.

== History ==
China Everbright Bank obtained a banking licence from the European Central Bank and clearance from Luxembourg's financial regulator, the CSSF, to open the subsidiary in 2017. Press coverage at the time framed the move partly as a way of securing a foothold in the EU single market ahead of Brexit, and partly as part of the bank's wider push to support trade tied to China's Belt and Road Initiative.

The bank marked the opening with a launch event in Luxembourg on 8 September 2017, held alongside the "Forum for Belt and Road Initiative and Investment of Chinese Enterprises in Europe". Those attending included Luxembourg's then prime minister Xavier Bettel, finance minister Pierre Gramegna, CSSF director general Claude Marx, China's ambassador to Luxembourg Huang Changqing, and China Everbright Group and Bank chairman Tang Shuangning.

Research on the sector has characterised such moves by Chinese state-linked banks as part of a broader, legally-structured pattern of foreign direct investment into the European Union, in which a Luxembourg subsidiary combined with a parallel branch is a common structural choice.

== Operations ==
The subsidiary is built around corporate banking rather than retail services. Its business centres on deposits and loans for corporate clients, multi-currency accounts (it handles euros, US dollars and renminbi), trade finance instruments such as letters of credit and guarantees, and international settlement and money-market activity. In practice, its client base consists mainly of European firms doing business in China, Chinese companies investing into the EU, and other banks needing a correspondent relationship in Luxembourg.

== Regulation ==
As a Luxembourg-licensed credit institution, the bank is supervised jointly by the European Central Bank under the Single Supervisory Mechanism and, at national level, by the CSSF, the country's financial regulator. The entity is listed in the CSSF's public register of authorised credit institutions and in the European Central Bank's official list of supervised entities. The licence also gives it EU passporting rights, so it can offer services across the wider European Economic Area without separate authorisation in each country. Deposits are covered up to €100,000 per depositor under Luxembourg's deposit guarantee scheme, the *Fonds de garantie des dépôts Luxembourg*.

Its identifying codes are: BIC/SWIFT EVERLULX; LEI 22210018MLEVW7CTGU78; Luxembourg trade and companies register (RCS) number B213668; and ECB monetary financial institution code LUB00401. The company's registration and corporate filings can be consulted through the official Luxembourg Business Registers portal.

== Financial position ==
As of 2025, the bank reported total assets of around €105 million and net profit of roughly €2 million, with a small workforce of six employees. Its registered office is at 10, Avenue Émile Reuter, in Luxembourg City.
