Draft: Kenneth Nelson (academic)

Draft text:
Kenneth Tommy Nelson is a Swedish sociologist and the Barnett Professor of Social Policy at the University of Oxford. He is head of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention and a fellow of St Cross College, Oxford. [ref: Professor Kenneth Nelson, Department of Social Policy and Intervention] [ref: Professor Kenneth Nelson, St Cross College] He also holds a professorship at the Swedish Institute for Social Research (SOFI) at Stockholm University. [ref: Kenneth Nelson appointed professor at the University of Oxford, Stockholm University]

Nelson's research concerns comparative social policy and the welfare state, particularly poverty, social inequality, minimum-income protection and social rights.

== Education and career ==

Nelson studied sociology and social work at Stockholm University and completed a doctorate in sociology there in 2004. His dissertation, Fighting Poverty: Comparative Studies on Social Insurance, Means-tested Benefits and Income Redistribution, examined the anti-poverty effects of different forms of social protection across welfare states. [ref: Fighting Poverty: Comparative Studies on Social Insurance, Means-tested Benefits and Income Redistribution, Stockholm University] He subsequently worked at the Swedish Institute for Social Research (SOFI), becoming professor of sociology in 2014.

In 2023, Nelson joined the University of Oxford as Barnett Professor of Social Policy and became a fellow of St Cross College, Oxford. He subsequently became head of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention.

Nelson has held a number of positions in academic organisations and publishing. He served as a board member and co-chair of the European Network for Social Policy Analysis (ESPAnet), and is a member of the Board of Governors of the Foundation for International Studies on Social Security (FISS). [ref: ESPAnet – European Network for Social Policy Analysis] [ref: Foundation for International Studies on Social Security] He is a co-editor of the Journal of European Social Policy. [ref: Journal of European Social Policy: Editorial Board, SAGE Publications] Nelson has also served on the board of the Swedish Sociological Association, including as its president from 2020 to 2022, and is a former president of the Nordic Sociological Association. [ref: Sveriges sociologförbund]

Nelson directs the Social Policy Indicators (SPIN) database, a cross-national collection of institutional social-policy data maintained at Stockholm University. [ref: Social Policy Indicators Database, Stockholm University] [ref: The Social Policy Indicators (SPIN) database, International Journal of Social Welfare]

== Research ==

Nelson's research focuses on the development and consequences of welfare states and social policy from a comparative perspective. His work has examined poverty, income inequality, social rights, minimum-income protection, health, employment and intergenerational relations.

A substantial part of his research concerns the comparative measurement of social policy, including the use of institutional indicators of social rights and benefit entitlements to analyse differences between welfare states. [ref: Social citizenship rights and social insurance replacement rate validity: pitfalls and possibilities, Journal of European Public Policy] Through SPIN, Nelson has contributed to comparative data on the institutional structure of social protection across countries. [ref: The Social Policy Indicators (SPIN) database, International Journal of Social Welfare]

=== Minimum income protection ===

Nelson has conducted comparative research on minimum-income benefits and the relationship between social assistance, poverty and broader welfare-state institutions. His work has examined the adequacy of social assistance in relation to poverty thresholds and the relationship between minimum-income benefits and material deprivation. [ref: Social Assistance and EU Poverty Thresholds 1990–2008: Are European Welfare Systems Providing Just and Fair Protection Against Low Income?, European Sociological Review] [ref: Counteracting material deprivation: The role of social assistance in Europe, Journal of European Social Policy]

With Ive Marx, Nelson edited Minimum Income Protection in Flux (2012), a comparative study of changes in minimum-income protection in Europe. [ref: Minimum Income Protection in Flux, Palgrave Macmillan] The book was subsequently discussed in the academic literature, including in an independent review in the Journal of Social Policy. [ref: Review of Minimum Income Protection in Flux, Journal of Social Policy]

Nelson's later work with Rense Nieuwenhuis developed a framework for analysing benefit coverage that distinguishes coverage from the generosity of social benefits. [ref: Towards a new consolidated framework for analysing benefit coverage, Journal of European Social Policy]

=== Intergenerational social policy ===

Nelson has also studied the distribution of social protection between generations. With Simon Birnbaum, Tommy Ferrarini and Joakim Palme, he co-authored The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes (2017), which examines how welfare states distribute social protection across childhood, working life and old age. [ref: The Generational Welfare Contract: Justice, Institutions and Outcomes, Edward Elgar]

Draft text:
Terrence Portelli is a Maltese politician and asset recovery manager [ref: Maltese voters have 39 candidates for Europe, 13 of which are independents, Malta Today] who served as leader of Imperium Europa, a far-right political party in Malta, from February 2025 to March 2026. He previously contested the 2024 European Parliament election as a candidate for the party.

== Political career ==
In September 2023, Portelli, alongside Normal Lowell (as planned candidates for the 2024 elections), spoke at an Imperium Europa press conference in front of the Great Siege Monument in Valletta. He presented the party as the only solution for Malta, highlighting the need to address forces dividing identity and to “rekindle the fire of masculinity and femininity in society”. [ref: Imperium Europa claims it is the only solution for Malta, [[TVM (Malta)]

=== European Parliament candidacy ===
Portelli contested the 2024 June European Parliament election in Malta as a candidate for Imperium Europa. [ref: 2024 elections: Malta heads to the polls for MEP and Local Council elections, BusinessNow.mt] [ref: CANDIDATES FOR MEP ELECTION 2024 - NATIONAL (MEP), Electrical Commission of Malta] [ref: Scandal-hit Malta struggles with next EU commissioner candidate, Euractiv] Malta elects six Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) using the single transferable vote system. [ref: 39 candidates, including 9 from PL, 8 from PN, to contest EP election, The Malta Independent]

Portelli’s campaign included opposition to further European Union integration. He advocated for Malta's withdrawal from the eurozone and the reintroduction of the Maltese lira, which he proposed should be backed by gold. He also supported changes to Malta's political system based on the model of Athenian democracy. [ref: Election Playbook: In the land of the F-Living, Malta Today]

In a May 2024 interview with the Times of Malta, Portelli criticized established political figures, referring to them as "puppet politicians" and "leeches". He spoke of rounding them up and handing them over to their “enemy,” and framed it in historical terms (comparing it to Arminius). He also opposed foreign military involvement and financial support in international conflicts and criticized European security policies. [ref: 'We will round you up': far-right MEP candidate's threat to political 'leeches', Times of Malta]

During debates organized by the National Youth Council in late May, Portelli raised issues concerning Malta’s current media transparency and allotted freedom of expression. [ref: ‘If someone says ABC, media has to report ABC’, says Imperium Europa candidate, Maltadaily.mt] He also argued that continued immigration could result in Malta's native population becoming a minority. [ref: Maltese becoming minority in their own country, says Imperium Europa’s Terrence Portelli, Malta Daily]

==== Results ====
Portelli himself received 147 first-preference votes (0.06%). He was eliminated early in the first-round counting process after receiving a small number of transferred votes, finishing with around 154–158 votes in total. [ref: Official: all the first-count votes in the European Parliament elections, Times of Malta] Nearly all of the party’s support went to Norman Lowell, who obtained 6,669 first-preference votes but was also eliminated later without reaching the quota required for election (37,180 votes). [ref: Norman Lowell Lost 1,569 Votes Since Last European Parliament Election, Lovin Malta]

=== Leadership of Imperium Europa ===
On 9 February 2025, Portelli became leader of Imperium Europa, succeeding the party's founder, Norman Lowell. His tenure followed a period of declining electoral support for the party.

Portelli resigned as party leader in March 2026, citing personal reasons and limited time. [ref: Terrence Portelli Resigns As Imperium Europa Leader, Eman Cross Takes Over, Lovin Malta] He was succeeded by Eman Cross, who was selected by the party's executive council. [ref: Expelled by Imperium Europa in 2021, Cross returns to lead far-right party, Times of Malta]

== References ==

Draft text:
Sylvia Netzer (born 1944) [ref: Artists' biographies, Confrontational Ceramics] [ref: Sylvia Netzer, Christopher Knowles, The New York Times] is an American sculptor, [ref: American Ceramics] art critic, and professor emeritus at the City College of New York. [ref: Christopher Knowles & Sylvia Netzer RELATiVE(s) at The Opening Gallery, [[Artsy (website)]

==Early life and education==
Netzer was born to Jenny Netzer and Hans A. Netzer in Manhattan, New York. She graduated from the City College of New York and later received her Masters in Fine Art in sculpture at Columbia University School of Fine Arts. [ref: S...as in Sylvia, A.I.R. Gallery] At City College, she was among the supporters of the 1965 March on Washington for Peace in Vietnam. [ref: Obervation Post, 1965-04-14, Observation Post]

==Career==
Netzer's abstract work Post-Toxic/Neo-Plastic, a room-sized installation of black and yellow figures, was described by Drew Shiflett as "remind[ing] one of a world in which genetic engineering has gone berserk or toxic wastes have influenced the gene pool"; [ref: In Three Dimensions: Women Sculptors of the '90s] it was followed up by her 1996 work Miasma Morph. [ref: Miasma Morph, A.I.R. Gallery] She later produced Glen Gary OLY in 2004, a sculpture of kiln-fired bricks carved to resemble herself in the lounging posture of Olympia, the 1863 oil painting. [ref: Pot People Recent Figurative Ceramic Sculpture, Sculpture Review] Two years later, she worked on site at a brick plant in York to create Glen Gary OLY II. [ref: Unusual guest at brick plant, The York Dispatch]

Netzer's work is represented by a collection at A.I.R. Gallery in Brooklyn, New York. She has curated several exhibits at the gallery and elsewhere. [ref: Education program, A.I.R. Gallery] She directed the ceramics program at City College from 1990 [ref: Sylvia Netzer, Reticulated Forms, A.I.R. Gallery] [ref: The Paper, 1993-03-18, The Paper] until her retirement in 2026.

==Personal life==
Netzer is married to theater director Robert M. Wilson. The two met in 1983 at Greenwich House Pottery, at which time Netzer was an instructor and Wilson a student, though he was not in her class. They married in August 2015.

The Boston Global Forum (BGF) is a Boston-based nonprofit think tank and international policy forum founded in 2012. Its work concerns international affairs, artificial intelligence governance and responsible technological development. [ref: Judea Pearl Named AI Pioneer by Boston Global Forum in Honor of America’s 250th Anniversary, UCLA Samueli School of Engineering] [ref: Boston Think Tank Brings Ethical AI Principles into Governance, Finance, Banking and Blockchain, Global Association of Risk Professionals] Its stated aims include peace, security, freedom, democracy and human dignity. BGF brings together political leaders, scholars, policymakers and technologists to develop proposals for global governance and the use of artificial intelligence. [ref: Boston Global Forum Announces the Evolution of AIWS: From AI World Society to AI Wisdom Society, Boston Global Forum]

== History and organization ==
BGF was co-founded by former Massachusetts governor Michael Dukakis, former VietNamNet editor Nguyen Anh Tuan, and Harvard professors Thomas E. Patterson and John Quelch. [ref: About, Boston Global Forum] In 2018, the Associated Press described Dukakis as its chair and Patterson as a board member. [ref: Dukakis: Global accord needed on use of AI by governments, KSL.com]

== Activities ==
=== Artificial intelligence governance ===
BGF's AI World Society initiative has developed proposals concerning AI ethics, government services and international cooperation. In 2018, its co-founders Dukakis and Tuan advocated international standards for AI use. The initiative proposed a United Nations body, modeled on the International Atomic Energy Agency, to coordinate agreements on the use of AI by governments.

A 2025 article in the Global Association of Risk Professionals' publication described BGF's subsequent proposals for AI-supported public services and financial governance, including AIWS Government 24/7 and the Boston Finance Accord. The article presented these initiatives through interviews with BGF representatives and descriptions of the organization's policy frameworks.

=== Cooperation with Club de Madrid ===
BGF and the Club de Madrid organized a policy lab on transatlantic approaches to digital governance on September 16–18, 2020. [ref: Policy Lab: Transatlantic Approaches to Digital Governance, MIT Media Lab] [ref: Club de Madrid and the Boston Global Forum advocate for a Social Contract for the AI Age, Club de Madrid] Its final report advocated a Social Contract for the AI Age, addressing the responsibilities of governments, technology companies and other participants in AI development and use. Recommendations included a code of ethics for AI developers and users and support for international cooperation on digital governance.

== Awards ==
BGF presents the World Leader for Peace and Security Award and the World Leader in AIWS Award. Recipients have included Shinzo Abe and Angela Merkel for the former, and Vint Cerf and Judea Pearl for the latter. [ref: World Leader for Peace and Security Award, Boston Global Forum] [ref: World Leaders in AIWS Award, Boston Global Forum]

In 2026, BGF and AIWS named 50 AI Pioneers in connection with the United States' 250th anniversary. UCLA reported that Pearl was among those recognized and that the honorees were celebrated at BGF's America at 250 conference in May.

Philippe Lamouris (born 1991) is a Hungarian-born composer, pianist and artistic researcher based in Belgium. He studied composition and piano at the Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel and completed a doctorate in the arts in 2021. His compositions include the community opera Leedberg, the oratorio Heavens, and Arctic Desert.

== Biography ==

Lamouris was born in Hungary in 1991. He studied at the Bartók Béla Conservatory in Budapest before moving to Belgium in 2009. At the Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel (KCB), he studied composition with Jan Van Landeghem and piano with Jan Michiels, receiving master's degrees in composition in 2014 and piano in 2015. [ref: Philippe Lamouris, Ars Musica]

He subsequently pursued doctoral research at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel. His doctorate in the arts, Beyond: A Pianist-composer's Thoughts on Musical Simplexity, Emotion and the Soul, concerned composition, performance, musical emotion and expression. [ref: Beyond. A pianist-composer's thoughts on musical simplexity, emotion and the soul, Brussels Arts Platform] He completed the doctorate in 2021.

Lamouris has taught at the Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel since 2016.

== Music ==

In 2017, Lamouris composed the community opera Leedberg, commissioned by the Immaculata Maria school in Roosdaal. A subsequent production at the Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel in 2018 brought together professional and amateur musicians, schoolchildren and local choirs. [ref: Opera met Brusselse ketjes en muzikanten in Conservatorium, BRUZZ]

His chamber work Ur was performed by the piano and saxophone duo Koi Collective. Reviewing the performance for Crescendo Magazine, Bernard Vincken described the work's combination of tenor saxophone, piano and electronic sounds. [ref: Koi Collective au Beeldenstorm d'Anderlecht, Crescendo Magazine]

In 2021, Lamouris composed the oratorio Heavens, with a text by Rozemarijn Vanwijnsberghe. The work incorporates religious and non-religious texts in several languages and was created in Schaarbeek in connection with the World Choir Games, with participation from singers in Belgium and abroad. [ref: Kinderkoor Sint-Jan repeteert voor Heavens, Koorklank]

The same year, Lamouris premiered his piano concerto at the Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel, performing as soloist with the symphoniaASSAI orchestra conducted by Wouter Lenaerts. The concert was presented as the final artistic result of his doctoral research. [ref: Beyond – Philippe Lamouris, Koninklijk Conservatorium Brussel]

In 2023, his composition Arctic Desert was selected as the laureate in the ACA category of the Andrée Charlier Composition Competition, organised in partnership with the Ars Musica festival. [ref: Concours de composition Andrée Charlier, Larsen]

Doro is a Canadian artificial intelligence chatbot designed to act as a mental-health coach for people experiencing early signs of anxiety and depression. It was developed by Razroze Inc., a startup founded in 2023 by brothers Rastin and Ramtin Rassoli and based at Velocity, the University of Waterloo's startup incubator in Kitchener, Ontario. The app conducts sessions by text or voice, draws on techniques from cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy, and assigns users small tasks between sessions.

== History ==
Rastin Rassoli began developing Doro in 2023 while studying computer science and psychology at the University of Waterloo, after earlier helping to build Joyi, an app delivering short psychology lessons to teenagers, during a co-op placement. He continued the work through the university's Enterprise Co-op program with the support of a CA$30,000 government grant. A first version was released to about 100 trial users in June 2024, followed by a wider release in September 2024, when the University of Waterloo's Campus Wellness service began offering the app to students.

By late 2024 the university reported that Doro had been deployed at some 30 mental-health clinics in Ontario and Alberta, and in January 2025 the student newspaper Imprint reported that the app had more than 2,000 users. Mobile apps for iOS and Android followed in 2025, and in August 2025 the Waterloo Region Record reported that the company had signed a contract with a chain of clinics in Alberta. By 2026 the company was working with hospital systems in Canada and the United States and collaborating with University of Waterloo researchers on clinical applications, according to the university.

== Features ==
Doro replaces questionnaire-style intake with a conversational assessment and delivers exercises drawn from about 20 psychotherapeutic techniques, such as journalling or the TIPP skill for managing panic, while tracking each session. It is positioned as an early-intervention tool for people whose symptoms have not reached a clinical diagnosis, rather than as treatment for diagnosed conditions. The developers state that the chatbot maintains a defined therapeutic stance and conversational boundaries rather than acting as a general-purpose assistant.

If a user's symptoms indicate a crisis, the app stops the session and directs them to a built-in directory of crisis helplines organized by country and province, or to a therapist in their region. Doro also partners with therapists, providing them with summaries of a user's prior conversations, and its exercises include prompts to attend social events and build connections outside the app.

== Reception ==
In September 2024, CBC News profiled Doro in a report on AI mental-health apps for students; experts quoted in the report said such apps cannot replace conventional treatment and raised concerns about safety, privacy and the lack of regulation of AI mental-health apps generally. In a 2025 episode of the TVO series Big If True on AI chatbots and therapy, host Molly Thomas tested the app; when she described thoughts of self-harm, it directed her to crisis resources. The Waterloo Region Record also covered the startup in 2025.

P & R Ginger Jo R (I.F.S.B. No. 127252; whelped 18 November 1973) was an American Foxhound owned and handled by Jacob “Jackie” Ryals of McRae, Georgia. In 1976 she won the United States Open (U.S.O.) and the National Field Trial Championship. The Chase and The Lumber City Log described those two titles, won in the same year, as unmatched in the sport. She remains the only foxhound, male or female, to win both events in the same calendar year.

== Early life and background ==
Ginger Jo R was whelped on 18 November 1973. She was sired by Allegany Ringo and out of Pittman Snow Bird. She was produced through a collaborative breeding program between Dr. C.W. Pittman of Raleigh, North Carolina and Ryals.  Ryals took the pick of the litter and raised her at his kennels in McRae.

The Chase quoted Ryals as saying she was “the sorriest looking little female you ever saw, but when she was turned loose at six months with older hounds that would not run a deer, she took right to foxhunting. At nine months of age she could hold her own with the other packs".

== Competitive career ==
At fifteen months age she was loaned to E. M. Cannon for the Mid-South Open and was scratched for running a deer.[2]

At the Western Hills field trial she did not have a score going into the last day, then came from behind to be crowned Western Hill Dual Champion.

In 1976 Ginger Jo R won the United States Open at Laurinburg, North Carolina, and the National Field Trial Championship at Panama City, Florida. Contemporary reports said more than 600 hounds were entered at the National. The Chase said she finished first in hunting, trailing, speed and drive, and endurance.

The Lumber City Log reported that the National win brought eight trophies, including challenge trophies, the Jasper Maupin Memorial Trophy, and the James Trophy.

In December of the same calendar year, she was entered into the U.S. Open Field Trial in Laurinburg, North Carolina. Despite freezing temperatures and frozen ground during the first two days of the event, she outperformed 353 other hounds to capture the High General Average (HGA) title and secure the U.S.O. championship. With this victory, she became the only hound in history to win both the National and the U.S. Open in the same calendar year [ref: List of National and U.S. Open Champions, The Chase]. [ref: N FCh Ginger Jo R. Wins Top USO Honors, The Chase]

== Sale and later life ==
In February 1977 Paul May purchased Ginger Jo R for $10,000, setting a record at the time for the highest price paid for a field trial hound. In 1978 she returned to the Ryals kennels in McRae. She was retired from field trial competition to be utilized for breeding with notable studs at the Ryals Kennels.

The Ryals kennels produced other champion hounds, including Jackie’s Scout, winner of the 1980 National Field Trial Championship. Ryals and that hound appeared on the cover of The Chase.[1]

== Burial ==
She is buried at the National Hall of Fame Cemetery of Fox Hounds at Boles Field in the Sabine National Forest, Shelby County, Texas. The headstone lists Western Hill Dual Champion, National Champion, and U.S.O. Champion.

== References ==

Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. (AOI) is an American company that designs and manufactures fiber-optic networking products and optical semiconductor components. It is headquartered in Sugar Land, Texas, and its common stock trades on the NASDAQ under the symbol AAOI. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. Common Stock (AAOI), Nasdaq] The company was founded in 1997 by Chih-Hsiang (Thompson) Lin and completed its initial public offering in 2013. [ref: Form DEF 14A (proxy statement), Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / SEC]

The company's products include optical transceivers for data centers, equipment for cable television (CATV) broadband networks, and lasers and components for telecommunications and fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) applications. [ref: Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission] As of December 31, 2025, the company had 4,691 employees. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics: Number of Employees 2012-2025, MacroTrends]

== History ==
Applied Optoelectronics was incorporated in Texas on February 28, 1997, by Chih-Hsiang (Thompson) Lin, who had worked as a research scientist and research associate professor at the University of Houston. The company reincorporated in Delaware in March 2013.

In 2000, AOI opened its headquarters and manufacturing facility in Sugar Land, Texas. [ref: AOI Opens New Manufacturing Facility, Moves Operations, Compound Semiconductor] Its early operations focused on semiconductor lasers and optical components.

AOI began trading on the Nasdaq on September 26, 2013, under the symbol AAOI. Its initial public offering was priced at $10 per share, below the proposed range of $13 to $15. The company sold 3.6 million shares and received approximately $33.5 million in net proceeds. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics sets pricing for IPO, PE Hub] [ref: Applied Optoelectronics shares fall after $36M IPO, www.ksl.com] [ref: Applied Optoelectronics - 10-Q quarterly report FY2013 Q3, companiesmarketcap.com]

In 2016, the company's two largest customers accounted for approximately three-quarters of its revenue, while its ten largest customers accounted for more than 95%. [ref: Microsoft is a big customer of Hortonworks and Applied Optoelectronics, CNBC]

In August 2017, AOI disclosed a slowdown in demand from a large data center customer, after which its stock price declined. [ref: Mad About Your Loss in Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) Stock? Don't Sue!, Nasdaq] The company subsequently disclosed quality issues involving certain lasers and transceivers. Shareholders filed securities class-action lawsuits against AOI and two of its officers. [ref: In re Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. Securities Litigation — Stipulation and Agreement of Settlement (S.D. Tex.), SEC filing / official settlement site] One consolidated action was settled for $15.5 million, with the settlement funded by the company's directors' and officers' insurance.

In December 2022, AOI entered a supply agreement with a technology customer to manufacture certain lasers, and in June 2023 it signed a further agreement covering design and assembly services. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) enters supply agreement with Microsoft Corporation, StreetInsider]

In March 2025, AOI entered into a transaction agreement with a customer that included a warrant to purchase up to 7,945,399 shares at an exercise price of $23.6954 per share, exercisable until March 13, 2035. [ref: Form 8-K (Amazon transaction agreement and warrant), Applied Optoelectronics, Inc. / SEC]

== Products ==

=== Optical transceivers ===
AOI manufactures optical transceivers for data center and networking applications. Its products include transceivers with data rates ranging from 40G to 1.6T and use form factors including SFP, QSFP, QSFP-DD and OSFP. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics demonstrating new transceiver product portfolio at OFC, www.semiconductor-today.com]

In the first quarter of 2026, the company reported its first volume shipment of 800G products. [ref: 1AAOI - Applied Optoelectronics Inc, Morningstar] In March 2026, AOI announced a volume order for 1.6T data center transceivers. [ref: AOI receives first volume order of 1.6T data center transceivers, Light Reading]

=== Semiconductor components ===
AOI manufactures semiconductor laser chips and optical components used in its products. It fabricates lasers using a combination of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) and metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD), and supplies lasers and laser subassemblies to other equipment and transceiver manufacturers.

=== Cable broadband ===
AOI supplies equipment for hybrid fiber-coaxial cable television networks. In September 2022 it introduced HFC products under the Quantum Bandwidth brand, including amplifiers and remote-management software. [ref: Applied Optoelectronics Showcases New Family of HFC Products Under Its 'Quantum Bandwidth' Brand Name, www.gophotonics.com] [ref: AOI adds smarts to cable amps with 'QuantumLink', Light Reading]

[[File:Edward Bird (1772-1819) - Idleness - FA.246(O) - Victoria and Albert Museum.jpg|upright=1.15|thumb|Idleness by Edward Bird, –1819]]

Lyadh (Bengali: ল্যাদ) is a word or concept in Bengali that describes the act of doing nothing, being relaxed, and lazing around. [ref: Panta Bhaat: How the humble fermented rice has become a summer weekend staple for me, Wion] [ref: The ultimate A to Z Bengali dictionary, [[The Telegraph (India)] [ref: On The Occasion Of Mahalaya, Here Are A Few Ways To Celebrate Durga Puja Like A Bengali, iDiva] Depending on the context, it can be translated as 'indolence', [ref: 2024 Reporter Diaries: A laid-back Bong finds love in the languid charm of domestic cricket - Santadeep Dey, Sportstar] 'sloth', [ref: Letters to the Editor: Oxford's Word of the Year 2022, [[The Telegraph (India)] [ref: ‘Lyadh’!, Varta Trust] 'sleepiness', [ref: Why Pradipta Bhattacharya’s musical short 'LYAD' is unique?, The Times of India] or a state of inactivity. It can also refer to a state of intentional unproductivity, lackadaisicalness, getting some rest, idling around, dawdling, or procrastinating. [ref: Untranslatable Words From Languages Across India, Homegrown] [ref: Tilottama at a glance, Ukiyoto Publishing] The Bengali expression lyadh khawa (Bengali: ল্যাদ খাওয়া; literally, 'consuming laziness' [ref: Review: In Praise of Laziness and Other Essays by Indrajit Hazra, Hindustan Times]) is often used to denote the act of experiencing, indulging in, or enjoying a state of idleness and relaxation. [ref: A true-blue Bengali guide to spending a ‘productive’ weekend, [[The Telegraph (India)] [ref: Please Remove Your Shoes: A Judgmental Guide to Surviving the World and the 30 United States of India]

Lyadh is an example of an untranslatable word, due to the lexical gap that prevents it from having a perfect equivalent in other languages.

== Etymology ==
Unlike the majority of words in the Bengali language, the etymology of lyadh is uncertain. It does not find mention in traditional Bengali dictionaries, and does not appear to share any roots or cognates with Sanskrit, Persian, or Arabic. The word, used as a slang or expression in Bengali, is believed to have originated during the late 2000s–early 2010s; it is possibly a corruption or adaptation of the English words 'laidback' or 'lethargy', albeit this is speculative and remains unconfirmed. [ref: ‘ল্যাদ’ পুজো, Eisamay Online]

== Culture and use ==
In Bengali culture, lyadh is considered an emotion or a state of mind, and a certain fondness for 'laziness' has become embedded in Bengali society. [ref: Lyaad -- A universal feeling, [[The Telegraph (India)] Unlike somnolence and lethargy, which sometimes carry negative connotations and are often associated with depression, apathy and weakness, lyadh is more intentional and guilt-free, and is usually associated with joy, pleasure and recreation. It is often described as the "art of doing nothing". [ref: Kolkata to Kurseong: Of mist and lazy days, mint] Bengalis tend to link indolence and idleness with the motto, "simple living, high thinking"; according to some, this inclination, however, arguably has adversely affected Bengal's economic output and entrepreneurial ethos. [ref: Poor, Lazy and Loving It, Open Magazine]

Lyadh can indicate a plethora of situations, such as lying on one's sofa, leisurely reading a book, taking a siesta, listening to music, and gazing out one's window, among others. It is also associated with adda culture, an informal Bengali tradition involving long, casual and unstructured conversations as part of a hang-out. [ref: This Bengali ritual is a cure for loneliness, 360]

== In popular culture ==
In 2020, Lyaad, a musical short film based on the concept was released. It was directed by Pradipta Bhattacharyya and stars Ritwick Chakraborty. [ref: শীতকালটা ‘ল্যাদ’ খেয়েই কাটালেন ঋত্বিক, Anandabazar Patrika]

== Similar words ==

* The Italian expression dolce far niente (literally, 'the sweetness of doing nothing') is close in meaning to lyadh, and refers to the joy derived from being idle, slowing down, or relaxing.
* The Dutch word niksen (literally, 'nothinging' or 'doing nothing') refers to the art of doing nothing and being idle, and has been explored as a method to combat work-related health problems such as stress and burnout.

==References==

Rubber Duc is a South African alternative-pop and acoustic dance music band formed in Johannesburg in 2014. The group is known for its fusion of folk, swing, pop, and brass instrumentation, as well as its upbeat comedic and observational lyrics. [ref: Local band getting ducks all in a row, [[Independent Online (South Africa)]

The band rose to national prominence following their 2014 breakthrough single "Ain't Nobody Got Time for That". Their debut studio album, The Secret Sunrise (2016), received two nominations at the 23rd South African Music Awards (SAMA 23). [ref: 2017 SAMAs: all the nominees, TVSA (Television South Africa)]

== History ==

=== Formation and breakthrough (2014–2015) ===
Rubber Duc was formed in Johannesburg in early 2014 by lead vocalist and guitarist Nick Jordaan, lead guitarist Brendan Campbell, saxophonist Sheldon Sham, and bassist Amiel Gopal. The band chose their name intentionally to distinguish themselves in search engines by omitting the letter "k".

In March 2014, the group released their satirical debut single, "Ain't Nobody Got Time for That", inspired by the viral video catchphrase of Sweet Brown. The track gained heavy rotation across national commercial radio stations in South Africa. The band followed this release with singles such as "It's Alright" and "Stay With Me", pioneering a style they described as "acoustic dance music" (ADM).

=== The Secret Sunrise and industry recognition (2016–2018) ===
In September 2016, Rubber Duc released their debut full-length studio album, The Secret Sunrise, which spawned several radio singles including "Are We There Yet?" and "Feet".

At the 23rd South African Music Awards in 2017, the album received two industry nominations: Best Alternative Music Album and Best Produced Album. [ref: SAMA23 nominees announced, Bizcommunity] In 2018, their composition "Avery" earned an Honourable Mention in the Folk/Singer-Songwriter category at the International Songwriting Competition (ISC), selected from over 16,000 worldwide submissions.

In late 2018, the band released the pop single "Through the Night", which reached number one on the Jacaranda FM Top 20 chart.

=== Subsequent releases and Old Money (2019–present) ===
In November 2020, Rubber Duc released the bilingual collaboration single "Come Again" with South African pop group ADAM.

In 2025, the group partnered with Virgin Music Group South Africa to release the extended play Old Money. [ref: Rubber Duc thrill Lyric Lounge audience with familiar hits and new songs, [[The Citizen (South Africa)]

== Musical style and performances ==
Rubber Duc's style combines acoustic folk instrumentation, syncopated rhythm guitars, saxophone hooks, and four-part vocal harmonies, blending elements of pop, swing, and dance music.

The band has performed on the main stages of prominent southern African music festivals, including Splashy Fen, [ref: American Authors set to headline at Splashy Fen, [[Independent Online (South Africa)] Oppikoppi, Rocking the Daisies, Up the Creek, [ref: It's great to be Up the Creek, [[Independent Online (South Africa)] and the Vic Falls Carnival in Zimbabwe. They have also performed as the primary opening act for German rock group Milky Chance during their South African tour.

Napleton is a small rural hamlet on the southern side of Kempsey, about 3–4 miles south of Worcester. It is part of Kempsey and is in the WR5 postal district.

Historical records have it as "Appelton" in 1275 and 1327, which directly translates to apple settlement or orchard. [ref: Worcestershire place names]

Napleton Grange is a substantial period house on Napleton Lane which was once the home of Edward Elgar (composer) who lived in Kempsey from 1923–1927. Napleton Grange dates back to around 1440 and is a property on the ‘Elgar Route’ which takes people through notable places and houses linked to the composer. Edward Elgar was appointed Master of the King’s music in 1924, during his time in Napleton, and the Civic Fanfare was composed whilst he was living there. [ref: https://elgarroute.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/Elgar-Route-Leaflet-Web.pdf? ]

Napleton House is the main house of the hamlet and is believed to have been built on the site of a roman villa. It was once owned by the Marquess of Blandford. [ref: Unspoilt Georgian country house]

Napleton House also has a Site of Special Scientific Interest in the grounds [ref: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/693153fc5b5198836f304020/annex-b-restrictions-relating-to-licensed-actions-on-or-around-protected-sites-in-worcestershire-2025.pdf ] - Napleton Meadows.

Yang Jung-won (Korean: 양정원; born February 9, 2004), known mononymously as Jungwon, is a South Korean singer, dancer, and the leader of the K-pop boy band Enhypen. Appointed to the leadership role at age 16, he drew media attention for being one of the youngest group leaders in the music industry. [ref: Youngest leaders taking charge in K-pop industry, The Korea Herald]

== Early life and education ==
Jungwon practiced Taekwondo for seven years prior to his training in the entertainment industry. [ref: Jungwon Weverse Magazine Interview, Weverse Magazine] He attended Namgang High School before transferring to Hanlim Multi Art School, where he graduated from the Department of Practical Dance in February 2023. He trained under SM Entertainment and Big Hit Music before joining Belift Lab.

== Career ==
=== 2020–present: Debut with Enhypen ===
In June 2020, Jungwon was introduced as a contestant on the reality survival competition show I-Land, created by CJ ENM and Big Hit Entertainment. [ref: 'I-LAND' unveils full lineup of 23 trainees, Newsen] During the live finale on September 18, 2020, he placed first in the global viewer voting with 1,417,620 votes, securing his spot in the final lineup of the boy band Enhypen. [ref: 'Global fan-made band' Enhypen debuts with album 'Border: Day One', Korea JoongAng Daily]

Following a comprehensive 40-day selection process that included interviews with staff and members, Jungwon was officially announced as the leader of the group on November 13, 2020. [ref: Enhypen selects Jungwon as group leader, newsen] Appointed to the position at 16 years old, his selection drew significant media attention as it made him one of the youngest group leaders in modern K-pop history, leading a team where the majority of the members were older than him. [ref: Jungwon chosen as leader, The Korea Herald]

=== Other activities ===
==== Hosting ====
Beyond his group activities, Jungwon has taken on solo hosting responsibilities. He served as a regular radio host (MC) for the Educational Broadcasting System (EBS) program Listen, co-hosting the weekly broadcast alongside fellow group member Sunoo. [ref: ENHYPEN Jungwon and Sunoo selected as new DJs for EBS radio 'Listen', Ilsan Sports]

==== Ambassadorships ====
On April 17, 2026, the Seoul Metropolitan Government officially appointed Yang Jungwon as an honorary ambassador for the 2026 Seoul International Garden Show held at Seoul Forest. [ref: Enhypen's Jungwon named honorary ambassador for Seoul International Garden Show, Korea JoongAng Daily] [ref: Enhypen's Jungwon named ambassador for Seoul International Garden Show, The Korea Herald] His appointment was heavily publicized due to his name being a homonym for the Korean word for "garden" (jeongwon). In this civic role, he was tasked with promoting urban sustainability and green initiatives through promotional videos and public audio guides for visitors.

As a member of Enhypen, Jungwon has also participated in several major global group brand ambassadorships, including Italian luxury fashion house Prada, Dunkin' Philippines, and Samyang Foods' MEP ramyeon campaign.

==== Recording Academy membership ====
In July 2025, Jungwon was invited to join The Recording Academy as a voting member for its 2025 class, granting voting rights for the 68th Annual Grammy Awards. [ref: Recording Academy Welcomes New Member Class Of 2025, The Recording Academy] [ref: Hybe CEO Lee Jae-sang named professional member of The Recording Academy, The Korea Herald] [ref: 16 K-pop artists, producers under HYBE added to Grammy Awards voting members list, Korea JoongAng Daily] The Academy highlighted his artistic contributions as a singer, dancer, and leader of Enhypen, alongside his budding songwriting work on tracks such as "Highway 1009" and "Hundred Broken Hearts."

Draft text:
Halcyon Veil is an American independent record label founded in 2015 by Rabit and Lane Stewart. Originally based between Houston, Texas, and Los Angeles, the label was associated with a hybridized style of club music sometimes described as "post-club," releasing work by artists including IVVVO, MHYSA, Angel-Ho, and 700 Bliss. The label's output has since broadened to include indie rock, hip-hop, and pop, continuing a consistent focus on music resistant to genre classification. Resident Advisor described the label as having grown from an outpost for experimental club music into a freeform, community-oriented network [ref: Label of the month: Halcyon Veil, Resident Advisor], while Bandcamp Daily characterized it as a distributed entity that, while rooted in Houston, has "always looked outward, almost like a pirate radio station. [ref: Halcyon Veil's Decade of Mutant Club Hybrids, Bandcamp Daily]"

== History ==
Halcyon Veil was formed in 2015, after Stewart and Burton met on Twitter, Burton proposing starting a label within minutes of meeting in person. [ref: A Houston Chorus: Mother Rabit Dreams a Garden, Fact (UK magazine)] The label's debut release was Angel-Ho's EP Ascension the same year. [ref: ANGEL-HO's New Track Is About the Lack of Safe Space for Queer People of Color in Cape Town Clubs, Vice] Its early catalog was closely associated with the "deconstructed" or "post-club" scenes of the mid-2010s, situating the label alongside a wider network of artists including Chino Amobi and Elysia Crampton. [ref: The Rise of Conceptronica, Pitchfork] Rabit and Chino Amobi's The Great Game: Freedom from Mental Poisoning, released on the label in 2015, was later cited by critic Matthew Phillips as a defining work of what he termed "neofuturism," an aesthetic he traced through artists including Arca, Lotic, and Holly Herndon. By the end of the decade, the label's roster had expanded to include artists such as IVVVO, whose 2019 single "Forever Your Mouth" was played by Aphex Twin during his Coachella set that year. [ref: Setlist.fm - Aphex Twin Setlist, Setlist.fm]

Underground Fire is a Swedish rock band formed in Karlstad, Sweden, in 2015 by musician Robert Fjällsby, better known as Rob Coffinshaker. The band's music incorporates elements of gothic rock, punk rock, post-punk, power pop and classic rock. [ref: Underground Fire, Bandcamp]

The band has released two studio albums, Ashes of Life (2020) and Hollow Grounds (2026), as well as several singles and other releases.

==History==

Underground Fire was formed in Karlstad in 2015 by Robert Fjällsby, who performs under the name Rob Coffinshaker. Fjällsby is also known for his work with the bands The Coffinshakers and Gehennah.

The band's early releases appeared in 2017, including the 7-inch singles Underground Fire and I Wasn't Made For This World. The singles "Summer Ends" and "End of the Night" followed in 2018.

The band's debut studio album, Ashes of Life, was released in 2020 by Critical Mass Recordings. It was recorded at Studio Cobra in Stockholm, with Martin "Konie" Ehrencrona involved in the recording and production. [ref: Ashes of Life, Bandcamp]

A 12-inch release titled Passage, featuring the songs "Passage" and "Poison Heart", was released by Critical Mass Recordings in 2021. [ref: Passage, Bandcamp]

The band's second studio album, Hollow Grounds, was released on 17 April 2026 by Critical Mass Recordings. [ref: UNDERGROUND FIRE releases second album!, Critical Mass Recordings]

==Musical style==

Underground Fire's music has been described as goth rock, incorporating elements of punk, power pop, post-punk and classic rock. Reviews of the band's releases have drawn comparisons with The Sisters of Mercy, The Leather Nun, Fields of the Nephilim, Blue Öyster Cult and Johnny Cash. [ref: Review - UNDERGROUND FIRE - Ashes Of Life, Ox Fanzine] [ref: Arvio: Underground Firen ajattomasti menneisyydestä lipuva musiikki kietoo kuulijan syleilyynsä kuin usva, jolla on tietoisuus, Soundi]

==Media coverage==

Swedish journalist and author Fredrik Strage has written about Underground Fire in connection with the band's second studio album. In a 2026 column for EFN, Strage included Hollow Grounds among new album releases and described the band's music as goth rock. [ref: Berlin är fortfarande som en injektion mousserande neon, EFN]

On 30 July 2026, Rob Coffinshaker appeared as a guest on Strage's podcast Hemma hos Strage in an episode titled "Rob Coffinshaker om mördarballader". The episode discusses Coffinshaker's musical career and his work with Underground Fire. [ref: Rob Coffinshaker om mördarballader, Acast]

Ana Khunjua is a Georgian boxer who represents Belgium in international amateur boxing. She previously represented Georgia. In 2019, she became the first Georgian female boxer to win a medal at a European boxing championship after taking bronze at the European Under-22 Boxing Championships. [ref: პირველი ქართველი მოკრივე ქალი ევროპის ჩემპიონატის მედლით, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty]

== Early life ==
Khunjua grew up in the village of Sajijao in Khobi Municipality, Georgia. She began training in boxing at the age of 12. According to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, she trained in a small local gym and was the only female boxer training there at the time.

== Boxing career ==

=== Georgia ===
In March 2019, Khunjua represented Georgia at the European Under-22 Boxing Championships in Vladikavkaz, Russia. Competing in the women's 54 kg division, she defeated Belarusian boxer Aliaksandra Karpovich by a 5–0 decision in the quarter-final. [ref: EUBC U22 European Boxing Championships Vladikavkaz 2019, European Boxing Confederation] She finished the tournament with a bronze medal, becoming the first Georgian female boxer to win a medal at a European boxing championship.

=== Belgium ===
Khunjua later began representing Belgium in international competition. In April 2025, she competed in the women's 54 kg division at the Brussels Capital Tournament in La Hulpe, Belgium. She defeated France's Kaelya Mopin in the semi-final. [ref: Les Bleu(e)s au tournoi de Bruxelles, Fédération Française de Boxe] In the final, she defeated Italy's Michel Nicol Vescovini to win the tournament. [ref: Brussels Capital Tournament – Brussels, Belgium – April 25–27 2025]

In 2026, Khunjua represented Belgium at the Gee-Bee Tournament in Helsinki, Finland. She competed in the women's 57 kg division against American boxer Deborah Grant. [ref: Brackets Set for USA Boxing Elite High Performance Squad at 2026 Gee Bee Boxing Tournament, USA Boxing] European Boxing reported that Khunjua had previously represented Georgia before switching to Belgium and had won international tournament titles for Belgium. [ref: News, European Boxing]

== Selected achievements ==
* 2019 European Under-22 Boxing Championships — Bronze medal, 54 kg (Georgia)
* 2025 Brussels Capital Tournament — Gold medal, 54 kg (Belgium) [ref: Brussels Capital Tournament – Brussels, Belgium – April 25–27 2025]

Draft text:
Arshad Pappu (c. 1972 – 16 March 2013) was a Pakistani underworld figure and gang leader based in Lyari, Karachi. [ref: Lyari 'gangster' Arshad Pappu, brother killed, [[Dawn (newspaper)] He led an influential criminal syndicate during the Lyari gang war, clashing primarily with factions led by Rehman Dakait and Uzair Baloch. [ref: Tortured to death: Gangster Arshad Pappu's body found in Lyari, The Express Tribune]

== Early life and background ==
Arshad Pappu was the son of Haji Lal Mohammad (known as Haji Laloo), a prominent drug dealer in Lyari. His brother was Yasir Arafat. Through family marriages, Pappu was connected to rival gang leader Rehman Dakait, as Dakait and Pappu's brother Arafat were married to sisters. [ref: Special report: Lords of misrule, [[Dawn (newspaper)]

== Criminal activities and gang war ==
During the 1990s, Pappu and Rehman Dakait operated together in Lyari before having a violent falling out over ransom money from an abduction. Following the split, Pappu established an independent syndicate.

A major turning point in the Lyari gang war occurred when Pappu was implicated in the kidnapping and murder of Faiz Mohammad (known as "Mama Faizu"), a local transporter and father of Uzair Baloch. After his father's death, Uzair Baloch allied with Rehman Dakait to launch a protracted feud against Pappu's faction.

Pappu was booked by police in over 50 criminal cases involving homicide, extortion, and narcotics. [ref: Uzair Baloch indicted in Arshad Pappu murder case, [[Dawn (newspaper)] He was imprisoned for five years in Karachi and the Gadani prison in Balochistan. Due to a lack of testifying witnesses, he was acquitted in all cases—including the murder of Faiz Mohammad—and released in early 2012. Following his release, he operated between Karachi and border areas of Balochistan.

== Death ==
On the night of 16 March 2013, Pappu, his brother Yasir Arafat, and an associate named Juma Shera (alias Shera Pathan) visited a flat in the Defence Housing Authority (DHA), where they were abducted by armed men. [ref: Key figure in Arshad Pappu's murder killed, The Express Tribune]

They were transported to Lyari, where all three were tortured and killed. [ref: Arshad Pappu murder: Police ordered to seize Uzair Baloch's properties within 10 days, The Express Tribune] Following orders from the Supreme Court of Pakistan, police registered a triple-murder case that indicted Uzair Baloch, Noor Muhammad (alias Baba Ladla), and several police personnel.

== In popular culture ==

* In Aditya Dhar's 2025 Hindi spy thriller film Dhurandhar, Arshad Pappu was portrayed by actor Ashwin Dhar. [ref: Ashwin Dhar on Arshad Pappu's viral 'football' scene in Dhurandhar, India TV]

Wuhan Airlines Flight 4211 was a domestic charter flight from Lanzhou, China to Xi’an, China. On 8 October 1992, the aircraft operating the flight crashed into a mountain range after suffering an engine failure on takeoff, killing 14 of the 35 people on board. [ref: Accident Avia 14 (Ilyushin Il-14) B-4211, Thursday 8 October 1992, aviation-safety.net] [ref: ]

Follow the crash, the Civil Aviation Administration of China had grounded the operation of all Ilyushin Il-14 aircraft. [ref: 难忘的历程——中国伊尔14飞机停飞15年纪念, ccaonline.cn]

== Aircraft ==
The aircraft involved was an Avia 14 manufactured in 1958 and registered as B-4211. At the time of the accident, the plane was considered to be unsuitable for standard conditions. [ref: 机组努力挽救至最后一刻，忆武汉航空旅游包机1992.10.8定西空难_腾讯新闻, new.qq.com]

There were 7 crew members: captain, first officer, navigator, radio operator, flight engineer, and two flight attendants. 28 passengers were on board, 14 of them were from Taiwanese "Silk Road Tour" group (11 Taiwanese and 3 Chinese), and 14 French passengers. [ref: 1992年10月8日 武航一旅游包机在甘肃坠毁-搜狐新闻, news.sohu.com]

== Accident ==
At 15:03, 45 minutes into the flight, the plane reached an altitude of 3,000 meters (9,840 feet). The left engine then lost power and failed for half a minute and its right engine didn't work properly. The crew requested for an emergency landing at Yuzhong Xiaguanying Airport. The plane only maintained its original altitude for 20 minutes before losing speed and descending. As the mountainside appeared, the crew determined that they would crash-landed into the hill. The left wing struck the ground first, ruptured the left landing gear and disintergrated with fire following the impact. Five crew member and nine French passengers died.According from a witness:It was around 3:30 PM. I was at my front door when suddenly a plane flew overhead from east to west. It flew very low and made a loud noise, but the sound was a little different from usual. At the time, I thought it was doing some kind of surveying, and that's why it was so loud at such a low altitude. Just as it passed, I heard a loud "bang" and then it disappeared. I figured it had just passed over a mountain and the noise had stopped abruptly, so I didn't pay much attention and went straight home. As soon as I entered the house, I heard someone crying from the mountaintop. I immediately ran out. It turned out to be a woman from our village named Wang Lan who was herding sheep. She had seen the plane crash and was crying out, "A plane has crashed! Go up and see!" My father heard it too and was shouting. As soon as I heard that, I immediately ran up the mountain. By then, all our neighbors had heard it and came running, and we all ran up the mountain together. [ref: 27年前遭遇空难，是定西的乡亲们救了这些台胞的命——中国·定西网, www.cndingxi.com]

== Investigation ==
The investigation concluded that the left-engine shutdown was caused by a punctured insulation layer of the engine generator. It damaged the ignition nozzle that lead to the failure. The plane was found to had been neglected for a long time due to lack of maintenance, and was in poor condition.

Draft text:
Frederick Louis Pache (9 May 1871 - 19 March 1910) was an Ocularist and heir of the prominent and award winning family firm Pache & Son [ref: The Ophthalmic Review, [Volume XII, Page 4], November 1893], which provided major UK hospitals with artificial glass eyes as well as the perfected Snellen "Reformed Eye". [ref: https://eyemuseum.ranzco.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/History_V4_2.pdf ] [ref: {{Cite web|url=https://www.college-optometrists.org/professional-development/college-journals/acuity/all-issues/summer-2025/an-art-and-a-science] [ref: A short history of the artificial eye by H.E Henkes & G K Van Leersum]

==Early Life==
Frederick was born in Birmingham in 1871, and the son of pioneering Ocularist Thomas Pache, during the city's booming industrial era. He was of Swiss-Huguenot ancestry, descending from an old historic bourgeoisie family of Morges in the Canton of Vaud, Switzerland. The family having ancestral records dating back centuries involving local artisans, merchants, and businessmen. [ref: {{Cite web|url=https://www.pastellists.com/Articles/Pache.pdf}] [ref: https://www.pastellists.com/Genealogies/Pache.pdf ]

His Grandfather Charles Lewis Pache, patriarch of the family, was the first to start the family business of Glassblowing during the late 1840's, specialising in artificial glass eyes, as well as Syringes, test tubes, foreign bird skins and insects. [ref: https://uncletomstales.com/a-virtual-tour-of-the-back-to-backs/a-virtual-tour-of-the-back-to-backs-part-25/] [ref: Slater's Business Directory for Birmingham 1852] He was also related to Charles Henry-Pache, his great-great Uncle, who was a famous Pastellist and supplier to the Royal Society of Arts.

As heir to the company Pache & Son, Frederick started working for the family firm when he was around 18 years old, learning the complex craftsmanship and skills involved in manufacturing and creating artificial glass eyes. [ref: The National Archives of the UK (TNA); Kew, Surrey, England; Census Returns of England and Wales, 1891; Class: RG12; Piece: 2408; Folio: 57; Page: 19; GSU roll: 6097518] [ref: The London Medical Record; Volume XII; Smith Elder & Co.; 15 Waterloo Place; 1884]

During the 1890's the family business had consolidated it's position as one of the countries leading artificial glass eye makers, and by 1900 had a complete monopoly in providing them to all major hospitals in the UK. This was mainly thanks to the quality manufacturing of their eyes and artistic details, as well as his father Thomas perfecting Snellen's "Reformed Eye" using English Glass, which at the time was considered extremely hard to achieve. [ref: Prosthetic Body Parts in Literature and Culture, 1832 to 1908 - Ryan Craig Sweet to the University of Exeter as a thesis for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in English] [ref: http://ndl.ethernet.edu.et/bitstream/123456789/12586/1/H.E.%20Henkes%20%282%29.pdf - History of Ophthalmology by H.E Henkes (Page 353)]

By this time, the firm had upwards of 4,000 eyes in stock and ready to be delivered to any of their principal hospitals. They created glass eyes in various colours, sizes, and even morbid conditions. Due to their exquisite design and detail, they even supplied models to universities so that the various examples of diseases and conditions of the eye could be examined by the students. [ref: The American Journal of Photography 1892 titled "ARTIFICIAL HUMAN EYES"] [ref: Showell's Dictionary of Birmingham, by Walter Showell.]

==Death==
It was between 1908 to 1910 that Frederick contracted Pulmonary Tuberculosis, commonly known as Phthisis during this era. This was probably the result of living and working in the densely populated urban areas of Birmingham, where this disease spread rapidly. [ref: Birmingham, England, All Saints Hospital Records, 1845-1931]

This lead to his rapid decline in mental and physical health during the next two years, being susceptible to bouts of delusion and aggression as his condition worsened, unfortunately resulting in a break-down of his marriage to Edith. [ref: Library of Birmingham, Birmingham City Council; Birmingham, England, UK; Court records: Quarter and Petty sessions; Reference: PS B/1/1/4/9]

It was in early 1910 that he had become profoundly emancipated, bedridden, and suffering from delusional insanity as a result of late-stage tuberculosis. It was because of this he was administered to the All Saints Hospital (Winson Green Asylum) on the 10th March 1910. However, he only survived for a further 9 days and passed away on the 19th March, aged only 38 years old. [ref: Library of Birmingham; Birmingham, England, UK; All Saints Hospital Records, 1845-1920; Reference Number: HC AS/10/1; Finding Number: MS 344/10/1]

Once Frederick had passed away, Thomas disinherited Frederick's family from the company fortune, because of him disapproving of his marriage to a "commoner", leaving Edith widowed with 6 children. However, Frederick's children eventually all received a sizable inheritance from their Aunt Ella Pache, who had taken over the company for a time after Thomas' death in 1918 until it ceased to exist sometime in the 1940's. [ref: Probate Record; 10 May 1919; Birmingham; and, hardcopy photocopy of Thomas Pache will.] [ref: Probate Record; Birmingham; 24 May 1930; to Ella Beatrice Grimson, widow; Effects £528 2s 8d.]

Ecce Homo or Behold The Man is a religous painting by 17th century Flemish painter Anthony Van Dyck. This painting depicts Christ being presented to the people before his crucifixion with ropes binding his hands together while wearing the crown of thorns and his waist covered in white and black cloth while a solider stands behind him holding a black cloth in both hands.

== Provenance ==
The painting may have been commisioned by the Baldi Family in 1625 and was first recorded in the collection of Francesco Maria Balbi in 1701. In 1805, it was aqquired by the painter and art dealer Andrew Wilson In 1807, it was sold at Coxe, London as lot 32 [ref: The catalogue of that most valuable and important selection of original paintings, the property of Andrew Wilson: purchased by him and brought to England from palaces of the first consequence at Genoa: embracing the finest works of those great masters, Claude le Loraine, Annibal Caracci, Agostino Caracci, Ludovico Caracci, Guido Rheni, Titian Vicelli, &c., Rubens, Tintoretto, Van Dyck, Perino del Vaga, Guercino, &c., Mazzolino di Ferrara, Jacomo Puntormo, Andrea Mantegna, Vadder, Dionysius Calvert, &c., [London]: Catalogues may be had of Mr. Peter Coxe and at the place of sale] and again in 1810 as lot 10. In 1825, the painting was sold by a man known as Mr. Berry to Sir Alexander Hope and was passed down through the Earls of Hopetoun (later the Marquesses of Linlithgow). It was finally sold at Christie's in 1954 to the Barber Institute of Fine Arts [ref: Anthony van Dyck (1599–1641), The Barber Institute of Fine Arts].

Ringgold Telephone Company (doing business as RTC) is an independent local exchange carrier and Internet service provider based in Ringgold, Georgia. Founded in 1912, the company provides fiber-optic broadband, telephone service, and managed IT services to residential and commercial customers in Catoosa County and adjacent areas in Northwest Georgia.

== History ==
The company was established in 1912 by Jim Evitt Sr., a Catoosa County pharmacist, with eight initial telephone lines. [ref: Ringgold Telephone marks century of service, Chattanooga Times Free Press] Following his death, his son, Jim Evitt Jr., assumed control of the utility. In 1950, RTC transitioned from manual switchboards to an automated dial exchange, serving approximately 250 subscriber lines. [ref: Annual Report of the Georgia Public Service Commission, State of Georgia]

Following the death of Jim Evitt Jr. in 1973, his daughter, Alice Evitt Bandy, became president of the company. [ref: Local family keeps Ringgold connected for three generations, The Catoosa County News]

During the late 1990s, the company expanded from basic analog telephone service into data transmission. In 2000, RTC completed a regional infrastructure upgrade making DSL broadband available across its 122-square-mile (320 km) exchange footprint. [ref: Rural Telcos Bridge the Digital Divide, Telephony Online] In 2003, RTC expanded into IPTV and digital television distribution over copper and hybrid infrastructure. [ref: RTC selects Amino for IP set-tops, Light Reading]

In June 2004, the company relocated operations from downtown Ringgold to an expanded operations facility on Evitt Parkway. In April 2025, RTC moved its corporate headquarters back to downtown Ringgold, acquiring and renovating the former Chrysler dealership building on Nashville Street. [ref: Ringgold Telephone Company returns to historic downtown hub, Chattanooga Times Free Press]

== Network and services ==
RTC operates an optical fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) network covering over 55 percent of Catoosa County. [ref: Broadband Deployment Data: Catoosa County, GA, Federal Communications Commission] Its network provides symmetric gigabit broadband, voice-over-IP (VoIP), hosted private branch exchange (PBX), and enterprise data links with service-level agreements.

The company also provides network hardware installation, commercial security integration, and structured cabling for regional businesses and public institutions in the greater Chattanooga metropolitan area.

Draft text:
Indoor skydancing is the performing art of choreographed bodyflight to music within a vertical wind tunnel, as well as a specific musical format within the sport of indoor skydiving. [ref: Indoor Skydancing: The Big Bang!, SkydiveMag] Rather than existing as a standalone sport with its own governing body, skydancing refers specifically to the artistic free routines where solo or group athletes—such as those in freestyle or dynamic disciplines—synchronize their aerial maneuvers to musical accompaniment. [ref: Indoor Solo Freestyle Competition Rules - 2025 Edition, Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI)] The term was coined by Mexican-Canadian competitor Lise Hernandez Girouard as a tribute to outdoor freestyle pioneer Deanna Kent, who was widely known as "Skydancer". [ref: Deana Kent "Skydancer", International Skydiving Museum Hall of Fame]

== History ==
=== Acoustic challenges and hardware integration ===
Before the integration of music, competitive indoor freestyle vertical wind tunnel (historically referred to as "Neo-Freestyle") was evaluated strictly on technical body positions, speed, and acrobatic maneuvers. [ref: Neo-freestyle competition at iFLY Hollywood, Extreme66] A primary barrier to incorporating music was the acoustic environment of vertical wind tunnels, which generate background noise exceeding 100 decibels at airspeeds over 200 km/h. [ref: Catching up with Lise Hernandez, SkydiveMag] Standard audio playback was inaudible to athletes, and extended exposure to such noise requires hearing protection.

To solve this, Hernandez Girouard developed a technical setup utilizing custom-moulded ear seals with integrated monitors, earmuffs, and a modified flight helmet. She also implemented a wireless multi-channel distribution system that transmitted the audio directly to the athlete's in-ear monitors, the on-site spectators, and the live broadcast feed simultaneously. The equipment was first successfully tested at the Aerokart wind tunnel in France in 2013. [ref: Lise Hernandez pionnière pour faire des figures au rythme d'une musique, Actu.fr]

=== Early performances and FAI rule updates (2014–2015) ===
The first public performance of indoor freestyle synchronized with live music occurred on March 23, 2014, during the 2nd Canadian Indoor Skydiving Championships at SkyVenture Montreal, where Hernandez Girouard competed in the Freestyle category. [ref: Music is in the Air, CanPara Magazine] In November 2014, she demonstrated the musical format internationally at the 1st Fédération Aéronautique Internationale (FAI) World Cup of Indoor Skydiving in Austin, Texas, acting as the only competitor using musical accompaniment. [ref: 1st World Cup in Indoor Skydiving - Day 2, FAI]

Prompted by these proof-of-concept performances, the FAI officially updated its global competitive regulations to permit music as an optional element in freestyle routines. However, at the inaugural FAI World Indoor Skydiving Championships held in Prague the following year in 2015, the option remained unused, and no freestyle competitors performed their routines to music.

=== The 2016 Wind Games ===
The integration of music gained significant global traction at the third edition of the Wind Games in January 2016 in Empuriabrava, Spain. Anne Maxwell, creator of the Wind Games, invited Hernandez Girouard to organize the event's first freestyle competition and mandated that it include a compulsory musical interpretation round.

Hernandez Girouard authored the new scoring criteria and served as Head Judge. The format required athletes to perform three rounds: low-speed flow, high-speed flight, and a mandatory musical interpretation round. To score the musical round fairly across both technical flight mechanics and choreographic expression, the judging panel was hybridized to include technical freeflyer Adam Mattacola, professional dance choreographer Dolo Yglesias, and Hernandez Girouard.

The 2016 musical routines achieved unprecedented viral publicity for the sport. Russian athlete Leonid Volkov won first place with a highly theatrical routine, while Polish athlete Maja Kuczyńska won second place. [ref: Wind Games winner will blow you away with astounding aerial dance moves, Today] [ref: Watch: Athlete dances in a wind tunnel, defies gravity, NBC News]. Volkov's routine went immediately viral, grabbing the media's attention. [ref: Watch: Athlete dances in a wind tunnel, defies gravity] A video of Kuczyńska's performance set to the song "Chandelier" amassed over 100 million views on social media, directly leading to her becoming the first indoor skydiving athlete sponsored by Red Bull, which subsequently became the primary title sponsor for the Wind Games. [ref: Maja Kuczyńska - Red Bull Athlete Profile, Red Bull] [ref: The Return of the Wind Games!, SkydiveMag]

== Formats and disciplines ==
Following the popularization of the musical round, indoor skydancing developed into two distinct branches: standardized competitive disciplines and theatrical performing arts exhibitions.

It is the fourth James Bond-themed pinball machine, following Gottlieb's James Bond 007 in 1980, Sega Pinball's Goldeneye in 1996, and another Stern Pinball James Bond 007 machine released in 2022.

Not be confused with James Bond 007 pinball machine designed by George Gomez and released by Stern Pinball in 2022, James Bond 007 60th anniversary Limited Edition is a completely different design and layout. The game is a single-level game with no ramps and only two flippers which differs from other Elwin designs. [ref: https://www.kineticist.com/news/stern-pinball-announces-james-bond-007-60th-anniversary-pinball] [ref: James Bond 007 (60th LE) Pinball Machine (Stern, 2023) | Pinside Game Archive, pinside.com] [ref: James Bond 60th Anniversary pinball machine | Stern Pinball | Preview] [ref: Stern Pinball reveals James Bond 007 - Pinball Magazine Stern Pinball reveals James Bond 007] [ref: Stern Pinball Announces New James Bond 007 Pinball Machines]

Production was limited to 500 units and features a custom-themed mirrored backglass, shaker motor, exclusive Union Jack shooter knob, 007-themed topper, numbered plaque, and a Certificate of Authenticity signed by Gary Stern, founder of Stern Pinball. The artwork is based on the first 25 James Bond films. [ref: Stern Pinball Celebrates 60 Years of James Bond with Limited-Edition Pinball Machine, License Global]

The game was advertised more as a collector's item than the 2022 George Gomez designed game, and encompassed all 25 Eon-produced James Bond films. There are six Villain modes connected to a kinetic spinning disc on the playfield shaped like Oddjob’s hat. [ref: JAMES BOND 60TH ANNIVERSARY, Pinball News] Once you complete all six villain modes, you activate Villain Multiball. In addition, you can collect gadgets and enable other multiballs by completing drop targets. [ref: 007 60th Anniversary Rulesheet, Pinball Rule Sheets]

Hassan Rilwan is a Nigerian public administrator who served as the Executive Secretary of the Kaduna State Scholarship and Loans Board from 2019 to 2022 under Governor Nasir Ahmad el-Rufai. [ref: El-Rufai appoints Hassan Rilwan as ES Kaduna Scholarship Board, Blueprint Newspaper] [ref: Kaduna spends N800m on 42 students to study overseas, Vanguard Newspaper] He subsequently served as Special Adviser to the Governor.

== Early life and career ==
Rilwan is an Associate Fellow of the Nigerian Leadership Institute and an alumnus of the Young African Leaders Initiative (YALI) fellowship. [ref: Hassan Rilwan Profile, The Future Awards Africa] In 2009, he served on the Federal Government Ministerial Committee on the establishment of the Almajiri Education System, which was established to integrate traditional Islamic education with modern school curricula across Northern Nigeria.

== Public service ==
In September 2019, Governor Nasir Ahmad el-Rufai appointed Rilwan as Executive Secretary of the Kaduna State Scholarship and Loans Board.

During his tenure, the board managed state-sponsored merit-based international scholarships for foreign postgraduate studies and implemented policy adjustments to protect educational funding during the COVID-19 pandemic. [ref: Kaduna says COVID-19 won't affect scholarships, loans, Punch Newspapers] In August 2021, under his leadership, the board coordinated the emergency security evacuation of tertiary institution students of Kaduna origin from Jos, Plateau State during inter-communal unrest. [ref: Jos crisis: Kaduna evacuates students from Plateau, Vanguard Newspaper]

Following his term at the scholarship board, Rilwan was appointed Special Adviser within the Kaduna State Government.

Itavia Flight 115 was a scheduled passenger flight from Rome to Genoa, Italy. On 14 October 1960, the aircraft operating the flight crashed into the slopes of Mount Capanne near the town of Elba at 728 meters (2,388 feet), killing all 7 passengers and 4 crew members. [ref: Accident de Havilland DH-114 Heron 2 I-AOMU, Friday 14 October 1960, aviation-safety.net]

== Aircraft and crew ==
The aircraft involved was an Itavia de Havilland DH-114 Heron 2, registration I-AOMU (serial no. 14090), manufactured in 1955. [ref: ] [ref: Il disastro aereo del 1960, Mucchio Selvaggio] The flight crew consisted of captain Ennio Scipione, aged 30, first officer Francesco Cossu, aged 44, and two flight attendants, Giovanna Pertusio, aged 25, and Grazia Candeloro, aged 20.

== Accident ==
The flight took off from Rome Urbe Airport at 15:02 pm local time. At 15:19, the crew contacted the tower in Genoa, stating that they were currently flying over the city of Civitavecchia. The controller, seeing the poor weather conditions along the flight's path, offered to divert them to either Turin or Nice. There was no response to this message from the crew. Moments later, the aircraft struck the slopes of Mount Capanne at 2,388 feet, exploding and breaking up on impact and killing all 11 occupants onboard. [ref: La Stampa (1960-10-15), Editrice La Stampa S.p.A.]
== Investigation ==
The investigation found that the crew was flying according to visual flight rules instead of instrument flight rules, which was required given the poor visibility on the flight's route. Why the crew chose to fly in VFR instead of IMC is unknown.

== Lawsuit ==
A court case followed the accident, with penal charges brought forward against the flight company, and responsible personnel of Civilavia and the Urbe airport. Among them were General Romolo Abbriata (director of the civil aviation authority), Luigi Petragnani (manager of Itavia), Renato Panini (technical organizer of Itavia) and Riccardo Rubbiano-Pivawere. However, they were acquitted of all charges in both instances (1965/66). [ref: La Stampa (1966-02-11), Editrice La Stampa S.p.A.]

== Memorial ==
=== 1960 ===
At the scene of the accident, a small white marble tombstone was built and placed against a rock formation, engraved with the star of David in memory of Silvio Sciunnach, a Jewish passenger who was onboard the flight and a victim of the accident.

=== 2013 ===
On October 13, 2013, on the evening preceding the 53rd anniversary of the accident, a monument was built on the accident site. [ref: Un Monumento sul Capanne in memoria del disastro aereo di 53 anni fa, www.elbareport.it]

Mohamed Sliten (25 January 1945 – 31 August 2026), also referred to in contemporary sources as Mohamed Slitane, was a Moroccan professional association football player who played as a winger.

During the 1960s, Sliten played in Europe for Belgian club Standard de Liège and Swiss club BSC Young Boys. [ref: Football: Décès de Mohamed Sliten, le roi du dribble, Maroc Hebdo] He later returned to Morocco to play for Union Sportive de Sidi Kacem in the Botola, where the club finished as league runners-up in 1970, and represented the Morocco national football team. [ref: Décès de l'ancien international Mohamed Sliten, "Le Roi du Dribble", L'Économiste] [ref: Morocco 1969/70, Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation]

== Early life ==
Sliten was born on 25 January 1945 in Marrakech. He developed as a youth player with local club Mouloudia Club de Marrakech in the Riad Zitoun quarter before moving abroad in 1963.

== Club career ==
=== Europe (1963–1968) ===
In 1963, Sliten moved to Europe and joined Belgian club Standard de Liège. In 1964, he transferred to Swiss Nationalliga A side BSC Young Boys. With Young Boys, he finished as runner-up in the 1964–65 Nationalliga A championship behind Lausanne-Sports. [ref: Switzerland 1964/65, Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation] During his tenure in Switzerland, he was nicknamed « Le Roi du Dribble » by the regional sports press in reference to his dribbling ability. [ref: أحد رواد الاحتراف المغربي في أوروبا "محمد سليتن" في ذمة الله, MFM Sport]

In the mid-1960s, during an international friendly fixture playing for Young Boys against English club Manchester United, Sliten scored three goals in a single match. [ref: Décès de l'ancien international Mohamed Sliten, Le Site Info]

=== Return to Morocco (1969–1978) ===
Sliten returned to the Moroccan domestic championship in 1969, signing with Union Sportive de Sidi Kacem (USK). During the 1969–70 Botola season, USK finished second in the Moroccan first division with 64 points (10 wins, 14 draws, 6 defeats), two points behind champions FAR Rabat, marking the highest league placement in the club's history. Sliten also competed with USK in the Coupe du Trône, reaching the semi-finals in 1971 and 1972. [ref: Morocco - List of Cup Finals, Rec.Sport.Soccer Statistics Foundation]

== International career ==
Sliten represented the Morocco national football team during the late 1960s and early 1970s. He took part in qualification matches for the 1970 FIFA World Cup, but was excluded from the final tournament squad in Mexico due to a knee injury sustained during domestic competition.

== Death ==
Sliten died in Marrakech on 31 August 2026, at the age of 81. His death was officially confirmed by the Fondation Mohammed VI des Champions Sportifs.
