Native Officer Ali D.C.M, ADC, was a native officer originally from Katsina in His Majesty King Edward the Seventh's Hausas [ref: ARIBA ALI V. ALHAJI MAMA ALI, judy.legal] who served in the British colonial forces in West Africa and the recognized Head of the Hausa community (Sarkin Hausawa) the year 1907 in the British colony, Gold Coast. [ref: The Power of Space in the Evolution of an Accra Zongo, Ethnohistory] [ref: Native Tribunals of the Akras (Continued from p. 330), Journal of the Royal African Society] [ref: The Muslim Association Party: A Test of Religious Politics in Ghana, Transactions of the Historical Society of Ghana]

== Early life and military career ==
Native Officer Ali enlisted in a military unit established by governor Sir John Hawley, known as "Glover Hausas or the "Hausa Force" in the year 1863 during a period of British expansion in West Africa and he subsequently served in several British military expeditions in West Africa. [ref: The Slaves of Salaga, The Journal of African History] He served as a Sargeant Major commanding troops at Prasu during the third Anglo-Ashanti War of 1873-1874. He and other officer were sent to the United Kingdom for further training in 1875-1876.

Ali later took part in several military campaigns and expeditions including one where he and 60 Hausa troops landed on an Island and searched it from end to end [ref: A History of the Gold Coast and Ashanti from the Earliest Times to the Commencement of the Twentieth Century, John Murray] He received a medal for his service during the Awuna expedition of 1885 and Denkyira expedition in 1890. [ref: Danborno, shardowfamilyweb] He served as an aide-de-camp to Gold Coast governors including Sir Matthew Nathan, Sir John Pickersgill Rodger and Frederick Mitchell Hodgson. He continued his military career into the early twentieth century, serving with the 2nd Gold Coast Regiment before retiring.

== Retirement and leadership ==
After Native Officer Ali retired from the service of Government in June 1902, and he was receiving a pension of £48 per anum. [ref: The Muslim Community in Accra (An Historical Survey), University of Ghana] Ali settled in Accra Ussher Town, Horse Road where he built his Zongo quarters, this location was where the current Accra General Post Office sits. [ref: A History of Accra's "Zongos": Heterogeneity and Social Change, Indiana University]

In 1907, the Hausa Community led by High Priest Mama Fulata Bornu, who was then the Chief Imam, together with Mallam Abubakare (Priest), Mallam DanJimba (Priest), Native Officer Harri Zanuah of (The Gold Coast Regiment) and Mallam Bukare (Priest) petitioned through the Colonial Government to officially recognize Native Officer Ali as Head Chief of the Hausa Community (Sarkin Hausawa), they wrote,

"As Hausas we have so far been under a great disadvantage in having no head chief, and whenever it has been necessary to wait upon the Government, it has always been difficult to obtain a spokesman.

"We are writing solely on behalf of the Hausas residing here. We have nothing to do with the Yorubas or other tribes who have their own head-chiefs."

On October 26, the Hausa community's request was approved by Governor John Pickersgill Rodger through Sir William Charles Fleming Robertson secretary for native affairs. [ref: Letter from the Acting Secretary for Native Affairs to Mama Fulata Bornu, Mallam Abubakare, Malam DanJimba, Native Officer Harri Zenuah, and Malam Bukare, Public Records and Archives Administration Department (PRAAD)] Native Officer Ali held the position until his death on 2nd day of February 1908. [ref: Migrant Chiefs in Stranger Communities in Ghana: The Challenge of their Inclusion into the Houses of Chiefs, Contemporary Journal of African Studies]

== Death and legacy ==
Native Officer Ali died on February 2, 1908. [ref: Gold Coast Leader] Remained Native Officer in the Gold Coast Regiment of the West African Frontier Force (also known as Native Officer in Chief of the Gold Coast Hausas) and Head Chief (or headman) of the Hausa community in Accra until his death.

He is regarded as one of the three principal early migrant leaders in the Gold Coast, alongside Mallam Naino (Nenu) and Alhaji Brimah

After his death, his name and ceremonial titles lived on in the person of his son by a Fanti woman from Elmina, Alhaji Mohammed Ali.

Draft text:
TAM Airlines Flight 540 was a domestic flight in Brazil from São Paulo to Bauru. On 12 February 1990, the Fokker F27 Friendship crashed while go-around after a failed attempt to land at Bauru Airport, killing the instructor and two individuals on ground. [ref: Accident Fokker F-27 Friendship 200 PT-LCG, Monday 12 February 1990, aviation-safety.net] [ref: ] [ref: Matéria para o Jornal Nacional sobre a queda do avião Fokker da TAM em Bauru, G1] [ref: JCNET: Queda matou 2 em 1990, sampi]

This plane crash was considered to be the most serious air accident in the Bauru region.

== Background ==

=== Aircraft ===
The aircraft involved was a Fokker F27 Friendship, manufactured in 1962. [ref: RELATÓRIO FINAL, CENIPA]

=== Crew member ===
On board was the instructor named Paulo Sérgio Espósito, who have acquired 5,706 flight hours with 3,578 of them were in the F27. He was the only fatality on the plane. [ref: Folha de S.Paulo - TAM diz que família não aceitou valor - 7/11/1996, www1.folha.uol.com.br]

The pilot flying was Minoru Kawakubo, who have acquried 10,010 flight hours with 1,286 of them were in the F27. He was under training during the flight. After the crash, he was fired and became a flight instructor for Pantanal Linhas Aéreas.

== Accident ==
At around 9:40 AM, at an altitude of 4000 feet, the crew decided to make a direct approach instead of the IFR plan. The plane was found to be too high for a proper descent but the instructor decided to continue the approach by pushing back the throttles and pushing the nose down steeply to bring back to the flight level. The plane touch down 775 meters from the threshold, nose gear first. The plane bounced and touched again 959 meters from the threshold. They realized they won't be able to stop the plane in time, so they initiated a go-around. However, the aircraft then stalled, fell down rapidly and crashed into obstacles. [ref: Queda de avião da TAM que matou mãe e filho em carro e marcou a aviação em Bauru completa 35 anos; relembre o caso, G1]

The plane struck a vehicle carrying Gisele Marie Savi Pinto and her son, Guilherme - all died at the scene. The captain initially survived, but was unconcious, trapped at the scene and died 27 days later due to smoke intoxication. Apart from the mother and child, other residents were not injured or affected. 25 passengers escaped unharmed, 11 passengers were injured. The co-pilot and flight attendant were also injured.

== Investigation ==
The investigation was conducted by CENIPA. On November 14, 1990, the final report was finalized. The reason for the stall during the go-around was found to be an abrupt throttle acceleration done by the instructor. This cause the engine combustion to gain too much fuel, insufficient air was received to ignite the kerosene-oxygen mixture and the temperature rose to a critical level, which hampered the propellor to produce energy for the lift. The flap was still retracted during the touchdown and go-around, lowering down the critical angle of attack. Those factors combined led to the aircraft's stalling condition.

== Lawsuit ==
Relatives of the victims demand compensation from the airline at Superior Court of Justice. The airline initially was ordered but then able to appeal as the crash was not the airlines' fault. Howevery, it was later denied after the court recognized the need for reimbursement of personal belongings damaged or lost in the accident. The company also need to cover funeral expenses not covered by social security institutions. In total, the airline had to pay 500 minimum wage per victims. [ref: G1 > Edição São Paulo - NOTÍCIAS - STJ mantém condenação a TAM por morte de mãe e filho atingidos por avião, g1.globo.com] [ref: TAM deve indenizar família por acidente em tentativa frustrada de pouso, Consultor Jurídico]

The airline also had to compensate R$116,000 for a passenger named Carlos Salles as he suffered from spinal injuries in the accident leading to a 20% loss of his work capacity. [ref: TAM é condenada a indenização por avião que bateu em carro, Exame]

== References ==

Solace Health is a healthtech platform that matches patients with healthcare advocates who help them navigate the U.S. healthcare system. Established in 2022, the privately held company is based in Redwood City, California.
== History ==
Jeremy Gurewitz and Sara Sargent co-founded Solace Health in 2022 after Gurewitz watched his mother struggle to navigate the healthcare system while she battled pancreatic cancer. His mother had difficulty even though she was a radiologist with an understanding of the medical system [ref: Solace Health expands care navigation services to commercially insured patients, Fierce Healthcare] who led a women's imaging center in Long Island, New York. [ref: Medicare Coverage Fuels Solace’s $60 Million Series B, Wall Street Journal]

Patients initially paid for Solace services out-of-pocket. This changed in 2024 when Medicare started covering patient advocacy services for chronic and complicated health conditions. [ref: VCs Give Solace Health $1 Billion Valuation for Patient Advocacy Tech, Bloomberg] Gurewitz told the Wall Street Journal that investor interest increased once patient advocacy was covered by Medicare. In April 2025, Solace announced a $60 million Series B, which was twice the amount they intended to raise. In February 2026, Business Insider reported that the need for help navigating the U.S. medical system had propelled the company to a $1 billion valuation.

In 2026, Solace announced additional insurance coverage from major health plans, including United Healthcare and Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield. Fierce Healthcare quoted Gurewitz that this expanded coverage extended the opportunity for patient advocacy to millions of Americans. The company also partnered with Disabled American Veterans (DAV) [ref: DAV announces new partnership with Solace Health supporting veterans’ care, DAV] and the American Legion [ref: Solace Health, American Legion announce partnership to help veterans navigate healthcare system, American Legion] to help U.S. military veterans navigate healthcare. They announced a partnership with Walmart’s Better Care Services in September 2026. [ref: Solace Health Expands Access to Healthcare Advocacy Through Walmart’s Better Care Services Platform, Businesswire]

== Advocacy services ==
Solace advocates include registered nurses and other healthcare professionals who, according to a 2026 press release have 16 years of experience on average. When Medicare reimburses advocates, Solace receives a share in exchange for use of its platform. In early 2026, Solace had more than 2,000 participating advocates providing services to more than 20,000 patients each month.

Advocate services include helping clients understand medical bills and treatment plans, as well as finding physicians, scheduling appointments, and coordinating care across multiple providers. Advocates can also go to appointments with patients, either virtually or in person. Gurewitz told MedCity News in 2026 that Solace advocates specialize in doing the work for patients, rather than simply providing advice on what patients should do.

Patients interact with advocates through text and phone calls as well as video calls embedded in the Solace platform. [ref: Solace Health Reaches Unicorn Status by Taking the ‘Homework’ Out of Care Navigation, MedCityNews] Solace's proprietary electronic health records system assembles a patient's health history. The platform also handles Medicare billing. Gurewitz informed Founder Brew in a 2026 interview that while the Solace platform incorporates AI to help advocates do their jobs, many aspects of the U.S. healthcare system cannot be completed by AI and still require human interaction.

“Mosley Lane” is the sixteenth episode of the fifth season of the American police procedural crime drama television series Criminal Minds. Written by Simon Mirren and Erica Messer and directed by series cast member Matthew Gray Gubler, the episode originally aired on March 3, 2010.

== Plot ==
At a winter festival in Ashburn, Virginia, eight-year-old Aimee Lynch disappears after her mother, Barbara, is distracted by a woman calling out for a missing child. The Behavioral Analysis Unit (BAU) begins investigating the abduction. Sarah Hillridge approaches Jennifer Jareau and claims that the person responsible for Aimee’s disappearance also abducted her eight-year-old son, Charlie, eight years earlier. Although Sarah has made similar claims following other child abductions, the team discovers similarities between Charlie’s and Aimee’s disappearances.

Penelope Garcia searches for similar disappearances and discovers a pattern of children who have vanished from public places over several years. The BAU concludes that the abductions are the work of the same offenders, who have been taking children and holding them for extended periods. As the team investigates the previous cases and interviews the families of the missing children, they work to identify a connection that could lead them to the abductors before Aimee disappears permanently.

Aimee is taken to the home of Roger and Anita Roycewood, where several other abducted children are being held. Among them are Charlie Hillridge, who has survived the eight years since his disappearance, and Stephen Shepherd. The Roycewoods force the children to live as members of their household and use the older children to help control the younger captives. Charlie and Stephen attempt to protect Aimee and teach her how to survive in the house without provoking the Roycewoods.

The BAU discovers that the Roycewoods have been abducting children for years and disposing of the bodies of those who die while in captivity. The investigation eventually leads the team to a funeral home and crematorium connected to the couple. Meanwhile, Anita decides that Stephen has become too difficult to control and kills him after he tries to protect Aimee. The discovery raises the urgency of the search as the team realizes that Aimee and the remaining children are in immediate danger.

As the BAU closes in on the Roycewoods, Roger and Anita prepare to kill the remaining children and destroy evidence of their crimes. Charlie manages to obtain a gun and shoots Anita before she can kill Aimee and the other children. Roger dies during the confrontation, and the surviving children are rescued. Charlie is reunited with his parents after eight years in captivity. He later tells Stephen’s parents that their son had survived until the previous day and died protecting Aimee, leaving them devastated by how close they had come to seeing him alive again.

== Cast [ref: ] ==

=== Main ===

* Paget Brewster as Emily Prentiss
* Shemar Moore as Derek Morgan
* Matthew Gray Gubler as Spencer Reid
* A. J. Cook as Jennifer “JJ” Jareau

=== Guest ===

* Bunny Levine as Martha Woodley

* Grace Savage as Jane
* Brooke Smith as Barbara Lynch
* Debra Sullivan as Mrs. Shepherd
* Owen Thayer as Police Sketch Artist

== Production ==
Gubler was also involved in selecting the episode’s guest cast, which included Brooke Smith, Bud Cort, Beth Grant, Ann Cusack and Toby Huss. He described the young performers appearing in the episode as among the most talented child actors he had encountered.

“Mosley Lane” marked Matthew Gray Gubler’s directorial debut. Gubler, who portrays Spencer Reid in the series, had studied film directing at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts before beginning his acting career. He had expressed an interest in directing Criminal Minds and approached executive producer and showrunner Ed Bernero about directing an episode near the end of the show’s fourth season. According to Gubler, Bernero told him that he was ready and only needed to ask. [ref: TV Guide, www.tvguide.com]

Gubler described “Mosley Lane” as a modern-day dark fairy tale inspired by Hansel and Gretel. Influenced by German Expressionist cinema, he chose to present parts of the story from a child’s perspective, giving the Roycewoods’ world an eerie, fantastical quality. For the Roycewoods’ home, Gubler selected a three-story Victorian mansion that he felt suited the episode’s unsettling atmosphere.

Redcoat Air Cargo Flight 103 was an international cargo flight from Massachusetts, United States to Shannon, Ireland. On February 16, 1980, the Bristol Britannia lost lift and stalled shortly after take-off. It crashed into a wooded area near Billerica, Massachusetts, leaving only the flight engineer survived of the eight on board. [ref: ] [ref: Bristol Britannia: the turboprop airliner and its legacy, Ready For Take-Off Book] [ref: Remembering the Billerica plane crash of 1980, Lowell Sun]

== Background ==

=== Aircraft ===
The aircraft involved was a Bristol Britannia manufactured in 1959. Before the accident, the plane had accumulated 21,963 flight hours and 8,310 hours.

=== Victims ===

* The captain of the flight was George William Coburn, aged 56, having certification for the Bristol Britannia and British Aerospace 125. He had acquired 11,600 flight hours, 7,600 of which were in the Bristol Britannia.
* The first officer of the flight was Jack Kingston Jones, aged 54, who had logged in 7,600 flight hours, 4,760 of which were in the Bristol Britannia.
* The flight engineer of the flight was Richard Alfred Creer, aged 59, who had logged in 20,000 flight hours, 12,000 of which were in the Bristol Britannia. He was the only survivor of the crash.
* The navigator of the flight was Anthony John Beckett, aged 49, who had logged in 14,000 flight hours, 8,000 of which were in the Bristol Britannia.
* The loadmaster was David Esmond Whike.
* The ground engineer was William Brady. [ref: ]
* The two passengers were Lionel Heady and Susan Parker.

== Accident ==
Before the accident, witness found that there were ice built up on the fuselage, wings, horizontal stabilizer, and the engine pipes. The ice were swept off before applying the deicing fluid. The aircraft was still parking for 20-25 minutes before being cleared to taxi at runway 15R. However, it was then changed to runway 33L. Following the traffic conflict, the flight had to hold position. During that time, witness found the accumulation of ice on the control surface.

At 14:08, the aircraft took off from Logan International Airport. As it reached an altitude of 1,700 feet, it suddenly lost altitude and crashed into a wooded area located in Billerica. Only the flight engineer survived with severe injuries. Numerous witnesses found the aircraft falling down in a nose-up configuration, exploded on impact and caught fire.

== Investigation ==
The final report stated that the probable cause of the crash was:

"Degraded aerodynamic performance, resulting from an accumulation of ice and snow on the airframe before take-off and a further accumulation of ice when the aircraft was flown into moderate to severe icing conditions following take-off.

Contributing were encounters with windshear, downdraughts and turbulence during the climb. The failure of the flight crew to obtain an adequate pre-flight weather briefing and the failure of the National Weather Service to advise the crew of a SIGMET for severe icing conditions were also contributing factors." [ref: AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT REPORT, NTSB] [ref: Accident Bristol 175 Britannia 253 G-BRAC, Saturday 16 February 1980, aviation-safety.net] [ref: When the sky fell over Billerica, Burlington Retro]

== See also ==

Draft text:
Monoethylene glycol reclamation (MEG reclamation) is an industrial process used to remove dissolved salts, corrosion products, hydrocarbons and degradation by-products from monoethylene glycol (MEG), allowing the glycol to be reused in hydrocarbon production systems. MEG is commonly used as a thermodynamic hydrate inhibitor in subsea pipeline systems, where it is injected into production fluids to prevent the formation of hydrates that could obstruct flowlines. [ref: Formation of Gas Hydrates in Natural Gas Transmission Lines, Industrial & Engineering Chemistry]

MEG reclamation is principally employed in offshore natural gas developments, long-distance subsea tie-backs, floating production storage and offloading facilities (FPSOs), and onshore gas-processing plants. The process is often integrated with MEG regeneration systems that remove water from the recovered glycol stream. [ref: Offshore MEG Regeneration and Reclamation Units: Lessons Learned from Their Design and Operation]
[ref: Power FPSO New MEG System Concept Select & PreFEED, io consulting]

== Background ==

Early Deepwater Projects relied primarily on methanol for hydrate inhibition. This was simple as it was injected and not recovered. Methanol solubility in gas and liquid hydrocarbon product streams is substantially higher
than MEG solubility. [ref: Offshore Hydrate Engineering Handbook, Center for Hydrate Research, Colorado School of Mines]

As subsea tie-back became longer and longer, in the 1990s, MEG began to use MEG as a hydrate inhibitor. Unlike methanol, MEG can be recovered, purified and re-used, reducing chemical consumption and operating costs. The first documented MEG Reclamation units were at Shell Todd in New Zealand [ref: Glycol Purification – A Novel Approach to an Old Problem, NZ Engineering] [ref: Advanced Design of Glycol Reclamation Plants] and Shell's Mensa field in the Gulf of Mexico. [ref: How to Select Best MEG Recovery Unit's Configuration?, Digital Refining]

As production fluids travel through pipelines, the recovered MEG becomes contaminated with dissolved salts, corrosion products, hydrocarbons, production chemicals and degradation compounds. Without reclamation, these contaminants can accumulate and adversely affect process equipment and flow assurance performance.

== Regeneration vs Reclamation ==

Although the terms are sometimes used together, regeneration and reclamation describe different stages of MEG recovery.

Regeneration

Lean MEG, which is typically a concentrated solution of 80-90 wt% MEG in water, is injected into the wellhead... The MEG Regeneration process is comprised of two sections: Pre-treatment where hydrocarbon vapour and liquids are separated from the Rich MEG in a low pressure three phase separator. Regeneration where MEG is regenerated by boiling off water in an atmospheric distillation column. [ref: Crawley-Boevey, S.; Jariwala, A. "Offshore MEG Regeneration and Reclamation Units; Lessons Learned from Their Design and Operation". GPA Europe Conference Proceedings.] These regeneration are similar to those for Gas Glycol Dehydration.

Reclamation

MEG reclamation is the process of removing dissolved salts (both monovalent and divalent), scale-forming species, corrosion products, and other contaminants from recycled monoethylene glycol. Unlike regeneration, which primarily removes water, reclamation prevents contaminant accumulation that can lead to scaling, fouling, corrosion, and reduced process performance. [ref: Odeigah, E.A.; Pojtanabuntoeng, T. (2022). "Regeneration and Reclamation of Mono-Ethylene Glycol (MEG) Used as a Hydrate Inhibitor: A Review". American Journal of Chemical Engineering. 10(2): 32-45. doi:10.11648/j.ajche.20221002.13.]

== Process configurations ==

MEG reclamation systems are generally configured using either a full-stream or a slip-stream reclamation process.

Full-stream reclamation
Full-stream reclamation is where the entire regenerated MEG recycle stream is treated to remove dissolved salts, suspended solids, corrosion products, and other contaminants. Unlike MEG regeneration, which removes water to restore glycol concentration, full-stream reclamation removes non-volatile contaminants that accumulate during operation and can lead to scaling, fouling, and corrosion.. [ref: Othman, A.; Khraisheh, M.; Almomani, F.; Al-Sobhi, S.A.; AlNouss, A.; Adham, S. (2020). "Design, Optimization and Economic Analysis of a Monoethylene Glycol Recovery Process: Salt Precipitation and Vacuum Operation". International Journal of Energy Research. doi:10.1002/er.5426.]

Slip-stream reclamation
In a slip-stream configuration, only a portion of the circulating MEG is treated for salt removal while the remainder undergoes conventional regeneration. The selection of reclamation philosophy depends primarily on anticipated formation-water production rates, salt loading, chemical management requirements and overall system economics. [ref: Hydrate Prevention Using MEG Instead of MeOH: Impact of Experience from Major Norwegian Developments on Technology Selection for Injection and Recovery of MEG, Offshore Technology Conference]

== Early life and high school ==

Leacock attended Millbrook High School in Raleigh, North Carolina, where he competed in sprint and hurdle events. During his high school career, he won the boys' 400-meter hurdles championship at The Outdoor Nationals, presented by Nike, in 2021, running 52.284 seconds at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. DyeStat reported that Leacock became the first male athlete from North Carolina to win the 400-meter hurdles title at the meet since 2008. [ref: Dillon Leacock 1st Place Boys 400m Hurdles Championship - The Outdoor Nationals, Presented by Nike 2021, DyeStat]

His University of Houston biography lists victories in the 400-meter hurdles at Nike Outdoor Nationals, the NACAC Championships and the USATF Outdoor Nationals, as well as a North Carolina state championship in the 300-meter hurdles. He was also runner-up in the North Carolina state 110-meter hurdles. [ref: Dillon Leacock - Track and Field, University of Houston Athletics]

== International career ==

In 2021, Leacock won the 400-meter hurdles at the NACAC Championships in San José, Costa Rica, in 53.45 seconds. Trinidad and Tobago Newsday reported that Leacock was among Trinidad and Tobago's gold medalists at the championships. [ref: Clement Campbell, Iantha Wright earn NACAC medals on final day, Trinidad and Tobago Newsday] [ref: NACAC U20 Championships, World Athletics]

The Trinidad Guardian later included Leacock's victory among Trinidad and Tobago's track and field highlights of 2021, reporting that he won the 400-meter hurdles in 53.45 seconds. [ref: Daniel, Horsford, Gittens and Warren track and fields bright spots for 2021, Trinidad Guardian]

Leacock was selected to represent Trinidad and Tobago at the 2021 World Athletics U20 Championships in Nairobi, Kenya. He was scheduled to compete in the men's 400-meter hurdles but withdrew before his heat after experiencing discomfort in training. [ref: Three-member Trinidad and Tobago team for World Athletics Under-20 Champs, Trinidad and Tobago Newsday] [ref: No medals for Trinidad and Tobago at U-20 World Championships, Trinidad and Tobago Newsday]

In 2025, Leacock represented Trinidad and Tobago at the 2025 Junior Pan American Games in Asunción, Paraguay. He competed in the men's 400-meter hurdles and was part of Trinidad and Tobago's men's 4 × 400-meter relay team, which finished fourth. [ref: Junior Pan American Games, World Athletics] [ref: Trinidad and Tobago men stumble to fourth in 4x400m final at Jr Pan Am, Trinidad and Tobago Newsday]

In June 2026, Leacock recorded a personal best of 49.83 seconds in the 400-meter hurdles at the LA Sprint Series at Notre Dame High School in Sherman Oaks, California. He finished second in the event. [ref: Leacock, Harrison shine in LA series, Trinidad Express] [ref: Dillon LEACOCK, World Athletics]

Later that month, Leacock won the men's 400-meter hurdles at the Trinidad and Tobago Championships, running 51.24 seconds. [ref: Trinidad & Tobago Championship, World Athletics]

== Collegiate career ==

=== Houston ===

Leacock competed collegiately for the Houston Cougars.

As a freshman in 2022, he finished eighth in the 400-meter hurdles at the American Athletic Conference Championships and recorded a personal best of 52.48 seconds. He also set a personal best of 49.70 seconds in the 400 meters at the Charlie Thomas Invitational. [ref: Dillon Leacock - Track and Field, University of Houston Athletics]

In 2023, Leacock qualified for the NCAA West Preliminary Round in the 400-meter hurdles. He finished seventh in the event at the American Athletic Conference Championships with a personal best of 52.15 seconds. During the indoor season, he ran 49.64 seconds in the 400 meters at the American Indoor Championships. [ref: Dillon Leacock - Track and Field, University of Houston Athletics]

In 2024, Leacock won the 400-meter hurdles at the Victor Lopez Classic in 51.33 seconds. At the Big 12 Outdoor Championships, he finished fifth in the 400-meter hurdles in 50.62 seconds and helped Houston finish seventh in the 4 × 400-meter relay. He subsequently qualified for the NCAA West First Round in both events. [ref: Dillon Leacock - Track and Field, University of Houston Athletics]

Leacock did not compete for Houston during the 2025 season. [ref: Dillon Leacock - Track and Field, University of Houston Athletics]

=== Missouri ===

Leacock transferred to the Missouri Tigers for the 2026 season. [ref: Dillon Leacock - 2026 Track & Field Roster, University of Missouri Athletics]

During the 2026 indoor season, he established a collegiate personal best of 47.61 seconds in the 400 meters at the Tyson Invitational. He also competed in the 60-meter hurdles and was part of Missouri's distance medley relay team. [ref: Dillon Leacock – Track and Field Results & Statistics, TFRRS]

At the Drake Relays in Des Moines, Iowa, Leacock won the men's 400-meter hurdles in 50.68 seconds, defeating a field of 20 competitors. The performance ranked third on Missouri's all-time list in the event. [ref: Track and Field Notches Three Champion Titles During Day Three of Drake Relays, University of Missouri Athletics] [ref: 116th Drake Relays - 400m Hurdles, TFRRS]

His Drake Relays performance qualified him for the NCAA West First Round. [ref: Fifteen Tigers Qualify for NCAA Track & Field West Regional Championships, University of Missouri Athletics]

Draft text:
Lyubov Nikolaevna Zapolskaya (;; 7 August 1871 – 3 November 1943) was a Russian mathematician and the first woman to receive a master's degree in mathematics from a Russian university.

== Early life and education ==
Zapolskaya was born on 7 August 1871 in the village of Bigildino in the Ryazan Governorate of the Russian Empire to secondary school teachers Sofya Zapolskaya (née Kochurova) and Nikolay Zapolsky.

When she was five years old, her family moved to St. Petersburg, where her father taught Russian language and literature at the Second Military Gymnasium, and her mother taught at Vasileostrovskaya Girls' Gymnasium.

In 1880, she enrolled in the after receiving financial support from her cousin. She studied there for seven years and completed her studies in 1887 at the age of sixteen, receiving a gold medal for her grades and academic achievements. She then took a three-year pedagogical course for women and received another medal for her efforts.

She then enrolled in the mathematics department of St. Petersburg Higher Courses for Women in late 1890. There, she studied analytic geometry, calculus, physics, and astronomy, and she developed an enthusiasm for higher algebra. She completed her studies in 1894. Russian universities did not admit women at the time, so Zapolskaya, inspired by Sofya Kovalevskaya, continued her education abroad. After obtaining permission from Ivan Delyanov, the Minister of Public Education, she traveled to Germany in October 1895 and attended the University of Göttingen.

At Göttingen, Zapolskaya studied under David Hilbert and Felix Klein. Her research focused on relatively abelian cubic number fields. Her research drew from Hilbert's prior work on algebraic number fields and his influential The Theory of Algebraic Number Fields. Her thesis defense took place in 1902, with Hilbert praising Zapolskaya's work, and she was awarded a Doctor of Philosophy in Mathematics, magna cum laude. She subsequently returned to Russia to pursue a career in teaching.

== Career ==
On 19 November 1902, Zapolskaya attended a meeting held by the Moscow Mathematical Society and presented her thesis. Her work impressed the attendees, including Nikolai Bugaev and Sergey Chaplygin, and she was made a member of the Moscow Mathematical Society.

From 1903, she taught at the Higher Women's Courses in Moscow and at the Imperial Moscow University. The university published her thesis in 1905 and invited her to defend it. She accepted and defended it on 8 March 1905, with and Dmitri Egorov acting as the examiners. She succeeded and was granted a master's degree, becoming the first woman to receive a master's in mathematics in Russia. Following her defense, she became a professor at the university.

== Later years and death ==
Zapolskaya died in Ryazan on 3 November 1943. She was buried at the Skorbyashchenskoye Cemetery.

Draft: Tokyo Peace Exhibition

Draft text:
The, also known in English as the Peace Memorial Tokyo Exposition and the Peace Commemorative Exposition, was an exposition held from March 10 to July 31, 1922, at Ueno Park, Tokyo, to commemorate the Allied victory in the First World War. Organized by an official exposition bureau (, Hakurankai Jimukyoku), it opened at the moment Japanese delegates were returning home from the Washington Naval Conference, becoming the largest and most popular Japanese exposition held to that time, with more than eleven million visitors—a record for a Taishō era exhibition.

== Background ==

According to historian Frederick R. Dickinson, the exposition grew out of the optimism of the early 1920s, when Japan's participation in the Washington Naval Conference of 1921–22 was seen at home as a triumph of international cooperation and disarmament, and The Tokyo Asahi described the fair as representing "the best of world culture" and "a harbinger of dazzling beauty." [ref: World War I and the Triumph of a New Japan, 1919-1930, Cambridge University Press] By the Taishō era the state-building exhibitions of the Meiji period had given way to exhibitions as entertainment and spectacle, and the Tokyo Peace Exhibition was conceived on a correspondingly grand scale: costing roughly 6 million yen, with almost fifty pavilions, two triumphal gates, and a natural lake covering some 110,000 square metres, it was described as the largest Japanese exposition to date. [ref: Peace Commemorative Exposition, Ueno Park, Tokyo, 1922, Old Tokyo]

The exposition opened on March 10, 1922, shortly after the conclusion of the Washington Naval Conference, timed to coincide with the return of Japan's delegates and with the annual cherry blossom season at Ueno. At the opening ceremony, festival chairman Prince Kan'in Kotohito, flanked by celebratory pine, plum and bamboo, tolled a dedicated "peace bell" and released doves, declaring that world sentiment was weary of "the ghastly evils of war" and full of "admiration for the happiness of peace." Official English-language materials dated the event "March 10–July 31, 1922". [ref: MeijiShowa]

== Grounds and exhibits ==

The grounds were divided into two sections. The first, laid out on the heights of Ueno Park, was dominated by a peace tower designed by the architect Sutemi Horiguchi, a leading figure of the Bunriha ("Secessionist") architecture group influenced by the Vienna Secession; the tower was modelled on the Wedding Tower at Darmstadt. The five entrances were arched in the shape of Mount Fuji. A second section surrounded Shinobazu Pond, around which clustered the exhibition's most popular attractions, from the Hokkaido pavilion and colonial exhibits to amusement rides; a contemporary account in The Japan Magazine likened the shoreline buildings to "architectural oddities, with unexpected humps in the roofs and extraordinary bumps in walls." [ref: The Tokyo Peace Exhibition, The Japan Magazine]

Pavilions and special buildings included those of Japan's colonies and overseas territories—Taiwan, Karafuto, Korea, Manchuria–Mongolia, and the South Seas mandate—as well as prefectural pavilions, industrial and machinery halls, an agricultural and sericulture hall, a "foreign lands" building, the Sumitomo pavilion, and a section of modern "culture houses" (, bunka jūtaku), together with airplane demonstrations and a touring hydroplane ride over the pond. [ref: Heiwa Kinen Tokyo Hakurankai (The Peace Memorial Tokyo Exposition), Unpinning History: Japanese Posters in the Age of Commercialism, Imperialism, and Modernism] Meiji-era and colonial pavilion architecture, photography, and even the exposition's official map—designed by Koijūrō Yoshida—were widely reproduced in commemorative postcards, albums, and administrative reports.

== Attendance and legacy ==

The exposition drew more than 11 million visitors, a record for a Taishō-period exhibition, making it the most popular Japanese exposition of its era. Its cherry-blossom backdrop fed a wider cultural shift identified by Dickinson, in which the cherry blossom became newly associated with the "culture of peace" of the 1920s. The exposition was commemorated in souvenir postcards, photographic albums, posters (including an official poster by the graphic designer Sugiyama Sueo), and map prints.

The opening of the exposition coincided with the debut on April 2, 1922, of Japan's oldest weekly magazines: the inaugural covers of Sunday Mainichi and its rival Shūkan Asahi both carried photographs taken at the fair. [ref: Japan's savvy, salacious shukanshi, Number 1 Shimbun] Images and printed records of the exposition are held in archives including the Library of Congress and the Stanford University Libraries. [ref: Formosa Bldg. (i.e. Building) Peace Expos., Tokyo, Library of Congress] [ref: Tōkyō Hakurankai Jimukyoku kyoka Heiwa Kinen Tōkyō Hakurankai ekibijō hikae, Stanford University Libraries]

Draft text:
== Introduction ==

Operational risk quantification refers to the statistical and analytical methods used to assess an organization's potential financial losses related to operational risk — losses arising from internal failures (fraud, processing errors) or from external events beyond the organization's control (natural disasters, pandemics). In banking, for example, a borrower's default is classified as credit risk rather than operational risk, whereas an error made in granting a loan is classified as operational risk.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision formally defined operational risk in the Basel II Accords (2004) as "the risk of loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems or from external events." [ref: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards, Bank for International Settlements] Basel II requires banks to quantify this risk in order to determine a portion of their regulatory capital and economic capital under Pillar 2 (ICAAP), the equity institutions must hold to absorb losses.

Institutions combine qualitative approaches, such as Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA), with quantitative approaches, such as the Standardized Measurement Approach (SMA) and the Loss Distribution Approach (LDA).

Since the 2020s, in response to the emergence of systemic threats linked to climate risks and dependence on technological service providers, these methodologies have integrated forward-looking scenario analyses. These practices are framed by new supervisory standards (such as the European regulation DORA, Digital Operational Resilience for the financial sector and Amending regulations) and rely technically on machine learning and Big data processing.

== Typology of methodological approaches ==

Financial institutions employ various methodological approaches to quantify their exposure to operational risk. The choice of model depends on the depth of historical data [ref: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards: A Revised Framework – Comprehensive Version, Bank for International Settlements], regulatory constraints [ref: 2023 EU-wide stress test – Methodological Note, EBA], and the institution's internal objectives regarding resilience [ref: Building operational resilience: Impact tolerances for important business services (PS6/21), Bank of England].

Quantitative models are divided into two main categories. Statistical methods jointly evaluate the frequency and severity of historical losses, while forward-looking scenario analyses estimate the impact of rare but critical events, such as cyberattacks, compliance litigation, or system failures [ref: Scenario Analysis in the Measurement of Operational Risk Capital: A Review, Journal of Operational Risk]. Both approaches frequently rely on modeling techniques, such as Monte Carlo simulation, to generate loss distributions [ref: Loss Distribution Approach for Operational Risk, SSRN Electronic Journal]. Under Basel III, banks using such models must calculate capital requirements at a 99.9% confidence level [ref: International Convergence of Capital Measurement and Capital Standards, Bank for International Settlements].

The implementation of these mathematical models raises several technical challenges documented by supervisory authorities [ref: Operational Risk: Supervisory Guidelines for the Advanced Measurement Approaches, Bank for International Settlements]:
*The scarcity of historical loss data and reporting bias in externally sourced data, which are especially pronounced for extreme, low-frequency events;
*The high sensitivity of capital requirements to distributional assumptions, notably the shape of the severity distribution's tail and the choice of dependence (correlation) structure between risk categories;
*The difficulty of combining statistical loss data with qualitative inputs, such as business environment and internal control factors (BEICFs).

To address these limitations, banking and insurance institutions no longer use these models in isolation. They combine quantitative measures with qualitative assessments within a comprehensive risk management framework.

=== Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) ===

The Loss Distribution Approach (LDA) estimates the total distribution of operational losses from historical data by modelling frequency and severity separately. Frequency is typically modelled with a Poisson or negative binomial distribution, while severity is fitted to heavy-tailed distributions such as the Lognormal, Weibull, or Pareto law [ref: Quantitative Risk Management: Concepts, Techniques and Tools, Princeton University Press].

The aggregate loss for a given period is modelled as:

: S = \sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i

where N is the (random) number of loss events, drawn from the frequency distribution, and each Xi is an individual loss severity, drawn independently from the severity distribution. Because this sum has no closed-form solution for most distribution choices, banks estimate it via Monte Carlo simulation, drawing repeatedly from both distributions to build an aggregated loss distribution and read off the capital requirement at the 99.9th percentile.
[truncated]

András Lénárd (born 6 September 1977 in Miercurea Ciuc) is a Szekler Hungarian businessman and investor from Szeklerland. [https://www.3szek.ro/load/cikk/94631/a-szekely-%E2%80%9Evilagrendszer%E2%80%9D-beszallitoja-lenard-andras-vallalkozoval-az-igazi-csiki-sorrol-es-davidnak-goliattal-valo-harcarol A székely „világrendszer” beszállítója – Lénárd András vállalkozóval az Igazi Csíki Sörről és Dávidnak Góliáttal való harcáról]. Retrieved 6 September 2026.]

His best-known business has been the Csíki Sör Manufactory in Sânsimion, which gained international attention through its trademark dispute with the Romanian subsidiary of Heineken. [ref: Karasz, Palko. [https://www.nytimes.com/2017/08/04/business/heineken-transylvania-beer.html Small Transylvania Brewer Stood Up to an Industry Giant, and Survived]. In 2024, he sold his 50 per cent interest in the corporate group that included the Csíki Sör and Csíki Csipsz production units founded by him. [ref: [https://mvm.hu/-/media/MVMHu/Documents/Media/Mediatartalmak/Jelentesek/EN/Archive/MVM_Group_Consolidated_Annual_Report_2014.pdf MVM Group Consolidated Annual Report 2014]. Section concerning the acquisition of the Valea Uzului hydropower project. Retrieved 15 July 2026.] Székelyhon reported, citing market information, that the buyout may have taken place at a corporate valuation of approximately €50 million.

== Early years and property development ==

Lénárd moved to the United States in the second half of the 1990s. In a 2020 interview, he said that he initially worked as a house painter before moving on to production and organisational roles in a sportswear company. He returned to Romania in 2001. [ref: Nagy, József. [https://24.hu/belfold/2020/06/19/lenard-andras-csiki-sor-interju/ Lénárd András: Elég sok bicskám van. S elég sok történetem]. 24.hu. 19 June 2020. Retrieved 15 July 2026.]

Starting in 2005, he was involved in property development in and around Miercurea Ciuc. Press reports have linked him to residential developments in the Jigodin and Șumuleu Ciuc areas and to the Hét vezér residential project. According to a Romanian press profile published in 2024, he was also involved in developing a four-star hotel in Budapest in 2015, which he later sold.

== Hydropower investments ==

Starting in the late 2000s, Lénárd became involved in hydropower projects. HydroEnergy Zrt., in which he held a majority interest, and related Romanian project companies developed power plants on the Vârghiș River and in the Valea Uzului area. [ref: Sipos, Zoltán. [https://atlatszo.ro/klimavalsag/torpe-vizeromu-oriasi-buktaval-a-magyar-allam-finanszirozza-a-csodot/ Törpe vízerőmű óriási buktával: a magyar állam finanszírozza a csődöt]. Átlátszó Erdély. 26 July 2019. Retrieved 15 July 2026.]

In January 2015, MVM completed the acquisition of a 90 per cent interest in Hivatalos SRL, the company that owned the Valea Uzului hydropower complex, from Winsland Holding Ltd. and HydroEnergy Zrt. MVM reported the total transaction value as €27.8 million.

The projects drew criticism regarding their environmental and economic aspects. Átlátszó Erdély reported that the Valea Uzului complex generated less electricity than initially estimated and that riverbed interventions raised environmental concerns. Lénárd responded that the projects had the required permits and that their environmental impact was limited.

The run-of-river hydropower technology used at Valea Uzului is commonly used in Europe. According to the European Small Hydropower Association, approximately 14,000 small hydropower plants operated in the old member states of the European Union, a further 2,800 in the new member states and approximately 400 in candidate countries, meaning that nearly 17,000 such facilities operated in Europe in total. [ref: [https://www.globalccsinstitute.com/archive/hub/publications/138218/State-art-small-hydropower-EU-25.pdf The State of the Art of Small Hydropower in the European Union]. European Small Hydropower Association. Retrieved 15 July 2026.]

Nate Hodges (born 1984) is an American professional timbersports competitor. He won the STIHL Timbersports Individual World Championship in 2024 [ref: North Fork native Nate Hodges crowned Timbersports world champion, ABC30] and the U.S. championship in 2024 and 2025. [ref: U.S. Championships Delivers World Records, Title Defenses, and Rising Stars, STIHL Timbersports] In 2025, he set a world record of 4.28 seconds in the Hot Saw discipline.

== Early life ==
Hodges grew up in North Fork, California, in Madera County. His family has a long involvement in the Mid-Sierra Loggers Jamboree; his father Patrick, mother Cathey, brother Jerry, and sister Amanda have also competed in the event. [ref: Hodges Carves Out Runner Up Finish At 2019 Stihl Timbersports Championships, Sierra News Online]

Hodges began competing at the Jamboree as a young adult, entering the axe throw. He tied for first place in his first competition and won a tiebreaker throw-off. [ref: Hodges Defends Title At 60th North Fork Loggers Jamboree, Sierra News Online]

== Career ==
Hodges entered the STIHL Timbersports national circuit in 2019. That July, he finished second at the U.S. Pro Championship in Milwaukee, one point behind Cassidy Scheer. Later that year, he competed for the United States at the World Championships in Prague. [ref: Hodges to Compete Next Month at Timbersports World Championships in Prague, Sierra News Online]

In 2022, Hodges was part of the U.S. team that won the silver medal at the Team World Championship in Gothenburg, Sweden. [ref: Australia dominate World Championships in Sweden, STIHL Timbersports] He won another team silver medal at the 2024 World Championships in Toulouse, France. [ref: Australia defend world title in Toulouse, STIHL Timbersports]

Hodges won his first U.S. championship in July 2024, defeating Matt Cogar by one point. [ref: STIHL Timbersports brings the heat to the U.S. Championship, STIHL Timbersports] The victory qualified him for the Individual World Championship in Toulouse, where he scored 67 points to win the title ahead of Jack Jordan of New Zealand and Ben Cumberland of Canada. [ref: Check-Nate! USA's Nate Hodges scoops his first STIHL Timbersports Individual World Championship, STIHL Timbersports]

In July 2025, Hodges won his second consecutive U.S. championship. During the semifinals, he set a world record of 4.28 seconds in the Hot Saw discipline. He finished sixth while defending his title at the 2025 Individual World Championship in Milan, after being disqualified in the Hot Saw for cutting outside the marked line. [ref: Wood you believe it?! New Zealand's Jack Jordan snatches his first solo world title, STIHL Timbersports]

In 2026, Hodges finished second at the North American Trophy and was runner-up to Matt Cogar at the U.S. Men's Pro Championship in Milwaukee. [ref: North American Trophy 2026, STIHL Timbersports] [ref: Breakthrough Champions, Record-Breaking Cuts and an Eight-Time Winner: STIHL Timbersports Crowns 2026 U.S. Champions, STIHL]

== Personal life ==
Hodges lives near North Fork, California, and has worked as a general contractor. In 2019, he opened Yosemite Axe Throwing in Oakhurst, California. [ref: Timber! New Axe Throwing Club Opening in Oakhurst, Sierra News Online]

Miguel Esparza is a Chicago-based sports broadcaster and voice-over artist known for his Spanish-language coverage of Major League Baseball and multiple Chicago professional sports teams, including the Cubs and the Blackhawks. [ref: Miguel Esparza is the Spanish voice of four Chicago sports teams, Block Club Chicago] [ref: Miguel Esparza: el reconocido narrador de Chicago MLB con raíces boricuas, Telemundo Puerto Rico] He has also worked in radio broadcasting as a news anchor and producer for WBBM 780 AM. [ref: How a Humboldt Park native became a Spanish voice for Chicago sports teams, CBS Chicago]

== Early life and education ==
Miguel Esparza was born and raised in Humboldt Park on the Northwest Side of Chicago. He is half Mexican and half Puerto Rican and he is the second of four children.

== Career ==

=== Early radio career ===
Esparza began his radio career in 2001 at La Ley 107.9 FM in Chicago, a regional Mexican music station, where he held various programming roles. In 2003, he began reporting on the Chicago Cubs and Chicago White Sox for a morning radio program.

In 2004, he joined Onda 92, a Spanish-language pop station, owned by the same parent company, but returned to La Ley after about a year and a half.

From 2009 to 2013, Esparza contributed remotely to talk shows for radio stations in Kentucky and Mazatlán, Sinaloa, Mexico, working the 10 a.m.-3 p.m. shift on both stations and working on the production side of the Kentucky station.

=== Chicago broadcasting and sports coverage ===
In 2014, Esparza went back to La Ley and began hosting a Spanish morning show and working as a Spanish-language play-by-play announcer for Chicago Bears broadcasts. He then moved to Mendota, Illinois and worked at regional Mexican station El Rey for four years before moving back to Chicago in 2018.

Esparza then joined Univision and WBBM 780 AM in Chicago. [ref: Meet Miguel Esparza, The Spanish Voice Of 4 Chicago Sports Teams, Block Club Chicago]At Univision, he contributed Spanish-language coverage of the Chicago Bulls, Chicago Bears, and Chicago Cubs. [ref: Miguel Esparza: el reconocido narrador de Chicago MLB con raíces boricuas, Telemundo Puerto Rico] He then added the Chicago White Sox to his roster in 2020.

A year later, Esparza took over Spanish-language play-by-play duties for the Chicago Cubs at Univison, gaining popularity by doing play-by-play coverage for multiple Chicago professional sports teams, including the Bears, Bulls, and Blackhawks. [ref: Miguel Esparza: el reconocido narrador de Chicago MLB con raíces boricuas, Telemundo Puerto Rico]

=== Current work ===
Since 2021, Esparza has served as the Spanish-language voice of the Chicago Cubs, gaining recognition from local media and other broadcasters for his passion of the job and his reporting on the teams.

Esparza has also provided Spanish-language play-by-play coverage for Grand Valley State University football. During the 2023 season, he was part of the inaugural Spanish-language broadcast team for the program, which was recognized by the Michigan Association of Broadcasters as the state's "Best" sports play-by-play broadcast. [ref: GVSU Football Spanish Language Broadcast Named Best Sports Play-By-Play in Michigan, Grand Valley State University Athletics]

He has appeared in media coverage related to the Chicago Cubs, including interviews at the team's annual Cubs Convention, podcasts with local news sites and a broadcast on Marquee Sports Network. [ref: Miguel Esparza loves Cubs' Alex Bregman, Edward Cabrera additions, Marquee Sports Network]

=== Community involvement ===
Outside of the radio booth, he has also worked to increase sports access and representation for and within the Latino community [ref: ], serving as an ambassador for both Chicago team franchises to get more Latino audiences into hockey and baseball. Latinos have historically not received a front-row seat to hockey compared to other nationalities, though the National Hockey League (NHL) has seen an increase in Latino fans since 2013. [ref: These NHL Players Are Changing Perceptions of Latinos in Hockey, Remezcla]

As part of that mission, Esparza has hosted events in partnership with the Blackhawks and the Cubs at the United Center and in various Chicago schools with predominantly Latino students, presenting them with checks for school supplies and hosting Mexican heritage nights. He always seeks to bring younger Latino sports fans into the Chicago sports world and inspire the next generation. [ref: Hockey eyes Hispanic fans for growth, www.espn.com]

Esparza has been involved in charitable work through St. Jude Children's Research Hospital since 2003 [ref: St. Jude radiothon volunteer is taking care of business, www.stjude.org], participating in annual radio fundraising radiothons that have raised about $300,000 every year. He has volunteered in both Chicago and Kentucky, helping coordinate volunteers, acting as the MC for the hospital’s golf outings and supporting on-air fundraising efforts. [ref: Miguel Esparza loves Cubs' Alex Bregman, Edward Cabrera additions, Marquee Sports Network - Home of the Cubs, Bears, Red Stars and Sky]

Liu Hanyuan (Chinese: 刘汉元; born December 1964) is a Chinese billionaire-businessman and is the founder and chairman of Tongwei Group. [ref: Liu Hanyuan, Forbes] He is the National People's Congress deputy and vice chairman of All-China Federation of Industry & Commerce. [ref: 刘汉元, All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce]

As of 2026, Liu has a net worth of US$5.9 billion.

==Early Life==
Liu was born in December 1964 to a peasant family background in Meishan, Sichuan. [ref: 通威40年变迁，如何穿越市场周期？, China Business Journal] He trained at Sichuan Fisheries School where he graduated in 1981, and worked as a technician in a state-run reservoir fishery. At age 19, he started an experimental fish cage initiative, where he developed the "flowing-water cage culture" technique, where he built mesh/metal cages and anchored them in a moving water source. [ref: 刘汉元：从网箱养鱼的年轻人到水产大亨, Yicai] At the time, aquaculture technology in China was limited to raising fish in an open pond, which limited yield based on the available oxygen and food in the water. Liu's development resulted in record yields, and his technique was later promoted nationwide by China's agriculture ministry. His success helped him realize that technique would require specialized feed, which inspired his founding of Sichuan Tongwei Feed Co., Ltd.

=== Founding of Tongwei ===
In 1992, Liu founded the company Sichuan Tongwei Feed Co., Ltd., which is the predecessor company of Tongwei Group. Under Liu's leadership, the company grew into China's largest producer of aquaculture feed. The company went public on the Shanghai Stock exchange in 2004.

=== Diversification into solar energy ===
Starting in 2006, Liu led the company to diversify into high-purity polysilicon production for the solar industry.

Tongwei was a latecomer to the PV industry in China. Liu led the company through a strategy that combined his expertise in aquatic fishing with solar energy. PV power stations were placed over aquaculture ponds to generate electricity while farmers harvested at lower costs with higher efficiency. [ref: 刘汉元"追光"40年创富950亿 通威股份抛650亿扩张欲再创奇迹, Sina Finance]

In 2013, Tongwei acquired LDK Solar Hi-Tech (Hefei) Co, a solar cell and module manufacturing unit from LDK Solar Co. [ref: Poly maker Tongwei acquires cell and module business, pv magazine] [ref: 8.7亿通威收购合肥赛维 布局光伏产业链, China Economic Net] The acquisition meant Tongwei could now manufacture solar cells and modules using its own polysilicon. [ref: 通威布局全产业链 光伏业频现"抄底"并购, China Securities Journal (CNStock)]

In 2019, Liu stepped down from operational leadership roles at the listed subsidiary Tongwei Co., Ltd., while remaining chairman and controlling shareholder of the unlisted parent, Tongwei Group. [ref: Chinese Silicon Giant Tongwei Names Founder's Daughter as New Chair, CEO, Yicai Global]

== Honors ==
In October 2018, Liu was named one of the "100 Outstanding Private Entrepreneurs of the 40 Years of Reform and Opening-up" (改革开放40年百名杰出民营企业家), an honor jointly conferred by central Chinese government and party bodies to mark the fortieth anniversary of China's reform era. [ref: 改革开放40年百名杰出民营企业家名单发布, All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce]

== Personal life ==
Liu is married to Guan Yamei; they have one daughter, Liu Shuqi (born 1989), who has served as chairwoman and chief executive of Tongwei Co., Ltd. since 2023.

== Philanthropy ==
In 2007, Liu established the "Siyuan–Sunshine Plan" with an initial donation of ¥50 million (around US$6.6 million at the time) to fund poverty-alleviation projects built around small-scale solar power, including installations in Sichuan's Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture and in Xinjiang. [ref: 以新质生产力创造新未来——访全国人大代表、通威集团董事局主席刘汉元, The Paper (澎湃新闻)]

Millard House II is an American educator and school administrator who has served as superintendent of the Houston Independent School District in Texas and Prince George's County Public Schools in Maryland. He previously served as director of schools for the Clarksville-Montgomery County School System in Tennessee, chief operating officer of Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools in North Carolina, and deputy superintendent of Tulsa Public Schools in Oklahoma.

== Early life and education ==

House is a native of Tulsa, Oklahoma, and grew up in a family of educators. His father, Millard House Sr., was a Tulsa Public Schools administrator, while his mother worked as a teacher and school counselor. [ref: He's firm, fair and unflappable, colleagues say. Can Millard House conquer Houston ISD?, Houston Chronicle]

House attended Booker T. Washington High School in Tulsa.

He graduated from the University of Montevallo in Alabama in 1995. He later earned a master's degree in school administration from Northeastern State University in Oklahoma and completed the Fisher School Leadership Program at the Haas School of Business at the University of California, Berkeley.

== Career ==

=== Tulsa ===

After graduating from college, House returned to Tulsa and began his education career as a physical education teacher.

After working as a teacher and assistant principal, House became principal of Anderson Elementary School in Tulsa. He later became the founding principal of KIPP Tulsa College Preparatory, a middle school developed through a partnership between Tulsa Public Schools and the Knowledge Is Power Program.

House subsequently moved into the central administration of Tulsa Public Schools, eventually serving as deputy superintendent.

=== Charlotte and Clarksville-Montgomery County ===

In 2012, House joined Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools in North Carolina as chief operating officer. His responsibilities included district operations such as facilities, transportation and security. [ref: Houston ISD trustees name Tennessee educator Millard House II as lone superintendent finalist, Houston Chronicle]

After leaving Charlotte-Mecklenburg Schools, House worked in education leadership development and consulting.

In 2017, House became director of schools for the Clarksville-Montgomery County School System in Tennessee. He led the district until 2021, when he was selected to lead Houston ISD.

=== Houston Independent School District ===

In May 2021, the Houston Independent School District Board of Education selected House as its lone finalist for superintendent. The board formally approved his appointment in June 2021, and he began serving as superintendent on July 1, 2021. [ref: Houston ISD trustees make it official, approve Millard House II as new superintendent, Houston Chronicle]

At the time, HISD enrolled approximately 200,000 students and was the largest school district in Texas. [ref: It's Day 1 for Millard House II, Houston ISD's new superintendent. Plenty of challenges await., Houston Chronicle]

In 2022, House presented a five-year strategic plan addressing areas including equitable access to school resources, teacher compensation, early childhood education, special education services and family engagement. [ref: Houston ISD's equity-based strategic plan calls for teacher raises, librarians at all campuses, Houston Chronicle]

During House's tenure, the number of HISD campuses receiving D or F state accountability ratings declined substantially. [ref: What we know about HISD Superintendent Millard House II now that the TEA has taken over the district, Houston Chronicle]

House's tenure coincided with a long-running dispute over a proposed state takeover of HISD. In March 2023, the Texas Education Agency announced that it would replace the district's elected board with a state-appointed board of managers and appoint a new superintendent.

House left HISD in June 2023 when the state intervention took effect.

=== Prince George's County Public Schools ===

In June 2023, Prince George's County Executive Angela Alsobrooks selected House to lead Prince George's County Public Schools in Maryland. [ref: Prince George's names former Houston superintendent as schools leader, The Washington Post]

House began serving as superintendent on July 1, 2023.

House and the Prince George's County Board of Education reached a mutual separation agreement in June 2025. [ref: Prince George's Schools superintendent stepping down, interim is named, The Washington Post]

His departure followed disputes involving district leadership and a no-confidence vote conducted by the county teachers union.

=== Region 4 Education Service Center ===

In 2026, House joined Region 4 Education Service Center in Houston as Director of Strategic Initiatives Services. [ref: Staff Directory, Region 4 Education Service Center]

Stark Future S.L. is a Spanish manufacturer of high-performance electric motorcycles headquartered in Sant Boi de Llobregat, near Barcelona. Founded in 2019 by Swedish entrepreneur Anton Wass and engineer Paul Soucy, the company is best known for the Stark VARG platform, a family of electric motocross, enduro and supermoto motorcycles. [ref: Spanish electric motorcycle company revolutionises motocross and mobility, European Investment Bank]

In 2025 the company reported its first profitable quarter and full-year revenue of €115 million, and in March 2026 it became the first electric manufacturer to win an FIM world championship title when it secured the Manufacturers' title in the FIM SuperEnduro World Championship.

== History ==

=== Founding (2019–2021) ===
Anton Wass, who grew up near Stockholm, had earlier co-founded the motorcycle parts e-commerce group Pierce AB, owner of the online retailer 24MX. [ref: A Peek Behind the Golden Ring: Visiting Stark Future Headquarters, Motorcycle.com] He founded Stark Future in Barcelona in 2019 with the stated aim of building electric motorcycles that outperform the best combustion-engined competitors rather than asking riders to compromise for sustainability. The company name derives from the Swedish word stark ("strong"); varg is Swedish for "wolf".

The Stark VARG was unveiled on 14 December 2021 as an electric motocross bike producing up to 80 hp, a figure the company claimed made it the most powerful production motocross motorcycle available. [ref: Stark Varg: This electric motocross bike from Sweden throws shade at its gas-powered competition, Notebookcheck] Wass later described the launch as the most successful of any motorcycle company in history.

=== Production ramp and Eicher investment (2022–2023) ===
Deliveries were originally scheduled for September 2022 but were delayed by production and quality problems; the company reportedly rejected roughly 90% of an initial batch of 1,000 frames from a supplier, and the first VARG MX customer units were delivered in May 2023.

On 29 December 2022 Eicher Motors, the Indian parent company of Royal Enfield, agreed to invest €50 million for an approximately 10.35% stake in Stark Future, taking a board seat and entering a technical collaboration agreement covering research and development, technology sharing and manufacturing. [ref: Eicher Motors to invest over Rs 440 cr in electric bike firm Stark Future, Business Standard] [ref: Eicher Motors Announces Strategic Investment in Stark Future, Cycle News] In June 2023 the company signed a €20 million loan with Banco Santander to expand production.

=== Expansion and profitability (2024–2025) ===
In September 2024 the European Investment Bank signed a €40 million credit facility with Stark Future, backed by the EU's InvestEU programme, to fund research, development and the scale-up of manufacturing capacity in Sant Boi de Llobregat over 2024–2027. [ref: Spain: EIB and Stark Future sign a €40 million loan to invest in innovation and new solutions for the electric motorcycle sector, European Investment Bank] [ref: Barcelona-based electric motorbike company Stark Future secures €40M from EIB, Silicon Canals] The street-legal VARG EX enduro model was launched in December 2024.

In April 2025 the company reported its first profitable month, with monthly revenue of €18.3 million and EBITDA of €2.8 million. [ref: Stark Future Achieves Record Profitability for All-Electric Motorcycle Manufacturer, RideApart] On 15 July 2025 Stark Future announced its first profitable quarter, reporting Q2 2025 revenue of €47 million and EBITDA of €4.5 million, with revenue more than doubling year on year; the company described itself as the fastest electric vehicle manufacturer to reach profitability. [ref: Stark Future Smashes EV Profitability Records in Q2 to Challenge Legacy Powersports, Cycle News] [ref: This electric motorcycle company just did what no one else could, Electrek] Electrek noted that the "largest electric-only motorcycle manufacturer" claim excludes large Asian scooter-focused makers such as Yadea and NIU.

A further equity round in 2025, drawn mainly from existing shareholders together with new investors connected to the MotoGP paddock, took total capital contributions past €100 million. [ref: Stark Future exceeds €100 million in total capital contributions with the latest equity investment round, The Pack] In October 2025 the company launched its third model, the road-legal VARG SM supermoto.

For the full year 2025 Stark Future reported revenue of €115 million, up 77% year on year, with fourth-quarter growth of 97% and profitability in five of the final nine months; the company said it had taken more than 3% of the global enduro segment within a year and around 50% of the enduro market in Germany. [ref: Stark Future Posts Record Growth and Profitability Accelerating Path to Global Scale, Cycle News] Revenue roughly tripled year on year in the first quarter of 2026. [ref: This EV Dirt Bike Startup Just Tripled Revenue, And Went Profitable, RideApart]

Miljan Krpić (Serbian Cyrillic: Миљан Крпић; born 3 July 2003) is a Serbian professional footballer who plays primarily as a centre-back for Nemzeti Bajnokság I club ETO FC Győr, where he has served as captain. He was part of the ETO side that won the 2025–26 Nemzeti Bajnokság I. [ref: „Ez egy újabb lehetőség, hogy bizonyítsuk, hogy képesek vagyunk újra bajnokságot nyerni” – az ETO csapatkapitánya bizakodva várja a Fradi elleni meccset, 24.hu]

== Club career ==
Krpić began playing football with Hajduk Kula, where he was a youth teammate of Miloš Kerkez. He subsequently spent time in the youth systems of TSC Bačka Topola and Hungary's Puskás Akadémia. [ref: Együtt fociztak gyerekként – Az ETO erőssége Kerkez nyomdokán járna a magyar válogatottban, Kisalföld] He started as a defensive midfielder before moving to centre-back. [ref: Mađari bi da nam ga "ukradu", a on sanja Partizan, B92.sport]

Krpić began his senior career with TSC under coach Žarko Lazetić. He played in the 2022–23 Serbian SuperLiga season, when TSC finished second, and later joined Voždovac. Following Voždovac's relegation from the SuperLiga, he moved to newly promoted ETO FC Győr in the summer of 2024.

Krpić initially had a limited role at ETO. During the winter preparation period of the 2024–25 season, coach Balázs Borbély reorganized the defence and used Krpić at centre-back. By the spring he had become a regular starter; Kisalföld described him as one of the club's leading players and noted his composure and ability to carry the ball out of defence. He suffered an ankle-ligament injury during a UEFA Conference League qualifying match against Rapid Wien in 2025 and was sidelined for about two months.

ETO won the 2025–26 Hungarian league title. In 2026, after the departure of Milán Vitális, Krpić took over as team captain. An independent Kisalföld match report also recorded him wearing the armband in ETO's 4–0 league win over Nyíregyháza on 2 August 2026. [ref: Lőttek, láttak, győztek – négygólos győzelemmel nyitott otthonában az ETO, Kisalföld]

== International eligibility ==
Krpić holds Serbian and Hungarian citizenship. In March 2026, Kisalföld examined why he had not been selected for Hungary despite public speculation about a call-up. The newspaper reported that his Hungarian ancestry was too distant to meet FIFA's ancestry requirement and that his periods of residence in Hungary had not been continuous. Under the residency route described by the newspaper, his five-year qualifying period restarted when he joined ETO in 2024, making 2029 the earliest point at which he could become eligible to represent Hungary. [ref: Miért nem játszhat Miljan Krpic a magyar válogatottban?, Kisalföld]

Rossin or Rossin Bicycles was the manufacturer of road-racing bicycles beginning in 1974 and was known for new racing and time trial bicycle designs.

== History ==
Vittorio Ghezzi, Giuseppe Ghezzi, Domenico Garbelli, and Alberto Inzaghi in 1973 recruited Mario Rossin to join in creating a new company to manufacture competitive bikes to supply their Italian amateur racing teams. [ref: Rossin Brand History, Registro Storico Cicli] [ref: Rossin Bikes, The Spoken]

Mario Rossin was formerly a bicycle racer and had served as chief builder at Colnago bicycles. His work with fitting top racers at Colnago including Eddy Merckx built his reputation for skilled craftsmanship.

The original five-member partnership reduced to Domenico Garbelli and Mario Rossin by 1980. Rossin acquired the Pogliaghi brand in November 1983 from Sante Pogliaghi when he retired, bringing the Pogliaghi production and Sante's expertise including road, track and tandem bike designs to the Rossin factory. [ref: Pogliaghi Super Record SLX, Bicycle Guide]
Later still, Alcide Basso of Basso Bikes bought the Poglaighi brand and remaining Pogliaghi production from Rossin in November 1989. [ref: Red-Hot Italian Iron, Bicycle Guide]

Rossin incorporated aerodynamic features into frame designs, developed new specialty time trial bikes designs such as the Futura CX, introduced the first disk wheels in 1983 and was among the first to add an onboard computer.
[ref: The High-tech Bicycle, Harper & Row]
[ref: Italian Racing Bicycles: The People, The Products, The Passion, Velo Press]
[ref: 1001 Bicycles to Dream of Riding, Universe Pub]
[ref: Cars, Trains, Ships, And Planes, A Visual Encyclopedia of Every Vehicle, DK Publishing]

In 1992 Rossin SRL was acquired by FINROSS SRL. GRUPPO BICI obtained the Rossin brand by 2000. Master frame builder Mario Rossin passed away in 2018. [ref: Cycling: Cavenago has said goodbye to Mario Rossin, bicycle manufacturer and sportsman, Cavenago Di Brianza, November 15, 2018]

==Trademark==
The Rossin brand logo design was influenced by the label on Royal-Cola bottles and by the wording on Rossignol skis. Rossingnol protested, so the logo design was changed in 1977. [ref: Rossin Brand History, Registro Storico Cicli]

Rossin advertising included the slogan "Biciclette per vincere" or "Bicycles to Win."

The trademark consists of the word "ROSSIN" in stylized characters, or two polygons, one inside each other, containing an artistic letter "R". [ref: Global Brand Database, WIPO]

==Production overview==
Rossin desiged and produced in Italy traditional steel racing bicycles, time trial bicycles specialized for triathlons and later, carbon fiber racing bicycles. [ref: The Bicycle Book-The Definitive Visual History, DK-Penguin Random House] Rossin was also the first Italian bicycle brand to produce in 1984 a distinct mountain bike model.

GRUPPO BICI reintroduced Rossin bicycles with a line-up of new design carbon fiber road bikes, along with traditional steel road bike frames and mountain bikes in 2011. The last Rossin bicycles were produced between 2017-2019.

Rossin bikes were used by racing champions including De Vlaeminck, Van Poppel, Berzin, Ugrumov, Virenque, Argentin, Kelly, and Kuiper.
