Draft: SCADS (Shipborne Containerized Air Defense System)

Draft text:
SCADS, or Shipborne Containerized Air Defense Systems, are a class of air defense systems. Typically composed of small, mobile modules of radar, command, and fire elements disguised within international standard intermodal containers, they are intended to be placed upon merchant ships being urgently pressed into military service at the outbreak of a conflict.

== Examples ==
After the conclusion of Falklands War in 1982, the British government investigated a SCAD system for their ships. The dramatic loss of the unarmed SS Atlantic Conveyer to Argentine Exocets demonstrated the need for self defense systems upon the ships of the STUFTS (Ships Taken Up From Trade) program. The British SCADS system was split between two concepts; SCADS A, which was to use a set of containers to convert the merchant ships to small anti submarine aircraft carriers (Similar to the join Anglo-American Arapaho Containerized Aircraft Handling System), and SCADS B, which would integrate vertical launch anti air and anti submarine systems, such as Seawolf and Ikara, along with ECM, chaff, and flares. [ref: SCADS A AND B - TWO VERSIONS FOR THE ASSIGNMENT OF PART OF THE LOAD TO WEAPONS SYSTEMS ON CONTAINERSHIPS, British Maritime Technology] [ref: This Containerized Missile Launcher Could Give Almost Any Ship Short-Range Air Defenses, The War Zone]

In the early 2000s, the United States Navy investigated the Affordable Weapon System, a containerized cruise missile similar to a miniaturized Tomahawk to be launched from standardized containers, however the project seems to have been cancelled during the budget cuts and cancellations of 2007-2008 as any information on the project past that point is scarce. [ref: ONR/Titan Affordable Weapon, www.designation-systems.net]

In early 2019, MBDA revealed SPIMM (Self-Protection Integrated Mistral Module), a small containerized system using their Mistral heat seeking MANPAD, which was derived from the existing SIMBAD-RC naval mounting for the missile. SPIMM is intended to be used aboard auxiliary ships. SPIMM will carry two missiles read for immediate fire, along with four more in a storage container which can be used to rearm the module. The system will be able to track and fire upon targets in any direction using 360 degree panoramic infrared cameras. Designed to fit within a 10 foot intermodal container, SPIMM only needs a place to be mounted and an electrical connection to the host ship to operate. The Mistral missile's 4 mile range limits its capabilities, however the system adds a useful layer of defense to otherwise large, undefended targets. It has the ability to be used against aerial or surface targets. MBDA is also investigating the possibility of using SPIMM in land mountings.

In October of 2020, at the Euronaval 2020 expo, Danish defense manufacturer SH Defence revealed their modular shipborne equipment system, The Cube. The Cube is intended to use more than 128 interchangeable modules to allow ships with the system to engage in air, surface, and submarine warfare, or perform other tasks such as search and rescue or delivering humanitarian aid. The system requires internal rails running through spaces within a ship to move the modules through the hull of a ship to perform their missions from various spaces. [ref: Euronaval Video: SH Defence Unveils Cutting Edge Equipment 'The Cube', Naval News] [ref: The Cube – SH Defence]

In 2023, the United States Navy test fired an RIM-174/SM-6 surface to air missile from a Mark 70 Payload Delivery System mounted on the flight deck of the Independence class littoral combat ship USS Savannah, significantly advancing the firepower of the littoral combat ships, which have been criticized for lacking in firepower. The Mark 70 system is also able to fire Tomahawk cruise missiles and Patriot PAC-3 land based surface to air missiles [ref: PAC-3 MSE launched from virtual Aegis ship hits cruise missile target, Defense News]. The Navy had previously used the Mark 70 system to fire another RIM-174/SM-6 from the unmanned vessel USV Ranger [ref: This "Ghost Fleet" Ship Firing An SM-6 Missile From A Modular Launcher Is A Glimpse Of The Future, TWZ]. The Mark 70 system is a naval variant of the US Army's Typhon Missile System, both of which are descended from the navy's Mark 41 Vertical Launch System [ref: SM-6 Missile Fired From Littoral Combat Ship, TWZ].

Khalid bin Abdullah bin Saidan is a Saudi real estate executive and civil engineer. He serves as Executive Director of Bin Saedan Real Estate Services and is a member of the boards of Abdullah Mohammed Bin Saedan & Sons Real Estate Company and Prime Estates.

== Education ==
Bin Saidan studied civil engineering at Leeds Beckett University in the United Kingdom, graduating in 2018. He later earned a master's degree in International Business Management with Project Management from Kingston University London in 2020. [ref: From Engineering to Real Estate: Khalid bin Abdullah bin Saidan on a Changing Saudi Property Market, Layali Al Riyadh]

== Career ==
Bin Saidan began his professional career within the Bin Saidan family's real estate businesses. His professional experience has included corporate operations, project management and real estate services.
He worked in project management at Affordable House Company before moving into senior leadership at Bin Saedan Real Estate Services. The company operates in areas including real estate marketing, brokerage, property management and real estate auctions. [ref: From Engineering to Real Estate: Khalid bin Abdullah bin Saidan on a Changing Saudi Property Market, Layali Al Riyadh]
Bin Saidan also serves as a member of the board of directors of Abdullah Mohammed Bin Saedan & Sons Real Estate Company and Prime Estates. [ref: About Us, Prime Estates] [ref: من نحن, شركة عبدالله محمد بن سعيدان وأولاده العقارية]

== Views on the Saudi real estate market ==
Bin Saidan has described the Saudi real estate market as becoming increasingly specialized, with greater emphasis on professional services, transparency, technology and data. He has also said that buyers and investors have become more informed in evaluating property and increasingly consider factors beyond the property itself, including accessibility, services, operating costs and long-term value. [ref: مدينة برايم الصناعية ترسم ملامح وجهة صناعية ولوجستية متكاملة على مساحة مليوني متر مربع جنوب الرياض, صحيفة المؤشر الاقتصادي]

Discussing his approach to real estate development, Bin Saidan has said that his education in civil engineering gave him a technical and analytical perspective, while his postgraduate studies in international business and project management provided a broader commercial and organizational perspective. [ref: Building on a Saudi Real Estate Legacy: A Conversation with Khalid Bin Seaidan, TechNewsArabia]

Draft text:
Chhabilal Rijal is a Nepali civil servant who served as the Chief District Officer (CDO) of Kathmandu District. He was Kathmandu's chief district officer during the 2025 Nepalese Gen Z protests in September 2025. [ref: Police arrest former Kathmandu CDO Chhabilal Rijal, The Kathmandu Post]

==Chief District Officer of Kathmandu==
Rijal served as Chief District Officer of Kathmandu during the Gen Z protests of 8 and 9 September 2025.. The protests began amid opposition to the government's ban on several social media platforms and wider concerns about corruption and governance. [ref: Nepal lifts social media ban after anti-corruption protests leave 19 dead, curfew imposed, Reuters]

On 8 September 2025, authorities imposed a curfew in parts of Kathmandu after clashes between protesters and security forces. Rijal was serving as Kathmandu's district administrator at the time. [ref: Curfew imposed in New Baneshwar area after Gen Z protesters break into restricted area, The Kathmandu Post]

On 9 September, an indefinite curfew was imposed in Kathmandu as the protests and unrest continued. [ref: Nepal lifts social media ban after anti-corruption protests leave 19 dead, curfew imposed, Reuters]

==Investigation and arrest==
Following the September 2025 protests, a government-appointed inquiry commission investigated the events and the response of government officials and security forces. The commission's recommendations included action against Rijal in connection with the handling of the protests. [ref: Former Kathmandu CDO Chhabi Rijal arrested, Setopati]

On 31 March 2026, police arrested Rijal in Kathmandu in connection with the implementation of the inquiry report concerning the Gen Z protests. He was detained from his residence in Baneshwar by a team from the Kathmandu Valley Crime Investigation Office. [ref: Police arrest former Kathmandu CDO Chhabilal Rijal, The Kathmandu Post]

The arrest was linked to allegations of negligence in the handling of the protests. Reporting on the inquiry commission said it recommended investigation and prosecution under provisions concerning causing death through negligent acts. [ref: Former Kathmandu CDO Chhabi Rijal arrested, Setopati]

==References==

Draft: Francesca Cordelia Merlan

Draft text:
Francesca Cordelia Merlan is an American-born Australian anthropologist whose research focuses on Indigenous-settler relations [ref: Dynamics of difference in Australia: indigenous past and present in a settler country, by Merlan, Francesca, HAL (Le Centre pour la Communication Scientifique Directe)], social transformation, land claims, gender, and linguistic documentation. [ref: Settlers and their land rights: Francesca Merlan, ‘Anthropology and change over the ‘land rights era’: Towards treaties?’ Australian Journal of Anthropology, 2025, settler colonial studies blog] [ref: Francesca Merlan, "Dynamics of Difference in Australia: Indigenous Past and Present in a Settler Country" (U Pennsylvania Press, 2018), New Books Network] in northern Australia [ref: ], Papua New Guinea [ref: Ku Waru: Language and segmentary politics in the western Nebilyer Valley, Papua New Guinea. By Francesca Merlan and Alan Rumsey. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1991. Pp. xviii, 387. Cloth $59.50., Language], and Germany. She is professor emeritus of Anthropology at the Australian National University (ANU) and Fellow of the Academy of the Social Sciences in Australia. [ref: ] In 2003 she was awarded the Centenary Medal from Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, Australia. [ref: ]

== Education and career ==
She completed her MA and PhD in anthropology at the University of New Mexico in 1975, conducting doctoral research on Native American and settler communities in the North American Plains. [ref: Moscow High School... Class of 1965, Francesca Merlan, www.mhs1965.com]

In 1976, Merlan was awarded a research grant from the Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies, bringing her to northern Australia for fieldwork that lasted from 1976 to 1979.

She joined the Australian National University as Professor of Anthropology in 1995 and has since been appointed professor emeritus. [ref: ] She has held a visiting fellowship at the Institute of Advanced Study, Princeton (2015–16). [ref: ]

== Scholarly works ==
Merlan's research focuses three geographic regions. In northern Australia, she has investigated the effects of Aboriginal people's movement into regional towns; Indigenous-settler relations [ref: Relative Autonomy Revisited: Reply to Francesca Merlan, American Anthropologist]; Aboriginal languages, socio-cultural significance and land claims. [ref: Power and Recognition: Australia's Indigenous People Today, University of Pennsylvania Press] Her book Caging the Rainbow: Places, Politics and Aborigines in a North Australian Town (1998), which examined the lives of Aboriginal people in Katherine, Northern Territory.

Her later book Dynamics of Difference in Australia: Indigenous Past and Present in a Settler Country (2018) investigated relations between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians from first contact to the present. [ref: Merlan, Francesca. 2018. Dynamics of difference in Australia: indigenous past and present in a settler country. Philadelphia, PA: University of Pennsylvania Press. 320 pp. Hb.: US$59.95. ISBN: 9780812250008., Social Anthropology] [ref: ]

Her co-authored work Ku Waru: Language and Segmentary Politics in the Western Nebilyer Valley, Papua New Guinea (1991) examined segmentary sociality, language, and politics. [ref: Gender as a Dimension in Changing Hegemonies, History of Anthropology Review] [ref: Children's Language Learning and the Making of Human Lifeworlds, School of Culture, History & Language]

Her other works include Mangarayi (1982), Ngalakan Grammar, Texts, and Vocabulary (1983) and A Grammar of Wardaman (1993). [ref: Review of A Grammar of Wardaman, a Language of the Northern Territory of Australia, Language]

==References==

Supratit Banerjee (born 23 February 2014) is an English chess player who holds the title of International Master (IM). He represented Scotland in international competition until February 2024, when he transferred to England.

In August 2026, at the age of 12, Banerjee completed his third IM norm and met the accompanying rating requirement, making him the youngest International Master in the United Kingdom. [ref: Chess prodigy Supratit Banerjee becomes Britain's youngest-ever International Master, ChessBase India] [ref: Genius Sutton boy, 12, becomes youngest Brit to get chess master title despite 'limited coaching', MyLondon]

== Early life and chess career ==
Banerjee began playing chess in Scotland in 2020, at the age of six, and continued with online chess lessons and inter-club matches. [ref: Supratit Banerjee, ChessKid] His first international tournament was the 2021 European Youth Chess Championship, where he represented Scotland in the Under-8 category. [ref: European Youth Chess Championship 2021 – Open 08, Chess-Results.com]

At the 2022 British Under-8 Championship, Banerjee won the title with a score of 6/7. [ref: Prizewinners' list 2022, British Chess Championships] Later that year, he also won the Under-8 section of the Delancey UK Schools' Chess Challenge Terafinal, scoring 10/11 to take first place on tiebreak. [ref: Terafinal 2022, Delancey UK Schools' Chess Challenge]

In 2023, Banerjee was named Chess Maestro at the BYITC Inspire Awards, recognising his early chess achievements. [ref: Sport Category Winners of BYITC Inspire Award 2023, British Youth International College] [ref: Edinburgh youngsters honoured at Holyrood in inaugural Inspire Awards, The NEN – North Edinburgh News] He was part of the Scotland team that won the Glorney Cup in 2023, the country's first victory in the event in 58 years. [ref: Scotland Win Glorney Cup, Chess Scotland] He was awarded the Candidate Master (CM) title that year. [ref: A New Titled Player – Supratit Banerjee, Chess Scotland]

Banerjee transferred his FIDE federation from Scotland to England in February 2024. [ref: FIDE federation transfer list 2024, FIDE] He played club chess for Coulsdon Chess Academy before joining Kingston Chess Club. [ref: David Maycock (Kingston) v Supratit Banerjee (Coulsdon), Kingston Chess Club] [ref: Supratit Banerjee v Simon Williams, Kingston Chess Club] In October 2024, he won the Under-10 section of the Delancey UK Schools' Chess Challenge Terafinal, scoring 9.5/11. [ref: 2024 Results, Delancey UK Schools' Chess Challenge] He plays for CSC/Kingston, the club's combined team in the 4NCL, and was a member of the squad promoted to the league's first division for the 2024–25 season. A review of that season named him the team's most valuable contributor. [ref: Measuring how individuals contribute to a team, Kingston Chess Club]

Banerjee received the FIDE Master (FM) title in 2025, at the age of 11. [ref: Banerjee, Supratit – FIDE Chess Profile, FIDE]

At the 2025 UK Chess Blitz Championship final, Banerjee qualified through a regional heat and finished eighth out of 16 players, in a field that included grandmasters, international masters and FIDE masters. [ref: Year 7 Student Shines at UK Chess Blitz Final, Sutton Grammar School]

At the 2026 British Rapid Championship in March, he finished joint third on points. [ref: Outstanding chess success for Supratit, Sutton Grammar School] Following his results in 4NCL matches, he was featured in a Financial Times article by Leonard Barden.

In 2026, he was invited through the English Chess Federation to training camps run by the Kasparov Chess Foundation in Munich and Zagreb, where he met Garry Kasparov. He also defeated Grandmaster Artem Uskov at the Menorca Chess Open. [ref: Supratit Banerjee: UK's Youngest International Master at 12, The Global Indian]

== International Master title ==
Banerjee earned his three IM norms between 2025 and 2026. The first came at the 2025 British Chess Championship in Liverpool, at the age of 11, where he scored 6/9. [ref: Supratit Banerjee Becomes UK's Youngest International Master at 12, ChessEver] [ref: 2025 Prizewinners, British Chess Championships] [ref: Michael Adams wins his ninth British Chess Championship; Yao and Mirzoeva tie for Women's title, FIDE] The second came in July 2026 at an IM norm tournament in Sheffield, where he scored 6.5/9 and finished joint first. [ref: Supratit Continues Remarkable Rise, Sutton Grammar School] The third came at the 2026 British Chess Championship in Coventry, where he scored 6/9 with a performance rating of 2503. Two days later, at the Stockholm GM Norm Invitation in Sweden, he crossed the 2400 FIDE rating threshold required for the title. Dr. Allison Matulli, a native of Trinidad and Tobago, is a Florida-based children's author, educator, legal scholar and First Amendment advocate. [ref: Dr. Allison Matulli, PEN America] She is the author of Your Freedom, Your Power: A Kid's Guide to the First Amendment (2023), published by Running Press Kids/Hachette Book Group, a book that highlights the true stories of brave kids that sparked change in their communities and left their mark on the legal history of the United States of America, as well as guiding young readers to be active and conscious citizens. [ref: Allison Matulli, Hachette Book Group] Her new Penguin RISE picture book, WE ARE FREE (September 2026), takes this mission a step further and aims to introduce children ages 0 to 5 to their First Freedoms [ref: ]

Dr.Matulli is the founder and executive director of The Little Lawyers, an award-winning organization that focuses on empowering children through the understanding of their constitutional rights, civic engagement and social justice. [ref: HOME, The Little Lawyers] As a former school administrator and first-ever Florida International University's Fulbright Global Scholar, she is now a fellow for the First Amendment at the Freedom Forum, where she shares her expertise on student free expression and digital speech rights. [ref: Dr. Allison Matulli, PEN America]

Allison Matulli is a graduate of the civic legacy of Howard University School of Law and works as a Pre-Law Technical Writing lecturer at the same institution, where she was elected for the first faculty cohort of the Google Career Launchpad Generative AI Leader Certification Program. [ref: ] Dr. Matulli has recently published her doctoral dissertation Free Speech and Digital Citizenship: A Qualitative Case Study with St. Thomas University, and is affiliate faculty at FIU's Maurice A.Ferre Institute for Civic Leadership. Her research about freedom of expression expands internationally, including landmark work in Colombia, Italy and Trinidad and Tobago. [ref: ]

Her advocacy work have led her to connect with families and young people as a keynote speaker at events and book readings, partnering with organizations like PEN America. [ref: Your Freedom, Your Power Hour! A Family Day of Stories & Creativity, PEN America] In 2023, Matulli was named one of Miami's most prominent and influential black women in business and industry by Legacy Magazine, [ref: Legacy Magazine Archives, M•I•A Media Group] and in 2024 one of South Florida's most prominent and influential black business leaders by the Miami Media Group. [ref: Archives, M•I•A Media Group]

Priyalal Sirisena (born 25 May 1979) is a Sri Lankan attorney-at-law and author who practices constitutional law and fundamental rights litigation in Sri Lanka. [ref: Lawyer sues cops for stifling his professional rights, Daily Mirror] In addition to his legal practice, he is a novelist whose literary work was shortlisted for the Swarna Pusthaka Awards. [ref: Swarna Pusthaka Awards 2025: Shortlisted Novels Announced, The Island]

== Early life and education ==
Sirisena was born in Kurunegala, Sri Lanka. He studied law at the University of Colombo, graduating with a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) in 2004, and was subsequently admitted to the bar as an Attorney-at-Law of the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka. He later completed a Master of Laws (LL.M.) at the same university.

== Legal career and human rights petitions ==
Sirisena has been involved in constitutional law and human rights cases in Sri Lanka. In June 2018, he filed a Fundamental Rights petition in the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka against senior police officers, alleging interference with his professional duties and rights as a legal counsel.

In May 2023, Sirisena filed formal complaints regarding intimidation and threats related to his ongoing legal proceedings in Kurunegala, which received coverage in national print media. [ref: 'Withdraw case or face the consequences': Lawyer files complaint, The Island] He has also represented clients in public interest litigations concerning administrative oversight and police accountability.

== Literary career ==
Sirisena is also active in Sinhala literature. He authored the Sinhala novel Deyyange Atha (The Elephant of the Gods). In 2025, the novel gained critical recognition and was selected among the shortlisted nominees for the prestigious Swarna Pusthaka Awards, one of Sri Lanka's primary literary honors for novel writing. [ref: Contemporary Sinhala Literature and the Swarna Pusthaka Nominees, Ceylon Today]

The Last Message is a 2026 Ukrainian documentary film directed by Andrii Voloshyn and Oleksii Liebiediev. The film follows Ukrainian-American singer and activist Kelsie Kimberlin as she travels to Ukraine following the death of her 21-year-old cousin, Andrii Rachok, during the Russian invasion of Ukraine. [ref: "The Last Message" Premieres in New York: A Personal Tragedy Becomes a Demand for Justice, EMPR]

In 2026, the film was one of eight films in Ukraine's national selection process for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards. [ref: Після продовження відбору вісім українських фільмів претендують на Оскар 2027, Suspilne Culture]

== Synopsis ==
The documentary follows Kimberlin's journey to Ukraine as she seeks to understand the circumstances surrounding the death of her cousin Andrii Rachok. During her journey, she meets Ukrainian soldiers, journalists, witnesses and civilians affected by the war.

The film develops from Kimberlin's personal search for answers into a broader examination of the effects of the Russian invasion of Ukraine and questions of accountability for the war.

== Production ==
The Last Message was directed by Andrii Voloshyn and Oleksii Liebiediev. Marharyta Vlasova is credited as writer and Andrii Samerkhanov as producer. The documentary was completed on January 10, 2026, and has a running time of 1 hour, 27 minutes and 19 seconds. It was filmed in Ukraine and is in English. [ref: The Last Message, FilmFreeway]

== Festival screenings and awards ==
In February 2026, The Last Message won Best Documentary Feature at the World Film Festival in Cannes. The festival lists the film as a Ukrainian production directed by Andrii Voloshyn and Oleksii Liebiediev. [ref: Winners Février 2026, World Film Festival in Cannes]

The film was a finalist in the Documentary Feature category of the 2026 Critics Society Awards. [ref: Critics Society Awards 2026 – Film Festival Results, Critics Society Awards]

The film was also selected in the Best Feature Documentary Film category at the Giraffe International Film Festival. [ref: Official Selections March – May 2026, Giraffe International Film Festival]

In August 2026, The Last Message was screened in New York as part of the Chain NYC Film Festival.

== Ukrainian Oscar selection ==
In August 2026, The Last Message was submitted to the Ukrainian Oscar Committee for consideration in Ukraine's national selection for the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards. [ref: Україна визначить фільм, який представить країну на 99-й премії «Оскар», Ukrainian State Film Agency]

Following an extension of the submission period, the Ukrainian Oscar Committee received eight eligible submissions. The Last Message remained among the eight films under consideration.

Dr. Ir. Justian Suhandinata, SE (20 November 1946 – 4 November 2022) was an Indonesian badminton administrator, businessman, and author. He held the position of Vice President of the International Badminton Federation (IBF), now known as the Badminton World Federation, across multiple terms from 1992 to 2002. In 2017, he became the tenth person in history — and the only Indonesian — to receive the Badminton World Federation Honorary Life Vice President award. [ref: https://bwfbadminton.com/news-single/2022/11/06/bwf-mourns-passing-of-justian-suhandinata Badminton World Federation, "BWF Mourns Passing of Justian Suhandinata", 6 November 2022] He is also credited with laying the groundwork for what became the Badminton World Federation World Junior Championships. [ref: https://www.antaranews.com/berita/3224965/justian-suhandinata-seorang-organisator-bulu-tangkis-kelas-dunia ANTARA News, "Justian Suhandinata, Organisator Bulu Tangkis Kelas Dunia", 2022]

== Early Life and Family ==

Justian Suhandinata was born on 20 November 1946 in Bandung, West Java. He was one of four sons of Suharso Suhandinata and his wife Sri Pandaliana (also known as Phan Tjoe Lian), who married in Bandung in 1941. [ref: [https://validnews.id/kultura/Suharso-Suhandinata--Diplomat-Pemersatu-Bulu-Tangkis-Dunia---cWD ValidNews, "Suharso Suhandinata, Diplomat Pemersatu Bulu Tangkis Dunia", 3 December 2018]] Suharso, together with Dick Sudirman, was instrumental in uniting the world's divided badminton bodies into a single organisation — a process that culminated in a landmark meeting in Tokyo in 1981. [ref: [https://www.kompas.com/badminton/read/2022/11/05/15000088/profil-justian-suhandinata-tokoh-bulu-tangkis-yang-bergelar-doktor-dari Kompas.com, "Profil Justian Suhandinata", 5 November 2022]]

He married Poppy Tumengkol, who represented Indonesia in the Uber Cup in 1969 and 1972. They had four children and seven grandchildren. [ref: https://golfmagz.id/dr-ir-justian-suhandinata-se/ GolfMagz, "Dr. Ir. Justian Suhandinata SE"]

== Education ==

Justian earned a degree in Engineering (Ir.) and a degree in Economics (SE) from Indonesian universities. He later completed a doctorate (Dr.) at Washington International University in Pennsylvania, United States, graduating in September 2002. [ref: https://golfmagz.id/dr-ir-justian-suhandinata-se/ GolfMagz, "Dr. Ir. Justian Suhandinata SE"]

== Badminton Playing Career ==

Justian took up badminton in 1957 and joined PB Tangkas as a club member the following year. [ref: https://www.antaranews.com/berita/3224965/justian-suhandinata-seorang-organisator-bulu-tangkis-kelas-dunia ANTARA News, "Justian Suhandinata, Organisator Bulu Tangkis Kelas Dunia", 2022] In 1964, he won the junior championship of DKI Jakarta and was subsequently selected for the national training centre (Pelatnas) of the Indonesian Badminton Association (PBSI). He was named to the Thomas Cup shadow squad in 1967 and represented DKI Jakarta at the Pekan Olahraga Nasional (National Sports Week) in Surabaya in 1969. [ref: https://www.kompas.com/badminton/read/2022/11/05/15000088/profil-justian-suhandinata-tokoh-bulu-tangkis-yang-bergelar-doktor-dari Kompas.com, "Profil Justian Suhandinata", 5 November 2022]

== Administrative Career ==

=== Domestic (PBSI) ===

Justian began his administrative work as Secretary of PB Tangkas. He progressed through PBSI's regional structure, serving as Head of Development and later Chairman of PBSI South Jakarta, before becoming Provincial Chairman of PBSI DKI Jakarta. At the national level, he served as Head of the Organisation Division of PP PBSI from 1985 to 1989, and as Vice Chairman General of PP PBSI from 1986. He later served as Secretary of the PP PBSI Supervisory Board from 1997 to 2001, and remained on the PP PBSI Advisory Board until his death. [ref: https://www.antaranews.com/berita/3224965/justian-suhandinata-seorang-organisator-bulu-tangkis-kelas-dunia ANTARA News, "Justian Suhandinata, Organisator Bulu Tangkis Kelas Dunia", 2022] He served as Chairman of PB Tangkas until 2022. [ref: https://bwfbadminton.com/news-single/2022/11/06/bwf-mourns-passing-of-justian-suhandinata Badminton World Federation, "BWF Mourns Passing of Justian Suhandinata", 6 November 2022]

=== International (IBF/Badminton World Federation) ===

Justian first joined the International Badminton Federation (IBF) as a Council Member in 1986. [ref: https://www.kompas.com/badminton/read/2022/11/05/15000088/profil-justian-suhandinata-tokoh-bulu-tangkis-yang-bergelar-doktor-dari Kompas.com, "Profil Justian Suhandinata", 5 November 2022] He went on to serve as Vice President of the IBF — later renamed the Badminton World Federation — across three consecutive terms: 1993–1995, 1996–1999, and 1999–2001. [ref: https://www.antaranews.com/berita/3224965/justian-suhandinata-seorang-organisator-bulu-tangkis-kelas-dunia ANTARA News, "Justian Suhandinata, Organisator Bulu Tangkis Kelas Dunia", 2022] During this period he also chaired the Development Committee during the establishment of the Badminton World Federation World Academy. He remained a Badminton World Federation Council Member until his passing. [ref: https://bwfbadminton.com/news-single/2022/11/06/bwf-mourns-passing-of-justian-suhandinata Badminton World Federation, "BWF Mourns Passing of Justian Suhandinata", 6 November 2022]

Draft: 1879–80 Birmingham Senior Cup

Draft text:
The 1879–80 Birmingham Senior Cup was the fourth season of the oldest county cup competition still active and the third oldest in the world overall. [ref: Birmingham County FA Cups, BCFA] [ref: The History of the Birmingham Senior Cup 1876 to 1905, Grorty Dick. ASIN:B00L3AL7YE] Aston Villa beat Saltley College 3–1 in the final.

Villa beat Excelsior 8–1 in the second round. On 14 February 1880, Aston Villa beat Newport (Salop) 7-0 in the third round [ref: Matches played on Saturday, Birmingham Evening Mail, 16 February 1880, p3] and Walsall Swifts in the semi-finals. [ref: "Gossip on rural pastimes", The Leeds Mercury, 26 March 1880, p2]

The Saltley Collegians reached the final, beating Stoke in the third round, in a tie delayed to allow the students to return to college after a mid-term break. [ref: Football jottings, Nottingham Evening Post] In the semi-finals the club lost 3–0 to Derby at the Aston Lower Ground, [ref: Birmingham Challenge Cup, Derby Daily Telegraph] but a protest was made that one of the Derby players was "cup-tied", having already played for Wednesbury Strollers in the Sheffield Challenge Cup, against the rules of the competition which barred any player from representing more than one side in competitive matches. [ref: Football, Birmingham Daily Gazette] The protest was upheld and the college team put into the final, where it faced Aston Villa at the Aston Lower Grounds in what was seen as a "certainty" for the Villans; [ref: Birmingham Association Cup, Nottingham Evening Post] the Aston side duly won 3–1. [ref: Birmingham Association Challenge Cup Final Tie, Birmingham Gazette] [ref: Aston Villa v Saltley College 3–1, Play Up Liverpool] The match was the college's high point in football.

Wednesbury Strollers reached the last six in 1879–80 losing heavily to the professional Walsall Swifts, by which time the Swifts were seen as the strongest side in Walsall. [ref: Football, Birmingham Evening Mail] The semi-final stage (because of an inequality of entrants) had three teams, but Swifts were doubly unlucky with the draw – they missed out on the bye to the final, and were drawn to face Aston Villa, by then the strongest side in the Midlands. Villa duly won 2–1 in front of 6,000 at the Aston Lower Grounds, scoring twice in two minutes. [ref: Birmingham Association Cup, Nottingham Evening Post]

Geir G. Greni (born 29 October 1970) is a Norwegian filmmaker, journalist, author and musician. He founded the production company Snurr Film AS. His work includes the feature films Umeå4ever (2011) and All Must Die (Alle må dø, 2020), the crime novel Jeg ser død (2019), and a series of short films.

== Journalism ==

Greni began his career as a journalist and television presenter for NRK. He has written for publications including Morgenbladet, Mann and Filmmagasinet, and has reviewed films for NRK P1.

== Short film career ==

During the late 1990s and early 2000s, Greni wrote, directed and produced a series of short films, including Afterwards (Etter filmen), Party, Que Serà, Serà, Xercise, The Part (Rolle) and Together (Sammen).

His short film Afterwards (Etter filmen, 1999) was written by Greni and Morten Abrahamsen. The Norwegian Federation of Film Societies praised the film's casting and dialogue, describing it as "a simple and brilliant film". [ref: [https://filmklubb.no/wp/film/etter-filmen/ "Etter filmen"], Norwegian Federation of Film Societies.]

The Norwegian Film Archive has described Greni's short films as humorous works characterised by psychological insight, and in a 2006 presentation described him as "one of the most talented contemporary Norwegian short film directors". [ref: [https://filmarkivet.no/content/news/article.aspx?id=1193 "Que sera sera"], Filmarkivet.no, 11 July 2006.]

In 2002, Que Serà, Serà, directed and produced by Greni from a screenplay by Bård Breien, won the Jameson Short Film Award at the Norwegian Short Film Festival in Grimstad.

The film subsequently appeared in the Jameson Short Film Awards programme presented during the 42nd Semaine Internationale de la Critique at the Cannes Film Festival in 2003. [ref: [https://www.semainedelacritique.com/uploads/edition/6032c000578a195c81a3fd781e95e769.pdf "Jameson Short Film Awards 2002"], Semaine Internationale de la Critique, Cannes 2003.]

== Feature films ==

Greni made his feature-film debut as writer, director and producer with Umeå4ever, released theatrically in 2011. In a commentary devoted to Greni and the film, author Erlend Loe called Umeå4ever "perhaps the bravest film project of the year".

Kristin Aalen of Stavanger Aftenblad wrote that Greni "lifts the comedy several notches above the predictable romantic stories of which dozens have been made", and highlighted his handling of the balance between caricature and seriousness as well as the film's dramaturgy. [ref: [https://www.aftenbladet.no/kultur/i/KlgzG/god-komedie-om-myk-mann Kristin Aalen, "God komedie om myk mann"], Stavanger Aftenblad, 1 April 2011.]

In 2020, Greni released the horror feature All Must Die (Alle må dø), written by Greni and Robert Næss. Greni directed and produced the film.

Cinema described the film as "a solid genre film that appeals to a young audience – and delivers", and highlighted its approach to the slasher genre. [ref: [https://cine.no/2020/03/05/alle-ma-do-utdrikningslaget-fra-helvete/ "Alle må dø – utdrikningslaget fra helvete"], Cinema, 5 March 2020.]

== Writing ==

Greni made his literary debut with the crime novel Jeg ser død, published by Vega Forlag in 2019. [ref: [https://booksfromnorway.com/books/1782-i-see-death "I See Death"], Books From Norway.]

Fædrelandsvennen described the novel as "remarkably good" ("oppsiktsvekkande god"), highlighting its plot, central characters and Greni's visual approach to storytelling.

Alongside his own productions, Greni has worked as a script doctor and script consultant, including on the NRK comedy series Hubert.

== Music ==

Greni is the lead singer, guitarist and songwriter of the band Norwegian Modesty. The band released the EP Happy Now and the album Mediocrity Rules in 2011.

Norwegian Modesty contributed music to the soundtrack of Umeå4ever, which was released as a separate soundtrack album in 2011. The band's music was later also used in All Must Die.

Greni has written, directed and produced music videos for Minor Majority, Superfamily and Norwegian Modesty.

== Acting ==

As an actor, Greni has appeared in both his own and other productions. He played one of the four leading roles in the stage production Papagayaekspressen by Torstein Bieler and Lars Kilevold.

He also starred in the short film Neon, directed by Simen Alsvik, which Greni produced. In addition, he has written and performed in comedy productions for NRK and appeared in an NRK radio drama production.

Draft text:
Tarek M. Elgindi is an Egyptian-American mathematician and a professor of mathematics at Duke University. His research concerns partial differential equations and mathematical fluid dynamics, particularly singularity formation and the long-term behavior of solutions to the incompressible Euler equations.

Elgindi established finite-time singularity formation in three-dimensional incompressible Euler flows without a physical boundary. His construction concerns initial velocity fields in the regularity class C^{1,\alpha}, rather than infinitely differentiable initial data. His analytical methods were subsequently adapted by Jiajie Chen and Thomas Y. Hou in further proofs of singularity formation for the Euler and Boussinesq equations. He received a Sloan Research Fellowship in 2020 and a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2026.

== Education and academic career ==

Elgindi studied mathematics at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, where he received a Goldwater Scholarship in 2008. He earned his doctorate at New York University in 2014, supervised by Nader Masmoudi and Fang-Hua Lin.

He was an instructor at Princeton University from 2014 to 2017 and an assistant professor at the University of California, San Diego from 2017 to 2020. He joined Duke University in 2020, and was appointed professor of mathematics in 2024.

== Research ==

=== Singularity formation ===

Elgindi's work on the incompressible Euler equations examines whether initially regular fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time. The equations describe an idealized fluid with no viscosity and constant density; a singularity can involve unbounded growth of vorticity, which measures local rotation within the fluid.

In work first circulated in 2019 and published in 2021, Elgindi constructed solutions on three-dimensional Euclidean space, \mathbb{R}^3, that develop finite-time singularities. The result demonstrated that short-time existence and uniqueness, known in the relevant regularity class since the 1920s, do not imply that solutions remain regular indefinitely. The construction uses axisymmetric flows without swirl: flows that are rotationally symmetric but have no velocity component around their symmetry axis. Their initial velocities belong to C^{1,\alpha} for sufficiently small positive \alpha, meaning that their first derivatives satisfy a Hölder continuity condition. The proof constructs self-similar solutions of a simpler model and uses their stability to obtain singular solutions of the Euler equations.

With Tej-Eddine Ghoul and Nader Masmoudi, Elgindi subsequently studied the stability of the blowup construction. They established the existence of finite-energy solutions with C^{1,\alpha} initial velocity that become singular in a locally self-similar manner.

== Honors and recognition ==

* Elgindi received a Sloan Research Fellowship in 2020.
* In 2024, he received a Frontiers of Science Award in mathematics from the International Congress of Basic Science for his work on finite-time singularity formation in the incompressible Euler equations.
* He was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 2026.

Assembly Atlanta is a film and television production campus and mixed-use development in Doraville, Georgia, built on the site of a former General Motors assembly plant. Its centerpiece, Assembly Studios, opened in October 2023 as a full-service production complex operated by NBCUniversal's Universal Production Services, and has since hosted network, streaming, and independent productions including Beyond the Gates, Fight Night: The Million Dollar Heist, Teacup, Grosse Pointe Garden Society, Murdaugh: Death in the Family, Cape Fear, and a pilot for a revival of The Rockford Files.

== History ==

=== Former General Motors plant (1947–2008) ===
General Motors opened the Doraville Assembly plant in 1947 under its newly created Buick-Oldsmobile-Pontiac division, on a roughly 165-acre site near what is now Interstate 285. [ref: GM Closing Georgia Assembly Plant, Manufacturing.net] The plant produced more than 9 million vehicles over 61 years, including Buick, Oldsmobile, Pontiac, and Chevrolet models, before GM closed it in September 2008 amid company-wide cost cutting. [ref: GM's Doraville plant built the cars America loved, ATLVault / Atlanta News First] [ref: Doraville GM plant closes, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]

=== Early redevelopment as "Assembly" (2014–2021) ===
Integral Group acquired the property in 2014 and proposed redeveloping the land as a mixed-use district known as Assembly. [ref: Major redevelopment of old GM site depends on public support, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] Portions of the property were sold for automobile dealerships, while another portion was developed as the corporate headquarters of Serta Simmons Bedding. [ref: Serta Simmons HQ boosts rebuild of General Motors Doraville site, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution]

Third Rail Studios, a film and television production facility occupying approximately seven acres and originally developed by The Integral Group, opened at the site in 2016. [ref: NBCUniversal will operate huge new Assembly film studio in Doraville, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] The studio hosted a number of high-profile productions, including the feature films Rampage, Mile 22, and Richard Jewell, the first season of NBC's Good Girls, and Netflix's Emmy-nominated series Ozark. [ref: Gray Television purchases Doraville's Third Rail Studios, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] [ref: Gray Television announces NBCUniversal deal for new studios, Gray News/Fox 34] Gray Television acquired Third Rail Studios in September 2021 and folded it into the larger Assembly site; it is now owned and operated under Gray Media. [ref: Gray Television purchases Third Rail Studios, 11Alive]

=== Gray Media acquisition and "Studio City" plan (2021) ===
Gray Media purchased the remaining property in March 2021 to pursue a new "Studio City" concept, with Gray chairman and CEO Hilton H. Howell Jr. leading the project. [ref: TV company to remake former GM plant into Georgia's largest "Studio City", Urbanize Atlanta] [ref: Former GM plant set to transform into massive film-production site, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] By 2022, Gray described the assembled 135-acre site as encompassing a 43-acre studio complex — featuring soundstages, production offices, warehouse and mill buildings, studio bungalows, event space, and a parking deck.

In June 2022, Gray announced a long-term agreement under which NBCUniversal would lease and operate new studio facilities at the site and manage all studio and production operations across the complex, including Gray's own facilities and Third Rail Studios.

=== Construction (2021–2023) ===
Construction broke ground in September 2021. At the time of the NBCUniversal deal, three soundstage walls had already been erected, with additional soundstages, production offices, mill buildings, event spaces, and warehouses still to come. [ref: NBCUniversal Media reached deal with Gray Television to film in Doraville, Fox 5 Atlanta] Steel for the project was purchased in 2021 to avoid pandemic-related shortages, and the contractor built a temporary on-site concrete plant; roughly 83 acres of the former GM plant's concrete floors were broken up over about a year and reused as fill.

=== Opening (October–November 2023) ===
Assembly Studios opened with 19 soundstages across roughly 43 of the site's 135 acres. [ref: Assembly Studios, Smith Dalia Architects] [ref: Build It, And Here They Come: Assembly Atlanta Set to Make Its Mark on Georgia's Film Industry, Georgia Entertainment] Gray marked the opening with a gala on October 21, 2023, featuring a commissioned mural by Atlanta artist Steve Penley, a drone show, and performances by Cee Lo Green, Gladys Knight, Dionne Warwick, and Sheryl Crow; the company said it had invested more than $400 million in the buildout. [ref: Gray opens Assembly TV/film studios with massive gala, The Atlanta Journal-Constitution] A formal grand-opening announcement followed on November 9, 2023. [ref: Gray Television's Assembly Studios Celebrates Grand Opening of Innovative Sound Stages in Georgia, GlobeNewswire]
[truncated]

Birpur Airport (IATA: none, ICAO: none) is a proposed domestic airport located at Birpur in the state of Bihar, India. [ref: Town Survey Report: Bihar. Forbesganj, Controller of Publications] [ref: Indian Aviation] [ref: Sattā ke sūtradhara: Ājādī ke bāda Bhārata, Sr̥shṭi Prakāśana] The airport is located on the India–Nepal border, this airport is close to Bhantabari in Sunsari district of Nepal and Bhimnagar in Supaul district of India. [ref: Why is India building an airport in Birpur near Nepal’s border?, Khabarhub] This airport will be built on a former Kosi project era airfield in Birpur, about from Supaul. [ref: Bihar To Get Airports And Heliports In Every District; CM Samrat Choudhary Highlights The Infrastructure Push In Legislative Assembly, ETV Bharat News] [ref: Regional air connectivity boost for Bihar, The Times of India] The Government of Bihar and the Airports Authority of India signed a Memorandum of Understanding for the construction of the airport in June 2025. [ref: AAI floats tender to upgrade Birpur airport for small aircraft operations, Hindustan Times]

== History ==
The former airfield was built during the 1950s-1960s to support the construction of Koshi Barrage. [ref: Birpur Airport Moves Closer to Take-Off with ₹28.42-Crore Runway Project, Drishti IAS] [ref: A Life for Water: A Memoir, Transactions, American Philosophical Society (Vol. 108, Part 4), University of Pennsylvania Press] The then Indian prime minister, Indira Gandhi landed on this airfield on January 3, 1975 to attend the last rites of Lalit Narayan Mishra, which was held in Baluwa village. [ref: Killing of Cabinet Minister Shocks India's Politicians, The New York Times]

== Development ==
The Airports Authority of India (AAI) issued a tender in March 2025 for the construction of a terminal building, air traffic control, fire stations, and other buildings. [ref: AAI accelerates Birpur Airport project with new tender for infra development, The Times of India] For the expansion of the runway, the Government of Bihar published a land acquisition notice on January 2, 2026. [ref: Notice regarding land acquisition for the development work of Birpur Airport] The initial plan was to upgrade the airport runway as a 2B category, which supports 19 seaters aircraft but recently the officials are planning to upgrade the runway for 70 seaters aircraft. Draft text:
Fatimah bint Aqil ibn Abi Talib (Arabic: فاطمة بنت عقيل بن أبي طالب) She was a daughter of Aqil ibn Abi Talib, the elder brother of Ali ibn Abi Talib, making her his niece. [ref: Nasab Quraysh] According to Musʿab al-Zubayri’s Nasab Quraysh, she was one of Aqil’s daughters, whose mothers were different ummhat awlad (enslaved women). Her sisters included Umm Hani (Ramlah), Zaynab, Zaynab al-Sughra, and Umm Luqman. [ref: Nasab Quraysh] She later married Ali ibn Yazid ibn Rukānah of Banu Abd al-Muttalib, [ref: The Ansab al-Ashraf of al-Baladhuri, University Press] and they had children.

==Elegies==
Ibn Abd Rabbih's al-ʿIqd al-Farīd attributes an elegy to an unnamed daughter of Aqil ibn Abi Talib, mourning Husayn ibn Ali and those killed with him. [ref: Ibn ʿAbd Rabbih, al-ʿIqd al-Farīd, vol. 5, p. 132.] A later report in al-Qunduzī's Yanabi' al-Mawadda identifies the daughter of Aqil who composed the elegy as Fatimah bint Aqil. [ref: al-Qunduzī, Yanabi' al-Mawadda, vol. 3, p. 153.]

The elegy begins:

“O my eyes, shed tears and lament,and mourn for the family of the Messenger.Six of them, all descended from Ali, were struck down,and five from the family of Aqil”. [ref: ʿAlī Ṣāliḥ Rasan al-Muḥammadāwī, ʿAqīl ibn Abī Ṭālib bayna al-ḥaqīqa wa-l-shubha, p. 145, citing al-Qundūzī, Yanābīʿ al-Mawadda, vol. 3, p. 153.]

Yokohama Triennale is an international contemporary art exhibition held every three years in Yokohama, Japan, since 2001. The first three editions (2001, 2005, 2008) were primarily organized by the Japan Foundation. Since 2011, the City of Yokohama has taken over the role of primary organizer. [ref: Yokohama Triennale 2011 will represent a significant shift in the event’s organization, primarily because the Japan Foundation has stepped down as the main organizer and the city of Yokohama has bolstered its participation as a result., Biennial Foundation] The Triennale hosts on average 60 to 90 national and international artists per edition [ref: About us｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale] with the exception of the 2017 triennial, which only hosted about 40 artists. [ref: Text von MIKI Akiko. Yokohama Triennale 2017, universes.art]

The Triennale's main venues are the Yokohama Museum of Art and the Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse.

== Chronology ==

=== 1st Yokohama Triennale ===
The exhibition, titled Mega Wave—Towards a New Synthesis, ran from 02 September 2001 to 11 November 2001. It took place in Pacifico Yokohama Exhibition Hall (C,D), Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse No.1, and was curated by Shinji Kohmoto, Akira Tatehata, Nobuo Nakamura, and Fumio Nanjo. [ref: YOKOHAMA 2001: International Triennale of Contemporary Art MEGA WAVE—Towards a New Synthesis｜Archive｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale]

=== 2nd Yokohama Triennale ===
The second edition, titled Art Circus [Jumping from the Ordinary], was held from 28 September 2005 to 18 December 2005 at the No.3 and No.4 warehouses of the Yamashita Pier. Its artistic director was Tadashi Kawamata, and its curators were Taro Amano, Takashi Serizawa, Shingo Yamano. [ref: YOKOHAMA 2005: International Triennale of Contemporary Art Art Circus [Jumping from the Ordinary]｜Archive｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale]

=== 3rd Yokohama Triennnale ===
The third edition, titled TIME CREVASSE, was held from 13 September 2008 to 30 November 2008 across several venues in Yokohama. The venues were Shinko Pier Exhibition Hall, NYK Waterfront Warehouse (BankART Studio NYK), Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse No.1, Sankeien Garden. The exhibition was directed by Tsutomu Mizusawa, and curated by Daniel Birnbaum, Fang Hu, Akiko Miyake, Hans-Ulrich Obrist, Beatrix Ruf. [ref: YOKOHAMA 2008: International Triennale of Contemporary Art TIME CREVASSE｜Archive｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale]

=== 4th Yokohama Triennale ===
The fourth edition, titled OUR MAGIC HOURーHow Much of the World Can We Know?ー, was held from 06 August 2011 to 06 November 2011 at the Yokohama Museum of Art, and the NYK Waterfront Warehouse (BankART Studio NYK). The triennial was directed by Eriko Osaka, and curated by Akiko Miki. [ref: Yokohama Triennale 2011 OUR MAGIC HOUR ーHow Much of the World Can We Know?ー｜Archive｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale] The 'magic' mentioned in the title was stated to be not of mystical kind, but rather a sense of wonder: "the show focused upon an ability to see the wonderful in the everyday that has long been popularly ascribed to artists." [ref: 4th Yokohama Triennale, "Our Magic Hour: How Much of the World Can We Know" - Criticism, e-flux]

=== 5th Yokohama Triennale ===
The fifth edition, titled Art Fahrenheit 451: Sailing into the sea of oblivion, was held from 01 August 2014 to 03 November 2014 at Yokohama Museum of Art, and the Shinko Pier Exhibition Hall. The Triennale's artistic director was Yasumasa Morimura. [ref: Yokohama Triennale 2014 ART Fahrenheit 451: Sailing into the sea of oblivion｜Archive｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale] The title was drawn from Ray Bradbury's dystopian novel Fahrenheit 451. Unlike the negative connotations of its title, the triennale was said to embrace "forgetting, destruction and failure as essential components of the creative process." [ref: Yokohama Triennale 2014: ART Fahrenheit 451: Sailing into the Sea of Oblivion, artreview.com]

=== 6th Yokohama Triennale ===
The sixth edition, titled Islands, Constellations & Galapagos, was held from 04 August 2017 to 05 November 2017 at the Yokohama Museum of Art, the Yokohama Red Brick Warehouse No.1, and the basement of Yokohama Port Opening Memorial Hall. The exhibition was directed by Eriko Osaka, Akiko Miki, Tomoh Kashiwagi [ref: Yokohama Triennale 2017 Islands, Constellations & Galapagos｜Archive｜Yokohama Triennale, Yokohama Triennale], and curated together with Rirkrit Tiravanija, Shuji Takashina, and Suhanya Raffel. [ref: 6th Yokohama Triennale, "Islands, Constellations and Galapagos" - Criticism, e-flux] This edition was said to read the world through 'connectivity' and 'isolation', making references to 'island mentality', Brexit, refugee crisis and online communities. [ref: Yokohama Triennale: Islands, Constellations & Galapagos, artreview.com]
[truncated]

Pediatric Neurorehabilitation Research Center (PNRC; Persian: مرکز تحقیقات توانبخشی اعصاب اطفال) is a research center at the University of Social Welfare and Rehabilitation Sciences in Tehran, Iran. The research center was established in 2008 with the approval of Iran'sMinistry of Health and Medical Education and is reported to be the first research center in dedicated to pediatric neurorehabilitation [ref: در دانشگاه علوم بهزيستي و توانبخشي نخستين مركز تحقيقات توانبخشي اعصاب اطفال كشور راه اندازي شد] [ref: نخستین مرکز تحقیقات توانبخشی اعصاب اطفال راه اندازی شد]

Considering the 6% prevalence of learning disorders among primary schoolers in Iran, Farin Soleymani, the head of the Pediatric Neurorehabilitation Research Center, highlights the importance of early detection of learning disorders in the success rate of rehabilitation attempts [ref: علائم اختلالات یادگیری/احتمال بروز در کدام کودکان بیشتر است؟]. Thus, with the aim of promoting the development of Iranian children and providing early intervention and rehabilitation for at risk children and children living with developmental disorders, the research center began its work. [ref: Pediatric Neurorehabilitation Research Center]

== Activities and collaborations ==
The Pediatric Neurorehabilitation Research Center was responsible for organizing the first National Pediatric Rehabilitation Congress in Iran, which was held in 2025 [ref: اولین کنگره ملی توانبخشی کودکان]. The congress brought together professionals working in the field of pediatric rehabilitation from across Iran, providing an opportunity for them to present and exchange their work and experiences.

The Pediatric Neurorehabilitation Research Center has close ties with Iran’s Ministry of Health and Medical Education. Through this collaboration, the center has been commissioned to undertake several projects, including the standardization of internationally recognized developmental assessment scales for Iranian children, such as the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development [ref: محتوای استاندارد آموزش مجازی و مهارتی آزمون تشخیصی تکاملی بیلی، تولید شد] [ref: آزمون تشخیصی «اختلالات تکاملی کودکان» بومی سازی شد], the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) and Denver Developmental Screening Tests [ref: آزمونهاي استاندارد شده توسط مركز], the development of early intervention protocols for children with language disorders [ref: مراسم رونمايي از مجموعه كتاب هاي مداخلات زودرس در اختلالات گفتار و زبان و بلع كودكان], and the design of a national developmental promotion program [ref: رئیس مرکز تحقیقات اعصاب اطفال دانشگاه علوم توانبخشی و سلامت اجتماعی از بررسی تدوین سند ملی جدید برای ارتقای تکامل کودکان از بدو تولد تا هشت سالگی خبر داد.].

The Pediatric Neurorehabilitation Research Center has established collaborations and agreements with several organizations and academic institutions, including the Iranian Red Crescent Society, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Tabriz University of Medical Sciences. [ref: همکاری مرکز تحقیقات توانبخشی اعصاب اطفال و سازمان هلال احمر کشور] [ref: تفاهم نامه ها]

One of the areas that the research center is actively promoting is research and education concerning childhood hearing loss and deafness. This began with the establishment of a hearing loss and deafness studies committee affiliated with the center in 2017. The committee's activities included support for research by students and researchers, public awareness, hearing screening, and early rehabilitation and educational programmes for deaf and hard-of-hearing children. [ref: کمیته مطالعات «ناشنوایی- کم شنوایی» آغاز بکار کرد] [ref: فعالیت کمیته مطالعات «ناشنوایی - کم شنوایی» آغاز شد]

Mid Devon Cycling Club (MDCC) is an amateur cycling club based at Abbrook Park in Kingsteignton, near Newton Abbot, Devon, England. Founded in 1930, it is one of the largest cycling clubs in South West England, with a membership of around 585 as of 2018, and has developed several riders who went on to national and professional honours.

== History ==
The club was formed in 1930 with 17 members under the name Newton Abbot Wheelers. [ref: Ride With... Mid Devon Cycling Club, Cycling Weekly] It is registered with British Cycling and organises competitive events across several disciplines in the local region, including time trials, hill climbs and road races, promoting the Totnes-Vire stage race and six open time trials as of 2018. [ref: 2025 Totnes Vire: day one report and results, The British Continental]

Since 2007 the club has organised the Dartmoor Classic sportive, an event started by then club vice-president Ron Keegan. [ref: GALLERY: More than 1,500 cyclists battle hills and changeable weather to take part in the Dartmoor Classic Sportive, plymouthsportsgazette.com] A 2009 review in Cycling Weekly described it as having become "the best organised sportive in the UK" within its first three years, citing its marshalling, signage and organisation, and it has continued to feature regularly in lists of the UK's leading sportives. [ref: Cyclo-Sportive: The Dartmoor Classic, Cycling Weekly]

MDCC runs a youth development programme and is the host club for coaching sessions at the Torbay Velopark; in March 2018 it hosted the opening round of the Youth National Circuit Series. As of 2018, five club riders had won British national titles across various age groups and disciplines.

== Notable alumni and members ==
Mid Devon Cycling Club has served as the development club or early team for several riders who went on to professional or international careers.

Colin Lewis (1942–2022) joined the club as a teenager and rode as an amateur for MDCC from 1958 to 1966 before turning professional, riding the Tour de France in 1967 and 1968 and winning the British National Road Race Championship in successive years (1967 and 1968). [ref: Obituary: GB Tour Rider Colin Lewis RIP, PezCycling News] He later served as MDCC president, a role he held from around 1998.

Jeremy Hunt, a two-time winner of the British National Road Race Championship (1997 and 2001) who went on to ride for professional teams including Banesto and Team Sky, was coached as a teenager in Devon by Colin Lewis. [ref: About cycling coach Jeremy Hunt, Formfinder]

Yanto Barker joined the club at 15 and won the Junior British National Road Race Championship in 1998 while riding for MDCC, before turning professional and later founding the cycling apparel brand Le Col. [ref: Yanto Barker, ProCyclingStats]

Harrison Wood became the club's first member in over a decade to sign a UCI WorldTour contract when he joined Cofidis in 2023, having previously taken a national championship podium in the junior 25-mile time trial while riding for MDCC. [ref: The next step for pro cyclist Harrison Wood, torbayweekly.co.uk]

Birger Corleis (20 October 1955 in Harsefeld-30 October 2012 at the same place) was a musician and a musical educator. He was most known for being one of the vocalists of Modern Talking forming the falsetto parts and singing the chorus of the song "There's too much blue in missing you". He has worked for artists like Rolf Köhler, Mary Roos and Taco. He has played in bands like Springflut, Straightflush, Junkband, Me & The Duckdivers and Kentucky.

==Early Life==
Birger Corleis was born and grew up in Harsefeld in Lower Saxony. In his youth he played in diffrent school bands. After his youth he studied to become a typesetter. [ref: Birger Corleis – early life]

==Career==
After his studies he devoted entirely to his music career. From the mid 1970s till the early 1990s he played in diffrent bands as a singer, bassist or guitarist. He played in bands such as Straight Flush, Springflut and Junkband. He also played in the band Kentucky. Kentucky was a popular live cover band in Germany. [ref: Birger Corleis with Kentucky] Together with Walter Vagts he wrote "Back in the highlands" for Rolf Köhler under his pseudonym "Marc De Ville" in 1978. In 1984 together with Rolf and Michael Scholz he created the band Straight Flush and released the single "Dancing In The Sunlight". Later he would create the band Junkband with Michael Scholz. He was also in the band Springflut together with Rolf, Michael and Detlef Wiedeke. [ref: The discography of Birger Corleis]

From 1984 till 1987 Corleis sang the and falsetto vocals for Modern Talking together with Köhler Scholz and Wiedeke. The falsettos became a iconic part of the sound of Modern Talking. Dieter Bohlen pretended to sing them in videos and concerts. Corleis also sang the chorus of "There's Too Much Blue In Missing You" in which Bohlen sang the verses. This only got revealed in 2001, due to some legal disputes with Dieter Bohlen. [ref: The real voices behind Modern Talking]
Modern Talking would sell 65 million records their first era and top the charts in many countries.Notably, Modern Talking were one of the first Western bloc bands sale of whose records was allowed in the Soviet Union. After four decades of Cold War censorship and import restrictions, Chairman Mikhail Gorbachev's glasnost reforms in the USSR in 1986 opened up the Soviet sphere to western bands, including Modern Talking at the height of their popularity. As a result, they have gotten a large, enduring fanbase in Eastern Europe. Other Euro Disco acts that entered the Soviet sphere are Joy, C.C.Catch and Silent Circle. [ref: Die Russen mögen's Anders, Der Spiegel] The Euro Disco acts Bad Boys Blue and Patty Ryan also entered the Soviet sphere and were inspired by Modern Talking. [ref: You're My Heart, You're My Soul vs You're A Woman] Popular tracks from Modern Talking which Corleis sang on were You're My Heart, You're My Soul, Cheri Cheri Lady, You Can Win If You Want, Brother Louie and Atlantis Is Calling (S.O.S. for Love).

He sang backing vocals for Mary Roos's album Leben Spür'n in 1987. He also sang backing vocals for Taco's album Swing Classics: In The Mood Of Glen Miller.

From the mid-1990s onwards, Corleis worked primarily as a musical educator, instructing at various music schools for almost two decades. [ref: Birger Corleis educator]He formed the band Me & The Duckdivers in 2007 with other members. [ref: Me & The Duckdivers]

==Lawsuit against Bohlen==
In 2001 Corleis sued Bohlen claiming he deserved more money for his contibutions to Modern Talking and for using recordings from the old Modern Talking albums for the 1998 album Back For Good Bohlen called it "typical parasitic behaviour" and told him that he would not get a cent. Corleis lost the lawsuit and had to pay the costs of the trial himself. [ref: Lawsuit against Bohlen]

==Death and Legacy==
In 2012 he died 10 days after his 57th birthday. He left behind one daughter. [ref: Death of Corleis] People on the internet started spreading tribute videos about his work. [ref: Tributes]

Lindsay LeBlanc (born 1989) is an American-born glass artist and educator based in County Leitrim, Ireland. She is known for flameworked glass botanical studies and installations that explore ecology, decay and transformation through what she terms an "ecogothic" lens. [ref: Lindsay LeBlanc — Artist in Residence, Leitrim Sculpture Centre]

== Early life and education ==
LeBlanc was born in the United States in 1989. She studied sculpture and glass at the Massachusetts College of Art and Design in Boston, completing a BFA, and later earned an MFA in art and ecology at Burren College of Art in County Clare. [ref: Artistic License: Glass Artist Lindsay LeBlanc, The Gloss]

== Career ==
LeBlanc has worked with glass since 2009, specialising in glassblowing, kiln-forming, flameworking, casting and large-scale installation. [ref: New Leitrim exhibition explores what survives in the boglands, Leitrim Observer] Her practice draws on scientific observation, ecological history and speculative thinking, and she describes an "EcoGothic" approach informed by folklore, environmental history and overlooked ecologies such as lichens, weeds and ruins.

Her solo exhibition The Long Pause: Ecology of Ruins I was held at the Leitrim Sculpture Centre in Manorhamilton from April to May 2026. The four-room installation explored a blanket bog in Kiltyclogher on the Irish border, working with reclaimed materials, foraged glass, moving image and sound to trace abandoned objects in the bogland landscape.

In 2026 she co-curated Of Sand and Ash, an exhibition of contemporary glass for the Glass Society of Ireland, with Ava Hayes at the National Design & Craft Gallery in Kilkenny. [ref: Of Sand and Ash — DCCI/NDCG, Design & Crafts Council Ireland] She serves on the board of the Glass Society of Ireland.

In August 2026 she curated THREADS: Time, Memory and Material at the Cashel Arts Festival. [ref: THREADS: Time, Memory and Material — curated by Lindsay LeBlanc, Cashel Arts Festival] Her glass botanical works are exhibited and sold through Blowfish Glass in Stourbridge, England, including in the gallery's international Fifteen x Fifteen 2026 exhibition. [ref: Lindsay LeBlanc — Blowfish Glass, Blowfish Glass] [ref: Fifteen x Fifteen 2026, Blowfish Glass]

== Awards ==
* 2024 Jutta Cuny-Franz Talent Prize [ref: The Jutta Cuny-Franz Memorial Award, Kunstpalast]
* Sculpture in Context Goodbody Award [ref: LooLooGlass — DCCI member directory, Design & Crafts Council Ireland]

Daniel Druhora (born 1982) is a Romanian-born American filmmaker and educator. He wrote, directed and produced the documentary Lives, Not Grades (2021), which received a Los Angeles Area Emmy Award in 2022. [ref: Los Angeles Area Emmy Awards, Television Academy] His other work includes Long Distance Swimmer: Sara Mardini (2023), Cloudwalkers: ISI and the Inventors of the Future (2024) and Flowing Forward, a documentary series about water security and reuse. He is a lecturer at the University of Southern California (USC) and resident filmmaker at the university's ReWater Center.

== Early life and education ==
Druhora was born in Romania in 1982. [ref: Solving the Puzzle of Ukraine, USC Viterbi Magazine] His family emigrated to the United States in the early 1990s, following the Romanian Revolution of 1989.

He studied international relations at the University of Washington and film and television production at USC.

== Career ==
Druhora began his career in motion-picture development and post-production at Warner Bros., working on Gangster Squad (2013) and The Lego Movie (2014).

In 2015 and 2017, his screenplays Climbers and Marjan were named semifinalists in the Academy Nicholl Fellowships in Screenwriting, an annual competition administered by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. [ref: 2015 Nicholl Fellowships in Screenwriting, Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences] [ref: 2017 Nicholl Fellowships in Screenwriting, Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]

Druhora wrote, directed and produced Lives, Not Grades, a documentary about university students developing responses to challenges faced by displaced people on the Greek island of Lesvos. The film was broadcast by the PBS member stations KCET and PBS SoCal, [ref: KCET and PBS SoCal Win 7 Los Angeles Area Emmy Awards, PBS SoCal] and received the Los Angeles Area Emmy Award for Independent Programming in 2022. [ref: Documentary by Romanian filmmaker Daniel Druhora among winners at 2022 Los Angeles Area Emmy Awards, Romania Insider] [ref: Documentarul „Vieți, nu note", regizat de românul Daniel Druhora, a câștigat premiul Emmy, în cadrul competiției regionale din Los Angeles, Observator Cultural]

He was a producer on Long Distance Swimmer: Sara Mardini (2023), which screened at Sheffield DocFest and the Raindance Film Festival, where it was nominated for best UK feature. [ref: Raindance Film Festival Best UK feature, Raindance]

Druhora wrote and directed Cloudwalkers: ISI and the Inventors of the Future (2024), a documentary about the USC Information Sciences Institute and its role in the development of early internet technologies, later released on Prime Video.

As resident filmmaker at USC's ReWater Center, Druhora created Flowing Forward, a documentary series about water security, reuse and infrastructure in the United States.

== Teaching ==
In 2018, with the USC faculty members Burcin Becerik-Gerber, David Gerber and Brad Cracchiola, Druhora co-created Innovation in Engineering and Design for Global Crises, an interdisciplinary USC program focused on humanitarian challenges. [ref: This USC Program Is Building Startups To Aid Ukrainian Refugees, dot.LA] [ref: Civil engineering course embraces innovation and real-world solutions, Civil Engineering]

Good Shepherd Rehabilitation is an independent, not-for-profit rehabilitation network headquartered in Allentown, Pennsylvania.Pediatric, adolescent and adult patients receive treatment at Good Shepherd for stroke; brain injury; spinal cord injury; bone and joint conditions; aches, pains and strains; cardiac and respiratory illnesses; chronic neurological conditions; and developmental disabilities.

Types of treatment include inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation for adults, adolescents and children; physical medicine and rehabilitation physician services; long-term care; long-term acute care; and supported independent living for people with disabilities.In all, Good Shepherd operates 30 facilities throughout eastern Pennsylvania.Good Shepherd is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation of Rehabilitation Facilities (CARF). Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital and Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital Pediatric Unit have a combined six CARF-accredited inpatient rehabilitation programs [ref: ] [ref: Find a Provider - Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital]
Good Shepherd is also accredited by the Joint Commission. [ref: About Us - Find Accredited Organizations - Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital]

== History ==

The Rev. John ("Papa") and Estella ("Mama") Raker founded the Good Shepherd Home in Allentown in February 1908 to care for orphaned children with disabilities. [ref: REV. OR. JOHN H. RAKER; Lutheran Minister Founded Good Shepherd Home, Allentown, Pa., The New York Times]While serving as the director of the Lutheran Orphan Home in Topton, Pennsylvania, the Rev. Raker met a local woman who had a disabled son. The woman said she had no way to provide care for her son. Despite his reservations, the Rev. Raker had to turn the mother and boy away because the home's charter allowed only "healthy children." [ref: History's Headlines: A Good Shepherd for over 100 years, WFMZ.com]In 1907, the Rev. Raker moved to Grace Lutheran mission in South Allentown but insisted that he be allowed to do mission work among children with disabilities as time allowed. His regular pastoral work with the church, however, did not leave much time initially.Then, his wife gave birth to a daughter, Viola, who passed away in infancy. Following the funeral, the Rev. Raker received a letter from another local minister about a child with a disability named Viola Hunt, who he hoped someone could take in.Seeing it as an omen, the Rakers took Viola Hunt in, and she became the first resident of what is now Good Shepherd.

=== Expansion ===
Good Shepherd opened its rehabilitation hospital in Allentown in 1967 and expanded the facility in 1983. [ref: ]In August 1980, Good Shepherd opened Good Shepherd Home - Raker Center on its South Allentown campus, providing a long-term care home for individuals with severe disabilities, such as cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, multiple sclerosis, spina bifida and traumatic brain injuries. Good Shepherd opened a second long-term care home in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania in 2000.

Good Shepherd announced a partnership in 2007 with Penn Medicine, forming Good Shepherd Penn Partners in 2008 to provide rehabilitation and therapy services in the greater Philadelphia area and parts of New Jersey. [ref: Penn, Good Shepherd to form partnership ** Philadelphia's Graduate Hospital will be transformed into a rehabilitation specialty center., The Morning Call] [ref: Good Shepherd Penn Partners Announces Administrative Team, Rehab Management] Good Shepherd Penn Partners changed names to GSPP Rehabilitation in 2024. [ref: ]Good Shepherd opened the region's first pediatric inpatient rehabilitation unit in Bethlehem in 2009. [ref: Samuel Miranda Jr.: Good Shepherd's pediatric unit reaches milestone, The Morning Call]

=== Good Shepherd Today ===
In 2023, Good Shepherd opened a free-standing, 123,000-square-foot, 76-bed inpatient rehabilitation hospital in Center Valley, Pennsylvania. [ref: Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Center opens new hospital in Upper Saucon Twp., WFMZ.com]Good Shepherd also opened the Fleming Center for Robotics in Rehabilitation in 2023.

In June 2026, Good Shepherd announced it would open the first Autism and Neurodevelopmental Wellness Center in the greater Lehigh Valley region in fall 2026. The center will be located on Cetronia Road in Upper Macungie Township. [ref: Good Shepherd Rehabilitation says it will open region's 1st Autism and Neurodevelopmental Wellness Center, WFMZ.com] [ref: ]

== Partnerships ==

Good Shepherd's partnership with the Temple University Hospital Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation (PM&R) Residency Program matches candidates in the field of physiatry for a training program at Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Hospital. [ref: Residency Program, Lewis Katz School of Medicine]In 2025, Good Shepherd and Lehigh University established a formal partnership, which included conducting a Community Health Needs Assessment to collect information on the needs of individuals with autism and other neurodivergent conditions in the greater Lehigh Valley [ref: Lehigh University and Good Shepherd Rehabilitation Join Forces to Advance Disability Health Equity, Lehigh University News], which led to the development of Good Shepherd's new Autism and Neurodevelopmental Wellness Center.
