It began as the BarCode podcast and later expanded into live events, documentary filmmaking, cybersecurity consulting, and other media projects. Its productions include the documentaries Inhuman (2024) and I Am Machine (2025), both directed by Glanden, and the narrative podcast FALLOUT, launched in 2026. [ref: From IT Help Desk to Cyber Storyteller: How Chris Glanden Built a Creative Career in Cybersecurity, CYBR.SEC.Media]

== History ==

=== 2020–2022: Podcast launch ===

BarCode launched as a podcast in September 2020, hosted by Newark, Delaware-based cybersecurity practitioner Chris Glanden. [ref: The BarCode podcast serves cybersecurity talk with a happy hour feel, Technical.ly] The show was created during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many in-person security conferences and networking events had been canceled. Glanden modeled the program after the informal conversations that take place at conference bars and hotel lobbies.

Early episodes included a recurring segment featuring Glanden and a fictional bartender named "Tony", who introduced a cocktail connected to the theme of the episode before the guest interview.

Within its first several months, the podcast featured guests including web security researcher Troy Hunt, cryptographer Bruce Schneier, Metasploit creator H.D. Moore, and former Tenable chief executive Ron Gula.

In 2021, BarCode won the Technology category at the People's Choice Podcast Awards. [ref: Past Winners, People's Choice Podcast Awards]

By 2022, BarCode was also producing live podcast and networking events in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware. [ref: 'Physical cybersecurity' is a thing, and other lessons from off the industry's beaten path, Technical.ly]

=== 2023–present: Expansion ===

In May 2023, Glanden announced Inhuman, a documentary examining the weaponization of artificial intelligence. The independently financed production marked BarCode's expansion into documentary filmmaking. [ref: This Delaware podcaster is behind 'Inhuman,' a documentary on AI weaponization, Technical.ly]

Later that year, Glanden left his cybersecurity consulting role to establish BarCode Security as a consulting business alongside the media operation. [ref: Delaware's BarCode expands into consulting, Technical.ly]

BarCode also continued recording podcasts in front of live audiences. In April 2023, it recorded CISOs Riff on the Latest in Cybersecurity at SecureWorld Philadelphia, featuring cybersecurity executives Krista Arndt, David Lingenfelter, and Bistra Lutz. [ref: InfoSec Leaders Share in Podcast Interview at SecureWorld Philadelphia, SecureWorld]

In 2024, Glanden co-founded the Cyber Circus Network, a collective of independent cybersecurity media creators and organizations.

The podcast recorded its 100th episode during a live event in Las Vegas in 2024. BarCode has also produced live programs in conjunction with cybersecurity events and conferences including BSides Philadelphia, SecureWorld, Hacker Halted, and events held during the annual Black Hat and DEF CON conference period in Las Vegas.

== BarCode podcast ==

The BarCode podcast consists primarily of long-form interviews with people working in cybersecurity and related fields, including security researchers, chief information security officers, penetration testers, social engineers, hackers, and technology executives.

The program combines technical discussions with personal interviews and elements drawn from Glanden's original conference "happy hour" concept. Many episodes have included a cocktail created around the episode's guest or subject.

Guests have included Bruce Schneier, Troy Hunt, H.D. Moore, Ron Gula, Jenny Radcliffe, Joe Grand, Graham Cluley, Sherri Davidoff, Ric Prado, Vivek Ramachandran, Anahi Santiago, John Kindervag, Jack Rhysider, Len Noe, and Higinio "W0rmer" Ochoa.

=== Selected episodes ===

* "SafeHouse" — Troy Hunt (October 6, 2020), founder of the data-breach notification service Have I Been Pwned?.
* "Full Disclosure" — Bruce Schneier (December 18, 2020), cryptographer, security technologist, and author.
* "Rumble" — H.D. Moore (January 22, 2021), founder of the Metasploit Project.
* "Checkmate" — Graham Cluley (May 14, 2021), cybersecurity writer and commentator.
* "Kingpin" — Joe Grand (June 4, 2021), hardware hacker and former member of L0pht Heavy Industries.

== Films ==

=== Inhuman ===

Inhuman is a 2024 documentary directed by Glanden about the weaponization and potential misuse of artificial intelligence. The documentary examines subjects including deepfakes, synthetic voices, generative artificial intelligence, autonomous vehicles, biometric tracking, and algorithmic bias.

=== I Am Machine ===

I Am Machine is a 2025 documentary directed by Glanden that profiles cybersecurity researcher Len Noe and examines the security, privacy, and ethical implications of human-machine augmentation.

The film was screened in several U.S. cities during 2025, including Philadelphia, Austin, Las Vegas, Houston, Grapevine, Texas, and Atlanta.

== Live events ==

Live events have been a recurring part of BarCode since 2022, when the organization began holding podcast recordings and cybersecurity networking events in the Delaware Valley.

The BarCode Live format places podcast interviews in bar and social-event settings rather than traditional studios.

Draft text:
Sammy Vashon Dyer (born 1905) was an American dancer, choreographer, and dance teacher. He performed in the Broadway musical Runnin’ Wild (1923) and toured the Black theater circuit before settling in Chicago, where he founded the Sammy Dyer School of Dancing in 1933. [ref: Ted Watson "Showfolks Mourn Death Of Dancing Sammy Dyer" (September 1, 1960) The Courier]

== Life and career ==
Dyer became a dancer who performed in Black cast Broadway shows, including Runnin’ Wild in 1923 [ref: Broadway Vet Teaches Adults, Kids Choreographic Intricacies, Chicago Tribune]. In Runnin’ Wild (by Flournoy Miller and Aubrey Lyles, with James Johnson) Sammy Dyer played a Dancing Red Cap.  That performance was credited with popularizing the Charleston on Broadway, and subsequently, all around the country [ref: The Makings of a Broadway Hit: the "Charleston," James P. Johnson, and San Juan Hill, Lincolncenter.org].

By 1931 Dyer had relocated to Chicago, and by 1933 he had rented a storefront on Michigan Avenue to start a children’s dancing school [ref: Our Legacy, Sammy Dyer School of the Theatre]. The Sammy Dyer School of Dancing taught jazz, ballet, tap, and acrobatics, with a focus on professional development. [ref: Muriel Foster: The Only Act of its Kind, Chicago Dance History]

Dyer also worked as a choreographer for prominent clubs and theaters in Chicago, like the Sunset Café, the Regal Theater, where he was ballet master, and managed the theater’s chorus dancers, the Regalettes, and the Palmer House, where he supervised Merriel Abbott's dancers, the Abbotteers. His most important position was at the Club DeLisa, where he managed the entertainment from its opening in 1934 until it closed in 1958 [ref: Earl Calloway “Sammy Dyer Stages Its 75th Anniversary with A Rhapsody in Black” (June 18, 2008) Chicago Defender]. Located on Garfield and State Street, DeLisa became a top entertainment venue in Black Chicago. Open 24 hours a day for much of its run, the club featured house bands led by Fletcher Henderson and Red Saunders. Dyer was DeLisa’s choreographer, stage producer, and was responsible for the chorus dancers [ref: Dance Notes: Julian Swain can still move a little bit, The Chicago Reader], the DeLisa Chorines. Because of his New York and touring history, and relationship with acts like Duke Ellington (whom he knew from his youth D.C., where Dyer worked for Ellington's sign painting business [ref: Jazz dance: the story of American vernacular dance, Da Capo]), Count Basie [ref: How It's Done, Jet], and Cab Calloway [ref: 25 Years of Cab Calloway, Jet], Dyer also handled some talent bookings. It was while working for Henderson at the DeLisa that pianist Herman Blount changed his stage name to Sun Ra, at Dyer’s suggestion [ref: Space is the Place: The Life and time sof Sun Ra, Pantheon].

In the early 1940s Dyer recruited some of the most talented dancers from his school to become the Dyerettes, an act that mixed dancing with comedy, acrobatics, and singing. As children Shirley Hall, Muriel Burns, Clarice White, Florence Saunders, Jean Cornell and Gloria Broussard performed at USO shows, and began appearing at Club DeLisa with the Saunders Orchestra, and playing early morning breakfast shows for overnight patrons. The Dyerettes would become an international touring act and from 1954-1958 were house openers at the Apollo Theater in New York. Ebony magazine declared them “one of the top dancing groups in the country.” [ref: Dyerettes Train Succesors, Ebony]

In addition to his work at the school and in nightclubs, Dyer also helped produce the Epic of a Race pageant at the 1933 Century of Progress World’s Fair at Soldier Field, and worked with prominent dance figures Katherine Dunham [ref: Chorus of 5,000 to be heard in Negro Pageant, Chicago Tribune] and Jeni LeGon [ref: Earl J. Morris “GRAND TOWN DAY AND NIGHT: HAPPY NEW YEAR! HERE'S Hoping That It Will Be Mellow” (Dec 29, 1934) The Pittsburgh Courier (1911-1950); Dec 29, 1934].  He helped organize Finnie’s Masquerade Ball, an annual Halloween drag show on the South Side that ran from 1935 until at least the 1970s [ref: What's the history of drag performance in Chicago?, WBEZ/Curious City]. 5000 people reportedly attended the 1958 Finnie’s Ball at the Trianon Ballroom [ref: Finnie's Ball Attracts 5000 in Chicago, Jet]. Dyer choreographed the 1938 musical The Swing Mikado, an all-black cast interpretation of Gilbert and Sullivan’s Mikado, a production of the WPA's Federal Theatre Project [ref: The Swing Mikado, Internet Broadway Database]. The show moved to Broadway where it competed with a production it inspired, The Hot Mikado (starring Bill “Bojangles” Robinson) which played at a theater across the street.

== Death and legacy ==
In 1959 Sammy Dyer became ill, and the Dyerettes ceased touring to help with his care. After a year-long illness, Dyer died in his native Washington D.C. on August 20, 1960. After a grand funeral at Chicago’s Bethel AME Church, with performances by Al Hibbler and Jo Ann Henderson, his body was returned to his city of birth for burial.

Konstantinas Šakenis (27 November 1881 – 7 July 1959) was a Lithuanian engineer, teacher and politician. He served as Lithuania's Minister of Education from 1927 to 1934, State Controller from 1934 to 1940, and Speaker of the Seimas from 1936 to 1940.

Educated at the Imperial Petersburg Institute of Technology in Saint Petersburg, Šakenis taught physics at various schools in Vilnius, Voronezh, Kaunas, Panevėžys from 1912 to 1926. In 1920, he published a three-part Lithuanian physics textbook for gymnasiums. He was active in the Lithuanian public life. During World War I, he was a member of the Lithuanian Society for the Relief of War Sufferers. He was a member of the central committees of the Party of National Progress (1920–1924) and its successor the Lithuanian Nationalist Union (1928–1933).

In December 1926, Šakenis became a member of the Third Seimas when he filled the vacancy left by Antanas Smetona who became the president of Lithuania. In April 1927, he became the Minister of Education. During his seven-year tenure, Lithuania implemented mandatory primary education and improved teachers' education and licensing. Šakenis was seen as a strong supporter of president Smetona and implemented educational policies favoring the Lithuanian Nationalist Union, most notably the prohibition of all political and social organizations in schools. After the ministry, Šakenis was the State Controller and the Speaker of the Fourth Seimas. He held both positions until the Soviet occupation of Lithuania in June 1940.

He was arrested by the Soviet NKVD during the June deportation in 1941. He was sentenced to ten years in prison and lifetime in exile, but was released in 1956 and returned to Lithuania. He wrote poetry and finished his memoir, which were posthumously published in 1990s after Lithuania regained independence.

==Biography==
===Early life and education===
Šakenis was born on in the village of, in the Vabalninkas volost of what was then the Kovno Governorate of the Russian Empire (now Biržai District Municipality, Lithuania). His family were royal peasants who had greater personal freedoms than serfs and sought education. His uncles Ferdinandas was deported to Siberia for participating in the Uprising of 1863, Juozas was a military doctor educated at Moscow University, and Pelicijonas worked for the railroad. Šakenis was the eldest of six siblings. His brother Julijonas became a Roman Catholic priest.

Šakenis was first educated by a daraktorius at a clandestine school at his home. In September 1892, he enrolled at Šiauliai Boys' Gymnasium. There he was friends with the future engineer and belonged to a small group of Lithuanian students that promoted the use of the Lithuanian language.

He graduated from the gymnasium with a silver medal in June 1900 and enrolled in the Faculty of Physics and Mathematics at the University of St. Petersburg. He joined a society of Lithuanian students that distributed and promoted Lithuanian press which was illegal due to the Lithuanian press ban and was its vice-chairman. He was expelled in early 1901 for taking part in an anti-Tsarist student unrest, but was able to get readmitted. In 1902, he voluntarily transferred to the Mechanics Faculty of the Imperial Petersburg Institute of Technology. There he studied with his friends Gravrogkas, Steponas Kairys, and.

His studies were temporarily interrupted by the Russian Revolution of 1905. He then worked at the Vilija factory of Petras Vileišis, as well as assisted in editing and publishing the first Lithuanian daily Vilniaus žinios. After completing his practicum at and as an assistant locomotive engineer at Radviliškis–Mažeikiai railway, Šakenis graduated in May 1910.

===Early career===
After graduation, Šakenis moved to Vilnius. In late 1911, he obtained teaching position at the 1st Vilnius Gymnasium and later at the Vilnius Girls' Gymnasium where he taught physics and cosmography. In 1912, he also worked as an engineer on the construction of the headquarters of the Saulė Society in Kaunas. During this time, he participated in the activities of the Lithuanian Mutual Aid Society of Vilnius.

At the start of World War I, Šakenis was elected to the audit committee of the Lithuanian Society for the Relief of War Sufferers. He organised trade workshops and schools on behalf of the Lithuanian Society. In 1915, the Russian gymnasiums along with Šakenis were evacuated to Russia. From September 1915 to June 1918, he served as an inspector of the Lithuanian gymnasium in Voronezh. For nearly a year, he was also an acting principal of the gymnasium while Pranas Mašiotas was recuperating. In late 1917, Šakenis helped edit published by the Party of National Progress.

Šakenis returned to Vilnius in June 1918 and became a teacher of mathematics and physics at the Vilnius Vytautas the Great Gymnasium. At the same time, he wrote a three-part textbook on physics in Lithuanian as there was an urgent need for Lithuanian-language educational materials. At the start of the Lithuanian–Soviet War, Šakenis evacuated to Kaunas.

Draft text:
----

The Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna (LGWA) is a proposed gravitational-wave observatory that would detect low-frequency gravitational waves by measuring vibrations of the Moon with an array of ultra-sensitive seismic sensors deployed on the lunar surface. It is intended to operate in the 1 mHz–1 Hz frequency band.

The project was proposed in 2020 and is intended to bridge the frequency gap between space-based detectors such as LISA and terrestrial observatories such as LIGO, KAGRA, the Einstein Telescope and the Cosmic Explorer.

== History ==

=== Early theoretical work ===
The idea of using an entire celestial body for detecting gravitational waves was proposed by Joseph Weber. Weber suggested that the Earth or the Moon could act as natural resonant antennas, with gravitational waves exciting their normal modes and the resulting motion being measured by sensitive gravimetric instruments.
Subsequent theoretical studies examined the response of planetary bodies to gravitational waves. Freeman Dyson derived the response of a free surface to an incident gravitational wave, while Ari Ben-Menahem later developed a treatment for a spherically symmetric Earth and showed that gravitational waves could excite low-order spheroidal modes of the planet.

=== Lunar seismology and experimental attempts ===
The Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package deployed seismometers on the Moon between 1969 and 1977, providing the first long-term record of lunar seismic activity. Among the instruments flown during the Apollo program was the Lunar Surface Gravimeter, which was partly conceived for gravitational-wave investigations.
The gravimeter suffered an engineering failure that prevented the experiment from operating as intended. Later analyses concluded that its sensitivity would not have been sufficient to detect astrophysical gravitational-wave signals, although Apollo seismic data were subsequently used to place limits on low-frequency gravitational-wave backgrounds.

=== Modern developments ===
Interest in planetary-body gravitational-wave detection was renewed with advances in seismology and precision sensing technologies. Studies explored the use of terrestrial seismic networks for low-frequency gravitational-wave searches and re-examined the response of the Earth and Moon to gravitational waves.
In the 2020s, detailed analyses of the lunar seismic environment, gravitational-wave response, and detector sensitivity led to the development of the Lunar Gravitational-Wave Antenna concept.

=== LGWA proposal ===
LGWA was proposed by Jan Harms and collaborators in response to a European Space Agency call for lunar science concepts. The proposal outlined a gravitational-wave observatory operating in the millihertz-to-hertz frequency range using the Moon as the detector test mass.

== Science objectives ==

=== Lunar science ===

A major component of the LGWA science programme is the study of the Moon's internal structure and seismic properties.

==== Seismic sources ====

Seismic observations conducted during the Apollo missions demonstrated that the Moon remains seismically active. More than 13,000 seismic events, collectively known as moonquakes, were identified from data acquired between 1969 and 1977.
Lunar seismic sources are generally classified into three categories: deep moonquakes, shallow moonquakes, and meteoroid impacts. Deep moonquakes are correlated with tidal stresses induced by the Earth-Moon system, while shallow moonquakes are less frequent and their origin remains incompletely understood.
Because the Moon lacks a substantial atmosphere, meteoroid impacts generate seismic signals that can be detected across the lunar surface and provide information on the present impact environment of the Earth-Moon system.
The distribution of seismic activity across the Moon remains only partially constrained because the Apollo seismic network operated exclusively on the lunar near side.

==== Internal structure ====

Data from the Apollo seismic experiments provided the first direct constraints on the Moon's internal structure, revealing a differentiated body composed of crust, mantle and core.
Seismic analyses led to the development of reference models of the lunar interior, including the Very Preliminary Reference Moon Model, which combines seismological and geodetic observations to describe the Moon's internal density and seismic velocity profiles.
Current models indicate a crust approximately 40 km thick and a small core with an estimated radius of about 380 km, although substantial uncertainties remain for the deepest regions of the Moon owing to the limited coverage of the Apollo seismic network.

==== Formation history ====

The Moon's internal structure provides important constraints on theories of its origin. Seismic, geodetic and geochemical evidence indicates that the Moon is a differentiated body with a crust, mantle and core, suggesting that it formed through a high-energy event followed by extensive melting and internal differentiation.
Several hypotheses have been proposed for the Moon's formation, including capture, co-accretion, fission and giant-impact models. Among these, the giant-impact hypothesis, in which the Moon formed from debris produced by a collision between the proto-Earth and a planetary body, is the most widely studied explanation.
The composition and internal structure of the Moon remain important tests of competing formation scenarios.

Dyala Khodary (Arabic: ديالا خضري; born 1979) is a Lebanese contemporary painter based in Beirut [ref: Dyala Khodary - Biography, Art on 56th]. Her work explores the city's people, architecture, infrastructure, and urban landscape through paintings depicting portraits, façades, tiled floors, manhole covers, electrical cables, and other elements of Beirut's environment. Although rooted in recognizable Beiruti scenery, her paintings often move toward abstraction through repetition, decorative pattern, and unusual perspectives [ref: Dyala Khodary répète Beyrouth à l’infini, L'Orient-Le Jour] [ref: Dyala Khodary, un regard sur les formes de Beyrouth, L'Orient-Le Jour].

Education and early career

Khodary graduated from the Lebanese University in 2002 with a degree in Plastic Arts.

Following her studies, she worked professionally in decorative painting. She has described this experience as influential in developing her approach to texture, material behavior, craftsmanship, and painted surfaces, elements that later became defining characteristics of her artistic practice [ref: Des bouches d'égout de Beyrouth à Menart Fair Paris: Le parcours artistique de Dyala Khodary, www.arabnews.fr].

Career

Before her first solo exhibition, Khodary participated in collective exhibitions, including three editions of the Salon d'Automne organized by Beirut's Sursock Museum.

Tailor-Made

Khodary's first solo exhibition, Tailor-Made, was held in 2015 in Beirut at Art on 56th, the gallery that has represented her since. The exhibition presented portraits drawn from the artist’s local surroundings, combining figurative painting with techniques influenced by her background in decorative painting, including patterns, collage, and layered surfaces [ref: ديالا خضري في "غاليري آرت أون 56" الفنانة الشابة ماهرة بتراكيبها ونضارة وجوهها الأنثوية, annahar.com] [ref: La mise en lumière de Dyala Khodary, L'Orient-Le Jour] [ref: " T a i l o r - M a d e " by Dyala Khodary, Lamasat Future TV].

Beirut in Patterns

Her second solo exhibition, Beirut in Patterns, opened in 2018 and marked a shift toward making Beirut's architecture the central subject of her work. Rather than depicting panoramic city views, the exhibition focused on architectural fragments such as balconies, façades, tiled floors, and abandoned buildings [ref: ] [ref: معرض ديالا خضري لدى غاليري 'آرت أون 56' إعادة اعتبار معمارية إلى بيروت أخرى بعيدة المنال, annahar.com].

Critics read the exhibition as a reflection on the disappearance of Beirut's historic architecture and the transformation of the city's urban identity. L'Orient-Le Jour described Beirut as the central subject of the series, while Annahar, Al-Akhbar, and Al Araby Al Jadeed emphasized architectural memory and the contrast between traditional and contemporary urban development [ref: مرثية لعمارات الزمن الوديع: ديالا خضري... الهمجية الزاحفة على بيروت, الأخبار] [ref: ديالا خضري: شبّاك قديم فتحه الهواء, العربي الجديد] [ref: ديالا خضري.. زوايا بيروت وانفعالاتها البصرية, العربي الجديد].

Le Corbeau et le Regard

In 2023, Khodary presented Le Corbeau et le Regard: Beyrouth en Motifs II (Corbels and Manholes: Beirut in Patterns II), a continuation of her investigation of Beirut's visual identity. The exhibition expanded her architectural vocabulary to include corbels, rooftops, staircases, pavements, drainage systems, and manhole covers. Around the same period, she also developed the Portals series, in which manhole covers became symbolic entrances to hidden layers of the city [ref: ].

Critics discussed the exhibition's relationship between realism and abstraction, as well as its use of overlooked urban details. Al Modon highlighted its elevated viewpoints and absence of human figures, while Al Mayadeen interpreted ordinary architectural objects as central components of Khodary's visual language [ref: Le Corbeau et le Regard by Dyala Khodary: Shades of Hyperrealism] [ref: ديالا الخضري: رحلة عابرة من تراث "الكوربو" إلى واقع "الريغار", شبكة الميادين] [ref: معرض «الغراب والنظرة» مجازية التعبير على طريقة لافونتين, aawsat.com].

Off the Grid / اشتراك

Khodary's fourth solo exhibition, Off the Grid / اشتراك, was presented in 2026. The exhibition focused on Lebanon's electricity crisis and the dense networks of electrical cables associated with privately operated neighborhood generators [ref: ] [ref: ]. Rather than functioning only as documentary representations, the cables became layered visual systems that moved between observation and abstraction. In some works, the cables remained recognizable as parts of the urban landscape. In others, they became lines, knots, grids, and overlapping forms that could be read independently of their original function [ref: معرض «اشتراك»... توصيلات المولّدات الكهربائية ندوب على وجه بيروت, aawsat.com] [ref: ] [ref: غابة الأسلاك والحلول المؤقتة بين الواقعية والتجريد: ديالا خضري... يوميات فوضى اسمها بيروت, الأخبار] [ref: OFF THE GRID by Dyala Khodary on MTV Sar El Wa2et] [ref: ].

Showaddywaddy is the eponymous debut studio album by English rock and roll revival group Showaddywaddy. Released on 8 November 1974 through Bell, the album peaked at number 9 on the UK Albums Chart and remained in the charts for 19 weeks, [ref: Showaddywaddy by Showaddywaddy, Official Charts] certifying Silver with the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) on 1st February 1975. [ref: BRIT Certified Award – Showaddywaddy – Showaddywaddy, British Phonographic Industry] The album was released and distributed in several European countries, as well as Australia, New Zealand, and Japan.

Unlike the group's later reputation as primarily a covers band, the album features nine original compositions alongside three covers of classic 1950s and 1960s tracks. [ref: Hey Rock 'n' Roll!, Isolation Records] It spawned two successful UK singles: "Hey Rock 'n' Roll" (which reached number 2) and "Rock 'n' Roll Lady" (which reached number 15). Prior to the album’s release the band appeared 5 times [ref: Showaddywaddy Artist Profile, Top of the Pops Archive] on the national British tv show Top of the Pops, miming to the 2 singles from the album.

== Critical reception ==

Record Mirror rated the album a good debut in its review on 16 November 1974, noting "a very solid side one" and that side two was "well played and sung". In a retrospective review for AllMusic, critic Dave Thompson awarded the album four out of five stars, praising the group as one of the finest and most enduring rock & roll revival bands of the 1970s. Thompson noted that while they emerged alongside other glam-era retro groups, their run of early material sounded remarkably pure and authentic, effectively balancing commercial pop appeal with true energy. The Encyclopedia of Popular Music gave the album a three-star rating, meaning the album was "good" by the groups "usual standards."

== Track listing ==
All tracks are written by Buddy Gask, Trevor Oakes, Al James, Romeo Challenger, Dave Bartram, Russ Field, Rod Deas, and Malcolm Allured, except where noted. Track lengths via MusicBrainz. [ref: Showaddywaddy release entry, MusicBrainz]

=== 2000 CD reissue bonus tracks ===
The 2000 reissue on 7T’s Records (GLAM CD 2) included the following bonus tracks, both written by Showaddywaddy:

# “You Will Lose Your Love Tomorrow” (first released on b-side of “Hey Rock ‘n’ Roll”)
# “I’m a Traveller” (first released on b-side of “Rock ‘n’ Roll Lady”)

Bahamas Airways was an airline based out of Nassau that operated from 1936 to 1970. It was a part of the BOAC group of companies and was one of the first airlines based out of the Bahamas. The company had a large impact during an important period in the development of tourism in the country. It was sold to the John Swire & Sons in 1968 but went out of business 2 years later.

== History ==

=== Establishment ===
Bahamas Airways was founded in 1936 [ref: Bahamas Air Holdings Ltd., Encyclopedia.com] by Charles Collar. [ref: Origins of Bahamian Aviation, The Nassau Institute] Collar was an American who had served in the US Naval Reserve and flown with Pan Am.

The airline took over the routes of Inter-Island Charter Services which had gone out of business after just three years. Millionaire Harry Oakes, one of Collar's customers, invested in the airline, allowing it to buy a Douglas Dolphin.

=== Operations (1941–1970) ===
In 1941, Collar returned to the US and sold the airline to Pan Am. In 1944, American Airways also took an interest in the fledgling airline. [ref: Index to vol. XLVI: July to December 1944, Flight and Aircraft Engineer] In 1947, the airline started flying to a cluster of islands nicknamed the French Leave islands.

In January 1949, the airline was acquired by H. G. Christie's British South American Airways. [ref: B.S.A.A. Acquire Bahamas Line, Gloucestershire Echo] [ref: ] In March 1956, the airline started flying to Grand Turk in the Turks and Caicos Islands via San Salvador, Mayaguana and Great Inagua. [ref: Bahamas Airways '59, Bluegrass Airlines]

In the 1950s, the government subsidised the airline. [ref: Air, Colonial Office Report on the Bahamas for the Years 1952 and 1953] [ref: Air, Colonial Office Report for the Bahamas for the Years 1954 and 1955] [ref: Air, Colonial Office Report for the Bahamas for the years 1956 and 1957]

In April 1959, the new Skyways (Bahamas) purchased a stake in the airline.

Bahamas Airways tried to break into the market flying to Florida, however, it didn't have a lot of success. It acquired bigger airplanes but American passengers still didn't fly with them and opted instead to fly with Pan Am and Mackey Airlines. In addition, the airline had to pay nearly double the cost of maintenance as other carriers. [ref: Flight 24 May 1962 (Britten-Norman Hovercraft Cutaway, Aurora, Bahamas Airways)] In 1958, the airline was also affected by the General Strike. [ref: B. O. A. C. 1957–58, Flight and Aircraft Engineer]

Several other airlines like Pan Am and British Eagle would propose replacements for Bahamas Airways around the same time as the crisis at Bahamas Airways.

However, the airline remained competitive in the domestic market with flights often being overbooked. [ref: ]

Parent company BOAC looked for a buyer for the airline. [ref: Bahamas Airways Pt2: Swire’s Flamingo -, Yesterday's Airlines] In 1961, questions were asked in the House of Commons when Bahamas Airways was sold by BOAC to Eric Rylands and David Brown and then bought back by BOAC in 1960. [ref: Air Commerce... Clearing the Bahamas Air, Flight (magazine)] MPs wanted to know the amount of money that exchanged hands.

The Bahamian government refused to take and interest and, in 1969, BOAC approached John Swire & Sons, which owned Cathay Pacific and had purchased Hong Kong Airways during the 1950s.

=== Collapse ===
In 1968, John Swire & Sons took an 80% stake in the airline, [ref: ] [ref: ] and set about rebranding the airline. [ref: New Image, Twin Falls Times News] The new flamingo motif and flight attendant uniforms, reminiscent of the Royal Bahamas Police Force, attracted attention. The airline ordered a couple of BAC 1-11s to allow it to carry more passengers and fly further. However, it was still bested by competitors flying Boeing 727. A long range BAC 1-11-500 was created by BAC especially for the airline. The airline took on 35 more flight attendants and, in July 1970, the airline announced that it was planning jet services to the Cayman Islands. [ref: Bahamas Airways to Introduce Jet Service, The Caymanian] In total, John Swire spent $30 million dollars. [ref: ]

On 9 October 1970, Bahamas Airways abruptly ceased operations, [ref: Airline going into liquidation, Shropspire Star] $35 million in debt.

The company cited the impact of a US recession on tourism; it had also failed to convince the Bahamian Government to invest in the airline. [ref: Bahamas Airways Ends Operation, Citing Recession, The New York Times] However, the Minister for Transport countered that the government had been been prepared to take a 51% interest in the carrier but the company insisted on a non-negotiable term that was unacceptable to the government and an immediate injection of cash. [ref: ] When the airline went out of business, 600 employees lost their jobs, including 80 pilots.

The airline was eventually wound up in 1973. The same year, the national carrier Bahamasair was born taking over the routes of Flamingo Airlines and Out Island Airways.

== Fleet ==
The airline would utilize a number of airlines during its lifetime:

* a Loening Air Yacht was the first aircraft in the Bahamas Airways fleet
* Douglas Dolphin in the 1930s and 1940s.
* six Vickers Viscounts. All of them removed from the fleet by the end of 1968.
* four Hawker Siddely HS 748; none of them the fleet by 1970 when the airline ceased operations.
* single Canadian Vickers Catalina was removed from the fleet in 1956.

Draft: Charge collection narrowing

Draft text:
Charge collection narrowing (CCN) is a mechanism used to obtain spectrally selective (narrowband) photodetection from a semiconductor that absorbs light over a broad spectral range, without an optical filter. Instead of restricting which photons are absorbed, CCN restricts which photogenerated charge carriers are collected: the active layer is made optically thick, so that strongly absorbed photons generate carriers in a region from which they cannot be extracted, while weakly absorbed photons near the absorption edge penetrate deeper into the device and are collected. The external quantum efficiency therefore peaks near the absorption onset, and the response to the main absorption band is suppressed.

== Principle of operation ==
The absorption coefficient of a semiconductor varies with wavelength, so the depth at which light is absorbed (the penetration depth) is wavelength dependent. In a device whose charge collection efficiency is not uniform across the active layer, this converts a spectral difference into a spatial one. Carriers generated in a poorly collecting region near the illuminated contact are lost, whereas carriers generated beyond it contribute to the photocurrent. Narrowband response is obtained by matching the thickness of the absorbing layer to the spectrally dependent penetration depth of the light. The mechanism has been described as selectively collecting long-wavelength photogenerated carriers by exploiting the difference between the carrier drift length and the penetration depth of the light, giving a narrow response at the absorption cut-off edge of the active material.

Reported origins of the non-uniform collection include electrical doping of the active layer and imbalanced charge-carrier mobilities.

== History ==
CCN was introduced in 2015 by Armin and co-workers, who reported organic photodiodes with optically thick bulk heterojunctions showing sub-100 nm full width at half maximum (FWHM), visible-blind red and near-infrared responses, and named the concept charge collection narrowing. Filterless narrowband visible photodiodes based on the same principle were reported in the same year. A 2018 review of organic near-infrared photodiodes lists manipulation of internal quantum efficiency via charge collection narrowing as one of three primary strategies for narrowband organic photodiodes, alongside truly narrowband absorbers and optical cavity structures.

== Implementations ==
CCN has been applied across several material systems:
* Organic semiconductors. Thick bulk-heterojunction photodiodes; a 2025 device based on a low-bandgap random terpolymer reached an FWHM of 68 nm at 916 nm, an effect attributed to a hole mobility exceeding the electron mobility by more than an order of magnitude.
* Doped organic junctions. Intentional n-type doping of an optically thick polymer:non-fullerene blend through an electron-donating amine interlayer produced a sub-50 nm response in the near-infrared.
* Metal-halide perovskites. The mechanism has been used to make perovskite narrowband photodetectors, with the spectral position tuned through the composition-dependent bandgap.
* Wide-bandgap semiconductors. A filterless narrowband 4H-silicon carbide photodetector using a sufficiently thick absorbing layer showed an FWHM of 14.5 nm at a peak wavelength of 355 nm.

== Limitations ==
Because the mechanism works by discarding the carriers generated by strongly absorbed light, narrowband response obtained through CCN is accompanied by a reduced external quantum efficiency, and the thick absorbing layers required lead to slower response times than thin-film photodiodes of the same materials.

== Comparison with other narrowband strategies ==
Alternative routes to filterless narrowband detection include semiconductors with intrinsically narrow absorption bands, optical microcavity and light management structures, and mechanisms based on exciton dissociation rather than charge collection.

== See also ==
* Photodetector
* Photodiode
* Quantum efficiency
* Organic semiconductor

Tahini's is a Canadian fast-casual restaurant chain specializing in Mediterranean fusion cuisine. [ref: Tahini's goes global: London restaurant chain expanding to the U.S., CBC News] [ref: A Small Restaurant Chain Is Plowing All of Its Profits Into Bitcoin, Markets Insider] Founded in 2012 in London, Ontario, the company operates franchise and corporate locations across Canada and the United States. [ref: Tahini's Bitcoin Treasury: How A Family Chain Outsmarted Inflation, Bitcoin Magazine] The chain is notable in corporate finance for converting its cash reserves into Bitcoin as a treasury reserve asset beginning in August 2020. [ref: Canadian Restaurant, Tahini's, Goes All-In With Bitcoin, BNN Bloomberg]

== History ==
Tahini's was established in 2012 by brothers Omar and Aly Hamam after acquiring a restaurant in London, Ontario. The company initially operated as a single local restaurant before expanding into a franchise business model across Canada.

In February 2025, the company began international expansion into the United States, opening franchise locations in Illinois with further regional development planned in Chicago and New Jersey.

== Corporate treasury strategy ==
In August 2020, Tahini's converted 100% of its corporate cash reserves into Bitcoin to hedge against potential currency inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic. Co-founders Omar and Aly Hamam cited past personal experiences with currency devaluation in Egypt and corporate moves by MicroStrategy as primary influences for the treasury adoption.

The company instituted a monthly dollar-cost averaging strategy, sweeping excess operational profits into Bitcoin while maintaining three to six months of working capital in cash. The company also introduced Bitcoin ATMs at select restaurant franchise locations.

== Media coverage ==
The company's non-traditional balance sheet strategy and international franchise growth have been featured in corporate broadcast coverage on BNN Bloomberg as well as dedicated business reporting by Markets Insider and CBC News.

Draft: Richard North (ethnomusicologist)

Draft text:
Richard North is an American ethnomusicologist, musician, and educator specializing in the traditional music traditions of Cirebon, an ancient kingdom on the north coast of West Java, Indonesia famous for its rich heritage of artistic traditions. Born on September 3, 1953 in Newport Beach, California, United State, he has been active in the research, teaching, documentation, and performance of Cirebon traditional music since 1976 in Indonesia, where he is known as Erik North (and affectionately as “Mama Erik”).

In addition to his activities in Indonesia, North is also the founder and director since 2002 of Gamelan Sinar Surya, a traditional Indonesian music ensemble based in Santa Barbara, California, United States, which focuses on teaching and performing Cirebon gamelan music. He is also a Continuing Lecturer and director of the University of California, Santa Barbara Gamelan Ensemble since 2015. [ref: Richard North, Department of Music, University of California, Santa Barbara] [ref: Gamelan Goes On at UCSB, The Santa Barbara Independent]

== Early life and education ==

North developed an interest in Asian culture and music as an Asian Studies major at the University of California, San Diego. It was there that he first learned gamelan music in 1972, studying under KRT Wasitodipuro, a famous master of the gamelan tradition of Central Java. [ref: Richard North, Department of Music, University of California, Santa Barbara]

In 1973 he continued his gamelan studies at the Center for World Music in Berkeley, California, where he became familiar with various regional forms of Indonesian gamelan from Sunda, Bali, and Central Java. He studied extensively with Undang Sumarna, a highly respected Sundanese gamelan teacher and performer who was active in teaching gamelan in California's academic community for over 50 years. [ref: Richard North, Department of Music, University of California, Santa Barbara]

North was introduced to the arts and culture of Cirebon by the famous scholar and performer of West Java performing arts Enoch Atmadibrata, who brought him to Cirebon on his first visit to Indonesia in 1976. Atmadibrata introduced him to a whole spectrum of Cirebon art traditions including not only Cirebon gamelan music, but also Cirebon style mask (Topeng) dancing, shadow puppet (Wayang Kulit) and rod puppet (Wayang Cepak) theatre, batik textiles, sacred heirloom daggers (Keris), reverse glass painting (Lukisan Kaca), traditional woodcarving and a host of other Cirebon arts. [ref: Richard North, Department of Music, University of California, Santa Barbara]

In addition to his formal education, North deepened his knowledge through direct study with the teachers and performers in the Cirebon arts community. He worked with traditional artists, including Cirebon legendary Topeng (mask) dancer Sujana Arja and local artists such as Pak Bulus, who introduced him to Cirebon's performance traditions at the community level. [ref: Cerita Profesor Amerika Pengajar Gamelan Cirebon di Universitas California, Liputan6.com] [ref: Sujana Arja, Maestro Topeng Cirebon, Liputan6.com]

In 1981, North received further training at the Kacirebonan Palace under the Lurah Seni Keraton (Palace Arts Director) Pangeran Haji Yusuf Dendabrata. This experience further deepened his understanding of Cirebon's musical traditions and practices. [ref: Gamelan Music of Cirebon, Indonesia: Volume 6 — Denggung, Lyricord Media]

As an ethnomusicologist, North combines academic study with performance experience. Under the guidance of P. H. Yusuf Dendabrata, he came to view gamelan not simply as an art form, but also as a complex, orderly, interdependent, and harmonious social and cultural system. This perspective became the basis of his approach to Cirebon music. [ref: Cerita Profesor Amerika Pengajar Gamelan Cirebon di Universitas California, Liputan6.com]

As part of his ethnomusicology work, North has shared his recordings, music notation and documentation of rare Cirebon art forms that were on the verge of extinction with Cirebon artists and communities to support the preservation of Cirebon's living cultural heritage. [ref: Gamelan of Thrones, University of California, Santa Barbara]

== Career and cultural activities ==
Since his first visit to Indonesia in 1976, North has returned to Cirebon more than 14 times to research, document, and study various forms of traditional music from the region, [ref: Yuk Kenalan dengan Richard North, Profesor Musik dari UCSB yang Cinta Gamelan Indonesia, Suara Merdeka Jakarta] including:

* Cirebon Gong Renteng [ref: Gong Renteng - A Brief History and Its Development Today]
* Cirebon Denggung
* Cirebon Gender
* Gong Sekati from the Kasepuhan and Kanoman palaces
* traditional Cirebon gamelan repertoires which were declining and approaching extinction in both the 5-tone Slendro tuning system (known in Cirebon as Prawa) as well as in the 7-tone Pelog tuning. [ref: Gamelan Cirebon: Its History and Present Condition]

Draft text:
Dove Viaggi (often simply Dove) is an Italian monthly travel and lifestyle magazine established in 1991 and published by RCS MediaGroup (ISSN 1121-1792). [ref: Dove, rcsmediagroup.it] [ref: Sito ufficiale Dove Viaggi, Corriere della Sera]

== History ==
The magazine was founded in May 1991 by journalist and publisher Luca Grandori (d. 2012), who had previously created other Italian travel publications, including Gulliver and Carnet. [ref: 25 anni di viaggi e sogni: l’editoriale del numero speciale di DOVE, Dove Viaggi] Its initial editorial office was located in Milan, with a founding team that included journalists Valeria Tegami, Mariella Grossi and Simona Tedesco.

During the 1990s, the magazine published themed print supplements, such as Speciale Weekend (focused on short itineraries) and Dossier Tropici (covering long-haul destinations). [ref: Cronologia e Linee di Sviluppo del Sistema DOVE, CairoRCS Media] In 2005, the publication released a series of spin-off magazines: DOVE Case, DOVE Eventi, and DOVE Auto. [ref: Dove negli anni, Corriere della Sera]

Valeria Tegami later became the magazine's director, followed by Carlo Montanaro. In January 2015, Simona Tedesco was appointed editor-in-chief, with an editorial focus on contemporary and sustainable travel.

In May 2017, the publication launched an annual Travel issue, distributed as a supplement with the daily newspaper Corriere della Sera.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the magazine temporarily shifted its editorial focus to domestic and local travel and launched digital initiatives allowing readers to share local content.

In 2026, Dove expanded its multimedia activities with vodcasts and the reader-focused DOVE Experience initiatives. In June, for its 35th anniversary, the magazine published a special issue with a commemorative cover and an editorial by Simona Tedesco centered on the manifesto "Andiamo sul posto. E raccontiamo", emphasizing the value of on-the-ground reporting over AI-generated content and unverified reviews. [ref: Buon compleanno Dove: 35 anni di viaggi da sogno, iO Donna]

== Monographic guides and special projects ==
Beyond its monthly print edition, the brand has developed several long-running editorial products and public initiatives. These include Le Guide di Dove, established as a structured series of monographic travel guides in 2006 following earlier pocket editions distributed with Corriere della Sera, which were later updated to incorporate digital features such as QR codes and geolocated podcasts.

The brand also organizes cultural festivals and public events focused on travel culture, most notably Il Tempo del Viaggio, produced in collaboration with Corriere della Sera at venues such as Sala Buzzati in Milan. [ref: Il Tempo del Viaggio Inverno, Corriere della Sera]

In the digital domain, the brand launched the portal doveviaggi.it in February 2014 as the travel section of the Corriere della Sera digital network. Over the years, the website expanded its online content to include narrative video reports, thematic newsletters, and dedicated podcasts launched in 2020, such as Brescia, che sorpresa! and I viaggi da film. This digital ecosystem was further extended in 2026 with the introduction of vodcasts and the DOVE Experience reader initiatives. [ref: I podcast di Dove Viaggi, Corriere della Sera] [ref: I Podcast di Dove 35 anni, Corriere della Sera]

As part of its commercial services, the brand launched DoveClub in February 2014, operating in parallel with the digital portal as an online travel booking and e-commerce platform. Originally focused on time-limited flash sales curated by the magazine's journalists, the platform subsequently consolidated its positioning in high-end tourism by offering customized travel packages and luxury experiences integrated within the newspaper's digital network.

== Editors-in-chief ==

* Valeria Tegami (1994–2003)
* Carlo Montanaro (2003–2015)
* Simona Tedesco (2015–present)

Lifestyle Gift Cards is a multi-retailer gift card platform, operated by Motivates Inc., a reward a recognition company in the United Kingdom. [ref: Red Letter Days Motivates is a new name to reflect a new strategy, reba.global]

The company provides gift card products for consumer gifting and corporate incentive programmes, including employee recognition, customer promotions an sales incentives. [ref: Red Letter Days launches a new corporate events division - Employee Benefits, Employee Benefits - Employee Benefits is the UK’s leading free-to-access website for HR, reward and benefits professionals.]

Lifestyle Gift Cards allows users to exchange prepaid gift card value for digital gift cards and vouchers from participating retailers through an online redemption platform. [ref: Lifestyle, www.lifestylegiftcards.co.uk]

== History ==
Lifestyle Gift Cards originated within Red Letter Days for Business, the corporate division of the UK experience gift company Red Letter Days.

The Lifestyle Gift Card product was introduced in 2011 as a multi-retailer gift card product that enabled recipients to exchange stored value for retailer-specific gift cards and vouchers from participating brands. [ref: The Perfect Gift has arrived just in time for Christmas - the Lifestyle Ultimate gift card!, ResponseSource Press Release Wire]

In 2018, Motivates Inc. was formed following a management buyout of the Lifestyle Gift Cards businesses from Red Letter Days for Business.

In 2020, Motivates Inc. partnered with InComm Payments to expand retail distribution of Lifestyle Gift Cards in the United Kingdom. [ref: InComm Payments Partners with Motivates to Launch a Multi-Choice Gift Card in the UK, www.prnewswire.co.uk] Following the partnership, the products became available through retail outlets including Sainsbury's, ASDA and TGJones.

In 2025, the company partnered with Small Business Sunday (#SBS), a small business network founded by entrepreneur Theo Paphitis, to launch the #SBS x Lifestyle Gift Card featuring independent businesses in the United Kingdom. [ref: ]

Motivates Inc. is a member of the Gift Card & Voucher Association (GCVA), the UK trade body for the gift card and stored value sector. [ref: Lifestyle, Gift Card & Voucher Association]

== Operations ==
Lifestyle Gift Cards operates multi retailer gift card products that can be redeemed online for digital gift cards and vouchers from participating brands.

The company's products are used in consumer gifting and corporate reward programmes, including employee recognition, customer incentives and promotional campaigns.

Lifestyle Gift Cards products are distributed through retail channels, corporate partnerships and online sales platforms.

The company also provides white-label gift card products to third-party brands and retailers such as Funky Pigeon. [ref: Funky Pigeon powered by Lifestyle Gift Cards, Funky Pigeon]

== Sustainability ==
Motivates Inc. became a Certified B Corporation in 2022. [ref: Motivates Inc. - Certified B Corporation - B Lab, www.bcorporation.net]

The company has introduced plastic-free packaging for selected gift card products and publishes information relating to environmental initiatives and carbon emissions reporting. [ref: Motivates-, Motivates]

Sara Mitich (born November 26, 1988) is a Canadian actress who is best known for her roles in Star Trek: Discovery, The Expanse, and Murdoch Mysteries. Mitich is the host of Gratitude & Growth, [ref: https://gratitudegrowth.com/about the website for Gratitude & Growth] and the author of 21 Days of Gratitude: Simple Exercises for a More Positive Life.

==Early life==
Sara Mitich was born in 1988 in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada [ref: https://youvebeenhooked.wordpress.com/2016/07/11/5x5-with-the-hook-sara-mitich/ an interview with Sara] and she is the youngest out of three girls. Her parents are from Serbia. She wanted to be a ballerina from a young age, and she attended the National Ballet School of Canada. As an adult, she attended the University of Toronto and Sheridan college for acting. She starred in various short films, such as Mind Games, Plastic, and Prick.

==Career==
===Murdoch Mysteries===
In Murdoch Mysteries, Mitich portrays Lillian Moss, a suffragette attempting to flee from her past life. Her character, Moss, and potential romantic partner, Emily Grace—played by actor Georgina Reilly —meet while protesting for women's rights, and the two grow close while working together. The pair decide to move to London, England, although Mitich's character is killed before the pair are able to leave Toronto.

===The Expanse===
In The Expanse, Mitich portrays a character named Gia, a prostitute who appears in four episodes of season one. In addition to her job, she also serves as a language tutor to Dimitri Havelock—portrayed by actor Jay Hernandez—a detective on the planet Ceres. She is later attacked by another character and is visited by Havelock while she recovers in the hospital. When asked about portraying Gia, Mitich has said that the "learning the language and gestural language was challenging." She also mentions that the role of Gia is one that she has learned keep perspective with and not to judge them. [ref: Revealed in an interview with Mitich on [https://starrymag.com/sara-mitich-the-expanse/ Starry Mag's website]]

===Star Trek Discovery===
Throughout the series Star Trek: Discovery, Mitich had the opportunity to play two different characters, Lieutenant Commander Airiam and Lieutenant Nilsson. She portrayed Airiam during the first season of the show, before being recast as Lt. Nilsson from season two onwards. Airiam was a female human cyborg, who also served as an officer aboard the USS Discovery. According to Darren Franich, a critic at Entertainment Weekly, Airiam is "the greatest background character in Trek history since the glory days of the Deep Space 9 bar." [ref: http://ew.com/tv/2019/01/11/star-trek-discovery-canon Entertainment Weekly]

As for Nilsson, her background is similar to Mitich's own—a ballerina who went to a prestigious school of dance, and ended up with a differing career path. [ref: Issue 204, Star Trek Magazine] Her character succeeds Airiam as a spore drives ops officer aboard the USS Discovery. Occasionally, Nilsson would be left in charge of the bridge of her ship. She later moves and serves aboard the USS Voyager, leaving her pet tribble behind.

===Control===

In Control, Mitich portrays a woman named Eileen. She wakes up in a room, where she is given numerous tasks to complete by an unseen entity. Failure to do so would result in her daughter, Eve, being killed. Working with her husband Roger, the pair must work together to save their daughter and uncover the secret behind her memory loss. Eileen has latent psychic abilities, and the organization that trapped her is determined to see what she can do. [ref: Revealed on [https://kemodoent.com/film/control/ Kemodo Entertainment's official website]]

==Personal life==
Mitich is an accomplished equestrian. She also enjoys kickboxing, yoga, and Pilates.

===Gratitude & Growth===
Mitich is the host of the self-growth brand named Gratitude & Growth, a personal development platform focused on mindfulness, emotional regulation, and presence. The project began as a podcast and later expanded into a broader brand offering written content, community resources, and tools for personal growth.Her work with Gratitude & Growth has been featured by publications including Tiny Buddha [ref: https://tinybuddha.com/author/sara-mitch/ Tinybuddha's website] and The Elephant Journal.

Zoopunk is an upcoming action role-playing video game developed and published by the Chinese studio TiGames. The game is a prequel to F.I.S.T.: Forged In Shadow Torch (2021), and changes the earlier game's side-scrolling Metroidvania format into a three-dimensional, third-person action role-playing game.

==Gameplay==
The game is played from a third-person perspective and combines melee and ranged combat with exploration. TiGames has described its areas as wider and more vertically layered than those in F.I.S.T., but not as a seamless open world. [ref: Zoopunk and the revival of wildness beyond wasteland aesthetics, IGN China] Three playable characters were announced: Rayton, an agile rabbit who specializes in close-range attacks; Braton, a rhinoceros who fights with heavy attacks and a large flame sword; and Trixie, a chipmunk who relies on acrobatics and hit-and-run tactics. Each character has a distinct combat role. [ref: Zoopunk shown in a spectacular new trailer, Gamereactor] [ref: ZOOPUNK Gamescom 2026 trailer screenshots, Gematsu]

== Premise ==
The story is set decades before F.I.S.T.: Forged In Shadow Torch, during the origins of Torch City. The discovery of Fire Seed energy accelerates technological development but also awakens mechanical debris, which becomes a self-aware mechanical empire. [ref: ZOOPUNK confirmed for PS5, Xbox Series, and PC; reveal trailer, Gematsu] [ref: Enter the Dieselpunk Chaos of Torch City in ZOOPUNK Coming to Xbox and PC, TheXboxHub] Rayton, Braton, and Trixie travel through territories controlled by competing animal factions as the First Torch War begins, with the characters shown pursuing an object called the Spark. [ref: Xbox Partner Preview November 2025 Everything Announced From Our Amazing Partners, Xbox Wire] [ref: 動物たちによるド派手なアクション『Zoopunk（ズーパンク）』の発売が決定。発売時期は明かされず【Xbox Partner Preview】, Dengeki Online]

== Development and release ==
TiGames began informal discussions about the project in early 2023 and began prototype development in 2024. Studio chief executive Tao Zhang said that the development team had grown from about 20 people to approximately 50, while retaining members of the earlier game's action-design team and composer Caisheng Bo. Chinese concept artist Su Jian was invited to contribute to the visual design. The game is being made with Unreal Engine 5, replacing the predecessor's use of Unreal Engine 4. TiGames cited the newer engine's handling of fur, feathers, lighting, and larger environments as reasons for the change. The term animal punk was used by the developers to describe the combination of anthropomorphic characters, industrial machinery, ruins, and resistance to technological domination.

The January 2025 Nvidia technology demonstration was the first public announcement of the game, which was then described as a project in the same setting as F.I.S.T. [ref: TiGames announces ZOOPUNK for console PC, Gematsu] In an interview published during CES 2025, Zhang called Zoopunk a provisional title and described it as a conventional PC and console game rather than an AI-focused experiment. [ref: Interview with TiGames CEO Tao Zhang on expanding the Animal Punk universe, TapTap] However, following the November 2025 gameplay reveal, the game's visual assets and an in-game tool allowing players to use generative AI for creating content sparked online discussion. TiGames publicly clarified that the core game is entirely human-made. [ref: Zoopunk Says The Game Is All Human Made But Lets Players Use Gen AI To Make Stuff, Kotaku] [ref: Rabbit action game Zoopunk was made by humans not AI says Chinese dev TiGames, Eurogamer]

TiGames formally revealed the game with a gameplay trailer during the Xbox Partner Preview on November 20, 2025. [ref: Every big announcement from the Xbox Partner Preview, Polygon] A second trailer premiered during Gamescom Opening Night Live on August 25, 2026, followed by an extended five-minute gameplay presentation. [ref: Animal Punk action RPG Zoopunk is coming to PC and consoles, RPG Site] [ref: All the Xbox and PC game announcements at Gamescom 2026 Opening Night Live, Windows Central] The game is set to be released for Windows, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X and Series S in 2027.

== Reception ==
Writing after the 2025 reveal, Alberto Zaragoza Lerma of MeriStation characterized the move from a Metroidvania to a three-dimensional action role-playing game as a substantial change from F.I.S.T.. [ref: A standout Chinese game makes the leap to 3D action in its prequel, MeriStation] Michael Hoglund of Windows Central praised the game's "grizzled combat and wondrous colors" but noted that certain visual elements felt off. [ref: ZOOPUNK showcases grizzled combat and wondrous colors but something feels off, Windows Central]

At Gamescom 2026, GamesRadar+ compared the presentation's premise and large-machine combat to other third-person action games, but commented that the density of the trailer made the action difficult to follow. [ref: Gamescom Opening Night Live 2026 Everything announced, GamesRadar+] Fabiano Uslenghi of GameStar called it his action game "surprise" of the event. [ref: Zoopunk was my action surprise of Opening Night Live, GameStar]

Prateek Gupta is an Indian film producer, writer, and editor. [ref: 'Hellaro' 1st Gujarati film to win top national award, The Times of India] He co-directed the documentary Goonga Pehelwan (2014), which won the National Film Award for Best Debut Film of a Director at the 62nd National Film Awards [ref: Complete list of 62nd National Film Award winners, ONMANORAMA] [ref: 62nd National Film Awards, 2014 announced, Press Information Bureau, Government of India, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting], and co-wrote, edited and co-produced Hellaro (2019), the first Gujarati film to win the National Film Award for Best Feature Film. [ref: Hellaro wins four awards at the Critics Choice Film Awards, The Times Of India]

==Early life and education==
Prateek Gupta graduated with a BCom (Hons) in accounting from the Amrut Mody School of Management at Ahmedabad University in 2010, and qualified as a chartered accountant in 2012 before entering filmmaking. [ref: Cannes Film Festival, Golden Lotus at National Film Awards for Ahmedabad Alumni, Ahmedabad University]

==Career==
Prateek Gupta co-directed Goonga Pehelwan with Mit Jani and Vivek Chaudhary, a feature-length documentary on the deaf wrestler Virender Singh (wrestler, born 1986). [ref: Goonga Pehelwan gets national award, The Indian Express] Alongside the film, the directors ran a campaign, Mission Rio 2016, seeking improved competition conditions for deaf wrestlers and the release of cash awards owed to Singh; the Wrestling Federation of India subsequently agreed to provide referees using visual and tactile cues for deaf competitors. [ref: Silent Strength, [[The Caravan (magazine)] [ref: A fighting chance, Bangalore Mirror]

Goonga Pehelwan won the National Film Award for Best Debut Film of a Director in the non-feature category at the 62nd National Film Awards, announced in March 2015. [ref: National award to Goonga Pahelwan, film on deaf-mute wrestler, Counterview] The directors attended the 46th International Film Festival of India in Panaji in November 2015, where the film was screened. [ref: The Directors of the Non-Feature film "Goonga Pehalwan", Vivek Chaudhary, Prateek Gupta and Mit Jani at a press conference, at the 46th International Film Festival of India, Press Information Bureau]

Prateek Gupta also worked on Hellaro (2019), directed by Abhishek Shah and made under the Saarthi Productions and Harfanmaula Films banners. He was a a co-producer, shared the screenplay credit with Shah, and worked as an editor. [ref: Hellaro: A journey from suppression to expression, Kartavya Sadhana] Set in the Rann of Kutch in the 1970s, the film won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film at the 66th National Film Awards, the first Gujarati film to do so, and its thirteen lead actresses jointly received a Special Jury Award. [ref: National Award Winning Gujarati Film Hellaro Gets A Hindi Release, The New Indian Express Indulge] [ref: 66th National Film Awards for 2018 announced, Press Information Bureau, Government of India, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting]

He went on to produce Kamthaan (2024), adapted from a novel by the Gujarati writer Ashwini Bhatt and directed by Dhrunad, [ref: Gujarati film 'Kamthan' a stress busting cop-comedy, South Asia Times] and Dhabkaaro (2026), written and directed by Shah and co-produced with Nadiadwala Grandson Entertainment. [ref: Makers of national award winning film Hellaro announce new Gujarati project: Dhabkaaro, Counterview] [ref: JOJO App Announces World Digital Premiere of the film 'Dhabkaaro' from August 27, Ahmedabad Mirror]

Shinn serves as chief strategy officer and has more than 20 years of experience in high-volume enterprise information systems; Solomonik serves as chief technology officer, with more than 20 years of software industry experience, including extensive experience in high-capacity billing information systems. [ref: Englewood-based BillingPlatform raises $18M Series A, announces new CEO]

The company grew organically for several years before seeking external funding, expanding its client base primarily through direct sales and word-of-mouth referrals.

In January 2026, Chris Bishop was named Chief Executive Officer, with Dennis Wall remaining on the company's board of directors. [ref: Chris Bishiop Named CEO of BillingPlatform]

==Funding==

In August 2017, BillingPlatform announced a $4 million Series A round led by Columbia Capital and Dennis Wall was named CEO. [ref: Englewood-based BillingPlatform raises $18M Series A, announces new CEO] Wall had previously co-founded Cloud Sherpas, a cloud advisory firm acquired by Accenture in 2015. [ref: Englewood-based BillingPlatform raises $18M Series A, announces new CEO]

In December 2019, BillingPlatform raised a $10 million Series B round from Columbia Capital. [ref: BillingPlatform Raises $10M in Series B Funding]
BillingPlatform announced a $90 million growth equity investment from FTV Capital, in January 2024. [ref: BillingPlatform lands $90m growth equity investment from FTV Capital] FTV Capital joined Columbia Capital as a minority institutional investor, and FTV Capital partners Kyle Griswold and Richard Liu joined the company's board of directors. [ref: BillingPlatform raises $90M growth round from FTV]

==Platform==
BillingPlatform's cloud-based software is built on a metadata-driven architecture that allows billing configurations to be defined through settings rather than custom code. It supports functions related to the order-to-cash process, including product catalog management, order intake, billing, invoicing, revenue recognition, payment processing, and collections.

The software supports several billing models, including one-time charges, subscriptions, usage-based pricing, and tiered pricing, as well as combinations of these models. It integrates with third-party payment gateways and enterprise systems such as ERP and CRM platforms, and includes functionality for ingesting usage data for consumption-based billing. [ref: BillingPlatform Enables Deployment of Pricing Models Designed for AI Services]

==Customers==
Notable customers include Carrier, DIRECTV, Instacart, J.P. Morgan and Panera. [ref: Auctane streamlines billing with expanded BillingPlatform use]

In November 2023, BillingPlatform announced a partnership with J.P. Morgan Payments to support billing needs across J.P. Morgan's Treasury Services and Trade Finance businesses, as part of J.P. Morgan's broader billing and pricing transformation. [ref: J.P. Morgan Payments integrates with BillingPlatform, IBS Intelligence]

Draft: Death Letter Blues (2023 film)

Draft text:
Death Letter Blues, originally titled The Banality, is a 2022 American Southern Gothic mystery thriller film written and directed by Michael Stevantoni and Strack Azar. It stars Sherman Augustus as a small-town Mississippi priest who becomes involved in the aftermath of the death of a teenager known locally as Feral Boy. Karole Foreman, Ramsay Midwood, Arianna Ngnomire and Keylor Leigh also star.

The film premiered at the Newport Beach Film Festival in October 2022 and played other festivals under its original title before Dark Sky Films released it in the United States as Death Letter Blues on August 8, 2025. Critics generally praised its atmosphere, cinematography and lead performance, with some finding its pacing slow and its ending unresolved.

== Plot ==
In a small Mississippi town, Father Moss, a priest struggling with his faith, arranges for a boy found living in the woods to be raised by a childless couple, Ed and Marcy. Eleven years later the boy, still known around town as "Feral Boy", is killed after a party in the woods. As Moss counsels the couple, he is also left a car and a letter of confession by a recently deceased parishioner, and begins to see parallels between the two deaths and his own recurring nightmares.

== Cast ==

* Sherman Augustus as Father Moss
* Karole Foreman as Marcy
* Ramsay Midwood as Ed
* Arianna Ngnomire as Riley
* Keylor Leigh as Jo
* Layton Miller as Feral Boy
* Woodrow Wilkins as Deacon Graham
* Diana Stevan as Ms. Webb

== Production ==
The film was Stevantoni's second feature and was shot in the Mississippi Delta, with many of the supporting roles cast from the local community. [ref: The Filmmakers, Comox Valley International Film Festival] [ref: Film Review: Death Letter Blues, CineGods] Augustus also served as a producer. Thomas Taugher was the cinematographer and Daniel McClure composed the score. [ref: Death Letter Blues, Dark Sky Films]

== Release ==
The film premiered as The Banality at the Newport Beach Film Festival in October 2022. [ref: The Banality, Newport Beach Film Festival] It went on to screen under that title at festivals including the Popcorn Frights Film Festival in August 2023 and the Woods Hole Film Festival in 2025, [ref: Mike's Review: The Banality (2023 Popcorn Frights Film Festival), The Scariest Things] [ref: The Banality, Woods Hole Film Festival] and won Best Mississippi Narrative Feature at the Oxford Film Festival. [ref: Death Letter Blues, Dark Sky Films]

Dark Sky Films released a trailer under the title Death Letter Blues in July 2025, [ref: Official Trailer for 'Death Letter Blues' Small Town Priest Horror Film, FirstShowing.net] and released the film in limited theaters and on digital platforms in the United States on August 8, 2025. [ref: Trailer for Death Letter Blues teases a supernatural mystery, Flickering Myth]

== Critical response ==
In Dread Central, the reviewer praised the film's cinematography and Augustus's performance as the tormented priest but found the pacing slow and the ending unresolved, with several characters' fates left unclear. [ref: 'Death Letter Blues' Review: A Southern Gothic Thriller That Burns Too Slowly, Dread Central] Australian critic Jim Schembri rated it three stars out of five, calling it an atmospheric Southern noir that plays subtly with genre conventions. [ref: A Stranger in the Woods: Death Letter Blues, jimschembri.com]

In a column for Crooked Marquee, Josh Bell gave the film a B, comparing it to the work of Flannery O'Connor and the early films of Jeff Nichols while finding its storytelling somewhat muddled and its pace slow. [ref: VODepths: What to See (and Avoid) on Demand This Week, Crooked Marquee] Tim Cogshell of CineGods was more positive, describing it as a sharp piece of Southern Gothic storytelling with a touch of magical realism. Louisa Moore of Screen Zealots praised its command of light, shadow and atmosphere, while noting that its lack of full resolution might frustrate some viewers. [ref: Death Letter Blues, Screen Zealots] Reviewing it at Popcorn Frights, Mike Campbell of The Scariest Things gave it four stars out of five, praising its cinematography and roots-music score and likening its contemplative approach to the films of Terrence Malick.

Draft text:
Maurice "Moe" Rubenstein (March 16, 1905 – February 3, 2001) was an American high school football, basketball and baseball coach, athletic director, and teacher at Ambridge High School in Ambridge, Pennsylvania. He coached Ambridge football from 1929 through 1950. His Pittsburgh Post-Gazette obituary reported a career record of 146–32–10. His teams never had a losing season. [ref: Feldman, Jacob. The Jewish Experience in Western Pennsylvania: A History 1755–1945. Pittsburgh: The Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania, 1986, p. 205; Snyder, Ron. The History of Ambridge Football 1919–2017; "Maurice Rubenstein." Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, February 6, 2001; Beaver County Sports Hall of Fame entry, https://bcshof.org/halloffamers/rubenstein1977.htm; Rauh Jewish Archives, "A. P. Moore Club," https://rauhjewisharchives.org/entries/a-p-moore-club/]

He coached Ambridge basketball from 1929 through 1946 and compiled a record of 260–99–1 with six section titles. His baseball teams won two sectional championships. [ref: New Castle News, November 14, 1946, p. 24.]

Rubenstein was inducted into the Beaver County Sports Hall of Fame, the Pittsburgh Jewish Sports Hall of Fame, the Pennsylvania Scholastic Football Coaches Association Hall of Fame, the Western Pennsylvania Sports Hall of Fame, and the Geneva College Athletics Hall of Fame. He received the Geneva College Distinguished Service Award. In 1977, Ambridge High School renamed its football stadium "Moe Rubenstein Stadium". [ref: Geneva College Athletics Hall of Fame, "Moe Rubenstein," https://athletics.geneva.edu/honors/geneva-college-athletics-hall-of-fame/moe-rubenstein/60; The Times.]

Rubenstein is credited with helping numerous high school athletes obtain college scholarships. [ref: Bires, Mike. "Moe Was a Legend." Beaver County Times, October 24, 2018. https://www.timesonline.com/story/sports/high-school/football/2018/10/23/moe-was-legend/8385622007/]

He married Sally Walters on August 18, 1929. His wife later owned the Stork's Nest Children's Clothing Store on Merchant Avenue in Ambridge. They had one child, Arlene. [ref: "Sally Rubenstein." Beaver County Times, April 19, 2009. https://www.timesonline.com/story/news/2009/04/19/sally-rubenstein/18307564007/]

==Early life==

Rubenstein was born on March 16, 1905, in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, the son of Lazar and Annie Rubenstein. Lazar was an immigrant from the Ukrainian village of Pliskov and worked as a carpenter. [ref: Birth record, Pittsburgh Department of Public Health. The record lists the father's first name as "Louis" and his occupation as carpenter. Other sources reference his name as Lazar; Louis was likely an Americanized form. The birth certificate also spells the surname as "Rubinstein."] As one of the original settlers from Pliskov around 1900, Lazar Rubenstein invited fellow villagers to come to Pittsburgh, where they stayed in the Rubenstein home until they found housing elsewhere. As a result of the Rubensteins' efforts, Pittsburgh subsequently had a large colony of families who immigrated from Pliskov. [ref: Feldman, Jacob. The Jewish Experience in Western Pennsylvania: A History 1755–1945. Pittsburgh: The Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania, 1986, p. 148.]

Rubenstein grew up in the Hill District of Pittsburgh and attended the now-defunct Fifth Avenue High School. He graduated high school having won nine letters and was named All-City in three different sports: baseball, basketball and football. [ref: Feldman, Jacob. The Jewish Experience in Western Pennsylvania: A History 1755–1945. Pittsburgh: The Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania, 1986, p. 205.]

Rubenstein attended Geneva College in Beaver Falls, Pennsylvania. [ref: Geneva College Athletics Hall of Fame, "Moe Rubenstein," https://athletics.geneva.edu/honors/geneva-college-athletics-hall-of-fame/moe-rubenstein/60] During his senior year, he was captain of the basketball and baseball teams. He did not letter in football. He graduated from Geneva College in 1928.

==Coaching career==

Upon graduation from college, Rubenstein was hired at Ambridge High School as head basketball coach and assistant football coach. He was named head football coach in 1929.

Rubenstein coached football until 1950. His football teams won a WPIAL title in 1932. He also coached basketball from 1929 to 1946, compiling a record of 260–99–1 with six section titles, and his baseball teams won two sectional championships. He had a reputation as a strict disciplinarian who never used profanity and required that his players maintain good grades. [ref: Barrickman, Bob. "Rubenstein Set the Coaching Standard at Ambridge." The Times/Beaver Newspapers, September 2, 1999.] In 19 years of coaching basketball, he was never assessed a technical foul.

Rubenstein is credited with helping numerous high school athletes obtain college scholarships, including players from neighboring schools. He contacted University of Alabama coach Paul "Bear" Bryant to recommend Beaver Falls High School quarterback Joe Namath, who went on to star at Alabama and for the NFL's New York Jets.
[truncated]
