Draft: Johnny Britt (musician)

Draft text:
Johnny Britt is an American singer, trumpeter, songwriter, producer, musical director and author. He is known as a founding member of the Motown/MoJazz R&B and jazz duo Impromp2, for his work as musical director for the Temptations, and for songwriting and recording collaborations with saxophonist Boney James. [ref: Impromp2, AllMusic] [ref: Johnny Britt, SoulTracks] [ref: Ride – Boney James, AllMusic]

== Early life and education ==
Britt was born in Louisville, Kentucky, and raised in Cleveland, Ohio, where he attended Cathedral Latin High School. [ref: Johnny Britt biographical materials.] [ref: Johnny Britt, WBSS Media] [ref: A Former Clevelander, Contemporary Jazz Star Johnny Britt to Perform in Cleveland This Weekend, Cleveland Scene] Gospel music was an early influence; he began singing in his uncle's church as a child and took up the trumpet at age 12.

As a teenager, Britt became friends with future television host Arsenio Hall, who was then a drummer, and the two played music together. Hall later discussed Britt and their long-standing friendship in his memoir. [ref: Arsenio: A Memoir] According to a photograph and caption reproduced in the book, the two met as students at R. H. Jamison Junior High School in Cleveland and started their first band together at age thirteen; Britt and Hall went on to play together in a group called the Soul Sophistications.

During a visit to France while still in high school, Britt attended a performance by French classical trumpeter Maurice André. Britt has described the experience as influencing his decision to pursue trumpet more seriously. [ref: 10 Questions with Johnny Britt, Connect Brazil]

Britt later returned to France and studied classical trumpet at the Conservatoire de Versailles under Roger Delmotte of the Paris Opera. In an interview with Connect Brazil, Britt said that during his time in France he became fluent in French, signed his first recording contract in Paris, and appeared on French radio and television.

After returning to the United States, Britt continued his music studies at Governors State University in the Chicago area, where he earned a bachelor's degree in music and received the Gerald Myrow Award for Outstanding Composer.

== Career ==

=== The Temptations ===
Britt's association with the Temptations began after meeting the group's founding member Otis Williams. Britt has recounted approaching Williams after a performance and presenting him with original songs; Williams subsequently hired Britt as the group's musical director.

Britt served as musical director for the Temptations for approximately three years. Multiple published profiles have described him as the group's youngest-ever musical director. [ref: Johnny Britt, EFG London Jazz Festival] [ref: Sitemap, EFG London Jazz Festival] [ref: Johnny Britt '75: A Multifaceted Talent Making Waves Across Industries, Latin Alumnotes] Arsenio Hall's memoir independently corroborates the general timing of the hire: Hall recounts that Britt, after the two reconnected following several years apart, told him that Williams had just hired him for the role.

Britt also worked as a songwriter and producer for the Temptations. He later served as a co-music producer on the NBC television miniseries The Temptations.

Britt subsequently worked as a co-music producer on the television film Little Richard, directed by Robert Townsend.

=== Impromp2 ===
After his work with the Temptations, Britt developed the concept for Impromp2 in Los Angeles, combining his vocals and trumpet with hip-hop and contemporary R&B influences. He partnered with rapper Sean E. Mac, and Impromp2 was formed in Los Angeles in 1993.

The duo signed with Motown's MoJazz label and released its debut album, You're Gonna Love It, in 1995, followed by Can't Get Enough in 1997.

After MoJazz was discontinued, Impromp2 released The Definition of Love through Big3 Records in 2003. JazzTimes described the group's combination of Britt's singing and trumpet with Sean E. Mac's rapping and singing; the album included guest appearances by Boney James and George Duke. [ref: Musicians find originality in mix of different styles, The Vindicator] [ref: Impromp2: The Definition of Love, JazzTimes]

The duo's fourth studio album, It Is What It Is, followed in 2008.

=== Songwriting, recording and solo career ===
As a songwriter, vocalist and musician, Britt contributed to several recordings by saxophonist Boney James. On James's 2001 album Ride, Britt co-wrote "Heaven" and "Grand Central" and contributed background vocals; AllMusic credits "Grand Central" to Johnny Britt and Boney James. [ref: Boney James Takes Guest Artists for a Ride, Billboard]

On James's 2004 album Pure, Britt co-wrote "Break of Dawn" (featuring Dwele) with James and Andwele Gardner, and co-wrote "It's On" with James. [ref: Pure – Boney James, AllMusic] "Grand Central" later received substantial smooth-jazz radio airplay, reaching the top 10 of the Radio & Records Smooth Jazz chart and finishing at No. 11 on the publication's 2003 year-end Smooth Jazz chart. [ref: Smooth Jazz airplay chart, Radio & Records] [ref: Year-End Smooth Jazz chart, Radio & Records]

Britt later co-wrote "The Total Experience," recorded by Boney James featuring George Duke; the song became James's first No. 1 on Billboards Smooth Jazz Airplay chart, spending four weeks at No. 1 in 2006. [ref: Shine – Boney James, AllMusic] [ref: Smooth Jazz Airplay chart, Billboard]

Shipsy, legally Llama Logisol Private Limited, is an Indian enterprise software company that develops cloud-based software for logistics and supply chain management. Founded in 2015, the company is headquartered in Gurugram, India.

== History ==
Shipsy was founded in 2015 in Gurugram by Soham Chokshi, Dhruv Agrawal, Harsh Kumar, Himanshu Gupta and Sahil Arora, graduates of the Indian Institutes of Technology; Chokshi became chief executive. An early angel round was led by Dheeraj Jain of Redcliffe Capital.

In April 2016, the courier company DTDC Express took a 20 percent stake in Shipsy for over US$1 million. A pre-Series A round led by Info Edge followed in November 2019, and in November 2020 the company raised a US$6 million Series A round co-led by Sequoia Capital India's Surge programme and Info Edge.

Shipsy raised US$25 million in a Series B round co-led by A91 Partners and Z3 Partners in February 2022.

In October 2023, Shipsy acquired the warehouse-management software provider StockOne to expand its fulfilment capabilities, and the same year launched an artificial intelligence assistant for logistics incident management called LIA. In 2025 it entered partnerships with logistics companies including Aramex and the UAE-based e7 Group, and in 2026 the company said it had crossed US$25 million in annual recurring revenue.

== Products and services ==
Shipsy develops cloud-based software that enterprises use to plan, execute and track the movement of goods across their supply chains. Its platform covers transportation management, warehouse management, last-mile delivery and route optimization, and multi-carrier management, and is used in sectors such as retail, manufacturing and automotive. Its warehouse-management capability was expanded through the 2023 acquisition of StockOne.

In 2026, Shipsy introduced AgentFleet, a set of artificial intelligence software agents designed to automate logistics workflows such as customer communication and invoice reconciliation.

== Recognition ==
Shipsy was positioned as a Niche Player in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Transportation Management Systems in 2026. In Gartner's 2026 Peer Insights Voice of the Customer for Transportation Management Systems, a report based on aggregated end-user reviews, Shipsy was named a Customers' Choice. Gartner has also listed the company as a representative vendor in its market guides for last-mile delivery technology (2025) and multicarrier parcel management (2026).

== Operations ==
Shipsy is headquartered in Gurugram and operates internationally, with customers in South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, Europe, Southeast Asia, Australia and the Americas. According to the company, it serves more than 150 enterprise customers in over 30 countries and employs around 300 people, with offices in India, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Singapore and Australia.

Since 2025, Shipsy has been a member of the Consultative Committee of the Universal Postal Union, a specialised agency of the United Nations.

Draft: Mansour Abdulreda Almail

Draft text:
Mansour Abdulreda Almail (; 1947–1997) was a Kuwaiti sports journalist, radio broadcaster, academic, and businessman. He founded the sports programming department at Radio Kuwait, the state radio service of the Ministry of Information, established the Youth and Sports Radio station, and was the licence holder and editor-in-chief of the magazine Dunya al Shabab wal Riyada ("World of Youth and Sport"). A commemorative media award was named after him at the 16th Arabian Gulf Cup in 2004.

== Early life and education ==
Mansour Abdulreda Hussain Almail was born in 1947 in the Sharq district of Kuwait City. He studied at Al Siddiq School and obtained a diploma from the Teachers' Institute, beginning his career as a physical education teacher with the Ministry of Education during the 1960s.

He competed internationally in gymnastics and later qualified as an international judge, eventually rising to head judge with the International Gymnastics Federation.

== Career ==

=== Business interests ===
Almail founded the Almail Group, which began trading in Kuwait in the early 1970s. Its commercial activities included general trading, contracting, transport, consumer goods, and industrial services. The business continued the commercial enterprise of his father, Abdulridha Almail, who had worked in transport and trade since the 1930s.

=== Radio ===
In 1969, Almail joined the Kuwaiti Ministry of Information in the radio sector, where he established and headed the sports programming department at Radio Kuwait. He served as controller of sports programming at the ministry from 1985 to 1994. In 1994, he founded the Youth and Sports Radio station and served as its first director, before being appointed assistant undersecretary for radio affairs in 1996.

=== Print journalism ===
Almail began working in sports journalism in the early 1970s and was a member of the Kuwait Journalists Association. He contributed to and managed sports desks for several Kuwaiti publications, including Al Rai Al Aam, Al Qabas, Mirat al Umma, and Al Imtiyaz. Regionally, he served as the first editor of the sports section for Al Taawun al Khaleeji and later launched Dunya al Shabab wal Riyada as its editor-in-chief.

=== Coverage of sporting events ===
Almail led Kuwaiti sports media delegations covering domestic, Gulf, Arab, and international athletic competitions. His commentary and reporting focused primarily on Kuwaiti football, including coverage of the Kuwait Premier League and the Kuwait national football team, alongside collaborative regional broadcasts across the Gulf.

=== Teaching and academia ===
From 1994 to 1996, Almail served as a seconded assistant professor at the College of Basic Education in Kuwait. During this period, he also acted as an external supervisor for master's and doctoral candidates in physical education.

== Recognition ==
Following his death, the Ministry of Information named a radio studio the "Mansour Almail Studio" in his honor. The Kuwait Olympic Committee also included him on its official list of ten pioneering figures in the history of Kuwaiti sports media.

=== Commemorative awards and tournaments ===
Ahead of the 16th Arabian Gulf Cup in 2003, the organizing committee established the "Late Mansour Almail Award for Best Journalist". At the conclusion of the tournament in January 2004, the honor was awarded to Qatari journalist Abdullah Al Marri.

In October 2005, the Ministry of Information and the Kuwait News Agency (KUNA) organized the inaugural media Ramadan football tournament competing for the "Late Mansour Almail Cup", establishing an annual tradition.

Draft: Mozambique Revolutionary Committee

Draft text:
The Mozambican Revolutionary Committee (Portugeuse: Comite Revolucionário de Moçambique), commonly known by its Portugeuse acronym COREMO, was an insurgent rebel group active in Mozambique between 1965 and 1982.

COREMO was founded in 1965 in Lusaka after splitting from FRELIMO over ideological differences due to the Sino-Soviet split. FRELIMO leader Samora Machel's internal party purges and close alignment with the Soviet Union had alienated many moderate socialists and anti-Soviet Maoists. [ref: Roots of Counter-Revolution: The "Mozambique National Resistance", Review of African Political Economy]
This caused a faction of FRELIMO under Adelino Gwambe to break away under the banner of COREMO.

It quickly became the second-largest independence movement in Mozambique during the Mozambican War of Independence. COREMO received significant financial and ideological backing from the People's Republic of China and Kenneth Kaunda's Zambia. [ref: Taylor, I. (2006) China and Africa: Engagement and Compromise, Routledge, p.95]

Its ideological base mainly consisted of a mix of Maoism, anti-Sovietism, a fierce opposition to the Machel administration, and moderate pan-African socialist politics. However, COREMO suffered from multiple intra-party ideological friction, with many factions leaning right-wing and anti-communist, preferring a closer alignment with RENAMO, during the Mozambican Civil War. [ref: Cabrita (2001) pp. 40-41]

Its leadership initially consisted of Gwambe but after an internal party purge in the mid-1960s, [ref: Marcum (2017) p.68] Paulo José Gumane became the Leader. He guided the group through the end of the Mozambican War of Independence, [ref: Marcum (2017) p.68] before being allegedly executed by FRELIMO loyalists in mid-1970s. [ref: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Africa report, Volume 2, 1998, p.371] Later leadership consisted of figures like Julius K. Ndozi who failed to stop the increasing factionalism, which ultimately culminated in the group's downfall.

Following the 1974 Lusaka Accord and the establishment of the People's Republic of Mozambique, a civil war started in the country. Backed by Malawi, Rhodesia, and apartheid South Africa, anti-communist RENAMO insurgents fought against the ruling FRELIMO government. COREMO opposed both sides and instead sought a non-aligned socialist state, continuing their own insurgency. [ref: Manning, C. (2002) The Politics of Peace in Mozambique: Post-conflict Democratization, 1992-2000, Greenwood, p.48]

By 1982, COREMO had completely fractured internally. Anti-communist and right-wing factions increased and fled to RENAMO, [ref: Cabrita (2001) pp. 40-41] and the significance of neutralism diminished as the Cold War reached its second-largest nuclear height. The group has been believed to have been either dissolved or merged into RENAMO around 1982.

Draft: Mereological Fallacy

Draft text:
The mereological fallacy is a conceptual error within the philosophy of mind, in which psychological capacities of a person or animal are attributed to the brain or another part of the organism. The argument is associated with neuroscientist Max Bennett and philosopher Peter Hacker, whose Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience (2003) criticises such attributions in cognitive neuroscience. [ref: Naming Our Concerns about Neuroscience: A Review of Bennett and Hacker's Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience, Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior]

Bennett and Hacker distinguish the cognitive processes that enable thinking, from the organism that exercises those capacities. Their argument has been disputed by various philosophers including Daniel Dennett and John Searle. [ref: What Is Cognitive Psychology?, Athabasca University Press]

== Argument ==
According to Bennett and Hacker, the circumstances under which psychological descriptions apply to people and other animals are part of what gives those descriptions their meaning. They argue that describing a brain as perceiving, or deciding, transfers these descriptions to something that does not meet their conditions of application. The resulting statements, on their account, are conceptually confused rather than empirically false. [ref: Philosophical Foundations of Neuroscience, Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews]

Bennett and Hacker accept that neural processes make psychological capacities possible. On their account, neuroscience investigates how neural activity enables an animal to see or remember. They claim that it doesn't explain those capacities by assigning sight or memory to the brain itself. They also argue that treating these expressions as harmless metaphors does not resolve the problem when the expressions are used when explaining phenomena like perception or memory.

Harry Smit and Hacker later clarified that the error isn't a strictly invalid inference, it is more precisely, an inappropriate attribution of a property, which may then produce mistaken inferences. In their usage, fallacy has a broader use than in formal logic. [ref: Seven Misconceptions About the Mereological Fallacy: A Compilation for the Perplexed, Erkenntnis Abstract and note 1.]

== Background ==

Bennett and Hacker's account draws on Ludwig Wittgenstein's discussion in Philosophical Investigations of the circumstances in which sensations and other psychological attributes can be ascribed to living beings. Smit and Hacker relate their terminology to Anthony Kenny's earlier discussion of the homunculus fallacy. They prefer the mereological terminology because the objection concerns part–whole relations, without requiring the postulation of a miniature person inside the organism.

The argument was debated in Neuroscience and Philosophy: Brain, Mind, and Language (2007), which included criticisms by Dennett and Searle and a reply by Bennett and Hacker. [ref: Minds, Brains, and Capacities: Situated Cognition and Neo-Aristotelianism, Frontiers in Psychology]

== Reception ==

Reviewing Bennett and Hacker's book, David W. Schaal welcomed its criticism of dualism and its attention to behavioural criteria for psychological concepts. He nevertheless questioned some restrictions the authors placed on the use of memory concepts in research on non-human animals.

Daniel Dennett defends a modified use of psychological vocabulary for subpersonal mechanisms. On his account, attributing simplified forms of belief to brain components can help explain a person's capacities without treating each component as a complete thinker.

John Searle challenges the role assigned to behavioural criteria. He argued that the evidence used to attribute a psychological state should be distinguished from the state itself, and that Bennett and Hacker's argument confuses these issues.

Paul Churchland appeals to information-processing descriptions in computer science, arguing that talk of storing, retrieving and manipulating information can have an intelligible technical use. Bennett and Hacker respond that producing results consistent with a rule differs from following that rule with understanding. Discussing this exchange, Michael R. W. Dawson argues that a functional explanation decomposes a system's capacities into simpler operations, which need not resemble the behaviour of the system as a whole.

Rom Harré questions whether brains, although parts of human bodies, should also be described as parts of persons. He proposes reformulating the issue through relationships between meanings and the roles of bodily organs in human activities. His account permits describing the hippocampus as an organ for remembering, without identifying neuroscience with psychology. [ref: Behind the Mereological Fallacy, Philosophy Abstract.]

Hans-Johann Glock defends the category-mistake objection to attributing cognition to brains and their parts, while rejecting the further claim that the brain cannot be described as the organ of cognition.

* Philosophy of neuroscience

Draft: History of Rajshahi

Draft text:
The history of Rajshahi, a city on the northern bank of the Padma River in northern Bangladesh, spans the ancient kingdom of Pundravardhana, successive Hindu and Buddhist dynasties, Muslim rule from the 13th century, the Mughal and British colonial periods, and the city's growth after Bangladeshi independence in 1971. The city is the headquarters of Rajshahi District and Rajshahi Division.

The surrounding Varendra tract was part of Pundravardhana, one of the earliest recorded state formations in ancient Bengal, and later came under the Maurya, Gupta, Pala and Sena rulers. Muslim rule was established in northwestern Bengal after the campaigns of Bakhtiyar Khilji in the early 13th century, and the spread of Islam in the surrounding countryside is traditionally associated with Sufi preachers, among them Shah Makhdum Rupos, whose arrival local tradition dates to 1288–89. Under Mughal rule the area was absorbed into the imperial revenue system, and the founding of the modern city is conventionally dated to about 1634. The name Rajshahi is usually explained as a compound of raj, denoting a raja or zamindar, and the Persian shahi, denoting royal status.

Under British rule the settlement, then known as Rampur-Boalia, became a centre of the silk and indigo trades; Rajshahi District was created in 1772 and the district headquarters moved to Rampur-Boalia in 1825. The founding of Rajshahi College in 1873 and of the Varendra Research Museum in 1910 established the town as an educational centre. Rajshahi became part of East Pakistan after the partition of 1947 and saw large-scale killings during the Bangladesh Liberation War of 1971, including at the University of Rajshahi. In 2016 the city attracted international attention for a sharp fall in airborne particulate pollution, although later reporting has described a deterioration in local air quality.

==Ancient period==
The Varendra tract of northern Bengal, which includes the area of present-day Rajshahi, has a documented history extending into antiquity. The region that now forms Rajshahi was part of the ancient territory of Pundravardhana, home to the Pundras, who are described in late Vedic literature as a non-Aryan people and who are said to have established one of the more prosperous Janapadas of ancient India by the 7th–8th centuries BCE. This early settlement lay within the Varendra (or Barind) tract, an elevated plateau of red clay soil bounded by the Ganges and Kosi rivers to the west, the Karatoya to the east and the Padma to the south. Archaeological evidence indicates that the riverine floodplains of Bengal have been inhabited for millennia, with sedentary settlement based on irrigated rice cultivation dating back at least 2,500 years.

The region's transition from a tribal polity to an imperial province began with the expansion of the Maurya Empire in the 3rd century BCE. The Mahasthangarh Brahmi inscription, the oldest written record found in Bangladesh, identifies the city of Pundranagara, at modern Mahasthan, as an administrative centre under Mauryan rule with a system for distributing grain during emergencies. Following the Mauryas the region came under the Gupta Empire of the 4th to 6th centuries CE, during which Pundravardhana became an administrative division known as a bhukti. Finds from this period in Rajshahi district include Gupta-style sculpture, such as a plainly carved Buddha image from Mandail.

The decline of the Guptas was followed by the rise of the Pala Empire in the 8th century, a period that O'Malley's gazetteer describes as a golden age of Varendra. The Pala kings, who were Buddhist, established an organised administration and supported the Varendra school of art, known for its black stone sculpture. Architectural work from the period includes the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, in the neighbouring area of present-day Naogaon District, built by King Dharmapala ( 770–810 CE), which became an important centre of Buddhist learning in South Asia. In the 12th century the Sena dynasty, originally from southern India, replaced the Palas and brought a shift toward orthodox Brahmanism; the Senas established a capital at Vijaynagara, near present-day Rajshahi city, and later moved it to Lakhnauti-Gaur.

==Medieval period==
Islam reached the Bengal delta by land at the start of the 13th century. In 1202–1204 CE Muhammad-i-Bakhtiyar Khilji, a Turkish officer, led a cavalry raid that overran northwestern Bengal. According to the traditional account, Bakhtiyar and his men entered the royal city of Nudiya disguised as horse dealers; the site of that city is disputed, and Van Schendel notes that it may have lain within the modern Rajshahi region rather than at Nabadwip. The Sena ruler Lakshmana Sena withdrew to eastern Bengal, and Bakhtiyar established a Muslim-ruled state with its capital at Lakhnauti-Gaur. For more than a century the region was administered by governors loosely subject to the Delhi sultans. Silk production in the area is recorded from this period, and the industry has continued into modern times.

Draft: Jaeyeol Han

Draft text:
Jaeyeol Han (; born 1983) is a South Korean painter who works between Seoul and Berlin. His principal bodies of work include Passersby, based on anonymous people encountered in cities, and Bystanders, which focuses on images of crowds. [ref: 선과 색의 총성, 한재열이 그리는 '얼굴 없는 얼굴', The Korea Economic Daily]

==Life and career==
In 2010, while serving in the South Korean military, Han volunteered for deployment to Haiti for earthquake-recovery work following the 2010 Haiti earthquake. After completing his service, he lived in Ireland and began drawing pedestrians, an activity that developed into the Passersby series.

In 2013, Han received an Excellence Award at the Seoul Digital University Art Awards for Passers-by, Repassage. [ref: '서울디지털대학교 미술상'에 이윤성, Kyunghyang Shinmun] In 2021, he presented the solo exhibition The Gathering, Bystanders at Gallery BK in Seoul, showing work that expanded his earlier individual figures into crowd imagery. [ref: 연말에 놓치면 안 될 회화 전시 4, Esquire Korea]

Han moved his main base to Berlin around the end of 2019 and has since maintained studios in Berlin and Seoul. His work appeared in the Schema Art Museum exhibition SM-Smash#1: Data Material in 2022. [ref: SM-Smash#1: Data Material, Schema Art Museum] Han participated in the group exhibition UNBOXING PROJECT 6: Reading, held at New Spring Project in Seoul from 23 October to 23 November 2025. [ref: Reading, UNBOXING PROJECT] He was selected for the VIRTUAL VITAL special exhibition at Kiaf SEOUL in 2026. [ref: '5년째 동행' 키아프·프리즈 “분리 개최해도 협력 유지…상생하며 발전”, Herald Business]

==Work and technique==
Han removes identifying facial features and indicators of age, gender, and race in order to emphasize anonymity. In a 2015 feature, the Korean art magazine Art in Culture described his use of oil sticks without brushes, noting the physical force of his mark-making and the thick masses of paint that give the work both painterly and sculptural qualities. [ref: [New Look] 한재열: 무명의 얼굴들, Art in Culture]

===Pigment bars===
Han makes and uses solid oil paint sticks that he calls "pigment bars" to obtain particular colors and textures. He holds the material directly against the canvas, applying friction and pressure rather than using a conventional brush; this produces heavily worked, sculptural surfaces. The pigment bars are used in both the Passersby and Bystanders series.

==Major series==
* Passersby: a series based on people observed in the streets of several cities, with individual identifying features broken down or removed.
* Bystanders: a series using montaged images of crowds associated with historical events, disasters, and wars to examine relationships between individuals and groups.

Draft: Debjit Mahalanobis

Draft text:
Debjit Mahalanobis is an Indian double bassist, composer, and instrument inventor who has incorporated the double bass into Hindustani classical music and Bengali folk. [ref: Meet Debjit Mahalanobis, the only full-time professional upright double bass artist in Bengal, Scroll.in] In 2018, he envisioned the Gajveena, a nine-string instrument combining elements of the double bass and the rudra veena, later which was one of the finalists at the 2026 Guthman Musical Instrument Competition at the Georgia Institute of Technology. [ref: Newly invented Gajveena makes it to the Guthman Musical Instrument competition in Atlanta, The Hindu] [ref: 2026 Finalists, Guthman Musical Instrument Competition] [ref: Check Out 10 Weird and Wonderful Finalists for the 'Pulitzer of the New Instrument World', Gizmodo]

== Early life and training ==

Mahalanobis’s paternal family includes statistician and scientist P. C. Mahalanobis, while his maternal lineage descends from Ramshankar Bhattacharya, founder of the Bishnupur Dhrupad-Dhamar gharana. [ref: About, Debjit Mahalanobis]

He started learning music informally at home on the harmonium. As a preteen, influenced by rock artists such as Led Zeppelin and The Who, he took up the guitar before moving to electric bass.

At the age of 17, he was introduced to Western classical music by his first teacher, Abraham Mazumdar. He initially studied the cello before moving to the double bass. After completing his education, he worked as a physics teacher before leaving the profession after three years to pursue music full-time.

He got mentorship under professor and conductor Hans Jürgen Nagel for a couple of years. [ref: Talented Debjit Mahalanobis and his Double Bass wonder!, GetBengal] Later he began studying Dagarvani dhrupad on the rudra veena under Bahauddin Dagar. [ref: Double the innovation: How musicians niftily weave in king-sized double bass into Indian compositions, The Hindu]

== Career ==

Mahalanobis was associated with the Calcutta School of Music. He has performed as a double bassist with several orchestras, including the Bombay Chamber Orchestra, the Indian National Youth Orchestra, the Indo-European Chamber Orchestra, the Kolkata Symphony, the South Asian Symphony Orchestra, and the Bangalore City Chamber Orchestra.

Mahalanobis recorded the main melody for the title track of the web series Taranath Tantrik after composer and filmmaker Q (Quashik Mukherjee) discovered a video of his double bass–sitar jugalbandi and approached him for the project. Mahalanobis played the melody in the studio, where it was recorded on the spot and subsequently used throughout the series. The series premiered on Hoichoi in January 2019.

Beyond orchestral performance, Mahalanobis has worked on a range of musical projects spanning contemporary music and television. In 2017, he performed on television as part of the Murshidabadi Project, a Sufi music initiative. In 2020, Sangeet Kala Mandir premiered Double Bass India, an online concert featuring his compositions. His commissioned work was also featured at the Favoriten Festival in Dortmund in 2022. In recognition of his work, he received the Chidakash Yuva Samman in 2021.

== Compositions and collaborations ==

Mahalanobis's work can be observed in Dakini 2025, an interdisciplinary short music film centred on Bengal's Bohurupi folk tradition, [ref: In 'DAKINI', Debjit Mahalanobis' Brings Double Bass Mastery To Bengali Performance Art, Homegrown] and Katha (2024), a solo double bass composition with Kathak. [ref: Debjit Mahalanobis' 'Katha' Video Tells an Unsettling Tale, Rolling Stone India]

Mahalanobis became a member of Hotel Kali, an Indo-German collaborative music project, after musician Varun Desai recommended him to Berlin-based musician Theresa Stroetges, who was seeking local collaborators during a two-month Kolkata residency organised with Goethe-Institut, Musicboard Berlin and BorderMovement. The group comprised Stroetges, Desai, Mahalanobis and Suyasha Sengupta, and released its self-titled debut album in 2021. [ref: Review: Hotel Kali Make A Stellar Case For Collaboration On Eponymous Debut Album, Wild City]

Mahalanobis has performed with DnA Machines, an electronic duo with Agnitray Chakrabarty, in which he plays a dismantlable upright electric bass. The duo performed at the World Music Day Festival at Kolkata’s Eastern Metropolitan Club in 2022. [ref: Eastern Metropolitan Club celebrates World Music Day, The Telegraph] He has also performed with JazzMahal, a Kolkata-based jazz trio featuring pianist Tazim Sheikh and drummer Aniruddha Saha, at JazzFest 2023 at the Dalhousie Institute, playing both electric and acoustic double bass. [ref: JazzFest 2023: Tunes from 'Epiphany' and a Ray-inspired 'Ode to Kolkata' shine on Day Two, The Telegraph] His performances have also explored the combination of the double bass with traditional Indian string instruments, including the Mattakokila veena and the Raas veena.

== The Gajveena ==

In 2018, Mahalanobis envisioned the Gajveena, a nine-string acoustic bass-veena designed to combine elements of the double bass and the rudra veena. Measuring 6 ft 11 in, the instrument has a 42-inch fretted fingerboard and dual resonators, and can be played with a bow or by plucking its strings. According to him, the name "Gajveena" was coined by his guru, Bahauddin Dagar.

Draft: Mallard x Pacific black duck hybrid

Draft text:
A mallard x pacific black duck hybrid is the hybrid offspring between a feral or domestic mallard (Anas platyrhynchos), and a pacific black duck (A. superciliosa) (abbreviated as PBD [ref: How Hybrid Ducks are Threatening the Future of Native Ducks, The Hobart + Launceston Independent Local] or sometimes called the grey duck). Hybrid ducks can result from the crossing of either a mallard drake x a female pacific black duck, or a pacific black drake x a female mallard. [ref: The breeding performance of Grey duck, Anas superciliosa, mallard, Anas platyrhynchos, and their hybrids in captivity, Academia] Though hybrid ducks are fertile, [ref: Identifying Mallard x Pacific Black Duck Hybrids, eBird] [ref: Ducks, Northern Midlands Council] [ref: Ducks, Derwent Estuary Program] they are not widely considered a unique species, and are classified under the same genus as their parent species. The mallard is known to hybridise with twenty-six species of waterfowl, with most being dabbling ducks of the genus Anas.

== History ==
Originally occurring in Eurasia and North America, the northern mallard was introduced to areas overlapping with the range of the Polynesian and Australasian occurring pacific black duck throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, being introduced to Australia in the 1860s (as early as 1862), and to New Zealand in 1867. The mallard was introduced to Australia and New Zealand as a gamefowl, but also through efforts by acclimisation societies as a means of creating an environment reminiscent of the native Europe of many settlers. [ref: Mallard, Australian Museum] Both species are dabbling ducks of the genus Anas that occupy ecologically similar niches in their respective ranges, and have naturally come into contact in areas of distributive overlap. In both Australia and New Zealand, its range increased rapidly in the 1950s as agricultural areas were developed in the post-war period. Historic records indicate that hybridisation increased significantly following this range expansion, with rates of hybridisation being less than 3% in New Zealand prior to 1958.

=== Introduction to Australia ===
The mallard was introduced to Australia as early as 1862, and saw prolific expansion into wetlands across the continent. The species was introduced incrementally to each state, first arriving in Victoria as early as 1864 with additional introduction efforts in 1971–72 where it has seen the most distributive expansion and success. It was introduced to Sydney and Perth before 1900 and before 1912 respectively, and has since become widespread in the proximity of each capital. The mallard has been noted to have spread throughout South Australia and Queensland too, occurring as far north as Maryborough in the latter, though it has only formed non-breeding populations in the state. The species can also be found uncommonly in Tasmania and the King and Flinders Islands north of the state. Lord Howe Island, Macquarie Island, and Norfolk Island all possess introduced mallard populations as well. While they occur here only in small densities, they have already contributed to a drastic decline in native pacific black duck populations regardless. Much of the hybrids present on Lord Howe Island in particular appear to be descended from New Zealand stock, and may have migrated from the mainland. [ref: The occurrence of hybridisation between the Pacific Black Duck (Anas superciliosa) and other dabbling ducks (Genus: Anas) in Australia, Victoria University] The lack of phenotypic expression and diversity of purebred pacific black ducks on the island may indicate that the species has become locally extinct there.

=== Introduction to New Zealand ===
The mallard is stated to have been introduced to New Zealand as early as 1867. Interbreeding with the native pacific black duck population began soon after introduction, with the first hybrid ducks being reported as early as 1885. The Natural History of Canterbury did not mention the mallard in its 1927 edition, indicating that the initial introduction of mallards may have been to some degree unsuccessful, though, the pacific black duck is noted as having declined in numbers due to hunting. [ref: Hybridisation, and the Conservation of the Grey Duck in New Zealand, UC Research Repository] Mallards were introduced from North America again in the 1920s–40s, and subsequent introduction of Australian feral populations occurred sometime in the 20th century as well. These later introductions were more significant, and may have been more successful due to the pacific black duck population having already been extricated from some areas due to hunting. New Zealand mallards have experienced significant introgression from hybridisation since their introduction, becoming no longer genetically consistent with the original stock of northern mallards introduced throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, constituting a novel genetic cluster (often referred to as a hybrid swarm) today.

Draft text:
Subuola Fasoyiro is a Nigerian food scientist and academic. She is a professor of Food Science and Technology and a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training (IAR&T), affiliated with Obafemi Awolowo University, Ibadan. [ref: Subuola Bosede Fasoyiro - About me, OWSD] [ref: Professor Subuola Fasoyiro, Bowen University] [ref: Prof. Subuola Bosede Fasoyiro, Institute of Agricultural Research and Training] Her work focuses on food processing, food safety, nutrition quality, product development, food preservation, and the utilization of underutilized legumes for food security.

== Early life and education ==

Subuola Fasoyiro was born on August 1, 1971, in Lagos State, Nigeria. She studied Food Science and Technology at the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta, where she obtained a Bachelor of Science degree in 1994. [ref: Why I chose career path in Food Science and Technology: Prof. Subuola Fasoyiro reflects on academic journey, The Nation] She later earned a Master of Science degree in Food Technology in 1997 and a Doctor of Philosophy degree in Food Technology in 2004 from the University of Ibadan.

[ref: FUNAAB Matriculates 6,356 Students, Highest intake in 4 decades, The Whistler]

== Career ==

Fasoyiro began research work at the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training (IAR&T) in 1998. She became a professor in 2014. She has also served as a professor in the Food Science and Technology Programme of Bowen University. Her academic and research work has been associated with food processing, product development, food preservation, food safety, and nutrition quality for food and nutrition security.

At IAR&T, her work has included research and extension activities in food processing technologies, value addition to agricultural produce, and training in food safety and processing for rural communities and extension personnel.

== Research ==

Fasoyiro's research interests include food processing, food preservation, food safety, food and nutrition quality, and food product development for food security. Specific areas of focus in her work include the processing and utilization of underutilized legumes, the nutritional improvement of indigenous staple crops through value addition, and the development of low-cost food technologies and natural food preservatives.

Her research, academic work and community service led to the delivery of the 372nd inaugural lecture at Obafemi Awolowo University in 2023. [ref: Hidden Treasures in Plants: For Food Security, Healthy and Wealthy Life, Obafemi Awolowo University Institutional Repository]

== Lectures ==

=== 372nd inaugural lecture of Obafemi Awolowo University ===

On 13 June 2023, Fasoyiro delivered the 372nd inaugural lecture of Obafemi Awolowo University, titled The Hidden Treasures in Plants: For Food Security, Healthy and Wealthy Life.

In the lecture, she discussed the role of food processing, value addition, and the use of underutilized plant resources in addressing hunger, malnutrition, and food insecurity. The lecture was reported by CEOAfrica, Independent and Nigerian Tribune. [ref: Prof. Subuola Fasoyiro is set to deliver 372nd Inauguration Lecture in OAU, CEOAfrica] [ref: OAU 372nd Inaugural Lecture: Prof Fasoyiro advocates for food security, healthy and wealthy life, CEOAfrica] [ref: Expert shares discoveries on reducing hunger, increasing food processing, Independent Newspaper Nigeria] [ref: How Nigeria can achieve sustainable food security by 2030 - Prof Fasoyiro, Tribune Online]

=== 13th commencement lecture, Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta ===

On 19 November 2025, Fasoyiro delivered the 13th commencement lecture of the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta during the institution's 2025/2026 matriculation ceremony. [ref: FUNAAB’s 2025/2026 Matriculation Ceremony: Prof. Fasoyiro to Deliver 13th Commencement Lecture, Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta] The lecture was titled Future Leaders of Character in Agriculture: Building Capacity Today for National and Global Impact Tomorrow. [ref: Future Leaders of Character in Agriculture: Building Capacity Today for National and Global Impact Tomorrow, ResearchGate] The event was also reported by The Whistler. [ref: FUNAAB Matriculates 6,356 Students, Highest intake in 4 decades, The Whistler]

== Community and institutional service ==

Fasoyiro has been involved in extension and community-based food technology work through IAR&T. Her institutional service has included technology transfer to adopted villages, training of extension agents and food vendors on food safety practices, and training of unemployed youth and processors in pigeon pea, soybean, cassava, and roselle processing technologies. She also mentors early career researchers.

She is the co-founder and vice-chairperson of Grace Reachfill Development Foundation (GRDF), an organization involved in education and empowerment initiatives for girls, youth and women. [ref: Prof Subuola Fasoyiro, Grace Reachfill Development Foundation]

Ignacio Orellana is a Chilean musician, drummer, photographer, videographer associated with Pirosaint and Quemasantos. [ref: A conversation with Pirosaint drummer/ NYC photographer/videographer Ignacio Orellana on new album ‘Know Thyself’, Metal Insider] [ref: Unearthing The Metal Underground: The Chilean Scene Part 2, Metal Underground]

== Background and early life ==

Orellana is from Santiago, Chile. Metal Underground reported that he began playing drums at age 14 and became involved in the Chilean metal scene during his teenage years. [ref: Unearthing The Metal Underground: The Chilean Scene Part 2, Metal Underground]

In 2002, Orellana moved to Poughkeepsie, New York, where he continued working on music with Pirosaint and developing media projects connected with Chilean metal in the United States. [ref: Unearthing The Metal Underground: The Chilean Scene Part 2, Metal Underground]

Orellana studied television production in Chile. In a 2021 interview with Metal Insider, he stated that he holds a degree in television and that his background in audio and video production contributed to his media work. [ref: A conversation with Pirosaint drummer/ NYC photographer/videographer Ignacio Orellana on new album ‘Know Thyself’, Metal Insider]

== Music career ==

In 2021, Pirosaint released Know Thyself. Metal Insider reported that the album was recorded during sessions held between 2013–2016 and 2020–2021 at Oily Sound Studios in NYC, and identified Orellana as Pirosaint's drummer as well as a photographer and videographer. [ref: A conversation with Pirosaint drummer/ NYC photographer/videographer Ignacio Orellana on new album ‘Know Thyself’, Metal Insider]

Orellana has also worked with Quemasantos. In 2026, Metal Insider reported that he composed the music and arrangements, as well as the recording, mixing, and mastering for the album Stranded in Hell at Oily Sound Studios in New York City, while vocalist Nelson Díaz developed the story and lyrical concept. [ref: Quemasantos announce new ambitious concept album ‘Stranded in Hell’, Metal Insider]

== Other musical work ==

In 2011, Orellana served as temporary touring drummer for Sacred Oath after its original drummer Kenny Evans suffered a back injury. Metal Underground reported that Orellana replaced Evans for several dates on the band's October–November 2011 tour. [ref: Pirosaint Working On First New Material In Fifteen Years, Metal Underground]

In 2017, Orellana joined the New York heavy metal band Metalfier as drummer. Metal Underground reported that he had already performed with the band in New Jersey and later appeared with Metalfier at Irving Plaza in New York City before the band formally announced him as a member. [ref: Metalfier Announce New Drummer Ignacio Orellana, Metal Underground]

== Media and photography ==

Orellana is a professional photographer, videographer, interviewer, and music-media producer in New York City. Metal Insider described him as a New York City photographer and videographer in addition to his work as a musician, and noted his work with music-media outlets. [ref: A conversation with Pirosaint drummer/ NYC photographer/videographer Ignacio Orellana on new album ‘Know Thyself’, Metal Insider]

His concert photography has been published by WPDH. In 2015, the station identified Orellana as a professional photographer associated with PoughkeepsieMETAL and published his photographs from performances by Testament and Extreme at The Chance Theater in Poughkeepsie, New York. [ref: Testament Rocks the Chance [PHOTOS], WPDH] [ref: EXTREME Rocks The Chance [PHOTOS], WPDH]

Orellana has also conducted artist interviews through ArmyOfOneTV. In 2010, Blabbermouth reported that he interviewed Cage vocalist Sean Peck at The Chance Theater in Poughkeepsie, New York. [ref: CAGE Frontman Interviewed By ArmyOfOneTV (Video), Blabbermouth.net] Blabbermouth later credited Orellana with recording an ArmyOfOneTV interview with Epica guitarist Mark Jansen in New York City. [ref: EPICA Guitarist On Group's Wide-Ranging Influences: 'Name It, And We Have Used It In Our Music', Blabbermouth.net]

Metal Underground documented Orellana's development of music-media projects including Chileanmetal, Digmetalworld, Bocasucia and ArmyOfOneTV. The publication described ArmyOfOneTV as an interview series featuring bands passing through New York City and discussed his efforts to provide exposure for Chileanmetal artists. [ref: Unearthing The Metal Underground: The Chilean Scene Part 2, Metal Underground]

Metal Underground separately described Digmetalworld as a New York metal label and distributor specializing in South American metal bands. [ref: Digmetalworld Offering Albums For Free Download, Metal Underground]

== Selected works ==

=== With Downfire ===
* Damnation (2010) – drums. [ref: Damnation – Downfire, AllMusic] [ref: Downfire – Damnation, Metal Temple]

=== With Pirosaint ===
* Know Thyself (2021) – drums and recording work. [ref: A conversation with Pirosaint drummer/ NYC photographer/videographer Ignacio Orellana on new album ‘Know Thyself’, Metal Insider]

=== With Quemasantos ===
* Stranded in Hell (2026) – composition, arrangements, recording, mixing, and mastering. [ref: Quemasantos announce new ambitious concept album ‘Stranded in Hell’, Metal Insider]

Draft text:
Germanair was a charter airline based in Germany. It started as a modest airline, but throughout the 1970s grew to become a sizeable operation, before merging with Bavaria Fluggesellschaft on March 1, 1977 to form Bavaria Germanair.

== History ==
The airline's origins date back to 1964, when Südwestflug GmbH was founded in Baden-Baden. The majority shareholder (50%) was Contracta, a leading German real estate company. The aim was to operate passenger charter flights catering to all travel and holiday agencies in the region. The first aircraft, three Douglas DC-6ss, were purchased in September 1965. [ref: World Airline Survey, Flight International] They were used by the company to fly potential customers to Spain and the Canary Islands for property viewings.

On September 1, 1968, the company name was changed to Germanair Bedarfsluftfahrt GmbH & Co. K.G., while ownership was acquired by the Goetz textile group and the headquarters moved to Frankfurt. [ref: World Airline Survey, Flight International] The operations continued positively and undisturbed to the point that in April of the following year the property was acquired by the fellow charter airline Transportflug. [ref: World Airline Survey, Flight International] The Douglas aircraft were phased out and replaced by three BAC 111 series 500 aircraft fitted with 114 seats during late 1969 into early 1970. The twin-engine aircraft were used extensively for inclusive tours and other charter flights throughout Europe and even North Africa. [ref: The One-Eleven Story, Air-Britain (Historians) Ltd.] A second-hand Douglas DC-9-10 was loaned from McDonnell Douglas as a stop-gap aircraft for a short time between April and August of 1969. In the 1970 fiscal year, the company transported approximately 470,000 passengers using an all-jet fleet.

At the beginning of 1971, the majority shareholding passed into the hands of Josef Schorgruber, who already held 26% of the fellow charter airline Bavaria with which a collaborative relationship was established in various fields. Shortly thereafter, in 1972, the airline incorporated into its fleet four Fokker 28s owned by the charter airline Bonair and operated on its behalf. [ref: World Airline Survey, Flight International]

Germanair was an early customer for the Airbus A300, acquiring the 12th example built. Nicknamed "Maximilian", she had appeared at the Paris Air Show just a few days before. "Maximilian" was delivered on May 23, 1975, entering service shortly thereafter in June of 1975. Germanair became the first German operator of this aircraft type. A second A300 was received a year later and both (fitted with 314 seats) spent a lot of flying hours shuttling passengers between Germany and the holiday centres in the Mediterranean basin and Canary Islands. [ref: Airbus A300, Airlife Publishing Ltd.] On May 12, 1976, both A300s arrived at Glasgow Prestwick Aiport, having been charted for the 1976 European Cup Final between Bayern München and Saint-Étienne.

At the end of 1974, Bavaria Fluggesellschaft also came under the sole ownership of the Schörghuber Group, leading to close cooperation with Germanair. In May 1975, Ernst Uhl was appointed joint managing director of the two companies. Although both airlines continued to operate under their own brand identities, they cooperated in all areas under the intent of an eventual merge. Although legally beginning on January 1, 1977, the merger was actually finalized on March 1, 1977. This resulted in the airline Bavaria Germanair, which has since (following further mergers) been absorbed into TUIfly.

Sahand Airlines is an Iranian Airline. [ref: Sahand Air]

== History ==
Founded in 2009 it is unclear exactly when they commenced operations though it is known in May of 2011, the Khorasan newspaper reported the explosion of an engine on a Boeing aircraft belonging to Sahand Airlines, which managed to make an emergency landing without any casualties. The aircraft in actuality was a McDonnel Douglas MD 82 operated by Khors Air on behalf of Sahand Airlines. [ref: Addition of Persons Acting Contrary to the National Security or Foreign Policy Interests of the United States to the Entity List; and Implementation of Additional Changes From the Annual Review of the Entity List] [ref: BIS Adds 9 Companies, 6 Individuals to Entity List]
[[File:Taban Air 1.jpg|thumb|The Sahand MD 80 now with Taban Air]]
After that, in 2017, Engineer Ashkan Ahmadi became the CEO and Deputy Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company and succeeded in activating two of the company's aircraft. [ref: Sahand Airlines history] In 2017 the airline added it's MD 83 fleet. [ref: Sahand Asia Airlines adds MD 83s] In 2018 the airline started domestic operations. [ref: Sahand Airlines start domestic operations] On October 18 2019 a Sahand Airlines MD 82 was seized as ordered by a Tehran court. [ref: Tehran Court orders seizure of MD 82] The court called off the seizure later the same year. [ref: Court calls off auction of Sahand Air Jet] Another aircraft was sold to Taban Air while one is owned by Sahand. There was also rumors that the Tehran court that seized the MD 80 also ordered the cessation of operations of Sahand Air. Draft text:
Nathaniel "Nate" Jacobs is a fictional character in the American teen drama television series Euphoria, created by Sam Levinson. He is portrayed by Jacob Elordi, with Gabriel Golub portraying a younger version of the character. Nate is introduced as a high school football player and the eldest son of Cal and Marsha Jacobs. He is characterized by his volatile temperament, controlling behavior, and preoccupation with masculinity and social status. His relationship with his father, whose secret sexual life he discovers as a child, becomes a central part of his character. [ref: Sam Levinson on Euphoria, Television Academy]

Nate's major storylines include his relationships with Maddy Perez, Jules Vaughn, and Cassie Howard, as well as his increasingly antagonistic relationship with Cal. He manipulates Jules under the alias "Tyler" after discovering her sexual encounter with his father, and later begins a relationship with Cassie while she is Maddy's close friend. Five years after graduating from high school, Nate is married to Cassie and becomes involved in his father's real-estate business. His financial difficulties lead to his involvement with loan sharks, who eventually kill him. [ref: 'Euphoria' Season 3 Episode 7 Recap: Nate Jacobs Dies, [[Variety (magazine)]

==Background==

Nate is the eldest son of Cal and Marsha Jacobs and grows up in East Highland, California. His father places considerable emphasis on physical strength, athletic achievement, and conventional masculinity during his childhood. Nate has a younger brother, Aaron, and an older brother, Derek, who dies before the events of the series.

At the age of 11, Nate discovers a collection of videos documenting Cal's sexual encounters with men and transgender women. The discovery profoundly affects his perception of his father and contributes to his later preoccupation with masculinity and sexuality. Sam Levinson has described Nate, alongside several other characters, as coming from a troubled home and attempting to fill emotional voids through sex, drugs, and adrenaline.

As a teenager, Nate becomes a star football player at East Highland High School. He develops a reputation for aggression and intimidation and begins an unstable relationship with Maddy Perez. Their relationship is repeatedly disrupted by jealousy, possessiveness, and violence.

Nate later discovers that Maddy possesses intimate photographs of Jules Vaughn and learns that Jules previously had a sexual encounter with Cal. Using the online identity "Tyler", Nate begins communicating with Jules and develops an emotional attachment to her while concealing his identity. After learning that Jules has evidence of his father's encounter with her, Nate threatens to expose her private photographs unless she remains silent.

During his senior year, Nate begins a secret relationship with Cassie Howard, despite her friendship with Maddy. Their relationship becomes public after Maddy discovers the affair and contributes to the breakdown of Cassie's friendship with her.

Following high school, Nate takes over his father's real-estate business and marries Cassie. Five years after the events of the second season, he experiences financial difficulties and becomes indebted to loan sharks. After being abducted and buried alive, Nate is rescued but subsequently killed by the men pursuing him. His death occurs in the seventh episode of the third season, "Rain or Shine".

==Personality==

Nate is portrayed as confident, physically imposing, and highly competitive, particularly in relation to football and his social position at school. He maintains a controlled outward appearance while frequently responding to perceived threats or challenges with anger and intimidation. His behavior toward his romantic partners is characterized by possessiveness, jealousy, manipulation, and violence.

A significant aspect of Nate's characterization is his relationship with masculinity. His father's emphasis on physical strength and traditional masculine behavior contributes to Nate's efforts to construct a similarly dominant public persona. His discovery of Cal's sexual encounters creates a conflict between his understanding of masculinity and the reality of his father's private life. Levinson has described Nate as one of several Euphoria characters who attempt to compensate for emotional difficulties through sex, drugs, or adrenaline.

Elordi has described Nate as a deeply conflicted character whose anger provides an outlet for problems he does not know how to confront directly. He has also characterized the role as substantially more complex than the version of Nate presented in the initial audition material, which he described as a stereotypical aggressive jock. [ref: Jacob Elordi Called Nate in "Euphoria" an "Emotional Terrorist", Teen Vogue]

Nate's relationships with Maddy, Jules, and Cassie each expose different aspects of his personality. His relationship with Maddy is marked by possessiveness and physical violence, while his relationship with Jules develops through an anonymous online identity that allows him to express feelings he is unwilling to acknowledge publicly. His relationship with Cassie similarly reflects his desire for control and his difficulty separating intimacy from possession.

Abdelaziz Taleb (born 1973) is a mixed-media artist, filmmaker [ref: Une seconde édition sous le signe de l'ouverture, Une seconde édition sous le signe de l'ouverture], producer and curator. He grew up in Agadir, Morocco. In 2002, Taleb and Moroccan filmmaker Abdellatif Benfaidoul established Videokaravaan, a nomadic media-art project focused on acquainting the Western audience with media art from Morocco, the Arab world and artists from the diaspora [ref: An Alternative Gaze: A Shared Reflection on Cross-Mediterranean Cooperation in the Arts, European Cultural Foundation]. His short film Ziyara Kassira (Short Visit, 2006) was presented at the International Film Festival Rotterdam in 2007 [ref: Short Visit, IFFR EN]

Early life and education

Taleb studied English literature at university in Agadir, Morocco. In 1999, he received a UNESCO-Aschberg bursary for artists and subsequently undertook a scholarship residency at the Academy of Media Arts Cologne (KHM) [ref: VIDEOKARAVAAN / Ateliers d'arts des médias - Agadir 2006, Maghress] in Germany. During 1999-2000, Taleb produced video works including Tests, Dangerous and Rauchen, which appeared in OVNI's 2000 Moroccan video programme in Barcelona [ref: ]

Career

In the early 2000s, Taleb and Benfaidoul brought the Videokaravaan project to Morocco, especially to Agadir [ref: Videokaravaan à Agadir, Maroc, universes-in-universe.de]. The project was about organising media art workshops series for Moroccan art students and led to the development of many video art works that were produced by Videokaravaan. Taleb was also involved in organising Digital Marrakech, a festival devoted to digital and media arts in Marrakech. In 2012, TelQuel [ref: Événement. Marrakech version Digital, Telquel.ma] identified Taleb and Benfaidoul as the filmmakers and organisers of the festival, whose programme included video, digital art, performances, workshops and discussions on media arts.

In 2003, the Spanish newspaper El País [ref: El extranjero, El País] published an article about the project Videokaravaan and its presentation of contemporary video from Morocco and other Arab countries in Europe. The newspaper identified Taleb as one of the project's founders and discussed the project in connection with contemporary Arab visual culture.

Film work

Taleb directed the short film Ziyara Kassira (Short Visit, 2006), which was presented at the International Film Festival Rotterdam in 2007 [ref: Short Visit, IFFR EN]. He also co-directed Astah (2006) with Abdellatif Benfaidoul. The film was included in the Moroccan retrospective of the Corto Cortissimo section [ref: Venezia, la sezione Corto cortissimo - Corriere della Sera, www.corriere.it] at the 64th Venice International Film Festival in 2007. Taleb participated in Berlinale Talents in 2007 [ref: Abdelaziz Taleb, Berlinale Talents] as a director and screenwriter.

Media art and curatorial work

Besides filmmaking, Taleb has curated many media art programmes and exhibitions. Through Videokaravaan, he developed programmes presenting moving-image work from Morocco, North Africa and the Arab world in European cultural institutions. Taleb also took part in the TransArab programme in Barcelona [ref: ], which brought together artists, filmmakers and cultural practitioners working across the Mediterranean.

In 2011, Taleb curated a series of artistic programmes and projects such as Arab Stereotypes in Western Cinema [ref: Orientalism in Moving images – Arab Media Lab // المختبر العربي لفنون الميديا], a programme also presented by Casa Árabe in Madrid [ref: ] in collaboration with Arab Media Lab. The programme examined representations of Arabs in Western cinema through screenings and public discussions. Taleb gave many seminars [ref: PROGRAM — Black Cloud - Kyiv Biennial 2019, blackcloud.info]and panel discussions around the subject of stereotypes in Western media. He co-directed Silent Film, Big Words (2011) a video work where many fragments from early Hollywood films ( 30's) were re-grouped and the Arab stereotypes is noticeable.

Taleb's recent work also includes multimedia and exhibition projects combining film, video, photography and installation. His solo exhibition Last Years in Babylon [ref: Last year in Babylon solo exhibition by Abdelaziz Taleb – Arab Media Lab // المختبر العربي لفنون الميديا] was shown in Marrakech, Morocco. The exhibition included photography and video installation.

Selected filmography

* Tazkiyat al-Nafs (Purification of the Soul)

Draft text:
The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present is a 2026 popular science book by American paleontologist Steve Brusatte. It presents a chronological account of the evolution of birds, from their origins among theropod dinosaurs to the diversity of living birds. [ref: The Story of Birds: An Evolutionary History of the Dinosaurs that Live Among Us, British Trust for Ornithology]

The book was published in the United States by Mariner Books on April 28, 2026. [ref: The Story of Birds, HarperCollins] A British edition was published by Picador on June 11, 2026, under the subtitle An Evolutionary History of the Dinosaurs That Live Among Us. [ref: The Story of Birds, Pan Macmillan]

==Background and writing==
Brusatte wrote The Story of Birds over several years alongside his work as a university teacher, laboratory manager, student supervisor and grant writer. In the acknowledgements, he described fitting the project around his professional and family responsibilities. His wife, Anne, a children's author and former teacher, read the complete manuscript and suggested revisions intended to make it more accessible to a general readership. [ref: The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present, Mariner Books]

Members of Brusatte's palaeontology group at the University of Edinburgh read portions or complete drafts of the book during weekly meetings, while students in his third-year palaeontology and sedimentology course commented on its opening chapters. Palaeontologist Daniel Field and members of his Cambridge research group read the complete manuscript and assisted with fact-checking its treatment of bird classification, anatomy and behaviour. Researchers associated with the "Deep Time Cognition" project reviewed the material concerning avian brains, neurons and cognition.

==Publication==
The American hardcover edition contains 448 pages and was published with the subtitle A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present. The British hardcover edition, also 448 pages, was published by Picador with a different subtitle.

An audiobook narrated by Patrick Lawlor was released by Harper Audio on April 28, 2026. [ref: The Story of Birds, Kirkus Reviews]

The first edition is illustrated throughout in black and white, combining drawings, photographs and diagrams. It contains illustrations by Cordula Marks Venters, Sarah Shelley and Todd Marshall, and photographs credited to palaeontologist Daniel Field. [ref: The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present, Mariner Books] Marshall also created the book's cover artwork. The front matter includes a chronological timeline of bird evolution and a simplified phylogenetic tree showing the principal relationships between dinosaurs, early birds and the major groups of living birds. [ref: The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present, Mariner Books]

==Contents==
The book is structured as a chronological history of birds and their ancestors. The main text comprises a prologue, nine numbered chapters and an epilogue. A timeline of bird evolution and a bird family tree precede the prologue, while notes on sources and an index follow the epilogue. [ref: The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present, Mariner Books]
[[File:Dinornis1387.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.7|Richard Owen beside a reconstructed moa skeleton in 1879. The photograph is reproduced in chapter 7, which discusses birds that lost the ability to fly.]]

The first four chapters trace the evolutionary origin of birds among theropod dinosaurs and the gradual development of characteristics associated with birds. These include small body size, feathers, wings, eggs, flight, changes to the digestive system, adaptations for living in trees, beaks, rapid growth, endothermy and bird sounds. [ref: The Story of Birds: A New History from Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present, Mariner Books]

Chapters five to seven examine the survival of some bird lineages during the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, the establishment and subsequent diversification of the modern bird family tree, and the repeated loss of flight in groups including ratites and penguins.

Chapter eight surveys extinct groups and species including terror birds, dromornithids, giant seabirds, the dodo, the passenger pigeon and the great auk. Chapter nine discusses bird intelligence, cognition, tool use, birdsong and continuing evolution among living species.

The epilogue turns to the human-driven decline of bird populations, discussing threats including habitat destruction, pesticides, invasive species, climate change, domestic cats and collisions with glass. It concludes on a cautiously optimistic note, emphasizing birds' evolutionary adaptability and resilience.

==Reception==
James Heywood, reviewing the book for the British Trust for Ornithology, gave it a highly positive assessment. He described Brusatte as one of the foremost palaeontologists working in the United Kingdom and praised his ability to make the subject exciting and engaging, as well as the book's engagement with recent research and its extensive notes. Heywood's only reservation concerned the illustrations: he suggested that additional phylogenetic diagrams and colour plates would have been useful, while noting that the book followed the same general approach as Brusatte's two preceding works.
[truncated]

Draft text:

Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART) is a brief, manualized form of psychotherapy developed by licensed marriage and family therapist Laney Rosenzweig in 2008. It uses imagery-based techniques, attention to physical and emotional responses, and therapist-directed eye movements while a person recalls distressing memories. Clients do not have to describe the details of a traumatic event verbally to the therapist. [ref: Treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A State-of-the-art Review, Current Neuropharmacology] [ref: USF Public Health awarded Army contract to train military clinicians in treatment of PTSD, USF Health News]

ART has been studied mainly as a treatment for Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and trauma-related symptoms. Clinical studies have reported reductions in PTSD symptoms as well as depression, anxiety, psychological distress, and sleep problems. A 2024 systematic review of five primary studies involving 337 enrolled adults described ART as a promising, time-efficient treatment for PTSD, while concluding that more high-quality research, particularly comparisons with established PTSD treatments, is needed. [ref: Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART) for the treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder in adults: A systematic review, PLOS Mental Health]

== History ==
ART was developed in 2008 by Laney Rosenzweig. She is a licensed marriage and family therapist who has worked in the mental health field since 1989. [ref: Introduction to Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART), National Association of Social Workers – California] The first clinical study of the therapy was published in 2012, [ref: Brief Treatment of Symptoms of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) by Use of Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART®), Behavioral Sciences] followed in 2013 by a randomized controlled trial involving U.S. service members and veterans. [ref: Randomized Controlled Trial of Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART) for Symptoms of Combat-Related Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Military Medicine]In 2015, ART was included in the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration's National Registry of Evidence-Based Programs and Practices (NREPP), which classified it as "effective" for psychological trauma and depression. [ref: Interventions with Special Relevance for the Family First Prevention Services Act (FFPSA), Ohio Department of Job and Family Services] In 2016, the U.S. Army awarded the University of South Florida a contract to train military mental health clinicians in ART at several Army installations.The first systematic review of ART for PTSD in adults was published in 2024.

== Technique ==
ART is a highly structured, manualized psychotherapy in which a therapist guides the client through the recall and processing of distressing memories while using sets of horizontal eye movements.The client brings a distressing event or image to mind while attending to associated emotional and physical sensations. ART places particular emphasis on processing physiological or somatic sensations associated with the recalled material. Detailed verbal narration of the traumatic experience is not required.

ART also uses a form of imagery rescripting known as Voluntary Image Replacement (VIR), in which distressing imagery associated with a memory is replaced with imagery selected by the client. The technique is intended to alter the distressing imagery without replacing the factual or narrative memory of the event.ART also incorporates visual imagery, metaphors, Gestalt-based techniques, and other prescribed interventions within its structured protocol. The client selects the replacement imagery, while the therapist guides the sequence of prescribed interventions. [ref: Practice comparisons between accelerated resolution therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing and cognitive processing therapy with case examples, Nurse Education Today]

ART and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) both use clinician-directed eye movements while distressing material is processed, but published descriptions identify differences in how the protocols structure reprocessing. ART uses different amounts of eye movements, incorporates attention to associated physiological sensations during processing, and uses Voluntary Image Replacement, in which the client deliberately rescripts distressing imagery. Published descriptions characterize ART's processing as more directive and less free-associative than EMDR.Several processes and mechanisms have been proposed to contribute to ART's effects, including exposure and imagery rescripting, along with hypotheses involving working memory and memory reconsolidation. It is not yet known which mechanisms or individual treatment components account for the clinical effects reported in studies. [ref: Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART): a Review and Research to Date, Current Psychiatry Reports]

== Research ==

=== Post-traumatic stress disorder ===
Most ART research to date has focused on PTSD.A 2012 prospective study of 80 adults with clinically significant PTSD symptoms reported reductions in PTSD symptoms and several related measures after one to five ART sessions. The study did not include a control group.

Deputy Under Secretary of the Army

The Deputy Under Secretary of the Army (DUSA) is a principal civilian advisor to the Secretary of the Army and Under Secretary of the Army and oversees special projects and policy initiatives as delegated by the Secretary of the Army. [ref: Army Publishing Directorate, armypubs.army.mil]The DUSA is a 3-Star Equivalent member of the Senior Executive Service (SES) and works alongside other senior members of Headquarters Department of the Army. The DUSA is assigned responsibility for:

a. assisting the Secretary of the Army in directing and supervising Army-wide transformation and reform initiatives

b. recommending to the Secretary of the Army policies, methodologies, and measurement criteria developed in consultation with the Secretariat and Army Staff to incorporate artificial intelligence (AI) into Army operations to synchronize, integrate, and coordinate optimal alignment in support of Department of War and Army missions

c. directing and supervising Civilian Senior Leader Management Office (CLSMO), as directed by the Under Secretary of the Army

The Position of Deputy Under Secretary of the Army (DUSA) was created in 1953, and at times multiple DUSA positions existed simultaneously. Although the mission for this role has changed throughout the decades, the DUSA’s portfolio adjusts according to the needs of the Army, directly supporting the Secretary of the Army’s oversight functions and Title 10 responsibilities.

Historical roles of the office include international affairs, manpower and reserve affairs, personnel management, operations research, and business transformation. In recent years, the portfolio of the Deputy Under Secretary of the Army included:

a.        Strategic Capital Initiative (SCI): Created in 2026, the Strategic Capital Initiative seeks strategic partners to co-invest in Army installations, technology, energy infrastructure, and the industrial base. The Army seeks to use creative financial and partnership models, such as joint ventures, long-term leases, and service agreements to create “value for value” exchanges in which the Army offers secure land and stable demand signal in return for resilient energy, re-shored supply chains, and modern facilities without relying solely on taxpayer dollars. The effort spans six pillars (energy resilience, the organic industrial base, logistics and supply chains, advanced manufacturing, real estate and facilities, and critical minerals). [ref: Strategic Capital Initiative, www.army.mil]

b.        Project ARIA (Army Rapid Integration of Artificial Intelligence): Announced March 5, 2026, Project ARIA pairs Army leaders with top private-sector firms to rapidly field cutting-edge technolgy to Army formations. The initaitve is organizaed into multiple teams, each of which is tasked rapidly prototype and field AI-solutions to solve specific Army problems, including both tactical and enterprise-level use cases. [ref: Harnessing AI for the future: Army unveils Project ARIA, www.army.mil]
