Erwin Lange (10 May 1914 – 30 October 1991) was a German politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). He was a member of the Bundestag from 1949 to 1980 and in the European Parliament from 1970 to 1984. In the European Parliament he chaired the economic committee and the budget committee. In 1937 a Nazi court convicted him of preparing high treason.

== Early life ==

Lange was born in Essen and was a Protestant. He left Mittelschule and started a commercial apprenticeship in 1930, then switched in 1931 to an apprenticeship as a typesetter. He joined the socialist youth movement in 1928 and the trade union movement in 1930.

== Persecution and war ==

Lange was arrested by the Nazi authorities in 1936 for political reasons. In 1937 he was convicted of preparing to commit high treason and sentenced to three and a half years in a penitentiary (Zuchthaus) and three years' loss of civil honour rights. After the sentence he did labour on moorland, was held in protective custody and was placed under police supervision. He is among the members profiled in Olaf Ihlau's 1969 study of the Rote Kämpfer (Red Fighters), a council communist resistance group broken up by the Gestapo in 1936–37.

In autumn 1942 Lange was conscripted into the punishment unit 999 and sent to Africa. He was taken prisoner by American forces in 1943 and released in 1946.

== Political career ==

After the war Lange passed the master's examination in his trade in 1947 and became manager of a printing company in Essen. [ref: Friedrich Ebert Foundation Library: Social Democratic Press Service: 1946–1995, library.fes.de] In the SPD he belonged to the Essen sub-district (Unterbezirk) and chaired the Niederrhein Bezirk.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

Lange was elected to the first Bundestag at the 1949 federal election and sat through the eighth legislative term, which ended in 1980. [ref: Biographisches Handbuch der Mitglieder des Deutschen Bundestages 1949–2002, Walter de Gruyter] Until 1969 he was on the executive committee of the SPD parliamentary group.

=== Member of the European Parliament ===

Lange sat in the European Parliament from 21 January 1970 to 23 July 1984. He chaired the economic committee until 1975 and then the budget committee. From 17 July 1979 to 23 July 1984 he was a member of the Socialist Group in the first directly elected Parliament, and from 20 July 1979 he chaired the Committee on Budgets. On 11 April 1983 he joined the delegation for relations with the United States.

== Death ==

Lange died in Essen on 30 October 1991.

== References ==

== Further reading ==
* Die Roten Kämpfer: Ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der Arbeiterbewegung in der Weimarer Republik und im „Dritten Reich", Anton Hain

Hardial Singh (1 February 1940 – 22 February 2018) was a Singaporean botanist and the former Deputy Commissioner of Parks and Recreation until his retirement.

== Education ==
Hardial graduated from the University of Malaya in Singapore with a Bachelor of Arts in Botany. He would later earn a master's degree in horticulture from the University of Hawai’i under an East-West Scholarship, specialising in the cloning of orchids. [ref: Rishpal Singh Sidhu. Hardial married Sudesh Kumari three days after meeting her. They have a son, Gino Hardial Singh, a criminal lawyer who has practised for more than two decades [ref: Sleepless nights, sad goodbyes: Seasoned lawyers and cops on the emotional toll of handling sex crimes, CNA]; and a daughter, Gina Hardy, a chocolate maker who works with Trinidad's cocoa beans. [ref: [https://www.nus.edu.sg/newshub/news/2019/2019-10/2019-10-06/MEDICINE-st-6oct-pA6pA7.pdf "Ultimate gift to medicine"]. The Straits Times. 06 Oct 2019. In 1975, he was transferred to non-research duties in the Parks and Recreation Department, a new organisation created by merging the Singapore Botanic Gardens and the Parks and Trees Unit under the Ministry of National Development [ref: [https://www.nas.gov.sg/archivesonline/government_records/agency-details/164 "Singapore. Parks & Recreation Department"]. National Archives Singapore. 2026. Retrieved 29 September 2026.]. Hardial briefly became the editor of The Gardens' Bulletin from 1978-1979 [ref: Wong, K.M. == Death ==
Hardial died a few weeks before what would have been his 78th birthday on 22 February 2018. However, his body would not be cremated until 30 August 2019 as he had donated his body to science under the National University of Singapore's Silent Mentors Programme.

Draft text:
On July 22, Unknown assailants attacked the Buketa Sami checkpoint killing five paramilitary personnel and injuring six others, no group claimed responsibility for the attacks; however, authorities suspected two men responsible for the attack.

== Background ==

The Provinces of Narathiwat, Yala province and Pattani province are Thailand's only Muslim majority provinces, in those regions an insurgency by Malay insurgents have claimed the lives of 7,000+ people since 2004 [ref: Thai authorities hunt for suspects after an attack in troubled south kills 5 soldiers, Manila Bulletin]

Thai spokeswoman, Ratchada Thanadirek stated that in the past two to three months that a series of violent attacks were perpetrated by a "terrorist network seeking to instil fear among the public and target state officials" [ref: Five soldiers killed in bomb attack in Thailand’s restive south, The Straits Times]

A day before the attack occurred, a car explosion occurred in front of a Police station causing minor injuries and property damage [ref: Five Thai soldiers killed in bomb attack, Dawn]

== Attack ==
The attack occurred on 6:45 PM, when unidentified assailants used pipe bombs and firearms during the attack, The attack resulted in the deaths of five Thai rangers while six civilians were wounded, including a ten-year-old boy [ref: Thailand: 5 soldiers killed in attack on security checkpoint, DW], a three-year-old girl and a senior citizen [ref: Five Thai rangers killed in armed attack in Narathiwat, Bernama], The attack also lasted for ninety seconds before ending [ref: CCTV shows nine attackers raiding Narathiwat checkpoint in 90 seconds, The Star] after the attack, Emergency teams immediately transported the wounded to hospitals [ref: 5 paramilitary troops killed in southern Thailand checkpoint attack, Anadolu Agency]

After the attack, The assailants seized three AK-47 rifles, Three bullet-proof vests and three cellphones from the paramilitary personnel [ref: Thai authorities hunt for suspects after an attack in troubled south kills 5 soldiers, The Washington Post]

Government forces reported that the pick-up truck used to transport the assailants was found abandoned and set on fire, 13 miles away from the attack site [ref: Thailand launches manhunt after 5 soldiers killed, civilians injured in deep south, South China Morning Post]

== Victims ==
The names of the victims killed were identified as [ref: Five rangers killed, civilians injured in Narathiwat checkpoint attack, Nation Thailand]

* Theerayut Somakerd
* Sakiriya Jena
* Wimon Dabthong
* Nattasit Kaewsena
* Salahuding Pi

Names of the Victims injured [ref: Five Thai rangers killed, civilians injured in Narathiwat checkpoint attack, The Star]

* Habib Hina
* Muhammad Ali Abrue
* Farhah Abrue
* Muhammad Hafit Hina
* Awatif Bueraheng

== Aftermath ==
Thai government forces sealed off the checkpoint after the attack and launched investigations to identify the assailants

On July 24, Thai authorities imposed martial law in Narathiwat following the attack as to pursue the assailants, this was issued by Major General Yod-Arwut Phuengpak [ref: Thailand imposes martial law in southern province after attack kills 5 paramilitary troops, Anadolu Agency]

Peacetalks with Insurgents in the area were also postponed indefinitely as a result of the attack [ref: Deadly raid puts peace talks on hold, Bangkok Post]

== Reactions ==
Thai Prime Minister, Anutin Charnvirakul condemned the attacks calling it a "brazen act of terrorism" and "a serious threat to national security"

Wes Parker is an American musician and songwriter from Richmond, Virginia. He wrote and performed with the indie rock band Camp Howard and recorded with his brother Jonathan Parker as the duo Ruth Good before releasing solo music under his own name in 2024. His solo releases include the EPs Splinter (2025) and fantom (2025), and the album Super Rare (2026). Parker also creates online comedy sketches featuring a recurring character named Skunk. [ref: From Band Life to Big Dreams: Wes Parker's Solo Journey, RVA Magazine] [ref: The many faces of Wes Parker, VPM] [ref: Yes, Wes Parker Can Feel Something Shifting Too, Zany Waves]

== Early life ==
Parker grew up in Richmond in a musical family. His father and older brothers played guitar, and Parker began learning the instrument as a child. He later played in a middle school band with Nicholás Perea, who would become his bandmate in Camp Howard. Parker has described a one-chord composition called "The Salamander Song" as his first song.

== Career ==
=== Camp Howard ===
Parker and Perea became songwriters in Camp Howard, a Richmond indie rock band that began performing in 2015. The group also included Matt Benson and Brian Larson. Parker played guitar and bass and contributed vocals. [ref: RVA #29: From house shows to Egghunt Records, a look at the rise of Camp Howard, RVA Magazine]

Camp Howard released a self-titled album in 2016 and the Juice EP through Egghunt Records in 2017. A live session recorded for Audiotree was released in 2018, followed by the band's second studio album, Cañón, in 2019. Camp Howard toured outside Richmond and reunited for a performance in 2023. [ref: Camp Howard - Audiotree Live, Bandcamp] [ref: Early Listen: Richmond's Camp Howard Unveils "Cañón", POND Magazine]

=== Ruth Good ===
Parker and his brother Jonathan, known as JP, formed the Richmond duo Ruth Good. Their seven-track Spliff EP was released through Citrus City Records in 2017. The brothers largely wrote and recorded their respective contributions separately, while their brother Alan played additional instruments on two tracks. All three brothers also played in the Richmond band Poser. [ref: Brothers from Richmond's Ruth Good Discuss Debut EP 'Spliff' Ahead of Smatter Show Tonight, RVA Magazine]

=== Solo recordings ===
Parker began releasing singles under his own name in 2024, including "Why Won't You Pick Up the Phone?", "Annie Moore", "Burn the House", "Tattoo" and "Den". He played every instrument on the recording of "Annie Moore". [ref: New Single "Den" By Wes Parker, Social Casualty] Reviewing "Den" for Social Casualty, Claire Johnson discussed its country-influenced guitar melody and changes in tempo.

His first solo EP, Splinter, was released in January 2025. Writing for The Auricular, a Richmond music publication, the reviewer connected Parker's earlier work with Camp Howard to Splinter, describing the EP's melodic pop-rock songwriting and retro-influenced arrangements. [ref: RVA Shows You Must See This Week: July 16 – July 22, The Auricular] RVA Magazine's "Sound Check!" column described Splinter as blending alternative country with indie rock, contrasting the title track's energetic sound with the country-influenced "Deadbolt". [ref: Sound Check! Wes Parker, Rubblebucket, Sweet Bahs, RVA Magazine] Parker followed it with fantom in October 2025. He described fantom as a fictional narrative inspired by the fall of Lucifer. [ref: Freedom and Fallen Angels: Journey into the World of Wes Parker's 'fantom', Atwood Magazine] In a review of the EP, Rachel Leong of Atwood Magazine discussed its alternative rock and early-2000s influences and the narrative connecting its songs. [ref: The Rise and Fall of an Angel: Wes Parker's EP 'fantom' & Defiant Artistry, Atwood Magazine] Leo Edworthy of EARMILK described the fantom single "Neck" as combining grunge influences, indie rock and falsetto vocals. [ref: Wes Parker tunes up his grunge sensibilities on "Neck", EARMILK] "Neck" appeared on filmmaker James Gunn's Spotify playlist of favorite songs from 2025, which he shared on Threads. [ref: Just a few of my favorite songs from 2025, Threads] [ref: James Gunn's favorite songs of 2025, Spotify]

Parker released his debut solo album, Super Rare, on June 5, 2026, through Big Machine Rock. It includes "Little Birdie", "Bad Doggie" and "Cut the Grass", the last of which features Jessica Lea Mayfield. [ref: New Music Mondays: Evanescence, Red Clay Strays and More!, Overtone] Overtone rated the album seven out of ten, discussing its mix of indie rock, folk and country and its radio-show framing.

In 2026, Parker placed second in the singer-songwriter category of Style Weekly Readers' Winners poll. [ref: Readers' Winners: Arts + Culture, Style Weekly]

=== Live performances ===
In 2025, Parker toured as a solo artist, including a 16-stop run noted by Flagpole ahead of a show in Athens, Georgia. [ref: Calendar Pick: Wes Parker, Flagpole] Parker also performed an in-studio set for WNRN's 2025 Holiday Showcase, playing original songs and a cover of "Last Christmas". The station published video and audio recordings of the session. [ref: 2025 WNRN Holiday Showcase, WNRN]

In May 2026, Parker and his band performed before a live audience at the DC101 Sound Stage in Rockville, Maryland. The appearance also included an interview with radio host Mike Jones. [ref: Wes Parker - DC101 Artist Session, DC101] [ref: INTERVIEW: Mike Jones Talks With Wes Parker!, ALT 107.3]

Kochchikade (; also spelled Kochchikada) is a town and locality in Negombo Divisional Secretariat, Gampaha District, Western Province, Sri Lanka.

Kochchikade is situated north of Negombo and forms part of an important road and railway corridor between the Colombo metropolitan area and north-western Sri Lanka. The locality is associated with the Colombo–Puttalam road, the Puttalam railway line, the Kochchikade railway station, and the Maha Oya bridge. [ref: [https://www.railway.gov.lk/web/index.php?Itemid=191&id=165&lang=en&option=com_content&view=article Sri Lanka Railways — Station Details]] [ref: [https://www.sundaytimes.lk/190324/news/pm-opens-new-maha-oya-bridge-342340.html The Sunday Times — PM opens new Maha Oya bridge]]

The official administrative code for Kochchikade is 1203015, and it is identified as Grama Niladhari Division 78 under the Negombo Divisional Secretariat and Negombo Municipal Council. [ref: [https://www.statistics.gov.lk/qlink/AdminDivCodes Department of Census and Statistics — Administrative Division Codes]]

The 2024 Census of Population and Housing recorded a population of 2,499 for Kochchikade GN Division, comprising 1,206 males and 1,293 females.

The locality should be distinguished from Kochchikade North and Kochchikade South in the Colombo municipal area, which have the same name but are separate localities.

== Name ==

The Sinhala name of the locality is කොච්චිකඩේ.

The English spelling Kochchikade is used in official administrative, railway, postal and municipal records. The alternative spelling Kochchikada also occurs in English-language material.

The locality has postal code 11540. [ref: [https://www.slpost.gov.lk/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/POST-CODE-BOOK-.pdf Sri Lanka Post — Post Code Directory]]

== Administrative status ==

Kochchikade is GN Division No. 78 within the Negombo Divisional Secretariat of Gampaha District.

The Department of Census and Statistics assigns Kochchikade the administrative code 1203015 and places it under Negombo DS Division and Negombo Municipal Council.

The 2012 Gampaha District GN atlas also lists Kochchikade as GN Division 78 of Negombo DS Division. [ref: [https://www.statistics.gov.lk/Resource/en/Population/DistrictAtlases/DCS_Population_Atlas_2012_D12_GampahaDistrict.pdf Department of Census and Statistics — Grama Niladhari Level Population Atlas of Gampaha District, 2012]]

== Negombo Municipal Council ==

Kochchikade is within the administrative area of Negombo Municipal Council.

The municipal council operates a Kochchikade Sub-Office as one of its two sub-offices. The council lists an officer-in-charge and identifies the Kochchikade sub-office as part of its local administrative service network. [ref: [https://www.negombo.mc.gov.lk/?lang=en&page_id=5540 Negombo Municipal Council — Sub-Offices]]

The council's published contact information lists the Kochchikade Sub-Office telephone number as 031-2277276. [ref: [https://www.negombo.mc.gov.lk/?lang=en&page_id=1643 Negombo Municipal Council — Contact Us]]

The council also lists a Kochchikade Ayurveda dispensary within its municipal health-service network.

Nizar Kiram is a Filipino former basketball player who played collegiate basketball for the St. Francis of Assisi College Doves and competed in the Philippine Basketball League (PBL) with John-O. He was also one of the applicants for the 2008 PBA draft.

== Basketball career ==

=== Collegiate career ===
Kiram played collegiate basketball for St. Francis of Assisi College. In March 2002, he was among the St. Francis players who participated in the Philippine Basketball League Rookie Camp. [ref: 158 aspirante sa PBL Rookies Camp, Pilipino Star Ngayon]

During the 2002 National Capital Region Athletic Association season, Kiram was part of a St. Francis team that entered the latter stages of the competition as defending champion. In December 2002, he scored 12 points in a 67–48 victory over La Salle-Manila, sharing second-highest scoring honors for St. Francis with Ervin Sotto behind Ranidel de Ocampo. [ref: PSBA rebounds, trips SS-Cavite, The Philippine Star]

In January 2003, Kiram contributed to St. Francis' 88–79 victory over Colegio de San Lorenzo in the quarterfinals of the NCRAA tournament, playing alongside Ranidel de Ocampo and Freddie Montelibano. [ref: St. Francis topples San Lorenzo five, The Philippine Star]

Later that year, Kiram led St. Francis with 15 points in a 75–72 victory over the Philippine School of Business Administration during the Universities and Colleges Athletic Association men's basketball tournament. Two of his three-point field goals helped St. Francis build a 19-point lead during the game. [ref: Doves soar past Jaguars; Generals up, The Philippine Star]

=== Philippine Basketball League ===
Kiram also played for John-O in the Philippine Basketball League. In September 2002, he was listed as part of a John-O lineup that included Ranidel de Ocampo, Jeff Napa, Archen Cayabyab, Bong Salvador and Mark Macapagal during the PBL–Cebu Basketball Federation Dual Meet. [ref: Casino vs John-O; Hapee kontra Blu, Pilipino Star Ngayon]

John-O subsequently competed in the 2002 PBL Challenge Cup, with Kiram and Ricky Calimag forming part of the team's frontline alongside PBL-CBF Most Valuable Player Ranidel de Ocampo. [ref: John-O Juzz team to beat, Pilipino Star Ngayon]

In June 2003, John-O defeated the Montana Jewels, 80–67, to finish third in the PBL Unity Cup. Pilipino Star Ngayon reported that Kiram and Emerson Oreta helped Richard Melencio during a decisive 19–0 third-quarter run. [ref: Hapee naisahan ng Viva, Pilipino Star Ngayon]

=== 2008 PBA draft ===
Kiram later applied for the 2008 PBA draft. He was included among the 45-player applicant pool reported by both The Philippine Star and GMA News. [ref: Norwood, Dillinger cleared for PBA draft, The Philippine Star] [ref: Welcoat to get Norwood as top PBA draft choice, GMA News Online]

The draft class included Gabe Norwood, Jared Dillinger, Jayson Castro, Beau Belga, Jeff Chan, Solomon Mercado and other players who later competed professionally in the Philippine Basketball Association. Kiram was not selected during the two-round draft.

== Family background ==
A genealogy maintained by members of the Kiram family identifies Nizar S. Kiram as the eldest listed son of Datu Ibrahim Dalus Kiram and Ruby Salcedo. [ref: Datu Ibrahim Dalus Kiram, Preservation of Sulu Sultanate – History and Rights]

Ibrahim Dalus Kiram belonged to the Kiram family associated with the historic Sultanate of Sulu. The same family genealogy identifies Ibrahim as a son of Punjungan Kiram and a brother of Jamalul Kiram III. Because succession to the Sultanate of Sulu has been disputed among different branches of the family, descriptions of royal titles and succession vary among sources.

Godfrey Nsereko is a Ugandan rally driver who competes in the two-wheel-drive (2WD) category of the National Rally Championship.

== Rallying career ==

Nsereko began his rally career as a co-driver before moving to the driver's seat in 2018. His debut as a driver was at the opening round of the 2018 National Rally Championship season in Mbarara, where he and co-driver Hamza Lwanga emerged as winners of the Clubman Rally Championship (CRC) category. Nsereko attributed his understanding of rallying fundamentals to his previous experience as a co-driver. [ref: Nsereko launches CRC title bid with victory in Mbarara, Kawowo Sports]

Later in the 2018 season, at the Kabalega Rally in Hoima, Nsereko and co-driver John Musisi won the CRC category. He was the only CRC finisher and secured the championship with two CRC events remaining. Kawowo Sports reported that the title was Nsereko's first rally championship. The Daily Monitor also identified Nsereko and Musisi as the CRC category winners. [ref: Nsereko draws several lessons after CRC success, Kawowo Sports] [ref: Pictorial: Alwi wins hotly contested Kabalega Rally, Daily Monitor]

For the 2019 season, Nsereko moved to the 2WD category. He emerged as the winner in the season-opening event in Mbarara after taking the lead following the retirement of Timothy Gawaya. Kawowo Sports reported that Nsereko and co-driver John Bosco Musisi took an early lead in the 2WD championship. [ref: Nsereko keen on more 2WD success, Kawowo Sports]

Nsereko continued competing in the 2WD category in subsequent seasons. Uganda Radio Network reported on his participation in the 2021 MOSAC Rally Championship and quoted him discussing the challenges of driving on muddy rally tracks. [ref: Drivers Decry Bad Weather During this Year's MOSAC Rally Championship, Uganda Radio Network]

In 2022, Nsereko was listed with 51 points in the final published 2WD standings of the National Rally Championship by the Daily Monitor. [ref: Rugomoka victory concludes NRC season that was, Daily Monitor]

Draft: Neo-Krautrock

Draft text:
----

Neo-Kraut Rock (later Neo-Krautrock) was invented and coined by the predecessor of Düsseldorf band Vibravoid, Lightshow Society Düsseldorf in the late 1980s. [ref: Vibravoid, Djournal] [ref: Kiss the Sun: Il lungo viaggio dell'heavy psych 1980–2000, Tsunami Edizioni] The first use of the designation is documented in 1988 to describe a new German-only Düsseldorf musical style that follows the original Kraut Rock tradition of the 1960s and 1970s but still draws on its ideas. [ref: Neo Psychedelic Neo Kraut Rock – Live at Casino, self-published] Later use extends the genre for international bands that focus on the Motorik rhythms of NEU! and Can.

== History ==
The word Kraut was used in world wars I and II to humiliate Germans as a derogatory term. [ref: kraut, Dictionary of Canadianisms on Historical Principles] In 1971 German agency Popo Music put ads in UK Melody Maker and US Billboard to promote the new German music named Kraut Rock spelled in 2 Words. [ref: Der Klang der Revolte: Krautrock und Pop avantgarde, Schott Music] The music was a German interpretation of psychedelic rock incorporating various styles. In the 1980s this term became derogatory and bands like Eloy hated by press and audience. [ref: Eloy, Progressive Rock & Progressive Metal E-Zine] German magazine Musikexpress repeatedly used Kraut Rock for sounds regarded as passé. [ref: Krautrock: German Music in the Seventies, University of Michigan Press] In 1997 David Bowie appeared on Germany's highest-rated television show Wetten, dass..?, where his question about Neu! received only one response from the audience, his question about Harmonia was met with complete silence. [ref: Don't Mention The War (41): David Bowie bei Wetten dass…? über Neu! und Harmonia, Die Tageszeitung Popblog]
In 1988 Düsseldorf band Lightshow Society Düsseldorf first introduced the designation Neo-Kraut Rock in the two word spelling on a concert flyer. In 1990 the group was renamed to Vibravoid who kept using the designation to describe their style which is rooted in the traditions of Düsseldof Kraut Rock that emerged around the first psychedelic club on mainland Europe, Creamcheese. [ref: Der "Lichtraum (Hommage à Fontana)" und das „Creamcheese“ im museum kunst palast: Zur Musealisierung der Düsseldorfer Kunstszene der 1960er Jahre, transcript Verlag] [ref: The Vibravoid – Neo Kraut Rock Psychedelia: Band Info, Vibravoid] In 1994 German magazine Intro reviewed the Vibravoid demo tape Void Forum and quoted “the band calls it Neo Kraut Rock”. [ref: Review of Vibravoid, Intro] In 1999, Smag Lifestyle Magazin described Christian Koch of Vibravoid as a "Neo-Kraut Rock Musiker". [ref: WP8: UFO CLUB, Smag Lifestyle Magazin] Another Düsseldorf group associated with the term Neo-Kraut Rock and Düsseldorf as a so called “Neo-Kraut Hub” was Kreidler who declined being part of that scene. [ref: Joachim Henn, review of Kreidler, Weekend, Intro, November 1996, reproduced in Kreidler's press archive.] In 2009 Vibravoid released the Kraut Rock Sensation EP which documents the first German release consisting solely of Kraut Rock coversongs. In the October 2009 issue of Prinz magazine reviewed the release in the context of the contrasting contemporary reception of Kraut Rock in Germany and Britain. The article noted that, “while entire Krautrock parties were being held in Britain, the music remained a niche phenomenon in its German country of origin” and that Vibravoid have load the cover songs with new “coolness”. [ref: Von Düsseldorfern... Hocherhitztes Kraut, Prinz]

== International use ==

Despite the German origin and the limitation to German music the designation was used in contrast for international bands from the 1990s onwards. British groups lke Stereolab and Loop incorporated Kraut Rock influences into their music and were described by press as a “Krautrock” revival, picking up the one word spelling. [ref: The Cambridge Companion to Krautrock, Cambridge University Press] [ref: Never Fade Out: Loop's Robert Hampson Interviewed, The Quietus]

In 1998 an early international occurrence of the exact expression "Neo-Krautrock" is documented in an interview with Cul de Sac. The interviewer applied the terms "Neo-Krautrock" and "Post-Rock" to the band's music, while the band rejected these classifications. [ref: Cul de Sac interview: Glenn Jones, Perfect Sound Forever]

== Contemporary use of “Neo-Krautrock” ==

The term “Neo Krautrock” was later also used beyond the historical West German scene, while the motorik sound associated with Neu! increasingly became a “shorthand for Krautrock” in international reception. [ref: 'I always wanted to be different', The Guardian]

In 2006, WDR produced the documentary Kraut und Rüben - Über die Anfänge deutscher Rockmusik as a history of the music that emerged in West Germany. The documentary describes "Kraut Rock" as German only phenomenon in the late 1960s and 1970s with a wide spectrum of musical styles. [ref: Kraut und Rüben – Über die Anfänge deutscher Rockmusik, WDR Rockpalast] In a later Rockpalast epsiode, WDR uses the designation for Tokyo-based group Minami Deutsch under the tile "Krautrock aus Japan" (Krautrock from Japan) although the band does not belong geographically and chronologically to the 1970s Kraut Rock scene in West Germany. [ref: Krautrock aus Japan: Minami Deutsch, WDR]

= Goudy Text =

Goudy Text is a blackletter typeface designed by American type designer Frederic W. Goudy and released in 1928. Goudy based it on an earlier alphabet called Goudy Black, which he had drawn for his 1922 book Elements of Lettering. He designed it in the tradition of the early blackletter used by Johannes Gutenberg, rather than the more decorative styles common in the 19th century. The name “Goudy Text” was suggested by the Lanston Monotype company. [ref: Anatomy of a Typeface, Godine]

Goudy Text follows the Textura style of blackletter. Type historian Alexander S. Lawson describes it as similar to Textura letters from 15th-century Italy, with some French influence. Goudy also designed Lombardic Capitals as an alternative set of capitals for the typeface.

A digital version of Goudy Text is available from Lanston through Adobe Fonts. [ref: ]

Adebola Akinola is a Nigerian gospel singer, songwriter, performer and choir director based in the United Kingdom. She began releasing recorded music in 2022 with the single “Wonderful God” and has also performed in theatrical and cultural productions incorporating Yoruba folklore. [ref: Adebola Akinola takes 'Wonderful God' global, Punch]

Akinola's performance work has included The Woman Whose Womb Carried the Village, a live music and storytelling piece presented at a Soap Box Spotlight event at the Showroom Cinema in Sheffield in March 2026. The work draws on Yoruba folklore and centres on a woman subjected to rejection because of infertility. A review in The Guardian Nigeria discussed Akinola's vocal delivery and the treatment of the story's themes of love, forgiveness and community judgment. [ref: Adebola Akinola delivers a Yoruba tale of love, hatred, forgiveness at soap box spotlight, The Guardian Nigeria]

== Early life and education ==

Akinola was born on the 7th of August in Lagos, Nigeria. She studied Music Education at Adeniran Ogunsanya College of Education and later studied Library and Information Science at Kwara State University, Malete. She also received musical training through the Musical Society of Nigeria (MUSON). [ref: About, Adebola Akinola]

Before relocating to the United Kingdom, Akinola was involved in church music in Nigeria, including work as a worship leader, choir director and music minister. [ref: About, Adebola Akinola]

== Music career ==

Akinola released “Wonderful God” in 2022. According to The Punch, the song was initially released on Boomplay and was subsequently made available on additional digital music services in 2026. The newspaper reported that the song had accumulated more than 8,000 listeners on Boomplay before its wider release. [ref: Adebola Akinola takes 'Wonderful God' global, Punch]

In May 2026, Vanguard reported on the wider release of “Wonderful God” and described Akinola as a UK-based Nigerian gospel artist, worship minister and choir director. The article also reported the 2023 release of the album Sovereignty. [ref: UK-based gospel artist Adebola takes worship global with 'Wonderful God', Vanguard]

New Telegraph likewise reported in May 2026 that “Wonderful God”, initially released in 2022, had subsequently been made available internationally. The article also described Sovereignty as an album released in 2023. [ref: Nigerian Gospel Artist, Adebola Akinola, Goes Global With Wonderful God, New Telegraph]

== Performance work ==

In March 2026, Akinola participated in The Woman Whose Womb Carried The Village, a live music work presented as part of Soap Box Spotlight at the Showroom Cinema in Sheffield. The production was created and performed by Akinola together with Toby Williams, Gideon Olajide and Segun Lawal. The programme was presented by SBC Theatre and was supported by Showroom Cinema, the Paul Hamlyn Foundation and Arts Council England. [ref: Soap Box Spotlight, SBC Theatre]

The performance draws on Yoruba folklore and tells the story of Morẹnikẹ, a woman who is rejected by her community because she is unable to have children. Reviewing the performance for The Guardian Nigeria, Michael Kolawole discussed Akinola's restrained and intense delivery, while also criticising the treatment of some elements of the story, including the character's unanswered prayer and the village's accountability. [ref: Adebola Akinola delivers a Yoruba tale of love, hatred, forgiveness at Soap Box spotlight, The Guardian Nigeria]

New Telegraph also reported on the Sheffield Soapbox event in April 2026, describing Akinola among the performers at the Showroom Cinema event. [ref: Standing Ovation At Sheffield Soapbox As Mayor Safiya Saeed Praises Adebola Akinola, New Telegraph]

== Awards and recognition ==

In 2023, Akinola received an Award of Excellence at the Kwara Province 1 Music Competition, where Punch reported that she was named Overall Best Winner and Best Vocalist. The information was included in the newspaper's coverage of the subsequent release of “Wonderful God”. [ref: Adebola Akinola takes 'Wonderful God' global, Punch]

In September 2026, THISDAY reported that Akinola received the Eko Best Female Vocalist / Best Vocal Performance Award at the sixth Eko Heritage Awards, held at the Lagos Oriental Hotel in Lagos. [ref: Adebola Akinola Wins Eko Best Female Vocalist Award at 2026 Eko Heritage Awards, THISDAY]

Takashi Isobe (Japanese: 磯部 孝, January 6, 1914 – October 7, 2001) was a Japanese physicist and engineer specializing in measurement and control engineering. He was a professor and later professor emeritus at the University of Tokyo. His research included underwater ballistics, flow measurement, correlation methods using random signals, and automatic control. He served twice as president of the Society of Instrument and Control Engineers (SICE) and was also a member of the science-writing group known as the. [ref: 磯部孝名誉教授, 学内広報]

== Early life and education ==
Isobe was born on January 6, 1914, in Ueno-Sakuragi, Tokyo, as the eldest of six children. He spent his childhood in Ikebukuro and attended the elementary school attached to Toyoshima Normal School, followed by Tokyo Prefectural Sixth Middle School, now Tokyo Metropolitan Shinjuku High School. [ref: Yasushi Ishii, "磯部孝先生の計測工学の歩み" [The development of Takashi Isobe's career in measurement engineering], in 磯部孝先生と計測工学, Isobe Takashi Sensei o Shinobu Kai, 2002, pp. 3–5. ]

In March 1930, after completing his fourth year of middle school, he entered the former Urawa Higher School. In 1933 he entered the Department of Physics at Tokyo Imperial University. He suffered from severe pneumonia while a student and delayed his progression by one year, graduating from the Department of Physics in March 1937.

After graduation, Isobe joined the Imperial Japanese Army Technical Headquarters as a civilian employee, initially working on ballistic calculations. From 1942 to 1944 he was dispatched by the Army Technical Headquarters to Tokyo Imperial University as a special graduate research student, where he studied underwater ballistics under Masaichi Majima.

== Academic career ==
In 1945, Isobe became a lecturer in the First Faculty of Engineering at Tokyo Imperial University. Following the establishment of the Department of Measurement Engineering, he became an associate professor in 1946 and a professor in 1948.

From September 1959, he spent approximately one year as a visiting professor at Cornell University in the United States. [ref: Ishii, "磯部孝先生の計測工学の歩み", 2002, pp. 10–11. ]

Isobe retired from the University of Tokyo in March 1974 and became professor emeritus. In April of that year, he became a professor in the Department of Photographic Engineering at Chiba University, where he worked on education and research in image measurement engineering. He retired from Chiba University in March 1979. [ref: Ishii, "磯部孝先生の計測工学の歩み", 2002, p. 15. ]

In 1979 he joined Chubu Institute of Technology as a professor. The institution was renamed Chubu University in 1984, and Isobe continued teaching and conducting research there for approximately ten years. [ref: Ishii, "磯部孝先生の計測工学の歩み", 2002, pp. 15–19. ]

He died on October 7, 2001, at the age of 87.

== Research ==

=== Underwater ballistics ===
While working at the Army Technical Headquarters, Isobe initially conducted ballistic calculations. Beginning in 1942, he pursued experimental studies of underwater ballistics at Tokyo Imperial University. His work examined phenomena including the ricochet of projectiles from the water surface and the motion of projectiles after entering water.

The University of Tokyo later described his work as having clarified in detail both ricochet at the water surface and projectile motion underwater, thereby opening a new field of research.

His results were later collected in the book Suichū dandō no kenkyū (水中弾道の研究, Studies in Underwater Ballistics), published by the University of Tokyo Press in 1975. [ref: 水中弾道の研究, Hanmoto.com]

A Chiba University Library publication described the book as a study of the motion of high-speed projectiles entering water, a specialized problem in fluid mechanics. [ref: 千葉大学附属図書館報, Chiba University Library]

=== Measurement engineering and flow measurement ===
After World War II, Isobe shifted the main focus of his research toward measurement engineering and its systematization. Together with Masaichi Majima, he edited the two-volume Keisokuhō gairon (計測法概論, Introduction to Measurement Methods), published in 1950–1951. [ref: 計測法概論, CiNii Books]

He also worked on industrial measurement, automatic control, and flow measurement. In 1956, he published a paper on problems in measurement and control technology in factories. [ref: 工場における計測及び制御技術の諸問題, Japan TAPPI Journal]

During the 1950s he developed a pulsating gas flowmeter. In 1958, Hiroo Hattori, Isobe, Takao Nomura, and Tositaka Hayasi published "Practical Tests of Pulsating Gas Flow Meter". The device had been developed into a commercial instrument and was tested under various experimental conditions. [ref: Practical Tests of Pulsating Gas Flow Meter, Journal of the Instrument Technology, Japan]

During his stay at Cornell University, Isobe presented his work on pulsating flow measurement at a meeting of the Instrument Society of America (ISA, now the International Society of Automation). The following year he received an award from the society for this work.

=== Correlation methods and control ===
During the 1960s, Isobe studied correlation methods that used random signals to determine the characteristics of control systems and other systems. The University of Tokyo later credited him with establishing correlation techniques that contributed substantially to the subsequent development of measurement and control engineering.

Draft: Ispmanager

Draft text:
ispmanager is a commercial web hosting control panel for Linux-based servers. It provides a web interface for administering web, apss, database and mail services without using the command line, and can be installed on physical servers or virtual machines.

Through its interface the panel manages common server software, including the Apache HTTP Server, Nginx and LiteSpeed/OpenLiteSpeed web servers; the MySQL, MariaDB, Percona and PostgreSQL database servers; and an Exim/Dovecot mail server.

== History ==
The first public release of the control panel appeared in 2004. [ref: ISPmanager 2004 announcement]

Version 5 was released in 2014, built on the developer's proprietary COREmanager framework and distributed as deb/rpm packages with data stored in SQLite or MySQL.

Version 6 was released in 2021, adding interface and update improvements, resource monitoring, an updated APS repository and Ansible support. [ref: New versions of the ispmanager panel are available, Introserv]

In March 2022 the product was spun off from its original developer, ISPsystem, into a separate company that focuses solely on the control panel. [ref: ISPmanager separates from ISPsystem and becomes an independent company, ispmanager]

== Editions ==
ispmanager is offered in three editions that differ mainly by the number of supported sites and the availability of features such as Docker virtualization and CloudLinux limits: lite (up to 10 sites), pro (up to 50 sites, with Docker and CloudLinux support) and host (unlimited sites). A 14-day free trial is available.

== Features ==
The panel can configure Apache, Nginx and LiteSpeed/OpenLiteSpeed web servers with per-site version selection for PHP, Python and Node.js. It supports one-click installation of content management systems such as WordPress, Drupal and Joomla, and works with the MySQL, MariaDB, Percona and PostgreSQL databases.

Security and maintenance functions include automatic issuing of Let's Encrypt SSL certificates, scheduled and manual backups to local or external storage, a configurable firewall, Fail2ban, WireGuard VPN, DNSSEC and integrations with third-party protection services. Mail functions cover mail domains, mailboxes, aliases, the Roundcube webmail client and spam/virus filtering.

The panel exposes an API and offers integration with billing systems including HostBill, [ref: ispmanager integration, HostBill] WiseCP, Blesta, ClientExec, WHMCS and BILLmanager. [ref: ispmanager shared hosting provisioning for WHMCS, WHMCS Marketplace] It can restore cPanel and Plesk backup files and transfer users between ispmanager installations.

== Supported operating systems ==
ispmanager supports current versions of Debian, Ubuntu, AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux.

Draft text:
Brent Bokovoy is an American filmmaker and screenwriter. He is known for the feature film Ronald's Little Factory (2023) and for the short horror film Monster in My Swimming Pool (2011), which won Universal's Halloween Horror Nights Short Film Competition in 2011. [ref: The Essential A&E Picks for Aug 3 - 9: Ronald's Little Factory, Park City Kimball Arts Festival, Ogden Pride, and more., Salt Lake City Weekly] [ref: Rants and Raves: Vote for San Diego Filmmakers, KPBS Public Media]

==Career==

In 2011, Bokovoy directed the horror short Monster in My Swimming Pool starring Lia Marie Johnson. [ref: The Sound of San Diego is...Kids' Music??, San Diego Reader] Bokovoy won Universal's Halloween Horror Nights Short Film Competition, and the film was screened during the Eyegore Awards at Universal Studios Hollywood. [ref: Stars, Screams And Scares At The 2011 “Eyegore” Awards, Neon Tommy] [ref: Event Report: The 2011 Eyegore Awards Celebrate the Best and Brightest of the Horror Genre, Dread Central] JoBlo.com described it as "curiously cute". [ref: EVENT: Universal's Hollywood Halloween Horror Nights 2011, JoBlo.com] KPBS arts reporter Beth Accomando wrote that the film was "smartly shot".

Bokovoy later wrote and directed Ronald's Little Factory, a dark comedy set within the culture of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. His use of a late-1980s horror aesthetic and the challenges of expanding the premise into a feature-length film were discussed in the Salt Lake City Weekly. Bokovoy made the film during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a 2024 essay about contemporary Mormon cinema for the Association for Mormon Letters, film scholar Randy Astle examined Ronald's Little Factory alongside films including Heretic and Plan 10 from Outer Space. He conferred on the film's exaggerated performances, its throwback setting, and its theology on sexuality. [ref: Heretic, Humanism, and the Modern Transcendental Mormon Film, Association for Mormon Letters] In 2025, Bokovoy directed the mockumentary short Deathline – The Juicy Hidden Truth Behind the Killer Tomatoes, a tribute to the cult film Attack of the Killer Tomatoes. [ref: San Diego arts roundup: Arsenio Hall brings stand-up show to Sycuan Casino, San Diego Union-Tribune]

Draft: Mark Harvey (political scientist)

Draft text:
Mark Harvey is an American political scientist, educator, and author whose scholarship spans political communication, international relations, popular culture, and political science pedagogy. His research examines celebrity influence, political persuasion, music and politics, and the use of games and simulations in political science and international relations education. He is Director of Graduate Business Programs at the University of Saint Mary.

== Education and career ==
Harvey earned a bachelor's degree in political science from Washburn University, master's degrees from the University of Missouri–Kansas City and the University of Wales Swansea, and a Ph.D. in political science from the University of Kansas. Harvey has taught at the University of Saint Mary, Baker University, the University of Birmingham, and the University of Kansas. He also taught in the Duke University Talent Identification Program, including appointments at the University of Kansas, Duke East Campus, and the London School of Economics. [ref: KU grad students give whiz kids head start on college, University Daily Kansan] [ref: Mark Harvey, University of Saint Mary]

== Research ==
Harvey's scholarship spans political communication, international relations, popular culture, and political science pedagogy. His work examines political influence, persuasion, and decision making in public life, particularly through celebrity advocacy, media, music, and experiential learning.

=== Celebrity influence and political communication ===
Harvey's research examines the role of celebrities in politics, public persuasion, issue advocacy, and media coverage. [ref: Celebrity Influence: Politics, Persuasion, and Issue-Based Advocacy, University Press of Kansas]

In Celebrity Influence: Politics, Persuasion, and Issue-Based Advocacy (2017), Harvey argues that celebrities derive political influence primarily through their ability to attract public and media attention to issues and their ability to persuade audiences through credibility, familiarity, and identification. [ref: Celebrity Influence: Politics, Persuasion, and Issue-Based Advocacy, University Press of Kansas]

His work explores the political activities of entertainers, athletes, and other public figures, analyzing how celebrities influence public agendas, shape media coverage, and participate in domestic and international policy debates. His research employs case studies, content analysis, surveys, and experimental methods.

A recurring theme in Harvey's scholarship is that celebrity influence depends not simply on fame but also on credibility, identity, expertise, and the perceived fit between a public figure and the issue or candidate being advocated. His work argues that endorsements are generally most effective when audiences perceive the celebrity as authentic and connected to the issue under discussion. [ref: Do celebrity endorsements matter? A look at the role of pop stars in modern politics, PBS NewsHour]

Harvey has argued that celebrity persuasion is often most effective on issues where public attitudes are not firmly established, while highly polarized political questions are less susceptible to influence from celebrity advocates. [ref: Do celebrity endorsements matter? A look at the role of pop stars in modern politics, PBS NewsHour] [ref: CBC News Network’s Aarti Pole speaks with author and professor Mark Harvey, CBC News] His research has examined celebrity advocacy in areas including foreign policy, development, human rights, international conflict, electoral politics, and public policy. [ref: Study shows Taylor Swift's endorsement may turn off voters Harris needs, The Hill]

Harvey has also examined the relationship between celebrity status, media coverage, and political influence. In a chapter analyzing media coverage of Donald Trump, he explored how celebrity and news attention can shape public perceptions of political leaders and contribute to political influence beyond traditional forms of political communication. [ref: The Hollywood Connection: The Influence of Fictional Media and Celebrity Politics in American Public Opinion, Lexington Books]

=== Music, media, and popular culture ===
Harvey's research examines the relationship between music, media, political communication, and political power. His work explores how musicians, performers, entertainment industries, and media systems influence public opinion, collective identities, and policy debates in both domestic and international contexts.

A significant portion of Harvey's scholarship focuses on the political and economic development of the recording industry. In studies of the long-playing (LP) record and the emergence of the album as an artistic format, he has examined how technological innovation, marketing strategies, industry structures, and cultural change transformed the music business during the second half of the twentieth century. Harvey has argued that the growing popularity of the album format was influenced not only by technological innovation but also by struggles within the recording industry over artistic autonomy, marketing practices, and control of creative production. [ref: The Rise of the LP: The Politics of Diffusion Innovation in the Recording Industry, Business History]

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh

Draft text:
Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh is a Palestinian-American journalist and media entrepreneur. He is the founder and editor-in-chief of @[user], a digital media publication and social media news outlet focused on news and culture for Muslim audiences. [ref: Meet the Accidental Editor in Chief of Muslim Media, Wired] [ref: Content creators surge past legacy media as news hits a tipping point, The Washington Post] He founded the publication while studying journalism at Rutgers University and was named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list in Media in 2021. [ref: Filling a Media Void for Young Muslims, Rutgers University Foundation] [ref: Ameer Al-Khatahtbeh, Forbes]

==Early life and education==

Al-Khatahtbeh is a first-generation Palestinian American. His mother was a Palestinian refugee and his father immigrated to the United States from Jordan.

He began his undergraduate studies at Rutgers University–Newark before transferring to Rutgers University–New Brunswick, where he studied journalism. He graduated from Rutgers in 2020 with a degree in journalism.

While a student, Al-Khatahtbeh became interested in creating media focused specifically on Muslim communities. According to Rutgers, after the 2017 executive order restricting travel from several Muslim-majority countries, he wrote an article about the policy for a journalism class and sought a Muslim-focused publication in which to publish it. His difficulty finding such an outlet contributed to his decision to develop his own publication.

==Career==

===Muslim===

Al-Khatahtbeh launched Muslim in February 2019 while he was a junior at Rutgers. The project initially included a weekly newsletter covering news related to Muslims before expanding into an online publication and social media network.

In April 2020, PAPER profiled Al-Khatahtbeh and the publication, describing Muslim as a media platform aimed primarily at Millennial and Generation Z Muslim audiences. Al-Khatahtbeh told the magazine that he created the platform in response to what he saw as a lack of Muslim-led coverage of issues affecting Muslim communities. [ref: Finally, a New Platform by Muslims for Muslims, PAPER]

Religion News Service also profiled Al-Khatahtbeh and Muslim in 2020, reporting that the publication was intended to reach young Muslims across different racial, sectarian and religious backgrounds. [ref: Meet Muslim, a new online publication for the Gen Z ummah, Religion News Service]

In 2020, Muslim drew wider attention after reporting on the use of a song containing a recitation of an Islamic hadith during Rihanna's Savage X Fenty fashion show. Forbes subsequently cited the story in its profile of Al-Khatahtbeh.

By 2021, the publication had expanded significantly on social media. Business Insider reported that the @[user] Instagram account had grown to more than 750,000 followers within two years and that the publication had expanded to platforms including TikTok, YouTube and Snapchat. [ref: How the 22-year-old who owns the @[user] Instagram handle used it to launch a disruptive media company, Business Insider]

Al-Khatahtbeh has also spoken publicly about the moderation of Palestinian content on social media platforms. During the 2021 Israel–Palestine crisis, the Columbia Journalism Review reported that Al-Khatahtbeh said he had documented thousands of instances in which Instagram users reported censorship or restrictions involving Palestine-related content. [ref: Social networks accused of censoring Palestinian content, Columbia Journalism Review]

In 2023, The Washington Post featured Al-Khatahtbeh in an article examining the growth of independent social-media news creators and their increasing role in how younger audiences consume news. The newspaper described him as one of a broader group of independent creators reshaping digital news consumption and reported that @[user] had accumulated millions of followers on Instagram and TikTok.

Al-Khatahtbeh was subsequently quoted by The Washington Post in its reporting on social-media moderation during the Israel–Gaza war, including concerns about restrictions affecting Palestinian and pro-Palestinian content. [ref: In Israel-Hamas war, social media isn't neutral, The Washington Post]

In May 2025, Meta restricted access to the @[user] Instagram account in India following a legal request from the Indian government. Agence France-Presse reported that users in India were shown a notice saying that access had been restricted because of a legal request. Al-Khatahtbeh publicly criticized the decision as censorship. [ref: Meta blocks major Muslim Instagram page in India amid rising conflict, The Guardian]

A 2026 profile in Wired examined Al-Khatahtbeh's development of Muslim from a student media project into a large social-first media operation. At the time of the profile, Wired reported that the publication had more than 12 million followers across its social-media platforms, including 6.7 million on Instagram.

==Recognition==

In 2021, Al-Khatahtbeh was included in Forbes 30 Under 30 list in the Media category for his work building Muslim. Rutgers later reported that he was the youngest person included on the Media list that year.

He also received grant support from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation for the development of Muslim.

== References ==

The Bernard Shaw was a pub in Portobello, Dublin open from 2006 to October 2019. Housed in a late 19th century protected structure, the pub previously known as Bambrick's was taken over in 2006 by Bodytonic who refurbished, reopened, and renamed it after writer George Bernard Shaw, who was born on nearby Synge Street. It became a popular venue, associated with alternative bohemian subcultures, and incorporated a basement venue, food yard, and beer garden in addition to a traditional style pub.

After the adjoining buildings had gradually been demolished or left fall into dereliction, the bar was refused planning permission to retain the beer garden in May 2019, and four months later announced the bar would close entirely in October of that year. The closure was polarising, with commentators lamenting a great loss to Dublin cultural life, while others celebrated it as eliminating a source of anti-social behaviour and an obstacle to regeneration and progress.

==Design==
The Bernard Shaw is in an old-fashioned pub with mahogany panels and a brass rail at the front entrance on South Richmond Street, that opened onto both a small 60-person venue space in the basement and an outdoor beer garden at the back; [ref: Bernard Shaw owner to open new pub on Dublin’s north side, The Irish Times] to the side of the pub was "Eatyard", an open area featuring food vendors and seating.

===Prior history===
The pub was included in the Record of Protected Structures maintained by Dublin City Council. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage dates the building to 1895, while a 2019 article in The Irish Times dates it to 1859, and a 2019 San Francisco Chronicle article reported claims of there having been a pub on the site since the 12th century. The 1862 Thom's Directory notes a spirit distiller at the site. A 2017 appraisal of the building by the National Built Heritage Service described it thusly:

The pub ran as 'Bambrick's' before Bodytonic refurbished and reopened it as The Bernard Shaw in 2006. [ref: Closure of Dublin's Bernard Shaw pub 'just another sign the city is changing', The Irish Times] The name of the pub refers to writer George Bernard Shaw, who was born on nearby Synge Street. [ref: The Bernard Shaw, 11-12 South Richmond Street, Dublin 2, DUBLIN, National Inventory of Architectural Heritage] They received planning permission in 2008 for a smoking area beside the pub, which they converted into the beer garden three years later.

===Dilapidated appearance and artwork===
[[File:EATYARD NEXT DOOR THE THE BERNARD SHAW -9-18 SOUTH RICHMOND STREET DUBLIN 2--134830 (25537978058).jpg|thumb|left|The pub was known for exterior, which featured street art and murals. Irish political leader Daniel O'Connell and the band 12 Sundays shown depicted on its northern face here in December 2017.]]
A mural by artist Aches of Savita Halappanavar adorned the wall adjacent to the pub's facade during the campaign around the 2018 referendum on abortion. It became a shrine to her memory in May 2018 when mourners left over a thousand messages at its base. [ref: Post-it notes left at a 'shrine' to Savita Halappanavar photographed and archived, The Irish Times] The notes were collected and archived by the Dublin City Library and Archive (DCLA) in collaboration with the Digital Repository of Ireland. After the pub's closure, a barrier over the former Eatyard entrance was painted by ESTR with a mural for Concern Worldwide with a QR code linking to a recording of a poem. [ref: Bodytonic to replace Bernard Shaw with new venue on Dublin's north side, Newstalk.com]

Christopher Jones of Dublin Live considered it to not look like much from the outside, but said it did have a charming and easygoing look, noting that it was a "reflection of many of the people that hung out there: scruffy but interesting".
Journalist Una Mullally of The Irish Times commented that it was "symbolic too because it revelled in its dilapidation", calling it a compelling visual environment"

==Activities and offerings==
[[File:Andrew Weatherall 9 Aug 2009.jpg|thumb|left|DJ Andrew Weatherall (pictured in 2006) was one of many artists to peform in the basement space]]
Acts who performed in the basement venue include Mr Saturday Night, [ref: Over 15K people have signed a petition to keep The Bernard Shaw's beer garden open, Nialler9] Andrew Weatherall, Acid Granny, [ref: Here's what's happening in the Bernard Shaw before it closes down this month, Nialler9] Optimo, Niall Byrne, Blue Niall, [ref: Blue Niall: “We are a nation of poets, we were destined to fully embrace hip hop eventually”, District Magazine] and Motor City Drum Ensemble.

The pub was also a centre of political activity, hosting events for Dublin Pride, International Women’s Day, and the Repeal the 8th abortion rights referendum campaign.

Draft: Kelvin wave

Draft text:
----

A Kelvin wave is a transverse wave of the narrow core of a vortex. As the wave propagates along the vortex, the core is displaced sideways in a direction that rotates along its length, producing a helical deformation. Kelvin waves were first described theoretically by Lord Kelvin in 1880 [ref: XXIV. Vibrations of a columnar vortex, The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science]. Although Kelvin's original argument assumes a homogeneous, incompressible, and inviscid fluid, Kelvin waves emerge in many different types of fluids, including water, superfluid helium, and cold atomic Bose–Einstein condensates. Kelvin waves are important because they influence the stability of vortices and the redistribution of energy in rotating flows. In classical fluids, Kelvin-wave dynamics is relevant to macroscopic vortices such as tornadoes and aircraft wake vortices.

== Kelvin waves in classical fluids ==
Kelvin waves were first observed experimentally in a classical fluid (water) in 1980 [ref: Theory and observations of waves on hollow-core vortices, Journal of Fluid Mechanics], followed in 1982 by a clearer manifestation of the helical deformation of a vortex core [ref: Vortex solitary waves in a rotating, turbulent flow, Nature]. Their basic properties, including the dispersion relation, were experimentally characterized much later, in 2026 [ref: Kelvin wave propagation along vortex cores, Nature Physics].

== Kelvin waves in superfluid helium-4 ==
Kelvin waves in superfluid helium-4 were first observed in 2014 [ref: Direct observation of Kelvin waves excited by quantized vortex reconnection, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences], followed by their controlled excitation, clear three-dimensional visualization, and quantitative characterization, including measurements of their dispersion relation and phase velocity in 2025 [ref: Direct excitation of Kelvin waves on quantized vortices, Nature Physics].

== Kevin waves in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates ==
Kelvin waves have been detected in ultracold atomic Bose–Einstein condensates [ref: Quadrupole Oscillation of a Single-Vortex Bose-Einstein Condensate: Evidence for Kelvin Modes, Physical Review Letters] [ref: Experimental Observation of the Tilting Mode of an Array of Vortices in a Dilute Bose-Einstein Condensate, Physical Review Letters], although propagating helical Kelvin waves have not yet been directly imaged.

Wanderlust (Serbian: Излет, romanized: Izlet) is a 2025 Serbian–British black-and-white drama film directed by Nenad Pavlović. It is based on the 1957 novel Izlet by Serbian painter, writer and filmmaker Mića Popović, with a screenplay by his son Jovan Popović. The film stars Stefan Vukić as Toma, a young artist who leaves the city and travels downriver in search of personal and artistic freedom. [ref: PRODUCTION: Serbian Director Nenad Pavlović Shoots Sophomore Feature Wanderlust, Film New Europe]

The film was made as a co-production between the British company Buca Productions and the Serbian company Digimedia. It is Pavlović's second feature film, following Trail of the Beast (2022). [ref: FNE Oscar Watch 2027: Serbia Selects Wanderlust as Oscar Contender, Film New Europe]

In September 2026, Wanderlust was selected as Serbia's official submission for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film at the 99th Academy Awards.

== Plot ==

Following his father's suicide, Toma, a young artist struggling with grief, leaves the city and travels downriver to escape the pressures of society. After encountering a succession of people during his journey, he reaches a deserted island, where he withdraws from society and begins creating art from natural materials. His search for personal and artistic freedom gradually confronts him with the limits of complete isolation.

== Cast ==

* Stefan Vukić as Toma
* Milena Radulović as the Girl
* Dragan Bjelogrlić as Toma's father
* Predrag Miki Manojlović as the Colonel
* Radoslav Milenković as the Blind Musician
* Denis Murić as the Young Worker
* Milena Pavlović as the Postwoman
* Jovo Maksić as the Cook
* Nenad Heraković as the Engineer
* Radoje Čupić as the Older Worker
* Igor Filipović as the Clerk

== Production ==

=== Development ===

Wanderlust is adapted from Mića Popović's 1957 novel Izlet. The screenplay was written by his son Jovan Popović. Production began in April 2024, with Stefan Vukić cast in the leading role. Filming took place in Petrovaradin, on the Danube and in Belgrade.

The film was produced by Predrag "Buca" Popović and Miloš Đukelić as a co-production between the British company Buca Productions and the Serbian company Digimedia.

=== Themes and style ===

The film draws on several movements in 20th-century Serbian and Yugoslav culture, including Zenitism, the Mediala art movement and the Yugoslav Black Wave. The latter is particularly relevant to director Nenad Pavlović, whose father, filmmaker Živojin Pavlović, was one of the major figures associated with the movement. [ref: Director Nenad Pavlović on his new film, the spirit of the times, despair, resisting the mundane, and a tribute to art, NIN]

The film connects the legacies of Mića Popović and Živojin Pavlović through their sons: Jovan Popović adapted his father's novel, while Nenad Pavlović directed the film.

Pavlović has said that the film deliberately avoids precisely defining its time and location. Its production design and costumes suggest the late 1950s or early 1960s, while the story addresses themes of individual freedom, social control and isolation.

=== Cinematography ===

Wanderlust was shot in black and white by cinematographer Bojana Andrić.

== Release ==

Wanderlust had its world premiere on 21 December 2025 at the Sava Centar in Belgrade, as part of the Najduža noć filma ("The Longest Night of Film") programme.

The film subsequently screened at several film festivals, including the Pula Film Festival in Croatia.

== Reception ==

Writing in the English edition of NIN, film critic Sandra Perović highlighted Bojana Andrić's black-and-white cinematography as the film's strongest achievement and discussed Wanderlust in the context of contemporary Serbian cinema and the legacy of the Yugoslav Black Wave. [ref: Reflection on the Film Year 2025: Notes on Serbian Film and Cinematography, NIN]

Goran Jovanović of Filmovi Preporuke gave the film four out of five stars, praising Andrić's cinematography, Stefan Vukić's performance and the adaptation of Mića Popović's novel. He considered the film stylistically more accomplished than Pavlović's previous feature. [ref: Izlet (2025), Filmovi Preporuke]

A more critical assessment appeared in Radar, which criticized the film's narrative coherence and length while praising Andrić's black-and-white cinematography. [ref: Najduža noć filma, Radar]
== Awards and recognition ==

At the 2026 Avant & Una Film Festival in Bihać, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Wanderlust received the award for Best Feature Film.

At the 2026 Niš Film Festival, Igor Filipović received the award for Best Supporting Actor for his performances in Wanderlust and Karmadonna. [ref: Završen Filmski festival u Nišu; poznati svi dobitnici svih nagrada, Mreža kinoprikazivača Srbije]

In September 2026, Wanderlust was selected as Serbia's official candidate for the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards.

The Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry is a public inquiry in the United Kingdom into the implementation and operation of the Horizon accounting system, and the actions taken by Post Office Ltd and others in response to apparent financial shortfalls recorded by the system. The inquiry was established on a non-statutory basis in September 2020 and was converted into a statutory inquiry under the Inquiries Act 2005 on 1 June 2021, with Sir Wyn Williams as chair. [ref: Terms of reference, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry]

The inquiry examined the development and operation of Horizon, the use of information generated by the system in investigations and prosecutions, the treatment of postmasters, compensation and access to justice, and the governance and oversight of the Post Office and its relationship with government. Its work was divided into seven phases. Public hearings began in February 2022 and concluded with closing submissions in December 2024. [ref: Key Documents, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry] [ref: British Post Office scandal, Wikipedia]

The first volume of the chair's final report was published on 8 July 2025 and dealt with the human impact of the scandal and financial redress. It contained 19 recommendations. As of July 2026, five further volumes remained in preparation; Sir Wyn Williams said that these would cover the period from the development of Legacy Horizon to events after the end of the litigation brought by Alan Bates and other claimants against the Post Office. [ref: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry Report: Volume 1, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry] [ref: Progress Update from Sir Wyn Williams, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry]

== Background ==

The inquiry arose from the wider British Post Office scandal, in which hundreds of postmasters were prosecuted and thousands more were held financially responsible for apparent losses recorded by Horizon. The system was developed for the Post Office by Fujitsu and began to be rolled out from 1999. Postmasters had reported discrepancies in branch accounts almost from the beginning of the rollout, but the Post Office continued to rely on Horizon data in seeking to recover alleged shortfalls and, in England and Wales, in criminal prosecutions.

In 2009, Computer Weekly reported allegations that Horizon could generate erroneous information, while the Justice for Subpostmasters Alliance was formed to campaign on behalf of affected postmasters. Subsequent investigations, the group litigation brought by 555 postmasters, and judgments of the High Court and Court of Appeal established the basis for challenges to convictions and increased pressure for an independent inquiry.

Following the settlement of the group litigation in 2019 and the beginning of successful appeals against convictions, campaigners and parliamentarians called for a judge-led investigation into the causes of the scandal and the conduct of the Post Office and government.

== Establishment ==

=== Non-statutory inquiry (2020–2021) ===

On 26 February 2020, the government indicated that it would establish an independent inquiry into the Horizon scandal. On 10 June 2020, the government announced an independent review of the Post Office's Horizon IT system and the use of information generated by it in criminal trials.

The review was established as a non-statutory inquiry in September 2020 under the chairmanship of Sir Wyn Williams. It issued a call for evidence on 1 December 2020, and its first public hearing took place on 15 January 2021. Two public hearings were held during the non-statutory phase, followed by a preliminary hearing on the provisional list of issues in November 2021. [ref: Key Documents, Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry]

The original review had a narrower remit than the later statutory inquiry. In particular, it did not include the Post Office's prosecution function, the settlement reached in the group litigation, or the conduct of current or future litigation.

=== Conversion to a statutory inquiry (2021) ===

On 19 May 2021, the government announced that the inquiry would be placed on a statutory footing. It was formally converted under the Inquiries Act 2005 on 1 June 2021, giving the chair additional powers to compel witnesses and require the production of evidence.

The statutory inquiry's terms of reference required it to establish what went wrong with Horizon and the Post Office's use of information from the system; obtain relevant evidence from the Post Office, Fujitsu, government departments and UK Government Investments; assess whether changes promised by the Post Office had been delivered; and examine governance, oversight and whistleblowing arrangements.

The terms of reference also required the inquiry to take account of the findings of the High Court in Bates & Others v Post Office Ltd and the Court of Appeal in R v Hamilton and others, as well as other judgments in which convictions had been quashed.

Coral Edge LRT station is a Light Rail Transit station in Punggol, Singapore. Coral Edge LRT station serves the east loop of the Punggol LRT line (PGLRT). Coral Edge is located along Punggol East, between Meridian and Riviera stations. Coral Edge station is designated [ref: https://www.lta.gov.sg/content/dam/ltagov/getting_around/public_transport/rail_network/pdf/SM_TEL4_Eng.pdf].

= History =

=== Punggol LRT line ===
Coral Edge station was first built as part of the LRT system that serves the Punggol area. The contract for designing and building the 13‑kilometre Punggol LRT system was awarded to a group that included Singapore Technologies Industrial Corporation [ref: https://www.sgpbusiness.com/company/Singapore-Technologies-Industrial-Corporation-Ltd], Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Mitsubishi Corporation for S$656 million. The contract also covered the Sengkang LRT line.

Coral Edge station opened on 29 January 2005 along with the east loop stations of the Punggol LRT. Coral Edge station is located inside the Coral Edge precinct, which gives it its name.

=== Incidents ===
On 9 January 2020 a crack was found on one of the plinths between Coral Edge and Riviera stations. Coral Edge station closed one platform early for maintenance while trains kept using the platform. [ref: https://www.straitstimes.com/singapore/transport/punggol-east-lrt-platform-closes-early-for-urgent-maintenance-works-after-crack?ref=search-results]

=== Details ===
Coral Edge station serves the east loop of the PGLRT Coral Edge station is located between Meridian and Riviera stations.

Like the stations on the Sengkang‑Punggol LRT [ref: https://www.lta.gov.sg/content/ltagov/en/getting_around/public_transport/rail_network/sengkang_punggol_lrt.html], Coral Edge station is wheelchair friendly. It has accessibility features such as lifts, wider fare gates [ref: https://www.sgtrains.com/technology-faregates.html] and tactile flooring.

Politrack Africa is a market research and opinion polling agency headquartered in Nairobi, Kenya. [ref: Wambua, Murungi and Methu top performing Senators in Politrack Africa poll, Capital FM]

== Research and polling ==

The firm evaluates public policy and political performance across Kenya's 47 counties. In September 2023, it surveyed 4,801 respondents to rank performance among county senators. A broader survey published in April 2024 evaluated Cabinet secretaries, governors, principal secretaries, and lawmakers across 290 constituencies. [ref: Kindiki, Linturi & Chelugui top performing CSs - Politrack Africa, KBC Digital]

Politrack's December 2024 rating index placed Mining and Blue Economy Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho as the highest-rated minister with 67.3% approval. [ref: Politrack Africa: Joho top perfoming CS with 67.3pc score, Capital FM] Early the following year, the company released a survey on Principal Secretaries based on responses from 1,068 citizens collected in January 2025. [ref: Politrak Report Unveils List of Top Ten Best Performing PSs, Kenyans.co.ke] It also hosted the 2025 Politrack Africa Star Leaders Awards in March to recognize elected and appointed officials. [ref: Babu Owino, Wandayi, Bitok Ranked Best MP, CS & PS at 2025 Politrack Africa Star Leaders Awards, Kenyans.co.ke]

In late 2025, Politrack published two nationwide studies: a performance evaluation of women representatives in November [ref: Nyandarua, Nyeri Woman Reps Lead as Politrack Africa Releases Best Performers List, Tuko] and a county governors index in December. In the governor survey, Kisii Governor Simba Arati and Kakamega Governor Fernandes Barasa tied for top performance at 65%, with Kirinyaga Governor Anne Waiguru placing third at 63.2%. [ref: Arati, Barasa and Waiguru ranked best performing governors in latest Politrack survey, [[TV47 Kenya]

Ahead of the 2027 general election, kenyan media reported on a Politrack africa poll conducted in September 2026 sampling 20,419 voters across 290 constituencies. [ref: Survey: Ruto commands lead, Sifuna surges, Daily Nation] The survey showed incumbent President William Ruto leading voter preference at 45.1%, followed by Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna at 19.6% and Kalonzo Musyoka at 10.3%. [ref: Politrack poll: Ruto leads presidential preference with 45.1%, Sifuna second at 19.6%, [[The Star (Kenya)] [ref: Ruto leads 2027 presidential preference poll at 45.1%, People Daily]

== Media coverage ==

In June 2026, Africa Check reported on a fabricated opinion poll attributed to Politrack Africa concerning the Machakos gubernatorial race. The fact-check found that the poll had not been published by Politrack Africa and that the firm had identified the circulating graphic as fake. [ref: Ignore fake pole, former chief of staff Nzioka Waita wasn’t ranked most popular candidate for Machakos governor, Africa Check]
