Rodriquez Wright II, also known by the stage name Rod212, is an American political organizer, media entrepreneur and hip-hop recording artist. He founded the Nashville-based political consulting and media firm Leo Operations and the publication Washington DC Magazine, and he served as Tennessee organizing director for Michael Bloomberg's 2020 presidential campaign.

== Early life and education ==
Wright studied English at Tennessee State University, a historically black university in Nashville, where he was named to the dean's list. During the 2012 session of the 107th Tennessee General Assembly, he served as a legislative intern for State Senator Ophelia Ford. The Tennessee General Assembly recognized his service in Senate Joint Resolution 905, which commended him for his service as a legislative intern. He also interned with the Tennessee Democratic Party.

== Political career ==
=== Nashville, 2012 to 2015 ===
Wright began working in Nashville politics while still a student. In 2012 he was a Davidson County field organizer for the Tennessee Democratic Party and a field organizer for Sharon Gentry's re-election campaign for the Metro Nashville school board, in which Gentry defeated 27-year board member Ed Kindall. [ref: Gentry Tops Kindall's 27-Year Experience, WPLN News] From 2013 to 2015 he worked for the Nashville public affairs firm Calvert Street Group, and in 2014 he managed Allegra Walker's campaign for Davidson County General Sessions judge and consulted for Kelvin Jones's campaign for Circuit Court judge.

In 2015 Wright was deputy campaign manager and then campaign manager for former vice mayor Howard Gentry's campaign for mayor of Nashville. Gentry finished fourth in the August 2015 general election. [ref: Nashville's Mayoral Runoff, Barry vs. Fox, Already Intense, WPLN News] Wright then served as community outreach director for David Fox in the September runoff, which Fox lost to Megan Barry. [ref: Megan Barry Elected Mayor of Nashville, Governing]

=== National field work, 2015 to 2020 ===
From 2015 to 2016 Wright was a campaign associate with Revolution Field Strategies, a Boston canvassing firm, directing petition drives and canvass programs in several states. They included the signature drive for a Massachusetts ballot initiative on hospital prices, which qualified for the 2016 ballot before its sponsors withdrew it as part of a legislative deal, [ref: Deal reached to avert ballot question on hospitals, The Boston Globe] and the drive for Montana's I-181, a proposed brain research bond program that qualified for the 2016 ballot and was rejected by voters. [ref: I-181 Has Consequences Beyond Brain Research, Montana Public Radio] He also worked on Hillary Clinton's 2016 New Hampshire primary campaign.

In 2017 he was field director for canvassing on Kansas City's $800 million general obligation bond package, which voters approved in April 2017. [ref: Tax ballot wins in St. Louis and Kansas City draw a favorable Moody's response, The Bond Buyer] From 2017 to 2018 he managed Omar Passons's campaign for the San Diego County Board of Supervisors; Passons was eliminated in the June 2018 primary and later endorsed Nathan Fletcher. [ref: Passons Endorses Fletcher in 4th District County Supervisor Race, Times of San Diego]

In 2018 Wright directed petition drives for Arizona's Invest in Ed income tax initiative, whose backers submitted about 270,000 signatures before the Arizona Supreme Court removed it from the ballot, [ref: Arizona Invest In Education Turns In Hundreds Of Thousands Of Signatures, KJZZ] and for All for Transportation's one-cent transportation sales tax in Hillsborough County, Florida, which voters approved that November. [ref: Group Gets Signatures For Hillsborough Transit Sales Tax Referendum, WUSF] Later that year he was Tennessee state project director for BlackPAC, and in 2019 he directed the Chicago canvass for The Black Institute's #KeepStarz campaign against Comcast.

In December 2019 the Bloomberg 2020 presidential campaign named Wright organizing director of its Tennessee operation, alongside outreach director London Lamar. The campaign opened its state headquarters in Nashville that month. [ref: Michael Bloomberg Opens Tennessee Campaign Headquarters In Nashville, WPLN News]

=== Leo Operations ===
Wright founded Leo Operations, a Nashville firm that provides campaign management, field strategy, media production and digital marketing for political campaigns, elected officials, nonprofits and businesses. Through the firm he was campaign manager for Nashville District Attorney Glenn Funk's 2022 re-election campaign, and digital consultant to Metro Council at-large members Zulfat Suara and Burkley Allen in 2019 and 2023 and to Sharon Hurt's 2026 campaign for Davidson County Clerk. In 2023 Suara and Allen were re-elected as part of the first at-large Metro Council delegation made up entirely of women. [ref: Women win all five at-large Metro council seats, WSMV]

Plucked is an upcoming American dark comedy period film written, produced, and directed by Usher Morgan and Katie Vincent. The film stars Vincent in the lead role, alongside Jared Canfield, J. Anthony Crane, Catherine Curtin, Susan Gallagher, Bryant Carroll, and Tony D. Head. [ref: Plucked Teaser Trailer: Stranger Things' Catherine Curtin Stars in Comedy Movie, Yahoo Entertainment]

The film was independently produced by Dark Passage Films and is scheduled to be released theatrically in the United States on November 13, 2026. [ref: Plucked Teaser Trailer: Stranger Things' Catherine Curtin Stars in Comedy Movie, ComingSoon.net] [ref: 'Plucked' Dark Comedy Film Stars Katie Vincent, Jared Canfield, J. Anthony Crane, Catherine Curtin – Trailer and Release Date, Movie Vine]

==Premise==
In Gilded Age New York, a rebellious woman (Vincent) is trying to divorce her emotionally unstable husband (Canfield). Consequently, a civilized evening violently spirals into pandemonium. [ref: Plucked (2026) film review, Screen Critix]

==Cast==

==Early reviews==
In early reviews, critics praised the film's dialogue, performances, and blend of period drama and dark comedy. [ref: Plucked, Rotten Tomatoes]

Carl Burgess of Screen Critix awarded the film 4.5 out of 5 stars, calling it "an impressive return from Morgan and Vincent" that showed "considerable growth in scale and visual confidence." Alton Williams, a critic with Battle Royale With Cheese described it as an "entertaining and increasingly unpredictable film that finds plenty of drama within the walls of a single home." Williams also praised Vincent's performance in the film. [ref: Plucked: Review, Battle Royale With Cheese]

The New York Amsterdam News "Curtain Raiser" critic Lapacazo Sandoval noted the film's $300K micro budget, and wrote that Plucked is "“a deliciously vicious dinner party in a world you can’t resist entering.” [ref: 'Plucked' Review: A Gilded Age Dinner Party Worth Crashing, AmNews Curtain Raiser]

Jason Knight of UK Film Review awarded the film 4 out of 5 stars, praising its period setting, cinematography, and performances, particularly those of Vincent and Canfield; noting that the first half of the film was somewhat slow-paced, he felt the remainder of the film made up for it. [ref: Plucked, UK Film Review]

Draft text:
Suzanne Scott is an American media scholar is an associate professor in the Department of Radio-TV-Film at the University of Texas at Austin. [ref: Suzanne Scott, The University of Texas at Austin: Moody College of Communication] Previously, Scott previously taught Film and Media Studies in the Department of English at Arizona State University, as well as undergraduate and graduate courses at University of California, Santa Cruz, University of California, Los Angeles, and the University of Southern California. She also served as a Mellon Digital Scholarship Postdoctoral Fellow in the Center of Digital Learning + Research at Occidental College.

Scott is the author of Fake Geek Girls: Fandom, Gender, and the Convergence Culture Industry (2019). She has also co-edited a number of books including The Routledge Companion to Media Fandom (2018) and Sartorial Fandom: Fashion, Beauty Culture, and Identity (2023).

== Education and personal life ==
Scott graduated from New York University with a B.F.A. in Cinema Studies and Journalism, she then earned her M.A. and Ph.D. in Critical Studies from the University of Southern California. Scott's doctoral dissertation, Revenge of the Fanboy: Convergence Culture and The Politics of Incorporation (2011) was supervised by Ellen Seiter, Tara McPherson, and Henry Jenkins.

Draft: Void Vibration

Draft text:
Void Vibration is the second studio album by Düsseldorf Neo-psychedelic and Neo-Kraut Rock band Vibravoid. The album was released in September 2002 by Berlin independent record label Nasoni Records. The album was named "CD of the Month" by major German music magazine Eclipsed. [ref: Vibravoid – Void Vibration, Eclipsed]

== Recording and production ==

The album was initially recorded on analogue tape at the Düsseldorf studio "Das Kleine Analoge" in November and December 2001 with a Fostex G24S 24-track tape recorder (1-inch). However, most of these recordings did not make it onto the album but were released later on Triptamine E.P. Volume 1. [ref: Triptamine E.P. Volume 1, Nasoni Records] The version of the title track Void Vibration from these sessions remains unreleased and is considered lost. [ref: Void Vibration (10th Anniversary Deluxe Edition), Krauted Mind Records] [ref: Eine kleine Reise ins elektrische Bewusstsein, eclipsed Rock Magazin]

The band re-recorded all tracks except Echovoid and Electrovoid in 2002 at the Institut für Wohlklangforschung in Hanover, assisted by Willi Dammeier on a Telefunken M15A 2-inch 24-track tape recorder and an Amek Angela mixing console. The album was mastered by Michael Schwabe at the Monoposto Studios. The album was produced in Dolby Surround quadraphonic sound. For the track Echovoid, two separate tape echo units were used, a Roland Space Echo and a Dynacord echo unit. [ref: Let's Take A Trip With… Nasoni Records, Rumble Skunk]

== Style and sound ==
Void Vibration is intended as an analogue counterpoint to the digital revolution in music production emerging in the 1990s. Stylistically, the album combines the experimental electronic influences of the Düsseldorf School with elements of classic flower power psychedelia and Kraut Rock. The overall sound is characterised by the use of analogue vintage effects, tape echo units, synthesizer and sitar sounds. Alongside psychedelic passages are noise-heavy walls of guitar sound that display influences from the early sound of Pink Floyd.

== Historical context of the songs ==
Void Vibration is retrospectively regarded as a document of the German underground of the 1990s and the emerging vinyl revival. [ref: Vibravoid, Slam] Other official releases of alternative versions date the songs during that decade. The track Adjustment was composed as early as 1992 and first recorded on 10 February 1994 at Potter's Work Studio in Essen, using a Fostex B16 reel-to-reel recorder and an ACE Audio Engineering mixing console. The original 1994 recording was first released on the demo tape One Nation Underground in the same year before appearing on the album Turned On Acid in 2003. [ref: Turned on Acid, Moonhead Records] A new recording of the song was released as a 7-inch single on Nasoni Records in 2001. This version had been recorded at the Düsseldorf studio "Das Kleine Analoge" using a Tascam 8-track tape recorder and was reviewed by contemporary press coverage. The single was released on grey marbled vinyl. [ref: Vibravoid – Void Vibration (review), Gew Gaw] [ref: Vibravoid – Adjustment, Prinz] Since this particular recording had already been released as a single, the band re-recorded the song in Hanover for the LP version of Void Vibration but included both songs from the 7” single as bonus tracks on the 2002 edition of the CD. [ref: Vibravoid – Void Vibration, Bad Acid Magazine]

The title track Void Vibration dates back to 1995 and is documented by historical demo tapes, live recordings from the period in which it was created and contemporary radio broadcasts. While the track Vivid Vision dates to 1996, the record credits identify Black And White and Creepy People as new compositions from 2001. [ref: Vibravoid Feature, Timemazine]

== Release and special editions ==
The CD edition was released in September 2002 on Nasoni Records and distributed by Swamp Room Distribution. The official record release party followed in December 2002 with a Vibravoid concert at the Duncker Club in Berlin. A recording of this show was released as Live At Duncker Berlin 2002 in 2025. [ref: Live At Duncker Berlin 2002 (Triptamine EP Vol. 8), Tonzonen Records] The vinyl edition of Void Vibration was released at the worldwide low point for vinyl records in 2003. [ref: Vinyl Revival, Journal of Popular Music Studies] The CD edition came in a black cover, while the LP was released in a white gatefold sleeve with blind embossing and a custom die-cut to be used for an optical effect. The LP was released in four different editions, including a DMM pressing in Dolby Surround quadraphonic sound on black 180-gram virgin vinyl, a white vinyl version, a regular black vinyl version and a black-and-white picture disc featuring an Op Art motif. This record is visually matched to the transparent inner sleeve printed with another Op Art graphic and being placed underneath the die cut opening. If the record is rotated inside the sleeve, moving Op Art effects are created. Production problems caused by an error during the die-cutting process delayed the regular delivery of the gatefold sleeves until February 2003. [ref: Vibravoid – Void Vibration (Master Release), Discogs]
[truncated]

Dr. Andrew Nathaniel Forde (born January 21, 1987) is a Canadian engineer, artificial intelligence researcher, management consultant, and violinist. He is a partner at KPMG and, since March 2026, the firm's inaugural head of AI research, a national role the firm described as the first of its kind in Canada's professional services industry.

Dr. Forde began his career as a materials scientist at NASA's Langley Research Center and later held roles at Boston Consulting Group, Deloitte, CGI, and IBM Consulting before joining KPMG in 2023. He is also an adjunct professor in the Faculty of Applied Science and Engineering at the University of Toronto, and testified before the Senate of Canada in 2026 as an expert witness on artificial intelligence.

Trained on the violin from early childhood, Dr. Forde has performed for United States presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush and has shared stages with Sting, Justin Bieber, Mary J. Blige, and Pitbull. His 2018 multimedia work Ideas of North, a reinterpretation of Glenn Gould's radio documentary The Idea of North, premiered to a sold-out audience at Koerner Hall in Toronto. He serves on the board of directors of the Tafelmusik Baroque Orchestra.

== Early life and education ==
Dr. Forde was born and raised in Toronto, Ontario, to a Jamaican mother and a Bajan father, and has credited his Caribbean family foundation with shaping his path toward higher education. He holds Canadian and Bajan citizenship. He was introduced to the violin at age three after watching an orchestral performance, and received his first instrument at age four.

He earned a Bachelor of Applied Science in materials science and engineering from the University of Toronto in 2011, and completed a PhD in industrial engineering and machine learning at the same institution in 2020 under the supervision of Mark S. Fox. His doctoral thesis, An Ontological Framework & Data Driven Approach for Measuring Radicalness, developed an innovation ontology for classifying radical and incremental innovation and for selecting ideas in the front end of innovation management. Fox, a Professor Emeritus of Industrial Engineering at Toronto and one of the first researchers to apply artificial intelligence to industrial systems, was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 2026. In 2014 Dr. Forde received a fellowship award from Mitacs (Mathematics of Information Technology and Complex Systems). While a graduate student, he was also chief executive of Sommerlink Solutions, a big-data consulting firm.

== Career ==

=== NASA and consulting ===
Dr. Forde began his professional career as a materials scientist conducting research at NASA's Langley Research Center. He subsequently worked as an associate at Boston Consulting Group, as global innovation lead for strategic modelling and analytics at Deloitte, and as a managing director at CGI, before becoming an associate partner in the data, AI, and technology transformation practice at IBM Consulting.

=== KPMG ===
Dr. Forde joined KPMG in 2023 as a partner in the firm's technology strategy and digital transformation practice, with a focus on digital healthcare, enterprise AI strategy, and large-scale transformation for clients across government, energy and utilities, healthcare, telecommunications, and financial services.

On March 24, 2026, KPMG Canada announced Dr. Forde's appointment as its first head of AI research, a newly established national role that the firm described as the first of its kind in Canada's professional services industry. The mandate focuses on bridging the gap between Canadian AI research and commercialization, building relationships with universities and research labs, and serving as the firm's leading voice on AI research and policy. Announcing the role, Dr. Forde argued that Canada helped pioneer modern AI research but has too often seen its breakthroughs commercialized elsewhere.

In April 2026, Dr. Forde appeared as an expert witness before the Standing Senate Committee on Transport and Communications, testifying on the opportunities and challenges of artificial intelligence in the information and communications technology sector. He has contributed to policy submissions to the Government of Canada on AI transparency, sovereign compute, and national AI strategy.

Dr. Forde is a frequent commentator on artificial intelligence in Canadian media. The Logic profiled him in May 2026 as KPMG's "AI whisperer", and in the Financial Post he has discussed the economics of enterprise AI token consumption and the competitive significance of Moonshot AI's open-weight Kimi K3 model. He has also spoken on AI trust and governance in The Logic and in an interview with Circuit Cellar at Web Summit Vancouver.

=== Academic work ===
Dr. Forde is an adjunct professor in the Faculty of Applied Science and Engineering at the University of Toronto, where he has taught since 2022. He has published in scientific journals and business literature on quantitative innovation and decision making under ambiguity.

== Music ==
A concert-trained violinist, Dr. Forde has performed for United States presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush, has performed alongside Sting, Justin Bieber, Mary J. Blige, and Pitbull, and has composed for film and commercial projects.

Los Lupeños de San José is a Mexican Folklórico dance company based in San Jose, California. Founded in 1969 by Susan V. Cashion and Ramón Morones Ortiz, it developed as a study and performance group dedicated to Mexican folk dance [ref: Did you know? Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]. The company operates under [http://CashionCulturalLegacy.org Cashion Cultural Legacy] and is based at the Mexican Heritage Plaza in East San Jose [ref: Did you know? Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]

== History ==

=== Foundation and early activities ===
Cashion and Morones met in Guadalajara, Mexico, where they studied folklórico. They established Los Lupeños in San José in 1969. Cashion also taught at Stanford University while continuing to direct the company. [ref: The Role of Folklorico and Danzantes Unidos in the Chican@ Movement, University of California, Merced]

The company's early activities included music education as well as dance. In a study of women in California mariachi, Cynthia Reifler Flores describes Cashion's efforts to establish a community mariachi ensemble to accompany the dancers. Instruction was open to interested participants, including women and musicians of different backgrounds. Barbara Pérez-Díaz, whose career is examined in the study, participated as both a dancer and musician. A surviving program documents the company's December 4, 1971 concert at the San Jose Civic Auditorium, with performances by Mariachi Tequilatlán and Mariachi Uclatlán. [ref: Barbara Perez-Díaz y Rebeca Gonzales. Women Pioneers of Mariachi in California. The Cultural and Transnational Implications, KARPA]

An April 1983 article in the San José newspaper Our Paper described the company as the oldest organized Mexican Folklorico dance company in the Nation. [ref: Los Lupenos Return Triumphantly to San Jose, Our Paper]

=== Folklórico organizations and collaborations ===
The founders participated in networks connecting folklórico practitioners across the United States. In a note about the early years of the Asociación Nacional de Grupos Folklóricos [https://angfdance.com/ (ANGF)], dance scholar Gabriela Mendoza-García identifies Cashion and Morones among the California practitioners contacted for the March 1974 national gathering at the University of New Mexico. Her account also reproduces a photograph of Los Lupeños performing Yucatán dances at ANGF in 1975. [ref: Creation, Growth, and Inspiration: The Beginnings of the Asociación Nacional de Grupos Folklóricos (1974–1976), Gabriela Mendoza-Garcia Ballet Folklorico]

Cashion and Morones organized collaborative folklórico concerts in San José in 1977 and brought visiting teachers from Mexico for performances and workshops. Eve Marie Delfin's history distinguishes these gatherings from the later Danzantes Unidos Festival, organized by John Estrada and Sue Welsh at UCLA in 1979. [ref: About Us, Danzantes Unidos] Delfin also documents Los Lupeños' subsequent role in hosting the festival in San José during the 1980s. [ref: The Role of Folklorico and Danzantes Unidos in the Chican@ Movement, University of California, Merced]

=== Transition to Cashion Cultural Legacy ===
In 2014, 501c3 Non profit organization [http://cashionculturallegacy.org Cashion Cultural Legacy] acquired Los Lupeños. A March 2015 interview in In Dance reported the appointment of Samuel Cortez as artistic director. Managing director Tony Ferrigno described the company's work as researching, learning, and staging folk dances, producing concerts, and providing community education through Los Lupeños Academy. [ref: Did you know? Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]

== Repertoire and performance ==
By 2026, the repertoire encompassed dances from almost every regions of Mexico and works based on early California history. Cashion described the company's interpretation as shaped by its California dancers' experiences as well as Mexican traditions. [ref: From Mexico to California and Back: A Look at Los Lupeños de San José, dancersgroup.org]

The founders created Mextizol, a dance drama about mestizo culture that premiered in the mid-1970s and toured the southwestern United States in several versions. [ref: Archiving Fellowships Blog: Cashion Cultural Legacy, Part 1, Dance/USA] A 2001 Los Angeles Times review examined the company's performance at Caltech. [ref: Ballet Folklorico Los Lupenos Whirls Through Regional Traditions, Los Angeles Times]

The Library of Congress documents musician Artemio Posadas's work accompanying the company and advising it on traditional son huasteco music and dance. [ref: Artemio Posadas: Mexican music and dance from California, Library of Congress]

=== Californio repertoire ===
The company's repertoire has included dances associated with Mexican California. A 2004 newspaper announcement listed its dancers in Fandango IV—Songs & Dances from Mexican California at the Presidio of San Francisco, alongside Coro Hispano de San Francisco, Conjunto Nuevo Mundo, and Cascada de Flores. [ref: Take a green tour through the city, SFGATE]

The Oregon State–Washington State football rivalry is an American college football rivalry game played in the states of Oregon and Washington between the Oregon State Beavers in Corvallis and the Washington State Cougars in Pullman.

First played in 1903, the game is one of the most played rivalries in NCAA football, historically being part of the Northwest Championship. The two schools have historically been apart of the same conference, with them being members of the Pacific Coast Conference from 1916 to 1959, the Athletic Association of Western Universities from 1964 to 1968, the Pac-8 Conference from 1968 to 1978, the Pac-10 Conference from 1978 to 2011, the Pac-12 North Division from 2011 to 2021, and the Pac-12 Conference from 2011 onwards.

The individual matchup between the two schools gained national attention after 10 out of the 12 original teams in the Pac-12 moved to other NCAA conferences in 2024, leaving the two teams as the only ones still in the conference. [ref: College football conference realignment breakdown for 2024-25: Teams in new conferences, NCAA] The matchup has not been officially named yet, with suggestions including "The Land-Grant Rivalry", "The Cascade Cup", "The War on I-84", or "The Columbia River Rivalry". [ref: Buddy-buddy time is over. Washington State-Oregon State is now a real rivalry., The Spokesman-Review] [ref: Rivalry game wins are meaningful, no matter who the opponent is, The Spokesman-Review]

Although the teams do not compete for a trophy on the field, the winning team's alumni association is given the "No Name Trophy", consisting of basalt and granite rock taken from the Columbia River, weighing more than 50 pounds. [ref: Take home the rock: WSU takes on the Beavers in Corvallis - A new trophy is introduced for the WSU vs. OSU rivalry, Daily Evergreen] [ref: ‘Let’s go win the rock’: Behind the new WSU-Oregon State rivalry trophy, Yakima-Herald Times] The concept of the trophy going to the winning team's alumni association is used by Oregon State in the Platypus Trophy.

Like many rivalry games, the game is played during the final week of the college football season, being played in that slot every year since 2025 following the collapse of the Pac-12.
==Series history==
The rivalry was first played in 1903, and has been played 111 times through 2025. They have played each other in 1903, 1905, and annually since 1910, except for in 1918, 1925, 1926, 1943, 1944, 1987, 1997, 1998, 1999, and 2002. Oregon State and Washington State played each other twice in 1945 and in 2025. Washington State leads the series [ref: Washington State-Oregon State, The Sideline]

The game is usually played at either Reser Stadium in Corvallis or Martin Stadium in Pullman. However, nine games were played in Portland, Oregon, and the 2011 game was played at CenturyLink field in Seattle in an effort to increase revenue for the two teams. [ref: Cougs pumped to play at CenturyLink, The Spokesman-Review]

Even though Washington State currently leads the series, Oregon State had several notable win streaks throughout it's history. Oregon State won the first four games they played against each other from 1903 to 1911, before Washington State broke the streak by winning 10-9 in 1912.

Oregon State had two notable win streaks, from 1960 to 1964, and from 1966 to 1971 under coaches Tommy Prothro and Dee Andros. The only time that Washington State won between 1960 and 1971 was in 1965, where they won 10-8 in Corvallis.

Washington State's largest win streak was from 1983 to 1993 under coaches Jim Walden, Dennis Erickson, and Mike Price, where they won 10 consecutive games until Oregon State beat them 21-3 on November 12, 1994. [ref: Oregon State vs Washington State, Fueled By Sports]

The 2023 Matchup, marred by rumors of conference realignment, and being jokingly dubbed the "Pac-2 Championship Game", was the first matchup in the rivalry's history in which both teams were ranked. The game was filled with pageantry, with the Washington State band playing the Oregon State fight song before the game. The Cougars would defeat the Beavers 38-35.

In 2024, Oregon State and Washington State became the only teams remaining in the Pac-12 Conference, [ref: Oregon State, Washington State last standing in depleted Pac-12, KGW8] leading to them being nicknamed the "Pac-2" by media outlets, to the point that a game between the two teams during the 2023 football season was jokingly dubbed the "Pac-2 Championship Game" by fans. [ref: How Pac-2 moves forward after leverage play as College Football Playoff updates 12-team expansion model, CBS Sports] [ref: What happens when realignment leaves a college football team behind, ESPN] [ref: College football abandoned them, but the Pac-2 refuses to go away, The Washington Post] The new attention to the game led to them forming a rivalry against each other. [ref: How the rebuilt Pac-12 looks to be 'in a tier of its own', ESPN] [ref: Washington State-Oregon State rivalry has some unexpected connections this year, Yahoo Sports] [ref: This Rivalry Is Really Weird., Youtube - Pac-12 Conference] Ahead of the game that year, Washington State head coach Jake Dickert said "Oregon State’s not our buddy." and "It’s one of our biggest rivals now". [ref: Abandoned rivals reunion pits Oregon State, Washington State, CBS Sports / Field Level Media] Washington State would lose in upset fashion 41-38.

Gilberto Q. Conchas is an American sociologist of education. He is the Wayne K. and Anita Woolfolk Hoy Endowed Professor of Education at Pennsylvania State University.

Conchas's first book, The Color of Success (2006), compared academies within an urban high school in northern California to examine the academic success of low-income students of color. His other books include Small Schools and Urban Youth (2008), on small learning communities; Streetsmart Schoolsmart (2012), on gangs and street socialization among boys; and The Chicana/o/x Dream (2020), on first-generation Chicana/o/x college students. He has also edited volumes on race and education policy, including When School Policies Backfire (2016) and Race Frames in Education (2022).

In 2022, Conchas received the Sylvia Hurtado University Faculty Award from the American Association of Hispanics in Higher Education.

==Early life and education==
Conchas is the son of Mexican immigrant farmworkers. [ref: Education as a Tool for Breaking the Cycles of Poverty, Teachers College, Columbia University] [ref: The Interview: Gil Conchas, The Boston Globe Magazine] After attending public schools in Ventura and graduating from Ventura High School in 1988, [ref: New Ventura schools chief begins year with pep talk, Thousand Oaks Star] he received a bachelor's degree in sociology from the University of California, Berkeley, and a master's degree and doctorate in sociology from the University of Michigan. [ref: Gilberto Q. Conchas To Give Talk, "Complicating Urban Success among Black and Chicano High School Boys: 1999, 2009, and 2019", Education and Inequality Workshop, University of Pennsylvania]

==Career==
Conchas was an assistant professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, [ref: Keynote speaker, Ventura County Star] where in 2001 he received a National Academy of Education/Spencer Postdoctoral Fellowship. [ref: Gilberto Conchas: Promoting Minority Academic Success: Understanding the Role of Institutional Mechanisms in Distinct School Contexts, National Academy of Education] He later moved to the University of California, Irvine, where by 2008 he was an associate professor of education and chancellor's fellow. [ref: Gates Program Officer to Speak on Breaking the Intergenerational Cycle of Poverty, Teachers College, Columbia University] During the same period he was a senior program officer at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in its postsecondary education program for low-income young people. He left UC Irvine as a full professor, [ref: Education professor's book recognized for focus on Hispanic issues, Penn State News] and in 2020 joined Pennsylvania State University as the Wayne K. and Anita Woolfolk Hoy Endowed Professor of Education. [ref: Education researcher outlines pathways for success for minoritized students, Penn State News] In 2022 he received the Sylvia Hurtado University Faculty Award from the American Association of Hispanics in Higher Education. [ref: Sylvia Hurtado Receives Major Awards from AIR and the University of Pennsylvania, UCLA School of Education & Information Studies]

==Research and work ==
===Student success in urban schools===
In his first book, The Color of Success: Race and High-Achieving Urban Youth (2006), Conchas studied low-income Black, Latina/o and Vietnamese American students at an urban high school in northern California, which the book calls Baldwin High School. He interviewed students and compared two academies within the school and its Advanced Placement track. [ref: A review of: The Color of Success: Race and High-Achieving Urban Youth. Gilberto Q. Conchas, Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk] The school's medical academy, which recruited "high-potential" students, produced cooperation across racial lines, while its more selective graphics academy produced competition. Conchas argued that social capital from peers and teachers shapes engagement and achievement, [ref: Book review: The Color of Success: Race and High-Achieving Urban Youth, Urban Education] and recommended small school-within-a-school programs. In Urban Education, Vichet Chhuon and Francisco D. Carranza recommended it for courses on minority education and school reform. D. Brent Edwards Jr. and Derek Tyler found it refreshing for showing that low-income minority students can achieve at high levels and recommended it as an example of context-specific research. However, they wrote that the book did not define success. Mei-Ling N. Malone called it an important resource for educators. She argued, however, that exclusive programs of the kind it recommends perpetuate tracking. [ref: Review: The Color of Success: Race and High-Achieving Urban Youth by Gilberto Q. Conchas, InterActions: UCLA Journal of Education and Information Studies] Conchas published a revised edition, The Color of Success 2.0, in 2024.

"Before You Break My Heart" is a song by the English singer Jade. It was released through RCA Records on 12 September 2025 as part of her first solo studio album That's Showbiz Baby!. The song was written by Jade, along with Pablo Bowman, and Mike Sabath, the latter of whom also produced it. Additional credits were given to songwriting and production team Holland–Dozier–Holland due to the song's interpolation of "Stop! In the Name of Love" (1965) by the Supremes.

==Background and composition==
[[File:The_Supremes_1966.JPG|thumb|"Before You Break My Heart" interpolates "Stop! In the Name of Love" by the Supremes (pictured).]]
"Before You Break My Heart" is described as a contemporary electronic pop song. [ref: Interview: Jade launches debut album That's Showbiz Baby: "I wanted this album to sound like chaos...I wanted you to listen to every track and be like oh god, what's coming next?", Women in Pop] The song samples vocals from 8-year-old Jade's audition for Stars in Their Eyes singing "Stop! In the Name of Love" by the Supremes. [ref: Curtain Call: Jade Steals the Spotlight on That's Showbiz Baby, The Honey Pop] [ref: Jade Thirlwall interview: life after Little Mix, [[Harper's Bazaar]

Following the song's release, Jade revealed that she is not receiving royalties from the song after being asked about how she was given permission to interpolate the Supremes' song on the track. [ref: Jade won't get royalties from 'Before You Break My Heart' due to Supremes sample, NME] She also explained that the song pays homage to Diana Ross, whom she described as her favorite artist, by prominently featuring the sample throughout the track. [ref: Jade Releases Debut Solo Album That's Showbiz Baby, PM Studio] [ref: Jade Thirlwall forfeits royalties to sample The Supremes on solo album, [[Contactmusic.com]

==Reception==
Puah Ziwei of NME described the song as "groovy" and noted Jade's vocal delivery as "oft-vulnerable." [ref: Jade – That's Showbiz Baby review: pop's star student is ready for the big leagues, NME] David Cobbald of The Line of Best Fit described the song as "more than well worth the listen" and highlighted its interpolation of "Stop! In the Name of Love", calling it a "perfect example of good sampling." [ref: Jade is the star of the show on That's Showbiz Baby, The Line of Best Fit] Jett Tattersall of Women in Pop praised the song for not being overly reliant on its interpolation and called it "an album highlight."

==Live performances==
On 25 July 2025, Jade performed an orchestral concert for BBC Proms at the Glasshouse, accompanied by the Royal Northern Sinfonia. [ref: Jade and Northern Sinfonia give packed crowd a musical masterpiece at BBC Proms in Gateshead, [[Evening Chronicle] After the show's radio broadcast, Jade was joined by her niece Amara to perform "Before You Break My Heart" before the song's release. [ref: A Northern Proms Debut: Jade Thirlwall and Finn Forster at The Glasshouse @ The BBC Proms, Classical Source] The performance was later broadcast as part of the BBC Two special Jade at the Proms: A Homecoming on 8 November 2025. [ref: TV tonight: Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande’s big Wicked night in, The Guardian]
It was also part of the setlist of Jade's first solo concert tour, That's Showbiz Baby: the Tour. [ref: The It Girl has arrived: Jade embodies showbiz perfection, Manchester Evening News]

==Visualiser==
On 12 September 2025, Jade premiered a compilation of visualisers for all tracks on That's Showbiz Baby, describing it as a visual album. [ref: Jade shines on debut solo album That’s Showbiz Baby, CelebMix] The visualiser for "Before You Break My Heart" features Jade and her niece, Amara, portraying a younger version of the singer. It was shot in South Shields by director Niyadre on the same day as Jade's BBC Proms show. [ref: Jade 'Before You Break My Heart' by Niyadre, Promonews.tv] [ref: Everything you need to know about Jade's solo music, [[Rayo (streaming)]

TREE Innovative Foundation (TREEI) is a not-for-profit company based in Pune, Maharashtra, India. It was founded in 2018 by mechanical engineer Tanveer Inamdar. [ref: Taking Electricity, Wherever They Go: Engineer's Portable Solar Units Power Huts of Tribal Migrants in Maharashtra, The Better India] The organisation works in Pune city and Pune district on clean energy, school education, women's livelihoods and health, nutrition and river restoration. [ref: About TREE Innovative Foundation, TREE Innovative Foundation] Its best-known project, Mission Urja, installs solar power systems in tribal hamlets that are not connected to the electricity grid, and since 2025 has installed solar lighting and CCTV cameras at hill forts in the Sahyadri. [ref: Forgotten Pune forts set to be solar-lit in effort to illuminate history, The Indian Express]

== History ==
Inamdar started the organisation in 2018 after working for multinational companies. The name TREE stands for "Technology Reuse Environment Empowerment". [ref: Neer Chakra helps rural women in fetching water, The Bridge Chronicle] It was formally registered in 2019 and was incorporated as a Section 8 company under the Companies Act, 2013 in 2023. [ref: Company master data: TREE Innovative Foundation (CIN U72200PN2023NPL220779), Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India]

Its first project was the Neer Chakra, a three-wheeled cart for carrying water over hilly ground. The cart holds 80 litres and has a filter and a tap. After a pilot in May 2019, carts were given to 25 families in Zhende Wadi, a village about 30 km from Pune, in August 2019. According to Inamdar, the water project showed that many of the same villages had no electricity, which led to Mission Urja in 2022.

The organisation started a school programme, Program Dhruv, in 2020. A river restoration programme and an integrated village development programme followed in 2026. [ref: Program DHARA, TREE Innovative Foundation]

== Programmes ==

=== Mission Urja ===
Mission Urja works mainly with the Katkari community in Haveli, Maval and Mulshi talukas of Pune district. [ref: Mission URJA: Village Edition, TREE Innovative Foundation] It uses two types of system: centralised solar installations of 15–20 kW that supply huts through individual meters, and portable foldable solar units of about 3 kg for migrant families without permanent homes. Small hydroelectric units are used where streams allow.

Each village forms a committee of three men and two women to manage its system. Households pay 10–50 a month into the committee's bank account to cover maintenance after the five-year equipment warranty, and local young people are trained to maintain the equipment.

In November 2024 the organisation began a project with Netcracker Technology and the Imerys group to supply solar and hydroelectric power to three Katkari villages, starting at Velvani. [ref: Mission Urja: TREEI Foundation's Green Power Initiative Reaches Underserved Villages, The Bridge Chronicle] The Better India reported in October 2025 that the programme had reached 945 households. [ref: Diwali Special: How 7 Indians Are Lighting Up Villages Across India With Solar, The Better India] The Marathi daily Sakal covered the programme in March 2026. [ref: Mission Urja Project: दुर्गम आदिवासी पाड्यांत सौरऊर्जेचा उजेड, Sakal] The organisation reported 41 villages and 1,398 households electrified, with 1,432 kW installed, as of 2026. [ref: Our Programs, TREE Innovative Foundation]

=== Hill forts ===
In April 2025 the organisation announced plans to light hill forts in Pune district that are not maintained by the state, starting with Tikona and Ghangad. The plan included solar street lights, floodlights, solar-powered CCTV cameras with footage shared with local police, and mobile charging points for trekkers. The organisation lists Tikona and Sudhagad as completed, with work under way at about ten other forts. [ref: Mission URJA: Fort Edition, TREE Innovative Foundation] In October 2026 Marathi newspapers reported that solar lighting and eight CCTV cameras had been installed at Asherigad. [ref: अशेरी गडावर सौर दिव्यांचा प्रकाश: सुरक्षेलाही बळकटी; आठ सीसीटीव्ही कॅमेऱ्यांची नजर, Sakal] [ref: अशेरी गडाच्या संरक्षणासाठी सोलर सीसीटीव्ही आणि एलईडी दिव्यांची सुविधा, Dainik Bhaskar]

=== Education ===
Program Dhruv, started in 2020, runs life-skills, counselling and career sessions for students in classes 5 to 12. According to the organisation, it works in about 80 government and rural schools in Mulshi, Maval, Purandar and Baramati talukas and in Pune city. [ref: Program DHRUV, TREE Innovative Foundation]

=== Women's livelihoods and health ===
Project Eklavya supports women-led small businesses in food processing and crafts. A production unit at Velhe, near Pune, was set up with support from Persistent Foundation; according to Persistent Foundation's 2023–24 annual report, the unit had 55 members and recorded a turnover of 18.94 lakh that year. [ref: 15th Annual Report 2023–24, Persistent Foundation] The same report describes a nutrition project addressing anaemia among women using locally made food. Project Garima provides counselling and support for women.

Draft: Triton (programming language)

Draft text:
Triton is an open-source domain-specific language and compiler for writing compute kernels for graphics processing units (GPUs). Triton is widely adopted in deep learning frameworks because of its portability and accessibility, including by notable LLM frameworks such as vLLM.

Kernels are written as decorated Python functions that operate on blocks ("tiles") of data, and it differs from lower level languages like CUDA in that much of the scheduling within a block is handled automatically.

Triton began as the doctoral research of Philippe Tillet at Harvard University and was further developed at OpenAI, which released version 1.0 in 2021. It is now the default GPU code-generation target for PyTorch's torch.compile. and the subject of a book by Harshwardhan Fartale, published by Manning.

Triton supports Nvidia and AMD GPUs, [ref: triton-lang/triton: Compatibility, GitHub] and Intel maintains an out-of-tree backend for its own GPUs. [ref: Learn How to Build and Run the Open Source OpenAI Triton Backend for Intel GPUs, Intel Developer]

== Example ==

The code below illustrates how a softmax kernel could be written in Triton.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def softmax_kernel(out_ptr, in_ptr, in_stride, out_stride, n_cols,
BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
row = tl.program_id(0)
cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
mask = cols torch.Tensor:
n_rows, n_cols = x.shape
out = torch.empty_like(x)
BLOCK = triton.next_power_of_2(n_cols)
softmax_kernel[(n_rows,)](out, x, x.stride(0), out.stride(0), n_cols,
BLOCK=BLOCK)
return out

Writing the kernel this way produces a single GPU kernel that computes the maximum, exponentials, sum and division in one pass, reading the input from memory once. A naive PyTorch implementation built from separate tensor operations launches each step as its own kernel, reading and writing intermediate results to memory between them. [ref: Fused Softmax, Triton documentation] In practice, PyTorch's built-in torch.softmax avoids this by calling a dedicated hand-written CUDA kernel. [ref: aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/SoftMax.cu, GitHub]

In CUDA, a row-wise softmax requires explicit synchronisation between the threads that cooperatively compute each row's maximum and sum; in Triton the compiler handles the synchronisation and shared-memory management.

== References ==

Manju Shivraj Singh (also published as Manju Kumari Singh) was an Indian cookery writer. She was the author of The Spice Box (1981), Royal Indian Cookery: A Taste of Palace Life (1987) and Shaakaahaari: Indian Vegetarian Cookery (1997).

== Early life ==
In 1964 she married Shiv Raj Singh, an entomologist then at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute; his career took the family to Ibadan, Nigeria, where he worked at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture from 1973 to 1990, to Ithaca, New York in 1979–80, and to Washington, D.C., where he joined the World Bank in 1991. [ref: Shiv Raj Singh, Prabook]

== Writing ==
Her first book, The Spice Box: Vegetarian Indian Cookbook, was published by the Crossing Press of Trumansburg, New York, in 1981. [ref: The Spice Box: Vegetarian Indian Cookbook, Crossing Press]

Royal Indian Cookery: A Taste of Palace Life followed in 1987, published by Windward in Britain and McGraw-Hill in the United States. [ref: Royal Indian Cookery: A Taste of Palace Life, Windward] [ref: Royal Indian Cookery: A Taste of Palace Life, McGraw-Hill] It was reissued in India by Zaika, Mumbai, in 2002. [ref: Royal Indian Cookery: A Taste of Palace Life, Zaika]

Writing as Manju Kumari Singh, she published Shaakaahaari: Indian Vegetarian Cookery with HarperCollins India in 1997, [ref: Shaakaahaari: Indian Vegetarian Cookery, HarperCollins Publishers India] and Vegetarian Indian Cooking with India Research Press, New Delhi, in 2002. [ref: Vegetarian Indian Cooking, India Research Press]

== Death ==
Manju Shivraj Singh died in 2020. Her husband survived her and died in Jaipur on 13 December 2022. [ref: Obituary: Dr. Shivraj Singh, The Times of India]

== Club Career ==

Vishnu Govindhan (also credited as Vishnu Govindan) is an Indian actor and film director known for his work in the Malayalam film industry. He is popularly known among Malayalam film audiences by the nickname "Jomy", after a supporting character he played in the 2017 film Oru Mexican Aparatha. [ref: History of Jomy, Deccan Chronicle] [ref: Director Vinayan's son Vishnu Vinay turns an actor; Oru Mexican Aparatha fame Vishnu Govindan to direct the movie, Onlookers Media]

== Early life ==
Govindhan is from Kottayam, Kerala. He moved to Kochi to pursue a B.Tech degree at the Cochin University of Science and Technology (CUSAT), a move that exposed him to the theatre and film community in the city and set him on the path toward acting, assistant direction, and later filmmaking.

== Career ==

=== Theatre and early film work ===
Before entering films, Govindhan worked as a theatre artiste in Kochi. He later worked as an assistant to filmmaker Tom Emmatty, having first met him during the making of Lord Livingstone 7000 Kandi, in which Govindhan had a small role. He went on to work with Emmatty on advertising films and later assisted him during the writing of Oru Mexican Aparatha. He had earlier had a minor acting role in Amal Neerad's Iyobinte Pusthakam.

=== Acting ===
Govindhan gained wider recognition for playing "Jomy" — a supporting, comic-relief role as the friend of the lead character — in Oru Mexican Aparatha (2017), starring Tovino Thomas. The role gave him his popular nickname.

=== Direction ===
Govindhan made his directorial debut with History of Joy (2017), a Malayalam coming-of-age drama produced under the banner of Sivaparvathi Films. He also co-wrote the film's story with Anoop P. [ref: Songs of 'History Of Joy', starring director Vinayan's son Vishnu Vinay, released, Onmanorama] The film starred Vishnu Vinay — son of director Vinayan — in his acting debut, alongside Vinay Forrt, Sai Kumar and Joju George. [ref: 'History of Joy' review: a take on second chances, Onmanorama] In its review, Onmanorama described the film as centring on a former convict's attempts to move past his history, and called Govindhan's work "commendable" for a directorial debut.

Draft text:
Linda Mwananchi is a Kenyan political movement established in 2026. The movement has been associated with opposition politics in Kenya and has participated in political mobilization and civic engagement activities ahead of the 2027 general election. In 2026, the movement adopted The Equitable Party as its political party vehicle and initiated a rebranding process under the name Linda Mwananchi. [ref: Political parties registrar approves Linda Mwananchi Movement Party name change - Breaking Kenya News] [ref: The Equitable Party to Rebrand to Linda Mwananchi Movement, Sifuna Confirms - Kenyans.co.ke, www.kenyans.co.ke]

== History ==

Linda Mwananchi emerged in 2026 amid political realignments within Kenya's opposition. The movement has been associated with Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, who has participated in its public activities and political engagements. [ref: Linda Mwananchi endorses Sifuna as 2027 presidential candidate, The Standard]
In September 2026, the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal issued a ruling concerning matters related to the movement's registration following a dispute involving the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties. [ref: ‘Linda Mwananchi movement’ name row heads to political parties tribunal, Citizen Digital]

== Activities ==

The movement advocates for citizen participation in governance, constitutionalism, accountability, and public involvement in democratic processes.

Linda Mwananchi has organized political rallies, public forums, and civic engagement events in different parts of Kenya. Its activities have focused on issues relating to governance, leadership, and preparations for the 2027 Kenyan general election.

Politicians associated with the movement have included Babu Owino, James Orengo, George Natembeya, and Bonny Khalwale. [ref: Linda Mwananchi group settles on Sifuna as its 2027 presidential candidate, Citizen Digital]

== Organization ==

The movement's activities have involved a combination of elected political leaders, party officials, and youth representatives. [ref: From broad-based to united opposition: How young women are shaping the 2027 General Election, Daily Nation] Media reports have identified Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna as one of the principal figures associated with the movement's public activities, alongside other politicians who have participated in its rallies and civic engagement programmes.

The movement has also incorporated youth representatives into its organizational structure. According to media reports, these representatives have participated in public outreach, civic education initiatives, and communication activities carried out under the Linda Mwananchi banner. [ref: Sifuna Picks Pauline Njoroge, Three Women For Linda Mwananchi Communication Team]

As of 2026, the movement's organizational structure continued to evolve alongside efforts to establish itself as a political organization ahead of the 2027 Kenyan general election. [ref: Linda Mwananchi endorses Sifuna as 2027 presidential candidate, The Eastleigh Voice]

== Reception ==

Linda Mwananchi has received media coverage in discussions concerning opposition politics, youth participation in governance, and political developments ahead of the 2027 general election. [ref: Linda Mwananchi leaders now prioritise individual interests ahead of 2027 elections, Daily Nation]

Draft text:
Netchex is an American human capital management and payroll software company headquartered in Covington, Louisiana. Founded in 2003 in Mandeville, Louisiana, by Will Boudreaux and Stuart Ethridge, the company provides cloud-based payroll processing, human resources administration, benefits management, time and attendance tracking, and recruiting services, primarily to employers with hourly and frontline workforces.

The company operated without outside investment until 2016, when it received a growth investment from Primus Capital. In June 2023, Netchex was acquired by the New York–based private equity firm GrowthCurve Capital, at which point it reported annual revenue of more than US$50 million, over 6,400 clients, and approximately 340 employees.

== History ==

=== Founding and early years ===
Boudreaux and Ethridge were roommates at Louisiana State University and later worked together for about twelve years in payroll and financial outsourcing at ADP. Following the collapse of the dot-com bubble, they founded Netchex in Mandeville in 2003 to offer payroll services over the web, financing the business with personal savings and a loan from the U.S. Small Business Administration. Boudreaux later said the two spent the early years "knocking on doors" along the Gulf Coast and bootstrapped the company for its first thirteen years before taking outside capital.

The company recorded first-year sales of between $600,000 and $700,000 against an initial target of $250,000. It concentrated on mid-market employers in sectors with large hourly workforces—restaurants, hotels, retailers, healthcare practices and automotive dealerships—which the founders considered underserved by payroll providers designed for corporate finance departments.

Netchex appeared on the Inc. 5000 list of fast-growing private companies in 2010 and 2016, and was included in the inaugural NOLA100 list in 2015 and in several editions of the LSU 100 list of fastest-growing businesses led by LSU graduates.

=== Louisiana expansion ===
In June 2015, Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal and Boudreaux announced a US$5.3 million expansion of the company's headquarters, supported by an incentive package from Louisiana Economic Development. The plan called for leasing 30,000 square feet of office space, retaining 86 existing jobs and creating 240 new positions at an average salary of $43,800 in St. Tammany Parish. Louisiana was selected over competing sites in Texas and Florida.

At the time, Netchex employed about 120 people, served more than 3,000 clients, and maintained offices in Dallas, Atlanta and Jackson, Mississippi. By 2016 the company reported annual revenue of about $14 million and 115 employees. The expansion took the company from its original offices on North Causeway Boulevard in Mandeville to a larger facility on U.S. Highway 190 in Covington, which remains its headquarters.

=== Primus Capital investment ===
In March 2016, Primus Capital, a private equity firm based in Cleveland, made a growth investment in Netchex for an undisclosed amount. The company then served more than 2,500 employers, concentrated in the southeastern United States.

=== Acquisition by GrowthCurve Capital ===
In June 2023, GrowthCurve Capital acquired a majority stake in Netchex from Primus Capital. Terms were not disclosed. Netchex reported annual revenue exceeding $50 million, more than 6,400 clients and approximately 340 employees, of whom about 200 worked at the Covington office. Boudreaux and Ethridge each retained an ownership stake and remained in executive roles.

=== Leadership ===
In September 2024, Boudreaux stepped down as chief executive after twenty-one years and joined the company's board of directors. He was succeeded by David Giannetto, previously chief executive of WorkWave. According to the company, Abhinav Agrawal, who had joined Netchex in 2023 as chief product and technology officer, became chief executive officer in 2025.

As of 2025 the company employed about 375 people, roughly 200 of them in the New Orleans metropolitan area, and reported serving more than 7,300 customers across all fifty states.

=== Mesh.ai acquisition and AI products ===
In 2025, Netchex acquired Mesh.ai, a Y Combinator-backed startup founded in 2020 that developed artificial-intelligence tools for performance management and employee engagement. Mesh.ai co-founder Saurabh Nangia joined Netchex as chief product officer.

In July 2026, Netchex launched Mesh, a set of six artificial intelligence assistants built on that technology and aimed at employers with deskless workforces. The company said the assistants identify issues such as missing timecards, expiring certifications and payroll discrepancies, that human approval is required before sensitive actions are completed, and that employees can access the platform through ChatGPT and Claude.

== Products and services ==
Netchex provides a cloud-based platform covering payroll processing and tax filing, human resources administration, benefits enrollment and Affordable Care Act reporting, time and attendance tracking, recruiting and onboarding, learning and performance management, and reporting and analytics. The company holds Nacha certification for ACH payment processing.
[truncated]

Houman Memarpanahi is an Iranian cultural manager, artistic director, and entrepreneur known for founding Emarat RooBeRoo (RooBeRoo Mansion), an independent multidisciplinary art center in Tehran. [ref: "Opening of RooBeRoo Mansion," Iran Theater. https://theater.ir/fa/73077] [ref: "Rooberoo Mansion Profile," Top Ten Tehran. https://toptenteh.com/art-galleries/item/592] As a cultural producer, he has been instrumental in bringing international neoclassical and contemporary musicians to Iran, facilitating major performances in Tehran and Shiraz.

== Career and Emarat RooBeRoo ==
In December 2016, Memarpanahi established Emarat RooBeRoo in a historic building near Tehran's Vali-e-Asr district. The center operates as a private cultural institution featuring a theater platform, art gallery, bookstore, and café. [ref: "Interview with Houman Memarpanahi," Tiwall. https://www.tiwall.com/theater/podcasts/interview.homanmemarpanahi] He later expanded the brand by opening a second branch in the Tajrish neighborhood of northern Tehran.

Memarpanahi has been a vocal advocate for the economic sustainability of private cultural institutions in Iran, discussing these challenges in national publications such as Arman Meli. [ref: "Economic Challenges of Art Centers," Arman Meli Newspaper Archive. https://www.pishkhan.com/Archive/1399/07/13990703/ArmanMeli6511411097109485551117351.pdf]

== International Concert Productions ==
Under the management of RooBeRoo Mansion, Memarpanahi has produced several high-profile concerts featuring international artists:
* Ólafur Arnalds: Produced the Icelandic composer's first concert in Tehran in December 2017. [ref: "Icelandic composer Ólafur Arnalds to give concert in Tehran," Tehran Times, 2017. https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/418995/]
* Evgeny Grinko: Managed the Russian pianist’s performance in Tehran in 2019. [ref: "Russian pianist Evgeny Grinko to give concert in Tehran," Tehran Times, 2019. https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/437040/]
* Sebastian Plano: Produced the "In Between Worlds" concert series featuring the Argentinian cellist and composer in Tehran. [ref: "In Between Worlds: Sebastian Plano’s sweet melancholic melodies," Tehran Times, 2019. https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/433876/]
* Federico Albanese: Organized the Italian pianist's performance of "The Blue Hour" in Shiraz & Tehran. [ref: "Albanese to perform Blue Hour in Shiraz," Tehran Times, 2018. https://www.tehrantimes.com/news/430243/]

== International Presence ==
In May 2017, Memarpanahi facilitated the "Theatricultural Exchange Program" in partnership with the Bohemi Theater Group, hosting international artists during the Iran International University Theater Festival. [ref: "Theatricultural Exchange Program Call," TINFO Finland. https://www.tinfo.fi/documents/tep_b.pdf] [ref: "Theatre/Cultural Exchange Program Document," Honar Online. https://cdn.honaronline.ir/servev2/eRX8BClkWnYH/1N9tRJb2yc-LeZ7lU0QoYEbuZiAZ2lKb2CkizeDhtRY,/theatricultural+exchange-2.pdf]

In May 2023, he represented RooBeRoo Mansion at the Volksbühne in Berlin during the "Artistic Work in Exile" panel, a side event of the Theatertreffen festival. [ref: "Auch das Publikum braucht einen Zugang," Theatertreffen-Blog, 2023. https://theatertreffen-blog.de/blog/auch-das-publikوم-braucht-einen-zugang/]

== Legal Issues ==
As a director of an independent cultural space, Memarpanahi has faced several regulatory challenges. In March 2025 (Esfand 1403), he was detained by security forces following a musical performance at RooBeRoo Mansion. [ref: "Detention of RooBeRoo Mansion Director," Iran International, March 2025. https://www.iranintl.com/fa/202503014357] [ref: "News of detention of Houman Memarpanahi," Balatarin. https://www.balatarin.com/permlink/2025/3/1/6306112] His subsequent release on bail was reported by outlets such as Shargh Daily and Aasoo. [ref: "Director of RooBeRoo Mansion Released," Shargh Daily, 2025. https://www.sharghdaily.com/fa/tiny/news-979879] [ref: "Independent Cultural Spaces and Recent Pressures," Aasoo. https://www.aasoo.org/fa/articles/5104]

Saleh Hasaballah (Arabic: صالح حسب الله) is an Egyptian lawyer at the Court of Cassation and writer. He is a member of the Egyptian Writers Union and the founder of the Egyptian Sports Lawyers Association.

== Career ==
Hasaballah practices law before the Egyptian Court of Cassation and the Supreme Constitutional Court. He is a member of the Egyptian Writers Union and has authored works in the legal field.

He founded the Egyptian Sports Lawyers Association (رابطة المحامين الرياضيين) in Egypt to promote sports activities among lawyers and to provide legal support in sports law.

== Legal activism ==
In 2011, following the 25 January Revolution, Hasaballah filed a complaint to Attorney General Abdel Meguid Mahmoud requesting an investigation into former interior ministers who served after the revolution, on suspicion of concealing incriminating evidence related to the killing of demonstrators.

According to Egypt Independent, the Attorney General ordered investigations into Mahmoud Wagdy and Mansour El-Essawy and the head of national security, based on the complaint filed by Hasaballah. [ref: Attorney general orders investigation into former interior ministers, Egypt Independent]

Their vermouth is called "La Fadrina and Lo Fadri" which roughly translates to "The young woman and the young man" in Catalan. Ol' Lonely, or "the lonely repairman", is a character in Maytag advertisements, created in 1967 by copywriter Vincent R. Vassolo of the Leo Burnett advertising agency for Maytag.

==History==
His character was initially played by Jesse White, who retained the role until 1988. [ref: North, Gary, What To Learn From Maytag, LewRockwell.com (2007)] [ref: [http://brandculturetalk.com/2009/01/09/maytags-brand-blunder-a-focus-group-of-one/ Early Maytag Repairman TV Commercial] Maytag's Brand Blunder, BrandCultureTalk.com, 9 January 2009]

In a time in which the laundry appliances of major manufacturers had reached maturity, differing mostly in minor details, the campaign was designed to remind consumers of the perceived added value in Maytag products derived from the brand's reputation for dependability. Maytag advertisements stated “Ol' Lonely’s predicament is testimony to the durability and reliability of Maytag appliances. Now if only he had something to do with his days.” Other ads stated, "Not all Maytag repairmen are this lonely, but we're trying." The campaign proved a huge success, allowing Maytag to set a substantial price premium, as well as strongly influencing consumer preference at the higher end of the laundry appliance market. [ref: Maytag's Brand Blunder, BrandCultureTalk.com, 9 January 2009]

In 1986, the repairman was joined by Newton, a Basset Hound named for Maytag's headquarters in Newton, Iowa. In 1989, after Jesse White retired from acting in 1988, character actor Gordon Jump first appeared as Ol' Lonely in the advertisement "Biker". [ref: Advertising: Been Lonely Too Long, Time] In total, Jump appeared in more than 77 Maytag commercials and print advertisements. He made appearances at events for employees and customers and also was actively involved in several philanthropic and charitable causes.

In January 2001, Maytag shifted the direction of its iconic "Ol' Lonely" campaign by hiring actor Mark Devine (which played the younger repairman known as the "Maytag Apprentice" from 2001 to 2007), while actor Gordon Jump continued playing the iconic senior repairman. [ref: The long-suffering and lonely Maytag repairman will get a new repairman, The New York Times]

Actor Hardy Rawls was hired to play Ol' Lonely after Jump's retirement in July 2003, although he appeared only in print advertising and personal appearances. [ref: Jump Retires as Maytag's 'Lonely' Repairman, ADWEEK] [ref: HE'S THE NEW MAYTAG MAN, New York Post] Gordon Jump died two months later on September 22, 2003. [ref: Gordon Jump, 71, 'WKRP' Actor Who Played Maytag's Repairman, The New York Times] [ref: [http://www.maytag.com/GJbiography.htm] ] In French-speaking Quebec, Ol' Lonely was played by Paul Berval. [ref: Paul Berval – Artisans — Emissions.ca, Archives.emissions.ca] However, in 2005 Maytag cancelled his contract. Maytag also elected not to renew Rawls' contract, instead holding open auditions. Indianapolis Colts backup quarterback Jim Sorgi was among those who auditioned. [ref: Maytag Casting for New 'Ol Lonely, The Washington Post] On April 2, 2007, Maytag announced that Clay Earl Jackson of Richmond, Virginia had been selected to fill the role of Ol' Lonely. [ref: Maytag Introduces New "Lonely" Repairman, CBS News] [ref: A Winning Audition for Maytag Repairman, The New York Times] [ref: Virginia man beats out 1500 for role of Maytag repairman, Sarasota Herald-Tribune]

By the end of the twentieth century, the "Maytag repairman" character had become an iconic metaphor for a professional whose services are rarely needed. Times were changing however, and events at Maytag and within the industry began to diminish the effectiveness of the long-lived Maytag repairman campaign. Consumer demand for innovative, expensive, and increasingly complex electronically controlled and computerized appliances, coupled with higher labor costs and complaints over Maytag product quality and service, influenced a decline in Maytag sales and profit margins. By 2004, the Maytag repairman character had become to some consumers a symbol of misplaced trust in aging marketing campaigns. [ref: Maytag's Brand Blunder (a focus group of one), Brand Culture Company] [ref: Rob Frankel – Branding Expert: The Maytag Repairman Gets Even Lonelier, Robfrankel.blogspot.com] As one commentator noted, "Unfortunately things change, and, after some major quality hiccups, now it's the Maytag salesman who is bemoaning his loneliness. Maytag's reputation has plunged to the bottom with costly consumer class action lawsuits and numerous quality complaints." [ref: Continental Quality Engineering, "The High Cost of Low Quality"; Anderson IA: The Continental Quality Newsletter] As a partial result of Maytag's quality problems, the company reported a loss of $9 million in 2004, according to Industry Week.

In January 2014, Maytag announced a "Generation Five" of the Maytag Repairman, currently played by Colin Ferguson. [ref: Maytag Ads Ditch That Old, Bored Repairman for a Younger Model, Business Week] But instead of commercials showing the repairman waiting around his shop for a Maytag appliance to break, he is playing the part of the actual appliance.
[truncated]

Uri Shanas (born April 16, 1961) is an Israeli professor of zoology and nature conservation Oranim College, and founder and CEO of the international nonprofit conservation organization This Is My Earth (TiME). [ref: Prof. Uri Shanas, Biology and Environment - Oranim campus] [ref: Israeli conservationist launching new platform to save at-risk global hotspots, Jerusalem Post]

== Biography ==
Uri was born in Beersheba, Israel, one of four children of Leib and Shoshana Shanas, environmental activists who initiated the fight against the construction of the nuclear reactor between Ashkelon and Ashdod in the 1970s. [ref: The activists who prevented the construction of a reactor in Nitzanim, Haaretz] [ref: Death Wants to Be Your Neighbor, Davar] His father worked for Mekorot, Israel’s national water company, and therefore, the family moved around the country when Uri was a child. From the age of 16, Uri and his family spent two years in Thailand, where his dad worked for Tahal, helping develop the water supply infrastructure in northeastern Thailand. When they returned to Israel, Uri enlisted in the Nahal, was a member of the Scouts' group that lived on Kibbutz Ketura, and participated in the establishment of Shizafon (now Neot-Smadar). [ref: Against Time: The Israeli Trying to Prevent the Greatest Disaster in History, NRG, Makor Rishon]

Shanas received a bachelor's degree in life sciences [ref: The George S. Wise Faculty of Life Sciences, en-lifesci.tau.ac.il] (1988), a master's degree in zoology (1991) and a doctorate with distinction in zoology (1997), all from Tel Aviv University. [ref: Israeli's crowdfunding effort seeks to save forests by buying a piece of them, The Times of Israel] The master's thesis was on the reproduction of the blind mole rat. [ref: Aspects of reproductive behavior of the mole rat Spalax ehrenbergi.] The doctoral thesis dealt with the morphology, chemistry, and pheromonal properties of the harderian gland of the blind mole rat. [ref: The morphology, chemistry, and pheromonal properties of the Harderian gland of the mole rat.]

In 1998, he did a postdoctoral fellowship at Columbia University and then joined the University of Haifa in 2001. From 2009 to 2013, he was head of the Biology and Environment department at the University of Haifa on the Oranim College campus.

Uri is married with three children and lives in Givat Ada, Israel.

== Environmental activism ==
In 2000, Shanas warned about the environmental impacts of the construction of the Trans-Israel Highway: the fragmentation of habitats, destruction of open spaces, roadkill, damage to vegetation, contamination of groundwater and air pollution. [ref: Amateur planning bordering on criminal negligence!, Green, Blue, and White: The Journal of the Economic and Business Forum for Environmental Quality] He pointed out shortcomings in the environmental-impact assessment phase and emphasized the difficulty of predicting in advance the true impacts of projects of this magnitude, warning that the damage could be irreversible. Shanas submitted a petition to the Supreme Court of Israel against the Trans-Israel Highway Company and the State of Israel in a lawsuit to address road runoff and protect the sources of the Yarkon River and water aquifers.

Shanas co-founded the Green Movement party. Two years later, he led the Green Movement’s submission of a petition to the Supreme Court of Israel demanding that the Turkel Committee reconsider Yoav Galant’s suitability for the position of the Israeli Defense Forces’ chief of staff, due to suspicions of land misappropriation. [ref: Green Movement Chief of Staff: Uri Shaines - the man behind the High Court of Justice Gallant, NRG, Makor Rishon] [ref: ] The Green Movement questioned “who gave Galant the extra 35 dunams [of public open space] and why no one else received it.” [ref: Turkel C'tee refuses to question Galant over land deal, The Jerusalem Post]

In 2011, Shanas was involved in research and the fight to protect the Samar Sands in the southern Arava, an area that is a unique habitat for rare and endemic species. [ref: Head to Head: Spiders Versus Tractors in the Samar Sands, Ynet] He worked to raise awareness of the ecological importance of the site and its biodiversity and warned against the harm caused by sand mining and habitat loss. As part of the conservation efforts, Shanas initiated the purchase of land by Israel Nature and Parks Authority, where he was a board member, to help save the last dunes in the area.

Draft: Mobile application security

Draft text:
Mobile application security (mobile AppSec) is the discipline of protecting mobile apps, the data, and backend services they connect to from reverse engineering, tampering, malware, and runtime attacks across an app's development lifecycle. It sits between two broader fields: application security, which covers building and verifying secure software generally, and mobile security, which covers protecting the device, operating system, and network layers a mobile app runs on. Mobile application security narrows that scope to the app itself. It focuses on the compiled binary sitting on a device the developer does not control, along with the code and secrets packaged inside it.

Standards bodies and industry analysts publish guidance specifically addressing mobile application security, distinguishing it from broader application security and mobile security concerns. The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) maintains "OWASP Mobile Application Security" as a separate dedicated project from its general Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS), on the grounds that mobile apps raise concerns, such as binary exposure and reverse engineering, that its web-focused standards do not fully address. [ref: Introduction to the OWASP Mobile Application Security Project - OWASP Mobile Application Security, mas.owasp.org] Gartner has similarly tracked "mobile application security testing" as a distinct technology category in its [https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/8151129 Hype Cycle for Application Security], along with Application Shielding. The analyst firm has published a dedicated market guide for it, separate from its general application security testing and mobile device management coverage. [ref: Gartner Mobile Application Security Testing Guide, NowSecure]

This distinction matters in practice because a mobile app, unlike a server-side web application, ships an executable copy of itself onto a device that is fully accessible to an attacker. The attacker can install the app, decompile it, attach a debugger, run it on an emulator, or modify and repackage it, without ever touching the developer's own infrastructure. Mobile application security therefore largely focuses on defending against this class of client-side attacks, on top of the concerns it already shares with web and API security, such as insecure data storage, weak authentication, and insufficient transport-layer protection.

== Overview ==

Smartphones are used to access sensitive personal and financial information, including banking and payment services, as well as enterprise systems and data. [ref: Guidelines for Managing the Security of Mobile Devices in the Enterprise, NIST] That has made mobile apps a target. Attackers steal credentials and payment data, extract and run fraud at scale through farmed emulators and automated bots, or take a legitimate app, repackage it with malicious code, and redistribute it. Academic work on mobile malware traced reverse engineering, tampering, and repackaging as recurring attack methods more than a decade ago; [ref: Suarez-Tangil, Guillermo; Tapiador, Juan E.; Peris-Lopez, Pedro; Ribagorda, Arturo (2014). "Evolution, Detection and Analysis of Malware for Smart Devices". IEEE Communications Surveys & Tutorials. 16 (2): 961–987.] mobile app security vendors have continued to report the same categories, along with API exploitation, as ongoing attack vectors. [ref: ]

Mobile application security is usually treated as spanning the entire software development life cycle, from secure design and coding through automated testing in continuous integration pipelines to hardening release binaries and monitoring apps once they reach stores such as the Google Play Store and the Apple App Store. Once an app is published, the developer has limited visibility into how it is used or attacked after it leaves the build pipeline, unless the app is built to report threat telemetry back.

== Why mobile apps require dedicated security practices ==

Several properties of the mobile environment set app security apart from traditional web or server application security.

* The client is untrusted and physically exposed. A mobile app binary can run on a device the attacker controls, so decompilers, disassemblers, and static analysis tools can be pointed directly at the compiled code. An attacker can read an app's logic, extract embedded API keys and cryptographic material from the binary, and reverse-engineer its business logic without ever touching a server.

* The binary itself can be patched and redistributed. Because the application binary is under the attacker's control, the app can be repackaged and republished under a different name, for example, to strip out license checks, bypass in-app purchases, inject malware, or intercept and alter data before it reaches the server. Academic literature has documented repackaging and cloning Android apps as a distinct malware-distribution route. [ref: Crussell, Johnathan; Gibler, Clint; Chen, Hao (2012). "Attack of the Clones: Detecting Cloned Applications on Android Markets". University of California, Davis. http://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~hchen/paper/esorics2012.pdf]

* The runtime environment is hostile by design. On a rooted or jailbroken device, or inside an emulator, debugger, or dynamic instrumentation framework, an attacker can watch and modify an app's behavior while it runs, even where the code itself resists static analysis.
