Draft: Ó Maol Phádraig

Draft text:
----

Ó Maol Phádraig is a historical Irish Gaelic surname, also recorded in anglicised forms including O'Mulpatrick, Mulpatrick and O Molpatrick. The name derives from the Irish personal name Maol Phádraig, meaning a devotee or servant of Saint Patrick, with the prefix Ó indicating descent.

The surname was historically associated particularly with Counties Cavan and Cork. Patrick Woulfe, in his 1923 work Irish Names and Surnames, described Ó Maolphádraig as formerly common in both counties and recorded Conor O Molpatrick as chief of his name in County Cavan in 1602. [ref: Irish Names and Surnames, M. H. Gill & Son]

Ó Maol Phádraig is distinct from Mac Giolla Phádraig, another Irish surname traditionally associated with Ossory in Counties Kilkenny and Laois. Both Gaelic surnames have been associated with the anglicised surname Fitzpatrick.

== Medieval references ==

A medieval reference to a kindred bearing a related name appears in the topographical poem attributed to John Ó Dubhagáin (died 1372). The poem identifies Teallach Maoilpatraig among the kindreds of Cenél Fearadhaigh, a branch of Cenél nEógain associated with the Clogher region of County Tyrone. [ref: The Topographical Poems of John O'Dubhagain and Giolla na Naomh O'Huidhrin, Irish Archaeological and Celtic Society]

The reference provides evidence of the use of the personal name Maol Phádraig in a medieval kindred designation. It does not, by itself, establish the ancestry of all later families recorded under the surname Ó Maol Robert Ó Maol Phádraig (1306)

== The Book of Fenagh and Cenél Luacháin ==

The Book of Fenagh preserves medieval genealogical, ecclesiastical and territorial traditions associated with the monastery of St Caillín at Fenagh in County Leitrim. The surviving compilation was prepared in 1516 by Muirgheas Ó Maolchonaire for Tadhg Ó Rodaighe, drawing upon earlier manuscript materials. It includes genealogies relating to the descendants of Conmhac and the families of the Breifne region. [ref: The Book of Fenagh in Irish and English, Alexander Thom]

Genealogical traditions associated with Cenél Luacháin identify Máel Pátraic, son of Maolgeann, as the ancestor from whom the Uí Maelpatraig took their name. Related material identifies Máelmochéirghe as the eponymous ancestor of Muintir Maelmochéirghe. These notices have been examined in connection with the medieval families Ó Maol Phádraig and Ó Maolmochéirghe.

The genealogies provide evidence of traditions concerning the origins and affiliations of these families. They do not independently establish the literal descent of every later bearer of the surnames, and the precise relationship between the surviving Fenagh material and the genealogies preserved by Dubhaltach Mac Fhirbhisigh requires further examination.

== Rathmulpatrick, County Sligo ==

Rathmulpatrick (Irish: Ráth Mhaolphádraig) is a townland in the civil parish of Kilmacallan, barony of Tirerrill, County Sligo. The Placenames Database of Ireland identifies its Irish name and explains the placename as referring to the ringfort of a person named Maolphádraig. The name contains the same Gaelic personal name from which the surname Ó Maol Phádraig was formed. [ref: Ráth Mhaolphádraig/Rathmulpatrick, Logainm.ie]

The placename is documented in early modern records. The Placenames Database records Rathmulpatricke in the Irish Patent Rolls of James I in 1617, Rathmolpatricke in estate rentals of 1633–1636, and Rath mullpatrick on the Down Survey maps of 1655–1657. In 1836, the Ordnance Survey parish namebooks recorded the Irish form Rath Mhaoil Patraic, interpreted as Mulpatrick's fort, and noted the existence of two ancient forts within the townland. [ref: Ráth Mhaolphádraig/Rathmulpatrick, Logainm.ie]

The archaeological inventory for County Sligo records two ringforts within Rathmulpatrick, numbered SL027-156 and SL027-159. Both are classified as ringforts (raths or cashels) in the published Record of Monuments and Places. [ref: Record of Monuments and Places: County Sligo, Sheet 27, National Monuments Service]

Although the placename and archaeological remains demonstrate the presence of an older settlement landscape associated with the personal name Maolphádraig, they do not establish that the townland was the original seat of the hereditary Ó Maol Phádraig surname or identify the families who occupied its ringforts.

== Robert Molpatrik (1306) ==

One of the earliest identified documentary references to an individual bearing the surname occurs in the Calendar of the Justiciary Rolls of Ireland for 1306. A man recorded as Robert Molpatrik, and elsewhere in the proceedings as Robert Omolpatrik, was among the jurors summoned in County Cork in a legal dispute involving Eustace le Poer and Philip de Barry.

The summoned jurors failed to appear, and subsequent proceedings identify Robert in connection with securing the attendance of Henry, son of Philip. The record places Robert within the administration of royal justice in medieval County Cork, where Gaelic and Anglo-Norman individuals participated in the same legal institutions. [ref: Calendar of the Justiciary Rolls of Ireland, 1305–1307, His Majesty's Stationery Office]

The proceedings do not identify Robert's residence, occupation or family relationships. No direct genealogical connection between Robert and the later Ó Maol Phádraig clerics at St Michael's Mount has been established.
[truncated]

Draft text:
----

Ajay B. Harish is a British-Indian computational engineer and Associate Professor in Computational Mechanics at the University of Manchester. His research aims at the development of numerical methods for computational mechanics, with applications in biomechanics and biomedical engineering. [ref: Ajay Harish, Research Explorer]

==Early life and education==
Harish graduated with a B.Tech in mechanical engineering from the National Institute of Technology Karnataka in 2007. He subsequently undertook masters' study in aeronautics at the California Institute of Technology and completed an engineer's thesis titled "simulation of dynamic interface fracture using a spectral boundary integral method", supervised by Nadia Lapusta in 2009. [ref: Simulation of Dynamic Interface Fracture Using Spectral Boundary Integral Method, CaltechTHESIS]. Subsequently he received a Dr.-Ing. from Leibniz University Hannover in 2018 under the supervision of Peter Wriggers. [ref: Micromechanics, fracture and contact behavior of nanoparticle reinforced polymers, Leibniz University Hannover Research Portal]. Harish was a group leader in Nanotribology at the Institute of Continuum Mechanics in Leibniz University Hannover between 2018-20. He joined the University of California, Berkeley in 2020 as a postdoctoral researcher with NHERI SimCenter. In 2022, he joined the University of Manchester as a lecturer in engineering simulation and data science and was later promoted to senior lecturer in 2025. Since Sep-2025, he serves as the Discipline Head of Education (Aerospace) / Deputy Head of Department (Mechanical & Aerospace engineering) at Manchester.

==Research and career==
Harish's work has spanned the development of numerical methods for modelling of tendon structures, abdominal aortic aneurysms and haemodynamics of the carotid.

== Recognition ==
Harish ss a recipient of a Ramanujan Fellowship in 2022 [ref: Ramanujan Fellowship, Research Explorer] and the UK-Italy Turing award by the Alan Turing Institute in 2024.

Shai Diego Hope (born 10 November 1993) is a Barbadian cricketer who has played for the West Indies cricket team. A right-handed batsman and wicket-keeper, he has scored 28 centuries in international cricket: 5 in Test cricket, 21 in One Day International (ODI) cricket and 2 in Twenty20 International (T20I) cricket.

Hope made his Test debut against England on 1 May 2015 at Kensington Oval in Bridgetown, Barbados. [ref: Shai Hope, International Cricket Council] He scored his maiden Test century during the 2017 tour of England, making 147 and an unbeaten 118 in the second Test at Headingley. [ref: Brathwaite, Hope reach career-best rankings, International Cricket Council] His two centuries made him the first batsman to score a century in each innings of a first-class match at Headingley. The West Indies won the match by five wickets after successfully chasing 322. [ref: Windies Test match defeat 'fresh in the minds' of England players - Trevor Bayliss, International Cricket Council] His highest Test score is 147.

Hope made his ODI debut against Sri Lanka in November 2016. [ref: 'If I had to open the bowling for West Indies, I'd do it' – Shai Hope, International Cricket Council] He scored his maiden ODI century against Zimbabwe in Bulawayo, scoring 101. [ref: Shai Hope, International Cricket Council] His highest ODI score is an unbeaten 170, which he scored against Ireland in 2019. [ref: Hope could be 'one of our best ODI players ever' – Jason Holder, International Cricket Council] In August 2022, Hope scored a century in his 100th ODI against India, becoming the tenth West Indies player to score a century in his 100th ODI. [ref: Axar keeps his cool to guide India to series-clinching victory, International Cricket Council] In February 2023, he was appointed captain of the West Indies ODI team. [ref: West Indies announce Pooran's replacements as ODI and T20I captain, International Cricket Council]

Draft text:
Hurricane Trudy is an active hurricane west of Mexico. It is the twenty-first named storm, twelfth hurricane, and tenth major hurricane of the 2026 Pacific hurricane season.

==Meteorological history ==

On October 6, at 06:00 UTC, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) stated a tropical wave entered the East Pacific south of Guatemala, and started monitoring it for development in the next 7 days. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/xgtwo/gtwo_archive.php?basin=epac&fdays=7¤t_issuance=202610060600] On October 12, the NHC noted the disturbance gained a surface low and stated it had a very high chance of development. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/xgtwo/gtwo_archive.php?basin=epac&fdays=7¤t_issuance=202610120600] The next day, at 15:00 UTC, the NHC upgraded the low pressure area to a tropical depression, designating it as Twenty One-E. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.001.shtml]Six hours later, the depression intensified into a tropical storm and was given the name Trudy. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.002.shtml] By October 14, Trudy had been upgraded to Category 1, and rapidly strengthened to Category 3 the next day, with it expected to further strengthen into a Category 4. [ref: Hurricane Trudy approaches Mexico’s coast: What you need to know about its path, El Cronista]

However, the eye started to decay and it was no longer visible around 18:35 UTC. At the same time The Hurricane Hunters flew into the storm, and noticed that Trudy rapidly weakened below major hurricane strength. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.update.10161833.shtml] [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.014.shtml]

== Preparations ==
On October 15, The National Hurricane Center issued Tropical Storm Watches for southern Mexico. [ref: Hurricane Trudy strengthens; warnings issued along Pacific Coast, nj] The next day they were upgraded into Hurricane Warnings, with tropical storm watches and warnings being issued for additional areas around the coast. [ref: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2026/ep21/ep212026.public.013.shtml]

Draft text:
The Glen Burn Colliery, known earlier as the Cameron Colliery and originally as the Gap mines, was an anthracite coal mine and breaker on the western edge of Shamokin, in Coal Township, Northumberland County, Pennsylvania. It lay in the Western Middle Anthracite Field. Coal was first mined in the Shamokin Creek water gap in the 1830s. Over the next century and a half the workings passed through a series of lessees, companies tied to the Pennsylvania Railroad, the Susquehanna coal companies and, from 1966, Kerris and Helfrick. The breaker shut down during a strike in 1984 and was demolished after the operation was liquidated in 1986. The colliery's culm bank still towers over Shamokin, and water from the old workings still drains into Shamokin Creek.

==History==
===Gap mines===
The first mines in the gap were opened in the late 1830s. On the east side, the landowners Dewart & Donnel drove several drifts beside the railroad and leased them to Yoxtheimer & Snyder of Sunbury, who failed after about a year. J. H. Purdy & Company began mining the west side at about the same time; their workings were later joined to those on the east side as part of the Cameron Colliery. The gap mines were among the four operations that shipped coal from the Shamokin district in 1839.

Fagely, Cleaver & Company took over the east-side mines in 1841. The partners, William and Reuben Fagely, Kimber Cleaver and William H. Kase, opened the Tape, or Skidmore, vein and soon became the district's leading shippers. The News-Item reports that William Cameron, a justice of the peace with experience building canals, tunnels, bridges and railroads, acquired the Gap mine in June 1841. In July 1855 the lessees, Kase, Reed & Company, sold their interest to Zimmerman & Pursell. The colliery's first breaker was built in 1857, a year in which Zimmerman & Pursell's "Lower Gap" shipped 14,887 tons.

===Cameron Colliery===
Haas & Bowen, who were already operating at Locust Gap, leased the Lower Gap in April 1862 and renamed it the Cameron Colliery. They sank a slope there, one of the first in the region. One archival record dates the name change to 1864 and says the colliery was named after William Cameron.

The colliery later passed to the Mineral Railroad and Mining Company, a Pennsylvania Railroad affiliate. Work on a new breaker began late in 1887 and was finished in January 1888, but the building burned that October. Its replacement, completed early in 1889, was described as "one of the largest and most complete structures in the State". That year the colliery shipped 101,418 tons.

Fire struck again in February 1890, this time in the gangway of the No. 1 slope, below the surface. The blaze was reportedly started by a miner's lamp and killed more than twenty mules. After weeks of firefighting, the company turned Shamokin Creek into the mine. By the officials' count, about a billion gallons of water flowed in over six days, eight hours and thirty minutes to fill workings that held more than of underground railroad. Pumping began in May, and the mine was dry again by November 2.

Another fire broke out on February 28, 1904, in the pump house on the second level of the No. 7 vein. Officials of the Mineral Railroad and Mining Company and the Susquehanna Coal Company closed off the area and smothered the fire with steam at for a full day, then spent three weeks putting out what was left with hoses. It was finally out on March 21.

The state mine inspectors' annual reports trace the mine's continued development. In 1910 a tunnel was driven from the No. 6 vein to the No. 1 Lykens Valley vein. In 1913 the company put up a concrete-block bathhouse,, with lockers and hot and cold showers, along with a reinforced-concrete emergency hospital for injured workers. In 1917 the No. 7 slope was extended and new jigs were installed in the breaker.

Cameron was one of seven Susquehanna Coal Company collieries in Northumberland County. Much of the company's stock was owned by the Pennsylvania Railroad and the Pennsylvania Canal Company, and the Pennsylvania State Archives call Cameron "one of the most famous mines in the Western Middle Coal Field". Bell's 1891 county history said much the same, calling it "one of the most famous collieries in the State". In 1917 the Susquehanna Coal Company transferred its mines to the Susquehanna Collieries Company, which was operating Cameron that year.

===Glen Burn===
The colliery's last breaker went up in 1939. In 1940 the colliery was renamed Glen Burn. Three miners were killed in an explosives detonation there on February 26, 1964.

Kerris and Helfrick, a Shamokin-area firm owned by Robert Kerris and Edward W. Helfrick, bought the colliery from the Susquehanna Coal Company on June 30, 1966. Working with the Lower Anthracite Regional Economic Development Organization (LAREDO), the new owners opened the mine to visitors on June 22, 1968. Tours ran on weekends and holidays, when the mine was idle, and were promoted as the world's first tour of a working anthracite mine. They continued until 1976.

Hugh Donald Clout (born 29 April 1944) is a British historical and rural geographer and emeritus professor of geography at University College London (UCL). His research focuses on the historical geography of France [ref: Book review essays: French historical geography: de Planhol, X. editor, 1978: Etudes de géographie historique. Bulletin de la Section de Géographie, Comité des Travaux Historiques et Scientifiques 82 (années 1975-77), 7-203. Paris: Bibliothèque Nationale. 203 pp. FF 90, Progress in Human Geography], rural landscapes [ref: An Overview of the Fluctuating Fortunes of Viticulture in England and Wales, EchoGéo] and regional development, postwar reconstruction, and the history of geographical scholarship. [ref: Hugh Clout, After the Ruins: Restoring the Countryside of Northern France After the Great War, Material Culture Review] He is an Emeritus Fellow of the British Academy [ref: Professor Hugh Clout FBA, The British Academy], a Fellow of University College London [ref: Hugh Clout, UCL Faculty of Social & Historical Sciences], and the Academia Europaea. [ref: ]

== Education and Career ==
He earned a BA, MPhil and PhD from University College London, a Doctorat from the Université Paris I, and a DLit from the University of London. Sorbonne University later awarded him an honorary doctorate. [ref: Sorbonne University honours eight outstanding achievers, Sorbonne Université]

Clout joined University College London's Department of Geography as a lecturer in 1967 [ref: Academy of Europe: Clout Hugh, www.ae-info.org] and later became professor of geography. He introduced rural geography teaching at UCL in the late 1960s and served as Dean of Social and Historical Sciences from 1995 to 2004. He was elected a Fellow of the British Academy in 1997 and a Fellow of UCL in 2008. In 2005, he shared the Newbigin Prize of the Royal Scottish Geographical Society with Iain Stevenson. [ref: Newbigin Prize, The Royal Scottish Geographical Society]

== Research and scholarly work ==
Clout's research has focused on rural and historical geography, particularly France and Western Europe. His books include Agriculture in France on the Eve of the Railway Age (1980) [ref: H. D. Clout. Agriculture in France on the Eve of the Railway Age, Norois], The Land of France, 1815–1914 (1983) [ref: Book Review: The Land of France 1815–1914, Progress in Human Geography] and After the Ruins: Restoring the Countryside of Northern France after the Great War (1996), which examined agricultural change and postwar reconstruction. [ref: Reconstitution des paysages dévastés par la Grande Guerre: H. Clout, After the ruins. Restoring the Countryside of Northern France after the Great War, Annales de géographie]

He has also written on French geographers, the history of geographical thought and the development of geography as an academic discipline. His other works include Histoire de Londres [ref: Clout H., Histoire de Londres, Géocarrefour] and The Times History of London. [ref: ]

Albert Spencer Aretz (Born June 11th, 1997), more known as Flamingo or MrFlimFlam, is an Amarican YouTuber. His videos focus on Gaming and Comedy.

== Early life and education ==
Albert Spencer Aretz was born on 11 June 1997. He was born in New Jersey and raised in Sarasota, Florida. He has kept his parents private only revealing his dad's name that is Ronald Gerard Aretz. Albert started to play videogames at the age of 10. [ref: Albert Aretz, Albertsstuff Wiki]

== YouTube career ==

=== Early years ===
Aretz initially uploaded Roblox videos under the name ROBLOXHub. In July 2012, he created the AlbertsStuff YouTube channel. He began regularly uploading to the channel in 2014. The AlbertsStuff channel became known for Roblox gameplay, commentary, dark humor, and unscripted interactions with other players. The channel eventually gained more than one million subscribers. Aretz's early content helped establish the style that would later become associated with his Flamingo channel. [ref: The Flamingo / Albert Q&A, Shorty]

=== Flamingo ===
In July 2017, Aretz created the Flamingo YouTube channel. The channel allowed him to focus on a more advertiser-friendly style of content while continuing to make Roblox videos. As Flamingo grew, Aretz gradually stopped regularly uploading to AlbertsStuff and focused his attention on Flamingo. The Flamingo channel reached one million subscribers in early 2018. It continued growing rapidly and passed 11 million subscribers in 2021. The channel has since grown to more than 14 million subscribers and billions of views. [ref: Flamingo (channel), Albertsstuff Wiki]

=== Content and style ===
Flamingo primarily produces Roblox gaming videos. His videos often combine gameplay with comedy and commentary. Common elements of his videos include:

* Roblox gameplay
* Comedy
* Roleplay
* Challenges
* Player interactions
* Reactions
* Memes
* Improvised situations

Aretz is known for changing his approach depending on the Roblox game he is playing. His videos can range from playing popular Roblox experiences to testing unusual games and interacting with random players. His style relies heavily on spontaneous humor and exaggerated reactions.

=== AlbertsStuff ===
AlbertsStuff was one of Aretz's earliest major YouTube channels. The channel became popular for its Roblox videos and more mature style of comedy. As Aretz's career developed, he shifted his focus toward Flamingo. In 2020, he removed or made private much of the older AlbertsStuff content because he no longer wanted the older material publicly available. The change allowed Aretz to concentrate on Flamingo and its more family-friendly style.

=== Flamingo's growth ===
Flamingo became one of the largest Roblox-focused YouTube channels. The channel's growth was helped by Aretz's frequent uploads and his focus on entertainment rather than competitive Roblox gameplay. In 2020, Flamingo was recognized as one of YouTube's top ten most-viewed gaming creators. The channel continued to gain millions of subscribers during the following years. By 2026, third-party tracking sites listed Flamingo at more than 14 million subscribers and over 12 billion views.

=== Face reveal ===
Aretz initially created videos without showing his face. He later began appearing on camera, with his face reveal becoming part of his transition toward the modern Flamingo channel. His videos have since included both gameplay footage and footage of himself.

=== Roblox ===
Roblox has remained the main focus of Aretz's online career. He began playing the platform in 2008 and has continued creating Roblox content for more than a decade. His videos have covered a wide range of Roblox experiences, including roleplay games, obstacle courses, social games, horror games, simulators, and games created by members of the Roblox community. Aretz has also used Roblox to create recurring characters and comedic situations that appear throughout his videos.

== Collaborations ==
Aretz has collaborated with other Roblox creators throughout his career. One of his notable recurring collaborators is Jayingee, who has appeared in videos with him. In November 2021, Aretz also appeared as a guard in MrBeast's real-life recreation of Squid Game.

Jon Gluyas (born Jonathan Gluyas) is a British geoscientist and energy entrepreneur. He is Emeritus Professor of Geoenergy, Carbon Capture and Storage at Durham University, and was President of the Geological Society of London from 2024 to 2026.

Gluyas spent around fifteen years at BP before moving into the independent oil sector and later academia. In 2015 he worked with Chris Ballentine of the University of Oxford to develop an exploration model used to confirm a large helium gas field in Tanzania, reported at the time as an unusual case of helium being found by deliberate exploration rather than discovered incidentally during oil and gas drilling.

== Early life and education ==
Gluyas traced his interest in geology to a Scout trip to the Yorkshire Dales as a schoolboy. He studied geology at the University of Sheffield and completed a PhD in geochemistry at the University of Liverpool in 1983.

== Career ==
Gluyas joined BP in 1981 as a sedimentologist and research geologist, holding technical and leadership roles in the UK, Norway, Venezuela and China over about fifteen years. He later worked at Monument Oil & Gas and Lasmo, before co-founding Acorn Oil & Gas in 2001, which redeveloped the previously abandoned Argyll/Ardmore oilfield in the North Sea. After Acorn was sold in 2005, he co-founded Fairfield Energy to redevelop mature North Sea assets, and has since founded or co-founded several further energy and earth-observation companies, including Geoptic, a muon-imaging spin-out from Durham, Sheffield and St Mary's University, Twickenham, which won a King's Award for Enterprise in 2025.

He joined Durham University in 2009 as the first holder of a chair in geoenergy, carbon capture and storage in Europe, later serving as Head of the Department of Earth Sciences (2011–2014) and Executive Director of the Durham Energy Institute.

== Research ==
Gluyas's early work focused on sedimentary diagenesis and its effects on sandstone reservoir quality, including a 1992 Nature paper co-authored with Michael Coleman. He has since worked on UK carbon capture and storage research and on deep geothermal energy, co-founding the BritGeothermal research consortium and later serving on the board of the UK National Geothermal Centre.

His 2015 helium work was followed by further research on nitrogen–helium gas field formation, published in Nature in 2023, and a 2025 review of natural hydrogen resource accumulation in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment. Gluyas has also contributed to research on human-induced earthquakes linked to hydraulic fracturing and geothermal operations, including work on the HiQuake database.

== Awards and honours ==
* Aberconway Medal, Geological Society of London (2000), for distinction in applied or economic geoscience.
* Industry Expert Award, SPE Aberdeen Offshore Achievement Awards (2025).
* King's Award for Enterprise, Innovation category (2025), awarded to Geoptic.
* Honorary Fellow, Geological Society of India (2023).

== Selected publications ==
* Gluyas, J. G., & Swarbrick, R. E. Petroleum Geoscience. Wiley-Blackwell.
* Kupecz, J. A., Gluyas, J. G., & Bloch, S. (eds.) (1997). Reservoir Quality Prediction in Sandstones and Carbonates. AAPG Memoir 69.
* Gluyas, J., & Coleman, M. (1992). "Material flux and porosity changes during sediment diagenesis". Nature, 356, 52–54.
* Wilson, M. P., Foulger, G. R., Gluyas, J. G., Davies, R. J., & Julian, B. R. (2017). "HiQuake: The Human-Induced Earthquake Database". Seismological Research Letters, 88(6), 1560–1565.
* Cheng, A., Sherwood Lollar, B., Gluyas, J. G., & Ballentine, C. J. (2023). "Primary N2–He gas field formation in intracratonic sedimentary basins". Nature, 615, 94–99.

His publications, cited more than 8,800 times, are listed on Google Scholar.

Somasekhar Sundaresan (born 23 December 1972) is an Indian jurist serving as a Permanent Judge of the Bombay High Court. After his appointment as an Additional Judge to that high court in November 2023, Sundaresan was confirmed as a Permanent Judge in September 2025. [ref: Hon'ble Sitting Judges: Somasekhar Sundaresan, J., High Court of Bombay] [ref: Advocate Somasekhar Sundaresan sworn in as additional judge of Bombay HC, The Indian Express] [ref: President appoints 6 Permanent Judges for Bombay High Court, SCC Online] He has also practiced as a regulatory and commercial lawyer giving advice on takeovers, securities laws and corporate insolvency rules in Mumbai. [ref: Somasekshar Sundaresan of JSA leaves the firm to begin counsel practice, The Economic Times]

== Early life and education ==
Sundaresan graduated with a Bachelor of Commerce from RA Podar College of Commerce & Economics in 1993. He then earned his law degree from Government Law College, Mumbai in 1996. While pursuing his law degree, Sundaresan worked in finance journalism as a business editor for The Times of India from 1994 to 1998. [ref: Somasekhar Sundaresan, Partner, J. Sagar Associates, on work of a transactional lawyer, responsibilites of a Partner, and his transition from Journalism to Law, SuperLawyer]

== Career ==

=== Legal ===
In 1999, Sundaresan joined Udwadia, Udeshi & Berjis (now Argus Partners) as a partner, advising on company law and foreign exchange regulations. From 2002 until August 2016, he served as a partner at J. Sagar Associates. Sundaresan's practice there had a focus on transactional governance and regulatory litigation before the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the Competition Commission of India and the Securities Appellate Tribunal.

=== Public policy and regulatory committees ===
Sundaresan has served on multiple Indian government advisory committees. He was a part of the SEBI Takeover Regulations Advisory Committee in 2010 to draft the revised substantial acquisition code. [ref: SEBI appoints committee to revamp Takeover Code; Achutan, Somasekhar Sundaresan and Kumar Desai represent the legal community, Bar and Bench] [ref: Report of the Takeover Regulations Advisory Committee, Securities and Exchange Board of India] Sundaresan provided advice to the Financial Sector Legislative Reforms Commission under Justice B.N. Srikrishna between 2011 and 2013, which prepared the draft Indian Financial Code. [ref: Who tried to clip the RBI governor's wings?, Mint] He was also a member of SEBI's High-Level Committee on Insider Trading Regulations in 2013, chaired by Justice N.K. Sodhi. [ref: Report of the High Level Committee to Review the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 1992, Securities and Exchange Board of India] Sundaresan was appointed by the Supreme Court of India to a six-member expert panel, reviewing securities market regulatory mechanisms after allegations against the Adani Group in 2023. [ref: Supreme Court forms expert panel to probe any regulatory failure on Adani issue, The Hindu]

=== Judicial ===
Sundaresan was recommended for elevation to the bench by the Bombay High Court Collegium in October 2021. The file was returned for reconsideration by the Union Government due to views expressed by Sundaresan on social media regarding pending court matters. In January 2023, the Supreme Court Collegium, headed by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud, strongly reiterated his name, stating that airing critical views on government policy does not compromise judicial independence or imply bias. [ref: Advocate Somasekhar Sundaresan appointed as an Additional Judge of the Bombay High Court, The Hindu] Sundaresan was then sworn in as an Additional Judge on 28 November 2023, before becoming a Permanent Judge on 18 September 2025.

Draft text:
Joseph B. Rasmussen is a Canadian aquatic ecologist. He is Professor Emeritus of Biological Sciences at the University of Lethbridge, where he held a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems and directed the Water Institute for Sustainable Environments. He developed stable-isotope methods now widely used to quantify food web structure and trophic position, and applied tracer-kinetic models to the study of contaminant biomagnification and in situ fish bioenergetics. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 2016.

Rasmussen was appointed in 2010 to a federal advisory panel reviewing environmental monitoring of the Athabasca oil sands, one of six scientists named by then-environment minister Jim Prentice. In 2024, University of Lethbridge researchers named a newly described species of parasite, Myxobolus rasmusseni, after him in recognition of his career in aquatic biology.

== Early life and education ==
Rasmussen studied zoology at the University of Alberta in the 1960s and 1970s, completing an honours BSc and an MSc in limnology, and went on to a PhD in aquatic ecology at the University of Calgary in 1983.

== Career ==
Rasmussen joined the Department of Biology at McGill University in 1984 as an NSERC postdoctoral fellow, and was later promoted to full professor. During his time at McGill, he worked on lake zoobenthos, stable-isotope food web ecology, and contaminant biomagnification, and in 1998 was among the faculty who established the McGill School of Environment.

He moved to the University of Lethbridge in 2003 to take up a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems, renewed in 2010, and to direct the Water Institute for Sustainable Environments. He later chaired the Department of Biological Sciences before retiring in 2019 as Professor Emeritus.

Later in his career, Rasmussen's group turned toward the conservation of native salmonids in western Canada, studying how introduced brook trout affect bull trout (Salvelinus confluentus) populations and how rainbow trout introductions affect the genetics of native westslope cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarkii lewisi), and tracing selenium from coal mining through mountain stream food webs. This work fed into his appointment to the federal oil sands review panel and to provincial panels on environmental monitoring and selenium impacts on Athabasca rainbow trout.

== Research ==
In the 1980s, whether persistent contaminants biomagnify up aquatic food webs was disputed; some chemists argued, from equilibrium partitioning, that it was thermodynamically implausible. Rasmussen and collaborators built kinetic models accounting for uptake, elimination, and bioenergetics to show that biomagnification is expected for contaminants that are readily assimilated but slowly eliminated, and that much lake-to-lake variation in fish PCB and mercury levels can be explained by food web structure.

His group adapted nitrogen stable-isotope (δ¹⁵N) methods, until then used mainly in marine geochemistry, to freshwater food webs, showing that δ¹⁵N signatures track trophic position more efficiently than traditional stomach-content analysis while also predicting mercury bioaccumulation; they also showed that comparing trophic position across different food webs requires correcting for variation in baseline isotope signatures. Combining isotope measurements with long-term lake data, the group traced how species introductions, such as smallmouth bass, reshaped the trophic position of native lake trout, and his student Anthony Ricciardi produced widely cited estimates of extinction rates among North American freshwater fauna. Rasmussen's group also extended radiotracer bioenergetics techniques to estimate feeding rates and metabolic costs of wild fish populations in the field.

== Awards and honours ==
* Fellow, Royal Society of Canada (Academy of Science, Earth, Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences division), 2016.
* Ingrid Speaker Award for Outstanding Research Achievement, University of Lethbridge, 2012.
* Frank H. Rigler Memorial Award, Society of Canadian Limnologists, 2010.
* Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Aquatic Ecosystems, 2003 (renewed 2010).

In 2024, a newly discovered myxozoan parasite infecting fathead minnows in southern Alberta was named Myxobolus rasmusseni in his honour by researchers Molly Tilley and Cameron Goater. Goater, a longtime colleague, described Rasmussen as one of the most decorated aquatic biologists in the country.
[truncated]

Mary Muriel Ludidi-Gaobepe is a South African-born educator, researcher, and activist who contributed significantly to women's vocational education and community development during her time in exile in Zambia.

== Early Life and Education ==
Mary Muriel Ludidi was born in Gwadu Village, Willowvale District, Eastern Cape to her parents, James Jubilee Ludidi and Dinah Siphunzi Ludidi. She grew up within the prominent Gaobepe and Ludidi family structures in the Eastern Cape. She pursued her primary and higher education in South Africa, qualifying as a professional educator before entering into political exile.

== Career and Exile in Zambia ==
During the South African liberation struggle, Ludidi-Gaobepe relocated to Zambia, which served as a major urban hub for the exiled liberation movement. She became a prominent lecturer at the Teachers' Training College in Kitwe, helping shape the landscape of regional education.

In the early 1970s, she participated in an international study visit to Australia sponsored by UNESCO to examine educational frameworks. [ref: UNESCO Study Visit: South African Educator in Australia, National Library of Australia (Trove)] In 1973, she co-authored and published a comprehensive country report on the social, educational, and economic conditions of women in Zambia for the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. [ref: Zambia, United Nations Economic Commission for Africa (Open Library / WorldCat)] During this period in exile, her home in Zambia also functioned as an important node of hospitality and support for active liberation leaders, including African National Congress (ANC) President Oliver Tambo.

== Personal Life ==
She was married to her husband, Godisang Au-Rheims Gaobepe. Together, they raised a family that included three children born in South Africa and during their time in Zambia. Her legacy continues through her children: Soga, Nomsa, and Neo. Her grandchildren, including Thandiwe Gaobepe, Godisang Nzo, Naledi Gaobepe, Nkululeko Nzo, Moranodi Gaobepe, Odueste Gaobepe, and Mthunziwabantu Alfred Nzo, maintain her archival history.

[ref: Watch Missy Elliott perform with "funky white sister" Mary Halsey, NME] [ref: Missy Elliott Praises Rhode Island Woman's Viral Rendition of "Work It", Exclaim!] She subsequently performed "Work It" on The Ellen DeGeneres Show on 13 September 2018, where Elliott surprised her on stage for a duet, performed live on Good Morning Britain, and served as a red-carpet correspondent for Ellen at the American Music Awards in October 2018 and the Grammy Awards in February 2019.

"Work It" became her regular karaoke song after a 2003 contest; she told Ellen DeGeneres that the positive reaction led her to study the lyrics until it became her go-to song. In 2018 she was working as a recreation assistant at Genesis HealthCare's Coventry Center in Rhode Island.

== Viral breakthrough in 2018 ==
In July 2018, Halsey performed "Work It" at "Karaoke Sunday" in Goddard Park, Warwick, Rhode Island, holding a shofar. Her best friend Pamela Wilsey filmed the performance, and Halsey posted it to Facebook that evening. The nickname "Missy's funky white sister" was Halsey's own self-description in her act, which Elliott adopted and amplified when she shared and praised the video on 8 August 2018.

Exclaim! reported that Elliott was among more than 7 million people who had viewed the performance, and quoted Elliott's post describing Halsey as her "FUNKY WHITE SISTER" and saying she "straight killed 'Work It' sound effects and all."

== Television appearances and coverage ==
On 13 September 2018, Halsey appeared on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. She performed "Work It" carrying the shofar, and Elliott surprised her on stage for a duet. [ref: Missy Elliott surprises viral video star who sang "Work It", The FADER] [ref: Missy Elliott Performs "Work It" on 'Ellen' With Viral Video Star, XXL] She received a signed shirt from Elliott and a "Missy's Funky White Sister" jacket from Ellen DeGeneres.

Halsey also performed live on Good Morning Britain. The programme's official clip is titled "Missy Elliot's Funky White Sister, Mary Halsey, Performs Live | Good Morning Britain". [ref: Missy Elliot's Funky White Sister, Mary Halsey, Performs Live, YouTube (Good Morning Britain)]

Two further national items were coverage of the Ellen moment, not separate studio interviews. TODAY published a PopStart video report, "See Missy Elliott surprise viral video star Mary Halsey on 'Ellen'". [ref: See Missy Elliott surprise viral video star Mary Halsey on 'Ellen', TODAY.com] Billboard News published a video segment, "Missy Elliott Surprises Viral Fan Mary Halsey on 'Ellen'". [ref: Missy Elliott Surprises Viral Fan Mary Halsey on 'Ellen', Billboard]

== Red-carpet correspondent work ==
Ellen DeGeneres sent Halsey as a red-carpet correspondent to the American Music Awards on 9 October 2018, accompanied by producer Andy Zenor, and to the Grammy Awards in February 2019. A contemporary American Music Awards report noted that DeGeneres sent Halsey to the AMAs as her special correspondent. [ref: The 46th Annual American Music Awards, Cal Times] Official Ellen videos document both assignments. [ref: Mary Halsey at the American Music Awards (Ellen), YouTube (The Ellen Show)] [ref: Mary Halsey at the Grammys (Ellen), YouTube (The Ellen Show)] In a second studio appearance on Ellen on 30 January 2019, Halsey performed "Anaconda" and received two Grammy tickets.

== Later work and recognition ==
Rhode Island Monthly named Halsey one of its Top Ten Rhode Islanders of the Year in its December 2018 issue. From 6 February 2019, she hosted "Skyline Karaoke Idol" on Wednesdays at Skyline at Waterplace in Providence. She appeared at Creators Live in Branson, Missouri, on 20 June 2020, and hosts The Magic Mary Podcast.

On 15 September 2026, a collaboration video with Nicki Marie was posted on Instagram by nickimarieinc, with Halsey (mary.halsey_) credited as collaborator. [ref: Nicki Marie collaboration reel with Mary Halsey, Instagram]

Anti-Rabid Fanbases (ARF) was an anti-fandom internet trolling group founded and owned by Princess Java McMan. Established in 2015, the group was created in response to widespread annoyance with the rapidly emerging Five Nights at Freddy's fandom on Youtube [ref: I ARE TECH: The Gayest Story Never Told] [ref: Click, M. A. (2019). Anti-fandom. NYU Press.]. Operating primarily across YouTube, Steam [ref: Steam Community:: Group:: Anti-Rabid Fanbases, steamcommunity.com], DeviantArt, Reddit, and the now-defunct Google+, ARF organized coordinated comment spam campaigns targeting prominent internet personalities [ref: Barnes, R. (2018). Uncovering online commenting culture. Springer.], including Markiplier. In addition to targeting individuals, the group orchestrated mass raids and harassment campaigns against various fandom-related communities [ref: Phillips, W. (2015). This is why we can’t have nice things. MIT Press.] [ref: Poland, B. (2016). Haters: Harassment, abuse, and violence online. Potomac Books.] [ref: Gorman, G. (2019). Troll hunting: Inside the world of online hate and its human fallout. Hardie Grant Books.]. ARF temporarily dissolved in 2017 after its Google+ group was deleted by Princess Java McMan [ref: What made your day? KAI - Page 18 - Toho Kingdom, www.tohokingdom.com], the organization later disbanded entirely in late 2019 due to leadership disagreements regarding its direction [ref: UTubeTrollPolice, UTubeTrollPedia] and the subsequent shutdown of Google+.

== Origins and history ==
In 2015, a YouTube channel named "Smilk" was created as a parody of prominent gaming YouTuber Smike. [ref: Smilk and Smike:: Five Nights at Freddy's 3 General Discussions, steamcommunity.com] The name originated from a internet nickname used by both fans and detractors combining "Smike" and "milk," reflecting a common perception at the time that Smike was "milking" Five Nights at Freddy's content for money.

Following the online traction of the Smilk channel, Princess Java McMan established the ARF Google+ group alongside Smilk. The primary objective to harass and troll fandoms they deemed rabid. [ref: Wright, K. (2016). Internet trolls and stalkers - nutjob atheists. Lulu Press, Inc.]

In June 2015, the group began vandalizing the Five Nights at Freddy's Fandom Wiki. As part of the coordination, members posted a warning message on the wiki's forums stating, "About 40 of us are going to raid your wiki. We're Anti-Rabid Fanbases, a google+ community. Anyway, better be prepared. The storm is coming." [ref: ]

During its time on Google+, Anti-Rabid Fanbases became involved in many conflicts with other users and online communities [ref: Eckstrand, N. (2018, November 29). The ugliness of trolls: Comparing the strategies/methods of the alt-right and the Ku Klux Klan.], It was a prime target for both fellow internet trolls and members of the fandoms they targeted, leading to an infiltration and mass banning of members by a user known as "Lizurdy" on July 15th, 2015. [ref: Anti-Rabid Fanbases Raided]

Hışva Han, also known as Lala Mustafa Pasha Inn, is a historic Ottoman inn in the Şahinbey district of Gaziantep, Turkey, south of Gaziantep Castle. The oldest surviving inn in the city centre, it was commissioned by Lala Mustafa Pasha in the second half of the 16th century. Although the building has no construction inscription, it is believed to have been built between 1563 and 1577. [ref: Gaziantep, TDV İslâm Araştırmaları Merkezi] [ref: Hışva Han – Gaziantep, Kültür Portalı]

Part of the Lala Mustafa Pasha külliye, Hışva Han is a single-storey building with a central courtyard, constructed from black and white dressed stone. Originally used for trade, accommodation and storage, it was restored by Gaziantep Metropolitan Municipality and reopened in August 2016 as a complex housing a hotel, restaurant and shops. [ref: Hışva Hanı, Tarihi ve Kültürel Eserler]

The California Flag Handicap is a Black type American Thoroughbred horse race for California-bred or sired horses aged three years old or older over a distance of about furlongs on the downhill turf course scheduled annually in mid-October at Santa Anita Park in Arcadia, California. It is part of the Golden State Series of races sponsored by the California Thoroughbred Breeders Association. [ref: California Thoroughbred Breeders Association - Golden State Series Schedule, California Thoroughbred Breeders Association] [ref: Kings River Knight Much The Best On Hillside Turf As He Rallies To Take $100,000 California Flag Handicap By 1 1/2 Lengths, Santa Anita Park] The event currently carries a purse of $100,000.

==History==

The event was inaugurated on 19 October 2013 at Santa Anita Park as the eighth race on the racecard over a distance of about furlongs on the downhill turf.

The event was named for California Flag, the 2009 Breeders' Cup Turf Sprint winner and Co-California Horse of the Year. [ref: Classy The Chosen Vron Heads Field Of 11 In Sunday’s $100,000 California Flag Handicap, Santa Anita Park]

In 2018, the race was shortened to 5 furlongs and excluded Santa Anita’s characteristic downhill. The race remained shortened at about 5.5 furlongs in 2019 and 2020 before returning to its original length in 2021.

Kerron Stark is an actor, television producer, teaching artist, musician, and author based in Omaha, Nebraska. He is the creator and host of Mister K's Clubhouse, a live-action educational children's television series that premiered in 2021. [ref: Omaha’s Kerron Stark may be the new face of educational children’s TV, The Reader] [ref: Mister K's Clubhouse aims to be a place of 'love, learning and imagination' for kids, KMTV 3 News Now] [ref: Omaha Wolf Trap Teaching Artists, Omaha Performing Arts]

== Background ==
Stark attended Omaha South High School, where he participated in theater and film productions. After graduating, he moved to Los Angeles to pursue acting. He later returned to Omaha and performed with local theater companies, including Radio Theatre Omaha, Blue Barn Theatre, Chanticleer, and SNAP! Productions.

== Career ==

=== Mister K's Clubhouse ===
Stark conceived the idea for his own children's television program in 2018. Mister K's Clubhouse debuted in 2021, with early episodes recorded in his basement. Production subsequently moved to KPAO, a public-access television station in Omaha.

Stark hosts the series as Mister K. The program uses songs, puppetry, dancing, and stories to introduce educational topics to young children. It features local children, puppets, and adult supporting characters, with episodes addressing themes such as feelings and friendship. Stark has cited children's programs including Mister Rogers' Neighborhood, Sesame Street, and Barney & Friends as influences on his work.

Stark personally financed the production of the pilot. In 2021, he received a Black American Artist Support Grant from Amplify Arts. The grant helped fund production of the series' first season. [ref: 2021 Annual Report, Amplify Arts] Amplify Arts' annual report also documented his performance of Mister K's Clubhouse LIVE! at Joslyn Art Museum. Stark also established the nonprofit organization Dreams V Reality.

In 2024, Stark presented Mister K's Toy Chest of Dreams, an interactive stage production based on the series, at Benson Theatre in Omaha.

=== Theater and arts education ===
Stark appeared in Witness for the Prosecution with Chanticleer Theater. His other theater credits include A Very Die Hard Christmas with Blue Barn Theatre and The Last Supper with SNAP! Productions. He has also worked with the touring theater organization RESPECT.

With Radio Theatre Omaha, Stark played Brad Wormrun in The Grinch Who Came to Dinner and Louis Wilkinson in Shadow Point in 2019. In 2020, he played Payload in the company's production of Atlas Slugged. [ref: Past Productions, Radio Theatre Omaha]

Stark has worked as a teaching artist providing social and emotional learning lessons in middle schools, as well as elementary schools. Omaha Performing Arts lists him among its Omaha Wolf Trap teaching artists. He has also served as a teaching artist for the organization's Disney Musicals in Schools program. [ref: Disney Musicals in Schools Teaching Artists, Omaha Performing Arts]

=== Writing ===
Stark is the author of the children's book Being Different Is Simply Amazing, illustrated by Marcus Murray. The educational organization RESPECT includes the book in its RESPECT Reads collection of recorded readings for teachers and parents. [ref: RESPECT Reads, RESPECT]

Stark co-wrote Carey the Car with Jenn Pollard, with illustrations by ARTPORTRA. A dramatized reading appeared on Mister K's Storybook Station in February 2024. [ref: Mister K's Storybook Station, Apple Podcasts] He also co-wrote The Adventures of Captain Epic with Mark Terrett, with illustrations by Tracie Mauk.

In 2022, Concordia University, Nebraska named Stark among the authors and illustrators scheduled to appear at its 26th annual Plum Creek Literacy Festival. [ref: Concordia University, Nebraska to host 26th annual Plum Creek Literacy Festival, Concordia University, Nebraska]

=== Music and audio productions ===
Stark began writing music during his senior year of high school. In a 2025 interview with The Reader, he described spending approximately ten years singing, rapping, songwriting, and performing before creating Mister K's Clubhouse.

Stark hosts Mister K's Storybook Station, a podcast featuring dramatized readings of children's stories. Its earliest listed episode was released in December 2023. In March 2024, author and former Romper Room presenter Karen Robbins joined him for a reading of her book I Think I Can.

He is also the creator of Do With That What You Will, a podcast whose introductory episode was released in December 2025. [ref: Do With That What You Will, Apple Podcasts]

== Barney fandom ==
Stark is an administrator and founding member of Barney History Fans, an online community focused on the children's television franchise. In a 2025 interview with The Pop Insider, he discussed his involvement in the community and his collection of Barney memorabilia. [ref: Barney's Tee-rific Comeback, The Pop Insider] The group was highlighted in the Peacock documentary I Love You, You Hate Me.

Karen Ocamb is an American journalist, editor, and photographer whose reporting has focused on LGBTQ+ civil rights, the HIV/AIDS epidemic, and LGBTQ+ political history. She began her career in broadcast journalism at CBS News before entering LGBTQ+ journalism in 1988. [ref: Frontiers news editor Karen Ocamb laid off by new owners – Press Pass Q, blog.presspassq.gay] [ref: ]

Ocamb worked for nearly three decades with Frontiers, a Los Angeles-based LGBTQ+ publication, and later became the founding news editor of the Los Angeles Blade in 2017. Her reporting has documented the AIDS epidemic, LGBTQ+ political movements, civil rights campaigns, and the development of LGBTQ+ organizations in Southern California and nationally. [ref: ] [ref: Lesbian reporter fired by prominent queer publication for being too old, LGBTQ Nation] [ref: Frontiers news editor Karen Ocamb laid off by new owners – Press Pass Q, blog.presspassq.gay]

Her work has received recognition from the California Legislative LGBT Caucus, GLAAD, the Los Angeles Press Club, and the City of West Hollywood. In 2020, she received a Special Recognition honor at the GLAAD Media Awards. She was also named the Los Angeles Press Club’s 2020 Print Journalist of the Year in the under-50,000-circulation category, with the award presented in October 2021. [ref: ] [ref: ] [ref: Former LA Blade Editor Karen Ocamb, journalist of the year awardee, Los Angeles Blade: LGBTQ News, Rights, Politics, Entertainment]

== Early Life ==
Karen Ocamb was born on January 24, 1950, at Maxwell Air Force Base in Montgomery, Alabama. Her father served in the United States Air Force, and her family moved several times before settling in Westport, Connecticut. [ref: Karen Ocamb: A Proud Eyewitness to LA AIDS/LGBTQ History, Los Angeles Blade: LGBTQ News, Rights, Politics, Entertainment]

During the 1960s, Ocamb participated in demonstrations against the Vietnam War and became involved in the civil rights and women’s liberation movements. She attended Skidmore College before beginning her journalism career in New York City. [ref: Karen Ocamb: A Proud Eyewitness to LA AIDS/LGBTQ History, Los Angeles Blade: LGBTQ News, Rights, Politics, Entertainment] [ref: Former LA Blade Editor Karen Ocamb, journalist of the year awardee, Los Angeles Blade: LGBTQ News, Rights, Politics, Entertainment]

== Journalism Career ==

=== CBS News & Early Career ===
Ocamb began her journalism career at CBS News in New York City in 1973. During her time with the network, she worked in broadcast production and editorial roles. Her career at CBS culminated in work producing coverage of the 1984 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles for CBS affiliates. [ref: ] [ref: Former LA Blade Editor Karen Ocamb, journalist of the year awardee, Los Angeles Blade: LGBTQ News, Rights, Politics, Entertainment]

Following her work in network journalism, Ocamb pursued theater and volunteered in the campaign for West Hollywood’s incorporation as an independent city. She subsequently worked for a Hollywood public relations firm. [ref: ]

== LGBTQ+ Journalism and AIDS Reporting ==
In 1988, Ocamb began reporting for Frontiers, a Los Angeles-based LGBTQ+ publication. Her first article concerned ACT UP’s October 1988 protests demanding expanded access to experimental AIDS treatments, including demonstrations directed at the Food and Drug Administration. [ref: Frontiers news editor Karen Ocamb laid off by new owners – Press Pass Q, blog.presspassq.gay]

Ocamb has described the deaths of friends during the AIDS epidemic as a major influence on her decision to enter LGBTQ+ journalism. Her reporting subsequently focused on HIV/AIDS, public health, LGBTQ+ political organizing, civil rights, and community organizations. [ref: Frontiers news editor Karen Ocamb laid off by new owners – Press Pass Q, blog.presspassq.gay] [ref: ]

Over the following decades, Ocamb reported on LGBTQ+ political developments in California and nationally. Her coverage included the 1994 election of Sheila Kuehl to the California State Assembly, the establishment of the California Legislative LGBT Caucus, and the election of John A. Pérez and Toni Atkins as speakers of the California State Assembly. [ref: ]

Ocamb also appeared as a commentator on radio programs discussing LGBTQ+ political and legal developments. She participated in coverage of California’s same-sex marriage litigation on KCRW’s public affairs program Which Way, L.A.?, hosted by Warren Olney. [ref: ]

Ocamb also contributed to other LGBTQ+ and progressive publications, including The Pride LA, Bay Area Reporter, Windy City Times, The Bilerico Project, and HuffPost. She established the LGBTQ+ news and commentary blog LGBT POV. [ref: Karen Ocamb: A Proud Eyewitness to LA AIDS/LGBTQ History, Los Angeles Blade: LGBTQ News, Rights, Politics, Entertainment] [ref: ]

In 2012, Ocamb contributed two chapters to Gay Press, Gay Power: The Growth of LGBT Community Newspapers in America, a historical collection edited by journalist Tracy Baim. Her contributions, “Headlines, Heroes and History” and “Frontiers Magazine,” examined LGBTQ+ journalism and the history of the Los Angeles publication Frontiers. [ref: ]
[truncated]

Meta Akita Inc. (Japanese: ) is a Japanese research and consulting firm based in Akita, Akita Prefecture. Its principal activities include research, regional development strategy, policy formulation, new business development, and the development and implementation of artificial intelligence and blockchain technologies. [ref: 事業内容：地域戦略、イノベーション支援、AI導入, Meta Akita]

In 2022, the company partnered with the Akita Inu Preservation Society to develop an international community of Akita dog enthusiasts using non-fungible tokens (NFTs) and metaverse platforms. [ref: 秋田犬で経済圏を 保存会公認 「メタ秋田」が設立 世界のファン拡大へ 地方創生目指す, Hokuroku Shimbun] [ref: 「秋田犬」がデジタルアートに 保存会×メタ秋田で１３日発売, Akita Sakigake Shimpo]

The company's stated philosophy includes the use of regional resources in domestic and international markets, the development of clients' businesses, and "strategic disruption and creation", which it describes as reconsidering existing structures and developing new industries. It also states that its approach combines data analysis and field research with support extending from strategy development to technology implementation.

== Business ==
=== Research and consulting ===
Meta Akita supports local governments and businesses in regional strategy, policy formulation and business development through research in Japan and overseas. Its work includes statistical analysis of regional economies, industrial structures and demographic trends, studies of initiatives in Japan and overseas, and stakeholder interviews. These inform its analysis of regional issues, business conditions, stakeholder needs and practical constraints, and the preparation of strategies, policies and business plans. [ref: 実績：政策提言、先端技術の社会実装、自治体・大学連携, Meta Akita]

Its services for businesses include planning new ventures, preparing business plans, commercialising regional resources and intellectual property, and supporting business development through collaboration among industry, universities and government.

In technology implementation, the company supports the design, deployment and adoption of AI, data applications and blockchain systems. Its services also cover business process digitalisation and workforce training.

=== AgeTech ===
The company conducts research and develops policy proposals concerning AgeTech, technology that supports the health, daily lives and social participation of older people. Its initiative covers four areas: health, daily living, social participation, and family and community. These include health management, dementia support, housing, mobility, learning, employment, social interaction, care and monitoring. [ref: AgeTech × 地方創生：秋田AgeTechHub構想, Meta Akita]

==== Akita AgeTech Hub Initiative ====
In August 2025, Meta Akita developed the Akita AgeTech Hub Initiative and submitted it to the Akita Prefectural Government. The proposal aims to establish the prefecture as a centre for AgeTech research and business development, addressing population decline and ageing while supporting local businesses and industrial development. [ref: Akita AgeTech Hub Initiative formulated and submitted to Akita Prefecture, Meta Akita]

Based on studies of initiatives in Japan and overseas, including industry support centres abroad, the proposal seeks to connect companies and researchers in Japan and abroad with businesses, local governments and universities in Akita. It identifies three functions:
* International conferences and information sharing to support business and research collaboration.
* Test sites in care and medical settings and local businesses to assess products and services and users' needs.
* Commercialisation and financing support, including a proposed public–private venture capital fund for businesses whose products and services have been evaluated through pilot projects. [ref: Our proposal selected for Akita Prefecture's longevity society conference project, Meta Akita]

==== Akita Prefecture conference project ====
In August 2026, the Akita Prefectural Government selected Meta Akita as the preferred contractor for a project to organise a conference on longevity and well-being. According to the company, it is responsible for planning and operating a prefecture-hosted symposium scheduled for January 2027, with keynote lectures and panel discussions on AgeTech.

The company describes the symposium as an initial stage of the Akita AgeTech Hub Initiative, intended to establish a shared understanding of ageing-related issues among residents and local businesses. Its proposed subsequent activities include recurring conferences, pilot projects in care and medical settings, and financing for businesses evaluated through those projects.

=== University collaboration ===
Meta Akita collaborates with Akita International University on the Tohoku Digital Archive initiative. Its corporate history dates the start of this joint research to October 2025. The company describes the initiative as using AI and blockchain technology to document and preserve regional folk culture for use in education, research and tourism.

=== Digital pedigree certificates ===
Meta Akita and the US company Heirloom Inc. jointly developed digital pedigree certificates for the Akita Inu Preservation Society. [ref: Japan Akita dog society issues digital pedigrees to combat forgery, Kyodo News] The company announced the system in February 2024, with introduction scheduled for March that year.

Red Rising is a dystopian science fiction series written by American author Pierce Brown. Set in a technologically advanced society organized around a rigid, color-coded social hierarchy, the series follows characters who challenge the political, social, and military systems governing humanity. The story begins on Mars and expands across the solar system as conflicts over oppression, revolution, power, loyalty, and freedom intensify. [ref: Red Rising by Pierce Brown, Penguin Random House]

The series began with Red Rising, published in 2014. The original trilogy consists of Red Rising, Golden Son (2015), and Morning Star (2016). [ref: Golden Son by Pierce Brown, Penguin Random House] [ref: Morning Star by Pierce Brown, Penguin Random House] Brown subsequently expanded the story with Iron Gold (2018), followed by Dark Age (2019) and Light Bringer (2023). [ref: Iron Gold by Pierce Brown, Penguin Random House] [ref: Dark Age by Pierce Brown, Penguin Random House] [ref: Light Bringer by Pierce Brown, Penguin Random House] The seventh novel, Red God, is planned to conclude the saga.

==Setting and themes==
The series takes place in a future in which humanity has colonized the solar system and society is divided into genetically and socially stratified groups known as Colors. Golds occupy the ruling class, while Reds occupy the lowest levels of the hierarchy, performing labor under conditions designed to preserve the established order.

The novels explore revolution, authoritarianism, class conflict, political legitimacy, military strategy, friendship, sacrifice, and the moral consequences of pursuing power. As the story progresses, the conflict expands from an uprising against an oppressive social order into a broader struggle over the future of human civilization.

==Plot==
===Original trilogy===
The original trilogy follows Darrow, a Red miner on Mars who discovers that the society he serves is built on deception. After undergoing a transformation that allows him to infiltrate the ruling Gold class, Darrow enters the institutions that govern the Society and works to undermine them from within.

In Red Rising, Darrow enters the Institute, a brutal proving ground where young Golds compete for status and power. Golden Son follows his rise through the political and military establishment, while Morning Star depicts the escalating conflict between the Rising and the Society.

===Second series===
The second series takes place approximately ten years after the events of Morning Star. The Rising has overthrown the old regime, but establishing a lasting political order proves more difficult than winning the war.

Iron Gold broadens the narrative through multiple perspectives, examining the consequences of revolution and the challenges of governing a fractured solar system. Dark Age depicts the escalating military and political crises confronting the Republic, while Light Bringer continues the struggle among rival powers as the future of the solar system remains uncertain.

Red God is intended to conclude the overarching story.

==Characters==
* Darrow — A Red-born revolutionary who infiltrates the Gold ruling class and becomes a central military and political figure in the Rising.
* Virginia au Augustus — Commonly known as Mustang, a Gold leader whose political judgment and commitment to the Republic shape the conflict.
* Sevro au Barca — Darrow's close ally and a prominent member of the Howlers.
* Cassius au Bellona — A Gold swordsman whose loyalties, relationships, and personal code place him at the center of several major conflicts.
* Adrius au Augustus — Known as the Jackal, he is a calculating political strategist and one of Darrow's most dangerous adversaries.
* Lysander au Lune — A central character in the second series whose competing ideals and ambitions influence the struggle over the solar system's future.
* Lyria of Lagalos — A Red whose experiences provide a perspective on the lives of ordinary people affected by the Rising and its aftermath.
* Ephraim ti Horn — A former soldier and criminal whose storyline explores survival, loss, and the consequences of political upheaval.

==Adaptations==
===Audiobooks===
The novels have been released in audiobook editions. The series' audio editions feature narrated performances that bring its extensive cast of characters, political conflicts, and military action to life.

===Board game===
A tabletop board game based on Red Rising was published by Stonemaier Games in 2021. The game uses characters and factions from the novels as the basis for a competitive card-driven strategy experience. [ref: Red Rising Standard Version, Stonemaier Games]

Will Green (born February 10, 1979) is an American entrepreneur and event promoter from Louisville, Kentucky. He founded Just Lit Candle Co., a scented candle business established in 2020, and created Trap-N-Candles, an event concept combining candle making with hip-hop and R&B music. Green has also participated in school supply fundraising in Louisville. [ref: Viral post sparks community effort to meet JCPS students' needs, The Courier-Journal]

== Early life ==

Green was born on February 10, 1979, in Louisville, Kentucky, where he grew up.Green was born on February 10, 1979, in Louisville, Kentucky, where he grew up. He later became involved in the local entertainment industry, working as an event promoter and planner.

== Career ==

=== Event promotion (2010–2020) ===

Green began working as an event promoter and planner in 2010. For approximately ten years, he organized and promoted parties, nightlife events, and other social gatherings.

In 2020, restrictions associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States affected in-person entertainment events. During this period, Green began exploring other business opportunities.

=== Just Lit Candle Co. (2020–present) ===

In 2020, Green founded Just Lit Candle Co., a scented candle business based in Louisville, Kentucky. During the pandemic, he began learning to make candles through instructional videos on YouTube and experimented with ingredients and fragrances before starting the business.

Green used marketing methods from his work in event promotion. The company's advertising has incorporated humor, popular culture, and suggestive themes.

According to Green, the company generated approximately $50,000 in sales during its first year, with sales increasing in later years. These figures have not been independently verified.

The company's fragrances have included Grey Sweatpants, Sunday Morning Mimosas, and Mr Teakwood.

=== Trap-N-Candles (2023–present) ===

In 2023, Green created Trap-N-Candles, an event concept combining candle making with music and entertainment. The events include candle-making activities, hip-hop, R&B, live DJs, and a nightclub-style setting. Some events include alcoholic beverages.

The concept combines Green's event promotion work with his candle business.

== Community involvement ==

Green has participated in efforts to provide school supplies to children in Louisville. In September 2026, The Courier-Journal published an article discussing his involvement in backpack fundraising and distribution efforts for local students. The article reported that he had been involved in backpack fundraising for approximately ten years and helped collect more than 3,000 backpacks ahead of the school year.

Epistle is an Indian public relations and communications consultancy headquartered in New Delhi, India. Founded in 2011 by architect Tanya Khanna, the firm specialises in strategic communications, brand development, and media relations for clients in the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry. It is recognised as South Asia's first and largest communications consultancy dedicated exclusively to the built environment sector. [ref: Alumni Q&As: Tanya Khanna is putting Indian design on the global map, UCL Bartlett Faculty of the Built Environment]

=== History ===

==== Founding ====
Epistle was founded in New Delhi in 2011 by Tanya Khanna, an architect trained at Sushant School of Art and Architecture and The Bartlett School of Architecture, University College London. Khanna established the firm with the aim of developing a professional communications infrastructure for architecture and design practices in India, a sector that lacked dedicated communications services at the time. [ref: The less-spoken field of architectural journalism, The Hindu]

==== Growth and expansion ====
From its founding as a sole proprietorship, Epistle expanded over the following decade into a multi-city operation. The firm grew to a team of over 80 professionals across six Indian cities. It has provided communications services to over 150 client organisations across the architecture, interior design, real estate, and design manufacturing sectors, with clients spanning twelve countries.

Epistle has been credited with pioneering the field of architectural communications in South Asia, developing editorial, public relations, content, and brand strategy services specifically for built environment practitioners.

=== Services ===
Epistle provides communications services exclusively to clients in the built environment sector. Its services include: [ref: ]

* Strategic communications: Development of communications strategies for architecture firms, design studios, real estate developers, and building product brands.
* Brand development: Positioning, identity, and messaging strategy for design practices and organisations.
* Media relations: Press outreach, project placement, and relationship management with architecture and design publications in India and internationally.
* Editorial services: Project documentation, architectural writing, award submissions, and content development.
* Digital communications: Online presence strategy, social media, and digital content for design practices.
* Education and training: The Epistle Academy offers structured training in design communication for architecture and design professionals. The Epistle Writing Prize is an open international competition for writing about architecture, design, and urbanism, which received 195 entries from 18 countries in its 2024 edition.

=== Leadership ===
Epistle is led by its founder, Tanya Khanna, who serves as Chief Executive Officer. The firm's senior leadership includes:

* Tanya Khanna — Founder and Chief Executive Officer
* Suneet Zishan Langar — Director, Editorial and Brand Strategy
* Mariyam Hassan — Director, Strategic Partnerships
* Sana Jhamb — Director, Public Relations

=== Recognition ===
Tanya Khanna and Epistle have received recognition from several industry organisations and publications:

* Khanna served as a juror for the Dezeen Awards in 2021. [ref: Tanya Khanna, Dezeen]
* Khanna served as a juror for the Frame Awards in 2022. [ref: The 15 design professionals leading May's Frame Awards jury, frameweb.com]
* Khanna was a speaker at NeoCon, Chicago, in June 2024. [ref: NeoCon Talks, NeoCon]
* Epistle and its work have been covered in The Hindu (February 2024) and the Journal of the Indian Institute of Architects (May–June 2023).

Ella Yurman (born ) is an American talk show host, writer, and comedian. She is known for hosting Going Down with Ella Yurman and Late Stage Live! With Ella Yurman, as well as for her 2025 Teen Vogue interview of Vivian Wilson.

Yurman has been cited as a prominent Gen Z influencer by Cosmopolitan, and her interview of Wilson earned her a GLAAD Media Award nomination in 2026 for outstanding journalism.

==Talk shows==
Late Stage Live! With Ella Yurman is a queer volunteer-run monthly show focusing on current events and politics for a primarily Gen Z audience. [ref: Late Stage Live! With Ella Yurman Wants to Be the Next Daily Show — But Make It LGBTQ+, Teen Vogue] The structure of the show follows the format set by The Late Show, opening with a monologue from Yurman, followed by a guest segment, and has a rapid-fire, irreverent tone throughout. The show is filmed at Brooklyn Information & Culture, airs on Brooklyn Public Access, [ref: Late Night Gets a Much-Needed Queer Makeover With ‘Late Stage Live!’, Jezebel.com] and episodes are published on YouTube for free.

Before creating the show, Yurman was writing for the YouTube series Some More News, and thought "there’s only so much I could be doing as a writer in a room writing for yet another cishet white guy." [ref: Ella Yurman, Teen Vogue] She was inspired to start the show having noticed there were no trans late night talk show hosts, or prominent trans commentators on politics. She approached playwright and comic Reid Pope and comedy writer Rima Parikh, whom she knew from New York stand up comedy circles, to write for the show. Neither Yurman nor head writer Pope had prior experience in television production. [ref: From a Tiny Studio in Brooklyn, Late Stage Live! Is Queering Late Night, [[Them (magazine)]

Guests who have appeared on Late Stage Live! show include New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé in October 2024. Topics covered include the marijuana industry and prison abolition, and it has a left-wing perspective with anti-capitalism and Palestinian liberation principles.

Yurman also hosts Going Down with Ella Yurman, the succession of Late Stage Live!, which was described as a "very good YouTube news series" by New York magazine's The Cut in 2025. [ref: What’s ‘Going Down’ With Ella Yurman: The Gen-Z New’s Cast Bringing Independent Journalism Back – Off Record Media]

T4T, an all-trans stand-up comedy show based in Brooklyn, was founded by Yurman and Terrence Dugan in 2022. [ref: T4T celebrates three years of transgender comedy, creating safe spaces at the Bell House, Brooklyn Paper] [ref: Trans Comedians Laugh Amidst the Horrors, Autostraddle] In 2024, Yurman left the show to focus on Going Down.

==Interview of Vivian Wilson==
[[File:Vivian Jenna Wilson - February 2025.jpg|thumb|Vivian Wilson, pictured a month before her March 2025 interview by Yurman in Teen Vogue]]
Yurman interviewed Vivian Wilson for Teen Vogue as the cover story for its March 2025 issue. [ref: Vivian Jenna Wilson on Being Elon Musk’s Estranged Daughter, Protecting Trans Youth and Taking on the Right Online, Teen Vogue] [ref: The 7 best takedowns of a chaotic 2025, Salon.com] The interview quickly gained attention on social media, and was covered by The New York Times, [ref: An Interview With Elon Musk’s Daughter Was Months in the Making, The New York Times] New York magazine's The Cut, [ref: 100 Days, 100 Small Victories: The political wins, works of art, and acts of defiance bringing us relief, joy, and even hope under Trump 2.0., [[The Cut (publication)] highlighted as a great read by Politico, [ref: The rival Biden forgot, Politico] and included by Salon in its list of "the 7 best takedowns of a chaotic 2025" for its impact on the public image of Elon Musk, Wilson's disowned father.

Yurman remarked to The New York Times of the interview that "I think a lot of coverage of trans people these days, even high-profile trans people, ends up centering their transness so much that it reduces them to two-dimensional figures without interiority. Most of all, I wanted this piece to give Vivian a chance to be herself in front of the world." The interview was nominated for the 37th GLAAD Media Awards in 2026 in the category Outstanding Online or Print Journalism Article in 2026. [ref: Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry Among Winners at 37th Annual GLAAD Media Awards, IGN.com]

==Reception==
In a 2024 article, Jezebel called Yurman "a generational talent with the sort of stage presence and charisma that make her one to watch". She was cited as a prominent gen Z influencer by Cosmopolitan in 2025. [ref: Introducing Cosmopolitan’s 2025 Z-Stars, [[Cosmopolitan (magazine)] She has also been featured in The New York Times, Politico, and Teen Vogue.
