Hayden High School is a public secondary school located in Hayden, Alabama, United States. Operated by Blount County Schools, the school serves students in grades eight through twelve. The school offers academic instruction, extracurricular activities, and interscholastic athletics.

The school's mascot is the Wildcats, and its school colors are black and Vegas gold.

== History ==

=== Early schools ===

The history of public education in Hayden, Alabama, predates the development of the present high school. According to the Encyclopedia of Alabama, the community's earliest school was a one-room log building. As the population grew, the school was expanded to a two-room, two-story building and later a four-room facility. [ref: Hayden, Encyclopedia of Alabama]

The Town of Hayden's historical account describes the earliest schoolhouse as a crude log structure with a dirt floor. School was initially held during the summer, when children were less needed for agricultural work. Winter classes were introduced later, and a fireplace was added to provide heat. As demand for education increased, the community constructed larger school buildings. [ref: Town History, Town of Hayden]

Following the construction of a four-room schoolhouse after World War I, additional rooms were added as enrollment increased. In the early 1920s, a larger site was acquired across the railroad, and a twelve-grade school building was constructed. The development marked an important stage in the expansion of educational facilities in the Hayden community. [ref: Town History, Town of Hayden]

=== Twentieth-century campus ===

According to Hayden High School's official website, a school building occupied by the institution had been in use since 1937. The building remained in use for decades, during which the campus expanded to include portable classroom trailers. [ref: About Us, Hayden High School]

=== New campus ===

On March 31, 2003, students, teachers, and staff moved from the older campus into a newly constructed school facility. The move ended the school's use of the building that had been occupied since 1937 and replaced a campus that included portable classrooms. The school described the new facility as a modern educational complex. [ref: About Us, Hayden High School]

== Academics ==

Hayden High School provides secondary education for students in grades eight through twelve. Its academic program includes academic support services, career and technical education, dual enrollment opportunities, and graduation planning. [ref: Academics, Hayden High School]

The school's educational mission emphasizes preparing students to become responsible, productive, successful lifelong learners. The school describes its educational approach as emphasizing cooperation, commitment, academic development, and preparation for participation in the wider community. [ref: Home, Hayden High School]

=== Academic support ===

Academic support is one of the services identified in the school's academic program. The school maintains a dedicated section for academic support to provide information about assistance available to students. Further details about specific interventions and services require additional documentation. [ref: Academics, Hayden High School]

=== Career and technical education ===

Career and technical education is part of Hayden High School's academic offerings. These programs provide a pathway for students interested in career-oriented learning alongside their broader secondary education. The school maintains a dedicated career and technical education page for program information. [ref: Career and Technical Education, Hayden High School]

=== Dual enrollment ===

Hayden High School lists dual enrollment as an academic opportunity for its students. Dual enrollment programs generally allow eligible high school students to take approved postsecondary courses while completing their high school education. Participation requirements, available courses, and arrangements with postsecondary institutions may vary. [ref: Dual Enrollment, Hayden High School]

=== Graduation requirements ===

The school publishes information about graduation requirements to guide students in completing the academic credits and other requirements necessary to graduate. These requirements are subject to applicable Alabama education regulations and local school district policies. [ref: Graduation Requirements, Hayden High School]

== Extracurricular activities ==

Hayden High School offers extracurricular programs intended to provide students with opportunities for leadership, academic competition, music, and service outside the classroom. The school's official extracurricular directory lists the Ambassadors program, Key Club, National Beta Club, the Pride of Hayden Band, and Scholars Bowl. [ref: Extracurriculars, Hayden High School]

=== Student leadership and service ===

The school's Ambassadors program provides an extracurricular opportunity associated with student representation and leadership. Key Club is a student service organization that emphasizes community service and volunteerism. The school also lists the National Beta Club, an organization that promotes academic achievement, leadership, character, and service among students. [ref: Extracurriculars, Hayden High School]

Thomson K. Mathew (1951 - ) is an American Pentecostal academic, author, and a globally recognized theological educator. He is professor emeritus and former Dean of the College of Theology and Ministry at Oral Roberts University ([https://oru.edu oru.edu]) and well-known conference speaker within the Spirit-empowered movement.

Career

Mathew began his career as the 16th pastor (1976-1981) of the historic Gospel Tabernacle of New Haven, CT (now Hope Christian Church) and later served as a chaplain at the (former) City of Faith Medical and Research Center in Tulsa, OK (1981-1989). In 1989, he joined the graduate (seminary) faculty of the College of Theology and Ministry at Oral Roberts University (ORU).

After thirty years of service at ORU as professor of pastoral care and concurrently holing various offices as Dean of Students, Director of Field Education and Assessment, Dean of Doctoral Studies, and Associate Dean of Academic Affairs at various times, he became the fifth Dean of the institution, serving sixteen years (2000-2016). He became professor emeritus in 2018 and has been serving as a volunteer academic consultant, doctoral program guide, and guest professor at several seminaries, including three in India - India Bible College, Kumbanad, Kerala; New Life College, Bangalore, Karnataka; and Filadelfia Institute of Global Studies, Udaipur, Rajasthan.

During his deanship, ORU Theological faculty was commissioned to help theological schools within the Spirit-empowered movement in England (Peniel College), Sweden (Livets Old, now Scandinavian School of Theology), Korea (Foursquare Gospel Theological Seminary, now Asia Life University), etc., modeling teaching courses from a Pentecostal/charismatic perspective and assisting to gain accreditation from their own regional jurisdictions.

Mathew has spoken at mega churches and major Pentecostal conferences in various parts of the world, including Sweden, Singapore, India, Russia, El Salvador, USA, UK, and Czech Republic.

Contributions to Theology and Theological Education

A major scholarly contribution was systematizing, clarifying, and historically interpreting Oral Roberts' theology for a new generation of scholars and ministry leaders. His work helped move Roberts' ideas from popular preaching into academically articulated theology. Rather than treating Roberts' theology as static, Mathew argued that it developed through three identifiable stages.

As dean, Mathew encouraged scholarship that remained faithful to Spirit-empowered perspective while engaging the wider evangelical and academic community. In this regard, he developed a new model of pastoral care by reframing pastoral care as "ministry between miracles."

Early Education and Family

Thomson K. Mathew was born in India as the eldest of six children. His parents (K. T. Mathew and Aleyamma Mathew) and grandparents (K. M. Thomas and Mariamma Thomas) were Pentecostal ministers in India. He attended CMS Primary School and St Thomas High School in Vechoochira and graduated from St Mary's High School, Niranam, all in Kerala. He migrated to the United States in 1972. He is married to Molly (George) Mathew. They are parents to two daughters.

Education and professional association

Thomson K. Mathew is a graduate of Bishop Moore College (Kerala University), India (BS, 1971), Yale University Divinity School (MDiv, 1975 and STM, 1977), Oral Roberts University (DMin, 1986), and Oklahoma State University (EdD, 1992). He is a professional member of the Association of Professional Chaplains (APC), Association for Clinical Pastoral Education (ACPE), and a charter member of the Association for Doctor of Ministry Education (ADME).

Books

Thomson K. Mathew is a prolific writer. His works include:

Ministry Between Miracles, revised edition: A Biblical Model of Spirit-led Pastoral Care

Spirit-led Ministry in the 21st Century, 3rd edition: Essentials of Ministry for Human Pastors Serving the AI Generation

Spiritual Identity and Spirit-empowered Life: Discover Your Identity in God's Family, Purpose in God's Call, and Power in God's Spirit

Spiritual Identity and Spirit-empowered Life Leader's Guide

What Will Your Tombstone Say? 52 Short Essays on Spirit-filled Church, Spirit-led Ministry, and Spirit-Empowered Discipleship

Membership to Discipleship: A Path to Spiritual Formation and World-Impacting Life

Prayer, Medicine and Healing: Why Ministers, Medical Professionals, and All Followers of Jesus Should Pray for the Sick

A Seminary Dean's Experiment with Servant Leadership: Stories and Lessons from My Journey Through Ivy League to Whole Person Education

Anatomy of a DMin Dissertation: A Guide to Develop, Implement, and Report a Doctor of Ministry Project

Small Group Ministry in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Guide to Extend Pastoral Care and Lead from Membership to Discipleship

Spirit-led Ministry in the 21st Century and Spiritual Identity and Spirit-empowered Live have been translated into Korean language, Spirit-led Ministry in the 21st Century has also been translated into Malayalam. He has written two other books in Malayalam.

Will Green (born February 10, 1979) is an American entrepreneur and event promoter from Louisville, Kentucky. He founded Just Lit Candle Co., a scented candle business established in 2020, and created Trap-N-Candles, an event concept combining candle making with hip-hop and R&B music. Green has also participated in school supply fundraising in Louisville. [ref: Viral post sparks community effort to meet JCPS students' needs, The Courier-Journal]

== Early life ==

Green was born on February 10, 1979, in Louisville, Kentucky, where he grew up. He later became involved in the local entertainment industry, working as an event promoter and planner.

== Career ==

=== Event promotion (2010–2020) ===

Green began working as an event promoter and planner in 2010. For approximately ten years, he organized and promoted parties, nightlife events, and other social gatherings.

In 2020, restrictions associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States affected in-person entertainment events. During this period, Green began exploring other business opportunities.

=== Just Lit Candle Co. (2020–present) ===

In 2020, Green founded Just Lit Candle Co., a scented candle business based in Louisville, Kentucky. During the pandemic, he began learning to make candles through instructional videos on YouTube and experimented with ingredients and fragrances before starting the business.

Green used marketing methods from his work in event promotion. The company's advertising has incorporated humor, popular culture, and suggestive themes.

According to Green, the company generated approximately $50,000 in sales during its first year, with sales increasing in later years. These figures have not been independently verified.

The company's fragrances have included Grey Sweatpants, Sunday Morning Mimosas, and Mr Teakwood.

=== Trap-N-Candles (2023–present) ===

In 2023, Green created Trap-N-Candles, an event concept combining candle making with music and entertainment. The events include candle-making activities, hip-hop, R&B, live DJs, and a nightclub-style setting. Some events include alcoholic beverages.

The concept combines Green's event promotion work with his candle business.

== Community involvement ==

Green has participated in efforts to provide school supplies to children in Louisville. In September 2026, The Courier-Journal published an article discussing his involvement in backpack fundraising and distribution efforts for local students. The article reported that he had been involved in backpack fundraising for approximately ten years and helped collect more than 3,000 backpacks ahead of the school year.

Draft text:
Hoodie Analytics is an American cannabis data and technology company based in Chicago, Illinois. The company collects and models retail data from licensed cannabis dispensaries in the United States and Canada, and sells market intelligence, sales and dispensary analytics software to cannabis brands, retailers, distributors and investors. Its data covers product pricing, promotions, stocking, distribution and share of shelf, and is drawn from dispensary menus and from point-of-sale (POS), ERP and seed-to-sale system integrations.

The company's data powers a shopping platform on the High Times website launched in 2025 and the magazine's Trans-High Market Quotations price index, and it was ranked on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of fast-growing private companies in the United States.

== History ==
=== Founding and seed funding (2020–2022) ===
Hoodie Analytics was founded in 2020 and is based in Chicago. Its chairman and chief executive, Wes Shepherd, previously founded Channel IQ, an e-commerce pricing and product content analytics firm that was sold to Numerator in 2016. At launch, the company said its executive team included former employees of the consumer data firms IRI, Nielsen, NPD and Numerator.

In April 2022, Hoodie Analytics announced the close of its first funding round, for an undisclosed amount. Investors included Greenlight Ventures, Satori Investment Partners, Entourage Effect Capital and individual investors including the actor Jim Belushi. The round was the first investment made by the Arcview Seed Fund, a vehicle of the cannabis investment and research firm The Arcview Group. Belushi, whose cannabis farm used Hoodie's data, joined the company's strategic advisory board alongside Lorne Gertner and Gregg Steinberg. Green Market Report noted at the time that competing cannabis data firms such as BDSA had raised more substantial outside funding.

At the time of the round, the company said it tracked about 3.5 million unique product offers daily across more than 8,000 dispensaries in the United States and Canada, and offered market data the day after it was collected, which it described as a first for the cannabis industry.

=== Partnerships and platform expansion (2022–2023) ===
In August 2022, the cannabis brand company Bhang announced that it would use Hoodie Analytics for retail sales insights. In September 2022, Hoodie Analytics and The Arcview Group announced a partnership under which Hoodie became Arcview's exclusive retail data provider and would supply data for Arcview's publications, events, consulting engagements and research. By then the company reported tracking more than 4 million daily offers in over 8,500 dispensaries. It also operated a consumer-facing product search site, Ask Hoodie.

In September 2023, the company launched an updated platform that added dispensary analytics, product velocity metrics, store-level segmentation by demographic and other attributes, and integration with wholesale systems. Cannabis companies 1906 and Good Day Farm were named as clients at the launch.

=== Series A funding (2024) ===
In June 2024, Hoodie Analytics closed a $5 million Series A round led by Measure 8 Partners, a firm founded by Boris Jordan, with participation from Entourage Effect Capital and Satori Investors. Earlier backers in the round included Greenlight Investors and OlsonUbben, an investment vehicle led by Tony Olson, the founder of the consumer packaged goods data company SPINS; a further $1 million was left open for follow-on investment. In connection with the round, David Navama, a co-founder of Vitamin Capital and former president of SPINS, and Timur Sultanov of Measure 8 Partners joined the company's board of directors, while Andy Sturner of Entourage Effect Capital and John Campbell of Satori Investors joined as board observers.

=== Media partnerships, e-commerce and recognition (2025–2026) ===
In April 2025, the cannabis publication Fat Nugs Magazine announced a partnership to use Hoodie's data in business coverage.

In late 2025, Hoodie Analytics and High Times, which had been acquired earlier that year by investors including Matt Stang and Josh Kesselman, launched a shopping and product discovery platform on the magazine's website. Built on Hoodie's data, it lets readers find legal products from articles and place orders for pickup at licensed retailers in their area, with sales completed in person to comply with state rules; at launch the platform supported retailers using the Dutchie and Blaze e-commerce systems, and High Times editors also gained access to Hoodie's analytics for market coverage. MJBizDaily reported that the ability to order a product from a link in an article appeared to be a first for the industry, and that Hoodie tracked more than 10,000 licensed retailers and 9 million product SKUs for the platform. Retailers could join a free Hoodie program, Hoodie Connect, for additional listing exposure and order referrals. Industry consultants quoted by MJBizDaily described the service as a step toward a mainstream online shopping experience, while the president of a premium edibles brand cautioned that e-commerce listings place premium products in direct price comparison with cheaper ones and bypass recommendations from dispensary staff.

Draft text:
CarOlé Flamenco (full name CarOlé Tachíria Acuña Flamenco; also credited as CarOlé Acuña and Tachíria Flamenco) is a fifth-generation flamenco and Spanish dancer, as well as a union actor, stand-up comedian, and mezzo-soprano singer. She is the director and principal artist of CarOlé Flamenco's Compañía FSDT (Flamenco Spanish Dance Theatre), carrying forward her family's Gitano flamenco legacy that began in 1894, as well as the professional company lineage, which Lola Montes started in 1955 and passed to her mother, Carolina Lugo, in succession in 1995 — the oldest flamenco and Spanish dance company lineage in the Americas. [ref: 'The healing power' of flamenco: How dancers are persisting amid a challenging arts landscape, San Francisco Chronicle] [ref: Fourth to Fifth Generation: What My Mother Gave to Me Lives on Through Me, In Dance]

== Early life and family ==

An essay published in In Dance traces her family flamenco tradition that began in 1894 and was practiced at home, running from her great-great-grandmother Domitila Herrera, through her great-grandmother Romelia and her grandmother Dora, to her mother, Carolina Lugo; Ms. Flamenco is the fifth generation.

== Early career and training ==

As a dancer, Ms. Flamenco turned professional at fourteen with Rosa Montoya's Bailes Flamencos. At seventeen, she joined her mother's company as co-director and principal artist, while also building her own solo career as a dancer and actor. In Seville, she was chosen as a private protégée of Pepa Montes, entering the lineage of Matilde Coral and Pastora Imperio; flamenco guitarist Gino D'Auri, who had toured with Lola Montes' company alongside her mother, brought her to Pepa. She trained in acting at the American Conservatory Theater and at the Meisner Technique Studio, where she completed a two-year Meisner program with Jim Jarrett, Sanford Meisner's last teaching protégée. At twenty-two, she became a professional actor, singer, and stand-up comedian. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in theatre and dance from San Francisco State University [ref: Commencement 2025, San Francisco State University] and is a Master of Fine Arts candidate at Saint Mary's College of California. [ref: CarOlé Flamenco, IMDb]

== Career ==

Ms. Flamenco is a professional union actor. She works in film, television, and live theatre, in both dramatic and comedic roles. Her film credits include the Academy Award-winning Milk, Wolf Mother, and Collisions, to name a few.

Sunset magazine profiled Ms. Flamenco, writing that she "brings the soul of Spain to San Francisco." [ref: Dance fever: flamenco star Carole Acuna brings the soul of Spain to San Francisco, Sunset] She was nominated for an Isadora Duncan Dance Award for Outstanding Achievement in Performance – Individual, for Unidad/Unity. [ref: 2016 Award Winners and Nominees, The Isadora Duncan Dance Awards] The San Francisco Chronicles Datebook section opened its feature "'The healing power' of flamenco" with her work reviving flamenco performance in San Francisco.

Her theatre work includes Lady Macbeth in The Dark Season; multiple lead roles at the San Francisco Dungeon; I Love You San Francisco; and Chardonnay Comedy at PianoFight, among others. As a stand-up comedian, she has performed at the Punch Line in San Francisco and Sacramento, Caroline's in New York, and the San Jose Improv, among others.

Following her mother's passing, Ms. Flamenco became director of Compañía FSDT. The company received a Cultural Dance Catalyst Fund grant through World Arts West, supported by the Wallace Foundation. [ref: WAW Cultural Dance Catalyst Fund 2026 Grantees, World Arts West] [ref: Wallace Foundation Provides Boost for Small Minority Art Groups, San Francisco Classical Voice]

== Reception ==

Ms. Flamenco performed with her mother as a mother-daughter duo. Reviewing the two of them dancing together, Oakland Tribune dance critic Ann Murphy wrote: "It is when Lugo and her daughter Carolé Acuña dance together that the women unearth a new dimension in dance…" [ref: Oakland Tribune] Of Ms. Flamenco's own dancing, Murphy wrote that she is "a mesmerizing young woman and a sensuous, generous dancer, as gifted in classical Spanish dance as in gypsy Flamenco." [ref: Oakland Tribune]

Chamisa Elementary School is one of the five elementary schools in the Los Alamos Public Schools district, and is the second one in the community of White Rock after Piñon Elementary [ref: Los Alamos Public School Sites, Los Alamos Public Schools]. The school was founded in 1968.

Unlike the other four elementary schools in the district, Chamisa had an open pod design, as opposed to an individual classroom layout. There were two main circular pods consisting of seven classrooms apiece and an open area in the center for various activities. The classrooms could be used in any combination or individually [ref: https://www.usmodernist.org/AW/AW-1967-05.pdf].

In 2024, construction began at Chamisa to replace the aging building on campus [ref: Groundbreaking Ceremony Held At Site Of New Chamisa Elementary School]. A new building was built next to the old one, and opened in time for the 2025-2026 academic year [ref: Brand New Chamisa Elementary School Welcomes Students]; and soon after the start of the school year, the old building was demolished [ref: Demolition Scenes Wednesday At Old Chamisa School, Los Alamos Daily Post].

Simdul  Shagaya (born 1975) known as Sim Shagaya is a Nigerian electrical engineer and technology business executive. He is the founder and chancellor of Miva Open University, a digital and distance learning higher institution,  uLesson - an educational technology company offering e-learning resources to African students, and  Konga, a Nigeria e-commerce company. [ref: How uLesson's present and past employees perceive Sim Shagaya's leadership style] [ref: ] [ref: "I look back now and I think I could have built this very differently." — Sim Shagaya on lessons learnt building Konga] [ref: Sim Shagaya: Entrepreneur Transforming Commerce, Education In Africa, Leadership] [ref: Konga ex-boss, Sim Shagaya started and failed at these 4 projects before finding success] [ref: Why ex-Konga boss, Sim Shagaya is now venturing into education with ed-tech startup, uLesson]

== Early life and education ==
Sim Shagaya was born in 1975 to John Nanzip Shagaya. His father was a Brigadier General in the Nigerian Army and served as commander of ECOMOG force in Liberia in 1993. [ref: Brig-General John Shagaya 1942-2018, Daily Trust] He was elected Senator for Plateau South Senatorial District in 2007 to the 6th Senate of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Senator Shagaya died on 11 February 2018 in a fatal auto crash in his home state of Plateau. [ref: UPDATED: Ex-senator John Shagaya dies in road accident, www.premiumtimesng.com]

Shagaya received his secondary school education at the Nigerian Military School, Zaria, and enlisted in the Nigerian Army where he had a stint before leaving to further his studies in the United States. [ref: The 9 companies Sim Shagaya built: From early failures to rewriting Nigeria's tech rules] He studied Electrical Engineering at George Washington University where he earned a bachelor of science degree. He attended Thayer School of Engineering, Dartmouth College for his master of science degree in Engineering Management, and Harvard Business School where he obtained a master of business administration (MBA) in 2003.

== Career ==
Shagaya’s career started in the late 1990s with several failed start-ups. In 2005, he founded his first successful company, E-Motion Advertising - an outdoor advertising agency. [ref: Business leaders who built empires from unlikely beginnings, Punch Newspapers] He ran the  company until 2019 when it was  acquired by Loatsad Promomedia. [ref: Konga founder Sim Shagaya's earliest company, E-Motion Advertising acquired by Seyi Tinubu's Loatsad Promomedia] [ref: Sim Shagaya enters venture capital space with “The Honey Badger Fund”] In 2011, Shagaya founded his second company, DealDey - a shopping website that tracks online discounts on popular goods and services for consumers. [ref: Ringier Africa acquires DealDey from Konga’s Sim Shagaya, Financial Nigeria International Limited]

In 2012, relying on his experience from the DealDey company, Shagaya diversified into e-commerce. He founded Konga, an online retail marketplace selling a wide range of consumer products. Konga was one of the early e-commerce start-ups in Nigeria and was initially impacted by lack of trust in online transactions, payment security, poor delivery infrastructure and low internet penetration. The company later became one of the popular online shopping companies in Nigeria. [ref: Konga Founder Had To Pay A Debt Of NGN 60 Mn That Wasn't His & Fake A Heart Attack To Save The Business, WeeTracker]  Shagaya stepped down from the company as its chief executive officer in 2016. In 2018, it was acquired by Zinox Group - a Nigerian technology company. [ref: Konga's former CEO, Sim Shagaya, establishes a new company 'uLesson', Nairametrics] [ref: Fall and rise of 48-year-old Sim Shagaya, brain behind Miva Open University, uLesson Group – Businessday NG]

Edtech

In 2019, Shagaya switched interest from e-commerce to education and founded uLesson Group - an educational technology company focused on making learning material accessible to African students online. uLesson's e-learning platform went live in 2020, initially focusing on primary and secondary school education offering curriculum based learning resources through digital devices such as recorded video lessons, quizzes, and assessments. [ref: With uLesson, Sim Shagaya is now top of the class, The Guardian Nigeria News - Nigeria and World News] [ref: Sim Shagaya the Serial Entrepreneur Behind Konga, Ulesson, Business Elites Africa]

Thomas Dörner

German physician-scientist and rheumatologist

Overview

Thomas Dörner is a German physician-scientist specializing in rheumatology, clinical immunology, hemostaseology, and autoimmune diseases. He is Professor of Innovative Therapies for Autoimmune Diseases at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, where he also leads Clinical Hemostaseology, and heads the B-Cell Memory research group at the German Rheumatism Research Center Berlin (DRFZ).

Education and career

Dörner studied medicine at Humboldt University and Charité in Berlin, receiving his medical doctorate in 1991 and completing his habilitation in rheumatology and clinical immunology in 1998. From 1996 to 1998, he conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. His specialist qualifications include internal medicine, rheumatology, hemostaseology, and transfusion medicine.

He has held senior academic and clinical positions at Charité and served as Professor and Head of Rheumatology at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich. Since 2009, he has held a professorship focused on innovative therapies for autoimmune diseases at Charité and has led its Clinical Hemostaseology service. His research group operates as a liaison between Charité and the DRFZ.

Research

Dörner’s research examines the roles of B lymphocytes, memory B cells, plasmablasts, and long-lived plasma cells in systemic autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), Sjögren’s disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and antiphospholipid syndrome. His early work used single-cell and immunoglobulin-gene methods to study B-cell receptor repertoires, receptor editing, and abnormal B-cell selection in lupus and Sjögren disease.

His group subsequently contributed to the characterization of circulating plasmablasts as correlates of disease activity, antigen-specific memory B-cell responses, extrafollicular immune activation, and distinct plasma-cell populations in human bone marrow. Later research addressed post-activated or functionally anergic B cells, immune-checkpoint pathways, plasma-cell heterogeneity, and CRISPR/Cas9-based manipulation of primary human B cells.

Clinical and translational work

Dörner has participated in the development and clinical evaluation of several B-cell- and immune-directed treatments. These include rituximab, epratuzumab, ianalumab, remibrutinib, baricitinib, iberdomide, and emerging approaches involving bispecific antibodies and CD19-directed CAR-T cells. He was the lead author of the initial clinical study of epratuzumab in patients with moderately active SLE, ianalumab (anti-BAFF-R) in Sjögren’s disease and led or contributed to other randomized studies of targeted therapies in lupus and Sjögren disease.

His clinical and translational work also encompasses autoimmune coagulation disorders, immune thrombocytopenia, antiphospholipid syndrome, vaccination responses in immunosuppressed patients, biomarker-guided monitoring, and the concept of deep B-cell targeting or “immune recalibration” in treatment-refractory autoimmune disease.

International collaborations and clinical standards

Dörner has contributed to international efforts to standardize the classification, assessment, and treatment of autoimmune disease. These activities include work on the 2019 EULAR/ACR classification criteria for SLE; the 2016 criteria followed by ESSDAI and ESSPRI disease-assessment instruments for Sjögren disease; the 2023 criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome; international definitions of remission and treat-to-target principles in lupus; and European treatment recommendations for SLE, Sjögren disease, antiphospholipid syndrome and related immune-mediated disorders.

Publications and recognition

Dörner has authored or co-authored an extensive body of original research, clinical studies, consensus statements, and review articles. His publications have addressed B-cell biology, autoantibody diagnostics, plasma-cell survival, biologic and targeted therapies, immune checkpoints, vaccination responses, and advanced cell-based treatments for autoimmune disease.

His honors include the American College of Rheumatology Senior Scholar Award, the Rudolf Schoen Prize of the German Society for Rheumatology, the Wolfgang Schultze Foundation Prize, and the Randy Fischer Prize. In 2023, he was named an Honorary Member of the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology (EULAR) for his contributions to rheumatology research, education, and international collaboration.

Before LemonLime, Zietz gained national attention as the 44th Stanford Tree, the university's unofficial mascot, a role from which he was suspended in 2022 for displaying a banner that read "Stanford Hates Fun" on the field during a football game. [ref: Jordan Zietz is solving the problem plaguing gamers nationwide, Kidpreneurs] [ref: Competing for College: South Florida high school senior creates esports league for students to earn scholarships, WSVN] [ref: A Startup Offered Job Interviews to Anyone Willing to Get Its Logo Tattooed. 7 People Took the Deal, Inc.]

== Early life and education ==
Zietz is a Florida native and attended Pine Crest School. [ref: Business Spotlight: Eau Resort & Spa managers give their best for Habitat, The Coastal Star] He studied management science and engineering at Stanford University, receiving a Bachelor of Science degree in 2024. [ref: 134th Commencement: List of Conferred Degrees and Degree Candidates, Stanford University] [ref: CEO apologizes for offering interviews to people who got tattoos of his AI company logo, San Francisco Chronicle] From 2021 to 2024, he was a member of the editorial board of The Stanford Flipside, a student satirical newspaper. [ref: Staff, The Stanford Flipside] In April 2023, he appeared as a contestant on Wheel of Fortune, representing Stanford during the show's College Week Spring Break episodes. [ref: College Week Spring Break 4]

=== Stanford Tree ===

During the 2022–23 academic year, Zietz served as the 44th Stanford Tree, the official mascot of the Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band and the unofficial mascot of the university. [ref: Stanford Tree gets the axe, suspended until January, The Stanford Daily] [ref: Meet the sapling: Bravery and new beginnings with Emily Rodriguez ’26, the 45th Stanford Tree, The Stanford Daily]

On October 22, 2022, during the Stanford University football game against Arizona State, Zietz and three other students, including Arizona State's mascot, carried a 40-foot banner across the field which read "Stanford Hates Fun". Following the stunt, the band's executive committee suspended Zietz from the role. The committee said the decision concerned his use of the position "for personal benefit" and was unrelated to the banner's message.

A student-led campaign protested Zietz's suspension and the university's social-life policies at the November 5 football game against Washington State, including the creation of a petition calling for Zietz's reinstatement which attracted over 700 signatures. [ref: ‘Stanford Hates Fun’ protests campus social life restrictions during football game, The Stanford Daily]

In 2023, Zietz judged auditions for the role and selected Emily Rodriguez as his successor.

Zietz started his first business, GameReef, through a Young Entrepreneurs Academy program supported by the Boca Raton Chamber of Commerce. In 2019, he founded the All-Star eSports League, which offered free, sponsor-funded competitions through which high school esports clubs could compete against one another and pursue college scholarships.

Zietz later co-founded Confetti, a social networking platform.

=== LemonLime ===
In early 2026, Zietz co-founded San Francisco artificial intelligence startup LemonLime alongside co-founder Daniela Muñoz. The company develops software to automate sales and marketing for small businesses. The company joined Y Combinator's Summer 2026 batch.

Duck, Duck, Gray Duck (also spelled Duck, Duck, Grey Duck) is a traditional children's game played primarily in the U.S. state of Minnesota. It is a regional variation of Duck, Duck, Goose, a children's chasing game played in schools, playgrounds, and recreational settings.

Although the two games share similar rules, the Minnesota variation commonly incorporates different duck colors, adding an element of anticipation and wordplay. The game has become a recognizable feature of Minnesota's regional culture and identity.

== Gameplay ==
Duck, Duck, Gray Duck is typically played by a group of children seated in a circle, facing inward. One player, designated as "it," walks around the outside of the circle, lightly tapping the other players on the head or shoulder while identifying them as ducks.

In the Minnesota variation, the player may use descriptive colors, such as "red duck," "blue duck," or "green duck," before selecting another player by saying "gray duck."

The player identified as the gray duck stands and attempts to catch the person who selected them before that person completes a circuit of the circle and occupies the empty space.

If the selecting player reaches the empty space without being caught, the selected player becomes the new person who is "it." Rules concerning what happens when the selecting player is caught may vary.

The use of different colors distinguishes this variation from the more widespread Duck, Duck, Goose game. Players may deliberately emphasize the beginning of a color, particularly the similar sounds of "green" and "gray," to create suspense.

== History and origins ==
The precise origins of Duck, Duck, Gray Duck are uncertain.

One theory attributes the Minnesota variation to Scandinavian immigration, particularly Swedish settlers who established communities throughout Minnesota during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Accounts of the game's possible Swedish origins describe two versions: Anka, Anka, Gås ("Duck, Duck, Goose") and Anka, Anka, Grå Anka ("Duck, Duck, Gray Duck"). According to this explanation, Swedish immigrants may have introduced the gray duck variation to Minnesota.

However, a direct historical connection between Swedish immigration and the Minnesota game's terminology has not been conclusively established.

A documented reference to "Duck, Duck, Grey Duck" appears in the 1936 educational publication Education in the Kindergarten, by Foster and Headley, both associated with kindergarten education in Minnesota. The book describes a circle game in which a player selects another child by saying "Grey Duck," prompting a chase.

This reference establishes that the gray duck terminology was in use in Minnesota educational settings by at least the 1930s, although it does not establish when or where the variation originated.

== Cultural significance in Minnesota ==
Duck, Duck, Gray Duck has become closely associated with Minnesota's cultural identity.

While most of the United States knows the game as Duck, Duck, Goose, many Minnesotans recognize Duck, Duck, Gray Duck as the familiar name from childhood. The distinction has become a subject of regional humor and friendly debate.

In March 2014, the Star Tribune published an article by Jeff Strickler examining the Minnesota variation and the public attention surrounding a map created by Christopher Pollard, a Minneapolis-area digital strategist. The map highlighted Minnesota's unusual terminology and gained attention through online sharing and coverage by BuzzFeed.

The discussion reflected the extent to which the game had become a symbol of Minnesota's regional distinctiveness.

The game has also been cited in discussions of Minnesota identity, alongside other regional traditions, expressions, and foods.

== Popular culture ==
The distinction between Duck, Duck, Gray Duck and Duck, Duck, Goose has appeared in Minnesota sports and popular media.

On October 9, 2017, Minnesota Vikings players performed a celebration based on the children's game following a touchdown against the Chicago Bears. The celebration attracted attention because the players used the more widely known "goose" terminology rather than Minnesota's "gray duck."

The event prompted renewed public discussion about the regional variation and inspired commemorative merchandise from a Minnesota apparel company.

Duck, Duck, Gray Duck has also appeared as a symbol of Minnesota identity in discussions surrounding the state's flag redesign. Some proposed flag designs submitted in 2023 incorporated references to the game.

== Relationship to Duck, Duck, Goose ==
Duck, Duck, Gray Duck and Duck, Duck, Goose share the same basic structure: players sit in a circle while one player walks around selecting another to give chase.

The primary differences are the terminology used to select the chasing player and the optional use of descriptive colors.

In Duck, Duck, Goose, the selecting player generally repeats "duck" until saying "goose." In Duck, Duck, Gray Duck, the selecting player may name differently colored ducks until announcing "gray duck."

The color-based variation allows for additional verbal misdirection and anticipation. Despite these differences, both games serve similar recreational purposes and involve running, listening, and group participation.

* Scandinavian American culture

== Marique B. Moss ==
Marique B. Moss (born June 29,1993) is an American Afro-Indigenous author, poet, educator, and community organizer. She is an enrolled citizen of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation (MHA) and is of African American, and Dakota ancestry. Based in Minneapolis, MN, she is nationally known for her work in Afro-Indignous literature, cultural education, Indigenous food sovereignty, and community orginizing. she is the author of Sweetgrass and Soul Food: A Memoir in Poems (2025). Sweetgrass and Soul Work: A Seld-Guided Journal for Reflection and Renewal (2026), and My Afro-Indigenous Superpower(2026).

She is also the co-founder of Mashkiki Studios, an Indigenous cultural education and creative business.

== Early life and family ==
Marique was born on June 29, 1993, in Rio Rancho, New Mexico. She is of African American ancestry through her father and Hidatsa an Dakota ancestry through her mother. She is the daughter of Dr. Margaret P. Moss, and Indigenous nursing scholar and professor at the university of Minnesota. Margaret P. Moss is known for her research in Indigenous health, nursing Education, aging, and health policy. Her Traditional Hidatsa name is Mirgua Miash, meaning "Woman in the Water". She is an enrolled citizen of MHA Nation, also know as the Three Affiliated Tribes.

== Education ==
Marique B. Moss attended Fort Lewis College in Durango, Colorodo, earnin a bacholor of arts in Native American and Indigenous studies.

In 2019, she received the college's Outstanding Student r of the year recognition in Native American and Indigenous Studies.During her undergraduate studies, she co-founded the Black Student Union and established the Black Student Resource Center, supporting initiatives related to student retention, campus inclusion and educational equity. In 2020, she earned a Master of Legal Studies in Indigeous Peoples Law from the University of Oklahoma College of Law. She has also served as vice president of the Native American alumni chapter at Fort Lewis College.

== Literary career ==
In 2025, Marique B. Moss published her debut poetry memoir, Sweetgrass and Soul Food: A Memoir in Poems.

The collection examines Afro-Indigenous identity, family history, cultural belonging, relationships, and personal experiences through poetry. The book has been incorporated into university curricula, including coursework examining Indigenous literature, identity, and cultural representation. It has also been distributed through independent bookstores, educational institutions, museums, and cultural organizations. The publication received coverage from Sahan Journal and Minnesota Native News. Sahan Journal profiled the author and discussed the cultural intersections explored in her writing, including the concept of "Blindian Country."

===== Sweetgrass and Soul Work: A Self-Guided Journal for Reflection and Renewal =====
In 2026, she published Sweetgrass and Soul Work: A Self-Guided Journal for Reflection and Renewal. The companion publication to her debut poetry memoir includes guided writing prompts and reflective exercises exploring personal identity, grief, emotional well-being, and renewal.

===== My Afro-Indigenous Superpower =====
In 2026, Marique B. Moss published My Afro-Indigenous Superpower, a children's book illustrated by Adair Carroll. The story follows Meeka, a young Afro-Indigenous girl exploring her African American and Indigenous heritage through family stories, cultural traditions, and intergenerational knowledge.

My Afro-Indigenous Superpower is one of fewer than five children's books written by Afro-Indigenous authors specifically about Afro-Indigenous identity and the experiences of Afro-Indigenous children. The publication received coverage from Minnesota Public Radio in February 2026, highlighting its focus on identity, representation, and the importance of children seeing their experiences reflected in literature.

== Indigenous education and cultural preservation ==
Marique B. Moss co-founded Mashkiki Studios with Theodore Marcil. The Minneapolis-based business focuses on Indigenous cultural education, traditional plant knowledge, arts programming, storytelling, and community-based learning. The studio provides educational workshops involving Indigenous foodways, herbal preparations, traditional crafts, plant identification, and cultural practices. Her work includes developing and facilitating programs for schools, community organizations, and cultural institutions, with an emphasis on connecting Indigenous knowledge with contemporary education.

===== University of Minnesota Landscape Arboretum =====
In 2026, she participated in the co-curation of the Hidatsa Earth Lodge Agriculture exhibit and the Original People's Garden at the University of Minnesota Landscape Arboretum. The exhibitions examine Indigenous food systems, agricultural traditions, and relationships between land, culture, and community. The Hidatsa Earth Lodge Agriculture exhibit incorporates traditional planting methods, including mound-based agriculture and the cultivation of corn, beans, squash, and sunflowers. Her work at the Arboretum was featured in a July 2026 article highlighting Indigenous agricultural knowledge and the preservation of ancestral traditions.

= Jay Stratton =
John "Jay" Stratton is a former American intelligence official and senior civilian official within the United States Department of Defense. He is best known for his role as the director and senior leader of several official military programs investigating Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP), formerly referred to as UFOs. Stratton served as the first director of the Pentagon's Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force (UAPTF).

== Early Life and Career ==
Stratton has an extensive background in the United States Armed Forces and intelligence community. During his tenure with the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA), he served as a senior executive, including as the Subject Matter Expert for Air and Space Warfare.

Throughout his government career, Stratton played a central role in initiating and managing three successive U.S. government UAP research efforts:

* AAWSAP (Advanced Aerospace Weapons System Applications Program)
* AATIP (Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program)
* UAPTF (Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force)

As head of these initiatives, Stratton led the initial internal Department of Defense investigation into the 2004 USS Nimitz "Tic Tac" incident. He was also instrumental in transitioning official terminology from "UFO" to "UAP" within government and defense policy contexts to reduce stigma and encourage formal reporting.

After retiring from government service, Stratton entered the private sector as an executive and consultant.

== Media Appearances and Claims ==
In October 2026, Stratton released his memoir, Out of the Shadows: Revealing the Truth About Non-Human Intelligence. In the book and subsequent public interviews, he stated that elements of the U.S. government and defense contractors have long been in possession of technology and material of non-human origin.

Official spokespersons for the Department of Defense and the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) have maintained that there is no verifiable evidence to support claims that the U.S. government possesses extraterrestrial technology or off-world craft.

Dhukal Wirrpanda (born 1957) is a Yolŋu elder and artist from the Dhudi-Djapu clan in North East Arnhem Land (associated with the Baniyala and Dhuruputjpi homelands). [ref: About the artist: Dhukal Wirrpanda, Annandale Galleries]

Dhukal Wirrpanda is the grandson (son in Yolŋu terms) of Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda, the Yolŋu leader at the centre of the landmark High Court of Australia case Tuckiar v The King (1934). Dhukal Wirrpanda is the protagonist and narrator of the documentary film Dhakiyarr vs The King. Nine ceremonial larrakitj hollow-log coffins) that Wirrpanda painted, along with seven other elders, were permanently installed in the foyer of Supreme Court of the Northern Territory during a Wukidi (reconciliation) ceremony at the end of the film. He has continued to advocate for Indigenous rights, reconciliation, and official recognition of historic Aboriginal deaths in custody. [ref: One of Australia's oldest cold cases: why after 90 years a family is still waiting for justice, The Guardian] [ref: Dhakiyarr Wirrpanda’s family calls for fresh probe into mystery disappearance, ABC News]

== Early life ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda was born in 1957 (some records cite 1955) to his father, Djungi.

He was born in North East Arnhem Land, Northern Territory, and raised on his ancestral Dhudi-Djapu clan homelands in Dhuruputjpi, approximately 200 kilometres southwest of Yirrkala. [ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda: Yalata (91x52cm Bark), Art Ark] [ref: Dhangultji at Dhuruputjpi, 1996 by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Galuma Maymuru, Art Gallery of New South Wales] Since the 1980s he has lived, worked and exhibited alongside his late wife, Galuma Maymuru.

== Artistic methods and themes ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda works include bark painting, wood carving and ceremonial hollow-log poles (larrakitj), using natural earth pigments and ochres sourced from his ancestral lands. His artistic practice is deeply connected with the ancestral stories, ceremonies and knowledge of the Dhudi-Djapu clan. [ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda: Yalata (91x52cm Bark), Art Ark]

His work frequently depicts the sacred ecology and seasonal transformations of his homelands around Dhuruputjpi in north-east Arnhem Land.

A portion of his mature practice centred on the Wukidi series, which depicts the ancient ancestral tsunami narrative and inland mortuary site integral to Dhudi-Djapu ceremonies. In this story, the ancestral hunters Balurruwuy and Yangamawuy were swept inland by a catastrophic wave and transformed into standing stone pillars. [ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda, Wukidi Tsunami, 2005, Deutscher and Hackett]
[ref: Dhukal Wirrpanda Sold at Auction Prices, Invaluable]

In addition to inland freshwater narratives, Wirrpanda's work engages deeply with sea country and maritime ecologies. In his contribution to the Saltwater collection, Gapuwarriku at Lutumba (1997-98), Wirrpanda depicts turtle hunters who successfully return with their catch. [ref: Djapu Turtle Hunt (1998) by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Australian National Maritime Museum] [ref: Gapuwarriku at Lutumba (1998) by Dhukal Wirrpanda, Australian National Maritime Museum] Anthropologist Howard Morphy noted that Wirrpanda uses the imagery the turtle shell, the connecting rope and the cleansing tide as a rich metaphor for Yolŋu mortuary ceremonies and the renewal of life. [ref: Saltwater Country – Paintings From Yirrkala, Art+Australia]

== Exhibitions ==
Dhukal Wirrpanda's early exhibition history includes participation in the 1984 Baniyala Artworks showcase at the Crafts Council Gallery in Sydney.

Alongside his late wife, fellow artist Galuma Maymuru, Wirrpanda co-created Dhangultji at Dhuruputjpi in 1996, a carved and painted wood installation that reflects the sacred ecology and ownership of their clan lands.

In 1997, he was featured in the landmark exhibition Native Title: Yirrkala Bark Paintings at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia in Sydney, highlighting the intersection of customary law, land rights, and contemporary bark painting. [ref: Native Title: Yirrkala Bark Paintings (1997), Museum of Contemporary Art Australia]

From 1998 to 1999, his work was included in A Material Thing: Objects from the Collection at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, showcasing sculptural works and cultural objects.

In 1998, Wirrpanda's bark paintings Djapu Turtle Hunt and Gapuwarriku at Lutumba were exhibited in the Saltwater: Yirrkala Bark Paintings of Sea Country project, created by Yolŋu artists to assert sea rights and sacred coastal ownership following illegal fishing intrusions at Garranali. These paintings then featured in the touring exhibition of the same name. [ref: Saltwater Country - Paintings From Yirrkala, Art+Australia]

Also in 1998, Wirrpanda and Galuma Maymuru held a joint exhibition titled In Memory of Narritjin – Bark Paintings and Carvings at the William Mora Gallery in Melbourne.

In 2000, Wirrpanda and Galuma Maymuru's collaborative carved sculpture Nyapalingu Wapitja Pair was exhibited at the 2000 Olympic Arts Festival in Sydney. [ref: Nyapalingu Wapitja Pair, Deutscher and Hackett]

In 2003, he was exhibited in the group showcase Buwayak (Invisibility) at Annandale Galleries in Sydney, which focused on the spiritual and cultural presence of Yolŋu art.

In 2025, he was featured in Yolŋu Power: The Art of Yirrkala at the Art Gallery of New South Wales, celebrating the enduring power and political agency of Yirrkala artistic traditions.

Mufti Khalil ur Rehman (1923 – 1977) was a Pakistani publishing administrator who served as the General Manager of the Taj Company in Lahore, a major publisher of Quranic literature in South Asia. He managed the company's executive administration and editorial operations.

== Early life and education ==
He was born in 1923 in Lohianwala, Gujranwala, British India. He did a Bachelor of Arts degree and a Munshi Fazil (Persian Honors) qualification from the University of the Punjab in 1945.

== Career ==
He joined the Taj Company in 1946, spending a professional career of 31 years with the firm, where he primarily served as General Manager based in Lahore. During his tenure, he traveled to various Arab and European countries to study Arabic calligraphy methods and modern printing technologies, focusing particularly on updates from Germany.

From 1966 to 1976, the publishing house undertook a multi-year project under his administrative guidance to produce a standardized 30-para collection of embroidered Quranic textiles crafted with gold and silver thread work, costing a total of 239,831 rupees. The project utilized 1,228 yards of green velvet across 1,228 pages, featuring threadwork containing 5% gold and 95% silver produced by United Industries Hyderabad. The primary calligraphy was executed by Hafiz Muhammad Azam of Mozang between July 1966 and November 1967, under the supervision of Hafiz Nazeer Ahmad and Mian Ata Muhammad. Following its completion, the embroidered collection was transitioned to permanent public display within the Tabarrukat-e-Qur'an Gallery located at the Badshahi Mosque museum in Lahore.

Lucy Bedingfield (1832 – December 19, 1910), born Finch, was an early Cherokee Indian mix landowner, farmer, and oral storyteller in North Alabama. Born into slavery, she went on to purchase 170 acres of land following emancipation, establishing a multi-ethnic agrarian enclave known as the Little Elk Community. Her legacy is physically commemorated in Limestone County, Alabama, by the geographic inlet known as Lucy's Branch in Athens, Alabama.

== Biography ==
Lucy was born into slavery around 1832 or 1833 on land that previously belonged to Cherokee settler John Melton, located in North Alabama. Family history and regional oral accounts document her as being of mixed heritage, born to an enslaved black-Indian and a Cherokee Indian father associated with the local Melton descendants who stayed in the Muscle Shoals region. According to historical marker accounts, her indigenous family name was "Finch". [ref: Lucy's Branch / Legacy of The Little Elk Community Historical Marker, www.hmdb.org]

== Career ==
In June 1888, she purchased 170 acres of land along the Elk River in Limestone County for $600, which was officially recorded under U.S. Land Patent #43463. [ref: About - Lucy's Branch Marina on Wheeler Lake in Athens, AL, lucysbranch.com] This property served as the cornerstone for the Little Elk Community, a unique regional settlement composed of Black, White, and Native American farmers. Known as an astute storyteller, she preserved early regional oral histories of the area's mixed-blood lineages. The Tennessee River inlet directly bordering this settlement was subsequently named Lucy's Branch in her honor. In her later years, Bedingfield migrated west to Oklahoma, joining a broader movement of families relocating to the region. She died on December 19, 1910, in Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and is buried at Oakwood Cemetery. [ref: Bicentennial Sightseeing, Visit Athens Alabama]

UserFerry is a WordPress plugin designed to export, import, and manage WordPress user data, including standard user information and custom profile fields. It supports multiple file formats and provides tools for transferring user records between WordPress installations, maintaining backups, and performing bulk user data operations.

The plugin includes user filtering, custom field detection, reusable export templates, import field mapping, batch processing, and export/import history management.

== Features and Functionality ==

=== 1. WordPress User Export ===
UserFerry allows administrators to export WordPress user information into structured files. [ref: ]

Users can be selected based on their assigned roles, registration dates, or individual accounts. The export interface also includes search, sorting, and a live user counter. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Administrators can select which fields to include and arrange their order before generating the export file.

=== 2. Multiple Export Formats ===
The plugin supports four data export formats:

* CSV: Suitable for spreadsheets, databases, and bulk data management.
* Excel (XLSX): Provides formatted worksheets with frozen headers and filtering options.
* JSON: Suitable for structured data exchange and development workflows.
* XML: Supports structured information exchange between systems.

=== 3. Custom User Field Support ===
UserFerry detects custom profile fields stored in WordPress user metadata. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

The plugin is designed to work with fields created by systems such as Advanced Custom Fields (ACF), Ultimate Member, WooCommerce, BuddyPress, Meta Box, and JetEngine. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Administrators can scan available custom fields and select which information should be included in exported files. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

=== 4. User Import and Migration ===
UserFerry provides functionality for importing user information from CSV, XLSX, JSON, and XML files. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Its import interface supports automatic column matching and manual field mapping. Administrators can create new users, update existing records, or skip matching users. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Existing accounts can be identified through email addresses, usernames, or user IDs. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

This functionality can be used when transferring user records between WordPress websites or updating user information in bulk. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

=== 5. Reusable Export Templates ===
The plugin includes a template management system that allows administrators to save export configurations. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Templates preserve selected fields and export settings, reducing the need to repeat the same configuration for recurring exports. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Saved templates can be edited, duplicated, deleted, or used to start another export. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

=== 6. Batch Processing ===
UserFerry processes import and export operations in batches. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

This approach is intended to reduce server timeouts and memory consumption when working with large numbers of WordPress users. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

The administration interface displays progress information during these operations. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

=== 7. Export and Import History ===
The plugin maintains a history of completed export and import operations. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Administrators can review previous operations and download retained export files. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Automatic file cleanup settings are available to manage stored export data. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

=== 8. Security and Data Protection ===
UserFerry includes several safeguards for handling WordPress user information. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

These include permission-based access, protected export file storage, import validation, role assignment restrictions, and spreadsheet formula injection protection. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

The plugin also includes a configuration check intended to identify situations where exported files might be publicly accessible. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

== Installation ==
UserFerry can be installed through the WordPress administration dashboard. [ref: UserFerry – Export & Import Users, WordPress.org]

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: TriTopic

Draft text:
TriTopic is an open-source method and Python library for topic modeling of text collections. It was introduced by Roman Egger in 2026. [ref: TriTopic: Tri-Modal Graph-Based Topic Modeling with Iterative Refinement and Archetypes] The method combines semantic text representations based on sentence embeddings with lexical information from tf–idf weighting and, optionally, document metadata in a single document graph. Topics are then identified through repeated graph-based community detection and consensus clustering. [ref: TriTopic – Graph-Based Topic Modeling, SmartVisions]

== Background ==
Topic modeling aims to discover recurring themes in large collections of text. Classical approaches include latent semantic analysis, non-negative matrix factorization and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA). [ref: Applied Data Science in Tourism: Interdisciplinary Approaches, Methodologies, and Applications, Springer] More recent methods such as BERTopic and Top2Vec cluster documents based on transformer-based text embeddings. [ref: A Topic Modeling Comparison Between LDA, NMF, Top2Vec, and BERTopic to Demystify Twitter Posts, Frontiers in Sociology]

TriTopic belongs to the embedding- and graph-based approaches. Unlike probabilistic models such as LDA, it does not rely on a generative model but represents similarities between documents as a graph. The original publication motivates the method with three limitations it attributes to existing embedding-based approaches: results that vary between runs, a loss of lexical precision, and reliance on a single view of the data.

== Method ==

=== Document representations ===
Documents are first encoded with a sentence embedding model, and the dimensionality of the embeddings is reduced with UMAP. In addition, a lexical representation based on tf–idf captures the actual vocabulary used. Optionally, metadata such as source or date can be included; according to the documentation, metadata only strengthens links between documents that are already similar in content and does not create new ones.

=== Graph construction ===
The representations are fused into a weighted document graph in which documents are nodes and similarities are edges. Neighbourhoods are determined using mutual k-nearest neighbors and shared nearest neighbors, and links that appear in more than one view receive a higher weight.

=== Consensus clustering ===
Communities in the graph are detected with the Leiden algorithm. [ref: From Louvain to Leiden: guaranteeing well-connected communities, Scientific Reports] Because the result depends on random initialisation, TriTopic runs the clustering several times and builds a consensus graph in which document pairs that are frequently assigned to the same community receive stronger links. This is intended to make the results more reproducible.

=== Number of topics and refinement ===
The number of topics can be specified or determined automatically. In automatic mode, several resolution parameters are tested and compared by the coherence of the resulting keywords. The document representations are then iteratively moved towards the centre of their topic and re-clustered until consecutive partitions agree.

=== Topic representation ===
Topics are described by characteristic keywords and representative documents; keyword selection takes into account both how frequent a term is within a topic and how many of the topic's documents contain it. The publication also describes an archetype-based topic representation that considers boundary cases in addition to central documents. Unlike density-based clustering methods such as HDBSCAN, every document is assigned to a topic.

== Further features ==
The library supports partially guided topic modeling, in which known categories are supplied as seed topics while further topics can still emerge from the data. It also provides functions for analysing how topics change over time, hierarchical topic structures, and analysis tools aimed at empirical research, such as topic stability under resampling, thematic saturation and group comparisons.

Large language models are not required to form the topics. They can optionally be used after clustering to name and describe topics.

== Evaluation ==
In the original publication, TriTopic was compared with LDA, non-negative matrix factorization and BERTopic on the 20 Newsgroups, BBC News, AG News and arXiv datasets. The author reports a mean normalized mutual information (NMI) of 0.575 for TriTopic, compared with 0.513 for BERTopic, 0.416 for NMF and 0.299 for LDA. No independent comparative evaluations have been published so far.

== Applications and limitations ==
The documentation lists open-ended survey responses, interviews, customer reviews, news articles, social media posts and support tickets as typical applications, for collections ranging from a few hundred to tens of thousands of texts. It describes the method as less suitable for very short text snippets, for long documents covering many themes (which should be split into sections first) and for corpora of millions of documents.

Draft: Sakibphobia

Draft text:
----

Sakibphobia is a social and psychological construct that refers to the constant fear, distaste, or hostility against people who seem to be better, more talented, more skilled, or more successful than the self. According to the Bangladeshi interdisciplinary scholar S M Nazmuz Sakib, the phenomenon derives from toxic comparative theory. He came up with the term and defined it as a form of phobia in his working paper titled S M Nazmuz Sakib's Toxic Comparative Theory: An Analysis of Sakibphobia that was published on the Cambridge University Press website on 12 April 2023.

In toxic comparative theory, which Sakib proposed as an alternative to normal social comparison theory, the victim is caught in a cycle of self-hatred and anxiety because of comparing him/herself to a person that seems to be better in terms of success. Contemporary societies, social media, education system, and business environment encourage this type of social competition, thus provoking feelings of inadequacy in individuals. To provide his theory with mathematical support, Sakib formulated an equation for estimating the extent of Sakibphobia in an individual or community.

Following the publication of the working paper, numerous peer-reviewed and preprint papers were published that addressed different aspects of Sakibphobia. In 2024, a journal article published at SSRN investigated the phenomenon's effects on people's mental health using the paradigms of structural functionalism, symbolic interactionism, and conflict theories. A study published in 2025 used qualitative data collection techniques to test whether toxic comparison fits into sociological models. In 2026, another paper discussed similarities between Sakibphobia, Emersonian self-reliance, and Sankara's Advaita Vedanta.

There have been critics of the concept since its inception. They claim that it pathologises a normal psychological process that can be explained with existing psychological disorders such as social anxiety disorder or low self-esteem. Moreover, some people find fault with the use of Sakib's name for the newly invented condition, arguing that it makes it difficult to separate scientific research from promoting the scholar himself. However, supporters say that there is a need for new terminology in this case.

Draft: William Gill (surgeon)

Draft text:
----

William Gill (1795 – 14 September 1863) was a British-born surgeon and naturalist who practiced in the Cape Colony. He is best known for the large bequest in his will that established Gill College in Somerset East (today KwaNojoli), one of the older educational institutions in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa [ref: Gedenkboek van die Nederduits-Gereformeerde Kerk Somerset Oos, Cape Times Beperk].

== Early life and training ==
Gill was born in Market Harborough, Leicestershire, in 1795. He completed a five-year medical apprenticeship (1810–1815) with Thomas Peck in Wellingborough, Northamptonshire, and studied medicine at the University of Glasgow. In 1818 he was admitted as a Member of the Royal College of Surgeons of England (MRCS) and as a licentiate of the Society of Apothecaries. He spent a year travelling in continental Europe, during which he developed a lasting interest in botany [ref: S2A3 Biographical Database of Southern African Science, www.s2a3.org.za].

== Career in the Cape Colony ==
Gill arrived at the Cape in June 1818 and was licensed to practise as a surgeon, accoucheur and apothecary later that year. He first served as district surgeon at Caledon and later settled in the Zwartland district (near present-day Malmesbury) in 1822, where he was noted for his work during a typhoid outbreak. [ref: South Africa: its medical history 1652-1898; a medical and social study, Struik]

In 1826 he undertook an expedition northward for hunting and natural-history collecting, reaching as far as Kuruman, where he met the explorer and geologist Andrew Geddes Bain. He suffered heavy losses when his wagons were destroyed and returned to Cape Town in 1827. Around the same period he collected plant and shell fossils along the Sundays River east of Uitenhage. [ref: Botanical Exploration of Southern Africa, SANBI]

On the recommendation of the Rev. George Thom, Gill was appointed district surgeon of the newly established settlement of Somerset (later Somerset East) in 1829. He maintained a private practice there for many years and became a respected member of the local community. When the district surgeoncy was abolished in 1845, Gill declined an alternative appointment as resident surgeon on Robben Island, instead continuing to practicing medicine in the town. He also acquired a number of farms in the district and became a wealthy merino sheep farmer.

He co-founded the Somerset Reading Society in 1832 and was a member of the Literary, Scientific and Medical Society of Grahamstown [ref: Grahamstown Journal, 15 March 1856, p. 2, "Literary, Scientific and Medical Society"]. He continued to collect botanical specimens, particularly orchids, and sold approximately 400 specimens that eventually reached the Herbarium at Kew Gardens. Several plant species, including Myrsine gillianus [ref: [https://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=2565-2 Threatened Species Programme | SANBI Red List of South African Plants]], Aspalathus gillii [ref: ] and Erica gillii [ref: ], were named in his honor.

== Death and legacy ==
Gill, unmarried, died of oedema on 14 September 1863 in Somerset East, aged 68 [ref: [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSQF-XS99-P?view=index&personArk=%2Fark%3A%2F61903%2F1%3A1%3AQGLF-GL2N&action=view&lang=en Cape Province. Probate Records 1861–1862, 1863]]. In his will dated 19 January 1863 he left the bulk of his estate, approximately £23,000, to “found and maintain an institution of higher education in the Eastern Province.” Local residents raised money for the buildings. The Gill College Corporation was formed, land was granted in 1867, and the college opened on 18 March 1869. Its architecture was modelled on that of the University of Glasgow. Originally intended as a university college, it later became a high school (from 1903) and continues today as a co-educational dual-medium school.

Gill’s remains were reinterred in front of the college in 1916.

== References ==

Joseph Kamusiime (born 5 March 1972) is a Ugandan businessman and retired military officer. He served in the Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) and was attached to the Joint Anti-Terrorism Taskforce (JATT). He owns Davanti Union Ltd, a company involved in real estate, construction, and agriculture.

=== Early Life and Education ===
Kamusiime was born on 5 March 1972 in Nyarushanje village, Rubabo County, Rukungiri District, Uganda.

He attended Katojo Primary School (1978–1981) and [https://www.mindat.org/feature-11669649.html Katurika Primary School] (1982–1984), completing his primary education in 1984. He then attended St Francis Secondary School Rutooma, Rukungiri (1985), and Kigezi High School, Kabale (1986–1988), graduating in 1988.

Kamusiime enrolled at Makerere University in 1991, earning a Bachelor of Arts in Social Administration and Literature in 1994, graduating on 20 January 1995. He later pursued a Bachelor of Laws at Kampala International University on a weekend programme, graduating on 25 November 2023.

=== Military Career ===
Kamusiime joined the Uganda People's Defence Force in 1995. He was attached to the Joint Anti-Terrorism Taskforce, and from 2001 to 2006 he served as special assistant to the Chief of Military Intelligence in charge of counter-terrorism. He retired on 31 July 2009 at the rank of Captain. [ref: ]

=== Authorship ===
Kamusiime is the author of Alcohol The Silent Killer, published by New Vision Printing and Publishing Company in 2022 (ISBN 978-9913-9800-0-5). [ref: Aristoc Bookstore, aristocbooklex.com]

=== Business Career ===
Kamusiime owns Davanti Union Ltd, which holds a 10% shareholding in Taifa Partners Ltd. Davanti Union was involved in financing a UGX 13 billion silo project for Uganda Prisons Services awarded to Taifa Partners. [ref: ]

Kamusiime is also Managing Director of Cacafe Agro Ltd, which engages in value addition for coffee and cocoa products. He is the authorised representative and attorney for [https://davantiunion.co.ug/ Davanti Union Ltd's] shareholding in Taifa Partners Ltd. [ref: URSB User Portal, eregistry.ursb.go.ug]

=== Farming ===
Kamusiime operates a farm at [http://www.lcmt.org/uganda/rukungiri/nyarushanje/burora/kyaruhotora Kyaruhotora, Rubabo County, Rukungiri District]. The farm engages in Ankole breed cattle keeping, goat and sheep rearing, and small-scale coffee farming on approximately 200 acres. [ref: Kyaruhotora Village, in Burora Parish, Nyarushanje Subcounty, Rukungiri District, Uganda, www.lcmt.org]

=== Legal and Public Controversies ===
Criminal Case No. 834/2023 (Uganda v Asiimwe Emmanuel) [ref: Shs13b silo project for Uganda prisons mired in controversy, Monitor]

Kamusiime, on behalf of [https://davantiunion.co.ug/ Davanti Union Ltd], lodged a criminal complaint against Emmanuel Asiimwe for forgery and utterance of documents in the name of Taifa Partners Ltd. Davanti Union holds 10% of Taifa Partners, while Asiimwe holds 90%. The case was before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrates Court. Asiimwe denied the charges.
