Ada Kate Uchegbu (born September 30, 1982) is a Nigerian journalist, author, media entrepreneur, and political figure. She is the founder and publisher of Distinguished Africans Magazine and the CEO of ADA Consolidated Nigeria Limited. In 2025, she declared her intention to run for the presidency of Nigeria in the 2027 general elections under the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), advocating for structural reforms, gender inclusion, and generational shifts in governance.

== Early life and education ==
Ada Kate Uchegbu was born on September 30, 1982, in Nigeria. She completed her higher education at the National Open University of Nigeria. Seeking further specialization in communications and language, she attended the National Broadcast Academy in Lagos and studied at Alliance Française in Lagos. She holds the traditional Igbo title of Iyom Omelorah.

== Career ==
=== Journalism and media ===
Uchegbu began her career in writing and media, focusing on investigative reporting across West Africa. Her coverage frequently addresses governance, systemic inequality, economic issues, and national insecurity. Notable among her editorial works is "Roads of Blood – The Kidnap Highway," an investigative piece dealing with kidnapping incidents in Nigeria.

She established the media firm ADA Consolidated Nigeria Limited and subsequently founded Distinguished Africans Magazine, serving as its Editor-in-Chief. The publication acts as a pan-African platform focused on celebrating local achievements, cultural promotion, and documenting the profiles of African leaders and innovators.

=== Literary works ===
As an author, Uchegbu has written across both non-fiction political commentary and creative fiction:
* Wings of Destiny: My Journey Through Power, Politics and the Dream of Nigeria's First Female President (2026) – A political memoir evaluating her experiences within the Nigerian political space and advocating for female political participation.
* Ada the Future President – A children's book series focusing on civic responsibility and leadership.
* Kidnapped and The Dark Testament – Fiction books exploring contemporary socio-political anxieties.
* African Short Horror Stories (Volume 1 and 2) – Fiction collections utilizing traditional African folklore, superstitions, and supernatural motifs.

== Political activism and 2027 presidential campaign ==
Uchegbu's political career spans over a decade of continuous participation, during which she contested positions including the Anambra State House of Assembly, the PDP National Women Leadership, and an APC gubernatorial primary in Anambra State.

In June 2025, Uchegbu officially declared her intention to run for the President of Nigeria in the 2027 general election under the platform of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP). Running under the campaign blueprint titled "The New Covenant," she argues that Nigeria's recurring socio-economic challenges stem from heavily recycled leadership and structural stagnation. She stands prominently as an advocate against the exclusion of women from major political party tickets, arguing that true democracy cannot be achieved without fair gender representation at the highest executive levels.

Her key campaign policy promises include:
* The establishment of a ₦150 billion Youth Enterprise Fund.
* Fully digitized public administration systems to counter institutional corruption.
* Standardized community health reforms and community-oriented policing.
* Increased representation of youth and women in the national cabinet.

== Media appearances ==
Uchegbu has utilized broadcast media platforms to advocate for structural reforms and greater inclusion of women within Nigeria's executive governance. Between late 2025 and 2026, she made several appearances on Silverbird Television and Radio Nigeria network news broadcasts. During these sessions, she argued against the political recycling of leadership and detailed her policy platform, "The Mother's Care," which calls for community-focused national safety nets and structural shifts in party primary nomination processes.

An independent story

== Built from the ground up. ==
The Last Recruit is an independent rock band from Leigh-on-Sea, founded by school friends brought together through a shared passion for music, recording and live performance. The band has evolved from performing grunge covers in local youth venues into writing, recording and independently releasing original music spanning pop, alternative rock, grunge and metal.

The short version

== A timeline ==

== of the noise. ==
Key points in the band's evolution, from the first name to the next chapter.

# 2024Celestial Horizon formed.
# 2025The Last Recruit name and new era began.
# 2026Life album released.
# 20262016 single released.
# 2026+The Descend era.

01

== The Genesis ==
The band's journey began in 2024 under the name Celestial Horizon. Inspired by bands such as Nirvana, Green Day and other alternative rock acts, the original lineup performed covers at school events, Music-on-Sea performances and local venues around Southend and Leigh-on-Sea. These early performances established the band's energetic live reputation and sparked an ambition to begin writing original material.

02

== Rebirth & the DIY philosophy ==
In 2025 the group adopted the name The Last Recruit, marking the beginning of a new era. Around the same time, the band experienced the departure of its founding bassist, Thomas Layton. Instead of bringing the project to an end, frontman Nicolas Rodrigues and drummer Sam Risbin continued writing together. They also welcomed a new bassist named Charlie.The philosophy was simple: create the best recordings possible using whatever equipment was available.Determined to learn every stage of music production, Nicolas spent months teaching himself recording, editing, mixing and mastering through experimentation rather than formal training.

03

== The making of Life ==
This approach led to the creation of the band's debut album, Life. Recorded almost entirely in Nicolas' bedroom over approximately six months, the project represented the band's first full-scale original release. Most of the album was recorded using microphones placed in front of amplifiers and vocal performances.

=== The Life tracking station ===
A glimpse into the original bedroom studio.

Early bedroom studio

Musically, Life surprised many people familiar with the band's live performances. While audiences knew The Last Recruit as a grunge and alternative rock band, the album explored a far more melodic and pop-influenced direction.

04

== Fog & friction ==
Among the songs featured on Life, “Field of Fog” and “Hole of the Bump” stand as the album's two defining pieces, together capturing its central themes and emotional identity.

“Field of Fog” reflects on memory, nostalgia and childhood. The song contrasts the warmth of early memories with the uncertainty of growing older. By contrast, “Hole of the Bump” explores physical pain and discomfort.The completion of Life marked a turning point. Every lesson learned during the album became the foundation for future releases.Although Life represented a major creative achievement, its commercial release proved to be the band's greatest logistical challenge. During digital distribution, repeated moderation issues forced the removal of two completed recordings: “50s Ghosts” and a professionally recorded version of “Life”.

05

== The 2016 bridge ==
Following the completion of Life, The Last Recruit entered a new stage of development. The knowledge gained from months of recording, mixing and experimenting during the album's production allowed the band to work with a much faster and more refined creative process. This evolution became clear with the standalone single 2016, a song that represented the connection between the melodic world of Life and the heavier direction of the upcoming Descend era.

Unlike the six-month production period of Life, 2016 was completed in approximately one week. The speed of the recording process demonstrated how much Nicolas' production workflow had developed, allowing the band to move from writing an idea to releasing a finished track far more efficiently. Shortly after completion, the song became available on streaming platforms, marking one of the fastest releases in The Last Recruit's history.

The production of 2016 combined the band's established bedroom recording methods with support from Belfairs Academy's music department. The majority of the track—including vocals, guitars, bass, editing, mixing and mastering—was completed by Nicolas inside his bedroom studio using his personal recording setup.

The drums were performed by Sam Risbin and recorded inside one of Belfairs Academy's music classrooms. With the assistance of a music teacher, two Zoom microphones were used to capture the drum performance before the recordings were combined into a stereo track and transferred back to Nicolas for editing and integration into the final production. This collaboration became another example of The Last Recruit's DIY approach: combining available resources, education and independent creativity to create original music.

=== The 2016 & Descend setup ===

Dr. Jamilu Isyaku Gwamna (MFR), known as the Sardaunan Gombe, is a Nigerian economist, businessman, and politician from Gombe State. Gwamna was born in Jekada Fari, Gombe Local Government Area, Gombe State.

Draft text:
The Last Letter is a romance novel including tragic elements by Rebecca Yarros, published by Entangled Publishing. The book came out in 2019 and alternates between letters and first-person viewpoints. Rebecca Yarros has written a lot of romance books, but her most popular work is the New York Times bestselling Empyrean Series, which is a romantic fantasy series.

== Plot description ==
Ella is a single mother of the twins Masie and Colt, and they live together at the Bed & Breakfast called Solitude, in Telluride, Colorado, which Ella runs. Chaos' whole life circles the military, and he’s in the same unit as Ella’s brother Ryan. Therefore he and Ella start having written correspondence, and they immediately find a connection, and ultimately fall in love.

Unfortunately Maise gets diagnosed with advanced neuroblastoma, and only has a 10 percent chance of surviving the year. Ella’s crushed and shortly after, she finds out that her brother died during a mission. When she doesn’t hear from Chaos, she believes that he died alongside her brother. But Chaos isn’t dead, he just couldn’t bring himself to answer Ella. When Ryan’s last wish is for him to go to Telluride and help Ella, he leaves the Army. But when he arrives at Solitude, he introduces him as Beckett Gentry, his real name, not revealing he’s Chaos. Ella's first response is to shut him out. She tells herself that she doesn’t need his help. But Beckett refuses to leave, and starts working with a search and rescue team in the mountains. Over time Ella let him in more and more, and when he meets the children, they immediately connect. With time Beckett earns her trust, and they eventually fall in love. Together they fight Maise’s cancer and take care of the twins.

But Masie’s treatments are expensive, and the insurance Ella signed for the kids isn’t enough to cover everything. Eventually they discover that Becketts' insurance is enough, and therefore Ella allows him to adopt the kids. But shortly after the papers are signed, the insurance company starts questioning the adoption. For them to believe that the adoption was an act of love, Beckett and Ella need evidence that Beckett knew the twins before Masie got sick. Beckett realises that the only way for his insurance to cover Maise’s treatments, is to show the company his and Ella’s letters. This is the evidence they need, but it also means that Ella will discover his lie.

Ella’s whole world breaks down once again. Beckett apologises deeply and tries to explain that his love isn’t a lie. But Ella doesn’t ever want to see his face again. The twins are incredibly sad that Beckett no longer is a part of their life. But when Beckett one afternoon needs to pick Colt up from suspension, since Ella is at the hospital with Masie, everyone realises how much the kids miss Beckett. Therefore he and Ella find a way to coexist, and they eventually find their way back together. At the same time, they find out that Masie is cancer free, which makes everyone unbelievably happy.

Unfortunately the unthinkable happens. During one of the twins’ field trips, Beckett and his rescue team find out that Colt is missing. While walking on the trail, he and his classmate Emma tripped off a steep cliff, and Colt risked himself to save Emma. They eventually find Colt in very bad condition, and there’s nothing Beckett can do to save him. Words can’t describe how big his, Ella’s and Masie’s grief are and together they mourn him. But with time that loss gets easier to carry, and in the end they manage to live through the pain.

== Major themes ==

=== Learning to trust ===
During her life, Ella has had a lot of experience with men leaving her behind. First her father and then her brother, who often promised to soon be out of the Army, but then ended up dead instead. Her ex husband Jeff, who she met at 18 years old and decided to marry in great haste, also left her after discovering that she was pregnant. Because of her trusting issues she also has a hard time with forgiving lies, and she doesn’t tolerate them. So when Beckett first arrives at Solitude, she believes that he’s the same as her brother and father, too restless to settle down and leaving as soon as reality gets too boring. But because Beckett already is in love with her, because of their written correspondence, and also promised Ryan to help her, he stays in Telluride. One step at a time he  finally earns her trust. But it takes a while, and she has a really hard time with letting him in and admitting to herself that she really is in love with him. But when the big lie is out, when Ella realises that Beckett and Chaos are the same person, and that Beckett has been lying to her during the eleven months that he’s been living at Solitude, her trust is broken. She’s mad at herself for letting Beckett in and believing and trusting him, since he was just like everyone else.
[truncated]

Constantime is an independent watchmaking brand and atelier founded in 2025 in Târgu Mureș, Transylvania, Romania, by Alin Constantin Mureșan. [ref: Het Dracula-horloge? Constantime zet Transsylvanië op de horlogekaart, 0024 Horloges] [ref: Mecanism elvețian, ADN transilvănean, După Afaceri Premium] Its first model, Constantime Genesis, was produced as a limited series of 25 pieces. [ref: Constantime: un atelier de ceasornicărie independentă construit în Târgu Mureș, Club Antreprenor]

Constantime makes small-series mechanical watches and uses references to Transylvanian architecture and history in their design. The watches use Swiss mechanical movements combined with components made and finished in the atelier, particularly the dials and hands; leather straps are made by a local artisan in Transylvania. [ref: CONSTANTIME Genesis participă la Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève 2026. Constantin A. Mureșan duce în premieră un brand românesc de orologerie de la Târgu Mureș pe scena internațională, LuxuryOnline]

== History ==

The first ideas that later developed into Constantime date to around 2017, when Alin Constantin Mureșan began considering the possibility of creating a watch that would carry his own design and personal imprint. [ref: Constantime Genesis: A Watch Born Beneath the Vaults of Transylvania, MrWatchMaster] The project developed over several years from an interest in watch design and mechanical movements into a dedicated watchmaking brand and atelier. [ref: Românul care a construit un ceas pentru Nadia Comăneci, iar acum și-a lansat propriul brand premium: CONSTANTIME, start-up.ro]

The name Constantime combines “Constantin”, part of the founder's name, with the English word “time”. [ref: Un orologer artizan român a creat un ceas pentru Nadia Comăneci cu primul 10 olimpic din istoria gimnasticii, Newsweek România]

== Transylvanian identity and Genesis ==

Transylvania became part of the identity of Constantime because the brand was created and developed in the region. Its architecture and history became a source of shapes and details used in the watches. [ref: Un ceas creat la Târgu Mureș duce simbolurile Transilvaniei la „Oscarurile” orologeriei, Cuvântul Liber]

The design of Genesis draws on the fortified architecture of Transylvania, including vaulted ceilings and arches found in medieval castles and fortified churches. Its sword-shaped hands and polished elements also refer to historical weapons associated with the region.

The name Genesis refers to the beginning of the Constantime project. The model was produced as a series of 25 numbered pieces; Constantime states that the number also refers to 2025, the year in which the brand was founded. [ref: Constantime Watches, Constantime]

== Watchmaking and production ==

The production process begins with raw brass used for the dial. The dial is machined, engraved, polished, coloured and finished in the Târgu Mureș atelier. The hands are also made and finished in the atelier.

These locally produced components are combined with a stainless-steel case, a Swiss mechanical movement and a leather strap made by a Transylvanian artisan. Constantime currently sources its cases externally, while developing its own case design with the aim of having future cases produced locally.

The atelier has stated that it intends to increase the proportion of components developed and produced locally and to expand its work on mechanical movements from finishing and customisation toward more complex modifications.

== Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève ==

In 2026, Constantime Genesis was entered in the Challenge category of the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG) and was included in the official selection. [ref: Un artizan din Târgu Mureș a creat un ceas unic pentru Nadia Comăneci, dedicat primului 10 din istoria gimnasticii, Revista LOR]

Alin Constantin Mureșan described the entry as an opportunity to present a project developed in Transylvania to an international watchmaking audience.

== Nadia Comăneci commemorative watch ==

In 2026, Constantime created a one-off mechanical watch for Romanian gymnast Nadia Comăneci to mark the 50th anniversary of the first perfect 10 in modern Olympic gymnastics, achieved at the 1976 Montreal Games. [ref: Mureș: Ceas personalizat pentru Nadia Comăneci cu primul 10 olimpic, creat de un artizan independent de ceasuri mecanice, AGERPRES]

The central design element was placed on the small-seconds subdial, which reproduced the “1.00” shown by the electronic scoreboard in Montreal. The scoreboard had not been designed to display a score of 10.00, so Comăneci's result appeared as 1.00. The design also incorporated her competition number.

The watch was personally presented to Comăneci by Alin Constantin Mureșan during anniversary events held in Onești, Romania.

== References ==

Draft text:
Ashirbek Kurbanovich Muminov (Kazakh: Әшірбек Құрбанұлы Муминов; born 18 July 1959) is a historian specializing in medieval Islam in Central Asia. His research includes Hanafi scholarship, Islamic manuscripts and the history of Islamic education.⁠[1]⁠[2]⁠[10]

= Early life and education =
Muminov grew up in Tashkent and attended Secondary School No. 1, where he studied Arabic from the second grade. He completed school in 1976 with a gold medal.⁠[1]⁠[10]

He entered the Arabic section of the Faculty of Oriental Languages at Tashkent State University in 1976 and graduated with honours in 1982. He qualified as an Arabic philologist and a teacher of Arabic and English languages and literature.⁠[7]

From 1987 to 1990, he undertook postgraduate research at the Leningrad branch of the Institute of Oriental Studies of the USSR Academy of Sciences under Stanislav Mikhailovich Prozorov. He defended his Candidate of Historical Sciences dissertation in Leningrad on 29 March 1991. It examined al-Kafawi’s Kata’ib a‘lam al-akhyar as a source for the history of Islam in Transoxiana.⁠[7] [ref: ИВР РАН (Санкт-Петербург) - Personalia, www.orientalstudies.ru]

On 24 June 2003, he defended his Doctor of Historical Sciences dissertation at Tashkent Islamic University. The study examined the significance of Hanafi scholars in the urban life of central Transoxiana.⁠[7]

= Academic career =
Muminov began his research career in 1982 at the Abu Rayhan Beruni Institute of Oriental Studies in Tashkent, working in the department responsible for source studies and cataloguing Oriental manuscripts. Detailed biographical accounts record research employment in 1982–1985 and 1990–1991.⁠[10] [ref: Ташкент-Алматы-Астана-Стамбул: Путь исламоведа, Qojalar.kz]

From 1991 to 1993, he headed the Department of Oriental Philology at Ahmed Yasawi University in Turkestan.⁠[10] He was an associate professor in the Department of Islamic Studies at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies from 1993 to 2005.⁠[8] [ref: ]

In 2005, he became deputy director of the R. B. Suleymenov Institute of Oriental Studies in Almaty, serving until 2013.⁠[8]⁠[10] From 2013 to 2016, he headed the Department of Religious Studies at L. N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University in Astana.⁠[8] In 2016, IRCICA identified him as consultant to its director general on Central Asian studies.⁠[2] [ref: ]

= International research appointments =
In 1998, Muminov was a visiting professor in the Fourth Section of the École pratique des hautes études (EPHE), at the Sorbonne in Paris, working with F. Déroche. He returned to the institution in 2002 as a visiting professor in its Fifth Section, working with D. Aigle.⁠[8]

The Alexander von Humboldt Foundation records a research fellowship at Ruhr University Bochum, hosted by Stefan Reichmuth, with sponsorship beginning on 1 October 1999. Muminov’s CV dates the research visit to 1999–2001.⁠[8]⁠[9]

In 2006, he was a visiting scholar at Indiana University, researching Islamization and sacred genealogies in Central Asia. He also held a visiting professorship at Zentrum Moderner Orient in Berlin in 2011.⁠[8]

He was a Fulbright Visiting Scholar at Indiana University Bloomington from September 2011 to June 2012. From September 2012 to June 2013, he held a senior fellowship at Koç University’s Research Center for Anatolian Civilizations in Istanbul.⁠[8]

In April–June 2015, he was a visiting scholar at Nanjing University in China.⁠[8]

= Research =
From 2001 to 2008, he participated in the “Manuscript heritage of Central Asia” project at CNRS in Paris, directed by Maria Szuppe. He subsequently participated in the project “Manuscript traditions of Iran, India and Central Asia” (2009–2012), directed by Szuppe and Nalini Balbir.⁠[8]

Muminov collaborated with Bakhtiyar Babadjanov and Anke von Kügelgen on the 2007 volume Disputes on Muslim Authority in Central Asia (20th Century). The collection presents texts documenting religious debates in Soviet Central Asia. In a 2008 review, Canat Mahaşeva discussed its use of manuscripts and printed works preserved in private collections.⁠[4] [ref: (XX.yy. Orta Asya Müslüman Din Adamlarýnýn Polemikleri: Kritik Edisyon ve Kaynak Araþtýrmasý),, Ankara Üniversitesi İlahiyat Fakültesi Dergisi]

He also conducted research with Devin DeWeese on the Islamization of Central Asia and sacred lineages, published in the two-volume work Islamization and Sacred Lineages in Central Asia (2008 and 2013).

He co-edited Saduaqas Ghïlmani’s biographical collection with Allen Frank and Aitzhan Nurmanova. Published by IRCICA in 2018, the two-volume edition contains the Arabic-script Kazakh text and an English translation.⁠[5] In 2026, he edited Galiya Kambarbekova’s catalogue of Turkic manuscripts in Kazakhstan’s National Library.⁠[6] [ref: Biographies of the Islamic Scholars of Our Times, shop.ircica.org]

= Recognition =
In 2016, his book Hanafi Madhhab in the History of Central Asia won first place in the Islam category of the regional Book of the Year competition for Russian-language scholarship on Islam and Iran. The award was presented on 1 December 2016.⁠[3] [ref: ]

= Languages =
His CV lists Kazakh, Uzbek and Russian as native languages, and Arabic, Turkish and English as fluent languages. It also records reading knowledge of German, French, Persian and the Turkic languages of Central Asia.⁠[8]
[truncated]

Malek Alshammari (Arabic: مالك عويد الشمري) is an orthopedic surgeon practising in Kuwait, specializing in hip and knee surgery. Al Salam Hospitals lists him as a consultant orthopedic surgeon whose clinical interests include hip and knee joint replacement, robotic-assisted knee replacement, arthroscopy, and the treatment of sports injuries and degenerative joint conditions. [ref: Dr. Malek Alshammari, Al Salam Hospitals]

== Education and postgraduate training ==
According to his official biography, Alshammari graduated from the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland. He subsequently completed specialty training and board qualification in orthopedic surgery before undertaking further clinical training in Canada. [ref: ]

His website describes three fellowships completed at McGill University in Montreal and the University of British Columbia in Vancouver. These covered hip and knee arthroplasty, joint reconstruction, arthroscopy, and sports surgery.

=== McGill University ===
Alshammari's official biography states that he completed a fellowship in hip and knee arthroplasty at McGill University, with clinical training at the Jewish General Hospital in Montreal. The training encompassed adult joint reconstruction, including primary hip and knee replacement and complex revision procedures.

The stated scope also included the management of infections associated with joint replacements and fractures around prosthetic joints.

=== University of British Columbia ===
According to the same biography, Alshammari subsequently completed a fellowship in hip and knee arthroplasty at the University of British Columbia. This training focused on adult reconstruction, complex revision joint replacement, and the management of bone loss.

He then undertook an additional fellowship in hip and knee arthroscopy, reconstructive procedures, and sports surgery. His biography describes training in hip preservation, femoroacetabular impingement, acetabular labral injuries, knee ligament reconstruction, and injuries involving multiple knee ligaments. It also lists training in meniscal surgery and the treatment of patellar conditions.

== Clinical practice ==
Al Salam Hospitals identifies Alshammari as a consultant orthopedic surgeon within its Orthopedic, Spinal Surgery and Sports Injuries Center. Its professional profile lists hip and knee replacement, robotic-assisted knee replacement, and hip and knee arthroscopy among his principal areas of practice.

His official website identifies his clinic as being at Al Salam Al Assima Hospital in Kuwait.

=== Joint replacement and reconstruction ===
The hospital profile lists hip and knee arthroplasty among Alshammari's specialties, together with robotic-assisted knee replacement. It identifies hip and knee osteoarthritis as conditions within his clinical practice.

His official biography additionally describes a practice encompassing both primary and revision hip and knee replacement. The revision component is consistent with the areas of postgraduate training described on his website.

=== Arthroscopy and hip preservation ===
Alshammari's hospital profile lists arthroscopy of both the hip and knee. It also identifies hip pain and femoroacetabular impingement among the conditions he treats.

His website describes further interests in hip preservation and the treatment of acetabular labral injuries. These areas are included in its account of his arthroscopy and sports surgery fellowship training.

=== Knee ligament and meniscal surgery ===
Al Salam Hospitals lists knee ligament injuries, meniscal injuries, patellar disorders, and patellar instability among his clinical interests.

His official biography describes a scope of practice that includes reconstruction of the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, collateral ligament reconstruction, and treatment of injuries involving multiple knee ligaments. It also lists high tibial osteotomy and procedures addressing patellar disorders.

== Professional activities ==
Alshammari is included on the published speaker list of the 4th Kuwait Orthopedic Conference. [ref: 4th Kuwait Orthopedic Conference, kworthoconf.com]

== Selected Publications ==

* Alshammari MO, de Petrillo G, Epure LM, Huk OL, Zukor DJ, Antoniou J. (2023). "Outcomes of Ceramic-On-Ceramic Bearing Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Minimum 10-Year Follow-Up Study." The Journal of Arthroplasty. 38 (7S): S146–S151. doi:10.1016/j.arth.2023.04.018. PMID:37084924. [ref: Outcomes of Ceramic-On-Ceramic Bearing Total Hip Arthroplasty: A Minimum 10-Year Follow-Up Study, The Journal of Arthroplasty]

Draft text:
Josh Pacewicz is an American sociologist, who is an Associate Professor of Sociology and Urban Studies at Brown University and a 2020 Guggenheim Fellow. [ref: ] His research interests are in the areas of political sociology, historical sociology, urban sociology, the sociology of law, and American political development. [ref: Pacewicz, Josh, vivo.brown.edu]

== Education and Career ==
Pacewicz holds a bachelor’s degree from The University of Texas-Austin, Plan II Honors program. He graduated from the University of Chicago with a Ph.D in Sociology in 2010. [ref: Pacewicz, Josh, vivo.brown.edu] His dissertation was supervised by Andrew Abbott, Elisabeth Clemens, Andreas Glaeser, and Susan Gal. [ref: Pacewicz, Josh, vivo.brown.edu]

From 2010 to 2012, Pacewicz was an ASA Postdoctoral Fellow on the Current Economic Crisis at Stanford University, under the supervision of Mark Granovetter. [ref: Pacewicz, Josh, vivo.brown.edu] He joined the faculty at Brown University in 2012. [ref: Pacewicz, Josh, vivo.brown.edu]

== Research Areas and Books ==
Pacewicz’s research focuses on American statecraft and subnational governance, especially the interplay between federal policy and party politics, municipal finance, political advocacy and expertise, and more generally the democratic process. His research relies primarily on interviews with legislators, state agency employees, municipal officials, and other policy workers. Pacewicz has written about qualitative case selection and comparison [ref: What Can You Do With a Single Case? How to Think About Ethnographic Case Selection Like a Historical Sociologist, Sociological Methods & Research] [ref: After Positivism: New Approaches to Comparison in Historical Sociology, Columbia University Press], and he is the author of two books about American political development and federalism.

In his 2016 book Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the post-Keynesian Society, Pacewicz examines municipal and partisan politics in two Rust Belt cities during the 2008 and 2012 election cycles. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press] The book shows how changes in American federalism—the corporate merger waves that followed 1970s-era financial deregulation and changes in the prevailing logics of inter-governmental finance—eroded the traditional base of both political parties, thus creating an opening for activists to take over grassroots politics, especially within the GOP. Partisans and Partners was a co-winner of the American Sociological Association’s Theory prize. [ref: Past Awards, ASA Theory Section]

His 2027 book, Divided States: Doing Federalism in Red and Blue America, centers officials who interpret and administer federal rights and programs in the states and documents their ongoing efforts to make real the promises of flagship social programs and civil rights guarantees. [ref: global.oup.com] In Republican states, this resulted in policies that were less extreme than legislators’ frontstage rhetoric, but also contributed to an extremist and antidemocratic reorientation among Republicans, who used the architecture of state government to decouple legislative initiatives from their street-level consequences.

== Awards ==
Pacewicz’s articles have received prizes from the American Sociological Association’s Historical-Comparative Section (2016) and Community and Urban Sociology Section (2015 and 2021). [ref: ] [ref: ] He has won an award from the Society for the Advancement of Socio-Economics (SASE) and was a 2020 Guggenheim Fellow. [ref: annual prize, Oxford Academic] [ref: Guggenheim Fellowships: Supporting Artists, Scholars, & Scientists, www.gf.org]

Draft: Brookie (food)

Draft text:
----

A brookie is type of bar cookie and hybrid dessert that combines aspects and ingredients from cookies and brownies. The batter of a brownie and the dough of a cookie are usually made separately and then combined before baking. This can either be done by layering the batter and dough or by scooping one after the other into the pan. [ref: The Vanderbilt Hustler, Reaching Out] [ref: brookie, dictionary.cambridge.org]

Brookies are usually baked in square or rectangular baking pans, like brownies. This causes brookies to be similar in size and shape to brownies. Brookies often have a fudgy or cakey texture, like brownies, while also keeping the chewy texture from cookies.

The brownie batter is often made with cocoa powder, sugar, eggs, flour and other ingredients. The cookie dough may include flour, eggs, brown sugar, and other ingredients. [ref: Turn leftover Creme Eggs into a gooey ‘brookie’ traybake, The Independent] [ref: The Vanderbilt Hustler, The New Gold Standard] In addition, they may also be made with chocolate chips, rolled oats, nuts, or dried fruits. Brookies are often baked and served like brownies, and they may be served with a variety of accompaniments such as milk, ice cream, fruit, coffee or whipped cream. [ref: ]

== Variations ==
Multiple variations of the brookie have been created. Many recipes substitute or add ingredients to have different flavors, textures or variations that meet dietary needs.

Vegan brookies are brookies made without any animal products. They are made to replace the butter, eggs, and milk chocolate chips using substitutes like apple sauce, vegetable oil, vegan butter and vegan chocolate chips.

Pumpkin swirl brookies are pumpkin or pumpkin spice flavored brookies. They are made with canned pumpkin puree and can additionally have cinnamon, nutmeg, allspice, pumpkin pie spice, ginger, cottage cheese, butterscotch chips and other spices. Pumpkin swirl brookies and typically more orange than regular brookies.

Peanut butter brookies are made by adding peanut butter to the brownie batter. Peanut butter brookies can also be made with various other nut butters like almond butter, walnut butter, cookie butter, and others nut butters. [ref: Pic's Really Good Recipe Book, Random House New Zealand]

Brookies themselves can also be made into ice cream by blending or cutting brookies and adding it to the ice cream as it is being churned. [ref: Carvel Drops New Brookie Ice Cream Flavor That´s a Mashup of Two Favorite Desserts] This ice cream can then be made into milkshakes by blending the brookie ice cream with milk. [ref: Milkshake Recipes: 100 Creamy and Irresistible Milkshake Recipes for Every Craving and Occasion, Brad Hoskinson]

== History & Popularization ==
The brookie was invented in the late 20th century, in the United States, the exact origins are unknown. Many restaurants and bakeries claim to have invented the brookie. The earliest known mention of a brookie was in 1988, where The Vanderbilt Hustler shows a menu from Rafferty's Bar & Restaurant with the brookie listed as a dessert. [ref: The Vanderbilt Hustler, Celebrating a Century of Service to the Vanderbilt Community.]

In 2006, Joanna Crumley's Praline Brookies, a brookie variant combining pecan pralines and brookies, placed as a top 100 finalist competing for the $1,000,000 grand prize in the 42nd Pillsbury Bake-Off. [ref: Hubbard resident wins 2019 Pillsbury Bake-Off dessert category, becomes finalist, Statesman Journal] [ref: Praline Brookies Recipe, Pillsbury]

In 2014, Milk and Brookies was founded by Jovon English, Marques Brooks, Naimah Harris and Tisa Smart-Washington. [ref: milk + brookies, Milk + Brookies] In 2015, Milk and Brookies went on season 7 of Shark Tank seeking $100,000 for 20% equity. This offer was turned down. [ref: Week 4: Table 87, EZ-Pee-Z, Milk + Brookies, Dude Products] Later, in 2016 Milk and Brookies participated in the 2nd annual CookieCon in Los Angeles, California. [ref: Visit milk + brookies at LA Cookie Con 2016, milk + brookies]

In 2016, Harry Foster baked brookies for MasterChef Australia Series 8. [ref: Team Challenge: Royal Children's Hospital Fête]

Draft text:
Sunset Paradise is an Australian independent-animated action-adventure comedy web series created by Kevin and Luke Lerdwichagul, produced and animated by Glitch Productions, and funded by Screen Australia for YouTube. Serving as a spinoff of the sketch comedy machinima web series SMG4, it focuses on Meggy Spletzer, a character from said series, who decides to take a vacation in order to find the calling she needs, while also fighting a variety of criminals and her inner demon, Shadow Meggy. Unlike Meta Runner, which focuses on Tari as the protagonist but is set in a separate continuity, Sunset Paradise is set within the SMG4 continuity, but remains in a standalone nature to put sole focus on Meggy's ongoing character arc.

Prio to the series, Meggy Spletzer first appeared as a major character in the machinima parody web series SMG4, also created by Luke Lerdwichagul. The series premiered on the GLITCH YouTube channel on 26 March 2021, with new episodes being released weekly from 4 June to 30 July of that year.

== Sypnosis ==
Sometime after winning the final Splatfest and fulfilling her promise to her friend Desti in the first SMG4 feature-length movie, "Meggy's Destiny," Meggy has found it increasingly hard to figure out what she wants to do with her life that gives her a purpose. To help sort herself out with some much-needed relaxation, she takes a vacation to Port Aurora, the island paradise home of the Aura Boras, and host to all manner of colorful tourists, leaving her dear friends behind. Unfortunately for her, the town has become plagued with criminal activity in the lead-up to its Phoenix Festival which takes place once every 100 years, and the closest thing the island has to an authority figure is the inept deputy Auri Bori who Meggy meets and befriends. If she wants to get any peace and quiet, Meggy will need to team up with Auri and lay down the law and bring justice as Port Aurora's new sheriff, leading to one heck of a crazy misadventure. Along the way, she not only has to battle a diverse cast of criminals including the Spud Buds, a rowdy gang of potato thugs, Whisk, a sly, but shy cat burglar, the Funky Fource, a team of super villainous robotic dancers, and the infamous criminal mastermind leading them, Sir Benedict Cumbersnatch, but also dealing with her inner demon self, Shadow Meggy.

== Characters ==

=== Main ===
* Meggy Speltzer (voiced by Lizzie Freeman) is an inkling-turned human and the main protagonist of the series. She goes on a vacation to Port Aurora to figure out what to do next in life, while also helping to fight criminals on the island. Freeman reprises her role as Meggy from SMG4.
* Auri Bori (voiced by Aimee Smith) is the secondary protagonist of the series, who is a young inept, but well-intentioned Aura Bora who is the self-proclaimed deputy of Port Aurora. In the penultimate episode, he sacrificed himself to save Meggy from the laser shot by Benedict at the top of the tower, but was later revived in the series finale.
* Mayora Bora (voiced by Jasmine Yang) is the tritagonist of the series. He is the mayor of Port Aurora. In "Mad Meggy", he was ultimately killed by the Funky Fource when he sacrificed himself to save Meggy and Auri.

=== Villains ===
* Benedict Cumbersnatch (voiced by Edwyn Tiong) is the main antagonist of the series. He is the crime boss of Port Aurora's criminal underworld who, after a confrontation with Auri's grandfather which resulted in the latter’s death, Benedict was cursed to be reduced into an egg-shaped form, forcing him to rely on the Goonies, alongside the Spud Buds, Whisk, and the Funky Fource. He wants to utilize Aloysius's ashes to bring him back to his original form, gain the Phoenix Egg to harness its power, and rule Port Aurora. However, he is defeated for good by Meggy and Auri.
* The Spud Buds (voiced by Kevin Lerdwichagul, Luke Lerdwichagul & Jasmine Yang) are major antagonists in the series. They are a gang of anthropomorphic potato bandits terrorizing Port Aurora and contribute to the crime occurring on the island, and are under the command of Benedict. Their names are Yam, Mash, Duke, & Russet.
* Whisk (voiced by Amber May) is the secondary antagonist in the series. She is a world-class cat thief who's always brimming with confidence and skill, whenever she's wearing her mask, that is. Without it, she turns into a literal scaredy-cat, and is under the command of Benedict.
* The Funky Fource (all voiced by Anthony Sardinha) are major antagonists in the series. They are a "funkalicious foursome of crime-fighting superheroes" who crush evil through the power of dance...or so they claim. In truth, they're frauds who harbor a dark secret behind their acts of derring-do, and are under the command of Benedict. After the fall of benedict, they are forced to fix the damage they caused. Their names are Frank Fresh, Freddy Fresh, Felix Fresh & Phil Fresh.
* Goonies - The recurring antagonsists of the series. They are silent, hulking Aura Boras serving under Benedict's whim as his army of henchmen. They are now working as ice-cream vendors with Aziz.
* Shadow Meggy (voiced by Lizzie Freeman) is one of the two overarching antagonists of the series. She is a mysterious entity and the dark counterpart of Meggy, who exists in her subconscious mind, serving as the manifestation of her negative thoughts and emotions, and the reason Meggy is even visiting Port Aurora in the first place.
[truncated]

Kh. Asadul Islam, also known as Kh. Asadul Islam Ripon, is a Bangladeshi financial executive and capital-market professional. He has served as the managing director and chief executive officer of Alliance Capital Asset Management Limited since June 2014. His previous positions include chief executive officer of IDLC Securities Limited, executive vice president and head of brokerage at The City Bank Limited, and managing director and chief executive officer of City Brokerage Limited. [ref: ]

His professional activities have included securities brokerage, investment management, institutional investor services, and commentary on Bangladesh's capital-market development. He also briefly served as a non-executive director of Asia Frontier Capital in 2013–2014. [ref: Asia Frontier Capital (AFC) - Asia Frontier Capital, www.asiafrontiercapital.com]

== Career ==

=== Early career ===
Islam began his professional career at Premium Securities Limited before moving to Peregrine Capital Limited and Union Capital Limited. In 2002, he became a director of SES Company Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of Union Capital, where he remained until 2006. He subsequently joined IDLC Securities Limited, serving as its chief executive officer. [ref: Kh Asadul joins City Bank as Head of Brokerage, today.thefinancialexpress.com.bd]

In July 2009, Islam joined The City Bank Limited as executive vice president and head of brokerage, following his tenure at IDLC Securities.

=== City Brokerage Limited ===
On 24 November 2010, The Financial Express reported Islam's appointment as chief executive officer of City Brokerage Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of The City Bank Limited. He was also described in subsequent reporting as the company's founding managing director and CEO. [ref: City Brokerage Limited appoints new CEO, today.thefinancialexpress.com.bd]

During his tenure, City Brokerage provided securities brokerage services to local and foreign investors. In January 2014, The Daily Star quoted Islam on the growth of foreign portfolio investment in Bangladesh during 2013. He attributed the increase partly to macroeconomic indicators and discussed the influence of interest rates, exchange rates, and international market conditions on foreign investment. [ref: ]

=== Alliance Capital Asset Management Limited ===
In June 2014, Islam was appointed managing director and chief executive officer of Alliance Capital Asset Management Limited, an investment management company operating in Bangladesh's mutual-fund industry. [ref: ]

In November 2014, Alliance Capital announced plans to introduce a Shariah-based equity index for institutional investors. The proposed index, developed using research from S&P Dow Jones Indices, was intended to help institutional investors identify Shariah-compliant investment opportunities. Islam discussed the proposed product and its investment objectives in an interview with The Daily Star. The announcement concerned a planned launch rather than a confirmed launch of the index. [ref: ]

In October 2022, Alliance Capital received second place in the asset-management category of the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission's Golden Jubilee of Bangladesh awards, which recognized market intermediaries for their performance in 2021. The award was presented to the company during Islam's tenure as its managing director and CEO. [ref: ]

== International financial activities ==
In October 2013, Asia Frontier Capital, an investment firm focused on frontier markets, announced Islam's appointment as a non-executive director. At the time, he was serving as the managing director and CEO of City Brokerage Limited. [ref: Asia Frontier Capital — October 2013 Newsletter, www.asiafrontiercapital.com]

In February 2014, Asia Frontier Capital's newsletter featured an interview with Islam concerning Bangladesh's economic conditions, investment environment, and opportunities for international investors. [ref: Asia Frontier Capital (AFC) - February 2014 Newsletter - Asia Frontier Capital, www.asiafrontiercapital.com]

In April 2014, Asia Frontier Capital announced that Islam had stepped down from his directorship for personal reasons. [ref: Asia Frontier Capital (AFC) - October 2013 Newsletter - Asia Frontier Capital, www.asiafrontiercapital.com]

His international professional involvement also included discussions of foreign portfolio investment in Bangladesh's securities market through his roles in brokerage and asset management. [ref: ]

== Contributions to capital-market discussions ==
Islam has participated in public discussions on Bangladesh's securities market, investment-product diversification, regulatory coordination, and the participation of institutional and foreign investors.

In December 2011, The Daily Star published his article "Stockmarket: what next?", which examined market instability following the 2010–2011 stock-market decline. The article advocated greater coordination between financial regulators, more transparent supervision, and the introduction of diversified investment instruments, including bonds and index-traded funds. [ref: ]

In December 2016, The Daily Star quoted Islam on the performance of Bangladesh's stock market and the need to address financial indiscipline and limited investment-product diversification. [ref: ]

Draft text:
Niklas Elmehed is a Swedish painter. He is known for his paintings of vinyl and gold leafed Nobel Prize illustrations and portraits which become feature of Nobel Prize ceremonies held every year in the month of October. [ref: Meet Niklas, the artist behind the Nobel Prize portraits, The Business Standard] [ref: Nobel Prize: Meet the artist behind laureates’ illustrations, Yahoo News Singapore]
== Career ==
Elmehed pursued fine arts in Sweden. [ref: Who is Niklas Elmehed: The man behind the iconic illustrations of the 2025 Nobel laureates, The Times of India] He also developed an interest in science, history and journalism. He developed sketch drawings using black and white charcoal, while pursuing his higher studies at the KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. [ref: Behind Niklas Elmehed’s gold portraits of Nobel Prize winners, The Hindu] It was through mastering the craft of sketch drawings using black and white charcoal, he was inspired to paint drawings with the element of gold foil. He obtained his master's degree at both KTH Royal Institute of Technology and Royal Institute of Art.

He began painting the official portraits of Nobel Prize laureates in 2012. It was revealed that the Nobel Committee had come up with the solution of using paintings instead of relying on photographs in order to publish the images of Nobel Prize laureates officially and in 2012, Niklas was hired as an art director by the Nobel Media as one of the fewest steps taken by the Nobel Committee to address the longstanding issues related to poor quality photographs, photographs with copyright issues and low resolution images of the award winners that usually circulate online. Niklas had been tasked with the visual content during the Nobel Prize ceremonies ever since he took charge as art director in 2012. In 2017, Niklas came up with the idea of using gold foil in his portraits, when the Nobel Committee had decided that the main color to be incorporated during the prize announcements would be gold in a landmark move, following the transition of Nobel Prize which went through a graphical rebranding procedure. [ref: Meet The Artist Behind Those Gold-Leafed Nobel Prize Illustrations, NDTV] His paintings on Noble Prize laureates are frequently displayed and featured in news media outlets after the announcement of Noble Prize winners. His job role is monitored under close supervision and the job role also inculcates on the concept of strict confidentiality as he is one of the fewest individuals to learn about the official Nobel Prize winners well in advance before the official public announcements.

In 2025, Elmehed unveiled “The Golden Wall”, where he displayed and exhibited the portraits of Nobel Prize winners at the Nobel headquarters located in Stockholm, Sweden. He conducted a live painting performance at the Nordic Pavilion of World Expo 2025 in Osaka, Japan. He also displayed his work at the TEDxPatras 2025, where he delivered glimpses of visual storytelling to a large target audience. [ref: ] He also serves as a freelance artist for the Sweden men's national football team.

Draft text:
Josh Pacewicz is an American sociologist, who is an Associate Professor of Sociology and Urban Studies at Brown University and a 2020 Guggenheim Fellow. His research interests are in the areas of political sociology, historical sociology, urban sociology, the sociology of law, and American political development. [ref: ]

== Education and Career ==
Pacewicz holds a bachelor’s degree from The University of Texas-Austin, Plan II Honors program. He graduated from the University of Chicago with a Ph.D in Sociology in 2010. His dissertation was supervised by Andrew Abbott, Elisabeth Clemens, Andreas Glaeser, and Susan Gal. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press]

From 2010 to 2012, Pacewicz was an ASA Postdoctoral Fellow on the Current Economic Crisis at Stanford University, under the supervision of Mark Granovetter. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press] He joined the faculty at Brown University in 2012.

== Research Areas and Books ==
Pacewicz’s research focuses on American statecraft and subnational governance, especially the interplay between federal policy and party politics, municipal finance, political advocacy and expertise, and more generally the democratic process. His research relies primarily on interviews with legislators, state agency employees, municipal officials, and other policy workers. Pacewicz has written about qualitative case selection and comparison [ref: What Can You Do With a Single Case? How to Think About Ethnographic Case Selection Like a Historical Sociologist, Sociological Methods & Research] [ref: After Positivism: New Approaches to Comparison in Historical Sociology, Columbia University Press], and he is the author of two books about American political development and federalism.

In his 2016 book Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the post-Keynesian Society, Pacewicz examines municipal and partisan politics in two Rust Belt cities during the 2008 and 2012 election cycles. [ref: Partisans and Partners: The Politics of the Post-Keynesian Society, University of Chicago Press] The book shows how changes in American federalism—the corporate merger waves that followed 1970s-era financial deregulation and changes in the prevailing logics of inter-governmental finance—eroded the traditional base of both political parties, thus creating an opening for activists to take over grassroots politics, especially within the GOP. Partisans and Partners was a co-winner of the American Sociological Association’s Theory prize. [ref: Past Awards, ASA Theory Section]

His 2027 book, Divided States: Doing Federalism in Red and Blue America, centers officials who interpret and administer federal rights and programs in the states and documents their ongoing efforts to make real the promises of flagship social programs and civil rights guarantees. [ref: global.oup.com] In Republican states, this resulted in policies that were less extreme than legislators’ frontstage rhetoric, but also contributed to an extremist and antidemocratic reorientation among Republicans, who used the architecture of state government to decouple legislative initiatives from their street-level consequences.

== Awards ==
Pacewicz’s articles have received prizes from the American Sociological Association’s Historical-Comparative Section (2016) and Community and Urban Sociology Section (2015 and 2021). [ref: ] [ref: ] He has won an award from the Society for the Advancement of Socio-Economics (SASE) and was a 2020 Guggenheim Fellow. [ref: annual prize, Oxford Academic] [ref: Guggenheim Fellowships: Supporting Artists, Scholars, & Scientists, www.gf.org]

== References ==

Draft text:
Mattappilly Raman (1885–1971), also known as Raman Master, was an Indian painter, sculptor and art educator from the Kingdom of Cochin, in present-day Kerala. He studied art in Calcutta, founded the Cochin School of Arts in Ernakulam in 1932, and was given the title of "Palace Artist" by the Maharaja of Cochin. Under his direction the school became known for casting life-size bronze statues, including one of Sree Narayana Guru. [ref: The artists we forgot, The Hindu] [ref: Census of India 1961, Volume VII: Kerala, Part VII-A: Selected Crafts, Manager of Publications, Government of India] His sons M. R. D. Dattan and M. R. Baburam also became artists. [ref: 'To make it better, State should support biennale', The Hindu]

== Early life and education ==
Raman was born in 1885 in Cochin. His family at first opposed his wish to study art. According to The Hindu, his father met Sree Narayana Guru at Alwaye, and the Guru encouraged the family to support him, giving him ten rupees towards his journey to Calcutta.

At the College of Art, Calcutta, he was taught by Percy Brown and Jamini Prasad Ganguly. He then spent time at Santiniketan before travelling across India painting portraits.

== Career ==
=== Cochin School of Arts ===
Raman returned to Cochin and founded the Cochin School of Arts in 1932, the first school of its kind in the region. [ref: Art tutors should be given freedom, The New Indian Express] The school taught wall-poster design, clay modelling, book illustration, Indian-style painting, and commercial and applied art. It prepared students for the Madras government technical examinations and awarded diplomas in drawing and painting, and at the time was the only aided fine-arts institution in the state to do so.

The 1965 Kerala District Gazetteer for Ernakulam listed the Cochin School of Arts as one of the district's three main schools of fine arts. The school was housed in the premises of the Ernakulam Public Library and received a government grant. Alongside drawing and painting classes leading to Group Certificates and a Diploma in Art, it specialised in teaching statue-making; the certificate course took three years and the diploma five. The Gazetteer described it as "the only institution in the whole of Kerala where a six-feet likeness statue in bronze has been tried successfully". [ref: Kerala District Gazetteers: Ernakulam, Government Press] By the early 1970s the school was run by Dattan and taught a realistic style of painting. [ref: Art and the man, The Hindu] Several artists from Kerala trained at the school, among them the painter T. Kaladharan, who studied there for a year around 1972, the painter and sculptor Jeevan Lal [ref: The human in the divine, The Hindu] and the graphic designer B. S. Satyaraj, who designed a 2014 Brazilian postage stamp marking 100 years of Indian cinema. [ref: A post from Brazil, The Hindu]
=== Palace Artist ===
The Maharaja of Cochin gave Raman the title of "Palace Artist". His works are held at the Hill Palace, the Guest House and the Port Trust buildings in Cochin.

=== Sculpture ===
Raman was also a sculptor. The Hindu credits him with one of the earliest bronze statues in India made by lost-wax casting. The 1961 Census of India's survey of Kerala crafts noted that the Cochin School of Arts, "run by Artist Sri. M. Raman", had made a valuable contribution to the manufacture of life-size statues. Among the school's works it described a six-foot standing statue of Sree Narayana Guru at Koorkancherry, which it said bore a close resemblance to the Guru and was "the only one of its kind". A statue of the Guru made by Raman and his sons was unveiled by S. Radhakrishnan in 1969, and later portraits and statues of the Guru have drawn on Raman's depiction.

== Family ==
Raman died in 1971. His sons M. R. D. Dattan (1935–2006) and M. R. Baburam trained at the Cochin School of Arts and became artists, and a younger son, M. Dilipkumar, is also an artist.

Dattan studied at the Madras School of Art and later became director of the Cochin School of Arts. His statues include those of Mahatma Gandhi, Swami Vivekananda, B. R. Ambedkar, R. Venkataraman and the elephant Guruvayur Kesavan, and he received a Kerala Lalithakala Akademi fellowship. [ref: Artist and sculptor M R D Dattan passes away, The Hindu]

Baburam was known for pastel portraiture and designed pavilions with theme murals for exhibitions and trade fairs in India and abroad. He was the founder of Pavilions and Interiors (India) Pvt. Ltd., an exhibition design and fabrication company established in 1972. [ref: About Us, Pavilions and Interiors]

* M. R. D. Dattan
* Narayana Guru
* Hill Palace, Tripunithura

== References ==

Cecelia (Band) is an American hard rock and glam metal band featuring singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Cecelia Casso. The band performs original music influenced by the sound and style of 1980s hair metal and hard rock. Originally based in Denver, Colorado, the band is now based in Las Vegas, Nevada. [ref: Cecelia Band, Cecelia Band]

= History =
Cecelia Casso began developing her musical career in Denver Colorado and began playing guitar in 2013. She began performing live in the Denver area in 2016. Her musical interests center on rock music of the 1960s, 1970s and 1980s, with a particular focus on hair metal and hard rock.

Cecelia (Band) developed as a vehicle for Casso’s original music and live performances. The band’s repertoire and recordings combine original material with the musical style and aesthetic associated with 1980s hair metal and hard rock. The Denver Post has described the Denver-based band as combining hard-rock covers with original songs in the style of 1980s hair metal. [ref: Colorado's cover bands and tribute acts make old music new again, The Denver Post]

Cecelia (Band) has performed the most throughout Colorado during 2021-2025, including appearances at Lost Lake in Denver [ref: Cecelia w/ Pocket Sauce, Twisted Escape + Anti- Omega, www.etix.com], the Rickhouse in Denver [ref: The Social Divide Tour CRASHING WAYWARD, THE ALMAS @ Francisco Studio Denver, CO - April 2nd 2025 7:30 pm, holdmyticket.com], and Moe’s Original BBQ in Englewood. [ref: Cecelia Band, Cecelia Band] The biggest show Cecelia (Band) has performed so far was July 18, 2025 at the Whisky a Go Go in West Hollywood, California, as part of a bill headlined by L.A. Guns. [ref: Whisky A Go Go L.A. Guns, Leila Harlac, Hooligan's Holiday (Motley Crue Tribute), Philthy Rych, Cutt, Tokyo Riot and Cecelia]

In July 2026, Casso relocated from Denver to Las Vegas, where she continued developing Cecelia (Band), writing original music and recording the band’s second release. [ref: Conversations With Cecelia Casso]

= Musical style and influences =
Cecelia (Band)’s music is rooted in 1980s hair metal and hard rock. Casso has cited bands including Stryper, Bon Jovi, Kiss, Def Leppard, Van Halen, Whitesnake, Journey, Europe, Y&T, Mötley Crüe, Dokken and Steelheart among her influences. She has also cited 1960s and 1970s rock artists including the Beatles, the Eagles and Queen as influences and the modern bands My Chemical Romance, the Struts and Pierce The Veil. [ref: Cecelia Band, Cecelia Band]

The band’s original material is characterized by its deliberate use of the musical style associated with 1980s hair metal. Casso told the Denver Post that she writes music to emulate the genre because of her longstanding affinity for it.

= Music And Discography =

Draft: Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience & Institution

Draft text:
Of Woman Born: Motherhood as Experience and Institution is a 1976 book by American poet, scholar, and essayist Adrienne Rich that examines motherhood from the lens of personal experience, anthropology, and feminist theory. Rich researched and wrote the book over a 4 year period because she felt that motherhood “was a crucial, still relatively unexplored, area for feminist theory.” [ref: Of woman born: motherhood as experience and institution, W. W. Norton & Company] It has been described by the Los Angeles Times as a landmark work in the literature of motherhood. [ref: Adrienne Rich dies at 82; feminist poet and essayist, Los Angeles Times]

== Summary ==

Of Woman Born begins with a foreword describing one of the book’s central aims: to begin to fill in the gap between the universal experience of motherhood and what is known about it: “We know more about the air we breathe, the seas we travel, than about the nature and meaning of motherhood.” The foreword also describes the book’s aim to create a distinction between motherhood as an experience, which Rich defines as “the potential relationship of any woman to her powers of reproduction and to children” and motherhood as an institution—the social and political systems that define, limit, and control the experience of motherhood.

=== Anger and Tenderness ===
Using entries from her journal, Rich illustrates the conflicting feelings she experienced as a young mother of three in the 1950’s: tenderness and anger, ambition and weariness, power and powerlessness. She describes how, from an early age,  she struggled to bridge the gap between the feminine ideals of the 1950’s, and her own vision of herself as a serious, independent poet. She describes the outline of her young adult life: married to a Cambridge academic at the age of 22, three children by the age of 29, her decision to be sterilized after her third child, her struggle to write while raising young children. Rich then examines the many assumptions her younger self had accepted as inevitable: that her experience as a mother was simply “the human condition;” that motherhood and child care had always looked this way; that mothers acted on instinct alone; that the only person developing in the mother-child relationship was the child. Rich ends the chapter citing her hope and belief that culture will come to see female biology “as a resource, rather than a destiny.”

=== The Sacred Calling ===
Rich traces the shifting roles of women in the United States and England over the 19th century, and illustrates how women went from essential, widely-skilled, productive members of their homesteads in pre-industrial eras to isolated individuals whose role was limited to “the specialization of motherhood.” She describes how the growth of factories in the Industrial Revolution separated the home from the “man’s world” of wage-earning, ambition, and power, and created the ideal of the home as the “woman’s sphere” of refuge and retreat, a relatively recent concept in human history. “The home thus defined had never before existed. It was a creation of the Industrial Revolution, an ideal invested with the power of something God-given, and its power as an idea remains unexpunged today.” She identifies the repercussions of this shift for women and mothers: isolation, loneliness, powerlessness, and a narrow definition of a woman’s capacities.

===The Kingdom of the Fathers ===
In this chapter, Rich explores the roots, characteristics, and consequences of patriarchy, which she defines as “the power of the fathers.” She identifies the advent of private property and inherited wealth as key foundations of patriarchal order, and a tendency to think in “positive-negative polarities”—rational/irrational, powerful/powerless—as key characteristics. Power itself, Rich states, and power over others, “is a primal relationship under patriarchy,” most often exemplified through a man’s control over his wife and children. Monotheism, in which an all-powerful, usually male god, causes this patriarchal power structure to become “internalized as ‘conscience,’ ‘tradition,’ ‘the moral law within.” Rich discusses how women have mostly experienced power as a negative force. She identifies the renewed interest in matriarchal and pre-patriarchal cultures that characterized feminist and counter-culture movements of the 1960’s and 1970’s as efforts “to reintegrate what has been named the unconscious, the subjective, the emotional with the structural, the rational, the intellectual.”

Oscar Robert Lindsey (born May 1, 2002) is an American singer, songwriter, and multi-instrumentalist. [ref: Oscar Lindsey on Apple Music, Apple Music] Born and raised in Nashville, Tennessee, to a musical family, Lindsey has released five studio albums. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Artist Page, Mom + Pop Music] He is best known for his indie folk-rock sound, characterized by introspective lyricism. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Interview, Official Charts] Alongside his music, Lindsey has documented an interest in liminal spaces, creating numerous videos exploring the concept. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Official YouTube Channel, YouTube]
== Early life ==
Raised by his father, Grammy-nominated American country music songwriter and record producer Chris Lindsey, and his mother, American author and songwriter Aimee Mayo, Lindsey gained experience with music at a young age, though he has admitted that he did not truly love music until he was in middle school. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Chats Blissfully Melancholic New Album 'Sunshine', Ones to Watch] [ref: Oscar Lindsey Live in the Library, WUTC] [ref: Tape Recorders, OCD and Bo Burnham: In Conversation with Oscar Lindsey, Strand Magazine] At age 14, inspired by Bo Burnham, he decided to learn all of Burnham's songs on the piano before later shifting to the guitar. [ref: Oscar Lindsey Instagram Post, Instagram] [ref: Oscar Lindsey on Sunshine, Virality and Life, The Music Box Media] In high school, he made comedy songs and rap music on GarageBand. His first self-released projects were the EP Tony Tapes and its single "23 to Go". Once Lindsey learned how to use DistroKid to distribute music onto Spotify, he took a short hiatus and began making more serious music in 2022 after discovering The Beatles. The Beatles became one of his biggest influences alongside Paul Simon, Ween, Todd Rundgren, Mac DeMarco, Elliott Smith, and Alex G—influences that became prominent in his work.
== Career ==
=== 2022–2025: Independent releases and Glitter ===
In 2022, Lindsey self-released the singles "Petals" and "All of My Friends", as well as the EP Airbag. In 2022, according to Lindsey, he was arrested for painting graffiti; he came out of the experience wanting to commit fully to music, and the following year he released his debut studio album, Look I Caught A Fish. [ref: Oscar Lindsey – Live set at the beach, YouTube]

Ahead of the album's March 8, 2023 release, he issued the lead single "Big Star". Recorded on a tape machine to achieve a lo-fi sound, Look I Caught A Fish began a prolific string of independent releases. He followed it later that year with his second album, Dinosaur (December 4, 2023), which included the single "If I Was a Bird", as well as the standalone single "If I Could Hold You Again" featuring his brother, Levi Lindsey. In 2024, he self-released his third studio album, Rocky Mountain Toast (April 11), and the EP Magic Eight Ball (September 7).

For his fourth album, Glitter, Lindsey decided to take a more serious approach by spending significantly more time on its production. As Lindsey stated, "Glitter was the first one where I was like, 'Okay, I want to step everything up.'" Self-released on July 19, 2025, Glitter was Lindsey's first project to be professionally mixed and recorded entirely on a computer, with the exception of the track "I Wanna Feel". [ref: Oscar Lindsey Instagram Post, Instagram] The album was supported by two singles, "Ruby" and "Forever's Such a Long Time", both of which were released with accompanying music videos. The music video for "Forever's Such a Long Time" was shot on 8mm film by Christian Modica, who also directed the video alongside Lindsey as co-director. [ref: Oscar Lindsey - Forever's Such a Long Time (Official Video), YouTube] Following the release of Glitter, from September 2025 to March 2026, Lindsey showcased his interest in liminal spaces and filmmaking by releasing a series of YouTube videos covering liminal spaces, nostalgia, and various niche topics.

=== 2026–present: Mom + Pop Music and Sunshine ===
In May 2026, Lindsey signed with the independent music booking agency Ground Control Touring, [ref: Oscar Lindsey Artist Page, Ground Control Touring] [ref: Oscar Lindsey Instagram Post, Instagram] and later that month, he signed with the New York-based independent record label Mom + Pop Music. While Lindsey's previous albums had been recorded on GarageBand, his next album, Sunshine, was recorded using Logic Pro. On June 12, 2026, Lindsey released "Metal Through Her Lips", the lead single from Sunshine, via Mom + Pop Music. [ref: Metal Through Her Lips - Single by Oscar Lindsey, Apple Music] The song went viral on TikTok, which helped further launch his career. Speaking about the song's social media popularity, Lindsey said, "It makes more sense looking at it retroactively, but I just had no idea that it was gonna happen. I always believed in myself and thought it would happen, but I'm just grateful that it happened now." Leading up to the release of Sunshine, he released the singles "Flip a Coin" and "Painting the Walls" under Mom + Pop Music. [ref: Oscar Lindsey to Release SUNSHINE LP, Shares New Single, BroadwayWorld] On October 16, 2026, Lindsey released the self-produced album Sunshine via Mom + Pop Music, marking his label debut. Draft text:
Turbo is a Dutch hard rock band from Arnhem, formed in early 1979 by former members of Dutch bands including Metal Voices, Long Tall Ernie and The Shakers, and the Speedtwins. The band released two albums on CBS Netherlands, Turbo (1979) and You Girl (1980).

== History ==

=== Formation ===
The line-up was singer and guitarist Leen "Lain" Barbier, guitarist Jos Jaspers, bassist Charles Schutters and drummer Eugène Arts. Jaspers, Schutters and Arts had previously played together in the science-fiction rock band Metal Voices; Barbier had been in the punk group Speedtwins and Splinterfunk, and Arts and Jaspers in Long Tall Ernie and The Shakers. According to regional press coverage, the band took a demo to CBS, whose staff at first believed it was an existing record, and the label signed them.

=== Turbo (1979) ===
Their self-titled debut album was completed in ten days and released on CBS in June 1979. Barbier wrote most of the lyrics, and some songs were by Floris Kolvenbach, a former Metal Voices member; "Time Traveller" dated from the Metal Voices period. A review in de Volkskrant of a concert at Amsterdam's Jaap Edenhal, where Turbo and Ted Nugent both played, described the band as playing "melodic hard rock" with more variety than ordinary "beton" (hard rock) and called them "a promise for the future", singling out Barbier's voice. A Groningen newspaper described the band as having been "heavily hyped" by CBS. The debut was also released in France, Germany and Canada.

A regional newspaper reported that the album's cover, showing the band appearing to steal a Porsche Turbo, was copied by another band, The Roadrunners, using a DAF, and that the car in the photograph was removed by someone else two days after the shoot.

=== You Girl (1980) ===
The second album, You Girl, appeared in early 1980, produced by the radio DJ Alfred Lagarde and including a cover of Jimi Hendrix's "Stone Free". Bassist Charles Schutters left after the recording sessions. “Algemeen Dagblad praised the album’s natural, carefully played rock, but found the title song somewhat forced, praising Barbier's singing, Jaspers' guitar solos and Lagarde's production, and noting that CBS Netherlands was actively developing Dutch talent with releases by Turbo, The Nits and White Honey.

=== Later activity ===
Turbo has continued to perform in the Netherlands in recent years under Barbier, with Dick Kemper and drummer Willem van der Aa. [ref: Dampend optreden Lain Barbier, Arnhemse Koerier] A planned show in Arnhem in July 2024 was cancelled when the drummer was injured.

== Discography ==

* Turbo (CBS, 1979)
* You Girl (CBS, 1980)

; Live albums

Red Rising is a science fiction novel series by American author Pierce Brown. Set in a future in which humanity has colonized the Solar System, the series depicts a hierarchical society divided into genetically and socially stratified groups known as Colors. The story follows a rebellion against the ruling class and the political, military, and social conflicts that result. [ref: Brown, Pierce, The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction]

The series began with Red Rising in 2014, followed by Golden Son (2015) and Morning Star (2016). Brown continued the narrative with Iron Gold (2018), Dark Age (2019), and Light Bringer (2023). [ref: Red Rising, Publishers Weekly] [ref: Iron Gold, Publishers Weekly]

== Publication ==
The first three novels form the original trilogy. The later novels continue the story after the rebellion against the Society and expand the narrative to include the political challenges of governing the newly established Republic.

== Setting and themes ==
The novels take place in a future in which humanity has colonized the Solar System. Society is divided into Colors, hereditary castes associated with different social roles. Golds occupy the ruling class, while Reds perform much of the labor that supports the established order. The hierarchy is maintained through political power, social conditioning, and the use of technology.

The first novel follows Darrow, a Red miner on Mars who discovers that the social order rests on a deception. He undergoes physical transformation and training to infiltrate the Gold elite, with the aim of undermining the ruling system from within.

The series combines elements of dystopian fiction and space opera with political intrigue, military conflict, and classical imagery. The Science Fiction Encyclopedia compares aspects of the first novel with earlier science fiction and with the young-adult dystopian genre, while noting its emphasis on action, personal sacrifice, and the protagonist's rise through the social hierarchy.

Recurring themes include class conflict, revolution, authoritarianism, loyalty, sacrifice, and the difficulty of creating a stable political order after the overthrow of an established regime.

== Plot ==
=== Original trilogy ===
The original trilogy follows Darrow, a member of the Red caste who works underground on Mars. After learning that the surface has long been habitable for the ruling Golds, he joins a revolutionary movement and undergoes extensive surgery and training to infiltrate Gold society.

In Red Rising, Darrow enters the Institute, an institution where young Golds compete in a violent test of leadership and survival. Golden Son follows his increasing involvement in Gold politics and military affairs. Morning Star continues the conflict between the rebellion and the Society.

=== Second series ===
The second series takes place after the initial rebellion has succeeded in overthrowing the Society's rule on Mars. The new Republic faces the challenge of extending its political order across the Solar System while confronting opponents of the revolution.

Iron Gold broadens the narrative through multiple points of view and examines the aftermath of revolution. Its plot includes military campaigns, political disputes within the Republic, and the experiences of people whose lives have not improved as much as the revolution promised.

Dark Age and Light Bringer continue the military and political conflicts among the competing factions of the Solar System.

== Characters ==
The novels feature characters from several castes and political factions. The later books expand beyond Darrow's perspective to portray the consequences of the rebellion for different groups within the Solar System.

* Darrow — A Red-born revolutionary who infiltrates the Gold ruling class and becomes a central military leader.
* Virginia au Augustus — Known as Mustang, a Gold leader associated with the Republic.
* Sevro au Barca — Darrow's ally and a prominent member of the Howlers.
* Cassius au Bellona — A Gold swordsman whose personal relationships and political loyalties affect the conflict.
* Adrius au Augustus — Known as the Jackal, a political strategist and adversary of Darrow.
* Lysander au Lune — A major character in the later novels whose political ambitions influence the struggle over the future of the Solar System.
* Lyria of Lagalos — A Red whose experiences offer a perspective on the effects of the revolution on ordinary people.
* Ephraim ti Horn — A former soldier whose storyline explores survival and the consequences of political upheaval.

== Reception ==
=== Critical reviews ===
Red Rising received reviews from professional book-review publications. Publishers Weekly described the novel as an action-driven science fiction story, but criticized its originality and plausibility. The review discussed Darrow's background as a Red miner, the caste system on Mars, and his recruitment to infiltrate Gold society.
