Draft: Cogitopic Principle

Draft text:
The “Cogitopic Principle” is a formal logical constraint expressing the necessary structural conditions for faithfully representing a cogito-capable Observer. Its starting premise is the assertion that “at least one experience occurs”. Experience is treated as a primitive predicate on Observer states: it holds for at least one state, but not for every state, and no further defining criterion is required for this formulation. With no assumed “prohibitor,” all finitely describable structures -including descriptions of noise- remain available without privileged status. A description represents a given cogito-registration only where its registered distinctions and specified continuation relations are in place. A description lacking that structure remains available but is cogito-incapable with respect to that registration. The principle is an analogue of the “Anthropic Principle” directed at the registering Observer. Its conditioning consists entirely in structural compatibility: no agent chooses descriptions, and no external process filters or removes them. Its formal content concerns the presence or absence of the structure identifying a registration, without requiring a philosophical interpretation of consciousness, an ontology of the Observer or an account of its physical constitution.

Rorisons (formerly Rorisons RMD) is a family owned agricultural lime and fertiliser company based in Mount Maunganui, New Zealand. It quarries limestone at Aria in the King Country and supplies lime, fertiliser and soil testing services to farms in the central North Island.

== History ==

The business traces its origins to I M Rorison Ltd, a transport company that Ian Marshall Rorison and his wife Nora started in Tokoroa in 1950, carting timber and fertiliser. [ref: Rorisons, RuralHQ]
In 1957 the family moved to Tauranga, where the company became a bulk haulage business and was soon renamed Rorison Mainline Limited. [ref: Progress, Power, Pride, New Zealand Trucking]

In the mid 1960s Rorison took over a lime and serpentine quarry at Aria, about nine kilometres inland from Piopio. Its lime was sold as Rorison Aglime, and its serpentine was supplied to fertiliser works as a source of magnesium for serpentine superphosphate.

During a farming downturn in 1971, the New Zealand Lumber Company took over Rorison Mainline. Rorison kept the Aria quarry through Rorison Mineral Developments Limited (RMD) and later rebuilt the trucking fleet. The restructured business was based at Mount Maunganui. He died in 1982, and his son Gary took over management of the business.

By 2009 the company, trading as Rorisons RMD under managing director Mike Rorison, described itself as a third generation family business. That year its lime and LimeMag, a lime and serpentine blend, received BioGro and Asure organic certification. The company said the Aria quarry held the only commercially quarried serpentine seam in the North Island. [ref: A soil solution to fit fertiliser budget, SunLive]

Rorisons Mainline truck at wharf.jpg|Rorisons Mainline truck No. 64 beside the ship Imperial Star, about 1970

== Operations ==
Rorisons has sites at Aria and on Aria Road near Piopio in the King Country, and its head office is in Mount Maunganui in the Bay of Plenty. [ref: Rorisons, Rorisons] It supplies farms in the Waikato, King Country, Taranaki, Bay of Plenty and Hawke's Bay regions, both directly and through rural consultants and spreading contractors.

Products include agricultural lime and lime based products such as CalciMag and CalciFeed, lime for aerial topdressing, limestone aggregates for farm tracks, fertilisers sourced in New Zealand and overseas, and custom fertiliser blends, including [https://www.biogro.co.nz BioGro] certified organic options. These are supplied for dairy, sheep and beef, and cropping farms, both conventional and regenerative. Draft: Abuqatrania

Draft text:
Abuqatrania is an extinct genus of parapithecid primates known from the Paleogene of North Africa. It was established in 2001 by Elwyn L. Simons, Erik R. Seiffert, Prithijit S. Chatrath and Yousry Attia for the type species Abuqatrania basiodontos, based on fossils from the late Eocene of the Fayum Depression in Egypt. [ref: Earliest record of a parapithecid anthropoid from the Jebel Qatrani Formation, northern Egypt, Folia Primatologica]

Its taxonomic status has been debated, as some authors have treated it as a synonym of the related genus Qatrania. [ref: A Companion to Paleoanthropology, Wiley-Blackwell] In 2024, isolated teeth from the earliest Oligocene of southern Morocco were tentatively referred to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos.

== Discovery and occurrence ==

The original fossils of Abuqatrania basiodontos came from Quarry L-41 in the Jebel Qatrani Formation of the Fayum Depression, northern Egypt. The species was described as a late Eocene anthropoid and provided evidence for the presence of Parapithecidae in the oldest productive vertebrate-bearing deposits of the formation.

A second, tentative occurrence was reported in 2024 from the Samlat Formation in the Dakhla region of southern Morocco, near the northern border of Mauritania. The material comes from locality DAK C2, in the uppermost part of the formation along the Atlantic margin of the Rio de Oro, east of the Dakhla peninsula. The fossil-bearing deposits date to the earliest Oligocene, approximately 33.5 million years ago. The specimens were recovered from estuarine sediments using wet-screening techniques. [ref: A new primate community from the earliest Oligocene of the Atlantic margin of Northwest Africa: Systematic, paleobiogeographic, and paleoenvironmental implications, Journal of Human Evolution]

== Description ==

The original description characterized Abuqatrania basiodontos as a parapithecid with no clear autapomorphies, or derived characteristics exclusive to the species. Its most parsimonious phylogenetic interpretation placed it as the sister taxon of a clade containing Qatrania, Parapithecus and Apidium.

Body mass estimates for specimens tentatively assigned to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos range from approximately 371 to 561 grams. These estimates were calculated from the dimensions of an isolated first lower molar and an isolated third lower molar from the earliest Oligocene of Morocco. This mass range is similar to that of New World Monkeys of the genus Callithrix. [ref: Quantitative assessment of grasping strength in platyrrhine monkeys, American Journal of Biological Anthropology]

The Moroccan material referred to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos consists of isolated teeth rather than an associated skeleton. The published specimen records include a lower canine, lower molars, an upper molar identified as either the first or second molar, a lower incisor tentatively identified as either the first or second incisor, two lower second premolars and an upper third molar. Some of the teeth are worn, corroded or broken. [ref: 3D models related to the publication: A new primate community from the earliest Oligocene of the Atlantic margin of Northwest Africa: Systematic, paleobiogeographic and paleoenvironmental implications, MorphoMuseuM]

== Taxonomic history ==

Simons and colleagues established Abuqatrania as a distinct genus in 2001. They interpreted A. basiodontos as closely related to other early parapithecids, particularly a clade containing Qatrania, Parapithecus and Apidium.

In their review of Paleogene anthropoids, Seiffert and colleagues (2010) recognized Abuqatrania separately from Qatrania. They also discussed the possibility that Abuqatrania basiodontos was close to the ancestry of other parapithecids, noting that its fossils were approximately one million years older than those of Qatrania wingi. [ref: Cenozoic Mammals of Africa, University of California Press]

The distinction between Abuqatrania and Qatrania was not accepted by all authors. In 2013, K. Christopher Beard treated Abuqatrania as a synonym of Qatrania, using the combination Qatrania basiodontos for the species. Under this classification, the species belongs to the same genus as Qatrania wingi and Qatrania fleaglei.

The name has continued to be used in subsequent scientific literature. Marivaux and colleagues (2024), for example, tentatively assigned the Moroccan material to Abuqatrania cf. basiodontos.

== Paleobiogeography ==

The Moroccan locality DAK C2 preserves a diverse primate community from the Eocene–Oligocene transition. Marivaux and colleagues identified at least eight primate species, including anthropoids assigned to Oligopithecidae, Propliopithecidae, Parapithecidae and Afrotarsiidae, as well as several strepsirrhine groups.

Comparisons between the primates and rodents from Dakhla and those from the Jebel Qatrani Formation in Egypt led the authors to propose that an east–west environmental connection existed across North Africa during the latest Eocene and earliest Oligocene. They also suggested that tropical habitats along the northwestern margin of Africa may have acted as refuges during the cooling associated with the Eocene–Oligocene transition. These interpretations concern the broader fossil assemblage and its environment, rather than Abuqatrania alone.

* Qatrania
* Parapithecidae

(description)When the city commission approved the Brentwood Hills Addition plans on June 1, 1953, it created the city of Kansas City, Kansas' first subdivision in Wyandotte County established for African Americans (west of 18th street). The stakeholders formed a Land Investors Group guided by Douglass State Bank.

Dr. Charles.W. Alexander and Dr. William M. Blount, both physicians in KCK; Harold Robbins and Wendell Robbins of Robbins & Robbins Construction Company; Henry W. Sewing, President of Douglass State Bank; Earl D. Thomas, an educator and Principal at Lincoln High School, KCMO;  Isadore Gross, a real estate broker and taxicab company owner in KCMO; Ernest W. Robbins, a retired railway mail clerk;  Atty. Elmer G. Jackson; Mrs. J.A. Hibbler; widow of a physician from KCMO and Rev. Isaiah H. Henderson Sr., pastor of Eighth Street Baptist Church, came together and brought their vision to life.

In total, 54 acres was purchased from Judge Norman B. Sorter. The original boundaries of the subdivision sat between 34th and Farrow and 38th and Farrow to 34th and Bell Crossing and 38th and Oak. It consisted of 143 homes.

According to the April 16, 1954 edition of the KC Call, 1200 people attended the open house. The official dedication was held on the Sunday afternoon of April 11, 1954 in Quindaro Park. Dr. George W. Snowden and William F. McKinney, both federal officials with the Federal Housing Administration, were in attendance.

The neighborhood became a village for the families that lived there. It consisted of doctors, teachers, beauticians and small business owners. It even had its own baseball team, The Quindaro Dragons, with Mr. Harold Rucker, as the coach and a Cub Scout Troop with Mrs. Lorraine Robinson as troop leader.

Missouri submitted Interstate 635 to the American Association of State Highway Officials (AASHO) as part of its proposed Urban Route Numbering on July 31, 1958 and it was approved on November 10, 1958. Construction of I635 began in 1969. Fourteen of the Brentwood Hills homes on 34th Street were acquired which changed the landscape of the subdivision, but not the pride of the people.

Faydor L. Litvin (January 21, 1914 – April 26, 2017) was a scientist who dedicated his life to the development of the modern theory of gearing and contributed to the theory of mechanisms. [ref: Celebrating the life of Distinguished Professor Emeritus Faydor Litvin, Mechanical and Industrial Engineering]

Born in Belarus, he emigrated to the United States in 1979 at the age of 65. He then worked as a professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and as the founding director of the Gear Research Center at the University of Illinois at Chicago. He continued his research until his retirement at the age of 93. [ref: Remembering UIC Distinguished Professor Emeritus Faydor L. Litvin, Gear Research Laboratory]

He was an expert in kinematics and the theory of gearing, with research on high-precision gear mechanisms used in the rotorcraft, aerospace, and automotive industries.

== Early life and education ==
Litvin was born in Belarus in 1914 to Jewish parents.

In 1928, at the age of 14, he moved to Leningrad, now Saint Petersburg, to pursue further education. He supported himself while continuing his studies.

He graduated from Leningrad Polytechnic Institute with distinction in 1937. He defended his PhD in 1944 and received his Doctor of Technical Science degree in 1954.

From 1963 to 1979, he served as department head and professor of mechanical engineering at the Institute of Precision Mechanics and Optics in Leningrad. There, he laid the mathematical foundations of his work on advanced gear geometry and kinematics.

== Career in the United States ==
In 1979, at the age of 65, Litvin fulfilled his long-standing wish to leave the Soviet Union. When asked how he could leave his prominent position and face an uncertain future, he replied: "It was easy. There was an ocean of blood between me and that country."

Born during World War I, he lived through the Russian Revolution, pogroms, Stalin's purges, World War II, and the Holocaust, in which his parents were killed.

He moved to the United States and joined the Department of Mechanical Engineering at the University of Illinois at Chicago as a professor. He founded and directed the Gear Research Center. There, together with his PhD students, he conducted research in collaboration with NASA, the U.S. Army, and the rotorcraft industry for 27 years. His technology helped reduce noise, vibration, and stress and was used in an upgraded attack helicopter operated by the U.S. Army.

Litvin mentored 100 PhD students, 50 in Russia and 50 in the United States, as well as visiting scholars from around the world. His students went on to hold teaching and research positions in the United States, Italy, Spain, Russia, Bulgaria, Poland, Hungary, China, Taiwan, and Australia. They described themselves as belonging to the "elite school of Litvin."

== Publications and inventions ==
Litvin had more than 350 publications, including 10 monographs, and held 26 patents. His monograph The Theory of Gearing went through six editions.

During World War II, he developed an invention that enabled the efficient transmission of radar coordinates to antiaircraft artillery instrumentation used by Soviet troops at the front. To test it, he traveled to Leningrad during the siege, crossing Lake Ladoga under heavy bombardment.

In his book Development of Gear Technology, he dedicated a chapter to scientists who had contributed to mechanical engineering, some of whom had received little recognition during their lifetimes. He researched their lives, sometimes contacting third-generation descendants. Portraits of these scientists formed a gallery in his Gear Research Center.

== Research and engineering contributions ==
Litvin's work replaced empirical trial-and-error gear design methods with mathematical models based on differential geometry.

His research focused on the simulation of meshing and tooth contact analysis. It introduced the localization of bearing contact and predesigned parabolic transmission functions. [ref: Generation and tooth contact analysis of spiral bevel gears with predesigned parabolic functions of transmission errors, NASA] [ref: Computerized Design and Generation of Low-Noise Gears with Localized Bearing Contact, NASA] His algorithms allowed computer numerical control machines to grind gears, reducing operational noise, wear, and vibration.

== Collaboration with NASA ==
In the 1980s, Litvin began collaborating with NASA's Glenn Research Center and the U.S. Army Research Laboratory. His geometric models were used to optimize planetary gear trains and spiral bevel gear drives to improve the reliability, safety, and acoustic performance of helicopter transmissions.

== Awards and honors ==
Litvin was an ASME Fellow, an associate editor of Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, and a member of the honorary editorial advisory board of Gearing and Transmissions.

His awards included 12 from NASA, the Thomas Bernard Hall Prize from the Institution of Mechanical Engineers in the United Kingdom, the Edison Award, and the IFToMM Merit Award from the International Federation for the Promotion of Mechanism and Machine Science.

Draft: Deep Structure Theory

Draft text:
Deep Structure Theory (DST), also known as Neuropsychological Deep Structure Theory, is a unifying analytical framework that models how mental states emerge as compiled electromagnetic oscillatory activity relating to the structure and function of underlying neural circuitry. It is a local instance of dynamic complex systems theory that applies to how the brain generates the mind and was introduced by the cognitive neuroscientist and psychotherapy researcher Oliver Boxell. [ref: Deep Structure Theory: An introduction to a unifying theoretical framework for the analysis of human neuropsychology., Journal of Mind and Behavior]

The term "deep structure" was popularized in formal linguistics by Noam Chomsky in his theory of generative grammar, although this referred only to a core syntactic structure that could be expressed as different surface sentence forms. Boxell radically extends and deepens the idea in DST by developing it into a standard model for the entirety of the mind in which core conceptual meaning representations can be re-coded into integrated language, mathematics, music and sound patterns, or visuospatial and sensorimotor patterns. Furthermore, while Chomsky viewed mental representation in isolation, DST describes deep structure as the product of integrated, co-evolved representational and real-time processing subsystems. As such, the DST paradigm is able to stipulate systems for memory, learning, and sustained developmental patterns over time, in which the emergence of consciousness appears and plays a mediating role. The relationship between micro- and macro- neural circuits and compiled oscillations as the encoding of deep structure also makes DST more explicit about how the mind emerges from the structure and function of the brain, although generative grammar also more loosely viewed deep structure as somehow relating to the structure of the brain.

=== Basic Technical Outline ===
Universal deep structure algorithms: Boxell imports three core algorithms from X-Bar Theory (namely the complement, specifier, and adjunct rules), as well as binary switches, but views them as domain-general faculty for core meaning rather than a language-specific one. As such, in DST these formal algorithms derive abstract mental information structure as encoded by compiled neural oscillations. In common with dynamic complex systems theories generally, these neurosymbolic structures are computed as branching computations of nodes (units of information) that form binary tree representations.

Phase transitions: The domain-general faculty for core meaning occurs in the Information-Phase (I-Phase) of deep structural computation. One of the main functions of the I-Phase is conceptual or thematic role assignment, in which the deep structural tree incorporates theta theory and predicate logic. As some of these I-Phase computations reach a neural activation threshold filter known as theta (Φ) they transition into the Spellout-Phase (S-Phase), where the core meaning derivations are re-rendered into modality-specific deep structural forms through the addition of abstract features to the nodes, producing language, mathematics, music and sound patterning, and visuospatial and sensorimotor patterning. The I-to-S phase transitions in DST subsume transformations and phase analysis from the Minimalist Program and extend it as per-propositional chunking to all neurocognitive domains as a general computational working memory constraint.

Linearization: Some I-Phase and especially S-Phase computations reach another neural threshold filter called omega (Ω) that precipitates the deletion of branches from the deep structural tree representations to create a linear string of nodes. Subsets of deep structures that undergo this transition become self-aware or conscious, in-line with fundamental neurobiological research on consciousness that finds it appears when activation thresholds are reached in conjunction with highly distributed macrocircuits. [ref: What is the readiness potential?, Trends in Cognitive Sciences] [ref: Unconscious determinants of free decisions in the human brain, Nature Neuroscience] [ref: Piercing of Consciousness as a Threshold-Crossing Operation, Current Biology] [ref: Neural correlates of evidence accumulation during value-based decisions revealed via simultaneous EEG-fMRI, Nature Communications]

Memory: The sustained strength of transient neural circuit structures upregulates the strength of branch connections between nodes in deep structural tree derivations. Using Marvin Minsky's typology, Boxell calls the strength of branch connections "k-lines" (knowledge lines). [ref: K-Lines: A theory of memory, Cognitive Science] Just as neural circuits upregulate k-lines, k-line strengths can downregulate neural circuit connectivity strength; at both the neurobiological and emergent neuropsychological levels, frequency, recency, and saliency are proposed as the main filters that determine connectivity strengths. The ephemeral nature of k-lines show how the processing subsystem is instrumental in forming part of the nature of the deep structures that are built along with the actual representational algorithms that constrain their nature.
[truncated]

Johnny O'Reilly (born 22 October 1970) is an Irish filmmaker and journalist. [ref: Our man in Moscow, The Irish Times] [ref: 'I want to see out the war': Irish filmmaker moved to Ukraine from Russia when 'the pessimists were proved right', The Irish Times] [ref: Red Letter Day, The Sunday Times] He wrote and directed the Russian-language feature films Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) and The Weather Station (2010), as well as the Academy Award-shortlisted short film The Terms (2002). [ref: The Terms Shortlisted for Oscars, IFTN] His feature documentary Kherson was shot over four years in southern Ukraine. As a journalist, he has spent two decades covering politics and culture in Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine for publications including The Times, The Sunday Times, Rolling Stone, and The Irish Times.

== Early life and education ==
O'Reilly grew up in Dublin, Ireland. He studied Russian and Classics at Trinity College Dublin. In 1993, while still a student, he worked in Moscow as a freelance reporter covering the Russian constitutional crisis. In 1996, he completed graduate film studies at New York University. He worked at The Sunday Times for two years before pursuing a full-time career in filmmaking. In 2006, he relocated to Moscow, where he lived for ten years.

== Career ==

=== Filmmaking ===
O'Reilly first gained international recognition with the short film The Terms (2002), based on a short story by Irish writer Mike McCormack. The film was shortlisted for the 74th Academy Awards and received multiple international festival awards.

His feature directorial debut was the Russian-language thriller The Weather Station (2010), described by Variety as a whodunit set in an arctic meteorological outpost and filmed near Simferopol in Crimea. [ref: The Weather Station, Variety]

In 2016, he wrote and directed Moscow Never Sleeps, an ensemble drama set during Moscow City Day celebrations that follows several interconnected stories over a single day and stars prominent Russian actors.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, O'Reilly began work on the documentary feature Kherson, following civilians, soldiers, and families living through the occupation and liberation of Kherson city.

=== Journalism and cultural initiatives ===
O'Reilly has spent more than two decades reporting from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and the wider former Soviet region, covering politics, culture, society, and conflict across Eastern Europe. His journalism has appeared in international media outlets, including The New York Times, Rolling Stone, The Sunday Times, The Times, The Irish Times, MarketWatch, and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

In 2008, he co-founded the Irish Film Festival in Moscow, an annual cultural initiative that ran for eleven years, evolving into a nationwide arts festival across multiple Russian cities.

=== Russian television incident ===
In August 2015, O'Reilly appeared live on Russian state television to discuss Moscow Never Sleeps. During the interview, he referred to the imprisonment of Ukrainian filmmaker Oleg Sentsov as a political imprisonment, after which the broadcast was abruptly cut short. [ref: Russian TV Cuts Away After Irish Director Backs Jailed Ukrainian Filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Russian TV cuts off Irish director after backing jailed filmmaker, The Irish Times] The incident received international media coverage in outlets such as The Irish Times and The Hollywood Reporter. [ref: Russian TV Cuts Away After Irish Director Backs Jailed Ukrainian Filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Russian TV cuts off Irish director after backing jailed filmmaker, The Irish Times]

== Filmography ==
* The Terms (2002) – Short film; writer, director
* CO/MA (2004) – Feature film; co-director
* The Weather Station (2010) – Feature film; writer, director
* Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) – Feature film; writer, director
* Kherson – Documentary feature; writer, director, producer

George Ergemlidze (, Giorgi Ergemlidze) is a Georgian singer, songwriter, multi-instrumentalist and record producer from Tbilisi. He works mainly in synthwave and alternative pop. He wrote the house song "My Queen", released in 2008 by Soulful Mood Recordings and in 2010 as a remix package with Portuguese DJ Ricky Teixeira on AudioBite Records, and fronted the Tbilisi band Mutual Friends. His solo albums include Eclectic (2012), Marsidan (2015), Dear WE (2020), Digitized (2022) and Looking Back in Time (2026).

== Early life ==
Ergemlidze is the son of Nugzar Ergemlidze, whom the music site beehype described as one of the foremost Georgian pop and rock composers of the Soviet era. Nugzar Ergemlidze, born in Batumi in 1955, is also a painter; he studied design at the Tbilisi State Academy of Arts and worked as an editor at Georgian state television and radio from 1982 to 2004.

Ergemlidze played the piano from early childhood. He has said that seeing Queen's performance at Live Aid when he was about ten shaped his musical taste, and that at 13 he taught himself to arrange and produce music on a computer.

== Career ==
=== "My Queen" (2008–2010) ===
In 2008, at the age of 20, Ergemlidze took part in the television talent show Star Academy, where, by his own account, he was told he did not have enough talent to succeed. The same year his song "My Queen" was released as a single by the Russian label Soulful Mood Recordings, under the name Darwin Marcus.

In 2010 My Queen (Remixes), credited to Ricky Teixeira featuring George Ergemlidze, was released on 28 September 2010 by AudioBite Records through its AudioBite Soulful imprint, with mixes by Teixeira, Groove Technicians, BBwhite, Ramiro Bernabela, and DJ Troby & Francesco Cofano. Ergemlidze is credited as vocalist, writer and composer.

=== Mutual Friends ===
At around the age of 20, Ergemlidze and a friend formed a band; he was the founder, leader and singer of Mutual Friends. In June 2011 the band played Alter/Vision's Tbilisi Open Air festival, alongside 19 other bands from Georgia and abroad. He later said the band became quite popular, but that he left to go solo because music was a hobby for the band but his career.

=== Solo work (2012–present) ===
He began his solo career under the name Ergland, releasing the album Eclectic in 2012, before switching to his own name for Marsidan, released on 3 March 2015.

From 2017 he moved toward synthwave. He sent his song "Violet Star" to the YouTube channel and label NewRetroWave, which then had about 300,000 subscribers; according to Ergemlidze, the upload received 20,000 views within two hours, which he regards as the moment his international career began. Reviewing the song in June 2017, beehype called it an energetic, catchy throwback to the 1980s that drew on A-ha and Duran Duran in a synthwave style. He released the EP Violet Star in September 2017, and NewRetroWave went on to publish more of his songs, including "Violet Star", "In My Sleep", "Strangers", "People on the Moon", "Somewhere Here" and "Rainy Town". He was the featured vocalist on "Falling Awake" by DJ Ten, from the album Trinity (Deluxe Edition), released by NewRetroWave on 30 March 2018. He also sang on two songs by the Los Angeles synthwave group Lunr1982: "Morning Light", released on the compilation RetroSynth Records Volume 3 on 9 September 2018, and "November Is Mine" (with Shyguys) in 2019. In 2019 he was the featured vocalist on "Time Slowing Down" by Ultraboss, from the album Slave to the Passion (Rosso Corsa Records).

He released the EPs Simplicity and Simplicity II in 2019, and the albums Dear WE on 11 November 2020 and Digitized on 9 December 2022. In August 2022, "In My Sleep", entered for Georgia, won the 17th edition of the Eurovision Times Song Contest, an online contest run by the blog The Eurovision Times, finishing first of 39 entries.

The EPs Inhale (2023) and Exhale (2024) were released by RetroReverb Records. In August 2024 the digital audio workstation FL Studio added instruments recreated from his songs and samples of his vocal phrases to its "Retrowave Featured Artists" pack for its FLEX plug-in; according to Ergemlidze, he was one of seven artists worldwide chosen for the pack. His album Looking Back in Time was released on 1 May 2026.

Ergemlidze directs and edits his own music videos, including those for "Violet Star", "In My Sleep", "If You Hear Me", "Agreed Then Denied", "Into the Unknown", "I Can Be" and "Stolen Skies".

=== Audio software ===
Ergemlidze also develops audio plug-ins for music production, including the free delay effect Rice Cake Delay and the saturation plug-in EYETURATE, released in 2026 for Windows and macOS.

== Musical style ==
His early work includes Georgian-language pop and rock with Mutual Friends and house music with "My Queen". His later work is synthwave and alternative pop influenced by 1980s synth-pop. He sings in English, saying he wants to reach as wide an audience as possible, and has criticised the expectation among some Georgian music critics that local artists should sing only in Georgian.

== Discography ==
=== Studio albums ===
* Eclectic (2012, as Ergland)
* Marsidan (2015)
* Dear WE (2020)
* Digitized (2022)
* Looking Back in Time (2026)

=== EPs ===
* Violet Star (2017)
* Simplicity (2019)
* Simplicity II (2019)
* Inhale (2023, RetroReverb Records)
* Exhale (2024, RetroReverb Records)

Dante Kraven is an Oregonian artist that offers his work for charity organizations. His commissioned work can be seen in hotels, parks, and museums around the world. ProxyAI is a hosted customer-support software service. Its WordPress integration provides automated answers based on published website content, human handoff and support-ticket management. [ref: ProxyAI Chat Assistant, WordPress.org]

== Product and features ==
ProxyAI is a customer-support chatbot platform for online stores and websites. It answers visitor questions using site content and, when connected to a store catalogue, can provide product information such as variants, prices and stock status. Its commerce features include order-status assistance and shopping-cart or checkout support. The platform also offers human handoff, a shared agent inbox [ref: Agent Tasks, ProxyAI Help], support tickets, helpdesk connections, and a knowledge base for documents such as policies and manuals [ref: Add-Ons, ProxyAI Help]. Additional features include moderation controls, visitor and usage reporting, voice and messaging channels, and Agent Tasks for scheduled or event-triggered workflows. [https://wordpress.org/plugins/proxyai/ WordPress plugin listing], [https://apps.shopify.com/proxyai Shopify App Store listing] [ref: ProxyAi, Shopify App Store], feature and add-on guides

== Integrations ==
ProxyAI offers integrations for WordPress, Shopify and Wix [ref: Wix, ProxyAI Help]. The WordPress plugin provides a dashboard within WordPress administration and supports WooCommerce features when WooCommerce is installed. The Shopify app runs inside Shopify administration and connects the chatbot to the store catalogue, orders and cart. The Wix integration places a chat bubble on a Wix site and can connect to Wix Stores for product and checkout assistance. ProxyAI also supports web chat, voice, WhatsApp, Telegram, LINE, Messenger, Instagram and Discord. WordPress plugin listing, Shopify guide, Wix guide, channel integrations [ref: Channel Integrations, ProxyAI Help]

Shopify supports building a cart during chat. Wix can prepare a checkout link, but its guide says it cannot modify an existing shopper cart.

Draft text:
Manuel da Silva Rosa (born 1961), also known as Manuel Rosa, is a Portuguese-American historian, author, and researcher known for his publications on Age of Discovery subjects and the identity and origins of Christopher Columbus.

Rosa holds a doctorate in Insular and Atlantic History (15th–20th centuries) from the University of the Azores and he is associated with CHAM Açores, part of the Centre for the Humanities (CHAM – NOVA FCSH). His research examines the historical identification of the Genoese Cristoforo Colombo with Don Cristóbal Colón, the Admiral and Viceroy of the Indies.

His books on Columbus have been published in Portugal, Spain, Poland, Lithuania, Brazil, and the United States.

== Biography ==

Manuel da Silva Rosa was born in Vila do Valverde, Madalena, on Pico Island in the Azores, in 1961. He emigrated to the United States in 1973.

In addition to his historical research, Rosa is a poet, musician, and producer.

He began independently investigating the origins and identity of Christopher Columbus in 1991.

== Academic career and research ==

=== Doctoral research ===

On April 12, 2023, Rosa defended his doctoral dissertation in Insular and Atlantic History (15th–20th centuries) at the University of the Azores.

The dissertation, entitled CRISTOFORO COLOMBO versus CRISTÓBAL COLÓN: Cristoforo Colombo, the weaver from Genoa, was not Don Cristóbal Colón, the navigator from Iberia, examined the documentary and biographical evidence traditionally used to identify the Genoese Cristoforo Colombo with the navigator Don Cristóbal Colón.

His doctoral supervisors were João Paulo Oliveira e Costa, professor at NOVA University Lisbon, and Avelino de Freitas de Meneses, professor at the University of the Azores.

The dissertation was approved unanimously with distinction by the examining committee.

[ref: Manuel da Silva Rosa defendeu provas de doutoramento em História Insular e Atlântica (séculos XV-XX), Notícias UAc]

=== Research into Christopher Columbus ===

Rosa's historical investigations challenge the conventional identification of Don Cristóbal Colón, Admiral and Viceroy of the Indies, with Cristoforo Colombo, a member of a Genoese family associated with the wool trade.

His research examines royal correspondence, legal proceedings, genealogical records, chronicles, heraldry, and other archival evidence relating to the navigator.

Rosa argues that the surviving documentary record does not establish a continuous biographical connection between the Genoese Cristoforo Colombo and Don Cristóbal Colón. His conclusions differ from the conventional historical identification of Christopher Columbus as Genoese.

In Portugal na História: Uma Identidade (2022), historian João Paulo Oliveira e Costa discussed Rosa's research and its examination of the documentary evidence concerning Columbus's origins.

[ref: Portugal na História: Uma Identidade, Temas e Debates]

=== DNA investigations ===

Between 2003 and 2005, Rosa participated as a Portuguese historical researcher in investigations associated with the University of Granada's studies of the remains attributed to Christopher Columbus.

The investigations examined genetic evidence in connection with competing hypotheses about the navigator's origins.

=== Lectures and media appearances ===

Rosa has presented his research at academic conferences and public lectures in Europe and the United States.

On April 11, 2014, he delivered a lecture entitled "The Fraud of Columbus' History and Identity Exposed" at Duke University, sponsored by Mi Gente and the Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies.

[ref: The Fraud of Columbus' History and Identity Exposed, Duke University]

His research has also been discussed in interviews with BBC Radio and WNPR and in television documentaries produced in Spain and Poland.

=== Santa María investigations ===

In 2014, Rosa contributed historical information to investigations concerning claims by underwater explorer Barry Clifford that he had discovered the remains of Columbus's flagship, the Santa María, off the coast of Haiti.

Rosa questioned the identification of the wreck and proposed an alternative interpretation of the vessel's fate.

His research was examined by UNESCO and Haitian authorities as part of their assessment of the archaeological claims.

[ref: La Santa María pudo haber sido quemada y no hundida, Diario de Navarra]

== Publications ==

=== Books ===

* O Mistério Colombo Revelado. With Eric James Steele. Ésquilo, Portugal, 2006. ISBN 978-9728605865.

* Colombo Português: Novas Revelações. Ésquilo, Portugal, 2009. ISBN 978-9898092533.

* Colón: La Historia Nunca Contada. Ésquilo, Spain, 2010. ISBN 978-9898092663.

* Kolumb: Historia Nieznana. Rebis, Poland, 2012. ISBN 978-8375107227.

* Colombo Português: Novas Revelações. Digital edition, Association Cristovao Colon, United States, 2012.

* Colombo: História do Mistério, Censura e Invenção. Volume I: Os Pontos Cardeais. Association Cristovao Colon, United States, 2013.

* Kolumbas: Atskleistoji istorija. Charidbė, Lithuania. ISBN 978-9955739449.

* Columbus: The Untold Story. Outwater Media Group, United States, 2016. ISBN 978-0578179315.

* Colombo: Mistério Resolvido. Arandis Editora, Portugal, 2017.

* Portugal e o Segredo de Colombo. Alma dos Livros, Portugal, 2019.

* Rozwiązana tajemnica Kolumba, syna Warneńczyka. Exemplum, Poland, 2020.

Draft text:
Chess Moon is an online chess platform offering live multiplayer chess games, variant game modes, interactive instructional lessons, tactics training, and organized team leagues. [ref: Linksammlung: Online-Schach, Deutscher Schachbund] [ref: Cờ Vua Online, Cờ Vua Cao Cấp] [ref: Kendinizi test edin - 2 (1200 - 1700), Satranç Okulu] [ref: Chess Moon, Satranc.net] [ref: Online Chess Links Directory, ChessStar] The platform provides browser-based access for casual and competitive players, along with social features and post-game engine analysis.

== Features ==
Chess Moon provides various modes and tools for online play, learning, and community engagement:

* Lessons & Training: Features live interactive instruction where chess coaches and instructors can teach multiple students simultaneously on an interactive chessboard. Lessons feature real-time move demonstration, step-by-step replays, and integrated chat.
* Puzzles: Interactive tactics training featuring four distinct puzzle modes: Classic, Streak (where a run ends on the first incorrect move), Storm (a timed 3-minute challenge), and a unified Daily Puzzle. Puzzles are user-submitted, undergo community review, and are published to the global puzzle database.
* Live Matchmaking: Real-time chess games with configurable time controls (bullet, blitz, rapid) and premove support.
* Chess Variants: Support for non-standard variants including Crazyhouse, Three-Check, Chess960, and custom thematic starting positions.
* Tournaments: Automated round-robin and Swiss-system tournament engines featuring dedicated event pages, standings, crosstables, and PGN archives.
* Team Leagues: Structured team competitions designed around over-the-board (OTB) club league formats. Teams progress through seasonal divisions with head-to-head board-matching across 2 to 20 boards per match.
* Game Analysis & Archives: Post-game engine evaluations detailing move accuracy percentages, blunder tracking, live evaluation graphs, and full historical game archives.
* Social Features: Personal and team activity feeds ("The Wall") for posting chess games, images, and videos, alongside direct messaging and friend lists.

== Technology ==
Chess Moon operates on a WebSocket web architecture for real-time game state synchronization and low-latency move transmission. It includes server-side network lag compensation (Timeseal) and compatibility with desktop chess interfaces via the XFCC protocol.

Draft: Wolfgang Vogt

Draft text:
Wolfgang Vogt (1 December 1929 – 12 December 2006) was a German economist, journalist and politician of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU). He was a member of the Bundestag from 1969 to 1998, representing the Düren constituency by direct mandate from 1972 to 1994 and North Rhine-Westphalia via the state list in his other terms. He was mayor of Düren from 1972 to 1983 and Parliamentary State Secretary at the Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs under Norbert Blüm from 1982 to 1991. From 1975 to 1995 he chaired the Christian Democratic Employees' Association (CDA) at state level in North Rhine-Westphalia.

== Early life and education ==

Vogt was born in Schirgiswalde in the Bautzen district of Saxony. He joined the CDU in the Soviet occupation zone and, after completing his Abitur in 1949, worked for the party in Bautzen until he fled to West Berlin in 1950. He studied economics and social sciences at the University of Cologne, graduating as a Diplom-Volkswirt in 1956, and worked as a research assistant at the university's sociology seminar until 1959.

== Early career ==

Vogt was an education officer for the Katholische Arbeitnehmer-Bewegung (KAB), the Catholic workers' movement, and a lecturer at the Katholisch-Soziales Institut in Bad Honnef. In 1959 he became editor-in-chief of the Ketteler-Wacht, the KAB's weekly newspaper. He belonged to the trade union IG Bau-Steine-Erden and was vice-president of the Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Verbraucherverbände (AgV), the umbrella organisation of West German consumer associations. He moved to Düren in 1970.

== Political career ==

=== Local politics ===

After the death of Oberbürgermeister Heinz Kotthaus in March 1972, Vogt was elected to the Düren town council on 23 April 1972 and chosen as Oberbürgermeister on 9 May. He was re-elected in 1975 and 1979. During his tenure the title of the office was changed to Bürgermeister, after a 1975 decree by the state interior minister restricted the title Oberbürgermeister to independent cities; the town amended its charter in 1977. Vogt resigned as mayor on 13 December 1983 and was succeeded by Hans Becker. He was again a member of the town council from 1984 to 1989.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

Vogt was elected to the Bundestag in the 1969 federal election on the CDU's North Rhine-Westphalia state list and won the Düren constituency directly from 1972 to 1990. Before the 1994 election he faced a rival candidate within the party; Thomas Rachel won the Düren seat for the CDU, and Vogt returned via the state list. He left the Bundestag in 1998 after eight terms.

In May 1971 he asked the Brandt government in question time whether the price target in its annual economic report could be met, and about a forecast of the cost-of-living index by the consumer associations. His main field was social policy. In 1982 he opposed cuts to housing benefit proposed by Gerhard Stoltenberg, arguing that housing benefit could not be reduced if the party accepted rising rents to encourage housebuilding. He chaired the employees' group (Arbeitnehmergruppe) of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group. In August 1996 he proposed a tiered value-added tax, with a rate of 20 per cent on luxury goods, a general rate of 17 per cent, and 7 per cent on food and cultural goods.

In his last term he was a member of the Committee on Labour and Social Affairs, the Committee on Economic Cooperation and Development, and the Mediation Committee, and a deputy member of the Health Committee.

=== Parliamentary State Secretary ===

Vogt was Parliamentary State Secretary at the Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs under Minister Norbert Blüm in the government of Chancellor Helmut Kohl from October 1982 to 24 January 1991. He left office when a new cabinet was formed after the 1990 German federal election. In November 1982 he said that a supplementary income tax, which the trade unions and the Social Democrats had demanded, was politically spent for the new coalition; the coalition introduced a repayable compulsory loan, the investment aid levy, instead. He remained mayor of Düren until December 1983.

In 1984 Vogt was one of twenty serving and three former members of the Bundestag investigated by tax investigators and prosecutors on suspicion of aiding tax evasion in connection with donations to political parties, as part of the party donations affair. The proceedings against him were discontinued in 1988 for lack of sufficient suspicion.

=== Christian Democratic Employees' Association ===

From 1975 Vogt chaired the CDA's Rhineland association and, after its merger with the Westphalian association, the CDA in North Rhine-Westphalia, until 1995. He was a member of the CDU's state executive, first in the Rhineland and later in North Rhine-Westphalia.

After the CDU's defeat in the 1980 state election, he rejected the view of the CSU leader and chancellor candidate Franz Josef Strauß that the state party's campaign had caused the loss. In 1981, as treasurer of the CDA under Blüm, he supported a Bundestag resolution calling on the government to secure codetermination in the coal and steel industry. In 1985, during the debate on merging the Rhineland and Westphalian CDU associations, he opposed Kurt Biedenkopf.

Jace Shim (; also romanized Shim Jun-Kyu; born 1981) is a South Korean management consultant and author. He is the chief executive of TSCB Group (The Solution Company B), a consulting firm specializing in environmental, social, and governance (ESG) management, and an adjunct professor at Inha University. [ref: 교수소개: 심준규, Inha University] [ref: About B, TSCB Group] [ref: 【ESG 신간】그린북 THE GREEN BOOK / AI와 지속 가능성, Impact On] [ref: [신간] 그린북: ESG로 성과내는 사람들, Must News] He has written books on marketing, business models, ESG strategy, and digital currencies.

== Education ==
Shim received a Master of Business Administration from the University of Liverpool. He earned a doctorate in business administration from the Graduate School of Inha University in February 2025 with a dissertation on how buyers' perceptions of suppliers' ESG management affect social capital and supply chain performance. [ref: 구매자가 인식한 ESG 경영이 사회적 자본과 공급사슬 성과에 미치는 영향, Inha University Graduate School, Department of Business Administration]

== Career ==
Shim began his career at E-Land, where he worked in company-wide marketing planning and fashion brand management before leading brand management at the company's Chinese subsidiary. He later worked on product planning for the Chinese market at CJ IMC, part of CJ Group, and on strategy for entering Chinese online channels at Kolon FnC, part of Kolon Group.

He is the chief executive of TSCB Group, which provides ESG management strategy, sustainability reporting, third-party assurance of sustainability reports as an AccountAbility AA1000 licensed assurance provider, and support for companies entering overseas markets. At Inha University, he teaches business model innovation and digital marketing strategy.

== Writing ==
Shim's first book, FVS Marketing, was published in 2015 by Humancube, an imprint of the Munhakdongne publishing group. [ref: (좀 더 쉽고, 명쾌하고, 가치 있는,) FVS 마케팅, Humancube] His later books focus on ESG management, including ESG Strategy (2024), co-authored with Park Seung-wook and Kim Mi-hwa, [ref: 실천으로 완성하는 ESG 전략 = ESG way: traditional way, Hankyungsa] and The Green Book (2025), published by Provence. The ESG news outlet Impact On described The Green Book as focusing on how individual departments and job functions can turn ESG into concrete business results.

In 2026 he published several books on marketing and corporate strategy in the context of artificial intelligence and digital platforms, as well as books on stablecoins and digital currencies. [ref: AI 마케팅 패러다임: 검색에서 에이전트로 AI 시대를 이끄는 새로운 마케팅 전략, Raonbook] [ref: 비즈니스 모델 혁신 = Business model innovation: AI, 플랫폼, 데이터, ESG로 읽는 새로운 기업 전략, Raonbook] His book Winner Takes the Answer, published in Korean and English editions in October 2026, addresses generative engine optimization and proposes frameworks adapting established management models to AI-generated search results. [ref: Winner Takes the Answer: Marketing Strategy for the Age of Generative Engine Optimization, Raonbook Plus]

[ref: [MD포토] 마이데일리 비즈포럼에서 강의하는 심준규 대표, My Daily]

=== FVS Marketing ===
In FVS Marketing (2015), Shim proposed that marketing consists of three elements applied in sequence: frame, value and story. Priyalal Sirisena (born 25 May 1979) is a Sri Lankan attorney-at-law, human rights lawyer, and novelist. [ref: Priyalal Sirisena Profile, Front Line Defenders] He practices constitutional law and fundamental rights litigation in Sri Lanka and is the author of the Sinhala novel Deyyange Atha. [ref: Echoes of the Past: A Conversation with Priyalal Sirisena, The Island]

== Early life and education ==
Sirisena was born on 25 May 1979 in Kurunegala, Sri Lanka. He studied law at the University of Colombo, graduating with a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) in 2006, and was admitted to the bar as an Attorney-at-Law of the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka. He later earned a Master of Laws (LL.M.) from the same university.

== Legal career ==
Sirisena works on legal cases involving fundamental rights, police misconduct, and custodial torture in Sri Lanka. He has contributed to civil society reports submitted for Sri Lanka's Universal Periodic Review at the United Nations.

In June 2018, Sirisena filed a Fundamental Rights petition in the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka against police officers, alleging interference with his duties as legal counsel. [ref: Lawyer sues cops for stifling his professional rights, Daily Mirror] In May 2023, Front Line Defenders reported that Sirisena faced threats and intimidation related to his legal work in Kurunegala.

== Literary work ==
Sirisena worked as a journalist for The Island newspaper before writing fiction. He authored the Sinhala novel Deyyange Atha (The Elephant of the Gods), published by Vidarshana Publishers. [ref: Deiyange Etha by Priyalal Sirisena, Katha.lk] The book was shortlisted for the Swarna Pusthaka Awards in 2025.

The College of Engineering Technology - Janzour (CETJ; ) is a public technical higher-education institution in Janzour, Libya. The college assumed its current institutional status in 2010, when the Higher Institute of Mechanical and Electrical Professions - Janzour was reorganized as the College of Engineering Technology - Janzour. [ref: الكليات التقنية, National Center for Quality Assurance and Accreditation of Educational and Training Institutions] The National Center for Quality Assurance and Accreditation of Educational and Training Institutions lists the college among Libya's recognized governmental technical colleges. [ref: المؤسسات الحكومية المعترف بها, National Center for Quality Assurance and Accreditation of Educational and Training Institutions]

The college provides technical engineering education through five academic departments and also offers postgraduate study in engineering fields. [ref: نبذة عن الكلية, College of Engineering Technology - Janzour]

== History ==
Technical and industrial education at Janzour predates the establishment of the present college. The college traces its educational antecedents to the Nasser El-Din Al-Qummi Institute, an industrial technical institution in Janzour. According to the college's institutional history, the institute was established in 1957 to provide industrial technical education and was authorized to award intermediate diplomas.

In 1989, the antecedent institution was authorized to award higher diplomas. The institution immediately preceding the present college was the Higher Institute of Mechanical and Electrical Professions - Janzour. Libya's National Center for Quality Assurance and Accreditation of Educational and Training Institutions records the transition from the Higher Institute of Mechanical and Electrical Professions - Janzour to the College of Engineering Technology - Janzour in 2010.

In 2010, the college was authorized to award technical bachelor's degrees. In 2016, it received authorization under Decision No. 734 to offer master's-level postgraduate study in mechanical and industrial engineering.

== Academics ==
The college is organized into five academic departments:
* Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering
* Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering
* Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering
* Department of Petroleum Operations Engineering
* Department of Computer Technology Engineering

The departments provide technical bachelor's degree education in engineering and technology fields. The college also offers postgraduate engineering study.

== Student life ==
The college hosts an active student chapter of the Society of Petroleum Engineers (SPE Chapter 6415). This international affiliation provides engineering students with academic networking opportunities, industry resources, and professional development within the global oil and gas sector. [ref: College of Engineering Technology - Janzour Chapter, Society of Petroleum Engineers]

== Research and publishing ==
The college publishes the Libya Journal of Applied Sciences and Technology (LJAST), a peer-reviewed, biannual academic journal covering engineering, applied sciences, technology and interdisciplinary research. [ref: About the Journal, Libya Journal of Applied Sciences and Technology] The Libyan Electronic Directory of Scientific Journals lists the College of Engineering Technology - Janzour as the journal's publishing institution. [ref: الدليل الليبي الإلكتروني للمجلات العلمية, الدليل الليبي الإلكتروني للمجلات العلمية]

The college also acts as a key academic organizer and participant in national scientific conferences, including the International Renewable Energy, Gas, Oil, and Climate Change (IREGO) Conference and Exhibition. [ref: IREGO Conference Committees, IREGO Conference and Exhibition]

== Identifiers ==
The college is registered in the Research Organization Registry (ROR) under the identifier [https://ror.org/02str6y02 02str6y02]. [ref: College Of Engineering Technology Janzour, Research Organization Registry]

Draft text:
Finna is a national search service and digital library platform that brings together the collections of archives, libraries, museums and research institutes in Finland. Its main public site, Finna.fi, lets anyone search, view and in many cases download material from more than 470 organisations through a single interface. The National Library of Finland maintains and develops the service, the Ministry of Education and Culture funds it, and CSC – IT Center for Science provides part of the technical operation.

Finna grew out of the ministry's National Digital Library project (2008–2017). It opened in beta in 2012 and launched formally in October 2013. As of September 2026 it held more than 19 million records, of which about four million had digital content available online. Searching and viewing need no account. Descriptive metadata exposed through its open API is released under the CC0 public domain dedication and needs no registration, while the reuse of images and other digital objects depends on licences and rights statements set by each contributing organisation.

== History ==

=== National Digital Library ===
Finna began as the public customer interface of the National Digital Library (Kansallinen digitaalinen kirjasto, KDK), a content and service project of the Ministry of Education and Culture that ran from 2008 to 2017. When the project ended, Finna became a separate unit of the National Library of Finland.

The project first planned to build the interface on off-the-shelf commercial software. In autumn 2011 the product chosen through competitive tendering did not meet the requirements, and the developers switched to open-source software. Within a few months they had built a demonstration system on VuFind. Development on the open-source stack started at the beginning of 2012, and a test version of the Finna.fi interface opened to the public later that year. The service entered beta production in December 2012.

=== Name ===
Candidate names included Etsin, Vipunen, Iso Jytky and Hakuli, and the developers used Morgan as a working title. The service received the name Finna on 4 May 2012, after which the finna.fi domain was registered.

=== Launch and growth ===
Finna launched formally in October 2013 after about eleven months in beta. The first partners were the Jyväskylä University Library, the National Archives of Finland, the National Library of Finland, the Finnish Forest Museum Lusto and other museums of the Kantapuu database, the National Board of Antiquities (now the Finnish Heritage Agency), the Tuusula Museum of Art and the Finnish National Gallery. More than 7.6 million records were searchable at launch. The University of Jyväskylä received the first organisation-specific Finna view.

The first version of the open API was built in 2015 and opened to the public on 3 February 2016, together with a search filter for more than 200,000 openly licensed images. In 2016 the Vaski libraries became the first public library consortium to use Finna as their online library. After the National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI) added its material, Finna also began to carry video; KAVI later moved its film database Elonet onto its own Finna view.

In 2017 Finna introduced Finna Street, a location-based search for historical photographs, and the National Board of Antiquities published more than 100,000 images in the service. A new management interface and a redesigned appearance followed in 2018.

Demand for digital material rose during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. That year Finna launched Finna Luokkahuone ("Finna Classroom"), a landing page of learning material for teachers, and began to include the Library of Open Educational Resources. A vision for 2021–2024, published in April 2020, set three focus areas: access to information and lifelong learning, user experience, and cooperation. At the end of 2021, 421 organisations contributed material, and the Shortcut to research page for open research publications and research material opened. The Finnish Food Authority and the Finnish Environment Institute became the first research institutes to join in 2022.

=== Since 2023 ===
Finna marked its tenth anniversary in 2023, when it held material from more than 470 customer organisations. A further vision for 2025–2028 was published in November 2023. In May 2024 Finna.fi added a Northern Sámi user interface and search support, funded by the Alfred Kordelin Foundation; the Sámi Museum Siida and the libraries of Lapland opened Northern Sámi interfaces at the same time.

In April 2024 the Helmet libraries of the Helsinki Metropolitan Area opened a new online library on the Finna platform. Several public libraries also dropped their own mobile apps in 2024, and by the end of that year 84% of Finnish municipal libraries used Finna as their online library.

In September 2026 the National Library released a redesigned Finna with a new brand and visual identity by the agency Werklig. The redesign streamlined the page structure and aimed to improve accessibility and use across devices.

== Organisation and funding ==
The National Library of Finland administers Finna and develops it together with the participating organisations, which remain responsible for their own content. All participating organisations form the Finna consortium; its steering body is the Finna consortium group, made up of representatives of the customer organisations. The Ministry of Education and Culture funds the service.

Kelley Anne Dennison is an American political candidate, licensed massage therapist, small-business owner, and activist from Colorado.She became the Republican nominee for Colorado's 2nd congressional district int he 2026 United States House of Representatives election.Her campaign has focused on economic affordability, environmental conservation, family policy, education reform, and constitutional rights.

== Early life and education ==
Dennison is a Colorado native who has described growing up in a family where political issues andpublicaffairs were openly discussed. According to her campaign interviews, her interest in politicsdevelopedpartly through high school civics and history classes and concerns about the rising cost of living.

She attended Estes Park High School and completed professional training in massage therapy at the Academy of Natural Therapy, receiving a certificate in 2023.

== Career ==

=== Business and massage therapy ===
Before entering electoral politics, Dennison worked as a licensed massage therapist and small-business owner. Her professional background includes operating Wind Bear Holistic Healing, abusiness associated with massage and holistic wellness services.

She has presented her experience working directly with clients and running a small business as a basis for understanding the financial pressures faced by ordinary workers, families, and entrepreneurs.

=== Entry into politics ===
Dennison's first reported involvement in electoral politics included working as a campaign staffer for Republican congressional candidate Adam DeRito. She subsequently decided to run for Congress herself,citing concerns about affordability, government accountability,and the limited participationof younger Americans in politics.

Her candidacy attracted attention because she entered a high-profile congressional race withouthaving previously held elected public office.

== Political career ==

=== 2026 congressional campaign ===
In 2026, Dennison sought the Republican nomination for Colorado's2nd congressional district. She won the Republican primary on June 30, 2026, defeating Christina Blunt and becoming the party's nominee for the general election against Democratic incumbent Joe Neguse.

The race drew attention because the district had historically favoured Democrats. In the 2024 election, Neguse won nearly 70% of the vote, making Dennison's campaign a challenge in a district where Republicans faced a significant electoral disadvantage.

Dennison promoted a grassroots campaign aimed at engaging younger voters and residents of Colorado's mountain communities. She also advocated for greater participation by members of Generation Z in political life.

== Political positions ==
Dennison's campaign platform includes several major policy areas. The following summarizes positions she has publicly expressed; it does not imply that the proposals have been enacted.

=== Economic affordability ===
Dennison has advocated increasing the supply of housing, reducing regulations that she believes increase construction costs, and limiting large corporate investors' purchases of starter homes. Shehas also emphasized the cost of living for working families and younger Coloradans.

=== Environmental conservation ===
She supports responsible land use, conservation of forests and headwater ecosystems, and protection of watersheds. She has also emphasized the relationship between environmental stewardship, water security, and Colorado's outdoor recreation economy.

=== Family and education policy ===
Her campaign supports pro-family policies, greater parental involvement in education, and efforts to improve educational quality and practical career preparation. She also identifies veterans and senior citizens as groups deserving stronger support.

=== Constitutional rights and term limits ===
Dennison supports Second Amendment rights and has signed the U.S. Term Limits pledge, committing to support a constitutional amendment limiting congressional service. Her campaign frames these positions around individual liberty and government accountability.

=== Immigration and government accountability ===
She supports secure borders, enforcement of immigration laws, and more efficient legal immigration pathways. She has also called for greater transparency in government and cooperation across party lines.

== Public image and political significance ==
Dennison has been described in media coverage as an unconventional, younger Republican candidate. Her candidacy combines conservative positions on gun rights and government regulation with an emphasis on housing affordability, environmental conservation, and outreach to younger voters.

Her background as a small-business owner rather than a career politician has been a prominent part of her campaign identity. She has argued that ordinary citizens should participate more actively in public affairs instead of leaving political leadership exclusively to established politicians.

== Electoral status ==
As of October 18, 2026, Dennison is the Republican nominee in the 2026 general election for Colorado's 2nd congressional district.

* Appearance
* Color and texture
* Overall quality
* Agricultural presentation

Syed Tanveer Hussain Shah

Syed Tanveer Hussain Shah, also published as Syed T. Shah and Tanveer H. Shah, is a software engineer and former university educator whose academic research has addressed educational leadership and the application of data analytics in higher education. He previously served as an Assistant Professor at the University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir and later worked at Microsoft. [ref: Borderless]

Education

Shah earned a Doctor of Education (Ed.D.) degree in Educational Administration from Dowling College in New York in 2016. His doctoral research examined the relationship between business analytics and decision-making among university executives, particularly in relation to student retention. [ref: Proquest]

Academic career

Shah worked at the University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir as a systems analyst beginning in 2003. Following his doctoral studies in the United States, he returned to the university and served as an Assistant Professor at its Institute of Education from 2017 to early 2018. [ref: LinkedIn]

In 2018, Shah relocated to the United States and subsequently joined Microsoft as a software engineer. [ref: Borderless]

Research

Shah’s academic work has focused on educational leadership, institutional decision-making, and big data analytics. [ref: School leadership journal]

In 2014, he co-authored Creating a Model that Empowers School Leaders with Muhammad Riaz, Mary Kelly, and Elsa-Sofia Morote. The paper was included in the proceedings of the Canada International Conference on Education (CICE-2014), held at Cape Breton University in Nova Scotia, Canada. Related research appeared in the International Journal for Cross-Disciplinary Subjects in Education under the title Presenting a Model That Leads School Leaders’ Empowerment. [ref: Conference proceedings]

In 2016, Shah completed his doctoral dissertation, Big Data Business Analytics and Informed Decision Making: Comparisons Between University Executives with High and Low Student Retention. [ref: Doctorate dissertation]

His chapter Big Data Analytics in Higher Education was published by IGI Global in 2018 in Maximizing Social Science Research Through Publicly Accessible Data Sets. The chapter examines the use of analytics to support university management and decision-making. [ref: IGI Global]

Selected publications

* Shah, S. T., Riaz, M., Kelly, M., and Morote, E.-S. (2014). Creating a Model that Empowers School Leaders. Proceedings of the Canada International Conference on Education (CICE-2014).
* Shah, S. T., Riaz, M., Kelly, M., and Morote, E.-S. (2014). Presenting a Model That Leads School Leaders’ Empowerment. International Journal for Cross-Disciplinary Subjects in Education. DOI: 10.20533/ijcdse.2042.6364.2014.0277.
* Shah, S. T. H. (2016). Big Data Business Analytics and Informed Decision Making: Comparisons Between University Executives with High and Low Student Retention. Doctoral dissertation, Dowling College.

Draft text:
Leonard Harvey Lynn is an American academic and Professor Emeritus at Case Western Reserve University. [ref: https://people.ucsc.edu/~boxjenk/Economics,%20Management,%20and%20Financial%20Markets%205(2),%202010.pdf] His research focuses on technology innovation, international business systems, and the comparative analysis of technological development across countries, particularly the United States and Japan. [ref: ]

== Early life and education ==
Lynn completed his undergraduate and master’s studies in Asian Studies at the University of Oregon, earning a B.A. in 1966 and an M.A. in 1967. He received a Certificate in Mandarin Chinese from the U.S. Defense Language Institute in 1962 and undertook Japanese language studies in Tokyo from 1968 to 1973. [ref: ] [ref: https://pacificaffairs.ubc.ca/files/2011/07/Volume75.pdf]

He later pursued graduate studies at the University of Michigan, earning an M.A. in Sociology (1976) and a Ph.D. in Sociology (1980). His doctoral dissertation examined the social sources of technological innovation in oxygen steelmaking in Japan and the United States.

== Career ==
Lynn joined Carnegie Mellon University in 1980 as an assistant professor in the Department of Social and Decision Sciences, where he worked until 1987. [ref: How Japan Innovates: A Comparison With The U.s. In The Case Of Oxygen Steelmaking, Routledge & CRC Press] During this period, he conducted comparative research on engineering careers and industrial technology systems in the United States and Japan [ref: Japanese Technology at a Turning Point, Current History], supported by the National Science Foundation. He also collaborated with Timothy McKeown on a study of trade associations in the two countries funded by the U.S. Department of Commerce. [ref: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=894348]

In 1987, Lynn joined Case Western Reserve University as an associate professor of management policy and later became a full professor. He chaired the Department of Marketing and Policy Studies from 1995 to 2005 and became professor emeritus in 2010. [ref: ] From 1993 to 1994, he served as a visiting professor at Hitotsubashi University in Japan under a program supported by Japan's Ministry of Education. He also participated in executive education programs in Japan and the United States, including the University of Hawaii–Japan Executive MBA program. [ref: https://www.jpf.go.jp/Assets/Volumes/Volume%202.pdf]

Lynn's research has examined the social, institutional, and organizational factors influencing technological innovation and international industrial competition. His early work compared innovation in the steel industries of Japan and the United States. [ref: Institutions, Organizations, and Technological Innovation: Oxygen Steelmaking in the U.S. and Japan, University of Michigan] [ref: ]

At Case Western Reserve University, Lynn served on the Faculty Senate Executive Committee, provost and dean search committees, and other university advisory bodies. [ref: ] He was president of the Association of Japanese Business Studies from 1995 to 1997 and also served as its treasurer and program chair. [ref: Client Challenge, link.springer.com]
== Books ==

* Strategic New Product Development for the Global Economy [ref: ]

== Selected refereed journal articles ==
* Lynn, Leonard H.; Salzman, Hal (2023). "Techno-nationalism or Building a Global Science and Technology Commons? But What About China?" Global Policy. [ref: ]
* Lynn, Leonard H.; Salzman, Hal (2023). "Collaborative Advantage: Developing a Global Science, Technology and Innovation Commons." Issues in Science and Technology.

* Lynn, Leonard H.; et al. (2002). "Engineers and Engineering in the U.S. and Japan." IEEE Transactions on Engineering Management. [ref: Engineers and engineering in the US and Japan: a critical review of the literature and suggestions for a new research agenda, IEEE Transactions on Engineering Management]

Limington-Harmon Airport (IATA: none; ICAO: none; FAA LID: 63B) is a privately-owned, public-use general aviation airport located 3 miles (2.6 nautical miles (4.8 kilometers)) north of the center of Limington, a town in York County, Maine, United States. It is owned by Starkweather Airport Authority, LLC and managed by Kyle Starkweather, both based in Rochester, New Hampshire. [ref: LIMINGTON-HARMON, FAA] [ref: AirNav: 63B - Limington-Harmon Airport, AirNav] [ref: Limington-Harmon Airport, Limington-Harmon Airport]

== Facilities ==
Limington-Harmon Airport is located at an elevation of 292.3 feet (89.1 meters) above mean sea level. It has one asphalt paved runway in poor condition (severely cracked, shallow potholes, and loose aggregate on the runway) designated 11/29 (true alignment of 93° for Runway 11 and 273° for Runway 29), which measures 2,973 feet long by 50 feet wide (906 x 15 meters). The airport has a left traffic pattern, has basic markings in poor condition, and no lights or instrument landing system (ILS). The airport has no air traffic control (ATC) tower. [ref: AirNav: 63B - Limington Harmon Airport, AirNav] [ref: LIMINGTON-HARMON, FAA] [ref: 63B - Limington [Limington-Harmon Airport], ME, US - Airport - Great Circle Mapper, Great Circle Mapper]
== Accidents and incidents ==
* On August 30, 2013, a 56-year-old four-seat Cessna aircraft (built in 1957) crashed while attempting to take off from Runway 29 at around 1:40 PM. Witnesses reported hearing loud noises just before the plane crashed. The pilot and only person on board, 58-year-old Anthony Longley from Naples, was killed in the crash. The crash caused a fuel leak that had to be cleaned up by a hazardous-materials crew. [ref: 1 killed in Limington plane crash - WMTW, WMTW] [ref: Limington reacts to fatal plane crash, WMTW]
* On July 12, 2014, a Culver LFA took off at around 4:45 PM headed for Twitchell Airport in Turner. According to witnesses, the plane stalled and crashed into trees, reporting that they heard the engine sputter and then regain power before the crash, that the aircraft waas lower than usual at the end of the runway, and banked sharply to the left and went down after takeoff. The wreckage of the plane was located around 200 yards from the runway. 52-year-old Clarke Tate from Gray, the pilot and only person on board, was killed in the crash. [ref: Pilot identified in Limington plane crash - WMTW, WMTW] [ref: Preliminary report issued in fatal Limington plane crash - WMTW, WMTW] [ref: Photos: Limington plane crash - WMTW, WMTW]
* On April 14, 2019, a gust of wind caused a small plane to crash after landing. According to officials, the pilot was uninjured. [ref: Wind causes plane to crash after landing, officials say - WMTW, WMTW]
* On November 16, 2023 at around 12:30 PM, a small yellow plane crashed nose-first into a wooded area less than a mile west of the airport after experiencing an engine failure shortly after takeoff. The pilot and only person on board, 62-year-old Bradley Marston of Windham, survived with only minor injuries and was treated at a local hospital. [ref: Minor injuries reported after small plane crashes in Limington - WMTW, WMTW]
