The Haggis Wildlife Foundation is a Scotland-based folklore, publishing and digital storytelling initiative whose work centres on the wild haggis, an animal associated with Scottish humour and folklore. The Foundation produces documentary-style films, illustrated species guides, fictional field reports, online publications and interactive community projects. Its stated purpose is to document, reinterpret and share the cultural legend for contemporary audiences, rather than to operate as a conventional wildlife conservation charity. [ref: About the Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Haggis Wildlife Foundation] [ref: Our Work, Haggis Wildlife Foundation]

Its activities span a main website, an online catalogue of films and books, an interactive sightings register, social-media and mailing-list communities, a related research-style publishing network, and a retail website. Although much of its work adopts the conventions of zoology, conservation and historical archives, those conventions are employed in a fictional and folkloric setting. [ref: Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Haggis Wildlife Foundation] [ref: About the Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Haggis Wildlife Foundation Official Shop]

== Purpose and organisational identity ==
The Foundations work is the preservation and continuation of a Scottish storytelling tradition. It uses encounters with wild haggis to encourage participation in folklore through watching, reading, sharing stories and submitting sightings. Its online About Us statement distinguishes this activity from conventional wildlife conservation and characterises the work as cultural storytelling and community-building.

The main website presents the Foundation as an archive of wild haggis lore. It organises material into areas such as species guides, videos, news, books, the Grand Survey and a map of reported sightings. The stated motto is To document and preserve, also rendered there as describendum et conservandum. Its Our Work statement identifies storytelling, documentary production and online discussion as its principal methods and places particular emphasis on the social communities formed around humorous folklore.

== Historical narrative ==
The Foundation's website contains an extensive fictionalised foundation history. Its Our Story page attributes an establishment date of 1892 to Sir Archibald MacTavish, described as the 7th Earl of Glenfinnan. It introduces a purported early team comprising photographer Neil McKinnon, zoologist Edwin McTaggart, and Highland guides Duncan and Harris MacLeod, and situates the fictional expeditionary programme around the Heatherlie estate and the Highlands. [ref: Our Story, Haggis Wildlife Foundation]

The narrative describes late nineteenth-century photographic expeditions, the use of glass-plate equipment, purported discoveries of haggis burrows and archival photographs. These episodes are elements of the Foundation's constructed history and are not independently established events in the organisation's actual legal or operational history. No independently corroborated nineteenth-century incorporation or continuous operating history is asserted here.

The historical framework extends beyond the Foundation's own website. Publications attributed to its fictional archives include photographs and purported field records dated to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Their historical dates describe the setting of the stories, not independently verified dates of the Foundation's real-world activities. [ref: Wildes Haggis, German-language Wikipedia]

== Activities and projects ==

=== Films and digital documentaries ===
Documentary-style video is one of the Foundation's principal forms of publication. Its website hosts a film catalogue covering imagined wild haggis species, habitats, seasonal migrations and encounters. Listed titles include White Tash Haggis Animal, The Round Woodland Haggis, Wild Forest Haggis, Subspecies of Wild Scottish Sea Haggis, The Great Return: Scotland's Wild Haggis Awaken, Winter Subspecies of Wild Haggis Animals, The Great Migration of Wild Scottish Haggis Animals and A Spotters Guide to Wild Scottish Haggis Animals. [ref: Videos, Haggis Wildlife Foundation]

The films use natural-history presentation techniques to describe impossible or invented animals as though they were subjects of wildlife photography. A September 2024 community-contributed article on Daily Kos discussed the Foundation's YouTube videos, including What Is Scotland's Wild Haggis Animal?, The Ancient Art of Scottish Wild Haggis Shearing and The Truth Behind Commercial Haggis Farming. The author described the documentaries as humorous fiction and commented on their computer-generated imagery and narrated presentation. [ref: Kitchen Table Kibitzing 9/3/2024: The Haggis Wildlife Foundation, Daily Kos]

=== Species guides ===
The Foundation publishes introductory descriptions of invented wild haggis varieties, including the Common Garden Haggis and the Stirling White Tash. Its website combines species names and illustrations with instructions framed as spotting advice, while linking to longer guides and films.

Hungered is a 2026 debut novel by Amanda Rizkalla, published by Henry Holt and Co. on May 19, 2026. Oprah Winfrey selected it for Oprah’s Book Club in October 2026, the club’s 125th pick. The novel follows a twelve-year-old girl named Sofia as she navigates homelessness and family instability after her mother leaves her father. [ref: Hungered By Amanda Rizkalla] [ref: ]

== Plot ==
Sofia is twelve when her mother wakes her and her younger brother at night, packs them into the car, and drives away from Sofia’s father called “baba” in the book. What follows is a stretch of parking lots, school mornings, fast food, and the effort to seem ordinary while the family is unhoused. Sofia narrates in short, diary-like sections. She remembers the girl now living in her old bedroom, a girl with a “belly bulging out of her shirt,” and tries to make sense of adults whose choices she can only partly see. The book stays close to Sofia’s view. Readers learn about her mother’s fear, her father’s absence, and the casual cruelty of teachers and classmates mostly through what Sofia notices, overhears, and misreads. [ref: Hungered, Literary Hub]

== Themes ==
Hungered addresses themes of poverty, housing insecurity, and class consciousness through the lens of a child's perspective. Kirkus Reviews noted that the novel encapsulates "the heaviness of class, race, and adolescence," and praised Rizkalla's ability to render "the gut-wrenching powerlessness Sofia often feels as she treads through a world rife with inequality". The novel also examines family bonds, memory, and the search for home in its various forms. Reviewers have described it as "a pointed social commentary" that captures the contradictions of Sofia's world through "spare, elegant prose". [ref: Oprah Wants You to Read The Book of Menopause, Oprah Daily]

== Reception ==
Kirkus Reviews called it "a heart-wrenching and powerful debut" and "a well-written and haunting look into a childhood marked by instability". Library Journal wrote that Rizkalla's "powerful debut captures the heartbreak of a family in crisis and the quiet resilience of a young girl who can't make sense of the world but still dares to dream". Writing for Shelf Awareness, Debra Ginsberg described the book as "thoughtful and wise" and "a powerful and resonant read".

Following its selection for Oprah's Book Club, The Independent reported that Winfrey praised the novel as "riveting" and said it "compassionately tackles the difficult subject of families who live outside the margins, living unhoused, and makes us see not only their struggles, but their hopes, dreams, and the perseverance it takes to face another day". [ref: Oprah Winfrey taps a 'riveting' debut novel for her book club, The Independent] USA Today noted that the pick was Winfrey's 125th selection, chosen during the 30th anniversary celebrations of her book club. [ref: Oprah's book club pick is a 'riveting' coming-of-age from a new voice. What is it?, USA TODAY]

== Author background ==
Amanda Rizkalla is a Los Angeles native who lives in the Bay Area. She was an undergraduate at Stanford University and received a Master of Fine Arts in creative writing from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where she was a Kemper Knapp Fellow. She is a recent Steinbeck Fellow and Wisconsin Institute for Creative Writing Fellow, and has been a writer-in-residence at Ragdale, Hedgebrook, Djerassi, and other arts organizations. Hungered is her first novel. [ref: Oprah Winfrey taps a 'riveting' debut novel for her book club] Rizkalla learned of her Oprah's Book Club selection after receiving a surprise call from Winfrey, and said in a statement that she was "so stunned I could hardly believe it was real". [ref: Oprah's book club pick is a 'riveting' coming-of-age from a new voice. What is it?, USA TODAY] [ref: ]

== References ==

Johnny O'Reilly (born 22 October 1970) is an Irish filmmaker and journalist. He wrote and directed the Russian-language feature films Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) and The Weather Station (2010), and the short film The Terms (2002), which was shortlisted for the 74th Academy Awards. Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, O'Reilly began developing a documentary project about events in Kherson and the surrounding region. [ref: Our man in Moscow, The Irish Times] [ref: 'I want to see out the war': Irish filmmaker moved to Ukraine from Russia when 'the pessimists were proved right', The Irish Times] [ref: Red Letter Day, The Sunday Times] As a journalist, he has covered politics and culture in Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine for publications including The Sunday Times, The Times, and The Irish Times.

== Early life and education ==
O'Reilly grew up in Dublin, Ireland. He studied Russian and Classics at Trinity College Dublin. In 1993, while still a student, he worked in Moscow as a freelance reporter covering the Russian constitutional crisis. In 1996, he completed graduate film studies at New York University. He worked at The Sunday Times for two years before pursuing a career in filmmaking. In 2006, he relocated to Moscow, where he lived for ten years.

== Career ==

=== Filmmaking ===

==== The Terms (2002) ====
O'Reilly directed the short film The Terms (2002). Based on a short story by Irish writer Mike McCormack, the film was shortlisted for the 74th Academy Awards and received multiple international festival awards. [ref: The Terms Shortlisted for Oscars, IFTN]

==== The Weather Station (2010) ====
O’Reilly’s feature directorial debut was the Russian-language thriller The Weather Station (2010). Described by Variety as a “whodunit straight out of the Agatha Christie school”, the film was set in an arctic meteorological outpost and filmed near Simferopol in Crimea, Ukraine. [ref: The Weather Station, Variety]

==== Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) ====
O’Reilly wrote and directed Moscow Never Sleeps (2016), an ensemble drama set during Moscow City Day celebrations. The film follows several interconnected stories over a single day and features actors including Mikhail Yefremov, Lyubov Aksyonova, and Aleksei Serebryakov.

==== Kherson ====
O'Reilly subsequently began developing a documentary project about events in Kherson and the surrounding region.

=== Journalism and cultural initiatives ===
O'Reilly has reported from Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and the wider former Soviet region, covering politics, culture, society, and conflict across Eastern Europe. His journalism has appeared in international media outlets, including The Sunday Times, The Times, and The Irish Times.

In 2008, he co-founded the Irish Film Festival in Moscow. According to The Sunday Times, the festival continued for eleven years and expanded to other Russian cities.

=== Russian television incident ===
In August 2015, O'Reilly appeared live on Russian state television to discuss Moscow Never Sleeps. During the interview, he described Ukrainian filmmaker Oleg Sentsov as a political prisoner, after which the broadcast was abruptly cut short. The incident received international media coverage in outlets such as The Irish Times and The Hollywood Reporter. [ref: Russian TV Cuts Away After Irish Director Backs Jailed Ukrainian Filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Russian TV cuts off Irish director after backing jailed filmmaker, The Irish Times]

== Filmography ==
=== Feature Films ===
* CO/MA (2004) – Writer, Director

* Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) — Writer, Director

=== Short Films ===

== Awards and Nominations ==
* **2001** – Ajijic International Film Festival: Winner, Los Charales Award for Best Short Film (under 16 minutes) — *The Terms*
* **2001** – Palm Springs International ShortFest: Second Place, Jury Award for Best Live Action Film (15 minutes and under) — *The Terms*

== History ==

Château Saint-Martin & Spa was established in 1954. [ref: A short history of Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Oetker Hotels] The site was previously occupied by a Roman fortification that later became a Crusader stronghold and a 12th-century Knights Templar commandery (including the Saint-Martin Chapel), which had fallen into ruins by the early 20th century. [ref: Hotel review: Chateau Saint-Martin & Spa offers blissful seclusion and medieval charm in the South of France, Tatler Asia] [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Forbes Travel Guide] [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa: saison jusqu'au 11 octobre, La Revue des Hôtels]

=== Development and construction ===

In 1935, the estate was bought by Fernand Genève, a Parisian businessman, who carried out extensive rebuilding and opened the first hotel on the property in 1954. [ref: Hotel review: Chateau Saint-Martin & Spa offers blissful seclusion and medieval charm in the South of France, Tatler Asia] Six private villas were added in 1960. [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa: saison jusqu'au 11 octobre, La Revue des Hôtels]

=== Ownership changes ===

In 1994, the Oetker family acquired the estate, and the building was fully restored in 1997. [ref: A short history of Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Oetker Hotels] [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa: saison jusqu'au 11 octobre, La Revue des Hôtels] A further renovation was completed in 2018 by the architect and interior decorator Bergit Gräfin Douglas of MM Design, based in Frankfurt. [ref: Hotel review: Chateau Saint-Martin & Spa offers blissful seclusion and medieval charm in the South of France, Tatler Asia]

On 10 October 2019, the hotel received the Palace distinction from Atout France. [ref: Atout France attribue la distinction Palace à six nouveaux hôtels, Déplacements Pros] The distinction was renewed on 24 June 2025 for three years under the label's revised criteria. [ref: Distinction Palace, Oetker Hotels]

== Architecture ==

The hotel stands on the foundations of a former Knights Templar commandery, and remains of the original ruins are still visible on the site. [ref: A short history of Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Oetker Hotels] A modern wing and the villas were later added to the original structure. The Michelin Guide describes the interior style as contemporary-classic, with soft Provençal colours. [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Michelin Guide]

The six villas are built in Provençal style on an olive-lined hillside above the château. [ref: 5-Star Hotel in the South of France, Oetker Hotels] The gardens were designed by the landscape architect Jean Mus and include centuries-old olive trees, from which the hotel produces its own olive oil. [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Forbes Travel Guide]

== Facilities ==

The hotel has one room, 39 junior suites, two suites and six villas. [ref: Questions & Answers, Oetker Hotels] The estate covers 14 hectares, and the hotel operates seasonally. [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa: saison jusqu'au 11 octobre, La Revue des Hôtels] The Michelin Guide awards the hotel one Michelin Key. [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Michelin Guide]

=== Restaurants ===

Le Saint-Martin: The hotel's gastronomic restaurant, with a panoramic terrace overlooking the Côte d'Azur. Romain Antoine became executive chef in 2026. [ref: Restaurant Le Saint-Martin in Vence, Nice Côte d'Azur Tourist Office]

L'Oliveraie: A summer restaurant serving Mediterranean cuisine in a garden of centuries-old olive trees. [ref: 5-Star Hotel in the South of France, Oetker Hotels]

The hotel also has a cocktail bar, Le Rossini, and a pool bar. [ref: Château Saint-Martin & Spa, Michelin Guide]

=== Amenities ===

Spa Saint-Martin by La Prairie has four treatment rooms, a duo suite and a beauty cabin, and treatments are also offered in a garden cabana. [ref: 5-Star Hotel in the South of France, Oetker Hotels] Other facilities include a swimming pool, a tennis court, a pickleball court, a pétanque ground, yoga classes and a fitness centre.

Draft: List of Middle Eastern tornadoes in 2026

Draft text:
The 2026 Middle Eastern tornado season is the current season of tornadoes and tornado outbreaks across the Middle East and the Caucasus in 2026. As of October, there have been 160 confirmed tornadoes across several countries, resulting in 1 fatalities and at least 30 injuries. [ref: European Severe Weather Database, ESWD]
*Note: Some tornadoes have been rated using different scales. They are counted as their closest IF-Scale equivalent on this table.

Many different meteorological organizations across the Middle East document tornado events, often using different tornado intensity scales, including the Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale, and the International Fujita (IF) scale. [ref: Tornado Rating in Europe with the EF-scale, Keraunos] For consistency, this list primarily uses the IF-scale, the preferred scale of the European Severe Storms Laboratory (ESSL) and its database, the European Severe Weather Database (ESWD). [ref: International Fujita (IF) Scale, European Severe Storms Laboratory]

==Climatology==

The Middle East sees significantly fewer tornadoes than the United States and Europe. Geography plays a major role in this discrepancy, with the unique features in North America making areas like Tornado Alley ideal for severe weather, while the Middle East relies on the heat from the Mediterranean, and the instability from the extreme heat of the deserts. However, the under-reporting of weaker tornadoes across the continent also contributes to this. [ref: Here's why the US has more tornadoes than any other country, CNN] [ref: A Climatology of Tornadoes in Europe: Results from the European Severe Weather Database, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society] This under-reporting primarily stems from a lack of Middle Eastern collaboration in monitoring tornadoes, and most tornadoes only being tracked by one database, resulting in less public awareness of them or their danger or the real threat they pose. [ref: Tornadoes in Europe: An Underestimated Threat, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society]

Tornado activity in the Middle East typically peaks in the spring, and is usually lowest during autumn, winter, and sometimes summer months. More specifically, Turkish and Syrian coastal areas peak in the spring and early summer, and most other coastal countries peak in months like January. Tornadoes over land most often occur in the late afternoon and early evening hours. On the other hand, waterspouts, which sometimes move ashore in coastal areas and become tornadoes, peak in late spring and typically occur earlier in the day.

==Season summary==

January was somewhat active, with 17 tornadoes confirmed, and 2 IF2 tornadoes reported. The first half of the month was very active, with 12 of the 17 tornadoes occurring in the first half. On January 8th, a strong IF2 struck Karacalar, Turkey, and a day later a waterspout in Bat Yam, Israel that made landfall, impacted 3 kitesurfers, one being killed after being thrown 150 meters and being struck by a large rock. The second half of the month was shockingly inactive, with only 5 tornadoes occurring, with most being part of a tornado outbreak lasting from January 26 to January 27. On January 26th, a strong IF2 struck Kumköy, Turkey. To end the season off, an IF1.5 tornado impacted Sarıçam and Ahatlar, Turkey.

February and March were both relatively inactive, with 11 tornadoes occurring in February and 12 in March. February was very inactive, with nearly every event being waterspouts. March was significantly more active in tornadic events, but still relatively inactive. On March 29th, an IF1.5 tornado impacted towns north of Aleppo, Syria.

April was slightly active, with 14 confirmed events occurring. The first half of the month was very active, with 12 of the 14 tornadoes occurring in the first half. An IF1.5 tornado struck Uzuncuk, Turkey. The second half was inactive, with 2 tornadoes occurring in the second half of the month. A long funnel cloud was observed in Nicosia, N. Cyprus, with touchdown being considered very likely.

May was an incredibly active month by a large margin, with 27 tornadoes being confirmed, with 8 IF2 rated tornadoes occuring. On May 3rd, a violent tornado outbreak tore parts of Turkey and Syria, with an extremely rare and violent IF4 tornado striking multiple villages along the Syria-Turkey border, and nearly striking a large city in the district of Oğuzeli, with the highest intensity being reported around Akçamezra, Turkey, with mansory houses being destroyed, and mature pistachio trees being entirely debarked. On the same day, 7 out of the 8 IF2 tornadoes occured on this day, and an IF2.5 struck a small rural village in southwestern Viranşehir, Turkey. This tornado outbreak holds multiple records, including strongest tornado in the Middle Eastern region and both Syria and Turkey, and first IF4 rated tornado to ever occur in an European country since 2021.

June and July are tied to be the most inactive months in this season, with both having 8 tornadoes. No significant events occured in the months, with nearly every tornado on this page being waterspouts. August and September were nearly as inactive as February, with 11 tornadoes occurring in August and 16 in September, with 24 of the 26 total events combined being waterspouts. No significant events occured in August or September.

==January==

Draft: The African insurance organization (AIO)

Draft text:
The African Insurance Organization (AIO) is a nongovernmental organization [ref: Organisation des Assurances Africains (OAA), MFW4A - Making Finance Work for Africa] representing Africa’s insurance and reinsurance industry. It was established in 1972 in Port Louis, Mauritius [ref: ], and its headquarters are in Douala, Cameroon [ref: ].

== Activities and role ==
The AIO organizes an annual conference and General Assembly, holds specialized meetings and seminars, and publishes studies on African insurance markets [ref: 52nd AIO conference kicks off in Cairo with more than 2,000 attendees] [ref: African Insurance Organization (AIO), Financial Afrik] [ref: ].

In 2026, its Africa Insurance Pulse report examined how limited insurance data contributes to the insurance protection gap in African markets [ref: Africa Insurance Pulse 2026 - Data-driven insurance catalyses inclusive growth in Africa, Africa Insurance Pulse]. An analysis discussed the challenges facing the AIO, including its limited financial resources, lack of regulatory authority and the diversity of insurance markets across Africa.

== History ==
In the early 1970s, insurance executives in Mauritius, including Robert Woodthorpe Browne [ref: Africa Insurance Organisation, The Paddy Ashdown Forum], proposed creating a forum where heads of African insurance companies could meet. The Insurers’ Association of Mauritius and Mauritius Re approached the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) to organize a conference in Mauritius.

The first meeting was held from 5 to 9 June 1972 [ref: Report by the Board of Direction of the African Reinsurance Corporation covering the period from 1st April, 1977 to 31st December, 1978, Report by the Board of Direction of the African Reinsurance Corporation covering the period from 1st April, 1977 to 31st December, 1978] at Le Réduit, Mauritius, with the support of the Mauritian government. It brought together 77 delegates from 28 African countries, including insurance companies, supervisory bodies and European observers. A sponsorship committee included René Adam, Sheikh S. M. Balala, Hedi Ennifer, Ephrem Marie Mba and Anthony Kobina Woode.

Discussions covered cooperation among insurance markets, insurance capacity, a possible African insurance congress and a proposed African reinsurance company. The meeting also considered the establishment of technical and training committees.

A second meeting, held in Nairobi, Kenya, from 25 to 29 June 1973, led to the formal establishment of the AIO. Tomas Okelo-Odongo, chairman of the board of Kenya Re, became its Secretary-General.

At the third conference, held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, in 1974, the AIO’s statutes were adopted. Kabisi Pene Yemba Milanga, Managing Director of the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s National Insurance Company (SONAS), was appointed the organization’s first Honorary Secretary-General.

=== The 1980s ===
Yosef Assefa was appointed Secretary-General in 1981 and held the position for 24 years. In July 1983, the AIO established its first insurance pool, the African Aviation Pool [ref: African Aviation Insurance Pool, pools.africa-re.com], in Libreville, Gabon. The organization’s headquarters moved from Nairobi to Douala in 1984. In June 1986, the AIO decided to establish the African Oil and Energy Pool [ref: African Oil and Energy Pool, pools.africa-re.com]. The pool began operations in January 1989.
=== The 1990s ===
The first African Reinsurance Forum was held in Lomé, Togo, in 1995.

=== The 2000s ===
After Assefa stepped down, Abdallah Badaoui became Secretary-General in July 2005 but left the position later that year. Roland Rasamoely served as acting Secretary-General until Prisca Soares was appointed in 2007; she served for 12 years [ref: AIO 2021: PILA Honours Prisca Soares With Award, businessstandardsng.com].

In 2005, the AIO, UNCTAD and the World Bank established the African Centre for Catastrophe Risks (ACCR), headquartered in Casablanca, Morocco.

=== The 2010s ===
In 2012, the AIO marked its 40th anniversary in Mauritius.

In 2016, the AIO published its first research report, Africa Reinsurance Pulse [ref: Africa Reinsurance Pulse - 2016, Africa Reinsurance Pulse], on trends and prospects in the African insurance market.

=== The 2020s ===
Jean Baptiste Ntukamazina became Secretary-General in 2019 [ref: New Secretary General for the African Insurance Organisation, www.cover.co.za]. In 2022, the AIO signed the Nairobi Declaration on Sustainable Insurance [ref: The Nairobi Declaration on Sustainable Insurance - EXPLAINER, The Nairobi Declaration on Sustainable Insurance].

== Members ==
According to the AIO’s 2025 annual report, as of June 2025 the organization had 421 corporate and institutional members from 47 African countries and 13 countries outside Africa [ref: African Insurance Organisation - Annual Report 2025, African Insurance Organisation - Annual Report]. The report lists insurers, brokers, reinsurers, regulators, associations, training institutions and InsurTech or support-service organizations among its members.

== Leadership ==
At the AIO’s 52nd Conference and Annual General Assembly in Cairo, Egypt, held from 5 to 9 June 2026, Alaa El-Zoheiry [ref: Alaa El-Zoheiry elected President of African Insurance Organisation for 2026-2027 term, Dailynewsegypt] was elected president for the 2026-2027 term.

Draft text:
Ido Naor () is an Israeli cybersecurity executive, former security researcher, and author. He is the co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of the cybersecurity company Security Joes, which he established in 2020 after leaving Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team. [ref: Ido Naor, Cyber Week 2025] [ref: Ido Naor — Experience, LinkedIn] He previously co-founded the malware-research platform VirusBay. [ref: VirusBay Aims To Make Malware Analysis More Social, BleepingComputer] His earlier research included banking malware, information exposed through online services, industrial control software, and threat actors targeting Israeli organizations. [ref: Zombies and mules: The inside story of the first-ever shekel bank hack, The Times of Israel] [ref: Flaws in Gas Station Software Let Hackers Change Prices, Steal Fuel, Erase Evidence, Vice]

== Early life and education ==
Naor was born in Kabri and raised in Afula. He served in Unit 504 of the Israel Defense Forces. [ref: האקר סטנדרטי, e-vrit] After active service he worked in security operations for the Israel Airports Authority at Ben Gurion Airport from 2009 to 2011.

During this period, Naor studied Computer Science at the College of Management Academic Studies. He graduated and returned as lecturer for cybersecurity studies between 2013–2015. [ref: מה אתם באמת יודעים על האקרים? הצצה לחייו של האקר, College of Management Academic Studies]

== Career ==
=== Early cybersecurity career ===
Naor began his cybersecurity career as an application-security researcher at CYCL, formerly known as Bugsec, in 2011. He subsequently worked as a security researcher at Cisco from 2012 to 2013 and at McAfee from 2013 to 2015. His earliest located magazine article, about the security of connected medical devices, appeared in the Israeli cybersecurity magazine Digital Whisper in June 2011, however prior to that he practiced Bug Bounty and was featured in Hall of Fame lists. [ref: Medical Hazardous Implants, Digital Whisper]

Naor maintained a personal security blog from 2011 to 2015. It included security-challenge walkthroughs and reports of web vulnerabilities that he disclosed to companies including LinkedIn, Google and Waze, eBay, AliExpress, and Meta's Facebook. [ref: Ido Naor, Blogger] Two posts from early 2014 display Naor's name in Google's application-security Hall of Fame for the fourth quarter of 2013; one of the posts focuses on multiple reported vulnerabilities in Waze, followed by Hall of Fame name appearance. [ref: Google Hall Of Fame – Multiple vulnerabilities in Google Waze GPS, Blogger] [ref: Google Hall Of Fame – Vulnerability in Google, Blogger]

=== Kaspersky ===
Naor joined Kaspersky's Global Research and Analysis Team in 2015. He worked as a senior security researcher and, from 2019 until leaving the company in August 2020, as a principal security researcher. His early work there included research into Grabit, an espionage campaign that targeted small and medium-sized organizations, [ref: Small-To-Mid-Sized Organizations Targeted By 'Grabit' Cyberspies, Dark Reading] and ATMZombie, a banking trojan used to steal money from Israeli accounts. [ref: כך גנבו האקרים מאות אלפי שקלים מחשבונות בנק בישראל, People and Computers]

In 2015, Naor disclosed a flaw in LinkedIn's mobile-comment and email-notification handling that could have facilitated targeted phishing. LinkedIn fixed the issue before publication. [ref: Kaspersky researchers warns Linkedin from potential spear phishing, Securelist] That year he also served as a mentor in Kaspersky's Security Startup Challenge, whose finals were held at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts. [ref: Taking A Break From Research To Accelerate Startups: SSC 2015, Securelist] [ref: Kaspersky Lab names the best startups of its first acceleration program, Kaspersky]

In June 2016, Naor investigated a Facebook-spreading malware campaign for which Kaspersky recorded almost 10,000 attempted infections in 48 hours. [ref: Facebook malware: tag me if you can, Securelist] He presented the research at CODE BLUE in Tokyo that October. [ref: Facebook Malware: Tag Me If You Can, CODE BLUE 2016]

In February 2017, Naor and the IDF's C4I and Information Security units published Breaking the Weakest Link of the Strongest Chain, an investigation of malicious Android applications and social engineering used to spy on more than 100 Israeli soldiers. [ref: Breaking The Weakest Link Of The Strongest Chain, Securelist] [ref: Israeli soldiers' personal Android phones hacked by spies, researchers say, CyberScoop] Initial media reports associated the campaign with Hamas. [ref: ViperRat – Mobile APT Targeting Israeli Defense Force, Lookout]

In mid-2017, Naor investigated an Instagram application programming interface flaw that exposed users' contact information. He reported the issue to the company and later demonstrated how information obtained through the flaw was being offered for sale. John Matthew Williams (born 1967) is an Australian legal scholar specialising in constitutional law, federalism and legal history. He serves as the deputy vice-chancellor (academic) of Adelaide University, where he also holds the Dame Roma Mitchell Chair of Law. His interests are centered on the Australian Constitution and the High Court of Australia.

Williams pursued political science and industrial relations at the University of New South Wales and later continued his education in law at the same university. He graduated from the University of Tasmania with the first-class honours Bachelor of Arts in 1991 and a graduate diploma in legal practice from the University of Technology Sydney in 1993. He earned his doctorate degree in law at the Australian National University (ANU) in 1997 after writing a thesis on the Protection of Rights Under the Australian Constitution: A Republican Analysis.

In 1997, Williams joined University of Adelaide (UofA) as a lecturer in law and later became a senior lecturer in 1999. From 2004 to 2005, he worked as a reader in law at ANU and returned to Adelaide to work as a professor of law in 2006. He was appointed founding director of the South Australian Law Reform Institute in 2010 and served as the dean of law from 2011 to 2016. He worked in several other important university administrative positions, including provost at UofA from 2023 to 2025.

== Early life and education ==
John Matthew Williams was born in 1967. [ref: Judicial federalism in Australia: history, theory, doctrine and practice, Catalogue] He was the first member of his family to attend university as his mother, Judith M. Williams, was a social justice activist who has volunteered with many councils and charities throughout her life. [ref: Judith M Williams OAM Scholarship for Humanities and Social Sciences, Adelaide University]

Williams joined the University of New South Wales between 1986 and 1988 and graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in political science and industrial relations. After that, he joined the same university for law between 1989 and 1992 and taught at Basser College in 1989 and 1990. In 1991, he earned a Bachelor of Arts in first-class honours from the University of Tasmania. [ref: Prof John Williams, Researcher Profiles]

== Academic career ==
=== Early career (1992–2003) ===
Between 1992 and 1993, Williams was a deputy dean of Basser College. In 1993, Williams attained a Graduate Diploma in Legal Practice from the University of Technology Sydney and enrolled for PhD at the Australian National University (ANU). He got an ANU postgraduate scholarship and became a research assistant to Philip Pettit in 1994. In 1995, he tutored in constitutional law via the Aboriginal Tutorial Assistance Scheme. He later worked as a consultant to the National Archives of Australia (NAA) from 1996 to 1997.

In May 1997, Williams graduated with his PhD in the Law Program at the Research School of Social Sciences of ANU and his thesis title was The Protection of Rights under the Australian Constitution: A Republican Analysis. [ref: Winterton’s Australian Federal Constitutional Law: Commentary and Materials, Third Edition — Select Bibliography, Lawbook Co.] Later that year, he became a lecturer in law at the University of Adelaide (UofA) and rose to the position of senior lecturer in 1999. He was the editor of the Australian Journal of Legal History between 1997 and 2001 and founded The New Federalist: The Journal of Australian Federation History, which he edited between 1998 and 2002.

Williams was an ambassador for the South Australian "Yes" campaign in the referendum about the 1999 Australian republic referendum. In 2000, he took part in a senior fellowship at the University of Melbourne and became a member of the Don Dunstan Foundation's management board. [ref: Member (AM) in the General Division of the Order of Australia: Media Notes (M–Z), Governor-General of the Commonwealth of Australia] Additionally, he assisted the NAA in developing its Documenting a Democracy website project, which was an electronic collection of documents relating to the legislation and constitution of Australia launched in June 2000. [ref: New website documents Australia's founding charters, Government of Western Australia]

Williams was an appointed professor at the University of Cape Town in 2001 and had the position of a Menzies Foundation Fellow at King's College London from 2002 to 2003. [ref: 'Swelling the ranks of the peripatetic unemployed': the first decade of the High Court of Australia, High Court of Australia] Moreover, he was on the council of the Australian Association of Constitutional Law (AACL) from 2001 to 2008 and associate dean of research at UofA from 2003 to 2004.

=== Professorship and law reform (2004–2014) ===
Between 2004 and 2005, Williams was a reader in law at ANU. He returned to UofA as a professor of law in 2006, serving as an associate dean for research till 2010. From 2006 till 2011, he edited the Adelaide Law Review while serving as the secretary of the Judicial Conference of Australia from 2006 to 2009. He had a visiting appointment at the University of Victoria in British Columbia in 2007.

Anthony Michael Glazer (born 1 May 1943) is a British crystallographer and Emeritus Professor of Physics at the University of Oxford. He is best known for developing the internationally adopted Glazer notation for octahedral tilting in perovskite structures. Glazer is also co‑founder of Oxford Cryosystems, a leading manufacturer of low‑temperature equipment for X‑ray crystallography.

Early life and education Glazer attended Christ’s College Finchley from 1954 to 1964. He earned a B.Sc. (Hons) in Physics from Queen’s College (University of St Andrews, Dundee) in 1965. He completed his Ph.D. in Crystallography at University College London under Kathleen Lonsdale between 1965 and 1968, working on mixed organic crystals. He later received M.A. degrees from the University of Cambridge (1974) and the University of Oxford (1976).

Academic career After a research fellowship at Harvard University (1968–1969) and research posts at the Cavendish Laboratory (1969–1976), Glazer joined the Clarendon Laboratory at Oxford in 1976 as Lecturer in Physics. He simultaneously became Official Fellow and Tutor in Physics at Jesus College, Oxford, positions he held until his retirement in 2010. He was appointed Professor of Physics in 1996 and is now Emeritus Professor of Physics at Oxford and Emeritus Fellow of Jesus College.

Research Glazer’s research focuses on the relationship between crystal structure and physical properties, particularly in ferroelectrics, perovskites, and phase transitions.

In 1972, he introduced a systematic classification of octahedral tilting in perovskite structures, now known as the Glazer tilt system. The notation is widely used in solid‑state physics, crystallography, and materials science.

In 1986, Glazer co‑founded Oxford Cryosystems with J. Cosier to commercialize cryogenic cooling systems for crystallography. Their Cryostream instrument became a standard tool for low‑temperature X‑ray diffraction worldwide.

He has also worked extensively on synchrotron radiation methods for X‑ray diffraction, birefringence measurement instrumentation, ferroelectric and antiferroelectric phase transitions, and crystallographic computing. He has delivered public lectures, including the Royal Institution Bragg Lecture on perovskites.

Publications Glazer is the author of several books, including:

* A Journey into Reciprocal Space (2nd ed., 2021)
* Crystallography: A Very Short Introduction (2016)
* Crystal Clear: The Autobiographies of Sir Lawrence and Lady Bragg (2015)
* Space Groups for Solid State Scientists (3rd ed., 2013)

He is also General Editor of the IUCr Newsletter.

Awards and honours Glazer has received numerous distinctions, including:

* National Medal of Polish Education (1992)
* Czochralski Medal, European Materials Research Society (2012)
* Spriggs Award, American Ceramic Society (2015)
* Vice President, International Union of Crystallography (2014–2017)
* President, British Crystallographic Association (1996–2000)

Draft text:
Big Little Truths is a 2026 novel by Australian author Liane Moriarty. It is the sequel to her 2014 bestseller Big Little Lies and was published by Crown on August 25, 2026. The book is set ten years after the events of the first novel and was selected as a Reese's Book Club pick. [ref: ] [ref: ]

== Plot ==
The novel returns to the fictional Pirriwee Peninsula, outside Sydney, where Madeline, Celeste, Jane, Renata, and Bonnie are now navigating the teenage years of their children. The story opens with a severed human finger mailed to the principal of the local high school, an act that unsettles the community and sets the plot in motion. [ref: Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty review – Big Little Lies sequel shoots for high drama but fails to deliver, The Guardian] [ref: ‘Big Little Lies’ Sequel Book Teases Storyline for HBO Series’ Season 3: What’s Going on With Madeline, Celeste and Jane in ‘Big Little Truths’, Variety]

Moriarty moves between the perspectives of the five women and a chorus of their teenage children, who are interviewed about the central events. A new history teacher, Melody, takes an unusual interest in the brightest students, and a stranger is soon spotted around the school asking questions. The narrative builds toward “D-Day,” a school presentation that exposes Melody’s connection to her husband, a predator who has used her position to access children at multiple schools. The finger, it turns out, belonged to a man who was already dead; it was sent by a former student trying to draw attention to Melody. [ref: ‘Big Little Lies’ Sequel Book Teases Storyline for HBO Series’ Season 3: What’s Going on With Madeline, Celeste and Jane in ‘Big Little Truths’, Variety] [ref: 'Big Little Lies' Author Liane Moriarty Teases Sequel Book & Season 3, Deadline]

== Background ==
Moriarty had long resisted writing a sequel. In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, she said she had told her team she was “not the sequel person,” a reference to authors who continue series indefinitely. [ref: Why Liane Moriarty Broke Her Own Rules and Wrote a Sequel to ‘Big Little Lies’, The Hollywood Reporter] She changed course after working on the first two seasons of the HBO adaptation, when she began to wonder what had become of the Pirriwee families. She had already started a separate novel set in a high school, and when interest in a third season of the show grew, she adapted that material into the Big Little Lies world.

The ten-year time jump was central to her approach. “You put your characters through so much and it just didn’t make sense to me to write something that followed on directly,” she told USA Today. “A time jump always made sense to me.” [ref: ‘Big Little Lies’ Sequel Book Teases Storyline for HBO Series’ Season 3: What’s Going on With Madeline, Celeste and Jane in ‘Big Little Truths’, Variety] The novel incorporates elements from the television adaptation, including the character Mary Louise, who was created for the show’s second season and did not appear in the original book. [ref: 'Big Little Lies' Author Liane Moriarty Teases Sequel Book & Season 3, Deadline]

== Reception ==
Kirkus Reviews gave the novel a starred review, calling Moriarty’s writing “sparkling” and noting that the book works even for readers unfamiliar with its predecessor. The Irish Independent described it as “sharp, funny and emotionally astute” and said it offered “a more satisfying continuation of the story than the divisive second season” of the HBO series. [ref: A severed finger, a charismatic teacher and a ‘creepy’ guy in Big Little Truths – Liane Moriarty’s sequel is busy and addictive, Irish Independent]

The Guardian’s Bec Kavanagh was more critical. She wrote that the novel, at over 400 pages, “fails to deliver” and that the lowered stakes of the sequel menopause, vaping teenagers, and a stalker do not generate the urgency of the first book. Kavanagh nonetheless acknowledged that Moriarty’s warmth and wit remain present. [ref: Big Little Truths by Liane Moriarty review – Big Little Lies sequel shoots for high drama but fails to deliver, The Guardian] The Cornell Sun faulted the sequel for abandoning the gossipy, dialogue-driven style that made Big Little Lies compelling, though it credited Moriarty with touching on the cyclical nature of domestic violence and the influence of online misogynist communities before dropping those threads. [ref: ‘Big Little Truths’ and the Bigger Little Problems with Sequels, ‘Big Little Truths’ and the Bigger Little Problems with Sequels - The Cornell Daily Sun] The Indian Express found the book “a little long at times” but said it “does not weigh you down,” and noted that it lacks the whodunit suspense of the original. [ref: Liane Moriarty’s sequel to Big Little Lies is big on sensitivity, low on suspense, The Indian Express]

The novel debuted at No. 1 on The New York Times bestseller list and appeared on Publishers Weekly’s hardcover fiction lists in the weeks after its release.

== References ==

Morgantown Mall is a shopping mall located in Westover, West Virginia, at the intersection of Interstate 79 and U.S. Route 19. It is the newer of the two malls located in Morgantown, the other being the Mountaineer Mall. Anchors are JCPenney, Dunham's Sports, Burkes Outlet, Home Centric, Ollie’s Bargain Outlet, and AMC Classic. The former Sears is used as a logistics and distribution center for WVU Medicine. [ref: 2 new anchor stores coming to Morgantown Mall, [[WBOY-TV] To the north lies The Morgantown Commons.

== History ==
Plans for the mall were announced in 1989 by Glimcher Realty Trust and site work began on June 12. [ref: Morgantown mall work under way, Cumberland Times News] It opened on September 13, 1990, with Elder-Beerman, JCPenney, Sears, and K-Mart (later Proffitt's) as anchors. The mall was a newer alternative to the Mountaineer Mall located across town along Greenbag Road. [ref: Morgantown complex poses no challenge, merchants say, The Pittsburgh Press] Due to its popularity, many anchors abandoned the Mountaineer Mall and began moving to the Morgantown Mall. [ref: Mountaineer Mall, more than just stores, The Dominion Post] Elder Beerman operated two stores in Morgantown in each mall before the closure of the Mountaineer Mall location in January 2008, due to lease expiry. [ref: Elder-Beerman to close its doors in January, Morgantown Dominion Post]

Proffitt's was converted to Belk on March 1, 2006. [ref: Proffitt's at Morgantown changes to Belk today, Morgantown Dominion Post] On November 1, Gabriel Brothers opened. [ref: Hosanna for bargain-hunters, Morgantown Dominion Post]

In 2016, The Gap and Hollister left the mall due to their owner companies restructuring. The Hollister was planned to be replaced with a Rue21. [ref: Morgantown Mall fills spaces fit for community needs, WV News] On October 15, 2018, Sears was announced to close as part of its national closure of 142 stores due to Chapter 11 Bankruptcy. [ref: Sears closing these 142 stores in bankruptcy filing and liquidation sale, CBS News] This followed the closures of Belk and Elder-Beerman the same year. [ref: Sears to close Morgantown Mall store as retailer continues to struggle, The Dominion Post] In 2020, AMC was renovated and Ollie’s Bargain Outlet and Dunham's Sports opened. In 2025, ownership was transferred from Washington Prime Group to Kohan Retail Investment Group. [ref: New ownership represents ‘pivotal moment’ for Morgantown Mall, [[The Dominion Post (Morgantown)] Their previous owner filed for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy protection after the COVID-19 pandemic. [ref: Morgantown Mall’s parent company files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, WBOY]

=== morgantownmall.com ===
On June 1, 2001, the domain name "morgantownmall.com" was disputed between Morgantown Mall Associates LTD. Partnership of Columbus, Ohio and the former domain holder located in Rio, Brazil via arbitration. Morgantown Mall Associates (owner of Morgantown Mall) stated that the domain name was identical to their current website and that it was used in "bad faith". It was decided that the domain name would be transferred to Morgantown Mall Associates. [ref: Morgantown Mall Assoc. Ltd. P’ship v. morgantownmall.com, adrforum.com]

Gadalla is associated with the food sector through Zulfa Food Industries [ref: Zulfa Factory Close to Completion, www.alushibenews.com]. The project was announced in 2024 and, across all its phases, is planned to produce roughly 8.1 million tons a year [ref: The Vietnam Trap: Why Libya’s Industrial Mega-Projects Must Build Supply Chains, Not Just Factories – OpEd, www.eurasiareview.com] [ref: What Asia’s Industrialization Lessons Can Teach Fragmented States] [ref: From Libya to the world: How international business can strengthen libya’s economy, Gulf Times].

Draft text:
Sam Slater is a British composer, music producer and sound designer based in Berlin. His work includes experimental recordings, solo work, film and television scores, video-game music and audiovisual performance. [ref: Sam Slater, CTM Festival] He collaborated with Hildur Guðnadóttir as score producer on Chernobyl and Joker, and as co-composer on Battlefield 2042. [ref: Chaos and Climate: Hildur Guðnadóttir and Sam Slater on scoring the near-future world of Battlefield 2042, MusicTech] The Recording Academy credits him with two Grammy wins, for Chernobyl in 2020 and Joker in 2021. [ref: Sam Slater, Recording Academy]

== Background and early career ==
Slater began producing recordings as a teenager and studied experimental composition at the University of Leeds. He moved to Germany in 2013. His early professional work included musical sound design and creative engineering for the Icelandic composer Jóhann Jóhannsson.

== Career ==

=== Film, television and video games ===
Slater worked with Guðnadóttir on the scores for the 2019 television miniseries Chernobyl and the film Joker, serving as score producer and musical sound designer. For the 2021 video game Battlefield 2042, the pair co-composed a score built around distorted textures and experimental sound-making. They received the Society of Composers & Lyricists award for Outstanding Original Score for Interactive Media in 2022. [ref: 3rd SCL Awards Held, Winners Announced, Society of Composers & Lyricists]

He composed the score for the Netflix series The Railway Men (2023), which concerns the 1984 Bhopal disaster. In an interview with Rolling Stone India, he discussed drawing on memories of the ravanahatha and railway sounds while developing the music. [ref: ‘The Railway Men’ Music Composer Sam Slater Takes Us Behind His Process, Rolling Stone India] The score won the Filmfare OTT Award for Best Background Music (Series) in 2024. [ref: Filmfare OTT Awards 2024: Who won maximum awards?, Filmfare]

His documentary work includes Mstyslav Chernov's 2000 Meters to Andriivka and Dmytro Hreshko's Divia, both released in 2025. [ref: 10th Annual Critics Choice Documentary Awards – List of Nominees and Winners (2025), Critics Choice Association] [ref: Exclusive: Trailer From Dmytro Hreshko’s Karlovy Vary-Premiering ‘Divia’, International Documentary Association] Chernov described how Slater incorporated battlefield recordings into the former's score, using gunfire and radio transmissions as musical material. [ref: Metric of Loss: Mstyslav Chernov Discusses the Ethical Responsibility of ‘2000 Meters to Andriivka’, International Documentary Association]

In 2026, Slater composed the music for Housemarque's Saros, combining electronic music with drone-metal influences. [ref: Saros, drone metal and the year's most stressful game soundtrack, NME]

=== Recordings and performance ===
Slater released Wrong Airport Ghost through Bedroom Community in 2018. Its development followed his work with musician Krishna Bhopa in Rajasthan and experiments with the sonic possibilities of a single string. [ref: Sam Slater Details Bedroom Community LP, ‘Wrong Airport Ghost’, XLR8R]

His second solo album, I Do Not Wish to Be Known as a Vandal, followed on the same label in 2022. The album assembled contributions from instrumentalists and vocalists. [ref: Sam Slater on bringing emotion into experimental composition, Composer] A related audiovisual work was developed with visual artist Theresa Baumgartner and dancer and choreographer Lukas Malkowski. [ref: I Do Not Wish To Be Known As A Vandal, Bedroom Community]

He is a member of Osmium with Guðnadóttir, James Ginzburg and Rully Shabara. The ensemble performs with custom-built instruments.

Slater's third solo album, Lunng (2026), features collaborators including Bendik Giske, Maria W. Horn, Adam Betts and Yair Glotman. GoMore is a Danish car-sharing company based in Copenhagen. It runs an online platform on which private individuals and businesses rent out cars, and it also offers car leasing. In Spain it operates under the brand Amovens. [ref: Getaround Europe and GoMore merge to create Europe's largest peer-to-peer carsharing network, Tech.eu] In 2026 it acquired the European operations of Getaround; the combined business reported more than five million users in 11 European countries. == History ==
GoMore was started in 2005 by Matias Møl Dalsgaard and Søren Riis and was relaunched in 2011 when further partners joined. [ref: Gomore: fem år og to millioner brugere senere, TechSavvy] It expanded to Sweden in 2014. [ref: Så blir bilsemestern billig, Dagens Nyheter] In March 2015 it acquired the Spanish ride-sharing service Amovens, founded in 2009 by Diego Hidalgo. [ref: Spanish car sharing platform Amovens acquired by GoMore, Novobrief] Later launches included Switzerland (2021) [ref: Geld verdienen mit dem eigenen Auto?, Luzerner Zeitung], Austria (2022) [ref: GoMore: So funktioniert die neue private Autovermietung in Österreich, Trending Topics] and Estonia (2024). [ref: Eestis alustab inimeselt inimesele autode jagamise platvorm GoMore, Raamatupidamisuudised] In 2021 the Swiss insurer Baloise invested about €5 million in the company. [ref: Baloise kauft sich bei dänischer Carsharing-Firma GoMore ein, cash.ch]

In February 2026 GoMore closed its ride-sharing service in Denmark, by then the only country where it was offered, to concentrate on car rental and leasing. [ref: Tak for turen, GoMore] [ref: GoMore dropper samkørsel i Danmark, TV 2]

In May 2026 GoMore acquired Getaround Europe, the European business of the US company Getaround, which operates mainly in France, Norway, Belgium and Germany. The purchase was financed with equity from existing investors and loans from EIFO and Nordea. The combined business reported about 70,000 shared cars, about 1.5 million rentals a year and net revenue of more than €50 million. [ref: GoMore übernimmt Getaround Europe und wird größte Carsharing-Plattform Europas, Trending Topics] Getaround continued as a separate platform after the purchase. [ref: Getaround and GoMore: a new chapter for carsharing in Europe, Getaround] In Austria, Getaround's cars later moved to the GoMore platform. [ref: Unsere Autos in Österreich sind jetzt bei GoMore, Getaround]

== Services ==
Car owners list cars on the GoMore website or app and renters book them. Many cars can be unlocked with the app, without a key handover. GoMore also offers leasing and a subscription, GoMore+, which gives a discount on rentals. [ref: New: Get a discount every time you rent a car with GoMore+, GoMore]

Draft text:
Friendly Captcha is a German computer security company based in Wörthsee, Bavaria, and the name of its CAPTCHA service. Founded in 2020 by Benedict Padberg and Guido Zuidhof, the company offers a service that, instead of asking visitors to solve image or text puzzles, has the visitor's browser complete a proof of work calculation in the background. Government accessibility guidance in Germany and Luxembourg has cited it as an example of proof-of-work CAPTCHAs. The company won the start-up category of the in 2023.

== History ==
Friendly Captcha was founded at the end of 2020 by Benedict Padberg and Guido Zuidhof. According to a 2024 profile in the magazine of the Munich and Upper Bavaria chamber of commerce, the founders financed the company from their own funds and from revenue rather than outside investment.

== Technology ==
When a user loads a page that embeds the Friendly Captcha widget, the widget presents the user's browser with a cryptographic puzzle. Solving it takes the browser a few seconds and usually requires no action from the user, while making automated mass submissions slower and more costly. The difficulty of the puzzle escalates when requests appear more likely to come from a bot. The underlying principle, proof of work, had been in use for decades before the company adopted it for CAPTCHAs.

== Reception ==
A guide published by the, the German federal body that monitors the accessibility of public-sector IT, lists proof-of-work methods among accessible alternatives to conventional CAPTCHAs, naming Friendly Captcha as an example. According to the guide, because the calculation runs in the background, such CAPTCHAs help users who are disadvantaged by incomprehensible, visual or audio tasks. A 2025 article on the Luxembourg government's accessibility portal likewise named Friendly Captcha as an example of proof-of-work CAPTCHAs, a family it said generally performs well on both accessibility and privacy and requires little or no user interaction. In a September 2025 survey of 821 Luxembourg public-sector websites, the same portal found Friendly Captcha on two sites, compared with reCAPTCHA on 98.

A 2024 article in Communications of the ACM, written by the developers of the competing mCaptcha system, included Friendly Captcha in a table comparing CAPTCHA services. The table noted that Friendly Captcha works over the Tor network and is accessible to screen reader users, but that it is not open source and its validation mechanism is undocumented. It listed application-specific integrated circuits and very large botnets as possible ways to bypass it.

== Awards ==
In September 2023, Friendly Captcha won the start-up category of the Deutscher Gründerpreis, a German award for founders, at a ceremony held at the ZDF capital studio in Berlin. The other finalists in the category were Edurino and Klim.

Draft text:
LabHost was a subscription-based phishing-as-a-service platform that operated from 2021 until April 2024, when it was shut down in an international police operation led by London's Metropolitan Police Service and coordinated by Europol. The service sold users templates for fake websites imitating banks, postal services and other organisations, along with hosting and tools for running SMS phishing campaigns. The Metropolitan Police said the platform had about 2,000 paying users who created some 40,000 fraudulent websites, and that it had been used to obtain about 480,000 payment card numbers, 64,000 PINs and more than one million passwords worldwide.

Between 14 and 17 April 2024, police in several countries searched about 70 addresses and arrested 37 people, including the service's original developer in the United Kingdom. In April 2025 the developer was sentenced to eight and a half years' imprisonment after pleading guilty to fraud and money-laundering offences. Prosecutions of individual users followed in other countries, including Canada and the Netherlands.

== Background ==
According to the Associated Press, LabHost was set up in 2021 and charged its users a monthly fee. Trend Micro, a security company that assisted the investigation, said the service appeared in late 2021 and mainly targeted customers of organisations in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. Australian police said the platform started in Canada before spreading to the UK, Ireland and elsewhere.

Subscriptions were paid in cryptocurrency. Trend Micro reported three membership tiers costing between US$179 and US$300 a month, the cheapest covering Canadian institutions and the most expensive covering more than 70 institutions in other countries. Users could choose among templates impersonating about 170 organisations, 47 of them based in the UK, according to police figures reported by the Press Association. The service also supplied tutorial videos.

Trend Micro described two built-in tools: "LabSend", for sending phishing text messages from customisable templates, and "LabRat", which used adversary-in-the-middle techniques to intercept credentials and two-factor authentication codes while a victim was entering them.

== Investigation and takedown ==
The Metropolitan Police investigation, named Operation Stargrew, began in June 2022 after the force received intelligence from the Cyber Defence Alliance, an information-sharing body of UK banks. Trend Micro said it began assisting the Metropolitan Police in June 2023. Europol's European Cybercrime Centre and the Joint Cybercrime Action Taskforce supported the case, and law enforcement agencies from 19 countries took part. In Australia, investigators began work on the platform's local users in October 2023.

Searches took place from 14 to 17 April 2024 at about 70 addresses worldwide, and 37 suspects were arrested. Europol said four of those arrested in the UK were linked to running the site, among them its original developer. UK arrests were reported at Manchester and Luton airports, in Essex and in London. On 18 April 2024 the Metropolitan Police replaced the LabHost website with a police notice.

In Australia, about 200 officers from the Australian Federal Police and four state police forces executed 22 search warrants in five states; two men from Melbourne and Adelaide were arrested and charged over alleged use of LabHost, and three others were arrested on drug charges during the searches. In Ireland, the Garda Síochána carried out 12 searches in Dublin, Kildare and Waterford, arrested two men and said it had linked 116 LabHost users to the country.

Private companies that assisted investigators included Trend Micro and Microsoft. The blockchain analysis company Chainalysis said wallets linked to LabHost received more than US$1.1 million in cryptocurrency between August 2021 and April 2024.

== Results ==
The Metropolitan Police said that up to 70,000 people in the UK had been victims of LabHost-based phishing. Police said they had contacted up to 25,000 UK victims to tell them their data had been compromised. About 800 LabHost users received a message from the police stating that their identities were known to investigators. The force said the platform had received just under £1 million in payments from users.

Australian police said the personal details of about 94,000 Australians had been obtained through the service, and estimated that it could have caused up to A$28 million in losses in Australia.

== Prosecutions ==
In September 2024 LabHost's developer, a man from Huddersfield, pleaded guilty to making or supplying articles for use in fraud, encouraging or assisting the commission of an offence, and transferring criminal property. On 14 April 2025 he was sentenced at Manchester Crown Court to eight and a half years' imprisonment. The Crown Prosecution Service said he had received about US$230,000 in cryptocurrency for creating and running the site between August 2021 and October 2023, and that it would seek confiscation of his assets.

In April 2025 the Sûreté du Québec and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police arrested 87 people in the Montreal area accused of carrying out phishing attacks with LabHost, following on from a server seized during the 2024 takedown. In November 2025 a court in the Netherlands convicted a LabHost user of phishing offences and imposed a partly suspended prison sentence and community service.

Tara Hernandez is an American television writer, producer and showrunner. She served as producer and wrote for the CBS sitcom The Big Bang Theory and its spin-off Young Sheldon. [ref: 'Big Bang Theory' EP Tara Hernandez Sets 19th-Century Sitcom Pilot Order at CBS, TheWrap] [ref: "Mrs. Davis" Receives New Series Order from Peacock, Warner Bros. Television] She co-created the Peacock science-fiction series Mrs. Davis (2023) with Damon Lindelof and served as its showrunner. [ref: Meet the cast and creators of Peacock's sci-fi series 'Mrs. Davis', Syfy Wire] She is writing a live-action adaptation of Captain Planet and the Planeteers for Netflix. [ref: CBS orders Tara Hernandez comedy pilot Regency, Deadline Hollywood]

== Early life and education ==
Hernandez graduated from Chapman University's Dodge College of Film and Media Arts in 2010 with a Bachelor of Fine Arts in film production. [ref: Alumni Spotlight – Tara Hernandez, Dodge College of Film and Media Arts]

== Career ==
=== The Big Bang Theory and Young Sheldon ===
After graduating, Hernandez was offered an interview with the executive producer and showrunner of The Big Bang Theory. She has said she was initially uninterested in television, describing herself as a "film snob". She was hired as an assistant to the show's executive producers, a role she held for two and a half seasons, during which she learned to pitch stories. After several of her pitches were produced, she was promoted to staff writer, and by early 2017 had become a co-producer.

Over her nine-year tenure on the series she progressed from assistant to writer and producer, eventually serving as a co-executive producer. She subsequently wrote for and co-executive produced the spin-off Young Sheldon from 2018 to 2021. By the time she left network comedy, she had written close to 200 episodes across the two series. [ref: "Mrs. Davis" – Wacky, Unpredictable, and Full of All Kinds of Surprises, Golden Globes] Hernandez also wrote an episode of the Nickelodeon series Henry Danger in 2015. [ref: Tara Hernandez, IMDb]

=== Mrs. Davis ===
Mrs. Davis grew out of a comedic spec script Hernandez had written about post-apocalyptic nuns. The script reached Susan Rovner, then an executive at Warner Bros. Television, who suggested Hernandez meet Lindelof; the pair met shortly before the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and developed the project together during that period. [ref: Mrs. Davis Co-Creator Tara Hernandez On Crafting Peacock's Wild New Sci-Fi Series [Exclusive Interview], /Film]

Rovner later brought the project with her to Peacock after leaving Warner Bros. to become chair of NBCUniversal's television and streaming division. [ref: Tara Hernandez, Variety500] In May 2021, Peacock gave the series a straight-to-series order of ten episodes in a competitive situation, with Hernandez as showrunner and executive producer; both she and Lindelof were then under overall deals with Warner Bros. Television. Starring Betty Gilpin as a nun set on destroying an all-powerful artificial intelligence, the series premiered at SXSW in March 2023 before its first four episodes were released on Peacock on 20 April 2023. It ran for a single season of eight episodes, [ref: Peacock Submits Genre-Bending Mrs. Davis as Limited/Anthology Series for 2023 Emmy Awards, Syfy Wire] and Peacock submitted it in the limited/anthology categories for the 75th Primetime Emmy Awards. The series was well received by critics. It was nominated for the TCA Award for Outstanding New Program. [ref: Mrs. Davis, TV Guide] Hernandez was named to the Variety500 for 2023.

=== Captain Planet and the Planeteers ===
As of 2025, Hernandez was writing a live-action series adaptation of the animated series Captain Planet and the Planeteers for Netflix, in development with Greg Berlanti's Berlanti Productions, Leonardo DiCaprio's Appian Way and Warner Bros. Television.
=== The Tillbrooks ===
In December 2025, CBS ordered a pilot for Regency, a multi-camera family sitcom written and executive produced by Hernandez for Warner Bros. Television, placing it in contention for the 2026–27 broadcast season. [ref: CBS comedy pilot Regency from Tara Hernandez, [[Variety (magazine)] The project put a period twist on the traditional family sitcom, following the upper-middle-class Tillbrooks family in 19th-century England. It was the network's second comedy pilot order of the cycle, after the single-camera Eternally Yours from Ghosts showrunners Joe Port and Joe Wiseman. Rhys Darby was cast as patriarch Arthur Tillbrook, [ref: Rhys Darby to Star in CBS Comedy Pilot 'Regency', [[Variety (magazine)] and Kate Walsh joined as matriarch Jocelyn after the project was retitled The Tillbrooks. [ref: Kate Walsh ("Grey's Anatomy") mit neuem Comedy-Projekt in der "Bridgerton"-Ära, Wunschliste] In April 2026, CBS declined to order the pilot to series, opting instead for the comedy Eternally Yours. [ref: Kate Walsh's new sitcom canceled at CBS, ARY News] [ref: CBS Orders Eternally Yours to Series, Passes on The Tillbrooks, The TV Ratings Guide]

Luxcara is an investment management company based in Hamburg, Germany. It manages investments in European energy infrastructure for institutional investors, including wind and solar power and hydrogen production. [ref: Hamburger Asset Manager übernimmt Anlagevermittler, Private Banking Magazin] It also invests in battery storage projects. [ref: Consortium kicks off 1.8GWh 'Battery Park' development in Germany, Energy-Storage.news] In 2024, its project company Waterekke Energy secured a 1.5 GW offshore wind concession in the German North Sea. [ref: RWE, Luxcara Winners of German 5.5 GW Offshore Wind Tender, OffshoreWIND.biz]

== Background and fund management ==

Alexandra von Bernstorff and Kathrin Oechtering established Luxcara in 2009. The business is owned by its management. Bernstorff, Marc Brehm and Philip Sander are its managing partners. [ref: The Team, Luxcara]

Flaveo I, one of Luxcara's early funds, closed in April 2010. [ref: Luxcara: Institution Profile, Infrastructure Investor] Its Luxembourg-based Flaveo S.A., SICAV-FIS fund held a solar power plant in France in 2012. [ref: Luxcara acquires 12MW PV plant in Aquitaine, France, PV Tech]

The company's funds receive capital from institutional investors, including insurance companies and pension funds. In 2023, the pension fund for Siemens employees in Switzerland committed capital to Luxcara's Flaveo IV Green Energy fund as part of its allocation to infrastructure. [ref: Swiss Siemens Pensionskasse commits to infrastructure via Aquila, Luxcara, Partners Group, IPE Real Assets] In 2024, the insurer Gothaer provided capital to a Luxcara fund, following a €150 million commitment made in 2022. [ref: Gothaer beteiligt sich an Luxcara-Fonds, dpn] [ref: Gothaer investiert in Offshore-Windpark und Wasserstoff-Projekt, Private Banking Magazin] In August 2024, Luxcara acquired Convexity, a Berlin financial services company authorised to provide investment brokerage, investment advice and asset management. The acquisition received approval from Germany's Federal Financial Supervisory Authority.

== Wind and solar investments ==

In May 2018, Facebook entered into a power purchase agreement with Luxcara for electricity from the Bjerkreim wind farm cluster in south-western Norway. The three projects covered by the agreement had a combined design capacity of 294 MW. Vattenfall contracted to provide electricity balancing and integration services. [ref: Facebook buys Norwegian wind power, Windpower Monthly] In 2019, Luxcara and MEAG arranged project bonds for two of the cluster's wind farms, Skinansfjellet and Gravdal. Investors in the bonds included Munich Re group companies and Uniqa Insurance Group, while a Luxcara fund provided equity financing. [ref: Munich Re and Luxcara create bond to finance Norwegian wind farms, IPE Real Assets]

Luxcara acquired the Guillena-Salteras solar project north of Seville, Spain, on behalf of institutional investors in January 2019. [ref: Greencoat, Sonnedix and Luxcara each expand solar portfolio via acquisition, IPE Real Assets] In April that year, it bought the Önusberget wind project in Sweden from Svevind for an undisclosed sum. [ref: Luxcara expands Scandinavian portfolio with Swedish wind farm project deal, IPE Real Assets] The wind farm forms part of the Markbygden wind power area near Piteå and has a capacity of 753 MW. [ref: Vindkraft vid Markbygden pressas av miljardförluster, ENERGInyheter.se] [ref: Windpower Intelligence Global Forecast: October 2023, Windpower Monthly]

Its German offshore investments include Waterkant and Waterekke. In August 2024, the Federal Network Agency awarded the N-9.3 North Sea site, with a capacity of 1.5 GW, to Luxcara.

== Waterkant turbine procurement ==

Waterkant is a 300 MW offshore wind development. [ref: Asset manager Luxcara shies away from using Chinese offshore wind turbines, Riviera Maritime Media] Its site lies approximately 90 km from the island of Borkum. [ref: Subventionierte China-Windräder vor Borkum geplant, Tagesschau]

In July 2024, Luxcara selected Ming Yang Smart Energy as the preferred turbine supplier for Waterkant. The agreement covered 16 turbines rated at up to 18.5 MW each. Germany's economy ministry announced that it would examine the implications for critical infrastructure and competition. The industry association WindEurope also criticised the agreement. [ref: Germany to examine security, competition impact of Chinese wind turbine deal, Reuters]

In August 2025, Luxcara entered a capacity into a reservation agreement with Siemens Gamesa for 97 turbines rated at 15.5 MW each for Waterekke. It also reserved 19 turbines of the same type for Waterkant. It attributed the possible supplier change to operational efficiencies between the projects and told Reuters that political debate had not been decisive. Ming Yang confirmed that it was no longer involved in Waterkant. [ref: German company is set to scrap politically sensitive Chinese turbine deal, Reuters]

Sir Horatio George Powys Townshend (6 February 1780 – 25 May 1843) KCH was a British politician and soldier. He sat as MP for Whitchurch from 13 August 1816 till 1826, and 25 February 1831 till 1832. [ref: TOWNSHEND, Hon. Horatio George Powys (1780-1843)., History of Parliament Online]

He was knighted and appointed Knight Commander of the Royal Guelphic Order (KCH) on 25 September 1835. At the time of his death, he served as lieutenant-governor of Windsor Castle.

== Military career ==
He served as ensign for the 1st Regiment of Foot Guards in 1795; he was promoted to lieutenant and captain in 1799; promoted to captain and lieutenant-colonel in 1809; promoted to brevet colonel in 1819; promoted to lieutenant-colonel of the 1st Regiment of Foot Guards in 1821.

== Family and education ==
He was the third son of Thomas Townshend, 1st Viscount Sydney by Elizabeth, the daughter and co-heiress of Richard Powys of Hintlesham, Suffolk. He was the brother of John Thomas Townshend and William Augustus Townshend. He was educated at Eton College from 1787 till 1791. He never married.

Rico Africa (born Robert Berry; 1964 – 2022) was an American painter, collagist, sculptor and performance artist active in the Cass Corridor art scene of Detroit, Michigan.

== Career ==
Africa emerged in the Cass Corridor art scene in the 1980s. He was self-taught, and was described by the Detroit News as well-versed in art theory, trends and criticism. His friend, the artist and curator Dave Roberts, described him as an outsider to art-school circles whose sociability gave him wide influence among other artists. Detroit singer-songwriter Audra Kubat credited Africa, whom she described as the host of a gathering at the Foyer House, a former artists' commune, with encouraging her first public performance.

His work was shown at the Motor City Brewing Works in Detroit, whose owner, artist John Linardos, exhibited the paintings under black light. In the 1990s Africa also worked as a performance artist; his project Transgendered Frankenstein combined spoken-word poetry with a live band.

== Style and themes ==
The Detroit News characterized Africa's style as pop-influenced expressionism. He worked in acrylic on canvas, collage, works on paper and welded steel sculpture. Many works combine collage with oil painting and use bright, almost radioactive color. Recurring subjects include consumerism and corporate America, Detroit politics and society, current events, and pure abstraction. Many of his paintings are self-portraits that address his identity as a Black and mixed-race man in America.

== Death and retrospective ==
Africa died of cancer in early 2022, aged 57. A posthumous retrospective of about 50 works, mostly dating from the 1990s to the 2010s, was held at the Cass Cafe in Detroit from April 23 to May 27, 2022, curated by Dave Roberts.

== References ==
