Moyo Ogunseinde began her career in architecture before moving into real estate development in Nigeria. She designed the Radisson Blu Anchorage Hotel on Victoria Island, Lagos, which opened in 2011, and later oversaw the renovation of its rooms and business lounge.

Moyo became an executive director of Uraga Real Estate Limited, a subsidiary of the Honeywell Group, contributing to design, land acquisition and planning.

=== Upbeat Recreation Centre ===
As an executive director of Uraga Real Estate, Moyo Ogunseinde led the development of the Upbeat Recreation Centre, a multi-purpose leisure facility on Admiralty Road, Lekki, which opened in December 2017 and was reported in the Nigerian media as West Africa's first trampoline park. The project was conceived during Nigeria's 2016 recession as a diversification into recreational real estate, aimed at the country's young population.

The centre set up a gymnastics club in February 2018 and held its first trampoline gymnastics competition in October 2018. In 2024 it hosted a fun day for underprivileged children in Lekki.

=== Aga Culture ===
In 2017 Moyo Ogunseinde founded Aga Culture (originally Àga Concept), an African lifestyle and design brand based in Lagos, and serves as its creative director. The name derives from the Yoruba word àga, meaning a chair or functional object. The brand produces clothing, furniture and homeware that combine Yoruba and wider African traditions with a contemporary, minimalist aesthetic, and emphasises slow fashion and ethically sourced materials such as Adire cotton and linen. Its furniture includes the Oko chair, drawn from traditional farming tools, and the Egungun accessories collection, inspired by Egungun masquerades; in 2020 the American trade magazine Hospitality Design named Moyo Ogunseinde one of six rising product designers. The brand's Mmanwu chair featured in Cultured magazine's 2021 survey of the Lagos design scene. Its work has also included the AADA clothing collection and participation in design exhibitions.

=== Hospitality ===
Moyo Ogunseinde has served as executive director of Anchorage Leisures Limited, owner of the Radisson Blu Anchorage Hotel, and sits on its board. She is also a board member of the Honeywell Group and an advisory board member of Wavecrest College of Hospitality, Lagos. In a 2022 interview, she argued that Nigeria could develop world-class tourism by investing in local infrastructure and emphasized local content in the hotel's operations, art and food sourcing.

In November 2025, she accepted the Best Corporate Hotel award at the World Luxury Awards in Barcelona on behalf of the Radisson Blu Anchorage, where she was described as a board member and key owner of the property. In 2025 she was included in a Nigerian trade listing of "Top 100 Women in Hospitality".

=== Club Concierge Africa ===

Moyo Ogunseinde founded Club Concierge Africa (CCA) during the COVID-19 pandemic, building a travel, hospitality and lifestyle group intended to serve African travellers. The group offers travel membership, travel management, hospitality partnerships and concierge services.

Its brands are:
* Club Concierge International (CCI), a travel club offering vacation-ownership membership for leisure travellers and, through Club Concierge for Business, corporate accommodation membership;
* GoTravelCC, a travel-management company offering flights, hotels and related travel services;
* MyTravelCC, a flights-first travel booking company for individuals;
* GoPartnerCC, the group's partnership brand;
* Concierge Resort, which manages resort destinations; and
* CSolute, a business-to-business travel affiliate arm.

As Group CEO, Moyo Ogunseinde oversees operations across several African and international markets.

In September 2026, she spoke on a panel on cross-border payments at the 22nd Akwaaba African Travel Market in Lagos, calling for closer cooperation between regulators, payment providers and tourism operators to reduce the cost of travel within Africa.

[https://cenrs.org/ The Center for Earth and Natural Resource Sciences (CENRS) is an autonomous, multidisciplinary research institution based in Rwanda. CENRS was officially established on 3 September 2025 under Rwandan Law No. 007/2021 of 5 February 2021. The Center conducts fundamental and applied research in environmental systems, Earth processes, natural hazards, natural resources, and technologies for pollution control and environmental remediation. It also provides research-based services to local communities. CENRS is currently focused exclusively on research and community services and does not engage in schooling activities]. [ref: ]

At 03:15 CST on 15 September 2016 (19:15 UTC on 14 September), Super Typhoon Meranti, a powerful tropical cyclone, struck Xiamen with measured two-minute sustained winds of 173 km/h]. At that time, Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro were in Xiamen conducting their doctoral research. [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969724062144 As young researchers specifically from inland Africa, where tropical cyclones have historically had little or no direct impact, they experienced a tropical cyclone firsthand for the first time and observed its extensive environmental, infrastructural, and societal impacts]. Schools and kindergartens in Xiamen and other coastal cities in Fujian were closed as a precaution. In China, [https://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2016-09/17/c_135692847.htm official assessments reported direct economic losses of more than ¥16.9 billion (2.6 billion USD) in Fujian Province, with additional losses in neighbouring] Zhejiang Province. [https://www.weather.gov.hk/en/publica/tc/tc2016/section3_5rpt.htm An earlier assessment by the Hong Kong Observatory reported at least 29 deaths in Fujian and Jiangxi and direct economic losses exceeding ¥11.7 billion (1.75 billion USD)]. Draft text:
Synopsys Verilog Compiler Simulator (VCS) [ref: EE 382N: VCS Manual, users.ece.utexas.edu] is a proprietary functional verification and Verilog simulator [ref: ] maintained by Synopsys. It also has integration with a GUI based waveform viewer called Synopsys Verdi [ref: Higher Productivity with Integrated MATLAB and Synopsys VCS Verification Workflows, in.mathworks.com], which superseded VirSim.
[[File:Synopsys-verdi-21mux.png|alt=Synopsys Verdi displaying a two-to-one multiplexer.|thumb|Synopsys Verdi displaying a two-to-one mux written in Verilog with its test waveform generated after simulating.]]

== History ==

VCS was developed by John Sanguinetti as part of Chronologic Simulation in 1992. Created from the ground up, VCS was developed by four people. Sun Microsystems gave the team a model called the "tsunami model", which, after 13 months of development on VCS, did not run. After ironing out the bugs, VCS was able to run the model successfully. Because of this, Sun Microsystems formed a contract with the team, promising an extra $480,000 of funding in three stages. [ref: [https://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/2015/06/102702042-05-01-acc.pdf Oral History of John Sanguinetti]. Computer History Museum. 26 February 2009.]

In November 1992, VCS was formally announced at the Tech Museum in San Jose. In January of 1993, the company received a $400,000 check from Cyrix, which allowed the company to further work on VCS.

Chronologic Simulation was acquired by ViewLogic in 1994 for $26.5mn, though there were complications with lawsuits until 1995 [ref: Chronologic Simulation, Inc. v. Sanguinetti, 892 F. Supp. 318 (D. Mass. 1995), Justia Law]. In 1997, ViewLogic as bought out by Synopsys for $500mn [ref: SYNOPSYS ACQUIRES VIEWLOGIC FOR $500M - Tech Monitor, Tech Monitor].

Draft: K. Abdul Kareem

Draft text:
K. Abdul Kareem is an Indian agricultural extension scholar and former professor of the Kerala Agricultural University (KAU). His work has focused on participatory agricultural extension, farmer-led innovation, group approaches to technology adoption, value addition and agricultural entrepreneurship. He served as Professor and Head of Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK), Kannur, and later held positions including Associate Director of Research and Associate Director of Extension in KAU.

== Career ==
Kareem worked in the Kerala Department of Agriculture before joining Kerala Agricultural University. At KAU, he worked in teaching, research and agricultural extension and served in the Department of Agricultural Extension at the College of Agriculture, Padannakkad. He later headed KVK Kannur and also served as Associate Director of Research and Associate Director of Extension.

During his tenure at KVK Kannur, the centre undertook programmes involving farmer innovations, group-based extension, value addition, agricultural entrepreneurship and collaboration among farmers, scientists and extension agencies. KVK Kannur received the National Best KVK Award for 2009 from the Indian Council of Agricultural Research.He served as Professor and Head of KVK Kannur from 1 January 2005 to 13 September 2013. [ref: Certificate concerning the tenure and extension initiatives of Dr. K. Abdul Kareem, Krishi Vigyan Kendra, Kannur, Kerala Agricultural University] He later served in positions including Associate Director of Research and Associate Director of Extension.

== Work in agricultural extension ==

=== Compact Area Group Approach ===
Kareem developed and field-tested the Compact Area Group Approach (CAGA), a farmer-participatory agricultural extension approach. as an on-farm extension experiment. The approach organised farmers within a compact geographical area for the coordinated adoption, testing and management of agricultural technologies. Dr. M. P. Giridharan, then Professor of Horticulture at Kerala Agricultural University, assisted in its conceptual development.

The model sought to move beyond isolated individual demonstrations by enabling neighbouring farmers to undertake related interventions collectively, exchange observations and support continuing field-level action.

=== Creative Extension ===
Kareem proposed the concept of Creative Extension, emphasising the use of locally appropriate and participatory communication methods in agricultural extension. These included exhibitions, audiovisual communication, farmer-led demonstrations, field programmes and other approaches intended to make technical information accessible to farming communities.

As part of this work, he produced the Malayalam short cine drama Thengukalude Nilavili (The Lament of the Coconut Palms), dealing with problems affecting coconut cultivation.

=== Farmers’ Science Congress ===
The Farmers’ Science Congress was conceived by Kareem and organised by KVK Kannur under his leadership on 4–5 February 2008. It provided a forum in which farmer-innovators presented their findings and practices before agricultural scientists, extension professionals, representatives of financial and developmental institutions, the media and other farmers.

The programme included presentations, discussions and an exhibition of farmers’ innovations. Proceedings documenting the innovations presented at the congress were also prepared. Farmer-inventor M. J. Joseph of Chemperi, known as Kunjetten, was honoured with the title “Dar” (Distinguished Agricultural Inventor) at the congress.

=== Farmers’ Science Museum ===
KVK Kannur subsequently established a Farmers’ Science Museum to document and display farmer-developed technologies and innovations. The initiative was intended to give public and institutional visibility to the experimental knowledge generated by farmers. [ref: A museum to showcase farmers’ innovations, The Hindu]

=== Paddy Task Force and agro-biopharmacy ===
The original ideas of the Paddy Task Force and agro-biopharmacy were mooted by Kareem’s colleague Dr. P. P. Moosa. During Kareem’s tenure as Professor and Head, KVK Kannur developed, demonstrated and promoted these models as part of its extension work.

The Paddy Task Force model involved trained groups undertaking operations connected with paddy cultivation. The agro-biopharmacy concept promoted the local availability and responsible use of biological inputs and plant-protection materials. [ref: Agro-bio pharmacy concept well received by Kerala farmers, The Hindu]

=== Coconut technicians and group approaches ===
Kareem promoted the formation and training of groups of coconut technicians to undertake skilled operations in coconut gardens. Group-based approaches were also used in programmes concerning crop health, farm services and collective action.

He was associated with field-level responses to diseases affecting coconut palms in northern Kerala and with programmes linking scientists, extension personnel and farmers. [ref: Tanjore wilt found in coconut palms in Kannur, The Hindu]

=== Value addition and agricultural entrepreneurship ===
At KVK Kannur, Kareem promoted value addition and agricultural entrepreneurship as components of extension work. Programmes included training, technology demonstrations, enterprise development and strategies intended to improve farm income. [ref: A slew of strategies to enhance income in Kannur, Kerala, The Hindu]
[truncated]

Draft: Jake Dunning (physician)

Draft text:
William Jake Dunning MBE is a British physician and clinical researcher specialising in emerging and high-consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs). He is a senior clinical research fellow at the Pandemic Sciences Institute, University of Oxford, and a consultant in infectious diseases at the Royal Free Hospital in London. He is NHS England's National Clinical Lead for Contact HCIDs and leads the HCID service at the Royal Free Hospital. [ref: Jake Dunning, Pandemic Sciences Institute] [ref: Britain's terrifying isolation tent for the world's deadliest diseases, The Daily Telegraph]

Dunning was the field lead for two clinical trials of experimental treatments during the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic. The trials were devised and led by Peter Horby. His work on the trials in Liberia and Sierra Leone was documented in a 2015 Guardian Long Read on experimental Ebola treatments. [ref: Ebola: the race to find a cure, The Guardian] His subsequent clinical and research work has encompassed Ebola virus disease, Lassa fever, mpox, influenza, MERS, COVID-19 and other emerging infectious diseases.

He is a co-director of the National Institute for Health and Care Research Health Protection Research Unit in Emerging and Zoonotic Infections, [ref: NIHR Health Protection Research Unit in Emerging and Zoonotic Infections, HPRU EZI] leads Oxford's clinically focused research contributions to the UK Public Health Rapid Support Team, and has served on World Health Organization (WHO) emergency committees and guideline-development groups. [ref: Who We Are, NIHR Health Protection Research Unit in Emerging and Zoonotic Infections] [ref: PSI's continued involvement in UK-PHRST to reinforce epidemic preparedness globally, Pandemic Sciences Institute]

Dunning received the Ebola Medal for Service in West Africa following his work during the West African Ebola epidemic and was appointed a Member of the Order of the British Empire (MBE) in the 2018 New Year Honours for services to clinical research. [ref: Uni honours staff who tackled Ebola, Oxford Mail] [ref: Dr Jake Dunning recognised in 2018 New Year's Honours list, University of Oxford]

==Career and research==

Between 2009 and 2013, Dunning worked on the Mechanisms of Severe Acute Influenza Consortium (MOSAIC). He undertook doctoral research in viral immunology at Imperial College London, under the supervision of Peter Openshaw, Jonathan Weber, and Anne O'Garra, and was awarded a PhD by Imperial. [ref: Determinants of severity in patients with pandemic influenza]

A principal output from this research was a first-author study published in Nature Immunology in 2018 examining whole-blood transcriptional responses in adults hospitalised with influenza. [ref: Progression of whole-blood transcriptional signatures from interferon-induced to neutrophil-associated patterns in severe influenza, Nature Immunology]

In 2014, Dunning joined the Epidemic diseases Research Group Oxford (ERGO) to work on clinical trials of potential treatments for Ebola virus disease in West Africa. During 2014 and 2015, he was clinical lead for Ebola treatment trials conducted by the Oxford group. The Guardian reported extensively on Dunning and the Oxford team's efforts to establish treatment trials across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, including his leadership of clinical trial teams in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

The research included trials of brincidofovir and TKM-130803, for which Dunning was lead author of the published reports. [ref: Experimental Treatment of Ebola Virus Disease with Brincidofovir, PLOS ONE] [ref: Experimental Treatment of Ebola Virus Disease with TKM-130803: A Single-Arm Phase 2 Clinical Trial, PLOS Medicine]

From January 2016 to April 2018, Dunning served as deputy lead of the NHS England High Consequence Infectious Diseases Programme, working with Sir Michael Jacobs. [ref: Second witness statement of Dr Michael Charles Prentice, UK Covid-19 Inquiry]

From 2015 until 2021, Dunning was a consultant at Public Health England (PHE), initially in the Respiratory Virus Unit and later becoming Head of the Enteric Virus Unit and Head of Emerging Infections and Zoonoses. He served as a national incident director, including during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom. In 2019, The Guardian identified him as PHE's head of emerging infections and zoonoses while reporting on the repatriation of British healthcare workers following potential exposure to Lassa fever in Sierra Leone. [ref: Three Britons brought back from Sierra Leone over Ebola-like virus, The Guardian]

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Dunning was co-lead of the NIHR-funded Assessment of Transmission and Contagiousness of COVID-19 in Contacts (ATACCC) study from 2020 to 2022, alongside Prof Ajit Lalvani at Imperial College London. [ref: Responsive Research, NIHR Health Protection Research Unit in Respiratory Infections] The prospective community study investigated SARS-CoV-2 transmission and infectiousness in UK households. Research arising from ATACCC included studies of infectiousness, viral-load kinetics and household transmission. [ref: Onset and window of SARS-CoV-2 infectiousness and temporal correlation with symptom onset: a prospective, longitudinal, community cohort study, The Lancet Respiratory Medicine]

Draft text:
Liz Tripodi is an Australian vocal coach, music educator, songwriter, podcast host and surrogacy advocate. She founded the Melbourne-based music school Vocal Art Studios and has worked in music education, performance and entertainment. She later became involved in international surrogacy advocacy following her experience of having children through surrogacy in Georgia. [ref: Georgia's surrogacy clinics attract hundreds of Australians but ethical questions remain, ABC News]

== Music career ==

Tripodi founded Vocal Art Studios in Melbourne in 2003. Australian Business Register records show Vocal Art Studios operating as a trading name from May 2003. [ref: Historical details for ABN 15 429 044 569, Australian Business Register]

Her work as Founder and Director from 2003-2023 through Vocal Art Studios included vocal coaching, music education, performance training and involvement in the Melbourne music and entertainment industry as well as work in America and Europe.

Tripodi has also worked as a mc, speaker, performer, adjudicator and judge at music competitions and eisteddfods. She has been heavily involved in Italian-Australian musical and cultural events, including festival and community performances as well as in Canada, America and Italy.

The Moonee Valley Foundation lists Tripodi among its past recipients, describing her as an "Italian musical producer". [ref: Past Winners, Moonee Valley Foundation]

== Songwriting ==

Tripodi has also worked as a songwriter. In 2019, her song Family placed ninth in the Folk/Acoustic category of the Australian Songwriting Contest. [ref: 2019 Top 10 List, Australian Songwriters Association]

The placing was also published in the December 2019 edition of The Australian Songwriter, the magazine of the Australian Songwriters Association. [ref: 2019 Australian Songwriting Contest Top 10, The Australian Songwriter]

== Awards and recognition ==

Tripodi was an individual recipient in the Service Delivery to Multicultural Victoria category of the Victorian Multicultural Commission's Multicultural Awards for Excellence. [ref: Annual Report 2008–09, Victorian Multicultural Commission]

In 2017, she received the Women's Small Business Champion award at the Northern Multicultural Small Business Awards for her work with Vocal Art Studios. [ref: Northern Multicultural Small Business Awards winners announced, Brotherhood of St Laurence]

Tripodi was also listed as a Westfield Airport West Local Heroes nominee in 2018. [ref: Recognising all of our 2018 Nominees, Westfield Local Heroes]

== Media and broadcasting ==

Tripodi has appeared in Australian media in connection with her work in music, business and surrogacy. Her media work has also included music broadcasting and interviews.

She has been featured in reporting concerning Italian-Australian cultural activities and has participated in radio and entertainment programs.

== Surrogacy advocacy ==

Tripodi and her husband experienced infertility for approximately 13 years before pursuing surrogacy in Georgia. Their twin daughters were born in Georgia through a surrogate.

ABC News reported in 2025 that Tripodi subsequently started a podcast about surrogacy in Georgia and became involved in supporting others considering international surrogacy.

The Georgian Surrogacy Podcast, hosted by Tripodi, began in 2022 and discusses international surrogacy, particularly surrogacy in Georgia. [ref: The Georgian Surrogacy, Great Australian Pods]

Tripodi has also participated in Australian surrogacy events. Growing Families has identified her as an Australian representative of Chachava Clinic in Georgia. [ref: Sydney Surrogacy and Donor Event, Growing Families]

She has contributed to public discussion concerning surrogacy regulation, including making a submission to the Australian Law Reform Commission. [ref: Submission – Liz Tripodi, Australian Law Reform Commission]

Team, Inc. (stylized in all caps) is a global industrial services company with its headquarters located in Sugar Land, Texas. Founded in 1973, the company provides specialty maintenance, inspection, and mechanical integrity services to facilities in the refining, petrochemical, power generation, and manufacturing sectors. The company's common stock is publicly traded on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol TISI.

== History ==
The company was founded in 1973 as an industrial maintenance services contractor primarily for petrochemical plants along the Texas Gulf Coast.

The company went public on the Nasdaq exchange in 1995, and moved its listing to the New York Stock Exchange in 2001, under the ticker symbol TISI.

In the 2000s and 2010s, TEAM, Inc. extended its geographic footprint and technical capabilities by acquiring regional inspection and specialty service providers. In February 2016, the Company acquired Furmanite Corporation, a leading competitor in specialized on-site industrial services and leak sealing, in an all-stock transaction.

The company had operational reorganization programs in the early 2020s to consolidate service lines and deal with debt from major transactions. In December 2022, the company completed a 1-for-10 reverse stock split to stay in compliance with exchange listing rules.

== Operations and services ==
TEAM, Inc. is a provider of asset integrity, inspection, maintenance and repair, and rope access services for industrial facilities and equipment. The company provides six core areas of service, including inspection, detection, repair, heat treating, digital services via OneInsight, and advanced asset and project solutions. [ref: Industrial Asset Integrity Services, TEAM, Inc.]

=== Inspection ===
TEAM performs traditional and advanced non-destructive testing, tank inspections and valve testing. It also possesses inspection capabilities, including robotics and drones, computed and digital radiography, laser inspection, infrared thermography, 3D imaging, and data collection to assess the state of industrial equipment and structures.Inspection and Testing (NDT/NDE), TEAM, Inc.

=== Detection ===
Detection services are designed to find and quantify leaks and emissions. These include: leak detection and repair (LDAR) programs, greenhouse gas measurement and control, methane emission reduction, and optical gas imaging. These services support emissions monitoring, repair coordination and environmental compliance reporting. [ref: Detection and Emissions Reduction, TEAM, Inc.]

=== Repair ===
TEAM offers specialty mechanical repair services including leak sealing on operating equipment, hot tapping and line stops, field machining, controlled bolting, valve repair and insertion, welding services and engineered composite repairs. It also provides vapor barrier and hydrostatic weld testing.On-Stream Mechanical Repair & Online Leak Sealing Services, TEAM, Inc.

=== Heat treating ===
Services include pre and post weld heat treatment, dehydrogenation, solution annealing, normalizing and curing of coatings and refractory materials. TEAM also provides equipment for thawing, expansion heating, temperature monitoring and mobile heat treatment.Heat Treating, TEAM, Inc.

=== OneInsight ===
OneInsight is TEAM’s digital platform for the collection, management and reporting of information associated with inspection, maintenance and repair activities. Its tools support field service management, remote monitoring, asset integrity records, repair documentation and turnaround co-ordination. The platform also includes dashboards, audit logs and mobile reporting.
OneInsight, TEAM, Inc.

=== Advanced asset and project solutions ===
TEAM provides industrial project support for maintenance, fabrication, shutdowns and asset integrity management Services include IRATA certified rope access for inspection & repair in hard to reach areas, custom component manufacturing, turnaround planning & execution and engineered line lifts to provide access to pipes and supports. Asset-integrity management services aid in risk assessment and maintenance planning. [ref: Industrial Project Support Services, TEAM, Inc.]

== Corporate affairs ==
Team, Inc. operates service locations across the United States, Canada, Europe, and Latin America. The company is governed by a board of directors and executive management led by Chief Executive Officer Gary L. Hill. As a publicly traded entity, it files annual (10-K) and quarterly (10-Q) reports with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

Dan Pinchbeck is a author, scriptwriter, and game developer. He is best known as co-creator of the video games Dear Esther and Everybody's Gone to the Rapture. Both games were nominated for several British Academy Games Awards with Everybody's Gone to the Rapture winning three along with winning the Writers' Guild of Great Britain Best Writing in a Videogame award. He is the co-founder of the British video game development studio The Chinese Room where he was creative director until 2023.

== Career ==
Pinchbeck started making games whilst undertaking a PhD and working as a lecturer at the University of Portsmouth. [ref: A very British disaster: How The Chinese Room made one of 2015's best video games, The Telegraph] After receiving a grant from the Arts & Humanities Research Council. [ref: UK Research and Innovation Gateway, UK Research & Innovation Gateway], he led a team that made a series of experimental game mods exploring different aspects of game design. Pinchbeck worked closely with the composer Jessica Curry on the development of the mods, which were released for free on the Moddb website. One of the mods, Dear Esther, was a breakout, if controversial, hit that has gone on to be a frequently cited title in conversations about the definition of games and the relationship between games and art. [ref: Game of the Week: Dear Esther, Eurogamer.net] [ref: ModDB Dear Esther, Moddb] [ref: Touched By The Hand of Mod, Rock, Paper, Shotgun].

In 2009, Pinchbeck and Curry were approached by game artist Robert Briscoe about creating a commercial version of Dear Esther. They secured investment from the US backer Indie Fund and the game was launched in 2012, paying back its investment in less than six hours [ref: Dear Esther has reached profitability, Indie Fund]. The game was an overnight cult hit. In his review for The Telegraph, Tom Hoggins described it as "oil painting, poetry, eulogy and video game all at once" [ref: Dear Esther review, The Telegraph]. For IGN, Keza MacDonald noted that "Dear Esther doesn't need puzzles or mechanics to draw you in. The strength of the writing and the world alone is enough", praising the writing's depth: "I can't give away anything of Dear Esther's story and premise without spoiling it, but it's layered enough to support multiple playthroughs. The writing is dense with intertextual references, most of them biblical, and there are clues and allusions in the narrator's musings that you won't notice the first time you play through.". She concluded that "Dear Esther can change your perspective on what games could be doing." [ref: Dear Esther review, IGN.com]. Dear Esther "is generally regarded as kick-starting the walking simulator sub-genre." [ref: Clash of Realities, Clash of Realities] It won an IndieCade award in 2012 for Best World/Story [ref: University of Portsmouth - Game, set and match, Times Higher Education (THE)] and was nominated for five British Academy Games Awards (BATFA).

At that point, under the brand name The Chinese Room, the development team had begun working on a sequel to Frictional Games' Amnesia: The Dark Descent.. The game, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs was released in 2013 [ref: How the Amnesia Sequel's sausage was made, www.eurogamer.net]. Pinchbeck stated that his aim with the game was to create a horror without simple morality and strong thematic links to 20th Century history. [ref: Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs writer Dan Pinchbeck talks about horror, genocide, and the scene so disgusting he had to cut it, Killscreen]

In his review of the game, Kirk Hamilton stated "Writer Dan Pinchbeck has stitched together literary influences both obvious and surprising, and the result is a wonderfully macabre indictment of the industrial revolution: Upton Sinclair‘s The Jungle meets H.G. Wells’ The Island of Doctor Moreau.” [ref: Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs review, Kotaku.com] The New York Times stated, "The game's writer, Dan Pinchbeck, is colorful and creative in the cruelty he describes" [ref: Rayman Legends, Total War: Rome II, Plants vs. Zombies 2, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs and Puppeteer, The New York Times]

By the time of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs release, The Chinese Room were working on a prototype for the openworld game Everybody's Gone to the Rapture. The story was inspired in part by Pinchbeck's experience of the Great storm of 1987 while growing up in a small village in Kent during the Cold War. In their review of the game, The Washington Post credited his "moxie" as creative director in helping The Chinese Room become a "vanguard in the industry." [ref: ‘Everybody’s Gone to the Rapture’ review: An arthouse movie in video game form, The Washington Post]

Kajeneri Mugenzi Christian is a Rwandan fintech executive and public official. He serves as the Chief Executive Officer of MTN MoMo Congo Brazzaville and as the Chairperson of the City of Kigali Council. [ref: Christian Mugenzi elected chair of City of Kigali council, [[The New Times (Rwanda)]

== Early life and education ==
Christian was born in Niamey, Niger, and spent his early childhood in West Africa before relocating with his family to Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo. He later moved to Kigali, Rwanda, where he completed his studies.

He graduated from the Science College of the University of Rwanda and completed post-graduate business management studies at the African Leadership University (ALU) School of Business.

== Career ==

=== Financial technology and banking ===
Christian has over 15 years of leadership experience in banking, telecommunications, and fintech across multiple African markets. He held senior positions at MTN Mobile Money Rwanda, Equity Bank, Airtel, and Ericsson.

He served as the Director of Payment Systems at the National Bank of Rwanda (BNR), where he led national payment system initiatives, financial inclusion strategies, and interoperability frameworks. [ref: National Bank of Rwanda Payment Systems Overview, [[The New Times (Rwanda)] He was later appointed Chief Executive Officer of MTN MoMo Congo Brazzaville, overseeing mobile money services and financial inclusion operations in Central Africa.

=== Public service ===
On 21 August 2024, Christian was appointed by President Paul Kagame as a councillor for the City of Kigali. [ref: President Kagame appoints six Kigali City councilors, IGIHE] On 22 August 2024, the council elected him as its Chairperson, succeeding Didas Kayihura Muganga. In this capacity, he oversees council governance, urban infrastructure policies, and the implementation of the Kigali City Master Plan. [ref: End of the City Council's five-year term: Key achievements in infrastructure and urbanisation, City of Kigali]

Draft text:
Peace, Death! is a pixel art simulation game developed and published for PC on March 24, 2017, by the Russian studio AZAMATIKA. The player controls Reaper, a novice worker of Death, who must guide people to their correct afterlife. [ref: Peace, Death! para PC - Linux, 3DJuegos] [ref: インディーズゲームの小部屋：Room＃474「Peace, Death!」, 4Gamer.net] [ref: Безумные игры: смартфонный президент, пес-суперагент и русские в Steam — Игромания, Igromania.ru] [ref: «Мир! Труд! Май!» — подборка игр, в которых можно попробовать необычные профессии, iXBT.games]. The game is currently available on PC, Android, iOS and Nintendo Switch.

== Gameplay ==
The gameplay consists of selecting who goes to Hell, Heaven or Purgatory, within a time limit. [ref: ]

In order to do it properly, the player must examine each individual and see what criteria they meet. [ref: SwitchArcade Round-Up: ‘SEGA AGES Out Run’ Releases January 10th, Upcoming NEOGEO Titles, the Latest Releases, a Huge List of Sales, and More – TouchArcade, TouchArcade] Initially it is as simple as sending demons down to Hell on the left elevator and humans up to Heaven on the right elevator. However, new rules are added every day and the process of checking them gets increasingly more complex. The player can be asked, for example, to verify if someone is carrying a weapon or if their body is stained with blood, with both cases meaning the character is meant to be sent to Hell. Some crucial elements might be hidden with objects such as hats or glasses, which must be removed in order to make a proper judgement.

Each day has a set number of people to verify, after which the player receives rewards depending on their performance. If enough mistakes are made, a day can be failed midway.

After a certain point, Purgatory is added as a third destination for those who cannot go to either Heaven or Hell. The criteria include, for example, letting go of a weapon (which would otherwise result in Hell) or renouncing holy text (which would otherwise lead to Heaven) when the player left-clicks the corresponding character.

During work, the player might answer phone calls from colleagues asking for advice on certain decisions. They receive the description of an individual and must discern what is important and what is superfluous.

The game often presents bizarre visitors, including celebrity references.

== Plot ==
The protagonist, a Grim Reaper, realizes they have no food to eat and decides to apply for a job at Apocalypse Corporation, working for Death. After successfully completing seven weeks of a trial period, they get paid and hired for a full-time job. [ref: Peace, Death!, Steam]

== Development ==
The head of the AZAMATIKA studio, Azamat Baizulaev (also known as Azamat Zage), revealed his original plan was to make a sequel to his Western game Gun Done, with the same hero, but it didn't work out. At the same time, he came across an online comment sarcastically asking his next game to not be called Peace, Death! (a Russian swear pun). [ref: «В играх я беру ник ULTRAG4Y». Интервью с создателем Peace, Death и Draw Chilly, DTF] The developer, instead, was motivated by the comment and began working on the title.

According to the creator, the central idea of the game remained mostly the same over the course of development. He highlights, however, how Reaper would originally give orders with a lever instead of his hands, which became visually problematic when Purgatory was added. [ref: Интервью с создателем игры Peace, Death! «А еще мы выпустили Gun Done» — Игромания, Igromania.ru]

When asked about comparisons to Papers, Please, Azamat described the similarities as coincidental, while acknowledging it helped boost the popularity of Peace, Death!

The game was localized in French by Sébastien Sosa and Mate Lichtle, in German by Thomas H. (also known as Kyron) and in Brazilian Portuguese by Ruffles, HDD and Fire Borealis. [ref: [Peace, Death! news and announcements], Steam]

Its Nintendo Switch edition, called Peace, Death: Complete Edition, was published by HypeTrain Digital. [ref: Nintendo Download: 22nd November (Europe), Nintendo Life]

== Reception ==
Peace, Death! was often compared to Papers, Please due to its similar gameplay loop.

Shaun Musgrave, writing for TouchArcade, praised the game's concept and the gameplay itself. However, he also drew attention to the humor, with some jokes he described as "a bit lame" and references he predicted might become dated.

An Igromania review, from Lena Pi, described the game as a rather entertaining time-killer.

== References ==

Draft text:
Letizia Murat (25 April 1802 - 3 December 1859) was a French noblewoman, notable for her salon at Palazzo Pepoli Campogrande or Palazzo Pepoli Vecchio on via Castiglione in Bologna, which led to her being nicknamed the Regina di Bologna ('Queen of Bologna').

Several portraits of her by notable artists such as Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres (Harvard University Art Museum [ref: Letizia Murat]), Benjamin Rolland (Reggia di Caserta) and
Louis Ducis (Musée de l'Histoire de France [ref: Musée de l'histoire de France]) survive.

== Life ==
[[File:Caroline_Murat_by_Vigee-Lebrun.jpg|thumb|left|Letizia as a child with her mother by Élisabeth Vigée-Lebrun.]]
Born in Paris to Joachim Murat and Caroline Bonaparte (the eldest of their four children), she had one sister, Luisa Giulia, and two brothers, Achille and Lucien. She was named after her mother's mother Letizia Bonaparte. She was made an imperial and royal prince of the First French Empire in 1804. [ref: Genealogische Tafeln zur Staatengeschichte des 19. Jahrhunderts, nebst einer genealogisch-statistischen Einleitung, F.A. Brockhaus]

Even after her father was made Grand Duke of Cleves and Burg by Caroline's brother Napoleon in 1806 the family remained in Paris. The same year she was made a princess of the Grand Duchy and on 28 October by imperial decree abbess of Elten, [ref: Das fürstliche Stift Elten: aus authentischen Quellen, Heberle'sche Buchhandlung] a former imperial territory annexed by the Grand Duchy. In 1808 her father was made King of Naples, making her princess of Naples. The family thus left the palais de l'Élysée in Paris for the Royal Palace of Naples. There she learned how to run a salon and received an education befitting her rank, learning singing, music, English, German and several other languages.

Her father was shot for his failed attempt to regain the Kingdom after Napoleon's second abdication and so she, her mother and her brothers moved to Trieste, where they benefitted from Metternich's support (Caroline had had a love affair with him years before while he was an ambassador in Paris [ref: Caroline Bonaparte: Princesse Murat, Reine de Naples, France-Empire.]). They lived near the town in villa Campo Marzo for a time before moving to Graz then to a suburb of Vienna and finally to Tuscany, where Caroline's sister Élisa lived.

The 1815 Congress of Vienna stripped them of the right to use their titles and banned them from returning to France and so in 1817 Caroline acquired the Frohsdorf Castle in Lower Austria, living there until 1819. [ref: Il était une fois...le château de Frohsdorf et le couvent de Kostanjevica, leretourdecharlesx.com] Although a liberal, Letizia later pushed her brother Lucien to claim his right to their father's throne in Naples. [ref: Pèpoli, Letìzia Murat, marchésa, www.sapere.it]

After her marriage she supported her husband's political career through her salon, travelled widely, wrote to figures all over Europe and wrote travel diaries. As well as their city residence, the couple also lived at Villa della Palata near the city. Her salon discussed art, culture and politics. In Rome she met the French salon-holder Julie Récamier, who wrote of the meeting "We were fascinated by Marquise Pepoli; I found her beautiful, spiritual and a perfect natural". [ref: Murat Letizia, www.storiaememoriadibologna.it]

[[File:Murat Bologna.JPG|thumb|upright|Her tomb monument, one of the masterpieces of the Certosa di Bologna.]]
She died in Bologna in 1859 after a long illness and was buried in the Certosa di Bologna cemetery there. Her tomb monument by Vincenzo Vela next to the Sala del Colombario is surmounted by a statue of her father.

== Marriage and issue ==
On 27 October 1823 she married Bolognese marquess Guido Taddeo Pepoli (1789-1852), count of Castiglione, who was from an ancient noble family from the city of Bologna. They had four children:

* Carolina (Bologna, 21 August 1824 – Bologna, 23 August 1892), married 1) count Angelo Tattini (1823-1878), with whom she had three children: Laetizia Guida (1846-1924) who married Francesco Isolani-Lupari, Giovanni Gioacchino (1846-1877) and Napoleone (1849-1870)
* Gioacchino Napoleone (Bologna, 1825 - Bologna, 1881) (Mayor of Bologna from 1866 to 1868), in 1844 married princess Friederike von Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, with whom he had three daughters: Letizia (1846-1902), in 1868 married count Antonio Gaddi (1842-1914), Antonietta (1849-1887), in 1872 married count Carlo Taveggi (1836-1902), and Napoleona Luisa (1853-1929), in 1872 married count Guarini Dominico-Mar Castelfalcino Matteucci (1848-1905)
* Elisabetta (1829-1892) married Ippolito Ruspoli, with whom he had two daughters: Laetizia (1849-1944; married Mario Rappini di Casteldelfino and then the Marquis di Casteldelfino); and Giacenta (1861-1862)
* Paolina (1831-1916), married for the first time to Gian Mauro Zucchini Solimei (1825-1854) and had one son 1) Giuseppe Gioacchino Zucchini (1854-1902) who married Carmelita Cagnola (1854-1936); second marriage to Tancredi Mosti Estense Trotti (1826-1903) by whom she had four children:1) Ercole (1864-?) married Rachel Verset and then Iole Fabbri (by whom he had a son called Tancredi); 2) Giovanna (1867-1945) married Alfonso Costabili Containi, with whom he had two children: Gian Battista and Maria Letizia; 3) Maria Letizia (1873-1951) married Andrea Carlo Guidi di Bagno, with whom she had one son, Guido Novello; 4) Ercole Guelfo (born 1876-1896)
[truncated]

Marcos da Matta Meira (born March 18, 1973), known as Parrumpinha or Parrumpa, is a Brazilian Brazilian jiu-jitsu black belt, retired mixed martial artist and mixed martial arts coach. A black belt under Carlson Gracie, he won the first IBJJF World Championship at purple belt in 1996 and the Brazilian national title at black belt in 2000. [ref: World Jiu-Jitsu IBJJF Championship 1996 – Results, International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation] [ref: Campeonato Brasileiro de Jiu-Jitsu 2000 – Resultados, Confederação Brasileira de Jiu-Jitsu] He moved to the United States in 2002 and is the head Brazilian jiu-jitsu coach of the American Top Team professional team in Coconut Creek, Florida. [ref: Pro Coaches, American Top Team] [ref: Inside American Top Team, Fighters Only]

He made his professional MMA debut at 34 and went 12–3 between 2007 and 2018, fighting for Strikeforce and Bellator. [ref: Treinador da ATT, Parrumpinha vence luta de despedida do MMA aos 45 anos, Combate] As a coach he has led Alexandre Pantoja since 2018, including Pantoja's run as UFC Flyweight Champion, and has worked with Petr Yan, Arman Tsarukyan, Renato Moicano, Amanda Nunes and Mayra Bueno Silva, among others. [ref: Marcos Parrumpinha condena polêmicas do MMA nas redes sociais: "Desrespeitam pessoas e nada acontece", ge]

==Early life==
Da Matta grew up in Copacabana, where he spent his days playing beach soccer and footvolley. [ref: Marcos da Matta "Parrumpinha", BJJ Heroes] Carlson Gracie's academy was in the same neighborhood, on Rua Figueiredo Magalhães. [ref: Num encontro marcante, pupilos lembram Carlson Gracie, Graciemag] By his account, Gracie met him on the beach when he was 11 or 12 and kept pushing him to train. He went "for a week or two to prove to him that I don't like it" and stayed. He began training regularly in 1987 and remained with Gracie until 2000. [ref: Interview with Marcos da Matta, American Top Team BJJ instructor, Bloody Elbow] [ref: Legendary Gym Stories: When Liborio Wiped Out The Carlson Gracie Competition Team, BJJEE]

His nickname reportedly comes from a well-known Copacabana local called "Parrumpa", whom he resembled, so friends called him "Parrumpinha" (little Parrumpa). Because of the number of Russian fighters he later began to coach, the Brazilian MMA community also took to calling him "Parrumpov". [ref: ATT Coach: Sean O'Malley Has Never Faced a Challenge Like Pedro Munhoz, Sherdog]

==Brazilian jiu-jitsu career==
===Carlson Gracie academy===
At Gracie's academy, one of his main influences was Amaury Bitetti, who got him to cross-train in judo and work on guard passing. He also practiced Álvaro Romano's Ginástica Natural, which he credits with helping him recover from injuries. [ref: Benefits of Ginastica Natural for Jiu-Jitsu, BJJEE] He calls Ricardo Libório his mentor, and names Renato Tavares as his most frequent training partner.

He was promoted to purple belt on January 1, 1994, and his first match at the new rank was against Leonardo Vieira, who was still unbeaten at purple belt. [ref: Parrumpinha - 100% Carlson Gracie, MMA Debate] The 20-minute match was part of a challenge between Carlson Gracie's academy and Romero "Jacaré" Cavalcanti's Academia Master, held at a nightclub in Leblon in February 1994. [ref: EP#25 Mente Blindada com Marcos "Parrumpinha" Da Matta, Gustavo Dantas] [ref: Exclusivo! Parrumpinha fala de seu início no jiu-jitsu e o começo da American Top Team, Só Papos MMA] Da Matta says he won by a wide margin on points. He had been a little-known blue belt until then and calls it the fight that most shaped his life, since the jiu-jitsu community began to take him seriously afterward. The two met again later, and each won once. [ref: Marcos Parrumpinha - Resenha PVT, Portal do Vale Tudo]

In 1996 he won the first IBJJF World Championship at purple belt, featherweight, entered as "Marcos Da Mata", with Fredson Junior taking silver. Gracie promoted him to black belt in 1997. [ref: It's Time! 'Parrumpinha' participa do podcast do Super Lutas, Super Lutas] At black belt he took silver at the 1999 Pan American Championship in the 70 kg division, losing the final to Royler Gracie on advantage. [ref: Marcos da Matta, Let's BJJ] During those years he also refereed as a center official for the Confederação Brasileira de Jiu-Jitsu. [ref: Parrumpinha comenta estreia no Strikeforce e lembra rivalidade com Robinho, Graciemag]

===Brazilian Top Team and the Robson Moura rivalry===
When Carlson Gracie's leading black belts broke with him in 2000, da Matta left with Libório and Bitetti for the newly founded Brazilian Top Team. Under the BTT banner he won the 2000 Brazilian Nationals at black belt featherweight, ahead of Marcos Loureiro. The same year he reached the featherweight final of the World Championship at the Tijuca Tênis Clube and lost 2–0 to Robson Moura. [ref: World Jiu-Jitsu IBJJF Championship 2000 – Results, International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation] [ref: Jiu-Jitsu: relembre Robinho Moura x Parrumpinha no Mundial de 2000, no Tijuca, Graciemag]

Draft text:
Assessment in the era of artificial intelligence

In the modern era of artificial intelligence (AI), evaluation means both using AI tools in evaluation and evaluating programmes, services or systems that use AI. Artificial intelligence can help with tasks such as sorting large datasets, analysing text and summarising documents. Its use also raises issues around the quality of evidence, bias, privacy, transparency and accountability. [ref: Artificial intelligence and big data-driven evaluation research and practices: A systematic literature review, Evaluation] Applications Machine-learning and artificial intelligence techniques have been used to analyse large data sets and detect trends in text and other information. Generative artificial intelligence can also assist with tasks at various stages of evaluation, including design, data structuring, analysis and reporting. Case studies of these applications and shifts in evaluation methods and practitioner skills are presented in the edited volume From Algorithms to Evidence: Using GenAI in Evaluation Practice. [ref: From Algorithms to Evidence: Using GenAI in Evaluation Practice, Routledge]

Methodological and ethical considerations: AI-assisted analysis may allow evaluators to work with more information or to perform some tasks more quickly. Outputs still need to be checked for accuracy, validity and relevance to the evaluation questions. A systematic review of the use of AI and big data in evaluation found unresolved methodological, ethical and data-ownership issues and recommended the combination of these tools with traditional approaches. [1] Researchers have also explored the possible effects of AI use on evaluation standards such as rigour, utility, fairness and independence. [ref: Sage Journals: Discover world-class research, Sage Journals] Responsible use guidelines on responsible AI use in evaluation typically encompass oversight by humans, transparency, sensitive data, and representation of different perspectives. In 2025, the United Nations Evaluation Group published ethical principles for the use of AI in United Nations evaluations. [ref: ]

The [https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/oa-edit/10.4324/9781003799139-33/frame-valentine-joseph-gandhi-kerry-bruce-steffen-bohni-nielsen?context=ubx&refId=eb11a85b-b358-4419-8ad1-0dc1e02d21a9 FRAME] framework (Framework for Responsible AI in Monitoring and Evaluation) offers guidance across seven phases of evaluation. It sets out five principles: accountability architecture; stakeholder engagement; epistemic integrity; transparency; and proportionality. The framework emphasises human responsibility for decisions and provides a checklist to record the use of AI in evaluation activities. [ref: ]]AI System Evaluation The evaluation of an AI system is a related but different task from the use of AI to perform an evaluation. It is about evaluating the system’s performance and effects in context. Evaluation researchers have also suggested criteria for thinking about how AI is used in evaluation practice and what its use leads to. [ref: Evaluation criteria for artificial intelligence, New Directions for Evaluation]

== Skura Style ==
Skura Style is an American company that sells kitchen cleaning products. Founded in 2017 by Linda Sawyer and Alison Matz, the company initially focused on kitchen sponges and later expanded its product range to include scouring pads, microfiber cloths, and kitchen towels. [ref: Two Rockland Natives Rethink The Kitchen Sponge, Daily Voice]

=== History ===
Skura Style was founded by Linda Sawyer, a former advertising executive, and Alison Matz, a media and publishing executive. The company launched in October 2017 with a kitchen sponge as its first product. Sawyer's previous career included serving as CEO and Chairman of the advertising agency Deutsch, while Matz spent the majority of her career as a media executive, serving as Publisher at Condé Nast and Meredith. Independent trade publication Digiday covered the founders' transition from advertising and publishing to consumer products in January 2018. [ref: Life After Advertising: From Deutsch CEO to cleaning supplies startup founder, Digiday]

In May 2022, actress Eva Mendes acquired an ownership stake in the company and became a co-owner and brand ambassador. Her involvement included collaboration on product design and marketing. The partnership subsequently expanded to include a collection of kitchen cleaning products associated with Mendes. [ref: Eva Mendes comes clean, Forbes Australia]

=== Products ===
The company's product range includes kitchen sponges, scouring pads, microfiber cleaning cloths, Swedish dishcloths, and cotton kitchen towels.

Its Skrubby Sponge incorporates a printed pattern that fades with use, providing a visual indication of when the sponge may need replacing. The product is also treated with an antimicrobial agent, according to descriptions of the product published by the company and media outlets.

Other products include Very Skrubby, a double-sided scouring pad; Wipe Envy, a microfiber cleaning cloth; and Towel Ta-Da, a cotton kitchen towel. The company has also released products in collaboration with Eva Mendes. [ref: Allow Eva Mendes to Explain Why She’s Bubbly Over Sponges These Days, Architectural Digest]

Draft text:
Gerald Jonas (born 1935) is an American writer, journalist, and literary critic. He was a staff writer for The New Yorker for approximately 30 years and a science fiction book critic for The New York Times Book Review. [ref: Selected Shorts: Anything But Politics with Tony Hale, Symphony Space] He wrote a number of nonfiction books, and his science fiction novelette The Shaker Revival was nominated for a Nebula Award in 1970. [ref: 1970 Nebula Awards, Nebula Awards]

== Early life and education ==
Jonas was born in 1935 [ref: Stuttering: the disorder of many theories - NLM Catalog - NCBI, www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov]. He attended the Horace Mann School in New York [ref: My Grandfather, the Writer, The Science Survey] and Yale University where he wrote for the Yale Daily News [ref: Elected to Yale News Board, The New York Times], graduating in 1957. He subsequently held a Henry Fellowship at the University of Cambridge, a Guggenheim Fellowship, and a Rockefeller Fellowship.

== Career ==
Jonas spent approximately three decades as a staff writer for The New Yorker [ref: Gerald Jonas, The New Yorker], writing about science, technology, psychology, and medicine. He served as a science fiction book critic for The New York Times Book Review for approximately 30 years, reviewing more than 900 works of science fiction and related literature. [ref: Science Fiction, archive.nytimes.com]

In 1977, science fiction critic John D. Berry criticised Jonas's New York Times column in the fanzine Karass. Berry considered Jonas a competent but unexceptional reviewer. [ref: Hot Corn, Cold Corn, Karass]

In a review of the second edition of The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction published in Fantasy Commentator, A. Langley Searles identified Jonas as one of several figures he believed warranted an entry. [ref: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, Fantasy Commentator]

In a 2006 discussion of science fiction reviewing in Publishers Weekly, Jonas' science fiction column was described as a near-monthly, one-page feature of capsule reviews that had become less frequent after Sam Tanenhaus became editor of The New York Times Book Review. [ref: ]

His later journalism included obituaries of science fiction writers Arthur C. Clarke [ref: Arthur C. Clarke, Author Who Saw Science Fiction Become Real, Dies at 90, The New York Times], Ray Bradbury [ref: Ray Bradbury, Who Brought Mars to Earth With a Lyrical Mastery, Dies at 91, The New York Times], and Ursula K. Le Guin [ref: Ursula K. Le Guin, Acclaimed for Her Fantasy Fiction, Is Dead at 88, The New York Times] for The New York Times.

=== Nonfiction books ===
Jonas has written six nonfiction books on subjects ranging from religion and psychology to scientific research, dance and natural history.

His first book, On Doing Good: The Quaker Experiment (1971), examined the history and principles of the Religious Society of Friends. Reviewing the book, Kirkus Reviews described it as "refreshingly objective". [ref: Book Reviews, Sites, Romance, Fantasy, Fiction, Kirkus Reviews]

His second book, Visceral Learning: Toward a Science of Self-Control (1973), concerned research into the control of physiological processes. It was reviewed by Bob Samples in The American Biology Teacher. [ref: Review: Visceral Learning: Toward a Science of Self-Control, by Gerald Jonas and The Psychology of the Consciousness, by Robert E. Ornstein, The American Biology Teacher]

Jonas's Stuttering: The Disorder of Many Theories (1977) combined scientific theories about stuttering with his personal experiences. A contemporary review in Kirkus Reviews praised the book's combination of personal experience and scientific investigation. [ref: Stuttering: The Disorder of Many Theories, Kirkus Reviews] In a 2012 essay in The New York Review of Books, Francine du Plessix Gray described the work as a "splendid memoir". [ref: The Paralysis of Stuttering, The New York Review of Books]

His 1989 book, The Circuit Riders: Rockefeller Money and the Rise of Modern Science, examined the role of Rockefeller Foundation philanthropy in the development of scientific research. The book was reviewed in several publications, including JAMA [ref: The Circuit Riders: Rockefeller Money and the Rise of Modern Science, JAMA], The New York Times Book Review [ref: BIG MONEY MEETS BIG SCIENCE, The New York Times], Science [ref: Modes and Agendas of Patronage: The Politics of Philanthropy. Abraham Flexner and Medical Education. Steven C. Wheatley. University of Wisconsin Press, Madison, 1989. xx, 249 pp. + plates. $37.50; paper, $14.95.; The Circuit Riders. Rockefeller Money and the Rise of Modern Science. Gerald Jonas. Norton, New York, 1989. 430 pp., illus. $22.95., Science], the Los Angeles Times [ref: Book Review: 'Circuit Riders': Giving Away Research Money Is an Art, Los Angeles Times], and The Quarterly Review of Biology. [ref: The Rockefeller Foundation: Warren Weaver and the Launching of Molecular Biology The Circuit Riders: Rockefeller Money and the Rise of Modern Science. Gerald Jonas, The Quarterly Review of Biology]

Jonas wrote Dancing: The Pleasure, Power, and Art of Movement (1992) as a companion to an eight-part television documentary series. The book and television series were reviewed in the Dance Research Journal. [ref: Dancing: The Pleasure, Power, and Art of Movement, byGerald Jonas. New York: Harry N. Abrams, 1992. 256pp., photographs, Bibliography, Index. 199.95., Dance Research Journal]

Andrea Monath Schumacher is an American interior designer and author. She is the founder of Andrea Schumacher Interiors, an interior design firm established in Denver, Colorado, in 1999. Schumacher has been featured in publications including Galerie, House Beautiful and 1stDibs, and was selected as a designer for the 50th Kips Bay Decorator Show House New York in 2025. Schumacher grew up in several locations in the United States and abroad, including Nigeria. She earned a bachelor's degree in interior design from Colorado State University and later studied universal design at the Harvard Graduate School of Design. [ref: Fashion and Travel Inspire This Former TV Set Designer’s Gutsy Interiors, 1stDibs Introspective]

=== Career ===
Schumacher began her career working in television set design in Los Angeles, including work associated with the NBC daytime series Days of Our Lives. She later returned to Colorado and established Andrea Schumacher Interiors in 1999. [ref: The Houzz Blog]

Her residential interiors have been characterized by layered combinations of color, pattern, vintage furnishings and objects collected through travel. Schumacher operates from Denver and Santa Barbara and has completed residential and hospitality projects in multiple regions of the United States. [ref: Meet Interior Designer Andrea Schumacher, Home & Garden Colorado]

In 2025, Schumacher participated in the 50th annual Kips Bay Decorator Show House New York, where she designed a guest apartment, kitchen and bathroom. [ref: Meet the Kips Bay Designer: Andrea Schumacher, Galerie Magazine]

=== Publications ===
Schumacher is the author of Vibrant Interiors: Living Large at Home, published by Gibbs Smith. The book received a Colorado Book Award in the pictorial category. [ref: Meet Interior Designer Andrea Schumacher, Home & Garden Colorado]

Samantha Storr is an American producer known for her work in virtual reality, augmented reality, and immersive media. She has served as Head of Content at Meta Reality Labs, overseeing the virtual reality fitness application Supernatural, and previously held leadership roles at Within and Here Be Dragons (formerly Vrse.works).

== Early life and education ==

Storr lives in Los Angeles with her husband and son. She attended the Hewitt School in New York City and earned a degree in Communications from Boston University. [ref: Samantha Storr – LinkedIn]

== Career ==

Storr began her career producing music videos and commercials, working with artists including the Beastie Boys and collaborating with film and commercial directors. Her early producing credits include Last Day Dream (2009), a short film directed by Chris Milk for the 42 Second Dream Film Festival; [ref: Last Day Dream, Vimeo] Fight for Your Right Revisited (2011), a short film directed by Adam Yauch that premiered at the Sundance Film Festival; [ref: Beastie Boys: Fight for Your Right Revisited, Radio Times] [ref: The House That Yauch Built, uDiscoverMusic] the Beastie Boys' "Don't Play No Game That I Can't Win" featuring Santigold (2011), directed by Spike Jonze; [ref: Advertising Age — 2011 to 2012, Advertising Age (via Internet Archive)] their "Make Some Noise" (2011), directed by Adam Yauch; [ref: 2011 MTV VMA Nominee List, HipHopWired] Demi Lovato: Stay Strong (2012), a documentary produced by RadicalMedia; [ref: Demi Lovato to Participate in Live Q&A Tuesday on MTV, NBC Today] The Legend of Hallowdega (2010), directed by Terry Gilliam; [ref: Craig DeLeon — Selected Credits, Evolution Music Partners] the 2013 YouTube Music Awards, directed by Spike Jonze; and Cathedrals of Culture (2013), a documentary series executive produced by Wim Wenders with an episode directed by Robert Redford. [ref: Cathedrals of Culture — Cast, TV Guide] [ref: Cathedrals of Culture — Credits, Box Office Mojo]

She also produced branded entertainment, including Toyota's "Project Endeavour" (2012), in which a Toyota Tundra towed the Space Shuttle Endeavour to the California Science Center; [ref: Tundra Endeavour 'Ultimate Journey', The One Club] Sony and Intel's "Project Shiphunt" (2011), an online adventure series; [ref: An @[user] Departure For 180LA: High School Students Go On Nautical Adventure For Sony VAIO, SHOOTonline] and the second season of GT Academy USA (2012), a Nissan and PlayStation reality competition series, on which she served as showrunner. [ref: Lauded Branded Entertainment, Part 2: GT Academy, SHOOTonline]

In 2013, Storr collaborated with director Chris Milk on Hello, Again, a virtual reality project featuring Beck. The interactive 360-degree concert film was commissioned by Lincoln and produced by RadicalMedia. [ref: A New Vision For Sound: Chris Milk Breaks Down How 'Beck: Hello, Again' Was Made, Fast Company] The project won two Cannes Gold Lions and one Bronze Lion in 2013, along with two Webby Awards. [ref: Beck "Hello, Again" — Awards, Zachary Richter] [ref: The Man Behind Beck's 360-Degree Sound and Vision, Billboard]

In 2014, Storr and Milk co-founded Vrse.works, a virtual reality production company that later became Here Be Dragons. She served as Vice President of Content from 2014 to 2017, overseeing documentary, branded, and narrative virtual reality productions. [ref: Evolution of Vrse, Webby Awards] [ref: FutureHero Samantha Storr: The heroine of virtual reality, Atlas of the Future] [ref: Vrse — Atlas of the Future, Atlas of the Future]

Projects produced during this period include Clouds Over Sidra (2015), created in collaboration with the United Nations and premiered at the World Economic Forum in Davos. The film, produced by Storr and directed by Gabo Arora and Chris Milk, follows a twelve-year-old Syrian girl in Jordan's Za'atari camp and was the first virtual reality film made for the UN. [ref: UN Launches Powerful, First Ever, VR Film following Syrian Refugee Girl, TechCrunch] [ref: UN Agencies team up to bring voices of Syrian refugees to world leaders through Virtual Reality, ReliefWeb (United Nations)] It won the Interactive Award at Sheffield Doc/Fest in 2015. [ref: 'Syrian Love Story' wins Sheffield Doc/Fest prize, Screen Daily]

She was also a key collaborator on Waves of Grace (2015), a virtual reality experience by Gabo Arora and Chris Milk following Ebola survivor Decontee Davis in Liberia, featured in the New Frontier program at the 2016 Sundance Film Festival. [ref: Sundance Institute Celebrates New Frontier 10th Anniversary at 2016 Festival, Sundance Institute]
[truncated]

Draft text:
Rodney Zelenka (born 1953) is a Panamanian painter and visual artist whose figurative and mixed-media work explores migration, violence, social exclusion and the exercise of power. He represented Panama at the centennial Venice Biennale in 1995, as part of the Istituto Italo-Latino Americano exhibition, and at the 23rd São Paulo Art Biennial in 1996. He was one of fourteen artists in Crosscurrents: Contemporary Painting from Panama 1968–1998 at the Americas Society in New York, and has since exhibited in Panama, the United States, Mexico and elsewhere.

== Early life and education ==
Zelenka was born in Panama City in 1953. He has said that his parents came to Panama from Europe to escape the Holocaust. From 1962 to 1969 he took courses with the painters Alfredo Sinclair and Guillermo Trujillo at Panama's Escuela de Bellas Artes. He studied at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, from 1971 to 1977, majoring in economics with a minor in Latin American politics and taking courses in studio art. According to his published curriculum vitae, he spent extended periods between 1979 and 1989 working alongside the artists Julio Zachrisson in Madrid, Rodolfo Abularach in New York and Jessy Patrick Allen in California.

== Career ==
=== Early exhibitions and international biennials ===
In 1979 Zelenka received a prize at the Gulf Oil Exhibition at Panama's Museo de Arte Contemporáneo, and in 1980 he held his first solo exhibition at Galería Arte 80 in Panama City. Writing in La Estrella de Panamá, the artist and writer Arístides Ureña Ramos placed Zelenka alongside Brooke Alfaro and Tabo Toral among the Panamanian artists who had spent time in New York in the 1970s and joined the local exhibition scene in the early 1980s.

In the late 1980s and early 1990s he exhibited at New York galleries such as Gallery Revel (1987) and Cast Iron Gallery (1993), and in Japan at Shone Okuda Gallery in Tokyo (1989) and at venues in Osaka and Nagoya (1990). In 1994 he took part in the Bienal de Cuenca in Ecuador and the Caribbean Biennial in Santo Domingo.

In 1995 Zelenka represented Panama at the 46th Venice Biennale, the centennial edition of the exhibition. He was one of nine artists from nine countries in the exhibition organized by the Istituto Italo-Latino Americano (IILA) at the Chiesa di San Giovanni Novo in Venice, for which Fernando Macotela served as commissioner, assisted by Alessandra Bonanni.

The following year he represented Panama at the 23rd São Paulo Art Biennial, held from 5 October to 8 December 1996 under the general curator Nelson Aguilar. The official catalogue devoted several pages to Zelenka and reproduced paintings including Asesino del Tiempo (1996), El Color de la Supervivencia (1996) and Escape en Cámara Lenta de Hueco Negro (1995). In an accompanying essay, the art critic Phyllis Braff described how the work combined tightly ordered patterns, figurative scenes and psychological tension.

Also in 1996, Zelenka held exhibitions at the Museo de la Nación in Lima, the Casa de la Cultura Ecuatoriana in Quito and the Museo Municipal de Arte Moderno in Cuenca. He later recalled that the Lima exhibition, Canto a la guerra y el fuego, used suspended mattresses to evoke the possessions carried by people fleeing disasters. His exhibition Tensión was shown at Panama's Museo de Arte Contemporáneo in 1997 and at the Museo de Arte Moderno in Santo Domingo in 1998.

In 1998 Zelenka took part in Crosscurrents: Contemporary Painting from Panama 1968–1998, curated by Mónica E. Kupfer and Edward J. Sullivan, which ran at the Americas Society in New York from 2 May to 31 July. The survey brought together fourteen Panamanian painters whose work had developed amid the political and cultural changes the country had undergone since 1968. His exhibition record also lists Panamanian art biennials up to 2002 and an international biennial in Buenos Aires that year.

=== Exhibitions since 2020 ===
In 2020 Zelenka took part in Everything Is Art, Everything Is Politics, an online group exhibition organized by Elga Wimmer PCC and curated by Wimmer and Berta Sichel. Writing about his paintings, Mark Bloch reported that the curators had compared Zelenka's treatment of the human body to the work of Leon Golub. According to the artist's exhibition history, the show was later presented at the Museo Casa Pintada of the Fundación Cristóbal Gabarrón in Mula, Spain, in 2021–2022.

Dominion and Frailty, curated by Wimmer and Thalia Vrachopoulos, was shown at the Tenri Cultural Institute in New York in November and December 2022. The paintings dealt with displacement, poverty and unequal relations of power. In their reviews, Mary Hrbacek and Bloch discussed how the show set grey human figures against brightly colored everyday belongings, and the journalist Lucy Komisar interviewed Zelenka about his use of suitcases and his concern with abusive power.

In Mexico, a run of exhibitions began in 2022 with Mística social at the Centro Estatal de las Artes in Tecate, Baja California, which later traveled to Ensenada and Tijuana. In 2023 the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez showed A ras de suelo, about 50 works dealing with migration, homelessness, violence and abuses of authority.

Also in 2023, Zelenka showed Rivers of Babylon at Lichtundfire in New York, co-curated by Wimmer and Priska Juschka. Reviewing the show, the art critic Robert C. Morgan related its works on paper to imagery of mass migration and discarded possessions.
[truncated]

The International Legal Technology Association (ILTA) is a non-profit trade association based in Chicago, Illinois, that provides education, networking, and research resources for legal technology professionals. [ref: International Legal Technology Association: ILTA, The National Law Review] Its activities include the annual ILTACON conference, the EVOLVE conference, the magazine Peer to Peer, and an annual technology survey of law firms.

== History ==
ILTA was founded in 1980 and was first incorporated in 1985. It is designated a 501(c)(6) nonprofit organization by the U.S. Internal Revenue Service.

== Membership and governance ==
ILTA's membership consists primarily of law firms, corporate legal departments, and law schools, and any employee of a member organization is eligible to participate. [ref: International Legal Technology Assoc., Idealist]

The organization is governed by a seven-member board of directors and supported by a professional staff. As of its most recent Form 990 filing, Joy Heath Rush serves as chief executive officer. [ref: International Legal Technology, Nonprofit Explorer]

== Activities ==
ILTA organizes educational conferences and events for legal technology professionals, including:

* ILTACON – ILTA's annual conference, which has been covered by legal trade press including Legaltech News and LawNext. [ref: 6 Things We Learned at this Year's ILTACON, Legaltech News] [ref: ILTACON 2021 Roundup: The Final Day, Legaltech News] [ref: Today on Legaltech Week: Our ILTACON Post-Mortem, LawNext] [ref: ILTACON Takeaways From a Legal Tech Newbie (and Litigation Beat Vet), Litigation Daily] [ref: Pre-ILTACON Legaltech Rundown, Legaltech News]
* EVOLVE – a conference on legal technology and operations that centers each year on two themes, most recently generative artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. [ref: EVOLVE, International Legal Technology Association] [ref: Legal tech education in the age of transformation: Insights ahead of ILTA EVOLVE 2025, Thomson Reuters Institute]
* ILTACON Europe – a regional community and event series for ILTA's European members. [ref: About ILTA Europe, International Legal Technology Association]
* Local socials – informal networking events in individual cities, often coordinated by volunteer member liaisons.

== Publications and research ==
ILTA's publications and programs include:

* Peer to Peer – a quarterly magazine on legal technology topics, published online and in a digital flipbook format. [ref: Peer to Peer Magazine, International Legal Technology Association]
* ILTA Technology Survey – an annual research report on technology use in law firms. The 2025 edition reported responses from 580 law firms representing more than 152,000 attorneys. [ref: 2025 Technology Survey, International Legal Technology Association]
* Distinguished Peer Awards – an annual awards program recognizing contributions to the legal technology field. [ref: ILTA Celebrates 16th Annual Distinguished Peer Awards, International Legal Technology Association]

Mindbreeze GmbH is an Austrian enterprise software company that develops enterprise search, knowledge management and artificial intelligence software. It was founded in Linz in 2005 by Daniel Fallmann and Jakob Praher. [ref: [https://www.mindbreeze.com/management "Management". Mindbreeze. Accessed 7 October 2026.]] [ref: [https://kompany.ie/p/at/262155y "Mindbreeze GmbH, FN 262155y". Austrian commercial register extract via kompany. Accessed 7 October 2026.]] The company operates in Austria and the United States. [ref: [https://www.mindbreeze.com/company "Company". Mindbreeze. Accessed 7 October 2026.]] It is majority-owned by the Austrian software company Fabasoft AG. [ref: [https://at.cloud.fabasoft.com/folio/public/0s5n1dd48kq2w2vz00fbpdjvw3/download "Fabasoft AG has increased its stake in Mindbreeze GmbH". Fabasoft AG, 20 April 2021.]]

== History ==

Mindbreeze was entered in the Austrian commercial register as a limited liability company (GmbH) on 13 April 2005. Its early software was marketed under the Fabasoft name, including Fabasoft Mindbreeze Enterprise, which searched information across corporate file systems, email and document management systems. [ref: [https://www.kmworld.com/Articles/Editorial/Features/Trend-Setting-Products-of-2010Fabasoft-and-FTI-Technology-69607.aspx "Trend-Setting Products of 2010: Fabasoft and FTI Technology". KMWorld, 2010.]]

Mindbreeze subsequently developed Mindbreeze InSpire, initially offered as enterprise search software preinstalled on dedicated hardware. The company later expanded its offerings to cloud and hybrid deployment. In May 2024, InSpire became available through Google Cloud Marketplace. [ref: [https://www.destinationcrm.com/Articles/CRM-News/CRM-Across-the-Wire/Mindbreeze-InSpire-Available-on-Google-Cloud-Marketplace-164213.aspx "Mindbreeze InSpire Available on Google Cloud Marketplace". Destination CRM, 24 May 2024.]]

In April 2021, Fabasoft increased its ownership interest in Mindbreeze from 76% to 85.5%. In a May 2026 article, Diginomica reported that Mindbreeze worked directly with approximately 2,000 large companies, with partners serving smaller customers. [ref: [https://diginomica.com/cast-setting-sail-enterprise-scale-ai-mindbreeze Ring, Katy. "Cast off! Setting sail for enterprise scale AI with Mindbreeze". Diginomica, 13 May 2026.]]

In 2024 the company introduced Mindbreeze Insight Workplace, a product built on its enterprise search technology. In August 2025, the company added multimodal large-language-model capabilities to InSpire, including processing of audio, video and image content. [ref: [https://www.destinationcrm.com/Articles/CRM-News/CRM-Across-the-Wire/Mindbreeze-Adds-Multimodal-LLM-Integration-to-InSpire-170822.aspx "Mindbreeze Adds Multimodal LLM Integration to InSpire". Destination CRM, 5 August 2025.]] [ref: [https://www.kmworld.com/Articles/News/News/Mindbreeze-adds-multimodal-LLM-integration-to-refine-enterprise-data-intelligence-171064.aspx Simone, Stephanie. "Mindbreeze adds multimodal LLM integration to refine enterprise data intelligence". KMWorld, 19 August 2025.]]

== Products ==

=== Mindbreeze InSpire ===

Mindbreeze InSpire is enterprise search and information-retrieval software designed to index structured and unstructured information from multiple business systems. The software supports search and question answering across connected sources and can be deployed on premises or through cloud infrastructure. Its newer functions use retrieval-augmented generation and multimodal large language models.

=== Mindbreeze Insight Workplace ===

Mindbreeze Insight Workplace is a software interface built on InSpire for accessing enterprise information and configuring AI-assisted workflows. Diginomica reported that its Insight Touchpoints can be configured by subject-matter experts through an Insight App Designer and that the software records information about user requests and responses.

== GenAI Confidence Index ==

Mindbreeze publishes a survey series called the GenAI Confidence Index, which examines business attitudes toward generative AI. In February 2026, Crowdfund Insider reported on findings from the company's survey, including differences in confidence between executive and implementation-focused roles. [ref: [https://www.crowdfundinsider.com/2026/02/264243-genai-focus-narrowing-mindbreeze-survey/ Zerucha, Tony. "GenAI Focus Narrowing: Mindbreeze Survey". Crowdfund Insider, 27 February 2026.]]
