Draft: Michelle Cook (sheriff)

Draft text:
Michelle Cook is an American law enforcement officer serving as Sheriff of Clay County, Florida since September 2020. She is the first woman to hold the office in the county's history and, as of 2026, is one of two women serving as sheriff in Florida, alongside Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz. [ref: She's the Sheriff: Michelle Cook starts early in Clay County, Florida Politics] [ref: Florida Sheriffs Association Celebrates Graduation of 2nd Annual Women's Leadership Academy, Florida Sheriffs Association] She was elected in 2020 after defeating incumbent Darryl Daniels, who had been suspended from office by Governor Ron DeSantis following his arrest, and was reelected in 2024 with about 80 percent of the vote. [ref: Daniels suspended as Clay County sheriff following arrest, Clay Today] [ref: Gov. DeSantis appoints temporary replacement for Florida sheriff, ABC Action News] [ref: Michelle Cook reelected as Clay County sheriff after defeating Darryl Daniels again, News4Jax]

== Early life and education ==
Cook is a native of Green Cove Springs, Florida, in Clay County, and a graduate of Clay High School. [ref: Clay Sheriff Michelle Cook lists her priorities for 2nd term, Jacksonville Today] She holds a bachelor's degree in criminal justice with a minor in public administration, and a master's degree in criminal justice, both from the University of North Florida, and is a graduate of the FBI-LEEDA Command Leadership Institute. [ref: Sheriff Michelle Cook, Clay County Sheriff's Office]

== Law enforcement career ==
Cook joined the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office in 1992. In 2016, she was promoted to head the agency's Department of Patrol and Enforcement. [ref: Michelle Cook leads by example at Sheriff's Office; recently promoted to run patrol and enforcement, Jacksonville Daily Record] She retired from the agency as director of patrol and enforcement in 2017, and became chief of the Atlantic Beach Police Department in 2017.

== 2020 sheriff election ==
Cook left the Atlantic Beach Police Department in early 2020 to run for Sheriff of Clay County. [ref: Michelle Cook launches bid for Clay County Sheriff, Florida Politics] The incumbent, Darryl Daniels, was arrested on August 13, 2020, and charged with tampering with evidence and giving false reports to law enforcement, charges that stemmed from an investigation into his relationship with a subordinate. Governor DeSantis suspended him the next day and appointed Florida Department of Law Enforcement agent Matt Walsh as interim sheriff. [ref: DeSantis names FDLE's Matt Walsh as interim sheriff of Clay County, News4Jax] Cook won the August 18, 2020, Republican primary, with Daniels finishing second with 29 percent of the vote. A write-in candidate withdrew from the general election race, leaving Cook as the next sheriff. [ref: Cook to be Clay County's next sheriff as write-in candidate withdraws, WJCT News] DeSantis asked Cook to take office ahead of the normal January inauguration date, and she was sworn in as Sheriff of Clay County on September 1, 2020, becoming the first woman to hold the office.

== Tenure as sheriff ==
In March 2021, the National Sheriffs' Association recognized Cook, at the time the only woman serving as sheriff in Florida, for Women's History Month. [ref: National Sheriff's Association recognizes Florida's only current woman sheriff: Michelle Cook, News4Jax] In 2023, she helped launch the Signal 35 Fund, a nonprofit that provides emergency financial assistance to first responders in Clay County. [ref: Clay County leaders announce launch of public safety initiative to help first responders facing personal emergencies, News4Jax] Cook and the Clay County Sheriff's Office are also founding partners of the Northeast Florida Inter-Agency Child Exploitation and Persons Trafficking (INTERCEPT) Task Force, a multi-agency initiative combating human trafficking and child exploitation. [ref: Leaders examine sex trafficking awareness, Clay Today]

Clay Today reported that crime rates in the county fell even as its population grew. [ref: Clay crime rates drop as county grows, Clay Today] In 2025, her office announced a collaboration with the state to help solve cold cases. [ref: Clay County Sheriff's Office announces collaboration with state to help solve cold cases, News4Jax]

In March 2026, Cook was recognized by President Donald Trump during a Women's History Month event at the White House. [ref: Clay County Sheriff Michelle Cook honored by President Trump at Women's History Month event at White House, News4Jax] [ref: Trump recognizes Clay County Sheriff Cook for Women's History Month, First Coast News]

== 2024 re-election ==
Cook filed for re-election in May 2023 and ran unopposed in the Republican primary. [ref: Michelle Cook files for re-election for Clay County Sheriff, Action News Jax] In the November 2024 general election, she again faced Daniels, who had been acquitted of all charges in 2022, and won with around 80 percent of the vote. [ref: Former Clay County sheriff acquitted of crimes against his mistress will be on 2024 ballot, First Coast News] [ref: Incumbent Clay County Sheriff Michelle Cook secures reelection, First Coast News]
[truncated]

Draft: Charles de Loupoigne

Draft text:
Charles de Loupoigne (14 March 1761 - 30 July 1799) was a man from the Southern Netherlands known for his resistance to the French occupation of that area. His acts of resistance inspired the Peasants' War. He was also known by the nom de guerre Charles François Jacqmin and the nicknames Cousin Charles or Charlepoeng.

== Family==
His father Jean Joseph Jacqmin was an eau de vie and brandy merchant, a gin distiller and corporal in Brussels' garde-bourgeoise. He was a son of Marie Virly and Jean Antoine Jacqmin, both based in Brussels. They were both buried in the parish of Saint Géry, Marie in 1758 and Jean Antoine in 1762. Almost all the Jacqmin family moved to live in Brussels. Jean Joseph and his two brothers were all born in Braine-l'Alleud and all three gained promotion to become Bourgeois of Brussels, Jean Joseph in 1752, Bartholomée in 1753 and Nicolas in 1772.

In 1752 Jean Joseph married Brigitte Josèphe Quertenmont in Saint-Nicolas parish in Brussels - she died in the parish of Saint-Géry in 1759. Again in the parish of Saint-Géry, Jean Joseph married Marie Josèphe De Glain or De Glin four months after his first wife's death. Charles François Jacqmin was born eighteen months after the marriage, followed by a second son, François Chrisostôme Jacqmin, in 1765. François later became a musician at the Théâtre des Arts in Rouen and had two marriages, one in Paris and another in Canteleu, both of which had issue. Jean Joseph Jacqmin died in Brussels on 21 May 1797. - Charles Francois's mother was still alive at the time.

A record from 1767 mentions Jean Joseph as an eau de vie maker at 30 Rue de l'Étuve, at its junction with Rue de l'Amigo, in section 30 of the city (Saint-Nicolas). Another from 1776 has him requesting a 'tolbrief' and giving his address as at the sign of 'Aen Sint Jan'.

==Life==
===Armed resistance===
He was born in Brussels and baptised at Saint-Géry church in the city on 14 March 1761. His family spoke French, but he learned Flemish with his playmates. He began but did not complete studies in surgery and unsuccessfully attempted to become a wine merchant on Rue du Lombard in Brussels.

In July 1789 he was made an excise officer in Brussels but lost that job on the outbreak of the Brabant Revolution and the French driving the Austrians out of the Southern Nerthlands, instead becoming a recruiting sergeant for the Franc Corps of Grün-Laudon, an Austrian regiment. When the Austrian forces crossed the Rhine at Neuss on 5 November 1794 he was captured and taken to Charleville.

He escaped in late December and headed for Brabant, but was arrested in his hiding place on 6 March 1795 and this time sent to the citadel in Doullens. He was freed a few months later in return for a security deposit. In June that year he was sheltered by Antoine Bève in Loupoigne. There Jacqmin took on the nickname Charles de Loupoigne, which misspelling transformed into Charlepoeng. He decided to oppose the French occupation of the Southern Netherlands and formed a group of forty armed men, calling it "The Belgian Army". His second-in-command was a distant relation, Antoine Lecoq, a slate worker in Baulers.

His force attacked a French-held foundry with an attached arms factory in Genappe on 3 January 1796, even though France and Austria had signed an armistice on 21 December the previous year. It was therefore a complete surprise to the French troops, who were all captured. The Tree of Liberty planted in front of the 'Le Roy d'Espagne' inn was cut down and the successful attack drew in new volunteers. The following day he and his force ambushed more French troops, this time at the Quatre Bras crossroads near Charleroi, capturing twenty-four men and 104 army horses. Near Gosselies he robbed a mail coach between Charleroi and Brussels, capturing three French travellers. One other traveller, Chapel, escaped and informed the French authorities in Brussels what had happened.

Those authorities immediately sent a garrison under commander Carette from Brussels to Gosselies. It attacked Charles' troops by night and - finding them asleep or drunk - easily defeated them. Lecoq was captured and interrogated, telling the French the true identity of 'Charlepoeng'. Lecoq was condemned to death and on 17 January shot in Place de la Liberté. The same sentence was passed on in absentia on 25 February on Charles and on Dom Guillaume de Chentinne, prior of the Cistercian abbey in Villers which sheltered Charles for a long period. de Chentinne was hidden in Charleroi by his brother and finally given an amnesty, dying a natural death in Jauche on 6 November 1811.

=== Peasants' War and death ===
From then on Charles lived a more clandestine life and changed tactics, terrorising and disarming French soldiers and stealing from the municipal coffers. On 18 April 1797 Austria and French agreed a treaty and Charles stopped his acts of resistance, failing to take an active part in the Peasants' War.

He took up arms again on 19 July 1799 and near Blanden captured Van Billioen, an old municipal agent in the village who had previously helped the brigands but had then been arrested for that supported. Charles avenged himself on him and on 23 July captured and for the same reason executed the former brigand Guilliam Bartholomeus, who had betrayed Charles and his troops and frequently given away their hiding places.

LVCRFT (pronounced "Lovecraft") is an American Halloween music group formed in Los Angeles in 2019 by songwriter Evan Bogart, songwriter and producer Amanda "MNDR" Warner, and producer Peter Wade. The group has released an album of Halloween-themed songs each year since its debut, This Is Halloween Vol. 1 (2019), and had written more than 100 Halloween songs by 2024. Its song "Skeleton Sam" was featured in the Disney+ film Hocus Pocus 2 (2022).

==History==
===Formation and early albums (2019–2021)===
LVCRFT was founded by Bogart, Warner and Wade, pop songwriters and producers whose credits include songs for Beyoncé, Rihanna, Charli XCX, Mark Ronson and Kylie Minogue. Members perform under pseudonyms, including "Lil Punkin" (Bogart), "DeepKutz" (Warner) and "Norman Crates" (Wade). Warner told Nylon that the group began in reaction to the same small set of classic Halloween songs being played every October.

The group's debut album, This Is Halloween Vol. 1, was released in 2019. Its second album, The Sequel (2020), contained 15 original songs and featured guest vocalists including Uffie, Bonnie McKee and Sarah Hudson, each credited under a horror-themed alias. Its lead single, a version of "Spooky Scary Skeletons", was used as the theme for Freeform's 31 Nights of Halloween programming block. The group's third album, The Return, followed in 2021, led by the single "Every Night". The song's music video, the group's first, was filmed inside a Spirit Halloween store.

===Hocus Pocus 2 and Scream Warriors (2022)===
"Skeleton Sam", sung by Sarah Barrios, is the first song heard in the present-day portion of Hocus Pocus 2 (2022). According to Luminate data reported by The New York Times, the song's U.S. streams nearly doubled between October 2022 and October 2023, and it had reached 14.3 million U.S. streams by October 2024. Later in 2022 the group released Scream Warriors, a 15-track album made in collaboration with film composer Christopher Young. Nylon described the album as darker and more immersive than the group's earlier work.

===V and Under the Covers (2023–2024)===
The group's fifth album, V, was released in 2023 and followed a "found audio" storyline about the character Skeleton Sam. In 2024 LVCRFT released Under the Covers, an album of Halloween-themed cover versions, preceded by the single "Halloween Hop" featuring actor David Dastmalchian.

===Skeleton Sam's Deadtime Stories (2026)===
The group's eighth album, Skeleton Sam's Deadtime Stories, was released on October 1, 2026, on the group's Spooky Never Sleeps label. Structured as a late-night horror broadcast with skits and fictional film trailers, it is hosted by Roger L. Jackson and features Robert Englund, Heather Langenkamp, Mick Garris, Robert Rodriguez, Bruce Campbell, Ernie Hudson, John Kassir, Jasmin Savoy Brown, Katharine Isabelle and Alyssa Sutherland, among others. A music video for "My Boo", featuring Brown, was released alongside the album. The group said an anthology series based on the album is in development.

==Other work==
LVCRFT's music has been used in Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, Hubie Halloween, Flack and Chucky. On October 31, 2023, Charity Lawson and Artem Chigvintsev performed a jive to "Skeleton Sam" on the "Monster Night" episode of Dancing with the Stars. The group scores mazes and live entertainment for the Queen Mary's Dark Harbor, and writes music for the LA Haunted Hayride. The group also creates ambient loops and custom scores for haunted attractions under the name Nightmare Soundworks.
The members also formed Spooky Never Sleeps, a company that serves as the group's record label and produces scores and immersive experiences; Bogart told The New York Times that the group hoped it would become a musical counterpart to the horror studio Blumhouse.

Doin' Damage is the debut LP by American hip-hop group JVC Force, released in 1988 through B-Boy Records. The album includes the song "Strong Island", one of the group's best-known recordings. The group consisted of MC's AJ Rok and B-Luv and DJ Curt Cazal. [ref: J.V.C. Force:: Doin' Damage, RapReviews]

== Reception ==

=== Contemporary ===

In its September 24, 1988 issue, Cash Box reviewed Doin' Damage in its "independant way" column. The review characterized JVC Force's approach as informal and humorous, highlighting the variety of vocal styles on the album. It also praised the range of its samples and beats, and described B-Boy Records as a promising independent label in the contemporary rap scene. [ref: The Independent Way, Cash Box]

=== Retrospective ===

In a 2008 review for RapReviews, Steve "Flash" Juon gave the album a score of 7.5 out of 10. He praised the chemistry between the group's members and the album's sampling and production, while noting that some of its rhymes could sound simplistic to modern listeners. Juon also discussed the later reissue of the album by Traffic Entertainment Group in 2005.

Carlos Jurado

Carlos Jurado is an American immigration attorney and the founder of The Jurado Firm. His practice focuses on family-based immigration, asylum, deportation defense, immigration waivers, and employment-related immigration matters. [ref: Meet Our Immigration Attorneys in Long Beach, The Jurado Firm]

Early life

Jurado was born in Los Angeles, California, to Mexican immigrant parents. His mother worked in a factory, and his father was a mariachi musician. He grew up in South Central Los Angeles, Long Beach, and Compton.

Jurado has described his family’s experiences with immigration and the passage of California’s Proposition 187 during his childhood as influences on his decision to pursue a legal career. He recalled the fear and uncertainty the measure created among his family and neighbors.

Education

Jurado earned an undergraduate degree in rhetoric from the University of California, Berkeley. He subsequently worked as a staff member in the United States House of Representatives in Washington, D.C.

He earned his law degree from the University of California, Hastings College of the Law. During his legal studies, he participated in community legal clinics serving small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and immigrant families.

Jurado also participated in a training program at Yale Law School’s Center for Community and Economic Development, where he provided legal assistance to mission-driven organizations.

Legal career

Jurado founded The Jurado Firm, an immigration law practice serving individuals, families, and employers. He is licensed to practice law in Michigan. [ref: Carlos Jurado, State Bar of Michigan Attorney Directory]

His practice includes family petitions, immigration waivers, asylum applications, deportation defense, and employment visas. He also represents artists, musicians, and athletes in immigration matters.

Selected cases

Carlitos Ricardo Parias

Jurado represented Carlitos Ricardo Parias, a Los Angeles citizen journalist known online as “Richard LA” and “Richard Noticias LA.” Parias was shot and wounded by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer during an attempted arrest on October 21, 2025. The U.S. Press Freedom Tracker identified Jurado as Parias’s attorney and reported his statements concerning the government’s treatment of his client. [ref: Journalist shot by federal agents in LA, taken into ICE custody]

José Mejía Hernández

Jurado also represented José Mejía Hernández, a Mexican immigrant who alleged that ICE officers seriously injured him during an encounter in Arlington, Virginia, on August 11, 2026. Working alongside civil rights attorney Denisse Gastélum, Jurado sought a criminal investigation into the incident. On August 28, Hernández appeared at Arlington County Police headquarters to report the alleged assault. His attorneys requested an investigation and preservation of evidence. The Department of Homeland Security disputed key elements of their account. [ref: Mexicano que acusa a ICE de una golpiza brutal presenta denuncia policial y pide investigación en Virginia] [ref: Mejía Hernandez Files Police Report, Seeks Criminal Investigation of ICE Officers]

The Spartanburg Youth Theatre is a community theatre founded in 1972 by Mary Nicholson. It operates on a “for youth, by youth,” principle. [ref: ]

Its productions are almost entirely produced by children. Children in the 3rd-12th grades can audition to be cast, and 7th-12th graders can apply to work as crew. It received the South Carolina Theatre of Distinction recognition in 2023 [ref: Previous Recipients, South Carolina Theatre Association].

== History ==
Founded in 1972, SYT originally performed in the Camp Croft Playhouse [ref: David W. Reid, Spartanburg Herald Journal] (later named the David W. Reid Playhouse) with its sister company, Spartanburg Little Theatre. Both companies moved to the Chapman Cultural Center in 2007.

The Youth Theatre is an extension of the Spartanburg Little Theatre, which was founded in 1964 [ref: ]. Their productions and offices reside entirely in the Chapman Cultural Center theatre building.

== Community Impact ==
SYT is highly involved in the local Spartanburg community, primarily in their outreach programs with local Title I schools. SYT board and educational members perform shows in Title I schools so as to curate an accessible introduction into the performing arts at a young age. They have performed True Story of the 3 Little Pigs, The Rainbow Fish, and more in these performances.

The theatre also provides school-time performances, in which local classes are able to come watch a show in the morning as an arts field trip [ref: ]. They average seven school time performances per Youth production.

Jacques Cory (Hebrew: יעקב קורי; born 1944) is an Israeli businessman, author, and lecturer on business ethics and corporate social responsibility. His publications address corporate governance and the protection of minority shareholders. He also helped initiate and edit a Ladino translation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. [ref: משוגעים, תרדו, Globes] [ref: Jacques Cory, Magnes Press] [ref: Deklarasion Universal de Derechos Umanos, El Amaneser]

== Early life and education ==

Cory was born in Cairo, Egypt, in 1944 and moved to Israel as a child. He studied economics and political science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and earned an MBA at INSEAD in France. [ref: About Jacques Cory, Business Ethics Cory]

In 2004, he completed a doctorate in management sciences at the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers (CNAM) in Paris, supervised by Yvon Pesqueux. His thesis, L’éthique des affaires et les actionnaires minoritaires, examined business ethics and the protection of minority shareholders. It was based on his two books published by Kluwer Academic Publishers in 2001. [ref: L’éthique des affaires et les actionnaires minoritaires, Theses.fr]

== Business and academic career ==

Cory worked at Elbit for fourteen years and held senior positions in the high technology industry. From 1987, he worked independently in international mergers and acquisitions.

He lectured at the University of Haifa on business ethics, corporate social responsibility, sustainability, globalization, and business administration. A contributor biography published in Sephardic Horizons also records teaching at INSEAD in 2006, the Technion in 2009–2010, and Tel Aviv University in 2010–2011. A 2013 notice from the University of Haifa’s junior academic staff organization identifies him as a teaching fellow. [ref: Komo deskuvri la sinagoga de Coria, Sephardic Horizons] [ref: University of Haifa junior academic staff newsletter, University of Haifa junior academic staff organization]

== Research and writing ==

In Business Ethics: The Ethical Revolution of Minority Shareholders, Cory examines the limitations of conventional safeguards for minority investors, including regulation, corporate boards, auditors, and financial intermediaries. He argues for greater transparency, investor associations, and ethical investment funds as additional means of protecting shareholders. The book includes case studies involving companies in France, Israel, and the United States. [ref: Business Ethics: The Ethical Revolution of Minority Shareholders, Springer Nature]

Reviewing Business Ethics in Transparency International Germany’s newsletter, Irene Wiegand praised its detailed case evidence and use of literature, while questioning its novelty and its analysis of ethical investment funds. [ref: Jacques Cory: Business Ethics. The Ethical Revolution of Minority Shareholders, Rundbrief]

His second book, Activist Business Ethics, develops an approach based on cooperation among businesspeople, academics, stakeholders, and minority shareholders to address unethical corporate conduct. [ref: Activist Business Ethics, Springer Nature]

His Hebrew book Selected Issues in Business Ethics and Social Responsibility was published by Magnes Press in 2008. It combines theoretical discussion and business cases with analyses of literary works, plays, and films. Its subjects include whistleblowing, corporate governance, corruption, environmental responsibility, and ethical questions in Israeli business. [ref: סוגיות נבחרות באתיקה עסקית ובאחריות חברתית, Magnes Press]

In a 2008 Globes discussion of business education, Cory advocated including integrity assessments in admissions to MBA programs. He proposed using simulations, case discussions, and role playing to examine applicants’ responses to conflicts between ethics and profitability. [ref: תסננו אותם, Globes]

In 2012, Cory and Eran Vigoda-Gadot contributed a chapter on the public responsibility of government and public administration to Public Responsibility in Israel, edited by Raphael Cohen-Almagor, Ori Arbel-Ganz, and Asa Kasher. [ref: Public Responsibility in Israel, Kotar]

== Literature and Ladino ==

Cory’s literary works include the play Nelly’s Choice, written with Amalia Eyal, and the Hebrew novel הישמרו מדורון יווני [Beware of Greeks’ Presents], published by Bimat Kedem in 2001. The novel concerns a businessman navigating a corrupt business environment. Cory has also published an essay in Ladino in Sephardic Horizons. [ref: הישמרו מדורון יווני, Bimat Kedem]

In 2011, Cory initiated a Ladinokomunita project to translate the Universal Declaration of Human Rights into Ladino. According to project participant Rachel Amado Bortnick, he and Bortnick co-edited the contributors’ translations, and Cory liaised with United Nations officials about submission. Her account was published in El Amaneser and on eSefarad. A Ladino translation is listed in the United Nations Regional Information Centre’s guide to translations of the Declaration. [ref: Deklarasion Universal de Derechos Umanos – en ladino, eSefarad] [ref: The Declaration in your language, United Nations Regional Information Centre]

== Recognition and personal life ==

Operations & Intelligence / O&I (Operatiën & Inlichtingen) was a Dutch stay-behind organization that originated in 1946/1947 from the resistance against the German occupation during World War II and was disbanded by Prime Minister Lubbers in 1992. [ref: Dr. D. Engelen, De Nederlandse stay behind-organisatie in de koude oorlog 1945-1992 Ministerie van Algemene Zaken, Ministerie van Defensie & Rijksarchiefdienst/PIVOT The Netherlands, National Archives, Institutional Investigation (Dutch). The Hague, 2005. ISBN 90-5909-0489.] [ref: https://www.rudi-harthoorn.nl/operatien-inlichtingen/] In fact, there were two separate organizations, namely Operations and Intelligence, which were eventually coordinated by a single person but each had its own task. [ref: https://www.defensiebond.nl/binnenland/erkenning-voor-ex-leden-stay-behind-organisatie/] Until approximately the mid-1980s, they were referred to simply as O and I; since then, service A and service B. In the media, O&I was often compared to the Italian Operation Gladio, although the Dutch network differed from it in important respects. [ref: Onderzoek naar Stay Behind-organisatie Ministerie van Defensie, NIMH, 2 February 2024.]

Operations & Intelligence was tasked with keeping the population as resilient as possible against communist propaganda and passing on information regarding political developments to the 'government in exile'. Furthermore, the organization was to attempt to disrupt and mislead the occupier's apparatus of authority wherever possible. Armed resistance was not the primary objective, but as the Soviets approached, members of the organization were to receive sufficient weapons from hidden depots to avoid being slaughtered defenseless. One such underground weapons depot, consisting of 19 crates, was discovered by chance in 1983 in the woods near Rozendaal. Three years earlier, in 1980, a similar weapons find had already been made in Haelen.

==History==

[[Image:LouisEinthoven.jpg|thumb|150px|Louis Einthoven]]
Operations & Intelligence originated from the Dutch resistance against the German occupier during the Second World War and was intended as a continuation of the work of the Intelligence Bureau (BI) and the Special Assignments Bureau (BBO). At the initiative of the head of the BI, Jan Somer, Section IIIC of the General Staff was established on May 13, 1946, of which he himself became the first head. Alongside the already existing Sections IIIA and IIIB of the General Staff, GS IIIC was responsible for setting up a stay-behind organization and gathering military intelligence in and about foreign countries.

GS IIIC consisted of Section I (Operations) and Section II (Preparation), with the head of Section I also becoming the head of the military section of the Foreign Intelligence Service (BID), established in February 1946, since formally only the BID was authorized to gather intelligence via foreign agents. In 1948, Section IIIC was renamed Section G7, and as of July 1, 1949, Section General Affairs (SAZ). This became the Intelligence branch (I, later B) of what had come to be called Operations & Intelligence since the early 1950s.

Former BBO agent Henk Veeneklaas, alias David van Eyck, also considered it advisable not to let the knowledge and experience gained during the war regarding operations in hostile/occupied territory be lost. As Commander of the Netherlands Armed Forces, Prince Bernhard referred him in the summer of 1945 to Louis Einthoven, who was then in the process of setting up the National Security Bureau (BNV).

Together with British officers of the Special Operations Executive (SOE), preparations were subsequently made for a stay-behind organization aimed at sabotage actions in case the Netherlands were occupied again. Funding for this was initially channeled through Einthoven's security service, which knew about Somer's General Command IIIC from the outset, whereas Somer only discovered the existence of the new organization led by Einthoven in the course of 1949. The latter became the Operations (O, later A) branch of Operations & Intelligence.

==Organization & structure==
For security reasons, both branches of O&I were heavily compartmentalized, and employees did not know each other's real names, partly as a result of the lessons learned from the Englandspiel. Coordination at the top was eventually established, but there was no close cooperation between the two organizations, let alone integration.

Since 1949, both branches of O&I were funded from the resources of the General Staff of the Department of War, later the Department of Defense, while until 1964 there was also a financial contribution from the CIA, which used the code name SYRUP-SYNTHOSIS for O&I.

The military and civilian personnel of the I-branch were formally employed by the Ministry of Defence, whereas (current or former military) employees of the O-branch were paid by Defence but were not employed by it. Because it was expected that the occupying forces would intern the intelligentsia, they recruited only people who did not hold a title or leadership position.

The implementing organization was formally housed within the General Staff of the Armed Forces and made use of the accommodation (Villa Maarheeze in Wassenaar) of the Foreign Intelligence Service (IDB).

Jackpot.com is an American lottery courier based in San Francisco. It has a website and app for ordering tickets for lottery draw games such as Powerball and Mega Millions, along with scratch cards, in seven US states as of January 2026. [ref: Jackpot.com secures $10m financing to fuel expansion, NEXT.io]

== History ==
In 2017, the Malta Gaming Authority approved the addition of a lottery messenger proposition to Jackpot.com's license. [ref: Jackpot.com secures secondary Maltese lottery licence, iGB] The company later began operating as a lottery courier in the United States. Its co-founders include chief executive Akshay Khanna, Roi More, and Yariv Ron. [ref: With New Jersey ties, Jackpot.com continues its rapid growth, NJBIZ]

In January 2023, Jackpot.com launched in Texas. [ref: The Couriers’ Race – La Fleur's Lottery World, lafleurs.com] Following its initial Series A funding round of $35 million in June 2022, [ref: Jackpot raises $35m to fund US expansion, Gaming Intelligence] [ref: Arctos, Kraft, Rubin Among Heavy Hitters in $35M Jackpot Raise, Yahoo Finance] the company secured an additional $7 million, [ref: Jackpot.com receives $42m investment to expand to Texas - SBC Americas] bringing total funding to $42 million. Investors included Bettor Capital, Aurum Partners, Detroit Venture Partners, the Tisch family, and the Dallas Cowboys and New York Yankees.

In 2023, Jackpot.com expanded its courier operations. It launched in Ohio in May [ref: Lottery site Jackpot.com launches in Ohio with help from Cleveland's three pro sports teams, Crains Cleveland] New York in August. [ref: Jackpot brings its lottery app, online ticket sales to NY, PIX11 News] In 2024 it continued its expansion, becoming available in Massachusetts in January, [ref: Jackpot.com enters fourth US market with Massachusetts launch - EGR North America] Arkansas in March, [ref: ] New Jersey in May, [ref: Lottery courier Jackpot.com launches in NJ, NJBIZ] and Colorado in November. [ref: Jackpot.com Launches in Colorado, Expanding To Seventh State] On January 7, 2025, Jackpot.com launched in Arizona, its eighth state. [ref: Arizona Now Eighth Market for Lottery Courier Jackpot.com]

In February 2025, the Texas Lottery Commission announced that it would prohibit lottery courier services. By early April 2025, Jackpot.com had suspended its operations in the state. [ref: How couriers changed the playing field of the Texas Lottery, The Texas Tribune] In June 2025, Texas enacted Senate Bill 3070, which made it a criminal offense to sale lottery tickets online or through apps, effectively banning courier services, and abolished the Texas Lottery Commission. [ref: Texas Lottery Commission to be disbanded as state game gets new restrictions, The Texas Tribune]

In January 2026, the company secured a $10 million revolving credit facility from Discerning Capital’s House Advantage Fund and PvX Capital.

In March 2026, the company introduced a loyalty program, Jackpot Rewards. [ref: Loyalty 360 - Jackpot.com Launches Loyalty Program to Reward Lottery Players]

== Operations ==

=== Courier service ===
Customers order lottery tickets through the Jackpot.com website or app. The company subsequently buys a physical ticket from a licensed retailers on the customer's behalf and uploads a scan of it to their account.

Winnings under $600 are credited directly to the customer's account. For larger prizes, the ticket is delivered to the player to claim from the state lottery.

== Partnerships and collaborations ==
In November 2024, 7-Eleven named Jackpot.com as its official lottery partner at more than 600 stores in Ohio and Massachusetts [ref: Jackpot.com named lottery partner of 7-Eleven, Gaming Intelligence].

In June 2024, the Associated Press (AP) named Jackpot.com as its official provider of lottery results. [ref: Associated Press Assigns Lottery Reporting, Ticket Sales To Jackpot.com, www.mediapost.com] [ref: The Associated Press taps Jackpot.com as official lottery partner - EGR North America]

Detlef Kleinert (26 July 1932 – 17 June 2016) was a German lawyer and politician of the Free Democratic Party (FDP). He was a member of the Bundestag from 20 October 1969 to 26 October 1998, representing Lower Saxony via the FDP state list, and worked on legal policy. From 1967 to 1996 he chaired the FDP district association for the city of Hanover.

== Early life and education ==

Kleinert was born in Essen and grew up in Schöningen, near the inner German border, and in Hanover. His father, a trained merchant, was a senior official of the Reichsbank and last headed its branch in Schöningen. He passed his Abitur in Schöningen in 1951 and studied law at the universities of Erlangen and Munich. He took the first state law examination in 1955 and the second in 1960. In Munich he joined a student corps. In 1952 he became a member of the Liberal Student Federation of Germany (Liberaler Studentenbund Deutschlands, LSD).

== Legal and business career ==

Kleinert began practising as a lawyer in Hanover in 1960 and later worked as a notary. During his time in parliament he was a board member of Wert-Garantie Technische Versicherung AG, an insurance company in Hanover. He was honorary chairman of the Vereinigung Liberaler Juristen (Association of Liberal Lawyers).

Kurt Jodexnis, a Hanover insurance businessman and a long-standing business associate of Kleinert, held a 20 per cent share in the casino company of Bad Bentheim and Bad Zwischenahn, which received its licence in 1975 from the FDP state interior minister Rötger Groß. In 1982 Jodexnis transferred half of this share to Kleinert. In August 1988 Kleinert testified about the stake before the Landtag of Lower Saxony's casino inquiry committee. He stated that he had received the share, with a nominal value of 300,000 Deutsche Mark, free of charge as compensation for a business deal with Jodexnis twelve years earlier. He also stated that he had only advised Jodexnis on the selection of the other partners, had never discussed the licence with Groß and had not donated any casino income to the party. Jodexnis largely confirmed his account.

== Political career ==

=== Party offices ===

Kleinert joined the FDP in 1957. From 1967 to 1996 he was chairman of the party's district association for the city of Hanover. In 1970 he became treasurer of the Lower Saxony FDP, a post he still held in 1988; during this time he consolidated the state party's finances. He took part in the FDP's 1974 coalition negotiations with the Social Democrats in Lower Saxony, whose delegation was led by Alfred Kubel. In November 1976 he was elected to the party's federal executive.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

Kleinert was elected to the Bundestag in the 1969 federal election on the FDP's state list for Lower Saxony and was re-elected at each subsequent election until 1994. He sat from 20 October 1969 to 26 October 1998, from the 6th to the 13th legislative term.

From the end of 1969 he chaired the FDP parliamentary group's Working Group IV, which covered home affairs and law and, at times, education and the environment. His work there included data protection, bureaucracy and the volume of legislation. In his last term he was a full member of the Legal Affairs Committee, the Judicial Selection Committee and the committee that elects judges of the Federal Constitutional Court, and a deputy member of the Committee on Internal Affairs. He supported the repeal of Paragraph 175, the criminal provision against homosexual acts between men, and took part in drafting the reform of divorce law.

In July 1979 the Bundestag debated the abolition of the statute of limitations for murder, prompted by the approaching expiry of the limitation period for Nazi-era murders. Kleinert spoke for the majority of the FDP parliamentary group in favour of retaining the existing law. He argued that criminal justice should be kept separate from the country's responsibility for its history, that few unidentified perpetrators remained, and that the Majdanek trial had shown that fair trials were no longer possible after so long a period.

In May 1989, in a Bundestag debate on the conviction of the Memmingen gynaecologist Horst Theissen for illegal abortions, Kleinert criticised the conduct of the trial and described the women concerned as more victims than offenders.

On 23 November 1994, in the debate on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government statement, Kleinert gave a short speech on legal and home-affairs policy while under the influence of alcohol. He spoke on whether electronic surveillance of private homes should be permitted, a question on which the FDP had not yet reached a decision, and his remarks drew repeated laughter from the opposition benches.

During the dispute over the German orthography reform of 1996, Kleinert, Norbert Geis and other members tabled a motion on German spelling, which the Bundestag debated on 18 April 1997.

Francesco Corvino is a British-Italian storyworld director and architect. He specializes in narrative worldbuilding, creative direction and IP development across film, television, videogames and experiential entertainment, for international clients.. [ref: About, Francesco Corvino / Eicon Design]

Corvino holds a Master of Architecture (M.Arch) and specializes in storyworld direction, a multidisciplinary design approach that integrates narrative, character design, setting, history, visual style, and internal rules to build cross-media franchises and intellectual properties.

Developing this workflow while freelancing across film and video game productions, Corvino structured the approach to address cross-departmental coordination challenges, production delays, and budget overruns. The primary objective of storyworld direction is to align creative decisions across departments to maintain narrative consistency and production efficiency.

=== Films ===

Corvino contributed to the storyworlds of films such as Edge of Tomorrow (2014), Maleficent (2014), Birdman (2014), The Martian (2015), Thor: Ragnarok (2017), and Blade Runner 2049 (2017). [ref: Francesco Corvino, IMDb] He helped shaping the world of Steven Spielberg's Ready Player One (2018), supporting the art department led by production designer Adam Stockhausen, which won the Art Directors Guild Award for Excellence in Production Design for a Fantasy Film. His film credits also span several of Disney's live-action reimaginings—including Cinderella, Beauty and the Beast, Dumbo, and Pinocchio, alongside Mary Poppins Returns—as well as major franchise tentpoles such as Lucasfilm's The Mandalorian and The Amazing Spider-Man 2.

Throughout his career, Corvino has collaborated directly with many filmmakers and production designers. He closely worked with production designer Gemma Jackson on major productions, including the biographical war drama Lee (2023), as well as the HBO Victorian science-fiction series The Nevers (2021), and the Netflix historical drama Death by Lightning. In television, Corvino's work includes select contributions to high-profile historical dramas and fantasy series. His other notable television work includes contributing digital matte painting to the fourth season of HBO's Game of Thrones (2014) through Rodeo FX, whose visual effects team won a Primetime Emmy Award [ref: Game Of Thrones – Awards & Nominations, Academy of Television Arts & Sciences]
, and serving as a concept designer for the second season of Netflix's Wednesday (2025).

=== Video games ===
In interactive media, Corvino contributed narrative and storyworld development to the Meta Quest gaming showcase 2023.

As of 2024, he works with Absurd Ventures, the multimedia company founded by Rockstar Games co-founder Dan Houser, and he's involved in the storyworld development of the studio's upcoming open-world video game project.

Outside of screen media, leveraging his architectural background, Corvino has designed environments for location-based entertainment and experiential installations. His projects include storyworld development for Pearl Quest, an immersive dark ride developed for China's Wanda Group in Qingdao, the Sphere in Las Vegas and the design of the visitor destination experience at the renovated Santiago Bernabéu Stadium in Madrid, in collaboration with Balich Wonder Studio. Corvino was also involved in the design of Netflix House, Netflix's permanent experiential entertainment and retail venues.

The **Social and Media Studies Institute** (French: Institut d'Études Sociales et Médiatiques; Arabic: معهد الدراسات الاجتماعية والإعلامية, acronym: SMS Institute) is an independent, non-profit think tank and research center headquartered in Casablanca, Kingdom of Morocco. Founded in mid-2019 by a collective of Moroccan researchers and academics specializing in economic, legal, political, and social sciences.

The institute produces field analyses and scientific public opinion polls on social, economic, and political transformations in Morocco, the Maghreb region, and Africa, as well as evaluations of public policies and the development of field observation tools.

== Creation and Objectives ==
The institute was founded with the aim of bridging theoretical academic research with public policy evaluation and providing empirical data for decision-makers and civil society actors. Its core statutory objectives include:
* Conducting quantitative and qualitative field studies on societal and media dynamics.
* Organizing public opinion polls on current political, economic, and social issues.
* Publishing peer-reviewed scientific journals and academic works via its publishing house, "African Academic Press". [ref: يوسف الحفيرة يقارب "الهوية السياسية", Hespress]
* Developing strategic notes and recommendations aimed at improving legislation and public policies. [ref: معهد الدراسات الاجتماعية يصدر مذكرة استراتيجية جديدة: نحو نموذج سياسي مغربي يقود التنمية, Journal 24]
* Promoting the values of transparency, combating discrimination, and anchoring ethics in media and scientific research.

== Structure and Governance ==
The governance of the institute relies on an executive management team and a scientific council composed of doctors and university professors affiliated with various Moroccan and international universities (including Mohammed V University in Rabat, Hassan II University in Casablanca, Cadi Ayyad University in Marrakech, Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University in Fes, Chouaib Doukkali University in El Jadida, Ibn Zohr University in Agadir, Mohammed I University in Oujda, as well as associate researchers from the University of Douala in Cameroon and Abderrahmane Mira University in Béjaïa, Algeria).

* Scientific Presidency: The institute is chaired by Dr. Younes Bennane, an economist and researcher specializing in public policies and geopolitics. [ref: Global South researchers to offer solutions to key world problems at ‘Future of the World’ Open Dialogue]
* Executive Management: Executive leadership and the development of international partnerships are overseen by Canadian researcher Dr. Brahim Meddeb. [ref: تنصيب الكندي براهيم مداب على رأس الادارة التنفيذية لمعهد الدراسات الاجتماعية و الإعلامية بالمغرب, Press Medias]

== Research Axes and Strategic Observatories ==

=== Political Sociology and Electoral Observation ===
The institute established the Interactive Legislative Election Results Observatory to monitor shifts in the electoral map, voting behavior in Morocco, and parliamentary performance [ref: المرصد التفاعلي للنتائج البرلمانية, BENNANE], while also formulating strategic memorandums containing proposals to reform the electoral system. [ref: معهد مغربي ينادي بإنشاء مجلس وطني مستقل للإشراف على الانتخابات, Hespress]

=== Public Policy and Institutional Evaluation ===
In its studies, the institute addresses the efficiency of national and constitutional institutions. It published an analytical report on the decisions of the Competition Council between 2020 and 2021 to assess its role in market regulation and the implementation of the New Development Model. [ref: دراسة: مجلس المنافسة لم يقبل أيّا من الإحالات المعروضة عليه باستثناء طلب رأي من وزير المالية, Lakome2] [ref: ] On the legislative front, the institute published a study addressing obstacles hindering parliamentary oversight of state budget execution within the framework of the organic law on finance laws. [ref: ] The institute has also conducted a study on the evolution of civil society functions in Morocco and its relationship with the state since independence.

=== Economic Foresight and Energy Security ===
The institute develops strategic dashboards, including a report dedicated to energy security [ref: ], shipping flows in Moroccan ports, and economic impact scenarios of closing the Strait of Hormuz. [ref: Google Scholar, scholar.google.com] In the summer of 2026, the institute published a critical study of the High Commission for Planning's (HCP) methodology regarding the labor market, demonstrating that the statistical decline in the unemployment rate does not necessarily reflect a reduction in social pressures and real precarity. [ref: ]

=== Social and Educational Issues ===
The institute has conducted several field opinion polls covering citizen trust in political parties (2021), Moroccan youth trust in the future and migration issues (2023), as well as a survey revealing that 80% of surveyed PhD holders doubt the transparency of selection criteria for assistant professor-researchers in Moroccan universities (2023).

= Benjamin Riley =

Benjamin Riley is an American education writer, policy advocate and former government lawyer. He is the founder of Cognitive Resonance, a self-described "think-and-do tank" that examines generative artificial intelligence through the lens of cognitive science.[1][3] Before that, he founded and for nearly a decade led Deans for Impact, a nonprofit that works to bring findings from the science of learning into teacher preparation programs.[1][6]

Riley is one of the more widely cited skeptics of AI in schools. He argues that large language models imitate the communicative side of human language without doing the thinking that language usually reports, and that heavy student reliance on chatbots can erode the mental effort learning depends on.[11][13] His writing on cognitive science, AI and education has appeared in outlets including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, The Washington Post, Le Monde, The Guardian, Education Week, Education Next, The 74 and NPR.[1]

Contents
# Education and legal career
# Education policy work
# Deans for Impact
# Cognitive Resonance
## Education Hazards of Generative AI
## Language and intelligence
## "Cognitive hot dog"
# Views
# Reception and criticism
# Selected works
# Media appearances
# References

== Education and legal career ==
Riley earned a bachelor's degree from the University of Washington and a Juris Doctor from Yale Law School.[1] His early career included about four years in private legal practice, a short period on Wall Street, and a summer clerkship with the Land Claims Court of South Africa.[5]

He later served as a deputy attorney general in the California Department of Justice. In that post he advised then–Attorney General Jerry Brown on California's first Race to the Top application and related education policy, helped draft legislation connected to the program, and represented the California State Board of Education, including a stint as the board's interim chief counsel. A Northern California legal publication named him one of two "Rising Stars" in education law in 2009.[5]

== Education policy work ==
After leaving state government, Riley became director of policy and advocacy at NewSchools Venture Fund, where he worked from Washington, D.C., on a policy agenda aimed at supporting education entrepreneurs.[5] He also carried out research on the New Zealand education system.[4]

== Deans for Impact ==
Riley founded Deans for Impact in 2015 and served as its executive director. Based in Austin, Texas, the organization brought together leaders of U.S. educator-preparation programs who wanted teacher training to draw more directly on research-backed principles of how students learn.[7][6]

The group's best-known early publication, The Science of Learning (2015), condensed findings from cognitive psychology into six questions every new teacher should be able to answer, each paired with classroom implications. It was produced by the organization's member deans with University of Virginia cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham and former middle-school science teacher Paul Bruno.[8] At its public launch, Riley urged educators to reconsider teaching one concept to mastery before moving on, and pointed to research-dissemination bodies in the United Kingdom as a model.[9] British education writer David Didau praised the document as clearer than comparable summaries.[10]

In April 2022, Deans for Impact announced that Riley would step down later that year, ending almost ten years with the organization. Board chair David Chard credited him with bold and creative leadership.[6]

== Cognitive Resonance ==
Riley has said his move into AI grew out of his own interest in deep learning in the years before ChatGPT, and from the view that AI belongs alongside psychology, neuroscience, linguistics and philosophy as one of the cognitive sciences.[12] He founded Cognitive Resonance to help people understand both human cognition and generative AI, and to replace hype with a clearer picture of how the systems work.[3][16] The venture publishes the Substack newsletter Build Cognitive Resonance, which had passed 3,000 subscribers, and runs a YouTube channel.[2][15]

=== Education Hazards of Generative AI ===
The organization's first publication, Education Hazards of Generative AI, was released on 7 August 2024 and co-written with Paul Bruno of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.[11][14] Aimed at teachers, administrators, parents and policymakers, it gives a plain-language overview of how large language models work and draws out practical consequences for classrooms. The report does not reject classroom AI outright but warns that the hype around it obscures real risks.[14] Riley told Education Week that schools need not adopt the technology simply because it exists.[11]

=== Language and intelligence ===
In late November 2025, The Verge published Riley's essay arguing that the AI boom rests on a basic error: treating fluency in language as if it were intelligence.[17] Drawing on a 2024 Nature paper by Evelina Fedorenko and colleagues, which concluded that language is primarily a tool for communication rather than thought, he argued that human reasoning depends largely on brain systems separate from language. On that view, scaling up language models would yield ever better text generation but not general intelligence or new scientific discoveries.[16][17] The piece drew wide international coverage.
[truncated]

Joyce Elane Westfall (1927 – June 2016), known professionally during her film career as Joyce Jarvis and later in academia as Professor Joyce Ramsay, was an American film actress, union representative, and associate professor of theatre at Michigan State University.

== Early life and education ==
Born Joyce Elane Westfall, she was raised in Michigan, the daughter of Roy A. and Mary Westfall. She attended Mackenzie High School in Detroit before enrolling at Michigan State University from 1949 to 1950. [ref: Joyce Jarvis - Biography, IMDb] In 1950, she married Arthur Murray Jarvis and relocated to California to pursue formal theatrical training at the Pasadena Playhouse College of Theatre Arts.

== Career ==
=== Hollywood and Film Career ===
Acting under her married name, Joyce Jarvis, she secured a screen test with Paramount Pictures and began working in commercial cinema and television. In February 1953, she appeared on a live broadcast of NBC's The Colgate Comedy Hour hosted by Eddie Cantor. [ref: The Colgate Comedy Hour (Season 3, Episode 22), IMDb]

Later that year, Jarvis co-starred as Valerie Creighton, a prominent rebellious student, in the Columbia Pictures exploitation melodrama Problem Girls (1953). [ref: Problem Girls (1953) Full Cast & Crew, IMDb] She followed this with a performance as Princess Arsinoe, the younger sister of Cleopatra, in the Technicolor historical epic Serpent of the Nile (1953), directed by William Castle. During her career in California, she also became actively involved with the Screen Actors Guild (SAG), serving in localized branch leadership and contract committee roles.

=== Academia and Later Career ===
Following her departure from the Hollywood studio system, she divorced and later remarried, adopting the surname Ramsay.

In the fall of 1979, she returned to Michigan State University's Department of Theatre as an Associate Professor and Artist-in-Residence under the name Joyce Ramsay. [ref: Feature: Spartans in Hollywood, MSU Spartan Story Hub] She spent more than two decades at the university teaching undergraduate and graduate courses in acting technique and physical improvisation. Her tenure overlapped with the final college years of future television star Jon-Erik Hexum, who studied in the Department of Theatre before graduating in May 1980.

In April 1980, Ramsay made her university mainstage directorial debut at the Fairchild Theatre with a production of Alan Ayckbourn's farce How the Other Half Loves, while concurrently appearing as a performer in the Michigan State University Performing Arts Company’s staging of Julius Caesar [ref: 'How Other Half Loves' opens tonight, The State News]. In addition to her studio instruction, she served on graduate Master of Fine Arts (MFA) thesis committees and introduced prominent guest creators for the MSU Celebrity Lecture Series, including playwright August Wilson. [ref: MSU Celebrity Lecture Series Archive: August Wilson, Michigan State University]

== Death and Legacy ==
Ramsay continued to teach at Michigan State University through the late 1990s and into the 2000s. She passed away in June 2016. Following her death, the Michigan State University Department of Theatre formally recognized her multi-decade impact as a "tremendous educator" who shaped generations of Spartan performers. [ref: MSU Department of Theatre Memorial Announcement, Facebook]

Draft: Warren Davis (video game designer)

Draft text:
Warren Davis is an American video game designer, programmer, actor and author. He designed and programmed the 1982 arcade game Q*bert at Gottlieb, working with artist Jeff Lee. He later worked on video digitizing tools used in arcade games including Mortal Kombat and NBA Jam. He has also worked as an actor, mainly in guest television roles, and in 2022 published a memoir about his career in the arcade industry.

== Early life and education ==
Davis attended high school in Brooklyn, New York, where he first learned to program in the 1970s. He earned a bachelor's degree in computer and systems engineering from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and a master's degree in electrical engineering from Ohio State University. He then worked at Bell Labs in Naperville, Illinois, leaving in 1981; afterwards he studied improvisational theatre in Chicago.

== Video game career ==
=== Gottlieb ===
Davis joined Gottlieb as a video game programmer at the start of 1982, after answering a newspaper job advertisement. Q*bert was his first game. It began as a programming exercise with bouncing balls, to which Davis added a player character, collision detection and the ability to jump off the pyramid. In Davis's account, the game's pyramid of cubes grew out of a cube-patterned screen Lee had drawn, and Davis wrote all of the game's code and made its design decisions; Lee designed the characters and is credited by Davis as a close collaborator, and David Thiel created the sound. Davis removed an early idea in which the main character shot at enemies, and rotated the joystick 45 degrees to match the game's diagonal movement, keeping the design despite objections from other staff.

Before release, Davis lowered the game's difficulty at management's request, which he later regretted. In 1983 he made a harder version, Faster, Harder, More Challenging Q*bert, which tested poorly and was not released; he later made its program available to the public. Davis declined Gottlieb's request to make a Q*bert sequel, and the follow-up, Q*bert's Qubes, was made by another programmer.

At Mylstar Electronics, as Gottlieb had been renamed, Davis was programmer and video editor on Us vs. Them (1984), a laserdisc video game combining live-action footage with game graphics. The finished game was smaller in scope than first planned, and laserdisc hardware proved too fragile for arcade use.

=== Williams, Midway and later work ===
At Williams Electronics Davis co-programmed Joust 2: Survival of the Fittest (1986) and began developing a system for bringing videotaped images into games, first used for NARC. At Williams he typically worked as part of larger teams rather than as lead designer. After leaving to develop the arcade game Exterminator for Premier Technology, he returned to Williams to work on Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991). His digitizing work was used in Williams/Bally/Midway games including Mortal Kombat and NBA Jam, and he also worked on Revolution X (1994). In the late 1990s he worked at Disney Interactive.

== Acting ==
Davis later turned to acting. His television guest roles include episodes of The Practice (1999), ER (2002), House (2005), Criminal Minds (2005) and The Middle (2015). He has also appeared as himself in documentaries about video games, including Video Games: The Movie (2014) and Insert Coin (2020), a film about Midway's arcade studio.

== Writing ==
Davis self-published a memoir, You Can't Call It @!#?@!, in 2019. Santa Monica Press then published it in 2022 as Creating Q*bert and Other Classic Video Arcade Games, with a foreword by Ed Boon and an afterword by John Newcomer. Publishers Weekly described the book as an entertaining debut that would fascinate gamers.

== Recognition ==
Davis was inducted into the International Video Game Hall of Fame as part of its class of 2017, in a ceremony in Ottumwa, Iowa, on October 6, 2018. In February 2019 he was one of twelve fans inducted into the White Castle restaurant chain's Cravers Hall of Fame, in its 18th annual class; his entry described eating the chain's burgers late at night while developing Q*bert.

Barak Bussel is an American venture capital investor and entrepreneur whose work focuses on emerging technologies, including quantum computing, semiconductors, and artificial intelligence. He is the managing partner of 7i Capital and chair of the strategic board of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Center for Quantum Science and Engineering. [ref: CQSE Strategic Board, UCLA Center for Quantum Science and Engineering]

== Education ==

Bussel received a Bachelor of Science in theoretical and mathematical physics from Harvey Mudd College. He subsequently earned a Master of Science in theoretical physics from UCLA in 1993 and a Master of Business Administration from the UCLA Anderson School of Management in 1995.

== Career ==

Bussel is the founder and managing partner of 7i Capital, a venture capital firm investing in early-stage technology companies in fields including quantum computing, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, semiconductors, robotics, energy, and space.

He has also served as a managing partner at Third Wave Ventures, a Los Angeles-based venture capital firm. From 2016 to 2019, Bussel was president of a photonics technology company in Third Wave Ventures' investment portfolio. Earlier in his career, he served on the board of Neven Vision, a machine-vision company subsequently acquired by Google.

== Academic and quantum technology activities ==

Bussel chairs the strategic board of UCLA's Center for Quantum Science and Engineering. He has participated in efforts to establish the UCLA Quantum Innovation Hub, an initiative associated with the university's Research Park and focused on quantum information science and technology.

In 2017, Bussel delivered an address at UCLA's Department of Physics and Astronomy commencement ceremony. [ref: UCLA College Magazine, Summer 2017, UCLA College]

In August 2026, Bussel appeared on The New Quantum Era podcast to discuss venture investment in quantum computing, fault-tolerant quantum technologies, and collaboration between universities and industry. [ref: Investing in the Quantum Frontier and the Road to Fault Tolerance with Barak Bussel, The New Quantum Era]

Trudy Tanzillo (born Trudy Ann Cauthen, 1946) is an American former beauty pageant titleholder and hereditary society officer. She was crowned Miss North Carolina USA in 1963 and represented North Carolina at Miss USA 1963. Since 2025 she has served as President General of the Descendants of American Prisoners of War (DAPOW), a national lineage society.

== Pageantry ==
Cauthen, of Newton, North Carolina, was crowned Miss North Carolina USA in 1963; contemporary newspaper coverage styled her "Miss N. C. Universe" and photographed her in a white ball gown waving from a flower-decked float. [ref: Contemporary newspaper photograph, 1963, captioned "MISS N. C. UNIVERSE, TRUDY CAUTHEN" (family collection).] She succeeded Brenda Smith of Charlotte in the title. As state titleholder she represented North Carolina at the Miss USA 1963 pageant, held in Miami Beach, Florida, on 17 July 1963. North Carolina sent no delegate to Miss USA in 1964; the next recorded state titleholder was Sandra Farmer of Greensboro in 1965.

== Education and career ==
Tanzillo earned a Bachelor of Arts in social sciences at Western Carolina University (1962–1966), where she was a member of Sigma Kappa and head cheerleader, and a Master of Arts in reading at Rider University (1979–1981), followed by certification in supervision and administration at Rutgers University (1984). [ref: Tanzillo, Trudy. Professional profile. LinkedIn.] Her career was in New Jersey public education: she taught in the Bordentown Township, East Windsor Regional, and Manalapan-Englishtown Regional school districts, served as assistant principal of West Windsor-Plainsboro High School South (1998–2002), and was an adjunct professor at Rider University (2002).

== Hereditary society leadership ==
Tanzillo has held office in several American hereditary and lineage societies. She was an officer of the Descendants of American Prisoners of War from its first administration, serving as Corresponding Secretary General (2021–2023), [ref: "Captive Thoughts" (DAPOW newsletter), Issue 2, 2022. Officer listing: "Corresponding Secretary General — Trudy Cauthen Tanzillo."] and in 2025 was elected the society's third President General, for the 2025–2027 term, succeeding Kimberly Ormsby Nagy. [ref: Descendants of American Prisoners of War (DAPOW) "President General (2025–2027): Trudy Cauthen Tanzillo."] [ref: Officers, Descendants of American Prisoners of War] She took office at the society's Fourth Annual Assembly on 6 April 2025 in Alexandria, Virginia. [ref: News & Photos, Descendants of American Prisoners of War]

She has also served as president of the Virginia Society of the National Society Southern Dames of America (2018–2020), [ref: "Virginia Society, Trudy Tanzillo, President 2018–2020." The Journal, National Society Southern Dames of America, Spring 2018.] president of the District of Columbia society of the National Society Daughters of Founders and Patriots of America (2019), [ref: CMM Past President Addresses Joint Meeting of DC OFPA and DC DFPA, Culpeper Minute Men Photo caption: "DC President, Daughters of Founders and Patriots, Trudy Tanzillo."] and chairman of the finance committee of the Sons and Daughters of Virginia Founding Fathers (2019–2021). She is a member of the Daughters of the American Revolution (from 2008), serving as Assistant Registrar of its Fairfax County Chapter in 2019, [ref: "Fairfax County Chapter Attends Turning Point Suffragist Memorial Groundbreaking." The Virginia View (Virginia Society DAR), Vol. V, Issue 2, November 2019.] a member of The National Society of the Colonial Dames of America (from 2017), and is recorded as an attendee at annual assemblies of the Order of the Steel Magnolias in 2019 and 2023. [ref: History, Order of the Steel Magnolias]

== Personal life ==
Tanzillo was born in Newton, North Carolina, in 1946.

Brunel Medical School was established as part of Brunel University of London's expansion into undergraduate medical education. Its MBBS programme began recruiting students for entry in 2022.

=== Undergraduate medicine ===
The school's principal programme is the five-year MBBS degree. The curriculum combines biomedical sciences, clinical skills, professional development and clinical placements.

== Teaching and learning ==
=== Team-based learning ===
Team-based learning is a principal teaching approach at the school. Students work in groups to apply medical knowledge and discuss clinical problems.

=== Clinical skills ===
Clinical and communication skills are incorporated throughout the programme, alongside simulation and supervised patient contact.

== Clinical training ==
Clinical placements take place in hospitals, general practices and community healthcare settings. The programme includes primary-care experiences and hospital-based clinical training.

== Facilities ==
Medical teaching takes place on Brunel University's campus, using anatomy teaching facilities, clinical skills laboratories and simulated hospital wards.

== Student support ==
The school operates a House system, with students allocated to one of five Houses.

Medical education in the United Kingdom is regulated by the General Medical Council. The programme's current regulatory status should be verified against the latest published GMC and university information.

Draft text:
Benjamin Basire is an Iranian-American legal and compliance professional, political analyst, writer, and media commentator based in Malibu, California. He writes articles and political analysis for media and academic outlets, specializing in Iran and Middle Eastern affairs, denuclearization, nuclear energy policy, and Iran's future democratic constitutional design. [ref: Integrating Denuclearization and Energy Accessibility: Policy Frameworks for a Sustainable Transition, SSRN] [ref: Rekindling the Discussion About Nuclear Power Usage, SSRN]

He has appeared multiple times on Fox News, on programs hosted by Trace Gallagher and Jonathan Hunter, and on Italy's RAI TG3 Mondo. He was the first political analyst in media to compare Secretary of State Marco Rubio's leadership style to that of Winston Churchill. [ref: Rubio's leadership is similar to Churchill, political analyst says, Fox News Video] Basire is also an active LGBT rights advocate and has worked with refugee populations.

He belongs to the Basire family, whose Sephardic branch resettled in Izmir (Smyrna) in the 15th century and later migrated to Persia (modern-day Iran), and whose British branch produced four generations of celebrated copper-plate engravers, including James Basire (1730–1802), the master of William Blake. [ref: James Basire, Wikipedia] [ref: James Basire, The Worshipful Company of Stationers and Newspaper Makers]

== Early life and family ==

Basire was born in Tehran, Iran to a Jewish family and grew up in Larnaca, Cyprus, where he was educated before relocating to the United States. He speaks six languages professionally and fluently: English, Persian (Farsi), Turkish, Greek, French, and Hebrew.

=== Sephardic heritage and the Basire dynasty ===

The Basire family is a Sephardic Jewish dynasty with branches across the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Europe. The branch to which Benjamin belongs resettled in Izmir (Smyrna) in the Ottoman Empire during the 15th century, part of the broader wave of Jewish migration following the expulsions from the Iberian Peninsula. The family later migrated eastward to Persia (modern-day Iran), where they became established within the country's ancient Jewish community, one of the oldest in the world, with roots extending to the Babylonian captivity of the 6th century BCE. [ref: Persian Jews]

On his mother's side, Basire comes from a well-respected Persian Jewish family.

=== The Basire dynasty ===

The British branch of the Basire family produced four generations of distinguished copper-plate engravers and is among the most prominent artistic dynasties in British history.

The dynasty began with Isaac Basire (1704–1768), the son of Jacques Basire, a Huguenot emigrant from Rouen, Normandy, who settled in Soho, London. Isaac trained as a silversmith before turning to copper-plate engraving, becoming renowned for his cartographic work. [ref: Isaac Basire (engraver), Wikipedia] [ref: BASIRE, Isaac, The Huguenots of Spitalfields]

His son James Basire I (1730–1802) became the most celebrated member of the dynasty. He served as Engraver to both the Royal Society and the Society of Antiquaries of London, and is best known for apprenticing the young William Blake at his Great Queen Street studio beginning 4 August 1772. His major works included the copperplate for the Field of the Cloth of Gold and extensive contributions to Vetusta Monumenta. [ref: James Basire, Royal Academy of Arts]

The tradition continued through James Basire II (1769–1822), who engraved the Oxford Almanack, and James Basire III (1796–1869), who expanded into lithography and produced scientific illustrations for the Philosophical Transactions and journals of the Royal Astronomical Society and Zoological Society of London. [ref: Drawing on Copper: The Basire family of copper-plate engravers and their works, Universitaire Pers Maastricht]

The broader Basire family also produced Claude Basire (1764–1794), a French Revolutionary politician from Dijon. He served as a deputy for the Côte-d'Or in the Legislative Assembly and the National Convention, where he voted for the execution of Louis XVI. He was tried before the Revolutionary Tribunal alongside Georges Danton and Camille Desmoulins and was guillotined in Paris in 1794. [ref: Claude Basire, Wikipedia]

== Education ==

Basire earned his Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) in International Affairs and Global Studies from Portland State University in Portland, Oregon. He then completed his LL.B./J.D. at Queen's University Belfast in Northern Ireland, followed by a Master of Laws (LL.M.) in Energy, Environment, and Natural Resources Law at Lewis & Clark Law School, also in Portland. He later enrolled at Pepperdine Caruso School of Law's Straus Institute for Dispute Resolution, where he is pursuing a second LL.M. in Dispute Resolution and completing a thesis on post-theocratic Iranian constitutional design. [ref: Straus Institute for Dispute Resolution, Pepperdine Caruso School of Law]

== Career ==

=== Legal and compliance ===

Basire has built a career in the legal and compliance field, with experience spanning litigation, regulatory compliance, dispute resolution, and enforcement matters in the United States. His work draws on his multilingual capabilities and international legal training across multiple jurisdictions.

Have I Been Squatted Inc. is a privately held cybersecurity company that works on domain intelligence. It builds a platform for finding typosquatted and lookalike domains, along with the websites and infrastructure tied to them, that may be used for phishing, brand impersonation, or other abuse. According to the company's documentation, its monitoring draws on domain permutations, Domain Name System (DNS) data, Certificate Transparency logs, registration data, website analysis, and passive infrastructure telemetry. [ref: Getting started with Have I Been Squatted, Have I Been Squatted Documentation]

The service started in 2022 as a public tool for spotting typosquatted domains. The company that now runs it, Have I Been Squatted Inc., was founded in 2024. [ref: About, Have I Been Squatted] [ref: Have I Been Squatted, LinkedIn]

The company also publishes research on phishing, malicious infrastructure, malware delivery, and domain-name security. Its work has been covered by BBC News, The Register, Recorded Future News, BleepingComputer, and FreightWaves. [ref: Phishing operation with links to Russia, Armenia compromised Western cargo companies, researchers find, Recorded Future News] [ref: Two characters open up a world of typosquatting opportunities in Chromium browsers, The Register]

== History ==

Have I Been Squatted began in 2022 as an experimental tool for finding possible typosquats. Users entered a domain name and the tool generated variations of it, showing registrations that could be used to impersonate the original organization. The company says the project was first released after an experiment was shared on Hacker News, and that it grew as security practitioners started using it. Part of the tool was built on twistrs, an open-source Rust library for generating domain-name permutations that the company still maintains on GitHub. [ref: Have I Been Squatted, GitHub]

Have I Been Squatted Inc. was founded in 2024 to develop and run the service on a commercial basis. [ref: Terms of Service, Have I Been Squatted]

The commercial service moved beyond one-off typosquatting searches to continuous monitoring and investigation of external infrastructure, and later added tools for investigations, alerts, and domain takedowns.

== Platform ==

The platform looks for internet infrastructure that may be impersonating an organization, its domains, or its brands. Customers add domains for monitoring, and the platform regularly generates permutations of them and checks for related registrations and infrastructure. It adds context to what it finds using DNS records, HTTP responses, WHOIS and RDAP registration data, Certificate Transparency observations, screenshots, classification data, and passive infrastructure telemetry.

Monitoring is not limited to typos of a protected domain. The platform also surfaces domains found through Certificate Transparency, passive DNS, and other infrastructure signals.

Separately from monitoring, the platform includes tools for investigating individual domains and larger datasets. Infrastructure it identifies can be classified, investigated, and linked to alerts or response work. The company later added workflows for submitting domain takedown requests and tracking their progress.

== Threat intelligence research ==

=== Diesel Vortex ===

In February 2026, Have I Been Squatted and the threat intelligence group Ctrl-Alt-Intel published an investigation into a cybercrime operation they called Diesel Vortex. The group went after freight and logistics companies in the United States and Europe, using phishing sites built to take over accounts on load boards, fleet-management systems, fuel-card services, and other logistics platforms. [ref: Russian cybercrime ring targeted freight firms in US, Europe, report says, FreightWaves]

According to Recorded Future News, Have I Been Squatted researchers found an exposed.git directory belonging to the operation. It held source code and the group's communications, which showed how the campaign was organized and indicated that the group was building a phishing-as-a-service platform to support a wider criminal operation.

FreightWaves reported that the campaign had compromised 1,649 unique credentials, drawn from 3,474 stolen login pairs. The investigation also identified 52 deployed phishing domains, more than 75,000 targeted contact email addresses, and 35 confirmed attempts at fraud using Electronic Funds Source checks.

The exposed material pointed to an organized operation, with separate roles and infrastructure for stealing credentials, communicating with logistics staff, and managing victim sessions. Recorded Future News reported that the compromised accounts could be used for freight diversion, double brokering, and check fraud.

Have I Been Squatted and Ctrl-Alt-Intel worked with technology and security companies to disrupt the campaign's infrastructure. Recorded Future News named Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), Cloudflare, GitLab, IPinfo, and Ping Identity among those involved.

In April 2026, BleepingComputer referred to the Diesel Vortex investigation in its report on an FBI warning about a sharp rise in cyber-enabled cargo theft. It cited Have I Been Squatted's finding that the group had used dozens of phishing domains against freight and logistics operators since 2025. [ref: FBI links cybercriminals to sharp surge in cargo theft attacks, BleepingComputer]
