These Smiths are an English tribute band based in Manchester that perform the music of the Smiths and Morrissey. Formed in 2015 by original vocalist Jim Thompson following his appearance on the television programme Stars in Their Eyes, the band has performed throughout the United Kingdom and internationally. The current line-up consists of Roy Barrow (vocals), Zander Sumner (guitar), Nigel Clare (bass) and Lee Summers (drums).

The band recreates the sound and stage presentation of the Smiths, including the guitar arrangements of Johnny Marr and the vocal style of Morrissey. The approach was discussed in a 2026 interview with the Spanish newspaper Última Hora.

== History ==

=== Formation and early years ===
These Smiths were formed in 2015 after original vocalist Jim Thompson performed as Morrissey on ITV's Stars in Their Eyes. His appearance was reported by the Manchester Evening News in February of that year.

The band's media archive lists subsequent press and radio appearances, including an interview with Thompson and guitarist Josh Smith in the Oldham Chronicle in 2016, a 2024 Bolton News review, a 2025 interview with the Polish publication Fakt, and a Radio Tameside interview with Roy Barrow and Zander Sumner. The group was also featured in a 2023 Dee Radio interview. [ref: Videos & media, These Smiths] [ref: These Smiths – The Smiths Tribute Band, Dee Radio]

In 2026, the group was profiled ahead of performances in Majorca and Galicia. The Majorca Daily Bulletin described its origins and current members, while El Ideal Gallego previewed a concert in A Coruña.

=== Line-up changes ===
The founding line-up consisted of vocalist Jim Thompson, guitarist Barry Eaton, bassist Nigel Clare and drummer Luke Williams. Josh Smith replaced Eaton in September 2016, remaining until January 2022, when Zander Sumner joined as guitarist. Thompson left in October 2024 and Roy Barrow succeeded him, making his first live appearance with the group in December 2024. Luke Williams departed in 2025; Dan Hough subsequently joined on drums and remained until November 2025. Lee Summers became the permanent drummer in December 2025, having previously performed as a deputy.

As in the original band, whose best-known line-up included Morrissey, Johnny Marr, Andy Rourke and Mike Joyce, each performer takes the corresponding role in the tribute group's stage presentation. [ref: Meet the band, These Smiths]

=== Zander Sumner's 2025 accident ===
In February 2025, guitarist Zander Sumner was seriously injured in a road collision on the A49 in Lancashire. Reports by Lancs Live and ITV News described injuries including a broken hip, broken collarbone and injuries to his hands, which affected his ability to perform during his recovery. [ref: The Smiths tribute guitarist left crawling from written-off car after hit-and-run crash, Lancs Live] [ref: Lancashire teenager spared jail after 'horror smash' leaves Smiths tribute act unable to perform, ITV News]

The band also used substitute performers during other members' absences, including bassist Kris Perry, who covered for Nigel Clare during March–May 2025 and at a performance in Germany in 2026.

=== Performances and touring ===
These Smiths perform at venues and festivals in the United Kingdom and abroad. British appearances have included The Cavern Club in Liverpool, Shepherd's Bush Empire in London and HMV Empire in Coventry. The band was included in the programme for the 2023 Made in Manchester festival. [ref: These Smiths – Live at The Cavern Club Liverpool, The Cavern Club] [ref: These Smiths at hmv Empire, Coventry, Eventim] [ref: Crowds enjoyed live music at Dukinfield's Made in Manchester festival, Tameside Reporter]

In 2026, Spanish newspaper reports previewed concerts in Santander, Ponferrada, A Coruña and Palma de Mallorca. The group performed at the Trui Teatre in Palma on 17 July 2026, with interviews and profiles appearing in the Majorca Daily Bulletin and Última Hora ahead of the concert.

The band also performed at Landei Lugau in Germany on 27 June 2026. [ref: These Smiths in Lugau, Eventim]

== Meeting members of the Smiths ==
In a July 2026 interview with the Spanish newspaper Última Hora, Sumner described meeting former Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr on two occasions and telling him about These Smiths. According to Sumner, Marr was aware of the band and had wished them well. Sumner also said members of These Smiths had met former Smiths drummer Mike Joyce at Christmas and had a photograph taken with him.

== 2026: The Queen Is Dead 40th anniversary ==
In 2026, These Smiths programmed performances marking 40 years since the release of The Queen Is Dead, the Smiths' third studio album. A June listing for the Marrs Bar in Worcester advertised a performance of the album in full, while a November concert at the Boileroom in Guildford was billed as an anniversary celebration. [ref: These Smiths, WeGotTickets] [ref: A celebration of The Smiths: 40 Years of The Queen Is Dead – These Smiths, The Boileroom]

== Band members ==

=== Current members ===

* Roy Barrow (Morrissey) – vocals (2024–present)
* Zander Sumner (Johnny Marr) – guitar (January 2022–present)
* Nigel Clare (Andy Rourke) – bass guitar (2015–present)
* Lee Summers (Mike Joyce) – drums (December 2025–present)

EnglishCentral is a provider of video-based English language learning tools, founded in 2009 by Alan Schwartz and based in Burlington, Massachusetts. The platform uses automated speech recognition with one-on-one live tutoring options to help non-native speakers practice speaking and listening.

== History ==
The company started operations in 2009 with funding from Google Ventures. It later expanded to schools and universities, mainly across East Asia and Europe, by partnering with educational institutions.

== Platform and Technology ==
The system offers video lessons paired with voice analysis tools. When users speak into the system, the speech recognition engine compares their pronunciation and fluency against target models to deliver feedback. Additionally, users can participate in live video sessions with tutors for direct conversational practice.

== Reception and Academic Evaluation ==
Scholars in computer-assisted language learning have studied the platform. A 2021 review by G. Strong in Language Learning & Technology noted that while the video and voice recognition setup helps practice speaking and listening, it has limited capacity for open conversational practice. Other journal studies have looked at its use in university settings regarding student engagement and pronunciation practice.

Tapas Chakraborty is an Indian computer scientist, researcher, and deep-tech entrepreneur. [ref: Can AI fix India's land record problem? This startup believes so, The Economic Times] He is the founder of Vixplor and its automated document intelligence platform, DocXplor. [ref: DocXplor extracts medical record, speeds up process in hospitals, insurance cos, The Hindu BusinessLine] His career spans a decade in the multinational software industry, peer-reviewed computational research in bioinformatics, and the deployment of artificial intelligence tools for public sector governance and healthcare infrastructure.

== Early life and education ==
Chakraborty completed his primary and secondary schooling at the historic Hindu School, Kolkata in Kolkata. He demonstrated early academic distinction under the West Bengal state boards, securing the 34th state rank in the Madhyamik examinations in 2001, and subsequently the 63rd state rank in the Higher Secondary examinations in 2003. He was named a recipient of the National Scholarship for his performances in both board tiers. Additionally, during his Higher Secondary board exam, he was awarded a Gold Medal from the Government of West Bengal for attaining a perfect score (200 out of 200) in mathematics.

He then attended Jadavpur University, graduating with a Bachelor of Engineering (BE) degree in 2007. Following a decade in corporate technology enterprises, Chakraborty returned to academia at Jadavpur University to pursue advanced computational research.

He completed his Master of Engineering (ME) degree in 2019. His master's research specialized in audio signal processing using deep learning frameworks, culminating in his thesis titled "Speaker identification on multimodal environment using deep learning" (2019). In 2026, he was awarded a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) in Computer Science from Jadavpur University. His doctoral work specialized in structural bioinformatics and computational biology. His dissertation, titled "Computational studies on protein protein interaction" (2026), proposed a series of deep neural network architectures introducing innovative approaches for predicting protein-protein interactions (PPI), protein self-interactions, and protein residue-residue proximity frameworks.

== Career ==
=== Enterprise technology (2007–2017) ===
After earning his engineering degree, Chakraborty spent ten years working within the enterprise software and technology consulting sectors. During this period, he held corporate engineering roles at global technology consulting firms, including IBM and PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers), where he designed enterprise application architectures and automated software data flows.

While at IBM, Chakraborty was assigned to highly specialized corporate optimization and data analytics projects:
* Severn Trent Water (Predictive Analytics): He contributed to the data analytics and predictive framework infrastructure for the UK-based water utility company Severn Trent. His work centered on building analytical modules to identify geographical "hot spots" in water distribution networks to isolate areas requiring immediate infrastructural intervention or targeted pipeline replacements.
* Philip Morris International (Research Infrastructure): He was integrated into the specialized technological research and development infrastructure team for Philip Morris International (PMI), assisting in building backend systems mapping data flows for their IQOS electronic nicotine delivery research programs.

=== Entrepreneurship and public sector utility (2017–present) ===
In 2017, Chakraborty left the multinational technology sector to establish his deep-tech startup, Vixplor, focusing on intelligent automation and character recognition. Under Vixplor, he developed **DocXplor**, an artificial intelligence platform utilizing specialized Deep Learning models and Large Language Models (LLMs) to read, interpret, and digitize highly variable printed and handwritten text records without requiring static templates.

The platform has been deployed in several public public infrastructure and private enterprise use cases:
* Land Records Digitization: The Finance Department of the Government of West Bengal contracted the platform to process, extract, and digitize legacy handwritten municipal registries and land deed repositories, algorithmically stitching together "chain deeds" to map real estate ownership lineage across multiple decades.
* Healthcare and Insurance Automation: The platform is used by national healthcare facilities and over a dozen insurance providers to instantly extract structured digital data from handwritten medical prescriptions and clinical invoices, reducing manual data entry delays and accelerating claim pre-authorizations.

In 2026, Chakraborty presented his document intelligence platform on zee TV Zee 24 Ghanta's startup program, Tigers Pitch (Season 1), securing institutional validation and ecosystem funding.. [ref: Tigers Pitch Season 1, Zee 24 Ghanta] He has also been invited as a domain specialist on state television networks, including Doordarshan DD Bangla's flagship economic and entrepreneurship programs, to speak on sustainable scaling and AI integration bottlenecks within emerging industrial corridors. [ref: Pratyasha: 2025-er Safalya 2026-er Pratashya, DD Bangla] and [ref: BARTAMAN ARTHONOITIK ABOSTHA EBONG START-UP BUSINESS, DD Bangla]

Pass Logistics is a British transport and logistics business based in Doncaster, South Yorkshire. Its services include road haulage, same day transport, warehousing and distribution.

The business developed from ParcelPass Transport Ltd, which was launched by Adrian Sullivan in 2017. [ref: Doncaster logistics firm scoops prestigious top prize at London business awards, Doncaster Free Press] The company was rebranded as Pass Logistics in 2020 alongside an acquisition of their logistics hub in Harworth, Nottinghamshire.

Adrian Sullivan founded ParcelPass Transport Ltd in 2017 after previously working in the electrical wholesale industry. An independent profile published in 2022 reported that the business began with one van and £1,500 and subsequently developed into a multi-site logistics operation. [ref: #DNBusinessTalks – Adrian Sullivan (Owner – Pass Logistics), Be More]

Pass Logistics was incorporated as a private limited company on 17 December 2020. Companies House lists its registered office at Suite 7, Spinner Point, Lakeside Boulevard, Doncaster. [ref: Adrian James SULLIVAN personal appointments - Find and update company information - GOV.UK, find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk]

In November 2024, Pass Logistics received the Customer Experience and Loyalty Award in the medium or large business category at the Growing Business Awards. The result was reported by the Doncaster Free Press and Business Doncaster. The same coverage reported the business had previously received the Start Up Business of the Year at the 2018 Doncaster Chamber Business Awards and the SME Business of the Year Award in 2022. [ref: Doncaster logistics firm scoops prestigious top prize at London business awards, Doncaster Free Press]

In March 2025, the company added twelve DAF XF tractor units to their fleet through contract-hire and rental agreements with Fraikin. At the time, industry publication Commercial Motor reported that the vehicles formed part of a program concerning the companies fleet of 18 trucks. [ref: A dozen new DAF XF tractor units for Pass Logistics, www.commercialmotor.com]

In September 2026, Pass Logistics acquired additional warehousing in Carcroft, Doncaster to support growing demand.

== Operations ==
Pass Logistics is a leading provider of transportation, warehousing and logistics services, serving clients across multiple sectors including retail, manufacturing and e-commerce. Known for its innovative approach to logistics solutions and its commitment to sustainability, Pass Logistics has grown rapidly in recent years, establishing a strong presence across the UK and beyond from its Doncaster base. [ref: Pass Logistics confirmed as Doncaster Rovers shirt sponsor, Yorkshire Post]

Pass Logistics provides transport, warehousing and logistics services. Reporting by Business Doncaster states that the company serves corporate and logistics customers in the United Kingdom and Europe. [ref: Doncaster logistics business scoops prestigious top prize at London business awards, Invest Doncaster]

== Doncaster Rovers Sponsorship ==
In December 2024, Pass Logistics entered a two-year agreement to become the front-of-shirt sponsor of Doncaster Rovers FC beginning with the 2025/26 season. The agreement covered the 2025/26 and 2026/27 EFL League One seasons.

Bdaily reported that the agreement followed an earlier relationship between the company and the club that began in 2023 when Pass Logistics sponsored the North Stand at the Club Doncaster Sports Village Stadium. The sponsorship announcement was also covered by The Yorkshire Post. [ref: Pass Logistics named Doncaster Rovers sponsor, Bdaily Business News]

Six HGV tractor units introduced in 2025 were given the names of former Doncaster Rovers legends [ref: PASS LOGISTICS TURNS TO FRAIKIN FOR THE FIRST TIME WITH BESPOKE CONTRACT HIRE AND RENTAL PACKAGE, Fraikin] as part of a campaign run by Pass Logistics' Marketing Manager, Harvey Travis. Pass Logistics supported the PassTheParcel Christmas donation campaign in partnership with Doncaster Rovers FC and Club Doncaster Foundation.

In December 2025, Doncaster Rovers reported that the campaign was collecting presents for children, as well as food and hygiene products for local food banks. The club stated that the campaign delivered presents to organisations including the children's ward at Doncaster Royal Infirmary, Foster for Doncaster and the Bluebell Wood Children's Hospice. [ref: www.doncasterroversfc.co.uk]

The 2025 campaign utilised Pass Logistics HGV's to support the collection and distribution operation.

Pass Logistics were recognised for their efforts as they were named finalist of Campaign of The Year at the 2026 Doncaster Business Awards.

Public statements from Pass Logistics noted the company's connection to the Harworth area through its warehousing operations and employees with linked to football club and community.

Rebel Reid is a Māori musician, guitarist, songwriter and producer from Aotearoa New Zealand. NZ Musician.] [ref: Conor Lochrie, “On ‘Hiria’, Rebel Reid Beautifully Memorialises Her Beloved Mum”. Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, 9 August 2023.]

== Early life ==
Rebel Reid was born on 4 June 1987 in Auckland, New Zealand, and grew up in Papatoetoe, South Auckland, with her mother, Leia Reid, who raised her as a solo parent. She attended Papatoetoe High School.

Her mother’s influence continued to shape Reid’s music throughout her career. In 2023, she released the solo EP Hiria in memory of her late mother. The project explores love, loss and remembrance, with the song “Leia” serving as a personal musical tribute to the woman who helped shape her life.

== Career ==

=== Valkyrie ===
Reid is the guitarist and songwriter for Valkyrie, a New Zealand band associated with South Auckland. The group developed a sound combining pop rock and alternative influences with a theatrical performance style. [ref: Sam Carswell, “Vallkyrie: Stirring the Pot”. NZ Musician.]

Reid and vocalist Omer Gilroy had known each other since childhood and later reconnected to pursue music together. Valkyrie subsequently developed its live performance profile and released its debut album, Joyride, in November 2022. [ref: “Aotearoa’s Valkyrie release smash debut album JOYRIDE”. Music Managers Forum Aotearoa, November 2022.]

In October 2023, Reid was included in the lineup for Aotearoa House at SXSW Sydney, a showcase featuring 30 New Zealand artists and supported by Creative New Zealand, Te Māngai Pāho and the New Zealand Music Commission. [ref: Levi Hartnett, “Aotearoa House to Bring 30 Kiwi Artists to SXSW Sydney”. Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, 3 October 2023.]

=== Solo career and Hiria ===
In July 2023, Reid released her debut solo EP, Hiria, coinciding with Matariki. The three-track project was dedicated to her late mother and features the songs “Leia”, “Cry Cry Cry” and “Dancing in the Stars”. [ref: “Rebel Reid shines on debut solo EP, ‘Hiria’, in memory of her beloved mum”. Muzic.NZ, 14 July 2023.]

In an interview with Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, Reid discussed her mother’s influence on her musical tastes and the personal significance of making Hiria. She described the EP as a gift to her mother and to her people and culture, connecting the release to Matariki and her experience of grief.

The EP blends English and te reo Māori with musical influences including blues, country, folk, pop and rock. Reid also discussed the influence of Witi Ihimaera’s book Navigating the Stars on the songwriting process.

The release received coverage from Rolling Stone Australia/New Zealand, Te Ao Māori News and Muzic.NZ. [ref: Mārena Mane, “Māori musician Rebel Reid releases new EP, an ode to her late mother”. Te Ao Māori News, July 2023.]

=== PROMISELAND ===
Reid is developing a music project titled PROMISELAND, drawing on blues and soul influences. In an August 2026 review of a Play It Strange fundraising concert at Auckland’s Tuning Fork, music journalist Paul Marshall described the blues and soul qualities of Reid’s voice and reported that she performed a song titled “Promised Land”. The review also quoted Reid expressing her ambition to record an album at Sun Records in Memphis, Tennessee. [ref: Paul Marshall, “Play It Strange”. Write Said Paul, 26 August 2026.]

The project’s wider concept, including its planned bilingual songwriting and cinematic elements, has not yet been independently documented in the sources identified for this article.

== Musical style and influences ==
Reid’s musical influences include blues, soul, country, folk, pop and rock. In coverage of Hiria, she discussed growing up listening to artists including Elvis Presley, David Bowie, Billy Idol, Pink Floyd, Queen and Prince. She also cited film composer Hans Zimmer among the music she listened to while recording the EP.

Her work with Valkyrie combines rock and pop influences with theatrical performance, while her solo work explores more personal themes through bilingual songwriting and acoustic arrangements.

Laguana was born in 1970. He spent part of his childhood as a foster youth, and experienced periods of homelessness as a young adult, [ref: SF homelessness advisor has first-hand experience with life on the street - CBS San Francisco, www.cbsnews.com] living in single-room occupancy hotels and working as a street performer in San Francisco. He later credited these experiences with shaping his later public service work. [ref: From street performer and ‘drifter’ to small business champion, San Francisco Examiner]

== Music career ==
In the mid-1990s, Laguana co-founded the indie rock band Creeper Lagoon in San Francisco. He played multiple instruments and contributed to the band's songwriting. Creeper Lagoon released two studio albums: I Become Small and Go (1998) on the Dust Brothers' NickelBag label, and Take Back the Universe and Give Me Yesterday (2001) on DreamWorks Records. [ref: Tonight Was Fun: The Quiet Odyssey of Creeper Lagoon, Under the Radar Magazine] The band received a Spin magazine Best New Artist award in 1998. [ref: 40 minutes to fame at Texas music fest, SFGATE] Their music appeared in films including Orange County, Vanilla Sky, and Hellboy, and in the television series The Sopranos. [ref: Sharky Laguana: Creeper Lagoon reunion 'feels right', Pass The Aux]

== Business career ==
Following the end of Creeper Lagoon, Laguana founded Bandago in 2003, [ref: Luxe van rental business Bandago makes sure all customers get the rock star experience, www.bizjournals.com] a van rental company marketed toward touring musicians. [ref: Bandago: Rock Star Van Rental, Forbes] The company expanded to U.S. locations and later transitioned to employee ownership in 2023. [ref: Bandago, Bandago]

He was also elected as president of American car rental association (ACRA) in 2020. [ref: Sharky Laguana – American Car Rental Assocation] [ref: ]

== Public service ==
In 2018, after a series of rental van thefts from his company. Liguana posted about thefts, [ref: SF man’s tweetstorm over stolen van leads to new state law, San Francisco Chronicle] lawmakers introduced AB 2620, which allowed rental companies to use GPS tracking to recover stolen vehicles under certain conditions. [ref: Can GPS tracking stop customers from stealing rental cars? In California, a new debate over privacy begins., The Washington Post] [ref: Twitter tale of SF van theft gets elected officials’ attention, San Francisco Chronicle]

Laguana was appointed to the San Francisco Small Business Commission in 2019 and served as its president from 2020 to 2022. During his tenure, he contributed drafting the city's Venue Recovery Fund, established in 2020 to support music and entertainment venues affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. He advocated for Proposition H [ref: He Survived the ‘Knife Fight’ of SF Politics. What’s Sharky Laguana’s Next Act?, The San Francisco Standard], a 2020 ballot measure make it easy for small businesses and community-serving organizations to operate in San Francisco, the “First Year Free” program that waived fees for new small businesses. [ref: SF Supervisor Proposes Pilot Program That Waives City Fees for New Small Businesses, NBC Bay Area]

In 2023, Laguana was appointed to the San Francisco Homeless Oversight Commission. [ref: Think you can solve SF’s homelessness crisis? Give it a try, The San Francisco Standard] [ref: New San Francisco study looks at data about homelessness with a different approach - CBS San Francisco, www.cbsnews.com]

== Personal life ==
Laguana lives in San Francisco. In 2000 He married Naomi Putterman; they have two sons. He has discussed his past experiences with homelessness and foster care in interviews and public appearances. [ref: Twitter tale of SF van theft gets elected officials' attention, San Francisco Chronicle]

Claudio Kaya is a Greek-Albanian actor, writer, director, and contemporary dancer. He works across feature films, television, and theater. He is best known for his breakthrough leading film role as Argiris in the 2024 psychological mystery thriller film Buzzheart, directed by Dennis Iliadis.

== Early life and education ==
Kaya was born in Albania and relocated to Greece with his family at the age of four, growing up in Athens. He pursued a professional career in the performing arts, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in Acting and Performance. During his academic studies, he completed intensive on-camera performance training under the mentorship of the prominent Greek television and film director Manousos Manousakis.

In 2024, Kaya made his feature film debut starring as Argiris, the central protagonist in the psychological thriller Buzzheart (original Greek title: Akouo tin Kardia sou). Directed by Hollywood genre filmmaker Dennis Iliadis, the film premiered in the Official Competition at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival. Kaya's performance as an introverted young man subjected to violent parental psychological screenings received favorable reviews from Greek cinematic publications such as Flix.gr.

Following his cinematic breakthrough, Kaya transitioned into television, securing guest roles on Greek National Television (ERT). He appeared as Vasilis Stefanidis in the comedy-drama series Mama sta Kryfa (Hidden Mother).

=== Theater and Other Work ===
Active within the independent Athens theater circuit, Kaya has expanded his work into writing and directing. He wrote and directed the original stage play Horny Fans, produced by Independent Artists in Athens. In addition to his acting career, Kaya is trained in contemporary dance and physical theater, and regularly participates in screenwriting workshops for stage and cinema.

Draft text:
David Alexander Plummer. [ref: SUSSEX WILDLIFE TRUST - Charity 207005, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk] is a British wildlife photographer, filmmaker, author, naturalist and conservationist. His work encompasses wildlife photography, natural history filmmaking, fieldcraft and conservation education [ref: Fieldcraft AKA how to watch wildlife without disturbing it - Sussex Wildlife Trust], with particular expertise in birds, especially owls, and butterflies.

Plummer's wildlife photographs have appeared in specialist publications and the national and international press [ref: 7 Years of Camera Shake, Discover Wildlife] [ref: I made the choice to grab life by the horns, The i] [ref: ProZone Interview: David Plummer, N-Photo]. He was shortlisted for Wildlife Photographer of the Year in 2016 and is the author of 7 Years of Camera Shake (2017) [ref: 7 Years of Camera Shake, The Times], which documents his photographic work following his diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in 2009. His television and film work includes contributions to BBC natural history productions, including Wild Isles (2023) [ref: Wild Isles], as well as wildlife consultancy and documentary filmmaking.

Plummer was the subject of 15 Years (2023) [ref: 15 YEARS - Living with Parkinson’s Disease as a Wildlife Photographer (Short Documentary)], a short documentary directed by Katie Mayhew that received a Golden Wing Grand Award at the [https://msmke.net Hungarian Special Film Festival] [ref: Ezen a fesztiválon három patkány is lehetett díjnyertes, index.hu]. He also appeared in Shaking Hands with the Devil [ref: Shaking Hands With The Devil – A documentary on Parkinson's & Witchcraft in Kenya, Africa], a documentary examining the stigma surrounding Parkinson's disease in Kenya [ref: ], which received a Bronze Judges' Award at the 2024 [https://smileymovement.org/charityfilmawards Smiley Charity Film Awards] [ref: Smiley Charity Film Awards, Smiley Charity Film Awards]. In 2025, he contributed to Super Nature, a feature-length documentary directed by Ed Sayers that premiered at the BFI London Film Festival [ref: Super Nature, Screen Scotland].

Plummer previously worked as a resident wildlife photographer at the [https://knepp.co.uk Knepp Estate] rewilding project in West Sussex. He has served as a trustee of Sussex Wildlife Trust since March 2024 [ref: Trustees and President - Sussex Wildlife Trust] and contributed to the Parkinson's UK garden at the 2026 RHS Chelsea Flower Show, which received the BBC/RHS People's Choice Award for Best Show Garden [ref: ].

== Early life ==
Plummer developed an interest in wildlife during childhood, spending time observing insects, breeding butterflies and studying animals in their natural habitats. His early interest in wildlife photography was influenced by the work of British bird photographer Eric Hosking, whom he heard interviewed on BBC Radio [ref: David Plummer: From Amateur to Professional, www.naturettl.com].

He began experimenting with photography using a second-hand Prinzflex 35mm single-lens reflex camera. Initially photographing wildlife and plants in his local surroundings, he developed his photographic techniques through observation and field experience [ref: Wildlife Photographer Proves Parkinson’s Is No Obstacle, Medium].

Plummer began his working career at the age of 17 as a police cadet, subsequently serving as a police officer for the Metropolitan Police. He then transferred to the Caribbean, where he continued working as a police officer, before pursuing a professional career in wildlife photography [ref: Woodland Bird Photography with David Plummer].

His early photographic work concentrated on British wildlife, particularly in Kent and Sussex, before expanding to international locations, including Africa, South America and the Galápagos Islands [ref: 7 YEARS OF CAMERA SHAKE - DAVID PLUMMER, wildimportance].

== Career ==

=== Wildlife photography ===
Plummer established his career photographing wildlife in Britain and internationally, with particular interests in birds, mammals and animal behaviour [ref: 6 world-class wildlife shots taken by a photographer with Parkinson's, Parkinson's Europe]. His work has taken him to locations including the Pantanal wetlands of Brazil, where he has photographed wildlife since the late 1990s.

He readily adopts fieldcraft, animal behaviour and the use of hides and camouflage into his photographic approach [ref: Fieldcraft AKA how to watch wildlife without disturbing it - Sussex Wildlife Trust].

He previously worked at the Knepp Estate in West Sussex, where he was involved in wildlife photography, photographic safaris and fieldcraft instruction [ref: The Knepp Estate, West Sussex, Bird Photographer of the Year].

Plummer’s observations of fallow deer at the Knepp Estate were featured in the companion book to the BBC natural history series Wild Isles. The book quotes his accounts of the annual deer rut and the behaviour of competing males. [ref: Wild Isles, William Collins]

In 2016, Plummer was shortlisted for Wildlife Photographer of the Year. The following year he published, 7 Years of Camera Shake: One Man's Passion for Photographing Wildlife, a collection of more than 200 photographs taken following his diagnosis of Parkinson's disease in 2009. The book features wildlife photographed in Britain and internationally, accompanied by accounts of his photographic experiences [ref: ].

Draft text:
Rethink Space (stylized up all caps) is an international space technology and infrastructure venture founded by German scientist and entrepreneur Karl Johannes Lierfeld. The organization develops architectural, neuro-technological, and robotic frameworks for the New Space Economy, focusing on long-term human presence in cis-lunar space and sustainable lunar habitats.

== History and Overview ==
Rethink Space was established as an interdisciplinary research and development project bridging artificial intelligence, brain-computer interfaces (BCI), robotics, and space architecture. Operating as Rethink Space Inc. (Delaware C-Corporation / foundation pending) with research activities in Germany, the venture collaborates with international academic and industrial partners.

The project addresses the key operational challenges of permanent human settlement on the Moon and deep-space environments. Rather than relying solely on terrestrial supply lines, Rethink Space focuses on in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), autonomous swarm robotics, and modular habitats.

== Research Areas ==

=== Lunar Habitat Design & Architecture ===
Rethink Space designs modular lunar habitats engineered to withstand extreme environmental hazards, including solar radiation, micro-meteorite impacts, and severe thermal fluctuations. The architectural concepts incorporate human-centered cognitive principles to mitigate psychological and physiological stressors during long-duration lunar missions.

=== Brain-Computer Interfaces & Neuro-AI ===
Drawing on founder Johannes Lierfeld's research in neurotechnology and artificial intelligence, Rethink Space explores brain–computer interface (BCI) applications in extreme environments. Focus areas include real-time neuro-monitoring of astronaut cognitive states and direct BCI systems for the teleoperation of surface robotics.

=== Swarm Robotics & ISRU ===
The project develops autonomous swarm robotics architectures designed for pre-deployment lunar operations, including regolith excavation, automated site preparation, and resource extraction prior to crew arrival.

== Collaborative Network ==
Rethink Space collaborates with academic researchers, space technology institutions, and start-up hubs, including:

* Valentina Sumini (Politecnico di Torino / MIT Media Lab) – Space architecture and swarm robotics.
* Tommy Nilsson (Fraunhofer FIT / European Space Agency) – Human-computer interaction and lunar digital twins.
* German Accelerator/Start2Group (selected Rethink Space for their "market discovery" and "market access" programs)
* ESA / ESTEC (selected Rethink Space for "Strategy forum on Space-Based Data Centers")

== Key Figures ==

* Karl Johannes Lierfeld – Founder and CEO. Lierfeld is a scientific author and entrepreneur working across artificial intelligence, cognitive neuroscience, and space technology.

Awasi is a Chilean hospitality company, headquartered in Santiago, that operates five small lodges in Chile, Argentina and Brazil. Founded in 2007 with the opening of Awasi Atacama in San Pedro de Atacama, it built lodges near Torres del Paine National Park (2013) and Iguazu Falls (2018), and acquired existing hotels in Santa Catarina, Brazil, in 2024 and in Mendoza, Argentina, in 2025. Each room is assigned its own guide and four-wheel-drive vehicle, and excursions are planned individually rather than on a fixed schedule. All five lodges hold Michelin Keys, with Awasi Patagonia holding three.

== History ==
The name Awasi derives from the Quechua word wasi, meaning "house". The company was founded by Matías de Cristóbal, an Argentine former banker. Its first lodge, Awasi Atacama, opened in 2007 as one of the first high-end hotels in the area, followed by Awasi Patagonia in November 2013 and Awasi Iguazú in 2018, the company's first property in Argentina. Since 2024, Awasi has been owned by the Argentine group Grupo Faro Verde.

At the end of 2024 Awasi acquired Ponta dos Ganchos, a resort that opened in 2002 in Governador Celso Ramos, Santa Catarina, and had been a Relais & Châteaux member from 2005 to 2014, and renamed it Awasi Santa Catarina. In 2025 it took over Cavas Wine Lodge in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza, which had opened in 2005 as one of the first hotels built within a winery, and renamed it Awasi Mendoza. Both properties adopted Awasi's fully hosted model, which includes meals, beverages and private guided excursions.

In 2025–2026 the company invested about R$20 million (US$4 million) in Awasi Santa Catarina, moving the pool to the cliff edge and adding a spa, gym, boats and a larger guiding team, and renewed vehicles and facilities at its other lodges.

== Properties ==

Awasi Atacama has 12 rooms built of stone, adobe and thatch in San Pedro de Atacama, a town at about 2,400 m at the foot of the Licancabur volcano; its architect worked with a local historian to model the rounded buildings on nearby pre-Inca ruins.

Awasi Patagonia, designed by Chilean architect Felipe Assadi, consists of 16 villas and a main lodge built of native lenga wood on a private conservation area northeast of Torres del Paine National Park, on a hillside above Lake Sarmiento facing the Torres del Paine peaks.

Awasi Iguazú has 14 villas on stilts, each with a private pool, set on a slope above the Iguazú River in a private Atlantic Forest reserve about 20 minutes from the falls. The lodge was designed by Argentine designer Eugenia Chorén with the Awasi team, using local stone and wood and decoration by nearby Guaraní communities.

Awasi Santa Catarina occupies a peninsula on the Emerald Coast, about 45 km from Florianópolis, with 25 standalone villas.

Awasi Mendoza has 17 villas on a vineyard estate in the Agrelo wine district, at the foot of the Andes.

== Operations ==
Awasi assigns each room a private guide and a four-wheel-drive vehicle, so guests set their own itineraries instead of joining group excursions. All five lodges are members of Relais & Châteaux. Awasi Santa Catarina, Awasi Iguazú and Awasi Mendoza offer guests the choice between a fully hosted stay and a bed-and-breakfast rate.

== Conservation and community ==
Awasi Iguazú and Awasi Patagonia together protect about 340 hectares of native forest, and the company describes its operations as carbon neutral. Awasi Patagonia runs on a combination of solar and diesel power, reuses wastewater for irrigation, and leases part of the surrounding ranch to move livestock off the land and restore wildlife habitat. In Misiones, the Iguazú lodge runs workshops with a local Guaraní community and sells its crafts to guests; in Patagonia, guides run nature and outdoor-skills workshops in rural schools. Awasi Santa Catarina keeps hives of native stingless bees, grows its own leafy greens and uses no pesticides on the property.

== Recognition ==
* Michelin Guide (2026 edition): three Keys for Awasi Patagonia and two Keys for each of the other four lodges; Awasi Santa Catarina rose from one Key to two in 2026. The guide lists Awasi Patagonia as one of two Three-Key hotels in Torres del Paine.
* Condé Nast Traveler: Readers' Choice Awards (2017) and Gold List (2019) for Awasi Atacama.
* Condé Nast Traveller Triple Crown (2026), awarded to hotels on its Hot List, Gold List and Readers' Choice Awards: Awasi Patagonia and Awasi Mendoza.
* Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards (2026): Awasi Atacama, Awasi Iguazú and Awasi Santa Catarina among the World's 100 Best Hotels; all five lodges among the Best Resorts in South America.
* Travel + Leisure Most Luxurious New Hotels in the World (2025): Awasi Santa Catarina.
* Travel + Leisure It List: Awasi Iguazú (2019) and Awasi Santa Catarina (2026).
* The Telegraph World's 50 Greatest Hotels (2024): Awasi Patagonia.
* La Liste Top 1000 Hotels (2026): Awasi Patagonia, with a score of 99.

Salah El Moncef (also written Salah el Moncef; full name Salah el Moncef bin Khalifa) is a writer, literary scholar, editor and visual artist born in Kuwait City and based in France. His publications include Atopian Limits (2002), The Offering (2015), Now and Then (2022), Benghazi (2022), The Woman from Warsaw (2026), and the long-form study Art as Pharmakon (2021). Independent criticism of his fiction has focused on memory, traumatic loss, diaspora and the effects of colonial and fascist violence. [ref: Nantes Université, "Salah EL MONCEF BIN KHALIFA," faculty profile, updated 12 May 2026.] [ref: Jean-Yves Pellegrin, review of Atopian Limits, Transatlantica (2004), DOI 10.4000/transatlantica.707.] [ref: Stephen Watt, "Memory, Trauma, and the Diasporic Subject," Los Angeles Review of Books, 4 April 2015.] [ref: Stephen Watt, "An Enormous, Enigmatic Signifier: Salah el Moncef's Benghazi," Michigan Quarterly Review, January 2023.] [ref: Stephen Watt, "The Art of World-Building: Salah el Moncef's The Woman from Warsaw," Michigan Quarterly Review, 20 February 2026.] [ref: Salah El Moncef, official author site (used only for routine biographical and publication data).]

At Nantes Université, Moncef is a Maître de Conférences in English studies and creative writing, with research interests in contemporary American literature and culture, diasporic literatures, migration and transnational identities. He is the General Issue Editor of Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities and an editor of the associated Routledge series Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities. Several Angelaki general issues have also used his paintings as cover and interior art. [ref: Nantes Université, institutional profile/CV: maître de conférences in English studies and creative writing; research on diasporic literatures, migration, and transnational identities.] [ref: Taylor & Francis, Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities, "About this journal" (editorial team).] [ref: Routledge, Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities, series page.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue I 2024." Angelaki 29.5 (2024), artwork list and acknowledgements.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue II 2025." Angelaki 30.6 (2025), artwork list and acknowledgements.]

== Education and academic career ==
A contributor biography published in the academic collection The Matrix in Theory records that Moncef received a Presidential Prize for Distinction in the Humanities in 1987 and was a Fulbright fellow at Indiana University Bloomington from 1988 to 1993. Indiana University lists him among its English PhD alumni, while a University of Colorado contributor profile likewise identifies him as a former Fulbright doctoral fellow there. [ref: University of Colorado Boulder, Genders archive, "Salah El Moncef" contributor profile.] [ref: Myriam Diocaretz and Stefan Herbrechter, eds., The Matrix in Theory (Rodopi, 2006), contributor note for Salah el Moncef bin Khalifa.] [ref: Indiana University Bloomington, Department of English, PhD alumni publications pages.]

Moncef later joined Nantes Université. The university's public profile lists him as a Maître de Conférences in the Department of English and identifies contemporary American literature and culture as his teaching and research field. A more detailed institutional profile describes his work as extending to creative writing, diasporic literature, migration and transnational identities.

== Scholarship and editorial work ==
Moncef's scholarship brings literary and cultural theory to modernist and postmodern American writing. His articles of the 1990s examined Ezra Pound in boundary 2, John Updike's Rabbit at Rest in Arizona Quarterly, Paul Auster's Moon Palace in Angelaki and Thomas Harris's Hannibal Lecter novels in Genders. This line of research was developed in Atopian Limits: Questions of Self, Complexity, and Contingency in Postmodern American Narrative (2002). [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Gold, Representation, and the Reversible Dynamic of Symptomatic Return in Ezra Pound." boundary 2 22.1 (1995): 117–142.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Sounding the Black Box: Linear Reproduction and Chance Bifurcations in Rabbit at Rest." Arizona Quarterly 51.4 (1995): 69–108.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Lecter Knows Worst: Justice, Marginal Value, and the Law in the Series of Thomas Harris's Silence of the Lambs." Genders, 5 July 1999.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Figures in (De)composition: The Genesis of the Paradoxical Self in Paul Auster's Moon Palace." Angelaki 4.3 (1999): 75–91.]

Reviewing Atopian Limits in Transatlantica, Jean-Yves Pellegrin described it as a wide-ranging study of postmodern American narrative organized around systems, limits, ethics and complexity, discussing writers including Paul Auster, Ken Kesey, John Updike, Thomas Harris, Gore Vidal and Kathy Acker. Moncef subsequently co-edited Présence et représentation (2005) with Jacques Gilbert and Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture (2006) with Michele Bottalico. In Aztlán, Antonio C. Márquez reviewed the latter as a collection on border identity and discussed Moncef's concluding contribution, "The Hybrid Self at the Crossroads." [ref: Antonio C. Márquez, review of Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture, Aztlán 32.2 (2007): 213–216.] [ref: WorldCat, bibliographic record for Présence et représentation, Jacques Gilbert and Salah El Moncef (Peter Lang, 2005).]

Niedax Holding GmbH serves as the parent company of the Niedax Group and is headquartered in Linz am Rhein, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany. The group has remained family-owned since it was established in 1920 and manufactures products for electrical and building installation technology. The Niedax Group operates at 81 sites, including 25 production facilities, in over 30 countries. It has joint ventures with FEMI-CZ and Steelline, both based in Italy, as well as with the R&M Electrical Group in Southampton, UK, and ABB in North America. [ref: ABB and Niedax’s joint venture—Abnex—ready to take on North America’s cable tray demands, Electrical Business]

The company develops and produces cable management systems for use in buildings, industrial facilities, and infrastructure projects. [ref: Niedax: Unabhängigkeit von Stahlindustrie, Wirtschaftswoche]

== History ==
Niedax was founded in Berlin in 1920 by engineers Alexander Niedergesäß and Fritz Axthelm as Niedergesäß & Co. OHG. The company initially manufactured fastening materials for the electrical industry. [ref: Mittelständler Niedax: „Mein Ziel war es, mit einer Milliarde Umsatz in Rente zu gehen. Jetzt will ich zwei.“, Wirtschaftswoche]

After World War II, the company was rebuilt and opened a branch in Linz am Rhein. [ref: Linz am Rhein. Die Geschichte der Stadt von der Frühzeit bis zur Gegenwart, Böhlau] A hot-dip galvanising facility began operations in St. Katharinen in 1975. By the end of the 1970s, production had been relocated to St. Katharinen, while the company's administration remained in Linz am Rhein. [ref: Niedax Group investiert kräftig in Linzer Standort, Rhein-Zeitung] [ref: Seit 1955 in Linz, Rhein-Zeitung] In 1995, Bruno Reufels and Egon Winggen took over the company's management from Franz Kolmer following his retirement. [ref: Ein Unbequemer geht, Rhein-Zeitung]

From 1995 onwards, Niedax began expanding its international operations. [ref: Niedax Group: Auf dem Weg zur ersten Umsatzmilliarde, Unternehmeredition] The company acquired Elektraplan in 1996 and the Dutch firm Alinco in 1999. [ref: Mit kleinen Klemmen zum Erfolg, Rhein-Zeitung] On 1 January 2000, it took over the Kleinhuis Group, based in Lüdenscheid, followed by Rico GmbH & Co. KG in 2004. [ref: Niedax steuert auf Expansionskurs, Rhein-Zeitung] [ref: Expansionskurs bringt neue Jobs, Rhein-Zeitung] Most of the larger acquisitions were made during periods of economic crisis, particularly the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. During this time, Niedax also bought two steel service centres.

Egon Winggen retired in 2007 and was succeeded by Alexander Horn, who joined Bruno Reufels as managing director. [ref: Egon Winggen prägte die Geschichte der Niedax-Gruppe, Rhein-Zeitung]

A new operational management team took up its duties on 1 January 2023. [ref: Niedax leitet den Generationswechsel ein, Elektrowirtschaft] Since the summer of 2023, the Niedax Group has been purchasing CO2-reduced steel from various suppliers and processed the material at its own production facilities. [ref: Die Niedax-Group bezieht CO2-reduzierten Stahl von Thyssenkrupp Steel, TGA-Fachplaner.de] [ref: UK steel maker delivers low-CO2-emissions steel to cable management firm, Envirotec Magazine]

In 2024, Niedax took over the Spina Group, an Italian manufacturer of cable management systems and distributor of electrotechnical materials for industrial facilities. [ref: Niedax übernimmt italienische Spina Group, Elektro.net] In November 2024, Niedax and ABB established the joint venture Abnex Inc., which brings together the two companies' North American cable tray businesses. [ref: ABB and Niedax Group Partner on Cable Tray Systems, Automation World] [ref: ABB, Niedax Launch Abnex Inc. for North American Cable Management, Mexico Business News] [ref: ABB and Niedax’s joint venture—Abnex—ready to take on North America’s cable tray demands, Electrical Business]

In 2025, Niedax opened a new site in Rahms, which primarily houses administrative and sales functions as well as a newly built technology campus. Since its completion, the site has served as the coordination centre for the group’s European infrastructure projects. Niedax Infrastruktur GmbH was established in connection with the development. [ref: Niedax Group erschließt neuen Standort in Deutschland, VG Asbach] [ref: Neuer Technologie Campus & Experience Center „Synnoscape“, I-Magazin]

In 2026, Niedax started working on a fibre-optic network for critical infrastructure in Germany. In April 2026, the Niedax subsidiary Netz33 GmbH began to work on a roughly 130-kilometre test route in Niedergörsdorf, Brandenburg. Along this route, Netz33 is testing technologies for the protection of data connections against sabotage, disruptions, and other security risks. [ref: Test für krisensicheres Glasfaser-Netz in Brandenburg, Süddeutsche Zeitung] [ref: Test Segment: Brandenburg Building Crisis-proof Fiber Optic Network, teltarif.de]

== Corporate structure ==
Niedax Holding GmbH, based in Linz am Rhein, serves as the parent company of the Niedax Group and has remained entirely family-owned since it was founded.

The group is organised in several corporate levels. Niedax Verwaltungs GmbH sits below the parent company and manages Niedax Beteiligungs GmbH & Co. KG. This company, in turn, holds a stake in Niedax GmbH & Co. KG, which consolidates most of the group's shareholdings.

Draft: Metamorphic solar cell

Draft text:
Metamorphic (MM) solar cells, also called lattice-mismatched solar cells are multijunction solar cells that incorporate materials with different lattice constants. These are contrasted with lattice-matched (LM) solar cells in which all subcells have the same crystal lattice constant. The main advantage of MM cells is the ability to optimize the band gaps of each subcell for maximum efficiency, a process known as band-gap engineering. Although band gaps can be modified in all multijunction solar cells, metamorphic semiconductors allow for greatly increased flexibility. [ref: ]

Having different lattice constants causes elastic deformation. To mitigate this, dislocations are purposefully created in the structure. This in turn increases the nonradiative recombination rate, which can decrease performance of the cell. A buffer layer can be used to relieve strain and reduce the dislocations. Another method is to grow the higher band gap subcells first and then grow the lower band gap subcells with a lattice-mismatch. Such cells are known as inverted metamorphic (IMM) cells. This also necessitates that the substrate is removed, which is done either through etching or epitaxial lift-off. [ref: ] The term upright metamorphic (UMM) cell is sometimes used to refer to cells that aren't inverted. [ref: ] [ref: ]

Patriot Pit Stop is an independently operated automotive repair and maintenance business located at Hill Air Force Base in Davis County, Utah, United States. The business operates adjacent to the Exchange Mini Mall at 7440 6th Street, providing automotive maintenance, diagnostic services, and mechanical repairs to military personnel, civilian employees, retirees, and other authorized visitors to the installation. [ref: https://patriotpitstophill.com/]

History

The automotive repair facility now known as Patriot Pit Stop, since Nov. 2025, originally operated as the separate company, Firestone automotive service center, before transitioning to Kwik Kar Complete Auto Care in July 2017. The location serves the Hill Air Force Base community as an automotive maintenance and repair facility. ref>https://www.loc8nearme.com/utah/hill-air-force-base/kwik-kar/4531611/

The Hill Air Force Base location subsequently transitioned from the Kwik Kar name to Patriot Pit Stop, establishing a distinct local identity while continuing to provide automotive maintenance and repair services. The facility retained its established location on the installation and continued serving the surrounding military community.

In September 2026, ownership of Patriot Pit Stop LLC transferred to Aaron Cleveland, marking a new chapter in the business's operations. The company continued operating as Patriot Pit Stop following the ownership transition.

Location

Patriot Pit Stop is situated at 7440 6th Street on Hill Air Force Base, near Ogden and Layton, Utah. The repair facility is attached to the Hill Air Force Base Exchange Mini Mall, a retail and service complex serving the installation's military and civilian population. [ref: https://www.loc8nearme.com/utah/hill-afb/hill-afb-mini-mall/7340475/]

Its location provides convenient access to automotive services for individuals working or conducting business on the installation. Because the facility is located within an active military installation, customer access is subject to Hill Air Force Base entry requirements.

Automotive services

Patriot Pit Stop provides general automotive repair, preventive maintenance, and vehicle diagnostic services for domestic and imported vehicles. Its operations include routine maintenance as well as more extensive mechanical repairs. [ref: https://patriotpitstophill.com/]

Services offered include oil and filter changes, brake inspection and repair, battery replacement, engine diagnostics, scheduled maintenance, tire rotation, wheel alignment, suspension and steering repairs, heating and air conditioning service, electrical system repairs, and replacement of starters, alternators, and timing belts. The staff has even been reported to drop off and pick up customers at their work.

The facility also provides vehicle inspections and fleet maintenance services. Its preventive maintenance program includes multipoint vehicle inspections intended to identify potential mechanical issues and support long-term vehicle reliability.

Operations

Patriot Pit Stop operates as a locally managed automotive service business serving the Hill Air Force Base community. The facility employs automotive technicians and service personnel responsible for vehicle diagnostics, maintenance, repairs, and customer assistance.

The business generally operates Monday through Friday, 8AM - 4PM, with scheduled appointments and repair services available during regular business hours. Its location within the Exchange Mini Mall area allows customers to access automotive maintenance services while they work without leaving the military installation.

HEF Group is a private surface engineering company, founded in 1953 by Jacques-Jean-Caubet. It was founded in the city of Saint-Chamond near Saint-Étienne (France) in the Loire department [ref: ]. In 2025, the group operates in 23 countries in Europe, North America, South America and Asia.

Since 1973, HEF is employee-owned, with 75% distributed among employees while the remaining shares are held by the founding family [ref: HEF, ingénierie des matériaux de surface et traitement de surface, HEF] [ref: HEF Group Acquires Abrisa Technologies, Abrisa Technologies].

== Sectors of activity ==
HEF Group's sectors of activity are the following:

* Surface finishing in ionic liquid;
* PVD and PECVD vacuum deposition technologies;
* The manufacturing of mechanical components such as bushings, pins and joints intended for industrial applications;
* Tribology and surface degradation mechanisms (wear, friction, corrosion and more);
* Hydrogen technologies (fuel cell [ref: A Saint-Etienne, HEF investit dans la production de matériaux pour piles à combustible, L'Usine Nouvelle]) since 2024 [ref: Saint-Etienne. Cette entreprise crée une usine unique au monde: 100 emplois prévus, actu.fr];

The group develops and sells surface coating services through processes such as nitriding or vacuum deposition [ref: HEF GROUPE, Hydrogen and Carbon Capture Technology World Expo 2026].

HEF manufactures friction components, notably metal and composite bushings. Depending on the intended application, these products can provide resistance to wear, friction, abrasion or corrosion, which serves industries such as mobility, energy, manufacturing and aeronautics [ref: HEF PEL Bushings, Agriculture XPRT] [ref: PEL 4.0].

== Acquisitions and diversification ==
As part of its strategy to extend its field of activity, HEF Group has acquired companies in the sectors of tribology, surface engineering and photonics.

In the friction components sector, the group acquired companies such as ACM Composite Bearings from the United Kingdom in 2024 and Drie-D from the Netherlands in 2026 [ref: ].

Beginning in 2021, HEF expanded into the photonics industry through acquisitions, and now owns the French companies Fichou (2021) [ref: Fichou, spécialiste de l’optique militaire demeure française, Portail de l'IE] [ref: Le fonds d'investissement du ministère des Armées se désengage de Fichou, spécialiste de l'optique de haute précision, Zone Militaire] [ref: Le ligérien HEF accélère sa diversification en reprenant des PME en Bretagne et en région parisienne - Le Journal des Entreprises, www.lejournaldesentreprises.com], Kerdry (2021) [ref: HEF becomes a major actor in the fields of photonics and defense] [ref: Le ligérien HEF accélère sa diversification en reprenant des PME en Bretagne et en région parisienne - Le Journal des Entreprises, www.lejournaldesentreprises.com], Acerde (October 2021) [ref: Startup ACERDE Anodes légères tournantes pour tubes à rayons X, www.myfrenchstartup.com] and Neyco (21 July 2022) [ref: ], as well as the American companies Abrisa Technologies (2021) [ref: Abrisa Technologies Joins HEF Photonics Business Unit, www.photonicsonline.com] [ref: ] and The Telic Company (2025) [ref: HEF Groupe annonce le rachat de la société TELIC by HEF GROUPEDirectIndustry, trends.directindustry.fr].

In 2024, the group invested €40 million into developing a new plant dedicated to the development of surface treatments for fuel cells, with the intention of providing an alternative to materials such as gold and platinum [ref: Hydrogène: le groupe HEF contraint de revoir sa copie faute d'un marché suffisant, www.latribune.fr] [ref: Plaques bipolaires: fabrication avancée, usinage CNC et revêtements de surface pour les piles à combustible de nouvelle génération, Shenzhen Tuofa Technology Co., Ltd.].

[ref: ] [ref: Nordstjernan's subsidiary Etac invests in Ki Mobility, Private Equity Wire]

In 2006, the Ax:son Johnson family's investment company Nordstjernan became the majority owner of Etac. [ref: RFSU och Nordstjernan i långsiktigt partnerskap om Etac, Cision News] In 2011, Nordstjernan acquired the remaining shares in Etac and became the sole owner. [ref: Nordstjernan takes the next step in building a global mobility Group – Etac acquires Convaid, Cision News]

Etac has received several design awards, including the Red Dot Award, Excellent Swedish Design, the Good Design Award, and the Award for Excellence. Etac's products are designed and/or manufactured in Scandinavia, North America, Austria, and Poland, and distributed from regional warehouses. [ref: About us, Etac]

Draft text:
The Falcon 23-4M Lightning, also styled FDI Falcon-23/4M Lightning, is a trailer-mounted short-range air defense and counter-unmanned aircraft system combining four ZU-23-2 twin-barrel 23 mm anti-aircraft gun mounts with radar, electro-optical sensors and centralized fire control.

Azerbaijani reporting attributes the design, development and manufacture of the system's main platform to FDI Falcon Dynamic Systems Azerbaijan. Other defence publications describe FDI Technology (Falcon Dynamic Systems) as a Turkish defence enterprise. These descriptions refer to the manufacturer and its reported national affiliations; they do not, by themselves, establish joint governmental development of the weapon.

The system was displayed at the ADEX 2026 defence exhibition in Baku, Azerbaijan, which took place from 30 September to 2 October 2026.

== Development ==

According to information supplied by the manufacturer and published by Editor.az, the main platform was designed and produced by FDI Falcon Dynamic Systems Azerbaijan, with BIRD radar components integrated as a separate technological module. The manufacturer said that integration, evaluation, proving-ground activity and live-fire trials were being carried out with support from Azerbaijan's Ministry of Defence. The company reiterated this account in an October 2026 announcement; these statements have not been presented as independently verified test results.

Times of Defence and Defence.Tech reported that a version of the system had been delivered to Azerbaijan in 2025 for integration and testing, describing the information as originating from the company. The reports do not establish the extent of any subsequent operational deployment.

== Design ==

The ADEX configuration mounts four ZU-23-2 gun assemblies on a multi-axle semi-trailer. Each assembly has two 23 mm cannon barrels, for a total of eight. Published descriptions also identify hydraulic stabilizing outriggers fitted to the carrier.

The concept reuses existing ZU-23-2 armament in a system intended for point defence, including the protection of airfields, logistics sites, command posts and other fixed or semi-fixed infrastructure. Defence reports list standard 23×152 mmB ammunition and a nominal combined cyclic rate of approximately 3,200–4,000 rounds per minute; these figures describe the weapon configuration, not a measured combat success rate.

AsiaToday described the displayed system as having a mast-mounted electro-optical station and a separate remote-control position with monitors. Azerbaijan's Ordu.az also published a feature about the four-mount arrangement in October 2026; its account closely resembles reporting by Army Recognition.

== Sensors and fire control ==

Reports describe the BIRD radar as providing surveillance and target cueing, while electro-optical and infrared equipment supports observation and target tracking. These inputs are reported to feed the FDI Falcon Eye Air Guard centralized fire-control system, allowing the four gun mounts to be directed as a coordinated installation.

The system has been described as using automated target tracking and computerized ballistic calculations while retaining remote operator control. In a report titled На ADEX в Баку представили Falcon-23M: ИИ следит, оператор стреляет, the Russian technology site Modelora used the designation Falcon-23M Lightning and, citing a NEWS.ru correspondent and an attributed developer statement, reported that artificial intelligence identifies and follows targets while the operator makes the decision to fire. The same report mentioned a radar detection range of up to 10 km and asserted that the underlying artificial-intelligence technology had been in development for seven years. Those details are uncorroborated descriptions of a differently designated system, not independently established specifications for the 23-4M variant; radar detection range is also distinct from weapon engagement range.

== Reported performance ==

Published manufacturer figures specify engagement against aerial targets travelling at speeds of up to 650 km/h, at ranges of up to 2.5 km and altitudes of up to 1,000 metres. Army Recognition, Defence Arabia and Vietnamese coverage note that the figures are manufacturer-stated or remain subject to validation; they are not verified here as achieved operational performance.

== Exhibition and media coverage ==

The Falcon 23-4M Lightning was depicted or discussed in ADEX 2026 coverage by NEWS.ru, AsiaToday and the Azerbaijani publication Ordu.az. Further Russian-language reporting included a brief item on Pressa24, which credited the Telegram channel @[user], and a comparative article in Conflictora discussing the Falcon alongside modernized ZU-23-family systems. Modelora also published a report on AI-related tracking and operator control.

Defence Review, Times of Defence, Army Recognition, Defence Arabia and Defence.Tech covered the system in specialist or defence-industry reporting. Defence.Tech explicitly credited Army Recognition for some of its information, while several reports repeated manufacturer technical figures.

Draft text:
St. John's Episcopal Church, known locally as St. John's Park Slope, is a parish of the Episcopal Church at 139 St. John's Place in the Park Slope neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York City. Founded in 1826 in what was then the village of Brooklyn, it is the second-oldest Episcopal parish in Brooklyn, after St. Ann's. Since 1870 the congregation has worshipped in a Gothic Revival brownstone church, attributed to the architect Edward Tuckerman Potter, which lies within the Park Slope Historic District, designated by the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission in 1973. The parish belongs to the Episcopal Diocese of Long Island.

== History ==

=== Founding ===
In 1826 the Rev. Evan Malbone Johnson sold his farm in Newtown to pay for a new church in Brooklyn. The first St. John's, a wooden building at Washington and Johnson Streets, opened for worship on September 24, 1826. The parish was incorporated on April 16, 1827, as "The Rector, Church Wardens and Vestrymen of Saint John's Church at Brooklyn", and the church was consecrated by Bishop John Henry Hobart on July 10, 1827. Its name was chosen by drawing lots. Johnson served as rector for twenty-one years without salary; known locally as "the Domine", he was said to have married some two thousand couples.

The young parish was active in the life of the village. In the 1820s it joined Presbyterian, Baptist and Dutch Reformed congregations in founding the Brooklyn Sunday School Union. By about 1837 its Sunday school kept a lending library of some 400 volumes open to the public, and in 1831 Johnson's wife, Maria, founded the Women's Benevolent Society, whose 1841 silver collection plates the parish still owns. Johnson also led the petition to open Myrtle Avenue, which succeeded despite some four hundred objectors.

In 1843, when pew rents were keeping poorer people out, Johnson asked the vestry that no one who came to the church "shall ever apply... and not be supplied with a seat", and the vestry agreed. The same year, in a private letter to John Jay, he wrote that, whatever his earlier opinions, he had come to believe that "God hath made of one blood" the whole human race. He befriended the Black priest Alexander Crummell, inviting him to preach, and between 1846 and 1853 he was among the clergy who argued that St. Philip's Church, a Black congregation in Manhattan, should be admitted to the convention of the Diocese of New York; St. Philip's vestry formally thanked him. He resigned from St. John's in 1847 to found St. Michael's, a free church in Brooklyn.

=== Dissension and recovery ===
After the death of the rector Thomas T. Guion in 1862, the parish was divided: vestrymen resigned, meetings failed to reach a quorum, and several priests declined calls to serve as rector. Bishop Horatio Potter asked George Franklin Seymour to recover the parish from "the distressing condition into which internal dissension had brought it". Seymour raised more than $13,000 in a single year, served until 1866, and later became Bishop of Springfield.

=== Move to Park Slope ===
In 1868 the parish sold its building and began holding mission services near Prospect Park. Under the rector Alexander Burgess, later Bishop of Quincy, it bought lots at Seventh Avenue and Douglass Street (now St. John's Place) in 1869, and the cornerstone of a new chapel was laid on June 15, 1869. The chapel opened on January 16, 1870, with about six hundred people present and Bishop Abram Newkirk Littlejohn preaching. The parish's histories attribute its design to Edward Tuckerman Potter, who had earlier been engaged to design a church the parish planned, and never built, on DeKalb Avenue. A larger church planned for the Seventh Avenue corner was never built, and the corner lots were later sold. The Brooklyn Theatre was built on the site of the first church and burned on December 5, 1876, in one of the deadliest fires in the city's history; the site was later occupied by the Brooklyn Daily Eagle building.

In 1885 the parish began enlarging the chapel with a nave and chancel, giving the building a cruciform plan. Trinity Church, Wall Street, which had helped the parish in 1832, lent it $8,000 in 1872 and forgave the loan in 1910. The parish carried a mortgage for forty-six years. During the Great Depression the rector's salary was small and sometimes paid in food, but the mortgage was paid off in 1931 and the church was consecrated by Bishop Ernest M. Stires on December 27 of that year.

=== Twentieth century ===
From the 1950s, Anglicans who had immigrated from the Caribbean became a large part of the congregation and sustained it as many earlier members moved away. The parish's own history acknowledges that the newcomers "were not always welcomed" at first. On December 16, 1960, the 1960 New York mid-air collision brought one of the airliners down at Seventh Avenue and Sterling Place, a block from the church. A new Hillgreen-Lane organ, the gift of an anonymous donor, was dedicated in 1962, and in 1963 a bequest of more than $400,000 from Mrs. Palen Nelson established the parish endowment. A series of sacrament windows by Payne Studios was installed between 1965 and 1971.

Aki Hayakawa (Japanese: 早川 アキ) is a fictional character from Tatsuki Fujimoto's manga series Chainsaw Man. Aki was a main character at the first part of the manga, and appeared as a professional devils hunter. Aki is voiced by Shogo Sakata in Japanese, and by Reagan Murdock in English. [ref: Aki Hayakawa, Behind The Voice Actors]

== Creation ==

Aki's Japanese name is written as "早川 アキ", where "アキ" uses katakana instead of the kanji "秋". Fujimoto has revealed that the origin of the name "アキ" has two layers. One is from the "Gun Fiend" form he ultimately turns into, where his arm becomes like an AK-47 assault rifle, taking its homophone "AKi". The other is representing the "空き" (Aki), meaning emptiness, hollowness. [ref: Analyzing "Chainsaw Man"'s Aki Hayakawa (早川アキ) from Japanese: The Tragedy Behind the Name and the Charm of "Kon", ANIHK] Hayakawa "早川" which consists of the characters for “already; now; by this time” and “river". [ref: Things You Didn't Know About Aki From Chainsaw Man, CBR]

Some concept art of what seems to be Aki, which shown on one of Tatsuki Fujimoto's alternate accounts, shows him with a slightly different older design with differences such as scars on his face. And there is a scrapped idea was that Himeno was going to be Aki's younger sister who would have lived longer. It was revealed that Aki's hairstyle is due to the nature of his contract with the Fox Devil. [ref: Chainsaw Man Creator Reveals the Secret Behind Aki's Top Knot Hairstyle, CBR]

=== Casting ===
Aki's role, played by Shogo Sakata, was Sakata's first major role in his acting career. Reagan Murdock, Aki's English voice actor, described Aki and said: “[Aki] is normally so very under control and he has such a firm... well, what he thinks is a firm grasp on his emotions when really he's just pushing his emotions down until they come exploding out". [ref: INTERVIEW: Chainsaw Man English Voice Actors for Denji and Aki Discuss What Makes a Good Dream, Crunchyroll news]

In an interview about Chainsaw Man – The Movie: Reze Arc, Sakata said that: "Aki Hayakawa had always been a part of me, so it didn't take long to get back into character. During the exchanges with Nomo, I received direction to "add a bit more familiarity," which was nice as it allowed me to explore new aspects of his character", and he also talked about his experience with Nomo, who voiced by Kenji Akabane-san, describing it as revealing a new side of Aki. [ref: "Chainsaw Man - The Movie: Reze Arc" Interview: Cast Discusses Aki's New Side, Makima's Unsettling Aura, and Denji's Summer Experience, Japan Wire by Kyodo News]

== Appearances ==
Aki is a tall man with blue eyes and medium-length black hair that he pulls back in topknot style. He has a serious, cold, and intelligent personality. He intensely hates devils, including those he contracts with within the organization, and advocates killing them mercilessly if they try to escape or betray the organization. However, he also harbors a kind and gentle side towards those he loves. Aki was born in Hokkaido to a family of his father, mother, and younger brother—who were all killed in a Gun Devil attack that completely destroyed their home. This instilled in Aki a deep hatred for devils from a young age. Aki joined the Public Safety Organization, where he met Himeno, his first colleague and close friend. Himeno, who harbored romantic feelings for Aki, tried to persuade him to resign from his job to save his life, but he refused. Aki treats Himeno as a close friend rather than a lover. Through Himeno, Aki was introduced to the world of smoking. [ref: Chainsaw Man, Viz Media]

With Denji's arrival, Makima asks Aki to look after him. Initially, Aki is harsh with Denji for his recklessness and lack of seriousness in his work as a devil hunter. [ref: Chainsaw Man, Viz Media] He tells Denji to quit his job to save his life and even threatens to kill him without hesitation if he betrays them or sides with other devils. However, as the story progresses, the two begin to form a friendship. Denji and Power live with Aki, and he treats them like that he is their older brother. After Himino sacrifices herself to save him from a Katana Man's attack, Aki is devastated. He quits smoking out of grief for Himino, but he refuses to resign, driven by his desire to avenge his family and Himino. As the story unfolds, Aki begins a friendship with Angel Devil and loses his arm in a battle with Darkness Devil. Aki's primary goal is to avenge his family and Himino. However, as the confrontation with the Gun Devil draws near, the Future Devil shows Aki a glimpse of the future, where he witnesses Denji and Power suffering a horrific and painful death. [ref: Chainsaw Man, Viz Media] This compels him to ask to withdraw the Public Safety Division 4's Devil Hunters from the upcoming battle with the Gun Devil to save their lives, even though killing the Gun Devil was his ultimate objective.
