Draft text:
Matija Strlič (born 1968) is a Slovenian heritage scientist and analytical chemist. He is Professor of Analytical Chemistry at the University of Ljubljana and Honorary Professor of Heritage Science at University College London (UCL). [ref: About Us, Heritage Science Laboratory Ljubljana, University of Ljubljana] [ref: People at the Institute for Sustainable Heritage, University College London]

His research focuses on the application of scientific methods to cultural heritage, including studies of degradation of historic paper and other heritage materials, effects of the environment and climate on collections, heritage values and the study of historical odours. [ref: The smell of history, Chemistry World]

Strlič studied chemistry at the University of Ljubljana and received a PhD in chemistry from the university in 2000. [ref: Prof Matija Strlic, University College London]

He joined University College London in 2007 and worked at UCL's Institute for Sustainable Heritage. In 2010, Strlič was course director of UCL's newly established MRes programme in Heritage Science. [ref: New Masters in Heritage Science at UCL Centre for Sustainable Heritage, Conservation DistList] He was a co-investigator on the Science and Engineering in Arts, Heritage and Archaeology (SEAHA) Centre for Doctoral Training, an EPSRC-funded centre established at University College London in partnership with the University of Oxford and the University of Brighton. [ref: Announcing SEAHA – Centre for Doctoral Training in Science and Engineering in Arts, Heritage and Archaeology, UCL Digital Humanities] He was also a member of the SEAHA Steering Committee. [ref: 2nd International SEAHA Conference: Book of Abstracts, University College London] He was Deputy Director of UCL Institute for Sustainable Heritage until 2019. [ref: Matija Strlic – About, University College London]

He also taught on the MSc in Conservation for Archaeology and Museums at UCL Institute of Archaeology (2008-2019). [ref: Matija Strlic – Teaching, University College London]

Strlič served as a Senior Research Fellow at the Smithsonian Institution's Museum Conservation Institute between 2020 and 2022. [ref: Good pollution: Smells in museums, Columbia University Graduate School of Architecture, Planning and Preservation]

At the University of Ljubljana, Strlič is Professor of Analytical Chemistry and leads the Heritage Science Laboratory Ljubljana. He is listed among the teaching staff of the Chair of Analytical Chemistry [ref: Chair of Analytical Chemistry, University of Ljubljana, Faculty of Chemistry and Chemical Technology], where he has taught courses in Analytical chemistry (since 1997) and Natural sciences for conservators (since 2019).

He heads the Centre of Excellence in Green Heritage Science [ref: GreenHer CoE, "[https://greenher.uni-lj.si/about-us/ About us]", University of Ljubljana. Accessed 19 September 2026.], an interinstitutional Centre established in Slovenia and funded by the European Commission through the Teaming instrument of the Widening programme. [ref: European Commission, "[https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101136457 GreenHer Centre of Excellence: Green Heritage Science]", CORDIS, grant agreement No. 101136457, 2025.]

He is member of the European Academy of Sciences and Arts [ref: European Academy of Sciences and Arts, "[https://euro-acad.eu/fileGreetings.php?path=JcjqsJxxDEVPYnM7ciBE New Members Elected by the Senate]", 2024.] and is Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry and the International Institute for Conservation of Historic and Artistic Works. Strlič has been included in the Stanford–Elsevier list of the world's top 2% of scientists, [ref: Top 2% Scientists, TOPSCINET] and his Scopus author profile records more than 190 publications. [ref: Author details: Strlic, Matija, Scopus]

In 2002, Strlič received the Zois award for outstanding scientific contributions in chemistry, [ref: Nagrade in priznanja za izjemne dosežke v znanstveno-raziskovalni in razvojni dejavnosti – 2002, Ministrstvo za šolstvo, znanost in šport] and in 2015, he received the Ambassador of Science of the Republic of Slovenia Award. [ref: Nagrade in priznanja za izjemne dosežke v znanstveno-raziskovalni in razvojni dejavnosti – 2015, Ministrstvo za izobraževanje, znanost in šport] In 2026, Strlič received the Research Collaboration Index Arts & Humanities Subject Award in recognition of his highly collaborative and cross-disciplinary research. Street Fighter (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack) is the soundtrack album to the 2026 film Street Fighter directed by Kitao Sakurai which is based on the Street Fighter video game series by Capcom. The album features original score composed by Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson and two original songs by the industrial rock band Health. The album was released through Milan Records and Paramount Music on October 16, 2026.

== Background ==
Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson composed the score for Street Fighter renewing his association with Sakurai after their collaboration in Twisted Metal. The composers admitted that the music for the video game has been their core musical foundation that shaped their career as composers, having listened to "Guile's Theme" composed by Yoko Shimomura for the video game. The newer version of "Guile's Theme" served as a nod to the original theme, and had attempted the reinterpretation to be heavily substantial for the film. [ref: ‘Street Fighter’ Soundtrack Takes ‘Guile’s Theme’ From Arcade to Big Screen: See the Full Tracklist, [[Billboard (magazine)]

The composers added that the primary goal for them was to present each character with a unique musical identity, and they went ahead with a fan-pleasing approach by creating distinct sounds for the characters and had incorporated most of them for nostalgic moments. He also admitted the action choreography for E. Honda was the most unique segments to score for and praised the director for allowing unconventional experimentations with the music. The duo also expressed on incorporating the music of 50 Cent to create a seamless "dovetail" between the licensed pre-existing music and original compositions. [ref: Cobra Kai Composers Zach Robinson and Leo Birenberg on pleasing fans in Street Fighter]

Besides the score, the industrial rock band "Health" contributed two original songs—"Negative Edge" [ref: EXCLUSIVE: Health Drops New Street Fighter Film Track, Bleeding Cool] and "Brainrot". [ref: Listen: HEALTH Drops Two New Songs Written For 'Street Fighter' Movie, Metal Injection] [ref: HEALTH Share Two New Songs From The 'Street Fighter' Soundtrack, Stereogum] Guitarist Charlie Robbins also worked on few of the musical pieces as one of the featured soloists. [ref: “A dream come true”: Street Fighter soundtrack guitarist has been revealed, Guitar World]

== Release ==
The new adaptation of "Guile's Theme" was released as a single on September 30, 2026. [ref: First Track from ‘Street Fighter’ Soundtrack Released, Film Music Reporter] The soundtrack album featuring the songs and score was released through Milan Records and Paramount Music on October 16, 2026. [ref: ‘Street Fighter’ Soundtrack Album Details, Film Music Reporter] [ref: Street Fighter (Original Motion Picture Soundtrack), Apple Music]

== Reception ==
Zanobard Reviews assigned the score 7.5/10 saying, "The sheer enthusiasm of Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson’s bombastically electric guitar-led score for Street Fighter is a thing to behold by itself, so that combined with a killer ’90s-styled orchestral/electronic sound and countless references to iconic themes makes it so worth a listen." [ref: Street Fighter (2026) – Soundtrack Review, Zanobard Reviews] Ayaan Paul Chowdhury of The Hindu added that "few composers are better equipped to soundtrack men punching through their feelings than Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson of Cobra Kai fame". [ref: ‘Street Fighter’ movie review: Fists, fetishes and a fighting chance at cult status, The Hindu] Kristy Puchko of Mashable India wrote "The score by composers Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson leans on electric guitar and synth keyboards that throw back to '90s action-movie sensibilities." [ref: 'Street Fighter' Review: What If It's Giving Super Mario Bros Live-Action, But I Love That?, [[Mashable] Dan Bayer of Next Best Picture called it "a kinetic techno score by Leo Birenberg and Zach Robinson". [ref: "STREET FIGHTER" - Review, Next Best Picture]

Muisbertus

== Achtergrond ==

Muisbertus is een internetmeme verspreid op Nederlandse meme pagina's vanaf 2025. De meme wordt veelal in verband gebracht met de memepagina [https://rtvvannelle.nl/ RTVVanNelle], hoewel niet met zekerheid gezegd kan worden of de meme hier ook voor het eerst is geplaatst.

De meme toont een karakter wat doorgaans half mens en half muis is, hoewel het visueel vooral een mannelijk, menselijk gedaante is met wat kenmerken van een muis zoals:

- Meer (grijs) haar dan natuurlijk voor een mens

- Een duidelijke verticale spleet in de bovenlip

- Oren in de vorm van die van een muis

Verder toont de meme een klein deel van een menselijk lichaam met overwegend overgewicht, een oud aandoende huidstextuur en neutraal starende ogen van achter een bril. In de originele afbeelding draagt Muisbertus een blauw t-shirt, hoewel vooral hierin veel variatie is aangebracht in latere memes.

== Verhaal ==

Verschillende verhalen rondom Muisbertus doen de ronde sinds de introductie in 2025, waarin vaak wordt beweerd dat Muisbertus zich bezighoudt met de productie en verspreiding van harddrugs op een manier die vooral doet denken aan de hitserie Breaking Bad.

Muisbertus komt volgens het verhaal uit Hoogeveen en heeft verschillende vijanden, dan wel kennissen die ook in verband worden gebracht met de onderwereld, zoals Kakeltinus, Miauwtinus en Grombertus.

The official website of the Council of Representatives of Iraq lists him among the representatives of Basra Governorate and as a member of the Iraqi Foundation Coalition. [ref: Members of the Council of Representatives of Iraq, Council of Representatives of Iraq]

According to the Iraqi Parliamentary Monitor, Al-Haidari is affiliated with the Wated Iraqi Gathering within the Iraqi Foundation Coalition. The same source states that he is a member of the Oil, Gas and Natural Resources Committee and holds a bachelor's degree. It also records two electoral terms and 7,117 votes. [ref: Alaa Sabah Marai Shahaf Al-Haidari, Iraqi Parliamentary Monitor]

== Political career ==

=== Membership of the Council of Representatives ===
By May 2022, Al-Haidari was a member of the Council of Representatives. At the time, Shafaq News described him as an independent representative from Basra Governorate. [ref: Parliamentarian puts forward Basra demands, including protesters' condition for voting on the food security law, Shafaq News]

On 19 May 2022, Shafaq News reported statements made by Al-Haidari during a press conference held at the Council of Representatives building. He called for the completion of the project to designate Basra as Iraq's economic capital and for the resolution of the governorate's petro-dollar issue. He also called for the demands of Basra's protesters to be included in the budget and the food security law.

The demands included the appointment of graduates of science colleges, as well as addressing the status of contract workers and daily-wage workers. Al-Haidari said that including these demands was a condition for voting on the Emergency Support Law or the budget, according to Shafaq News.

=== Chairmanship of the Iraqi Foundation Coalition parliamentary bloc ===
On 5 January 2026, the National Iraqi News Agency (NINA) reported that Al-Haidari, a representative from Basra Governorate, had been chosen as chairman of the Iraqi Foundation Coalition parliamentary bloc during the sixth legislative term of the Council of Representatives. [ref: Al-Haidari named chairman of the Foundation Coalition parliamentary bloc, National Iraqi News Agency]

On 3 June 2026, the President of Iraq received a delegation from the Iraqi Foundation Coalition parliamentary bloc, headed by Representative Alaa Al-Haidari, at Al-Salam Palace in Baghdad. GoMore is a Danish car-sharing company based in Copenhagen. It provides a platform for private individuals to rent out cars and also offers car leasing. In Spain, it operates under the name Amovens. [ref: Getaround Europe and GoMore merge to create Europe's largest peer-to-peer carsharing network, Tech.eu]

In May 2026, GoMore acquired the European operations of the American car-sharing company Getaround. The two businesses reported a combined total of more than five million users across 11 European countries. [ref: GoMore Becomes Europe's Largest Peer-to-Peer Car-Sharing Platform After Acquiring Getaround Europe, Øresund Startups]

== History ==

GoMore began in 2005 as a non-profit ride-sharing website, founded by Matias Møl Dalsgaard and Søren Riis. [ref: Gomore: fem år og to millioner brugere senere, TechSavvy] It became a for-profit business in 2011 and introduced peer-to-peer car rental and leasing services in 2014. [ref: Business model diversification in the sharing economy: The case of GoMore, Journal of Cleaner Production]

GoMore expanded into Sweden in 2014. [ref: Så blir bilsemestern billig, Dagens Nyheter] In March 2015, it acquired Amovens, a Spanish ride-sharing service founded by Diego Hidalgo in 2009. [ref: Spanish car sharing platform Amovens acquired by GoMore, Novobrief] It launched in France in 2016.

By 2017, GoMore had become Denmark's largest ride-sharing service, with more than 645,000 Danish members. [ref: Deleøkonomien i Danmark]

GoMore launched in Finland in late 2020. [ref: Oman auton voi vuokrata tuntemattomalle jopa ilman, että on itse paikalla, Yle] In April 2021, the Swiss insurance company Baloise invested approximately €5 million in GoMore. [ref: Baloise kauft sich bei dänischer Carsharing-Firma GoMore ein, cash.ch] GoMore launched in Switzerland in October 2021, [ref: Geld verdienen mit dem eigenen Auto?, Luzerner Zeitung] Austria in 2022 [ref: GoMore: So funktioniert die neue private Autovermietung in Österreich, Trending Topics] and Estonia in March 2024. [ref: Eestis alustab inimeselt inimesele autode jagamise platvorm GoMore, Raamatupidamisuudised]

GoMore closed its ride-sharing service in Denmark in February 2026. By then, Denmark was the only country where GoMore still offered ride-sharing. The company said it would focus on car rental and leasing. [ref: GoMore dropper samkørsel i Danmark, TV 2] [ref: GoMore dropper samkørsel: Ikke nok opbakning til idéen, Ingeniøren]

In May 2026, GoMore acquired Getaround's European business, which operated in several countries, including France, Norway, Belgium and Germany. The purchase was financed through investments from existing shareholders and loans from EIFO and Nordea.

At the time of the acquisition, the companies reported approximately 70,000 shared cars, 1.5 million annual rentals and net revenue exceeding €50 million. [ref: GoMore übernimmt Getaround Europe und wird größte Carsharing-Plattform Europas, Trending Topics] Getaround continued to operate as a separate platform. [ref: Getaround and GoMore: a new chapter for carsharing in Europe, Getaround]

== Services ==

GoMore allows private individuals to list cars for rent through its website and app. Renters can book available cars, some of which can be unlocked through the app without meeting the owner.

The company also offers car leasing. [ref: Nya tjänster för delad mobilitet, Trafikanalys] Its GoMore+ subscription provides discounts on car rentals. [ref: New: Get a discount every time you rent a car with GoMore+, GoMore]

Kirk T. McDonald is an American experimental physicist specializing in high-energy physics and strong-field quantum electrodynamics. He is a professor emeritus in the Department of Physics at Princeton University.

== Biography ==

=== Education ===
McDonald first studied at the University of Arizona, where he earned his Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in physics in 1966. He pursued his graduate studies at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), completing his PhD titled Inelastic Photoproduction of Pi Mesons from Hydrogen and Deuterium at Energies Between 1.3 and 1.8 GeV in 1972 under the supervision of Clemens A. Heusch. [ref: Inelastic Photoproduction of Pi Mesons from Hydrogen and Deuterium at Energies Between 1.3 and 1.8 GeV, Caltech / ProQuest Dissertations]

=== Academic career ===
From 1973 to 1975, he conducted postdoctoral research as a Fellow at CERN in Geneva, before becoming a researcher at the Enrico Fermi Institute at the University of Chicago.

In 1976, he joined the faculty of Princeton University as an assistant professor. He was granted tenure in 1980 and spent the remainder of his academic career there at the Joseph Henry Laboratories. [ref: Kirk McDonald's Research Interests, Princeton University] He is currently a professor emeritus.

== Research and contributions ==
McDonald's research focuses on major international experimental programs in particle physics and the development of innovative detectors.

=== Strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) ===
In the 1990s, he led the notable SLAC E-144 experiment at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC). This experiment successfully produced matter directly from light-by-light collisions (nonlinear Breit–Wheeler process) by colliding a 46.6 GeV electron beam with an ultra-intense picosecond laser pulse, [ref: Observation of Nonlinear Effects in Compton Scattering, Physical Review Letters] thereby validating fundamental predictions of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. [ref: Positron Production in Multiphoton Light-by-Light Scattering, Physical Review Letters]

=== Neutrino physics and flavor ===

Kirk T. McDonald is an American experimental physicist who works in high-energy physics and strong-field quantum electrodynamics. He is a professor emeritus in the Department of Physics at Princeton University.

== Biography ==

=== Education ===
McDonald studied at the University of Arizona, earning a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in physics in 1966. He completed his PhD in experimental high-energy particle physics at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) in 1972, under the supervision of Clemens A. Heusch. [ref: Inelastic Photoproduction of Pi Mesons from Hydrogen and Deuterium at Energies Between 1.3 and 1.8 GeV, Caltech / ProQuest Dissertations]

=== Academic career ===
From 1973 to 1975, he was a postdoctoral Fellow at CERN in Geneva, and subsequently worked as a researcher at the Enrico Fermi Institute at the University of Chicago.

In 1976, he joined the faculty of Princeton University as an assistant professor. He was granted tenure in 1980 and conducted his research at the Joseph Henry Laboratories. [ref: Kirk McDonald's Research Interests, Princeton University] He later became a professor emeritus.

== Research and contributions ==
McDonald's research involves experimental programs in particle physics and detector development.

=== Strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) ===
In the 1990s, he led the SLAC E-144 experiment at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC). This experiment studied the production of matter from light-by-light collisions (the nonlinear Breit–Wheeler process) by colliding a 46.6 GeV electron beam with a picosecond laser pulse, [ref: Observation of Nonlinear Effects in Compton Scattering, Physical Review Letters] providing data for predictions in strong-field quantum electrodynamics. [ref: Positron Production in Multiphoton Light-by-Light Scattering, Physical Review Letters]

=== Neutrino physics ===
McDonald has participated in several neutrino and CP violation experiments:
* He was a member of the Daya Bay Reactor Neutrino Experiment in China, which measured the neutrino mixing angle θ13. [ref: Observation of Electron-Antineutrino Disappearance at Daya Bay, Physical Review Letters] As a member of this collaboration, he shared the 2016 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. [ref: Laureates: Daya Bay Collaboration, Breakthrough Prize]
* He worked on the BaBar experiment at SLAC, which studied CP violation in B meson decays. [ref: Observation of CP Violation in the $B^0$ Meson System, Physical Review Letters]
* He has contributed to research regarding neutrino factories, targetry for muon production, [ref: High-Power Targets for Muon (and Neutrino) Production, arXiv] and the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE).

=== Electromagnetism physics notes ===
McDonald maintains a collection of educational problems and technical notes in classical electromagnetism. He has authored over 1,200 scientific notes addressing physics problems related to Maxwell's equations, radiation reaction forces, and the dynamics of relativistic charges.

Johnny O'Reilly (born 22 October 1970) is an Irish filmmaker and journalist. He wrote and directed the Russian-language feature films Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) and The Weather Station (2010), and the short film The Terms (2002), which was shortlisted for the 74th Academy Awards. [ref: Our man in Moscow, The Irish Times] [ref: 'I want to see out the war': Irish filmmaker moved to Ukraine from Russia when 'the pessimists were proved right', The Irish Times] [ref: Red Letter Day, The Sunday Times] As a journalist, he has reported from Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine for publications including The Sunday Times, The Times, and The Irish Times.

== Early life and education ==
O'Reilly grew up in Dublin, Ireland. He studied Russian and Classics at Trinity College Dublin. In 1993, while a student, he worked in Moscow as a freelance reporter covering the Russian constitutional crisis. In 1996, he completed graduate film studies at New York University. He worked at The Sunday Times for two years before focusing on filmmaking. In 2006, he moved to Moscow, where he lived for ten years.

== Career ==

=== Filmmaking ===

==== The Terms (2002) ====
O'Reilly directed the short film The Terms (2002), based on a short story by Irish writer Mike McCormack. The film was shortlisted for the 74th Academy Awards. [ref: The Terms Shortlisted for Oscars, IFTN]

==== The Weather Station (2010) ====
His feature directorial debut was the Russian-language thriller The Weather Station (2010). The film was set in an arctic meteorological outpost and filmed near Simferopol in Crimea. [ref: The Weather Station, Variety]

==== Moscow Never Sleeps (2016) ====
O’Reilly wrote and directed Moscow Never Sleeps (2016), an ensemble drama set during Moscow City Day celebrations. The film follows interconnected stories over a single day.

==== Kherson ====
O'Reilly subsequently began work on a documentary project focused on events in Kherson and the surrounding region.

=== Journalism and cultural initiatives ===
O'Reilly has reported on politics and culture in Eastern Europe. His reporting has appeared in outlets including The Sunday Times, The Times, and The Irish Times.

In 2008, he co-founded the Irish Film Festival in Moscow, which ran for eleven years and held events in multiple Russian cities.

=== Russian television incident ===
In August 2015, O'Reilly appeared live on Russian state television to discuss Moscow Never Sleeps. During the interview, he described Ukrainian filmmaker Oleg Sentsov as a political prisoner, after which the broadcast was cut short. [ref: Russian TV Cuts Away After Irish Director Backs Jailed Ukrainian Filmmaker Oleg Sentsov, The Hollywood Reporter] [ref: Russian TV cuts off Irish director after backing jailed filmmaker, The Irish Times]

Draft text:
EuroNatur is a German foundation based in Radolfzell that supports nature conservation projects in Europe. The foundation was established in 1987 by Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland (BUND), Environmental Action Germany (DUH) and Naturschutzbund Deutschland (NABU). EuroNatur is a member of the Deutschen Naturschutzring.

== Mission ==
The foundation's mission is to protect Europe's diverse natural heritage. Its projects focus on wild animals such as wolves, brown bears, lynxes and endangered migratory birds, as well as valuable natural and cultural sites. The foundation's motto is “connecting nature and people”, which reflects its belief that restoring nature, conserving wildlife and improving biodiversity are fundamental to human quality of life. Working with local people helps ensure the long-term success of their projects to protect endangered animals and their habitats in Europe.

EuroNatur is heavily involved with the European Green Belt initiative, a collaborative cross-border project which aims to create a wild, biodiverse corridor along the route of the former Iron Curtain. Since 2004, EuroNatur has coordinated the conservation efforts along the Balkan Green Belt, the southernmost section of the European Green Belt. [ref: EGB: Home, www.europeangreenbelt.org]

== Operations and administration ==
The foundation works with scientists, conservationists, farmers, politicians and entrepreneurs from across Europe. A key part of the foundation’s work takes place in the Balkans, for which they work with local conservationists and volunteers to plan and establish a large network of nature reserves, along with species conservation projects for wolves, bears, lynxes and migratory birds based on scientific research. EuroNatur organises workshops, seminars and training programmes to share knowledge and experiences that help protect Europe’s wild animals. EuroNatur also engages in political lobbying in EU institutions.

EuroNatur's first president was Claus-Peter Hutter, followed by Hartmut Vogtmann between January 2008 and early July 2011. Christel Schroeder served from October 2011 to the end of 2019, and Thomas Potthast has been president since 1 January 2020. Gabriel Schwaderer is the executive director of EuroNatur. [ref: Gabriel Schwaderer, EuroNatur]

== Funding ==
The foundation is funded through donations, third-party funding and income from foundation capital. EuroNatur has been awarded the DZI Donation Seal by the German Central Institute for Social Issues (DZI).

== European Stork Villages ==
The European Stork Village network was set up by EuroNatur in 1994 as a way of publicly recognising communities across Europe that are making a significant contribution to protecting their local white stork populations. Representatives from each of the Stork Villages meet every year in one of the member villages to discuss and develop solutions for the conservation of white storks. There are currently 16 recognised European Stork Villages. [ref: “European Stork Villages” initiative, EuroNatur]

The most recent village to be recognised and added to the network was Knepp Wildland and Storrington in 2025, the first and only Stork Village in the UK. [ref: European Stork Villages Network, White Stork Project] The village was honoured in recognition of its conservation and rewilding programme which led to the return of the white stork to the area. The village of Storrington holds its White Stork and Nature Festival each year to celebrate its conservation efforts and the return of its white stork population.

== Awards ==
The foundation has been running its EuroNatur Award since 1992. [ref: Award for Environmental Excellence, EuroNatur]

EuroNatur runs an annual photography competition called European Treasures of Nature in partnership with the NaturVision film festival, Natur magazine and German utility company Gelsenwasser. The winning entries are displayed in a year-long touring exhibition titled Fascinating Nature and featured in the next year's EuroNatur calendar. [ref: European Treasures of Nature, EuroNatur]

== References ==

The album 10 Pujaan Malindo was recorded in two volumes, released in 1986 and 1987. This album series was launched in 1986 by Life Records (Hup Hup Sdn. Bhd.).

== Background ==
After taking part in an audition organised by RTM, the winner of the 1985 RTM Bintang competition, Noraniza Idris, was approached by Hamidi, the publisher and producer at Life Records, who wanted her to become a recording artist because he was captivated by the sweetness of her voice; The offer first arose whilst she was still participating in the 1985 RTM Star competition, which had not yet concluded. At the time, she was with her father, Idris Ahmad, enjoying a meal at the Angkasapuri canteen—the venue where she had taken the RTM talent test. Eventually, after much consideration, she agreed to sign a contract with Life Records on 1 January 1986 and officially became a recording artist – marking the first recording contract of her career. She also released her debut album, a compilation titled Melayu Deli, alongside a legendary singer of the 1980s on 1 January 1986. Meanwhile, he had taken part in the 1985 Bintang RTM competition, though he only reached the semi-finals; however, he remained resilient, and perhaps Hamidi’s arrival and his official status as a recording artist served as the remedy he had been seeking all along. [ref: NORANIZA IDRIS: 12 LAGU PALING POPULAR SEPANJANG ZAMAN, GALAKSIVIRAL]

The release of the album 10 Pujaan Malindo Vol.1 in 1986 on the Life Records label (Hup Hup Sdn. Bhd.) marked a highly significant milestone in Noraniza Idris’s professional discography. This major project was released at a time when the regional music market was witnessing a vibrant wave of cultural exchange between Malaysia and Indonesia (the acronym for ‘Malindo’). As a new singer establishing her name in the 1980s, Noraniza was sent to Jakarta, Indonesia, to undertake the vocal recording and musical arrangement process on location. This strategic move by the record company was taken to ensure that the resulting archipelago-inspired music possessed authentic aesthetic value and high production standards. The album’s extraordinary success in the market not only placed her on the mainstream industry’s radar but also paved the way for the production of its sequel, 10 Pujaan Malindo Vol.2, which was released the following year. [ref: A local dad behind an acclaimed Amazon Prime documentary becomes patron of the children's hospice that cared for his son, Wigan Today]

== Early life and education ==
Paul went to Latham high school in Skelmersdale and then attended Wigan and Leigh College where he studied electrical engineering. It was a year later that he decided drama would be his chosen path so he switched to St Helens College to study theatre performance and then eventually gained a degree under the University of Central Lancashire UCLAN. Early is his acting career, Paul starred in two British independent feature films The Treasure of Albion 2006 and The School that Roared in 2009. Those films were produced by the co-operative British film Academy or the BYFA. [ref: Paul Woodward, Derian House Children's Hospice]

Paul stepped away from the creative industries for several years to care for his son who needed 24/7 care at the time. In 2017, Paul decided to join the Academy of Live and Recorded Arts ALRA in Wigan, where he gained a masters in professional acting, this was the start of his journey creating Old Swan Films.

== Career ==
Early in his career, Paul cut his teeth in many disciplines from cabaret to UK stage tours and short films, after gaining his master’s in 2018 he created Old Swan Films with Thomas Elliott Griffiths. Old Swan Films is a Liverpool based film production company, the pair often work on socially impactful films and also work towards developing talent behind the camera.

In 2025 Paul produced The Little Things feature documentary which was directed by Thomas Elliott Griffiths and saw multi-BAFTA winning actor and writer Steve Pemberton joint as an executive Producer. The film was created from Paul's own experience after his son attended Derian House Children's Hospice for several years. The film was picked up by American distribution company Buffalo 8 and then was globally released on Amazon Prime. In early 2026 Paul then produced and directed Voice Again an 18 minute documentary which was in support of other father's who had lost a child, as-well as men's mental health charities, this short documentary took Paul to the BBC morning sofa.

Paul also produced the satirical feminist thriller Time to Go which was directed by Thomas Elliott Griffiths this film was in support of RASA Merseyside, a sexual abuse charity. The film has gone on to win multiple awards and be seen on the film festival circuit across the UK. Paul also had a support role in the film. [ref: Thomas Elliott Griffiths, Edge Hill University]

== Advocacy and philanthropy ==
Paul was made a patron of Derian House Children's Hospice after creating The Little Things, it is very much a place close to his heart as his son spent several years at the hospice before passing away in 2019. This experience has inspired much of his documentary work to date and Paul continues to look for powerful stories to tell. [ref: BBC News] [ref: BBC News]

Since becoming a Patron, Paul has had many opportunities to speak and share his work at major health events across the country, early in 2026 Paul was able to show The Little Things at the 2026 Royal College of Nursing annual conference in Liverpool. [ref: Derian House documentary moves healthcare workers to tears, Lancashire Telegraph]

There was also a special screening by Hospice UK at the Everyman Cinema at Kings Cross, London in September 2026. [ref: Derian House documentary screened at London cinema, Lancashire Telegraph]

In June 2026, during Children’s Hospice Week and in partnership with Together for short Lives, Paul gave a speech at the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) in Westminster and spoke about the vital need for more funding for our UK children's hospices. [ref: Paul’s story: Our most precious moments, Together for Short Lives]

Draft text:
HURR is a UK fashion rental and resale platform founded by Victoria Prew in 2018 [ref: How HURR Became The Go-To Place To Create The Perfect Vacation Wardrobe, Forbes]. The platform supports peer-to-peer rentals between users as well as managed rentals, with garments supplied by fashion brands and retailers. Lauren Roberts is HURR's current CEO after Prew stepped away from her role [ref: Hurr co-founder Victoria Prew steps down as CEO, Drapers].

History

HURR was founded by Victoria Prew in 2018, who said the idea for the company came from the growth of sharing-economy businesses such as Airbnb and Uber. The platform launched during the 2018 Christmas period as a peer-to-peer fashion rental service.

In 2020, HURR opened a rental pop-up at Selfridges in London. The pop-up stocked around 200 garments from brands including Rixo, Ganni, Mara Hoffman and Gucci, that customers could rent for either 4 or 8 days. [ref: Hurr Collective is launching the first in-store wardrobe rental pop-up at Selfridges, The Standard].

HURR later began providing rental services for fashion brands and retailers. In 2021, the company developed a white-label service called HURR Enterprise where retailers could operate rental services under their own brands. Selfridges Rental was an early client of the service

Forbes included founder Victoria Prew in its 30 Under 30 list and in 2021, HURR was named among the world's top 50 retail technology start-ups [ref: HURR: The Tech Start-Up Leading The UK’s Fashion Rental Revolution, Forbes]. The company has also received venture capital investment as part of its growth within this industry (fashion technology and circular fashion) [ref: Leading UK fashion rental platform HURR joins our portfolio, Praetura Ventures]. They secured £7.9m in a fundraising round led by Praetura Ventures [ref: Hurr secures $10m in funding, Drapers].

By 2022, HURR was working with more than 130 fashion brands and operating rental services for retailers including Selfridges, John Lewis and Matches Fashion [ref: ‘It’s more sustainable – and I still get to wear something new every weekend’: how rental fashion became big business, The Guardian]. In the same year, the company became the first fashion rental platform to achieve B Corporation certification [ref: Hurr co-founder Victoria Prew steps down as CEO, Drapers].

Business Model

HURR operates a fashion rental marketplace with brands such as Fendi, Ganni and The Row having been listed as available to rent through the platform [ref: 20 pledges for 2020: Renting clothes could be the trick to help me curb my fast fashion habits, Independent].

The company offers peer-to-peer (P2P) rentals, where users can rent their clothing directly to other users, and managed rentals, where stock is supplied by fashion brands and partners. Customers can rent items for 4, 8, 16 or 30-day options [ref: Hurr launches bundle rental service, Drapers].

In May 2024, HURR Flex launched, a credit-based rental service. Customers can purchase bundles of rental credits to use on items available through the marketplace by spending £99 for £170 credit points or £125 for £225 [ref: Hurr launches bundle rental service, Drapers].

Alongside P2P rentals, HURR provides rental services to fashion brands and retailers through HURR Enterprise. The service allows brands to operate rental platforms under their own branding, with HURR providing the technology and operational services.

HURR launched a resale service in 2023 where users could make offers to purchase garments listed on the platform [ref: Rental platform Hurr launches resale, Drapers].

Partnerships

Vogue has reported that HURR works with more than 100 brands and retailers. Its retail partnerships have included Selfridges, John Lewis, Matches Fashion and Flannels [ref: The 6 Best Fashion Rental Sites In The UK, British Vogue].

In 2023, HURR partnered with Depop to launch “The Loop by HURR”, where the collection consisted of previously rented garments offered for resale. In the same year, Net-a-Porter also launched its first rental edit on the platform [ref: Net-A-Porter debuts rental collection with By Rotation and Hurr, Drapers].

In November 2024, HURR partnered with Deliveroo on a rental delivery service within central London where customers could receive their rental orders in under 20 minutes by bike couriers [ref: HURR teams up with Deliveroo to deliver dresses in just 20 minutes, The Industry Fashion] [ref: Hurr taps Deliveroo for same-day fashion rental delivery, Drapers].

Reaction and Impact

A HURR user has earned more than £100 000 from renting clothing through the platform after starting to list items in 2021 [ref: How fashion became the go-to side hustle for working mothers, Bazaar].

In October 2026, HURR partnered with Sky to allow customers to rent original designer pieces worn by Sienna Miller and other cast members in the drama series, War [ref: Want to Dress Like Sienna Miller in the New Sky Series ‘War’? Hurr Rentals Can Make It Happen, WWD].

== Green Mountain Gringo ==
Green Mountain Gringo is an American brand of salsa and tortilla strips owned by TW Garner Food Company, also known as Garner Foods, a food manufacturer based in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. The brand was founded in Vermont in 1989 and is known primarily for its line of all-natural jarred salsas made with ingredients including tomatoes, tomatillos, onions, peppers, garlic, herbs and spices. [ref: Our Story, Green Mountain Gringo]

Green Mountain Gringo products include traditional, roasted and cantina-style salsas in multiple heat levels, as well as corn tortilla strips. The brand's products are sold through grocery retailers in the United States and through its online store.

=== History: ===
Green Mountain Gringo was founded in 1989 in Vermont by Christine and David Hume. [ref: Green Mountain Gringo, Vermont Roots, Inc]

The Humes developed the original Green Mountain Gringo salsa recipe at their farm in Chester, Vermont, initially making salsa in small batches using produce and a simple combination of vegetables, herbs and spices. As demand increased, the brand expanded beyond its local origins. [ref: Green Mountain Gringo, Vermont Roots, Inc]

Green Mountain Gringo was subsequently acquired by TW Garner Food Company, a family-owned food manufacturer headquartered in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. TW Garner Food Company is also the maker of the Texas Pete brand of hot sauces and condiments. [ref: Our Story, Green Mountain Gringo]

Following the acquisition, production of Green Mountain Gringo expanded and the brand developed national retail distribution while retaining salsa as its primary product category.

== Products: ==
Green Mountain Gringo's principal product line is jarred salsa. Its salsa portfolio has included:

* Mild Salsa
* Medium Salsa
* Hot Salsa
* Roasted Garlic Medium Salsa
* Roasted Chile Pepper Medium Salsa
* Cantina Mild Salsa
* Cantina Medium Salsa
* Cantina Roasted Garlic Salsa
* Cantina Salsa Verde Salsa
* Mango Habanero Hot Salsa

The brand also produces tortilla strips, including yellow corn, multigrain, blue corn and white corn varieties. Some varieties of its tortilla strips are made with organic corn. [ref: All Products - Complete Product Listing, Green Mountain Gringo]

Green Mountain Gringo salsa varieties range from mild to hot. The brand uses combinations of jalapeño, pasilla and serrano peppers to produce different heat profiles.

=== Ingredients and certifications: ===
Green Mountain Gringo positions its salsa around relatively simple ingredient formulations. Ingredients found across its salsa varieties include tomatoes, onions, tomatillos, apple cider vinegar, jalapeño peppers, pasilla peppers, serrano peppers, cilantro, parsley, garlic, sea salt and cumin. [ref: Medium Salsa, Green Mountain Gringo]

Green Mountain Gringo salsas are Certified Gluten-Free, Non-GMO Project Verified, and certified kosher. The company's salsas are also certified by the American Vegetarian Association. [ref: FAQs, Green Mountain Gringo]

The company's salsa products do not contain the major food allergens identified on their ingredient labels, although they are manufactured on a line that also produces products containing soy. [ref: FAQs, Green Mountain Gringo]

=== Ownership and manufacturing ===
Green Mountain Gringo is owned by TW Garner Food Company, which operates under the Garner Foods name and is headquartered in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. [ref: Our Story, Green Mountain Gringo]

Garner Foods traces its history to 1929 and is best known as the manufacturer of Texas Pete hot sauce. The company manufactures and markets products under both the Texas Pete and Green Mountain Gringo brands.

Green Mountain Gringo products are manufactured in Winston-Salem, North Carolina. [ref: Our Story, Green Mountain Gringo]

=== Brand development ===
In 2025, Green Mountain Gringo introduced redesigned packaging and a broader brand refresh. The redesign included updated salsa and tortilla-strip packaging, a redesigned website, new retail materials and a marketing campaign using the phrase "Let's Gringo!"

The company also expanded its salsa portfolio with a line of Cantina salsas, developed to provide a smoother, restaurant-style consistency than the brand's traditional salsa varieties.

The Cantina range includes mild, medium, hot and roasted garlic varieties. [ref: All Products - Complete Product Listing, Green Mountain Gringo]

=== Distribution ===
Green Mountain Gringo products are distributed through grocery and food retailers in the United States as well as through [https://Greenmountaingringo.com Greenmountaingringo.com] and Amazon.

At the introduction of its expanded Cantina salsa line in 2025, the company reported that the products were available through more than 2,600 retail stores nationwide.

Draft text:
EuroNatur is a German foundation based in Radolfzell that supports nature conservation projects in Europe. The foundation was established in 1987 by Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland (BUND), Environmental Action Germany (DUH) and Naturschutzbund Deutschland (NABU). EuroNatur is a member of the Deutschen Naturschutzring.

== Mission ==
The foundation's mission is to protect Europe's diverse natural heritage. Its projects focus on wild animals such as wolves, brown bears, lynxes and endangered migratory birds, as well as valuable natural and cultural sites. The foundation's motto is "connecting nature and people", which reflects its belief that restoring nature, conserving wildlife and improving biodiversity are fundamental to human quality of life. Working with local people helps ensure the long-term success of their projects to protect endangered animals and their habitats in Europe.

EuroNatur is heavily involved with the European Green Belt initiative, a collaborative cross-border project which aims to create a wild, biodiverse corridor along the route of the former Iron Curtain. Since 2004, EuroNatur has coordinated the conservation efforts along the Balkan Green Belt, the southernmost section of the European Green Belt. [ref: EGB: Home, www.europeangreenbelt.org]

== Operations and administration ==
The foundation works with scientists, conservationists, farmers, politicians and entrepreneurs from across Europe. A key part of the foundation's work takes place in the Balkans, for which they work with local conservationists and volunteers to plan and establish a large network of nature reserves, along with species conservation projects for wolves, bears, lynxes and migratory birds based on scientific research. EuroNatur organises workshops, seminars and training programmes to share knowledge and experiences that help protect Europe's wild animals. EuroNatur also engages in political lobbying in EU institutions.

EuroNatur's first president was Claus-Peter Hutter, followed by Hartmut Vogtmann between January 2008 and early July 2011. Christel Schroeder served from October 2011 to the end of 2019, and Thomas Potthast has been president since 1 January 2020. Gabriel Schwaderer is the executive director of EuroNatur.

== Funding ==
The foundation is funded through donations, third-party funding and income from foundation capital. EuroNatur has been awarded the DZI Donation Seal by the German Central Institute for Social Issues (DZI).

== European Stork Villages ==
The European Stork Village network was set up by EuroNatur in 1994 as a way of publicly recognising communities across Europe that are making a significant contribution to protecting their local white stork populations. [ref: Ferger, Stefan & Schwaderer, Gabriel. (2016). The European Stork Villages - a successful combination of nature conservation and sustainable development of rural areas.] Representatives from each of the Stork Villages meet every year in one of the member villages to discuss and develop solutions for the conservation of white storks. There are currently 16 recognised European Stork Villages.

The most recent village to be recognised and added to the network was Knepp Wildland and Storrington in 2025, the first and only Stork Village in the UK. [ref: European Stork Villages Network, White Stork Project] The village was honoured in recognition of its conservation and rewilding programme which led to the return of the white stork to the area. The village of Storrington holds its White Stork and Nature Festival each year to celebrate its conservation efforts and the return of its white stork population.

== Awards ==
The foundation has been running its EuroNatur Award since 1992. [ref: Award for Environmental Excellence, EuroNatur]

EuroNatur runs an annual photography competition called European Treasures of Nature in partnership with the NaturVision film festival, Natur magazine and German utility company Gelsenwasser. The winning entries are displayed in a year-long touring exhibition titled Fascinating Nature and featured in the next year's EuroNatur calendar.

Ada Kate Uchegbu (born September 30, 1982) is a Nigerian journalist, writer, and political figure. Born in Ebute Metta, Lagos State, she serves as the Chief Executive Officer of ADA Consolidated Nigeria Limited and the Editor of Distinguished Africans Magazine. Over a multi-decade career in public life, she has worked as an investigative reporter covering regional security, managed diversified corporate portfolios, and contested multiple electoral positions, culminating in a declaration for the 2027 presidential election cycle.

== Early life and education ==
Ada Kate Uchegbu was born on September 30, 1982, in the Ebute Metta area of Lagos State, Nigeria. She began her secondary education at Command Secondary School in Ipaja, Lagos, and later completed her secondary studies at Apata Memorial High School in Isolo, Lagos. She completed her higher education at the National Open University of Nigeria. To specialize in communication and language, she undertook vocational courses at the National Broadcast Academy in Lagos and studied at Alliance Française Lagos. She holds the traditional Igbo title of Iyom Omelorah.

== Career ==
=== Media and corporate leadership ===
Uchegbu worked as an investigative reporter focusing on regional insecurity, economic disparities, and institutional governance across West Africa. Her written work includes the investigative report "Roads of Blood – The Kidnap Highway", which examined systemic highway kidnapping infrastructure within Nigeria.

She directs commercial operations as the Chief Executive Officer of ADA Consolidated Nigeria Limited, a conglomerate operating across real estate, media publishing, and the oil and gas sectors. As part of her media portfolio, she serves as the Editor of Distinguished Africans Magazine, a pan-African publication that documents regional leadership, corporate enterprise, cultural promotion, and profiles of contemporary African innovators.

=== Literary works ===
As an author, Uchegbu has published both non-fiction political works and fiction:
* Wings of Destiny: My Journey Through Power, Politics and the Dream of Nigeria's First Female President (2026) – A memoir analyzing female political inclusion and party ticket dynamics in contemporary Nigeria.
* Ada the Future President – A children's book series centered on civic responsibility and leadership development.
* Kidnapped and The Dark Testament – Fiction novels dealing with modern socio-political anxieties.
* African Short Horror Stories – A multi-volume fiction anthology incorporating traditional folklore, superstition, and supernatural motifs.

== Political career and recognition ==
Uchegbu has engaged in local and national politics for over fifteen years. She began her electoral career by contesting the 2011 elections for the Anambra State House of Assembly. The following year, she entered national party politics during the March 2012 Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) National Convention, running as an aspirant from Anambra State for the position of National Women Leader. On May 30, 2017, she received recognition from the National Youth Council of Nigeria (NYCN), winning an award in the emerging youth category. Later that year, she joined the All Progressives Congress (APC) and stood as one of only three female aspirants out of twenty-six total candidates cleared to contest the August 2017 APC gubernatorial primary election ahead of the Anambra State governorship election.

In mid-2025, Uchegbu announced her intention to run for the President of Nigeria in the 2027 general elections under the PDP banner, presenting a policy blueprint titled "The New Covenant". Her campaign platform emphasized breaking recycled leadership patterns through digitized public administration, establishing a ₦150 billion Youth Enterprise Fund, and decentralizing policing systems. After the 2026 party selection cycles favored male candidates for major tickets, she transitioned into wider policy advocacy. In late 2026, she spoke on electoral inclusion and African female leadership at the African Women Summit in Croydon, England.

== Media appearances ==
Uchegbu has used television and radio broadcast segments to critique national security frameworks and support gender parity in politics. Between late 2025 and 2026, she completed a series of interviews on Silverbird Television and Radio Nigeria network news updates. Her media commentary focused on public community health reforms, economic restructuring, and structural changes to political primary nomination rules.

== Family ==

Nomenclature & Classification

Full Name: H5N1 influenza virus, clade [ip]b

Virus Family: Orthomyxoviridae (influenza)

Genetic Lineage: Emerged from H5N8 (clade [ip]) during 2016–2020 H5N8 outbreak

Timeline

2020: Clade [ip]b first detected; marks beginning of 2020–2026 global outbreak

2020–2023: Rapid global expansion across avian populations

2023–2026: Spillover into mammalian species; expanded ecological range

2024: Detected in Antarctica (Danger Islands penguin deaths)

Geographic Distribution

Primary: Asia, Europe, North America, Africa

Recent: South America, Antarctic region

Status: Pandemic strain; circulating on all inhabited continents

Key Characteristics

Dominance: Primary circulating H5N1 clade globally since 2020

Adaptation: Enhanced capacity to infect diverse bird species and mammals

Severity: High mortality rates in poultry and wild birds; increasing mammalian spillover

Transmission: Primarily via direct contact and contaminated environments; limited human-to-human transmission

Affected Species

Primary: Domestic poultry (chickens, turkeys, ducks); wild waterfowl

Secondary: Penguins, seabirds, marine mammals (seals, sea lions)

Spillover: Terrestrial mammals (minks, foxes, raccoons); occasional human infections

Public Health Impact

Human Cases: Sporadic, rare; limited human-to-human transmission documented

Mortality (Human): High case fatality rate when infections occur (~50%)

Economic: Billions in poultry culling and trade losses

Pandemic Risk: Monitored by WHO; intermediate zoonotic threat (lower than pandemic influenza risk)

Surveillance: WHO, FAO, OIE coordinate global monitoring

Genomic Tracking: Continuous sequencing reveals sub-lineage evolution

Poultry Deaths/Culls: Hundreds of millions

Wildlife Deaths: Millions documented (particularly seabirds)

Status: Ongoing endemic circulation in wild populations

Molecular & Genetic Features

Surface Proteins:

Hemagglutinin (HA): H5 subtype; contains multiple basic amino acids at cleavage site (high pathogenicity marker)

Neuraminidase (NA): N1 subtype

Key Mutations: Polybasic cleavage site; N66S and other residues linked to mammalian adaptation

Genetic Stability: Relatively stable compared to seasonal influenza; limited reassortment risk with human seasonal strains

Species-Specific Mortality Rates

Species Mortality Rate Notes

Domestic chickens 90–100% Highly susceptible; rapid spread in flocks

Wild waterfowl 30–70% Variable by species; some tolerance

Preemptive and reactive depopulation of infected flocks

Billions of birds culled globally since 2020

Farm quarantine protocols

Equipment disinfection; movement restrictions

Personal protective equipment (PPE) for handlers

Wildlife Management:

Limited intervention; monitoring and surveillance primary strategy

Human vaccine candidates under development; limited stockpiles available

Antivirals:

Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir) effective in vitro; clinical efficacy in human cases variable

Monoclonal antibody treatments in research phase

Draft text:
OC Japan Fair is a Japanese cultural festival held in Orange County, California, United States, since 2009. The event showcases traditional Japanese culture alongside contemporary Japanese popular culture. It is primarily held at the OC Fair & Event Center in Costa Mesa, California. [ref: ABOUT US / CONTACT, OC Japan Fair] [ref: OC Japan Fair: a festival of tradition with a pop culture twist, Daily Pilot]

== Overview ==

OC Japan Fair presents various aspects of Japanese culture, including cuisine, traditional performing arts, music, anime, manga, and fashion. The festival features live performances, food vendors, merchandise exhibitions, and cultural activities.

The event is organized by Japan Product Promotion and operated by Adentope, Inc. Its programming combines traditional Japanese cultural activities with contemporary entertainment, attracting local residents and visitors interested in Japanese culture. [ref: Traditional and contemporary Japanese culture celebrated at OC Japan Fair in Costa Mesa, Daily Pilot]

== History ==

OC Japan Fair was established in 2009 in Orange County, California, under the organization of Japan Product Promotion.

The ninth edition was held in October 2018, featuring Japanese cultural activities such as Awa Odori dancing, taiko drumming, and tea ceremonies. The event was covered by the Daily Pilot, a regional publication of the Los Angeles Times. [ref: OC Japan Fair brings slices of culture to Costa Mesa fairgrounds, Daily Pilot]

The 13th OC Japan Fair was held from October 27 to 29, 2023. According to the organizers, approximately 220 booths were planned, with an anticipated attendance of 45,000 visitors. The announced performers included Japanese boy band Travis Japan, singer Chris Hart, entertainer Ai Haruna, and comedian Tonikaku Akarui Yasumura. [ref: The 13th OC JAPAN FAIR is bringing Japan to SoCal October 27th to 29th, 2023, Japan Product Promotion]

The 18th edition took place from April 3 to 5, 2026, featuring more than 200 booths. The spring festival was held alongside the Japanese music event Freedom LA, whose announced performers included Minmi, Naoto Inti Raymi, Genki Iwahashi, and Yuriyan Retriever.

== Festival activities ==

=== Traditional Japanese culture ===

The festival features demonstrations and performances of traditional Japanese arts, including tea ceremonies, taiko drumming, traditional dance, and kimono-related activities.

During the spring 2026 event, an area inspired by Nakamise Street in Tokyo's Asakusa district featured Bon Odori dancing, koto performances, calligraphy, and ikebana demonstrations. The autumn 2026 event included naginata martial arts demonstrations and traditional Japanese dance performances.

=== Music and live entertainment ===

The festival hosts live performances featuring Japanese pop music, traditional performing arts, dance, and comedy. In 2023, Travis Japan was among the announced performers, drawing attention to the festival's entertainment lineup.

In spring 2026, the event was held alongside Freedom LA, a Japanese music festival featuring artists including MINMI.

=== Anime and cosplay ===

Japanese anime, manga, and video game culture are represented through themed activities, merchandise vendors, and cosplay competitions.

In spring 2026, an area called "Akihabara Electric Town", inspired by Tokyo's Akihabara district, featured a maid café and vendors selling anime-related merchandise.

=== Food and merchandise ===

Food vendors offer a variety of Japanese dishes, including yakitori, takoyaki, ramen, and wagyu beef. The festival has also featured tuna-cutting demonstrations.

Merchandise vendors sell Japanese traditional crafts, accessories, and anime- and manga-related products.

== Organization ==

OC Japan Fair is organized by Japan Product Promotion and operated by Adentope, Inc., doing business as Japan Product Promotion. According to the festival's official website, the company's president is Masataka Taguchi and its producer is Ryuji Yamakita.

== Venue ==

The festival is primarily held at the OC Fair & Event Center, located at 88 Fair Drive in Costa Mesa, California.

The event uses several areas of the fairgrounds, including the Anaheim Building, Los Alamitos Building, Main Mall, and OC Promenade. [ref: OC Japan Fair, OC Fair & Event Center]

Vanessa Ragland is an American comedian, actress and theater producer. She is the co-owner and co-artistic director of Dynasty Typewriter, a comedy and performance venue in the Westlake neighborhood of Los Angeles, and co-hosts the podcast Pop My Culture.

== Early life and education ==
Ragland grew up in a rural area with little access to the arts. She earned a bachelor's degree in acting from Virginia Tech and briefly studied toward an MFA in poetry at the University of North Carolina Wilmington before moving to Los Angeles.

== Career ==
=== Performing ===
Ragland performed with The Groundlings, including as a member of its Sunday Company. Her television credits include The Office, Men of a Certain Age and New Girl. She played Chastity, a teacher's assistant, in the 2010 independent comedy Jeffie Was Here; a review from the Phoenix Film Festival singled out her brief comic performance. She played Jenny in The Late Bloomer (2016), a comedy directed by Kevin Pollak. In October 2014, several outlets reported on similarities between a Tina Turner impersonator sketch Ragland and Kimberly Condict had written and performed with the Groundlings and a Saturday Night Live sketch that aired that month; an unnamed source close to SNL attributed the resemblance to parallel thinking. With Cole Stratton she co-hosts Pop My Culture, an interview podcast about film, television and music; in 2011 Rolling Stone ranked it second on its list of the ten best comedy podcasts. She has also co-hosted Totally Mommy, a comedic parenting podcast that The Washington Post included in a 2016 list of recommended parenting podcasts.

=== Dynasty Typewriter ===
Ragland met Jamie Flam more than a decade before founding the venue, when she interned at the comedy theater where he worked and the two joined the same improv team. In 2010 they staged a comedy benefit at the Hayworth Theatre for the Leukemia & Lymphoma Society. Over about a year and a half, they wrote a business plan, negotiated a lease on the Hayworth Theatre, and ran a $100,000 Kickstarter campaign to open Dynasty Typewriter, which held its first performance on November 16, 2017. Ragland and Flam co-own the venue and serve as co-artistic directors, curating its programming together.

In 2019, The New York Times reported that the venue had established itself within two years as a home for unconventional comedy programming, hosting performers including Sarah Silverman, Bob Odenkirk and Margaret Cho, with residencies by Marc Maron, Eddie Izzard and Hannah Gadsby. In 2022 the Los Angeles Times featured Ragland among women booking the city's stand-up venues, noting her role in booking the club and growing it into a leading local comedy venue.

== References ==

Hopecore is a social media trend where participants share content intended to inspire hope and optimism. [ref: What is TikTok's new 'hopecore' trend and is it exactly what we need right now?, The Independent] It typically features montages or slideshows of inspirational quotations and images, often accompanied with music. Common hopecore-themed videos include acts of kindness, personal achievements, and scenes from nature. [ref: Is Hopecore the Last Gasp of a Less-Toxic Internet?, GQ]

Hopecore was started on TikTok as an optimistic offshoot of corecore. After gaining popularity on TikTok, it spread to Instagram, YouTube, Reddit, and X. By 2024, it was also being used ironically for videos that paired cheerful imagery and music with captions about personal problems. [ref: TikTok's 'hopecore' trend shows the best-and worst-of internet optimism, Fast Company]

A 2026 study in the Journal of Documentation examined hopecore posts and user comments on Instagram. [ref: "Needed this": understanding hopecore content and engagement on Instagram, Journal of Documentation]

== Reception ==
Kieran Press-Reynolds of GQ criticised hopecore's simplistic reassurances and its commercial exploitation by influencers: "In a godless internet landscape full of dodgy influencers and grifters, it has morphed into the algorithmic equivalent of a role model for kids, who comment about how the videos have changed their mindset and leave praise like, 'This video is cleaning my ["For You" Page]!'"

Draft text:
The Salaspils Research Reactor () is a former pool-type research reactor in Salaspils, Latvia. It was built for the Institute of Physics of the Latvian Academy of Sciences and operated from 26 September 1961 to 19 June 1998. [ref: Development of nuclear energetics in Latvia] [ref: Par Salaspils kodolreaktora likvidēšanas un demontāžas koncepciju, Likumi.lv] Research at the reactor covered nuclear physics, radiation chemistry and radiobiology.

The facility was partly dismantled after its closure, but decommissioning was still in progress in August 2025. [ref: IAEA Mission Says Latvia Committed to Safe and Responsible Management of Radioactive Waste, Sees Areas for Further Enhancement, International Atomic Energy Agency] [ref: Republic of Latvia National Report on the implementation of the obligations under the Convention on Nuclear Safety for the 10th Review Meeting of the Contracting Parties]

== Establishment and research ==
The Soviet government authorised construction of the reactor in 1958. It was based on the IRT design developed at the Institute of Atomic Energy in Moscow. The reactor first reached criticality on 26 September 1961. Reconstruction in the mid-1970s increased its thermal power to 5 MW. [ref: 60 gadi kopš Salaspils kodolreaktora iedarbināšanas, LSM.lv]

Alongside research in nuclear physics, radiation chemistry and radiobiology, the reactor was used to develop radiation dosimeters and produce radioactive preparations for medical use. Latvian scientists also developed a radiation loop that supplied gamma rays for irradiation experiments and work on industrial irradiation processes.

The reactor provided training for specialists from North Korea, Iraq and Libya, which had acquired IRT reactors from the Soviet Union.

== Closure and decommissioning ==
In May 1995, the Latvian government ordered preparations to dismantle the reactor and prohibited further purchases of nuclear fuel. [ref: Par pasākumiem Salaspils zinātniski pētnieciskā atomreaktora likvidācijas sagatavošanai, Likumi.lv] The reactor shut down permanently on 19 June 1998. The government approved a decommissioning plan on 26 October 1999 and revised it in 2004.

Unused nuclear fuel was returned to Russia in 2005, followed by the spent fuel in 2008. By 2019, the reactor had been partly dismantled and was awaiting final decommissioning, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Funding shortages and the need for additional capacity at the Radons radioactive waste repository near Baldone delayed completion of the dismantling work. [ref: Salaspils reaktoram aprit 60; līdz demontāžai vēl vismaz 10 gadi, LSM.lv] Decommissioning remained in progress in August 2025, when Latvia's radiation regulator reported delays in completing the dismantling design.

# Raj Gond

The **Raj Gond** (also spelled **Rajgond** or **Raj-Gond**; Hindi: राजगोंड; Telugu: రాజ్ గోండ్) are the historically dominant, aristocratic lineage and ethnolinguistic branch of the Gondi people, an Adivasi community primarily inhabiting the Gondwana region of Central India. They are distributed across the states of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra (chiefly in Vidarbha), Telangana (concentrated in Adilabad and Kumuram Bheem Asifabad district), Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, and Karnataka.

Between the 14th and 18th centuries, Raj Gond dynastic houses established four major sovereign kingdoms in Central India: Garha-Mandla, Chanda (Chandrapur), Deogarh, and Kherla. The ruling houses adopted aspects of Rajput court culture, statecraft, and ritual patronage—a sociopolitical process often cited in anthropological literature as a classic example of "Rajputisation" or "Kshatriyaisation"—while retaining their distinct Dravidian language, religious system, and totemic clan organization.

Raj Gond society is internationally renowned in anthropology due to the foundational field ethnographies of Austrian anthropologist Christoph von Fürer-Haimendorf, whose works, including *The Raj Gonds of Adilabad* (1948) and *The Gonds of Andhra Pradesh* (1979), documented their four-phratry social structure (*sagas*), the ritual veneration of clan deities (*Persa Pen*), and their symbiotic relationship with the Pardhan hereditary bards. In modern India, the Raj Gond are constitutionally recognized as a Scheduled Tribe under the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950.

---

## Infobox

| **Raj Gond (राजगोंड / రాజ్ గోండ్)** | |:--- | | **Total population:** Approx. 4–5 million (sub-group of the ~13 million Gondi population) | | **Regions with significant populations:** India: Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Karnataka | | **Languages:** Gondi language (Adilabad Gondi, Northern Gondi), Hindi, Marathi, Telugu | | **Writing systems:** Historically Gunjala Gondi script, Masaram Gondi script; modern usage in Devanagari and Telugu script | | **Religion:** Gondi Punem (worship of *Persa Pen*, *Aki Pen*, ancestral *Sanal*), alongside syncretic Hinduism | | **Related ethnic groups:** Gondi people, Pardhan, Kolam, Maria, Muria, Baiga |

---

## Etymology and Identity

The compound name *Raj Gond* derives from Sanskrit/Hindi *Rājā* (राजा, meaning "king", "royal", or "ruling") and *Gond*, literally signifying the "Royal Gonds" or "Ruling Gonds." Historically, the term denoted the landed nobility, hereditary chieftains (*zamindars*), village headmen (*patels* or *mokashis*), and royal houses of Gondwana, distinguishing them from ordinary cultivators and pastoralists (frequently termed *Dhur Gond*, literally "dust Gonds" or commoners, in colonial-era gazetteers).

Like other branches of the Gond confederation, the Raj Gond refer to themselves endonymously as ***Kōītōr*** (or *Koitur*, *Koya*), which translates in the Gondi language to "human beings" or "people of the hills/earth."

During the height of their political power in the medieval era, Gond rulers patronized Brahmin scholars and genealogists, observed ritual dietary codes, adopted the sacred thread (*janeu*), and contracted political marriages with established Rajput ruling houses—most notably illustrated by the marriage of King Dalpat Shah of Garha-Mandla to the Chandel Rajput princess Rani Durgavati. Despite these outer adoptions of Hindu martial norms, the Raj Gonds remained endogamous within the broader Gond social fabric, maintaining ancestral clan totems, village shrines, and customary laws outside the orthodox fourfold varna system.

---

## History

### Medieval Origins and Rise of Gondwana

Prior to the 12th century, the Central Indian highlands—geographically dominated by the Satpura Range, Vindhya Range, and the basins of the Narmada River and Godavari River—were sparsely documented in imperial Sanskrit and Persian chronicles. As regional empires such as the Kalachuris of Tripuri and the Paramaras fragmented, indigenous Gond chieftains consolidated territorial bastions (*garhs* or hill forts) and established political authority over the region, which came to be known as **Gondwana** ("Country of the Gonds").

Muslim historians of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire noted the rise of substantial Gond kingdoms by the 14th century, documenting their fortified capital cities, standing armies, cavalry, and extensive agricultural revenue systems.

What Part of "Get Thee Gone" Don't You Understand? is a 1997 compilation/reissue by The Geraldine Fibbers, the Los Angeles alt-country band fronted by Carla Bozulich.

It originated as an expanded reissue of the band's self-titled 1994 EP, which featured their early signature song "Get Thee Gone." The reissue was put out in 1997 to showcase the band's earliest days staking out their elegant, often intense country-rock sound.

It was released on February 11, 1997, on Sympathy for the Record Industry (catalog SFTRI 481).

The album contains 16 tracks, and draws from several sources:

Tracks 1–7 were originally released as the earlier EP Get Thee Gone.

Tracks 8–9 come from the Big Jesus 7".

Track 10 is an unreleased demo from November 1994.

Tracks 11–13 were recorded live on KCRW-FM in Santa Monica, and

Tracks 14–15 were recorded live at the El Rey Theatre in Los Angeles in June 1996.

Track 16 was recorded live at the Foothill Club, Long Beach in September 1996

681 is the genre of music that consist of exactly vocals and percussion instruments. It combines a capella with minimalist dance music. An example is the song Crabapples by Bruce Peninsula. [ref: Bruce Peninsula climbing the musical ladder, Interrobang]

It follows that this is the alternative name of the genre of minimalist vocal dance music.

Many genres have a given alternative name. For example, an alternative name trance is given to usually minimalist ambient rhythmic dance music with tempo between 120 and 150 BPM.

== Name origin ==

The name 681 originates from the list of natural numbers. We have a=1 because of the existence of vocals as the primary element of most vocal songs. [ref: Musical Texture, Fundamentals: Music in World Cultures] Then we skip 2 because there are no instruments other than percussion in this genre to function as the secondary element of most vocal songs. Hence we take b=3 as the next notable number because there is percussion in this genre and is the tertiary element of most vocal songs. The formula of the square of a binomial is (a+b)^2=a^2+2\cdot a\cdot b+b^2. If we square the exponents of b in each addend, i.e., raise them to the 2nd power, because 2 is the skipped natural number, we get the addends a^2, 2\cdot a \cdot b and b^4, respectively. The addends are equal to 1, 6 and 81, respectively. The ratio when the second addend is divided by the first addend is 6/1=6, while the ratio when the third addend is divided by the first addend is 81/1=81. Its concatenation gives 681.

Headquartered in Clearwater, Florida, Advanta IRA Services, LLC is a private U.S.-based company that provides administrative and recordkeeping services for self-directed individual retirement arrangements (IRAs) and other qualified plans and savings accounts. [ref: Tampa Bay Business Journal, Tampa Bay Business Journal]

In 2024, the Tampa Bay Business Journal described Advanta IRA as a multibillion-dollar self-directed retirement account administrator. As of mid 2026, the company reports holding approximately $4 billion in assets under administration. [ref: Why Advanta IRA, Advanta IRA]

== History ==
Jack Callahan is the founder and president of Advanta IRA. With decades of experience in financial services and real estate, Callahan has spoken on self-directed retirement strategies and regulatory compliance. [ref: ]

Advanta IRA was originally founded in 2003 and began operating as an affiliate of The Entrust Group under the name Entrust of Tampa Bay. Callahan added another location, Entrust of Georgia, located in Atlanta, in January 2009. [ref: ADVANTA IRA SERVICES, LLC - LEI: 254900VLUCG2CCN7N325, Bloomberg LEI]

The company changed its name to Advanta IRA Services, LLC in December 2011. It became independent of The Entrust Group’s franchise program in January 2012. [ref: The Entrust Group Announces the Dissolution of its Franchise Program, www.theentrustgroup.com]

Throughout its 20+ year history, Advanta IRA has grown in both client base and assets under administration. Advanta IRA was named to Florida State University's Seminole 100 list of fastest-growing alumni-owned or alumni-led businesses in 2020, 2021, and 2022, ranking 58th, 71st, and 55th, respectively. [ref: ] [ref: ] [ref: ] The Seminole 100 list, which recognizes the fastest-growing companies owned or led by alumni of Florida State University, is presented annually by the Jim Moran Institute for Global Entrepreneurship at Florida State University.

In 2024, the company relocated its corporate headquarters from Largo to Clearwater, Florida. According to the Tampa Bay Business Journal, the move followed a period of operational growth.

In 2025, Callahan formed Advanta Trust Company, Inc., a Nevada-chartered trust company established to serve as a qualified custodian for self-directed accounts. [ref: Retail Trust Companies as of April 20, 2026, Nevada Financial Institutions Division] As of 2026, client assets administered by Advanta IRA are held in custody by Advanta Trust Company. [ref: Advanta Trust Company Launches as Nationwide Custodian for Self-Directed IRAs and Tax-Advantaged Accounts, Yahoo Finance]

== Services ==
Advanta IRA provides administrative services for self-directed IRAs and other retirement and savings plans. These accounts include traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs, solo 401(k)s, health savings accounts (HSAs), and Coverdell education savings accounts (ESAs). [ref: Types of Self-Directed IRA Accounts, Advanta IRA]

The firm administers accounts used for alternative investments in real estate, gold, private placements, private lending, and limited liability company (LLC) structures (commonly referred to as checkbook IRAs). [ref: IRA Alternative Investments, Advanta IRA]

Advanta IRA facilitates account setup, documentation, and compliance reporting in accordance with Internal Revenue Service (IRS) regulations. The company does not offer investment advice or sell investments. Clients maintain full control over their investment choices and decisions. [ref: Beyond Stocks and Bonds: Is a Self-Directed IRA Right for You?, pro.thestreet.com]

== Educational Resources and Outreach ==
Advanta IRA produces educational content related to self-directed accounts and  alternative investments, including webinars, podcasts, articles, and frequently asked questions addressing investment structures and IRS regulations. Representatives of the company participate as speakers on third-party podcasts and webinars focused on alternative investments and self-directed accounts. [ref: ] [ref: Retiring soon? Expert explains how IRAs and 401(k) work, The Independent] [ref: REIAGC Speaker Profile for Larissa Greene, www.cincinnatireia.com] [ref: Bitcoin Q&A for Business Owners – Tax, Mining, and Retirement]

== Regulatory Compliance ==
Self-directed accounts administered by Advanta IRA are subject to federal tax laws and regulations governing individual retirement accounts and qualified plans, including contribution limits, required minimum distributions (RMDs), prohibited transactions, and reporting obligations. [ref: ] [ref: ]

In an interview with TheStreet, Advanta IRA’s Vice President of Sales, Scott Maurer, stated that Advanta IRA performs administrative functions in accordance with these regulations, but does not sell or vet investments. Account holders and their financial team are responsible for due diligence and compliance.
