10 Pujaan Malindo Vol.1 [ref: ] is Noraniza Idris’s debut studio album, and the songs she performs are cover versions of tracks previously popularised by local artists as well as those from neighbouring countries (Indonesia). The album 10 Pujaan Malindo was recorded in two volumes, released in 1986 and 1987. This album series was launched in 1986 by Life Records (Hup Hup Sdn. Bhd.).

== Background ==
After taking part in an audition organised by RTM, the winner of the 1985 RTM Bintang competition, Noraniza Idris, was approached by Hamidi, the publisher and producer at Life Records, who wanted her to become a recording artist because he was captivated by the sweetness of her voice; The offer first arose whilst she was still participating in the 1985 RTM Star competition, which had not yet concluded. At the time, she was with her father, Idris Ahmad, enjoying a meal at the Angkasapuri canteen—the venue where she had taken the RTM talent test. Eventually, after much consideration, she agreed to sign a contract with Life Records on 1 January 1986 and officially became a recording artist – marking the first recording contract of her career. She also released her debut album, a compilation titled Melayu Deli, alongside a legendary singer of the 1980s on 1 January 1986. Meanwhile, he had taken part in the 1985 Bintang RTM competition, though he only reached the semi-finals; however, he remained resilient, and perhaps Hamidi’s arrival and his official status as a recording artist served as the remedy he had been seeking all along. [ref: NORANIZA IDRIS: 12 LAGU PALING POPULAR SEPANJANG ZAMAN, GALAKSIVIRAL]

The release of the album 10 Pujaan Malindo Vol.1 in 1986 on the Life Records label (Hup Hup Sdn. Bhd.) marked a highly significant milestone in Noraniza Idris’s professional discography. This major project was released at a time when the regional music market was witnessing a vibrant wave of cultural exchange between Malaysia and Indonesia (the acronym for ‘Malindo’). As a new singer establishing her name in the 1980s, Noraniza was sent to Jakarta, Indonesia, to undertake the vocal recording and musical arrangement process on location. This strategic move by the record company was taken to ensure that the resulting archipelago-inspired music possessed authentic aesthetic value and high production standards. The album’s extraordinary success in the market not only placed her on the mainstream industry’s radar but also paved the way for the production of its sequel, 10 Pujaan Malindo Vol.2, which was released the following year. [ref: ]

== Album summary ==
In terms of track selection, 10 Pujaan Malindo Vol. 1 presents a compilation studio album concept based on cover versions of popular songs that once propelled the original singers to fame in both countries. Released on physical cassette format and widely distributed in Malaysia and Singapore, the album features a selection of songs in the creative pop and contemporary folk genres. The album’s standout track, which achieved the greatest commercial impact, was the upbeat song titled “Anak Tani” (or better known by its original Indonesian title, “Singkong dan Keju”). The song became a radio phenomenon on local stations, sparking a unique cultural impact; the commercial impact of these cover versions even led some fans to dub Noraniza with the somewhat derisive nickname “Queen of Covers" or “Queen of Plagiarism” early in her career, due to her vocal prowess in breathing new life into these songs whilst imbuing them with her own distinct identity. In today’s digital age, a significant portion of the key repertoire from this classic 1986 cassette album series has been officially re-compiled by Life Records into a digital streaming album titled Nostalgia Malindo. Furthermore, several tracks from this album that became hits have been included in a compilation album entitled 16 Pujaan Malindo.

Draft text:
Marcus Sim (born in 23rd October 1997) is a professional squash player from Kuching,Sarawak, Malaysia. Sim represented Malaysia at the international stage. In 2015, Sim won the gold medalist for Malaysia in Men's Doubles Squash at the Commonwealth Youth Games in Samoa. In 2016, Sim represented Malaysia at the World Junior Championship in Poland where the Malaysia finished 13th in the world. [ref: Major upset as Malaysia loses to South Africa in World Junior Squash, Malay Mail] In the same year, he also won the Malaysian Games (SUKMA) in Men's Doubles [ref: ] and Malaysia Nationals in Men's Doubles with his partner Jess Tay on their homecourt. In 2017, he helped Malaysia secured the gold medal in the Southeast Asia Cup [ref: Malaysia banking on crowd support for 3rd SEA Squash C’ship, Borneo Post Online], making Malaysia the powerhouse of squash in Southeast Asia.

Sim has a career high world rank of 263 [ref: ] in the singles squash circuit.

Later in 2017, Sim was recruited to play for the YellowJackets the college squash circuit in the United States. [ref: Malaysian trio head to US for college squash, Squash Mad] [ref: Marcus to miss SEA Games for US studies, Borneo Post Online]

== College Career ==
In his first year, Sim was named Rookie of the Year by the Liberty League [ref: Liberty League announces 2017-18 Men's Squash Award Recipients, libertyleagueathletics.com] and was also named Rookie of the week multiple times. [ref: Sim Receives Liberty League Rookie Honor for Second Week Straight, University of Rochester Athletics]

During his second year, Sim had a record of 16 wins and 2 losses; which makes him the 7th in single season program win percentage (.889) [ref: Marcus Sim - Men's Squash, University of Rochester Athletics]

In the 2019-2020 season, Sim had a record of 17 wins and 4 losses, and was named First Team All Liberty League and was the semi-finalist in CSA Individual Squash Championship.

Sim accumulated an impressive overall singles record of 47-12 across his three primary active seasons, making him one of the top player to have the highest winning record in Rochester squash history.

== Post College ==
After the pandemic, Sim continue his squash career on the World Hardball Doubles circuit in America. Sim signed with the Heights Casino as his home club where he currently trains in. With his doubles expertise, Sim won the Creek Challenge Cup; making him the first Malaysian to win a title in the SDA tour. [ref: Parkhurst/Sim Wei Jie Take Creek Challenge Cup, SDA Pro Tour] Sim has a career high ranking of 33 in the world. [ref: Rankings, SDA Pro Tour]

Draft text:
Joshua’s Confusion is a 1977 children's television special produced by Multimedia Program Productions. It is part of a series called Young People's Specials, a series of specials locally produced in Cincinnati [ref: Young People's Specials - Joshua's Confusion entry form, letters, study guide, press release, clipping, and photos, 1977, University of Georgia] that tackled cultural issues through the lenses of children. The special originally aired on WLWT-TV, but would be syndicated in other areas, including on Nickelodeon's Special Delivery. [ref: Monday Movie Ratings, Eugene Register-Guard] [ref: Sunday TV, Mohave Daily Miner] [ref: Daily TV Time Table, Williamson Daily News] The film was produced with help from the Amish community of Berlin, Ohio.

==Plot==
The special follows Joshua, an Amish boy who gets invited to a sleepover by one of his friends at school. His parents forbid Joshua from going since it goes against their beliefs. Joshua sneaks out of his bedroom window and goes to the party anyway. Throughout the party, Joshua thinks about what his father told him as he plays with the kids. Joshua’s parents find out Joshua left and pick him up. On the way home, Joshua jumps out of their buggy and retreats into the woods. Joshua sleeps in the woods and the special ends with him returning home the next day.

==Awards==
In 1977, Joshua's Confusion won a Peabody Award for Children's & Youth. [ref: Joshua's Confusion - Peabody Awards, peabodyawards.com] Charles Goetz won a regional Emmy for his role as Joshua's Father. [ref: 42nd Street Lights Up Stage, The Western Star] [ref: Charles Joseph Goetz Jr. Obituary, weilkahnfuneralhome.com]

= Susantha Salgado =
Shihan J. Susantha Salgado (born 17 November 1962) is a Sri Lankan karate instructor, coach, and martial arts administrator. He is known for his involvement in the promotion of Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai in Sri Lanka and has served as the Head Master and Chief Instructor of the organization. Salgado holds a 7th Dan Black Belt recognized by Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai, Japan, and has been active in karate training, coaching, and administration for several decades.

== Early Life ==
Susantha Salgado was born on 17 November 1962 and is from Negombo, Sri Lanka, where he has been involved in martial arts training and instruction throughout much of his life.

== Martial Arts Career ==
Salgado is associated with Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai Sri Lanka, serving in leadership and instructional roles within the organization. He has been identified as:

* Chairman and Director of Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai Sri Lanka
* Chief Instructor of Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai Sri Lanka
* Representative Branch Manager of Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai, Japan
* Senior A Grade Coach
* Member of the Sri Lanka Karate Do Federation
* Life Member of the Sri Lanka School Karate Do Association

He has conducted karate training programs, black belt examinations, and coaching activities aimed at developing karate practitioners in Sri Lanka.

== Training in Japan ==
In 2013, Salgado was among a group of Sri Lankan karate instructors who participated in a specialized training program in Japan under the invitation of Japan Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai. Media coverage reported that Salgado and other instructors underwent advanced technical training and grading activities during the visit.

The training initiative was highlighted in the Daily Mirror article "Karatekas return after training in Japan", which reported on representatives of the Sri Lankan Kenshukai organization attending a 25-day training program in Japan.

== Leadership of Kenshukai Sri Lanka ==
Under Salgado's leadership, Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai Sri Lanka has organized karate training programs, coaching seminars, grading examinations, and black belt certification programs. Social media records from the organization's official pages identify Salgado as the Head Master of the Sri Lankan branch and reference his supervision of black belt examinations and instructor development activities.

== Ranks and Recognition ==
Salgado is reported to hold:

* 7th Dan Black Belt in Nihon Karate Do Kenshukai, Japan
* 8th Dan Black Belt in Wano Michiryu Karate and Kobudo U.S.A.

He has been recognized within karate organizations in Sri Lanka for his contribution to technical instruction and the development of karate practitioners.

== Personal Life ==
Salgado resides in Negombo, Sri Lanka.

Bix Pix Entertainment is an American animation studio specializing in stop-motion animation, based in Burbank, California and was founded in 1998. [ref: Local Stories - Meet Kelli Bixler of Burbank, CA, VoyageLA]

== History and Work ==
Bix Pix Entertainment has provided original and work-for-hire production services across new media, television, commercials and short films for clients including Disney, NBC, Cartoon Network, Hasbro, Amazon Studios and Applet TV+. [ref: Bix Pix Clicks with Amazon, Kidscreen Magazine] [ref: Podcast: Creating Stop Motion Animation, WAMC Northeast Public Radio] The studio's credits include several award-winning productions, among them the preschool series Tumble Leaf, which received a BAFTA, an Annecy International Animation Film Festival Jury Award, Annie Awards, Emmy Awards and a Peabody nomination; Adventure Time episode "Bad Jubies," which earned an Annie Award; and Apple TV+'s Shape Island which received an Annecy Jury Award and nominations for a Peabody and an Emmy Award.

Founder, Kelli Bixler discovered stop motion while working as a live-action director in Chicago, IL and Bix Pix was established shortly after that. [ref: Reel Chicago, Reel Chicago] The studio's early productions were created in traditional clay animation and included a 23-minute video Doh-Doh Island Adventures for Hasbro, the "NBC Memories" commercial, and Miss Twiggley's Tree, based on Dorothea Warren Fox's children's book. [ref: The Big Picture, Animation Magazine] In 2005, the studio produced a Saturday Night Live "TV Funhouse" segment Christmastime for the Jews. [ref: (https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0694918/companycredits/?ref_=tt_dt_cmpyv)] [ref: Stop-Motion ‘Community’ Special Airs Thursday, Animation Magazine]

The studio relocated to Los Angeles in 2006 and began production on the ABC special Holiday: The Christmas That Almost Didn't Happen. [ref: Wal-Mart Taps Bix Pix for Holiday Toons, Animation Magazine] In 2013, Bix Pix developed the preschool show Tumble Leaf for Amazon Studios. [ref: Bix Pix Brings Handcrafted Approach to Amazon's Tumble Leaf, Animation World Magazine] In between seasons, Bix Pix worked with director Kirsten Lepore to produce her stop-motion episode "Bad Jubies" for Cartoon Network's Adventure Time [ref: Kirsten Lepore Lends Stop-Motion Skill to Tonight’s ‘Adventure Time’, Cartoon Brew] [ref: Adventure Time: Good Jubies – Making Of Bad Jubies, Stop Motion Magazine]and in 2017, they worked with Fred Rogers Productions and The Fred Rogers Center to create the Google Doodle "Celebrating Mister Rogers." [ref: Watch Google's beautiful tribute to Mister Rogers, USA Today] In 2021, Bix Pix moved to Burbank, CA to create Shape Island for Apple TV+, adapting Mac Barnett and Jon Klassen's Shape books. [ref: Bix Pix Brings Great ‘Form’ to Apple TV+’s ‘Shape Island’ Kids’ Series, Animation World Network]

Freshdi is an online multi-category business-to-business (B2B) marketplace connecting global suppliers and buyers. [ref: About Us, Freshdi] Its earlier documented activities focused on supply chain traceability and agricultural distribution in Vietnam. [ref: Ứng dụng nền tảng số để kết nối tiêu thụ nông sản Việt, VOV2]

== History and activities ==

=== Traceability and agricultural supply chain (2022–2023) ===
In February 2022, Vietnam's National Numbering and Barcodes Center (NBC) announced a cooperation agreement with Freshdi to apply barcode standards, blockchain technology, and big data to supply chain management and product traceability. [ref: Ký kết hợp tác giữa NBC và Freshdi, National Numbering and Barcodes Center]

During this period, Vietnamese media outlets including VietQ and VOV2 reported on Freshdi's implementation of digital tools to connect agricultural producers with distributors and to verify supply chain participants. [ref: Ứng dụng công nghệ Blockchain trong truy xuất nguồn gốc, Journal of Intellectual Property and Innovation] In February 2023, the Thanh Hóa youth organization collaborated with Freshdi Vietnam to establish a QR code-integrated portal introducing local specialty agricultural products. [ref: Tỉnh đoàn, Hội LHTN tỉnh Thanh Hóa phối hợp Freshdi Việt Nam hỗ trợ xây dựng Cổng đặc sản Thanh Hóa ứng dụng công nghệ 4.0, Thanh Hóa Youth Union]

=== Digital transformation initiatives ===
In June 2023, at the launch event for a digital transformation handbook for the food processing and distribution sector, Freshdi representatives presented sales management solutions and tools for marketing Vietnamese agricultural products to small and medium-sized enterprises. [ref: Ra mắt sổ tay chuyển đổi số ở lĩnh vực chế biến và phân phối thực phẩm, VietnamPlus] [ref: Sổ tay chuyển đổi số – Cẩm nang hữu ích cho doanh nghiệp nhỏ và vừa trong lĩnh vực chế biến và phân phối thực phẩm, Kinh tế và Dự báo]

In December 2025, Nhân Dân reported Freshdi Vietnam's participation in the VietLeap business matching event within the artificial intelligence ecosystem. [ref: Kết nối, tăng cường hợp tác cho hệ sinh thái trí tuệ nhân tạo tại Việt Nam, Nhân Dân]

== Corporate structure ==
According to the terms of use on its official website, the platform is operated by Freshdi Asia Pte. Ltd., a company registered in Singapore. [ref: Terms of Use, Freshdi] Operations and domestic partnerships in Vietnam are conducted through Freshdi Vietnam Joint Stock Company.

== References ==

Draft text:
Alexander "Alex" Pongrass (10 November 1923 – 9 June 2000) was a Hungarian-born Australian businessman and football administrator. Co-founder of the National Soccer League (NSL) alongside Frank Lowy. Pongrass was a long-time chairman of St George-Budapest Soccer Club.

== Early life ==
Born into a Jewish family in 1923, he was the second of three brothers. He began a textile apprenticeship and studied bookkeeping.

In 1939, following the outbreak of World War II, 16-year-old Pongrass left home to work in his uncle’s newspaper distribution business. His parents later perished in the Auschwitz concentration camp. His brother, George, survived internment in the Dachau concentration camp.

In 1944, during the German occupation of Hungary, Pongrass joined the Jewish underground resistance. Utilising forged identity papers, he posed as a liaison officer with the SS guards command. He successfully escorted Hungarian Jews to the protection of Raoul Wallenberg, the Swedish diplomat who saved thousands of Jews from execution and forced death marches by issuing protective Swedish passports. [ref: Obituary - Alexander (Alex) Pongrass - Obituaries Australia, oa.anu.edu.au] [ref: Biographies of 22 outstanding Hungarian migrants, Hungarian Immigration in Australia.]

== Business career ==
Partnering with his brother George, Alex established an engineering works in Sydney (later Pongrass Brothers Pty Ltd). During the 1960s and 70s, the company expanded into commercial boatbuilding, metal furniture, and plumbing, eventually employing over 600 people.

== Football administration ==
=== St George-Budapest ===
Pongrass served as a benefactor and chairman of the St George-Budapest Soccer Club. In 1958, he became president for over 40 years until the late 1990s. Under his leadership, the club became an powerhouse in Australian football, constructing its own rectangular venue, St George Stadium at Barton Park, which hosted local and international fixtures. [ref: Australian Professional Leagues, SFCU] [ref: The impact of football 'visionary' and recent Hall of Fame inductee Alex Pongrass AM, Football Australia] [ref: Alex Pongrass AM into the Football Australia Hall of Fame, St George Football Club] [ref: From Socceroos and Pele to a drug den. Now this stadium has been reborn, The Sydney Morning Herald]

Pongrass is credited with elevating the professional standards of the sport in Australia by actively recruiting top-tier, professional coaching talent. He hired national team manager Rale Rasic and Hungarian-Australian coach Frank Arok. During his tenure, St George-Budapest won five NSW First Division championships and captured the National Soccer League title in 1983. Pongrass also acted as a long-time mentor to Australian football legend Johnny Warren.

=== Foundation of the National Soccer League ===
On 5 April 1975, Pongrass and Hakoah's Frank Lowy convened a meeting of clubs where attendees signed a resolution of intent that led to the launch of the National Soccer League (NSL) in 1977. [ref: Minutes of Special Meeting on the Australian National Soccer League, Soccer News via Facebook] The NSL became the first national club competition of any football code in Australia.
== Honours ==
* In the 1988 Australia Day Honours, Pongrass was awarded the Member of the Order of Australia (AM) in recognition of his services to the game.
* In November 2024, he was posthumously inducted into the Football Australia Hall of Fame as a participant at Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium. [ref: Football Australia Hall of Fame, Wikipedia]

== Death ==
Pongrass passed away in Sydney on 9 June 2000. [ref: Family notices, The Sydney Morning Herald]

Salah El Moncef is a writer, literary scholar, editor and visual artist. He was born in Kuwait City and is based in France.His books include [https://journals.openedition.org/transatlantica/707 Atopian Limits] (2002), [https://www.atoponbooks.com/the-offering The Offering] (2015), [https://www.forewordreviews.com/reviews/now-and-then/ Now and Then] (2022), [https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/mqr/2023/01/an-enormous-enigmatic-signifier-salah-el-moncefs-benghazi/ Benghazi] (2022) and [https://www.atoponbooks.com/the-woman-from-warsaw The Woman from Warsaw] (2026). He also published the study [https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0969725X.2021.1988410 Art as Pharmakon] in 2021. Reviews and scholarly discussions of Salah El Moncef’s fiction have focused on memory, loss, migration, and the effects of colonial rule and fascist violance. [ref: Salah EL MONCEF BIN KHALIFA, Nantes Université] [ref: Review of Atopian Limits, Transatlantica] [ref: Memory, Trauma, and the Diasporic Subject, Los Angeles Review of Books] [ref: An Enormous, Enigmatic Signifier: Salah el Moncef's Benghazi, Michigan Quarterly Review] [ref: The Art of World-Building: Salah el Moncef's The Woman from Warsaw, Michigan Quarterly Review] [ref: Salah el Moncef, official author site (used only for routine biographical and publication data).]

Moncef teaches English studies and creative writing at Nantes Université, where he works as a Maître de Conférences. His research focuses on contemporary American literature, diasporic writing, migration, and transnational identities. He is also the General Issue Editor of Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities and an editor of the Routledge series Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities. The journal has featured his paintings on its covers and included his artwork as illustrations in its issues. [ref: Nantes Université, institutional profile/CV: maître de conférences in English studies and creative writing; research on diasporic literatures, migration, and transnational identities.] [ref: Angelaki: Journal of the Theoretical Humanities – About this journal, Taylor & Francis] [ref: Routledge, Angelaki: New Work in the Theoretical Humanities, series page.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue I 2024." Angelaki 29.5 (2024), artwork list and acknowledgements.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Editorial Introduction: General Issue II 2025." Angelaki 30.6 (2025), artwork list and acknowledgements.]

== Education and academic career ==
A biographical note in The Matrix in Theory states that Moncef recieved the Presidential Prize for Distinction in the Humanities in 1987. It also mentions that he held a Fulbright fellowship at Indiana University Bloomington from 1988 to 1993. Indiana University also lists him among its alumni who completed a PhD in English.. [ref: Salah El Moncef, Genders archive] [ref: Myriam Diocaretz and Stefan Herbrechter, eds., The Matrix in Theory (Rodopi, 2006), contributor note for Salah el Moncef bin Khalifa.] [ref: Benghazi, PhD alumni publications]

Moncef later started teaching English and creative writing in Nantes, France. His work focuses on American literature and culture, along with migration, diasporic writing, and the experiences of people living between different cultures.

== Scholarship and editorial work ==
During the 1990s, Moncef wrote articles on Ezra Pound, John Updike’s Rabbit at Rest, Paul Auster’s Moon Palace, and Thomas Harris’s Hannibal Lecter novels. His work appeared in journals such as boundary 2, Arizona Quarterly, Angelaki, and Genders. In 2002, he published Atopian Limits: Questions of Self, Complexity, and Contingency in Postmodern American Narrative, bringing together some of his work on postmodern American fiction. [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Gold, Representation, and the Reversible Dynamic of Symptomatic Return in Ezra Pound." boundary 2 22.1 (1995): 117–142.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Sounding the Black Box: Linear Reproduction and Chance Bifurcations in Rabbit at Rest." Arizona Quarterly 51.4 (1995): 69–108.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Lecter Knows Worst: Justice, Marginal Value, and the Law in the Series of Thomas Harris's Silence of the Lambs." Genders, 5 July 1999.] [ref: Moncef, Salah el. "Figures in (De)composition: The Genesis of the Paradoxical Self in Paul Auster's Moon Palace." Angelaki 4.3 (1999): 75–91.]

Jean-Yves Pellegrin reviewed Atopian Limits in Transatlantica. He discussed how the book looks at American fiction and the work of writers such as Paul Auster, Ken Kesey, John Updike, Thomas Harris, Gore Vidal, and Kathy Acker.

In 2005, Moncef co-edited Présence et représentation with Jacques Gilbert. The following year, he co-edited Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture with Michele Bottalico. Antonio C. Márquez reviewed the second book in Aztlán and discussed Moncef’s chapter, “The Hybrid Self at the Crossroads." [ref: Antonio C. Márquez, review of Borderline Identities in Chicano Culture, Aztlán 32.2 (2007): 213–216.] [ref: WorldCat, bibliographic record for Présence et représentation, Jacques Gilbert and Salah el Moncef (Peter Lang, 2005).]

His later work included chapters on mestiza and cyborg identeties and The Matrix trilogy. He also wrote about The Truman Show, Gloria Anzaldúa, and Don DeLillo’s novels Underworld and Falling Man. In 2020, he wrote the entry “Minor Literature” for the Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Literature.

Wesley Schokker (born March 24, 2006) is a Dutch author, public speaker, and digital personality. Nationally known for his deeply personal autobiographical books on overcoming hardship and peer pressure, Schokker has simultaneously achieved internet renown as the "Clown Emoji King" within his communities and His Story Basement Discord server.
== Early Life and Literary Career ==
Born in Dedemsvaart, Netherlands, Schokker began writing in his late teens. He used writing as a powerful outlet to navigate severe online and offline bullying, and he has spoken openly in public forums about his lived experiences with autism and navigating life with a speech impediment.

In 2025, his writings gained national media attention after an online essay garnered over 200,000 views. This led to his debut book, 24 Maart: Gevallen, maar niet gebroken (2025). He followed this up with Iedereen Maakt Fouten (2026), a raw reflection on peer pressure and personal growth. Today, when he is not writing, he tours secondary schools across the Netherlands to speak against cyberbullying.

== Discord Lore and Server Culture ==
In digital spaces, Schokker acts as the absolute owner of a dedicated Discord story server. Within this public community, his digital persona is defined by a mix of vulnerable transparency and eccentric internet humor.

=== The "Clown Emoji King" and Trademark Lore ===
Schokker operates under the absolute title of the "Clown Emoji King". Within Discord culture, he is famously known as a joke, as the "person who trademarked the clown emoji." According to community members, this legendary status stems from his compulsive habit of relentlessly spamming the 🤡 emoji across every available text channel.

The server's central running joke dictates that Schokker has a biological dependency on the symbol, with members frequently stating that "he needs the clown emoji like humans need oxygen to breathe." If chat goes too long without a clown emoji, Schokker will reportedly flood the channels to restore order to his digital empire.
Disclaimer: Schokker does not directly own or have any legal right towards the clown emoji, the information from this category was told by members who have met him. This was said as an inside joke due to his excessive clown emoji usage.

=== Bot Developer Relations and Server Incidents ===
A major recurring dynamic in the server revolves around Schokker's relationship with his technical staff. He is widely recognized for his immature management style, which frequently involves aggressively pleading with and begging his Bot Developers to fix, update, or code brand-new custom features for the server's automated bots.

Community logs show that these requests are often accompanied by intense spamming of the trademark clown emoji until the developers comply with his demands.

=== Mental Health and Autism Advocacy ===
Unlike many internet personalities who separate their digital personas from reality, Schokker heavily integrates his real life into his Discord server. He frequently uses his public channels to candidly discuss his daily life with autism, turning his server into an interactive extension of his books. This space allows followers to hear his raw, unfiltered thoughts on neurodiversity, coping mechanisms, and his day-to-day routines.

Draft text:
Courtney Grace is an American actress and former television journalist. She worked for about seven years as a reporter, producer and news anchor, most recently at WTSP in Tampa, Florida, before leaving the news business in 2023 to act full-time. [ref: 'Disclosure Day' Anchor Courtney Grace Signs With Gersh (EXCLUSIVE), Deadline] [ref: Courtney Grace, "Disclosure Day," and the One-Scene Wonder, www.rogerebert.com] Her breakout role in a one-scene performance as an unnamed NBC News anchor towards the end of  Steven Spielberg's 2026 science-fiction film Disclosure Day gained widespread attention and press coverage. [ref: ‘Disclosure Day’ Anchor Courtney Grace on Delivering That Final Broadcast and Quitting Her Job to Pursue Acting: ‘It Felt Like Home’, Variety] [ref: Disclosure Day’s Climactic Scene Is Stolen by an Unknown Actor Who Had No Idea Her Part Was So Big, Slate]

== Journalism career ==
Grace was a reporter, producer and anchor in local television news for about seven years. Her last on-air job was at WTSP, the CBS affiliate in Tampa. She said she decided to leave the news business after a conversation with a mentor during an interview training. The mentor sensed that she didn't truly want to be a journalist and asked her what she really wanted to do. She replied: "I want to be an actress." Grace quit her job about a month after that fateful conversation in 2023 to start an acting journey. At that time, she had only a single $500 booking lined up. [ref: Courtney Grace Left Her News Anchor Job 3 Years Ago to Pursue Acting, Now Stars in Spielberg's “Disclosure Day”, Yahoo Entertainment]

== Acting career ==

=== Early roles ===
After leaving news business, Grace acted in several small television parts, including credits on Netflix’s Stranger Things and Sweet Magnolias, Hulu's Murdaugh: Death in the Family, Paramount+'s Tulsa King. She also appeared in David Michôd’s boxing drama Christy starring Sydney Sweeney as boxer Christy Martin. Five of her first seventeen screen roles were playing journalist.

=== Disclosure Day ===
Grace initially auditioned for another role in Disclosure Day, but didn’t get it. But casting director Cindy Tolan, who cast Rachel Zegler and Oscar winner Ariana DeBose in Spielberg's West Side Story, kept Grace in mind and proposed the NBC anchor role to her. [ref: 'Disclosure Day' Gave Former News Anchor Courtney Grace Its Most Emotional Moment, and She Didn't Even Know It, TheWrap]

The scene was shot in New York at 30 Rock, on an NBC set. Grace, who had spent years at a real news anchor desk, described the experience of filming on an NBC set as a full-circle moment. [ref: Courtney Grace had no idea how critical her role would be before watching 'Disclosure Day', NBC New York] She met Spielberg for the first time after filming her role had already started. Spielberg approved of her performance and encouraged her to keep going.

In the finished film, Grace's character appears in the last several minutes. She is presenting a live broadcast about escalating tension on the Korean peninsula when the broadcast is interrupted. Footage released by the characters played by Emily Blunt and Josh O'Connor documenting decades of contact with aliens concealed by the U.S. government was then broadcast. Over the course of the scene, the anchor moves from routine delivery to apology for the images, then to visible distress, before addressing the audience directly with the line "You are not alone."

Grace first saw the completed film at a cast-and-crew screening in New York. She said she expected her scene to show up in the first half an hour of the film. She described the experience of waiting till the end of the film and then realizing the weight of her role in the film as being on two rollercoasters at once.

=== Reception ===

Some of the coverage of Disclosure Day singled out Grace's performance. Writing for RogerEbert.com, Richard Roeper argued that casting a largely unknown actor was the right choice, since a famous actor "would have taken us out of the moment and shifted focus from the intensity of the scene in favor of us chuckling and nodding in recognition." Slate described the ending as being "stolen by an unknown actor" and stated that the scene's plausibility was largely due to Grace's journalist background. Variety noted that while Emily Blunt and Josh O’Connor received their fair share of recognition from critics, Grace had generated some of the strongest online buzz.

=== Subsequent roles ===

In July 2026, Grace signed with Gersh for representation in all areas. She is set to appear in Ally Clark, a thriller directed by Phillip Noyce, and starring Viola Davis for Amazon MGM Studios.

Draft: Pealeism

Draft text:
Pealeism, known by its namesake as Practical Christianity, or more commonly Positive Thinking, is a non-denominational Christian revivalist and new religious movement based on the preaching of Norman Vincent Peale’s ministry, especially his book The Power of Positive Thinking. It emerged in the 1940s advocating for Christian revival in the United States, primarily emphasizing the practical aspects of Christian faith to improve daily life. Pealeism reached its height during the early Fourth Great Awakening before declining throughout the 1960s. [ref: Surge of Piety: Norman Vincent Peale and the Remaking of American Religious Life, Yale University Press]

== History ==
=== Opposition to the New Deal ===
From 1942 on, Norman Vincent Peale’s contacts in business, politics, industry, and religion developed in to a movement around his ministry. In 1945, Peale and his wife, Ruth Stafford Peale, established Guideposts magazine, which featured personal accounts of how faith had helped people confront difficulty.

Peale associated Christian faith with American civic life, capitalism, anti-communism, opposing U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, and participated in conservative organizations including the Committee for Constitutional Government and Spiritual Mobilization. [ref: Norman Vincent Peale Was A Conservative Hero Known Well Beyond His Era, NPR] He belived Christian revival could counter the influence of communism by encouraging Americans to treat Christian faith as integral to personal wellbeing.

=== Post-World War II era and Cold War ===
After World War II, the Pealeist movement grew to include the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic and Foundation for Christian Living, which was the administrative arm of Peale’s ministry. The two organizations allowed Peale to preach to business executives, industrial workers, and youth outside his immediate congregation. In 1951, Peale renamed the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry and served as its president until 1962. The foundation promoted cooperation between clergy and psychiatrists, supported pastoral counselling, and sought to establish Christian faith as integral to mental health.

These approaches were further popularized by books his books, The Real Art of Happiness in 1950, and seminally, The Power of Positive Thinking in 1953.

Peale’s relationships with Federal Bureau of Investigation director J. Edgar Hoover and U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, increased his public visibility and brought his views on religion and national identity to influential circles. He supported campaigns presenting the United States as “one nation under God,” which was part of a broader political and cultural trend towards the prominence of religious language in public life during the 1950s. Peale’s emphasis on rugged individualism and success also appealed to business audiences, since he argued that prayer could inform business decisions, strengthen workplace relations, and address professional challenges.

=== Decline and institutional reorganization ===
Peale’s ministry remained active after the 1950s, but growth in public religious observance declined during the 1960s. In contrast, debates about secularism, science, and societal role of religion became more prominent. The foundation’s claims that Christianity was important to mental health were increasingly criticized by intellectuals.

Peale stepped down as president of the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry in 1962. The foundation subsequently faced financial difficulties by the late 1960s and struggled to maintain the level of support in had the decade prior, reflecting broader changes in the relationship between Christian revivalism and mental-health care.

In 1972, the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry merged with the Academy of Religion and Mental Health to create the Institutes of Religion and Health. However, the organization ended in 1975, though a substantially altered counselling institution continued.

Peale continued to lecture, write, and participate in religious and media activities until he retired as senior minister of Marble Collegiate Church in 1984. He also received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the United States’ highest civilian honour. He died on 24 December 1993 at the age of 95 at his home in Pawling, New York.

In 1995, the Peale Center for Christian Living merged with Guideposts under the leadership of Peale’s wife.

=== 2016 United States presidential election and influence on Donald Trump ===
Peale’s influence received renewed attention during Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign through the latter’s public accounts of his religious upbringing. Trump attended Marble Collegiate Church with his family, and repeatedly identified Peale as a significant spiritual influence. [ref: How Trump got religion — and why his legendary minister’s son now rejects him, The Washington Post] Peale’s influence continues to be relevant in discipline about Christianity’s role in contemporary American conservatism. [ref: ]
[truncated]

Draft text:
The University at Buffalo Student Association Inc., commonly known as the Student Association or SA, is the undergraduate student government of the University at Buffalo (UB), a public university in New York. It represents undergraduate students, recognizes and funds student organizations, and operates campus events and services. [ref: About us, University at Buffalo Student Association] Under its bylaws, every UB undergraduate is a member of the association. [ref: University at Buffalo Student Association Inc. By-Laws, University at Buffalo Student Association]

SA is incorporated separately from the university and has federal 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status. [ref: Student governments become not-for-profit, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)] [ref: University At Buffalo Student Association Inc, Nonprofit Explorer] In 2026, it oversaw more than 200 undergraduate clubs and operated on an annual budget of approximately $4.5 million, funded primarily by a mandatory student activity fee. [ref: UB students vote to increase $109 mandatory student activity fee to $115, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

== History ==

=== Early history and student control of funds ===

The exact founding date of the Student Association is not established in published sources. University Archives holds a collection of SA minutes, correspondence, and other records dating from 1961 to 1967, showing that the organization was active by the early 1960s. [ref: Student Association Records, 1961–1967, University at Buffalo Libraries] The university's Black Student Union, founded in 1967, was recognized by SA in 1968 and had approximately 1,000 members by 1969. [ref: Black Student Union Collection, University at Buffalo Libraries]

In 1970, students established Sub-Board I (SBI), a corporation that administered funds for UB's student governments. SBI was created to move control of student activity-fee money away from the Faculty Student Association (FSA), and it later operated services including legal consultations, a safety shuttle, an off-campus housing service, and student radio. [ref: UB to replace Sub-Board I with Faculty Student Association as student government fiscal agent, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

=== Nonprofit incorporation and fiscal-agent transition ===

In March 2013, the SA Senate voted 13–0, with two abstentions, to seek student approval to incorporate SA as an independent nonprofit. Supporters said that incorporation would separate the association's liabilities from the university and allow SA to enter contracts in its own name. [ref: SA pushes to become not-for-profit, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)] A subsequent student referendum approved incorporation with 90 percent support.

The organizational change was completed in 2019. UB replaced SBI, which had served as fiscal agent for 49 years, with the FSA on July 1, and UB's student governments incorporated as nonprofit organizations legally separate from the university. SA's Senate became the corporation's board of directors. The Internal Revenue Service recognized SA as tax-exempt in December 2019.

=== Recent governance changes ===

In January 2025, the Senate voted 17–0, with one abstention, to divide the existing vice-presidential office into three positions responsible for advocacy, clubs, and events. The change expanded the executive board from three elected officers to five beginning with the 2025–26 term. President Samin Bhuya argued that the change would broaden representation, while vice president Killian Hannigan said that dividing the portfolio would create a clearer chain of command. Senator Jack Koscinski initially questioned whether the additional offices were necessary. [ref: SA Senate splits VP role into three positions: advocacy, events and clubs, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

In October 2025, the Senate voted 19–1, with two abstentions, to permit the president and treasurer, acting jointly, to remove a club-council coordinator. President Aisha Adam supported the change as a way to address coordinators who did not perform their duties. An earlier version had failed the preceding spring amid concerns that it would concentrate too much authority in the executive board. [ref: SA council coordinators now subject to removal by e-board, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

The REAL party swept all five executive offices in April 2026 in an election with 4,937 voters, which then-president Aisha Adam described as record turnout. The elected board consisted of Jack Koscinski as president, Na'Dia Carter as vice president for advocacy, Pranavan Balachandran as vice president for clubs, William Dong as vice president for events, and Laron Fomby as treasurer. [ref: 'REAL' party sweeps SA's 2026–27 e-board elections, [[The Spectrum (University at Buffalo)]

== Knox Studios ==

Knox Studios is an independent American software development studio based in Valley, Alabama. Founded in May 2026 as a subsidiary of Knox Holdings LLC, the company specializes in mobile applications, utility software, "offline-first" business tools, and video games for iOS and Android platforms. The studio is known for its "local-first" architectural approach, which prioritizes data privacy; this involves utilizing on-device machine learning alongside hybrid, web-native frameworks. == History ==
Knox Studios was founded by its managing partner, Connor, with an explicit focus on the craftsmanship of its products and the user experience, rather than on the size of the company. Operating independently from Valley, Alabama, the studio handles the entire development, technical implementation, and publishing of its software. As of the end of 2026, the company manages more than 30 active applications on the Google Play Store and maintains an extensive pipeline of software projects currently in development for iOS and Android. [ref: Knox Studios — Apps & Games, Knox Studios]

== Software and Applications ==
The studio has developed several end-user-facing discovery apps based on swipe-driven user interfaces:

== Tools and Utilities ==
A large portion of the Knox Studios portfolio is dedicated to practical tools and calculators for field work, with a strong emphasis on offline functionality:

* Trade Tools: Applications such as PlumbSync (a digital precision spirit level) and the Fraction Calculator (designed specifically for carpenters to accurately interpret measurements from a tape measure) are tailored for the construction and skilled trades sectors.
* Quote Estimation Apps: The studio offers a range of offline-optimized estimation apps for various service industries, including HydroBid (pressure washing), TurfQuote (landscaping), CaterBid (catering), and FenceBid (fencing).
* Privacy and Security Apps: Applications such as Scrambl (password-protected photo obfuscation) and Quantext (AES-256-GCM text encryption) focus on keeping user data stored locally on the device, with no user account required.

== Health and Family Care ==
Knox Studios develops the Sync suite and other health apps, with a focus on data privacy and user-friendliness. Currently available applications include BackSpace (isometric exercises for back pain), EveSync (menstrual cycle and ovulation tracking), and NestSync (an offline timer for newborn care). This category also includes tools that have not yet been released: ElderSync, designed for senior care, and SproutSync, for comprehensive tracking of child development. [ref: Apps & Games, Knox Studios]

== Video Games ==
In addition to utility software, Knox Studios also develops mobile games that explicitly eschew real-money gambling mechanics.

* Puzzle Games: The studios live gaming portfolio includes puzzle games that can be played offline, such as DinoDoku (a logic puzzle similar to Star Battle), Bubble Pop Quest, and Jewel Journey.
* Knox Gems Collection: This collection of classic casino and card games including Knox Blackjack, Three Card Poker, Knox Baccarat, and Knox Solitaire is currently in development and utilizes a unified in-app currency system called "Gems."

Ferdowsi's Grandeur (Persian: ) is a sculpture of the Persian poet Ferdowsi, made by Mohsen Saraji and commissioned by Hossein Sabet for the science square of Ferdowsi University of Mashhad, Iran. A May 2025 report in The Independent Persian described it as a 38-metre fibreglass statue that had not been installed. [ref: مجسمه‌ای‌ که هرگز نصب نشد؛ قامت ایستاده فردوسی، خط قرمز گنبد, The Independent Persian]

== Construction ==
Work began in autumn 2019. According to the Saraaj centre's project account, fabrication was completed in Azar 1399 (November–December 2020) and involved more than 250 components. [ref: فردوسی, Saraaj]

== Proposed installation ==
In May 2020, the Iran Book News Agency reported objections by university academics and students to the proposed scale and location. Critics questioned its suitability for an educational setting and argued for prioritising university facilities. The report also covered university president Mohammad Kafi's defence of the project and his explanation that a private donor was financing it. [ref: ماجرای ساخت مجسمه 40 متری فردوسی در دانشگاه فردوسی مشهد چیست؟, Iran Book News Agency]

In May 2024, Iran International reported that Ahmad Alamolhoda characterised the proposed university statue as an attempt to present Ferdowsi in opposition to Imam Reza. [ref: نماینده خامنه‌ای در خراسان رضوی: برخی می‌خواستند فردوسی را مقابل امام رضا مطرح کنند, Iran International]

In a Mehr News Agency report republished by Expressna on 31 August 2025, Razavi Khorasan governor Gholamhossein Mozaffari supported installing the statue and said there was no obstacle to doing so. He rejected comparisons between the monument and the Imam Reza shrine, while calling for consideration of the location and implementation details. [ref: استاندار خراسان رضوی: نصب مجسمه فردوسی هیچ مانعی ندارد, Expressna]

Didban Iran reported that Mohammad Javad Khosravi, mayor of Tehran's District 22, said the municipality had sought to transfer the statue from Mashhad for installation in the Chitgar heights or at Chitgar Lake, but that the statue had not been made available to it. [ref: مدیران شهری پایتخت: مجسمه فردوسی در حال از بین رفتن است/ نه در مشهد از آن استفاده کردند، نه آن را به تهران دادند, Didban Iran]

Thomas Bonham (by 1482 – 1532) was an English politician. He sat as MP for Essex in 1529. [ref: BONHAM, Thomas (by 1482-1532), of Stanway, Essex., History of Parliament Online]

== Family and education ==
He was educated at the Inner Temple. In 1508/9, he married Catherine, the daughter of Henry Marney, 1st Baron Marney, the widow of Edward Knyvet and they had five sons (including William Bonham) and two daughters.

== Offices held ==
He served as receiver-general of the Duchy of Lancaster from 1509 till his death, and steward of Savoy manor from 1523 till his death; justice of the peace for Essex from 1510 till possibly his death; recorder of Colchester from 1511 till 1529; commissioner of subsidy in Essex in 1512, 1514, 1515, 1523, 1524, and in Colchester in 1523, and 1524; he served in other commissions from 1512 till 1530; as keeper of writs and rolls, captain of common pleas in 1520; Sheriff of Essex and Hertfordshire from 1520 till February 1522, 1526 till 1527; and bencher of the Inner Temple in 1530.

Stun Siva (also credited as Stun Shiva) is an Indian stunt choreographer and actor who works mainly in Tamil cinema, and also in Hindi, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada films. He received the Tamil Nadu State Film Award for Best Stunt Coordinator for Kannukkul Nilavu (2000) and, with Peter Hein, the IIFA Award for Best Action for the Hindi film Ghajini.

== Career ==

=== Stunt choreography ===
Siva began his career in the Tamil film industry as a stunt performer and assistant. In a 2018 interview with The Times of India, he said that he became a stunt master with the 1997 film Love Today. A 2008 India Today feature on Chennai's stunt directors included him among the city's leading action choreographers and described how stunt professionals progressed in the industry. In 2016, The Times of India discussed his work and experience in an article on Tamil cinema's action choreographers.

He received the Tamil Nadu State Film Award for Best Stunt Coordinator for Kannukkul Nilavu (2000). For the 2008 Hindi film Ghajini, he and Peter Hein won the IIFA Award for Best Action at the 2009 IIFA technical awards.

His later work includes the action sequences of Nelson Dilipkumar's Jailer (2023); a review in Odisha Plus said that the film relied heavily on his action direction and that the action complemented the narrative.

=== Acting ===
Siva has also appeared as an actor, including in Vettaiyaadu Vilaiyaadu (2006). In Champion (2019), directed by Suseenthiran, he played the antagonist. In an August 2019 interview with The Times of India, he discussed his performance in Goli Soda 2 and said it led to him being cast as a lead actor.

=== Directing ===
In 2015, Siva announced his directorial debut, an action film with a romance track, launched in the presence of producer Kalaipuli S. Thanu and director Prabhu Solomon. The film, titled Karate Karan (also spelled Karatekaaran), was described as a Tamil remake of The Karate Kid, with his sons Kevin and Steven in the lead roles; Siva said that Jackie Chan had sent his good wishes to the team. In 2018, The Times of India reported on his continued work on the film.

== Personal life ==
Siva's sons, Kevin Kumar and Steven Kumar, are also stunt choreographers and martial artists.

Usman Iqbal is a Pakistani-born health informatics researcher and academic. He is a Professor of Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence at Bond University, where he leads the Evidence-Based Practice Professorial Unit at Gold Coast Hospital and Health Services.

== Education ==

He also holds a postgraduate certificate in global health informatics from the Harvard–MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology.

== Academic career ==
Usman held academic positions at Taipei Medical University and co-founded the Taiwan chapter of the Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) collaborative. He subsequently worked in government on digital health initiatives before joining Bond University. He also holds an adjunct academic appointment at the University of New South Wales.

His research focuses on digital health, biomedical informatics, patient safety, and artificial intelligence in healthcare. In 2020, he co-authored a paper proposing "earlier medicine", an approach that uses artificial intelligence and predictive analytics to support earlier identification of health risks and intervention. In 2026, he was the lead author of an evidence gap map of digital health interventions for patient engagement, published in npj Digital Medicine.

Usman was elected a Fellow of the International Academy of Health Sciences Informatics in 2023. In 2019, he received Taiwan's Plum Blossom Card in recognition of his contributions as a high-level foreign professional.

Terenc Pepa (born 8 October 1987) is an Albanian landscape and cultural heritage photographer, certified commercial drone pilot, and information technology engineer. [ref: Terenc Pepa, fotografi profesionist që profesionalisht na sjell Shkodrën në çdo hir të saj adhurues, Albert Vataj]

== Early life and education ==

Pepa was born in Shkodër, Albania, on 8 October 1987. He received artistic training during his secondary education at the Prenkë Jakova artistic school (Shkolla Artistike "Prenkë Jakova") in Shkodër before pursuing formal studies in computer engineering and information technology.

Pepa later completed European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) certification as an unmanned aircraft (drone) pilot, incorporating specialized high-altitude aerial photography and videography into his documentation of the mountainous terrain of the Albanian Alps. [ref: About – Terenc Pepa Photography, terencpepa.com]

== Photography and visual promotion ==

Pepa has documented landscapes, architectural sites, and cultural heritage across Northern Albania for over a decade. His imagery frequently highlights regional landmarks including Rozafa Castle, Lake Shkodër, the Shala River, Theth, Valbona Valley National Park, the Kelmend region, and the historic urban core of Shkodër.

Journalist and cultural critic Albert Vataj has written multiple profiles detailing Pepa's photographic style, emphasizing his technical use of drone cameras at dawn and dusk to record natural light patterns over historical ruins, rivers, and national parks in Northern Albania.

Pepa's visual work has been utilized in destination marketing campaigns, institutional archives, and promotional projects supported by public institutions and international development bodies:
* Government and regional institutions: The Municipality of Shkodër (Bashkia Shkodër), the Shkodër Regional Council (Këshilli i Qarkut Shkodër), the National Agency of Protected Areas (Agjencia Kombëtare e Zonave të Mbrojtura – AKZM), and projects backed by the Minister of State for the Protection of Enterprise (Ministria e Shtetit për Mbrojtjen e Sipërmarrjes).
* International and non-governmental organizations: Visual production and heritage documentation for the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the Institute for Habitat Development (Co-PLAN), and the Italian humanitarian organization VIS Albania.

== Information technology and digital media ==

Parallel to his work in photography, Pepa has worked in system administration, web development, and broadcasting infrastructure. He has provided IT and video transmission support for regional broadcaster Star Plus TV and served as digital media administrator and webmaster for the multi-sports club KF Vllaznia Shkodër. He is also the founder and developer of the regional portal Shkodër.info.

* Shkodra Tourism Awards: Awarded "Tourism Influencer of the Year" for regional digital promotion and travel photography of Northern Albania.

Dharmendra Jai Narain, also known as DJ Narain, is an Indian musician, singer, composer and also a former civil servant. Started as the lead singer and composer of the Indian pop-rock band Aryans. The group became popular in the late 90 and 2000s with popular songs including Aankhon Mein Tera Hi Chehra, Yeh Hawa Kehti Hai Kya and Dekha Hai Teri Aankhon Ko. [ref: Aryans: Bald and the dutiful!, The Times of India] [ref: Tera Naam: Aryans' DJ Narain makes a grand comeback with soulful number, Hindustan Times]

Besides being a musician, he has been a civil servant with Government of India. Alongside his music career, Narain had a career in the Indian Information Service for long and served as director of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII) from 2011 to 2015. [ref: D J Narain takes charge as director of FTII, The Times of India] [ref: Ex-NFAI director Prashant Pathrabe appointed as director of FTII Pune, The Indian Express] His last few months as director of FTII were eventful and in news for the students strike over appointments to the institute's governing bodies. [ref: FTII director draws hard line to students: End strike or face rustication, The Indian Express]

After taking voluntary retirement from government service, Narain returned to releasing music as a solo artist and musician in 2022. [ref: DJ Narain is back, to shoot a song in hometown Lucknow, Hindustan Times]

==Early life and music==

Narain studied at the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur. [ref: Aryans: Striking the right notes, The Times of India]

He was involved with music before the formation of Aryans and was associated with the Lucknow student music scene and was a member of the band Dreams in 1988 who later became DJ Narain of Aryans. [ref: Bands which had a bond with LU, The Times of India]

Narain subsequently became associated with Aryans while also pursuing a professional career as a Civil servant outside music. In 2003 while being part of the band Aryans, he was also working with the Directorate of Film Festivals in New Delhi.

==Music career==

===Aryans===

Aryans emerged as part of India's independent-pop scene around the turn of the century. Narain was one of the principal members of the group and was widely known for being its lead singer.

The group produced songs including Aankhon Mein Tera Hi Chehra, Yeh Hawa Kehti Hai Kya and Dekha Hai Teri Aankhon Ko. The music video for Aankhon Mein Tera Hi Chehra featured Shahid Kapoor before his emergence as a Hindi film actor.

Narain continued to pursue music while working in government as a civil servant. Early 2000s, various media reports profiled Aryans lead singer Narain's connection with the music and his simultaneous professional career. There were Reports about the band's music and international performances. Aryans had also contributed the song Kyun to the Hindi film Woodstock Villa in 2008.

The band later went off the radar as the members pursued individual career and DJ Narain focusses on his professional career as a Civil Servant with goverment.

===Solo return===

He spent more than a decade being away from music, and after his voluntary retirement from government service, Narain returned as a solo artist in 2022.

His single Tera Naam was released by Times Music. Narain wrote, composed and sang the song.

==Civil service career==

Before joining the civil services, Narain worked in advertising inductry. He subsequently joined the Indian Information Service as part of its 1990 batch.

His association with FTII began in 1993, when he undertook a film and television production course at the institute as part of his Indian Information Service training.

During his government career, Narain served as the spokesperson for the Southern Command, Ministry of Defence in 1997–98 and later taught mass communication at the Indian Institute of Mass Communication.

===Film and Television Institute of India===

Narain took charge as director of the Film and Television Institute of India in July 2011, succeeding Pankaj Rag.

After an inatial three-year term, he subsequently received a one-year extension. [ref: FTII director to be picked in July 13 meet, The Indian Express]

====2015 FTII strike====

The final months of Narain's tenure coincided with a major dispute at FTII following the appointment of actor Gajendra Chauhan as chairman of the institute's governing council and the appointment of other members of the FTII Society. Students began an indefinite strike in June 2015 opposing the appointments.

Narain, as director, became actively involved in a bid to manage the dispute. As the strike continued into its second month, he issued a formal notice directing students to resume academic activities and warning that continued defiance could result in disciplinary action, including rustication. But the students rejected the warning and continued their protest, publicly criticising the administration's response. [ref: Now, FTII director comes under criticism for rustication threat, The Indian Express]

Draft text:
EasyAudit is an American information security compliance company headquartered in Miami Beach, Florida. It provides a managed compliance service that combines a dedicated human compliance lead with an AI-based platform to help organizations prepare for third-party audits and certifications against frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, NIST Cybersecurity Framework and ISO 9001. The company was founded by Christian Khoury, a former Deloitte risk advisory consultant, who serves as chief executive officer.[1]

The company describes its approach as "Autonomous Compliance" and positions the service as an alternative to both compliance automation software, such as Vanta and Drata, and to readiness assessments sold by consulting firms.[2] EasyAudit does not perform audits or issue certifications; those remain the responsibility of independent auditors and accredited certification bodies.

History

EasyAudit was founded in 2023 by Christian Khoury and Tyson Graham. Khoury previously worked in risk advisory at Deloitte.[1] According to the company, it was started because its founders were unable to hire the compliance expertise they needed and built a service to replace it.[2]

The company initially launched as an AI-based compliance software product that generated self-assessment reports, security controls and policy documents from a company questionnaire.[3] It later repositioned from selling software to delivering an outcome-based managed service, in which a named compliance lead manages each engagement and the platform executes recurring work.[2]

In 2026, EasyAudit introduced a free diagnostic engagement it calls the Compliance Simulation, and a guarantee under which customers do not pay if they are not audit-ready by an agreed date.[2]

Products and services

EasyAudit sells a single managed service built from three parts: a dedicated compliance lead who owns the engagement and coordinates with the customer and its auditor; an AI assistant the company calls the AI Compliance Officer, which collects evidence, drafts documentation and monitors controls; and an underlying platform that stores controls, evidence, mappings and audit history.[2]

The platform is organized around a single framework-agnostic control library, called the EasyAudit Framework, into which each supported standard is mapped. The company states that one control in the library can satisfy requirements from up to seven frameworks, so that evidence collected once applies across all of them.[4] Supported frameworks include SOC 1, SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-53, and NIST SP 800-171.[4]

Other platform functions include an onboarding questionnaire that builds a company profile, AI-generated controls and policies tailored to that profile, continuous monitoring through read-only integrations with Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Microsoft 365, risk assessment, vendor risk management, a public trust center, and a Model Context Protocol connection that lets third-party AI assistants read the compliance data.[4]

Before a contract, prospective customers can take part in the Compliance Simulation, a diagnostic in which EasyAudit reviews existing policies and connected systems and returns a gap analysis, scope, timeline and price. Where eligible, the timeline is backed by a guarantee that the customer does not pay if it is not audit-ready by the agreed date.[2] The company states that formal certification and audit opinions remain with the independent auditor.[2]

Business model and market

EasyAudit charges a subscription fee for the managed service rather than billing by the hour, and ties part of that fee to delivering audit readiness by an agreed date.[2] The company has said it competes mainly with compliance consulting firms, including the Big Four accounting firms and specialist firms such as Coalfire, and A-LIGN, whose paid readiness assessments it aims to replace with its free Simulation, and secondarily with compliance automation software vendors such as Vanta, Drata and Secureframe.[2]

Its customers are mid-market organizations in regulated industries, typically with 500 to 10,000 employees, including insurance, data centers, business process outsourcing, pharmaceutical services and companies pursuing ISO 42001 for AI management systems. The company primarily serves the United States, with secondary markets in Canada and Latin America, and supports English and Spanish.[2]

== Sunkind India Limited ==
Sunkind India Limited is an Indian renewable energy company headquartered in Gurugram, Haryana. The company works in the solar energy sector, delivering engineering, procurement, and construction (solar EPC services), operations and maintenance (O&M), and commercial renewable energy project solutions for industries and institutions. Its business activities also include solar mounting structures and photovoltaic module manufacturing, with planned expansion into battery energy storage systems. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, official website.]

The company operates under the brand of Sunkind Energy and describes its activities as covering several stages of the renewable energy value chain, including solar project development, equipment manufacturing and renewable power generation. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Sunkind Energy: EPC operations and project portfolio.]

== History ==
Sunkind Energy was established in Sept 2019 to develop solar energy solutions for industrial and commercial customers in India. Its early operations included rooftop photovoltaic installations and hybrid rooftop systems. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, About Us: company history and leadership.]

2020: In 2020 the company completes its first set of hybrid rooftop systems, laying the foundation for execution excellence. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Investor information and financial disclosures.]

2021: Company delivers a major 3 MWp rooftop project, expanding its capabilities and building trust across sectors.

2022: Company launches Strucmax and establishes in-house mounting structure manufacturing, completing 18+ MWp of projects in a single year. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Strucmax: solar mounting structures.]

2023: Sunkind recorded strong growth, delivered 20+ MWp of solar projects, and moved into a new corporate headquarters.

2024: Company executes 75+ MWp of projects and completes its first project under an operating expenditure (OPEX) model.

2025: Sunkind crosses 150+ MWp in project capacity, expands group manufacturing capabilities, and strengthens its position as a future-ready clean energy company.

== Business activities ==

=== Solar engineering, procurement, and construction ===
Sunkind's principal business as of 2026 is providing Solar EPC services. The company provides turnkey solar power installations services including engineering, equipment procurement, construction, installation and commissioning.

Its project portfolio includes rooftop solar systems, ground-mounted photovoltaic installations and off-site solar projects. The company also provides solutions under capital expenditure (CAPEX) and operating expenditure (OPEX) arrangements.

Under the CAPEX model, customers finance and own their solar installations. Under OPEX arrangements, solar assets may be developed and operated under contractual structures designed to reduce the customer's initial capital requirement.

=== Operations and maintenance (O&M) ===
Sunkind India Limited provides integrated and external operations and maintenance services for solar power plants. These services include plant inspections, module cleaning, remote monitoring, equipment repairs and performance management. The services are designed to support system availability, energy generation and long-term plant performance.

=== Solar mounting structures ===
Strucmax is the part of Sunkind Energy group's and a solar mounting structure manufacturing business. It manufactures mounting systems used to support photovoltaic modules in solar power installations.

The company describes its products as modular, in-house-engineered structures designed for installation efficiency and structural durability. The business is part of the group's efforts to integrate equipment manufacturing with solar EPC operations.

=== Photovoltaic module manufacturing ===
Sunkind Photovoltaics is a part of Sunkind energy group and photovoltaic module manufacturing business. Its activities focus on manufacturing solar modules for use in renewable energy installations. [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Sunkind Photovoltaics.]

The company describes its manufacturing approach as including automated production processes and quality control. Its published product information includes high-efficiency TOPCon and bifacial solar module technologies. [ref: pv magazine India, Sunkind India Limited secures long-term supply access to 1 GW TOPCon DCR solar cells, 29 May 2026.]

=== Battery energy storage ===
Batt-Li is the part of Sunkind Energy group's plan for building lithium-ion batteries for renewal energy storage business. The company is actively investing in commercial and industrial energy storage solutions (BESS). [ref: Sunkind India Limited, Batt-Li: battery energy storage.]

=== Project portfolio ===
Sunkind's solar EPC portfolio includes installations for industrial, commercial, institutional and power-sector customers. The company's project listings identify clients across industries such as steel, textiles, automotive manufacturing, packaging, aluminium, healthcare, hospitality and food processing.

The company lists projects in more than 16 states and union territories. Its published portfolio includes both commissioned installations and projects under execution.

He was an author of a 2008 study in Science describing inhibitors of the bacterial cell-division protein FtsZ, and lead author of a 2016 review in The Lancet Infectious Diseases assessing non-traditional approaches to treating bacterial infection.

== Education ==
Czaplewski received a first-class B.Sc. in biological sciences from the University of East Anglia and a Ph.D. in molecular genetics from the University of Glasgow, where his research concerned Streptomyces molecular genetics. [ref: Streptomyces molecular genetics thesis record, University of Glasgow] He subsequently held a postdoctoral position at the University of Leeds studying gene regulation in Bacillus subtilis. [ref: Biography for Lloyd Czaplewski, World Health Organization]

== Career ==
Czaplewski has held research and development roles at British Biotech, Prolysis, Biota Europe and Persica Pharmaceuticals. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry. [ref: Lloyd Czaplewski, CF AMR Syndicate] [ref: Lloyd Czaplewski, REVIVE, Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership]

== Antibacterial drug discovery ==
Czaplewski was one of the authors of a 2008 study in Science describing a class of synthetic antibacterials, exemplified by the compound PC190723, that inhibit FtsZ and prevent bacterial cell division. The compounds showed bactericidal activity against staphylococci, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. [ref: An inhibitor of FtsZ with potent and selective anti-staphylococcal activity, [[Science (journal)] The work arose from antibacterial research at Prolysis, [ref: New approaches to overcoming antimicrobial resistance, The Pharmaceutical Journal] which subsequently received funding for antibacterial discovery research through the Wellcome Trust's Seeding Drug Discovery initiative. [ref: Wellcome Trust issues first grants to encourage drug discovery, Pharmafile]

== Antimicrobial resistance research and policy ==
From around 2010 Czaplewski worked on initiatives concerning antimicrobial resistance. He took part in activities associated with the British Society for Antimicrobial Chemotherapy's "The Urgent Need" programme, which examined challenges in antibacterial research and development. [ref: Antibiotic resistance: what, why, where, when and how?, British Medical Bulletin] He chaired a review commissioned by the UK Department of Health and the Wellcome Trust examining alternatives to conventional antibiotics, including bacteriophages, antimicrobial peptides and host-directed approaches. The review was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases in 2016 as "Alternatives to antibiotics—a pipeline portfolio review", with Czaplewski as lead author. [ref: Alternatives to antibiotics—a pipeline portfolio review, The Lancet Infectious Diseases] Its findings informed the alternatives-to-antibiotics section of the Review on Antimicrobial Resistance chaired by Jim O'Neill; Czaplewski is listed among the report's acknowledged contributors.< [ref: Tackling Drug-Resistant Infections Globally: Final Report and Recommendations, Review on Antimicrobial Resistance)] He was lead author of a study of global public and philanthropic investment in antibacterial therapeutic research from 2017 to 2023, published in The Lancet Microbe in 2026. The analysis, based on data from the Global AMR R&D Hub, found that 130 funders had invested US$2.51 billion over the period, that funding was concentrated among a small number of sources, and that it had declined since 2020. [ref: An overview of global public and philanthropic investments into antibacterial therapeutics (2017–23), The Lancet Microbe]

== Later translational research ==
Czaplewski is chief scientific officer of Persica Pharmaceuticals, which developed PP353, an intradiscal antibiotic therapy for chronic low back pain associated with Modic change type 1. A phase 1b randomised, sham-controlled trial reported in eClinicalMedicine in 2026 found that two intradiscal administrations of PP353 were well tolerated and reduced pain and disability relative to the sham procedure at twelve months. [ref: Intradiscal linezolid (PP353) treatment for chronic low back pain associated with Modic change type 1: an international, first-in-human, randomised, sham procedure-controlled, double-blind, phase 1b clinical trial, eClinicalMedicine] [ref: New drug for lower back pain could be ‘a gamechanger’, The Guardian] [ref: Therapeutic approach could treat chronic low back pain, Drug Discovery World (DDW)].

== Advisory roles ==
Czaplewski has served on advisory bodies concerned with antimicrobial resistance research and funding, including the World Health Organization's Antibiotic Advisory Group and advisory panels for CARB-X [ref: Advisory Board, Carb-X] and the Global Antibiotic Research and Development Partnership. He served on the scientific selection board of the Novo REPAIR Impact Fund and later chaired it, and has chaired an advisory group of the Pathways to Antimicrobial Clinical Efficacy (PACE) programme. [ref: PACE Scientific Projects Advisory Group, PACE] Since 2021 he has been a non-executive director of Curza. [ref: Curza leadership and board information, Curza]

== Research impact ==
As of October 2026, Czaplewski's publications had received over 6,000 citations with an h-index of 32, according to Google Scholar. [ref: Lloyd Czaplewski, Google Scholar]

Before this, he was founding CEO of the World Kabaddi League (WKL) and founder of the sports-media company Sports Flashes. Raheja has worked in the entertainment and events industry and later contributed in development of sports leagues, sports media, marketing and research in India. [ref: Exclusive: Sports Flashes raises pre-Series A funding, TechCircle]

Through LLC, he was also involved in hosting some noteworthy cricket matches featuring former international players in Jammu and Srinagar, cities which were deprived of international cricket for several decades. Raheja served as the founding chief executive officer of the World Kabaddi League (WKL), a professional circle-style kabaddi competition launched in 2014. The league was part of Kabaddi's growth in India along with Pro Kabaddi League

The competition was conceived as an international touring sports property as its structure had been modelled on Formula One, with plans for teams to compete in cities across several countries. The inaugural season began in London before subsequently staging matches in India. [ref: World Kabaddi League, Times of India]

In 2016, Raheja was part of sports research organisation Super Insight, and was instrumental in the launch of Indian Sports Salaries Report 2016. Media stories described it as India's first sports salaries report [ref: India's first ever Sports Salary Report reveals startling facts, The Sports Mirror] with compensation details across eight professional sports leagues in India, including the Indian Premier League, Indian Super League, Pro Kabaddi League, Hockey India League, International Premier Tennis League, Premier Badminton League, Champions Tennis League and Pro Wrestling League.
