Drew Smith (born 1950) is an English food writer, critic, editor, broadcaster and translator. He was The Guardian restaurant columnist, editor of The Good Food Guide, and presenter and investigative journalist of Channel 4’s Food File TV programme. His books include Oyster, a Gastronomic History of the World (with Recipes); Soupology, Six Broths for 70 Soups; and Modern Cooking: From the First Backstreet Bistros of Lyons to the Finest Restaurants. He also translated La Mère Brazier: The Mother of Modern French Cooking, by Eugénie Brazier into English and acted as a consultant editor on the first translation of The Talisman of Happiness, by Ada Boni.

== Food journalism and broadcasting ==
Smith was appointed editor of The Good Food Guide in 1981, [ref: ] after winning the restaurant writer of the year award at the Glenfiddich Food and Drink Awards. [ref: ] He held the post of editor until 1989 [ref: FOOD & DRINK / Undercover with a guide leader: 'The Good Food Guide', The Independent].
Whilst at The Good Food Guide [ref: All Consuming: The instant Sunday Times bestseller: Why We Eat the Way We Eat Now, Random House], Smith coined the term Modern British Cooking to describe regional and traditional British cuisine.. He had strong views on some regional cuisine, describing in 1982 that the lack of good food options in the North East England was a "black hole of gastronomy". [ref: A Geordie gourmet, The Independent]

In 1981 he was appointed restaurant columnist for The Guardian [ref: Drew Smith, Caterer & Hotelkeeper], where he stayed until 1990. When Smith inspected the London branch of Maxim's restaurant in 1983 without wearing a tie, the door staff presented Smith with a selection of public school ties to borrow while dining. The Guardian's headline on the resultant review went: "Sunshine, at £18, I’ll eat it stark naked with chopsticks if I like." [ref: From veggie fritters to fish ice-cream: 200 years of Guardian food, The Guardian]

In 1991 Smith launched Channel 4’s investigative food programme Food File. [ref: Channel 4 8:30: Food File, The Times] Notable episodes include one that explored The Mediterranean diet for the first time on British TV, and an exposé of the potential harm of saturated fats. [ref: Television - Eschewing the fat: Food File, Channel 4, The Times]

Smith is also known for his radio and podcast work. He presented A beginner’s guide to the oysters on BBC Sounds and was featured on the BBC’s The Food Programme. [ref: A beginners guide to the oyster, BBC]

Smith has contributed to newspapers and magazines, including The Sunday Times, The Guardian and The Independent, as well as being cited in several books [ref: The Sociology of Tourism: Theoretical and Empirical Investigations, Routledge] and articles about food and hospitality.

== Books ==
Smith is a book author and editor. His works include Oyster, a Gastronomic History of the World (with Recipes) [ref: A potted history of the oyster in London, The Standard] – voted one of American Vogue’s books of the year – Soupology, Six Broths for 70 Soups [ref: Broth to Bowl by Drew Smith] and Modern Cooking: From the First Backstreet Bistros of Lyons to the Finest Restaurants.
He was instrumental in bringing two European classic recipe books to English audiences for the first time: La Mère Brazier: The Mother of Modern French Cooking, a French classic by Eugénie Brazier [ref: La Mère Brazier, Elwin Street Productions] [ref: The Queen of the French Kitchen, The Daily Beast], the first woman awarded six Michelin stars [ref: Mère Brazier, guide.michelin.com], which Smith translated into English and was named the 2018 book of the year by The Observer. He also published
The Talisman of Happiness by Ada Boni [ref: The Book That Taught Nonna to Cook Is Coming to America, The New York Times], for which he served as consultant editor on the first English translation of the Italian cooking book.
Smith also collaborated on a series of books with Dr Stephan Domenig of the FX Mayr clinic in Austria, exploring the benefits of the alkaline diet.
He is currently editor-at-large for book publisher Elwin Street Productions.

== Other work ==
Smith is one of the founders of the Guild of Food Writers and acted as Head of Food Policy at the London Docklands Development Corporation from 1999 to 2001.

== Awards ==
Glenfiddich Food and Drink Awards, restaurant critic of the year 1979, 1982, 1985.

== Student-Centered, Technology-Rich Learning Environments (SCenTRLE)==
Student-Centered, Technology-Rich Learning Environments (SCenTRLE) is an instructional design model developed by educational researcher Atsusi Hirumi. Hirumi developed the model in the 1990s and formally published it in 2002. Hirumi's model uses eight instructional events to facilitate student-centred learning grounded in constructivist principles. The model largely focuses on active participation, knowledge construction and learner independence, and uses technology to support the learning process. [ref: Student-Centered, Technology-Rich Learning Environments (SCenTRLE): Operationalizing Constructivist Approaches to Teaching and Learning, Journal of Technology and Teacher Education]

== Theoretical background ==

The SCenTRLE model is rooted in constructivist learning theory, which depicts learners as active participants in the expansion of knowledge. Hirumi identified four foundations for the model: societal, psychological, epistemological and pedagogical. These four principles are also addressed in other research on technology-enhanced student-centred learning environments.. [ref: The Foundations and Assumptions of Technology-Enhanced Student-Centered Learning Environments, Instructional Science]

Hirumi posits that the societal foundation is based on the growing role of information and technology in education. He argued that increased access to information requires learners to develop various competences other than subject knowledge such as problem-solving skills, communication and independent learning.

Secondly, the psychological foundation draws on constructivist perspectives of Jean Piaget, Jerome Bruner and Lev Vygotsky. It explains how learners acquire knowledge through experience, cognitive development and social interaction.

Thirdly, the epistemological foundation is rooted in pragmatism. This perspective claims that individuals construct knowledge through experience, prior understanding and interaction with others while recognising an external reality.

Finally, the pedagogical foundation integrates student-centred learning, generative learning, situated cognition, problem-based learning and performance assessment. Together, they foster active participation, authentic learning and the practical application of knowledge.

In SCenTRLE, learners contribute to decisions about their learning, while instructors provide continuous guidance and feedback.

== The eight instructional events ==

The SCenTRLE model comprises eight instructional events that guide student-centred learning. The events provide a framework that learners use to establish objectives, select learning strategies and assess their progress. The events are presented sequentially but learners may revisit earlier activities as their understanding develops. [ref: Vicarious Interactions and Self-Directed Learning of Students by Course Delivery Strategy, Texas A&M University]

# Set Learning Challenge:The instructor sets a learning challenge that identifies what students should be able to accomplish and provides the overall direction.
# Negotiate Learning Goals and Objectives: Learners collaborate with the instructor to determine the knowledge and skills needed to complete the challenge. This may include assessing prior knowledge, identifying areas for improvement and creating individual learning objectives.
# Negotiate Learning Strategies: Students identify the activities and resources they will use to achieve their learning objectives while instructors provide guidance and encourages learners to determine which activities best address their needs.
# Construct Knowledge: Learners then apply their strategies, individually or collaboratively, to develop knowledge and skills. The instructor monitors progress and provides support when needed.
# Negotiate Performance Criteria: Learners and instructors establish criteria for assessing whether the learning objectives have been met. Assessment rubrics may be developed to help learners review the quality of their work.
# Conduct Self, Peer and Expert Assessments: Students evaluate their work based on the agreed rubrics and receive feedback from peers and individuals with relevant expertise.
# Monitor Performance and Provide Feedback: Monitoring and feedback occur throughout the learning process. Instructors review students' work, respond to questions, provide feedback on their progress while students monitor their own progress.
# Communicate Results: The final event involves presenting the outcomes of learning. Students may use portfolios, presentations or other samples to demonstrate their achievements.

The eight events promote learner independence while preserving the instructor's role as a facilitator.

== Applications and case studies ==

=== Initial implementation in higher education ===

Hirumi's first field test of SCenTRLE was a 15-week undergraduate course on the educational applications of computer technology. The course included 30 students with different levels of computer experience: seven novice users, 17 apprentices and six more proficient users. The model was introduced to address these differences and allow students to pursue learning objectives aligned with their existing knowledge and interests.
[truncated]

== Injury and death ==

In September 2026, Kawanthissa was reportedly found with an injury to his right foreleg in the Galgamuwa area. Wildlife officials and veterinarians treated the injury and monitored his condition. [ref: Ailing tusker Kavanthissa in critical condition, public urged to stay away, Daily Mirror]

Subsequent reports described a deterioration in the elephant's condition, including reduced food intake and diarrhoea, while veterinary treatment continued. [ref: Ailing tusker Kavanthissa in critical condition, public urged to stay away, Daily Mirror]

Kawanthissa died in October 2026 while receiving veterinary care. His death prompted public concern and calls for an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his treatment. [ref: Outrage and calls for investigation following tragic death of iconic Kawanthissa, The Sunday Times]

== Investigation ==

Following Kawanthissa's death, Sri Lanka's Environment Ministry announced an independent investigation into the circumstances of his treatment and whether any errors or deliberate wrongdoing had occurred. [ref: Independent probe into tusker Kawanthissa's death, Daily Mirror]

On 19 October 2026, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake appointed an expert committee to investigate the elephant's death, examine its possible causes, and determine whether lapses or negligence had occurred during treatment. The committee was also tasked with making recommendations concerning wild elephant welfare and conservation. [ref: President appoints committee to probe Kavanthissa's death, Daily Mirror]

The Bieler School of Environment (BSE), known until 2020 as the McGill School of Environment (MSE), is an interfaculty undergraduate teaching and research unit of McGill University in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Founded in 1998, it offers interdisciplinary environment programs on both McGill's Downtown campus and its Macdonald Campus. [ref: About the McGill Bieler School of Environment, McGill University] The school was renamed in 2020 in recognition of a $15-million gift commitment from McGill alumnus and agri-food entrepreneur Marc Bieler. [ref: McGill receives $15-million gift commitment from agri-food entrepreneur Marc Bieler, McGill University Newsroom]

== History ==
=== McGill School of Environment (1998–2020) ===
The school was established in 1998 as a joint initiative of three McGill faculties: Agricultural and Environmental Sciences, Arts, and Science. [ref: Bieler School of Environment welcomes new director, McGill University] [ref: The MSE Newsletter, Issue 3, McGill School of Environment] The Faculty of Law later joined as a partner faculty. [ref: McGill School of Environment, Programs, Courses and University Regulations 2015–2016]

Its first full-time director was Peter G. Brown, an environmental ethicist and former founding director of the School of Public Affairs at the University of Maryland. [ref: McGill School of Environment: A new director takes the helm, McGill Reporter] Later directors included parasitologist Marilyn Scott, who led the school in the early 2010s. [ref: McGill School of Environment Newsletter, Spring 2012, McGill School of Environment] The school marked its 20th anniversary in 2018 with a homecoming lecture and alumni events. [ref: MSE 20th Anniversary Homecoming Newsletter, McGill School of Environment]

=== Renaming and the Bieler gift (2020) ===
In October 2020, McGill announced a $15-million gift commitment from Marc Bieler (DipAgr'58, BA'64) and his wife Marie Bieler (BSc(Agr)'80), and renamed the school the Bieler School of Environment. [ref: The cranberry king donates $15M to McGill University's school of the environment, CTV News Montreal] The gift consists of an initial cash contribution followed by a 25-year commitment from Bieler and his estate, and was described as the largest ever made by a graduate of the Macdonald Campus. [ref: A new chapter for Environmental Studies at McGill, McGill University Advancement] According to McGill, the funds were directed at three areas: expanding academic programs (particularly graduate training and doctoral recruitment); strengthening interdisciplinary research capacity, visiting scholars and international partnerships; and expanding internships, mobility awards and other experiential-learning opportunities.

At the time of the gift, the school was described as a joint initiative of the Faculties of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences, Arts, Engineering, Law and Science, with 18 jointly appointed faculty members and 53 associate members. Administratively, it reports through the Dean of the Faculty of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences. [ref: 00408 – Bieler School of Environment, McGill University Academic Personnel Board]

=== Recent developments ===
Atmospheric scientist Frédéric Fabry served as director from 2020 to 2025. In January 2025, invasion ecologist Anthony Ricciardi, a member of the school since 2001, was appointed director; directors serve five-year terms.

== Academic programs ==
The school's approach is to expose students to a broad range of disciplines early in their studies before they specialize. [ref: Environment, Bieler School of, McGill Course Catalogue] Many programs can be taken entirely on either campus or across both.

=== Undergraduate ===
Programs offered include: [ref: Université McGill – Programmes offerts en environnement, Gouvernement du Québec]
* B.Sc. Major in Environment, with concentrations including Atmospheric Environment and Air Quality; Biodiversity and Conservation; Earth Sciences and Economics; Ecological Determinants of Health; Environmetrics; Food Production and Environment; Land Surface Processes and Environmental Change; Renewable Resource Management; and Water Environments and Ecosystems
* B.Sc.(Ag.Env.Sc.) Major in Environment (Macdonald Campus)
* B.A. Faculty Program in Environment, with concentrations including Economics and the Earth's Environment, Environment and Development, and Ecological Determinants of Health in Society
* B.A. & Sc. Interfaculty Program in Environment
* Honours and Joint Honours options
* Minor in Environment and Diploma in Environment

=== Graduate ===
The school administers a graduate Environment option that can be added to master's and doctoral programs in participating departments, including Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences, Biology, Bioresource Engineering, Geography and Philosophy. Students in the option must be supervised or co-supervised by a BSE faculty or associate member. [ref: Environment, Bieler School of (Graduate), McGill Course Catalogue]

The plant is endemic to Australia and is found in Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland.

Draft text:
Reconomy is a British circular economy and waste management company headquartered in Telford, Shropshire, England. Founded in 1994 as an outsourced waste management business, it expanded through a series of acquisitions in the United Kingdom, mainland Europe and North America, and provides waste and resource management, extended producer responsibility (EPR) compliance, take-back and reverse logistics services. It operates through a number of specialist brands, including Valpak, Reverse Logistics Group (RLG), Noventiz, Advanced Supply Chain, ReBound and Lincoln Waste Solutions.

The company has been owned by the private equity firm EMK Capital since 2017. Its revenue grew from about £111 million in 2016 to more than £1 billion in 2022, largely through acquisitions.

== History ==

=== 1994 to 2016: Founding and early growth ===
The company's main UK trading entity, Reconomy (UK) Limited, was incorporated on 22 July 1994 as Critical Resource Limited and adopted its current name in 2012. The business provided outsourced waste management services for commercial customers, delivering a national service through a network of independent local waste operators.

In July 2006 the private equity firm Bregal Capital acquired a majority stake in the business. In 2015 Reconomy bought Countrywide Waste Management in January and Just Hire UK, which traded as Network Waste, in October. At that time it employed about 180 people, worked mainly in the construction and business and industrial sectors, and expected annual turnover of about £90 million. It acquired Skippy Nationwide in 2016.

=== 2017 to 2021: EMK Capital ownership and diversification ===
In August 2017 Reconomy was acquired by EMK Capital, a London-based private equity firm founded by Bregal's former managing partner Edmund Lazarus. The company then employed about 300 people, had sales of £111 million in the previous year and managed about three million tonnes of waste a year. In 2018 it refinanced its debt with a £70.7 million facility from Macquarie Bank, reporting turnover of £122 million for 2017.

During 2018 Reconomy acquired the waste broker Waste Check, the resource management consultancy Helistrat and, in December, Valpak, which it described as the UK's largest compliance scheme provider, which continued to operate under its own brand. Group revenue was forecast to exceed £250 million in 2019.

The company began to expand outside the UK in 2020. It acquired Noventiz, a waste disposal provider based in Cologne, Germany, in October 2020, and agreed in December 2020 to acquire Reverse Logistics Group, a Munich-based provider of outsourced resource management and environmental services operating in more than 80 countries. The RLG deal took the group's pro-forma revenue for 2020 to more than £465 million. In late 2021 it bought the British recycling businesses Casepak and Oceala.

=== 2022 to present: Further acquisitions and North America ===
In 2022 Reconomy and RLG acquired Rene AG, a German compliance services provider for electronics, packaging and batteries. Group revenue more than doubled to over £1 billion in 2022, from £490 million in 2021, through a combination of organic growth and acquisitions.

Guy Wakeley succeeded Paul Cox as chief executive on 1 January 2023, with Cox moving to the role of founder director on the group board. In 2023 the company acquired the Danish recycling and waste management company Combineering and the Newark-based waste broker UK Waste Solutions, whose brands included Novati, AMA, Click Waste and Evolution.

In the first half of 2024 Reconomy made four acquisitions, including its first two in North America (Lincoln Waste Solutions of Windsor, Connecticut, and Vermilion), the German metal recovery business Sudamin Rohstoff and the UK waste management provider Circle Waste. It continued to expand in the United States through Lincoln Waste Solutions, acquiring Complete Solutions & Sourcing and Waste Focus in January 2025, American Outsourced Waste and Recycling in April 2025, and Integrated Waste Analysts and National Waste Associates later that year. In 2026 it acquired the German industrial waste management company GfAW and, in its ninth North American acquisition, Waste Disposal Solutions of Greensboro, North Carolina.

== Operations ==
Reconomy organises its services into three areas, which it calls loops: Recycle, covering outsourced waste and resource management; Comply, covering producer responsibility and environmental compliance; and Re-use, covering returns management, reverse logistics and supply chain services. The Re-use loop includes the specialist brands Advanced Supply Chain and ReBound. The group's businesses are based in locations including Telford and Stratford-upon-Avon in England, Munich and Cologne in Germany, Denmark, and Connecticut and North Carolina in the United States.

According to the company, it served more than 25,000 customers in over 175 countries in 2025, with about 32% of revenue from the UK, 42% from the European Union and 23% from North America.

Matthew Bernard Laur (born February 14, 1999), is an American football player, with most of his professional snaps being at wide receiver. Born in Minneapolis, Minnesota, Laur played college football for the University of Minnesota Morris Cougars. After graduating in December, 2021, he continued his football career in Germany. He is the first player in the history of the Minnesota Morris Cougars football program to be a member of the XFL draft pool.

== Early years ==
Matthew Laur was born in Minneapolis, Minnesota. He attended Irondale High School in New Brighton, Minnesota from the fall of 2013 until graduating in the spring of 2017, where he was a letterman in football and weight lifting. In football, he played wide receiver and outside linebacker for the Knights football team. Laur played center as a freshman, but changed to wide receiver and outside linebacker his sophomore season, when he started practicing with JV and varsity. After going 0-10 as a freshman, his sophomore year didn't go any better, as both varsity and junior varsity went winless. Laur started receiving more playing time on special teams units, especially kickoff. As a junior, he became a full time starter for junior varsity going both ways as a wide receiver and outside linebacker. At the end of his junior season (2015), Laur received the Most Improved JV Player award from the team. In the fall of 2016, Laur's senior year of high school, he was placed back on junior varsity instead of being promoted to varsity. He would never start a high school varsity football game, outside of special teams, only getting to start the second half of his senior night at outside linebacker. Laur recorded 1 tackle and 1 fumble recovery as a member of the kickoff team against Park Center Senior High School during his senior night. He would only add a handful more tackles to his high school varsity career stats, all from special teams.

Laur was also a member of his high school's track and field team during his freshman and sophomore years. He competed in the 100m, 800m, shotput, and discus during his two years with the team.

During his junior year of high school, Laur went out for the tennis team. He participated in both singles and doubles during the season for the junior varsity team. This would be his only season of high school tennis.

As a high school senior, Laur joined the Mounds View rugby club. Laur played lock during the rugby season, and wing during the rugby sevens season. Rugby is where Laur learned how to drop kick field goals.

Laur enrolled in the delayed entry program for the Marine Corps during the summer of 2016, wanting to pursue military police. In March of 2017, Matthew was called by the University of Minnesota Morris, and they recruited him to play football for them as a wide receiver. He committed to Morris shortly after to be a student athlete and get his Bachelor of Arts degree in human services: criminal justice. Minnesota Morris was the only school to recruit Laur for athletics.

== College career ==
Laur played his entire college career [ref: Matt Laur - Football, University of Minnesota Morris Athletics] for the University of Minnesota Morris. From the fall of 2017 to the fall of 2021, Laur attended the University of Minnesota Morris as a student athlete. He played wide receiver and special teams for their football program, while earning his bachelor's degree in human services: criminal justice.

In addition to playing football during his time at the University of Minnesota Morris, Laur also played for their tennis team. [ref: Matt Laur - Men's Tennis, University of Minnesota Morris Athletics] He participated in both singles and doubles for his college tennis team. Laur finished his collegiate tennis career with a record of 2-1 in singles, and 1-1 in doubles, for a 3-2 (.600) overall record.

Laur was also a member of the rugby club at Minnesota Morris. He participated in an alumni match his freshman year and played the wing position. After a rugby tournament was canceled during his freshman year, Laur decided to step away from rugby to focus more on football.

=== 2017 season ===
As a freshman at the University of Minnesota Morris, Matthew Laur appeared in 4 games of 10 games. He made his collegiate debut on September 9th, 2017 at Westminster College. The following week on September 16th, 2017, Laur would get his first snaps on offense during a home game against Eureka College. The following week, September 23rd, 2017, Laur recorded his first collegiate reception playing at the College of St. Scholastica, for a seven yard gain and a first down. The cougars would finish this season 1-9 overall, only winning their homecoming game against Crown College.

Shaz Saleem – Full Biography

Shaz Saleem

British community leader, charity founder and former local politician

Shaz Saleem is known for his involvement in local government, charitable fundraising, youth development and community initiatives across Dudley, Kingswinford and the wider West Midlands.

1. Early life and personal background

Shaz Saleem has strong connections to the Black Country, particularly Kingswinford and the Dudley borough. He was the Chairman of Dudley Private Hire and Taxi Association which had over 2000 members.

Family and community have played an important role in shaping his public activities. One particularly significant influence was his grandfather, whose memory inspired the establishment of The Saleem Foundation in 2019.

His public profile has centred on helping others, bringing communities together and encouraging young people to get involved in positive activities.

Detailed information about his age, education and early childhood is not widely documented in reliable public sources.

2. Education and professional background

Saleem's public LinkedIn profile lists the University of Wolverhampton as his place of study between 2006 and 2009.

His profile also identifies experience in the taxi industry, business enterprise advice and community organisations.

3. Political career

Saleem became involved in local politics through the Conservative Party.

# 2021 – Elected councillor

Elected as a Conservative representative for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council.

# 2022 – Cabinet appointment

Appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm, with responsibilities relating to local roads, highways and public spaces.

# 2023 – Departure from Conservative group

Following his suspension from the Conservative Party in February 2023, he left his cabinet position and continued serving as an independent councillor.

# 2025 – Court proceedings

Saleem stood trial over two charges concerning messages allegedly sent over a public communications network. He denied both charges and was found not guilty by the district judge in March 2025.

# 2026 – Return to Conservatives

He announced his return to the Conservative Party and indicated that he would support candidates rather than stand in the 2026 local elections.

4. The Saleem Foundation

The Saleem Foundation was established in 2019 in memory of Saleem's grandfather, Al-Haj Master Mohammad Saleem, who died in 2016.

The organisation supports people experiencing financial hardship, disability, illness, social isolation and other difficulties across Birmingham and the Black Country.

Its registered charity number is 1183167, according to the Charity Commission.

Its community initiatives have included:

* TSF Youth Club: Activities and opportunities for local young people.
* TSF Kuppa Club: Social gatherings intended to reduce loneliness, particularly among older residents.
* Kingswinford and Wall Heath Litter Pick Group: Volunteer-led environmental improvements. They won the Black Country Heroes Award for Environment in 2026.
* Mental health awareness: Campaigns, films and support for community conversations.
* Emergency and charitable assistance: Food deliveries, food banks and fundraising for other charities.

In an interview published by the University of Derby's StoryHub in March 2026, Saleem explained that his grandfather's death had been a major turning point in his life. He described how establishing the charity helped him turn personal difficulties into community action.

5. Fundraising and charitable achievements

£240,000+

Reported cumulative fundraising for various charitable causes

2019

Year The Saleem Foundation was established

Saleem's fundraising activities have included a 15,000-foot skydive, bungee jumping, abseiling and charity boxing. Local reporting credits him with raising more than £240,000 for various charitable causes, although that figure is not an independently audited lifetime total.

The Foundation has also supported West Midlands Air Ambulance and organised smaller community fundraising events, including coffee afternoons.

6. Awards and recognition

One of his notable honours was the High Sheriff Award in 2025, recognising his contribution to community life.

The award was presented by Douglas Wright MBE DL at a West Midlands ceremony in Sutton Coldfield.

The recognition highlighted his voluntary activities, community groups, charitable fundraising and work supporting local residents.

7. Community values and public profile

A recurring theme in Saleem's interviews is his belief that residents share responsibility for improving the places where they live.

He has spoken about the importance of helping people who experience loneliness, supporting mental wellbeing, engaging young people and encouraging residents to volunteer.

His work combines grassroots community activity with political experience, although the two are distinct parts of his public career.

8. Recent activities in 2026

In 2026, Saleem continued to be publicly associated with charitable fundraising and community projects.

Dudley Council also publicised a charity boxing event involving Saleem and council leader Patrick Harley, planned to raise money for the Mayor of Dudley's charities. The council's announcement set a fundraising target of £30,000, which should not be confused with a confirmed amount raised.

9. Overall profile

CE-103 is an analog of modafinil, a member of a series of structurally related heterocyclic derivatives. [ref: Structure-Activity Relationships of Novel Thiazole-Based Modafinil Analogues Acting at Monoamine Transporters, Journal of Medicinal Chemistry]

CE-103 inhibits dopamine reuptake with an IC50 of 14.73 μM, an IC50 of 420.1 μM at the norepinephrine transporter (NET), while its effect on serotonin transporter (SERT) is negligible, therefore it is a modestly selective dopamine reuptake inhibitor. Sprague Dawley rats given CE-103 at doses 1 and 10 mg/kg showed an increased working memory index in a radial arm maze. Administration of the compound also decreased levels of complexes containing phosphorylated dopamine transporter (pDAT) and D1 receptor, while significantly increasing levels of complexes containing D2 receptor and D3 receptor. [ref: A heterocyclic compound CE-103 inhibits dopamine reuptake and modulates dopamine transporter and dopamine D1-D3 containing receptor complexes, Neuropharmacology]

It is closely related to CE-123, being a positional isomer.

Frédéric Worms was born on 30 January 1964 [ref: Connaissez-vous Frédéric Worms ?, www.marianne.net] in Boulogne-Billancourt, Hauts-de-Seine, Île-de-France. Worms is a French contemporary philosopher, a professor at the University of Lille and director of the École normale supérieure since 2022. He is known for his specialization in the history and thought of Henri Bergson. He is the author of several books and periodicals, and has directed much editorial work. In 2018, he was awarded the Prix Moron for his entire body of work.

== Education ==
Worms received his education at École normale supérieure in Paris from 1982-1986, at which time and place he earned the Agrégation in Philosophy. [ref: Frédéric Worms: “Le refus de la mort sous toutes ses formes est la seule façon de fonder la morale”, philomag] He completed a doctoral thesis in 1995 at Blaise Pascal University, a that is titled in English translation, "The problem of mind: psychology, koowledge theory, and metaphysics in the philosophy of Bergson," and researched under the supervision of Jean-Claude Pariente. [ref: Le problème de l'esprit: psychologie, théorie de la connaissance et métaphysique dans l'oeuvre de Bergson, Theses] He also obtained a Habilitation to direct research in 2004. His work for that qualification was published as Bergson ou Les deux sens de la vie: étude inédite by Presses Universitaires de France (PUF) in 2004. [ref: Bergson ou les deux sens de la vie: étude inédite, Presses universitaires de France]

== Academic career ==
He is a professor at the University of Lille since 2004, director of the ENS since 2022, [ref: Frédéric Worms: "Bien organisé, notre emploi du temps est un instrument contre la panique qui menace le monde", L'Express] [ref: Décret du 12 mars 2022 portant nomination du directeur de l'Ecole normale supérieure - M. WORMS (Frédéric), Journal officiel de la République française] [ref: « L’urgence la plus vitale »: quand tout devient urgent, que faut-il sauver d’abord ?, up-magazine] and a visiting professor at several institutions in the United States and United Kingdom, including: Worms is a visiting professor at several institutions, including UC Berkeley, UCLA, the University of Chicago, Ritsumeikan University, and the University of Essex. [ref: Entretien avec Frédéric Worms - Philosophe et professeur de philosophie contemporaine à l’École normale supérieure, membre du Comité consultatif national d’éthique pour les sciences de la vie et de la santé Marie Gaille and Jean-Luc Teillaud Med Sci (Paris), 35 2 (2019) 157-162 DOI: https://doi.org/10.1051/medsci/2019012]

Since 2006, he has been the founding honorary president of the (Society of Friends of Bergson). He co-authored a biography of the philosopher with Philippe Soulez. He directed the first critical edition of Bergson's works for Presses Universitaires de France (2007–2012)—a collection comprising all of lectures, articles, correspondence, and previously unpublished lectures from the Collège de France. [ref: La première édition critique de Bergson, www.puf.com] It included volumes of the Annales bergsoniennes in the "Épiméthée" series directed by Jean-Luc Marion. Worms directed the Annales bergsoniennes, a PUF collection, and also currently directs the "Questions de soin" [ref: Questions de soin, www.puf.com] and "Philosophie française contemporaine" book series. [ref: Philosophie française contemporaine, www.puf.com] He is a co-editor of the journal Bergsoniana.

Since 2004, he is the director of the (International Center for the Study of Contemporary French Philosophy, abbreviated as CIEPFC), a component of the "Republic of Knowledge: Letters, Sciences, Philosophy" research unit (UMR 3608 ENS / CNRS / Collège de France). [ref: Frédéric Worms – République des Savoirs, republique-des-savoirs] [ref: Approches de l’individuel: Épistémologie, logique, métaphysique. France: Éditions Rue d’Ulm via OpenEdition, 2022.]

In 2007, at the University of Lille III, he established the "Ethics of the Living" Master's program, which he directed until 2013. [ref: Frédéric Worms Institut-ENS, institutens]

From 2012 to 2014, he served as director of the USR 3308 Cirphles (ENS / CNRS). In September 2015, he became the deputy director of the École normale supérieure. [ref: Frédéric Worms, Philomonaco]

From 2013-2021, he served on the Comité consultatif national d'éthique (National Ethics Advisory Committee, [ref: Arrêté du 26 décembre 2017 portant nomination au comité consulta, ccne-ethique] investigating bioethical issues in the sciences.

Prior to his appointment as director at the ENS, he was the institution's deputy director (from 2015) under the directorship of Marc Mézard.

Ekonómia ľudskou rečou () is a Slovak educational media project that explains economics, personal finance and economic policy in non-technical language. It was started in April 2020 by analyst Martin Lindák as a YouTube channel and later expanded into a podcast, a website and an Instagram account. [ref: Slovákom na Youtube vysvetľuje ekonomické témy. Jeho rady odoberajú najmä muži, Forbes Slovensko] [ref: Analytik Lindák: Na YouTube sa dá zarobiť, ale s mojimi témami sa človek neuživí, Forbes Slovensko]

== History ==
Martin Lindák, a native of Rožňava, studied finance, banking and investment at the University of Economics in Bratislava. He was an external contributor to the F. A. Hayek Foundation, worked at Index, the business section of the daily SME, and as an analyst at the Slovak Business Agency, and later became an analyst at the business-information company FinStat. [ref: Martin Lindák – Rebríček 30 pod 30: Forbes predstavuje členov pre rok 2024, Forbes Slovensko]

He launched the channel during the COVID-19 pandemic while working from home. He cited Slovak popular-history and popular-science channels such as Dejepis Inak and Vedátor as inspiration, saying that nobody in Slovakia had done something similar for economics.

The channel grew fastest during the 2020–2023 global chip shortage and after the start of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, when it published videos on the Russian economy, sanctions, the SWIFT system and whether Europe could replace Russian gas. In April 2023, Forbes Slovakia reported that the channel had about 45,000 subscribers, more than 120 videos and 4.6 million views, with almost 16,000 followers on Instagram.

== Content ==
The project covers macroeconomics, public finance, taxes and social contributions, pensions, housing and mortgages, investing, inflation, entrepreneurship and the world economy. [ref: Ekonomika a osobné financie ľudskou rečou, Ekonómia ľudskou rečou] Its most-watched videos have included an overview of the Russian economy published on 22 February 2022 (over 350,000 views), a video on the chip shortage, two videos on the economy of Vatican City released around Pope Francis's 2021 visit to Slovakia, and a documentary-style video on the economic history of the Gemer region.

=== Podcast ===
A podcast of the same name has been produced since 2022 by the Slovak podcast network skpodcasty.sk. Besides Lindák, it has been hosted by Nikola Šuliková Bajánová and Jana Kubalová. As of October 2026, Apple Podcasts listed 188 episodes. [ref: Ekonómia ľudskou rečou, Apple Podcasts]

== Audience and funding ==
According to Lindák, the audience is mostly aged 25 to 50; on YouTube it is predominantly male and includes a significant share of pensioners, while the Instagram audience is balanced by gender. The project is funded through YouTube advertising, sponsored segments and supporter contributions. Lindák has said he does not provide investment advice.

== Reception ==
In 2024, Lindák was included in the Forbes Slovakia 30 Under 30 list in the Science and Education category for the project, and appeared as a guest on episode 29 of the Forbes 30 pod 30 podcast. As the channel's author he appears in Slovak media as a commentator on economic issues. In March 2022, shortly after the Russian invasion began, the news site Startitup interviewed him about the state of the Russian economy, [ref: Putinovo Rusko môže o 2 týždne zbankrotovať, hovorí Martin z kanálu Ekonómia ľudskou rečou, Startitup] and in May 2026 he was a guest on Startitup's interview show Dírerov filter, discussing the sustainability of the Slovak pension system and housing affordability for young people. = Shaz Saleem =
Shaz Saleem (also known as Shazada Saleem) is a British community activist, charity founder and former Conservative Party politician. He served as a councillor for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council from 2021 and was appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm in May 2022.[1][2] [ref: ]

Saleem founded The Saleem Foundation, a charitable organisation registered in 2019 that supports individuals and community groups across Birmingham and the Black Country.[3][4] His community activities have included charitable fundraising, youth engagement, mental health awareness and environmental projects. [ref: ]

== Background ==
Saleem has longstanding connections with Kingswinford and the Dudley borough in the West Midlands. [ref: ]

Before entering local government, he was involved in the private hire and taxi industry and community organisations. [ref: ]

In a March 2026 interview with the University of Derby's StoryHub, Saleem described his grandfather as an important influence on his involvement in charitable activities. His grandfather died in 2016, and Saleem subsequently established a foundation in his memory.[4] [ref: ]

== Political career ==

=== Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council ===
Saleem was elected as a Conservative councillor for Kingswinford North and Wall Heath in the 2021 local elections.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

In May 2022, he was appointed cabinet member for highways and public realm on Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council. His responsibilities included matters relating to highways and public spaces within the borough.[1] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

In February 2023, Saleem was suspended from the Conservative Party and resigned from his cabinet position. He subsequently served as an independent councillor.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

=== Legal proceedings ===
In March 2025, Saleem appeared at Walsall Magistrates' Court charged with two offences relating to allegedly threatening or offensive voicemail messages sent in June 2023. [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

Saleem denied both charges. On 6 March 2025, District Judge Michael Wheeler found him not guilty.[6] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

=== Return to the Conservative Party ===
In February 2026, the Express & Star reported that Saleem had rejoined the Conservative Party. He stated that he intended to support Conservative candidates in the 2026 local elections rather than stand as a candidate himself.[2] [ref: 'Politicians used these ridiculous charges to sabotage community projects' fumes cleared former Dudley councillor, Express and Star]

== Charitable activities ==

=== The Saleem Foundation ===
Saleem founded The Saleem Foundation in 2019 in memory of his grandfather, who died in 2016.[4] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

The foundation was registered with the Charity Commission for England and Wales on 29 April 2019 under charity number 1183167.[3] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

According to its registered charitable objectives, the foundation supports charities, voluntary organisations and disadvantaged individuals across Birmingham and the Black Country. Its activities include assistance relating to health, disability, financial hardship, age and other circumstances affecting personal welfare.[3] [ref: THE SALEEM FOUNDATION - Charity 1183167, prd-ds-register-of-charities.charitycommission.gov.uk]

In a March 2026 interview with StoryHub Derby, Saleem described the foundation's involvement in food distribution, mental health awareness campaigns, charitable fundraising and community activities.[4] [ref: ]

=== Community projects ===
Saleem has been associated with a number of community initiatives, including activities aimed at reducing loneliness, engaging young people and improving local environments. [ref: ]

These include The Saleem Foundation's Cuppa Club, established to provide opportunities for social interaction, particularly among older residents experiencing isolation.[4] [ref: ]

Other activities have included litter-picking initiatives, food assistance and awareness campaigns concerning mental health and domestic abuse.[4] [ref: ]

=== Fundraising ===
Saleem has participated in charitable fundraising activities, including boxing events. [ref: Councillor hoping to deliver a knockout for Mayor’s charities, Dudley Council News]

In March 2022, Dudley Council publicised his participation in a charity boxing event at Kingswinford School in support of PAPYRUS Prevention of Young Suicide and the Mayor of Dudley's charities.[7] [ref: Councillor hoping to deliver a knockout for Mayor’s charities, Dudley Council News]

Draft text:
Duncan A. Buell (born October 17, 1950) is an American mathematician and computer scientist whose research and professional work have included computational number theory, high-performance computing, information retrieval, digital humanities, and election data analysis. He is Professor Emeritus at the University of South Carolina, where he previously held the NCR Chair in Computer Science and Engineering. [ref: ] He has also worked in government research environments, including the Institute for Defense Analyses’ Center for Computing Sciences. [ref: https://www.purplebreezepress.com/duncan-buell] [ref: Frontiers of Supercomputing II: A National Reassessment, University of California Press]

== Early life and education ==
Duncan A. Buell was born in Detroit, Michigan, United States. He received a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from the University of Arizona in 1971 [ref: https://www.fitsnews.com/wp-content/uploads/securepdfs/2024/12/Report_of_Dr_Duncan_Buell_on_Senate_District_29_Results_for_2024_General_Election.pdf], a Master of Arts in mathematics from the University of Michigan in 1972, and a Ph.D. in mathematics from the University of Illinois Chicago in 1976. His doctoral specialization was in number theory. [ref: ] [ref: ]

== Career ==
After completing his Ph.D., Buell worked as a research associate at Carleton University from 1976 to 1977. He then held assistant professor positions at Bowling Green State University from 1977 to 1979 and Louisiana State University from 1979 to 1985, where he subsequently became a tenured associate professor. [ref: https://www.amazon.in/Duncan-Buell/e/B005LYRXXW/ref=dp_byline_cont_book_1]

During this period, his research focused on number theory, algebraic structures, and computational methods in mathematics. His publications addressed topics including quadratic fields, class numbers, and computational aspects of algebraic number theory. [ref: Algorithmic Number Theory: 6th International Symposium, ANTS-VI, Burlington, VT, USA, June 13-18, 2004, Proceedings, Springer Berlin Heidelberg] [ref: Duncan Buell, scholar.google.com]

From 1986 to 2000, Buell worked at the Center for Computing Sciences, an institution operated by the Institute for Defense Analyses. The center, formerly known as the Supercomputing Research Center, conducted computational research in support of the U.S. National Security Agency.

His work involved high-performance computing, parallel computation, and large-scale algorithmic implementations. He also participated in research projects involving large-scale computations, including one described as the largest computation performed in the history of the U.S. intelligence community. [ref: Duncan A Buell, ACM Digital Library]

In 2000, Buell joined the University of South Carolina as Professor of Computer Science and Engineering. He served as department chair for nine years and as interim dean of the College of Engineering and Information Technology (2005–2006). [ref: https://www.hpcwire.com/2006/01/06/thats_why_its_called_research-1/]

== Selected Publications ==

* Binary Quadratic Forms: Classical Theory and Modern Computations [ref: https://www.amazon.de/-/en/Duncan-Buell/dp/1461245435]
* Fundamentals of Cryptography [ref: Fundamentals of Cryptography: Introducing Mathematical and Algorithmic Foundations, Springer International Publishing]
* Multiple peer-reviewed articles in journals including Journal of Number Theory, Information Processing and Management, and Fuzzy Sets and Systems (1979–present)

Draft text:
Richardson Robertson III, professionally known as Rick Robertson, is an American architect and principal of Robertson Partners Architects. His work includes private residences and proposals for large-scale urban development drawing on Neoclassical, Beaux-Arts, and other classical architectural traditions. His projects include the Fleur de Lys estate in Los Angeles and proposed residential developments in California and New York.

== Career and residential architecture ==

Robertson designed Fleur de Lys, a French-inspired estate in Los Angeles, which was featured in Matt Tyrnauer’s 2002 Vanity Fair article “Versailles on the Pacific”. [ref: Tyrnauer, Matt. “Versailles on the Pacific.” Vanity Fair, April 2002.] The Los Angeles Times also reported on the estate and Robertson’s work. [ref: Ryon, Ruth. “Now Anchored in Hollywood.” Los Angeles Times, December 13, 1998.]

Jeff Hyland’s The Legendary Estates of Beverly Hills includes a chapter on Fleur de Lys describing its site, architecture, construction, and landscape. [ref: Hyland, Jeff. The Legendary Estates of Beverly Hills. New York: Rizzoli, 2008. Chapter: “Carolwood Drive: Fleur de Lys.”] The property was assembled from six adjacent parcels to create a site of approximately five acres.

In 2014, the Los Angeles Times reported that Fleur de Lys had sold for $102 million. The article identified Robertson as its architect and quoted his description of the house as a Neoclassical design conceived as a decorative arts museum rather than one based on a traditional French floor plan. [ref: Beale, Lauren. “Westside mansion sells for $102 million, highest Southland price.” Los Angeles Times, April 1, 2014.]

In April 2007, C Magazine published Degen Pener’s profile “Classical Artist,” examining Robertson’s career, architectural philosophy, and use of classical precedents in residential and urban design. [ref: Pener, Degen. “Classical Artist.” C Magazine, April 2007.]

Robertson designed a Mediterranean-style house in Tulsa, Oklahoma, for Bobby and Leslie Lorton. Southern Accents featured the residence in “Together in Tulsa” in its May–June 2007 issue, discussing its limestone exterior, classical detailing, and the clients’ interest in historical architectural accuracy. [ref: Fox, Marion Laffey. “Together in Tulsa.” Southern Accents, May–June 2007.]

In January–February 2014, Veranda published “Glamorous Texas Home,” featuring a Dallas residence designed by Robertson. The article credited Beverly Field with the interior design, Nancy Perot with the text, and Max Kim-Bee with the photography. [ref: Perot, Nancy. “Glamorous Texas Home.” Veranda, January–February 2014. Interior design by Beverly Field; architecture by Richardson Robertson III; photography by Max Kim-Bee.]

In 2010, the Los Angeles Times featured a French Normandy-style residence designed by Robertson at Lake Arrowhead, California. [ref: Marshutz, Scott. “Home of the Week: Chateau on Lake Arrowhead.” Los Angeles Times, September 5, 2010.] In 2019, the newspaper identified him as the architect of a Mediterranean-style residence in Los Angeles’s Bird Streets neighborhood offered for sale by former motorcycle racer John Kocinski. [ref: Flemming, Jack. “Retired motorcycle racer John Kocinski asks $30 million for Bird Streets abode.” Los Angeles Times, January 16, 2019.]

== Classical architecture and urban design ==

In December 2007, Angeleno published Gaby Baum’s “The Limestone Cowboy,” a feature examining Robertson’s design for City House, a proposed residential tower in downtown Los Angeles. [ref: Baum, Gaby. “The Limestone Cowboy.” Angeleno, December 2007, pp. 102–103.] The article discussed the project’s limestone cladding, bas-relief decoration, and granite cobblestone motor court in the context of Robertson’s approach to classical architecture.

Baum examined Robertson’s preference for a prominent entrance and a formal motor-court arrival sequence, contrasting this arrangement with modern buildings whose service functions are organized around rear alleys. The article also discussed his architectural philosophy in relation to contemporary modernist architecture and architects including Thom Mayne and Frank Gehry.

The feature presented City House as an example of Robertson’s advocacy of what he called a “New Beaux Arts” approach, incorporating historical architectural references, traditional materials, and ornamental detail into a contemporary high-rise design. The article documented his application of these principles to proposed urban development as well as residential architecture.

In 2009, Robertson published The Future of Classicism: New Beaux Arts, The Architecture of Richardson Robertson III, a 300-page book documenting his architectural work, including houses, estates, new towns, and proposed skyscrapers. [ref: Robertson, Richardson III. The Future of Classicism: New Beaux Arts, The Architecture of Richardson Robertson III. Blurb, 2009. [https://www.blurb.com/b/728925-the-future-of-classicism-new-beaux-arts-the-archite Book listing].]

Draft: JBOY (artist)

Draft text:
----

JBOY is a street artist based in London. In 2010, JBOY changed a Banksy artwork in Bermondsey to include a reference to The Simpsons. [ref: Banksy's artwork gets Simpsons makeover, ShortList] [ref: Simpsons Themed Parody of Bansky [sic] by JBOY, Laughing Squid] More recent work has appeared in group exhibitions in London and on outdoor screens abroad.

== Early work ==
In October 2010, JBOY made a Simpsons-themed version of Banksy’s tribute to Keith Haring in Bermondsey, south London. This happened shortly after Banksy made the opening sequence for an episode of The Simpsons. ShortList covered the piece and described JBOY as a London street art group. JBOY told the magazine that the work had received complaints as well as compliments.

== Later work ==
In July 2024, JBOY took part in Let’s Live With Less Plastic, organised by Le Good Society for Plastic Free July. The exhibition showed work on outdoor screens in Times Square in New York and across the Netherlands. [ref: 'Let's Live With Less Plastic' Art Exhibition Inspires Global Action, The Ethicalist] JBOY returned in 2025 with Seafood, a work about plastic pollution. That year, the exhibition ran in New York, the Netherlands and London. FAD Magazine included a photograph of Seafood on a screen in Chelsea. [ref: Global Exhibition aims to help tackle Plastic Pollution, FAD Magazine] [ref: Pixels for the Planet: Global Outdoor Art Exhibition Tackles Plastic Pollution, The Ethicalist] In October 2026, JBOY took part in Wrestle Room, a group exhibition about British wrestling at Atom Gallery in Stoke Newington. Other artists in the exhibition included Peter Blake and Luke Haines. [ref: Wrestle Room, Atom Gallery]

== Style ==
On the artist’s website, JBOY describes working mainly with charcoal, pencil and paint. The work is often black and white with one strong colour. JBOY names cartoonist Gary Larson and illustrator Guy Billout as influences, and says the idea behind a piece matters more than its style or finish. The website also describes using tags, stickers and other forms of street writing, with humour that is often directed at the artist’s own work. JBOY uses the term détournement to describe changing familiar images or everyday things to give them a different meaning. [ref: About JBOY, JBOY] A series called Drip Works uses uncontrolled paint drips as the basis of the work. [ref: Drip Works, JBOY]

== Auctions ==
JBOY’s prints have appeared at auctions in the United States and the UK. In 2019, Heritage Auctions offered Selfie (Silver), a print from 2018, and Very Little Helper, which was released in 2010. [ref: Jboy, Selfie (Silver), 2018, Artsy] [ref: Jboy, Very Little Helper, 2010, Artsy] A copy of Very Little Helper was sold at Chiswick Auctions in London in March 2021. [ref: Very little helper, MutualArt] The prints Blinky and Yoots were also offered by Adam Partridge Auctioneers in September 2024. [ref: Blinky, MutualArt] [ref: JBoy, MutualArt] In October 2026, the painting The Standard was sold at McTear’s in Glasgow. It was included in a charity auction raising money for Glasgow Children’s Hospital Charity. [ref: Lot 40 – JBOY, The Standard, McTear's]

Robilant is an art gallery based in London, founded in 2026 by art dealer Edmondo di Robilant. The gallery was founded following the separation of the gallery Robilant+Voena, and specialises in European Old Masters, 20th Century art with a focus on the Italian Post-War period, and Contemporary art. [ref: Robilant, Robilant]

The gallery is located on Dover Street, in Mayfair, the former premises of Robilant+Voena. Robilant offers a varied exhibition programme, presenting curated shows on art from the 16th century to the present. The gallery also participates in fairs internationally, including TEFAF Maastricht and TEFAF New York, Frieze Masters in London, NOMAD in St. Moritz and its inaugural edition in the Hamptons.

=== Exhibitions ===
Robilant launched its exhibition programme with a group show of five contemporary artists in May 2026, titled Nor here, Nor there. The artists represented in the exhibition were Yoan Capote, Isaac Chong Wai, Hung Fai, Raya Kassisieh and Vittorio Marella. [ref: ]

In October 2026, the gallery opened a survey of 400 years of still life painting, Still Life, Then and Now. The exhibition featured paintings from the 16th century to the present, by artists such as Osias Beert the Elder, Willem Claesz. Heda, Sebastian Stoskopff, Michelangelo Cerquozzi, Francisco de Zurbarán, Giovanni Battista Recco, Anne Vallayer-Coster, Giovanni Segantini, Henri Fantin-Latour, Victoria Dubourg, Odilon Redon, Pablo Picasso, Juan Gris, Pierre Bonnard, Nicolas de Staël, Andy Warhol, Poppy Jones and Asher Liftin. [ref: ] The exhibition was featured by ARTNews and House & Garden as one of the top exhibitions to see in London in October 2026. [ref: 7 Exhibitions to See in London During Frieze Week, From Shocking ’90s Artworks to Renoir Masterpieces, ARTnews.com] [ref: The art exhibitions you need to see in London in October 2026, House & Garden]

Gould Property Company is associated with the Gould family, an American family whose prominence dates to the 19th century through the railroad and financial activities of Jay Gould [ref: ]. Earlier generations of the Gould family were associated with railroad and financial enterprises, while later generations became involved in real estate and related businesses. The family lineage relevant to the company runs from Jay Gould to his son George Jay Gould, his grandson Kingdon Gould Sr., and his great-grandson Kingdon Gould Jr. [ref: About, Gould Property Company] [ref: DC's Top 10 Real Estate Dynasties, Bisnow] The Gould family's business interests have extended beyond Gould Property Company. Earlier generations were associated with railroad and financial enterprises, while later generations developed interests in real estate and related businesses.

Kingdon Gould Jr. established Gould Property Company in the 1950s. The company subsequently became one of the family's principal real estate businesses in the Washington, D.C., and Baltimore metropolitan areas. The company's own history identifies Gould Jr. as its founder and traces its origins to land acquisitions made during the 1950s.

Kingdon Gould III, the son of Kingdon Gould Jr., subsequently became owner and vice president of Gould Property Company [ref: DC's Top 10 Real Estate Dynasties, Bisnow]. He has also served in leadership roles with the DowntownDC Business Improvement District [ref: Our Team, Downtown DC].

It is located near the National Security Agency, Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, Goddard Space Flight Center, and the University of Maryland. Development of Konterra has proceeded in phases, with construction on the current phase beginning in April 2026 and a groundbreaking ceremony held on May 14, 2026, in anticipation of the future Konterra Town Center East, an approximately 400-acre mixed-use district withing Konterra [ref: Konterra breaks ground on first residential project » The Business Monthly, The Business Monthly]. Early career

Vibin Baskar composed the songs and original background score for the Tamil legal drama web series Sattamum Neethiyum, released on ZEE5 in 2025. The series received positive reviews, with several critics highlighting Baskar's music as one of its major strengths.

Reviewers noted that:

* the background score effectively complemented the emotional tone of the story;
* the courtroom sequences were enhanced by the music;
* the climax episode featured an emotionally impactful musical score;
* the background music strengthened the portrayal of the lead character.

A review published in Cinema Murasam described the music and cinematography as the "pillars of support" for the series.

Angusam praised the emotional integration of the score with the narrative, particularly during the climax.

A review in Hindu Tamil Thisai identified the music as one of the most significant strengths of the series after its screenplay and direction, while also noting that the opening "heroism"-styled title song ("Yaar Ivan?") appeared somewhat inconsistent with the otherwise realistic tone of the drama.

The series has been regarded as an important milestone in Baskar's career, introducing his work to a wider Tamil audience.

Douglas Alexander Paul is an American Army National Guard officer and Special Forces officer who served as commanding general of the Colorado Army National Guard and assistant adjutant general of Colorado from 2019 to 2022. He deployed to Afghanistan and Iraq several times and received the Purple Heart after being wounded in Iraq.

== Early life and education ==
Paul earned a Bachelor of Science in economics from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, a Master of Science in computer information technology from Regis University, and a Master of Strategic Studies from the United States Army War College, which he attended from 2012 to 2013. He is also a graduate of the United States Army Command and General Staff College.

== Military career ==
=== Early career and Afghanistan ===
Paul was commissioned a second lieutenant through the Reserve Officers' Training Corps on December 12, 1992. After the Engineer Officer Basic Course, he completed the Special Forces Detachment Officer Qualification Course. From 1993 to 2001 he commanded a Special Forces detachment ("A-Team") in Company C, 5th Battalion, 19th Special Forces Group (Airborne), based in Fort Collins, Colorado.

From December 2001 to November 2002 he was a detachment commander with Task Force Dagger/Crossbow in Gardez, Afghanistan, during Operation Enduring Freedom. He then commanded a detachment in Company B, 5th Battalion, 19th Special Forces Group, in Pueblo, Colorado, until August 2003.

=== Iraq ===
From August 2003 to August 2004 Paul was joint operations center director for Task Force Legion, Combined Joint Special Operations Task Force – Arabian Peninsula, in Baghdad. He was wounded in Iraq and received the Purple Heart. In January 2005 Governor Bill Owens recognized Paul for his wounding during the State of the State address to a joint session of the Colorado General Assembly.

After serving as operations officer of Special Operations Detachment – Korea from 2004 to 2006, he commanded Company B, 5th Battalion, 19th Special Forces Group, at Fort Carson from 2006 to 2007. From September 2007 to November 2008 he commanded the Special Forces advanced operating base of Special Operations Task Force North in Mosul.

=== Battalion command and staff assignments ===
Paul was executive officer of 5th Battalion, 19th Special Forces Group, from 2008 to 2009, and a contingency, exercise and plans officer with the Colorado Army National Guard's mobilization element at United States Northern Command from 2009 to 2010. He commanded 5th Battalion, 19th Special Forces Group (Airborne), in Watkins, Colorado, from June 2010 to July 2012.

After the Army War College, he was an operations officer with U.S. Northern Command J32/Special Operations Command – North in Colorado Springs from June to October 2013, and then deputy commander of Special Operations Detachment – Korea. From February to December 2014 he was senior Ministry of Defense advisor for the NATO Special Operations Component Command/Special Operations Joint Task Force – Afghanistan in Kabul. On his return he served as G3 (operations) of the Colorado Army National Guard from 2014 to 2016. He was qualified as a Joint Qualified Officer Level III in 2015 and promoted to colonel that December.

=== Korea and Afghanistan ===
From October 2016 to September 2018 Paul commanded Special Operations Detachment – Korea, based in Aurora, Colorado. From 2018 to 2019 he deployed as deputy commander of the Combined Joint Special Operations Task Force – Afghanistan, leading a task force of U.S., NATO and Afghan special operations forces.

=== Colorado Army National Guard command ===
Paul was promoted to brigadier general with a date of rank of August 20, 2019, and took command of the Colorado Army National Guard from Brigadier General Laura Clellan on October 19, 2019, at Fort Carson. The position also carries the title of Assistant Adjutant General, Army.

During his command the Colorado National Guard carried out the largest activation in its history in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, including building an alternative care site at the Colorado Convention Center in Denver and supporting assisted-living facilities across the state. Guard members also supported the 59th presidential inauguration and responded to the Marshall Fire, and the 1st Battalion, 157th Infantry deployed overseas for the first time since World War II.

On October 19, 2021, President Joe Biden nominated Paul for promotion to major general in the Reserve of the Army, and the Senate confirmed the nomination by voice vote on October 28, 2021. Official biographies published in 2022 continued to list his rank as brigadier general.

Paul relinquished command to Brigadier General Bren Rogers on February 5, 2022, in Loveland, Colorado, and became deputy commanding general for the Army National Guard at the Army's Combined Arms Center at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

Intellihelp was built to move quickly enough to meet immediate urgent needs by allowing direct exchanges between the people in need, and the people able to provide help, while protecting the dignity of those asking for help.

Intellihelp's initiative grew beyond its original municipal scale and became associated with broader crisis assistance, utilizing volunteer-based help during the pandemic.

The colonial fascism is a term used to describe various historical regimes in Haiti, such as the presidency of Louis Borno or the subsequent government of François Duvalier. [ref: The Roots of Haitian Despotism, Lynne Rienner Publishers]

== Development ==
There is significant controversy regarding which political movements and governments in Africa, if any, can be considered fascist. The American historian and political scientist Robert Paxton, a scholar on the subject of fascism, rejects the view that Idi Amin’s government in Uganda was fascist in nature. [ref: Robert O. Paxton, The Anatomy of Fascism, 2004, p. 191] The Coalition for the Defence of the Republic and the larger nascent Hutu Power movement, an ultranationalist and Hutu-supremacist movement that organized and carried out the Rwandan genocide with the aim of exterminating the Tutsi people of Rwanda, has been described as an example of “tropical fascism” in Africa. [ref: Judging war, judging history: behind truth and reconciliation, Stanford University Press] Other examples of colonial fascism are the Brazilian Integralist Action party, Egyptian militarism, [ref: Fascism and Nasserism: Ideological Influence or Alternative Explanations?] [ref: Egypt’s New Constitutional Amendments: Moving toward Totalitarianism, Arab Center Washington DC] [ref: The record of collaboration of King Farouk of Egypt with the Nazis and their ally, the Mufti] and the Integralist movement in Brazil, one of the far-right movements that had the greatest impact in its place of origin. [ref: UN ENSAYO BIBLIOGRÁFICO SOBRE EL INTEGRALISMO BRASILEÑO, Revista Ayer] [ref: EL FASCISMO TROPICAL: LITERATURA Y AÇÃO INTEGRALISTA BRASILEIRA, Revista Ayer]

= The Scientific Achievements of Professor Sh. S. Kamoliddin and His Contribution to Scholarship =
One of the principal strengths of Sh. S. Kamoliddin’s scholarly work is that, despite his foundational education in Oriental studies, which provided him with knowledge of several Eastern languages and the skills needed to work with primary sources, he has never confined his research interests to historiography and historical source studies alone.

While working on his doctoral dissertation between 1990 and 1993, following the joint recommendation of Orientalist P. G. Bulgakov and archaeologist E. V. Rtveladze, he began employing an interdisciplinary research approach. This approach incorporated written sources and archaeological findings, as well as evidence from historical toponymy, cartography, numismatics, anthropology, ethnography, and other auxiliary historical disciplines.

The comprehensive study and comparative analysis of different types of sources, together with his distinctive methodological approach, have enabled him to develop research conclusions that sometimes differ from positions widely accepted in international historiography. Examples of his research findings include the following:

1. The Early Presence of Ancient Turks in Central Asia

According to the document, a prevailing view in international historiography holds that the ancient Turks arrived in Central Asia during the Turkic Khaganate period, from the mid-sixth to the mid-eighth century. Kamoliddin’s toponymic and linguistic research into the historical place names of Central Asia led him to conclude that ancient Turkic populations had lived in the region since at least the Bronze Age and formed part of its early indigenous population.

He proposed that, following the arrival of Aryan-speaking groups, some of these populations were displaced beyond Central Asia, mainly to the north and east, while a larger portion remained in the region under Aryan rule.

2. The Contribution of Ancient Turks to Settled and Urban Culture

The document describes a view in historiography that ancient Turks lived exclusively nomadic lives, primarily engaged in animal husbandry, and made no contribution to settled agricultural and urban culture.

Through interdisciplinary research and comparative analysis of historical terminology in Turkic and Iranian languages, Kamoliddin concluded that ancient Turks had developed traditions in agriculture, horticulture, metallurgy, handicraft production, and urban construction. He argued that they made a significant contribution to the development of settled agricultural and urban culture in Central Asia.

3. The Role of Medieval Turks in the Cultural Development of the Muslim World

The document discusses the view that medieval Turks were primarily associated with raids and warfare and made little contribution to world culture and civilization.

Kamoliddin’s research in historiography and historical source studies led him to argue that medieval Turks played an active role in the cultural flourishing of the Muslim world commonly referred to as the “Muslim Renaissance.” He considered them initiators and important participants in this process, which he attributed to the interaction of different cultures within the Islamic world. He further argued that the experience acquired by Turkic peoples during the Turkic Khaganate period, from the mid-sixth to the mid-eighth century, contributed to their role in the later cultural development of the Abbasid Caliphate, which existed from the mid-eighth century to the early thirteenth century.

4. The Origins of the Samanid Dynasty

The document notes that the Samanid dynasty, which ruled Transoxiana and Khorasan during the ninth and tenth centuries, is generally regarded in historiography as having Iranian origins.

Based on a comprehensive examination of written, archaeological, numismatic, ethnographic, and other historical evidence, Kamoliddin proposed that the Samanids had Oghuz-Turkic origins.

According to his interpretation, the dynasty’s ancestor, known as Saman-Khudat or Saman-Yabgu, descended from the Turkic yabghus of Tokharistan, whom he associated with the Ashina clan, the ruling family of the Turkic Khaganate. Kamoliddin further proposed that this ancestor bore the Turkic name Arkuk and practiced Buddhism or Manichaeism before converting to Islam. The document also states that, according to its interpretation, he wore his hair in a braid in accordance with an ancient Turkic custom and was nicknamed “Kakuldar” by the surrounding Iranian population, a term interpreted as “the possessor of a braid.”

5. The Historical Development of the Terms “Uzbek” and “Uzbekistan”

The document discusses the claim that the ethnonym “Uzbek” and the place name “Uzbekistan” were introduced by Russian Bolsheviks during the national-territorial delimitation of Turkestan in 1924.

Kamoliddin’s research in historical geography and cartography led him to argue that the term “Uzbek” was already used among Turkic peoples as a personal name in the twelfth century.

According to his interpretation, the names “Uzbek,” “Uzbekia,” or “Uzbekistan” began to be used in the fourteenth century in connection with the Golden Horde during the reign of Öz Beg Khan, when his subjects came to be known as Uzbeks.

Jim Gloyd is an American writer, actor, producer, director and author. He wrote, produced, co-directed and starred as Bruce in the 2020 drama The Wager. His other screen credits include the voice role of Tsayid in Cadia: The World Within (2019) and Dr. Molder in Clay Zombies (2021). [ref: The Wager, Rotten Tomatoes] [ref: The Wager, Apple TV] [ref: Jim Gloyd, IMDb]

== Career ==
Gloyd developed The Wager from a short story he had written. In 2018, the Scioto Post reported that the film was being produced by Clean Screen Productions, a company created by Gloyd, and that filming was planned in Circleville, Ashville and Columbus, Ohio. The report also covered the casting of former heavyweight boxing champion James "Buster" Douglas. [ref: "Buster" Douglas Cast in Local Film "The Wager", Scioto Post]

Pickaway County Board of Commissioners minutes from April 2019 document Gloyd's request to use the county Engineer's Office in Circleville for filming The Wager. [ref: April 2, 2019 Minutes, Pickaway County] The film was released in 2020. Apple TV and Rotten Tomatoes credit Gloyd as a director and actor, while Rotten Tomatoes also credits him as producer and screenwriter.

The Wager received local television coverage on Good Day Columbus on ABC6, where Gloyd appeared to discuss the film. Dove.org later reviewed the film and identified Gloyd among its actors, writers, directors and producers. The production and release were also covered by the Circleville Herald. [ref: Local filmmaker talks about his movie "The Wager", ABC6 / Good Day Columbus] [ref: The Wager, Dove.org] [ref: Ashville man to shoot inspirational film in Pickaway, Circleville Herald] [ref: Locally sourced movie to be released next week, Circleville Herald]

In addition to The Wager, Gloyd voiced Tsayid in the fantasy film Cadia: The World Within, which also featured Corbin Bernsen and James Phelps. He later appeared as Dr. Molder in the 2021 horror-comedy Clay Zombies. [ref: Cadia: The World Within, Apple TV] [ref: Cadia: The World Within Cast, TV Guide] [ref: Clay Zombies, Apple TV] [ref: Clay Zombies, Tubi]

== Books and children's projects ==
Gloyd's published works include Becoming Free from the Judas in Me, co-authored with Shawn Harper and published in 2010, and The Wager: And 11 Other Short Stories, co-authored with William C. Canfield and published by Glory Publishing in 2025. His bibliography also includes the children's title Sammy the Witness: The Fish That Outlived Methuselah!. [ref: Jim Gloyd, Goodreads] [ref: Saving Satan's Backsliders: Becoming Free From the Judas in Me, PR.com] [ref: The Wager: And 11 Other Short Stories, AbeBooks]

Gloyd is also credited as a writer on the animated television project The Chronicles of the Tiny Ones: Sammy the Witness, listed as a current project on his IMDb profile. The related published children's title Sammy the Witness: The Fish That Outlived Methuselah! is listed in his Goodreads bibliography.

== Music ==
Gloyd releases independent music under the project name 100 Days Ahead. Public listings under his name include the tracks "Warning Lights", "Burned Again" and "My Superhero". [ref: 100 Days Ahead tracks, Slaps]

== Awards and recognition ==
At The Actors Awards in September 2020, Gloyd received Best Performance of Fest and Best Actor in a Drama for The Wager. [ref: September 2020 Winners, The Actors Awards] The Vegas Movie Awards' August winners archive lists The Wager and Gloyd for Best 1st Time Producer. [ref: August Edition — Winners of Excellence, Vegas Movie Awards]
