Kishan Dholakia (FAA) is a physicist and professor specialising in optics and photonics. He holds positions at the Adelaide University in Australia and the University of St Andrews in Scotland. His research centres on the development of optical manipulation techniques, including optical tweezers and structured light beams, and their applications in biology and medicine.

In 2026, Dholakia was elected a Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science [ref: Photonics leader named Australian Academy of Science Fellow, University of Adelaide]. He is an Australian Research Council (ARC) Laureate Fellow (2021-2026) and is a Node Leader and Chief Investigator for the Australian Research Council [https://www.combs.org.au/ Centre of Excellence Optical Microcombs for Breakthrough Science (COMBS)]. He also Director for the [https://www.adelaide.edu.au/centre-of-light-for-life/ Centre of Light for Life] at Adelaide University.

== Early Life and Education ==
Dholakia completed his Bachelor of Arts in Natural Sciences (Physics) from Churchill College, University of Cambridge, in 1988. He then pursued postgraduate studies at Imperial College London, obtaining an MSc with distinction in Applied Optics in 1990, followed by a PhD in Laser Physics in 1993, focusing on laser cooling and trapping of ions [ref: Kishan Dholakia CV].

== Career ==

=== University of St Andrews ===
In 1997, Dholakia joined the University of St Andrews as a Royal Society of Edinburgh Research Fellow. He was a lecturer in the School of Physics and Astronomy in 2000 and became a full Professor of Physics in 2003. At St Andrews, he established the [https://biology.st-andrews.ac.uk/biophotonics/ Centre of Biophotonics] and founded the James Mackenzie Institute for Early Diagnosis in 2019 [ref: Sir James Mackenzie Institute for Early Diagnosis]. He is the head of the [https://opticalmanipulationgroup.wp.st-andrews.ac.uk/ Optical Manipulation Group], with Graham Bruce. The group specialises in many areas of optics, namely Raman spectroscopy, speckle metrology, structured light fields, bioimaging, optical tweezers and levitated optomechanics.

=== Adelaide University ===
In 2020, he joined the University of Adelaide as a Visiting Professor. In 2022, he became a full Professor and the Director for the Centre of Light for Life, together with Deputy Director Associate Professor Kylie Dunning. The Centre vision is "To use light to reveal, measure and understand life and the world around us, and translate these insights into meaningful impact." [ref: Centre of Light for Life Vision Statement, University of Adelaide]. The Centre laboratories house numerous specialised optics, including light sheet fluorescence microscopy, speckle metrology, levitated optomechanics, optical tweezers, quantum imaging, digital holographic microscopy, optical coherence tomography, and Raman spectroscopy. The group consists of approximately 20 researchers, ranging from undergraduate to graduate students, and postdoctoral researchers [ref: Centre of Light for Life researchers, adelaide.edu.au]. The Centre also collaborates with researchers from institutes with Adelaide University: the [https://adelaide.edu.au/research/institute-for-photonics-advanced-sensing-and-quantum-technologies/ Institute of Advanced Sensing and Quantum Technologies] and the [https://adelaide.edu.au/research/robinson-research-institute/ Robinson Research Institute]. Dholakia is Chief Investigator for the Australian Research Council [https://www.combs.org.au/ Centre of Excellence Optical Microcombs for Breakthrough Science (COMBS)], the Australian Research Council [https://arcquantumcentre.com.au/ Training Centre for Current and Emergent Quantum Technologies (QuTech)], and Australian Research Council [https://ai-grainhub.org/researchthemes Industrial Transformation Research Hub in Responsible AI for a Sustainable Grain Industry (grAIn)].

== Research ==
Dholakia's research is widely cited (over 49,000 citations, [https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=OlD7pJoAAAAJ& Google Scholar]) and encompasses:

* Optical Manipulation: Developing optical tweezers which use lasers to trap and manipulate matter at microscopic scales, such as microscopic particles, biological specimens, and molecules [ref: Shaping the future of manipulation, Nature Photonics] [ref: Roadmap for optical tweezers, Journal of Physics: Photonics].
* Structured Light: Exploring Bessel beams [ref: Bessel beams: Diffraction in a new light, Contemporary Physics], Airy beams [ref: Light-sheet microscopy using an Airy beam, Nature Methods], and Laguerre-Gaussian beams [ref: Second-harmonic generation and the conservation of orbital angular momentum with high-order Laguerre-Gaussian modes, Physical Review A] for applications in biological imaging and material analysis, such as multiphoton imaging to improve imaging at depth [ref: All-Optical Methods to Study Neuronal Function: Widefield Multiphoton Imaging at Depth with Temporal Focusing, Springer].

Atomos Wealth is a British wealth management and financial planning company headquartered in London and Bristol. It was formed in 2022 following the acquisition of the UK wealth business of the Sanlam Group by funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management, and trades under the brand "atomos". The firm provides advice-led financial planning alongside discretionary investment management, and is authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

== History ==
The business has its origins in the UK expansion of the South African financial services group Sanlam, which built a wealth advisory and asset management presence in Britain over a period of around two decades. In September 2021, Sanlam agreed to sell its UK wealth management business to funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management in a transaction reported at around £140 million. The deal completed in 2022, after which the business was rebranded from Sanlam Wealth to atomos.

The rebrand was announced in 2022, with the business commencing trading under the atomos name. Jonathan Polin, who had been chief executive of Sanlam's UK group, continued to lead the company following the change of ownership.

== Corporate structure ==
Atomos Wealth operates through several regulated and non-regulated entities registered at Companies House in England and Wales. Regulated activities are carried out principally through Atomos Investments Limited, which holds FCA permissions for discretionary investment management (FCA firm reference number 122588), and Atomos Financial Planning Limited, which is authorised to arrange and advise on regulated financial products (FCA firm reference number 193503).

The group is owned by funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management, which took control following the 2022 carve-out from Sanlam. In October 2024, the professional-services and advisory firm Willis Towers Watson (WTW) acquired a minority equity stake in the business.

== Operations ==
The company describes its model as advice-led, combining face-to-face financial planning with discretionary fund management and a client-facing digital platform. It operates from offices in London and Bristol alongside a network of regional offices across England.

In November 2022, Atomos entered a sub-advisory arrangement under which Willis Towers Watson took over management of the firm's retail multi-asset portfolios. The commercial relationship between the two firms was extended when WTW took its minority stake in 2024.

== Acquisitions ==
Following its separation from Sanlam, Atomos pursued a programme of acquiring regional financial advisory firms. Acquisitions have included Shore Financial Planning in Devon and Define Wealth in Surrey, both in 2023, and the City of London advisory firm Cartlidge Morland in 2026.

In September 2026, Atomos acquired MWA Financial from its founder and the private equity firm Coniston Capital, in a transaction reported to add almost £1 billion in assets. According to trade press, the acquisition brought the group's total assets under administration to around £8.7 billion.

== Recognition ==
Atomos has been named in the WealthBriefing Wealth for Good Awards. Coverage of the firm and its transactions has appeared in financial trade publications including Professional Adviser, Investment Week and International Adviser.

== References ==

devicenow GmbH is a German information technology services company that rents end-user IT hardware to businesses under a device-as-a-service (DaaS) model. It was founded in 2022 as a subsidiary of the technology leasing company CHG-Meridian and is headquartered in Weingarten, Baden-Württemberg.

== History ==
CHG-Meridian announced the formation of devicenow in April 2022, alongside a second new company, the Berlin-based refurbished-hardware reseller circulee. According to a report by the Deutsche Presse-Agentur, the parent company expected that the increase in home working during the COVID-19 pandemic had raised demand for IT equipment, and that short product cycles would lead many companies to prefer renting devices over buying them. At launch, CHG-Meridian stated that the service would be available in 190 countries and would operate on a non-captive basis, that is, independently of specific hardware manufacturers.

The Nuremberg-based IT service company Hemmersbach acted as the service and logistics partner for the offering from its launch. The trade magazine DV-Dialog described devicenow as having been established together with Hemmersbach. In August 2022 the Federal Cartel Office listed a notification (file no. B7-75/22) under which CHG-Meridian planned to acquire shares in, and joint control of, Hemmersbach Holding GmbH and Hemmersbach Worldwide GmbH.

In February 2024 the Norwegian company Techstep announced a partnership with devicenow to offer Techstep's device lifecycle management software to devicenow customers; Techstep reported in October 2024 that the first devicenow customer had been onboarded to the platform.

== Services ==
devicenow rents laptops, desktop computers, tablets and smartphones to companies for a fixed monthly fee per device. The contracts bundle the hardware with services across the device lifecycle, including procurement, pre-configuration, international logistics, a next-business-day replacement service for defective devices, certified data erasure and the reuse of returned devices. According to DV-Dialog, the service is aimed primarily at multinational corporations and larger Mittelstand companies.

Within the CHG-Meridian group, devicenow is operated as a separate brand from the parent company's individually structured leasing business, offering a standardized rental product for workplace IT.

Center for Earth and Natural Resource Sciences

[https://cenrs.org/ The Center for Earth and Natural Resource Sciences (CENRS) is an autonomous, multidisciplinary research institution based in Rwanda. Its headquarters are located in Mukamira, Nyabihu District, Northern Rwanda, with a community service branch in Nyabugogo, Kigali City. CENRS was officially established on 3 September 2025 under Rwandan Law No. 007/2021 of 5 February 2021. The Center conducts fundamental and applied research in environmental systems, Earth processes, natural hazards, natural resources, and technologies for pollution control and environmental remediation. It also provides research-based services to local communities. CENRS is currently focused exclusively on research and community services and does not engage in schooling activities].. [ref: ]

History

[https://cenrs.org/ The origins of CENRS can be traced back to 15 September 2016 in Xiamen], where two Rwandan scientists, [https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1244-3434 Jean Claude Ndayishimiye] and [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9686-5177 Pascaline Nyirabuhoro], [https://web.archive.org/web/20160914193505/http://www.nmc.cn/publish/typhoon/warning were pursuing doctoral degrees at the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and conducting research at the Institute of Urban Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences[2,3]. At 03:15 CST on 15 September 2016 (19:15 UTC on 14 September), Super Typhoon Meranti, a powerful tropical cyclone, struck Xiamen with measured two-minute sustained winds of 173 km/h]. At that time, Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro were in Xiamen conducting their doctoral research. [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969724062144 As young researchers specifically from inland Africa, where tropical cyclones have historically had little or no direct impact, they experienced a tropical cyclone firsthand for the first time and observed its extensive environmental, infrastructural, and societal impacts]. [https://www.climatesignals.org/headlines/china-top-alert-ocean-waves-typhoon-meranti-approaches China’s National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center issued a red ocean-wave warning, the highest level in China’s four-tier warning system]. More than 331,000 people were relocated in Fujian Province, and [https://www.weather.gov.hk/en/publica/tc/tc2016/section3_5rpt.htm widespread power outages affected millions of households]. Schools and kindergartens in Xiamen and other coastal cities in Fujian were closed as a precaution. In China, [https://www.xinhuanet.com/english/2016-09/17/c_135692847.htm official assessments reported direct economic losses of more than ¥16.9 billion (2.6 billion USD) in Fujian Province, with additional losses in neighbouring] Zhejiang Province. [https://www.weather.gov.hk/en/publica/tc/tc2016/section3_5rpt.htm An earlier assessment by the Hong Kong Observatory reported at least 29 deaths in Fujian and Jiangxi and direct economic losses exceeding ¥11.7 billion (1.75 billion USD)]. Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro were deeply impressed by the effectiveness of China’s early warning systems, coordinated evacuation measures, and resilient infrastructure. [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969724062144 Their experience extended beyond these observations, as their direct exposure to Super Typhoon Meranti immediately shaped their research interests, with climate extremes and environmental disturbances becoming central areas of their scientific work. Notably, under the supervision of Professor Yang Jun at the Institute of Urban Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Ndayishimiye examined the effects of typhoon-driven disturbances on drinking-water reservoirs and testate amoeba communities] [ref: Community responses of testate amoebae (Arcellinida and Euglyphida) to ecological disturbance explained by contrasting assembly mechanisms in two subtropical reservoirs, Science of the Total Environment]. When Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro began their postdoctoral research at Shenzhen MSU-BIT University in February and September 2021, respectively, Africa was grappling with the devastation shaped by tropical cyclones. [https://web.archive.org/web/20190812000713/http://thoughtleadership.aonbenfield.com//Documents/20190723-analytics-if-1h-global-report.pdf Notably, Intense Tropical Cyclone Idai affected Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi from 4 to 21 March 2019, causing catastrophic flooding and widespread destruction across the region, with 1,593 deaths, 2,452 injuries, and 3.1 million people affected[14], along with total damages estimated at 2.2 billion USD]. == Roofing calculator ==
A [https://roofertx.net/tools/ roofing calculator] is a calculation tool used to estimate roof surface area, roofing material quantities, or project costs. Depending on its purpose, it may use measurements supplied by the user or property information processed by an estimating system. Area calculators can account for roof slope and overhangs, while cost estimators may incorporate location, roof size, and complexity. [ref: https://www.gaf.com/en-us/plan-design/homeowner-education/roof-cost/calculator]
== Area estimation ==
Roof surface area differs from the horizontal area covered by a building. On a sloping roof, the surface follows the incline rather than the horizontal projection.

Some roofing calculators estimate this surface using a building’s base area, roof pitch, and eave dimensions. A slope correction factor converts horizontal measurements into an estimated sloping area. [ref: https://roofertx.net/tools/roof-area-calculator/]

For roofs with several sections or different slopes, the individual sections may be measured separately and their areas added together. A single base-area measurement cannot fully describe a complex roof.
== Material estimation ==
Material calculators use an estimated or measured roof area to calculate quantities of roofing products. Their outputs depend on the material assumptions built into the tool.

In roofing estimates, area may be expressed in square feet or roofing squares. A roofing square represents 100 square feet of roof surface. This unit is also used when describing material and installation costs.
== Cost estimation ==
Roofing cost calculators produce estimates using selected project characteristics. For example, GAF describes its residential replacement-cost calculator as using information including property address, roof size, slope, and complexity to generate a non-binding estimate. [ref: https://www.gaf.com/en-us/plan-design/homeowner-education/roof-cost]

Roof replacement costs also depend on the selected materials and the circumstances of the project. Roof slope can affect installation labor, while location influences local costs and applicable requirements.

A calculator’s estimated price and a contractor’s final price may differ. Existing roof layers or damaged decking can require additional work that becomes apparent during removal.

=== Limitations ===
The usefulness of a roofing calculation depends on the measurements and assumptions supplied to it. A calculator based on a simplified roof shape may not account adequately for a roof with multiple intersecting sections. Calculator.net’s documentation recommends measuring individual sections when estimating more complex roofs.

Cost estimates also have a defined scope. GAF characterizes its calculator results as informational and non-binding; they do not constitute a project-specific contract price. [ref: https://www.gaf.com/en-us/plan-design/homeowner-education/roof-cost]

The Ceylon Examiner (originally The Examiner) was an English-language bi-weekly newspaper published in Colombo, British Ceylon. After it was bought in 1859 by a syndicate led by the lawyer Charles Ambrose Lorenz, it has been described as arguably the island's first genuinely local newspaper. [ref: In search of Charles Ambrose Lorenz, [[The Sunday Times (Sri Lanka)]

== History ==
=== Founding ===
The paper was founded in 1846 as The Examiner. [ref: Newspaper publishing in Sri Lanka, [[Sunday Observer (Sri Lanka)] Accounts differ on the exact date: the Sunday Observer places its launch in January 1846, while another account gives 7 September 1846, with Bessell as editor and John Capper as chief contributor. [ref: John Capper: A life in old Ceylon, [[The Sunday Times (Sri Lanka)] Along with the Observer and the Times, it was one of only three English-language newspapers on the island at the time. [ref: Some Notable Burgher Personalities of the Past, VMSL Library]

=== Lorenz era (1859–1871) ===
In 1850–52, a group of Burgher intellectuals, including Lorenz, George and Frederick Nell, John Prins and Charles Ferdinands, published the literary magazine Young Ceylon. [ref: People Inbetween: Ethnic and Class Prejudices in British Ceylon, Thuppahi's Blog] In 1859 the same circle organised the purchase of an English newspaper to serve as a critical voice against the colonial government. Under Lorenz's syndicate, The Examiner was renamed the Ceylon Examiner.

Francis Beven became a co-proprietor at the age of 23, alongside Lorenz and Leopold Ludovici. In 1861 Lorenz succeeded Louis Nell as editor. Until his death in 1871, he edited and largely wrote the paper. He used it to argue for social reform and democratic causes, and to criticise the Governor and the Executive Council. [ref: Some Burgher personalities of the past in the arenas of public debate and politics, WorldGenWeb Sri Lanka]

=== Later years ===
Leopold Ludovici, formerly of the Ceylon Survey Department, later became editor and then proprietor of the paper. [ref: Ludovici, Leopold, Persons of Indian Studies] Robert Farrance also served as its editor, for ten years. [ref: List of Inscriptions on Tombstones and Monuments in Ceylon, of Historical or Local Interest, Government Printer]

== Legacy ==
The Ceylon Examiner has been described as carrying forward the Young Ceylon circle's idea of a shared "Ceylonese" identity from 1859 onwards. [ref: The Cricketing Universe of Sri Lanka: A Short History written in 2007, Thuppahi's Blog] Lorenz himself is credited with coining the term "Ceylonese". The paper was known as a lawyers' paper, and George Wille was among its regular contributors.

== References ==

= Siriusim =
Siriusim is the name used by an alleged cyber threat actor that claimed to possess and release data associated with the State Bank of India (SBI), India's largest public-sector bank by assets. The actor came to public attention in October 2026 after reports of a suspected data exposure involving records found on the dark web. Public reporting has associated the name with claims posted on an online cybercrime forum. The identity, membership, origins and broader activities of Siriusim have not been independently established. [1][2] [ref: Hacker group claims access to 3.8 lakh SBI data entries, The Times of India]

== Background ==
Siriusim became publicly associated with the SBI data exposure in October 2026. According to media reports, the actor claimed to possess approximately 375,000 rows of data and 2,722 PDF documents allegedly related to banking customers and applications. The claims reportedly included personal information and loan-related and account-opening documents. The authenticity, origin and completeness of the entire dataset remain subject to investigation. [1][2] [ref: State Bank of India reports cyberattack involving nearly 3,900 customer records, Reuters]

== Alleged SBI data exposure ==
On 21 October 2026, the State Bank of India disclosed an incident involving the loss of certain data. The bank said a preliminary examination of approximately 375,000 records found on the dark web identified 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information. The exposed information reportedly included names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, residential addresses, branch details, customer identifiers and metadata associated with loan and lead records. [1][3]

SBI stated that it had received alerts concerning the suspected exposure on 16 October 2026 from its threat-intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In). The bank activated its cyber incident response procedures and appointed an independent cybersecurity agency to investigate the incident. [1][3] [ref: SBI probes suspected data breach after 3.75 lakh records surface on dark web, The Economic Times]

SBI said the incident had not materially affected its core business operations, financial performance or business continuity. The bank also stated that customer balances remained safe. The investigation was intended to establish the authenticity and extent of the exposed information and determine its potential source. [1][3]

Although reports associated Siriusim with the data leak, SBI's public disclosure did not identify the actor as responsible for the incident. The available reporting does not establish precisely how the data was obtained or whether all the material claimed by Siriusim originated from SBI systems.

== Identity and organisation ==
As of October 2026, reliable public information about Siriusim's operators, membership, location, organisational structure and motivations is limited. Its use of a particular name in online claims does not independently establish whether it represents an organised group, an individual operator or a shared online identity.

No independently verified public evidence cited here establishes its founding date, leadership, affiliations with other cyber threat actors or involvement in incidents beyond the reported SBI allegations.

== Cybersecurity implications ==
The alleged exposure illustrates the risks associated with the unauthorised disclosure of personal and financial information. If genuine, information such as names, telephone numbers, dates of birth and residential addresses can be used in impersonation attempts, targeted phishing and other forms of fraud.

The incident also highlights the importance of investigating how sensitive information is stored, accessed and shared across organisations and third-party service providers. Determining the source of the exposure requires technical investigation rather than relying solely on claims made by an alleged threat actor.

Ulaa Browser [ref: ] is a privacy-focused web browser developed by Zoho Corporation, an Indian technology company known for products such as Zoho Books, Zoho Mail and Zoho Workplace. It is designed to provide a safer, more private and more productive browsing experience by combining regular web browsing with built-in privacy protection, advertisement blocking, tracker prevention and productivity features. Like Google Chrome, Ulaa is based on the Chromium browser engine, which means most modern websites should work similarly in both browsers. However, Ulaa adds its own features and customisations to improve privacy and help users manage their online activities. It is available for Windows, Linux, macOS, Android and iOS, making it suitable for personal computers, office systems and mobile devices. One of its main attractions is that users can access many privacy and productivity features without having to install several separate browser extensions. [ref: https://ulaa.com/#privacy] [ref: Zoho launches privacy-centered browser ‘Ulaa’ to challenge Google, Microsoft and Apple, BusinessLine] [ref: https://www.business-standard.com/technology/tech-news/privacy-centred-web-browser-ulaa-to-remain-free-for-end-users-without-ads-123051000818_1.html]

== Privacy and Advertisement Blocking ==
One of Ulaa's principal features is its built-in advertisement and tracker blocking functionality. Websites may use advertisements, tracking scripts, cookies, and other technologies to display content, measure visitor activity, or personalise services. Ulaa's protection mechanisms are intended to block certain advertisements and tracking elements, reducing some forms of online tracking and potentially improving page-loading performance. [ref: https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/startup/government-agencies-enterprises-keen-on-adopting-zohos-ulaa-web-browser-10731491.html]

The browser provides privacy settings that allow users to adjust the level of protection. More restrictive settings may interfere with website functionality when a website depends on scripts or other resources that are blocked. Consequently, users may occasionally need to adjust protection settings for particular websites. [ref: After Arattai, Zoho's Google Chrome killer tops App Store charts. Here's what makes Ulaa browser special, mint] [ref: Zoho CEO Sridhar Vembu launches new 'Private Browser' in India; forays into AI tools powered by ChatGPT - BusinessToday, Business Today]

Advertisement blocking does not guarantee that all advertisements will be removed. Similarly, tracker prevention does not provide complete anonymity or prevent every method of collecting information about browsing activity. [ref: Zoho launches Ulaa web browser, unveils AI strategy, The Times of India] [ref: 'Trust me, bro': Zoho's Sridhar Vembu promises user privacy security in Arattai Messenger soon, Deccan Herald] [ref: Ulaa: Everything you need to know about Zoho’s Google Chrome rival, The Indian Express]

== Family and education ==
He was the second son of John Egerton, 2nd Earl of Bridgewater and the brother of Charles Egerton. He was admitted into the Inner Temple in 1673. On 23 September 1674, he married Honora, the daughter of Sir Thomas Leigh and they had one son (whom predeceased him) and four daughters.

Draft text:
Fabio Albano is an Italian-American battery scientist and technology executive. He is a co-founder of Sakti3, the solid-state battery company acquired by Dyson in 2015, and has served as chief technology officer of NantG Power, a NantWorks company developing silicon-anode lithium-ion batteries. Albano led the solid-state battery program at Fisker Inc., where the technology he brought to the company formed the basis of its announced "super battery" effort. Over a career spanning more than two decades in advanced battery research and manufacturing, he has been granted 16 patents in North America and Europe. In 2016 he was named to Midwest Energy News 40 Under 40 list of emerging clean-energy leaders. [ref: 2016 Midwest Energy News 40 Under 40, Midwest Energy News (via ZEF Energy)]

== Early life and education ==
Albano was born in Sanremo, Italy. He received his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering from the University of Michigan, where his doctoral advisor was Ann Marie Sastry and his research centered on microarchitectured energy devices; his earliest patents, assigned to the University of Michigan, date from this period. His doctoral research on power supplies for wireless integrated microsystems — including implantable medical devices — was published as a monograph, Power Supplies for Wireless Integrated Microsystems (WIMS): Design and Optimization, in 2009. [ref: ECS Detroit Section Presents Fabio Albano, The Electrochemical Society] [ref: Deposited microarchitectured battery and manufacturing method — US8231998B2, Google Patents]

== Career ==
=== Sakti3 ===
In 2007, Albano co-founded Sakti3 in Ann Arbor, Michigan, with Sastry and Chia-Wei Wang, to commercialize solid-state lithium-ion batteries built from deposited, microarchitectured (three-dimensional) electrodes rather than conventional planar thin films. The architecture was intended to raise energy and power density by roughly an order of magnitude over 2D designs and to allow water-based processing and the use of a non-flammable solid electrolyte. [ref: Arbitration Award Confirmation for Fisker — LA County Case 20TRCV00731, Scribd (court filing)] Sakti3's work attracted funding including U.S. Department of Energy grants, and in 2015 the company was acquired by Dyson. [ref: Will we soon be able to charge electric cars in just a minute?, The Irish Times] Albano, who had departed before the sale, was later among the former employees reported by Quartz to have criticized the company's subsequent technical direction, including its use of a stacked-cell configuration they regarded as unscalable. [ref: Sakti3's quest for a better battery: Hype, funding, promises, and then a surprise sale, Quartz]

=== Dow Kokam / XALT Energy and Energy Power Systems ===
In 2011 Albano became a founding member of Energy Power Systems (EPS), a Michigan battery company, and chief technology officer of Dow Kokam — the lithium-ion cell manufacturer later renamed XALT Energy — a role he held from 2011 to 2016. [ref: ECS Detroit Section Presents Fabio Albano, The Electrochemical Society] In September 2016 he was named to Midwest Energy News 40 Under 40, which cited his Sakti3 co-founding, his 16 issued patents in North America and Europe, two R&D 100 award nominations, and awards in France and Italy. [ref: 2016 Midwest Energy News 40 Under 40, Midwest Energy News (via ZEF Energy)]

=== Fisker Inc. ===
After leaving Sakti3, Albano joined Fisker Inc. as vice president of battery systems, heading its battery team. [ref: Fisker Aims To Unleash The Potential Of Solid-State Batteries, & Stun With EMotion, CleanTechnica] Under an agreement dated 10 January 2017, he transferred his solid-state battery patent to Fisker, together with three research grants (two from the U.S. Department of Energy and one from Ann Arbor SPARK) totaling $797,000, in exchange for stock options. [ref: Arbitration Award Confirmation for Fisker — LA County Case 20TRCV00731, Scribd (court filing)] In November 2017, Fisker announced it had filed patents on flexible solid-state battery designs based on Albano's work, projecting energy densities more than twice those of conventional lithium-ion cells; Henrik Fisker credited Albano publicly, saying "the breakthrough that Fabio brought to me" was a solid-state design that overcame the surface-area limits of thin-film batteries. [ref: Will we soon be able to charge electric cars in just a minute?, The Irish Times] Inc. magazine described his approach as turning "a one-story solid-state battery into a multistory one" — a three-dimensional "bolt battery" with over 25 times the surface area of a thin-film cell. [ref: How a Failed Car Company Gave Rise to a Revolutionary New Battery, Inc.] A prototype was displayed at the Consumer Electronics Show in January 2018. Albano said at the announcement: "This breakthrough marks the beginning of a new era in solid-state materials and manufacturing technologies." [ref: Fisker gives up on solid-state batteries after announcing 'breakthrough', Electrek] Fisker abandoned its solid-state battery program in 2021. Albano's relationship with Fisker ended in a legal dispute over the 2017 agreement, which he pursued in arbitration; in 2022 he petitioned the Los Angeles County Superior Court to confirm the arbitration award. [ref: Arbitration Award Confirmation for Fisker — LA County Case 20TRCV00731, Scribd (court filing)]
[truncated]

Dove Viaggi (often simply Dove) is an Italian monthly travel and lifestyle magazine established in 1991 and published by RCS MediaGroup (ISSN 1121-1792). [ref: Dove, rcsmediagroup.it] [ref: Sito ufficiale Dove Viaggi, Corriere della Sera]

== History ==
The magazine was founded in May 1991 by journalist and publisher Luca Grandori (d. 2012), who had previously created other Italian travel publications, including Gulliver and Carnet. [ref: 25 anni di viaggi e sogni: l’editoriale del numero speciale di DOVE, Dove Viaggi] Its initial editorial office was located in Milan, with a founding team that included journalists Valeria Tegami, Mariella Grossi and Simona Tedesco.

During the 1990s, the magazine published themed print supplements, such as Speciale Weekend (focused on short itineraries) and Dossier Tropici (covering long-haul destinations). [ref: Cronologia e Linee di Sviluppo del Sistema DOVE, CairoRCS Media] In 2005, the publication released a series of spin-off magazines: DOVE Case, DOVE Eventi, and DOVE Auto. [ref: Dove negli anni, Corriere della Sera]

Valeria Tegami later became the magazine's director, followed by Carlo Montanaro. In January 2015, Simona Tedesco was appointed editor-in-chief, with an editorial focus on contemporary and sustainable travel.

In May 2017, the publication launched an annual Travel issue, distributed as a supplement with the daily newspaper Corriere della Sera.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the magazine temporarily shifted its editorial focus to domestic and local travel and launched digital initiatives allowing readers to share local content.

In 2026, Dove expanded its multimedia activities with vodcasts and reader initiatives. [ref: I Podcast di Dove 35 anni, Corriere della Sera] In June, for its 35th anniversary, the magazine published a special issue with a commemorative cover and an editorial by Simona Tedesco centered on the manifesto "Andiamo sul posto. E raccontiamo", emphasizing the value of on-the-ground reporting over AI-generated content and unverified reviews. [ref: Buon compleanno Dove: 35 anni di viaggi da sogno, iO Donna]

== Monographic guides and digital projects ==
Beyond its monthly print edition, the publication produces Le Guide di Dove, a series of monographic travel guides established in 2006, and co-organizes public events on travel culture, such as the festival Il Tempo del Viaggio in Milan. [ref: Il Tempo del Viaggio Inverno, Corriere della Sera]

In February 2014, the brand expanded online with the launch of doveviaggi.it as the travel section of Corriere della Sera. Over time, the website expanded its content to include narrative video series, thematic newsletters, and dedicated podcasts launched in 2020, such as Brescia, che sorpresa! and I viaggi da film. [ref: I podcast di Dove Viaggi, Corriere della Sera] In parallel with the website's launch in 2014, the brand also introduced DoveClub, an online travel booking and e-commerce platform.

== Editors-in-chief ==
* Luca Grandori (1991–1994)
* Valeria Tegami (1994–2003)
* Carlo Montanaro (2003–2015)
* Simona Tedesco (2015–present)

Kenneth Tetteh Akiti

Kenneth Tetteh Akiti is a Ghanaian electrical and electronics engineer, researcher, and inventor whose work encompasses embedded systems, magnetic-field measurement, and battery energy storage technologies. He is a doctoral researcher at Edith Cowan University in Western Australia, where his research focuses on the reuse of retired electric mining vehicle batteries in stationary energy storage applications. [ref: Kenneth Tetteh Akiti, ECU] [ref: Responsible management of retired mining vehicle batteries to address environmental and economic challenges ​, Minerals Research Institute of WA]

In 2025, Akiti was awarded the Odwyn Jones PhD Scholarship by the [https://www.mriwa.wa.gov.au/ Minerals Research Institute of Western Australia (MRIWA)] for research into the responsible management of retired mining vehicle batteries. He is also a named co-inventor of a patented optical-pumping-based magnetic-field measurement device. [ref: Device and method for measuring scalar magnetic field based on pulsed optical pumping]

Early life and education

Akiti was born in Ghana and attended Presbyterian Boys' Senior High School in Accra, where he studied General Science and joined the robotics club.

He studied Electronics and Communication Engineering at All Nations University in Koforidua, Ghana, graduating with a Bachelor of Engineering degree with First Class Honours in 2017.

He subsequently studied at Zhejiang University of Science and Technology in Hangzhou, China, where he obtained a master's degree in Intelligent Manufacturing and Control Engineering. His postgraduate work included research on laser stabilization and magnetic-field measurement systems. [ref: A kilohertz bandwidth and sensitive scalar atomic magnetometer using an optical multipass cell, Measurement]

Akiti later enrolled in a doctoral programme in Electrical and Electronic Engineering at Edith Cowan University in Perth, Australia. His doctoral research concerns battery management, optimization, and the repurposing of retired electric vehicle batteries for secondary energy storage applications.

Engineering career

Akiti has worked in embedded systems engineering, electronic circuit design, and autonomous systems development.

During his early career in Ghana, he worked at Syngle Electronics Bay, where his engineering activities included microcontroller-based systems, electronic prototyping, and embedded hardware development.

He subsequently worked at Robsense Technology in Hangzhou, China, developing embedded systems for unmanned aerial vehicles and related control technologies.

His professional and research interests include microcontroller programming, autonomous systems, electronic instrumentation, and energy storage system design.

ResearchMagnetic-field measurement and instrumentation

During his postgraduate studies in China, Akiti participated in research involving atomic magnetometers and optical instrumentation.

He co-authored the 2022 paper "A kilohertz bandwidth and sensitive scalar atomic magnetometer using an optical multipass cell", published in the journal "Measurement". The study investigated a scalar atomic magnetometer designed to achieve high measurement bandwidth and sensitivity through an optical multipass cell.

Akiti is also listed as a co-inventor of United States patent US11486945B1, "Device and method for measuring scalar magnetic field based on pulsed optical pumping", granted on 1 November 2022. The patent describes an optical-pumping-based system for measuring magnetic fields.

Second-life battery systems

At Edith Cowan University, Akiti's doctoral research examines the technical challenges associated with reusing retired batteries from electrically powered mining vehicles.

The project, titled "Responsible management of retired mining vehicle batteries to address environmental and economic challenges", investigates methods of repurposing batteries for stationary battery energy storage systems.

His research includes predictive modelling, battery-cell performance assessment, and dynamic reconfiguration of electrical connections within battery packs. These approaches are intended to address cell heterogeneity, performance degradation, and the operational limitations of conventional fixed-configuration battery systems.

The project has potential applications in renewable energy integration and energy storage for mining operations and remote communities.

In 2026, Akiti and colleagues authored "Switching configurations for reconfigurable battery packs: A review", a study examining switching architectures used in reconfigurable battery systems, including their complexity, fault tolerance, and implementation characteristics. [ref: Switching Configurations for reconfigurable battery packs: A review, Journal of Energy Storage]

Awards and recognition

In 2025, Akiti received the MRIWA Odwyn Jones PhD Scholarship, supporting his research at Edith Cowan University.

The award and associated research project were documented in the Minerals Research Institute of Western Australia's 2024–25 annual report, which identified his project as part of the institute's research and workforce development programme.

Akiti was also featured among the researchers presenting at MRIWA's 2025 scholarship programme events. [ref: Speakers 2025, Minerals Research Institute of WA]

== Overview ==
The [https://eachccp.eu/ European Association of CCP Clearing Houses (EACH)] is a Belgian not-for-profit organisation that represents the interests of Central Counterparty Clearing Houses (CCPs) across Europe. Established in 1992, the association contributes to the safety, transparency, and efficiency of financial markets by coordinating policy engagement, developing standards, and supporting the role of CCPs in reducing systemic risk.

EACH acts as the collective voice of European CCPs, representing 19 members from 15 European countries as of 2026 [ref: About us, EACH - European Association of CCP Clearing Houses]. The organisation is registered in the EU Transparency Register under the number 36897011311-96.

CCPs play a crucial role in modern financial systems by interposing themselves between buyers and sellers in financial transactions and managing counterparty credit risk [ref: Central Clearing of OTC Derivatives: bilateral vs multilateral netting, Statistics & Risk Modeling]. EACH supports these institutions by facilitating dialogue with regulators, providing industry expertise, encouraging harmonisation of best practices and representing them in discussions concerning financial market infrastructure, clearing, risk management and financial regulation with several entities in the EU bubble [ref: The European central counterparty (CCP) ecosystem] [ref: Standards of Risk Management Controls used by Central Counterparty Clearing Houses].

== History ==
EACH was established in 1992 to facilitate and strengthen cooperation among European CCPs and contribute to a more resilient financial system. In 2001, the association published a set of risk management standards for CCPs. According to EACH, these standards contributed to later international work on CCP regulation, including discussions leading to the development of international standards for financial market infrastructures by the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS, now CPMI) and the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO).

Following the 2007–2008 global financial crisis and the adoption of the European Market Infrastructure Regulation (EMIR), EACH became a regular participant in consultations conducted by the European Commission, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the European Banking Authority (EBA), the European Central Bank (ECB) and international standard-setting bodies like CPMI, IOSCO and Financial Stability Board (FSB) on the regulation and supervision of central counterparties [ref: Setting EU CCP policy – much more than meets the eye] [ref: CCP Policy, www.esma.europa.eu], which has lead to the association subsequently contributing to consultations relating to EMIR reviews, CCP recovery and resolution, operational resilience, cyber security, digital assets and the transition to T+1 securities settlement [ref: ESMA CONSULTS ON EMIR REPORTING GUIDELINES, www.esma.europa.eu] [ref: ].

== Activities ==
* Preparing industry responses to consultations issued by European and international authorities.
* Facilitating cooperation among member CCPs on technical and regulatory issues.
* Organising working groups on legal, operational, technological and risk-management matters.
* Publishing reports, position papers and technical guidance relating to clearing and market infrastructure.

EACH's consultation responses are part of the broader stakeholder input considered by [https://www.esrb.europa.eu/about/orga/list/html/index.en.html European macroprudential authorities] when reviewing financial market infrastructure regulation [ref: A system-wide approach to macroprudential policy].

== Governance ==
As stated on their website, EACH is governed by its General Assembly, Board and a number of specialised committees and working groups [ref: Governance, EACH - European Association of CCP Clearing Houses].

=== General Assembly ===
The General Assembly is the association's highest decision-making body. It approves amendments to the Articles of Association, elects the Board, approves the annual accounts and decides on the admission of new members.

=== Board ===
The Board is responsible for overseeing the implementation of the association's strategic objectives and supervising its activities between meetings of the General Assembly [ref: Board, EACH - European Association of CCP Clearing Houses].

=== Committees and Working Groups ===
EACH maintains permanent committees and working groups [ref: Committees, EACH - European Association of CCP Clearing Houses] covering regulatory, legal, operational and technical matters. These include:

* Policy Committee
* Risk Committee
* Legal Committee
* Energy Clearing Working Group
* EMIR Trade Reporting Working Group
* EMIR Risk-Free Rates Working Group
* Securities Operations Working Group
* DORA Task Force
* Cyber Security Task Force

These bodies internally coordinate technical analysis and prepare common industry positions on regulatory developments affecting CCPs.

== Membership ==
As of 2026, EACH's members comprise:

Legends League Cricket (LLC) is a Twenty20 cricket competition featuring former international cricketers. The competition began in January 2022 with an international-format tournament and later expanded to include a franchise-based competition in India.

The league was co-founded by Raman Raheja and Vivek Khushalani and is organised by Absolute Legends Sports Private Limited. [ref: Uncertain times: Legends League Cricket caught in 'ownership' row, The New Indian Express]

== History ==

=== Establishment and Ravi Shastri's appointment ===

In November 2021, former India cricketer and national team head coach Ravi Shastri was appointed commissioner of Legends League Cricket ahead of its inaugural tournament. The competition was planned as an international event involving former players from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Australia, England and other cricket-playing nations. [ref: Ravi Shastri joins upcoming Legends League as Commissioner, The Indian Express]

The first edition was staged in Muscat, Oman, in January 2022. It featured India Maharajas, Asia Lions and World Giants, with World Giants winning the tournament. [ref: Legends League Cricket 2022: Full list of players signed up for season two of LLC T20, Wisden]

The international-format competition subsequently operated under the name LLC Masters, while a separate franchise-based tournament was established in India.

=== Franchise competition ===

The franchise tournament began in September 2022 with four teams: India Capitals, Manipal Tigers, Bhilwara Kings and Gujarat Giants. The inaugural season featured former India cricketers Virender Sehwag, Gautam Gambhir, Harbhajan Singh and Irfan Pathan as team captains. [ref: Virender Sehwag, Irfan Pathan, Gautam Gambhir and Harbhajan Singh appointed captains in Legends League Cricket, Hindustan Times]

India Capitals won the first franchise championship, defeating Bhilwara Kings by 104 runs in the final in Jaipur. [ref: Legends League Cricket: India Capitals Champions After Ross Taylor, Mitchell Johnson Fireworks, NDTV Sports]

The competition expanded to six teams in 2023. Manipal Tigers won the championship, defeating Urbanrisers Hyderabad in the final. [ref: Harbhajan Singh's Manipal Tigers clinch LLC T20 2023 title after beating Suresh Raina's side, The Times of India]

The 2024 season was won by Southern Super Stars, who defeated Konark Suryas Odisha in a Super Over at Bakshi Stadium, Srinagar. [ref: Southern Super Stars vs Konark Suryas Odisha, Final, Legends League Cricket 2024, Cricbuzz]

The fourth franchise season took place in March 2026. Royal Riders Punjab defeated Konark Suryas Odisha by 41 runs in the final at Haldwani. [ref: Legends League Cricket 2026, Cricbuzz]

== Notable participants ==

The league has featured former international cricketers from India, Australia, England, Sri Lanka, South Africa, New Zealand, Pakistan, the West Indies and other cricket-playing nations.

Among the former Indian players associated with the competition are Virender Sehwag, Gautam Gambhir, Harbhajan Singh, Suresh Raina, Irfan Pathan, Yusuf Pathan, Mohammad Kaif and Robin Uthappa.

International participants have included Chris Gayle, Jacques Kallis, Brett Lee, Shane Watson, Muttiah Muralitharan, Dale Steyn, Eoin Morgan, Mitchell Johnson, Ross Taylor and Darren Sammy. [ref: Legends League Cricket press releases, Legends League Cricket]

== Matches in Jammu and Kashmir ==

In November 2023, Legends League Cricket staged matches at Maulana Azad Stadium in Jammu. The event brought former international players to a venue that had not hosted international cricket for approximately 35 years. [ref: After 35 years, Jammu witnesses return of international cricket, The Indian Express]

In October 2024, the league held matches at Bakshi Stadium in Srinagar. The tournament received international media coverage for bringing former international players to Kashmir after nearly four decades. Al Jazeera reported both enthusiasm among spectators and concerns expressed by some local observers about the long-term development of cricket in the region. [ref: Legends League allows long-deprived fans to enjoy cricket again in Kashmir, Al Jazeera]

== Commercial and legal developments ==

In 2022, the league became involved in an ownership dispute concerning an earlier memorandum of understanding. The New Indian Express reported that the matter reached the Delhi High Court following a petition seeking arbitration. The league's representatives disputed the validity of the agreement.

History

Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society Ltd. (MCRCMS) is a farmer-owned cooperative society based in Mulkanoor village in Hanumakonda district, Telangana, India. Established on 27 July 1956 under the Hyderabad Cooperative Societies Act, 1952, it was initially known as Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Bank and was later renamed Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society. [ref: The Story of Mulkanoor cooperative Rural credit and marketing society, International cooperative Alliance Asia and Pacific]

The society was formed to improve the socio-economic conditions of farmers in Mulkanoor and surrounding villages. It was established in response to challenges faced by cultivators, including limited irrigation facilities, high interest rates on loans, inadequate access to agricultural inputs, distress sales of agricultural produce and dependence on moneylenders. Initially, the cooperative was  established with a membership of 373 farmers.with a share capital of ₹2,300. [ref: New Member: Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society, International Cooperative Alliance Asia and Pacific]

Its services include agricultural credit, agricultural inputs, agricultural produce procurement and marketing, consumer services and welfare-related activities. Over the following decades, it expanded its membership and developed integrated services in agricultural credit, agricultural production, finance, marketing, value addition and rural development, with the objectives of improving agricultural productivity, increasing farmers' incomes and reducing dependence on moneylenders and intermediaries. [ref: Mulkanoor Light of Indian's Cooperative Movement]

== Area of operation ==
The society's area of operation covers 14 revenue villages across the Bheemadevarapally, Elkathurthy and Velair mandals. These include Mulkanoor, Mutharam, Bheemadevarapally, Gatla Narsingapur, Kothapally, Koppur, Vangara, Rathnagiri, Mallaram, Kothakonda, Mustafapur, Gopalpur, Jeelugula and Errabelly. [ref: The Harvest of Trust, International Cooperative Alliance Asia and Pacific]

Historical government material has also described the cooperative as operating across 14 revenue villages surrounding Mulkanoor and providing agricultural credit, agricultural supplies and agricultural marketing services. [ref: The Harvest of Trust - The Story of Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society, International Cooperative Alliance Asia and Pacific]

Objectives

The cooperative was established primarily to provide financial and agricultural services to its farmer members. Its activities developed around the following objectives:

* Agriculture credit to members [ref: Agriculture input services, Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society]
* Procuring and marketing agricultural produce value-addition facilities [ref: Agri Produce Procurement, Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society]
* Assisting members with agricultural production extension services [ref: Title: Mulkanoor Cooperative Society: A Model of Member - Centric Rural Development Publication: Hindu Dhayashankar Author: Dr.S.L.N.T. Srinivas Date: 20 May 2026]
* Providing consumer and welfare activities [ref: Impact of Institutions on Economy of Farmers-A Case Study of Mulkanoor Co-operative Rural Bank and Marketing Society in Telangana, Indianjournals.com]
* Supplying agricultural inputs
* Supporting agricultural extension and farmer education.

These activities have allowed the society to operate across several stages of the agricultural value chain

== Services ==

=== Agricultural credit ===
MCRCMS provides agricultural and other forms of credit to its members. Its lending activities include short-term seasonal crop loans, medium-term agricultural loans, long-term loans and general-term loans for specified purposes. Agricultural finance supports crop cultivation, the purchase of farm machinery, irrigation facilities and other agricultural activities. The society also provides loans for allied agricultural activities, including dairy farming, poultry farming, sheep rearing, horticulture, sericulture and protected cultivation. [ref: Impact of Institutions on Economy of Farmers-A Case Study of Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Bank and Marketing Society in Telangana, Researchgate]

The society also provides loans to support the purchase of agricultural equipment and the development of irrigation infrastructure [ref: Impact of Institutions on Economy of Farmers – A Case Study of Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Bank and Marketing Society in Telangana, Research Gate]

=== Agricultural inputs and extension ===
The cooperative supplies agricultural inputs and provides technical and extension-related assistance to its members. Its agricultural services include the supply of seeds, fertilizers, pesticides and other farming inputs intended to support farm productivity. The International Cooperative Alliance describes the society's agricultural input and extension services as being supported by technical experts. [ref: Agriculture Input Services, Mulkanoor Cooperative Rural Credit and Marketing Society]

Wiki: English Wikipedia
Draft: Glub (artist)

Draft text:
Glub, art name of Manuel Ramos (born 1969), is a Spanish
graffiti writer and painter. He is regarded as one of the pioneers of
native Madrid graffiti, the style known as "flechero", alongside
Muelle and Bleck la Rata. Since 2010 he has worked in
geometric abstraction, developing the lines he terms "Rigid Geometry", "Minimum Abstract
Geometry" and "Transparent Abstract Geometry". He is also a typeface designer and a
musician. [ref: La intuición geométrica de Manuel Ramos, Geometricae]

== Biography ==

Ramos was born in Madrid in 1969 and began painting the streets of the city in 1986,
when the local graffiti scene was barely emerging. [ref: La historia de Glub, el grafitero amigo de Muelle..., El Mundo] He lived near
the Pacífico neighbourhood, between Atocha and Puente de Vallecas, and signed the
advertising posters of the Madrid Metro, a traditional surface of the city's native
graffiti movement. [ref: BTR#20: Glub, una vida de graffiti, Breaking The Rules]

In 1989 he adopted the elaborate aesthetics of New York graffiti, joining the emerging
Spanish hip hop scene; as a result he is considered a forerunner of the Spanish
"old school". In that period he painted with writers such as Larry 88, Rafita, Tifón
and Carmona, with whom he founded the ACT Crew in 1991. He also acted as a link
between the Madrid and Alicante scenes. [ref: GLUB y su «Top 10 Canciones», El Ritmo de la Calle]

He graduated in Fine Arts (painting) from the Complutense University of Madrid in
1998. [ref: Manuel Ramos, ArteInformado] He has lived in Valencia for a number of years, where he
painted with the local writers Ove, Noke, Tabe and Pike as a member of the Yes crew.

== Work ==

=== Madrid native graffiti ===

Glub's signature, an arrowed pictogram drawn with fine calligraphic strokes, is part of
the history of Madrid graffiti. It is documented in the reference volume
Madrid Graffiti 1982–1995 (Figueroa-Saavedra and Gálvez, 2002) [ref: Madrid Graffiti 1982-1995, Megamultimedia]
and in Nicholas Ganz's international survey Graffiti. Art of the Five Continents
(2004). [ref: Graffiti. Art of the Five Continents, Gustavo Gili] The Spanish Graffiare archive keeps photographs of his work
from the 1990s (Pacífico, Ventilla, Alcorcón, Plaza de Castilla) and a 2000 interview. [ref: Entrevista a GLUB, Spanish Graffiare]
In 2001 the magazine Geometricae published the photograph
Muelle (left) + Glub — signatures on a wall, Madrid, 2001, showing the two pioneers
signing the same wall.

=== Geometric abstraction ===

Since 2010 Ramos has painted geometric abstractions on traditional supports. A 2025
review by the geometric art magazine Geometricae describes his work as a bridge
between the immediacy of urban art and the conceptual depth of geometric abstraction,
and identifies three personal lines: "Rigid Geometry", "Minimum Abstract Geometry" and
"Transparent Abstract Geometry". In the latter he applies spray paint and the stencilling
technique to create soft colour gradations on canvas, an inheritance from his graffiti
practice.

His solo exhibitions include Geometries Cromàtics (Espai Llimera, Valencia, 2016),
Modulaciones (Ama-Gi Club, Valencia, 2016), Abstracción geométrica (Ama-Gi Club,
Valencia, 2018), Nuevas Geometrías (Espai Llimera, Valencia, 2020) and
Exposition de peinture abstraite géométrique (Colegio de España, Paris, 2018). [ref: Curriculum - Manuel Ramos, ArteInformado]

== Collection and recognition ==

A work by Glub was acquired by the Museum of European and Mediterranean
Civilisations (MuCEM) in Marseille, France, and shown in the exhibition
Graff en Méditerranée (Fort Saint-Jean, 2017–2018); the museum publishes a photograph
of the piece, credited to Yves Inchierman, on the exhibition page. [ref: Graff en Méditerranée, MuCEM]
Another work belongs to the Colegio de España in Paris (2018), and a third one to the
Junta Municipal de Arganzuela in Madrid (1999); he also received the acquisition prize of
the "Premios de Arganzuela" painting competition in 1999.

Since 2017 he has been a member of the editorial team of the geometric art magazine
Geometricae, which published the monographic catalogues of his work
Geometría Abstracta Transparente (2018, 36 pp., with texts by Ramos himself) and
Nuevas Geometrías (2020), and dedicated an extensive review to his painting in
2025. [ref: Geometría Abstracta Transparente – Manuel Ramos, Geometricae]

== Other activities ==

=== Typography ===

Under his own name, he has published seventy typefaces on the site DaFont,
with more than 2.6 million downloads, including graffiti-based scripts such as
"Graffont" and "Arsone" and the popular designs "Metropolis" and "Alameda". [ref: Manuel Ramos (fonts), DaFont]

=== Music ===

In 2026 he released the album Rizomatic on the dub house label Haibt,
distributed digitally on YouTube with tracks such as "KEF" and "Genesis". [ref: Rizomatic – Glub (album), YouTube]

== Publications ==

* Memorias en graffiti (2007, self-published, edition of 100 copies; updated edition
available since 2022).
* Relatos de un escritor de graffiti (2009, free online publication, with
contributions by Trase, El Niño de las Pinturas, Suso 033, among others).
* Geometría Abstracta Transparente – monographic catalogue, Geometricae, 2018.
* Nuevas Geometrías – exhibition catalogue, Geometricae, 2020.

== References ==

Draft: DeskTime

Draft text:
DeskTime is an automatic time-tracking software that analyzes employee productivity. [ref: DeskTime employee monitoring, TechRadar] First released in 2011 by the Latvian tech company Draugiem Group, the software was initially developed for internal use within the group before becoming a standalone product.

The software allows users to categorize the applications and websites used during working hours as productive, unproductive, or neutral, providing insight into how time is spent throughout the day. The collected data is available to both employees and managers. [ref: Kā darbojas produktivitātes mērīšanas rīks "DeskTime", un vai to iespējams apmānīt, Delfi] [ref: Latvian Economics Ministry to watch employees' screen time, eng.lsm.lv] The software is mostly used in the private sector, however some pilot projects in the public sector have also been set up.

DeskTime's user base exceeds over 100,000 employees worldwide, with the United States and India as the biggest markets. [ref: Trīs mēneši ar "DeskTime" – jaunā realitāte Ekonomikas ministrijā, Delfi] [ref: Uzņēmums ķer “laika zagļus”, LA.LV]

== Productivity research ==
The company that develops DeskTime has published several studies on workplace productivity based on aggregated user data. A 2014 analysis of its most productive users found that they typically worked in 52-minute intervals followed by 17-minute breaks - a pattern that became known as the 52/17 rule, a time-management method comparable to the Pomodoro Technique. [ref: What the most productive workers have in common, The Washington Post] [ref: The Exact Perfect Amount of Time to Take a Break, According to Data, TIME] [ref: The Exact Amount Of Time You Should Work Every Day, Fast Company]

In 2017, a study drawing on data from 65,000 employees in the United States found that productivity declines after extended working hours: output dropped by 11% immediately after eight hours of work, with an additional 19% decrease for each subsequent hour. [ref: New Data Proves Staying Late in the Office Is Pointless, Observer]

== References ==

Draft: BookMyShow (ticketing platform)

Draft text:
BookMyShow is an Indian online ticketing and entertainment platform operated by Big Tree Entertainment Private Limited. It provides ticketing services for films, concerts, theatrical performances, sporting events and other entertainment activities. The company was founded in 2007, with its headquarters in Mumbai, Maharashtra. [ref: India's BookMyShow pulls in $100M to grow its online ticketing business, TechCrunch] [ref: About Us, BookMyShow]

The company has expanded from online ticketing into live-event promotion, production and event infrastructure. Its live-events business has become a significant part of its operations, alongside its ticketing business. [ref: Going-out economy: No longer a one-man show, [[The Financial Express (India)] [ref: BookMyShow moves up the live-events chain, [[The Financial Express (India)] [ref: KKR Backs BookMyShow As Live Entertainment Becomes Its Next Growth Engine, Inc42]

== History ==

=== Establishment and acquisitions ===

Big Tree Entertainment was established in 1999 by Ashish Hemrajani, Rajesh Balpande and Parikshit Dar. The company initially provided software and inventory-management services to the cinema industry before launching BookMyShow as a consumer-facing online ticketing service in 2007.

BookMyShow expanded its ticketing and event-related operations through a series of acquisitions. In 2013, Big Tree Entertainment acquired Chennai-based online ticketing company TicketGreen. It acquired a majority stake in Bengaluru-based Eventifier, a social media analytics company, in 2015 and Chennai-based sports fan relationship management company Fantain Sports in 2016. [ref: BookMyShow.com acquires Chennai-based Ticketgreen.com, Business Standard] [ref: Bookmyshow buys majority stake in Eventifier for $2 million, ETRetail] [ref: BookMyShow buys Chennai-based startup Fantain Sports to expand user base, The Economic Times]

In 2017, BookMyShow acquired Hyderabad-based online ticketing platform MastiTickets and acquired a 75% stake in Pune-based event-registration platform Townscript. It also acquired the restaurant-discovery platform Burrp from Network18 through its subsidiary Foodfesta Wellcare and acquired the digital entertainment company Nfusion, using technology from the latter to develop its audio-entertainment offering Jukebox. [ref: BookMyShow buys Hyderabad-based MastiTickets in all-cash deal, Business Standard] [ref: Bookmyshow picks up 75% stake in Townscript, [[Mint (newspaper)] [ref: BookMyShow acquires Mumbai-based Burrp, The Economic Times] [ref: BookMyShow acquires digital entertainment firm Nfusion, Business Standard]

=== Regional and international expansion ===

In October 2017, BookMyShow expanded the language options available on its website and Android application to include Marathi, Malayalam, Gujarati and Punjabi, alongside Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and English. [ref: बुकमायशो आता मराठीसह अन्य ३ भाषांत उपलब्ध, Maharashtra Times]

The company expanded into Southeast Asia during the late 2010s. In November 2018, it joined Grab Ventures Velocity, an accelerator programme associated with Southeast Asian technology company Grab, as part of its international expansion. In December 2019, BookMyShow separated its Southeast Asian operations into a distinct business headquartered in Singapore. [ref: BookMyShow Joins Grab Ventures Velocity Program With An Eye On Southeast Asia, Inc42] [ref: BookMyShow separates SE Asia Arm, The Economic Times]

=== COVID-19 pandemic ===

Restrictions on cinema screenings and live events during the COVID-19 pandemic significantly affected BookMyShow's operations. During 2021, as cinemas and entertainment venues remained closed owing to the pandemic, the company reduced its workforce. [ref: തിയറ്ററുകളും ഷോകളും ഇല്ല; ബുക്ക് മൈ ഷോ 200 ജീവനക്കാരെ കൂടി പിരിച്ച് വിട്ടു, Madhyamam]

It looked into pursuing other business avenues in response to the pandemic's impact on cinema and live-event ticketing. Its recovery strategy included diversification beyond the traditional ticketing business. [ref: Streaming now: BookMyShow and its fight back, Forbes India]

The company performed further restructuring that resulted in reducing its workforce from approximately 1,600 employees before the pandemic to around 600 afterwards. [ref: How BookMyShow Is Helping Turn India Into A Global Concert Market, Pollstar]

== Business development ==

BookMyShow expanded beyond ticketing into live-event promotion, production and infrastructure. By the 2020s, these activities had become a significant part of its business alongside online ticketing. [ref: A Strategic Analysis of Online Movie and Event Ticketing Platform: BookMyShow, Journal of The Gujarat Research Society]

In 2026, live events accounted for a substantial share of the company's business. The expansion has included investments in staging equipment, venues, production capabilities and entertainment properties, reducing the company's reliance on external event infrastructure and increasing its involvement across the live-events value chain. [ref: Beyond Attention. Into Immersion, [[Ernst & Young]

The company's live-events revenue increased from ₹24.6 crore in the 2021–22 financial year to ₹237.5 crore in 2022–23, ₹455 crore in 2023–24 and ₹756 crore in 2024–25.

Draft text:
GameBanana is an online community and repository platform made for sharing, and downloading various mods made by other users for a specific video game. Users can share custom 3D Model, Audio, Texture, GUI, Script, and Tool mods. It includes Forums, Work-In-Progress (W.I.P.) Mods, Requests, Questions, Jams, and Tutorials.
== History ==
It was founded in the mid-2000s under the name CSCentral (which stands for Counter-Strike Central) by Sebastian and originally functioned as a community for modding Counter-Strike. The website achieved significant success by offering free user-generated content for other gamers to use. When the site launched, [https://gamebanana.com/members/1382 Tom] was included on the administrator list, and since then, more people have been added to the moderation and administration team; however, Tom is the only one who has had access to the code since Sebastian left. [ref: https://gamebanana.com/wikis/1917]

As time passed, the community grew larger and expanded into a wider range of topics.

In July 2005, it briefly went to banana.nu, then shortly reverted to CSbanana.com as a result of SEO problems and user confusion.

After that, in 2005 until January 1, 2011, the community agreed the site would be named FPSBanana (Short for First-Person-Shooter Banana); Bananas were chosen as the official mascots of the site because bananas had similarities to a hand-held gun. [ref: https://gamebanana.com/wikis/1917]
==News Coverage==
Nintendo issued more than 60 separate DMCA takedown notices directed to [https://gamebanana.com/members/1676542 Waikuteru], other gamebanana Nintendo game mods have also been targetted by Nintendo. [ref: https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2024/06/nintendo-issues-multiple-dmcas-on-the-modding-site-gamebanana]

PC Gamer covered a [https://gamebanana.com/mods/440088 gamebanana mod]. The mod also includes new costumes/models, animations, textures, voice lines, field dialogue, and more. [ref: https://www.pcgamer.com/you-can-finally-be-a-woman-in-persona-5-royal-thanks-to-a-massive-mod-project/]

Draft: The way I used to be

Draft text:
The way I used to be is a 2016 young adult realistic fiction novel with themes of romance and sexual assault. It’s written by Amber Smith [ref: Amber Smith – bestselling author of young adult & middle grade books] and is published by Margaret K. McElderry Books. The novel is about a girl, named Eden, who gets sexually assaulted and how her life gets affected by that. This is a book series with two other books after this one.

== Plot summery ==
The novel begins right after Eden, who is the main character, wakes up after she got raped and sexually abused by Kevin who is her brothers best friend, a person close to her family. She wants it to be a dream, but it’s not. She starts questioning herself for example she think “I don’t know why I didn’t hear the door click shut, why I didn’t lock the damn door to begin with, why I didn’t scream when I opened my eyes and saw him crawling between my sheets, or why I didn’t try to fight him when I still stood a chance”. Eden's mom came into her room in the morning and saw the blood in the bed but she just thought Eden got her period, so she didn’t make a big deal about it. Eden knew in her mind that she should tell somebody, but she couldn’t, instead she kept it a secret. She tries to continue her normal life at school, but she struggles with her feelings and becomes a different person. In school Eden and her friends Mara and Stephen are seen as “nobodys” and are bullied. To get away from that she starts a bookclub, not just because she’s bullied but also because she thinks it will help her get over her trauma. Which it doesn’t.

During the middle part, she starts sophomore year and some time has passed since she was raped and sexually assaulted. Now Eden has changed her looks, it’s like she has become a new person. She doesn’t want to be the shy, “dorky” girl anymore. Instead she tries to appear self-confident and like nothing has happened.

She tries to get control over her life after what Kevin did to her. She still doesn't tell the truth though about what happened and she tries to hide how bad she feels. She has important people around her but still feels lonely and can't tell anyone what happened.

Eden starts talking to a boy in her school who is one year older than her, Josh Miller. He is one of the “popular” boys and they get interested in each other. But she finds it hard to trust others, difficult managing her emotions and letting anyone get close to her. She tries to keep the relationship on her own terms and does not want to show how vulnerable she is. She lies about things, her terms leads to a difficult relationship between them and even though Josh shows love to her she still feels alone. She still continues to keep the abuse a secret.

As the book goes on Eden grows up, she's in senior year and she has become even more emotionally shut off. Eden tries to cope with her pain by partying, drinking alcohol, smoking cigarettes and having casual sexual relationships. But all she wants, even though the abuse was several years ago, is still for someone to ask her if she’s doing fine and to acknowledge her. But no one does and she can’t bear to tell people either. Eden's relationship with her best friend Mara is falling apart, because Eden feels left out, has it hard to show what she needs and behaves kinda bad.

Close to the end, Eden finds out that Kevin has been accused of rape by another girl and the police get involved. Eden then calls Josh again after years of not talking and meets him again and tells him everything about the abuse. Then she also tells her brother Caelin and the book ends with her going to the police and telling them what happened and report Kevin for rape. In the end, she chose to make her voice heard and don't carry this all by herself anymore. She regained control of her life again.

== Major themes ==
There is quite a lot of major themes in the book The way I used to be, but the biggest theme that the whole plot relies on is that Eden gets raped by her older brothers best friend Kevin. This becomes a big theme not only because it's an awful thing but also because Eden doesn’t tell anyone, not even her best friend, and we get to read how much this affects her life considering she changes herself to a completely different person than she was before it all happened and she even starts hating herself.

The book is therefore not just about the assault itself, it’s also very much about what happens to Eden afterwards. The trauma affects her self-image, sexuality, schooling, way of handling emotions and relationships. It affects her for a very long time and we get to read about the consequences that follow her.

Another major theme in this book is Eden’s silence about the assault. The fear, shame and anxiety she feels causes her to keep it to herself instead of telling anyone and get the help she deserves, which causes the isolation and it forces her to navigate this trauma on her own. The author wants to show by this, how important it is to talk to someone if something like this happens. It doesn’t matter who, it could be a parent, a friend, the police or someone you don’t know, but just telling and asking for help is important!
