Draft text:
Ernst August Rudolf Schellenberg (20 February 1907 – 6 June 1984) was a German economist, social insurance administrator and politician of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). After the Second World War he headed the unified social insurance institution for Berlin, the Versicherungsanstalt Berlin (VAB). He was a member of the Bundestag for Berlin from 1952 to 1976 and chaired its committee on social policy from 1957 to 1976.

He was the SPD's spokesman on pensions in the debate on the 1957 pension reform and chaired the committee during the social legislation of the grand coalition and the first social–liberal coalition.

== Early life and education ==

Schellenberg was born in Berlin, the eldest of three children of Paul Schellenberg, a legal adviser, and his wife Anna, who ran a flower shop in Schöneberg. He attended the Paulsen-Realgymnasium in Steglitz from 1913 to 1922. After his parents divorced, his mother could not pay for further schooling, and he left with an intermediate certificate.

At fifteen he began an apprenticeship in social insurance at the Schmiede-Berufsgenossenschaft, the accident insurance association for the metalworking trades in Berlin. He then worked as a welfare worker and received state recognition as a Wohlfahrtspfleger in 1930.

In the mid-1920s he joined the Zentralverband der Angestellten, a union of salaried employees, and led its working group on social policy. In the last years of the Weimar Republic he did voluntary work for Rote Hilfe and was a sympathiser of the Communist Party of Germany.

From 1927 to 1929 he attended the social policy seminar of the Deutsche Hochschule für Politik. He then attended economics lectures at the University of Berlin as a guest student, and in 1931 he was admitted to regular study without the Abitur after passing a special examination. He also studied for a time in Heidelberg. In early 1933 he received a doctorate (Dr. rer. pol.) from the University of Berlin under Emil Lederer, with a dissertation on the voluntary labour service, Der freiwillige Arbeitsdienst auf Grund der bisherigen Erfahrungen.

== Nazi period ==

After the Nazis came to power, Schellenberg was briefly unemployed. In September 1933 he became a statistician with Allianz in Stuttgart. His attempt to obtain the habilitation at the University of Tübingen failed in 1936; the university cited his wife's Jewish family background and the Nuremberg Laws.

In 1938 he moved to Berlin as head of the calculation department of the national association of private insurers. From 1940 he also taught at the Hochschulinstitut für Versicherungswissenschaft of the University of Berlin, and after 1942 he acted for a time as deputy to its director, Theodor Süss. The education ministry refused on political grounds to extend his teaching. In 1944 he was released from military service after a few months as a recruit, having been found unfit.

== Social insurance in post-war Berlin ==

In May 1945 Ottomar Geschke, head of the social welfare department of Berlin's new Magistrat, appointed Schellenberg as his deputy. On 18 June 1945 Schellenberg proposed to the Magistrat that the city's fragmented insurance funds be replaced by a single institution. Ferdinand Sauerbruch, the councillor responsible for health, supported the proposal, and the Magistrat adopted it.

The Versicherungsanstalt Berlin began operating on 1 July 1945 under Schellenberg's direction. It combined health, pension and accident insurance. All employed persons were compulsorily insured, and a single contribution of 20 per cent of earnings was shared equally by employers and employees. Pension payments, suspended at the capitulation, resumed in August 1945 and were initially limited to 35 Reichsmarks a month. In January 1947 the Soviet Military Administration extended the Berlin model to the provinces of the Soviet occupation zone.

Schellenberg left the Magistrat in 1946. From the winter semester of 1946/47 he lectured on social insurance and social policy at the University of Berlin, later the Humboldt University, and in 1947 he was appointed extraordinary professor and director of its Institute for Social Policy and Insurance.

The SED-dominated Magistrat planned to change how the VAB's self-governing bodies were appointed. In February 1949 Schellenberg moved the VAB's headquarters from Mitte to Wilmersdorf in the western sector, and the institution split into eastern and western bodies. In May 1949 the Humboldt University announced that he was no longer a member of its teaching staff.

After West Berlin adopted federal legislation, the unified insurance was divided into separate branches in the early 1950s. Schellenberg headed the western institution's successor, the Krankenversicherungsanstalt Berlin, and became the first director of the AOK Berlin, the city's general local health insurance fund. He held these posts until 1958.

== Political career ==

Schellenberg joined the SPD in 1948.

=== Member of the Bundestag ===

In February 1952 Otto Suhr resigned his Bundestag seat, and the Abgeordnetenhaus of Berlin elected Schellenberg as his successor. He represented Berlin in the Bundestag until 1976.

From 1952 he worked with Ludwig Preller and Walter Auerbach on the SPD's Sozialplan für Deutschland, a programme for reorganising the social security system. He held constituency surgeries in Spandau and Kreuzberg.

This book consists of 39 short stories or essays by G.K. Chesterton that were originally published as newspaper pieces in The Daily News. Later, these were collected and published as a book by Methuen & Co in 1909. [ref: Tremendous Trifles, Methuen & Co.]

== Contents and themes ==

The 39 pieces in this book explores and expounds on everyday occurrences or objects from a unique light and re-enchants them.

== Reception ==

In his commentary dated October 7, 1909, writer Arnold Bennet gives a mixed review in his criticism of Chesterton's work noting his unnuanced assertions and overly-religious worldview. However, praising Chesterton's imagination and prose. This review was later collected in Bennet's 1917 book Books and Persons. [ref: Books and Persons: Being Comments on a Past Epoch, 1908–1911, George H. Doran Company]

A later critic, Dale Ahlquist describes his appreciation of the collections for its attention to ordinary wonders. [ref: Lecture 14: Tremendous Trifles, Society of Gilbert Keith Chesterton]

Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight is a 2026 children's novel written and illustrated by American author Jeff Kinney. It is the 21st book in the Diary of a Wimpy Kid series. The book was published by Amulet Books, an imprint of Abrams Books, on October 20, 2026. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight, Wimpy Kid]

== Premise ==
Greg Heffley has compiled a three-ring binder filled with notes on his middle school's biggest bullies and strategies for avoiding them. When the binder falls into the wrong hands, Greg finds himself targeted and must decide how to respond. His best friend Rowley Jefferson has been taking karate lessons, giving Greg some support, though an unexpected complication arises. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight (Book 21), Penguin Books]

In interviews, Kinney described the book as addressing bullying through humor. He noted that Greg begins by viewing himself as part of a "long line of cowards" and proud of avoiding confrontation, only to attract the attention of the school's worst bully. [ref: Jeff Kinney Launches 'Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight', Fun 107]

== Development and publication ==
The book continues the series' pattern of annual releases established in recent years. The cover features a scrambled-eggs background with Greg depicted as a chicken wearing a boxing glove, surrounded by feathers. An earlier version of the cover used a bacon-patterned spine, which was later changed to burnt toast. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight, Diary of a Wimpy Kid Wiki]

The title and cover were publicly revealed in early 2026, including an appearance related to The Kelly Clarkson Show. Kinney supported the launch with a multi-city tour featuring an interactive stage show themed around the book. [ref: Fight or Flight Tour Wimpy Kid Press Release, Abrams Books] [ref: 'Wimpy Kid' at Home and on the Road: Jeff Kinney's Wildly Busy Year, Publishers Weekly]

== Reception ==
As a newly released title, critical reception is still emerging. Early reader responses on platforms such as Goodreads have been generally positive, consistent with the series' established popularity. [ref: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Fight or Flight, Goodreads] The broader Diary of a Wimpy Kid series has sold more than 300 million copies worldwide.

Draft: Bogos

Draft text:
Bogos (Bogo; associated with the Bilen people) is a historical region in present-day Eritrea, centered on the area around Keren. The region is known for its unique social institutions, customary laws and historical traditions. Werner Munzinger, a nineteenth-century explorer and ethnographer, documented the customs, legal practices and political history of the Bogos in his work Über die Sitten und das Recht der Bogos, published in 1859.

Bogos developed within the larger historical context of the northern Horn of Africa, where highland communities, pastoral societies and regional powers maintained fluctuating political and commercial relationships. Munzinger's writings, along with the historical and linguistic research of Leo Reinisch, provide accounts of the region's traditional history, kinship structures and customary institutions.

In the nineteenth century, Bogos became increasingly involved in the political rivalries affecting the northern Ethiopian and Eritrean borderlands. The region's history was linked to the expansion of Egyptian authority, the policies of Ethiopian rulers and the changing balance of power in the surrounding territories. Historical accounts by Munzinger and later studies of Eritrea provide sources for examining these developments and their effects on local communities.

The social organization of Bogos was closely linked to customary law, kinship and community traditions. Munzinger's account describes rules regarding marriage, inheritance, property, family relations and compensation for injury and homicide, making it an important early source for the study of the region's traditional legal institutions.

Aaron Hertzmann is a computer scientist who works in computer graphics, computer vision, and machine learning, and on the perception and theory of art. He is a principal scientist at Adobe Research and was previously a professor of computer science at the University of Toronto. [ref: Computer Graphics Achievement Award, ACM SIGGRAPH] [ref: Aaron Hertzmann, ACM SIGGRAPH History Archive] His research has included non-photorealistic rendering, the Image Analogies method for example-based image stylization, machine-learning models of human motion for character animation, and computational photography. He received the ACM SIGGRAPH Computer Graphics Achievement Award in 2024 and is a Fellow of the Association for Computing Machinery and of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers. [ref: Announcing ACM SIGGRAPH Award Winners, ACM SIGGRAPH] [ref: Aaron Hertzmann – ACM Fellows (2018), Association for Computing Machinery]

== Education ==
Hertzmann received a bachelor's degree in computer science and art and art history from Rice University in 1996. [ref: Aaron Hertzmann, CS-Can/Info-Can] He received a PhD in computer science from New York University in 2001, supervised by Ken Perlin and Denis Zorin.

== Career ==
After a year as a postdoctoral researcher in the Graphics and Imaging Laboratory (GRAIL) at the University of Washington (2001–2002), [ref: Ras Bodik, Alec Wolman, and Aaron Hertzmann recognized as Fellows of the ACM for outstanding contributions to the field of computing, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, University of Washington] Hertzmann joined the Department of Computer Science at the University of Toronto in 2003. He was a professor there until 2013. He joined Adobe in 2012 and became a principal scientist in 2016. He has held an affiliate faculty appointment at the University of Washington since 2005.

Hertzmann was conference co-chair, with Craig Kaplan, of the 2004 Symposium on Non-Photorealistic Animation and Rendering (NPAR). [ref: Proceedings of the 3rd International Symposium on Non-Photorealistic Animation and Rendering, Association for Computing Machinery] He served as the first Conference Papers Director at SIGGRAPH 2022, for a conference track he had advocated creating. He is the editor-in-chief of the journal Foundations and Trends in Computer Graphics and Vision. [ref: Foundations and Trends in Computer Graphics and Vision, Emerald Publishing]

== Research ==
Hertzmann's early work concerned non-photorealistic rendering (NPR), including algorithms for painterly rendering of images and video and for producing line drawings from 3D models. [ref: Paint by Pixel, Science News] His 2001 paper Image Analogies, with Charles Jacobs, Nuria Oliver, Brian Curless and David Salesin, described a method for learning an image filter or artistic style from an example pair of images and applying it to new images. [ref: Image Analogies] [ref: Computer mimics great masters' style, BBC News] [ref: Virtual Virtuosity, [[MIT Technology Review] [ref: Smooth Moves, Computer Graphics World] The SIGGRAPH award citation credits the paper with beginning a new era of machine learning for image authoring and stylization, with influence extending to later image-editing methods based on generative adversarial networks and diffusion models.

Hertzmann's work combining computer graphics with machine learning has included models of character motion learned from motion capture data, capturing non-rigid motion from video, and rotoscoping. [ref: Innovators Under 35: 2004, MIT Technology Review] [ref: A Matter of Style, Computer Graphics World] He also worked on controlling physically simulated human motion. [ref: Walk like a human, New Scientist] The SIGGRAPH award citation describes this as laying groundwork for later uses of reinforcement learning in physics-based animation. His other work includes image deblurring, portrait segmentation and depth-aware photo editing in computational photography, and early machine-learning approaches to graphic design and geometry processing.

Hertzmann has written position articles on the science of art and on art made with generative artificial intelligence, drawing on art history, philosophy and psychology. In them he argues that art is a social activity, and that AI systems act as artistic tools in the way earlier technologies such as photography did, rather than as artists in their own right. [ref: Can Computers Create Art?, Arts] He was a co-author of a 2023 article in Science on art and generative AI. [ref: Art and the science of generative AI, [[Science (journal)]

He has also proposed theories of how people perceive perspective and shape in pictures. These theories seek to explain phenomena that linear perspective theory does not account for. [ref: Toward a Theory of Perspective Perception in Pictures, Journal of Vision] Hertzmann is also a painter. [ref: About the Cover: Music to the Eyes, IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications]

Joseph "Joe" Lee Swanson [ref: A Hero Sits Next Door] is a fictional character from the American adult animated sitcom Family Guy. He is a neighbor and friend of the Griffin family, best known for being an intensely muscular, short-tempered paraplegic police officer who is confined to a wheelchair. The show's creator, Seth MacFarlane, designed the character, who is voiced by actor Patrick Warburton. Joe lives at 33 Spooner Street in Quahog, Rhode Island, and completes the core neighborhood friend group alongside Peter Griffin, Glenn Quagmire, and Cleveland Brown.

==Role in the show==

Joe works as a dedicated police officer for the Quahog Police Department. He lives on Spooner Street with his wife, Bonnie Swanson, with whom he shares a deeply strained and mutually exhausting marriage. Together they have two children: Kevin, a troubled Iraq War veteran, and Susie, an infant daughter. [ref: Family Guy: "Believe it Or Not, Joe's Walking On Air" Review, IGN] [ref: Family Guy: “Thanksgiving.”, The A.V. Club] Joe is one of Peter Griffin's best friends and is frequently seen drinking with Peter, Quagmire, and Cleveland at their local hangout, The Drunken Clam. [ref: Family Guy: “Joe's Revenge”, The A.V. Club]

The origin of Joe's disability has been a recurring plot point throughout the series. He originally claimed that he was paralyzed after faking a fight with the Grinch on Christmas Eve. [ref: Review: Family Guy "Joe's Revenge", Bubbleblabber] However, the episode "Joe's Revenge" later revealed the true story: Joe was shot in both legs by a heroin dealer named Bobby Briggs during an undercover operation. Despite his paralysis, Joe possesses extraordinary, near-superhuman upper-body strength and is a highly capable hand-to-hand combatant.

In early seasons of the show, Joe was characterized as a fiercely competitive, respected, and highly confident hero who frequently intimidated Peter. As the series progressed, his characterization shifted dramatically. In later seasons, Joe is often depicted as severely depressed, emotionally vulnerable, and insecure. He is frequently subjected to dynamic shifts in the group, often acting as the resident "punching bag" whose disability and domestic misery are the butt of his friends' jokes. [ref: Family Guy: The 4 Best (& 5 Worst) Recurring Characters, Screen Rant]

In addition to his routine police work, Joe's health and physical condition have served as the focal point for several major storylines. In the episode "Believe It or Not, Joe's Walking on Air," he undergoes an experimental spine transplant surgery that successfully restores his ability to walk. However, his newly regained mobility causes him to become arrogant and abusive toward his friends, leading Peter, Quagmire, and Cleveland to team up and re-break his spine to return him to his status quo. Joe has also participated in various high-stakes neighborhood misadventures, including traveling overseas with the guys and assembling his paraplegic friends to combine their wheelchairs into a giant, Voltron-style functional robot known as "Crippletron." [ref: Family Guy: "No Meals on Wheels" Review, IGN]

==Creation and design==

Joe Swanson was created by Seth MacFarlane and writers Mike Barker and Matt Weitzman for the fifth episode of the first season of Family Guy, titled "A Hero Sits Next Door." [ref: Inside Family Guy: An Illustrated History, HarperDesign] To contrast with the rest of the neighborhood characters, Joe was designed as an overly intense, athletic alpha male whose physical limitations were intentionally juxtaposed against his incredible determination and "super-cop" persona. [ref: How Family Guy's Characters Are Completely Different Now, CinemaBlend] Actor Patrick Warburton was cast to voice the character, using his signature loud, booming, and hyper-masculine inflection to drive home the aggressive, intense authority required for the role. [ref: Random Roles: Patrick Warburton, The A.V. Club]

MacFarlane cast Patrick Warburton for the role after becoming a fan of his deadpan comedic timing and deep, booming baritone voice, which Warburton had previously popularized as David Puddy on Seinfeld. [ref: ‘We do need humour in our lives’: Seinfeld’s Patrick Warburton slams cancel culture, Evening Standard] In behind-the-scenes interviews, Warburton has noted that Joe's voice is essentially a heightened, high-energy extension of his own natural speaking register, made to match the character's relentless intensity and physical over-compensation. [ref: A 'Family Guy' Voice Actor Once Refused to Record an Episode Over a Joke He Said Went Too Far, Vice]

==Reception==

Joe Swanson has generated significant analysis from television critics who widely praised his addition as an essential fixture on Spooner Street. In an early-season retrospective for IGN, television commentator Ahsan Haque lauded the character's conceptual debut, writing that the narrative-driven story serves as a "great introduction for Joe" and successfully establishes his unique dynamic within the regular neighborhood roster. Haque particularly praised the physical comedy surrounding the character's narrative heights, characterizing the sequence where Joe combines his wheelchair-bound friends into a massive, Voltron-style functional robot known as the "Cripple-Tron" as a brilliant display of "sheer creativity". [ref: Family Guy: Top 10 Fights, IGN]
[truncated]

Parneet Kaur Khaira, known professionally as Parneet Khaira, is an Australian model, children's author, youth advocate and social media content creator based in Brisbane, Queensland. Her work has focused on youth empowerment, cultural diversity, environmental awareness and community engagement. In 2025 she won the title of Miss Australia Legacy International 2025.

== Early life and education ==
Khaira moved to Australia at the age of three and grew up there. She has spoken publicly about her Punjabi heritage and about her upbringing in Australia and her strong connection to the country she calls home. Khaira has expressed an interest in Australian public life, community affairs and contributing to the country through public service and civic engagement.

== Career ==

=== Modelling and pageantry ===
Khaira began modelling at a young age and has taken part in Australian pageants. In July 2025, she won the title of Miss Australia Legacy International 2025. In 2026, StarCentral Magazine profiled her as one of the finalists in its coverage of the National Miss Australia competition. StarCentral Magazine also published an earlier article about candidates for Queens of Australia 2025.

=== Writing ===
Khaira is a children's author whose books address confidence, kindness, self-belief and environmental responsibility. Her titles include You're Too Young and It Starts With You. Earlier reporting also identified Fearless and Fierce as a children's book associated with her youth advocacy initiative.

=== Digital media ===
Khaira creates social media content about fashion, beauty, modelling and lifestyle. She has also used her platforms to promote advocacy initiatives, community projects and youth empowerment. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com]

== Advocacy and community work ==
Khaira began volunteering for charitable causes in her early teens. Her community interests have included youth empowerment, disability inclusion, cultural understanding, environmental sustainability and education.

She founded Fearless Future, an initiative that addresses bullying, racism and self-doubt and encourages confidence and inclusion among young people. Earlier media coverage referred to the initiative as Fearless Vibez. Media reports have also described book donations to schools in India, environmental initiatives and awareness efforts on social issues affecting young people.

== Political involvement ==
Khaira has taken part in political and community activities in Queensland, including involvement with the Liberal National Party (LNP) and its youth organisation, Young LNP. [ref: Instagram, www.instagram.com]

== Youth diplomacy ==
Khaira has plans to take part in the Change the World Academy programme in New York City in 2027. [ref: ] The programme runs Model United Nations conferences, in which students debate international issues, practise negotiation and explore diplomacy.

Siddhartha Lahiri, known as Sid Lahiri, is a cricket coach and former club cricketer from Kolkata, India. He has worked as a performance coach with Rajasthan Royals in the Indian Premier League, as a batting coach with Paarl Royals in SA20 and Barbados Royals in the Caribbean Premier League, and as an assistant coach with Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred. [ref: Gautam Bhattacharyya. [https://www.nationalheraldindia.com/cricket/sid-lahiri-a-journey-from-kolkata-maidan-to-global-coaching-role Sid Lahiri: A journey from Kolkata maidan to Royals' global coaching role]. National Herald. 17 March 2026.] [ref: [https://www.edgbaston.com/media-article/birmingham-phoenix-announce-coaching-staff-for-2026 Birmingham Phoenix announce coaching staff for 2026]. Edgbaston. 10 March 2026.]

In February 2025, Royals Sports Group appointed him head of international player development, with responsibilities for its academies and coaching across its overseas franchises. [ref: [https://www.rajasthanroyals.com/latest-news/siddhartha-lahiri-royals-head-of-international-player-development-appoint Royals Sports Group appoints Siddhartha Lahiri as Head of International Player Development]. Rajasthan Royals. 4 February 2025.]

== Early life and playing career ==
Lahiri trained under Gopal Bose in Kolkata and played as an opening batter in local cricket. His clubs included Dakshin Kalikata Sansad, Milan Samity, Anandabazar Sports Club and Customs, which competed in Cricket Association of Bengal tournaments. [ref: Shayan Acharya. [https://sportstar.thehindu.com/cricket/siddhartha-lahiri-interview-rajasthan-royals-ipl-royal-sports-group-paarl-sat20-star-cricket-academy/article69167362.ece From maidans of Kolkata to leading the ‘Royals way’ of coaching - the Siddhartha Lahiri story]. Sportstar. 1 February 2025.] [ref: [http://starcricketacademy.co.uk/about-us/ About – The Rajasthan Royals Academy]. Rajasthan Royals Academy Surrey. Undated. Accessed 21 October 2026.]

He moved to England in 2003 to gain coaching qualifications. He completed England and Wales Cricket Board Level 1 and Level 2 courses through Middlesex and later qualified at Level 3. [ref: Sandip Sarkar. [https://bengali.abplive.com/sports/ipl/abp-exclusive-know-about-siddhartha-lahiri-of-rajasthan-royals-plays-a-major-role-in-mustafizur-rahman-s-comeback-814163 ABP Exclusive: Know about Siddhartha Lahiri of Rajasthan Royals plays a major role in Mustafizur Rahman's comeback]. ABP Ananda. 11 May 2021. In Bengali.]

== Coaching career ==
In Surrey, Lahiri played for Stoke d’Abernon Cricket Club. At Parkside School in Cobham, he initially worked as a groundsman and later began coaching young cricketers.

Lahiri established a cricket academy at Parkside School in 2005. It later became known as Star Cricket Academy, moved to Reed’s School in September 2018 and partnered with Rajasthan Royals in February 2019.

The responsibilities announced with his appointment in 2025 covered academies in Jaipur, Surrey, Pune and New Jersey. They included developing player pathways and coordinating coaching across the Royals academy network.

In March 2026, Birmingham Phoenix named Lahiri one of three assistant coaches for its men’s team under head coach Shane Bond. The other assistants were James Foster and Graeme Welch.

National Herald reported that month that Lahiri had worked on developing Royals Hub, an online course for cricket coaches.

== Player development ==
Lahiri’s pupils included Ollie Pope, Ryan Patel and Amir Virdi. [ref: Barney Ronay. [https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2019/oct/01/rajasthan-royals-academy-ipl-cricket-future Rajasthan Royals’ English academy: a glimpse of cricket’s future?]. The Guardian. 1 October 2019.]

Sportstar reported that he had also worked with Phil Salt and Shoaib Bashir. Lahiri told the magazine that he worked with Riyan Parag when Parag joined Rajasthan Royals in 2019.

In 2025, Lahiri described clear communication and trust as important to coaching. He said his academy work included training plans, regular calls and masterclasses for coaches.

He also coached West Indies cricketer Justin Greaves. [ref: Sayak Banerjee. [https://www.telegraphindia.com/sports/cricket/justin-greaves-epic-test-turnaround-draws-praise-as-mindset-shift-fuels-west-indies-comeback-prnt/cid/2136705 Mentorship and mindset shift spark Justin Greaves’ rise after match-saving double hundred]. The Telegraph. 8 December 2025.]

Alec Stewart, a former England captain, praised Lahiri’s coaching and relationships with players in 2020. [ref: Sayak Banerjee. [https://www.telegraphindia.com/amp/sports/behala-boy-who-laid-pitch-for-pope/cid/1746111 Behala boy who laid pitch for Pope]. The Telegraph. 17 February 2020.]

== Personal life ==
In a 2021 interview with ABP Ananda, Lahiri said his wife had encouraged him to travel to England for coaching courses in 2003.

Draft text:
Regent International School is a private, co-educational British-curriculum school in The Greens, Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Operated by Fortes Education, the school provides education from Foundation Stage 1 through Year 13, serving children aged approximately 3 to 18. It follows the National Curriculum for England, leading to General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE), International General Certificate of Secondary Education (IGCSE) and A-level qualifications. [ref: Regent International Private School L.L.C, Knowledge and Human Development Authority] [ref: Regent International School, Get Information about Schools] [ref: IGCSE or GCSE – What is the Difference?, Regent International School]

The school was rated Very Good overall in its 2023–24 inspection by Dubai's Knowledge and Human Development Authority (KHDA). The UK Department for Education also lists a British Schools Overseas inspection report for the school dated 12 February 2026; Regent states that it received an Outstanding judgement under that framework. [ref: Regent International Private School L.L.C: Summary of Inspection Findings 2023–2024, Knowledge and Human Development Authority] [ref: British schools overseas: accredited schools inspection reports, UK Department for Education] [ref: Principal's Message, Regent International School]

== History ==

Regent International School was established in the early 1990s. The KHDA's current school directory and a 2015 British Schools Overseas inspection report give its opening year as 1992, although a 2016–17 KHDA report gives 1993. [ref: Regent International School, Dubai: British Schools Overseas inspection report, CfBT Education Trust] [ref: Regent International Private School: Inspection Report 2016–2017, Knowledge and Human Development Authority]

Regent was originally a school with both primary and secondary education. In 2016, the secondary division was relocated to the newly opened Sunmarke School, another Fortes Education institution. Regent subsequently offered a primary-focused programme, before expanding again into secondary education and Sixth Form provision. [ref: Sunmarke School: Value-for-money premium school, Gulf News] [ref: Making the move from Primary to Secondary? Here's how we do it!, Regent International School]

The school is led by principal David Williams, who previously held teaching and leadership roles at Regent, including Head of Lower School and Vice Principal. [ref: Mr. David Williams, Regent International School]

== Curriculum ==

Regent International School follows the English National Curriculum through its Foundation Stage, Primary, Secondary and Sixth Form phases.

=== Early Years Foundation Stage ===

The Early Years Foundation Stage (FS1 and FS2) serves children aged approximately three to five. Teaching follows the British EYFS framework and incorporates play-based learning, language development and opportunities for independent exploration. The school describes its early years provision as informed by the Curiosity Approach. [ref: Early Years Foundation Stage, Regent International School]

=== Primary education ===

Primary education covers Years 1 to 6, including Key Stage 1 (Years 1–2) and Key Stage 2 (Years 3–6). The curriculum includes English, mathematics and science, alongside humanities, creative subjects, computing and physical education. Regent also provides cross-curricular projects and extracurricular activities. [ref: Primary School, Regent International School]

=== Secondary education ===

Secondary schooling includes Key Stage 3 (Years 7–9) and Key Stage 4 (Years 10–11). Students study the National Curriculum for England and work towards GCSE or IGCSE examinations. Assessment during Key Stage 3 includes classroom testing and end-of-year examinations. [ref: How Is Progress Measured in Years 7 to 9? A Parent's Guide to Key Stage 3 Assessment, Regent International School]

=== Sixth Form ===

In Years 12 and 13, the school offers A-level courses as part of its post-16 British curriculum pathway. Its Sixth Form provision includes university and career guidance. [ref: Regent International School, Regent International School]

== Educational approach ==

=== Positive Education ===

Regent integrates Positive Education into its teaching and pastoral provision. The approach incorporates student wellbeing, resilience, character development and social and emotional learning alongside academic studies.

=== Technology and creative education ===

The school's programmes cover science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics (STEAM), including activities involving coding, robotics and design technology. It also offers opportunities in music, drama, media and performing arts. [ref: Our Campus, Regent International School] [ref: Free Extracurricular Activities, Regent International School]

=== Extracurricular activities ===

Regent runs sports, science, creative arts, language and enrichment clubs. Its published extracurricular programme includes football, basketball, netball, swimming, Model United Nations, debating, robotics, musical theatre, visual arts and the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award.

== Campus and facilities ==

Draft text:
The United States Boomerang Association (USBA) is an American nonprofit organization that promotes the science and sport of boomerang throwing. [ref: United States Boomerang Association Records, National Air and Space Museum Archives] It sanctions competitions in the United States, holds national championships, and organizes the national teams that represent the country at the World Boomerang Championships.

== History ==
Newspaper accounts give 1980 as the year the USBA was established. [ref: Boomerang, [[The Daily Herald (Everett)] [ref: Michael 'Gel' Girvin: boomerang master, Federal Way Mirror] The Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum describes it as a nonprofit organization incorporated in 1983 in Connecticut and Ohio. Its members voted to donate the organization's files to the museum through annual compilations of its records; the museum's archives hold USBA correspondence, by-laws, competition information and financial records dating from 1983 to 1987, received as a gift in 1987.

In 2001 the USBA gave a Lifetime Achievement Award to Michael "Gel" Girvin, a former member of the U.S. national team.

== Activities ==
The USBA has held national championships annually. Sports Illustrated published a photo feature on the 2014 U.S. National Boomerang Championships, held in Delaware, Ohio. [ref: U.S. National Boomerang Championships, Sports Illustrated] The 2019 championships were held in Boise, Idaho. Earlier championships were held in Delaware, Ohio, in 2009, [ref: National Boomerang Championships, Sports Illustrated Kids] and the 2023 championships took place at Lorain County Community College in Elyria, Ohio. [ref: What goes around comes around: Elyria's Kenny Barr leads defending champs as national boomerang championships return to LCCC, The Chronicle-Telegram] It was the third consecutive year the event was held there; the championships are open to all ages and include open, novice and women's divisions, with events in accuracy, trick catch, maximum time aloft, fast catch, endurance, Australian round and long distance. In its early years members received a quarterly newsletter, Many Happy Returns, and were ranked according to their performance in sanctioned competition; the association also kept files on boomerang manufacturers, materials and clubs. It sanctions local tournaments, such as the Bellingham Boomfest in Bellingham, Washington, first held in 2025. [ref: Boomerang sport grows with help from Western students, professor, Cascadia Daily News]

National team members are chosen at team trials. The 2026 U.S. Boomerang Team Trials were held in Arlington, Washington, selecting two teams and a developmental youth team for that year's world championships. [ref: Event Recap: 2026 US Boomerang Team Trials glide into Arlington, Snohomish County Sports Commission]

== International competition ==
U.S. teams have won the team title at the World Boomerang Championships in 1994, 2002, 2010 in Rome (regaining the Uncle Toby's Oats Cup from Germany), [ref: Local throwers headed to World Boomerang Championships, The Delaware Gazette] 2016 in Kiel, 2018 in Albuquerque [ref: Boomerang champ Logan Broadbent hopes the sport catches on in Cleveland, [[Ideastream Public Media], 2022 in France and 2026 in Bandung, Indonesia. [ref: WWU Boomerang Club, led by professor, places sixth at world championships, Cascadia Daily News]

The United States hosted the 2024 World Boomerang Championships at Westminster City Park in Westminster, Colorado. [ref: World Boomerang Championships make their way to Colorado, Denver7] It was the first time Colorado hosted the event, which drew about 80 throwers. [ref: Colorado hosts the Boomerang World Championships for the first time, Colorado Public Radio] At that event a U.S. team finished second to a team from Brazil. The U.S. also entered a national adult developmental team at the 2024 championships.

Caleb Landon is an American real estate investor and entrepreneur. He is the founder of Landon Capital Group, a firm that acquires and operates manufactured housing communities through investor syndications, and the president and co-founder of Lotly Software, a property management software company for mobile home parks. [ref: Why Mobile Home Parks Continue to Outperform with Caleb Landon] [ref: About Lotly, Lotly]

== Early life and education ==
Landon began taking classes at Jessup University in Rocklin, California, at age 11, and later graduated from the university. [ref: Featured Online Stories, Jessup Magazine]

== Career ==
After high school, Landon worked as an intern and analyst at a mobile home park syndication firm for about two years, underwriting acquisitions. [ref: How He Built 250 Mobile Home Park Units From a College Dorm, Investor Fuel] [ref: Efficient Mobile Home Park Syndications with Caleb Landon] He left in early 2023, while still in college, to start his own firm, Landon Capital Group. He raised just under $400,000 from friends, family and other investors for his first acquisition.

As of 2026, Landon Capital Group operated seven communities, three in Michigan, three in Iowa and one in Texas, totaling more than 250 home sites, with Landon as sole general partner. Its most recent acquisition at that time was a $2.8 million purchase funded in part by about $1.1 million raised from roughly 20 investors.

Landon is the president and co-founder of Lotly Software LLC, a company based in Rocklin, California, that develops property management software for mobile home parks, covering functions such as tenant screening, rent collection, maintenance requests and resident communication. At Lotly he leads product, engineering and Fair Credit Reporting Act compliance. Lotly Software also operates RentalApplication.ai, a pay-per-report tenant screening service for landlords and property managers, [ref: About, RentalApplication.ai] and MHPSales.ai, an AI voice agent that handles sales inquiries for manufactured homes by phone, text and email. [ref: MHPSales.ai, Lotly Software LLC] In an interview, Landon said the company's software products were developed using AI-assisted programming.

[ref: Electrolux names appliances veteran Fierling as new CEO, Reuters] [ref: Yannick Fierling, un Français nommé à la tête d'Electrolux, L'Usine Nouvelle]

Fierling holds two master's degrees in mechanical engineering from the Université de Technologie de Compiègne in France and Virginia Tech in the United States. [ref: European Commission - Brussels Economic Forum 2025 - Yannick Fierling, ec.europa.eu] He also holds a degree in finance for executives from INSEAD in France. Recepta.dk (stylised in lowercase as recepta) is a Danish online medical clinic operated by Recepta ApS, a private limited company based in Copenhagen. It provides consultations with licensed Danish doctors by video or telephone for medical weight loss, erectile dysfunction, low testosterone and male hair loss. When a doctor approves treatment, the prescription is sent electronically to a pharmacy of the patient's choice; the company does not sell medicines itself.

The clinic employs only doctors, and each patient is followed by the same doctor throughout treatment. It is registered as a treatment site under the supervision of the Danish Patient Safety Authority (Styrelsen for Patientsikkerhed).

== History ==
The arrival of GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide (Wegovy) as prescription treatments for obesity led a number of clinics in Denmark to offer consultations and prescriptions over the internet. In 2024 the consumer programme Kontant on DR showed a reporter of normal weight obtaining a Wegovy prescription from one such clinic after a short telephone call, having given a false weight. Shortly afterwards the Danish Patient Safety Authority tightened its requirements, so that online clinics must see the patient by video before prescribing Wegovy.

Recepta ApS was registered in the Danish Central Business Register in 2026 under industry code 862100, general medical practice activities. The clinic opened the same year, initially offering medical weight loss and treatment of erectile dysfunction, and during 2026 added assessment of low testosterone, treatment of male hair loss and an English-language version of the service for English-speaking residents of Denmark. A Swedish-language site, recepta.se, registers interest ahead of a planned launch in Sweden.

== Services ==
Consultations for weight loss take place by video and those for erectile dysfunction by telephone. Patients choose the time of the consultation, including evenings and weekends, and the company states that most patients can start within 24 hours on weekdays. Prescriptions are sent electronically to the pharmacy chosen by the patient, and the medicine is bought there at the pharmacy's price.

* Medical weight loss: video consultation with a view to treatment with GLP-1-based medicines such as semaglutide and tirzepatide, following the Danish criteria of a body mass index over 30, or over 27 with a weight-related condition.
* Erectile dysfunction: telephone consultation with a view to treatment with sildenafil or tadalafil.
* Low testosterone: doctor-led assessment with blood tests taken at a hospital laboratory, initially for patients in the Capital Region and Central Denmark Region.
* Hair loss: treatment of male pattern hair loss with finasteride.

Payment is by a membership billed every four weeks, which covers the consultation, the prescription, renewals, dose adjustments and written follow-up. The doctor's consultation itself is free of charge, and patients are charged only once a doctor has approved treatment; the medicine is bought separately at the pharmacy.

== Regulation and patient data ==
The clinic is a registered treatment site (behandlingssted) supervised by the Danish Patient Safety Authority and states that it keeps patient records under the same rules as a general practice. Patient data are stored within the EU in accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation, and the clinic's doctors are bound by professional confidentiality.

EMU Express (legal name Express Mail Universal LLC; ) is a private courier, express mail and logistics company headquartered in Tashkent, Uzbekistan. Founded in 2016, it provides domestic and international parcel delivery, cargo transport and fulfillment services for individuals and businesses, including online retailers. As of 2026 the company reported more than 200 branches and service points in Uzbekistan, a fleet of over 250 vehicles and more than 500 employees, as well as a branch network in Kazakhstan.

== History ==

=== Founding ===
EMU Express was founded by Murod Jumaev, who had studied postal communication technologies at the Tashkent University of Information Technologies and from 2008 worked at the Bukhara branch of the national postal operator Oʻzbekiston pochtasi. The idea for the company originated in 2016 as a business-planning project developed by a group of six students during Jumaev's master's studies at the Higher School of Business and Entrepreneurship () in Tashkent; the company was established on 7 November 2016. In its early years the company marketed itself as EMU (ekspress pochta) ("EMU express mail") and used the emu bird as its emblem.

=== Early growth (2017–2020) ===
In 2017 the company offered delivery of documents and parcels within Uzbekistan with a stated delivery time of 24 hours between Tashkent and regional centres. By that year it had offices in regional centres including Andijan, Bukhara, Navoiy, Samarkand, Qarshi, Termez, Nukus, Urgench, Fergana, Namangan, Jizzakh and Gulistan. In January 2018 the company's head office was located in the Yakkasaray district of Tashkent, and its regional network also included Kokand.

By March 2020 the company reported more than 150 employees and a fleet of 30 vehicles, and described itself as a licensed courier operator serving both individuals and businesses, including online shops. In mid-2020 it offered discounted rates for e-commerce businesses depending on shipment volume.

=== Expansion (2021–present) ===
In 2026 the company marked its tenth anniversary. By that year it reported more than 200 branches and service points across Uzbekistan, more than 250 vehicles and over 500 employees, and a network of offices in Kazakhstan, its first market outside Uzbekistan. The same year it launched a mobile application for ordering courier pickups.

== Operations ==
EMU Express operates a network of branches and pickup/delivery points across all regions of Uzbekistan, including the Republic of Karakalpakstan. The company's registered office is at 35/1 Shota Rustaveli Street in the Yakkasaray district of Tashkent.

According to the company, shipments are processed through an automated system in which each parcel is scanned at every stage, allowing customers to track shipments online in real time; customers receive SMS notifications on the status of their shipments. The company offers a mobile application for iOS and Android. Some branches are equipped with fitting rooms for customers of online clothing retailers.

=== Kazakhstan ===

Kazakhstan is the company's first market outside Uzbekistan. By 2026 it had opened offices in 17 regions of the country and in three major cities, including Almaty and Astana.

== Services ==
The company's services include:
* express mail and courier delivery within Uzbekistan;
* international mail and courier delivery;
* door-to-door delivery;
* cargo transport and consolidation;
* e-commerce logistics for online stores and marketplaces;
* fulfillment and warehousing;
* B2B and B2C logistics.

== Management ==
As of 2026, the company is headed by its director and founder Murod Jumaev. Jumaev has commented publicly on business regulation in Uzbekistan; in April 2018, during discussion of a proposed 25% tax on dividends, he criticised the measure as a blow to entrepreneurs. He has also published conference papers on youth employment in the digital economy and on regional innovation policy.

== Certification ==
Since November 2021 the company's quality management system has been certified to ISO 9001:2015 for the scope "courier deliveries and truckings" (certificate no. GIUZ-1031-QC, initial certification 10 November 2021; current certificate issued 2 December 2025 and valid until 9 November 2027, subject to annual surveillance). The certificate was issued by G-CERTI, a Seoul-based certification body accredited by the International Accreditation Service.

Draft text:
Asif Hasan (born ) is a retired British cardiothoracic surgeon who specialised in congenital heart surgery and paediatric heart and lung transplantation at the Freeman Hospital in Newcastle upon Tyne. He joined the hospital in 1991, was appointed a consultant in 1995, and went on to lead its paediatric cardiac surgery and paediatric transplant services and to direct its cardiopulmonary transplant programme, retiring in 2026. Over his career he performed more than 4,000 open-heart operations, around 3,000 of them as lead surgeon, and estimates that he carried out approximately 400 transplants.

In October 2026 he received the Lifetime Achievement Award at the Pride of Britain Awards.

== Early life and education ==
Hasan graduated in medicine (MBBS) from Dow Medical College in Karachi in 1979. He moved to the United Kingdom from Pakistan in 1981, and obtained the Fellowship of the Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh (FRCSEd) in 1984 and the intercollegiate specialty fellowship in cardiothoracic surgery, FRCS (C/Th), in 1994. Before joining the transplant team in Newcastle he had trained in surgery for congenital heart disease.

== Career ==

=== Freeman Hospital ===
Hasan joined the Freeman Hospital in 1991 as a surgeon in cardiopulmonary transplantation, and was appointed a consultant cardiothoracic surgeon there in 1995. He has described the combination of congenital heart surgery and transplantation in one post as an unusual opportunity, and has said that Newcastle became the largest centre in Europe for transplantation in patients with congenital heart disease. The Freeman is one of only two centres in the UK performing heart and lung transplants in children.

He led the hospital's paediatric transplant programme, and by 2018 was described as director of the Freeman's cardiac and pulmonary transplant programme, having succeeded John Dark, who retired in 2017. In that role he was quoted in 2017 on the 30th anniversary of the hospital's paediatric heart and lung transplant programme, which by then had performed 308 paediatric transplants. He and Dark were guest editors of a 2018 issue of the Annals of Cardiothoracic Surgery devoted to transplantation and mechanical circulatory support.

Hasan co-led Newcastle's "bridge to transplant" programme, which uses the Berlin Heart, a paracorporeal ventricular assist device, to keep infants and children alive while they wait for a donor heart. He was also involved in the Freeman's early experience of ABO-incompatible heart transplantation in infants, published in 2004. Hospital colleagues and patients' families have described his willingness to operate on very high-risk children, including patients whom other cardiac centres had declined.

Among his patients was Max Johnson, whose heart transplant at the Freeman in 2017 was filmed for the BBC Two documentary Heart Transplant: A Chance to Live (2018). Johnson and his donor, Keira Ball, gave their names to "Max and Keira's Law", the Organ Donation (Deemed Consent) Act 2019, which introduced an opt-out system of organ donation in England.

Hasan retired from clinical practice in 2026, at the age of 70. Sources give his length of service at the Freeman variously as 30, 35 and 36 years, reflecting the difference between his time as head of the paediatric service and his total time at the hospital since 1991.

=== Surgical technique ===
With Mohamed Nassar and Bari Murtuza, Hasan described a "bootlace" technique for gradual delayed sternal closure after paediatric cardiac surgery, published in the World Journal for Pediatric and Congenital Heart Surgery in 2017. The method is intended for cases in which closing the chest in one step is difficult, particularly after transplantation with a donor heart that is large relative to the recipient; it allows some children to receive donor hearts that would otherwise be too big for them.

=== International work and teaching ===
Hasan has been involved in setting up paediatric cardiac surgery units and supporting surgeons in several countries, and has written about the successes and failures of developing such services in Pakistan. For many years he used his annual leave to travel to Pakistan, where he operated on children and trained local surgical teams on a voluntary basis. Newcastle Hospitals has said he contributed to charity surgical camps overseas and helped train surgeons abroad, and that surgeons he trained now work as consultants around the world. He has been listed as faculty by the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery, which describes his current interest as teaching and mentoring congenital heart surgeons internationally.

== In the media ==
Hasan's work featured in the BBC Two documentary Heart Transplant: A Chance to Live (2018), filmed at the Freeman Hospital's Institute of Transplantation. In 2023 he appeared in the second series of the Channel 4 documentary series Geordie Hospital, in an episode first broadcast on 13 September 2023 that followed him replacing a heart valve in 13-year-old Seb Hollingsworth, on whom he had first operated as an infant.

Jaijit Bhattacharya is an Indian technology policy researcher, author and entrepreneur. He was recognized by MIT Sloan Management Review India in its Policy 50 list, Which highlights 50 influential leaders, thinkers and policymakers shaping India digital economy and technology policy. He is the president of the [https://c-dep.org Centre for Digital Economy Policy Research] and has previously held positions at the World Economic Forum and KPMG. [ref: Jaijit Bhattacharya, MIT Sloan Management Review Middle East] His work has focused on technology, governance, digital transformation and technology policy, including the coining of the terms "Digital Colonization" and "Technological Sovereignty". [ref: ICANN announces digital policy expert Jaijit Bhattacharya as ccNSO Council member, ETGovernment]

== Career ==

Bhattacharya is the president of the [https://c-dep.org Centre for Digital Economy Policy Research]. He has worked in technology, consulting and public policy. He served as a partner in the Economics and Policy Practice at KPMG India.

During his tenure at KPMG, Bhattacharya worked on infrastructure, government services, regulatory policy and urban development. [ref: Why smart cities need smarter urban governance model, Business Standard] He later headed the Centre for the Fourth Industrial Revolution in India at the World Economic Forum.
[ref: ICANN announces Dr. Jaijit Bhattacharya, President C-DEP.org as ccNSO Council member, PTI]

In 2015, the Government of India established an expert committee to examine ways to reduce the number of regulatory permissions required by businesses. Bhattacharya, then a partner at KPMG, was appointed as a member of the committee. [ref: Government sets up panel to reduce permissions for investors, The Economic Times]

In 2024, he became a member of the Country Code Names Supporting Organization (ccNSO) Council of the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN). ICANN lists his term as running from March 2024 to October 2027 and identifies his areas of expertise as technology policy, multilateral negotiations and artificial-intelligence frameworks. [ref: Council Members, Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers]

The committee considered replacing multiple prior approvals with a simplified regulatory process. Bhattacharya supported simplifying business regulations and removing redundant legislation. [ref: India Inc petitions govt: From land laws to levy, ease it all, The Indian Express]

Bhattacharya also participated in policy discussions on smart cities and infrastructure. During his time at KPMG, he publicly discussed governance and institutional issues related to India's smart-cities programme.

In 2026, Bhattacharya advocated greater international cooperation between India and other governments in addressing cybersecurity threats. [ref: India needs to collaborate with other governments on cyber threats: C-DEP President, Asian News International]

== Academic and research ==

Bhattacharya received a Bachelor of Technology degree in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur and an MBA from the Indian Institute of Management Calcutta. He later received a PhD in computer science and engineering from the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi.

Bhattacharya has also conducted training at the Asian Development Bank Institute in Tokyo on public expenditure management. [ref: Jaijit Bhattacharya, Finnacle Capital Advisors]

In 2013, Bhattacharya co-authored a paper published in "PLOS Medicine" examining the use of rapidly deployable eHealth centres for healthcare delivery and data collection in rural India. [ref: Integrating Health Care Delivery and Data Collection in Rural India Using a Rapidly Deployable eHealth Center, PLOS Medicine]

Bhattacharya's work has addressed the concepts of "Digital Colonization" and "Technological Sovereignty". MIT Sloan Management Review Middle East credits him with coining both terms. ETGovernment has also credited him with coining the terminology.

In 2010, Bhattacharya published Technology Standards: A Route to Digital Colonization in the IETE Journal of Education. The paper examined the relationship between information and communications technology standards, public policy and dependence on particular technologies. [ref: Technology Standards: A Route to Digital Colonization, IETE Journal of Education]

His subsequent policy work and commentary have continued to address technological sovereignty and questions concerning domestic technological capabilities, technology standards and dependence on foreign technologies.

Bhattacharya has written books and academic and policy articles concerning e-governance and technology policy.

His books include e-Gov 2.0: Policies, Processes and Technologies, published by McGraw Hill Education in 2010. [ref: e-Gov 2.0: Policies, Processes and Technologies, McGraw Hill Education]

Bhattacharya's research publications include Technology Standards: A Route to Digital Colonization in the IETE Journal of Education and the co-authored Integrating Health Care Delivery and Data Collection in Rural India Using a Rapidly Deployable eHealth Center in PLOS Medicine.

== Awards and recognition ==

Bhattacharya has received the APJ Abdul Kalam Award for Innovation in Governance.

He has also received the Global Corporate Affairs Leadership Award for a decade of contribution. [ref: Corporate Affairs Leadership Award, World CSR Congress]

Michael Mansouri is an American technologist, entrepreneur, and cinematography technician. He co-founded the digital cinema and custom engineering company Radiant Images alongside his wife and business partner, Gianna Wolfe. Currently serving as CEO of the cloud collaboration platform MeetMo.io, his work focuses on digital cinematography, virtual reality (VR), volumetric capture, and live 360-degree broadcast technology.

== Early and Personal Life ==
Born in Tehran, Iran, to filmmaker parents, he and his older brother, Babak, worked as child actors prior to the revolution. They starred in their mother's educational television programs, Halghe Jado and Vajhe O Bazi, for Iran's National Television Station in the 1970s. [ref: Cooking for Hollywood, a documentary about Tony Kerum at Kino Croatia, Los Angeles, Cinema Without Borders] The family emigrated to the United States in 1977, settling in the Los Angeles area. His father later passed away in 2015. [ref: Camera Maker Has New Takes on Action Scenes, Los Angeles Business Journal]

== Career and Technology Innovation ==
Early in his career, he worked in technology startups across Silicon Valley and Japan before transitioning to the entertainment industry under the mentorship of American Society of Cinematographers (ASC) member Bob Primes. [ref: Management - Maya Global Solutions, Maya Global Solutions] [ref: Revolutionary Approach to Rogue Filmmaking in Cuba with Piel, The American Society of Cinematographers]

Establishing Radiant Images to provide digital cinema equipment and custom lens modifications, the company gained early industry recognition by supplying custom rigs utilizing the SI-2K digital camera for Danny Boyle's Academy Award-nominated film 127 Hours (2010). [ref: Cameras Used In The End Of Watch Movie, Cinescopophilia] His brother, Babak, joined as an inventor to help develop custom modifications for major studio films. For example, during the production of David Ayer's 2012 film End of Watch, Babak designed the SI-2K Nano, a palm-sized 2K uncompressed RAW camera system built specifically so actors Jake Gyllenhaal and Michael Peña could wear them on their chests for POV shots without restricting movement. [ref: Cameras Used In The End Of Watch Movie, Cinescopophilia] [ref: Cooking for Hollywood, a documentary about Tony Kerum at Kino Croatia, Los Angeles, Cinema Without Borders] The brothers also developed the NOVO, a cinema-modified GoPro capable of utilizing interchangeable professional C-mount lenses. [ref: Cooking for Hollywood, a documentary about Tony Kerum at Kino Croatia, Los Angeles, Cinema Without Borders]

=== Immersive Media and Volumetric Capture ===
Expanding into immersive media formats, the team explored virtual reality, augmented reality, and 360-degree camera arrays. [ref: Going 360 With Radiant Images, The American Society of Cinematographers] This led to the development of the AXA immersive capture system, a modular, hexagon-shaped rig built to accommodate various digital cinema cameras for spherical image capture, earning US Patent 10,860,296. [ref: Radiant Images issued patent on immersive capture system for holographic imaging, Auganix] While acting as a principal for Hawkeye Systems in 2019, the AXA Volumetric Light Field Stage was recognized with a Lumiere Award by the Advanced Imaging Society for Best Holographic Video Technology. [ref: Hawkeye Systems Subsidiary Honoree of the Prestigious Lumiere Award for Best Holographic Video Technology, Hawkeye Systems]

=== Broadcast and Cloud Technology ===
Shifting toward cloud-based real-time video collaboration, the MeetMo.io platform was launched with Gianna Wolfe serving as Vice President. [ref: AI and Software-Defined Infrastructure for Live Media, NVIDIA] [ref: NASA's Artemis Marks First-Ever 8K Immersive Live Broadcast, MeetMo.io] Interactive broadcasting efforts have led to major institutional partnerships, including providing the immersive technical infrastructure for a 2018 NASA and JPL VR project that won an Emmy Award for Outstanding Original Interactive Program. [ref: Reimagining Cinema with Radiant Images' Michael Mansouri - XR, XR for Business]

During the 2022 Artemis 1 launch, MeetMo.io and Felix & Paul Studios delivered an 8K ultra-high-resolution 360° live VR broadcast of the event, streamed globally to Meta Horizon Worlds venues and physical planetarium domes. [ref: NASA's Artemis Marks First-Ever 8K Immersive Live Broadcast, MeetMo.io] A subsequent 2025 partnership with T-Mobile at the Las Vegas Grand Prix integrated augmented reality (AR) overlays over live Formula 1 racing, securing another Lumiere Award for Best Interactive Experience. [ref: T-Mobile, MeetMo, and NantStudios Win Prestigious 2025 Lumiere Award, StockTitan] Additionally, he co-founded Maya Global Solutions in 2019 to focus on network optimization for enterprise video conferencing, where he currently serves as Chairman. [ref: Management - Maya Global Solutions, Maya Global Solutions]

The company provides production services for international broadcasters, streaming platforms, corporations, and news organizations filming in Israel, the Palestinian territories, and across the Middle East. It is one of the longest-operating production services companies in Israel.

In 2009, Highlight Films produced Jerusalem 3D, an IMAX documentary film, described as one of the first IMAX productions made in Israel. [ref: Jerusalem The Movie — Production Notes]

==Services==

Highlight Films provides production services for visiting international crews and for remote productions. Services include camera crews, equipment rental (including 4K and HD cameras, aerial drone rigs, IMAX, VR 360, and 3D), producer and fixer services, research, logistics, location scouting, security coordination, film permits, post-production, uplink and satellite feed services, and remote production including live video and audio feeds.
The company maintains a stock footage library and also operates the filminisrael.com resource for international production information.

[ref: Kattalan OTT Release Date: When and Where to Watch This Antony Varghese and Sunil Starrer, Esquire India]

=== Live performances ===
Shaah performs at live concerts and stage programmes in Kerala and abroad, including in the United Arab Emirates. [ref: Kerala street singer Anish Bhai performs with Braille lyrics, takes stages and social media by storm, Onmanorama] In 2026 he shared the stage with Anish, a blind street singer whose videos had gone viral, at a shop inauguration in Perinthalmanna; the appearance brought wider recognition to Anish's troupe, Malabar Blind Voice.

==== 2025 Kasaragod concert incident ====
On 23 November 2025, a concert featuring Shaah, held as part of an expo at a ground near the private bus stand in Kasaragod, was stopped by police after severe overcrowding. [ref: Hanan Shaah's concert stopped in Kasaragod after overcrowding triggers chaos, Deccan Herald] A stampede-like rush led to several attendees fainting or suffering breathing difficulties; reports of the number hospitalised or injured ranged from around 16 to over 30, and no deaths were reported. [ref: Overcrowding at Hanan Shaah concert sends 16 to hospital; organisers booked, Madhyamam] [ref: Stampede-like crowd surge injures 20 at Kasaragod concert, The South First] [ref: Five booked after music concert rush leaves several injured in Kasaragod, Onmanorama] Police registered a case against the event's organisers; according to the FIR, police had permitted an audience of 3,000, but the organisers allegedly sold tickets to more than 10,000 people despite a written warning.

Draft text:
Dan Priddy is a songwriter, record producer and multi-instrumentalist based in London. He has worked with Rag'n'Bone Man, Bastille, Mika, James Arthur and Louis Tomlinson, frequently collaborating with producer Mark Crew. [ref: Abbey Road Amplify: The Craft of Hitmaking, Abbey Road] [ref: FM Premiere: Dan Priddy's Dopamine, Fame Magazine] He co-founded Best Laid Plans Records with Crew and Bastille singer Dan Smith. [ref: 'We're open to anything': Bastille's Dan Smith on his Best Laid Plans label, Music Week] His songwriting and production credits also include recordings by Shania Twain and Ashnikko. [ref: Queen of Me — Shania Twain: credits, Qobuz] [ref: Deal With It (feat. Kelis) by Ashnikko — Credits, Muso.AI]

== Career ==

=== Early work ===
Priddy began playing piano and singing at the age of six, later learning drums, bass and guitar. He initially worked with his brother Reuben under the name Mannequin, developing songs and production with J. R. Rotem and Zach Katz. He focused on songwriting and production while at university, where he met Crew.

=== Best Laid Plans and Rag'n'Bone Man ===
Priddy, Crew and Smith established Best Laid Plans Records to develop and release music by artists they knew. The label released Rag'n'Bone Man's Wolves and Disfigured, followed by his 2017 album Human in partnership with Columbia Records. Other artists associated with the label included Rationale, Kianja, the Dawn of May and Akine.

Priddy worked with Crew on the development of Rag'n'Bone Man's early recordings. According to Abbey Road's profile, he contributed to ten songs on Human and four songs on the 2021 album Life by Misadventure. He co-wrote "Anywhere Away from Here", a duet by Rag'n'Bone Man and Pink. [ref: Anywhere Away from Here (Rag'n'Bone Man & P!nk) — Credits, Muso.AI]

His later work with Rag'n'Bone Man included co-writing and co-producing "Rush of Blood", "Feeding All These Fires" and "Put a Little Hurt on Me" for the 2024 album What Do You Believe In?. [ref: What Do You Believe In? — Rag'n'Bone Man: credits, Qobuz]

=== Bastille and other collaborations ===
Priddy became a regular songwriting and production collaborator of Bastille alongside Crew. [ref: Bastille's Dan Smith On Technological Mania & The "Totally Bizarre" Timing Of Their New Album, 'Give Me The Future', Grammy.com] His production work includes "Doom Days" and "Another Place" from the band's 2019 album Doom Days. [ref: Dan Priddy, Eaves Music Group] On Give Me the Future (2022), he co-produced "Thelma + Louise", "No Bad Days" and "Stay Awake?", and co-wrote "No Bad Days". [ref: Give Me the Future — Bastille: credits, Qobuz]

In 2019, Priddy worked with Crew on Mika's My Name Is Michael Holbrook. Reviewing the album for PopMatters, Brice Ezell discussed their production of "Platform Ballerinas" and "Tomorrow", praising the clarity of the arrangements while finding parts of the album's production overly polished. [ref: Mika Delivers Undeniably Catchy Hooks on 'My Name Is Michael Holbrook', PopMatters]

Priddy co-wrote and co-produced "Brand New" and "Best Friend" on Shania Twain's 2023 album Queen of Me. He also worked with Birdy on Portraits, which she described as a project made with a small group of collaborators including Priddy and Crew. [ref: Birdy — Interview, Bedroomdisco] His production credits include Lovejoy's 2023 single "Call Me What You Like". [ref: Call Me What You Like by Lovejoy — Credits, Muso.AI]

In 2025, Priddy was credited as a producer on Maddie Zahm's "Sheets" and Tom Grennan's "Somewhere Only We Go". His contributions to the latter also included drums, guitar, keyboards and programming. [ref: Sheets — Maddie Zahm: credits, AllMusic] [ref: Somewhere Only We Go — Tom Grennan: credits, Qobuz]

=== Solo recordings ===
Priddy previously released music under the name Braque, including the EP V1CES. [ref: Surfacing: Dan Priddy's Demonstrates His Pop Chops On Debut Single 'Dopamine', Faded Glamour] In June 2019, he released "Dopamine" under his own name. Fame Magazine reported that he wrote, produced, mixed and mastered the recording himself. He released the single "liar" on 19 June 2026 through Enzino Records. [ref: liar — Dan Priddy, Amazon Music]

Draft: Xerocomellus atropurpureus

Draft text:
Xerocomellus atropurpureus is a mushroom in the family Boletaceae found along the west coast of North America. Its conservation status is listed as Least Concern according to the IUCN Fungal Redlist.
==Taxonomy==
X. atropurpureus is one of several species within the Xerocomellus genus that were previously considered to be the single species Boletus zelleri. Field studies as well as genetic evidence compiled by J.L. Frank, N. Siegel & C.F. Schwarz between 2016 and 2020 supported the move of many former Boletus species into related various genera and split zelleri into a number of highly similar species.

==Description==
Cap: 4-11 cm; convex to flat; dark brown to near black, often with reddish-purple tones; texture smooth to bumpy or velvety, not developing extensive cracking with age; white bloom sometimes present on young specimens.

Stipe: 4-12 cm; equal or slightly enlarged at base; mostly red, but may be yellow with red striations; may stain blue unpredictably when cut or bruised.

Pore surface: Yellow when young fading to olive-yellow with age; rarely staining blue slowly when bruised.

Spores: Spore print olive brown. Under microscope spores are 11-15 x 4-6 µm and fusiform.

==Habitat and distribution==
Distributed throughout the Pacific Northwest region of the United States and Canada from British Columbia through Northern California, amongst the Cascade and coastal ranges. Mycorrhizal with various conifer species, including but not limited to Douglas fir, Monterey pine, bishop pine, western hemlock, Sitka spruce, and coast redwood. X atropurpureus primarily grows on the ground but may occasionally be found on well-rotted wood.

==Similar species==
X. zelleri - the type species of the genus, X. zelleri is less common than previously believed, and the most likely to be confused for X. atropurpureus. X. zelleri is best differentiated by the cap which is smooth, not bumpy or velvety, and trends medium brown to olive toned rather than reddish-purple, with a distinctive light band at the edge. It is less substantial with a narrower stipe and shows a stronger affinity for growing on wood.

X. diffractus is another of the more common Xerocomellus species on the west coast. It can be easily differentiated by the namesake "cracked cap", which is a lighter olive-brown and develops extensive cracks across the surface with age, often with pink shading. The stipe is primarily yellow with red striations limited to the lower half.

X. mendocinensis, X. rainisiae, and X. amylosporus are all highly similar to X. diffractus in overall appearance and difficult to tell from each other, but may be differentiated from other Xerocomellus species by their aggressive blue staining on both stipe and pore surface when cut or bruised.

The date range for these opinion polls are from the 2026 Russian legislative election, held on 18–20 September, until the time next election will be held.

== Biography ==
Laimonas Vilčinskas is a Lithuanian digital content creator, influencer. He is best known as the founder, owner, and creative director of the global TikTok humor and meme channel [https://www.tiktok.com/@[user] @[user]]. As of 2026, Laimonas has accumulated a multi-million audience of over 1.1 million followers and more than 32.2 million likes on the platform. [ref: https://ecommercefastlane.com/how-tiktok-creators-get-paid-outside-the-us-laimonas-vilcinskas/]

== Career and Brand Collaborations ==
Operating from Lithuania, a market outside of TikTok's Creator Rewards Program, Laimonas sustains his digital media enterprise, Laimonas Vilčinskas Media, through direct commercial partnerships and brand integrations. Because creators in non-monetized European markets receive zero direct platform payouts regardless of viral traffic, direct brand integrations constitute the entirety of his channel's income.

As an influencer and content creator at this scale, he has executed high-profile advertising campaigns for global retail platforms like Temu and artificial intelligence (AI) video generation companies, including Kling AI and Hailuo AI. [ref: https://tynmagazine.com/laimonas-vilcinskas-on-viral-videos-ai-and-humour-in-advertising/] He has also collaborated with international entertainment brands such as Nickelodeon.

Beyond his career as a social media creator, Laimonas works on film sets and is active in electronic music production. He is pursuing higher education in digital marketing and communication at Mykolas Romeris University in Vilnius. Laimonas Vilčinskas has also been cited in European media as an expert commentator on cybersecurity and online safety, specifically regarding digital scams and phishing operations targeting creators. [ref: https://www.dziennikwschodni.pl/artykul/393375,tworcy-internetowi-na-celowniku-oszustow-jak-rozpoznac-falszywe-oferty-i-phishing]

Stars College () is a private school network in Lebanon with four campuses, in Tyre (Abbasiyeh), Zebdine in the Nabatieh Governorate, Ghaziyeh near Sidon, and Dibbiyeh in the Chouf.
