Draft text:
The place Akkarapadam is part of Vaikom taluk in Vadakkemuri Village of Kottayam district. It comes under the Udayanapuram Grama Panchayath. For administrative purpose Vaikom Taluk is divided into sixteen villages, and Vadakkemuri is one among them. Vaikom is situated in the north west of Kottayam district in the state of Kerala. Vaikom gained its fame on a national level during Vaikom Satyagraha, a civil right movement aimed at securing freedom of movement for lower caste people (untouchables) through the public roads leading to Vaikom temple.

Vaikom is believed to be a part of kingdom called Venmalanadu in the past. When Venmalanadu was split into Vadakkumkoor and Thekkumkoor Vaikom became part of Vadakkumkoor dynasty. Later when the Maharaja of Travancore, Anizham Thirunal Marthanda Varma annexed Vadakkumkoor to his kingdom in 1742, Vaikom became part of Travancore.

=== History ===

It is very difficult to trace out the root or the origin of the family in the absence of authentic depositions. As per available information passed on by ancestors, it is believed that sometime during 16th century AD, a small Christian family with their only son, from the eastern part of the present Ernakulam District called Kothamangalam came and settled down at South Paravoor (Thekkan Paravoor). Who were they, what were they and the reason which forced them to leave Kothamangalam were not exactly known. Thus they reached South Paravoor, a distant Christian belt under the Travancore dynasty, where the church desired an able leadership for their laity who was mostly ordinary people. The family who came from Kothamangalam, having an impeccable charisma were welcomed at South Paravoor with a warm heart and they got the same prominence as at Kothamangalam. This period was very crucial for the Christian Community in Kerala (Malankara or Malabar Christians). Following the oath of the “Coonen Kuriz” of 1653, the single church of pre-Portuguese days had lost its unity in a threefold way. Two groups of the Malabar Christians continued functioning in allegiance with Rome (one in alliance with the Portuguese and the other directly under Rome, guided by missionaries of the Society for the propagation of the faith). A third body sought to keep its independent existence without any devotion to Rome. They soon realized that the validity of its ministerial succession could be questioned and needed rectification with the assistance of a Church from outside. With this aim in mind the leaders approached several Eastern Churches with an appeal for assistance. The Antiochene Syrian Church responded by sending metropolitan Mar Gregorios of Jerusalem in 1665, without insisting any pre condition for cooperation. The Indian Church received him with open arms. Those who accepted the East Syrian theological and liturgical tradition of Mar Gregorios were later known as Jacobites and those who continued with West Syrian theological and liturgical tradition and stayed faithful to the Synod of Diamper are known as Syro-Malabar Catholic Church. Thus, 72 out of 116 churches were claimed by Catholics, 32 by others and 12 being shared. This vertical split of the Christian community had its effect in South Paravoor too and the family which came from Kothamangalam stood strongly with the fraction associated with Antiochene Syrian Church. Consequently a new church was built on the eastern side of the main road opposite to the old church (present Catholic Church) for which the family had a pivotal role. This is the old Jacobite Church at South Paravoor. The family from Kothamangalam became stronger in the church and the community. This is evident from the fact that the family held 2 of the 7 keys of the church strong room (mempootu) of the church. [ref: From archives and information passed down from generation to generation]

It was during this period the young man from this family, believed to be one Mathulla, who had three brothers and a sister moved around in search of some fertile land suitable for agriculture, because Christians in general were engaged in agriculture and or trade during those days. At that time South Paravoor was not an ideal place for agriculture. He reached a remote village in the western banks of river Ithipuzha (branch of Muvattupuzha River) where there was vast area of wet and marshy land ideal for cultivation. He acquired lot of property; say almost half of the village along with plenty of servants and slaves. There he had built a palatial house, nearly four centuries ago, at an elevated portion of the land (“chira”) on the riverbank which stood as a testimony to the wealth of the family. Since the house was built on a “chira” the family got the name “Chirayil”. Brothers of Mathulla continued to stay at South Paravoor itself in separate properties namely Parakkattu, Koluthakottil and Kanjirakkattu after giving their ancestral house to their only sister. It is believed that “Chirayil Tharavad" about was the first permanent house in the village made of stone about 400 years ago.This fact aligns perfectly with the socio economic evolution of the Vaikom region. During that era the construction of a permanent tiled or stone structure rather than a thatched house was a major status symbol. It required special permission from the local rulers or the Kingdom of Travancore and indicated immense land-owning prominence. = Giuseppe Ambrosio =
Giuseppe Ambrosio is an international accountant and auditor based in Monaco, where he is licensed as Tax advisor and Tax representative. Ambrosio is the founder of Ambrosio Audit, an audit and professional services organization that includes Ambrosio Audit LLP and Ambrosio Audit STP SRL as its operating entities. He is the Fellow Chartered Accountant of the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales (ICAEW), the institute’s Contact Member for Monaco and the Honorary Consul of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines in Monaco. [ref: Monaco's contact member, www.icaew.com] [ref: AmbrosioAudit] [ref: [https://ambprincipatomonaco.esteri.it/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Elenco-Commercialisti.pdf Elenco-Commercialisti.pdf]]

=== Career ===
Ambrosio qualified as an Italian chartered accountant and statutory auditor in 2000. He worked for Price Waterhouse, then PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) after his recruitment as a financial-services auditor. In an interview with Monaco Life in 2017, he described his professional background, including the secondment to the United Kingdom and later a position in Madrid before his move to Monaco. [ref: Match Point with Giuseppe Ambrosio, President Monaco Family Office Association, Monaco Life] Ambrosio is a Fellow Chartered Accountant of ICAEW and holds a Practice Certificate and Audit Qualification. The Arab Cycling Federation (ACF) is an Arab federation concerned with the sport of cycling. It was founded in 1975 by a group of national Arab cycling federations and operates under the umbrella of the Union of Arab National Olympic Committees. Its headquarters was originally in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, before moving to Cairo, Egypt, then to Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and finally to Sharjah. [ref: الشهراني نائباً أول لرئيس الاتحاد العربي للدراجات, Okaz] In July 2018 the Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI) officially recognized the federation's championships and races.

== Members ==
* Iraq – 1976
* United Arab Emirates – 1975
* Saudi Arabia – 1975
* Syria – 1975
* Jordan – 1982
* Palestine – 1983
* Bahrain – 1983
* Kuwait – 1977
* Qatar – 2002
* Lebanon – 1977
* Yemen – 1988
* Oman – 1987
* Egypt – 1975
* Somalia – accession pending
* Libya – 1975
* Algeria – 1975
* Morocco – 1975
* Tunisia – 1975
* Sudan – 1975
* Mauritania – 2017

== Presidents of the Federation ==
* Prince Bandar bin Abdulrahman
* Dr. Khalid Al-Turki
* Sheikh Faisal bin Hamid Al Qasimi
* 2025 – present: Dr. Yasser Omar Al-Dokhi [ref: Yasser Al Doukhi elected President of Arab Cycling Federation, Sharjah 24] [ref: Arab Cycling Federation General Assembly elects new leadership, The Peninsula]

== Board members ==
President of the Federation: Dr. Yasser Omar Al-Dokhi

First Vice President: Abdulaziz Al-Shahrani

Second Vice President: Mohammed Katem

Third Vice President: Fatima Al-Ghanem

Members: Dr. Tarek Al-Khayyat, Youssef Harb, Dr. Ahmed Jaber, Jamal Al-Kuwari, Mohammed Aidaroos

Secretary-General: Dr. Ashraf Mohammed Sayed Imam

== History of the Federation ==
The Arab Cycling Federation was the first Arab sports federation to come into being. The idea of establishing it was brought to the first Arab Cycling Tour of Lebanon in 1955 by the Syrian administrator Rashid Dashan, and after the tour ended it was taken forward with Ismail Taher (Egypt), Abdel Hafiz Al-Turki (Libya), Saadi Al-Douri (Iraq) and Nassif Majdalani (Lebanon).

The Arab Federation was founded on Wednesday, 11 January 1956, in Cairo, during the third Egypt International Cycling Race. Its administrative committee was formed of Ismail Taher (Egypt) as president; Tayseer Mashnouq (Syria), Nassif Majdalani (Lebanon), Saadi Al-Douri (Iraq) and Masoud Al-Zentouni (Libya) as vice-presidents; Joseph Saadeh (Lebanon) as deputy for motorcycles; Sayed Zaki (Egypt) as secretary-general; Shaker Abdel Hay (Egypt) as assistant secretary-general; and Abdullah Abdel Hay as assistant secretary for motorcycles.

Several meetings were held to activate the federation's role and activity, the last of which took place in Beirut in April 1966, but they did not achieve the desired goals, and the federation's activity subsequently ceased after an unsuccessful experience.

Following an invitation from the Saudi Cycling Federation to the presidents of Arab cycling federations, the founding conference to re-establish the Arab Federation was held in Riyadh from 28 to 30 October 1975. The meeting was a complete success and the federation was re-founded, with Prince Bandar bin Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud (Saudi Arabia) chairing the board of the new Arab Federation. He was succeeded as president by Dr. Khalid Ibrahim Al-Turki (Saudi Arabia), and then by Sheikh Faisal bin Hamid Al Qasimi (UAE) from June 1997.

Following an invitation from the Egyptian Cycling Federation and a number of Arab federations to hold an extraordinary general assembly in Cairo in 1997, to discuss reviving the Arab Federation, which had been inactive for more than six years, the general assembly elected a new board of directors and moved the headquarters to Cairo. This continued until 2003, when the general assembly in Tunis decided to attach the headquarters to the presidency in the United Arab Emirates, which has headed the federation since 1997. The signs of change in the federation's course soon became clear to all, reflecting everyone's desire to activate its role, support its progress and achieve the goals of raising the standard of Arab cycling to the best levels. The federation saw a qualitative leap thanks to the redrafting of many regulations in line with the new stage, and the regular implementation of championship and course programs.

== Objectives of the Federation ==
To spread and promote the sport in the Arab countries.

To prepare technical and administrative cadres.

To work on raising the technical level of the Arab player.

To strengthen relations among member federations, offering advice and counsel and settling any disputes that may arise between them.

To consolidate relations with the Union Cycliste Internationale and with continental and international federations.

To coordinate among member federations and unify their positions at Arab and continental meetings.

To support member federations when they take part in international and continental events.

To encourage scientific research and authorship, and to enrich the Arab library with books and translations on the sport, supporting authors and translators.

== References ==

Pathya Health (legally Pathyahealth Digital Private Limited) is an Indian preventive-health and women's health company based in Gurugram. Its main product is CycleIQ, an at-home hormone testing system that combines test strips with a smartphone app. [ref: CycleIQ by Pathya: At-home hormone testing for PCOS, Ovulation & Menopause, Pathya Health]

== Background ==
Pathya Health describes itself as a movement in preventive healthcare. The company states that its aim is to help people use health data to act earlier on risks, with an emphasis on chronic and metabolic conditions and, through CycleIQ, on hormonal health. [ref: About Pathya, Pathya Health] It organises its approach around four stated foundations: preventive healthcare, empowerment, data-driven insight and scientific rigour.

The operating company, Pathyahealth Digital Private Limited, is registered in Gurugram, Haryana. [ref: Trust & compliance: Certifications, Pathya Health]

== Products ==
=== CycleIQ test kits ===
CycleIQ is offered as three kits:
* a hormone-tracking kit using luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) strips, intended for people with irregular cycles or polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS);
* an ovulation testing kit using LH strips, intended for fertility prediction; and
* a menopause detection kit using FSH strips, intended to detect hormonal changes associated with the menopause transition.

The company states that the kits are for in-vitro diagnostic use only and that the results are for educational purposes and are not a medical diagnosis.

=== CycleIQ platform ===
Users photograph the test strip with the CycleIQ web app, which reads the strip and records the result against the user's menstrual cycle. According to the company's app, features include period logging and a cycle calendar with estimated ovulation and fertile-window dates, a test history with LH and FSH charts, a hormonal health report, a PCOS assessment that includes the modified Ferriman–Gallwey score for hirsutism, and a question-and-answer assistant that responds with passages from published research. [ref: How to use CycleIQ, Pathya Health]

== Regulatory status ==
The company states that it holds a medical device registration (Form MD-42) in Haryana for its test kits, and that its kits are registered with India's Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

== Distribution ==
CycleIQ is sold through the company's website and through a brand store on Amazon India.

== Media ==
Pathya Health publishes video series on YouTube, including Pro Talk with Pathya, featuring conversations with doctors, and Real Talk with Pathya, featuring personal stories. [ref: The Pathya Podcast Series, Pathya Health]

== Leadership ==
Charu Mathur (also reported as Charu Sachdeva Mathur) is the founder and chief executive officer. Before founding the company she worked in banking and consulting. According to the company's founder's message page, she completed a postgraduate programme at the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad (2008–2010), worked as a consultant at the Boston Consulting Group (2010–2013) and then at IndusInd Bank from 2013 to 2025, most recently as chief digital officer. [ref: Founder's message, Pathya Health] In 2025 she was named in the press as head of digital banking and strategy for the existing business at IndusInd Bank. [ref: IndusInd Bank expands INDIE app to all retail customers, SME Street] In the same message she states that she spent over a decade leading strategy, digital transformation and data and decision-science work in banking before founding Pathya Health.

Draft: Justinian's wars

Draft text:
Justinian I's reign (527–565) was marked by numerous wars that recovered extensive territories in the western Mediterranean lost by the Roman Empire in the 5th century. As a Christian emperor, Justinian considered it his duty to restore the state's former borders. In the east he continued the war with Persia begun under Justin I, with intermittent conflict lasting until 562. In the west, his campaigns against the barbarian kingdoms succeeded in conquering the Vandal Kingdom in North Africa (533–534) and in bringing Italy under Byzantine control after the war with the Ostrogoths (535–554), while less successful wars with the Visigothic Kingdom expanded Byzantine possessions in Spain. Thanks to the works of Procopius and other Byzantine historians, these wars are well studied. The Byzantine army resembled the earlier Roman army, with its field army (comitatenses) and frontier troops (limitanei), and numbered around 150,000 men, with barbarians playing a significant, though debated, role.

Although Justinian's conquests destroyed several barbarian kingdoms, including the Vandals, Ostrogoths and Visigoths, the empire proved unable to defend itself against new and more dangerous peoples such as the Slavs, Avars and Lombards. Even Constantinople was threatened by attacks from the north in the final years of his reign, and under his successors Justin II, Tiberius II and Maurice the empire increasingly struggled with a shortage of manpower. Researchers attribute this to declining discipline in the "barbarised" army, demographic losses from devastating epidemics and fewer available barbarian mercenaries. By straining resources without accounting for the changed realities of the sixth century, Justinian's campaigns are widely held to have contributed to the subsequent decline of Byzantium.
== Main directions of foreign policy ==
In the beginning of Justinian's reign, the empire's neighbors in the west were the so-called "barbarian kingdoms" of the Germans, which had formed in the 5th century on the territory of the Western Roman Empire. In all of these kingdoms the conquerors made up an insignificant minority, and the descendants of the empire's inhabitants, who had inherited Roman culture, could attain high social standing. At the beginning of the 6th century these states flourished under their outstanding rulers — the Franks in northern Gaul under Clovis I, the Burgundians in the Loire valley under Gundobad, the Ostrogoths in Italy under Theodoric the Great, the Visigoths in southern Gaul and Spain under Alaric II, and the Vandals in Africa under Thrasamund. By 527, when Justinian came to the throne, these kingdoms found themselves in a difficult situation. In 508, the Visigoths had been expelled from most of Gaul by the Franks, whose kingdom was later divided among the sons of Clovis. In the first half of the 530s the Burgundians suffered defeat at the hands of the Franks. With the death of Theodoric in 526, a crisis began in the Ostrogothic Kingdom, although even during that ruler's lifetime the conflict between the parties favoring and opposing rapprochement with the Byzantine Empire had already sharpened. A similar situation developed in the early 530s in the Vandal Kingdom.

In the east, Byzantium's only opponent was the Sasanian Empire, with which the empire, with brief interruptions, had waged war since the beginning of the 3rd century. By the beginning of the 6th century, this was a prosperous and developed state, roughly equal in area to Byzantium, stretching from the Indus in the east to Mesopotamia in the west. The main challenges facing the Sasanian state at the beginning of Justinian's reign were the ongoing threat of invasions by the Hephthalite Huns, who had first appeared at the borders in the second half of the 5th century, as well as internal instability and struggles for the shahanshah's throne. Around this time a popular Mazdakism movement arose, directed against the aristocracy and the Zoroastrian priesthood (magi). At the beginning of his reign, Khosrow I (531–579) supported this movement, but by the end of his reign it had come to represent a threat to the state. Under Justin I no significant military events connected with Persia took place. Among the diplomatic events of note is the initiative of Shah Kavad, who in the mid-520-s proposed that Justin adopt his son Khosrow and make him heir to the Roman Empire. This proposal was rejected.

EuroNatur is a German foundation based in Radolfzell that supports nature conservation projects in Europe. The foundation was established in 1987 by Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz Deutschland (BUND), Environmental Action Germany (DUH) and Naturschutzbund Deutschland (NABU). EuroNatur is a member of the Deutschen Naturschutzring.

== Mission ==
The foundation's mission is to protect Europe's diverse natural heritage. Its projects focus on wild animals such as wolves, brown bears, lynxes and endangered migratory birds, as well as valuable natural and cultural sites. The foundation's motto is "connecting nature and people", which reflects its belief that restoring nature, conserving wildlife and improving biodiversity are fundamental to human quality of life. Working with local people helps ensure the long-term success of their projects to protect endangered animals and their habitats in Europe.

EuroNatur is heavily involved with the European Green Belt initiative, a collaborative cross-border project which aims to create a wild, biodiverse corridor along the route of the former Iron Curtain. Since 2004, EuroNatur has coordinated the conservation efforts along the Balkan Green Belt, the southernmost section of the European Green Belt. [ref: EGB: Home, www.europeangreenbelt.org]

== Operations and administration ==
The foundation works with scientists, conservationists, farmers, politicians and entrepreneurs from across Europe. A key part of the foundation's work takes place in the Balkans, for which they work with local conservationists and volunteers to plan and establish a large network of nature reserves, along with species conservation projects for wolves, bears, lynxes and migratory birds based on scientific research. EuroNatur organises workshops, seminars and training programmes to share knowledge and experiences that help protect Europe's wild animals. EuroNatur also engages in political lobbying in EU institutions.

EuroNatur's first president was Claus-Peter Hutter, followed by Hartmut Vogtmann between January 2008 and early July 2011. Christel Schroeder served from October 2011 to the end of 2019, and Thomas Potthast has been president since 1 January 2020. Gabriel Schwaderer is the executive director of EuroNatur.

== Funding ==
The foundation is funded through donations, third-party funding and income from foundation capital. EuroNatur has been awarded the DZI Donation Seal by the German Central Institute for Social Issues (DZI).

== European Stork Villages ==
The European Stork Village network was set up by EuroNatur in 1994 as a way of publicly recognising communities across Europe that are making a significant contribution to protecting their local white stork populations. [ref: Ferger, Stefan & Schwaderer, Gabriel. (2016). The European Stork Villages - a successful combination of nature conservation and sustainable development of rural areas.] Representatives from each of the Stork Villages meet every year in one of the member villages to discuss and develop solutions for the conservation of white storks. There are currently 16 recognised European Stork Villages.

The most recent village to be recognised and added to the network was Knepp Wildland and Storrington in 2025, the first and only Stork Village in the UK. [ref: European Stork Villages Network, White Stork Project] The village was honoured in recognition of its conservation and rewilding programme which led to the return of the white stork to the area. The village of Storrington holds its White Stork and Nature Festival each year to celebrate its conservation efforts and the return of its white stork population.

== Awards ==
The foundation has been running its EuroNatur Award since 1992. [ref: Award for Environmental Excellence, EuroNatur]

EuroNatur runs an annual photography competition called European Treasures of Nature in partnership with the NaturVision film festival, Natur magazine and German utility company Gelsenwasser. The winning entries are displayed in a year-long touring exhibition titled Fascinating Nature and featured in the next year's EuroNatur calendar.

== References ==

The Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter (MPSD; ) is a non-university research institute of the Max Planck Society (MPG). It is located in the Hamburg district of Bahrenfeld, on the campus of the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY). The institute primarily conducts basic research in the natural sciences, in experimental and theoretical physics and chemistry. Its focus is on very fast physical processes and chemical reactions that can be studied by ultrafast spectroscopy using pulsed radiation sources such as the nearby free-electron lasers FLASH and European XFEL.

== History ==
The institute grew out of an existing Max Planck Society research group for structural dynamics at the University of Hamburg. The decision to establish an independent institute with five research departments was announced in November 2012. The institute was officially founded on 1 January 2014 and initially consisted of two departments, headed by its two founding directors: Condensed Matter Dynamics, led by Andrea Cavalleri, and Atomically Resolved Dynamics, led by R. J. Dwayne Miller. The Theory Department under Ángel Rubio was added on 1 November 2014. Miller's department was dissolved when he left the MPSD on 30 June 2020. On 15 June 2021, Philip Moll was appointed director of the Microstructured Quantum Matter Department.

In 2024, Jie Shan and Kin Fai Mak were recruited as further directors. They joined the institute fully on 1 January 2025 and lead two jointly run departments of Nanoscale Quantum Materials, focusing on optics (Shan) and transport (Mak), bringing the number of departments to five.

Konidela Venkat Rao (c. 1937 – 24 December 2007) was an Indian government official and occasional actor, best known as the patriarch of the Konidela–Allu family, one of the most prominent film dynasties in Telugu cinema. He was the father of actors Chiranjeevi, Nagendra Babu, and Pawan Kalyan, and the paternal grandfather of actor Ram Charan.

== Personal life ==
Venkat Rao was born in Mogalthur, located in the West Godavari district of Andhra Pradesh. He worked professionally as a government excise inspector and was frequently transferred across different regions during his service. He married Anjana Devi, and the couple had three sons and two daughters:
* Chiranjeevi (born Konidela Sivasankara Varaprasad Rao), prominent actor and politician.
* Nagendra Babu, film producer and actor.
* Pawan Kalyan (born Konidela Kalyan Kumar), actor and Deputy Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh.
* Vijaya Durga, mother of actors Sai Durgha Tej and Panja Vaisshnav Tej.
* Madhavi Rao, who maintains a private profile; there is no publicly known information regarding her husband or children.

He passed away due to illness at the age of 70 on 24 December 2007 in Hyderabad.

== Acting career ==
Though primarily dedicated to his career in public service, Venkat Rao had a deep passion for the arts and acted in brief roles. He made his acting debut with a minor role in the 1969 film Jagat Khiladi. Due to family and government duties, he did not pursue full-time acting but strongly encouraged his eldest son, Chiranjeevi, to enter the film industry. Later, he made a notable appearance alongside Chiranjeevi, playing the role of a minister in the 1983 film Mantri Gari Viyyankudu, directed by Bapu.

== Legacy and descendants ==
Through his children, Venkat Rao established the lineage of the "Mega Family" in Tollywood. His prominent grandchildren and notable direct descendants include:
* Grandsons: Ram Charan, Varun Tej, Sai Durgha Tej, Panja Vaisshnav Tej, and Akira Nandan.
* Granddaughters: Sushmitha Konidela, Sreeja Konidela, and Niharika Konidela.
* Great-granddaughters: Klin Kaara Konidela (daughter of Ram Charan), among others.

== Biography ==

=== First years and education ===
Mariana Conti Takahashi was born on 23 July 1985 in the city of Campinas, in the interior of São Paulo. She is one of four children born to an electrical engineer and a sociologist. [ref: Mariana Conti critica violência política de gênero dentro da Câmara, Correio Popular] She grew up in Americana, a city bordering Campinas, and enrolled at the State University of Campinas (Unicamp) in 2004 to study social sciences. Draft: Healthcare in Abu Dhabi

Draft text:
Healthcare in Abu Dhabi covers the health system of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates. Since a reform programme begun in 2005–2006, health services in the emirate have been funded mainly through compulsory health insurance for all residents, with regulation separated from the provision of public services. The sector combines government-owned hospitals operated by SEHA with a larger private sector, which accounted for more than 75% of the market in 2020. Researchers and the regulator have identified cost growth, workforce needs and preventive care as priorities for the health system.

== History ==
In 2005 Abu Dhabi's leadership began restructuring a health system whose design, according to a 2012 study in Health Policy, had not met its aims. The reforms introduced compulsory tiered health insurance for all residents, a single standardised payment system, and an independent regulator responsible for licensing and inspecting health professionals, facilities and insurers. [ref: Benefits of a single payment system: Case study of Abu Dhabi health system reforms, Health Policy] From 2006 the regulator, the Health Authority – Abu Dhabi, was separated from the provision of services, which became the responsibility of the Abu Dhabi Health Services Company (SEHA). [ref: Progress and outcomes of health systems reform in the United Arab Emirates: a systematic review, BMC Health Services Research] The regulator now operates as the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi (DoH). [ref: 2 stroke centres of excellence named in Abu Dhabi, Gulf News]

Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, owned by Mubadala Healthcare and modelled on the Cleveland Clinic in the United States, began opening in March 2015 with 364 beds on Al Maryah Island. [ref: Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi opens its doors for patients, The National] In July 2019 the emirate's health information exchange, Malaffi, became operational, the first such platform in the UAE; by September 2020 it connected 40 hospitals and 403 clinics. [ref: More than 60% of Abu Dhabi hospitals now digitally connected, Healthcare IT News] In December 2019 the DoH launched a genome programme to produce an Emirati reference genome, carried out by Group 42 with the sequencing companies BGI and Oxford Nanopore Technologies, with a first phase of 100,000 samples. [ref: Abu Dhabi launches genome programme, Gulf News] [ref: Abu Dhabi teams with BGI, Oxford Nanopore on population sequencing project, GenomeWeb]

== Financing and insurance ==
Health insurance is compulsory for all residents. UAE nationals are covered by the Thiqa programme, while expatriates are covered by Basic or Enhanced plans. At the end of 2017 Thiqa covered about 600,000 members (20%), Basic plans 1.3 million (43%) and Enhanced plans 1.1 million (37%). [ref: Doctor's orders: Preventive medicine, digitisation and innovative technologies revitalise Abu Dhabi's medical offerings, Oxford Business Group]

Insurance claims rose from 15.3 million, worth US$1.6 billion, in 2011 to more than 22 million, worth US$2.9 billion, in 2014. A 2017 systematic review noted that some researchers saw the rise as a sign that further change was needed to keep the system financially sustainable, and that limited regulatory control and insurer competition had been identified as obstacles to cost efficiency.

== Facilities ==
In April 2020 the DoH reported 3,114 licensed health facilities in the emirate, including 64 hospitals, 759 clinics and 746 health centres, and 7,032 hospital beds (2.7 per 1,000 people) in 2019. SEHA, the largest public provider, operated at least 12 hospitals with 2,644 beds. Private providers accounted for more than 75% of the market, and the speed of private-sector growth raised concerns about oversupply in some specialities. About 70% of outpatient visits and 40% of inpatient care took place in private facilities.

=== Centres of Excellence ===
Since 2023 the DoH has designated selected hospital programmes as Centres of Excellence, assessed on clinical outcomes, patient experience, patient safety and quality, staff competency, and medical education, research and residency programmes, as well as accreditation. In July 2023 Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi and Sheikh Shakhbout Medical City were designated for stroke care; other facilities able to give emergency stroke treatment were designated "stroke ready" and transfer patients to the two centres once stable. Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi was designated for adult cardiac surgery in October 2023 [ref: Department of Health – Abu Dhabi appoints Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi as centre of excellence for cardiac surgery, Abu Dhabi Media Office] and for adult multi-organ transplants in December 2025, by which time the hospital reported more than 1,000 organ transplants since its programme began in 2017. [ref: Department of Health – Abu Dhabi designates Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi as Centre of Excellence for Adult Multi-Organ Transplants, Department of Health – Abu Dhabi] Other designated specialities include paediatric heart care, burn care and stem cell transplantation. In June 2026 the DoH stated that the centres had treated more than 3,000 complex cases and reduced the need for treatment abroad by 60%. [ref: DoH's Designated Centres of Excellence Deliver Specialised Care to More Than 3,000 Complex Cases, Department of Health – Abu Dhabi] In 2013 the regulator had sponsored more than 1,400 patients for treatment abroad.

Pemamek Oy is a Finnish engineering company that designs and manufactures welding automation and production automation systems for heavy metal fabrication. Its products are sold under the PEMA brand. The company is headquartered in Loimaa, Southwest Finland, and has been owned by the Heikonen family since the late 1980s. [ref: Leadership And Governance - Pemamek] [ref: ”Ei riitä, että olemme Suomen paras – pitää olla champions league -tasoa”, Perheyritysten liitto] Its customers include shipyards, manufacturers of wind turbine towers and foundations, and makers of heavy equipment, boilers and pressure vessels. [ref: ] [ref: ]

In the financial year ending March 2026, the parent company Pemamek Oy reported revenue of €155.2 million and had 386 employees. [ref: Pemamek - yritystiedot, päättäjät, taloustiedot, Finder] The company states that around 90 per cent of its sales are exports.

== History ==

=== Origins and ownership changes (1970 to 1989) ===
Pemamek was founded in 1970 in Loimaa. The company describes its origins as a small business making welding positioners, devices that hold and rotate a workpiece during welding. According to Pekka Heikonen, the current chairman, the company had about ten employees when he joined in 1978.

In 1982 Pemamek became part of Korpivaara Oy, and Heikonen became its factory manager. The conglomerate Amer acquired Korpivaara in 1984. In late 1988 Amer decided to divest three of its metal industry businesses, and Pemamek's business passed to Heikonen.

=== Automation and growth (1980s to 2010s) ===
Pemamek began developing robotic solutions in the 1980s. During the 1990s automation became its core product line. Through the 2010s, demand from shipyards was a major driver of growth, and staff numbers passed 200. Customers in this period included the Meyer Turku shipyard. [ref: Pemamek kasvaa aimo askelin Loimaalla, Loimaan Lehti]

A factory extension completed in early 2017 increased production space by half. Jaakko Heikonen had become chief executive in spring 2016. In the 2017-18 financial year the company expected revenue of about €50 million, compared with €35-40 million in earlier years, and employed 190 people.

On 1 May 2019 Juha Mäkitalo, previously chief executive of the sheet metal machinery maker Finn-Power, succeeded Jaakko Heikonen as CEO. Heikonen remained vice chairman of the board. Revenue for the financial year 2018-19 was €77 million, with 230 employees. [ref: Juha Mäkitalo Appointed As New CEO Of Pemamek - Pemamek]

=== Diversification into wind energy (2016 onwards) ===
In 2023 Yle reported that the company had decided some six or seven years earlier that it depended too heavily on the cyclical shipbuilding industry, and had turned to the growing wind power market. [ref: Kan Finland bli en stormakt för grön teknik? Vi besöker familjeföretaget som ser enorm efterfrågan, Svenska Yle] In June 2022 Pemamek announced €15 million of investment in a factory extension and product development, aimed at demand from the wind industry. The extension brought the Loimaa factory to 27,000 square metres. [ref: Windtech International - Pemamek invests in factory expansion and R&D to meet demand from the wind market, www.windtech-international.com] The new hall, completed in December 2022, has a ceiling five metres higher than the older halls, to accommodate production lines for large offshore wind foundations.

In spring 2023 Pemamek announced orders for production lines for XXL monopile foundations from Sif Holding of the Netherlands and Haizea Wind Group of Spain. Staff numbers grew from just over 200 to nearly 350 within a few years.

=== Recent developments (2024 to present) ===
In June 2026 Pemamek acquired the business operations of Mach Machines, a North American robotic welding integrator. The combined operation was to move to a larger facility in Blue Ash, Ohio. [ref: Pemamek X Mach Machines - Pemamek Joins Forces With Mach Machines] In October 2026 Jaakko Heikonen and Pemamek were named among the finalists of the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year competition in Finland. [ref: Pemamek kisaa kovassa seurassa, Loimaan Lehti]

== Operations ==
Pemamek's headquarters and factory are in Loimaa, beside Finnish national road 9, with engineering offices in Tampere and Turku. [ref: Contact - Pemamek] Design, manufacturing and testing of its systems take place in Finland. Export contracts often include installation, commissioning and maintenance at the customer's site.

=== International presence ===
In 2023 Finnvera reported that Pemamek had subsidiaries in the United States, Germany, Spain and Italy, and sales companies in Brazil and Poland. As of 2026 the company lists sales or service offices in Germany, the United States, Brazil, Poland, Spain, Italy, and the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Its Spanish operation trades as Pemamek Iberia.

The June 2026 purchase of Mach Machines' business added a team in Ohio; the combined US operation was to relocate to Blue Ash, Ohio.

Max Shelton is an Australian agricultural scientist and former Associate Professor at the University of Queensland. He is known for his research on tropical pastures and the development of a new insect-resistant cultivar of Leucaena leucocephala, a variety called Redlands [ref: Insect-resistant forage crop almost ready for commercial release, ABC News], which is used in cattle farming. In 2022, Shelton was awarded the AW Howard Medal for significant contributions to the advancement of pastures in Australia. [ref: Leucaena research pioneer Max Shelton receives national honour, Beef Central]

== Research and career ==
Shelton graduated with honours from a degree in agricultural science at the University of Queensland in 1968. He then completed a PhD at the University of Queensland in 1972 [ref: Factors influencing competition between upland rice (Oryza sativa Linn.) and undersown stylo (Stylosanthes guyanensis Aubl.), The University of Queensland] on the integration of stylo pasture in farming systems in North-East Thailand. He returned to the University of Queensland in 1978 in the Department of Agriculture, taking up a tenured lectureship in pasture science in 1986. He retired in 2016 as associate professor. [ref: Celebrating the contribution of Dr Max Shelton, Beef Central]

Shelton's career focused on the development and management of forage tree legumes in livestock production. With colleagues he bred a new psyllid-resistant variety of Leucaena called Redlands. [ref: 'Redlands' leucaena lifts beef productivity and profitability in coastal Queensland, Beef Central] [ref: Associate Professor Max Shelton on his pest resistant Leucaena forage research, ABC Rural] He was also involved in the release of three other new pasture plant varieties (Sesbania cv Mt Cotton and Leucaena cvv Tarramba, and Wondergraze). Shelton worked with smallholder farmers in Indonesia to improve nutrition for cattle through better pasture management. [ref: Improving smallholder cattle fattening systems based on forage tree legume diets in eastern Indonesia and northern Australia, Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research]
He has delivered a series of courses to graziers in northern Queensland and advised them on the establishment and management of grazed leucaena pastures. [ref: Five decades of leucaena R&D: Is it time to move on?, Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation]

Shelton has also carried out research on the environmental impact of cattle production, including methane production [ref: Leucaena: The productive and sustainable forage legume, Meat & Livestock Australia] and how leucaena-based grazing systems can be used to sequester carbon. [ref: Soil organic carbon and total nitrogen under Leucaena leucocephala pastures in Queensland, Crop & Pasture Science] [ref: The sequestration and turnover of soil organic carbon in subtropical leucaena-grass pastures, Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment] In addition, Shelton has investigated the drought-resistance potential of leucaena for farmers in dry, tropical regions. [ref: Drought fodder crop takes centre stage, UQ News]

== References ==

The Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter (MPSD; ) is a non-university research institute of the Max Planck Society (MPG). It is located in the Hamburg district of Bahrenfeld, on the campus of the Deutsches Elektronen-Synchrotron (DESY). The institute primarily conducts basic research in the natural sciences, in experimental and theoretical physics and chemistry. Its focus is on very fast physical processes and chemical reactions that can be studied by ultrafast spectroscopy using pulsed radiation sources such as the nearby free-electron lasers FLASH and European XFEL.

== History ==
The institute grew out of an existing Max Planck Society research group for structural dynamics at the University of Hamburg. The decision to establish an independent institute with five research departments and up to 120 permanent positions was announced in November 2012. The institute was officially founded on 1 January 2014 and initially consisted of two departments, headed by its two founding directors: Condensed Matter Dynamics, led by Andrea Cavalleri, and Atomically Resolved Dynamics, led by R. J. Dwayne Miller. The Theory Department under Ángel Rubio was added on 1 November 2014. Miller's department was dissolved when he left the MPSD on 30 June 2020. On 15 June 2021, Philip Moll was appointed director of the Microstructured Quantum Matter Department.

In 2024, Jie Shan and Kin Fai Mak were recruited as further directors. They joined the institute fully on 1 January 2025 and lead two jointly run departments of Nanoscale Quantum Materials, focusing on optics (Shan) and transport (Mak), bringing the number of departments to five.

== Building ==
Since its founding, the MPSD has used space in the neighbouring Center for Free-Electron Laser Science (CFEL) building, which it shares with DESY and the University of Hamburg. A separate institute building next to the CFEL, designed by hammeskrause architekten, was completed in 2023; a foundation slab up to 1.5 metres thick keeps its laboratories free of vibrations. The building was officially opened on 13 May 2024. Of its total construction cost of €54 million, the City of Hamburg contributed €37 million and the Max Planck Society the rest. The extension allowed the institute to grow from three to five departments.

== Doctoral training ==
The MPSD hosts the International Max Planck Research School for Ultrafast Imaging and Structural Dynamics (IMPRS-UFAST), a structured doctoral programme founded in 2011 for doctoral students with backgrounds in physics, chemistry and biology.

William D. Oliver is an American physicist and electrical engineer. He is the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a professor of physics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), director of the MIT Center for Quantum Engineering, and associate director of the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE). His research focuses on superconducting qubits and on cryogenic control electronics for quantum and classical high-performance computing.

== Early life and education ==
Oliver received a B.S. in electrical engineering and a B.A. in Japanese from the University of Rochester in 1995. He earned an S.M. in electrical engineering and computer science from MIT in 1997, working with Tod Machover at the MIT Media Lab, and a Ph.D. in electrical engineering, with a minor in physics, from Stanford University in 2003 supervised by Yoshihisa Yamamoto.

== CareerYoshihisa Yamamoto ==
Oliver joined MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 2003 as a member of its Quantum Information and Integrated Nanosystems Group. He became a principal investigator at RLE in 2006 and later led its Engineering Quantum Systems Group. He spent 2013 as a JSPS Visiting Researcher at the University of Tokyo, and the MIT Department of Physics appointed him Professor of the Practice two years later. Lincoln Laboratory named him a Fellow in 2017. He was also appointed associate director of RLE, where he leads quantum information science research and is the liaison between RLE and Lincoln Laboratory.

MIT promoted Oliver to Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and of Physics in 2021 and named him the Henry Ellis Warren (1894) Professor. He is the founding director of the MIT Center for Quantum Engineering and holds Lincoln Laboratory Fellow Emeritus status.

Oliver was a co-author of the 2019 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine consensus study report Quantum Computing: Progress and Prospects. He is a member of the U.S. National Quantum Initiative Advisory Committee and the U.S. Committee for Superconducting Electronics.

Oliver and several current and former members of the Engineering Quantum Systems Group founded Atlantic Quantum in 2022 to develop superconducting quantum-computing hardware. The company raised a $9 million seed round led by The Engine and joined Google Quantum AI in October 2025. In a 2026 Scientific American feature on the state of the field, Oliver estimated that larger-scale quantum computers could arrive in about 20 years.

== Research ==
Oliver's research covers the materials growth, fabrication, design and measurement of superconducting qubits and their use in quantum processors. He also works on cryogenic packaging and on control electronics based on cryogenic complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) and single-flux-quantum digital logic.

His group studies the coherence of superconducting flux and fluxonium qubits. A 2016 paper in Nature Communications described a redesigned flux qubit with improved coherence and more reproducible fabrication. A separate 2016 study in Science showed that qubit relaxation could be suppressed by quasiparticle pumping.

== Awards and honors ==
* Fellow, American Association for the Advancement of Science (2023) [ref: ]
* Thornton Family Faculty Research and Innovation Fellowship, MIT (2021)
* Fellow, American Physical Society (2016), "for pioneering contributions to the physics and associated engineering of robust, reproducible, superconducting quantum systems and high-performance cryogenic control electronics" [ref: Division of Quantum Information Fellowship, www.aps.org]
* Fellow, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (2025) [ref: ]

== Selected publications ==

* Suppressing relaxation in superconducting qubits by quasiparticle pumping, Science
* National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2019). Quantum Computing: Progress and Prospects. Washington, DC: The National Academies Press.

The Cancer Research Society (CRS;, SRC) is a Canadian charitable organization dedicated exclusively to funding research on all types of cancer in order to better prevent, detect, and treat the disease. [ref: Our mission, Cancer Research Society] It was founded in 1945 in Montreal. [ref: 100% Research for 80 Years, Cancer Research Society]

== History ==

The Cancer Research Society was founded in 1945 by Betty Caplan and her three friends, Etta Kastner, Hattie Rolbin, and Mildred Singer. Faced with her mother's cancer, Betty Caplan realized that no Canadian organization was then dedicated exclusively to cancer research, and decided to act. From its inception, the organization set itself the mission of funding research exclusively into all types of cancer in order to better prevent, detect, and treat the disease.In 1946, the CRS awarded its first four grants of $600 each, for a total of $2,400, an amount that would represent more than $40,000 today. In 1948, three years after its founding, the organization comprised more than one hundred member units organizing various fundraising activities. A first Medical Advisory Board, composed of physicians responsible for selecting the researchers to be funded, was established in the early years. [ref: In 1945, Betty Caplan changed cancer research in Canada, Hub SRC]

=== Development ===
Over the decades, the CRS expanded its support for research on all types of cancer across Canada. Since its founding, the organization reports having allocated more than $450 million in research grants and fellowships. In 2024-2025, according to the organization, the CRS invested $17 million and awarded 316 grants across its various programs. [ref: Our impact, Cancer Research Society]In 2025, the CRS marked its 80th anniversary.

=== Growth of activities ===
In 2010, the CRS created the Challenge Against Cancer program, in which charity trips are organized and enable participants to raise funds for research. [ref: Notre histoire, Société de recherche sur le cancer]

== Organization ==

=== Headquarters and administration ===
The Cancer Research Society is headquartered in Montreal. It is a registered charitable organization (registration number 11915 3229 RR0001). [ref: Société de recherche sur le cancer / Cancer Research Society (119153229RR0001), List of charities] According to the organization, it has a staff of about thirty employees. Its governance rests on a board of directors composed of volunteer members, a management team responsible for guiding the team's actions, and a Scientific Advisory Committee. [ref: Our team, Cancer Research Society]

=== Board of directors ===
Founder Betty Caplan served as president of the organization from 1945 to 1954. A number of people succeeded her in this role over the decades. Christian M. Paupe, a member of the board of directors since 2021, [ref: Christian M. Paupe appointed to the Board, Cancer Research Society] chairs it as of 2026. [ref: Board of directors, Cancer Research Society]

=== Scientific Advisory Committee ===
The Scientific Advisory Committee is composed of experts in cancer research from diverse backgrounds.Actor and host André Robitaille serves as the CRS's spokesperson.

== Funding ==
The Cancer Research Society funds its activities through donations from individuals, contributions from partners, and funds raised at its events. [ref: Our mission, Cancer Research Society]According to the independent charity evaluator Charity Intelligence Canada, the CRS reported total revenues of $40.4 million for the 2024-2025 fiscal year, of which $34.2 million came from donations and special-events revenue, and $6.2 million from investment income. According to the same source, the CRS devoted $17.0 million to its grants and their management during that same fiscal year. The organization publishes impact reports and audited financial statements accounting for its management. [ref: Cancer Research Society, Charity Intelligence Canada]

== Activities ==
The CRS organizes several fundraising events across Canada. [ref: Events, Cancer Research Society]One of its main events is the Urban BBQ, presented by RBC Royal Bank since 2014 and held at the Grand Quai of the Port of Montreal. According to the organization, the event has raised more than $6.3 million since its first edition, [ref: Urban BBQ 2026, Cancer Research Society] and its 12th edition, in 2026, brought together more than 1,000 guests and raised $850,000 net. [ref: Urban BBQ 2026: a collective success for cancer research, Cancer Research Society]Among the organization's other events are Accords Célestes, an evening pairing fine dining, wines, and music, held in Montreal, [ref: Accords Célestes 2026, Cancer Research Society] as well as Christmas Carols for Research, a holiday-season concert whose 2026 edition supports breast cancer research. [ref: Christmas Carols for Research 2026, Cancer Research Society] The CRS is also associated with charity races across the country. [ref: Nos événements, Société de recherche sur le cancer]The Challenge Against Cancer program, created in 2010, offers charity trips to various destinations around the world during which participants take on physical challenges while raising funds for cancer research. [ref: Challenge Against Cancer, Cancer Research Society] The Challenge rose, announced in 2025, is an edition dedicated entirely to breast cancer research. [ref: Challenge rose 2026, Cancer Research Society]

In 2017, Raymundo made his acting debut as ‘Oscar’ in the television series,
La Quinceanera, directed
by Gigi Saul Guerrero for Stage 13 Network, the digital content division for Warner Bros. Digital Networks. [ref: La Quinceanera, IMDb]

In the same year, Raymundo guest-starred as ‘Enrique’ on multiple episodes of the CBS American drama television series, Zoo; directed by Michael Katleman, based on the novel by James Patterson and Michael Ledwidge.

In 2018, Raymundo joined the American science fiction drama television series, The X-Files, and American science fiction action film, The Predator; where Raymundo shared the screen with the likes of, David Duchovny and Boyd Holtbrooke in their corresponding stunt sequences.

Raymundo then returned to The CW Network as 'Hugo', on American television drama series, The 100, executively produced and directed by Jason Rothenberg for the 100 series; shortly after Raymundo guest-starred as 'Brant Moore' on various episodes of the science fiction television series, Travelers, created by Brad Wright for Netflix International.

2019, Raymundo focused his efforts on being a stuntman as he joined a number of television shows with such notable mentions as Deadly Class for the Syfy network, sharing the screen with British actor Benedict Wong; and Disney's Siren where Raymundo performed as a stunt double for three different actors including Ian Verdun, Hugo Ateo and Luc Roderique. Raymundo finished 2019 guest-starring as the role of 'Motorman' in multiple episodes of the American science fiction television series, Lost in Space, for the Netflix Network.

In 2020, Raymundo joined the Marvel Cinematic Universe as a stuntman for Hulu Network's American television series, Helstrom; later that year Raymundo joined the Paramount+ Network as BO, on the American television mini-series, The Stand, an adaption of the post-apocalyptic dark fantasy novel written by Stephen King, where Raymundo shares the screen with James Marsden and Owen Teague.

After sharing the screen with actress Juliette Lewis on the television series Yellowjackets, Raymundo focused his efforts on acting. [ref: ‘Fire Country’ Episode 9 “No Good Deed” Photos, Plot, Cast and Air Date, Showbiz Junkies] Shortly after, Raymundo took on the role of 'Mike Garcia', the father of Isaac Garcia, played by Isaac Arellanes and Lee Garcia, played by Myles Perez for the Netflix Network's teen drama, My Life with the Walter Boys, Starring Nikki Rodriguez, Ashby Gentry, Noah LaLonde, Sarah Rafferty and Johnny Link an adaption of the novel written by Ali Novak.

In 2025 Raymundo, joined the cast of the American Western drama television series, Billy the Kid, as "Miguel Otero" for MGM+.

TX2 was born as Timothy Evan Thomas in Cort Collins, CO. He is most widely known as the American alternative rock singer and songwriter TX2. He gained attention in the early 2022 through a combination of social media promotion, viral singles, and touring within the alternative rock and metalcore scenes. TX2’s music mixes pop punk, emo, alternative rock, rap, numetal, metalcore and electronic music, often focusing on themes of mental health, identity, alienation, criminalisation of the queer in the USA, internet culture, and social criticism.

TX2 signed with Hopeless Records in July 2023 and later toured with artists including Ice Nine Kills, In This Moment, The Word Alive, and Beartooth.

TX2 originally released music independently as a solo artist before launching TX2 as a band with multiple members. Early releases built a following online, particularly on TikTok, where TX2 became known for his often over the top videos and provacative song lyrics.

In 2023, the single “I Would Hate Me Too” became one of TX2’s breakout songs online and helped expand the band’s audience beyond social media. During this period, TX2 released several singles and EPs while touring nationally and expanding into Europe.

In 2023, TX2 toured with Magnolia Park on a United States tour, before featuring on their track 'Life In The USA'.

In June of 2024 TX2 played Download Festival in the United Kingdom, and Aftershock Festival in California. That same year, TX2 appeared on the Kiss of Death Tour Part 2 tour alongside Ice Nine Kills, In This Moment, and Avatar.

TX2 released the single “MAD” featuring Spencer Charnas of Ice Nine Kills on August 28, 2024.

Additional collaborations during this period included “Vendetta”, featuring Johnny 3 Tears of Hollywood Undead, and “THIS ISN’T ABOUT DRUGS (I SWEAR)”, featuring From First to Last.

In 2025, TX2 joined the touring festival Summer of Loud alongside Beartooth, Parkway Drive, Killswitch Engage, I Prevail, The Devil Wears Prada, The Amity Affliction, and Alpha Wolf. TX2 also performed at the Vans Warped Tour stop in Long Beach, California.

In July and August of 2025 TX2 toured with The Word Alive and later announced the project’s first headline tour across Europe and the United Kingdom.

TX2 frequently collaborates with other artists. Recent collaborations include "Feed" featuring DeathByRomy, "Nice Guy" featuring Ekoh, "The End Of Us" featuring Andy Biersack of Black Veil Brides, and "Murder Scene" featuring Joshua Roberts of Magnolia Park.

TX2 released his debut album End Of Us in February 2026 on Hopeless Records, before allegedly parting ways to release under an independent name.

On April 25, 2026 TX2 kicked off their North American tour with Black Veil Brides, As December Falls, and From Ashes To New.

TX2 has received polarized reactions within the alternative and metalcore scene. Supporters have praised his openness about mental health, identity, and online harassment, while critics have pointed out his heavy use of social media and his confrontational online persona.

Kerrang! described Evan Thomas as a “much-hyped altrock icon-in-waiting” in a feature discussing TX2’s debut album End Of Us. Revolver included TX2 in its 6 Best New Songs Right Now feature in 2025.

TX2’s music combines alternative, emo, pop punk, rap, numetal, metalcore, and electronic influences. His sound and style has been associated with the emo revival, metalcore, and TikTok alternative music scenes. More recent music has shown a shift in TX2's style, with their song 'Evil Is Contagious' being made with a ska punk instrumental co-created with Reel Big Fish.

TX2 lists Green Day, My Chemical Romance, Linkin Park, Limp Bizkit, and Eminem as his influences.

Toden is an identity verification and risk-management software company. [ref: KYC & Identity Verification Platform, Toden]

Its platform combines Know Your Customer (KYC), Know Your Business (KYB), biometric authentication, anti-money laundering (AML) screening, fraud detection, transaction monitoring and automated risk decisioning. These services are delivered through application programming interfaces (APIs), software development kits (SDKs) and a web-based management platform. [ref: The Platform: trust infrastructure for digital businesses, Toden]

== Products and services ==

=== Identity verification ===

Toden provides Know Your Customer (KYC) infrastructure that enables businesses to verify individuals using government-issued identity documents, official records and biometric authentication. [ref: Identity Verification (KYC), Toden]

The platform supports identity document and facial verification across 240 countries and regions. Government database verification is available in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, South Africa and Côte d'Ivoire.

Through facial deduplication technology, Toden can identify potential matches between newly submitted biometric records and identities previously verified within the same customer's organisation. This capability is designed to support the detection of repeated registrations, identity misuse and certain forms of multi-account fraud. [ref: Face Search, Toden]

=== Business verification ===

Toden's Know Your Business (KYB) services enable organisations to verify companies and assess the identities of individuals associated with them. [ref: Business Verification (KYB), Toden]

The system combines company registry searches, corporate documentation checks, director verification, beneficial ownership assessment and compliance screening.

=== Risk intelligence and fraud prevention ===

The system combines information from customer identities, devices, network activity, transactions, behavioural patterns and compliance screening results to support risk assessment.

Its capabilities include transaction risk scoring, device and IP intelligence, suspicious activity detection, cryptocurrency wallet screening, sanctions screening, politically exposed person (PEP) screening and adverse-media monitoring. [ref: Risk Intelligence, Toden]

The platform supports configurable decision rules that allow businesses to approve transactions, decline high-risk activities, request additional verification or refer cases for human review.

Toden also provides investigation and case management tools that record alerts, evidence, decisions and reviewer actions. These records can help businesses with compliance reviews and preparing suspicious activity reports.

=== Automated compliance and continuous monitoring ===

The platform supports ongoing sanctions and watchlist screening, transaction monitoring, activity-based alerts, customer re-verification and risk-based investigation workflows.

Its visual workflow builder allows compliance and risk teams to configure verification steps and decision policies without modifying their application's source code.

== Technology ==

The company provides SDKs for React, React Native and Flutter, alongside hosted verification sessions, server-side APIs and signed webhooks. [ref: Toden KYC and identity verification documentation, Toden]

The platform also incorporates audit trails, configurable access controls and data protection mechanisms for handling sensitive identity and financial information. [ref: Privacy Policy, Toden]

== International coverage ==

NFC chip verification supports documents issued by up to 138 countries, according to the company's developer documentation.

In Africa, Toden provides government-record verification in five markets: Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, South Africa and Côte d'Ivoire.

The platform also supports business registry verification in multiple international jurisdictions, although the depth of available information differs by market.

== Business model ==

Its pricing is primarily usage-based, allowing customers to pay for individual verification, screening and risk management components.

The modular model enables businesses to select specific services, such as identity verification, business checks, biometric authentication or transaction monitoring, rather than purchasing a fixed combination of products.

Toden also provides a sandbox environment for developers to test integrations before processing live verification requests.

Julie Tobiason is an American ballet dancer, choreographer, and dance educator. She performed with Chicago City Ballet, as a principal dancer with Pacific Northwest Ballet (PNB), and co-founded Seattle Dance Project with Timothy Lynch in 2008. [ref: Performance at ACT Theatre tonight launches Seattle Dance Project, Seattle Post-Intelligencer]

== Early life and training ==
Tobiason began studying dance at age four in Lyndhurst, New Jersey. She subsequently trained with The Studio Workshop, Garden State Ballet, and the School of American Ballet (SAB) in New York City. [ref: Fifteen years of 'Nutcracker' keeps dancer on her toes, Seattle Post-Intelligencer]

== Career ==
=== Chicago City Ballet ===
Tobiason joined Chicago City Ballet in January 1983, under artistic directors Maria Tallchief and Paul Mejia. [ref: Chicago City Ballet: Cinderella] She performed in Mejia's Favorita, which was reviewed by the Chicago Tribune in September 1985. [ref: 2 Short Works Highlight City Ballet's Lively Show, Chicago Tribune]

=== Pacific Northwest Ballet ===
Tobiason joined Pacific Northwest Ballet in 1986 and was promoted to principal dancer in 1992. She performed with the company until 2002. [ref: PNB can't make 'Seven Sins' work, Seattle Post-Intelligencer] She also appeared in the film Nutcracker: The Motion Picture (1986), directed by Carroll Ballard. [ref: Nutcracker: The Motion Picture (1986), AFI Catalog]

Her repertory included traditional major roles such as Swanhilda in Coppélia, Dream Clara in Kent Stowell's production of The Nutcracker, Hermia in George Balanchine’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream (1999 BBC film). [ref: A Midsummer Night's Dream, HDVDARTS]. She danced in works by Paul Taylor, William Forsythe, Nacho Duato, and Val Caniparoli. In a 1992 review of PNB at the Kennedy Center, The Washington Post discussed her performance in George Balanchine's Rubies alongside Brent Davi. [ref: Dance, The Washington Post]

=== Seattle Dance Project ===
Tobiason and former PNB dancer Timothy Lynch launched Seattle Dance Project in 2008, a company of experienced dancers performing contemporary choreography. The debut performance at ACT Theatre included works by Donald Byrd, Molissa Fenley, Pat Catterson, and Olivier Wevers. [ref: Project One: A PNB Spin-Off Debuts, Seattle Weekly]

In a review of the company's debut, The Seattle Times critic Moira Macdonald singled out Tobiason's performance in Donald Byrd's Tatum Dance #2. [ref: Seattle Dance Project finds new moves, The Seattle Times]

Seattle Dance Project presented a full-evening dance production titled Project Orpheus. [ref: Review: SDP's 'Project Orpheus' benefits from roomier setting, The Seattle Times]. In 2009, she danced in Edwaard Liang's Flight of Angels with Oleg Gorboulev, receiving coverage in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer and Seattle Met. [ref: Seattle Dance Project's 'Project Two' is a real crowd pleaser, Seattle Post-Intelligencer]

== Choreography ==
Tobiason has choreographed many student performances as a faculty member at PNB and for Seattle International Dance Festival. Her 2018 work kairos received a favorable review from Marcie Sillman, who highlighted its combination of classical ballet and contemporary dance. [ref: Dance Diary – SIDF June 14, 2018, Seattle International Dance Festival]

== Introduction ==
Tijori Robo Investing is a Pakistani digital investment advisory platform operated by Shaikha Robo Securities (Private) Limited, a securities adviser licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP). The platform provides risk-based investment portfolios and securities advisory services, with brokerage execution and custody services provided through Chase Securities. [ref: ]

Tijori is designed primarily for individuals seeking to participate in Pakistan's equity markets through a structured investment approach without independently selecting and allocating every security in their investment portfolios. The platform incorporates features commonly associated with robo-investing technology, including investor risk profiling, model portfolio allocation, proportionate investment calculations and portfolio rebalancing tools. [ref: ]

Brokerage and custody services associated with the platform are provided through Chase Securities Pakistan (Private) Limited, a securities broker registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan (SECP) and a Trading Rights Entitlement Certificate (TREC) holder of the Pakistan Stock Exchange. Shaikha Robo Securities provides the technology platform and investment interface, while Chase Securities provides the brokerage infrastructure through which client securities transactions are processed. [ref: Shaikha Robo Securities Pvt Ltd Securities Advisor License]

The platform operates through a non-discretionary transaction model in which users retain responsibility for reviewing and authorizing securities transactions. Investment allocations and transaction calculations may be generated through software, but orders require client authorization before submission for execution.

Tijori's investment approach focuses on portfolio construction, diversification, periodic contributions and long-term participation in the equity market. The platform also provides educational resources intended to explain financial markets and investment concepts to retail users. [ref: ]

== History ==

=== Corporate background ===
Tijori Robo Investing was developed as a digital investment initiative intended to make participation in Pakistan's capital markets more accessible to individual investors.

The platform is associated with Shaikha Robo Securities (Private) Limited, a private company incorporated in Pakistan. Its founder and chief executive officer, Shahzeb Shaikha, has professional experience in financial services, securities brokerage and wealth management, including roles at Prudential Financial and Oppenheimer & Co. Inc. His professional background includes United States FINRA Series 7 and Series 66 registrations and Accredited Portfolio Management Advisor (APMA) credentials. [ref: IAPD - Investment Adviser Public Disclosure - Homepage, adviserinfo.sec.gov] [ref: IFMP Financial Advisors Certification] [ref: APMA Certification]

The development of Tijori was influenced by the challenges encountered by retail investors when entering securities markets, including the need to select individual companies, assess investment risk, determine appropriate allocations and monitor securities holdings.

The company sought to address these challenges by developing a digital platform combining model portfolio methodology with securities brokerage infrastructure.

=== Platform development ===
Development of the Tijori software platform took place during 2026, encompassing web and mobile applications, backend services, portfolio management tools and integration with brokerage systems.

Software development was undertaken by a Pakistan-based software development firm. The project included the implementation of account-opening workflows, subscription management, portfolio allocation calculations, order-processing interfaces, investment activity monitoring and administrative functions.

The portfolio management engine was designed to calculate stock allocations based on predefined portfolio models and available investment amounts. Because securities on the Pakistan Stock Exchange are generally traded in whole shares, the software incorporates calculations accounting for share quantities, market prices and residual cash.

Additional functionality was developed to support proportionate investments, partial portfolio liquidation, cash withdrawals and portfolio rebalancing.

The company also developed administrative workflows for reviewing investor information, processing account-related requests and coordinating activities with the executing brokerage firm.

=== Relationship with Chase Securities ===
Tijori established a technology and brokerage integration arrangement with Chase Securities Pakistan (Private) Limited to provide access to regulated securities-market infrastructure.

Chase Securities was incorporated in April 2021 and holds Pakistan Stock Exchange TREC No. 526. It is registered as a securities broker with the Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan. [ref: About Us - Chase Securities, chasesecurities.com]

Under the operating arrangement, Chase Securities is responsible for brokerage account infrastructure, trade execution, custody arrangements and relevant broker-side compliance functions.

Tijori provides a separate digital interface through which investors can access portfolio construction tools, account information and transaction functionality.

Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co., Ltd. (SSE: 688139) is a Chinese medical technology and life sciences enterprise operating under the healthcare ecosystem of Haier Group. [ref: Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co Ltd Company Profile, Reuters] Headquartered in Qingdao, Shandong, the company manufactures cold-chain storage equipment, biological safety equipment, automated laboratory equipment, and digital healthcare solutions. [ref: Listing Announcement: Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co., Ltd. (688139), Shanghai Stock Exchange]

Its systems are utilized globally across academic research institutes, biopharmaceutical companies, medical institutions, blood donation centers, and public health agencies. In October 2019, Haier Biomedical completed its initial public offering on the Science and Technology Innovation Board (STAR Market) of the Shanghai Stock Exchange.

== History ==
Qingdao Haier Biomedical Co., Ltd. was established on October 28, 2005, under the former name Qingdao Haier Special Electrical Appliances Co., Ltd. The company initially focused on biomedical refrigeration and subsequently expanded its operations into biobanking, healthcare cold-chain management, molecular diagnostics, and laboratory solutions.

* 2008: Provided biobanking solutions to the China Marrow Donor Program.
* 2011: Secured World Health Organization (WHO) Performance, Quality and Safety (PQS) prequalification for medical refrigerators and freezers; a company-developed refrigerator was carried aboard the Shenzhou-8 spacecraft.
* 2015–2017: Initiated research and development into internet-connected monitoring solutions and entered the point-of-care testing market.
* 2019: Completed its initial public offering on the Shanghai Stock Exchange STAR Market under stock code 688139.
* 2020–2023: Acquired Chongqing Sandawell Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. in 2020 and a stake in Suzhou Houhong Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd. in 2023 to expand pharmacy and cold-storage automation.
* 2024–2026: Expanded research into automated laboratory instruments and bioprocess technology applications.

== Operational Sectors and Product Categories ==
Haier Biomedical designs, manufactures, and distributes laboratory and medical equipment across four primary sectors:

=== Sample and Biobanking Solutions ===
* Cryogenic storage systems, including ultra-low temperature freezers operating at -86°C and -150°C, and hydrocarbon-based ecological freezers.
* Automated full-temperature-range biobanking systems for high-throughput sample preservation and retrieval.
* Specialized cryogenic systems deployed in research facilities and specialized environments.

=== Research and Biomanufacturing Solutions ===
* Cell processing workstations, cell culture systems, and cell preservation equipment.
* Laboratory safety and biosafety equipment, including CO₂ incubators, refrigerated centrifuges, Class II biological safety cabinets, and laminar flow clean benches.
* Biopharmaceutical consumable tracking systems and sterile preparation equipment.

=== Healthcare and Hospital Pharmacy Solutions ===
* Automated hospital pharmacy dispensing systems and medication management cabinets.
* Digital medical imaging equipment and clinical workflow support software.

=== Blood Management and Public Health Networks ===
* Internet-connected blood bank refrigerators and plasma freezers for inventory tracking across blood centers and hospitals.
* Solar-powered vaccine refrigerators, mobile vaccination vehicles, and immunization clinic equipment designed for public health infrastructure. [ref: Cold Chain Equipment Guide, UNICEF Supply Division]

== Global Operations and Partnerships ==
Haier Biomedical operates across more than 160 countries and territories. The company maintains regional technical support hubs and distribution networks in North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, the Middle East, and Africa.

The company has collaborated with international organizations—including the World Health Organization, UNICEF, and GAVI—to supply solar-powered vaccine refrigeration equipment and cold-chain infrastructure to health systems in developing economies.

== Sustainability ==
Haier Biomedical publishes annual environmental and governance performance disclosures. Its sustainability initiatives focus on:
* Transitioning refrigeration product lines to natural hydrocarbon refrigerants to lower global warming potential.
* Manufacturing zero-electricity, solar-direct-drive cold-storage equipment for off-grid medical infrastructure.
* Implementing green manufacturing processes certified under international environmental management standards.
