Draft text:
The Alleys () is a 2021 Jordanian crime thriller film written and directed by Bassel Ghandour in his feature directorial debut. Set in a neighbourhood of East Amman, the film follows a small-time hustler whose secret relationship sets off a chain of blackmail, gossip and violence. It stars Emad Azmi, Baraka Rahmani, Munther Rayahnah, Nadira Omran and Maisa Abd Elhadi.

The film had its world premiere in the Piazza Grande section of the 74th Locarno Film Festival in August 2021, the first Jordanian feature to screen at the festival. It was released in Jordanian and Saudi cinemas in June 2022. Its uncensored version was released on Netflix in January 2023, where it became one of the most-watched films in Jordan; its profanity and its portrayal of Jordanian society provoked criticism from conservative members of the Jordanian parliament.

== Plot ==
In a gossip-ridden neighbourhood of East Amman, Ali, a young hustler who earns fees by steering tourists to an escort bar, is secretly in love with Lana. They hide the relationship from Lana's mother, Aseel, a beauty salon owner who disapproves of Ali's lower-class background. When Aseel receives a surveillance video of the couple in a compromising position, along with a demand for hush money, she turns to Abbas, a local gangster, to suppress the video and drive Ali away from her daughter; in exchange, she agrees to make up Abbas's call girls in her salon. As Aseel pressures Lana to accept another suitor, Ali urges her to elope with him and, before they flee, robs Abbas of the protection money he collects from the neighbourhood, cutting out the gangster's tongue in the fight. When Lana finds Ali's gun and the stolen cash, she abandons him, and Abbas and his loyal lieutenant Hanadi set out for revenge, leading to further violence.

== Cast ==
* Emad Azmi as Ali
* Baraka Rahmani as Lana
* Munther Rayahnah as Abbas
* Nadira Omran as Aseel
* Maisa Abd Elhadi as Hanadi

== Production ==
The Alleys is the first feature directed by Bassel Ghandour, who previously co-wrote and produced Theeb (2014), which was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film at the 88th Academy Awards and won the BAFTA Award for Outstanding Debut. The film was produced by Rula Nasser of The Imaginarium Films and Yousef Abed Alnabi of Bayt Al Shawareb, with Shahinaz El-Akkad's Lagoonie Film Production as co-producer. It is a co-production between Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It was filmed in Jabal Al Natheef, a densely built neighbourhood of East Amman.

The project was developed through the EAVE Producers Workshop and received support from the Jordan Film Fund of the Royal Film Commission, the Doha Film Institute, Dubai Film Connection and the Red Sea Lodge. At the 2020 Cairo Film Connection, the co-production platform of the Cairo International Film Festival, it won the Badyã Award and the New Century Productions Prize, each worth US$10,000. Earlier that year it received the Works in Progress Post-production Development Award at the Eastern Promises industry programme of the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival.

The cinematography is by Justin Hamilton, the editing by Eyad Hamam, and the original score by Nasser Sharaf. A soundtrack album was released in September 2022.

== Release ==
The Alleys premiered in August 2021 in the Piazza Grande at the 74th Locarno Film Festival. It was the first Jordanian feature selected for the festival and the first Arab film shown in the Piazza Grande since 2008. It then competed for the Sutherland Award for best first feature at the BFI London Film Festival, and had its Arab premiere at the inaugural Red Sea International Film Festival in Jeddah in December 2021. In January 2022 it became the first Jordanian film selected for the International Film Festival Rotterdam.

The film was released commercially on 9 June 2022 in Jordan, through Arab Media Network, and in Saudi Arabia, through Rowad Media, opening in four Jordanian and 21 Saudi cinemas. The theatrical version had scenes with explicit language either removed or bleeped. It was released in the United Arab Emirates on 6 October 2022 and in Egypt in November 2022. MAD Solutions handled distribution in the Arab world, and the Paris-based company Elle Driver handled international sales.

The uncensored version was released on Netflix on 5 January 2023. In July 2024 it was added to the Arabic streaming service Shahid.

== Reception ==
=== Critical response ===
Reviewing the film from Locarno for Variety, Jay Weissberg found it "unattractively shot and weighed down by too many unappealing, witless characters", though he praised Nadira Omran's performance as Aseel. Screen Daily described the film as "by turns dark comedy, mystery thriller and crime drama". After its Netflix release, The New York Times recommended it as an international streaming pick, describing it as "somewhere between a mafia movie and a comedy of errors". Writing for Arab News in February 2023, William Mullally called it "the best-received film set in Jordan" since Theeb.

Christodoulos Constantinou was born in 2007, in Paphos, Cyprus. He emerged in the Cypriot classical music scene at a young age, composing music for the theatre - ancient and modern drama, and mainly concert classical music. His music is often characterized as expressionistic, neoromantic, and surrealistic. Major influences on him are literature, poetry, and cinema, but mainly his personal experiences and social perceptions. He studies Composition at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

At the age of 16, he completed the Composition intensive at The Juilliard School, where his first major pieces were performed and he had masterclasses with John Corigliano, Wynton Marsalis, Eric Whitacre, John Mackey, Tania León, Amy Beth Kirsten and others, and continued studying with Daniel Felsenfeld.
Pieces of his have been performed in Cyprus, Greece, Slovenia, the USA, the Netherlands and Italy. He has been awarded the first prize in the Brahms Competition(2025) and also won first and third prizes in the 6th International Music Olympiad in Cyprus(2024) and the 5th International Music Olympiad in Slovenia(2021). He also served in the military band of the Cypriot National Guard (ΣΜΕΦ), as a trumpet player.

Jonathane Ricci

Jonathane Ricci is a lawyer licensed in New York and Michigan. The New York State Unified Court System lists Jonathane Michael Ricci as a currently registered attorney. The State Bar of Michigan's attorney directory lists Jonathane M. Ricci as an active member in good standing.[1][2]

JR Wealth Management identifies Ricci as its founder and chief executive officer.[3] Because this description comes from the company's own website, it is used here only as an attributed statement and not as independent evidence of notability.

Education and student leadership

Ricci studied at the Detroit College of Law at Michigan State University. The law school's Spring 1998 issue of Amicus identified him as a member of the class of 1998 and as president of the Detroit College of Law/Michigan State University Student Bar Association during the 1997–1998 academic year.[4]

The issue appeared during a period of institutional transition for the law school. Its cover story described the Detroit College of Law at Michigan State University and the dedication of a new law-school building in East Lansing on April 21, 1998.[4]

Student Bar Association presidency

In “Forging Traditions of the Future,” published in Amicus, Ricci described the Student Bar Association as a longstanding part of student life at the law school. He wrote that the organization had previously been known as the Student Senate and discussed changes to its structure, executive positions, and constitution during the school's transition to Michigan State University.[4]

The article described Ricci's role as president during 1997 and 1998 and referred to the association's work representing students, organizing student participation, and developing the structure of student government. It also discussed the election of student officers and the creation or clarification of executive responsibilities within the association.[4]

Ricci's article addressed the relationship between student leadership and the future direction of the law school. It emphasized student involvement, participation in school affairs, and the importance of preserving institutional traditions while adapting to the law school's new affiliation.[4]

1998 building dedication and speech

An archival video held by Michigan State University's University Archives and Historical Collections documents the April 21, 1998, dedication of the Detroit College of Law building at the Wharton Center on the MSU campus. The archive identifies former United States president Gerald R. Ford as the event's keynote speaker and lists the recording as part of the Media Communications Records, resource identifier A008293.[5]

In the recording, the dean introduces Ricci as the president of the Detroit College of Law at Michigan State University Student Bar Association and as a member of the law school's graduating class of 1998. The introduction occurs at approximately 57 minutes and 22 seconds into the recording. Ford is introduced later as the 38th president of the United States and keynote speaker.[5]

Ricci then addresses the audience from the platform at approximately 57 minutes and 40 seconds. He identifies himself as a graduating student and Student Bar Association president, thanks the platform guests, and explains that he was invited to speak on behalf of the students. He discusses his perspective as a student who began his legal education at the Detroit campus and completed it at the East Lansing campus, and describes the law school's traditions, faculty, students, and expected opportunities at Michigan State University. He concludes by thanking those attending and inviting them to join the procession to the new law-college building. His remarks continue until approximately 61 minutes and 57 seconds.[5]

The recording shows Ricci speaking on the same platform at which Ford is present. It therefore provides direct archival evidence that Ricci and Ford appeared at the same building-dedication event and shared the platform during the ceremony.[5]

Legal career

The New York State Unified Court System attorney record lists Ricci's date of admission as July 19, 2011, and identifies the Third Department as his department of admission. The record lists his registration status as “Currently registered.”[1]

The State Bar of Michigan directory lists Ricci's Michigan license number as P58740 and his admission date as November 20, 1998. It describes his status as “Active Member in Good Standing.”[2]

JR Wealth Management

JR Wealth Management's website describes Ricci as the firm's founder and identifies the organization with wealth-management and related strategic services.[3] As a company-controlled source, the website is suitable for documenting the company's own description of its leadership, services, and branding, but it does not by itself establish independent recognition or Wikipedia notability.

Ivan Fernando Rodríguez Huerta is a Mexican-born global operations executive, supply chain strategist, and author based in the United States. == Early Life and Education ==

Rodríguez was born in Mexico and pursued academic training focused on industrial operations. He attended the Tecnológico de Monterrey before continuing his professional business management studies at the University of Phoenix.

== Career ==

Rodríguez's career spans more than 25 years of leadership within international industrial, manufacturing, and technology sectors. Lewis Raven Wallace (they/ze/he) is an award-winning journalist, author, and activist for trans rights. His first book, The View from Somewhere: Undoing the Myth of Journalistic Objectivity [ref: The View from Somewhere: Undoing the Myth of Journalistic Objectivity, University of Chicago Press], explores how the ideology of "objective" news reporting in the United States has been a tool of gatekeeping, exclusion, and complicity with racism and transphobia. His second book, Radical Unlearning: The Art and Science of Creating Change from Within [ref: ], draws on the science of neuroplasticity and trauma healing to show how people create the conditions to let go of deeply held beliefs and transform harm. Lewis previously worked in public radio and is a long-time activist engaged in prison abolition, racial justice, and queer and trans liberation.

Career:

Early on in his career, Wallace was the economics reporter and managing editor at WYSO Public Radio in Yellow Springs, Ohio. After his time there, Wallace worked for public radio's Marketplace in the New York bureau. At WYSO, he founded a prison radio project and worked closely with youth radio and community voices programs, teaching community members to make radio stories.

In early 2017, Wallace, then a reporter at American Public Media’s Marketplace, published a piece on his personal blog in which he considered the role of an “objective” press as the country transitioned into a new presidential administration, one that had brought with it transphobia, racism, and regular attacks on the press [ref: Truth-Telling - Columbia Journalism Review, www.cjr.org]. Wallace was fired when he refused to take down the post, which sparked the idea for his first book, The View from Somewhere. He was fired because the post violated Marketplace’s ethics code of journalistic objectivity.

Wallace wrote The View from Somewhere, published in 2019 by the University of Chicago Press [ref: The View from Somewhere: Undoing the Myth of Journalistic Objectivity, University of Chicago Press], an exploration of objectivity in the newsroom and how it has historically silenced marginalized perspectives.

In 2025, Beacon Press published his second book, Radical Unlearning, a guide to unlearning harmful beliefs and changing minds (source).

His third book, Journalism as Resistance, is set for release in May 2027.

Personal life:

Wallace was born and raised in the Midwest. He is currently based in Durham, North Carolina. He is currently a student of history at Duke University [ref: Scholars@Duke publication: Journalism as Resistance: How to Fight Authoritarianism with Movement Media and Grassroots Reporting, scholars.duke.edu].

Awards and nominations:

Wallace has been the recipient of numerous awards and nominations, including the Nieman Visting Journalism Fellow at Harvard University in 2020 [ref: about, Lewis Raven Wallace] and the Abolition Fellowship in 2025. [ref: Lewis Raven Wallace, Interrupting Criminalization]

== Richardson Sales Performance ==
Richardson also known as Richardson Sales Performance is a global sales training and performance company headquartered in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. It develops and delivers sales training programs, including facilitator-led workshops, individual coaching, and technology-based learning platforms, built around Consultative Selling and Challenger methodologies. Richardson's clients span across industries including healthcare, financial services, technology, manufacturing, insurance and retail banking.

=== History ===
Richardson was founded in 1978 by Linda Richardson [ref: About Linda], a Wharton educator and author who's credited with the movement toward "Consultative Selling", an approach to sales training that emphasizes understanding a customer's needs before presenting a product or solution.

Linda Richardson wrote several books on effective sales technique and process over the following decades. Her first, "Stop Telling, Start Selling: How to Use Customer-Focused Dialogue to Close Sales [ref: Stop Telling, Start Selling: How to Use Customer-Focused Dialogue to Close Sales]" (McGraw-Hill [ref: McGraw-Hill Homepage]), was the first. Published in 1993, re-published with a revised edition in 1997. She followed this with "Sales Coaching: Making the Great Leap from Sales Manager to Sales Coach [ref: Sales Coaching: Making the Great Leap from Sales Manager to Sales Coach]" (McGraw-Hill), first published in 1996 with a revised edition in 2008.

Additionally, in 2008, Linda Richardson published "Perfect Selling: Open the Door. Close the Deal" [ref: Perfect Selling] (McGraw-Hill), a book on consultative selling techniques that became a noted release landing on a spot on the New York Times, [ref: Richardson's Perfect Selling Book Listed on New York Times Best Seller List, Learning News - the learning sector's newswire'] USA Today [ref: Richardson's Perfect Selling Book Reaches USA Today Best Seller List, Learning News - the learning sector's newswire']and BusinessWeek [ref: Richardson's New Book Perfect Selling on the BusinessWeek Best Seller List, Learning News - the learning sector's newswire']bestseller lists, respectively.

By 2010, Richardson received a growth investment from ClearLight Partners; [ref: ClearLight Partners Homepage] Linda Richardson moved into the role of executive chairman while David DiStefano moved into the role of chief executive officer.

In 2019, Richardson merged with Sales Performance International (SPI) [ref: Sales Performance International And Richardson To Merge Forces, Forrester], a portfolio company of private equity firm Kartesia. This merger combined Richardson's primarily U.S. client base with SPI's presence in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Then in 2022, Richardson acquired DoubleDigitSales [ref: Richardson Sales Performance Acquires DoubleDigit Sales] (DDS) to expand its Canadian footprint and product offerings.

In 2023, Los Angeles-based private equity firm TrueLink Capital acquired Richardson as its second portfolio company. According to the Los Angeles Business Journal, [ref: Truelink Capital Adds to Portfolio, Los Angeles Business Journal] talks between the two organizations began in October 2022 and the deal closed in June 2023.

Richardson purchased UK based e4enable in February 2024 [ref: Truelink Raises $875M Fund, Los Angeles Business Journal]to expand its technology offerings, and in September 2024, acquired Challenger, a sales and marketing strategy firm known for its "Challenger Sale" [ref: ] methodology.

Richardson is currently under the leadership of President and CEO, John Elsey since 2015.

=== Recognition ===
Richardson was one of nine vendors evaluated in Forrester's "The Forrester Wave: Sales Training and Services" Q1, 2020 and later, the Gartner Magic Quadrant in 2022 as a "Leader" in its 2022 Magic Quadrant for Sales Training Providers. The organization has been included in Training Industry's annual "Top 20 Sales Training Companies" lists in multiple years, most recently in 2026.

The Behring Foundation (Fundação Behring) is a Brazilian family philanthropic foundation focused on education and technology, founded in 2020 by Alex Behring and Daniele Behring. Alex Behring is a co-founder and partner of 3G Capital and serves on the Board of Dean's Advisors of Harvard Business School. The foundation runs three programs for young people in technology, Behring Academy, Behring Scholars and Behring Founders, and a fourth initiative, Behring Network, through which it funds partnerships with academic and research institutions. According to the foundation, it also supports research initiatives at Hospital Pequeno Príncipe, a pediatric hospital in Curitiba.

== History ==
The foundation was established in 2020. It has funded scholarships at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio) since the early 2020s. In December 2024 it donated R$ 35million (about US$ 5.8 million) to the university for the creation of the PUC-Behring Institute of Artificial Intelligence; it was the largest single donation PUC-Rio had received since its founding in the 1940s. [ref: PUC-Rio establishes institute for teaching and research in Artificial Intelligence and will offer a degree in the field by 2025, O Globo] [ref: PUC-Rio recebe da Fundação Behring maior doação de sua história - Vatican News, www.vaticannews.va]

In 2022 the foundation co-founded Instituto Rio Aquatics, a Rio de Janeiro non-governmental organisation that works with children and adolescents in situations of social vulnerability through swimming and water polo. [ref: Projeto carioca une natação e educação para transformar vida de jovens em vulnerabilidad, Educação básica]The organisation opened its first site at Vasco da Gama in May 2022 and a second at the Júlio Delamare aquatic park in April 2023. The foundation is listed as one of its sustaining partners.

== Programs ==

=== Behring Academy ===
Behring Academy is a free online technology program for students from the ninth grade of Brazilian lower secondary school through the end of secondary school. Participants have won 24 medals at the Brazilian Informatics Olympiad (Olimpíada Brasileira de Informática) since the program began; six of them in its first year. More than 3,500 students have applied to the program and 101 have been selected. [ref: Fundação Behring abre inscrições para formação online e gratuita em tecnologia, Estudar Fora] [ref: Behring Academy – Fundação Behring]

=== Behring Scholars ===
Behring Scholars awards undergraduate scholarships in technology fields in Brazil and abroad. At Carnegie Mellon University, the foundation funds two Brazilian students a year enrolled in the School of Computer Science or the Electrical and Computer Engineering Department; the award may cover up to the full cost of attendance for the duration of their undergraduate education, depending on financial need. [ref: Behring Foundation gift supports international undergrads in tech, engineering.cmu.edu] The university described the gift as the first of its kind there. [ref: International Student Funding Opportunities - Student Financial Services - Division of Enrollment Management - Carnegie Mellon University, www.cmu.edu] As of 2026, the foundation reported more than 200 scholarships granted, over 180 of them active, at more than 40 universities in Brazil and abroad. [ref: The Behring Foundation-OBMEP Tech Scholarship Supports Medalists in STEM Courses, IMPA - Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics] [ref: Behring Foundation awards 10 scholarships of R$ 900 to OBMEP medalists - IMPA Tech, IMPA Tech - O programa de graduação do IMPA] [ref: Fundação Behring lança bolsa exclusiva para brasileiros na melhor faculdade de Ciência da Computação dos EUA, Estudar Fora] [ref: Behring Scholars – Fundação Behring]

=== Behring Founders ===
Behring Founders, launched in 2025, supports young technology entrepreneurs through mentorship, networking and funding. According to the foundation, participants may receive up to R$ 200,000 (about US$ 37,000) without the foundation taking equity in their companies. [ref: Behring Founders – Fundação Behring]

=== Behring Network ===
Behring Network funds partnerships in science and technology. These include the PUC-Behring Institute of Artificial Intelligence at PUC-Rio, which will be housed in the Behring Building, a 3,300 m² facility on the university's Gávea campus designed pro bono by Bernardes Arquitetura; construction began in August 2025. = Eytmolophile (/ˌɛtɪˈmɒləʊfaɪl/, noun) =

=== (eh-tih-MOH-lo-file) ===

== Definition: A person who loves, collects, or is deeply fascinated by the origins, histories, and evolutions of words. ==

==== Etymology: Formed within English by compounding etymolo- (representing Greek etymología "study of the true meaning of words") + -phile (representing Greek phílos "loving, dear"). ====

Part 1: The Anatomy of Etymolo- [ref: ]

The first element derives from the Ancient Greek compound noun ἐτυμολογία (etymología), which breaks down into two distinct Proto-Indo-European (PIE) ancestral branches:

# The Core (Etymo-):
#* Ancient Greek: Comes from ἔτυμος (étumos), meaning "true, real, or factual."
#* The PIE Root: This traces back to the Proto-Indo-European root *es- (meaning "to be"). This is the exact same prehistoric root that gave English the words is, am, and essence. To the ancient Greeks, finding a word's origin wasn't just a hobby—it was an attempt to find the "true, essential being" of the thing itself.
# The Suffix (-logia):
#* Ancient Greek: Comes from -λογία (-logía), denoting a branch of study or speak. This comes from λόγος (lógos), meaning "word, reason, or speech."
#* The PIE Root: Traces back to *leǵ-, meaning "to gather or collect." (The logic being: you gather your thoughts, collect words, and speak them). This same root gave us collect, lecture, and elegant.

Part 2: The Journey Through Latin [ref: -phile - Etymology & Meaning of the Suffix, etymonline]

When the Romans conquered Greece, they adopted Greek intellectual terms.

* The Greek etymología was transliterated directly into Classical Latin as etymologia.
* In Latin, it kept the exact same meaning: "the explanation of the origin of words."
* It passed into Old French as ethimologie, and English borrowed it in the late 14th century, eventually streamlining the spelling back to its cleaner Latin/Greek roots: etymology. [ref: ]

Part 3: The Anatomy of -phile

The second element is a classic English combining form that allows us to turn any concept into a passion.

* Ancient Greek: Comes from φίλος (phílos), meaning "dear, beloved, or friendly," and the suffix -φιλία (-philía), meaning "affectionate love."
* The PIE Root: It stems from the root *bili-, which meant "good, friendly, or kind" in ancient dialects.
* Unlike eros (romantic love) or agape (spiritual love), philos is the love of deep affinity, companionship, and intense intellectual attraction.

FOR MORE IN-DEPTH READING ABOUT ETYMOLOGY [ref: THE EVOLUTION OF ETYMOLOGY: WORDS AS WINDOWS INTO HISTORY, SHOKH LIBRARY] Abdulazizova Maftuna, The Evolution of Etymology (PDF Available): SHOKH LIBRARY (Vol. 1 November, 2025).

[ref: hms.harvard.edu] Christy DeSmith, Ancient-DNA: Study Identifies Originators of Indo-European Language FamilyFindings resolve “steppe hypothesis” enigma (Harvard Gazette: 5 February, 2025).

[ref: ] Vinayak, Logesh, Proto Indo European Roots and their Descendants, papers.ssrn.com (12 January, 2024).

Mountain Wizard is an American independent apparel brand founded in June 2024 by [https://www.kruizechristensen.com Kruize Christensen], a seventh-generation Montanan. The company originated in Fairfield, Montana, and operates primarily through an online store. The brand produces graphic apparel inspired by Montana landscapes, outdoor experiences, and personal storytelling.

== History ==
Mountain Wizard was established in June 2024 in Fairfield, Montana, by Kruize Christensen. The brand began as a personal creative project, evolving from the founder’s interest in combining art, photography, and digital design into wearable products.

Christensen’s background in drafting, 3D printing, photography, and graphic design contributed to the development of the brand’s visual style. Early production focused on limited-run designs distributed through the company’s online platform.

== Founder ==

Kruize Christensen is the founder and owner of Mountain Wizard. A seventh-generation Montanan, Christensen draws inspiration from his upbringing and environment in Montana.

His creative background includes experience in drafting, 3D printing, photography, and digital design tools such as Adobe Photoshop. These skills influence the brand’s emphasis on stylized and silhouette-based artwork.

== Designs ==

=== Hidden Bay Lovers ===

Hidden Bay Lovers was the first design released by Mountain Wizard. The design was inspired by a personal experience in which Christensen met his girlfriend, later his wife, while paddleboarding in Hidden Bay on Swan Lake in Montana.

The design aimed to capture the scene through silhouette artwork rather than traditional photography, establishing the brand’s focus on creating evocative and symbolic imagery.

=== Other designs ===
Following its initial release, Mountain Wizard expanded its catalog to include additional T-shirt and apparel designs centered on themes such as:

* Mountain Silhouette
* Buckin' Montana
* Montana Heritage
* Montana Horror
* Norwegian Heritage
* Personal and relationship-based narratives

== Company name ==
The name Mountain Wizard is derived from a combination of personal nicknames associated with the founder.

"Mountain" references both the Spanish origin of the word Montana, meaning "mountain", and a nickname Christensen received as a football player, where he was known as "Mountain Man" for his physical strength.

"Wizard" originates from a nickname earned during his school years, where he was referred to as a "Tech Wizard" due to his aptitude for working with and repairing technology.

== Business model ==
Mountain Wizard operates as a direct-to-consumer brand, selling products primarily through its official website. This model allows the company to maintain creative control over design and production while reaching a broader audience.

{AfC submission|t||ts=20261023183752|u=BioPhilosophyGuy|ns=118|demo=}}

Omer Gokcumen is an evolutionary anthropologist and geneticist. He is a professor of biological sciences at the University at Buffalo, part of the State University of New York system. His research examines the evolution of genetic variation in humans and other primates, particularly structural variation involving the deletion and duplication of DNA sequences. [ref: Gokcumen, Omer, University at Buffalo]

His work has addressed archaic human ancestry, the maintenance of genetic polymorphisms by natural selection, and the evolution of genes associated with dietary adaptation. His research on the evolution of human salivary amylase genes has received coverage in The New York Times, The Scientist, and Smithsonian Magazine. [ref: How Early Humans Evolved to Eat Starch, The New York Times] [ref: How did Humans Adapt to Digest Starchy Foods?, The Scientist] [ref: Can't Get Enough Carbs? That Craving Might Have Started More Than 800,000 Years Ago, Smithsonian Magazine]

== Education and academic career ==

Gokcumen earned a bachelor's degree in molecular biology and genetics from Boğaziçi University in Istanbul in 2002. He subsequently earned a PhD in anthropology from the University of Pennsylvania in 2008, where he studied with Theodore G. Schurr. [ref: Omer Gokcumen – ORCID record, ORCID] His doctoral research investigated the relationship between cultural practices and patterns of human genetic variation in communities in Anatolia. [ref: BioNews 2013, University at Buffalo, Department of Biological Sciences] [ref: Omer Gokcumen: Faculty Profile, University at Buffalo]

From 2008 to 2013, Gokcumen undertook postdoctoral research in genomics with Charles Lee at the Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School Department of Pathology. [ref: People, Gokcumen Lab] The two co-authored a 2009 methodological review of copy-number variation analysis in primates. He was also involved in studies of genomic structural variation in primate evolution and ancient balancing selection in human regulatory DNA. [ref: Copy number variants (CNVs) in primate species using array-based comparative genomic hybridization, Methods] [ref: Primate genome architecture influences structural variation mechanisms and functional consequences, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences] [ref: Balancing Selection on a Regulatory Region Exhibiting Ancient Variation That Predates Human–Neandertal Divergence, PLOS Genetics]

He joined the University at Buffalo as an assistant professor in 2013, became an associate professor in 2019, and was promoted to professor in 2023.

At Buffalo, Gokcumen established a research group investigating evolutionary and anthropological genomics, with an emphasis on the origin, evolutionary history, and functional consequences of genomic structural variants.

== Research ==

=== Genomic structural variation and human evolution ===

Gokcumen's research focuses on structural changes in the genome, including deletions, duplications, and copy-number polymorphisms. His laboratory studies how these forms of genetic variation arise, persist in populations, and influence phenotypes and adaptation.

In 2017, Gokcumen and colleagues published a study of variation in MUC7, a gene encoding a salivary mucin. The researchers identified associations between genetic variation at the locus and the composition of the oral microbiome. Population genetic analyses also suggested that a divergent MUC7 haplotype may have originated in an unidentified archaic African hominin lineage and entered the ancestors of present-day humans through interbreeding. [ref: Archaic Hominin Introgression in Africa Contributes to Functional Salivary MUC7 Genetic Variation, Molecular Biology and Evolution]

In 2023, Gokcumen co-authored a study examining ancient deletion polymorphisms shared between modern humans and archaic hominins. The researchers reported evidence that balancing selection contributed to the maintenance of some deletion variants over extended evolutionary periods, including variants associated with immune and metabolic traits. [ref: Balancing selection on genomic deletion polymorphisms in humans, eLife]

=== Evolution of amylase genes and dietary adaptation ===

Another area of Gokcumen's research concerns the evolutionary history of amylase, an enzyme involved in starch digestion. In a 2019 study published in eLife, Gokcumen and collaborators investigated amylase gene copy-number variation across mammalian species. They found that independent expansions of amylase gene families were associated with dietary preferences, particularly starch consumption. [ref: Independent amylase gene copy number bursts correlate with dietary preferences in mammals, eLife]

Brandi Morin is an acclaimed French, Cree, and Iroquois journalist. == Career ==

=== Reporting ===
In 2013 Morin worked as a freelance writer at Indian Country Today. In April 2015 she began her work as a journalist across various television stations and media companies, including Aboriginal Peoples Television Network, CBC/Radio-Canada, and Canada's National Observer. === Memoir ===
While doing her freelance work, Morin wrote her debut memoir, "Our Voice of Fire: A Memoir of a Warrior Rising," which was published August 2, 2022 by House of Anansi Press, in which she uses her experience as a survivor of the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls crisis to tell the stories of those who did not survive. The book became a national bestseller shortly after its release and received both the Memoir of the Year and the Wilfrid Eggleston prizes at the 2023 Alberta Literary Awards. SynchronoGeometry is a novel theoretical framework in geometry and the philosophy of time, introduced by Saadat Samadi, an independent researcher, in 2025. The theory defines time not as an external dimension, but as an intrinsic, rhythmic, and local property at every point in space.

== Definition of the Theory ==
In SynchronoGeometry, every point on a spatial manifold has its own specific temporal frequency. This perspective causes geometric structures such as geodesic paths, surfaces, and triangles to change dynamically and in a time-dependent manner. Unlike classical geometries such as Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian geometry, this theory enables the modeling of non-causal relations and meaningful synchronies. [ref: ]

== Difference from Classical Geometries ==
In traditional geometries, time is considered an external and universal parameter. However, in SynchronoGeometry, time is defined intrinsically and locally at every point in space, which leads to structures that deform in response to temporal rhythms.

== Applications ==
SynchronoGeometry may find application in the following areas:

* Theoretical physics: Redefining spacetime structures in quantum models
* Cognitive science: Modeling temporal rhythms in neural networks
* Philosophy of science: Understanding meaningful synchronies in human systems
* Interactive media design: Spatial structures with local temporal responses

Draft: Multiple Listing Organ Transplantation

Draft text:
Multiple listing is the practice by which a candidate for organ transplantation registers on the waiting list at more than one transplant program. In the United States it is permitted under the policies of the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN), which first allowed it in 1987. Supporters describe it as a way for patients in areas with long waits to reach programs with shorter ones; critics argue that it mainly benefits patients who can afford to travel and to undergo more than one evaluation.

== Policy ==
OPTN Policy 3.4.F allows a candidate to be registered at more than one transplant program. Under Policy 3.2, programs must inform patients of this option and of whether the program itself accepts candidates who are registered elsewhere. Each program decides for itself whether to accept such candidates. Guidance for patients published by the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS), which has operated the OPTN under federal contract, also addresses transferring accumulated waiting time from one program to another.

== History ==
The OPTN board adopted a resolution on August 10, 1987, allowing patients to be added to the waiting lists of more than one transplant program. The practice was prohibited from January to March 1988 and survived repeal attempts in 1988, 1994 and 2001; the board last considered modifying the policy in 2003. Media coverage of the 2009 liver transplant of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs in Tennessee brought wider public attention to the practice.

In January 2023 the OPTN Ethics Committee released a white paper for public comment that recommended removing multiple listing as an option except for candidates who are difficult to match. Feedback was mixed, and professional societies including the American Society of Transplant Surgeons and the American Society of Transplantation raised concerns. The committee removed its recommendations before presenting the paper to the board, and on June 26, 2023, the OPTN board declined to approve it.

== Use ==
Registry analyses summarized in a 2025 article in Frontiers in Transplantation found that 3.3% of liver transplant candidates listed from 1995 to 2000, and 2.3% of those listed from 2005 to 2011, were multiply listed. An OPTN snapshot found 1.5% of liver candidates multiply listed on December 31, 2021.

The Ethics Committee's 2023 analysis found that multiply listed liver candidates were more likely than singly listed candidates to have private insurance (68.8% versus 50.8%) and less likely to be covered by Medicaid (5.7% versus 20.1%). It concluded that the policy, although formally open to every patient, does not give patients a fair and equal opportunity to use it. The same analysis found that multiply listed liver recipients had a longer median waiting time than singly listed recipients, and stated that the data were insufficient to show that the practice increases the number of transplants performed.

== Debate ==
Supporters have presented multiple listing as a response to geographic disparities in access. A 2014 perspective in The New England Journal of Medicine described geography as destiny for transplant candidates. A modeling study published in Management Science in 2017, conducted under the earlier kidney allocation system based on donation service areas, found that multiple listing could substantially improve geographic equity and that the inequity would disappear if enough patients could multiply list; its authors proposed an affordable private-jet service, OrganJet, to make this practical. A 2020 registry study reported that listing in more than one region increased transplant rates for liver candidates with MELD scores below 15.

Critics have focused on equity and system effects. An editorial in the same issue of Transplantation as the 2020 study argued that multiple listing helps a few patients but does not address the organ shortage. The authors of the 2025 Frontiers article stated that the United States is the only country known to allow multiple listing and argued that its use should be confined to defined situations in which it is justified. They also noted that multiple listing can substantially improve access for candidates with low MELD scores whose local program does not use extended-criteria livers, such as older or donation-after-circulatory-death organs.

* Liver transplantation
* Organ procurement organization

Draft: Yazid ibn Muawiya's tomb

Draft text:
The destruction of the tomb of Yazid ibn Muawiya refers to the reported loss and destruction of the burial site of the second Umayyad caliph Yazid I (c. 647 – 683).

== Background ==
Yazid I ruled as caliph from 680 to 683 CE. He died in November 683 CE in the town of Hawwarin, between Damascus and Palmyra, during the expedition to suppress the revolt of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. [ref: The Arab Kingdom and its Fall, University of Calcutta]

== Burial ==
Early Islamic historians including al-Tabari report that Yazid was buried in Hawwarin. [ref: The History of al-Tabari, Volume 20: The Collapse of Sufyanid Authority, SUNY Press] Later traditions place a commemorative grave in the Bab al-Saghir cemetery in Damascus.

== Tomb location ==
Two locations are traditionally associated with Yazid I:
* Hawwarin: The contemporary historical burial place.
* Bab al-Saghir, Damascus: A later traditional grave within the historic cemetery, where several Umayyad figures are buried. The exact identification is disputed.

== Reports of destruction and loss ==
Medieval sources do not describe a formal monumental tomb surviving from the Umayyad period. Over the centuries, the grave in Damascus became unmarked and was reported by travelers and local historians as lost, ruined, or destroyed due to neglect, urban expansion of the cemetery, and periodic conflicts in Syria. [ref: Le Califat de Yazid Ier, Imprimerie Catholique]

There is no archaeological evidence of a surviving structure. Modern surveys of Bab al-Saghir list the site as unidentified or no longer extant. [ref: Bab al-Saghir Cemetery - Islamic Heritage Sites]

== Historical debate ==
Historians note that early Umayyad graves were typically simple and unmarked, following early Islamic burial customs. The absence of a marked tomb is therefore consistent with contemporary practice, rather than a single documented act of intentional destruction. [ref: The First Dynasty of Islam: The Umayyad Caliphate AD 661-750, Routledge]

[ref: Steve Ditko in the 1960s: In His Own Words, in His Interviews, in the Words of the Fans Who Knew Him, Totalmojo Productions] [ref: Founders of Comic Fandom: A Biographical Who's Who of Publishers, Dealers, Collectors, Writers, Artists, and Other Luminaries of the 1950s and 1960s, Pulp Hero Press] Weingroff published the fanzine Whiz-Bang and wrote articles for fan publications including Rocket's Blast Comicollector, focusing on early Spider-Man comics by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko. [ref: Blasts from the Readers, Rocket's Blast Comicollector] [ref: Forbush Gazette #1 Review, SpiderFan.org]

Weingroff studied at the University of Maryland, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in English. [ref: Richard F. Weingroff Biography, Federal Highway Administration] After graduating from college, he served in the United States Air Force from 1968 to 1972. Stationed at Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio, Texas, he worked as a reading skills instructor.

== History career ==
In 1973, Weingroff joined the Federal Highway Administration as a technical writer and information specialist, handling public inquiries, congressional correspondence, and agency speeches.

In the 1980s, he began writing articles and historical overviews on American road development. His research covers U.S. highway systems, President Dwight D. Eisenhower's role in the Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, [ref: Eisenhower and the Interstate, The Cupola: Student Publications] [ref: Vast Interstate Highway System Marks Half a Century, Voice of America] the Bureau of Public Roads, [ref: Have Truck, Will Drive: The Trucking Industry and the Use of Independent Owner-Operators Over Time, Transportation Law Journal] [ref: Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1921, EBSCO] and local urban planning battles—including documenting how local citizen pushback and freeway revolts reshaped proposed highway routing through the District of Columbia. [ref: FHWA Highway History, Federal Highway Administration] [ref: Roads Not Traveled: DC Pushes Back Against Freeway Plans, Boundary Stones] [ref: Washington's Main Street: Consensus and Conflict on the Capital Beltway, 1952-2001, University of Maryland, College Park] These agency writings formed the backbone of the FHWA's public "[https://highways.dot.gov/highway-history Highway History]" web portal.

Weingroff's historical research is referenced in academic studies, peer-reviewed journals, and books, including Earl Swift's history of the Interstate System, The Big Roads. [ref: The Big Roads: The Visionaries, Wrecks, and Whistle-Blowers Who Built the Superhighways, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt] [ref: Peer-Reviewed Transportation Scholarship, SAGE Journals] [ref: The American Highway: The History and Culture of Roads in the United States, McFarland & Company] [ref: Freeway Revolts! The Quality of Life Effects of Highways, The Review of Economics and Statistics] Weingroff’s articles have also been cited in legal filings, law review articles, think tank assessments, and National Register of Historic Places documentation. [ref: Stanford Law Review Article Citations on Infrastructure, Stanford Law Review] [ref: Historic Resources of the Santa Fe Trail (Amended), Kansas Historical Society / National Park Service] [ref: Supreme Court of the United States Docket No. 23-51 (Filing), Supreme Court of the United States] [ref: Infrastructure Costs, Brookings Institution] In addition, he has contributed to media retrospectives on American urban transit and appeared on television documentary series such as the History Channel's Modern Marvels. [ref: Richard Weingroff Filmography, IMDb] [ref: "Traffic". Modern Marvels. Season 6. Episode 19. June 22, 2000. The History Channel.]

After serving as the agency's informal historian for several decades, Weingroff was officially appointed as the FHWA's agency historian in 2017 while continuing his duties as an information specialist. [ref: On Being Federal Highway Administration's Official Historian: Public Roads 100th Anniversary, Federal Highway Administration]

Draft: Advertising in Azerbaijan

Draft text:
Advertising in Azerbaijan comprises the creation, production and media placement of advertising in Azerbaijan. According to the State Statistics Committee of Azerbaijan (SSC), revenue from advertising activity in the country amounted to 292.4 million manat in 2025, about 3.9 times the 75.6 million manat recorded in 2020. [ref: Azərbaycanda reklam bazarı sürətlə böyüyür – RƏQƏMLƏR, Sfera.az] [ref: Mətbuat öldü! Yaşasın media!, Pressklub.az] The SSC figure covers the creation and production of advertising as well as its placement. Official statistics and industry estimates differ considerably: for 2023 the SSC reported 201 million manat, while the ICT Market Participants Public Union estimated the market at about 140 million manat.

Banks are the main group of advertisers whose budgets are publicly disclosed; their advertising and marketing expenses totalled 92.8 million manat in 2025. National television audience measurement has been carried out by MARSA since 2023, and since September 2026 foreign digital service providers have been registering for value-added tax in Azerbaijan.

== History ==
A modern advertising market began to form in the 1990s, following independence, the transition to a market economy, the emergence of private broadcasters and the arrival of foreign brands. The first law "On Advertising" was adopted in 1997 and remained in force until 2015. [ref: "Reklam haqqında" Azərbaycan Respublikasının Qanunu (№ 1281-IVQ, 15 may 2015-ci il), e-qanun.az]

=== 2012–2019 ===
According to the SSC, revenue from advertising services rose from 48.4 million manat in 2012 to 72.5 million manat in 2014. During the economic difficulties of 2015–2016 it fell to 43.5 million manat, a decline of about 40%, and returned to its 2014 level only in 2019. [ref: Azərbaycanda reklama nə qədər pul ödənilir?, [[Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty]

=== 2020s ===
In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, revenue from advertising activity grew by 4.4% to 75.6 million manat. Advertising revenue of the mass media that year was 11.84 million manat, of which 10.54 million went to television and radio and 1.02 million to periodical print media. Growth accelerated in the following years: revenue reached 99 million manat in 2021, 201 million in 2023 and 292.4 million in 2025. Annual growth was about 40% in 2023, 30% in 2024 and 12% in 2025.

=== Structure by activity ===

Outdoor advertising was the largest placement segment. Placement in the media and at mass events amounted to 68 million manat, of which 40.2 million went to television and radio and 20 million to digital channels. Revenue from advertising on vehicles was 20 million manat.

In 2022, advertising revenue of the mass media was 16.1 million manat, of which 15 million went to television and radio. Outdoor advertising revenue that year was about 30 million manat, roughly three times the previous year's level. [ref: Mətbuat günü: İqtisadi kollaps, media ağırlaşdı, ANS Press]

=== Industry estimates ===

According to the ICT Market Participants Public Union, advertising investment grew by 14% in 2023 to about 140 million manat. Television accounted for 46 million manat (about 33% of the market), digital platforms for 33 million and radio for 7.2 million; outdoor advertising grew by 6%, while the share of print media continued to decline. [ref: Azərbaycanda reklam bazarının həcmi 140 mln. manata çatıb, APA] This estimate is considerably lower than the SSC figure for the same year (201 million manat). The union has not published its methodology, while the SSC figure includes the creation and production of advertising in addition to placement.

== Channels ==
=== Television ===
Speaking at a seminar in Baku on 4 November 2022, Zaur Ismayilov, chairman of the advertisers' committee of the Digital and Audiovisual Broadcasting Industry Public Union, said that the annual turnover of the television advertising market had not exceeded 45 million manat for seven years. According to him, the total rating value of the market was 1.6 million, the average price of a rating point was 28 manat, and the market was at a "stalemate". [ref: Azərbaycanda televiziya reklamı bazarının illik dövriyyəsi açıqlanıb, Report.az]

Draft text:
----

Kloster Arenberg is the Mutterhaus of the Arenberg Dominican Sisters—Sisters of Saint Catherine of Siena within the Order of Saint Dominic located in the district Arenberg of the city Koblenz in the German state Rhineland-Platinate.
The sisters state that they aim to shape their "daily life in community through the power of the Gospel" and to remain open to those seeking peace and quiet. Consequently, the convent—located in the Koblenz district and pilgrimage site of the district Arenberg includes a guesthouse and offers a diverse range of educational programs.

Since 2002, Arenberg Convent and its associated pilgrimage site have been part of the UNESCO World Heritage site "Upper Middle Rhine Valley," marking its northernmost point.

== History ==

Parish priest Johann Baptist Kraus—who commissioned the creation of the pilgrimage grounds that now bear his name, the "Pfarrer-Kraus-Anlagen"—had a small convent building constructed in 1864. In 1868, following Pope Pius IX’s approval for the establishment of a convent focused on schooling and nursing, Kraus brought two sisters from Switzerland to Arenberg. They were tasked with residing there, maintaining the pilgrimage grounds, and carrying out social work within the local community. Also arriving in Arenberg in 1868 was Anna Maria Josepha Willimann, who had previously worked as a convent porter in Switzerland. Shortly thereafter, she received the religious name Maria Cherubina. Later, she signed her name as "Cherubine." [ref: Anja Ostrowitzki: [https://www.rheinische-geschichte.lvr.de/Persoenlichkeiten/cherubine-willimann/DE-2086/lido/57c931ce409182.20986779 Cherubine Willimann.] In: rheinische-geschichte.lvr.de. Retrieved August 1, 2022.]

Within the religious order and among the sisters at Arenberg, tensions arose between those who favored a life devoted exclusively to contemplation and those who saw their primary mission as social work. These conflicts—which threatened the very survival of the convent—ultimately led to the Arenberg convent becoming independent, with the Bishop of Trier, Michael Felix Korum, appointing Sister Cherubine Willimann as prioress. In 1877, the community at Arenberg joined the Dominican Order. [ref: Dana Kim Hansen-Strosche: Time-Out für die Seele: zu Besuch bei den Dominikanerinnen auf dem Arenberg. In: Herder Korrespondenz Spezial, 2021, Issue 2: Fromm und frei? Spiritualität heute, pp. 26–28, here p. 28.] Under Sister Cherubine, the convent grew and established branch houses. Cherubine Willimann passed away on December 18, 1914, at the age of 72. A short time later, the Arenberg Convent had 42 branches in addition to its motherhouse. In 1914, the congregation of the "Sisters of Saint Catherine of Siena of the Order of Saint Dominic in Arenberg" received papal recognition.

== Description ==

For about 50 years, the sisters operated a Kneipp sanatorium on their premises before transforming it, in the early 2000s, into a center for religious retreat—combining medical treatments and health cures with educational and recreational offerings. The facility includes a wellness area with a swimming pool and sauna, as well as group sessions for gymnastics, dew-walking, and aqua fitness. Guests are welcome to join the Dominican sisters for prayer services and may also engage in personal conversations with them if desired. The convent library is likewise open to guests.

Every summer, a "promenade concert" (Wandelkonzert) takes place, featuring sacred music and choral performances from various eras. The event incorporates both the church of the Arenberg Dominican convent and the pilgrimage church of St. Nicholas (St. Nikolaus). For this occasion, the outdoor grounds are illuminated.

To the west of the Dominican motherhouse lie an expansive park and a herb garden. The sisters are happy to explain the various plants and offer tea to interested visitors. An "insect hotel"—a multi-level nesting structure—has been built to accommodate the insects drawn to the flowering plants. There are also display cases dedicated to apiculture (beekeeping), and the convent produces its own honey. At the western edge of the park, which transitions into orchards high above the Rhine Valley, a second Lourdes grotto—complete with a resting area and a statue of the Virgin Mary—has been reconstructed; it serves as a counterpart to the one located in the Pfarrer-Kraus-Anlagen (Father Kraus Grounds).

== Literature ==

St. Nikolaus in Arenberg: A Pilgrimage Site of the Catholic Late Romantic Period in the Rhineland (1845–1892). Doctoral dissertation, University of Frankfurt. – Frankfurt am Main: Kunstg

Nina Linh

Nina Linh is an American non profit executive, education advocate, entrepreneur. Independent political candidate, and founder of the WonderSeed Foundation. [ref: https://wonderseedfoundation.org/] in 2026, she ran as an Independent candidate for the United States House of Representatives in California's 40th congressional district, after beginning her campaign as a Democrat and leaving the part in November 2025. [ref: Linh is 5th Democrat to enter California's 40th Congressional District race for 2026, Inland Valley Daily Bulletin]

Linh is the founder and CEO of WonderSeed Foundation, a nonprofit organization founded in 2018 that applied neuroscience, trauma-informed practices, immersive technology, and artificial intelligence to behavioral health, education, and workplace development. [ref: Nina Linh - Ballotpedia, Ballotpedia]

Early Life

Linh was born in Da Nang, Vietnam, during the Vietnam War. Her father was killed during the war, and her mother fled Vietnam with her three children.

After arriving in the United States as refugees, the family passed through Fort Chaffee, a major processing center for Vietnamese refugees following the fall of Saigon in 1975. They were subsequently sponsored by a Catholic organization and resettled in American Midwest. [ref: 497 - Can An Independent Vietnamese-American Actually Win A Seat In Congress? - Nina Linh]

Linh has cited her family's experience with war, displacement, immigration, and rebuilding their lives in the United States as influences on her later work in education and public services.

Education and public-policy advocacy, including work at the federal level and participation in efforts involving proposed federal education legislation.

Her advocacy has focused on educational opportunity, workforce readiness, emotional and social development, and improving outcomes for underserved young people.

WonderSeed Foundation

Linh founded the WonderSeed Foundation in 2018, driven in part by the struggles of her only child and her search for more effective approaches to behavioral and mental health.

From its early years, WonderSeed explored and applied immersive environments, virtual reality and AI- enabled simulations, ahead of their board mainstream adoption as tools for experimental learning and behavioral change. The organization used these technologies to create interactive experiences in which participants could practice emotional regulation, communication, decision making, and real world behavioral responses.

The approach draws on neuroplasticity, using repeated immersive experiences and simulations to help participants practice and reinforce healthier, more adaptive behavioral patterns over time.

WonderSeed's theory of change is based on the premise that unaddressed trauma can contribute to emotional dysregulation, which can turn contribute to behavioral, educational, employment, and broader social difficulties.

Its program combine neuroscience and trauma-informed practices with emerging technology, education, and workforce preparation. The organization has developed programming for young people facing significant barriers, including youth involved in the juvenile-justice system, and has undertaken initiatives involving Los Angeles County Probation.

Linh's work places her at the intersection of behavioral and mental health, neuroscience immersive technology, artificial intelligence, education and workforce development, with an emphasis on translating emerging technologies into practical tools for sustained behavioral change.

Independent congressional campaign

In 2025, Linh launched a campaign for the U.S. House of Representatives in California's 40th congressional district. She initially entered the race as Democrat but changed her political registration to Independent on November 11, 2025.

Her decision to run as an Independent became a defining feature of her congressional campaign. Linh framed her candidacy around independent from the two major political parties and the principle the elected representatives should be accountable primarily to their constitute rather than partisan institutions.

Her campaign combined positions often associated with different sides of the traditional political spectrum. Its priorities included education and workforce development, healthcare affordability and transparency, housing, mental-health services, early -childhood education, immigration reform and boarder security, government efficiency, emerging technology, and protection of Medicare and Social Security. [ref: Linh, Nina – Candidate overview, Federal Election Commission]

Linh competed as an Independent in California's June 2026 primary election but did not advance to general election.

Political Approach

Linh has characterized her political approach as independent and pragmatic rather than conventionally partisan.

Her positions have combined support for expanded access to healthcare, education, and mental-health services with an emphasis on fiscal accountability, government efficiency, entrepreneur, boarder security, workforce development, and private-sector innovation.

Her 2026 congressional candidacy represented a departure from traditional party politics and became an extension of her broader emphasis on problem-solving across political and institutional boundaries. [ref: Nina Linh, Ballotpedia]

Personal Life

Ben McDonnell (born 1991 or 1992) is an American actor, podcaster, photographer and barrel racer. He is a contestant on The Traitors: New Blood, the 2026 all-civilian season of the NBC reality competition series The Traitors. [ref: 'The Traitors: New Blood' Expands 'Traitors' Fandom to NBC Viewers, NBCUniversal] He hosts the comedy podcast It's Ben A Week, which he launched in 2024. [ref: 'The Traitors: New Blood': Inside Ben McDonnell's Hidden Hollywood Past, TheThings]

== Early life ==
McDonnell was born in Maplewood, Minnesota. [ref: North Texan will compete for $250,000 on NBC's 'The Traitors: New Blood', Fort Worth Star-Telegram] He later moved to Los Angeles to pursue an acting career, training at The Groundlings and with acting coach Lesly Kahn.

== Career ==
=== Acting ===
One of McDonnell's first roles was in the 2015 Will Smith film Concussion. He went on to appear in a number of short films, and in episodes of The Bay, Class Act and What Would You Do?. He also appeared on The Ellen DeGeneres Show and The Late Late Show with James Corden.

McDonnell produced the 2019 miniseries Class Act and executive produced the short film Dear Dad (2018). He made his directing debut with the short film I (2016), an official selection of the Twin Cities Film Festival.

=== Podcasting ===
In 2024, McDonnell launched It's Ben A Week, a solo comedy podcast.

=== Photography ===
McDonnell works as a headshot, corporate and conference photographer in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, and has said his own experience as an actor shaped his approach to headshots. [ref: Meet Benjamin McDonnell, CanvasRebel]

=== The Traitors: New Blood ===
In August 2026, McDonnell was announced as one of 22 contestants on The Traitors: New Blood, the first American season of The Traitors cast entirely with non-celebrities, selected from more than 60,000 applicants. [ref: The Traitors: New Blood Introduces This Season's All-Civilian Cast, Bleeding Cool] Hosted by Alan Cumming and filmed in the Scottish Highlands, the season premiered on NBC on September 17, 2026. [ref: Meet the Cast of 'The Traitors: New Blood', TV Insider] [ref: How a barrel racer from North Texas plans to out-lie everyone on 'The Traitors', Dallas Observer] He competes as a Faithful. [ref: Your Guide to the Normies in 'The Traitors: New Blood' Cast, Yahoo Entertainment]

== Personal life ==
McDonnell lives in Granbury, Texas, where he competes in barrel racing. According to the Dallas Observer, he keeps around 70 animals.

----AutoForecast Solutions LLC (AFS) is an American automotive industry forecasting, business intelligence, and advisory services company headquartered in Chester Springs, Pennsylvania. The company provides global vehicle production forecasts, powertrain and drivetrain data, business planning software, and automotive market analysis to vehicle manufacturers, automotive suppliers, financial institutions, government agencies, and other industry participants. [ref: AutoForecast Solutions, AutoForecast Solutions]

AFS combines automotive databases with forecasting software and industry analysis. Its services support production planning, capacity assessment, revenue forecasting, competitive analysis, and evaluation of market opportunities and risks. [ref: Global Forecasting, AutoForecast Solutions]

== History ==
AutoForecast Solutions was established in 2014, according to the company's LinkedIn profile. [ref: AutoForecast Solutions LLC, LinkedIn] Its founder and chief executive officer, Joseph McCabe, previously held positions in automotive forecasting, strategy, and competitive assessment. [ref: Joseph McCabe, Center for Automotive Research]

The company developed services combining vehicle production forecasts with information on powertrains, drivetrains, alternative propulsion technologies, and manufacturing programs. Its software and advisory services are intended to help automotive businesses connect industry forecasts with commercial planning and revenue objectives.

== Products and services ==

=== Automotive production forecasting ===
AFS provides historical automotive production data and forward-looking forecasts covering vehicle manufacturers, vehicle platforms, model programs, assembly plants, and powertrain applications. Its forecasting services cover multiple global regions and include light vehicles, engines, transmissions, electric motors, and alternative propulsion systems.

The company's forecasts are used to evaluate expected production volumes, manufacturing capacity, changes in vehicle programs, and shifts in powertrain technology.

=== Business intelligence and planning software ===
AFS offers business intelligence and planning applications for automotive companies. These tools support sales and revenue forecasting, capacity planning, market-share analysis, competitive assessment, and the development of alternative production scenarios. [ref: Solutions and Services, AutoForecast Solutions]

The company's planning services also support tracking sales opportunities and customer programs at the component or part-number level.

=== Market analysis and advisory services ===
AFS provides industry reports, market alerts, special studies, and consulting services addressing developments in automotive manufacturing and technology. Its areas of analysis include production trends, electrification, powertrain development, vehicle programs, competitive positioning, and changes in the automotive supply chain.

The company also publishes automotive industry commentary and analysis through its website and related media channels.

== Customers and industry coverage ==
AFS serves businesses and institutions involved in the global automotive industry, including original equipment manufacturers, component suppliers, financial institutions, government agencies, industry associations, and academic organizations.

Its forecasting databases cover vehicle production across multiple countries and include conventional internal combustion engines, hybrid vehicles, plug-in hybrid vehicles, battery electric vehicles, and other propulsion technologies.

== Publications and industry commentary ==
AFS publishes automotive market analysis and forecasting commentary through its reporting services. Its coverage addresses production outlooks, manufacturing capacity, vehicle launches, powertrain trends, and changes in the competitive landscape.

The company's analysts also participate in industry events and media discussions concerning automotive manufacturing and supply-chain developments.

== Headquarters ==
AutoForecast Solutions is headquartered in Chester Springs, Pennsylvania, United States.

Athanasios Papastyliadis

Athanasios Papastyliadis (Αθανάσιος Παπαστυλιάδης in Greek, 1875–1939) was a master builder, practical architect, building contractor, and merchant in Western Macedonia and Romania. He participated in the Macedonian Struggle in 1904 as an organizer and collaborator of Pavlos Melas, alongside other members of his family.

Origin and Early Life

Athanasios Papastyliadis was a scion of the Styliadis family, descendants of priest Kostas (son of Stylos or Stylianos), who over time adopted the surnames Stylou, Stylianou, and Styliadis. (Athanasios was the only one who used the surname Papastyliadis to indicate his descent from priests [papa-].) The family included well-known builders and icon-painters [ref: Ζωγράφοι του Βιτσίου, Prefectural Committee for Popular Education (Ν.Ε.Λ.Ε) of Florina].

Priest Kostas, Athanasios's grandfather, set out after 1840 from Plikati in Konitsa —the northernmost of the area's builder villages (mastrochoria)— at the head of about 50 families and his four brothers. After a long journey, they reached the region of Florina, where in 1843 they purchased a large tract of land in the forest [ref: Μπελκαμένη. Χωριό του νομού Φλώρινας. (Εκατό χρόνια ζωή), Διογένης - Πέτρος Κουλουφάκος] from Bey Osman Ismail Passou for 3,000 gold sovereigns [ref: Η ζωή και οι περιπέτειες στη Δροσοπηγή. Λαογραφικά - ιστορικά ενθυμήματα, "Politis" newspaper]. They were bilingual (Greek-speaking and Albanian-speaking), all stone artisans, and founded the villages of Belkameni (present-day Drosopigi) in 1844 and Negovani (present-day Flampouro) in 1861, building houses with very thick walls and a sewage system.

He was born in 1875, the son of Dimitrios Styliadis or Stylianou, son of Priest Kostas. (In the family, he was known as Nasi-Miti —Thanasis [son of] Dimitris.) He married Agora Giankou at a very young age and had 18 or 19 children with her, seven of whom died in infancy or early childhood. The first, Zacharia, was born in 1894.

Alongside the craft of stonemasonry learned from his ancestors, he also engaged in trade with Romania. Many craftsmen from Belkameni worked seasonally in Bucharest, leaving the village on the Feast of Saint George and returning for the Feast of Saint Demetrius. Athanasios established a commercial store in Brăila, trading mainly in woolen goods, which he procured from surrounding villages and Mount Athos. As early as 1897, he used letterhead featuring his name in Latin script, as evidenced by eight of his letters to [https://www.pemptousia.gr/2014/06/agiorites-mikrasiates-igoumeni-to-2/ Archimandrite Neofytos—abbot of the Monastery of Simonopetra on Mount Athos]— and monk Galaktion, a fellow villager living there. The letters date between 1897 and 1904 and are preserved at the monastery.

Macedonian Struggle and Flight to Romania

With the onset of the Macedonian Struggle, Papastyliadis became active and established ties with the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which awarded him the rank of First Class Agent. On July 25, he went to Kozani to meet Pavlos Melas during Melas's second entry into Macedonia. Melas wrote to his wife: "...Athanasios Papastyliadis came from Belkameni, a good brave fellow of the area. We brought him to make arrangements for men and hideouts, so they are ready at once." [ref: Παύλος Μελάς, Δωδώνη]

Papastyliadis organized the necessary arrangements for the struggle. Melas entered Ottoman-ruled Macedonia for the third time a month later (August 28, 1904) with 35 armed men, becoming the first Greek officer involved in combat in Macedonia. On September 17, the group entered Belkameni secretly and lodged in an empty house. There, they met the village committee, including Papastyliadis, [https://macedonian-fighters.com/index.php/%CE%A0%CE%AD%CF%84%CF%81%CE%BF%CF%82_%CE%A3%CF%84%CF%85%CE%BB%CE%B9%CE%AC%CE%B4%CE%B7%CF%82 Priest Petros Styliadis] (his father's first cousin and also a First Class Agent of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs), and the volunteer Filippos Kapetanopoulos. The group left for the forest at 3:00 a.m. to avoid incriminating Papastyliadis, while Melas and his second-in-command, Lakis Pyrzas, were hosted at Papastyliadis's home. In the morning, the troop entered the village triumphantly and departed later.

Following the death of Pavlos Melas on October 13, 1904, the komitadjis sought to eliminate his associates. They assassinated Priest Petros Styliadis, forcing Athanasios to flee in 1905 to Kastoria and then to Brăila, where he stayed until shortly after the Young Turk Revolution. Upon leaving, he left his shop to Athanasios Giokas, the husband of his daughter Elisabeth. (During his stay in Romania in 1907, the komitadjis also assassinated Apostolos Styliadis, his father's brother and a Third Class Agent, and imprisoned his relative Nikolaos Styliadis, a First Class Agent of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.) [ref: Αφανείς γηγενείς μακεδονομάχοι (1903 – 1913), University Studio Press]

==2026 B.C. Conservative leadership election campaign==
Caroline Elliot was one of five candidates in the May 2026 Conservative Party of British Columbia leadership election. [ref: Has right's rise primed B.C. politics for a party that breaks the binary?, The Globe and Mail]
She was described as a "real conservative"
since she argued that while economic issues are "critically important", it is necessary to take on "cultural" issues like the catch-and-release criminal justice system, [ref: PODCAST: Caroline Elliott: 'This province is at a crucial time', Northern Beat] [ref: Can't fix B.C. without a culture war, says Conservative leadership runner-up, Vancouver Sun]

[ref: Will the B.C. Conservatives now become MAGA North?, The Globe and Mail]
She received the endorsement of former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell, [ref: Former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell back in the political game, The Globe and Mail] [ref: Campbell, Day throw support behind Elliott in race for BC Conservative leadership, The Castanet] and Harman Bhangu, a longtime B.C. Serpent's Curse is a steel roller coaster currently under construction at Paultons Park in Hampshire, England. Manufactured by Mack Rides, the ride is a custom-designed water coaster; the first of its kind in the UK. [ref: ] The attraction is expected to open in 2027 in the park's Viking-themed land: Valgard: Realm of the Vikings.

== History ==
The ride was announced to the public during Paultons Park's annual Super Fans day on 16 May 2026. [ref: LIVE: Super Fans Day 2026 & Big New Plans for 2027!]

The ride's lift hill was topped off on 13 July 2026, with the first drop being completed the following day. [ref: ] The ride's track, up to the splashdown element was completed on 17 July 2026.

== Characteristics ==

=== Ride experience ===
Upon exiting the station, riders take a right-hand turn before ascending the chain lift hill. The ride then executes a left-hand banked drop into a twisted airtime hill. Riders then experience a steep-banked turn over the lift hill before another airtime hill. The ride then rises up into a top-hat element before a small airtime hill into the ride's splashdown. The ride vehicle then floats, pushed by the water, back to the station.

=== Ride vehicles ===
The ride's 4 boats are arranged with riders sitting 2 across in 4 rows for a total of 8 riders per car. [ref: ]
