Draft text:
The Acceleration Consortium (AC) is a research consortium based at the University of Toronto focused on accelerated materials and molecular discovery using "self-driving labs," robotic research workflows that use artificial intelligence and advanced computing to autonomously design, run, and characterize experiments.

The consortium is directed by chemist and computer scientist Alan Aspuru-Guzik and develops self-driving labs for applications in medicine, energy, plastics, electronics, and construction [ref: Experts say $200-million grant awarded to U of T will drive ‘big science’ via the Acceleration Consortium]. In 2023, the Acceleration Consortium received a $200 million award from the Canada First Research Excellence Fund (CFREF), issued by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC), National Science and Engineering Research Council (NSERC), and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) [ref: New Acceleration Consortium at University of Toronto applies artificial intelligence to discovery of advanced materials, U of T Engineering News].

== History ==
The consortium traces its origins to a 2018 project that was using robotic research workflows for new organic laser materials, which Alan Aspuru-Guzik says was what the AC was originally designed for [ref: Acceleration Consortium 2025, acceleration.utoronto.ca]. The University of Toronto then launched the AC in April 2021 as an Institutional Strategic Initiative. It described the Acceleration Consortium as a global coalition that would use materials acceleration platforms (i.e. self-driving labs) to discover and design new materials.

A significant portion of the Acceleration Consortium's projects come from industry partners and collaborations. Merck KGaA was one of the consortium’s first partners. The two organizations collaborated on open-sourcing Merck’s Bayesian Back End (BayBE) experiment planner, which the AC’s self-driving labs later adopted in their automated workflows [ref: Acceleration Consortium cements partnership with global technology leader Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany].

In April 2025, BASF signed a master research agreement with the University of Toronto, the company’s first with a Canadian university. The collaborations cover crop protection, coatings that extend the life of architectural materials, and targeted drug delivery. One project, led by formulations lab co-lead Frank Gu, uses plant-derived biopolymers to regulate soil moisture and to slowly release pesticides or fertilizers near the plant [ref: BASF signs its first Canadian Master Research Agreement with the University of Toronto].

AC researchers worked with the AI drug discovery company Insilico Medicine on the 2023 Chemical Science study that used AlphaFold to design a potential liver cancer drug. Aspuru-Guzik is an adviser to Insilico. The two groups later co-authored the 2025 Nature Biotechnology study that used quantum computing and generative AI to design molecules targeting the cancer protein KRAS [ref: Acceleration Consortium, Institutional Strategic Initiatives].

The AC also maintains projects with Sanofi, Amgen, Procter & Gamble, Bristol Myers Squibb, IBM, Amazon Web Services, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Mettler Toledo, Sekisui, and others [ref: Partners, acceleration.utoronto.ca].

== Operations ==

=== Network of self-driving labs ===
The AC built a network of self-driving labs, each focused on one particular class of applications, that collaborate on projects with other SDLs while having a mandate of advancing one particular field. The labs are numbered from SDL 0 to SDL 7. SDLs 0 to 6 are housed at the University of Toronto whereas SDL 7 is at the University of British Columbia [ref: AC Labs and Facilities, acceleration.utoronto.ca].

==== SDL 0: AI and Automation ====
SDL 0 focuses on overcoming robotic and equipment bottlenecks in self-driving labs by integrating robot manipulation, computer vision, and learning-based agentic reasoning into a unified autonomy stack. Its projects include a GPU-accelerated multiscale digital twin framework for simulating autonomous lab workflows, a general orchestrator for executing closed-loop experiments, and equipment API integrations [ref: SDL0: AI and Automation, acceleration.utoronto.ca].

==== SDL 1: Inorganic ====
SDL 1 focuses on designing inorganic materials. It focuses on solution-based, solid-state, and electrochemical synthesis pathways with real-time data collection, adaptive process control, and AI-guided planning to further a property-driven optimization with mechanistic understanding. Its projects include the closed-loop discovery of electrocatalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) for green hydrogen, an automated electrolyzer workflow for CO2 conversion, high-throughput optimization of aqueous battery electrolytes, and fully automated solid-state synthesis of oxides and alloys [ref: SDL1: Inorganic, acceleration.utoronto.ca].

==== SDL 2: Organic ====
SDL 2 builds automated, data-driven platforms to design, execute, and optimize complex organic synthesis, with a focus on pharmaceuticals, catalysis, and functional materials. Current projects include an autonomous liquid-liquid extraction platform for solvent-efficient purification and a self-driving workflow for high-throughput solubility measurement and crystallization studies [ref: SDL2: Organic, acceleration.utoronto.ca].

The Ji-Paraná Tornado was an strong tornado phenomenon occurred on September 24, 2007, causing destruction in the region of Ji-Paraná, in Rondônia. The tornado caused over 1 million reais (BRL) in damages. [ref: ]

== Synoptic Setup ==

The tornado and storms were caused by a Cold front that came from the south. Before the tornado, it was a warm 80⁰F, indicating the possibility of storms. When the Cold front arrived, it caused a line of instability in the state, thus causing the tornado. [ref: ]

== Damage in the city and information ==

The tornado ripped roofs off houses and businesses, overturned cars, knocked down power poles near a gas station, hurled road signs a distance away, and uprooted large trees, suggesting an E/F2 classification. [ref: ]
and left more than 10 families homeless. [ref: ]
The tornado also caused an estimated 1 million reais in damage at the time.
Shortly after the tornado, a Microburst with winds of 149 km/h (92 mph) hit the city. [ref: ]
It possibly hit Rondolândia, which also suffered electrical power outages.

== Trajectory ==

The tornado started in the Ji-Paraná River and quickly moved towards the eastern part of the city, uprooting trees, knocking down power poles, etc.
The tornado traveled more than 8km to Nova Colina, affecting a rural area before dissipating.
[ref: ]

----

Vidani (Marathi: विडणी) is a prominent and heavily populated village located in the Phaltan taluka of Satara district in the Indian state of Maharashtra. Situated in the agrarian heartland of the Deccan Plateau, the village is renowned for its intensive sugarcane cultivation, its historical ties to the Maratha Empire, and the ancient Uttareshwar Temple. It also serves as a critical rural hub for agricultural research, acting as an implementation site for institutions like the Nimbkar Agricultural Research Institute (NARI). [ref: Census of India 2011: Data from the 2011 Census, including cities, villages and towns, Census of India]

== History ==

The history of Vidani is deeply intertwined with the broader history of the Phaltan region, which was a prominent Maratha princely state ruled by the Nimbalkar dynasty prior to Indian independence. Historical records from the Satara District Gazetteer suggest that Vidani, alongside neighboring agrarian settlements, served as an important revenue-generating village for the Phaltan state due to its proximity to the fertile Nira River basin. [ref: Satara District Gazetteer, Gazetteers Department, Government of Maharashtra]

The village's most significant historical monument is the Uttareshwar Temple, believed to date back several centuries. Local lore and architectural evidence suggest the temple faced vandalism in the 17th century by the Bijapur general Afzal Khan during his military campaign against Shivaji Maharaj.

== Geography and Climate ==

Vidani is geographically positioned at, sitting at an average elevation of 550 meters (1,800 feet) above sea level. It is located 72 kilometers northeast of the Satara district headquarters, 11 kilometers east of Phaltan city, and approximately 242 kilometers southeast of the state capital, Mumbai.

The village spans a total geographical area of 2,186.6 hectares (21.87 sq km). Rather than a single densely packed core, the settlement is distributed among a primary center and several decentralized hamlets (locally referred to as wadis or vastis), including Mazeri, and Pawarwadi.

=== Climate ===

Vidani experiences a hot semi-arid climate. The region falls squarely within the rain-shadow zone of the Western Ghats, making it relatively dry for most of the year.

* Summer (March to May): Extremely hot and dry, with daytime temperatures frequently exceeding 38°C (100°F).

* Monsoon (June to October): Characterized by erratic and generally low rainfall, averaging between 400 mm to 500 mm annually. Due to the scant rainfall, the village relies entirely on canal irrigation. [ref: Climate and Rainfall Data for Satara District, India Meteorological Department, Pune]

* Winter (November to February): Mild and pleasant, with nighttime temperatures dropping to around 12°C to 15°C.

== Demographics ==

As per the 2011 Census of India, Vidani has a total population of 10,439 individuals, spread across 2,080 households. It is one of the most heavily populated rural centers in the Phaltan subdivision.

* Gender: The population consists of 5,398 males and 5,041 females, yielding a sex ratio of 934 females for every 1,000 males, which is roughly on par with the regional average.

* Children: The population of children aged 0-6 years is 1,124, making up 10.77% of the total population. The child sex ratio stands at 855.

* Literacy: The overall literacy rate in Vidani is an impressive 80.44%, which is higher than the national average. Male literacy is 86.08%, while female literacy is 74.43%.

* Social Stratification: Scheduled Castes (SC) constitute 13.84% of the population, while Scheduled Tribes (ST) account for 0.34%.

== Economy and Agriculture ==

The economy of Vidani is heavily reliant on agriculture and allied agro-industries.

=== Cash Crops and Irrigation ===

Sugarcane (Saccharum officinarum) is the dominant cash crop. Despite being in a drought-prone region, sugarcane cultivation thrives here due to a robust network of artificial irrigation supplied by the Neera Right Bank Canal, which draws water from the Veer Dam. [ref: Irrigation and Water Management in the Nira Basin, Water Resources Department, Maharashtra] The harvested sugarcane primarily supplies the cooperative and private sugar mills in the taluka, notably the Shriram Sahakari Sakhar Karkhana and New Phaltan Sugar Works.

Other secondary crops include sorghum (jowar), pearl millet (bajra), onions, maize, and wheat.

=== Dairy and Allied Sectors ===

Dairy farming is a critical supplementary source of income. Almost every farming household maintains livestock, and the village features several milk collection centers that supply major state cooperatives like Govind Milk and Milk Products, headquartered in Phaltan.

Vidani also serves as an important field-testing ground for the Nimbkar Agricultural Research Institute (NARI). NARI's interventions in the village include the introduction of high-yield sweet sorghum varieties and the distribution of the "Nari Suvarna" sheep breed, which has significantly improved the economic resilience of marginal farmers.

== Civic Administration and Utilities ==

Vidani is governed by a Gram panchayat (village council) under the Panchayati Raj system. The village is divided into multiple wards, each electing a Gram Panchayat member. The Sarpanch serves as the head of the village administration.

== [user] ==
Muayad "Mo" Abbas is a real estate development executive and university lecturer known for his involvement in residential, hospitality, and mixed-use developments in the United States and international markets. He is Managing Director of Development at OKO Group and a lecturer at the University of Miami School of Architecture. [ref: Bisnow's Hurricane Irma Miami State of the Market, Bisnow] [ref: Former Ritz president leads new North Miami project, The Real Deal] [ref: Rafael Moneo Reveals Design of His First Condo Tower in Miami, ArchDaily]

== Career ==

=== Related International ===
Abbas previously served as Vice President of Related International, the international development arm of the Related Group, overseeing real estate operations in Panama, Colombia, and Argentina. [ref: Bisnow's Hurricane Irma Miami State of the Market, Bisnow]

=== Urbanis Advisors and Apeiron Living ===
Abbas founded Urbanis Advisors, a real estate development and advisory firm. He subsequently co-founded Apeiron Living, a luxury residential and hospitality venture conceived in collaboration with Horst Schulze, co-founder and former president of the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company, and Michael Bedner, co-founder of Hirsch Bedner Associates (HBA). [ref: Former Ritz president leads new North Miami project, The Real Deal] [ref: Rafael Moneo Reveals Design of His First Condo Tower in Miami, ArchDaily] [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club wins approval, plans to launch sales, The Real Deal]

The founders conceived Apeiron as a hospitality and residential brand combining luxury living with personalized service, health and wellness, preventive medical care, and arts and cultural programming. The concept was designed primarily for affluent, active older adults seeking a residential environment that supported independent living and aging in place -- coined as Limitless Living.

The brand emphasized architecture, hospitality, wellness, and curated experiences as pillars of an integrated residential lifestyle. Apeiron's proposed wellness program included medical services coordinated with the Cleveland Clinic. [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club wins approval, plans to launch sales, The Real Deal]

Apeiron at the Jockey Club in Miami, Florida, was the venture's flagship development and a model for potential expansion into other U.S. markets. The proposed redevelopment of the historic waterfront property included serviced residences, hospitality amenities, wellness facilities, dining, cultural programming, and a marina. [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club wins approval, plans to launch sales, The Real Deal]

The architectural design was led by Pritzker Architecture Prize recipient Spanish architect Rafael Moneo. [ref: Rafael Moneo Reveals Design of His First Condo Tower in Miami, ArchDaily]

The development faced legal challenges from existing condominium associations seeking to block construction. In June 2020, Florida's Third District Court of Appeal upheld the trial court's rulings, affirming Apeiron Miami LLC's development and its property rights at the Jockey Club. [ref: Jockey Club residents reignite lawsuit against next-door landowner, The Real Deal] [ref: Apeiron at the Jockey Club Developer Wins Key Ruling from Appeals Court, Carlton Fields] [ref: Developer Wins Key Ruling from Appeals Court in Miami-Dade, Council on Vertical Urbanism]

=== Mast Capital ===
Abbas subsequently served as Senior Vice President of Development at Mast Capital, a Miami-based real estate investment and development firm.

During his tenure, he led the development of Cipriani Residences Miami, an 80-story, 397-residence luxury condominium tower in Miami's Brickell neighborhood, designed by Arquitectonica. [ref: Mast Capital, www.mastcapital.com] [ref: ] [ref: Mast Capital, www.mastcapital.com]

The project was in collaboration with the Cipriani family. Led by Giuseppe Cipriani, the family's hospitality organization partnered with Mast Capital to establish its first ground-up residential development in the United States.

=== OKO Group ===
In 2025, Abbas joined Vlad Doronin's OKO Group as Managing Director of Development, overseeing a portfolio of luxury residential, hospitality, and mixed-use developments. New Earth Ascension is a concept from the New Age movement. It is the belief that Earth is transitioning to a new spiritual stage, with greater spiritual awareness and impact on every aspect of human life. The idea appeared in Spiritism and Theosophy in the mid 19th century and gained popularity in the New Age movement in the 1980s. The concept can be considered a fringe theory of eschatological nature, and is commonly associated to UFO religions.

Because the New Age movement is heavily decentralized, this same concept can be reffered by different terms, like The 3D to 5D Shift, The Collective Consciousness Shift, The Timeline Split and others.

== Definition ==

=== Earth as a life school ===

According to the New Age point of view, human beings are spirits with a physical body. The spirits are created simple and ignorant. For their development, spirits are born on Earth through multiple incarnations. Human experiences on Earth promote the evolution of the spirit.

It is also believed that there are several planets with intelligent life in the Universe. Each planet has a different level of spiritual and technological development. A young soul will incarnate in a less developed planet and, as it progresses, will be transferred to more advanced ones. Eventually, when the spirit assimilates everything that has to be learned, it will graduate as a Pure Spirit. [ref: Journey of souls: Case studies of life between lives., Llewellyn Publications] [ref: Between death and life: Conversations with a spirit, Ozark Mountain Publishing]

=== A call for help and the volunteers ===

According to the New Earth theory, human greed, war, environmental destruction, and fear-based control systems have pushed the Earth to its absolute limit. The breaking point was the creation of the atomic bomb in the 1940s. Because of free will, the caretakers of the Earth could not interfere from outside. So they found a way to interfere from inside. A desperate call for help was sent across the Universe, and millions of advanced souls volunteered to be born on Earth. These souls are known as starseeds or volunteers.

Some of the starseeds are former aliens from advanced planets, and some are Pure Spirits. They live ordinary lives, but unconsciously work as "anchors of light", reducing the density of the planet and transmitting the necessary energy for the creation of the new Earth. Due to the nature of Earth, volunteers go through the "veil of forgetfulness" when they are born, so they forget about their real nature. Because of this, there is the risk of a volunteer getting lost in the density of the Earth. If a volunteer yields to selfishness, hatred, or generates too much negative karma, they may end up becoming trapped in Earth's reincarnation cycle, instead of returning home by the end of their life.

In his books "Gods of Aquarius" and "The star people", Brad Steiger described psychological and physical characteristics of the starseeds, which include: [ref: Gods of Aquarius: UFOs and the transformation of man, Berkley Publishing Corp] [ref: The star people, Berkley Publishing Corp]

* Feeling of not belonging: From childhood, they feel that "this world is not their home" or that they were left on the wrong planet.

* Social alienation: They have extreme difficulty adjusting to rigid social structures, competitive political systems, or purely material ambitions.

* Initial amnesia and awakening: Forgetting of real identity and purpose during childhood, followed by a gradual or abrupt process of "awakening".

* Physical symptoms and allergies: Because they have a mix of terrestrial and extraterrestrial lineage, starseeds have greater propensity for allergies, sleep disorders, chronic fatigue, or hypersensitivity to loud noises, bright lights, and heavy environments.

* Intrinsic desire to help: Even without knowing why, they possess an internal moral compass oriented towards healing, caring for nature, animals, or the well-being of others.

* Paranormal and Spiritual Experiences: They commonly see UFOs, have vivid dreams of spaceships and traveling to other planets, and possess latent or active psychic abilities, such as telepathy, precognition, or hands-on healing.

In the book "The Three Waves of Volunteers and the New Earth", Dolores Cannon identified three waves of volunteers: [ref: The three waves of volunteers and the new Earth, Ozark Mountain Publishing]

* The First Wave arrived from the 1950s to the 1960s as a pioneering force. Their task was to break through the planet's dense, negative vibration following the advent of nuclear weapons. Because they were the first to arrive, they suffered the most from intense feelings of alienation, severe depression, and a painful, lifelong homesickness for their true spiritual homes.

* The Second Wave arrived from the 1970s to the 1980s, acting as passive "energetic antennas". Their primary mission is simply to exist and anchor light on the planet. They need no active effort, nor do they need to change the world through career achievements. ==Plot==
When Oscar makes the life-altering decision to leave behind his modest background and economic hardships in Bosnia, he carries with him a singular, unwavering dream: to attend medical school and build a secure, meaningful future. Arriving in the pristine and seemingly immaculate city of Lund, Sweden, he expects an orderly transition into European university life. Instead, he quickly discovers that reality is far more eccentric, unpredictable, and chaotic than he ever could have imagined.
Plunged headfirst into a whirlwind of high stakes academics, stark cultural shifts, and sudden independence, Oscar finds his daily routine instantly upended by a colorful ensemble of personalities. He moves into a quirky, lived in apartment shared with Erik a laid back engineering student sporting a distinct California accent and strong, unyielding opinions on pizza toppings. Between Erik's mischievous pranks and culinary debates, Oscar's home life is never dull. Adding to the turbulence is Nora, a deadpan, scheming letting agent who treats housing like a high-stakes chess match and thrives on absolute administrative chaos. Under their watch, Oscar learns that nothing in Sweden goes quite according to plan.
Meanwhile, his deep, lifelong bond with his childhood best friend, Selma, faces entirely new tests across geographic borders and shifting distances. As they navigate the complexities of life apart, buried feelings inevitably bubble to the surface. But everyday life brings its own absurd hurdles, from bizarre local traditions emerging from the shadows to disrupt their peace to the persistent, haunting echoes of a mysterious recurring dream that blurs the delicate line between fate and reality.
As old boundaries are crossed and unexpected foundations are built, Oscar must learn to navigate a complex labyrinth of personal and professional choices. Tom Nesher (; born December 17, 1996) is an Israeli film director, screenwriter, and journalist. She is an Ophir Awards winner for Best Film and Best Director to 2024 for Come Closer.

== Biography ==
Nesher was born in 1996, the eldest daughter of director Avi Nesher and the artist and photographer Iris Nesher. Her younger brother, Ari, was killed in 2018 at the age of 17 in a hit and run accident caused by footballer Manamto Asefa in Tel Aviv. [ref: https://www.haaretz.co.il/gallery/cinema/2020-12-02/ty-article-magazine/.highlight/0000017f-dc63-df62-a9ff-dcf7c44e0000] [ref: Soccer player released after 2 years in prison for deadly hit-and-run, The Times of Israel] In high school, she studied at the Thelma Yellin High School In Givatayim.

In 2014, Nesher served as an announcer on Galei Tzahal. [ref: https://www.israelhayom.co.il/celebrities/local-celebrities/article/7481993] After this, she studied screenwriting at the Sam Spiegel Film School, and history and literature at Tel Aviv University. [ref: תום נשר - ביוגרפיה, אידיבי]

In 2020, Nesher joined Channel 13 News as an investigative reporter. [ref: https://www.israelhayom.co.il/celebrities/local-celebrities/article/7343134]

In 2024, Nesher released her debut feature film, Come Closer, a drama heavily inspired by her own personal experience. The film follows Eden, a young woman who, after the tragic death of her brother, embarks on an intense emotional journey to find his secret girlfriend, navigating complex themes of youth, intimacy and healing. [ref: Interview: Tom Nesher on "Come Closer", The Moveable Fest] The film winning four major awards at the 2024 Ophir Awards, including Best Feature Film and Best Director for Nesher, and Best Actress for Lia Elalouf. It was subsequently selected as the Israeli entry for Best International Feature Film at the 97th Academy Awards. [ref: Tom Nesher’s ‘Come Closer’ wins Ophir, becomes Israel’s choice for Oscar nomination, The Times of Israel]

== Awards and recognition ==

* 2024 - Tribeca Film Festival: Viewpoints Award (Come Closer) [ref: Israeli filmmaker Tom Nesher’s debut feature wins prize at Tribeca Film Festival, The Times of Israel]
* 2024 - Jerusalem Film Festival: GWFF Award for Best Israeli First Feature (Come Closer) [ref: 2024 JFF Winners, Jerusalem Film Festival]
* 2024 - Ophir Awards: Best Feature Film and Best Director (Come Closer)

In 2025, Nesher was elected for Verietys prestigious "10 Directors to watch" list. [ref: ‘The Substance,’ ‘The Piano Lesson,’ ‘Babygirl’ Filmmakers Selected for Variety’s 2025 Directors to Watch, Variety]

== Personal life ==
Since 2016, Nesher has been in relationship with Guy Kornowski, and in April 2026, they had their first son. [ref: "טריפ של אינסוף אהבה": תום נשר ובן זוגה הביאו לעולם את בנם הבכור, mako]

The Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), known until 2005 as the Nuclear Science Centre (NSC), is an autonomous research institute in New Delhi, India, that operates particle accelerators and associated experimental facilities as a national user facility for researchers from Indian universities, colleges and research institutions. It was the first Inter-University Centre set up by the University Grants Commission (UGC), and is funded by the UGC. [ref: Inter University Accelerator Centre (formerly Nuclear Science Centre), University Grants Commission] [ref: About IUAC, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

The centre's main accelerator is a 15 UD Pelletron tandem electrostatic accelerator, which has delivered ion beams to users since 1991 and is supplemented by a superconducting linear accelerator booster, several smaller accelerators, and a compact free-electron laser producing terahertz radiation. It also hosts a PARAM Rudra supercomputer under India's National Supercomputing Mission. [ref: Nuclear reaction and structure studies using experimental facilities at Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), The European Physical Journal A]

== History ==
The UGC conceived the Inter-University Centre model in the early 1980s to give university researchers access to expensive research infrastructure that individual universities could not afford. The proposal for an accelerator-based centre was approved by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in 1984, and the institute was set up that year as the Nuclear Science Centre, the first of the UGC's Inter-University Centres. [ref: Historical dates of events, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

The centre was built as a greenfield project on about 25 acres of land provided by Jawaharlal Nehru University, in the institutional area near the Qutub in south Delhi. [ref: Inter-University Accelerator Centre (IUAC), New Delhi, Vikaspedia] Construction began in December 1986. The centre was registered as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 30 September 1988 and became autonomous on 19 December 1988.

The Pelletron accelerator was commissioned and dedicated to the nation by the Minister of Human Resource Development on 19 December 1990, and the first user experiment was carried out on 8 July 1991, from which date the centre has functioned as a national user facility.

Through the 1990s and 2000s the centre added beamlines and detector systems for nuclear physics, materials science and radiation biology, and developed a superconducting linear accelerator (LINAC) to boost the energy of beams from the Pelletron. Its first LINAC module was commissioned in September 2004. In June 2005 the Nuclear Science Centre was renamed the Inter-University Accelerator Centre, reflecting its role as a multidisciplinary accelerator facility rather than a nuclear physics laboratory alone. [ref: Inter-University Accelerator Centre (Formerly Nuclear Science Centre), Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

== Accelerators ==
=== 15 UD Pelletron ===
The centre's principal machine is a 15 UD Pelletron, a vertical tandem electrostatic accelerator capable of terminal voltages of about 15 MV. It accelerates beams of ions ranging from protons to heavy ions to energies of tens to hundreds of MeV, and has been in near-continuous operation as a user facility since 1991. [ref: IUAC information brochure 2020, Inter-University Accelerator Centre]

=== Superconducting LINAC ===
To reach higher beam energies, the centre designed and built a superconducting linear accelerator that boosts ions from the Pelletron. It uses niobium quarter-wave resonators, a number of which were fabricated in-house at the centre's resonator fabrication facility, and is cooled by liquid helium from an on-site cryogenic plant.

Patrick Mathias, professionally known as Password, is an African songwriter, record producer, singer-songwriter, and Creative Architect whose work bridges mainstream African music, contemporary gospel, and culture-shaping creativity.

His own artistic expression is rooted in the conviction that music should do more than entertain—it should awaken hope, inform identity, and leave a lasting imprint on people and culture. This philosophy informs his evolving body of work, including Cogitations, an Urban Gospel album exploring faith, purpose, identity, and the realities of a generation through an authentic contemporary sound.

As an artist and creative entrepreneur, Password is committed to building work and platforms that transcend trends, expand the possibilities of African music, and demonstrate that faith and cultural relevance can coexist with excellence, innovation, and global ambition.

.werkkzeug ("werkkzeug" is german for "tool") - procedural content generation program for demos. It was developed between 2000-2007 by a German group called ".theproddukt" (a branch of Farbrausch). Only 3 releases of the program were made,.werkkzeug 1.200,.werkkzeug 1.201, and.werkkzeug 3 TE (Texture Edition). In April of 2012, the Source Codes for.werkkzeug 3 and.werkkzeug 4 were released on Github, along with other tools and libraries used for their demos.

This software is mostly known for the award winning game, ".kkrieger", it is also known for ".detuned™" for playstation 3, and other competition winning demos, such as "fr-041: debris"

==.werkkzeug 1.200-1.201 ==
.werkkzeug 1 was the first edition of the program, having a fast and powerful 3d engine, ability to import from.JPEG and.OGG files, an advanced texture and mesh generator, ability to export as.exe and.kk1 files, and other features. [ref:.theprodukkt, www.theprodukkt.com]

The source code for.werkkzeug 1.200-1.201 hasn't been released.

==.werkkzeug 3 ==
.werkkzeug 3 was first released as.werkkzeug 3 TE (Texture Editon) [ref: An archive of theprodukkt's website, talking about.werkkzeug 3 TE.] [ref: The downloads for.werkkzeug 3 TE on the werkkzeug.com website linked on theprodukkt.com.], a limited edition that only had the capability to create textures and test them on simple 3d models. The full version of.werkkzeug3 features a macro-language that allows to make interactive programs, such as video games instead of just demos. In 2004, with the help of a special branch of.werkkzeug 3, a first-person shooter game under the name ".kkrieger" was made, with only 96KB of size.

.werkkzeug 3 is one of the most powerful tools for procedural texturing, having some even appear photorealistic.

The source code for.werkkzeug 3 is open, one having the general version of the program, and another having one built specifically for the making of.kkrieger. [ref: The general.werkkzeug 3 repository., GitHub] [ref: The.kkrieger branch of.werkkzeug 3., GitHub]

==.werkkzeug For mobile ==
.werkkzeug for mobile [ref:.theprodukkt, www.theprodukkt.com] has never been released publicly, but the source code for it has been released. It was built for making small demos or commercial games for mobile devices, altough.theprodukkt hadn't used this version for anything. This version was seemingly a branch of.werkkzeug 3, as the source files for it are in the /werkkzeug3 repository.

==.werkkzeug 4 ==
.werkkzeug 4 is the most recent version of the program, having the most realistic and low in file size results. Many projects such as fr-041: debris and Detuned have been made in it. It was built on the "Altona" framework found in the github repository [ref: fr_public/altona_wz4/altona at master · farbrausch/fr_public, GitHub].

Ilaria Bernardini (born 1977) is an Italian novelist and screenwriter who writes in both Italian and English. Her works include several collections of short stories and graphic novels. [ref: Bernardini, Ilaria, Treccani] She has written screenplays for TV shows such as In Treatment, [ref: In treatment 2, Wildside] Citadel: Diana and along with several films including Chalk, Te l'avevo detto, Amata and The Echo Chamber. [ref: Citadel: Diana, Amazon MGM Studios] [ref: Te l'avevo detto – Commissione Nazionale Valutazione Film, Commissione Nazionale Valutazione Film] [ref: Amata - 2025 - films released 2000 - 2025, Filmitalia] [ref: The Echo Chamber, Cinema/Chicago] She co-authored the screenplay for the short film Chalk, which was nominated for the BAFTA Award for Best Short Film in 2012. [ref: Film Awards 2012, British Academy of Film and Television Arts] She also wrote the screenplay for Morten Tyldum's upcoming film Ibelin. [ref: Charlie Plummer, Stephen Graham, Toni Collette, Anthony Hopkins Starring in 'Ibelin,' Inspirational 'World of Warcraft' Drama, [[Variety (magazine)] [ref: Bill Nighy Joins 'Ibelin' As Production Begins In Oslo, Deadline]

== Early life and education ==
Born in Milan in 1977, Bernardini graduated in Philosophy of science. [ref: Domenica - Ilaria Bernardini - Feltrinelli Editore, feltrinellieditore.it] Her thesis was based on a year-long interview with the poet Alda Merini. [ref: Film card - Torino Film Fest, Torino Film Festival] [ref: La fine dell'amore, Artribune]

== Literary career ==
Bernardini's first novel, Non è niente, was published by Baldini Castoldi Dalai in 2005. [ref: Ilaria Bernardini: Libri e opere in offerta, Gruppo Feltrinelli] The short-story collection La fine dell'amore came out in 2006 and was a finalist for the Premio Chiara in 2007. [ref: Albo d'oro del Premio Chiara, Premio Chiara] Her other works are I supereroi (2009), Corpo libero (2010), Domenica (2012), another short-story collection L'inizio di tutte le cose (2015), [ref: ] Faremo foresta (2018), Il ritratto (2020), Il dolore non esiste (2024) and Amata (2025). Domenica made the finalist of the Premio Letterario Chianti. Faremo foresta was translated into English by Livia Franchini as We Will Be Forest. It was published in 2024 by Whitefox Publishing in London. [ref: We Will Be Forest [Translation], Goldsmiths, University of London]

Her first novel in English, The Portrait, was published by Atlantic Books in the UK in 2020 [ref: The Portrait – Atlantic Books, Atlantic Books] and by Pegasus Books in the US in 2021. [ref: ] Publishers Weekly called it a "mournful English-language debut". [ref: The Portrait, Publishers Weekly] Corpo libero, published in Italy by Feltrinelli and Mondadori, was acquired by HarperCollins for the UK and HarperFiction for the US as The Girls Are Good in 2022. [ref: HarperFiction pre-empts Bernardini's 'gripping' thriller set in world of elite gymnastics, The Bookseller] [ref: The Girls Are Good, HarperCollins Publishers] The book Il dolore non esiste (2024) deals with her relationship (in absence) with her missing father. [ref: «Mio padre non mi parla più. Volevo usare la mia storia per interrogare i vuoti di tutti», Domani] HarperCollins Italia published Amata in 2025. [ref: Amata – Premio Strega 2026, Premio Strega] Bernardini said that Amata was inspired by reporting about a newborn left at a hospital baby hatch in Milan and the public pressure subsequently placed on the child's mother. [ref: "Amata" da libro a film: La scrittrice Bernardini: narro echi di maternità, Avvenire]

Three of her novels have been proposed for the Strega Prize: Faremo foresta in 2018 by writer Caterina Bonvicini; [ref: I titoli proposti dagli Amici della domenica per concorrere alla LXXII edizione, Premio Strega] Il ritratto in 2020 by film director Paolo Sorrentino; [ref: Il ritratto, Premio Strega] and Amata in 2026 by journalist Simonetta Sciandivasci.

=== Graphic novels ===
In 2014, Hop! Edizioni published La fine dell'amore graphic short stories, an illustrated adaptation of stories from Bernardini's first collection with artwork by thirteen illustrators. [ref: La fine dell'amore, Linkiesta.it] [ref: "La fine dell'amore": tredici graphic short stories per tredici talenti italiani – Lo Spazio Bianco, Lo Spazio Bianco] Hop! also published the children's book Facciamo foresta! (2019), which was written together with Lorenza Tonani and inspired by Faremo foresta, narrating the story as a child's diary [ref: Rosicchialibri Facciamo f(or)esta!, Il Rosicchialibri] and a graphic-novel version of Corpo libero (2022), scripted by Chiara Barzini, Bernardini, Ludovica Rampoldi and Giordana Mari, with artwork by Giulia Rosa. [ref: Corpo libero, Hop! Edizioni] [ref: "Corpo libero", un thriller psicologico che svela il lato oscuro della ginnastica artistica, Fumettologica]

== Columnist ==
Bernardini has written for the Italian editions of Rolling Stone, Vogue, [ref: Il nuovo sesso, Vogue Italia] GQ, Amica and also for Vanity Fair. [ref: Ilaria Bernardini – Atlantic Books, Atlantic Books]

Adrian Crutchfield is an American saxophonist, flutist, composer, and horn arranger from Roanoke, Virginia. Working across jazz, funk, R&B, hip-hop, and pop, he is best known as the final saxophonist and horn arranger to perform and record with Prince and The New Power Generation from 2012 to 2016. [ref: Bio – Adrian Crutchfield, adriancrutchfield.com] Fellow saxophonist Dave Koz has called him "one of the most highly anticipated up-and-coming musicians of his generation." [ref: Bio: Adrian Crutchfield, Music Mentor Group]

==Early life and education==

Crutchfield was born and raised in Roanoke, Virginia, where his passion for the saxophone was ignited at age four. During a concert, jazz artist Kenny G noticed the young Crutchfield in the audience, invited him on stage, and gifted him his first saxophone after playing a childish melody on it for the boy. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, Antigua Winds]

Around age ten, Crutchfield and his family relocated to Charlotte, North Carolina, where he was able to pursue his musical education more formally. He attended the Northwest School of the Performing Arts from sixth through eleventh grade. He subsequently graduated from the North Carolina School of the Arts (Conservatory) in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

He went on to pursue higher education at Florida State University, graduating in 2008 with a Bachelor of Arts in Music with a concentration in jazz, contemporary media, and commercial music.

==Career==

===Work with Prince===

Crutchfield served as the final saxophonist and horn arranger for Prince and The New Power Generation from 2012 until Prince's death in 2016. He was featured on several of Prince's later works, including the 2017 Grammy-nominated album Hit-N-Run Phase 2. In 2026, he was credited for overdubbing horn parts on the posthumous Prince album Timeless, a contribution that became the subject of controversy, as Prince's estate had initially stated the album would feature no new overdubs. [ref: Timeless (Prince album)]

===Other collaborations===

Beyond his work with Prince, Crutchfield has performed and toured with a diverse roster of artists including Lionel Richie, Bette Midler, CeeLo Green, Anthony Hamilton, Fantasia Barrino, KC and JoJo, Adina Howard, Regina Belle, Bootsy Collins, Young Jeezy, Jonathan Butler, Peter White, The Avett Brothers, Kenny Lattimore, Maysa Leak, Paul Jackson Jr., and Nathan East. Bette Midler has described his performance style as "divine." [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, ArtistCard]

He is featured as both a soloist and section player on Bootsy Collins' album World Wide Funk. In the jazz world, he has performed alongside Branford Marsalis, Brian Culbertson, Kim Waters, Mike Phillips, Alex Bugnon, Jeff Lorber, and the groups Fourplay and The Gap Band featuring Charlie Wilson. He also appears on the 2025 re-release of Brian Culbertson's Sensuality, contributing tenor saxophone.

Crutchfield collaborated with rapper Big K.R.I.T. on the 2022 neo-soul/hip-hop studio album Digital Roses Don't Die, playing flute on two tracks. On "Wind (Interlude)," he provides the backing flute instrumentation for the poetic, atmospheric interlude; on "More Than Roses," his flute arrangements appear alongside a live horn section and strings that form the song's lush, soulful soundscape. He is also a featured artist on the track "Dishonest Mistake" from the 2017 studio album Resurrection by Adina Howard. [ref: Resurrection (Adina Howard album)]

===Solo career===

Crutchfield released his debut album, Private Party, in 2009, blending jazz, neo-soul, and hip-hop influences. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, Légère Reeds] His second album, Leap, followed in 2017 and was described as a genre-defying project showcasing his neo-soul sound. He released his third album, Lover, in 2022.

In 2025, Crutchfield signed with Trippin 'n Rhythm Records and released Slick, his fourth studio album and label debut. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield – Slick, Smooth Jazz Daily] His single "Sooo Good" reached number one on the Billboard charts in August 2026, holding the position for three consecutive weeks. [ref: Adrian Crutchfield, adriancrutchfield.com] He subsequently achieved a second number-one single with "Hypnotic." His collaborative single "Colors," featuring saxophonist BK Jackson, guitarist Lemek, and multi-instrumentalist Ryan La Valette, also reached number one on the Billboard charts.

Kei Kim (born August 13th, year is unknown) is an New Zealand-based faceless alternative-pop/shoegaze artist, whose fame originates from popular tracks like "for her [ref: ]" and "snakelike (the stars collide) [ref: ]". He has an average of 650,000 monthly listeners on Spotify. He is an independent artist who produces his own tracks on the music production platform BandLab. He writes, produces, and releases his own songs independently. [ref: whatsaheart Lyrics, Songs, and Albums, Genius]

Whatsaheart began his music career in early 2023 with the single "formyslxts", followed by "pxssesive" a month later in early February, along with a remix of the same track with featured artist "SSJ Twiin" two weeks later. Later in summer 2023, he released his 2nd most streamed single on Spotify [ref: whatsaheart, Spotify] titled "for her", totalling over 30 million streams. He then beat his own record with the single "snakelike (the stars collide)" in spring 2024 that reached over 55 million streams, making it his most famous track. In winter 2024, he released his 3rd most streamed single on Spotify, "taking over me". He is however also known for other tracks like "WHXRE" (unreleased) and "lovesick", a song that is the first track on the "lovesick EP", released in 2024. Whatsaheart has a wide variety of unreleased songs, most of which can be found on music streaming platforms like SoundCloud, Audiomack, or YouTube.

== Early Life ==
Kei Kim was born in a small town in New Zealand, on August 13th. The exact birth year is unknown. Kim explained his first real interest in music was in his early childhood, when a soundtrack from famous video-game franchise Sonic the Hedgehog titled "I Am... All Of Me" by Japanese-American rock band Crush 40. A vivid childhood memory of his was playing the song with an air-guitar, while standing on his bed. Growing up, he developed a growing interest in the music group Daft Punk and was a big fan of theirs for a long time. He also mentions that Daft Punk was one of his main inspirations to become a faceless artist. As Kim's music taste evolved, he became a big fan of American rapper and singer XXXTentacion. Kim said he admired Onfroy's self-awareness, talent, and how he wanted to change himself for the better. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

He then went on to discover famous Australian band Chase Atlantic. He explained attending a live performance and being in awe of their performance. He said he wished to be in the band's position and how he would've enjoyed performing live on stage also. Kim highlights that witnessing that performance hadn't necessarily been a direct inspiration for him to begin making music of his own, but rather that it helped him develop the idea in his head. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

== Musical career ==
Kim's musical history dates back to his early childhood. As he was part of a musically-involved family, he had easy and direct access to various musical instruments. His first ever experience with a real instrument was when he played the drums when he was part of his school's band. Kim's involvement with music didn't stop there, however. Before that, Kim recalls covering songs from his PlayStation and recording these covers on his phone. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

Later on, he would again record these covers on the music producing platform BandLab and post said covers to the public. As he stayed consistent with his covers, he started building himself a small community around his identity and music. And although Kim enjoyed the community of people he'd managed to form, he kept believing he could achieve something bigger. This belief led him to opening a TikTok account to advertise his music. He however then took the page down after receiving negative backlash. Approximately a month after closing his first page, Kim decided to try again and opened a second TikTok account, which is a major checkpoint in Kim's musical career. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

When asked in an interview, Kim explained he didn't have any songs he liked more than others, and believed all of his tracks were individually valuable for his career and where he is now. He did however note that he considers "for her" and "pxssesive" important releases in his career. [ref: HISTORY OF WHATSAHEART (DOCUMENTARY)]

== Musical style and discography ==
Whatsaheart's musical genres generally include alternative pop and rock, shoegaze, with occasional alternative metal influences. When asked about influences and inspirations, Kim hightlighted the popular anime Bleach and Japanese video game Kingdom Hearts. He also mentions being a big anime fan overall and enjoying video games. [ref: the whatsaheart interview]

He occasionally uses Light Yagami's (main character in popular manga and anime "Death Note") laugh as an element in some of his tracks like "WHXRE" and "pxssesive".

Reoccurring topics in his tracks are love, heartbreak, and romantic obsession. Some tracks that highlight these topics well are "pxsession", "obsessixn", "toxic", "LOVE GUN", and "sky (falling for you)". Albums with similar focuses are the "lovesick" EP and "katsubō". [ref: whatsaheart - discography]

Ahmed Sajidan Jarjis Rafsan (born 1 July 2003), who also uses the name Sajidan Rafsan, is a Bangladeshi social entrepreneur, humanitarian organizer, researcher and student activist. He is the founder and executive leader of the Shirin Sajmila International Foundation (SSIF), a nonprofit that works in disaster relief, disability rehabilitation, maternal healthcare, civic engagement and youth mobilization in South Asia, the Middle East and Africa. He also founded ApexStride, a company that develops prosthetics for flood-prone regions.

Rafsan is a senior at St. Olaf College in Minnesota, in the class of 2027. He also works on cancer genomics as a data scientist at the Dana–Farber Cancer Institute.

==Early life and education==
Rafsan was born in Chittagong, Bangladesh, and grew up mostly in the Mehedibagh area of the city. His mother, Shirin A. Chowdhury, was a professor of management at the University of Chittagong and had survived cancer three times. She later suffered from uterine carcinosarcoma. His sister, Sajmila Jishmam Uzma, was a third-year electrical and electronic engineering student at the university.

He went to school in Chittagong, mainly at Cantonment English School and College and Chittagong Cantonment Public College. At 13 he started a small school for local children in the yard of the family home. It grew into a nonprofit that taught children from low-income families and offered rehabilitation services and inclusive education models. The initiative was first called Dream Foundation, and SSIF is its later form. In 2018 he spoke on the entrepreneurship panel at the Glocal International Teen Conference, which is organized in Nepal. He was invited as a ninth-grade student.

The United World Colleges (UWC) are an international network of schools that teach the International Baccalaureate to students chosen through national committees. After his SSC examinations in 2019, Rafsan won a full scholarship to UWC Changshu, in the city of Changshu near Shanghai in China, and began there in August 2019. He took a year out when his mother's cancer returned, and he finished the second year at UWC Maastricht in the Netherlands. He then received a full scholarship to St. Olaf College. He is a Davis UWC scholar there, and in 2023 he was named a Weber Scholar at the college's Buntrock Institute for Freedom and Community. In November 2025 the college described him as a junior studying economics and political science, and the Davis scholars report lists him under quantitative economics. He studied data science and economics.

==Family loss and healthcare==
On 10 July 2022 Rafsan was in India with his mother and sister, who were hit by a bus as they crossed a street. He and his brother were on the other side of the road. The accident happened in Kolkata, and his mother was badly hurt. His sister died of her injuries. His mother, partly paralyzed and still ill, died on 22 August 2022, within 40 days of the accident. She died at Imperial Hospital in Chittagong.

Rafsan has said that his time in public, local and private hospitals in Bangladesh and India showed him inequalities in access, cost and care, and that this shaped his later public health and humanitarian work. After the deaths he renamed the organization the Shirin Sajmila International Foundation, after his mother and sister.

==Humanitarian and social work==
SSIF is a United States 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Rafsan founded it in 2016. SSIF says it has reached more than 700,000 people through programs in disaster response, disability rehabilitation, maternal healthcare, education, public health and civic engagement. It works in Bangladesh and has led refugee support in Egypt for Sudanese and Syrian communities. It also works in Kashmir, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and other countries.

SSIF worked with the World Health Organization, local government and military partners during the 2024 floods in Bangladesh, giving emergency relief, medical care, menstrual hygiene supplies and rehabilitation support to families in districts including Feni and Noakhali. Its website says a 15-member medical team runs regular camps in flood-affected areas with the Bangladesh Army, and that it sent 20 tons of medicine to Feni with the World Health Organization and the government.

Rafsan was one of the key young organizers of protest mobilization during the July 2024 uprising and a medical-response coordinator, and SSIF gave medical and legal help to injured student protesters. During and after the uprising, SSIF launched Bir Chattala Shajai, a civic and public art movement. It mobilized more than 100,000 young people, mainly in Chittagong and Dhaka, for murals, graffiti and other civic work.

In July 2025, after a plane crashed into Milestone School and College in Dhaka, Rafsan wrote on Facebook about Sabuja Begum, a school employee who was badly burned while rescuing children. SSIF said it was paying for her care and her family's expenses.

==ApexStride==
Rafsan started ApexStride in 2023 to build repairable prosthetic systems for humid, flood-prone places. It also works on mobility rehabilitation and accessibility for people with disabilities. A Bangla feature article described his aim as restoring "freedom of movement" and dignity for people with disabilities. He has talked about the work on Bangladeshi television, including Channel 24's Prosongo Chattogram in September 2026.

== References ==

Sam Ven () is a Cambodian social work administrator and child protection advocate. [ref: Management Team - This Life Cambodia, This Life Cambodia] He serves as the Children and Families Section Lead at This Life Cambodia (TLC), a non-governmental organization specializing in community-led developmental programs. Ven is recognized for directing structural social assistance programs focused on juvenile rehabilitation, diversionary alternative sentencing, and family preservation for marginalized populations affected by parental incarceration. [ref: Sam Ven - Global Social Service Workforce Alliance, Global Social Service Workforce Alliance] Community programs managed under his administration have provided social support, case tracking, and integration services to approximately 3,000 families throughout Cambodia. [ref: Celebrating Recognition: Sam Ven's Impact on Social Service..., This Life Cambodia]

== Early life and education ==
Ven was raised in a rural village in Cambodia during the post-Khmer Rouge reconstruction period. His early formal education was disrupted by localized civil conflicts and geographic displacement. Despite prevailing socio-economic barriers in his community, he completed his secondary education and subsequently graduated with a Bachelor's Degree in Business Administration. His early exposure to community instability influenced his later career pivot toward professional social welfare and advocacy systems.

== Career ==

=== Non-governmental organization work ===
Ven entered the non-profit sector by volunteering for localized non-governmental organizations (NGOs) targeting substance harm reduction and urban marginalized populations. In 2012, he formally joined the professional staff of This Life Cambodia (TLC).

He initially served as a Program Officer for three years, tracking legal case management for minors entangled in the provincial criminal justice system. He was subsequently promoted to Program Coordinator, where he led the "This Life Beyond Bars" team, before being appointed to the organization's Senior Management Team as a section leader.

=== Program management and strategy ===
As the Section Lead for Children and Families, Ven oversees five operational community initiatives and manages a department of approximately 30 professional social service workers. His administrative portfolio focuses heavily on the "This Life in Families" (TLIF) and "This Life Beyond Bars" (TLBB) frameworks.

Operating across several provinces—including Siem Reap, Banteay Meanchey, and Phnom Penh—these initiatives concentrate on:
* Institutionalization Prevention: Administering structural family livelihood assessments and educational grants to prevent the placement of children into residential care institutions (orphanages) when primary caretakers face imprisonment.
* Kinship Care Optimization: Developing strategic case management networks to safely retain vulnerable minors within extended family or biological structures.
* Juvenile Reintegration: Coordinating life skills, vocational training, and post-release support metrics inside juvenile correctional spaces to mitigate youth recidivism rates.

== Advocacy and public engagement ==
Ven frequently acts as a civil society liaison to Cambodian state judicial and correctional bodies concerning statutory reforms for minor offenders. In December 2023, he represented TLC at the Annual Meeting of the Siem Reap Provincial Administration, engaging in policy talks with Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Tea Seiha. [ref: On 25th and 26th December 2023, Mr. Sam Ven..., This Life Cambodia Official Communication] Ven advocated for structural alternatives to detention at the immediate point of youth arrest, alongside educational reforms inside prisons to alleviate structural institutional overcrowding.

Additionally, he coordinates public human rights broadcasts detailing juvenile justice frameworks alongside national ministries, such as the Department of Juvenile Rehabilitation under the Ministry of Social Affairs, Veterans and Youth Rehabilitation (MoSVY). [ref: Rights of the child in the conflict with the law and the progress, Cambodian Center for Human Rights] According to organizational performance indexes, programs under his managerial oversight have systematically verified the community tracking and safe reintegration of more than 1,500 vulnerable children.

Pealeism, known by its namesake as Practical Christianity, or more commonly Positive Thinking, is a non-denominational Christian revivalist and new religious movement based on the preaching of Norman Vincent Peale and his book The Power of Positive Thinking. It emerged in the 1940s advocating for Christian revival in the United States, primarily emphasizing the practical, rather than creedal, aspects of Christian faith to improve daily life. Pealeism reached its height during the early Fourth Great Awakening before declining throughout the 1960s. [ref: Surge of Piety: Norman Vincent Peale and the Remaking of American Religious Life, Yale University Press]

Pealeism’s legacy remains politically, scientifically, and theologically controversial. Its approach to Christian faith, mental health, and politics has been respectively criticized as unbiblical, scientifically flawed, and having provided religious justification for conservatism and radical anti-communism during the Cold War.

The movement’s philosophy received renewed public attention during Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and first presidency, with Peale being cited by biographers and Trump himself as a formative influence on the latter’s worldview.

== History ==
=== Opposition to the New Deal ===
Beginning in 1942, Norman Vincent Peale travelled across the United States to court contacts in business, politics, industry, and religion, which would become a movement around his ministry. In 1945, Peale and his wife, Ruth Stafford Peale, established Guideposts magazine, which featured personal accounts claiming how Christian faith helped overcome personal difficulty.

Peale associated Christianity with American civic life, capitalism, anti-communism, opposing U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, and participated in conservative organizations including the Committee for Constitutional Government and Spiritual Mobilization. [ref: Norman Vincent Peale Was A Conservative Hero Known Well Beyond His Era, NPR] He belived Christian revival could encouraging Americans to treat faith as integral to personal wellbeing and thus be a counter to communist influence.

=== Post-World War II era and Cold War ===
After World War II, the Pealeist movement grew to include the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic and Foundation for Christian Living, which was the administrative arm of Peale’s ministry. The two organizations allowed Peale to preach to business executives, industrial workers, and youth outside his immediate congregation. In 1951, the Religio-Psychiatric Clinic was renamed the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry, [ref: Dr. Smiley Blanton Dead Here; Psychiatrist and Author Was 84; Co-Founder With Dr. Peale of Clinic to Aid Distressed Wrote 'Love or Perish', The New York Times] with Peale serving as its until 1962. The foundation promoted cooperation between clergy and psychiatrists, supported pastoral counselling, and sought to establish Christian faith as integral to mental health.

Peale’s relationships with Federal Bureau of Investigation director J. Edgar Hoover and U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower, increased his public visibility and brought his views on religion and national identity to influential circles. He supported campaigns presenting the United States as “one nation under God,” which was part of a broader political and cultural trend towards the prominence of religious language in public life during the 1950s.

=== Decline and institutional reorganization ===
Peale’s ministry remained active after the 1950s, but growth in American religious observance started declining in the 1960s.

Peale stepped down as president of the American Foundation of Religion and Psychiatry in 1962. The foundation subsequently faced financial difficulties by the late 1960s and struggled to maintain the level of support in had the decade prior, reflecting broader changes in the relationship between Christian revivalism and mental-health care.

In 1972, the foundation merged with the Academy of Religion and Mental Health to create the Institutes of Religion and Health.

Peale continued to lecture, write, and participate in religious and media activities until he retired as senior minister of Marble Collegiate Church in 1984. He also received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the United States’ highest civilian honour.

=== 2016 United States presidential election and influence on Donald Trump ===
Peale’s influence received renewed attention during Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign through the latter’s public accounts of his religious upbringing. Trump attended Marble Collegiate Church with his family, and repeatedly identified Peale as a significant spiritual influence. [ref: How Trump got religion — and why his legendary minister’s son now rejects him, The Washington Post] Peale’s influence continues to be relevant in public discourse about Christianity’s role in contemporary American conservatism. [ref: ]
[truncated]

Julian Lual

**Julian Lual** (born April 16, 2002) is a Canadian college basketball player who most recently played for the Alcorn State Braves of the Southwestern Athletic Conference (SWAC). He previously played for McCook Community College and the Arkansas State Red Wolves.

## Early life and high school career

Lual was born in Canada and grew up in Calgary, Alberta, where he attended Central Memorial High School. He later moved to the United States to complete his high school career at Central Pointe Christian Academy in Kissimmee, Florida.

## College career

### McCook Community College (2020–2022)

Lual began his collegiate career at the junior college (JUCO) level with McCook Community College in Nebraska. As a freshman in the pandemic-shortened 2020–21 season, he appeared in 25 games, averaging 10.0 points and 5.7 rebounds per game. He broke out during his sophomore season (2021–22), starting all 31 games and averaging 14.1 points, 8.9 rebounds, and 1.9 assists per game. He recorded 15 double-doubles on the year, earning All-Region IX accolades and attracting Division I recruiting interest.

### Arkansas State (2022–2024)

In 2022, Lual transferred to NCAA Division I program Arkansas State under head coach Mike Balado, later playing under Bryan Hodgson. During the 2022–23 season, he appeared in 32 games (six starts), averaging 4.9 points and 3.0 rebounds in 18.2 minutes per game. The following season (2023–24), he retained a rotational role on a Red Wolves team that reached the Sun Belt tournament championship game, averaging 4.5 points and 2.2 rebounds over 32 appearances.

### Alcorn State (2024–2025)

For his final year of collegiate eligibility, Lual transferred to Alcorn State for the 2024–25 season. He appeared in 22 games for the Braves, contributing 5.2 points and 3.0 rebounds per game before concluding his collegiate career.

Mamoon Abdel Halim Mohamed Wagih (; born 13 November 1960) is an Egyptian linguist and academic specializing in Arabic grammar, morphology and lexicography. He is a professor emeritus at Fayoum University, a former dean of its Faculty of Dar Al-Uloom, and a member of the Academy of the Arabic Language in Cairo. He has served as scientific director of the Historical Dictionary of the Arabic Language. [ref: مأمون وجيه, مجمع اللغة العربية بالقاهرة] [ref: مأمون عبد الحليم محمد وجيه, Fayoum University] [ref: صلاح فضل ومأمون وجيه ضمن تشكيل مؤتمر مجمع اللغة العربية بالشارقة, أخبار اليوم]

== Early life and education ==
Wagih was born on 13 November 1960 in a village in the Tanta district of Gharbia Governorate, Egypt. He studied at Tanta University, receiving a bachelor's degree in Arabic language in 1984 and a master's degree in Arabic grammar in 1989. In 1996, he earned a doctorate in Arabic grammar from Cairo University through a joint-supervision programme involving the School of Oriental and African Studies at the University of London.

== Academic career ==
Wagih joined the Faculty of Dar Al-Uloom at Fayoum as an assistant lecturer in 1990. Following his doctorate, he became a lecturer in 1996. From 1999 to 2009, he held academic appointments at the Faculty of Sharia and Islamic Studies in Al-Ahsa, part of Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University in Saudi Arabia.

He returned to Fayoum University in 2009 and was promoted to professor in September 2011. He subsequently headed the Department of Grammar, Morphology and Prosody and served as dean of the Faculty of Dar Al-Uloom from 2012 to 2015. He also served as editor-in-chief of the faculty's academic journal. Fayoum University records his appointment as professor emeritus in August 2021. [ref: أ.د. مأمون عبد الحليم محمد, Fayoum University]

== Academy of the Arabic Language ==
In October 2013, Wagih was appointed an expert on dictionary committees at the Academy of the Arabic Language in Cairo. He was elected to membership in 2016, succeeding Mahmoud Ali Makki. His work at the Academy has included committees concerned with the Great Arabic Dictionary, Arabic poetic vocabulary and historical lexicography.

== Historical Dictionary of the Arabic Language ==
Wagih has served as scientific director of the Historical Dictionary of the Arabic Language (), a project documenting the historical usage and semantic development of Arabic vocabulary. The project has involved Arabic language academies and received support from the Emirate of Sharjah. [ref: مقدمة المدير العلمي, المعجم التاريخي للغة العربية]

The first eight volumes were presented in Sharjah on 5 November 2020. In a November 2021 interview with Youm7, Wagih discussed the dictionary's methodology, including its treatment of word origins and changes in meaning across historical periods. [ref: المدير العلمى للمعجم التاريخى للغة العربية فى حواره لـ"اليوم السابع", Youm7]

== Research and publications ==
Wagih's research includes Arabic syntax, morphology, grammatical analysis of classical poetry and comparisons between classical Arabic grammatical traditions and modern linguistic approaches. His publications have addressed metathesis, ellipsis, syntactic ambiguity, constituent ordering and grammatical evidence in pre-Islamic poetry.

=== Selected books ===

* دراسات في علم التصريف (Studies in Arabic Morphology).
* ظاهرة الإعلال والإبدال: دراسة تحليلية (The Phenomena of I'lal and Ibdal: An Analytical Study).
* العروض والقافية بين التراث والتجديد (Arabic Prosody and Rhyme: Between Tradition and Renewal).
* منصوبات الأسماء: دراسة في ضوء التراث النحوي (Nouns in the Accusative Case: A Study in the Light of the Arabic Grammatical Tradition).

=== Selected research ===

* القلب المكاني في البنية العربية — research on metathesis in Arabic morphology.
* قرائن الحذف في البنية والتركيب — research on ellipsis in Arabic linguistic structures.
* مسوغات التقديم الإجباري في التراكيب العربية — research on obligatory fronting in Arabic syntax.
* شواهد امرئ القيس في التراث النحوي — research on grammatical evidence from the poetry of Imru' al-Qais.
* أثر الرواية الشفهية للشعر الجاهلي في تعديل الحكم النحوي — research on oral transmission of pre-Islamic poetry and grammatical judgments.

== Poetry ==
Wagih is also the author of a poetry collection titled غضبة النيل (The Wrath of the Nile), which contains 26 poems according to the Academy of the Arabic Language.

== Michael S. Oberlaender ==
Michael S. Oberlaender is a cybersecurity executive and author. In March 2021 he was appointed chief information security officer (CISO) of LogMeIn. He is the author of the Global CISO series of books on CISO leadership, strategy and communication with boards.

== Career ==
Coverage of Oberlaender's 2021 appointment at LogMeIn described him as a 30-year industry veteran who had held CISO and advisory positions at other organizations, including Vodafone Deutschland, Cisco and Netskope. The coverage did not give his titles or dates at those companies.

== LogMeIn ==
In March 2021, LogMeIn named Oberlaender its chief information security officer. He was described as leading a global security team covering IT security, security operations, assurance, engagement, governance, risk management and compliance, and as responsible for the security of the company's internal systems and software products. LogMeIn's chief information officer, Ian Pitt, described him as a strategic partner for improving the company's software development lifecycle.

== Board and advisory roles ==
At the time of his LogMeIn appointment, Oberlaender was reported to serve on the board of the ISACA Greater Houston Chapter. In July 2024, Netenrich named him among the founding members of its Security Advisory Council. He is also listed as a speaker by SecureWorld.

== Certifications and memberships ==
Coverage of his 2021 appointment listed professional certifications including CISM, CISSP, CISA and CRISC, and memberships in (ISC)², ISACA, ISSA and InfraGard. These details are reported as of March 2021.

== Books ==
Oberlaender is the author of the Global CISO series.

* Global CISO — Strategy, Tactics, & Leadership: How to Succeed in InfoSec and CyberSecurity. Security Management reviewed the book in October 2020. The reviewer, Ben Rothke, described it as a playbook-style guide for new and experienced CISOs covering strategy, people, regulation, business goals and budgets, and noted its emphasis on security as an ongoing effort rather than a one-time project.
* Premier CISO — Board & C-Suite: Raising the Bar for Cybersecurity. Security Management reviewed the book in February 2025, describing it as the third volume in the series and as a practical guide to working with boards and executives. The review presented its central idea as CISOs earning board trust by communicating in business terms. Help Net Security discussed the book in a September 2024 interview with Oberlaender and included it in a March 2025 list of ten books for security leaders.

== Media appearances ==
In a September 2024 interview with Help Net Security, Oberlaender discussed fitting security into business processes, building a security strategy from scratch, and aligning with frameworks such as ISO, NIST and CIS. In March 2026, Fortra published a question-and-answer interview with him covering how he entered cybersecurity, the evolution of the CISO role, security culture, threats from artificial intelligence and quantum cryptography, limited CISO access to boards, and reliance on outsourced virtual CISOs.

== References ==

= Kenneth “K” Morrow =

Kenneth (Ken) “K” Morrow is an American author/writer/inventor specializing in the production, cultivation and study of the cannabis plant, hashish production, terpene/cannabinoid/flavonoid isolation and pharmaceutical applications. He is the founding owner of Trichome Technologies, a molecular research and development company.

Kenneth Morrow, who has also written under the pen name “K,” is an author/writer, botanist, horticulturist, agronomist, cannabis formulation specialist, consultant, and the founding owner of Trichome Technologies. His book [https://www.amazon.com/Marijuana-Horticulture-Fundamentals-Comprehensive-Cultivation-ebook/dp/B0HJMWBD32 Marijuana Horticulture Fundamentals: A comprehensive guide to cannabis cultivation and hashish production] is a highly regarded informational source. He has written for multiple periodicals for decades and is considered a respected information source (see list below). Informational links to many of the articles and media interviews and programs mentioned in the detailed biographical notes compiled by @[user]. More information and articles can be found at [https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/magazine CannabisBusinessTimes.com] and [https://muckrack.com/kenneth-morrow Morrow’s Muckrack profile].

= Kenneth Morrow’s Early Years =
To understand what Kenneth “K” Morrow has built you have to understand the world he built it in. Not the world of licensed dispensaries and compliance departments and seed-to-sale tracking software — that world didn't exist yet. Not the world of venture capital and celebrity strains and Instagram marketing. That world was decades away.

The world Morrow came from was completely illegal. Every transaction happened in cash. Every relationship depended on trust. Every pound moved was a risk taken in service of something the people taking the risk genuinely believed in. Morrow operated in this world and was thirteen years old when he started.

In 1978, in the ninth grade, with his mother's permission, Morrow began cultivating cannabis hydroponically. He ordered a Hydropot system from the back of a [https://hightimes.com/ High Times Magazine] — a busboy tray, lava rock, a fish aquarium aerator, a little Miracle-Gro. It was the only hydroponic system he ever purchased. Everything after that he built himself.

Morrow had access to cannabis that most people his age had never encountered. And he wasn't just consuming it. He was studying it. Between 1978 and 1981, his early experiences with the plant ranged across blond and red hashish from Lebanon, Afghan hash, and multiple old world cultivars — Panamanian, Mexican, Columbian, Thai. These were not recreational curiosities. They were reference points. Each one told him something about what the plant was capable of, each raised the bar on what he was trying to achieve.

In 1980 or 1981, he took his first hit of an unusually clean, clear amber honey oil. The flavor was extraordinary. The cleanliness was extraordinary. The potency was extraordinary. That oil became the defining standard of everything that followed — the reference point that set the bar for flavor, cleanliness, and potency that he would spend the next four decades building toward and ultimately surpassing.

By the mid-1980s, as growers were introducing commercial scale operations and high quality trim was becoming more abundant, Morrow began trafficking cannabis. He was fifteen years old and continued through the late eighties and into the early nineties. But trafficking was never the point. The plant was the point. His focus was moving steadily away from flower and toward the trichome — toward what lived in the resin, toward what the plant was actually capable of when you knew how to capture it properly.

He continued his dry sieve education throughout this period, pursuing super refined extracts with the particular obsession of someone who has tasted what is possible and cannot accept anything less. And through all of it — the trafficking, the cultivation, the extraction experiments — he was doing something that would define his legacy more than any single technique: he was documenting everything, developing repeatable and consistent and predictable processes, and building a foundation of knowledge that could be passed forward.

In a world where there was no patent office to run to, no institution to credential him, no legal framework to protect what he was building — Morrow built it anyway. And he gave it away.

= The 1990s =
In the early 1990s, Morrow continued learning while pushing further into the question that consumed him: what was the best possible way to capture the active ingredients in the trichome?

Then in 1994, Morrow received very basic water hash isolation instructions. What he did with those basic instructions was entirely his own. He employed a titanium water chiller to replace ice, maintaining the water at precise temperatures throughout the extraction process. He utilized fresh frozen plant material — harvested and immediately frozen rather than dried — to minimize contamination and preserve the aromatic terpene compounds that the drying process destroyed. The result was a superior aromatic and flavorful isolate of extraordinary quality. He was producing it years before any commercial separation equipment existed for this process, because that equipment hadn't been invented yet. He was building everything himself because he had to.
[truncated]
