Draft text:
A. J. Ramirez is an educator, licensed professional counselor, researcher, and United Methodist lay minister in Georgia. She works at Valdosta State University in sociology and Women's and Gender Studies. Her work includes teaching and research on gender, sexuality, social inequality, and the experiences of marginalized groups. [ref: Dr. A. J. Ramirez - Directory Profile - Valdosta State University, www.valdosta.edu]

Education and academic career

Ramirez earned a bachelor's degree in sociology from the University of North Georgia. She later earned a master's degree in marriage and family therapy and a Doctor of Education degree from Valdosta State University. [ref: Dr. A. J. Ramirez - Directory Profile - Valdosta State University, www.valdosta.edu]

At Valdosta State, Ramirez works in sociology and Women's and Gender Studies. In 2022, she participated in a university program on women's suffrage supported by a grant from the American Library Association. The program included a discussion of Women Making History: The 19th Amendment Book, a collection of essays compiled by the National Park Service. [ref: VSU Wins American Library Association Grant for Women’s Suffrage Project, Valdosta CEO] [ref: Valdosta State University's Odum Library & Women's & Gender Studies Program Receive Grant for Women's Suffrage Book Discussion Project, Georgia Library Quarterly]

Ramirez has also taught in the department of Women's Studies at Florida State University. [ref: ]

Counseling

Ramirez owns and leads L.E.A.F. Therapy Services, a counseling practice in South Georgia. The practice provides counseling for individuals, couples, and families. Its stated mission focuses on well-being, relationships, and healthier communities, and it welcomes clients from different backgrounds, including people who have experienced discrimination or marginalization. [ref: Home, My Vxw Site Drdccu 1]

Research

Ramirez has collaborated with sociologist Nancy L. Malcom on research about LGBTQ+-affirming members of The United Methodist Church. Their work examined why some LGBTQ+ people and their allies remain in the denomination despite disagreements over LGBTQ+ inclusion.

Their research included “Worth Fighting For”: Research Findings on Affirming United Methodists’ Decision to Stay or Leave and the series “Why Do They Stay? Queer Voices Share Their UMC Experiences.” The publications discuss the experiences and decisions of people navigating questions of inclusion within the church. [ref: Sociologists Find LGBTQ United Methodists, Allies Stay in UMC Out of Hope, United Methodist Insight] [ref: Why Do They Stay? Queer Voices Share Their UMC Experiences, United Methodist Insight]

Media appearances

In May 2023, Ramirez appeared with Malcom on Faith Revisited, a podcast hosted by the Reverend Ben Gosden. The episode, titled “Why Stay: Research on Marginalized Voices in the UMC,” focused on their research and the experiences of LGBTQ+-affirming United Methodists. [ref: Faith Revisited Podcast, Faith Revisited Podcast]

Ramirez was also interviewed for In Between, a student documentary directed by Adison Oliver and associated with students in Florida State University's media department. [ref: THE IN•BETWEEN]

Mosaic United Methodist Church and LGBTQ Advocacy

Ramirez has advocated for LGBTQ+ inclusion in the South Georgia Conference of The United Methodist Church. Ramirez and her wife, Gayle, helped establish an LGBTQ+-affirming United Methodist community in Valdosta, Georgia. The initiative received support from Centenary United Methodist Church in Macon, initially under the leadership of the Reverend Timothy Bagwell and later with support from the Reverend Sara Pugh Montgomery. The community developed into Mosaic United Methodist Church. The denomination's directory records the congregation's start date as March 1, 2023. [ref: ]

Lay ministry

Ramirez became a certified lay minister in the South Georgia Conference in December 2024. In December 2025, Centenary United Methodist Church announced a congregational process concerning her advancement toward candidacy for ordained ministry as a deacon. [ref: Called Charge Conference, Centenary Church] The 2024 General Conference of The United Methodist Church removed longstanding restrictions on LGBTQ+ people serving as clergy. Ramirez's ministry developed during this period of change in the denomination.

Draft: Abdelrahman Mohamed (AI Researcher)

Draft text:
Abdelrahman Mohamed (also written Abdel-rahman Mohamed); is an Egyptian-American computer scientist working in the United States, known for his research on deep learning for speech recognition and self-supervised speech representation learning. As a doctoral student at the University of Toronto under Geoffrey Hinton and Gerald Penn, he was part of the group that first applied deep belief networks to acoustic modelling, work that is credited with starting the deep learning era in speech recognition. He later created the HuBERT model and co-developed wav2vec 2.0 at Meta AI. He is a co-founder and chief AI scientist of the advertising-technology company Rembrand.

== Education ==
Mohamed received a bachelor's degree (2004) and a master's degree (2007) in computer science from Cairo University. After a research position at KU Leuven in Belgium, he began doctoral studies at the University of Toronto in 2008, where he was supervised by Gerald Penn and Geoffrey Hinton, receiving his PhD in 2014.

== Career ==
In 2009, Mohamed, George E. Dahl and Hinton showed that deep belief networks could outperform the Gaussian mixture models then standard in speech recognition on the TIMIT phone-recognition benchmark. The result was extended to large-vocabulary recognition by groups at Microsoft, Google and IBM, and Mohamed was a co-author of the 2012 overview paper in IEEE Signal Processing Magazine that summarised the shared findings of the four groups. With Alex Graves and Hinton he also published early work on deep recurrent neural networks for speech recognition, and with Ossama Abdel-Hamid and others on convolutional neural networks for speech.

Mohamed was a researcher at Microsoft Research in Redmond, Washington, from 2014 to 2017, and a principal scientist and manager in the Amazon Alexa AI group from 2017 to 2018. From 2018 to 2022 he was at Meta's Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) laboratory in Seattle, where his group worked on learning speech representations from unlabelled audio. He co-developed wav2vec 2.0, a contrastive self-supervised framework for speech, and led the development of HuBERT (Hidden-Unit BERT), which learns speech representations by predicting clustered "hidden units" of masked audio segments; both models are widely used as pre-trained foundations for speech systems. His group extended the approach to audio-visual speech with AV-HuBERT and co-organised SUPERB, a benchmark for evaluating self-supervised speech models. He was first author of a 2022 review of self-supervised speech representation learning in the IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing.

In December 2022 Mohamed left Meta, where he had been a director of AI research, to co-found Rembrand, a Palo Alto, California company that uses generative AI to insert virtual product placement into video, serving as its chief AI scientist. The company, led by Omar Tawakol, raised an $8 million seed round in 2023 and a $23 million Series A in 2025.

== Awards ==
* IEEE Signal Processing Society Best Paper Award, 2016, for "Convolutional Neural Networks for Speech Recognition" (with Abdel-Hamid, Jiang, Deng, Penn and Yu).
* IEEE Signal Processing Magazine Best Paper Award, 2022, for "Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition: The Shared Views of Four Research Groups".

== Selected publications ==
* Deep belief networks for phone recognition
* Acoustic Modeling Using Deep Belief Networks, IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
* Deep Neural Networks for Acoustic Modeling in Speech Recognition: The Shared Views of Four Research Groups, IEEE Signal Processing Magazine
* Speech recognition with deep recurrent neural networks
* Convolutional Neural Networks for Speech Recognition, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
* wav2vec 2.0: A Framework for Self-Supervised Learning of Speech Representations
* HuBERT: Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning by Masked Prediction of Hidden Units, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing
* Self-Supervised Speech Representation Learning: A Review, IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing

The Newton Novices' Hurdle is a Grade 2 National Hunt hurdle race in Great Britain which is open to horses aged four years or older. It is run at Haydock Park over a distance of about 1 mile 7½ furlongs (1 mile 7 furlongs 144 yards, or 3,149 metres), and during its running there are nine hurdles to be jumped. [ref: Haydock Course Map, Racing Post] The race is for novice hurdlers, and it is scheduled to take place each year in November.

The race was inaugurated in 2004, run in early December at Listed level. The following year, it was moved to November and formed part of the undercard for the new Lancashire Chase, a role the race still performs today. However, the race was held on the day before (the Friday) from 2011 to 2016, when it returned to the Saturday. [ref: Haydock Results, Racing Post] It was upgraded in 2023 to Grade 2. [ref: Package of changes agreed to help strengthen performance of British Jump racing, BHA] The race is currently sponsored by Betfair.

Luca Camilleri (born 2005) is a Maltese podcaster and content creator. He is the founder and host of Champions Connect, a long-form interview podcast founded in 2024, whose guests have included Prime Minister of Malta Robert Abela and former Prime Minister Joseph Muscat.

== Early life ==
Camilleri grew up in Malta and played football as a goalkeeper before leaving the sport. He has described himself as a disruptive pupil at school and has cited his parents' separation as a turning point.

== Career ==
Camilleri founded Champions Connect in 2024. The podcast features long-form conversations, usually one to two hours, with entrepreneurs, executives, athletes, politicians and artists, and is aimed mainly at listeners aged 15 to 25. The first episode was released on 1 February 2025, and 43 episodes had been released by October 2026.

Guests have included Robert Abela (2025), Joseph Muscat (2026), European commissioner Glenn Micallef, tenor Joseph Calleja, boxer Joe Cordina, and footballers Andrew Hogg, Gilbert Agius and Matthew Guillaumier. In a 2026 episode, Camilleri interviewed EBO chief executive Gege Gatt about the next five years of artificial intelligence. The show is published on YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts, with clips on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook. Camilleri also edits much of the show's video content himself.

= Leif Halvorsen =
Leif Christian Halvorsen (born July 20, 1954) is an incarcerated individual whose convictions include three counts of murder and retaining a concealed deadly weapon. [ref: ]

== Crimes ==
In January 1983, in Lexington, Kentucky, Halvorsen and his accomplice, Mitchell Willoughby, shot Joe Norman, Joey Durrum, and Jacqueline Greene to death while under the influence of painkillers, cocaine, and marijuana. The event took place at Jacqueline Greene's residency, where she and Joe Norman resided. [ref: Halvorsen v. Com. (Ky. 1987), Justia Law]

In July 1983, the Fayette Circuit Court tried Halvorsen and Willoughby for their involvement in the triple homicide of Norman, Durrum, and Greene. During this trial, Mitchell Willoughby took all the blame for the shootings. However, upon the court's consideration of Halvorsen and Willoughby making errors in their assertions, it was determined that both were to blame for the shootings. On September 15th, 1983, Halvorsen and Mitchell Willoughby were convicted for three counts of murder. Leif Halvorsen's charges included a death sentence for the killing of Greene and Durrum and a life sentence for the killing of Norman. In addition, Halvorsen was convicted for retaining a concealed deadly weapon, which led to him being sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment as well as being fined $500. [ref: Halvorsen v. Com. (Ky. 1987), Justia Law]

In Kentucky, lower courts are required to have their death penalty rulings appealed to the Kentucky Supreme Court for confirmation. Thus, on July 2nd, 1987, the Kentucky Supreme Court confirmed the Fayette Circuit Court's decision for Halvorsen and Willoughby's death penalties. [ref: Halvorsen v. Com. (Ky. 1987), Justia Law]

== Administrative Exception ==
On December 21st, 2001, in a memo from Warden Parker of Kentucky State Penitentiary, Parker provided his rationale on why Halvorsen would be a benefit to the Kentucky Department of Correction's Youth Awareness Program. Due to security risks, the Kentucky State Penitentiary did not typically allow death-row inmates to serve on the Youth Awareness Program's panel. In the same memo, Parker clarified that he made an exception for Halvorsen to serve as a panel member for the Youth Awareness Program due to his consideration of a variety of factors such as Halvorsen's remorse for his actions and his persistent intent in preventing future generations from being incarcerated. As a consequence, Halvorsen became the first and only death-sentenced inmate in the history of the Kentucky Department of Corrections to be allowed to participate in its Youth Awareness Program. In the following years, numerous memos detailed accounts of individuals benefitting from Halvorsen's advocacy efforts. [ref: Application for Executive Clemency for Leif Halvorsen]

== Appeals ==

=== Halvorsen v. Parker (2012) ===
In 2012, Halvorsen filed a motion to amend his writ of habeas corpus in order to assert eleven new claims. For these eleven claims, Halvorsen contended that during his state post-conviction proceedings, there was an ineffective assistance of counsel, in which his post-conviction counsel failed to acknowledge that the trial counsel in his original defense had failed to raise questions for several unconstitutional claims used against him. On November 19th, 2012, the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Kentucky denied Halvorsen's motion to amend his petition for his writ of habeas corpus. The rationale behind this decision was that three years prior, Halvorsen had the ability to assert ineffective assistance of counsel when he filed his original petition, and how amending this petition would have been unfairly prejudicial to the current defendants who worked on the case as well as presenting an unnecessary delay for the proceedings. [ref: Halvorsen v. Parker]

=== Halvorsen v. White (2018) ===
In 2018, Halvorsen petitioned for a writ of habeas corpus, in which he claimed that trial court error, ineffective assistance of counsel, and prosecutorial and juror misconduct violated his constitutional rights. On August 20th, 2018, due to the Kentucky Supreme Court presenting reasonable evidence corroborating their justifications, the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit denied Halvorsen appeal. [ref: HALVORSEN v. WHITE (2018), FindLaw]

=== Halvorsen v. Commonwealth of Kentucky (2023) ===
In 2023, Halvorsen requested for post-conviction relief, claiming that the jury instructions used for his original convictions were biased in suggesting that the jury act on the account of a combined decision, thus rendering the final verdict as non-unanimous. On March 23, 2023, Kentucky's Supreme Court denied Halvorsen appeal. The rationale behind this decision was that cases at bar were final and upon elaborating on CR 60.02 and CR 60.03, clarified that those rules prohibit a defendant to circumvent the time limitations of a RCr 11.42 motion. In addition, the Supreme Court of Kentucky utilized Teague v. Lane to determine that the Teague rule cannot be applied retroactively on collateral review to convictions finalized prior to 2010. [ref: Halvorsen v. Commonwealth (Ky. 2023), Justia Law]
[truncated]

Draft: Yohannes Tekle Haymanot

Draft text:
Yohannes Teklehaimanot Tesfaye (; 1941 – February 1976) was an Ethiopian Tigrayan nationalist and teacher. With Gebre Kidan Asfaha, he led the Political Association of Tigrayans, a clandestine group that advocated the independence of Tigray and later emerged as an armed organisation, the Tigray Liberation Front (TLF; ). [ref: The Origins of the Tigray People's Liberation Front, African Affairs] In December 1975 the TLF's leadership was detained by forces of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) following a merger ceremony, and Yohannes is reported to have been executed in February 1976.

== Early life and education ==
Yohannes was born in 1941 in the village of Assai, near the town of Gendebta in Feresmay woreda, Adwa awraja, to Teklehaimanot Tesfaye, an Orthodox Christian priest and farmer, and Weleteyesus Abreha. He was the seventh of thirteen siblings.

He did not attend school until the age of twelve. In 1953 his elder brother, Woldegebriel Teklehaimanot, who worked for Ras Imru and later became a businessman in Addis Ababa, took him to Addis Ababa to be educated, and he began primary school at the Prince Asfaw Wossen School. When Woldegebriel left for India with Ras Imru, who had been appointed ambassador there, Yohannes was placed in the care of Kassa Hagos, a Merkato businessman, with a monthly allowance for his schooling.

After completing seventh grade he visited Tigray for the summer and learned that his mother had died several years earlier. He decided not to return to Addis Ababa and enrolled in Grade 8 at Queen Sheba School in Adwa. He then entered the Evangelical Mission boarding school in Debre Zeit (now Bishoftu), where he learned to play the guitar.

He completed the Ethiopian School Leaving Certificate examination in June 1963 and in 1964 entered Haile Selassie I University (now Addis Ababa University), where he studied history and graduated in June 1969.

== Career and political activism ==
At university Yohannes took part in student political meetings and discussion groups, including gatherings at the Genfele (Ginfelle) house in Addis Ababa where he lived with his siblings Kidanemariam, Aberash and Sahleselassie Teklehaimanot. Participants and visitors reportedly included Gidey Gebrewahid, Yoseph Gebregziabher, Gebrekidan Asfaha, Rezene Tekle and Netsanet Asfaw.

After graduating in 1969 he worked for an American-founded international organisation in Addis Ababa, travelling regularly to Tigray, and reportedly declined a scholarship to study in the United States. He wrote a manuscript on Tigrayan history in Tigrinya, titled, copies of which were circulated among friends; the original reportedly went with him when he joined the armed struggle in 1975, while a copy left with relatives was destroyed out of fear of Derg house searches.

In 1971 he moved to Mekelle and taught history and English at Emperor Yohannes Secondary School.

== Tigray Liberation Front ==
=== Origins ===
According to Aregawi Berhe, a founding member of the TPLF, the Political Association of Tigrayans (PAT), led by Yohannes Teklehaimanot and Gebre Kidan, carried out underground political mobilisation of Tigrayans against the Ethiopian government. The association advocated the outright independence of Tigray and later emerged as an armed organisation known as the Tigray Liberation Front. The date of the TLF's founding is given as 1972 in some accounts. Reported founders and early members include Gidey Gebrewahid, Rezene Tekle, Gebrekidan Asfeha, Yemane Gebremeskel, Tadesse Tilahun, Hailekiros Asgede, Amare Tesfaye, Mussie Kidane, Tekeste Birhane and others.

Yohannes is reported to have served as the organisation's chairman while remaining in Mekelle and Addis Ababa to organise underground activity, while other members went to the mountains of Eastern Tigray near Aiga, along the Eritrean border.

=== Ideology ===
The TLF was grounded in Tigrayan nationalism rather than Marxism–Leninism. Yohannes is reported to have admired earlier Tigrayan rulers such as Yohannes IV and Ras Alula, in contrast to contemporary revolutionary groups that viewed traditional rulers as an oppressive class. He also reportedly envisaged a shared "Tigray-Tigrigni" state uniting Tigray and Eritrea.

=== Relations with the Eritrean Liberation Front ===
By the time the Tigrayan National Organization, the precursor of the TPLF, approached the Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF) for support, the TLF had already established a working relationship with the ELF. Berhe suggests that the ELF may have regarded the TLF as more truly nationalist because it upheld the independence of Tigray, similar to the Eritrean position. Yohannes reportedly attended an ELF congress in the Barka region of Eritrea, where he proposed a joint Tigray-Tigrigni state; the ELF leadership did not respond favourably.

=== Move to the field ===
After the Derg formally took power on 12 September 1974, Yohannes remained in Addis Ababa for several months. After the Derg's security services uncovered the underground network, he reportedly left the capital in early 1975 and joined TLF forces in Eastern Tigray.
[truncated]

== New York Chinese School est. 1909 [https://www.nychineseschool.org/home------.html New York Chinese School Homepage] Official Website ==

The New York Chinese School (NYCS) is a non-profit 501(c)(3) community language school located on Mott Street in the Chinatown neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City. [ref: New York Chinese School – Museum of Chinese in America, www.mocanyc.org] Established in the early 20th century, the school is one of 60 member organizations affiliated with the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association (CCBA) [ref: The History of the Oldest Chinese School in NYC, Documented] and has been chartered by the New York State Education Department since 1967. [ref: New York Chinese School – Museum of Chinese in America, www.mocanyc.org]

==== History and Facilities ====
Founded as one of the earliest overseas Chinese language schools, NYCS initially opened with approximately 20 students. The school has since expanded to serve over 3,000 [ref: During Pandemic, Taiwanese Donations Help Keep Chinese Language School Afloat, Columbia News Service] students annually across its weekend, after-school, and summer camp sessions.

Its facility includes 22 classrooms, a 400-seat auditorium, an indoor gymnasium, two dance studios, and a music practice room. [ref: about, New York Chinese School]

==== Academics and Programs ====
NYCS offers language instruction in Mandarin and Cantonese for K–12 students and adults, covering beginner through advanced proficiency levels. Curriculum materials incorporate both Traditional and Simplified Chinese characters, with primary emphasis on Simplified script. In addition to language coursework, the curriculum includes Chinese cultural studies, such as calligraphy and traditional poetry. [ref: New York Chinese School – Museum of Chinese in America, www.mocanyc.org]

The school also provides elective and academic support programs, including:

* Arts & Music: Visual arts, dance, piano, and violin [ref: The History of the Oldest Chinese School in NYC, Documented]
* Academic Enrichment: Mathematics, English, computer coding, and Specialized High Schools Admissions Test (SHSAT) preparation

Qualified language students can sit for the Standards-based Measurement of Proficiency (STAMP) examination. Passing scores on the STAMP test qualify students to earn the New York State Seal of Biliteracy.

==== Partnerships and Student Support ====
NYCS collaborates with local higher education institutions, including Columbia University’s Teachers College and Hunter College, to place university students as teaching assistants. [ref: The History of the Oldest Chinese School in NYC, Documented]

The school assists eligible students in registering for national youth recognition frameworks, including the Congressional Award program. Financial assistance and academic scholarships are provided through community donations, including support from Wonton Food Inc. and local civic leaders. [ref: The History of the Oldest Chinese School in NYC, Documented]

Go Brewing is an American brewery in Naperville, Illinois, that produces only non-alcoholic beer. It was described at its opening as the first brewery in Illinois dedicated to non-alcoholic and low-alcohol beer. [ref: Go Brewing opening state's first nonalcoholic, low-alcohol brewery in Naperville, Daily Herald]

== History ==
Go Brewing was founded by Joe Chura. [ref: An entrepreneur finds a niche in high-quality no-alcohol beer, Crain's Chicago Business] [ref: Down to Business: Naperville's Go Brewing finds its niche by tapping into audience that wants beer taste, no alcohol, Naperville Sun] Its taproom opened on October 15, 2022. [ref: Naperville's Go Brewing Opens for Business on Oct. 15, NCTV17] The brewery operates a taproom in Naperville that serves only non-alcoholic beer. [ref: Dry January, not Beerless January, at Go Brewing in Naperville, Chicago Sun-Times] [ref: A Naperville Taproom Is Changing the Way Customers Think About Nonalcoholic Beer, Eater Chicago]

Go began distributing outside Illinois in 2023 and 2024, including Wisconsin [ref: Nonalcoholic brewery Go Brewing's taproom in Naperville, Illinois, is a rarity, Milwaukee Journal Sentinel] [ref: Go Brewing's NA beers arrive in Milwaukee just in time for Dry January, OnMilwaukee] and northwest Indiana. [ref: Non-alcoholic craft beer Go Brewing, founded by a Chicago assembly plant worker, now distributed in Northwest Indiana, The Times of Northwest Indiana] In 2024 the Naperville Sun reported on its plans to grow through new partnerships. [ref: Naperville's Go Brewing seeks to build on its nonalcoholic beer success with new partnerships, Naperville Sun] According to the trade newsletter Beer Marketer's Insights, Go produced about 21,600 barrels in 2025, the most of any brewery newly reaching regional-brewery size that year. [ref: Non-Alc Co Go Brewing Tops Short List of New Regionals in 2025, Doubled to 21.6K Bbls, Beer Marketer's Insights]

In October 2026 the company launched Cold Standard, a non-alcoholic light lager whose packaging de-emphasizes the "non-alcoholic" label, which Food & Wine covered. [ref: This New NA Beer Is Making Its Nonalcoholic Label Harder to Notice, Food & Wine]

== Products and reception ==
Go Brewing's range includes IPAs, pilsners, sours, a chelada-style lager and seasonal beers, all under 0.5% ABV. [ref: Tasting: 7 Non-Alcoholic Craft Beers from Go Brewing, Paste] Chicago magazine named the taproom the city's best place to "drink beer and not get drunk" in 2023. [ref: Best of Chicago 2023, Chicago] Wirecutter named Salty AF Chelada its top pick for non-alcoholic fruited lager. [ref: The Best Non-Alcoholic Beer, Wirecutter]

Nate Isaacman (October 14, 1898 – November 22, 1957), also known by the ring names Joe McCabe and Joe Isaacman, was an American professional boxer from Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. He competed in regional lightweight and welterweight divisions during the 1910s and 1920s.

== Early life ==

Nate Isaacman was born in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania. He was raised in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, where his family resided on Conoy Street. Prior to and during the early stages of his boxing career, he was employed locally as a railroad laborer for the Pennsylvania Railroad.

He grew up in Harrisburg, was a dancer and an athlete. Dancing led him to take his dancing talents into the boxing ring.

== Boxing career ==
Nate Isaacman competed primarily in Pennsylvania and regional East Coast venues, securing wins across professional bouts. His most high profile bouts were against Tim Droney, Jack Silver and Jack Stone.

Nate Isaacman fought a lot over a nine-year boxing career. In June 1918 he fought Sammy Schiff in Harrisburg. Here is information on fights under his birth name Nate Isaacman as shown in BoxRec.

In 1919 Nate Isaacman fought Bobby Williams at the Power Motive show. [ref: Nate Isaacman fights Bobby Williams at the Power Motive Show, Harrisburg Telegraph]

In 1922 Joe McCabe won a bout in Philadelphia. [ref: JOE McCABE WINS, Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger]

In 1923 Nate Isaacman fought and won against Tim Droney. [ref: Tim Droney Loses to Joe McCabe, Philadelphia Inquirer]

He fought the lightweight champion of the West Coast in 1923 in the Oakland, California Coliseum. He lost.

Nate Isaacman fought in the west coast in the Bay Area, as shown in this article, Geo. Gilmore, fought with Joe McCabe who had previously lost in a fight. [ref: Joe McCabe returns to box Geo. Gilmore, Oakland Tribune]

Though it was expected that he would win, from the fights in Oakland, later he lost the title as shown in the Oakland Tribune, March 6, 1924. [ref: Joe McCabe Can Claim Welterweight Title, Oakland Tribune]

There were fights that he won in California, such as the fight against Jack Powell. [ref: Sports Told in Paragraphs, The Bakersfield Californian]

== Personal life ==

After his boxing days were over, he got married, fathered five children: Miriam, Sylvia, Eileen, Max and Terri.

== Later life and death ==

Following his retirement from sports, Isaacman continued working as a laborer. He died on November 22, 1957, at Harrisburg State Hospital.

Draft text:
Hotta Studio is a Chinese video game developer based in Suzhou, Jiangsu, China. It is wholly owned by Perfect World (完美世界股份有限公司, SZSE: 002624). The studio specializes in developing free-to-play open-world action RPGs with anime-inspired aesthetics for mobile platforms, PC, and consoles. It is best known for creating Tower of Fantasy (幻塔) and Neverness to Everness (异环).

The name "Hotta" is a phonetic transliteration of the Chinese 幻塔 (huàn tǎ, "phantom tower"), the title of the studio's debut game. In international markets, the company also operates under the trade name Hottagames Co., Ltd., which is used for contracts with overseas partners and press materials.

== History ==

=== Origins and founding (2018) ===

The studio's founder and long-standing head is Zhang Yu (张御, also known as Kee Zhang). Before founding Hotta Studio, Zhang Yu worked for many years at Snail Games, where he led Black Gold Studio (黑金工作室). Under his leadership, projects included Voyage Century (航海世纪), the first three entries in the Taichi Panda (太极熊猫) series, and the Chinese localization of Lineage 2. Zhang Yu has around 19 years of professional experience in game development [ref: [https://www.unrealengine.com/developer-interviews/tower-of-fantasy-leverages-unreal-engine-to-bring-open-world-action-to-mobile-pc-and-playstation Tower of Fantasy leverages Unreal Engine to bring open world action to mobile, PC and PlayStation] ].

In 2018, having decided to focus on developing next-generation open-world games, Zhang Yu left Snail Games and joined Perfect World. There, he was tasked with establishing a completely new in-house studio, and the team that would later become known as Hotta Studio was founded [ref: [https://en.namu.wiki/w/Hotta%20Studio Hotta Studio]]. The project was initially launched as a game under a codename derived from 幻塔 (huàn tǎ, "phantom tower"), which later also gave the studio its name. The legal entity, 苏州幻塔网络科技有限公司, was registered in Suzhou in November 2018 [ref: 苏州幻塔网络科技有限公司].

=== Development of Tower of Fantasy (2018–2021) ===

Development of Tower of Fantasy began in 2018, almost immediately after the studio was founded. The project was Perfect World's response to the success of miHoYo's Genshin Impact. Perfect World viewed the rapidly growing anime-style open-world gacha RPG market as a strategic priority and funded several parallel in-house projects, one of which was Hotta Studio's Tower of Fantasy [ref: 幻塔].

From the outset, the team focused on:

* An open world with large-scale locations and vertical traversal, including parkour and flying vehicles;
* Multiplayer features, including co-op dungeons and PvP zones, distinguishing it from Genshin Impact and its primarily single-player focus;
* A science-fantasy setting combining science fiction and fantasy, which was unconventional for Chinese gacha games;
* A weapon system instead of a traditional character-based system: players obtain weapons, each with a unique combat style [ref: Tower of Fantasy — Weapons].

The game was first publicly showcased at ChinaJoy 2020, where concept trailers featuring anime-inspired art direction were presented. The first closed beta test (CBT-1) took place on 28 October 2020. The results were mixed: the game's overall architecture and design received positive assessments, but its execution was criticized. In response, the studio published what it called a "list of issues to fix" (头秃清单), an initial document containing hundreds of optimization tasks [ref: [https://baijiahao.baidu.com/s?id=1863044756225920058 专访幻塔制作人张御：杨受德是个狠人，对话还原一个真实的Hotta Studio]].

After CBT-1, Zhang Yu and his team worked intensively to improve the game. The second closed beta test (CBT-2) took place on 15 April 2021 and showed a marked improvement in quality. The "List of Issues to Fix 2.0" contained 30% more items than the first version. The third closed beta test (CBT-3) was held on 15 July 2021 and added the Simulacra system (SSR Simulacra) to the game.

=== Chinese and global release of Tower of Fantasy ===

On 16 December 2021, Tower of Fantasy entered public beta in mainland China for iOS and Android. Revenue on the first day was approximately 50 million yuan, and exceeded 500 million yuan (5亿) in the first month, while the number of new users surpassed 10 million [ref: [https://web.archive.org/web/20220305053635/http://notice.10jqka.com.cn/api/pdf/fb900faf62d1691a.pdf 完美世界2022年1月投资者关系活动记录]].

Following the success of CBT-3, Perfect World increased its investment in the project. The studio's staff grew to around 200 people, and funding for marketing and server infrastructure was increased. In January 2022, Perfect World officially announced plans for a global release in mid-2022.

The Friedrich Katz Prize is an annual book prize of the American Historical Association. It is awarded for "the best book published in English focusing on Latin America, including the Caribbean," and is named in honor of Friedrich Katz, a distinguished historian of Latin America.

The AHA announced the creation of the prize in November 2013. The Katz Prize succeeded the earlier John E. Fagg Prize, which had only received a ten-year bequest. Major donors at the inception of the prize included the Katz family, El Colegio de México, and the Tinker Foundation. [ref: AHA Establishes the Friedrich Katz Prize – AHA, https://www.historians.org/] The first award was given in 2014. [ref: Friedrich Katz Prize, American Historical Association]

Meletius Peter Dutkewich (1871–1939) was an American photographer. [ref: US Passport Application, Family Search] He was known as an adventurer, big game hunter, and for his attempt to climb Mount Kilimanjaro with Peter MacQueen in 1909.

==Early life==
Dutkewich was born in Warsaw in 1871 and emigrated to the United States as a teenager. He became a US citizen in 1895. [ref: Another Dimension: Stereoscopic Photography and the Press, c. 1896–1911, Doctoral thesis, Durham University]

==Early African travels==
Between 1908 and 1909, Dutkewich and Peter MacQueen plotted an expedition from the Nile to East Africa and Kilimanjaro, for the purpose of recording their adventures. The excursion was later published in a book titled In Wildest Africa: The record of a hunting and exploration trip through Uganda, Victoria Nyanza, the Kilimanjaro region and British East Africa, with an account of an ascent of the snowfields of Mount Kibo, in East/Central Africa, and a description of the various native tribes, [ref: In Wildest Africa PDF] which contained sixty-four of Dutkewich's photographs along with MacQueen's narrative. [ref: In Wildest Africa, Seattle Post-Intelligencer] The book was published in advance of Theodore Roosevelt's travels to Africa which heightened American interest in the region. [ref: New Books, Etc., Scientific American]

During their expedition, Dutkewich was reported lost in Central Africa for three weeks, fell into animal traps, and suffered a fall on Kilimanjaro where he broke three ribs. [ref: Peter Dutkewich, The Times-Union] [ref: Rev Peter M'Queen is a Climber Too, The Buffalo News] [ref: Kilimanjaro: To the roof of Africa, National Geographic Society] They completed their Kilimanjaro ascent on July 17, 1908. [ref: Peter McQueen on the Heights, Vermont Journal] Some of Dutkewich's photographs of his African travels – big game hunters, ceremonies and dances, mountain peaks and other African scenes – were published as stereographs by Underwood & Underwood. [ref: In Advance of Roosevelt, Ottawa Daily Republic] He was described in 1909 as having "a genius for adventure". Dutkewich was said to have made more than 12,000 negatives of the African continent and his photography was used to illustrate other contemporary books about Africa and appeared in the Burr McIntosh Monthly. [ref: My African neighbors: man, bird, and beast in Nyasaland, Little, Brown, and Company] [ref: Peter MacQueen: "the fighting parson", Puzzlebox Press]

==Later career==
In the 1920s, Dutkewich met Bert Underwood of Underwood & Underwood while both were traveling in Athens during the Greco-Turkish War. According to his memoir, Underwood offered Dutkewich a job on the spot, but was turned down until Dutkewich fulfilled his ongoing contract with another photographic house. He continued to do freelance work for Underwood & Underwood and other American stereoscopic companies such as B.W. Kilburn & Co., of New York. Over the course of his life, Dutkewich took photographs of many countries and territories, including Australia, New Guinea, New Zealand, Japan, India, China, Siberia, Turkey, the Philippines, the Canadian Rockies, Mexico, Zimbabwe, and Kenya.

Padel Pingpong was invented in Sweden in 2020. As the name indicates Padel Pingpong is a racket sport that combines influences from table tennis and padel tennis. [ref: Padel Pingpong, Padel Pingpong] It all started during an after work where Magnus Willner and Erik Magnarsson played table tennis in a conference room and the walls came into use. [ref: Jörgen Persson bakom ny sport – lanserar padelpingis, Hallandsposten] A company named Padel Pingpong International AB was later founded to develop the concept. Cofounders are Johan Edfors, professional golfer and Jörgen Persson professional table tennis player, amongst a couple of others.

== The Court and equipment ==
The court is made up by a rectangular box, made of security glass measuring 3.208 by 6.100 m and 2.075 m high. The short sides have a 17 degree angle to make the ball bounce back easier. In the middle of the court is a table (measuring 1.45 by 2.44 meters). The table has rounded corners designed to easier move around inside the court and to avoid injuries. [ref: Padel Pingpong, Padel Pingpong]

The ball is 55 mm in diameter (compared to a table tennis ball that is normally 40 mm in diameter) and the rackets are made of wood or plastic without friction (meaning no spin). The net measures 21 cm in hight. [ref: Padel Pingpong, Padel Pingpong]

== Rules ==
The game has influences from other racket sports when it comes to the rules like using the walls as in padel tennis. Also the counting, first to 11 points in each set wins, like in table tennis. But it also has it's own rules ie. the possibillity to gain bonus points within a rally and not being allowed to smash the ball out of the cage. [ref: Padel Pingpong, Padel Pingpong]

== International expansion ==
Padel Pingpong has received millions of views across social media platforms, including Tiktok and Instagram. [ref: Padel Pingpong on Tiktok, Tiktok] [ref: Padel Pingpong on Instagram, Instagram]

The sport has also been promoted through international events such as Waldner cup in Oslo and The 2023 European Table Tennis Championship in Malmö. [ref: Padel Pingpong on Pingispågarna youtubechannel, YouTube] [ref: Padel Pingpong, Padel Pingpong]

By 2026 the sport is available in 16 countries. [ref: Padel Pingpong, Padel Pingpong]

== Media ==

United States

The recording of the Padel Pingpong Championship has been broadcasted on several occasions on ESPN networks, including ESPN2 and ESPN8. [ref: Padel Pingpong Championship, Disney+] [ref: ESPN. "Padel Pingpong Championship (7/18/26)." Broadcast on ESPNNews. First streamed on July 18, 2026. Link originally available on WatchESPN.] [ref: ESPN. "Padel Pingpong Championship (10/19/25)." Broadcast on ESPNNews. First streamed on October 19, 2025. Link originally available on WatchESPN.] [ref: ESPN Deportes. "Padel Pingpong Championship (2/14/26)." Transmitido por primera vez el 14 de febrero de 2026 en ESPNNews. Enlace originalmente disponible en ESPN Deportes.]

Sweden

Hallandsposten wrote an article in 2022 when the first prototypes got in place and the sport was launched. Jörgen Persson and Johan Edfors, both from the region Halland, was interviewed and it was mentioned in the text that the idea of the concept came from an afterwork where Magnus Willner and Erik Magnarsson played table tennis using the walls. [ref: Jörgen Persson bakom ny sport – lanserar padelpingis, Hallandsposten]

Italy

The concept was shown on a large and popular Italian show named Tú Sí Que Vales in 2024, giving a larger audience a glance of the sport. [ref: Vincenzo, Matteo, Cristian, Adam – Prima puntata]

The proposed hepatitis B vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau, also known as the HBV-NSE trial, was a proposed randomized controlled trial assertedly intended to investigate the effects of administering the hepatitis B vaccine to newborn infants in Guinea-Bissau. The study was developed by researchers affiliated with the Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, and funded by an award of US$1.6 million from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, under the authority of Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. [ref: Notice of Award of a Single Source Unsolicited Grant To Fund University of Southern Denmark (SDU), Federal Register] [ref: Controversial HBV vaccine trial in Guinea-Bissau halted, The Lancet Infectious Diseases] [ref: CDC awards $1.6 million for hepatitis B vaccine study by controversial Danish researchers, Center for Infectious Disease Research & Policy-CIDRAP] It was ostensibly intended to evaluate whether administration of the vaccine at birth affected childhood mortality, illness, and development beyond its established protective effect against hepatitis B infection, [ref: US awards no-bid contract to Denmark scientists studying hepatitis B vaccine in African babies, Associated Press] but experts questioned the intent of the experiment, and the ethics of its design. [ref: The Hepatitis B Foundation and The African Hepatitis B Advocacy Coalition denounce the unethical HepB birth dose study in Guinea-Bissau, Hepatitis B Foundation] [ref: Guest post: The CDC hepatitis B study is unethical and must never be published, Retraction Watch] [ref: The U.S. Health Research Project Rejected by Guinea Bissau was Absurd and Deadly, CounterPunch.org] [ref: Every accusation is a confession (or a statement of intent): MAHA’s new Tuskegee experiment, Science-Based Medicine] [ref: The US must never support research and policies that inflict harm on Black communities, BMJ] [ref: US-funded Guinea-Bissau vaccine study to undergo ethical review, African health officials say, Reuters] The proposed trial was ultimately formally rejected by the government of Guinea-Bissau in October 2026, and the country's judicial police subsequently searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project and seized vaccine supplies intended for the study. The trial was never conducted, and no participants were enrolled.

==Background==
===Hepatitis B vaccination===
Hepatitis B is a viral infection that can cause chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Infection acquired during infancy is particularly likely to become chronic, with approximately 90% of newborns infected during childbirth developing chronic infection. The hepatitis B vaccine, first approved in 1981, has an established record of safety and effectiveness in preventing infection and its complications. Serious adverse effects are rare, and studies have found that vaccination can provide protection against clinical disease and chronic infection for at least 30 years. [ref: Hepatitis B vaccines: WHO position paper – July 2017, Relevé Épidémiologique Hebdomadaire] [ref: Ask the Experts: Hepatitis B, Immunize.org]

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all newborns receive an initial dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours, followed by two or three additional doses. The birth dose is particularly important in preventing vertical transmission of the virus from an infected mother to her infant. According to the WHO, timely birth-dose vaccination prevents an estimated 70–95% of mother-to-child hepatitis B transmission. For newborns whose mothers are infected, administering hepatitis B immune globulin in addition to vaccination provides greater protection than vaccination alone. [ref: Hepatitis B immunisation for newborn infants of hepatitis B surface antigen-positive mothers, The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews]

Guinea-Bissau has a high prevalence of hepatitis B infection, with the WHO estimating in 2026 that more than 12% of adults were living with chronic infection in 2022 and that approximately 2% of children younger than five were infected in 2020. At the time of the proposed trial, the country's routine childhood immunization schedule did not include a hepatitis B birth dose, with infants instead receiving their first hepatitis B vaccination at approximately six weeks of age. In 2024, Guinea-Bissau decided to introduce universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth, with implementation planned by 2028. The WHO identified the timely introduction of the birth dose as an important measure for reducing hepatitis B transmission in the country.

===Questioning of Bandim Health Project research practices===
The Bandim Health Project has investigated the possible non-specific effects of vaccines, including effects on health outcomes other than the diseases against which vaccines are intended to protect. Researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn have contributed to this line of research, which has also been the subject of scientific criticism.
[truncated]

Melvyn Wilkes is a British-born, Australian based football (soccer) coach, sporting director, coach educator, and youth development specialist. His professional career encompasses football coaching, academy management, technical direction, and the development of international pathways for aspiring professional players. Wilkes has worked in youth coaching and development roles associated with English football clubs including Manchester City FC, West Bromwich Albion FC, and Nottingham Forest FC. His professional background also includes coach education at Manchester Metropolitan University and work connected with England's Football Association and Professional Footballers' Association.

Evgeniy Puzyrevskiy (; born 17 February 1987) is a film director and screenwriter, best known for the interactive film She Sees Red (2019) and the television series Crazy House (2023) and My Friend AI (2026).

== Early life and education ==
Puzyrevskiy was born in Weimar, East Germany, where his father was serving in the military, and moved to Russia before the age of one. He grew up in Kamyshlov, Sverdlovsk Oblast, and studied for three years at the Sverdlovsk Regional College of Arts and Culture in Yekaterinburg. He has no formal film education and is self-taught. In Moscow he directed commercials and music videos (including for Oleg Gazmanov and the band Torba-na-Kruche) and worked in the DVD stores Novoe Iskusstvo and Mir Kino.

== Career ==
=== Short films ===
Puzyrevskiy began with short films. He Was His Friend (2015), which he wrote and directed, won the Audience Award for Best Long Form Narrative Short at the Nevermore Film Festival and the Masters of Genre award at the Lublin Film Festival, and was one of five Russian short films presented by ROSKINO in the Global Russians programme at the 2016 Cannes Film Festival. [ref: LXIX Cannes Film Festival, ROSKINO] The film stars Sergey Pokhodaev, Kirill Polukhin and Ivan Mulin.

His horror short Mom Is Always There for You (2016) stars Angelina Strechina and Denis Shvedov. Underwater (2018), starring Ksenia Radchenko in the lead role, was nominated for Best Short Film at the Boca do Inferno festival in Brazil.

=== She Sees Red ===
In 2019 Puzyrevskiy wrote and directed She Sees Red (), an interactive thriller developed by Rhinotales and described by Rossiyskaya Gazeta as the first interactive film in Russia. [ref: «Она сердится»: первый российский интерактивный триллер, Rossiyskaya Gazeta] The film was released on Steam, GOG, PlayStation, Nintendo Switch, Xbox, iOS and Android, with a full English dub and subtitles in 19 languages. It was included in the Los Angeles Times list of "8 defining interactive TV games" (2020) [ref: Schlocky ‘Night Trap’ to absurdly fun ‘Kimmy Schmidt’: 8 defining interactive TV games, Los Angeles Times] and in Polygons selection of indie gems (2019). [ref: Buried treasure: Unearthing the hidden indie gems from beneath the sea of games, Polygon] On Steam it holds a "Very Positive" rating, with 78% of more than 3,100 user reviews positive. [ref: She Sees Red on SteamDB, SteamDB]

=== Television ===
In 2023 Puzyrevskiy directed the comedy series Crazy House (), produced by the Tritamata creative bureau for the Friday! channel and Premier; the series starred Aleksey Maklakov, Denis Kosyakov, Anna Kotova-Deryabina, Dmitry Lysenko, Roman Kurtsyn, Alyona Yakovleva and Elena Simonova. The same year he directed the pilot episode of the series Chef (), presented at the Pilot television festival. In 2024 he served as creative producer on the series Teenagers in Space ().

His series My Friend AI (), released in 2026 on Okko and Wink, was made by the creators of the series Difficult Teenagers (). [ref: Смотрим трейлер сериала «Мой друг ИИ», Sobaka.ru] It stars Kai Getz, Svyatoslav Rogozhan, Mariya Markova, Oleg Vereshchagin and Ekaterina Morgunova.

=== Other work ===
Puzyrevskiy is the author of the novel The Seventh Summer (, 2012); an audiobook version, narrated by Alexander Vodianoy, is available on LitRes.

Since 2021 he has hosted the YouTube programme Zapakh napalma po utram (, "The Smell of Napalm in the Morning"), in which film-industry professionals discuss films from the perspective of their crafts; guests have included visual effects supervisor Arman Yakhin, director Roman Karimov and director Viktor Shamirov.

He has been a member of the Directors' Guild of Russia since 13 June 2023.

Gary Meier (born 10 September 1955) is an Australian former soccer player who played as a goalkeeper. He spent his entire senior career with Sydney Olympic FC (originally known as Pan-Hellenic), and holds the club's record for most appearances. He was capped once for the Australian national team in 1978. [ref: Former Roos receive caps, FTBL]

== Club career ==
Meier joined Pan-Hellenic, later renamed Sydney Olympic, in the early 1970s. He was in goal for Sydney Olympic during the club's first season in the National Soccer League in 1977, including a 2–0 win over Brisbane Lions at Perry Park on 25 April 1977. [ref: NSL 1977 Round 4, OzFootball] In 1978 he made 24 appearances in all competitions and kept four clean sheets. [ref: 1978 Sydney Olympic FC season, Wikipedia]

Meier played for Sydney Olympic until 1994, making 412 appearances, a club record. [ref: Sydney Olympic FC, Wikipedia] He won the NSL Cup with the club in 1983 and 1985. [ref: Gary Meier, worldfootball.net] He is a member of the Sydney Olympic Hall of Fame.

After leaving Sydney Olympic, Meier played for Killarney District Soccer Club on the Central Coast. [ref: Gary Meier, National Football Teams]

== International career ==
Meier earned one cap for Australia, becoming Socceroo No. 276. He came on as a 66th-minute substitute in a 1–1 friendly draw against Greece in Sydney on 18 June 1978. [ref: Socceroo caps, OzFootball]

== Coaching career ==
Meier briefly managed Sydney Olympic in 1995. [ref: Gary Meier, worldfootball.net]

Paul Kenny  –  A Life in Music. Beginnings The story of Paul Kenny begins in a house where silence was never truly silent. Even in the quietest hours of early morning, before the world stirred awake, sound lived there, the faint hum of the wind through a window crack, the rhythm of rain on a tin roof, the soft, steady breathing of a family still asleep. To a child attuned to the subtleties of the world, these were not random noises; they were the first fragments of music. From the earliest days, Paul seemed to hear differently. Where others heard routine, he heard patterns. Where most would pass by a songbird's tweet without notice, he paused to catch its phrasing, its pauses, its echoes. This gift, or perhaps this calling, would shape the course of his entire life. There was an old piano in the corner of his grandparents home, one that had seen better days. Its wood bore scratches and its keys had yellowed slightly with age. Yet for Paul, it was an entire universe waiting to be discovered. He would sit before it long before he was formally taught, stretching his small hands across the keys, pressing down gently at first, and then with growing curiosity. The notes, however uneven, stirred something deep within him, a sense of purpose that transcended the moment.

Music became his first language. It spoke to him in ways words could not. The harmonies he found by accident seemed to reveal truths beyond expression, beauty, longing, and an unexplainable peace. As the years passed, the piano was no longer simply an instrument. It became a friend, a confidant, and later, a mirror through which Paul would come to understand himself and the world around him.  Formal lessons began soon after. Teachers noticed quickly what his family had already seen, that this was not an ordinary student. Paul absorbed theory, technique, and interpretation with rare ease. Paul's natural learning and understanding of the language of writing music, music theory and performance meant that he outgrew teachers extremely quickly as they simply could not keep up with the Maestro in the making. Yet even as he mastered scales, études, sonatas and concertos his imagination reached beyond the printed notes. He wanted to understand why music moved people, why a certain chord could summon joy, or a modulation could bring tears. That question would become the quiet pursuit of his life. The Maroochy River holds a special place in his childhood, shaped by long, unhurried days spent with my grandparents along its banks. Fishing was never rushed. Lines were cast gently into the moving water, and we waited together in comfortable silence, watching the river breathe with the tide. The mangroves framed the day, alive with birds and the soft sounds of water against mud. In those moments, time seemed to slow, and Paul learnt that patience was not something you forced, it arrived naturally when you allowed yourself to be still. Mud crabbing was both exciting and grounding. Paul remembers lifting the heavy pots from the river, thick with mud and anticipation, Paul's grandfather guiding and reminding him to be careful. He showed Paul how to handle the crabs properly, which ones to keep and which to return, and why respect for the river mattered. These were practical lessons, but they carried something deeper, an understanding of responsibility, balance, and gratitude for what nature provided. Chess belonged to a different world, taught by his grandfather on his mothers side, far from the river's edge. With him, the lessons were quieter and more deliberate. Sitting across a small board, he explained the logic behind each move, encouraging me to think ahead and consider the whole picture rather than chasing quick wins. His teaching was calm and thoughtful, shaping the way Paul approached not only the game, but problem-solving itself. Together, these memories form two distinct threads of his early life, one rooted in river mud and sunlight, the other in quiet rooms and careful thought. Each grandfather taught Paul in his own way, and both left lasting impressions. One gave him a love of the natural world and its rhythms; the other gave him a way of thinking that would guide Paul long after the board was packed away. Paul's grandfather carried his history quietly, never with show or ceremony, but with a steady sense of gravity that made you listen when he spoke. Through him, Paul became aware of the family's long association with the Masonic lodge, a lineage bound not by power or secrecy, but by values: discipline, service, knowledge, and moral responsibility. Freemasonry, as he described it, was less about what was hidden and more about what was expected of a man, integrity in private, fairness in public, and loyalty to something greater than oneself. He spoke of the Freemasons and the Lodge with respect, emphasising their role as custodians of tradition and symbolism rather than holders of authority. The rituals, the tools, and the language all pointed toward self-improvement and the shaping of a person's character. Listening to him, Paul understood that the lodge was a place of reflection and fraternity, where men were reminded to build their lives as carefully as a mason shapes stone, deliberately, honestly, and with purpose. Alongside this Masonic heritage was the deeper, older thread of the Knights Templar, spoken of not as myth, but as an ancestral memory. To Paul's grandfather, the Templars represented

Stumble Guys is a 2020 free-to-play platform battle royale game developed by the american game developer Scopely and was published by the former developer Kitka Games. The game tends to be heavily inspired by the 2020 video game Fall Guys although Stumble Guys tends to not use the bean-like characters from Fall Guys. The game was first released on Android on 24 September, 2020, but was then released on iOS on 12 February, 2021 and was released on Steam on 7 October, 2021. The game was released on consoles like Xbox One, Xbox Series X and Series S in January 2024, [ref: Mobile smash hit Stumble Guys is coming to consoles, Polygon.com] [ref: Mobile Hit 'Stumble Guys' Will Be A Timed Console Exclusive For Xbox, Pure Xbox] [ref: Stumble Guys trips onto console, first to Xbox, GAMINGTREND] [ref: ] [ref: “Stumble Guys” is bringing its massively multiplayer mayhem to Console, www.scopely.com] PlayStation 4, and PlayStation 5 in May 2024, [ref: Stumble Guys Debuts On PS4 And PS5 Today, Cross-Progression Update Now Live, GameSpot] [ref: Stumble Guys confirmed for PS5, PS4, Gematsu] and was last released on Nintendo Switch on August 2024. [ref: ]

== Gameplay ==
Similar to Fall Guys, about 24 to 32 players are put in battle royal matches where the players must pass through obstacles without trying to not get knocked out or fall. When they finish all of the obstacles, up to 12 people will win if they make it to the finish. Progressively, the same gameplay happens but with less players and different maps. Players can dive, slide, and more, just like Fall Guys. The aim is to qualify for subsequent rounds by successfully completing each of the randomly selected mini-games from a spinning wheel-like selector which many of have randomly selected variations.
====Currency====
The game uses a currency called Gems where players can buy spinning wheels, avatar skins, and change their username.
====Features====
There are features in the game such as prize wheels where players can use 9 free spins on the Free prize wheels before they have to wait 12 or 24 hours to get those free prize wheel spins again. Players can buy prize wheels with the currency Gems which may cost around 99 or 149 Gems. Players can also get free Stumble Boxes where it contains points where when the player gets enough points, they will get a avatar skin.

== Development ==
The game was originally developed and published by Kitka Games with a small team. The idea was to make a mobile version of Fall Guys since Android and iOS didn't have Fall Guys and it wasn't available on Android and iOS. [ref: Stumble Guys Analysis: How a Clone Game Became a Massive Success, [[Medium (website)] Since the rise of Fall Guys, Kitka Games made Stumble Guys, a highly inspired version of Fall Guys but on mobile. The game was made from using the video game engine Unity just like Fall Guys. The game didn't get popular until 2021 when it grew viral growth in parts of regions in India.

In September 2022, Scopely officially acquired the game from Kitka Games. [ref: Welcome “Stumble Guys” to the Scopely portfolio!, www.scopely.com] [ref: Scopely acquires Stumble Guys battle royale game from Kitka Games, GamesBeat]

====Collaboration events====
On 15 December, 2022, the game collaborated with Hot Wheels, releasing a hot wheels track which allowed players to race other players. [ref: “Stumble Guys” players can now tear up the race track with new driving mode powered by Mattel's Hot Wheels™, www.scopely.com] [ref: Stumble Guys hits the tracks with Hot Wheels, GamesBeat] This was Stumble Guys first ever official brand partnership between a major company called Mattel.

On 25 April, 2023, the game collaborated with Nerf, an American toy company that is known for making Nerf Blasters released an update where players would be in a first-person shooter map where the players would have to shoot other players. [ref: New first-person game mode, powered by NERF, is launching into “Stumble Guys”, www.scopely.com] [ref: Grab your blaster! 🔫 @[user] is officially here!!! 🔥 Check out our newest trailer and play our new Blaster Base level in the Nerf Arena NOW! 😎🎉 #StumbleGuys]

On 27 July, 2023, the game collaborated with MrBeast, releasing MrBeast avatar skins and oversized obstacle courses were added in the update. On November 2023, a new part of the update was released, releasing a stage called MrBeast's Dangerous Traps was introduced, mimicking his channel's high-stakes endurance challenges. The final update was in February 2024 where a music-themed elimination level named Disco Drop. Alongside this level, the developers launched the Stumble Workshop MrBeast Toolkit, allowing players to use lasers, blimps, and giant fans to build their own custom MrBeast obstacle courses. [ref: Stumble Guys launches the Stumble Workshop MrBeast Toolkit and other collab goodies in latest update, www.pocketgamer.com] [ref: Design your own MrBeast course in “Stumble Guys” with the Stumble Workshop MrBeast Toolkit, www.scopely.com]
[truncated]

He also wrote for artists associated with The Rachidia, a respected musical institution, notably for the artists Khemais Tarnane and Hedi Jouini.

Draft: Lemonaid Health

Draft text:
Lemonaid Health is an American telehealth company based in San Francisco that provides online medical consultations, prescriptions and laboratory testing directly to consumers for a flat fee. Founded in 2013 and launched in 2014, it was acquired by the genetic-testing company 23andMe for US$400 million in 2021. In 2025, following 23andMe's bankruptcy, the business was sold to the investment firms Bambu Ventures and Innova Capital Partners for US$10 million.

== History ==
=== Founding and early growth ===
Lemonaid Health was founded in San Francisco in 2013 by Paul Johnson, who became chief executive, and Ian Van Every, who became president. Johnson had previously run online retail businesses in the United Kingdom. The service launched in 2014 in California and Pennsylvania, expanding to Michigan and New York in late 2015, and offered consultations by text chat, telephone or video for a flat fee, with physicians responding within two hours of a patient completing an online questionnaire. Early services were limited to a small number of conditions, with birth control the most requested, followed by treatments for conditions such as urinary tract infections, high cholesterol and hair loss and a small number of laboratory tests including screening for sexually transmitted infections.

In May 2017 the company raised an US$11 million Series A round led by Novartis Venture Fund and Hikma Ventures, the venture arms of Novartis and Hikma Pharmaceuticals, at which point it was available in 14 states. By April 2018 it had handled more than 100,000 patient visits, employed 26 people including three full-time physicians, and operated in 18 states; a STAT News profile that year described state-by-state licensing rules as the main constraint on its expansion. The same profile reported that Lemonaid had filed complaints with state medical boards against competitors including Nurx, alleging improper use of online questionnaires; Nurx denied wrongdoing.

=== Expansion and Series B ===
In July 2020 the company raised a US$33 million Series B round led by Olive Tree Ventures, with participation from Artis Ventures, Correlation Ventures, Hikma Ventures and Sierra Ventures, bringing total funding to US$55 million. It said it would use the round to add treatment for asthma, hypertension and type 2 diabetes and to expand its mental health services. By 2021 the company operated in all fifty states and ran its own pharmacy.

=== Acquisition by 23andMe ===
In October 2021, 23andMe agreed to acquire Lemonaid Health for US$400 million. 23andMe said the purchase would allow it to offer medical consultations and prescriptions alongside its genetic testing, moving the company toward a subscription health service. Johnson became general manager of 23andMe's consumer business following the acquisition.

=== Bankruptcy of 23andMe and sale ===
23andMe filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in March 2025. In September 2025, Bambu Ventures, in partnership with Innova Capital Partners, agreed to buy all of Lemonaid Health's stock from 23andMe for US$10 million in cash. Bambu said it intended to expand Lemonaid's on-demand telehealth and online pharmacy services.

== Services ==
Lemonaid provides online consultations for conditions including birth control, hair loss, mental health, and urinary tract infections, with prescriptions filled through its own pharmacy or sent to a pharmacy of the patient's choice. Patients pay a flat fee per visit rather than billing insurance.

Paul David Johnson (born 1984) is a British-American entrepreneur, venture capitalist, and author. He co-founded the telehealth company Lemonaid Health and led it as chief executive until its US$400 million acquisition by 23andMe in 2021. He is a general partner and chief executive of the San Francisco venture capital firm Flex Capital.

== Early life and education ==
Johnson was born in England in 1984. He studied computer science and business management at the University of Worcester. [ref: Paul Johnson – General Partner, Flex Capital, yespress.io] Before founding Lemonaid Health he sold sports equipment and pet supplies online, served as UK managing director of the online pet retailer Zooplus, and was head of online at McKesson UK, where he was responsible for the group's digital business including Lloyds Pharmacy.

== Career ==
=== Lemonaid Health ===
Johnson co-founded Lemonaid Health in San Francisco with Ian Van Every; the company launched in 2014 offering virtual doctor visits by chat, phone, or video for a flat fee, initially focused on a small number of conditions such as birth control and sexually transmitted infection testing. [ref: A startup promised to make health care 'refreshingly simple.' Building the business has been anything but, [[Stat (website)] By 2018 the company had handled more than 100,000 patient visits across 18 states.

In July 2020 Lemonaid raised a US$33 million Series B round, with Johnson as chief executive. [ref: Lemonaid Health expanding services with $33M, Sun Life invests in Dialogue Technologies and more digital health funding news, MobiHealthNews]

In October 2021, 23andMe agreed to acquire Lemonaid Health for US$400 million, paid 25 percent in cash and the remainder in 23andMe stock. [ref: 23andMe to buy telehealth firm Lemonaid Health for $400 mln, Reuters] [ref: 23andMe jumps into telehealth, prescription drug delivery with $400M buyout of Lemonaid Health, Fierce Healthcare] Following the acquisition, Johnson became general manager of 23andMe's consumer business, continuing to run Lemonaid's services, [ref: DNA testing giant 23andMe expands into telemedicine with $400 million Lemonaid acquisition, [[Fortune (magazine)] and later served as chief operating officer of that business.

=== Flex Capital ===
In February 2025 Johnson joined Flex Capital, a seed-stage venture capital firm founded by Auren Hoffman and Tod Sacerdoti, as a general partner. [ref: Announcing Our New GP — Paul Johnson, Flex Capital] He serves as the firm's chief executive. [ref: About Flex Capital, Flex Capital]

=== Board roles and other work ===
In May 2024 Johnson was appointed an independent non-executive director of Closed Loop Medicine, a British precision-medicine company. [ref: Closed Loop Medicine Appoints Paul Johnson as Non-Executive Director, Business Wire] He also works as a coach to chief executives and is an angel investor.

== Writing ==
Writing as Paul D. Johnson, he has published two biographies of artificial intelligence researchers: Move 37: The Life of Demis Hassabis (2026) [ref: Move 37: The Life of Demis Hassabis] and Not Insects: The Life of Geoffrey Hinton. [ref: Not Insects: The Life of Geoffrey Hinton]

== Personal life ==
Johnson lives in San Francisco. He became a United States citizen in February 2021. [ref: Gold medal pickleball player stumbled onto the popular game at Glen Park Rec, Glen Park Association] He is a competitive pickleball player who won a singles gold medal at the 2019 West Regional tournament.

Mynul Islam () is a Bangladeshi-American journalist, broadcast news editor, and international affairs correspondent based in New York City. Over a career spanning more than 15 years in television and digital media, he has covered global diplomacy, United Nations proceedings, Bangladesh–United States relations, and affairs concerning the Bangladeshi diaspora. [ref: সাংবাদিকতায় বিশেষ অবদানে ফোবানা সম্মাননা পেলেন মাইনুল ইসলাম, 71 Sangbad]

Islam currently serves as a Special Correspondent for Channel i USA, Editor of The Bangla Hour, and Head of News at BHTV. [ref: Channel i, Impress Telefilm mark 28th anniversary in New York, The Business Standard] He is also the International Affairs Secretary of the International Relations Reporters Forum (IRRF) in Bangladesh.

== Early life and education ==
Islam completed his higher education in Bangladesh, earning degrees in business and law, including a Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA), a Master of Business Administration (MBA), and a Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.).

== Career ==

=== Television journalism in Bangladesh (2009–2023) ===
Islam began his career in television journalism in 2009 when he joined Ekushey Television (ETV) as a news reporter. During his tenure at ETV, he covered national politics, economic affairs, and social issues, eventually being promoted to Staff Reporter. In 2014, he received ETV's Best Reporting Award.

In 2016, Islam joined GTV as a Staff Reporter. He covered major national assignments and was promoted to Assignment Editor in 2023, where he managed newsroom assignments, field reporter deployment, and live news coordination. [ref: সাংবাদিকতায় বিশেষ অবদানে ফোবানা সম্মাননা পেলen মাইনুল ইসলাম, 71 Sangbad]

Parallel to his broadcast work, Islam served as a part-time instructor at the Bangladesh Institute of Journalism & Electronic Media (BIJAM) from 2014 to 2023, training aspiring reporters in broadcast presentation and field journalism.

=== International journalism and U.S. media (2024–present) ===
Following his relocation to the United States, Islam expanded his focus toward international diplomacy and diaspora journalism. In 2025, he joined Channel i USA as a Special Correspondent and presenter. Based at the United Nations Headquarters in New York City, he has reported on multiple sessions of the United Nations General Assembly, including UNGA 2019, 2023, 2024, and 2026.

In addition to broadcast journalism, Islam serves as Editor of The Bangla Hour and oversees news production as Head of News for BHTV. In October 2026, he was honored at the United Nations Plaza during the Global Summit on Paid Period Leave for his journalism and coverage of social welfare issues. [ref: Global Summit on Paid Period Leave Held in New York: Journalist Mynul Islam Honored, The Bangla Hour]

Cong An Nhan Dan Baseball Club (), also known as CAND BC is a Vietnamese amateur baseball club based in Hanoi. They regularly compete at the annual Vietnam Baseball Championship.

== History ==

=== Before MPS affiliation ===
CAND BC's origins can be traced back to a youth club called Hanoi Capitals. Founded by an American lawyer in 2008, the club had been a prominent pioneer of baseball in Hanoi as a member of PONY Baseball and Softball Asia-Pacific division, having made its Colt World Series in 2016. [ref: 2015 Baseball WS Archive, www.pony.org]

After the founding of the Vietnam Baseball and Softball Federation (VBSF) in late 2021 and the advent of a national competition, the a senior Capitals team was established for its inaugural tournament in 2022. Consisting of members of the 2015 Colt World Series team, the team finished the tournament in third place.

In 2023, the senior Capitals got restructured into an independent amateur club called the Hanoi 29ers. Under the management of former Cincinnati Reds prospect Lucas Benenati, the team won the inaugural Hanoi Major Series, after finishing fifth in the 2023 national tournament.

=== MPS affiliation ===
In 2024, it was announced that a baseball club, consisting of the former Capitals/29ers core, was established under the Ministry of Public Security's People's Public Security Sports Association. Aptly named the Cong An Nhan Dan Baseball Club, the club won their first national championship title in their first time under the police banner, becoming the first non-HCMC club to do so. [ref: People’s Police secure National Baseball Clubs Championship trophy, vietnamnews.vn]

During the following years, CAND has remained highly competitive at both the local and national level, regularly trading top finishes with local rival Hanoi Archers as well as regularly sending players to the national team roster. They won their first Hanoi league title in 2025, before finishing runner-up in the 2026 national championship, falling short to Southern powerhouse Saigon Storm. [ref: Câu lạc bộ bóng chày Công an nhân dân giành ngôi Á quân giải vô địch quốc gia 2026, Báo Nhân Dân điện tử]
