Based in Bengaluru, Karnataka, the company sells traditional and contemporary Indian clothing, including sarees, kurtas, salwar suits and lehengas. It operates physical retail stores and online sales channels. [ref: Ethnic wear brand Soch looking to spread beyond Indian shores, FashionUnited]

== History ==
According to FashionUnited, Soch was launched in 2003 by Vinay Chatlani. The business initially operated as a multi-brand clothing retailer before expanding its own-label range and developing dedicated stores. In October 2017, the company opened its 100th exclusive brand outlet in India at Inorbit Mall in Hyderabad. At that time, FashionUnited reported that Soch had a presence in 39 Indian cities and also sold products through shop-in-shop arrangements and e-commerce platforms. [ref: Soch opens its 100th store in India, FashionUnited] In November 2018, FashionUnited reported that private equity firm CX Partners planned to acquire an approximately 30% stake in Soch in a transaction valued at slightly more than ₹300 crore. [ref: PE firm CX Partners to buy 30 per cent stake in Soch, FashionUnited]

== Retail and online operations ==
Soch sells women's Indian ethnic clothing for everyday wear and special occasions. Its retail model combines branded stores with online distribution.

== International expansion ==
In January 2018, FashionUnited reported that Soch was planning to test international markets through online sales, with potential expansion into countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and the United Arab Emirates. The company subsequently expanded into Canada. In June 2026, Retail Insider reported the opening of a store in Surrey, British Columbia, describing it as Soch's second Canadian location and fifth international store. The report also noted that the company had entered Canada in 2024 with a store in Brampton, Ontario. [ref: India's Soch Expands to Surrey as Canadian Growth Strategy Continues, Retail Insider]

== Financial performance ==
In May 2026, The Economic Times Retail reported that Soch had recorded revenue exceeding ₹500 crore in the 2025–26 financial year. The report stated that its online sales had increased by 65% year on year to ₹88 crore and that the company operated more than 175 stores across over 70 cities in India, Canada and Malaysia. == Sunkind India Limited ==
Sunkind India Limited is a renewable energy company based in Gurugram, Haryana. [ref: Sunkind India Limited — Company Profile & CIN Registration, CompanySeekers] It provides solar energy solutions through engineering, procurement and construction (solar EPC) operations and maintenance and commercial renewable energy solutions to industrial and institutional clients. [ref: About Sunkind — Best Solar EPC Companies in India, Sunkind India Limited] It also offers solar mounting structures through Strucmax, and photovoltaic modules through Sunkind Photovoltaics. They will be expanding into battery energy storage systems (BESS). [ref: Sunkind plans to enter solar module manufacturing; signs Rs 1,500-cr cell-procurement pact, The Economic Times] [ref: Sunkind India Files DRHP for NSE Emerge IPO; 100% Fresh Issue, HDFC SKY News]

Sunkind Energy offers solar energy solutions at various points across the value chain.

== History ==
Sunkind Energy was registered as a private limited company (Sunkind India Private Limited) on the 19th of September 2019. It offered solar solutions for commercial and industrial uses. Initially they focused on Photovoltaic Rooftop and Hybrid Rooftop systems.

* 2020: Complete Hybrid Rooftop Systems.
* 2021: 3 MWp Rooftop System
* 2022: Launch of Strucmax (in house manufacturing of solar mounting structures). Over 18MWp of system installations.
* 2023: Over 20MWp of solar systems installed. Relocated to new head office in Gurugram.
* 2024: Over 75MWp of solar systems installed. First project completed using operating expenditure (OPEX) model.
* 2025–2026: Over 200MWp of systems completed. 1GW Solar Module line launched in Jaipur, Rajasthan. Draft documents submitted for IPO on NSE Emerge. [ref: Sunkind India Limited files DRHP for IPO on NSE EMERGE, IPO Platform]

== Business activities ==

=== Solar engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) ===
Sunkind provides Solar EPC solutions. This involves engineering, procurement, construction, installation and commissioning of solar systems. They offer both capital expenditure (CAPEX) and operating expenditure (OPEX) arrangements. In CAPEX solar systems are paid for by the client and owned by them. In OPEX the solar systems are built and operated by Sunkind with an agreement in place to limit the amount of money the client needs to pay upfront. [ref: Draft Red Herring Prospectus: Sunkind India Limited, Sunkind India Limited / National Stock Exchange of India]

=== Operations and maintenance (O&M) ===
Sunkind provide in house and out of house operations and maintenance solutions for solar systems. This includes inspecting the systems, cleaning solar modules, monitoring performance, repairing equipment and managing outputs.

=== Solar mounting structures (Strucmax) ===
Strucmax is the solar mounting structure manufacturing arm of the group. They manufacture engineered structures for photovoltaic solar installations. They manufacture modular structures for efficient installation.

=== Photovoltaic module manufacturing (Sunkind Photovoltaics) ===
Sunkind Photovoltaics is the solar module manufacturing arm of the company. They manufacture high efficiency TOPCon and bifacial photovoltaic solar modules. [ref: Sunkind India Limited secures long-term supply access to 1 GW TOPCon DCR solar cells, pv magazine India] In May 2026 they launched a 1GW solar module line in Jaipur, Rajasthan. They have also signed a procurement deal worth between twelve to fifteen hundred crore for solar cells in India.

=== Battery energy storage (Batt-Li) ===
Batt-Li is the lithium-ion battery energy storage arm of the company. They provide battery energy storage solutions for commercial and industrial use.

== Project portfolio and geographical presence ==
Sunkind provides Solar Engineering Procurement & Construction solutions for Commercial, Industrial, Institutional and Power Sector clients. They have worked with clients in the steel, textiles, automotive manufacturing, packaging, aluminium, healthcare, and food processing.

Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Limited (DOSCEL) is an Australian Catholic education organisation responsible for the governance and operation of Catholic primary and secondary schools with in Diocese of Sale in Victoria, Australia. [ref: education - Catholic Diocese of Sale, www.cdsale.org.au] Established in 2018, the organisation provides system leadership, governance and educational support to schools across south-eastern Victoria and the Gippsland region. [ref: Governance - Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Ltd]

DOSCEL is a company limited by guarantee, with the Bishop of Sale its sole member. Is governance is overseen by a board of directors, supported by an executive leadership team. The organisation's central office is Sion House, Warragul.

== History ==
Before the establishment of DOSCEL, the governance of Catholic schools in the Diocese of Sale was traditionally the responsibility of parish priests. In 2018, school governance was transferred to DOSCEL which was newly established. [ref: Priests out of school admin, Latrobe Valley Express] The transition was intended to provide coordinated governance and support for schools while allowing parish priest to focus more closely on their pastoral and spiritual responsibilities. Under the new structure, DOSCEL assumed responsibility for the employment of school staff and the governance of the schools under its authority.

Maria Kirkwood served as the organisation's inaugural chief executive officer and Director of Catholic Education. She retired in December of 2022 after a decade as Director of Catholic Education in the diocese. [ref: Catholic Education leader to retire after 50 years of service, Dandenong Star Journal]> Paul Velten was appointed as her successor in 2022. [ref: Announcement of Director Catholic Education, CEO of DOSCEL, www.cdsale.org.au]

== Governance and structure ==
DOSCEL operates as a company limited by guarantee. The Bishop of Sale is the company's sole member and appoints a board of directors to oversee its governance. The executive leadership team manages the organisation's day-to-day operations and provides leadership and services to schools within its jurisdiction.

Its responsibilities include school governance, educational improvement, staff support, child safety, regulatory compliance and the maintenance of Catholic identity across its schools.

== Curriculum ==
All DOSCEL schools are required to complete Religion Education through the use of the Diocesan curriculum 'To Live in Christ Jesus'. This curriculum aims to teach from the Catholic perspective through the invitation of other faiths along the journey. The 'To live in Christ Jesus' framework is based on four core learning strands; Triune God, The Life and Mission of Jesus, Sacramental Church and Christian Life and Catholic Social Teaching. [ref: Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Limited (DOSCEL), Catholic School Parents Victoria]

== Schools ==
DOSCEL governs and operates 44 Catholic schools, comprising 39 primary schools and five secondary colleges, according to its official website in 2026. [ref: Overview, Victorian Catholic Education Authority] The organisation's schools are distributed across south-eastern Victoria, extending from the outer south-eastern suburbs of Melbourne, including Narre Warren and Cranbourne, through Phillip Island and Gippsland to Orbost. [ref: About - Diocese of Sale Catholic Education Ltd]

Two Catholic secondary colleges within the Diocese of Sale are governed separately from DOSCEL: Lavalla Catholic College, which is governed by Marist Schools Australia, and Catholic College Sale, which is governed by Catholic College Sale Limited. Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools (MACS), legally known as Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools Ltd, is a Catholic education organisation responsible for the governance and operation of Catholic schools within the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Melbourne in Victoria, Australia. Established in 2021 by Archbishop Peter Comensoli, MACS oversees approximately 300 Catholic schools across metropolitan Melbourne and regional areas within the archdiocese. [ref: Our mission, Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools]

MACS provides system-wide leadership, governance and educational support to its schools, including services relating to curriculum, professional learning, child safety, employment, finance and Catholic identity. [ref: Annual Report 2023, Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools]

== History ==

=== Establishment ===
Before the establishment of MACS, many Catholic schools within the Archdiocese of Melbourne were governed at the parish level, with parish priests and local school communities playing significant roles in school administration and governance.

In 2021, Archbishop Peter Comensoli established MACS to assume responsibility for the governance and operation of approximately 293 Catholic schools owned by the archdiocese, its parishes or associations of parishes. The change introduced a centralised governance structure intended to strengthen accountability, improve coordination and support collaboration between schools while maintaining their Catholic mission. [ref: New era for Catholic education in Melbourne, Melbourne Catholic]

The establishment of MACS formed part of a broader restructuring of Catholic education governance in Victoria. Statewide coordination and representation were subsequently undertaken by the Victorian Catholic Education Authority, which replaced the Catholic Education Commission of Victoria in 2023. [ref: Overview, Victorian Catholic Education Authority]

=== MACS 2030 ===
In 2023, MACS began implementing its MACS 2030 strategy, titled Forming Lives to Enrich the World. The strategy established four principal areas of focus: Inspired by Faith, Flourishing Learners, Enabled Leaders and Enriched Communities.

The strategy provides a framework for the organisation's work in Catholic identity, teaching and learning, leadership development and support for school communities.

== Governance and structure ==
MACS operates as a company limited by guarantee and is responsible for the governance and operation of Catholic schools within the Archdiocese of Melbourne that fall under its authority.

The organisation is governed by a board of directors, supported by an executive leadership team. The board oversees strategic direction and organisational governance, while school principals are responsible for the day-to-day leadership and management of their schools within the system's governance framework. [ref: Governance, Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools]

MACS works with parish priests, principals, school advisory councils, families and local communities. Under the Working Together in Mission charter, parish priests and principals have distinct responsibilities and collaborate to maintain the Catholic identity and mission of their schools. [ref: Working Together in Mission, Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools]

== Schools ==
MACS governs and supports approximately 300 Catholic schools within the Archdiocese of Melbourne, including parish primary schools, regional secondary colleges and archdiocesan secondary colleges.

The schools operate across metropolitan Melbourne and parts of regional Victoria within the boundaries of the archdiocese. They provide primary and secondary education and form part of the wider Catholic education sector in Victoria.

Not all Catholic schools in Victoria are governed by MACS. Other diocesan education authorities, religious institutes and independent Catholic school proprietors govern schools in their respective jurisdictions.

== Educational mission ==
The mission of MACS is centred on Catholic education and the formation of the whole person. Its educational framework seeks to combine academic development with spiritual, moral, social and emotional formation, drawing on the teachings of the Catholic Church.

The organisation supports schools through system-wide educational frameworks, including its Vision for Instruction, Vision for Engagement and Vision for Leadership initiatives. These frameworks address teaching practice, student engagement, school leadership and the development of learning environments that support students' educational and personal growth.

Child safety, student wellbeing, inclusive education and professional development are also among the areas addressed through the organisation's policies and support services.

== Funding ==
MACS schools receive funding from government sources, school fees and other income, including fundraising activities. Government funding arrangements operate within the regulatory frameworks governing Australian non-government schools. [ref: Who is MACS? Our role in Catholic education, Melbourne Archdiocese Catholic Schools]

Victorian Catholic Education Authority (VCEA), formerly the Catholic Education Commission of Victoria (CECV), is the peak body for Catholic education in Victoria, Australia. It works with Catholic school proprietors across the state on matters including government funding, school regulation, industrial relations, policy advocacy, Catholic identity and educational research. [ref: Overview, Victorian Catholic Education Authority] [ref: Our role, Victorian Catholic Education Authority]

The organisation was established as the Catholic Education Commission of Victoria in 1973 by the Archbishop of Melbourne and the bishops of the dioceses of Ballarat, Sale and Sandhurst. It was incorporated in 2006 and adopted its current name in 2023 following a review of its governance and operations.

== History ==

=== Establishment ===
The Catholic Education Commission of Victoria was established in 1973 by the Catholic Church's senior leadership in Victoria to support and represent Catholic school education across the state. The organisation was subsequently incorporated in 2006 as a company limited by guarantee.

=== Governance review and renewal ===
In 2021, the Bishops of Victoria commissioned an independent review of the Catholic Education Commission of Victoria's role, governance and operations. The review led to a renewal process intended to strengthen its governance arrangements, operating model and accountability. [ref: Annual Report 2023, Victorian Catholic Education Authority Limited]

As part of this process, the organisation adopted the name Victorian Catholic Education Authority in 2023. The renewal was completed in December 2023, with changes to its governance structure and operating model.

== Role and responsibilities ==
VCEA provides services and undertakes functions for Catholic school proprietors and Catholic schools throughout Victoria. Its responsibilities are established through its constitution and relevant legislative and regulatory arrangements.

=== Government funding ===
VCEA is the approved authority for government funding of Catholic schools in Victoria and serves as a non-government representative body and block grant authority under the Australian Education Act. It receives and allocates government funding for eligible Catholic schools, including recurrent funding for school operations and capital grants for infrastructure and facilities.

Funding allocations are made through established models and processes designed to distribute resources in accordance with applicable requirements and arrangements agreed by representatives of Catholic education.

=== School registration and compliance ===
VCEA acts as the review body for Catholic schools in Victoria, including school boarding premises, in relation to compliance with the minimum standards and requirements for school registration. Its responsibilities include reviewing compliance with child safety requirements in accordance with arrangements involving the Victorian Registration and Qualifications Authority.

=== Industrial relations ===
VCEA represents Catholic school employers in statewide enterprise bargaining. It works with Catholic school proprietors to negotiate employment agreements and support consistency in employment arrangements across the sector.

The organisation also administers the Catholic Education Long Service Leave Scheme in Victoria, which supports the portability of long service leave entitlements between participating Catholic education employers.

=== Policy and advocacy ===
VCEA represents the interests of Catholic school education in Victoria in discussions with the Victorian and Australian governments, school regulators and other relevant organisations. Its work includes policy development, advocacy on school funding and engagement in national discussions concerning Catholic education.

=== Catholic identity and educational research ===
Under the oversight of the Catholic bishops, VCEA supports the Catholic identity of schools and their connection to the mission of the Catholic Church. It also undertakes research and data analysis concerning school funding, educational quality, sustainability and other issues affecting Catholic education in Victoria.

== Governance ==
VCEA is governed by a board of directors and works with representatives of Catholic education providers throughout Victoria. Its governance arrangements include a consultation committee that provides a forum for collaboration between the authority and Catholic school proprietors. [ref: Governance, Victorian Catholic Education Authority]

The organisation's company members include the Archbishop of Melbourne, the bishops of Ballarat, Sale and Sandhurst, and a representative of religious life. The board oversees the organisation's governance, while its executive leadership manages its operations.

August Olsen Storbugt (born 29 April 2000) is a Norwegian handball player who plays as a line player. Born in Fredrikstad, Norway, he has played for Halden Topphåndball and Drammen HK in Norway's top division. In 2025, he signed a two-year contract with Danish club Nordsjælland Håndbold.[1][2][3]

== Career ==

=== Early career ===
Storbugt is originally from the Sarpsborg area in southeastern Norway. He played for Halden Topphåndball for four seasons before joining Drammen HK. During his time at Halden, he represented Norwegian youth national teams and participated in the under-21 World Championship alongside players from an older age group.[1]

=== Drammen HK ===
In January 2021, Drammen HK announced that Storbugt would join the club after completing the season with Halden. He signed an initial two-year contract and was recruited for his physical playing style and ability to contribute in both attack and defence.[1]

In February 2023, Drammen extended his contract for a further two seasons. During his time at the club, Storbugt developed into an important defensive player and a counterattacking threat, while also contributing to the team's scoring.[2][3]

In the 2024–25 season, he was among Drammen's leading scorers. In April 2025, he finished the regular season as the club's top scorer with 116 goals from open play. His final match for Drammen was the second leg of the Norwegian league quarter-finals against Elverum, after which he prepared to move to Denmark.[3][4]

=== Nordsjælland Håndbold ===
In February 2025, Nordsjælland Håndbold announced that Storbugt had signed a two-year contract beginning with the 2025–26 season. The Danish club recruited him primarily for his defensive versatility, physical strength and ability to contribute to fast-break attacks.[3][5]

== International career ==
Storbugt represented Norway at youth international level. According to Drammen HK, he had played nearly 50 age-group international matches by January 2021 and had served as captain of Norway's 2000-born youth cohort.[1]

Draft text:
Iya Agbebi System in Pre-Colonial Lagos

Iya Agbebi system in precolonial Lagos refers to the traditional Yoruba institution of midwifery and maternal healthcare as it operated in the Lagos region before the British colonization of 1861, and its role in trade and economic development. The system was maintained by women known as Iya Agbebi or Iya Abiye, who provided childbirth care, herbal medicine, and postnatal support.

The Iya Agbebi were part of a wider network of female economic actors in precolonial Lagos, alongside women potters, traders, and market leaders.

== Historical background ==
In precolonial Awori and Yoruba societies of Lagos, midwifery was a hereditary female occupation transmitted within family compounds. Training was by apprenticeship, from mother to daughter or from senior female relative to junior wife, similar to other craft guilds. [ref: Nigerian Women in Historical Perspective, Sankore] Their practice combined herbal knowledge, spiritual rites, and practical obstetric care.

== Relationship to trade and economic development ==

=== Labor preservation and population growth ===
The economy of precolonial Lagos relied on human labor for fishing, farming, boat-building, and long-distance trade across the Lagos Lagoon. By providing maternal and infant care, Iya Agbebi contributed to the preservation of human capital and the maintenance of household labor, which supported market expansion. [ref: Slavery and the Birth of an African City: Lagos, 1760-1900, Indiana University Press]

=== Economic role and compensation ===
While anchored in communal welfare, Iya Agbebi were compensated through gifts, agricultural produce, cowries, and specialized trade goods. This exchange contributed to local circulation of currency and goods. Many midwives also engaged in market trading, using the social networks built through their healthcare work to establish customer bases. [ref: Women Traders, Chiefs and the Market, Journal of African History]

=== Support for women's productivity ===
Community-based prenatal and postnatal care reduced periods of incapacity for female traders and artisans, enabling them to return to productive activities. The apprenticeship model of the Iya Agbebi mirrored other female occupational guilds in Yorubaland. [ref: Where Women Work: A Study of Yoruba Women in the Marketplace and at Home, University of Michigan]

=== Medical supply chain ===
The practice relied on medicinal plants, roots, bark, and palm oils, collectively known as egbogi. Sourcing these materials involved herbal merchants and medicine suppliers (onisegun) and created demand for forest products from the Yoruba interior, linking coastal Lagos with inland communities. [ref: Yoruba Medicine, Oxford University Press]

== Decline and transformation ==
With the introduction of colonial biomedical services and Christian missionary maternity centers in late 19th and early 20th century Lagos, the formal role of the Iya Agbebi declined, though the practice continued informally.

The website does not name a Saint Lucia financial regulator for this entity. Clients are introduced through the South African company and then enter a trading agreement with the Saint Lucia company.

Draft text:
Luciano Perrone è un medico chirurgo italiano attivo nei campi della chirurgia generale, della chirurgia del seno e della medicina e chirurgia estetica. [ref: Dott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

== Formazione e carriera ==
Perrone si è laureato in Medicina e Chirurgia presso l'Università degli Studi di Roma Tor Vergata nel marzo 2008. La sua tesi riguardava la correlazione tra fibrosi epatica e infiammazione nei pazienti sottoposti a trapianto di fegato per epatite C; lo stesso argomento è stato trattato in una pubblicazione scientifica alla quale ha partecipato come coautore. [ref: Correlation between liver fibrosis and inflammation in patients transplanted for HCV liver disease, PubMed]

Tra il 2008 e il 2010 ha lavorato nell'unità di trapianto di Tor Vergata, occupandosi di chirurgia epatobiliare e trapianti di fegato e rene. Successivamente ha svolto attività presso l'Aurelia Hospital di Roma e, dal 2013, ha maturato esperienze in chirurgia del pavimento pelvico, chirurgia laparoscopica e chirurgia colorettale. Tra il 2014 e il 2016 ha proseguito la formazione in chirurgia epatobiliare e laparoscopica presso strutture italiane e britanniche, tra cui il Noble's Hospital, il Colchester Hospital e l'ICENI Centre. [ref: Curriculum vitae del dottor Giovanni Domenico Tebala, Azienda ospedaliero-universitaria Sant'Andrea]

Nel 2012 ha completato un percorso di perfezionamento in Medicina Estetica presso l'Università di Camerino. Nel luglio 2015 ha conseguito la specializzazione in Chirurgia Generale e Chirurgia del Seno presso Tor Vergata. [ref: Dr. Luciano Perrone, Chirurgo Plastico, iDoctors]

La successiva formazione in chirurgia estetica ha incluso periodi presso il Dolan Park Hospital di Bromsgrove e nell'area di Harley Street a Londra, oltre a esperienze formative a Buenos Aires sotto la supervisione del chirurgo J. C. Pavani. [ref: Dott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

== Attività professionale ==
Dal 2013 Perrone ha svolto attività in chirurgia estetica nel Regno Unito, con esperienze professionali a Londra, Birmingham e Manchester. I suoi ambiti di attività comprendono la chirurgia del seno, del viso e del corpo, la chirurgia intima, i trattamenti non chirurgici di medicina estetica e il trapianto di capelli. [ref: Dott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

In Italia è direttore sanitario delle Cliniche Dr. Peròn, con sedi a Parma, Milano e Bologna. I profili professionali disponibili lo indicano iscritto all'Ordine dei Medici di Parma con il numero 7488 e a quello di Roma con il numero 56818. È inoltre indicato come membro dell'Associazione Italiana di Chirurgia Plastica ed Estetica (AICPE) e registrato presso il General Medical Council britannico. [ref: Chi siamo, Cliniche Dr. PerònDott. Perrone Luciano, Federazione Italiana Medici Estetici]

Perrone presenta un approccio alla mastoplastica additiva denominato Mastoplastica Argentina, associato alle sue esperienze formative in Argentina. In un'intervista pubblicata da Guidaestetica ha descritto un percorso che comprende la valutazione delle aspettative della paziente, l'esame delle caratteristiche anatomiche e la scelta dell'impianto. La tecnica chirurgica descritta prevede il posizionamento della protesi secondo la tecnica dual plane, con scelte adattate alle caratteristiche individuali. [ref: Il metodo della Mastoplastica Argentina del Dr. Luciano Perrone, un seno naturale su misura senza sorprese, Guidaestetica]

== Attività scientifica ==
L'attività scientifica di Perrone si è concentrata prevalentemente sulla chirurgia dei trapianti, la chirurgia laparoscopica e la chirurgia colorettale. Tra le pubblicazioni a cui ha contribuito figurano studi sulla fibrosi epatica dopo trapianto, sui regimi immunosoppressivi nei pazienti sottoposti a trapianto renale e sui programmi di recupero postoperatorio. [ref: Correlation between liver fibrosis and inflammation in patients transplanted for HCV liver disease, PubMedEarly Discharge After Colorectal Resection: The Positive Impact of an Enhanced Recovery Program on a Rural Colorectal Surgery Service, PubMed]

=== Pubblicazioni selezionate ===

The Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West is a 2025 book by international relations scholar Amitav Acharya,. [ref: ] published by Basic Books in April 2025. [ref: The Once and Future World Order, John Murray Press] The book explores the historical development of world order across different civilizations and regions, beginning with ancient Sumer and Egypt and extending through Persia, Greece, India, China, Rome, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, and Europe to the contemporary international system. [ref: The once and future world order: why global civilization will survive the decline of the West, Basic Books] The book examines the development of political ideas, institutions, and practices associated with relations among states and societies, including diplomacy, trade, political organization, war, and interstate cooperation, and concludes with a discussion of the changing international order and the implications of declining Western dominance.

== Contents ==
The book traces the development of different world orders and interactions among societies throughout history, before turning to the contemporary international system and its possible future.

The book starts by examining the different ideas and institutions commonly associated with the "Western" world order emerged in non-Western civilizations thousands of years before the rise of the West. These range from peace treaties and interstate cooperation to freedom of the seas and environmental protection. Acharya argues that these contributions have often been overlooked in the mainstream history.

The book examines how the dominance of the European perspective over the last 500 years has contributed to two forms of historical misrepresentation: the sin of commission and the sin of omission. The sin of commission is largely the misinterpretation or distortion of the achievements of non-Western cultures and civilizations. The sin of omission occurs when facts about them are overlooked. The book also considers the achievements and failures of both Western and non-Western civilizations. [ref: Review of the Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West, International Studies Review]

The book also explores three fears in the West today about the end of the American-led Western order: the fear of the rise of the "civilization states," the fear of the Chinese-built and Chinese-led order, and the fear of "chaos, violence, and conflict."

== Reception ==
Writing in The New York Times, historian Abhishek Kaicker reviewed the book together with historian William Dalrymple’s The Golden Road. He discussed the two works as attempts to reconsider conventional accounts of how the international order developed. [ref: Worried the World Is Falling Apart? That's OK. It's Happened Before., The New York Times] In The Christian Science Monitor, it appeared on the 10 best books of April 2025 [ref: 10 best books of April 2025 make a bouquet of great reads, The Christian Science Monitor] and Abhijnan Rej examined Acharya’s claim that the principles and institutions of political order arose across several civilizations rather than exclusively in the modern West. [ref: Democratic ideals and the rule of law have persisted across nations and eras, Christian Science Monitor]

The book was included in Foreign Policy’s The Most Anticipated Books of 2025. [ref: The Most Anticipated Books of 2025, Foreign Policy]

Academic reviews include International Studies Review [ref: Review of the Once and Future World Order: Why Global Civilization Will Survive the Decline of the West, International Studies Review] and Commonwealth & Comparative Politics [ref: The once and future world order: why global civilization will survive the decline of the West: by Amitav Acharya, New York, Basic Books, 2025, 464 pp., $32.50 (hardback), ISBN 9781541604148, Commonwealth & Comparative Politics]

== References ==

=== Ian McBride (cyclist) ===

* Subject Description: Ian McBride (born c. 1970s) is a New Zealand-born, London-based ultra-distance and audax cyclist who has competed internationally in premier long-distance randonnées. After moving from New Zealand to the UK in the late 1990s, he transitioned from triathlons to ultra-endurance cycling, joining the night-riding group "The Fridays". He completed the 1,200 km Paris–Brest–Paris (PBP) event in 2019, and returned in the 2023 edition to finish with a time of 51 hours and 39 minutes, cementing his record as the fastest New Zealander in the event's history. He also finished the 1,540 km London–Edinburgh–London (LEL) event in 2022 in joint 2nd with 2x winner Dutchman Anco De Jong, despite suffering from Shermer's neck in the final stages. Following his cycling achievements, he was voted by the membership and awarded the 2025 Audax UK Male Merit Award (The Paul Castle Cup), given annually to the cyclist whose performance is considered the most meritorious of the year.

McBride achieved widespread national and international cycling media coverage during the August 2025 iteration of the London–Edinburgh–London event. Setting off at 4:00 AM on 3 August 2025, McBride intentionally paced his ride to outrun an impending severe weather system. He successfully crossed into Scotland and reached the Edinburgh turnaround point, with a 3 hour lead over the 2nd placed rider, just before event organisers officially suspended the brevet due to 100 mph winds brought by Storm Floris. Because thousands of trailing participants were ordered to stop or turn back from wherever they had reached, McBride became the only rider out of 2,500 entrants to complete the full, original 1,500 km scheduled route back to London. His feat is a primary subject of the 2025 non-fiction book "Riders of the Storm: The Inside Story of London Edinburgh London".

Tom Joel Obengo is a Kenyan bioethicist, philosopher, educator and academic administrator. He is Vice-Principal for Academic Affairs and Senior Lecturer at Moffat Bible College, Kijabe, Kenya, and a recent Postdoctoral Research Fellow in Epidemic Ethics in the Department of Medicine at the University of Cape Town.

== Early life and education ==

Obengo earned a Bachelor of Theology (B.Th.) from Scott University in 1994 and an Honours Bachelor of Arts (Hons.B.A.) in Ethics and Philosophy from the University of South Africa in 1999.

He completed his Master of Theology (M.Th.) in Medical Ethics (Systematic Theology) at Stellenbosch University in 2013 with a thesis titled The quest for human dignity in the ethics of pregnancy termination: a theological-ethical evaluation of the church's approach in Kenya, which was supervised by Professor Chris Jones.. [ref: Browsing by Author Obengo, Tom Joel, SUNScholar, Stellenbosch University] [ref: The quest for human dignity in the ethics of pregnancy termination, SUNScholar]

He undertook M.Phil. courses in Philosophy specialising in Applied Ethics at Stellenbosch University (2016–2017) and completed his Doctor of Philosophy (D.Phil.) in Applied Ethics in March 2020 with a dissertation titled A Utilitarian Assessment of the Relevance of Genetic Therapies for HIV-AIDS in Africa, with Special Reference to the Situation in Kenya, supervised by Professor Anton A. van Niekerk, Distinguished Professor of Philosophy at Stellenbosch University. [ref: A Utilitarian Assessment of the Relevance of Genetic Therapies for HIV-AIDS in Africa, with Special Reference to the Situation in Kenya, University of Stellenbosch, Department of Philosophy, Faculty of Arts & Social Sciences]

== Academic career ==

Since 2014, Obengo has served as Vice-Principal for Academic Affairs and Senior Lecturer at Moffat Bible College, Kijabe, where he teaches ethics, philosophy, critical thinking, apologetics and theology. [ref: Faculty, Moffat Bible College]Some pPublic records list him as Rev. Tom Obengo (Vice Principal Academics) explaining courses offered at the college. [ref: Moffat Bible College, Moffat Bible College via Haylla]

He previously served as Academic Registrarsuccessively at Scott University, at International Leadership University–Kenya, and at Great Lakes University of Kisum.uHe once served ass Academic Dean and Acting Principal at Ahero Bible Training College.

From 2021 to 2024, he was Post-Doctoral Research Fellow in Epidemic Ethics in the Department of Medicine at the University of Cape Town, based at the EthicsLab, where he focused on epidemic ethics and published articles and a book chapter. [ref: Dr Tom J. Obengo, University of Cape Town EthicsLab]

His university teaching and examination roles include:

* External examiner in bioethics, University of Nairobi and University of the Witwatersrand
* Adjunct teaching roles, University of Virginia and Stellenbosch University
* Postgraduate teaching in bioethics, Kabarak University and Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI)

== Research and publications ==

Obengo is the author of:

* The Quest for Human Dignity in the Ethics of Pregnancy Termination (Wipf and Stock, 2016)

and co-author of:

* Research Ethics in Epidemics and Pandemics: A Casebook (Springer Nature, 2024) – Chapter 2. [ref: Research Ethics in Epidemics and Pandemics: A Casebook, Springer Nature]

His research interests include utilitarian bioethics, genetic therapies for HIV-AIDS, epidemic ethics, human dignity, and African Christian ethics.

== Professional service ==

* Managing Editor, African Christian Theology Journal [ref: Editorial Team, African Christian Theology Journal]
* Editorial board member, Journal of Interdisciplinary Ethical Research [ref: Editorial Team, Journal of Interdisciplinary Ethical Research]
* Member, Institutional Scientific and Ethical Review Committee (ISERC), AIC Kijabe Hospital (since 2015)
* Member, Epidemic Ethics Team, The Global Health Network
* Member, Bioethics Society of Kenya

PiEEG is a neurotechnology company based in Edinburgh, Scotland, that develops low-cost, open-source brain–computer interface (BCI) hardware for researchers, developers and hobbyists. Its devices measure electroencephalography (EEG), electromyography (EMG) and electrocardiography (ECG) signals.

== History ==
The company's first product, an EEG board for the Raspberry Pi, was developed after the 2020–2023 global chip shortage made an earlier standalone design too expensive. It launched on Crowd Supply in 2023 at US$250–$350. A 16-channel model followed in 2024. In 2026 the company announced PiEEG XR, an EEG face interface for Meta Quest headsets.

== Products ==

* PiEEG – an 8-channel EEG board for the Raspberry Pi 3 and 4.
* PiEEG-16 – a 16-channel board for the Raspberry Pi 5.
* IronBCI – a standalone wearable 8-channel BCI.
* PiEEG XR – a sensor face interface for the Meta Quest 3, aimed at developers, including for VRChat avatars.

== Reception ==
IEEE Spectrum presented PiEEG as an example of open-source hardware bringing BCI to makers. UploadVR called PiEEG XR a developer kit that still has to solve problems of fit, noise and calibration.

GameBoost is an online marketplace for video game digital goods, operated by the Croatian company Global Gaming Services d.o.o. The platform connects buyers with third-party sellers of game keys, gift cards, game accounts, in-game currency and items. The company was founded by Kristijan Salijević and registered in 2022 in Strmec Stubički, Krapina-Zagorje County.

== History ==
According to Salijević, the activity that became GameBoost began around 2017–2018 as a hobby during his university studies, with small initial earnings and no long-term business plan. The operating company, Global Gaming Services d.o.o., was entered in the Croatian court register on 28 February 2022.

In April 2022, the venture capital fund Fil Rouge Capital invested €500,000 in the company. In March 2023, Fil Rouge Capital and the impact investment fund Feelsgood Capital Partners closed a second round of €2 million, co-invested in equal shares, intended to fund expansion into new markets and additional games. At the time, the company reported more than 20 employees and around 700 freelancers, with most of its freelancers and customers based outside Croatia.

== Products ==
GameBoost operates as a marketplace on which verified third-party sellers list digital goods for video games, while the platform handles checkout, payments and customer support. Its main product categories include game keys, gift cards, game accounts, in-game currency, virtual items and account top-ups.

Game keys are sold for PC storefronts such as Steam, GOG, EA app and Ubisoft Connect, as well as for Xbox, PlayStation and Nintendo Switch consoles. Gift cards and subscription cards are offered for services including Steam, Xbox, PlayStation Network and Amazon.

The account category covers pre-made accounts for more than 200 games, including Fortnite, Valorant, Grand Theft Auto V, Clash of Clans and Counter-Strike 2. According to the company, sellers must pass verification before listing, and purchased accounts carry a 14-day warranty. The platform also has a marketplace for Counter-Strike 2 skins and items.

== Finances ==
According to financial data filed with the Croatian Financial Agency (FINA), Global Gaming Services reported the following results:

== Recognition ==
GameBoost has been featured in several Croatian and European startup and business rankings.

In January 2024, the European startup publication EU-Startups included GameBoost in its list of ten innovative Croatian startups to watch in 2024, describing it as an "all-in-one platform designed to cater to the diverse needs of gamers". The company was again included in the publication's January 2025 list of ten promising Croatian startups, which noted that it had raised €2.5 million in funding.

In November 2024, founder Kristijan Salijević was named to the "30 Under 30" list compiled by the Croatian technology magazine VIDI. The list recognises people under the age of 30 for achievements in startups, science and information and communications technology, and was presented at the VIDI Awards ceremony, with previous honourees serving as the jury.

In April 2026, the business weekly Lider featured Salijević in its "40 Under 40" series on successful Croatian entrepreneurs. To be considered for the ranking, entrepreneurs had to be founders holding an active director-level role in a company with annual revenue above €1 million.

Mt. Kili is an American indie folk duo from Asheville, North Carolina, consisting of singer-songwriter and guitarist Rick Sichta and drummer and percussionist Matt Shepard. Violinist and vocalist Laney Barnett is featured on the group's second album. [ref: Mt. Kili – The Noticer, Obscure Sound] [ref: Mt. Kili releases new album, Plastic Magazine] [ref: The Noticer Is a Rich, Natural Evolution for Mt. Kili, Rotate Magazine] [ref: Discover Mt Kili's The Noticer, York Calling]

The project's second studio album, The Noticer, was recorded at Echo Mountain Studio in Asheville and expanded the home-recorded approach of its debut into a collaborative studio arrangement.

== History ==
Plastic Magazine reported that Sichta introduced the project with the single "Tomorrow" in 2023 and followed it with the home-recorded debut album Ten Songs for My Girls, for Now and Later in 2024. The publication described the debut as centered on voice and classical guitar and written for Sichta's twin daughters.

For The Noticer, the project developed into a fuller-band collaboration with Shepard and Barnett. Plastic Magazine, York Calling, Echo Mountain Recording, and La Caverna credited Julian Dreyer with engineering and David Glasser with mastering, while multiple reviews described the contrast between the debut's home recording and the second album's studio production. [ref: So Far in 2026: New Music From Echo Mountain Artists, Echo Mountain Recording] [ref: De la Cruda Identidad Urbana al Folk de Autor y Ritmos Híbridos, La Caverna]

A third album, Ikigai, is scheduled for release on 1 May 2027. Sichta wrote the album during a summer spent alone in Costa Rica; Songwriter Safari described its songs as questions "about where we came from, what we're doing here, where we're going", completing an arc across the three records in which the debut was "giving", The Noticer is "seeing", and Ikigai is "asking". [ref: From Mountain Trails to Mt. Kili, Songwriter Safari (Late Bloomers Rock)]

== Reception ==
Obscure Sound published a track-by-track review and called the album "one of the strongest folk albums of 2026 so far", while describing the songwriting and gradually developing arrangements. Plastic Magazine also reviewed the record track by track, focusing on the transition from solo home recordings to an ensemble studio production and describing "The Weather Report" as using "hypnotic instrumentation".

Clout characterized the album's flow as hypnotic and ambitious, discussed the title track's gradual build, and noted the restrained acoustic treatment of "The Road Isn't as Long as It Seems". [ref: Album Review: Mt. Kili – The Noticer, Clout] Rotate Magazine framed the album as a fuller development of the debut, crediting Barnett's violin and vocals and Shepard's rhythmic role, and described the result as "deeply human".

Dave Franklin, writing for Dancing About Architecture, compared the use of space in "Don't Start a War" to Damien Rice and connected the record's intimate scale with songs informed by Sichta's reported travels in China, Tibet, and near Mount Everest. [ref: The Noticer – Mt. Kili, Dancing About Architecture] The Slow Music Movement reviewed the album track by track and characterized Sichta's voice as a "roots music lifeline" in contrast with derivative folk music. Barrett Business Services, Inc. (BBSI) is an American professional employer organization (PEO) headquartered in Vancouver, Washington. The company provides payroll, human resources, workers' compensation coverage, and related administrative services to small and mid-sized businesses through a co-employment arrangement, and also operates a staffing business. It is listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol BBSI.

The company traces its origins to a temporary-staffing business founded in Baltimore in 1951 and was incorporated in Maryland in 1965. It became a public company through an initial public offering on the Nasdaq in June 1993. The company reported revenue of $1.14 billion for 2024.

== History ==
The business that became Barrett Business Services was founded in Baltimore in 1951 by Nancy Barrett, who operated a temporary-help office there for about two decades. The company was incorporated in Maryland in 1965, and in 1971 it merged with Barry Temporary Services, a Portland, Oregon, temporary-employment firm led by William W. Sherertz, who became president of the combined company. BBSI became publicly traded through an initial public offering on the Nasdaq in June 1993. Sherertz led the company until his death in 2011; he was succeeded as chief executive by Michael Elich, and in 2020 by Gary Kramer.

== Operations ==
BBSI operates primarily as a professional employer organization, entering into a client services agreement to establish a co-employment relationship with each client company and assuming responsibility for payroll, payroll taxes, workers' compensation coverage, and certain other administrative functions. It reports its services in two categories, professional employer services and staffing. In a 2024 interview, chief executive Gary Kramer said the company operated in 68 markets and that its average client employed about 26 people.

== References ==

Bayou Boy is a 1971 American television adventure film produced by Walt Disney Productions. [ref: The Wonderful World of Disney Television, Hyperion Books] [ref: Disney A to Z: The Official Encyclopedia: Third Edition, Disney Editions] Directed by Gary Nelson and written by Louis Pelletier, it originally aired in two parts on NBC's The Wonderful World of Disney on February 7 and February 14, 1971. [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23] [ref: Louis Pelletier; Wrote 500 Episodes of 'FBI' Radio Series, Los Angeles Times] The film was rebroadcast by NBC in 1979 under the title The Boy from Dead Man's Bayou. [ref: The Magical World of Disney Season 17 Episodes, TV Guide] [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23]

== Plot ==
Jeannot Boudreau is determined to locate a sunken silver church bell that is lost in Dead Man’s Bayou in the Louisiana backwoods, after a hurricane destroyed the church it was located in. [ref: Bayou Boy (television), D23] He wants to retrieve it to honor his father, who helped cast the bell. [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] To find the bell he must contend with a giant alligator who patrols the bayou. [ref: The Magical World of Disney Season 17 Episodes, TV Guide]

== Cast ==

* Mitch Vogel as Jeannot Boudreau
* Mike Lookinland as Claude
* Vito Scotti as Mr. Bob
* Paul Fix as Captain Pierre
* John McIntire as Father Boudreau
* Jeanette Nolan as Tante Louise
* Marcel Hillaire as M. Verret
* Frank Silvera as Uncle Maxim
* Percy Rodrigues as Charbot
* Michael Ontkean as Alcide
* Brad David as Phillipe

== Production ==
Co-stars John McIntire and Jeanette Nolan were married in real life, and often appeared in the same shows and movies. [ref: Husband, Wife Acting Team in 'Bayou Boy', Idaho State Journal] [ref: Behind the Scenes, The Daily Herald]

Filming took place at Pine Island Point at Caddo Lake, on the Texas-Louisiana border near Shreveport. [ref: Disney filming at Caddo Lake, Shreveport Times] [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] [ref: Louisiana to be Spotlighted in Disney TV Series on NBC, The Marksville Weekly News] [ref: Page 28, The Jeffersonian] In one instance when a stuntman failed to show up, a local highway patrolman was asked to fall 25 feet in a lake. [ref: City Beat, The Mexia Daily News] After filming Governor Preston Smith made the cast of the film honorary Texas citizens. [ref: 'Bayou Boy' Cast Honorary Texas Citizens, The Salt Lake Tribune]

A $12,000 replica of the bayou was constructed at Disney Studio in Burbank for the alligator fight scene. [ref: Bayou Boy, Chronique Disney] [ref: Prehistoric Caddo Lake is Setting for Disney's 'Bayou Boy' Adventure, The Robesonian] [ref: TV Scout, The Index-Journal]

== Music ==
The musical score was composed by Buddy Baker. [ref: Norman "Buddy" Baker Collection, NYU Special Collections Finding Aids] The opening title song, "Bayou Boy", was written by Terry Gilkyson and performed by his daughter Lisa. [ref: Dynamite, cowboy boots, horse falls, and toupee hijinks with Steve McQueen's costar Mitch Vogel, Medium]

== Reception ==
The Robesonian called it an “exciting two-part action adventure drama,” [ref: Percy Rodrigues Fights Alligator on 'Disney World' Bayou Drama, The Robesonian] and The Oneonta Star felt that it was “suitable family fare.” [ref: Top TV, The Oneonta Star] The Daily Herald referred to it as a “mystery adventure,” [ref: Mitch Vogel in Title Role for Disney's 'Bayou Boy', The Daily Herald] and the Albuquerque Journal wrote that “kids should eat it up.” [ref: TV Key Previews, Albuquerque Journal]

Kha Ma Harun (also known as K. M. Harun Al Rashid; born 26 October 1953) is a Bangladeshi television director, filmmaker, media executive, educator and author. He serves as the Principal and Head of the Department of Film and Television at Pathshala South Asian Media Institute, an affiliate of the University of Dhaka. [ref: Faculty Member, Pathshala South Asian Media Institute] [ref: Kha Ma Harun, Pathshala South Asian Media Institute] [ref: Reform from ground up needed for media to speak for nation, The Daily Star] During his three-decade career at Bangladesh Television (BTV), he held senior executive roles-including Director, Deputy Director General (programme), and Acting Director General [ref: Poet Abu Zafar made BTV DG, The Daily Star] while producing and directing television dramas, serials, telefilms, documentaries, and cultural broadcasts. He is also the author of three published books. [ref: প্রযুক্তি সহজ হলেও ভালো কনটেন্ট তৈরি সহজ হয়নি, The Daily News Paper Ittefaq]

== Early Life and Education ==
Harun was born on 26 October 1953 in Khulna, in what was then East Pakistan (now Bangladesh). He studied Philosophy at the University of Dhaka, where he earned a Bachelor of Arts (Honours) and a Master of Arts degree. During his university years, he also studied Political Science and History. As a first-year student, he participated in the Bangladesh Liberation War in 1971. After completing his master's degree in 1976, Harun received a Government of India scholarship to study at the National School of Drama (NSD) in New Delhi. He completed a three-year postgraduate diploma in Drama in 1979, specializing in theatre design.
== Career ==
Harun joined Bangladesh Television (BTV) as a producer on 17 July 1980. [ref: Former BTV deputy DG recalls a sweet and conflicted Tazin Ahmed, Dhaka Tribune] During his 30 years at BTV, he worked as a Producer, Executive Producer, Programme Manager, Director, and Deputy Director General until his retirement in 2010. At BTV, his work involved television production, programme planning, dramas, telefilms, documentaries, serials, musical shows, and public affairs broadcasts. He also served as Executive Director and Chief of Programmes at RTV, [ref: Revolution Television, The Daily Star] and as Director of the National Institute of Mass Communication (NIMC), the Government of Bangladesh's media training institution. His directorial work includes Firiye Dao Aronnyo (1989), featuring Tauquir Ahmed, Munira Yusuf Memi, and Abdul Barik Mukul [ref: MEMI Versatility and verve, The Daily Star] [ref: কেমন আছেন অভিনেতা আবদুল বারিক মুকুল, Jugantor] and the series Shongkito Podojatra (1992) written by Mansurul Aziz. He also produced Shohor, Jhor, Nilpania, Rupali Nodir Dheu, and Kichuto Bolun. Harun authored Shongkito Podojatra (2023), [ref: Shongkito Podojatra, pathakshamabesh] a memoir detailing his experiences in the Bangladesh Liberation War and his broadcasting career. The book shares its title with a 1992 television series he previously directed for Bangladesh Television. Harun authored two additional books: Sabinoye Jante Chai (সবিনয়ে জানতে চাই) from Sahitya Prakash in 1997 [ref: সবিনয়ে জানতে চাই, Sāhitya Prakāśa] and Diary 1972 Ebong Koyekti Din (ডায়েরি ১৯৭২ এবং কয়েকটি দিন) from Panjeri Publications, 2026. [ref: ডায়েরি ১৯৭২: কয়েকটি দিন, Samakal]

Following his retirement from Bangladesh Television, Harun entered academia as an Adjunct Professor in the Department of Television, Film and Photography at the University of Dhaka, teaching television production, broadcasting management, and media studies. He was later appointed Principal and Head of the Department of Film and Television at Pathshala South Asian Media Institute, an institute affiliated with the University of Dhaka. He also served as a member of the Strategic Plan Team of the Asia-Pacific Institute for Broadcasting Development (AIBD), where he participated in regional broadcasting and media development initiatives, [ref: আন্তর্জাতিক সম্প্রচার কৌশল পরিকল্পনা টিমে খ ম হারুন, Daily Inqilab] the Commonwealth Broadcasting Association (CBA), and the SAARC Audio Visual Exchange (SAVE). He has also participated in international broadcasting conferences, workshops, and media forums in Asia and Europe. In 2017, he attended the 14th Asia Media Summit in Qingdao, China, as a member of the Bangladeshi delegation. During his visits to China, he also produced documentary films for Bangladeshi television and participated in professional exchanges with Chinese broadcasting organizations.[https://www.ekusheypatrika.com/archives/17469] [ref: খ ম হারুন-চীনা বেতারের ভ্রমণ কথোপকথন, Ekushey Patrika] Harun contributed archival photographs and historical information to a feature published by Prothom Alo on the history of Bangladesh Television. [ref: বিটিভির যাত্রা শুরুর রোমাঞ্চকর নেপথ্য কাহিনি, প্রথম আলো বাংলা নিউজ পেপার]

Oreoluwa Finnih, (born 11 March 1973) is a Nigerian physician, public-sector official and grassroots politician whose work spans healthcare administration, public health and sustainable development. She has held several positions in the Lagos State Government, including Senior Special Assistant on Health and Special Adviser on Sustainable Development Goals to the governor. Her work has included public-health programmes, human capital development, women's financial inclusion and initiatives aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

== Education ==
Finnih attended Queen's College in Yaba, Lagos, from 1984 to 1990. She subsequently studied dentistry at the University of Lagos College of Medicine between 1990 and 1998.

She later attended Lagos Business School, part of Pan-Atlantic University, where she completed an Executive Master of Business Administration programme from 2008 to 2009. [ref: Oreoluwa Finnih-Awokoya, SA on SDGs & Investments to Governor of Lagos State, BusinessDay]

Her professional development has included training in agribusiness, export administration, public-sector transformation, governance, public health and leadership. In 2015, she attended agribusiness training through the Dream Business Club and the Songhai Regional Centre in Porto-Novo, Benin. She subsequently completed export-related training organised by the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry in 2016.

In 2018, she undertook master-trainer training through the Lagos State Office of Transformation, Creativity and Innovation's Growth Mindset Initiative. In 2019, she participated in training related to good governance and resilient health systems at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. Her later courses included the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health programme Applied Risk Communication for the 21st Century in September 2021 and Harvard Medical School's Career Advancement and Leadership Skills for Women in Healthcare in November 2021. She also completed the [https://sdgacademy.org SDG Academy]'s Global Public Health Programme, receiving a verified certificate in June 2021.

== Career ==

=== Healthcare ===
Finnih began her professional career in the health sector. From 1999 to 2000, she worked as a medical officer with the Lagos State Health Management Board. She subsequently worked as a dentist at [https://www.schubbsdental.com Schubbs Dental Clinics] from June 2001 to March 2002.

She later held management positions at [https://finnihmedicalcentre.com Finnih Medical Centre], including Head of Human Resources from January 2002 to August 2005, Head of Administration and Finance from September 2005 to May 2007, and Chief Operating Officer from June 2007 to December 2011. She served as the centre's chief executive officer from December 2011 to April 2015.

Finnih Medical Centre was established in 1983 by physician Oluyomi Finnih. [ref: Sanwo-Olu celebrates veteran gynaecologist, Oluyomi Finnih, at 80, The Punch]

=== Agribusiness ===
In November 2015, Finnih founded Helix Farms, where she served as chief executive officer. Her work in the sector followed training in agribusiness, farming and export administration.

=== Lagos State public service ===
Finnih returned to public service in 2016, when she worked as a Research and Statistics Officer at the Lagos State Health Service Commission from December 2016 to June 2017. Between February and June 2017, she also served as Personal Assistant to the Permanent Secretary of the Lagos State Primary Health Care Board.

From June 2017 to December 2019, she worked as a Senior Medical Officer in the Directorate of Medical Services. From February 2018 to December 2019, she also served as an Infection Prevention and Disease Control Officer.

In December 2019, she became Senior Special Assistant on Health to Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. In that role, she worked within the state's health administration and public-health framework. A profile published by BusinessDay reported that she led the risk-communication pillar of Lagos State's COVID-19 response in 2020.

In September 2023, following a change in her cabinet designation, she was appointed [https://lagossdg.com Special Adviser] on Sustainable Development Goals to the governor of Lagos State. [ref: Cabinet: Sanwo-Olu redeploys Finnih-Awokoya, Olowu as special advisers, Independent Nigeria]

== Sustainable development work ==

=== Sustainable Development Goals ===
As Special Adviser on Sustainable Development Goals, Finnih has been involved in programmes intended to align state initiatives with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals. These goals address areas including poverty reduction, health, education, gender equality, economic opportunity, sustainable cities and partnerships for development.

In September 2024, she participated in discussions on building a more resilient and sustainable Lagos. She also took part in activities around the United Nations General Assembly's seventy-ninth session, where Lagos State promoted its sustainable-development agenda and partnerships. [ref: Oreoluwa Finnih leads discourse in charting path for building resilient, sustainable Lagos, BusinessDay] [ref: UNGA79: Lagos advances agenda on attaining SDGs, TheCable]
[truncated]

= Jump Branding & Design Inc. =
Jump Branding & Design Inc. is a Canadian multidisciplinary branding and design agency headquartered in Toronto, Ontario. Founded in 2004, the privately held company specializes in brand strategy, visual identity, packaging design, restaurant and retail environments, digital design, and marketing communications.

The agency works with businesses across the food and beverage, hospitality, retail, consumer packaged goods, and commercial sectors. Its practice combines graphic design and brand development with the design of physical environments and customer experiences.

Jump has received recognition through Canadian and international design competitions, including the Association for Retail Environments (A.R.E.) Design Awards, Packaging Association of Canada (PAC) Leadership Awards, Transform Awards, and Digital Signage Awards.

== History ==
Jump Branding & Design Inc. was established in Toronto in 2004 as an independent branding and design agency.

The company developed a multidisciplinary practice combining brand strategy, graphic design, packaging, and environmental design, with a particular focus on restaurant and retail businesses.

Over the following two decades, the agency undertook projects for Canadian and international businesses, including restaurant chains, retail operators, consumer product companies, and commercial property organizations.

The agency's work has included brand identity development, restaurant concepts, retail environments, product packaging, environmental graphics, and digital communications.

Jump is led by founding principals Eric Boulden and Jason Hemsworth, who serve as co-presidents.

== Services and operations ==
Jump provides design and consulting services across several disciplines.

=== Branding and visual identity ===
The agency develops brand strategies, corporate identities, naming systems, brand architecture, visual identities, and brand guidelines for established businesses and emerging brands.

=== Restaurant and retail design ===
Jump designs restaurant, hospitality, and retail environments, including interior concepts, space planning, signage, environmental graphics, customer circulation, merchandising, and design documentation.

Its work includes individual locations, restaurant prototypes, and design programs intended for implementation across multiple locations.

=== Packaging design ===
The company's packaging practice includes consumer product packaging, product identity, packaging systems, and brand extensions for food, beverage, retail, and other consumer goods.

=== Digital design and marketing ===
Jump also provides digital brand applications, website design, marketing communications, advertising creative, and photography.

== Notable projects ==

=== South St. Burger Co. ===
Jump developed retail and environmental design work for South St. Burger Co., including a restaurant at Toronto's Shops at Don Mills.

The project incorporated sustainable design strategies, energy-efficient equipment, and environmentally responsible material selections.

The restaurant received recognition through the Association for Retail Environments' design awards, including sustainability-related honours. The project was featured in Retail Design Blog in March 2012.

=== Union Station Food Court ===
Jump was involved in the development of digital signage and branded environments for the food court at Toronto's Union Station.

Working with Osmington and participating food-service operators, the agency helped develop digital signage standards and branded content for the food hall.

The project included environmental graphics, digital menu boards, and digital signage for multiple food-service tenants.

The Union Station Food Court project was recognized in the Restaurants, Bars and Foods category of the Digital Signage Awards, with winners announced in January 2021.

=== Frank – Canadian Tire ===
Jump Branding & Design worked with Canadian Tire to redesign the packaging for Frank, its private-label brand spanning household essentials, cleaning products, and snack foods. The agency developed a packaging system incorporating humour, playful illustrations, and product-specific messaging to establish a consistent brand personality across more than 100 SKUs.

The work received a Silver Davey Award in 2018 and a Best in Class award at the 2021 PAC Global Leadership Awards in the Brand Marketing – Revitalized Food category, recognizing the Frank snack food packaging.

=== Bento Sushi / Bento Brave ===
In 2025, Jump developed the creative concept and visual identity for Bento Sushi's Bento Brave rebranding initiative.

The rebranding introduced updated typography, graphics, colours, and a dragon motif intended for use across the company's retail and food-service locations.

The initiative was covered by Retail Insider and Adnews, which identified Jump as the agency responsible for the new visual identity.

=== Other clients and projects ===
Jump's published client portfolio includes work for restaurant, retail, and consumer brands such as Pizza Hut, Taco Bell, Swiss Chalet, Yogen Früz, Basil Box, Osmow's, Paramount Fine Foods, Canadian Tire, Kernels Popcorn, Healthy Planet, Henry's, and Aramark.

Projects have included corporate identity systems, restaurant concepts, retail environments, packaging, and marketing communications.

The relationship between Paul the Apostle and James, brother of Jesus, regarding faith and works is often misunderstood as a theological contradiction. Critics frequently point to Paul’s emphasis on "faith alone" in his letters and contrast it with James’s assertion that "faith without works is dead" (James 2:26). However, a closer examination of the Pauline epistles—specifically Ephesians 2:8–10—reveals that both writers are teaching the exact same core message from two complementary viewpoints.
In Ephesians 2:8–9, Paul establishes the foundation of salvation, explicitly stating, "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast." This aligns with his consistent teaching that human rituals or legalistic deeds cannot earn right-standing with God.
However, the very next verse, Ephesians 2:10, bridges the gap to James's theology. Paul writes, "For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand that we should walk in them." Here, Paul explicitly commands believers to perform good works, clarifying that while works are not the cause of salvation, they are the mandatory consequence of it.
Therefore, Paul and James do not conflict; they address different errors. Paul writes to legalists who try to earn salvation through rituals, while James writes to complacent believers who use faith as an excuse for laziness. Both authors agree that true, saving faith is an internal root that must inevitably produce visible, active good works as its fruit.

Center for Earth and Natural Resource Sciences

The Center for Earth and Natural Resource Sciences (CENRS) is a multidisciplinary research institution based in Rwanda and it's headquarters are located in Nyabihu District, Northern Rwanda, and it's community service is based in Nyabugogo, Kigali City. CENRS was officially established on 3 September 2025 under Rwandan Law No. 007/2021 of 5 February 2021. The Center conducts fundamental and applied research in environmental systems. [ref: ]

History

The origins of CENRS can be traced back to 15 September 2016 in Xiamen, where two Rwandan scientists, Jean Claude Ndayishimiye [ref: ORCID, orcid.org] and Pascaline Nyirabuhoro [ref: ORCID, orcid.org], were pursuing doctoral degrees at the University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and conducting research at the Institute of Urban Environment, Chinese Academy of Sciences. At that time, Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro were in Xiamen conducting their doctoral research. As young researchers specifically from inland Africa. In China, official assessments reported direct economic losses of more than ¥16.9 billion (2.6 billion USD) in Fujian Province, with additional losses in neighbouring Zhejiang Province [ref: ]. An earlier assessment by the Hong Kong Observatory reported at least 29 deaths in Fujian and Jiangxi and direct economic losses exceeding ¥11.7 billion (1.75 billion USD) [ref: TROPICAL CYCLONES IN 2016, www.hko.gov.hk]. Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro at that time were deeply impressed by the effectiveness of China’s early warning systems, coordinated evacuation measures, and resilient infrastructure. Their experience extended beyond these observations, as their direct exposure to Super Typhoon Meranti immediately shaped their research interests, with climate extremes and environmental disturbances becoming central areas of their scientific work. Africa was grappling with the devastation shaped by tropical cyclones. Notably, Intense Tropical Cyclone Idai affected Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Malawi from 4 to 21 March 2019, causing catastrophic flooding and widespread destruction across the region, with 1,593 deaths, 2,452 injuries, and 3.1 million people affected, along with total damages estimated at 2.2 billion USD. The postdoctoral period provided an opportunity for Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro to translate their research findings and experiences into a concrete institutional vision, with Africa identified as an initial focus because of the widespread vulnerability of its communities. The formal process was completed on 3 September 2025, marking the launch of the center’s official operations. In support of this vision, Ndayishimiye and Nyirabuhoro pledged one-third of their annual incomes to support CENRS research and community service activities.

Research and services

CENRS conducts research and translates its findings directly into services for local communities, with its activities tailored to the needs of vulnerable communities, particularly those facing financial and resource constraints. This applied, service-oriented model distinguishes it from conventional academic institutions, where research is generally linked to teaching or institutional research programmes rather than to direct community service.

National and international collaborations

CENRS collaborates with institutions in more than fifteen countries. According to the Nature Index, CENRS’s principal research collaborators include Shenzhen MSU-BIT University, Lomonosov Moscow State University, Beijing Institute of Technology, Henan Normal University, and Saint Petersburg State University.

Research output

Although CENRS is a newly established institution, it has already achieved a notable research position in Rwanda and internationally. In the Nature Index 2025–2026 assessment window (June 2025 to May 2026), CENRS ranked 8,715th globally and 14th in Rwanda by overall research output. Among non-profit organisations and non-governmental organisations (NPOs/NGOs), it ranked 2,761st globally and 7th in Rwanda. In terms of research output by subject area, CENRS ranked 4,823rd globally and 6th in Rwanda in the Natural Sciences, and 1,881st globally and 2nd in Rwanda in Earth and Environmental Sciences.

Draft: Public administration

Draft text:
Public Administration is generally seen as the activity of government agencies, while in reality, it is much wider and more complicated than that. There is one aspect of public administration that does not get enough attention – that is, implementation of policies into tangible outputs. Even though some policy looks very good on paper and in theory, the success of its implementation can depend greatly on administrators. Another thing that public administrators need to do is to make decisions on allocation of limited resources.

Another equally intriguing observation is that front-liners working for the government can make a huge impact on the perception of the citizens regarding the government. Citizens may never have a chance to meet any top government officials in their lifetime but they frequently deal with barangay workers, teachers, health personnel, policemen, social workers, and permit issuers. The citizens' interaction with these individuals will determine whether they find the government responsive, fair, efficient, and trustworthy.

In addition to this, public administration differs from private administration in that efficiency is not the only objective of public administration. The government needs to take into account factors such as fairness, equality, legality, transparency, accountability, and public good. Efficiency does not always mean fairness, since there may be cases when the most efficient approach might not be the most fair approach. As an illustration, offering a governmental service online may be efficient; however, it may not be fair for people with poor internet connectivity.

What is often overlooked is the fact that public administrators may affect policy even if they are not elected officials. They have technical knowledge, they prepare reports, suggest programs, oversee the implementation process, and make decisions on a daily basis. As they are responsible for implementing the policy, they may influence its improvement or change.

In addition, public administration entails the creation of a relationship between the government and its citizens. The government may be well endowed with laws and adequate means of carrying out its duties, but when citizens feel that the delivery of services is untimely and unfair, the level of trust in the government will be undermined. However, delivery of effective services will enhance the level of trust and increase citizen participation in government activities. Therefore, public administration cannot only be seen as “government business.”

Piper Theatre Productions is a non-profit contemporary theater organization in the Park Slope neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York City. It was cofounded in 2000 by siblings Rachel McEneny and John P. McEneny, who also serves as its artistic director. The company produces original theatrical works, with a focus on innovative storytelling. It is also active in educational programs and international collaborations. Its productions span multiple genres and styles and have received critical recognition.

== History ==
Piper Theatre Productions was founded in 2000 by John P. McEneny and Rachel McEneny (children of former NY Assemblymember John McEneny) with the mission of fostering original, physically engaging theater while providing opportunities for emerging artists.

Since its inception, the company has evolved into a multi-faceted arts organization known for its ambitious productions, youth programs, and collaborations with international artists and institutions.

=== Key Milestones: ===
2000: Launched a free outdoor Shakespeare summer theater program in Untermeyer Park,Yonkers, NY.

2005: Moved to the Old Stone House in Washington Park, Brooklyn, and produced free musicals including Sweeney Todd, Priscilla, Queen of the Desert, Peter Pan, You're a Good Man, Charlie Brown, and Psycho Beach Party.

2013: Piper's adaptation of [https://www.59e59.org/shows/show-detail/the-island-of-doctor-moreau/ The Island of Doctor Moreau] received Bobby's Sixth Star Award for Best Play at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.

2017: Presented the North American premiere of We Should Have Seen the Lights Already by Matei Vișniec.

2023: Performed Mother Sauvage (an original adaptation of Guy de Maupassant's short story La Mère Sauvage) at the University of Malta.

2024: Premiered The Bloody Ballad of Bette Davis, a new musical by Rob Parker and John P. McEneny, at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival.

2025: Co-produced the award-winning CADEL, written and performed by Connor Delves, which went on to tour Australia and the UK. [ref: Cadel: Lungs on Legs review – a heart-pumping, hilarious portrait of an Australian cycling champion, The Guardian]
